shelves.title: CDK4/6 inhibitors in early breast cancer: abemaciclib and ribociclib work — palbociclib failed twice; an agent effect, not a class effect
shelves.question: In HR-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, does adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy prevent recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival · Receptors, Estrogen · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases
shelves.balance: Four large trials, two answers, split cleanly by drug. Abemaciclib (monarchE, high-risk node-positive disease): 5-year iDFS HR 0.68, with the absolute benefit still deepening after treatment ends — and its harms on the same card (VTE 2.5% vs 0.6%). Ribociclib (NATALEE, broader stage II–III disease): iDFS HR 0.75 at 3 years, 0.72 at 4 years. In both positive trials overall survival remains immature and is stated as such. The fence, carded with equal weight: palbociclib failed twice — PALLAS (final HR 0.96) and PENELOPE-B (HR 0.93), the second in the highest-risk residual-disease population. Nothing on this shelf licenses 'CDK4/6 inhibitors prevent recurrence' as a class sentence; the evidence names two drugs, two regimens, and two populations. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: monarchE: abemaciclib in high-risk early breast cancer — 5-year invasive disease-free survival HR 0.68; overall survival NOT significant; VTE 2.5% vs 0.6% on the same card
cards.summary: 5,637 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative, node-positive, high-risk early breast cancer: 2 years of abemaciclib + endocrine therapy vs endocrine therapy alone. At 5 years (median follow-up 54 months): invasive disease-free survival HR 0.68 [0.60–0.77], relative , with the absolute benefit deepening over time — 7.6 percentage points at 5 years (6.0 at 4 years, 4.8 at 3). Distant relapse-free survival HR 0.68. Overall survival: fewer deaths (208 vs 234) but NOT statistically significant — immature, stated as such. The harm ledger: venous thromboembolism about 2.5% vs 0.6% , and diarrhea is common on abemaciclib.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label phase 3 trial (monarchE), J Clin Oncol 2020; preplanned 5-year efficacy / overall-survival interim analysis, J Clin Oncol 2024. Registry verified against the records' own databank: NCT03155997.
cards.people: 5,637 patients randomly assigned with four or more positive nodes, or one to three nodes plus tumor ≥5 cm, grade 3, or Ki-67 ≥20%; all had surgery and, as indicated, radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy. The records do not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At the first efficacy interim analysis, abemaciclib plus endocrine therapy showed superior invasive disease-free survival (HR 0.75 [0.60–0.93]; 2-year iDFS 92.2% vs 88.7%). At the 5-year analysis, the benefit persisted beyond the 2-year treatment period: HR 0.680 [0.599–0.772] for iDFS and 0.675 [0.588–0.774] for distant relapse-free survival, with 5-year absolute improvements of 7.6 and 6.7 percentage points. Deaths were fewer with abemaciclib (208 vs 234) but overall-survival significance was not reached. No new safety signals were observed.
cards.watchOut: Recurrence prevented is the proven claim; survival is the open one — monarchE's OS analysis remains an interim look and the shelf does not let the deepening iDFS curves borrow certainty they have not yet earned. The widening absolute benefit after treatment ends (a 'carryover' pattern the authors describe) is the most encouraging feature in this drug class's adjuvant data — and it belongs to this agent and this high-risk population, not to the class (References 3–4).
cards.source: Johnston SRD et al. Abemaciclib combined with endocrine therapy for the adjuvant treatment of HR+, HER2-, node-positive, high-risk, early breast cancer (monarchE). J Clin Oncol. 2020;38:3987–3998. PMID 32954927 · NCT03155997 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1200/JCO.20.02514. Five-year outcomes: Rastogi P et al. J Clin Oncol. 2024;42:987–993. PMID 38194616.

cards.headline: NATALEE: ribociclib in stage II–III early breast cancer — iDFS HR 0.75 at 3 years, 0.72 at the 4-year analysis; overall survival immature
cards.summary: 5,101 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative stage II or III early breast cancer — a broader, lower-risk population than monarchE, including some node-negative disease: 3 years of ribociclib (400 mg) + a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor vs the inhibitor alone. 3-year invasive disease-free survival 90.4% vs 87.1% — HR 0.75 [0.62–0.91], relative; P=0.003. At the exploratory 4-year analysis: HR 0.72 [0.61–0.84] ; 4-year iDFS 88.5% vs 83.6% (a 4.9-point absolute difference). Overall survival remains immature (HR 0.83 [0.64–1.07] — a trend, not a result).
cards.type: Randomized, open-label phase 3 trial (NATALEE), N Engl J Med 2024; exploratory 4-year outcomes, JAMA Oncol 2025. Registry verified against the records' own databank: NCT03701334.
cards.people: 5,101 patients (median age 52 years; 99.6% women) with anatomic stage IIA (with risk factors or node involvement), IIB, or III disease; premenopausal women and men also received goserelin. The NEJM record carries no age/sex detail; age and sex are from the 4-year record.
cards.result: At the prespecified interim analysis (426 iDFS events), invasive disease-free survival significantly favored ribociclib plus NSAI (3-year iDFS 90.4% vs 87.1%; HR 0.75 [0.62–0.91]; P=0.003); distant disease-free and recurrence-free survival also favored the combination. At the exploratory 4-year analysis (median follow-up 44.2 months, all patients off ribociclib), the iDFS benefit persisted (HR 0.72 [0.61–0.84]; 3-year rates 90.8% vs 88.1%; 4-year rates 88.5% vs 83.6%). Overall survival remained immature (HR 0.83 [0.64–1.07]). No new safety signals emerged.
cards.watchOut: NATALEE tests a different bet than monarchE: a lower dose (400 mg, the adjuvant dose) for longer (3 years) in a broader population — so its absolute benefit per patient is smaller (about 3–5 points) spread over many more eligible patients, and its survival answer is further away. Both positive trials on this shelf are agent-and-regimen specific; the class fence is Cards 3–4.
cards.source: Slamon D et al. Ribociclib plus endocrine therapy in early breast cancer. N Engl J Med. 2024;390:1080–1091. PMID 38507751 · NCT03701334 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2305488. Four-year outcomes: Fasching PA et al. JAMA Oncol. 2025. PMID 40996773.

cards.headline: The class fence, part 1 — PALLAS: palbociclib FAILED in early breast cancer (final iDFS HR 0.96; 4-year iDFS 84.2% vs 84.5%)
cards.summary: 5,796 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer: 2 years of palbociclib + endocrine therapy vs endocrine therapy alone. At the final protocol-defined analysis (median follow-up 31 months): iDFS events 8.8% vs 9.1%; 4-year iDFS 84.2% vs 84.5% — HR 0.96 [0.81–1.14]; P=0.65 . No secondary time-to-event endpoint differed, and no subgroup showed a difference. A null, carded with the same weight as the shelf's positives. (An earlier interim futility analysis, the source of the round 'HR 1.00' sometimes quoted for PALLAS, was superseded by this final analysis — the gate states the final record.)
cards.type: Randomized, open-label phase 3 trial (PALLAS), J Clin Oncol 2022 (final analysis). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02513394.
cards.people: 5,761 patients in the intention-to-treat population (of 5,796 enrolled at 406 centers in 21 countries) with HR-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy for at least 5 years. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At the final analysis, iDFS events occurred in 253 of 2,884 patients (8.8%) on palbociclib plus endocrine therapy and 263 of 2,877 (9.1%) on endocrine therapy alone (4-year iDFS 84.2% vs 84.5%; HR 0.96 [0.81–1.14]; P=0.65). No significant differences were observed for secondary endpoints, and subgroup analyses showed no differences. There were no new safety signals. The authors conclude that adjuvant palbociclib did not improve outcomes over endocrine therapy alone.
cards.watchOut: Same target (CDK4/6), same setting, opposite answer from Cards 1–2 — which is why this shelf's stamp is agent-specific. Palbociclib's adjuvant failure, twice over (Reference 4), also disciplines the metastatic-setting intuition that the class is interchangeable: dose intensity, schedule, and adherence differed across these trials, and whatever the mechanism, the empirical fact is two wins and two nulls, split by drug.

cards.headline: The class fence, part 2 — PENELOPE-B: palbociclib FAILED again, in the highest-risk post-neoadjuvant population (iDFS HR 0.93, NS)
cards.summary: 1,250 women with HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer and residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — a population at high risk of relapse: 13 cycles of palbociclib + endocrine therapy vs placebo + endocrine therapy. Invasive disease-free survival HR 0.93 [0.74–1.17] — not significant (P=0.525) , with 308 events at a median follow-up of 42.8 months and no subgroup difference. If any adjuvant population should have shown a palbociclib effect, it was this one; the second null closes the class question for this agent.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (PENELOPE-B), J Clin Oncol 2021. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01864746.
cards.people: 1,250 women randomly assigned; median age 49.0 years (range 19–79); the majority were ypN+ with Ki-67 ≤15%; 59.4% had a clinical-pathological staging score ≥3; 50.1% received an aromatase inhibitor.
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 42.8 months, 308 iDFS events were confirmed. Palbociclib did not improve iDFS vs placebo (stratified HR 0.93 [repeated 95% CI 0.74–1.17]; two-sided P=0.525). There was no difference among subgroups. The most common related serious adverse events were infections and vascular disorders (113 patients, 9.1%, no between-arm difference); eight fatal serious adverse events were reported (2 palbociclib, 6 placebo).
cards.watchOut: PENELOPE-B is the stronger of the two fence posts: double-blind, placebo-controlled, and run in residual-disease patients whose recurrence risk dwarfs PALLAS's — and still null. Read together, Cards 1–4 say the adjuvant CDK4/6 story is written drug by drug: abemaciclib and ribociclib earned their indications in their trials; palbociclib, tested twice, did not.
cards.source: Loibl S et al. Palbociclib for residual high-risk invasive HR-positive and HER2-negative early breast cancer — the Penelope-B trial. J Clin Oncol. 2021;39:1518–1530. PMID 33793299 · NCT01864746 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1200/JCO.20.03639

shelves.title: DOACs for cancer-associated VTE: the class is split by agent — apixaban without a bleeding excess, edoxaban and rivaroxaban with a gastrointestinal one
shelves.question: In cancer-associated venous thromboembolism, can a direct oral anticoagulant replace daily dalteparin injections — and which agent?
shelves.mesh: Venous Thromboembolism · Anticoagulants · Dalteparin · Neoplasms · Hemorrhage · Factor Xa Inhibitors
shelves.balance: All three trials beat or matched dalteparin on recurrence, and the shelf's split is the bleeding column. Apixaban (CARAVAGGIO): recurrence HR 0.63 — noninferior, and stated as NOT superior (P=0.09) — with major bleeding HR 0.82 and no gastrointestinal excess (1.9% vs 1.7%). Edoxaban (Hokusai-VTE Cancer): composite HR 0.97, a figure that pools fewer recurrences with more major bleeds (HR 1.77, GI-driven). Rivaroxaban (SELECT-D): recurrence HR 0.43, clinically relevant non-major bleeding 13% vs 4%, and a mid-trial protocol amendment excluding esophageal cancers, noted on its card. Stated across the shelf: no trial showed a mortality difference. All three cards are re-cards of trials whose home is Shelf #156; they are counted once, there. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CARAVAGGIO (Agnelli 2020): apixaban noninferior — recurrence HR 0.63, and NOT superior (P=0.09 for superiority, stated); major bleeding HR 0.82 [re-card — home Shelf #156]
cards.summary: 1,155 patients with cancer and acute proximal DVT or PE: apixaban vs dalteparin for 6 months. Recurrent VTE 5.6% vs 7.9% — HR 0.63 [0.37–1.07], relative : noninferiority met (P<0.001); superiority NOT shown (P=0.09) — the shelf states both, because 'noninferior' keeps being misquoted as 'better'. Major bleeding 3.8% vs 4.0% — HR 0.82 [0.40–1.69] ; gastrointestinal major bleeding 1.9% vs 1.7% — the GI-bleed excess seen with the other agents on this shelf did not appear with apixaban. Mortality did not differ between the arms. Re-card: home Shelf #156, counted once there.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label noninferiority trial with blinded outcome adjudication (CARAVAGGIO), N Engl J Med 2020. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03045406. Re-card; home Shelf #156.
cards.people: 1,155 consecutive patients with cancer who had symptomatic or incidental acute proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism (576 apixaban, 579 dalteparin), treated for 6 months. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 32 of 576 patients (5.6%) in the apixaban group and 46 of 579 (7.9%) in the dalteparin group (HR 0.63 [0.37–1.07]; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.09 for superiority in the trial report). Major bleeding occurred in 22 patients (3.8%) vs 23 (4.0%) (HR 0.82 [0.40–1.69]; P=0.60). The authors conclude that oral apixaban was noninferior to subcutaneous dalteparin without an increased risk of major bleeding.
cards.watchOut: Apixaban is the only agent on this shelf whose major-bleeding point estimate sits below 1.0 — with a confidence interval (0.40–1.69) wide enough to include meaningful harm, so 'no excess shown' is the claim, not 'proven safer'. The noninferiority/superiority pair on this card is the shelf's standing lesson: a trial can clear its noninferiority margin and still not be better (see the Noninferiority trial definition).
cards.source: Agnelli G et al. Apixaban for the treatment of venous thromboembolism associated with cancer. N Engl J Med. 2020;382:1599–1607. PMID 32223112 · NCT03045406 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1915103

cards.headline: Hokusai-VTE Cancer (Raskob 2018): edoxaban noninferior on the composite (HR 0.97) — with major bleeding HR 1.77, driven by gastrointestinal bleeds [re-card — home Shelf #156]
cards.summary: 1,046 patients with cancer and acute VTE: edoxaban (after ≥5 days of heparin) vs dalteparin for 6–12 months. Primary composite (recurrent VTE or major bleeding) 12.8% vs 13.5% — HR 0.97 [0.70–1.36], relative; noninferiority met . The composite's two halves moved in opposite directions, and the shelf states them separately: recurrence 7.9% vs 11.3% (−3.4 points); major bleeding 6.9% vs 4.0% (+2.9 points) — HR 1.77, relative, driven by gastrointestinal bleeding , concentrated in patients with GI cancers. Mortality did not differ between the arms. Re-card: home Shelf #156, counted once there.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label noninferiority trial (Hokusai-VTE Cancer), N Engl J Med 2018. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02073682. Re-card; home Shelf #156.
cards.people: 1,046 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (of 1,050 randomized) with cancer and acute symptomatic or incidental venous thromboembolism, treated for at least 6 and up to 12 months. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 67 of 522 patients (12.8%) in the edoxaban group vs 71 of 524 (13.5%) in the dalteparin group (HR 0.97 [0.70–1.36]; P=0.006 for noninferiority; P=0.87 for superiority). Recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 41 patients (7.9%) vs 59 (11.3%) (risk difference −3.4 points [−7.0 to 0.2]). Major bleeding occurred in 36 patients (6.9%) vs 21 (4.0%) (risk difference +2.9 points [0.1 to 5.6]; HR 1.77 in the trial report). The authors conclude that edoxaban was noninferior on the composite, with a lower recurrence rate but a higher major-bleeding rate than dalteparin.
cards.watchOut: This card is the library's composite-endpoint lesson in one trial (see the Composite endpoint definition): HR 0.97 'noninferior' pools fewer clots with more bleeds and calls the mixture equal. For a patient with a luminal GI cancer, the halves are not interchangeable — the bleeding half is the one that lands in hospital. Agent choice on this shelf is a bleeding-site decision before it is a convenience decision.
cards.source: Raskob GE et al. Edoxaban for the treatment of cancer-associated venous thromboembolism. N Engl J Med. 2018;378:615–624. PMID 29231094 · NCT02073682 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1711948

cards.headline: SELECT-D (Young 2018): rivaroxaban cut recurrence (4% vs 11%; HR 0.43) — clinically relevant non-major bleeding 13% vs 4% [re-card — home Shelf #156]
cards.summary: 406 patients with active cancer and symptomatic or incidental PE or proximal DVT, rivaroxaban vs dalteparin for 6 months (a pilot trial, sized for estimates, not proof): VTE recurrence 4% vs 11% — HR 0.43 [0.19–0.99], relative . Major bleeding 6% vs 4% (HR 1.83 [0.68–4.96]); clinically relevant non-major bleeding 13% vs 4% — HR 3.76 [1.63–8.69] . Mortality did not differ (6-month survival was similar in both arms). Trial-conduct note, stated as the shelf requires: mid-trial, the protocol was amended to exclude patients with esophageal and gastroesophageal cancers after an interim signal of excess bleeding in that subgroup. Re-card: home Shelf #156, counted once there.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label pilot trial (SELECT-D), J Clin Oncol 2018. Registries verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN86712308 · EudraCT 2012-005589-37. Re-card; home Shelf #156.
cards.people: 406 patients randomly assigned (203 per group) at UK centers with active cancer and symptomatic pulmonary embolism, incidental PE, or symptomatic lower-extremity proximal DVT; 58% had metastases. The record does not state a mean age or sex split. The sample size of 400 was chosen to estimate a 10% recurrence rate to within ±4.5% — a pilot design.
cards.result: Twenty-six patients had recurrent VTE (dalteparin 18, rivaroxaban 8); the 6-month cumulative recurrence rate was 11% [7–16%] with dalteparin and 4% [2–9%] with rivaroxaban (HR 0.43 [0.19–0.99]). The 6-month cumulative major-bleeding rate was 4% [2–8%] vs 6% [3–11%] (HR 1.83 [0.68–4.96]). Clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding: 4% [2–9%] vs 13% [9–19%] (HR 3.76 [1.63–8.69]). The authors conclude that rivaroxaban was associated with relatively low VTE recurrence but higher clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding than dalteparin.
cards.watchOut: SELECT-D's mid-trial exclusion of esophageal/gastroesophageal cancers is stated because it is the moment the GI-bleeding pattern on this shelf stopped being a statistic and changed a protocol — and because a reader comparing trials deserves to know SELECT-D's later population was selected differently. As a pilot, its recurrence HR (0.43) is the least precise on the shelf; its bleeding signal is the one that replicated.
cards.source: Young AM et al. shelves.title: Early palliative care in advanced cancer: better quality of life, mood, and satisfaction — survival POSSIBLE, never proven
shelves.question: In advanced cancer, does introducing palliative care early — alongside oncology care — improve quality of life, mood, and end-of-life care?
shelves.mesh: Palliative Care · Quality of Life · Neoplasms · Depression · Patient Satisfaction · Terminal Care
shelves.balance: The honest summary of this literature is outcome-by-outcome. Quality of life, mood, and satisfaction: LIKELY better — Temel's trial improved quality of life and halved depressive symptoms (16% vs 38%), and Zimmermann's improved satisfaction with care, though Zimmermann missed its primary quality-of-life endpoint (P=0.07) and ENABLE III's patient-reported outcomes were null, both stated on their cards. Survival: POSSIBLE — Temel (11.6 vs 8.9 months) and ENABLE III (1-year survival 63% vs 48%) both found survival differences, and in both trials survival was a secondary outcome ; the label travels with the number everywhere on this shelf. Less aggressive end-of-life care: POSSIBLE (Temel 33% vs 54%; ENABLE III's resource use was null). And the boundary: RESPECT-Meso found no benefit of routine early referral in mesothelioma centers with good on-demand access — a null carded at full weight. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Temel 2010: early palliative care in metastatic NSCLC — depression 16% vs 38%, aggressive end-of-life care 33% vs 54%, and survival 11.6 vs 8.9 months as a SECONDARY outcome, labeled so
cards.summary: 151 patients with newly diagnosed metastatic NSCLC: early palliative care integrated with standard oncology care vs standard care alone. Quality of life at 12 weeks was better (FACT-L 98.0 vs 91.5, P=0.03); depressive symptoms 16% vs 38% (P=0.01) ; aggressive end-of-life care 33% vs 54% (P=0.05) . Median survival was 11.6 vs 8.9 months (P=0.02) — stated here with its label: survival was a secondary outcome of a 151-patient, single-center trial whose primary outcome was quality of life. The survival figure may be quoted only with that label attached.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (Temel 2010), N Engl J Med 2010. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01038271.
cards.people: 151 patients who underwent randomization with newly diagnosed metastatic NSCLC at a single center; 27 died by 12 weeks and 107 (86% of the remaining) completed the 12-week assessments. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Patients assigned to early palliative care had better quality of life at 12 weeks (mean FACT-L score 98.0 vs 91.5; P=0.03). Fewer patients in the palliative care group had depressive symptoms (16% vs 38%, P=0.01). Despite fewer patients in the early palliative care group receiving aggressive end-of-life care (33% vs 54%, P=0.05), median survival was longer with early palliative care (11.6 vs 8.9 months, P=0.02) — a secondary outcome. The authors conclude that early palliative care led to significant improvements in quality of life and mood, with less aggressive care at the end of life but longer survival.
cards.watchOut: 'Less aggressive care, longer survival' is the most quoted sentence in palliative-care research, and this shelf protects it by labeling it: one center, 151 patients, survival secondary. The finding deserves its influence on practice — earlier conversations, better symptom control — but any agent that upgrades it to 'palliative care prolongs life, proven' has left the record behind. The shelf's survival stamp is POSSIBLE for exactly this reason.
cards.source: Temel JS et al. Early palliative care for patients with metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer. N Engl J Med. 2010;363:733–742. PMID 20818875 · NCT01038271 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1000678

cards.headline: ENABLE III (Bakitas 2015): early vs delayed palliative care — patient-reported outcomes NULL; 1-year survival 63% vs 48%, also a secondary outcome
cards.summary: 207 patients with advanced cancer: palliative care (consultation plus structured nurse-coaching telehealth) started early vs delayed by 3 months. The patient-reported outcomes were not significant — quality of life P=0.34, symptom impact P=0.09, mood P=0.33 — stated first, because ENABLE III is the shelf's discipline against Temel-only citation. One-year survival was 63% early vs 48% delayed (difference 15 points; P=0.038) — again a secondary outcome , labeled so. Resource use (hospital and ICU days, emergency visits, chemotherapy in the last 14 days, home death) did not differ significantly.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (ENABLE III), J Clin Oncol 2015. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01245621.
cards.people: 207 patients with advanced cancer at an NCI cancer center, a VA medical center, and community outreach clinics, randomized October 2010 to March 2013 to early palliative care or initiation delayed by 3 months. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Overall patient-reported outcomes were not statistically significant after enrollment (quality of life P=0.34; symptom impact P=0.09; mood P=0.33) or before death. Kaplan–Meier 1-year survival rates were 63% in the early group and 48% in the delayed group (difference 15%; P=0.038). Relative rates of resource use were similar between groups (hospital days 0.73 [0.41–1.27]; ICU days 0.68; emergency visits 0.73; chemotherapy in the last 14 days 1.57; home death 54% vs 47%). The authors note that understanding the mechanisms by which palliative care may improve survival remains a research priority.
cards.watchOut: The delayed-start design is this trial's subtlety: the control group got palliative care too, three months later — so ENABLE III tests timing, not palliative care vs none, and its null patient-reported outcomes may mean three months of delay costs little on those measures while its survival gap says timing mattered for something else. Both readings are stated; the shelf's split stamp (POSSIBLE survival) is built from this ambiguity, not despite it.
cards.source: Bakitas MA et al. Early versus delayed initiation of concurrent palliative oncology care: patient outcomes in the ENABLE III randomized controlled trial. J Clin Oncol. 2015;33:1438–1445. PMID 25800768 · NCT01245621 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1200/JCO.2014.58.6362

cards.headline: Zimmermann 2014: the primary quality-of-life endpoint was MISSED (P=0.07) — satisfaction with care improved; the 4-month secondaries favored the intervention
cards.summary: 461 patients with advanced cancer in a cluster-randomized trial (24 oncology clinics): early palliative care consultation and monthly follow-up vs standard cancer care. The primary endpoint — change in FACIT-Sp quality-of-life score at 3 months — was NOT significant: difference 3.56 points [−0.27 to 7.40], P=0.07 , stated first as this shelf's rule requires. Symptom severity (ESAS) also did not differ at 3 months (P=0.33). What did improve: quality-of-life-at-end-of-life scores (QUAL-E, P=0.05) and satisfaction with care (FAMCARE-P16 difference 3.79 [1.74–5.85], P=0.0003) ; at 4 months, all outcomes except one interaction scale favored the intervention.
cards.type: Cluster-randomized controlled trial, Lancet 2014. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01248624.
cards.people: 461 patients who completed baseline measures (228 intervention, 233 control) with advanced cancer, performance status 0–2, and a clinical prognosis of 6–24 months, at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, Toronto; 393 completed at least one follow-up assessment. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At 3 months, there was a non-significant difference in the primary outcome, change in FACIT-Sp (3.56 points [−0.27 to 7.40], P=0.07); a significant difference in QUAL-E (2.25 [0.01–4.49], P=0.05) and FAMCARE-P16 satisfaction (3.79 [1.74–5.85], P=0.0003); and no difference in symptom severity (ESAS −1.70 [−5.26 to 1.87], P=0.33) or in problems with medical interactions (P=0.40). At 4 months, significant differences favored the intervention for all outcomes except the interaction scale.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary endpoint with positive secondaries is the most over-quoted shape in medicine, and this shelf handles it the same way it handled Temel's survival: state the miss first, state the real wins (satisfaction, end-of-life quality) accurately, and let the stamp say POSSIBLE-to-LIKELY by outcome rather than 'proven'. The 4-month pattern suggests the intervention's effects grow with exposure — a hypothesis the trial can raise but, with its primary missed, cannot settle.

cards.headline: RESPECT-Meso (Brims 2019): early specialist palliative care in mesothelioma was NULL — no quality-of-life or mood difference at 12 or 24 weeks
cards.summary: 174 patients with newly diagnosed malignant pleural mesothelioma at 20 sites: early referral to specialist palliative care (review within 3 weeks, then every 4 weeks) vs standard care. The primary outcome — change in EORTC global health status at 12 weeks — showed no significant difference (mean difference 1.8 [−4.9 to 8.5], P=0.59) ; no difference at 24 weeks (−2.0 [−8.6 to 4.6], P=0.54), and no difference in depression or anxiety at either point. Carers' quality of life and mood also did not differ, though carers consistently preferred the intervention arm's care. The null is carded at full weight: it bounds the shelf's claim by disease and by setting.
cards.type: Multicentre randomized controlled trial (RESPECT-Meso), Thorax 2019. Registration ISRCTN18955704, stated in the record; the record carries no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry.
cards.people: 174 participants with newly diagnosed malignant pleural mesothelioma randomized at 19 UK hospital sites and one large site in Western Australia, April 2014 to October 2016; main carers were additionally recruited. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: There was no significant between-group difference in quality-of-life score at 12 weeks (mean difference 1.8 [−4.9 to 8.5]; P=0.59) or at 24 weeks (mean difference −2.0 [−8.6 to 4.6]; P=0.54). There was no difference in depression or anxiety scores at 12 or 24 weeks. In carers, there was no difference in quality of life or mood, although there was a consistent preference for care favoring the intervention arm. The authors conclude there is no role for routine referral to specialist palliative care soon after diagnosis of mesothelioma for patients cared for in centers with good access to specialist palliative care when required.
cards.watchOut: Context is the honest reading of this null: RESPECT-Meso ran in centers where standard care already included good access to palliative care on request — the trial tested routine-early vs available-on-demand, and in that comparison routine-early added nothing measurable. It narrows the shelf's claim; it does not erase Temel or Zimmermann, whose control arms were thinner.

shelves.title: G-CSF primary prophylaxis in chemotherapy: febrile neutropenia roughly halved, early deaths fewer — inside the ≥20% risk fence
shelves.question: Does giving granulocyte colony-stimulating factor from the first chemotherapy cycle prevent febrile neutropenia and early death?
shelves.mesh: Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor · Neutropenia · Fever · Neoplasms · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Primary Prevention · Humans
shelves.balance: Two independent meta-analyses agree: primary G-CSF prophylaxis roughly halves febrile neutropenia in relative terms (RR 0.54, Kuderer; RR 0.51, Cooper), and Kuderer's adds the outcome that earns this shelf its Tier C stamp — fewer infection-related deaths (RR 0.55, relative) and fewer early all-cause deaths during chemotherapy (RR 0.60, relative), printed beside the one absolute harm the source states, bone pain in 19.6% vs 10.4%. The fence prints on the shelf's face: primary prophylaxis is standard when a regimen's febrile-neutropenia risk is ≥20%; this shelf makes no claim below that threshold , where baseline risk is too low for a halving to buy much. Nor does the shelf claim any cancer-survival benefit — Kuderer states the data were insufficient for disease-free or overall survival. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Kuderer 2007 (17 trials, 3,493 patients): febrile neutropenia RR 0.54, infection-related mortality RR 0.55, early mortality RR 0.60 — all relative; bone pain 19.6% vs 10.4%
cards.summary: Across 17 randomized trials of primary G-CSF prophylaxis vs placebo/no prophylaxis in adults receiving chemotherapy for solid tumors or lymphoma: febrile neutropenia RR 0.54 [0.43–0.67] , infection-related mortality RR 0.55 [0.33–0.90] , and early (on-treatment) all-cause mortality RR 0.60 [0.43–0.83] — each a relative effect; the meta-analysis reports the relative risks without arm-level absolute rates, and this card does not invent them. The cost, in absolute terms: bone or musculoskeletal pain 19.6% vs 10.4% (RR 4.03). Data were insufficient to judge disease-free or overall survival.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 randomized controlled trials (Kuderer 2007), J Clin Oncol 2007. A meta-analysis; no registry entry applies.
cards.people: 3,493 adult patients with solid tumors or malignant lymphoma receiving chemotherapy, across 17 randomized trials of primary prophylactic G-CSF vs placebo or untreated controls. The record does not state a pooled mean age or sex split.
cards.result: For infection-related mortality, the relative risk with G-CSF vs controls was 0.55 (95% CI 0.33–0.90; P=0.018) — a 45% relative reduction; for early mortality (all-cause mortality during the chemotherapy period), RR 0.60 (0.43–0.83; P=0.002) — a 40% relative reduction; and for febrile neutropenia, RR 0.54 (0.43–0.67; P<0.001) — a 46% relative reduction. Average relative dose-intensity was significantly higher with G-CSF (P<0.001). Bone or musculoskeletal pain was reported in 19.6% of G-CSF patients vs 10.4% of controls (RR 4.03 [2.15–7.52]; P<0.001). There were insufficient data to assess impact on disease-free and overall survival.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks on a rare outcome can look larger than the lives they count: infection-related deaths are uncommon in modern chemotherapy trials, so RR 0.55 acts on a small absolute base the source does not print — which is exactly why the ≥20% febrile-neutropenia-risk threshold (see shelf balance) does the practical work: prophylaxis is aimed where the baseline risk makes the relative effect worth having. Nothing here supports G-CSF to improve cancer survival; the claim is fewer neutropenic fevers and fewer early deaths during treatment.
cards.source: Kuderer NM, Dale DC, Crawford J, Lyman GH. Impact of primary prophylaxis with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor on febrile neutropenia and mortality in adult cancer patients receiving chemotherapy: a systematic review. J Clin Oncol. 2007;25:3158–3167. PMID 17634496. DOI 10.1200/JCO.2006.08.8823

cards.headline: Cooper 2011 (20 trials): any primary G-CSF cut febrile neutropenia (RR 0.51, relative) — pegfilgrastim 0.30, filgrastim 0.57, lenograstim 0.62
cards.summary: A second, independent meta-analysis reaches the same place: across 20 trials in adults receiving chemotherapy for solid tumors or lymphoma, primary G-CSF prophylaxis vs none gave a febrile-neutropenia relative risk of 0.51 [0.41–0.62] — pegfilgrastim 0.30 [0.14–0.65] , filgrastim 0.57 [0.48–0.69] , lenograstim 0.62 [0.44–0.88] . In the five head-to-head studies, pegfilgrastim beat filgrastim (RR 0.66 [0.44–0.98]). This review's question is febrile neutropenia only — the mortality case rests on Card 1 — and arm-level absolute rates are again not stated in the record.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cooper 2011), BMC Cancer 2011 — 20 trials comparing primary G-CSF prophylaxis with no primary prophylaxis. A meta-analysis; no registry entry applies.
cards.people: Adults undergoing chemotherapy for solid tumours or lymphoma, across 20 randomized studies (five of pegfilgrastim, ten of filgrastim, five of lenograstim vs no primary prophylaxis). The record does not state a pooled mean age or sex split.
cards.result: All three G-CSFs significantly reduced febrile-neutropenia incidence: relative risks 0.30 (95% CI 0.14–0.65) for pegfilgrastim, 0.57 (0.48–0.69) for filgrastim, and 0.62 (0.44–0.88) for lenograstim. Overall, the relative risk of febrile neutropenia for any primary G-CSF prophylaxis vs no primary prophylaxis was 0.51 (0.41–0.62). In five studies comparing pegfilgrastim with filgrastim directly, febrile-neutropenia incidence was significantly lower with pegfilgrastim (RR 0.66 [0.44–0.98]).
cards.watchOut: Two meta-analyses agreeing on the direction and rough size of the febrile-neutropenia effect (RR ≈0.5) is the spine of this shelf's LIKELY stamp — for preventing febrile neutropenia. Cooper's pegfilgrastim estimate (0.30) rests on five trials with a wide interval, and the head-to-head advantage over filgrastim is a further, softer claim; neither extends the shelf below the ≥20% risk threshold, and neither says anything about mortality.
cards.source: Cooper KL, Madan J, Whyte S, Stevenson MD, Akehurst RL. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factors for febrile neutropenia prophylaxis following chemotherapy: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Cancer. 2011;11:404. PMID 21943360. DOI 10.1186/1471-2407-11-404

shelves.title: How long should androgen deprivation run with radiation for prostate cancer? Six months is too short; 18 may be enough for some; high risk earns the long course
shelves.question: With radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer, how much androgen deprivation is enough — and for whom?
shelves.mesh: Prostatic Neoplasms · Androgen Antagonists · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Radiotherapy · Quality of Life · Survival Rate · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: The gradient is the shelf. At the bottom, short courses fail where disease is locally advanced or high-risk: 6 months was inferior to 3 years (EORTC 22961 — 5-year mortality 19.0% vs 15.2%, prostate-cancer deaths 47 vs 29), and 4 months was inferior to 28 months with high-dose radiation (DART 01/05 — 5-year survival 86% vs 95%, the benefit concentrated in high-risk disease). At the top, the returns flatten: PCS IV found 36 months not superior to 18 in high-risk men (deaths 147 vs 143; quality of life clearly better at 18) — carded with its logic intact, as a failed superiority test rather than a proven equivalence. So the risk-stratified reading: high-risk disease earns a long course (roughly 18–36 months; 4–6 months is undertreatment), and for selected men 18 months is a defensible stop. This is the library's prostate ADT shelf; later urology topics are checked against it before they are proposed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: EORTC 22961 (Bolla 2009): 6 months of ADT was INFERIOR to 3 years with radiation — 5-year mortality 19.0% vs 15.2%
cards.summary: 970 men with locally advanced prostate cancer, all radiated and given 6 months of androgen suppression, then randomized to stop or continue to 3 years total: deaths 132 (short) vs 98 (long) ; 5-year overall mortality 19.0% vs 15.2% (HR 1.42 for short vs long); prostate-cancer deaths 47 vs 29 . Short-term suppression failed its noninferiority test outright (P=0.65 for noninferiority). In locally advanced disease, six months is not a short cut — it is undertreatment.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (EORTC 22961), N Engl J Med 2009. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00003026.
cards.people: 970 men randomly assigned (483 short-term, 487 long-term) of 1,113 registered, with locally advanced prostate cancer, after external-beam radiotherapy plus 6 months of androgen suppression; median follow-up 6.4 years. The record does not state a mean age.
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 6.4 years, 132 patients in the short-term group and 98 in the long-term group had died; deaths due to prostate cancer numbered 47 vs 29. Five-year overall mortality was 19.0% (short-term) vs 15.2% (long-term); the observed hazard ratio was 1.42 (upper 95.71% confidence limit 1.79; P=0.65 for noninferiority, against a required HR above 1.35 to declare short-term noninferior). The authors' conclusion: radiotherapy plus 6 months of androgen suppression provides inferior survival to radiotherapy plus 3 years. Adverse events in both groups included fatigue, diminished sexual function, and hot flushes.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's floor, stated as plainly as its ceiling: the comparison is against 6 months, in locally advanced (largely high-risk) disease, with the radiation of its era. It does not prove every man needs 3 years — Cards 2 and 3 map where shorter can still be long enough — but no reading of EORTC 22961 supports 6 months as adequate here.
cards.source: Bolla M et al. Duration of androgen suppression in the treatment of prostate cancer. N Engl J Med. 2009;360:2516–2527. PMID 19516032 · NCT00003026 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0810095

cards.headline: DART 01/05 (Zapatero 2015): 4 months vs 28 months with high-dose radiation — 5-year survival 86% vs 95%, benefit concentrated in high-risk disease
cards.summary: 355 men with T1c–T3b prostate cancer (intermediate- and high-risk) receiving high-dose radiotherapy, randomized to 4 months of ADT or 4 months plus 24 more: 5-year overall survival 95% (long) vs 86% (short) (HR 2.48 [1.31–4.68] for short vs long, P=0.009); metastasis-free survival 94% vs 83%; biochemical disease-free survival 90% vs 81%. The authors state the effect was more evident in high-risk than intermediate-risk disease — the gradient inside a single trial. Late rectal/urinary toxicity did not differ, and no treatment-related deaths were reported.
cards.type: Randomized controlled phase 3 trial (DART 01/05 GICOR), Lancet Oncol 2015 — open-label. Registry as stated on the record's own databank: NCT02175212 (registered retrospectively, after the trial's 2005–2010 accrual).
cards.people: 355 patients with clinical stage T1c–T3b N0M0 prostate adenocarcinoma with intermediate- or high-risk features (2005 NCCN criteria) at ten Spanish university hospitals: 178 short-term, 177 long-term ADT with high-dose radiotherapy (minimum 76 Gy). The record does not state a mean age.
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 63 months, 5-year biochemical disease-free survival was 90% [87–92] with long-term vs 81% [78–85] with short-term androgen deprivation (HR 1.88 [1.12–3.15]; P=0.01); 5-year overall survival was 95% [93–97] vs 86% [83–89] (HR 2.48 [1.31–4.68]; P=0.009); and 5-year metastasis-free survival was 94% [92–96] vs 83% [80–86] (HR 2.31 [1.23–3.85]; P=0.01) — hazard ratios as printed in the record, for short-term relative to long-term treatment. The effect was more evident in high-risk than in intermediate-risk disease. Grade 3 late rectal toxicity occurred in 2% (long) vs 1% (short); grade 3–4 late urinary toxicity in 3% in each group; no deaths were related to treatment.
cards.watchOut: DART's long arm is 28 months, not 36, and its radiation was high-dose and modern — the combination that makes its survival gap (9 points at 5 years) the shelf's strongest 'long beats short' result after EORTC. Its own caveat is in the abstract: whether men with intermediate-risk disease benefit from more than 4 months needs longer follow-up. The shelf therefore reads DART as a high-risk result with an intermediate-risk question attached.
cards.source: Zapatero A et al. High-dose radiotherapy with short-term or long-term androgen deprivation in localised prostate cancer (DART01/05 GICOR): a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol. 2015;16:320–327. PMID 25702876 · NCT02175212 (as stated on the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(15)70045-8

cards.headline: PCS IV (Nabid 2018): 36 months was NOT superior to 18 — deaths 147 vs 143, quality of life better at 18 (in high-risk disease)
cards.summary: 630 men with localized high-risk prostate cancer, all radiated, randomized to 36 vs 18 months of ADT: after median 9.4 years, deaths were 147 (36 months) vs 143 (18 months) ; 5-year overall survival 91% vs 86% (P=0.07) — a numerical gap favoring 36 that did not reach significance in a superiority trial, so '36 is better' was not shown and '18 equals 36' was not formally tested either. Quality of life is the clean result: six scales and 13 items significantly favored 18 months , two by a clinically relevant ≥10 points. The authors: 18 months is a valid option in selected men.
cards.type: Randomized phase III superiority trial (PCS IV), Eur Urol 2018. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 630 patients with localized high-risk prostate cancer randomized between 2000 and 2008: 310 to pelvic and prostate radiotherapy with 36 months of ADT, 320 to the same radiotherapy with 18 months. Median follow-up 9.4 years. The record does not state a mean age.
cards.result: With a median follow-up of 9.4 years, 290 patients had died (147 long arm vs 143 short arm). The 5-year overall survival rates were 91% for the long arm (95% CI 88–95%) and 86% for the short arm (83–90%), P=0.07. Quality-of-life analysis showed a significant difference (P<0.001) in six scales and 13 items favoring 18 months of ADT, two presenting a clinically relevant difference in mean scores of ≥10 points. The authors conclude that 36 months is not superior to 18 months, and that ADT with radiotherapy can potentially be reduced to 18 months in selected men without compromising survival or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Two disciplines on one card. First, the population: PCS IV enrolled high-risk men — summaries that file it as an intermediate-risk trial misstate the record. Second, the logic: this was a superiority trial that failed to show superiority, which is weaker than a noninferiority proof — the 5-year point estimates still favor 36 months (91% vs 86%), and the trial cannot exclude a real, modest benefit. What it settles is that 18 months is a defensible option for selected high-risk men who pay heavily for ADT — not that the extra 18 months are worthless for everyone.
cards.source: Nabid A et al. Duration of androgen deprivation therapy in high-risk prostate cancer: a randomized phase III trial. Eur Urol. 2018;74:432–441. PMID 29980331. DOI 10.1016/j.eururo.2018.06.018

shelves.title: Multi-cancer blood tests: a signal in 1.4% of adults — benefit not yet tested in a randomized trial
shelves.question: Do multi-cancer early detection blood tests help asymptomatic people live longer or avoid advanced cancer?
shelves.mesh: Cell-Free Nucleic Acids · Early Detection of Cancer · Hematologic Tests · Humans · Mass Screening · Neoplasms · Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: What is proven: the tests can be run at scale, a signal appears in about 1.4% of screened adults, 38% of signals in PATHFINDER were cancers, and the diagnostic cascade that follows is usually tolerable — a median 79 days to resolution, longer for the 62% whose signal was false. What is not proven is everything that makes screening worthwhile: no randomized comparison, no stage-shift or mortality result, no measure of overdiagnosis or of cancers falsely reassured. Both prospective studies are carded in full because they are honest feasibility work; the shelf’s grade is the library’s lowest, as briefed: MAYBE (weak evidence). Proposed stamp MAYBE (weak evidence) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: PATHFINDER (Schrag 2023, Lancet): a multi-cancer blood test in 6,621 adults — signal in 1.4%, cancer in 38% of signals, 79 days to an answer
cards.summary: 6,621 adults aged 50+ without symptoms of cancer, tested with a methylation-based multi-cancer early detection (MCED) blood test across seven US health networks. A cancer signal was detected in 92 (1.4%) : 35 (38%) were diagnosed with cancer (true positives); 57 (62%) had no cancer (false positives) . Median time to diagnostic resolution was 79 days (57 days for true positives; 162 days for false positives ). Most participants underwent laboratory tests and imaging; procedures were done in 82% of true positives and 30% of false positives; surgery in 3 true positives and 1 false positive.
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (PATHFINDER), Lancet 2023. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT04241796. Funded by GRAIL, the test’s maker, as stated in the record.
cards.people: 6,662 participants recruited (6,621 with analyzable results): adults aged 50 years or older without signs or symptoms of cancer, at oncology and primary care clinics of seven US health networks. 63.5% women; 91.7% White.
cards.result: A cancer signal was detected in 92 (1.4%) of 6,621 participants with analyzable results. 35 (38%) participants were diagnosed with cancer (true positives) and 57 (62%) had no cancer diagnosis (false positives). Median time to diagnostic resolution was 79 days (IQR 37–219): 57 days in true-positive and 162 days in false-positive participants. Most participants had both laboratory tests (79% of true-positive and 88% of false-positive participants) and imaging (91% and 93%); fewer procedures were done in false-positive (30%) than true-positive (82%) participants, and few had surgery (one false-positive, three true-positive). The authors concluded the study supports the feasibility of MCED screening and underscores the need for research into its clinical utility.
cards.watchOut: Feasibility is the ceiling of this design — no control group, no mortality or stage outcome, and a positive predictive value of 38% means the typical positive result begins months of testing for a cancer that is not there (median 162 days to resolution for false positives). Note also what the study cannot see: cancers the test missed declare themselves later, outside this report’s frame, so sensitivity for real-world screening cannot be computed from it.
cards.source: Schrag D et al. Blood-based tests for multicancer early detection (PATHFINDER): a prospective cohort study. Lancet. 2023;402(10409):1251–1260. PMID 37805216 · NCT04241796. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)01700-2

cards.headline: DETECT-A (Lennon 2020, Science): blood test plus PET-CT in 10,006 women found 26 cancers — 1% had false-positive imaging, 0.22% a futile invasive procedure
cards.summary: 10,006 women not previously known to have cancer, screened with a multi-protein/mutation blood test (CancerSEEK), positives confirmed and localized by PET-CT. 26 cancers were detected by blood testing ; of these, 15 underwent PET-CT and 9 (60%) were surgically excised. Standard screening found 24 further cancers, and 46 cancers were found by neither approach during the study. 1% of participants underwent PET-CT based on false-positive blood tests, and 0.22% underwent a futile invasive diagnostic procedure.
cards.type: Prospective, interventional feasibility and safety study (DETECT-A), Science 2020. The record carries no registry ID; none is printed here.
cards.people: 10,006 women not previously known to have cancer, enrolled through a single US health system. The record’s abstract does not print an age range or further demographic detail, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Twenty-six cancers were detected by blood testing. Of these, 15 underwent PET-CT imaging and nine (60%) were surgically excised. Twenty-four additional cancers were detected by standard-of-care screening and 46 by neither approach. One percent of participants underwent PET-CT imaging based on false-positive blood tests, and 0.22% underwent a futile invasive diagnostic procedure. The authors concluded that multicancer blood testing combined with PET-CT can be safely incorporated into routine clinical care, in some cases leading to surgery with intent to cure.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one health system, no control group, and no follow-up long enough to ask whether the 26 detected cancers were found earlier than they would have been — or whether finding them changed any outcome. The safety numbers are genuinely reassuring for the workup cascade; they are not evidence of screening benefit, and nearly twice as many cancers (46) surfaced outside both the test and standard screening as the test itself found (26).
cards.source: Lennon AM et al. Feasibility of blood testing combined with PET-CT to screen for cancer and guide intervention. Science. 2020;369(6499):eaabb9601. PMID 32345712. DOI 10.1126/science.abb9601

cards.headline: Reading the multi-cancer evidence together: feasibility proven twice — clinical utility proven zero times
cards.summary: The two prospective studies agree on what these tests do today: they can be deployed safely at scale (10,006 women; 6,621 adults), they return a signal in about 1.4% of screened adults, roughly 4 in 10 signals is a cancer , and the workup cascade is manageable, with futile invasive procedures under 1%. Neither study randomized anyone, and neither can answer the questions screening must answer: fewer advanced cancers, fewer cancer deaths, and how much overdiagnosis and false reassurance ride along.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states why this shelf carries the library’s lowest grade.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: asymptomatic adults aged 50+ in US health networks (PATHFINDER) and women in a single US health system (DETECT-A) — both without prior cancer diagnoses.
cards.result: Both studies are single-group feasibility cohorts: they measure signal rates, predictive value in the tested population, workup burden, and safety of the diagnostic cascade. By design they cannot estimate screening benefit (no comparison group), stage shift, overdiagnosis, or mortality effects. Large randomized trials of MCED screening have been mounted (for example, the NHS-Galleri trial) but had reported no outcome results when this shelf was built — the shelf will be re-graded when one does.
cards.watchOut: The commercial availability of these tests has run far ahead of this evidence: a patient can buy the test today, but no one can honestly tell them it has been shown to help anyone live longer. That gap — between feasibility and utility — is exactly what MAYBE (weak evidence) is for.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 37805216; PMID 32345712).

shelves.title: HPV vaccination and cervical cancer: the registries deliver the endpoint the trials could not wait for
shelves.question: Does HPV vaccination prevent invasive cervical cancer?
shelves.mesh: Cohort Studies · Humans · Immunization Programs · Incidence · Papillomavirus Vaccines · Registries · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms · Vaccination
shelves.balance: The trials proved precancer prevention (Shelf #216); the cancer endpoint could only come from registries, and two of the world’s best now agree. In Sweden, invasive cervical cancer’s adjusted rate ratio for vaccinated women was 0.37 [0.21–0.57] — and 0.12 [0.00–0.34] when vaccination came before age 17. In England, cohorts offered the vaccine at 12–13 had 87% lower cervical cancer rates than unvaccinated cohorts, with a clean gradient by age at offer. Both effects sit far beyond this library’s 0.5 observational floor, with the age gradient confounding would struggle to fake. LIKELY rather than the top tier because the design is observational and the cohorts are still young: lifetime magnitude is not yet in any record. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: The Swedish nationwide registry (Lei 2020, NEJM): quadrivalent vaccination and invasive cervical cancer — adjusted rate ratio 0.37, and 0.12 when vaccinated before 17
cards.summary: Sweden’s registries followed girls and women aged 10–30 (2006–2017) to their 31st birthday. Invasive cervical cancer was diagnosed in 19 vaccinated women and 538 unvaccinated women ; cumulative incidence was 47 cases per 100,000 vaccinated vs 94 per 100,000 unvaccinated . Adjusted for age and then for parental and demographic covariates, the incidence rate ratio was 0.37 [0.21–0.57] . By age at vaccination the gradient was steep: vaccinated before age 17, rate ratio 0.12 [0.00–0.34] ; vaccinated at 17–30, 0.47 [0.27–0.75] .
cards.type: Nationwide registry cohort study, N Engl J Med 2020. No registry ID — an observational registry study; none on the record.
cards.people: Girls and women 10 to 30 years of age in Sweden, 2006 through 2017, followed for invasive cervical cancer until their 31st birthday; vaccination was with the quadrivalent HPV vaccine.
cards.result: After adjustment for age at follow-up, the incidence rate ratio for cervical cancer in the vaccinated population compared with the unvaccinated population was 0.51 (95% CI, 0.32 to 0.82); after additional adjustment for other covariates it was 0.37 (95% CI, 0.21 to 0.57). After adjustment for all covariates, the incidence rate ratio was 0.12 (95% CI, 0.00 to 0.34) among women who had been vaccinated before the age of 17 years and 0.47 (95% CI, 0.27 to 0.75) among women vaccinated at 17 to 30 years. The authors concluded that quadrivalent HPV vaccination was associated with a substantially reduced risk of invasive cervical cancer at the population level.
cards.watchOut: Registry evidence, with registry limits: vaccination was not randomised, vaccinated women differ from unvaccinated women in ways registries capture imperfectly, and the endpoint counts are small on the vaccinated side (19 cancers) because the cohorts are still young — the cancers prevented at 40 and 50 are not yet in this record. The effect sizes, however, sit far outside the range confounding usually manufactures (0.37 overall; 0.12 for pre-17 vaccination, both beyond this library’s 0.5 observational floor), and the age-at-vaccination gradient is the pattern a real preventive effect produces.
cards.source: Lei J et al. HPV vaccination and the risk of invasive cervical cancer. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(14):1340–1348. PMID 32997908. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1917338

cards.headline: The English programme evaluation (Falcaro 2021, The Lancet): cervical cancer rates down 87% in the cohort offered vaccine at 12–13
cards.summary: England introduced bivalent HPV vaccination in 2008 (routine at 12–13, catch-up to 18). Comparing vaccinated cohorts with earlier unvaccinated cohorts in the national cancer registry (13.7 million person-years of follow-up in women aged 20 to under 30), the estimated relative reductions in cervical cancer were 87% [72–94] for those offered vaccine at age 12–13 , 62% [52–71] at 14–16 , and 34% [25–41] at 16–18 ; for CIN3 the reductions were 97%, 75% and 39% respectively. By mid-2019 the authors estimated 448 fewer cervical cancers than expected in the vaccinated cohorts.
cards.type: Observational programme evaluation (age-period-cohort modelling of national cancer-registry data), The Lancet 2021. No registry ID — an observational study; none on the record.
cards.people: Women aged 20–64 in England, with diagnoses of cervical cancer and CIN3 from 2006 to mid-2019; the effect estimates are for women aged 20 to under 30 across 13.7 million person-years of follow-up, in three cohorts defined by the age at which vaccine was offered.
cards.result: The estimated relative reduction in cervical cancer rates by age at vaccine offer was 34% (95% CI 25–41) for age 16–18 years, 62% (52–71) for age 14–16 years, and 87% (72–94) for age 12–13 years, compared with the reference unvaccinated cohort. The corresponding risk reductions for CIN3 were 39% (36–41), 75% (72–77), and 97% (96–98). The authors estimated that by June 30, 2019 there had been 448 (339–556) fewer than expected cervical cancers and 17,235 (15,919–18,552) fewer than expected cases of CIN3 in vaccinated cohorts in England.
cards.watchOut: An ecological cohort comparison, not an individual-level linkage: the ‘vaccinated cohorts’ are birth cohorts defined by the offer, secular changes in screening are modelled rather than measured, and the oldest vaccinated women were still under 30 at the end of follow-up. The same three fences as Card 1 — and the same answer to them: a dose-response gradient by age at offer (87/62/34) is very hard for confounding to counterfeit, and two independent national systems agree.
cards.source: Falcaro M et al. The effects of the national HPV immunisation programme in England, UK, on cervical cancer and grade 3 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia incidence: a register-based observational study. Lancet. 2021;398(10316):2084–2092. PMID 34741816. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(21)02178-4

cards.headline: A fenced secondary claim — MAYBE (weak evidence): HPV vaccination and cardiovascular outcomes, read against the HPV infection signal
cards.summary: A separate, weaker claim sits beside the cancer evidence. In one retrospective TriNetX study of adults aged 20–40 (propensity-matched, ~59,423 pairs), HPV vaccination tracked with less new-onset cardiovascular disease (HR 0.90 [0.847–0.957]), cerebrovascular disease (0.605) and heart dysfunction (0.833). Swedish registers point the other way for infection : incident cardiovascular disease adjusted HR 1.07 [1.05–1.08], spiking to 1.43 in the first year after diagnosis then attenuating to 1.02. Graded MAYBE (weak evidence) on its face — a secondary claim, fenced from this shelf’s LIKELY cancer claim.
cards.type: Retrospective database cohort study (TriNetX) read against a nationwide register cohort with sibling analysis. A separate secondary claim, graded on its face MAYBE (weak evidence); it does not change this shelf’s approved cancer claim (LIKELY) or its stamp. No registry ID — observational studies; none on the records.
cards.people: TriNetX: adults aged 20–40, propensity-matched ~59,423 pairs. Swedish study: a nationwide register cohort of people diagnosed with HPV infection, with a sibling comparison.
cards.result: HPV vaccination and new-onset cardiovascular disease: HR 0.90 [0.847–0.957]; cerebrovascular disease: HR 0.605 [0.484–0.754]; heart dysfunction: HR 0.833 [0.708–0.98] (TriNetX, retrospective, propensity-matched). HPV infection and incident cardiovascular disease: adjusted HR 1.07 [1.05–1.08] overall, HR 1.43 [1.38–1.48] in the first year after diagnosis attenuating to 1.02 thereafter; cardiovascular mortality HR 1.25 [1.16–1.34] (Swedish registers).
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence), and fenced. The vaccination claim rests on a single retrospective database study. Its headline effect (HR 0.90) sits inside this library’s 0.5–2.0 not-solid band for observational evidence. Healthy-vaccinee bias — vaccinated young adults differ from unvaccinated adults in health behaviour, screening and care contact in ways matching cannot fully remove — is the standing alternative explanation. On the infection side, the first-year spike (1.43) decaying to 1.02 is the signature of detection and surveillance around a new diagnosis, not of a durable vascular effect. Nothing on this card changes the shelf’s cancer claim or its LIKELY stamp.
cards.source: Yang et al. J Health Popul Nutr. 2025. PMID 40390149 (TriNetX retrospective cohort). Deng et al. PLoS Med. 2026. PMID 42678931 (Swedish register cohort with sibling analysis).

cards.headline: Reading the cancer evidence together: the endpoint the trials could not wait for, delivered by two registries
cards.summary: The randomised trials on Shelf #216 proved the vaccine prevents the precancerous lesions that precede cancer (PATRICIA: 92.9% efficacy against vaccine-type CIN2+ in HPV-naive women) — but a trial powered on invasive cancer would have needed decades, so the cancer endpoint was always going to arrive by registry. It has: Sweden (individual-level linkage, rate ratio 0.37; 0.12 before age 17) and England (programme cohorts, 87% lower rates when offered at 12–13) point the same way with the same age gradient, and both effect sizes clear this library’s observational floor with room to spare. What remains genuinely open is magnitude at older ages and durability into the decades when cervical cancer peaks — the vaccinated cohorts have not yet lived them.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together, with the precancer trials at their own home (Shelf #216).
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: Swedish girls and women vaccinated at 10–30, and English birth cohorts offered vaccination at 12–18, each compared with unvaccinated counterparts in national registries.
cards.result: The evidence establishes that HPV vaccination, especially before age 17, is followed at population level by substantially fewer invasive cervical cancers within the first decades of follow-up. It does not yet quantify lifetime protection, protection from vaccination in the late 20s and beyond, or the effect in settings without organised screening.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is deliberately the cancer-outcome companion to Shelf #216’s precancer shelf: cite #216 for what the trials proved about lesions, and this shelf for what the registries show about cancer — and keep the observational label on the latter, however strong the numbers look.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 32997908; PMID 34741816); precancer trial evidence at Shelf #216 (PMID 19586656; PMID 17494925).

shelves.title: Finasteride and prostate cancer prevention (PCPT): fewer diagnoses, mostly low-grade — and no survival difference at 18 years
shelves.question: Does finasteride prevent prostate cancer, what did the high-grade signal amount to, and did prevention change survival?
shelves.mesh: Prostatic Neoplasms · Finasteride · 5-alpha Reductase Inhibitors · Neoplasm Grading · Incidence · Survival Rate · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Medicare · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: The PCPT itself — Thompson 2003: prostate cancer in 18.4% on finasteride vs 24.4% on placebo over 7 years, a 24.8% relative reduction in prevalence, with Gleason 7–10 tumours more common on finasteride (6.4% vs 5.1% of men analysed) — is carded on Shelf #218 (finasteride and dutasteride prevention), and the PSA-screening frame around it is Shelf #212; neither is re-carded here. This shelf adds what #218 does not carry: the long view. At up to 18 years (Thompson 2013), cancer had been diagnosed in 10.5% on finasteride vs 14.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.70), high-grade cancer in 3.5% vs 3.0% (relative risk 1.17, P=0.05) — and 15-year survival was 78.0% vs 78.2% (HR for death 1.02), with no survival difference after diagnosis in either grade group. A Medicare-claims extension (Unger 2018; median follow-up 16 years) found the diagnosis reduction persisted (HR 0.79) with no rebound after the drug stopped (HR 1.10 beyond 7.5 years) — observational linkage, corroborating the trial, and fenced as such. Prevention here means fewer diagnoses, concentrated in low-grade disease, with no demonstrated survival gain and a high-grade signal that shrank but never fully vanished. Proposed stamp SPLIT: LIKELY fewer prostate-cancer diagnoses, mostly low-grade / LIKELY no demonstrated survival benefit at 15–18 years — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Thompson 2013 (NEJM), PCPT long-term: diagnoses 10.5% vs 14.9% (RR 0.70), high-grade 3.5% vs 3.0% (RR 1.17) — and 15-year survival identical (78.0% vs 78.2%)
cards.summary: Long-term follow-up of the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (18,880 men randomised to finasteride 5 mg or placebo for 7 years), with one additional year of incidence data and survival through the Social Security Death Index to October 31, 2011 (up to 18 years). Prostate cancer diagnosed: 989/9,423 (10.5%) finasteride vs 1,412/9,457 (14.9%) placebo (relative risk 0.70 [95% CI 0.65–0.76], P<0.001). High-grade (Gleason 7–10) cancer: 333 (3.5%) vs 286 (3.0%) (relative risk 1.17 [1.00–1.37], P=0.05). Deaths: 2,538 vs 2,496; 15-year survival 78.0% vs 78.2% (unadjusted HR 1.02 [0.97–1.08], P=0.46). Ten-year survival after a low-grade diagnosis: 83.0% vs 80.9%; after high-grade: 73.0% vs 73.6%.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up analysis of a randomised, placebo-controlled trial (PCPT), N Engl J Med 2013. The record carries no registry ID (the parent trial is pre-registration-era), and none is printed.
cards.people: 18,880 eligible men aged ≥55 years randomised (9,423 finasteride, 9,457 placebo) with normal digital rectal examination and PSA ≤3.0 ng/mL at entry. The record's abstract does not print a mean age for this follow-up.
cards.result: Prostate cancer: 10.5% finasteride vs 14.9% placebo (relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.65 to 0.76; P<0.001) — about a one-third relative reduction, 4.4 percentage points absolute in cumulative diagnoses. High-grade cancer: 3.5% vs 3.0% (relative risk 1.17; 1.00 to 1.37; P=0.05). 15-year overall survival: 78.0% vs 78.2% (HR 1.02; 0.97 to 1.08; P=0.46).
cards.watchOut: This card is the fence around the whole prevention idea: a real, durable reduction in diagnoses that bought no measurable survival difference in 18 years, because most prevented cancers were low-grade. The residual high-grade excess (RR 1.17, P=0.05, 0.5 percentage points absolute) is smaller than the 2003 alarm but is reported here as printed — neither dismissed as pure detection artefact nor upgraded to proven harm.
cards.source: Thompson IM et al. Long-term survival of participants in the prostate cancer prevention trial. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(7):603-10. PMID 23944298

cards.headline: Unger 2018 (JNCI): Medicare-linked PCPT follow-up — diagnosis reduction persisted to 16 years (HR 0.79), with no rebound after finasteride stopped
cards.summary: PCPT participants linked to Medicare claims (9,423 finasteride, 9,457 placebo); median follow-up 16 years. Overall, finasteride-arm participants had a 21.1% relative decrease in the hazard of a prostate-cancer diagnosis (HR 0.79 [95% CI 0.74–0.84], P<0.001), strongest in the first 7.5 years (HR 0.71 [0.66–0.77]); after 7.5 years there was no increased risk (HR 1.10 [0.96–1.26], P=0.18). The authors conclude the benefit was maintained after the end-of-study biopsy period, with no strong evidence it diminished after discontinuation.
cards.type: Observational claims-linkage extension of a randomised trial cohort, J Natl Cancer Inst 2018. The record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 18,880 PCPT participants (9,423 finasteride, 9,457 placebo) with Medicare-linked follow-up; median follow-up 16 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Prostate-cancer diagnosis hazard: HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.84; P<0.001) overall; HR 0.71 (0.66 to 0.77) in the first 7.5 years; HR 1.10 (0.96 to 1.26; P=0.18) after 7.5 years.
cards.watchOut: Observational by design after randomisation ends: diagnoses come from a claims algorithm, not protocol biopsies, and an HR of 0.79 sits inside the library's 0.5–2.0 zone where observational associations are not, on their own, solid evidence. Its job on this shelf is narrow — checking for a post-treatment rebound — and on that question it agrees with the randomised record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: PCPT prevents diagnoses, not deaths — the 2003 trial is on Shelf #218; this shelf is its 18-year verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–2, with the one-home pointer stated plainly: the PCPT primary report (Thompson 2003, PMID 12824459 — prevalence 18.4% vs 24.4% over 7 years; Gleason 7–10 in 6.4% vs 5.1% of analysed men; sexual side effects more common on finasteride, urinary symptoms more common on placebo) is carded on Shelf #218 and is not re-carded here. Read together: finasteride for 7 years durably reduces the chance a man is diagnosed with prostate cancer (RR 0.70 at 18 years), the reduction is concentrated in low-grade disease, the high-grade excess attenuates to 0.5 percentage points, and overall survival is unchanged. Any counselling that presents finasteride as preventing prostate-cancer death goes beyond every record on this shelf.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–2 together with the Shelf #218 pointer stated in the summary.
cards.people: 18,880 men randomised in PCPT, followed to 18 years (Reference 1) and through Medicare linkage to a median 16 years (Reference 2).
cards.result: Diagnoses at longest follow-up: 10.5% vs 14.9% (RR 0.70). High-grade: 3.5% vs 3.0% (RR 1.17). Survival at 15 years: 78.0% vs 78.2% (HR 1.02). Post-discontinuation diagnosis hazard: HR 1.10 (0.96–1.26) — no rebound.
cards.watchOut: 'Prevention' on this shelf means delayed or avoided diagnosis of mostly low-grade cancer — the developer's delay-not-prevention framing for prostate disease applies with full force, and overdiagnosis (Shelf #212) is the cost side of the same ledger.

shelves.title: Low-risk localised prostate cancer: monitoring vs surgery vs radiation (ProtecT) — cancer death ~3% at 15 years in all three arms
shelves.question: In men with PSA-detected localised prostate cancer, how do active monitoring, radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy compare on death, metastases and progression?
shelves.mesh: Prostatic Neoplasms · Watchful Waiting · Prostatectomy · Radiotherapy · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Neoplasm Metastasis · Follow-Up Studies · Quality of Life · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Aged
shelves.balance: ProtecT randomised 1,643 men with PSA-detected localised prostate cancer to active monitoring, prostatectomy or radiotherapy. At 15 years (Hamdy 2023), prostate-cancer death was 3.1% on monitoring, 2.2% on surgery and 2.9% on radiotherapy (P=0.53) — about 3% in every arm — and death from any cause was 21.7% overall, similar across arms. What radical treatment bought was not survival but spread: metastases developed in 9.4% on monitoring versus 4.7% (surgery) and 5.0% (radiotherapy); clinical progression in 25.9% versus 10.5% and 11.0%; long-term androgen deprivation in 12.7% versus 7.2% and 7.7%. And monitoring was often not treatment deferred forever but treatment chosen: 24.4% of the monitoring group were alive without any prostate-cancer treatment at 15 years. The harms are asymmetric and durable (Donovan 2016): prostatectomy worst for sexual function and continence throughout; radiotherapy worst early for bowel function, with bloody stools increasing over time. A 2025 secondary analysis adds a biological fence: cribriform-positive disease carried a much higher metastasis risk (HR 3.61), and cribriform-negative men did well on any strategy. TIER C — this shelf carries mortality claims and is flagged for the developer's personal ruling. Proposed grade: LIKELY. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: ProtecT 15-year (Hamdy 2023, NEJM): prostate-cancer death 3.1% monitoring vs 2.2% surgery vs 2.9% radiotherapy (P=0.53) — metastases 9.4% vs 4.7% vs 5.0%
cards.summary: Between 1999 and 2009, 82,429 UK men aged 50–69 had a PSA test; 2,664 were diagnosed with localised prostate cancer and 1,643 randomised to active monitoring (545), prostatectomy (553) or radiotherapy (545); follow-up complete for 1,610 (98%) at a median 15 years. Prostate-cancer deaths: 45 total (2.7%) — 17 (3.1%) monitoring, 12 (2.2%) surgery, 16 (2.9%) radiotherapy (P=0.53). Deaths from any cause: 356 (21.7%), similar across groups. Metastases: 51 (9.4%) monitoring, 26 (4.7%) surgery, 27 (5.0%) radiotherapy. Long-term ADT started in 69 (12.7%), 40 (7.2%) and 42 (7.7%); clinical progression in 141 (25.9%), 58 (10.5%) and 60 (11.0%). In the monitoring group, 133 men (24.4%) remained alive with no prostate-cancer treatment. More than a third of the cohort had intermediate- or high-risk disease at diagnosis on later stratification.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 15-year outcomes (ProtecT), N Engl J Med 2023. Registries verified against the record's own databank/abstract: ISRCTN20141297 · NCT02044172.
cards.people: 1,643 men aged 50–69 with PSA-detected localised prostate cancer randomised (545 monitoring, 553 prostatectomy, 545 radiotherapy), United Kingdom; median follow-up 15 years (range 11–21); follow-up complete for 98%. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Death from prostate cancer: 17/545 (3.1%) monitoring, 12/553 (2.2%) prostatectomy, 16/545 (2.9%) radiotherapy (P=0.53 for the overall comparison). Death from any cause: 356/1,643 (21.7%), similar numbers in all groups. Metastases: 9.4% vs 4.7% vs 5.0%. Clinical progression: 25.9% vs 10.5% vs 11.0%. Initiation of long-term ADT: 12.7% vs 7.2% vs 7.7%. Alive without any treatment at 15 years: 133 men (24.4%) in the monitoring group.
cards.watchOut: TIER C card — mortality claims, developer's personal ruling required. Two fences: (1) 'low-risk' in the shelf title is the trial's popular label, but the record states over a third of randomised men had intermediate- or high-risk features on risk stratification — do not quote the 3% mortality as a pure low-risk figure; (2) monitoring in ProtecT was a 1999–2009 protocol, less intensive than modern MRI-guided active surveillance, so its metastasis excess may overstate today's surveillance risk.
cards.source: Hamdy FC et al. Fifteen-Year Outcomes after Monitoring, Surgery, or Radiotherapy for Prostate Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(17):1547-1558. PMID 36912538 · ISRCTN20141297 · NCT02044172

cards.headline: ProtecT 10-year (Hamdy 2016, NEJM): the same pattern a decade in — 17 prostate-cancer deaths total, no significant difference; progression and metastases already higher on monitoring
cards.summary: First randomised report of ProtecT (1,643 men; median follow-up 10 years). Prostate-cancer deaths: 8 on monitoring (1.5 per 1,000 person-years), 5 on surgery (0.9 per 1,000) and 4 on radiotherapy (0.7 per 1,000) — 17 total, no significant difference (P=0.48). All-cause deaths: 169 overall, no significant difference (P=0.87). Metastases: 33 men on monitoring (6.3 per 1,000 person-years) vs 13 on surgery (2.4) and 16 on radiotherapy (3.0) (P=0.004). Disease progression: 112 (22.9 per 1,000) vs 46 (8.9) and 46 (9.0) (P<0.001).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 10-year outcomes (ProtecT), N Engl J Med 2016. Registries verified against the record's own databank/abstract: ISRCTN20141297 · NCT02044172.
cards.people: 1,643 men aged 50–69 with clinically localised, PSA-detected prostate cancer randomised (545 monitoring, 553 surgery, 545 radiotherapy); median follow-up 10 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Prostate-cancer mortality rates per 1,000 person-years: monitoring 1.5 (95% CI 0.7 to 3.0), surgery 0.9 (0.4 to 2.2), radiotherapy 0.7 (0.3 to 2.0); P=0.48. Metastases per 1,000 person-years: 6.3 vs 2.4 vs 3.0 (P=0.004). Progression per 1,000 person-years: 22.9 vs 8.9 vs 9.0 (P<0.001). All-cause deaths 169, P=0.87.
cards.watchOut: Kept on the shelf because it shows the metastasis/progression gap was already present at 10 years while mortality was not — the 15-year report (Reference 1) supersedes it for every number, and the two must never be averaged. Event counts at 10 years are small (17 cancer deaths), which is why the mortality comparison needed the longer follow-up.
