shelves.title: Perioperative pembrolizumab in early triple-negative breast cancer (KEYNOTE-522)
shelves.question: Does adding pembrolizumab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy and continuing it after surgery improve event-free and overall survival in high-risk early triple-negative breast cancer?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Neoadjuvant Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claim): A single pivotal trial, reported twice. KEYNOTE-522 event-free survival at 36 months was 84.5% versus 76.8% (hazard ratio 0.63, relative), and overall survival at 60 months was 86.6% versus 81.7% (P=0.002). One trial, however large, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the library's single-trial rule; the two records are sequential reports of one trial and are counted once as evidence.

cards.people: 1174 patients with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer, randomised 2:1 to pembrolizumab-chemotherapy (784) or placebo-chemotherapy (390), with pembrolizumab or placebo continued after surgery. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 39.1 months, estimated event-free survival at 36 months was 84.5% (95% CI 81.7 to 86.9) with pembrolizumab versus 76.8% (72.2 to 80.7) with placebo (hazard ratio for event or death 0.63; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.82; P<0.001) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates. Adverse events occurred predominantly during the neoadjuvant phase and were consistent with the known profiles of pembrolizumab and chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Interim report of a single trial; the hazard ratio of 0.63 sits inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band on its own, supported here by a 7.7-point absolute difference at 36 months.

shelves.title: Immunotherapy added to chemotherapy in advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer: RUBY and NRG GY018
shelves.question: In primary advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, does adding dostarlimab (RUBY) or pembrolizumab (NRG GY018) to carboplatin-paclitaxel improve progression-free and overall survival — in dMMR and pMMR disease?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claim in RUBY): Two double-blind phase 3 trials agree on progression-free survival, largest in dMMR disease (hazard ratios 0.28 in RUBY and 0.30 in GY018, both relative) and present in pMMR disease too (GY018 hazard ratio 0.54, relative). RUBY also showed an overall-survival difference at 24 months (71.3% vs 56.0%; hazard ratio 0.64, relative); GY018's survival data were still immature in its 2025 update (hazard ratios 0.55 dMMR and 0.79 pMMR, both non-significant), and the balance does not claim survival for GY018.

cards.headline: Mirza 2023 (RUBY): dostarlimab plus chemotherapy — 24-month progression-free survival 61.4% vs 15.7% in dMMR disease (hazard ratio 0.28), and survival 71.3% vs 56.0% overall
cards.summary: RUBY (2023): dostarlimab plus chemotherapy — 24-month progression-free survival 61.4% vs 15.7% in dMMR disease (hazard ratio 0.28).
cards.people: 494 patients with primary advanced stage III/IV or first recurrent endometrial cancer, randomised 1:1 to dostarlimab or placebo plus carboplatin-paclitaxel, then dostarlimab or placebo maintenance; 118 (23.9%) had dMMR/MSI-H tumours. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In the dMMR-MSI-H population, estimated progression-free survival at 24 months was 61.4% (95% CI 46.3 to 73.4) versus 15.7% (7.2 to 27.0), hazard ratio 0.28 (0.16 to 0.50; P<0.001) — a relative measure. In the overall population, 24-month progression-free survival was 36.1% versus 18.1% (hazard ratio 0.64; 0.51 to 0.80) and overall survival at 24 months was 71.3% versus 56.0% (hazard ratio for death 0.64; 0.46 to 0.87), both relative measures beside their absolute rates. Severe and serious adverse events were more frequent with dostarlimab; the commonest events were nausea (53.9% vs 45.9%), alopecia (53.5% vs 50.0%) and fatigue (51.9% vs 54.5%).
cards.watchOut: The headline dMMR subgroup is 118 patients; the overall-population hazard ratios (0.64) sit inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band and lean on their absolute-rate differences.

shelves.question: In high-risk locally advanced cervical cancer, does pembrolizumab given with and after chemoradiotherapy (KEYNOTE-A18) — or induction chemotherapy before standard chemoradiotherapy (INTERLACE) — improve survival versus chemoradiotherapy alone?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two independent phase 3 trials beat chemoradiotherapy alone on overall survival by different routes. KEYNOTE-A18: 36-month survival 82.6% versus 74.8% (hazard ratio 0.67, relative). INTERLACE: 5-year survival 80% versus 72% (hazard ratio 0.60, relative) with 5-year progression-free survival 72% versus 64%. cards.headline: Lorusso 2024 (KEYNOTE-A18, overall survival): pembrolizumab with chemoradiotherapy — 36-month survival 82.6% vs 74.8%, hazard ratio for death 0.67
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-A18 (2024): pembrolizumab with chemoradiotherapy — 36-month survival 82.6% vs 74.8% , hazard ratio for death 0.67.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial (overall-survival report)
cards.people: 1060 patients with newly diagnosed high-risk locally advanced cervical cancer (FIGO 2014 stage IB2-IIB node-positive, or stage III-IVA), randomised 1:1 to pembrolizumab-chemoradiotherapy (529) or placebo-chemoradiotherapy (531), pembrolizumab/placebo continuing after chemoradiotherapy. cards.result: Median overall survival was not reached in either group; 36-month overall survival was 82.6% (95% CI 78.4 to 86.1) versus 74.8% (70.1 to 78.8), hazard ratio for death 0.67 (0.50 to 0.90; p=0.0040) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates, meeting the protocol-specified objective (progression-free survival had been positive at the first interim analysis). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 78% versus 70%; potentially immune-mediated events in 39% versus 17%.
cards.watchOut: Survival medians are immature (not reached in either group), so the claim rests on the 36-month landmark difference of 7.8 points and a hazard ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band.

shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two phase 3 trials of checkpoint inhibitor plus platinum-etoposide versus the same chemotherapy agree on a survival gain of about 2-2.7 months median — IMpower133: median 12.3 versus 10.3 months (hazard ratio 0.70, relative); CASPIAN: median 13.0 versus 10.3 months (hazard ratio 0.73, relative), with 18-month survival 34% versus 25% in CASPIAN. shelves.title: HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer: trastuzumab deruxtecan versus trastuzumab emtansine (DESTINY-Breast03)
shelves.question: In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane, does trastuzumab deruxtecan beat trastuzumab emtansine on progression-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Ado-Trastuzumab Emtansine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy,mortality,pathology · Camptothecin/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Immunoconjugates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY (on progression-free survival): The head-to-head trial is large and its effect is below the solid-evidence threshold — DESTINY-Breast03 hazard ratio for progression or death 0.28 (relative), with 75.8% versus 34.1% alive without progression at 12 months — and a second randomised trial of the same drug in a later line (DESTINY-Breast02, hazard ratio 0.36, median 17.8 vs 6.9 months) points the same way. Ruling on the Tier C candidate: NOT Tier C — the shelf's claim is progression-free survival; DESTINY-Breast03's overall-survival analysis at this report had not reached its prespecified significance boundary (hazard ratio 0.55, 94.1% vs 85.9% alive at 12 months) and no survival claim is made, exactly as with Shelf #851.

cards.headline: Cortés 2022 (DESTINY-Breast03): trastuzumab deruxtecan versus emtansine — 75.8% vs 34.1% progression-free at 12 months, hazard ratio 0.28; response 79.7% vs 34.2%
cards.summary: DESTINY-Breast03 (2022): trastuzumab deruxtecan versus emtansine — 75.8% vs 34.1% progression-free at 12 months, hazard ratio 0.28.
cards.people: 524 patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and a taxane, randomised to trastuzumab deruxtecan or trastuzumab emtansine. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The percentage alive without disease progression at 12 months was 75.8% (95% CI 69.8 to 80.7) with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus 34.1% (27.7 to 40.5) with trastuzumab emtansine (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.28; 0.22 to 0.37; P<0.001) — a relative measure below the 0.5 solid-evidence threshold. Overall response occurred in 79.7% versus 34.2%. The percentage alive at 12 months was 94.1% versus 85.9% (hazard ratio for death 0.55; 0.36 to 0.86) but the prespecified significance boundary for survival was not reached, so no survival claim is made. Drug-related grade 3 or 4 events: 45.1% versus 39.8%; adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 10.5% versus 1.9%, none grade 4 or 5.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the drug's signature harm is on this card: interstitial lung disease in about one in ten patients on trastuzumab deruxtecan in this report.
cards.source: Cortés J et al. Trastuzumab Deruxtecan versus Trastuzumab Emtansine for Breast Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2022;386(12):1143-1154. PMID: 35320644. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03529110, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: First-line nivolumab or pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric and gastro-oesophageal cancer
shelves.question: In HER2-negative advanced gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, does adding nivolumab (CheckMate 649) or pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-859) to chemotherapy improve survival — and does the benefit track PD-L1 CPS?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/drug therapy · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Esophageal Neoplasms/drug therapy · Esophagogastric Junction · Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Nivolumab/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two phase 3 trials agree. CheckMate 649 (PD-L1 CPS ≥5 primary population): hazard ratios 0.71 for death and 0.68 for progression or death (both relative; the abstract gives no absolute median survival for that population, and the card says so). KEYNOTE-859 (intention-to-treat): median survival 12.9 versus 11.5 months (hazard ratio 0.78, relative), rising with CPS — 13.0 versus 11.4 months at CPS ≥1 and 15.7 versus 11.8 months at CPS ≥10 (hazard ratio 0.65). Yes, the benefit tracks PD-L1 CPS; and every hazard ratio here sits inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band, carried by concordance and the CPS gradient.

cards.summary: CheckMate 649 (2021): nivolumab plus chemotherapy improved survival in PD-L1 CPS ≥5 disease — hazard ratio for death 0.71 .
cards.people: 1581 previously untreated patients with unresectable, non-HER2-positive gastric, gastro-oesophageal junction or oesophageal adenocarcinoma in the two groups reported here — nivolumab plus chemotherapy (789) or chemotherapy alone (792) — from 175 centres in 29 countries, enrolled regardless of PD-L1 expression. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In patients with PD-L1 CPS of five or more, nivolumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival (hazard ratio 0.71; 98.4% CI 0.59 to 0.86; p<0.0001) and progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.68; 98% CI 0.56 to 0.81; p<0.0001) versus chemotherapy alone — relative measures; this record's abstract does not give the absolute median survival for the CPS ≥5 population, so none is printed. Significant survival improvement was also reported at CPS ≥1 and in all randomised patients. Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 59% versus 44%; treatment-related deaths in 2% versus 1%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label; the primary claim is biomarker-restricted (CPS ≥5), and printing a median survival for it would require a figure this abstract does not contain — so the card does not.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two double-blind phase 3 trials are positive but modest. cards.people: 685 patients with previously untreated unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer, or recurrent disease, randomised 1:1 to durvalumab (341) or placebo (344) with gemcitabine-cisplatin, then durvalumab or placebo monotherapy. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.80 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P=0.021) — a relative measure; estimated 24-month survival was 24.9% (95% CI 17.9 to 32.5) versus 10.4% (4.7 to 18.8), with 58.1% versus 65.7% of patients having died at cutoff. The hazard ratio for progression-free survival was 0.75 (0.63 to 0.89); objective response rates were 26.7% versus 18.7%. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events: 75.7% versus 77.8%.
cards.watchOut: The 24-month landmark rests on wide confidence intervals (the placebo estimate spans 4.7% to 18.8%), and the hazard ratio of 0.80 is inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band — a tail difference, not a median transformation.
cards.source: Oh DY et al. Durvalumab plus Gemcitabine and Cisplatin in Advanced Biliary Tract Cancer. NEJM evidence. 2022;1(8):EVIDoa2200015. PMID: 38319896. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03875235, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: KEYNOTE-966 (2023): pembrolizumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin — median survival 12.7 vs 10.9 months , hazard ratio 0.83.

shelves.title: First-line therapy for advanced urothelial cancer: enfortumab vedotin-pembrolizumab and nivolumab-chemotherapy
shelves.question: In untreated advanced urothelial carcinoma, does enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab (EV-302) — or nivolumab added to gemcitabine-cisplatin (CheckMate 901) — improve survival versus platinum chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Transitional Cell/drug therapy,pathology,secondary · Cisplatin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Urinary Bladder Neoplasms · Gemcitabine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Carboplatin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, overall-survival claims): Two phase 3 trials beat platinum chemotherapy. EV-302 is the large effect: median survival 31.5 versus 16.1 months, hazard ratio for death 0.47 (relative, below the 0.5 solid-evidence threshold), progression-free survival 12.5 versus 6.3 months (hazard ratio 0.45). CheckMate 901 is the modest, concordant one: median survival 21.7 versus 18.9 months (hazard ratio 0.78, relative, inside the caution band). Together they support LIKELY that first-line therapy has moved beyond chemotherapy alone, with EV-302 carrying the grade.

cards.headline: Powles 2024 (EV-302): enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab — median survival 31.5 vs 16.1 months (hazard ratio 0.47), progression-free survival 12.5 vs 6.3 months (hazard ratio 0.45)
cards.summary: EV-302 (2024): enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab — median survival 31.5 vs 16.1 months (hazard ratio 0.47); progression-free survival 12.5 vs 6.3 months.
cards.people: 886 patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, randomised 1:1 to enfortumab vedotin-pembrolizumab (442) or platinum chemotherapy (444; gemcitabine with cisplatin or carboplatin); median follow-up for survival 17.2 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was longer with enfortumab vedotin-pembrolizumab (median 12.5 versus 6.3 months; hazard ratio for progression or death 0.45; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.54; P<0.001), as was overall survival (median 31.5 versus 16.1 months; hazard ratio for death 0.47; 0.38 to 0.58; P<0.001) — relative measures below the 0.5 threshold, beside large absolute median differences. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 55.9% versus 69.5%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and follow-up is still short (median 17.2 months) for a median survival estimate of 31.5 months in the experimental group — the direction is clear, the exact median will move.
cards.source: Powles T et al. Enfortumab Vedotin and Pembrolizumab in Untreated Advanced Urothelial Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2024;390(10):875-888. PMID: 38446675. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04223856, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: van der Heijden 2023 (CheckMate 901): nivolumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin — median survival 21.7 vs 18.9 months (hazard ratio 0.78), response 57.6% vs 43.1%
cards.summary: CheckMate 901 (2023): nivolumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin — median survival 21.7 vs 18.9 months (hazard ratio 0.78).
cards.people: 608 patients with previously untreated unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, randomised 1:1 (304 per group) to nivolumab plus gemcitabine-cisplatin then nivolumab maintenance, or gemcitabine-cisplatin alone; median follow-up 33.6 months. cards.result: Overall survival was longer with the nivolumab combination (hazard ratio for death 0.78; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.96; P=0.02), median 21.7 months (18.6 to 26.4) versus 18.9 months (14.7 to 22.4) — a relative measure beside its absolute medians. cards.headline: Synthesis: chemotherapy alone is no longer the first-line benchmark — LIKELY, proposed (Tier C)
cards.summary: Chemotherapy alone is no longer the first-line benchmark — LIKELY, Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EV-302 (886 patients, versus platinum chemotherapy) and CheckMate 901 (608 patients, cisplatin-based, versus gemcitabine-cisplatin).
cards.result: Both strategies improved overall survival over platinum chemotherapy; EV-302's effect (hazard ratio 0.47 relative; median 31.5 vs 16.1 months) is roughly double CheckMate 901's (0.78; 21.7 vs 18.9 months), and there is no head-to-head trial between them. shelves.title: Sentinel-node-positive melanoma: completion lymph-node dissection versus observation
shelves.question: After a positive sentinel-node biopsy in melanoma, does immediate completion dissection improve survival or regional control versus ultrasound observation (MSLT-II, DeCOG-SLT)?
shelves.mesh: Disease-Free Survival · Intention to Treat Analysis · Lymph Node Excision/adverse effects · Lymph Nodes/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Lymphatic Metastasis/diagnosis · Lymphedema/etiology · Melanoma/mortality,pathology,secondary,surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on survival): Two randomised trials agree that immediate completion dissection does not improve survival. MSLT-II (1934 evaluable patients): 3-year melanoma-specific survival 86% in both groups (P=0.42), with dissection improving regional nodal control (92% vs 77% at 3 years) at the cost of lymphoedema in 24.1% versus 6.3%. DeCOG-SLT (473 analysed): 3-year distant metastasis-free survival 77.0% on observation versus 74.9% with dissection. A null carried by two concordant trials, one very large, earns LIKELY; there is no survival-benefit claim, so the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Faries 2017 (MSLT-II): completion dissection did not improve melanoma-specific survival — 86% vs 86% at 3 years — but raised lymphoedema from 6.3% to 24.1%
cards.summary: MSLT-II (2017): completion dissection did not improve melanoma-specific survival — 86% vs 86% at 3 years — but lymphoedema was 6.3% on observation and far higher with dissection.
cards.people: 1934 patients with sentinel-node metastases in melanoma evaluable in the intention-to-treat analysis (1755 per-protocol), randomised to immediate completion lymph-node dissection or nodal observation with ultrasonography; median follow-up 43 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the per-protocol analysis, mean 3-year melanoma-specific survival was 86±1.3% with dissection and 86±1.2% with observation (P=0.42). Disease-free survival was slightly higher with dissection (68±1.7% vs 63±1.7% at 3 years; P=0.05), based on regional nodal control (92±1.0% vs 77±1.5%; P<0.001) — results the authors say must be interpreted with caution. Nonsentinel-node metastases (found in 11.5% of the dissection group) were a strong prognostic factor for recurrence (hazard ratio 1.78 — a relative measure inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band, printed as prognostic, not as a treatment effect). Lymphoedema occurred in 24.1% versus 6.3%.
cards.watchOut: The dissection group's disease-free-survival edge is a regional-control artefact the authors themselves flag; it did not convert into melanoma-specific survival.
cards.source: Faries MB et al. Completion Dissection or Observation for Sentinel-Node Metastasis in Melanoma. The New England journal of medicine. 2017;376(23):2211-2222. PMID: 28591523. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00297895, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Leiter 2016 (DeCOG-SLT): no difference in distant metastasis-free survival — 77.0% (observation) vs 74.9% (dissection) at 3 years
cards.summary: DeCOG-SLT (2016): no difference in distant metastasis-free survival — 77.0% (observation) vs 74.9% (dissection) at 3 years.
cards.people: 473 patients with sentinel-node-positive cutaneous melanoma analysed as intention-to-treat (observation 233, complete lymph-node dissection 240) at 41 German centres; 311 (66%) had sentinel-node metastases of 1 mm or less; median follow-up 35 months (IQR 20-54). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Distant metastasis-free survival at 3 years was 77.0% (90% CI 71.9 to 82.1; 55 events) in the observation group and 74.9% (69.5 to 80.3; 54 events) with dissection — no difference. In the dissection group, grade 3 and 4 adverse events occurred in 6% and 8% of patients, including lymphoedema (grade 3 in seven patients, grade 4 in 13). No serious adverse events were reported in the observation group as the abstract presents it.
cards.watchOut: The trial closed early and was underpowered (fewer events than required) — its null agrees with the much larger MSLT-II, which is what allows the shelf's LIKELY-the-null stamp; alone it would cap lower.
cards.source: Leiter U et al. Complete lymph node dissection versus no dissection in patients with sentinel lymph node biopsy positive melanoma (DeCOG-SLT): a multicentre, randomised, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: observe the nodal basin; dissection adds staging information and lymphoedema, not survival — LIKELY the null
cards.summary: Observe the nodal basin; dissection adds staging information and lymphoedema, not survival — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MSLT-II (1934 evaluable patients) and DeCOG-SLT (473 analysed), both sentinel-node-positive melanoma.
cards.result: Survival is the same either way in both trials (86% vs 86% melanoma-specific at 3 years; 77.0% vs 74.9% distant metastasis-free, favouring observation numerically). What dissection buys is regional control (92% vs 77%) and prognostic information from nonsentinel nodes; what it costs is lymphoedema (24.1% vs 6.3% in MSLT-II). Adjuvant and metastatic melanoma DRUG therapy (drafted Shelves #761, #764) are different questions and stay home there.
cards.watchOut: DeCOG-SLT's population was mostly micrometastases of 1 mm or less; MSLT-II is the card to read for larger sentinel-node burdens.

shelves.title: Sentinel-node-positive breast cancer: axillary dissection versus radiotherapy or no further axillary treatment
shelves.question: In early breast cancer with one or two positive sentinel nodes, can axillary dissection be safely omitted (ACOSOG Z0011) or replaced by axillary radiotherapy (AMAROS)?
shelves.mesh: Axilla · Breast Neoplasms/mortality,pathology,therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Lymph Node Excision · Lymphatic Metastasis · Mastectomy, Segmental
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials support de-escalation in their stated populations. Z0011: omitting axillary dissection in women with T1-T2 tumours, breast-conserving therapy and 1-2 positive sentinel nodes was noninferior on 10-year overall survival (86.3% without dissection vs 83.6% with; hazard ratio 0.85, relative). AMAROS: axillary radiotherapy matched dissection on axillary control (5-year recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43%, on very few events) with significantly less lymphoedema. Non-inferiority on survival with less harm is the claim — no survival-benefit claim is made, so the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Giuliano 2017 (ACOSOG Z0011, 10 years): no axillary dissection was noninferior — 10-year survival 86.3% vs 83.6%
cards.summary: ACOSOG Z0011 (2017, 10 years): no axillary dissection was noninferior — 10-year survival 86.3% vs 83.6% .
cards.people: 891 women with clinical T1 or T2 invasive breast cancer, no palpable axillary adenopathy and 1 or 2 positive sentinel nodes, all planned for lumpectomy, tangential whole-breast irradiation and adjuvant systemic therapy (median age 55 years); 856 (96%) completed the trial — sentinel-node dissection alone (446) or axillary dissection (445) as randomised groups are reported.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 9.3 years, 10-year overall survival was 86.3% with sentinel-node dissection alone versus 83.6% with axillary dissection (hazard ratio 0.85 [1-sided 95% CI 0 to 1.16]; noninferiority P=.02 against a margin of 1.3) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates. Ten-year disease-free survival was 80.2% versus 78.2% (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.17). Between years 5 and 10 there was one regional recurrence in the no-dissection group and none with dissection; 10-year regional recurrence did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A tightly specified population: breast conservation with whole-breast irradiation and systemic therapy, 1-2 positive sentinel nodes, no palpable adenopathy. The result does not license omission after mastectomy or neoadjuvant therapy on this card's evidence.
cards.source: Giuliano AE et al. Effect of Axillary Dissection vs No Axillary Dissection on 10-Year Overall Survival Among Women With Invasive Breast Cancer and Sentinel Node Metastasis: The ACOSOG Z0011 (Alliance) Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017;318(10):918-926. PMID: 28898379. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00003855, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Donker 2014 (AMAROS): axillary radiotherapy gave comparable control to dissection — 5-year axillary recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43% — with significantly less lymphoedema
cards.summary: AMAROS (2014): axillary radiotherapy gave comparable control to dissection — 5-year axillary recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43% — with significantly less lymphoedema.
cards.type: Open-label, randomised, multicentre, phase 3, non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 1425 patients with T1-2 primary breast cancer, no palpable lymphadenopathy and a positive sentinel node, in the intention-to-treat population (744 assigned axillary dissection, 681 axillary radiotherapy), from 4806 eligible randomised patients at 34 European centres; median follow-up 6.1 years (IQR 4.1-8.0). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Axillary recurrence occurred in 4 of 744 patients after dissection and 7 of 681 after radiotherapy; 5-year axillary recurrence was 0.43% (95% CI 0.00 to 0.92) versus 1.19% (0.31 to 2.08). The planned non-inferiority test was underpowered because of the low number of events (one-sided 95% CI for the hazard ratio 0.00 to 5.27 against a margin of 2). Lymphoedema in the ipsilateral arm was noted significantly more often after dissection than after radiotherapy at 1, 3 and 5 years. Of patients who had dissection, 33% had additional positive nodes.
cards.watchOut: Both recurrence rates are under 1.2% — the trial shows both strategies control the axilla well, but its formal non-inferiority test was underpowered, and the card says so rather than claiming the test was met.

shelves.title: Small peripheral lung cancer: segmentectomy versus lobectomy
shelves.question: For peripheral stage IA non-small-cell lung cancer 2 cm or smaller, is anatomical segmentectomy non-inferior to lobectomy on survival (JCOG0802) — and is sublobar resection non-inferior on disease-free survival (CALGB 140503)?
shelves.mesh: Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung · Lung Neoplasms · Mastectomy, Segmental · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/pathology · Neoplasm Staging · Pneumonectomy · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/mortality,pathology,surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: overall survival is JCOG0802's primary endpoint and the trial claims a survival advantage, so under the brief's rule this candidate IS Tier C). The evidence: JCOG0802 found segmentectomy non-inferior and superior on 5-year overall survival (94.3% vs 91.1%; hazard ratio 0.663, relative) with identical relapse-free survival but more local relapse (10.5% vs 5.4%); CALGB 140503 found sublobar resection non-inferior on disease-free survival (hazard ratio 1.01) with similar overall survival (80.3% vs 78.9% at 5 years; hazard ratio 0.95, relative). Less lung removed, no survival penalty in either trial — and a survival claim in one, which is why the developer rules personally.

cards.headline: Saji 2022 (JCOG0802): segmentectomy beat lobectomy on 5-year overall survival — 94.3% vs 91.1%, hazard ratio 0.663 — with more local relapse, 10.5% vs 5.4%
cards.summary: JCOG0802 (2022): segmentectomy beat lobectomy on 5-year overall survival — 94.3% vs 91.1% , hazard ratio 0.663 — with more local relapse (10.5% vs 5.4%).
cards.people: 1106 patients with clinical stage IA non-small-cell lung cancer (tumour diameter 2 cm or smaller, consolidation-to-tumour ratio above 0.5) at 70 Japanese institutions, randomised to lobectomy (554) or segmentectomy (552); median follow-up 7.3 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 94.3% (95% CI 92.1 to 96.0) with segmentectomy versus 91.1% (88.4 to 93.2) with lobectomy; non-inferiority and superiority were both confirmed (hazard ratio 0.663; 0.474 to 0.927; one-sided p<0.0001 for non-inferiority, p=0.0082 for superiority) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates, and many deaths were from other diseases (63% of deaths after lobectomy, 47% after segmentectomy). Five-year relapse-free survival was 88.0% versus 87.9% (hazard ratio 0.998). Local relapse was more frequent after segmentectomy (10.5% vs 5.4%; p=0.0018). The 1-year difference in FEV1 reduction (3.5%) did not reach the predefined 10% clinical-significance threshold. No 30-day or 90-day mortality occurred.
cards.watchOut: The survival advantage coexists with double the local relapse and largely non-cancer deaths — read it as 'no survival penalty for segmentectomy, with a survival signal', not as proof segmentectomy treats cancer better; the lung-function gain also fell short of the trial's own significance threshold.

cards.headline: Altorki 2023 (CALGB 140503): sublobar resection was non-inferior on disease-free survival — hazard ratio 1.01; 5-year survival 80.3% vs 78.9%
cards.summary: CALGB 140503 (2023): sublobar resection was non-inferior on disease-free survival — hazard ratio 1.01 ; 5-year survival 80.3% vs 78.9%.
cards.people: 697 patients with peripheral non-small-cell lung cancer clinically staged T1aN0 (tumour 2 cm or smaller), randomised after intraoperative confirmation of node-negative disease to sublobar resection (340) or lobar resection (357); median follow-up 7 years. cards.result: Sublobar resection was noninferior for disease-free survival (hazard ratio for recurrence or death 1.01; 90% CI 0.83 to 1.24) — a relative measure; 5-year disease-free survival was 63.6% versus 64.1%. shelves.title: Minimally invasive versus open oesophagectomy
shelves.question: Does minimally invasive (TIME) or hybrid minimally invasive (MIRO) oesophagectomy reduce pulmonary and major complications versus open resection for oesophageal cancer, without compromising oncological outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Esophageal Neoplasms/surgery · Esophagectomy/methods · Esophagogastric Junction/surgery · Esophagoscopy/methods · Length of Stay · Lung Diseases/etiology · Postoperative Complications/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials using different minimally invasive techniques agree on fewer pulmonary/major complications. TIME (totally minimally invasive): pulmonary infection in the first 2 weeks in 9% versus 29% (relative risk 0.30). MIRO (hybrid — laparoscopic abdomen, open chest): major complications in 36% versus 64% (odds ratio 0.31, a relative measure), major pulmonary complications 18% versus 30%, with 3-year overall survival 67% versus 55% and disease-free survival 57% versus 48% — reported as not compromising oncological outcomes, not as a survival benefit. Both relative effect measures are below the 0.5 solid-evidence threshold and the absolute differences are large.

cards.headline: Biere 2012 (TIME): minimally invasive oesophagectomy cut early pulmonary infection to 9% from 29% (relative risk 0.30)
cards.summary: TIME (2012): minimally invasive oesophagectomy cut early pulmonary infection to 9% from 29% (relative risk 0.30).
cards.people: 115 patients aged 18-75 with resectable cancer of the oesophagus or gastro-oesophageal junction at five centres in three countries, randomised to open transthoracic (56) or minimally invasive transthoracic (59) oesophagectomy.
cards.result: Pulmonary infection within the first 2 weeks occurred in 5 of 59 patients (9%) in the minimally invasive group versus 16 of 56 (29%) in the open group (relative risk 0.30; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.76; p=0.005) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates. In-hospital pulmonary infection was 12% versus 34% (relative risk 0.35; 0.16 to 0.78). In-hospital mortality: one death in the open group (anastomotic leakage) and two in the minimally invasive group (aspiration and mediastinitis after anastomotic leakage).
cards.watchOut: A small trial (115 patients) with an infection endpoint — its estimate is imprecise, and the two deaths on the minimally invasive side are printed here so the complication win is not read as a mortality win.
cards.source: Biere SS et al. Minimally invasive versus open oesophagectomy for patients with oesophageal cancer: a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2012;379(9829):1887-92. PMID: 22552194. Registry ID: Netherlands Trial Register: NTR TC 2452, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

shelves.title: Total neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal cancer: RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23
shelves.question: Does moving all systemic therapy before surgery — short-course radiotherapy then chemotherapy (RAPIDO), or induction FOLFIRINOX then chemoradiotherapy (PRODIGE 23) — improve disease-free survival versus standard preoperative chemoradiotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/mortality,secondary,therapy · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chemoradiotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects,mortality · Digestive System Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,mortality · Disease Progression · Dose Fractionation, Radiation · Europe
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruling: PRODIGE 23's long-term report carries an overall-survival claim — 7-year survival 81.9% versus 76.1%, P=0.033 — so under the brief's mortality-claim rule this candidate IS Tier C, per the CHALLENGE precedent noted in the topic file). The disease-free evidence: RAPIDO's 3-year disease-related treatment failure was 23.7% versus 30.4% (hazard ratio 0.75, relative); PRODIGE 23's 7-year disease-free survival was 67.6% versus 62.5% and metastasis-free survival 79.2% versus 72.3%. cards.summary: RAPIDO (2021): short-course radiotherapy then chemotherapy cut 3-year disease-related treatment failure to 23.7% from 30.4% (hazard ratio 0.75).
cards.people: 912 eligible patients with high-risk locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma (at least one of cT4, extramural vascular invasion, cN2, involved mesorectal fascia or enlarged lateral nodes), randomised to experimental total neoadjuvant therapy (462) or standard chemoradiotherapy (450) at 54 centres; median follow-up 4.6 years. cards.result: At 3 years, the cumulative probability of disease-related treatment failure was 23.7% (95% CI 19.8 to 27.6) in the experimental group versus 30.4% (26.1 to 34.6) in the standard group (hazard ratio 0.75; 0.60 to 0.95; p=0.019) — a relative measure beside its absolute rates, sitting inside the 0.5-2.0 caution band. Grade 3 or higher diarrhoea during preoperative therapy occurred in 18% versus 9%; serious adverse events in 38% versus 34%; treatment-related deaths numbered four in each group.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a composite (locoregional failure, distant metastasis, new colorectal primary, or treatment-related death), not overall survival — this card makes no survival claim for RAPIDO.

shelves.title: Scalp cooling to prevent chemotherapy-induced alopecia (SCALP)
shelves.question: In women receiving taxane/anthracycline chemotherapy for breast cancer, does scalp cooling prevent hair loss versus no cooling?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alopecia/chemically induced/prevention & control · Anthracyclines/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Bridged-Ring Compounds/adverse effects · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Female · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods · Middle Aged · Primary Prevention/instrumentation/methods · Quality of Life · Scalp · Taxoids/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one randomised trial plus a large prospective cohort, with a correction to the topic file disclosed here: the file named the Rugo 2017 JAMA paper as 'the SCALP randomised clinical trial'; Rugo is a prospective cohort study, not a randomised trial. The randomised SCALP trial is Nangia 2017, and it leads this shelf: hair preservation (less than 50% hair loss) in 50.5% of cooled women versus 0% of controls at the end of four cycles. The Rugo cohort, carded second and labelled as a cohort, found Dean-scale success in 66.3% versus 0% on non-anthracycline regimens. The two studies use different success scales (CTCAE grade 0–1 versus Dean 0–2), so their percentages are not interchangeable. The randomised trial was stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy, which tends to flatter effect sizes; even allowing for that, a 0% control rate makes the direction secure. LIKELY.

cards.headline: SCALP randomised trial (Nangia 2017): hair preservation in 50.5% with scalp cooling versus 0% without, after four cycles
cards.summary: SCALP randomised trial (Nangia 2017): hair preservation in 50.5% with scalp cooling versus 0% without, after four cycles
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (7 US sites); stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy
cards.people: 182 women with stage I–II breast cancer requiring chemotherapy were randomised to scalp cooling (119) or control (63); 142 were evaluable at the interim analysis. Mean age was 52.6 years (SD 10.1); 36% received anthracycline-based and 64% taxane-based chemotherapy.
cards.result: Successful hair preservation (CTCAE grade 0–1, i.e. less than 50% hair loss not requiring a wig, assessed by a clinician unaware of assignment) after four cycles occurred in 48 of 95 women (50.5%; 95% CI 40.7–60.4) with cooling versus 0 of 47 (0%; 95% CI 0–7.6) in controls — a success-rate difference of 50.5% (95% CI 40.5–60.6). The one-tailed P value (Fisher exact test) was <.001, crossing the prespecified superiority boundary (P=.0061), and the data and safety monitoring board recommended termination on 26 September 2016. No quality-of-life scale differed between groups. 54 adverse events were reported in the cooling group, all grade 1–2, with no serious device events.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions ride on this card: the reported P value is one-tailed, as the record states; and early stopping for efficacy is known to overestimate effects, so the true preservation rate is probably below 50.5% — though not near the 0% seen in controls. Results cover stage I–II disease and four cycles.
cards.source: Nangia J et al. Effect of a scalp cooling device on alopecia in women undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer: the SCALP randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28196254. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01986140, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Rugo 2017 (prospective cohort, not randomised): Dean-scale success in 66.3% with cooling versus 0% in controls on non-anthracycline regimens
cards.summary: Rugo 2017 (prospective cohort, not randomised): Dean-scale success in 66.3% with cooling versus 0% in controls on non-anthracycline regimens
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (5 US centres) — carded second and labelled as non-randomised evidence
cards.people: 122 women with stage I–II breast cancer receiving adjuvant or neoadjuvant chemotherapy (106 scalp cooling, 16 controls, 14 of them matched by age and regimen); mean age 53 years (range 28–77). Regimens excluded sequential or combination anthracycline-plus-taxane, and no cooling patient received anthracyclines.
cards.result: Hair loss of 50% or less (Dean score 0–2, self-estimated from photographs four weeks after the last chemotherapy dose) occurred in 67 of 101 evaluable cooling patients (66.3%; 95% CI 56.2–75.4) versus 0 of 16 controls (P<.001). Three of five quality-of-life measures were significantly better one month after chemotherapy in the cooling group, and fewer cooled patients felt less physically attractive (27.3% versus 56.3%; P=.02). Mild headache occurred in 3.8% and 2.8% discontinued cooling because of cold.
cards.watchOut: Not a randomised trial — the topic file mislabelled it as one, corrected here and in the balance. Hair loss was self-estimated by unblinded patients, and the control group is tiny (16 patients) and unmatched in the main analysis; treat its 66.3% as supportive of, not equal to, the randomised estimate. Anthracycline-containing regimens are essentially untested in this cohort.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Association between use of a scalp cooling device and alopecia after chemotherapy for breast cancer. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28196257. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01831024, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: scalp cooling preserves hair in roughly half of women on taxane/anthracycline chemotherapy — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: scalp cooling preserves hair in roughly half of women on taxane/anthracycline chemotherapy — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Nangia 2017 randomised trial (182 randomised, 142 evaluable) and Rugo 2017 prospective cohort (122 patients).
cards.result: Cooling the scalp during chemotherapy converts near-certain major hair loss (0% preservation without cooling in both studies) into a coin flip or better (50.5% randomised; 66.3% in the cohort on gentler regimens), with only minor cold-related adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the two percentages: different designs, different regimens, different hair-loss scales. Evidence for anthracycline-heavy and sequential regimens remains thin.

shelves.title: Palifermin for oral mucositis in transplant conditioning
shelves.question: In patients undergoing haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, does palifermin reduce severe oral mucositis versus placebo — and does the answer depend on the conditioning regimen?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Combined Modality Therapy/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor 7 · Fibroblast Growth Factors/therapeutic use · Hematologic Neoplasms/complications/therapy · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouth Mucosa · Neutropenia/prevention & control · Parenteral Nutrition, Total/statistics & numerical data · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Stomatitis/drug therapy/etiology/prevention & control · Transplantation Conditioning/adverse effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY in total-body-irradiation conditioning / MAYBE (weak evidence) in melphalan-only conditioning. The question is widened from the topic file's TBI-only framing to cover both randomised settings, with the split stated on the face of the shelf. In the TBI-plus-high-dose-chemotherapy trial (Spielberger 2004, n=212), palifermin cut WHO grade 3–4 mucositis from 98% to 63% and grade 4 from 62% to 20% (both P<0.001), with less opioid use and less total parenteral nutrition. In the chemotherapy-only high-dose melphalan setting (Blijlevens 2013, n=281), palifermin showed no significant effect on maximum mucositis severity (severe mucositis 37% placebo, 38% pre/post-transplant dosing, 24% pre-transplant-only dosing) and more infections and fever in the pre/post arm. The topic file's 'DOUBLE-A' label is therefore misleading as filed: the second trial does not confirm the first — it bounds it to the irradiation setting. Quote the split, never a single pooled claim.

cards.headline: Spielberger 2004 (TBI conditioning): grade 3–4 mucositis 63% on palifermin versus 98% on placebo; grade 4, 20% versus 62%
cards.summary: Spielberger 2004 (TBI conditioning): grade 3–4 mucositis 63% on palifermin versus 98% on placebo; grade 4, 20% versus 62%
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (autologous HSCT after fractionated TBI plus high-dose chemotherapy)
cards.people: 212 patients with haematologic cancers (106 palifermin, 106 placebo); palifermin 60 µg/kg/day intravenously for three days before conditioning and after transplantation. Mucositis was assessed daily for 28 days after transplant. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: WHO grade 3–4 oral mucositis occurred in 63% on palifermin versus 98% on placebo (P<0.001); grade 4 in 20% versus 62% (P<0.001). Among affected patients the median duration was 6 versus 9 days; across all patients, 3 versus 9 days (P<0.001). Patient-reported mouth and throat soreness (AUC 29.0 versus 46.8; P<0.001), opioid use (median 212 versus 535 mg morphine equivalents; P<0.001) and total parenteral nutrition (31% versus 55%; P<0.001) all favoured palifermin. Adverse events (rash, pruritus, erythema, mouth and tongue disorders, taste alteration) were mild to moderate and transient.
cards.watchOut: The near-universal placebo rate (98%) reflects TBI-based conditioning; it cannot be carried into chemotherapy-only regimens, as the melphalan trial below shows. This is a single trial in its setting, large and decisive as it is.
cards.source: Spielberger R et al. Palifermin for oral mucositis after intensive therapy for hematologic cancers. N Engl J Med. 2004. PMID: 15602019. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Blijlevens 2013 (melphalan-only conditioning): no significant reduction in mucositis severity — severe mucositis 37% placebo, 38% pre/post dosing, 24% pre-only
cards.summary: Blijlevens 2013 (melphalan-only conditioning): no significant reduction in mucositis severity — severe mucositis 37% placebo, 38% pre/post dosing, 24% pre-only
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (39 European centres; high-dose melphalan autologous SCT for multiple myeloma)
cards.people: 281 patients (mean age 56 years, SD 8) randomised to placebo (57), palifermin before and after high-dose melphalan (115), or palifermin before melphalan only (109), at 60 µg/kg/day for three days.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in maximum oral mucositis severity between palifermin and placebo. Severe mucositis occurred in 37% (placebo), 38% (pre/post dosing) and 24% (pre-only dosing). Patient-reported outcomes and medical resource use did not differ significantly, and more infections and fever during neutropenia were reported in the pre/post arm than on placebo (for example, 51% versus 26%). The authors conclude palifermin was unable to reduce mucositis or its burden in this setting.
cards.watchOut: A genuine null in a different conditioning biology — melphalan without irradiation. The numerically lower 24% in the pre-only arm was not significant and should not be quoted as a trend toward benefit without the trial's overall null beside it.
cards.source: Blijlevens N et al. In a high-dose melphalan setting, palifermin compared with placebo had no effect on oral mucositis or related patient's burden. Bone Marrow Transplant. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: palifermin works where irradiation drives the mucositis, not in melphalan-only conditioning — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: palifermin works where irradiation drives the mucositis, not in melphalan-only conditioning — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Spielberger 2004 (212 patients, TBI conditioning) and Blijlevens 2013 (281 patients, melphalan-only conditioning) — two trials, 493 patients, opposite results by setting.
cards.result: Palifermin's benefit is setting-specific: a large reduction in severe mucositis under total-body-irradiation conditioning (98% to 63%), and no demonstrable benefit under high-dose melphalan alone. Any use or summary that ignores the conditioning regimen misstates the evidence.
cards.watchOut: The split is the finding. A single-stamp summary of 'palifermin for transplant mucositis' would be wrong in one direction or the other for roughly half the transplant population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Spielberger R et al. N Engl J Med. 2004 (PMID: 15602019) and Blijlevens N et al. Bone Marrow Transplant. 2013 (PMID: 23241739). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Oral cryotherapy for chemotherapy-induced mucositis
shelves.question: In patients receiving bolus fluorouracil or high-dose melphalan, does oral cryotherapy (ice chips) during infusion prevent oral mucositis versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Alkylating/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cryotherapy · Female · Humans · Male · Melphalan/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy/therapy · Pain/prevention & control · Peripheral Blood Stem Cell Transplantation · Prospective Studies · Stomatitis/chemically induced/prevention & control · Transplantation, Autologous
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — two small randomised trials in different regimens, both positive, each with reporting limits stated on its card. In high-dose melphalan transplant conditioning (Lilleby 2006, n=40), cryotherapy cut grade 3–4 mucositis from 74% to 14% (P=0.0005). In bolus fluorouracil-plus-leucovorin (Mahood 1991, n=95), mucositis was significantly reduced by both physician (P=.0002) and patient (P=.0001) assessment — but that abstract prints no event rates at all, so the size of the 5-FU effect cannot be carded, only its significance. Small samples, an unblindable intervention, and one rate-free record cap the stamp at POSSIBLE despite the dramatic melphalan figures.

cards.headline: Lilleby 2006 (high-dose melphalan): grade 3–4 mucositis 14% with cryotherapy versus 74% with saline rinses
cards.summary: Lilleby 2006 (high-dose melphalan): grade 3–4 mucositis 14% with cryotherapy versus 74% with saline rinses
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (autologous stem-cell transplantation for multiple myeloma)
cards.people: 40 patients receiving melphalan 200 mg/m² followed by autologous stem-cell transplantation, randomised to oral cryotherapy or room-temperature saline rinses, from 30 minutes before to 6 hours after high-dose therapy. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Grade 3–4 mucositis (National Cancer Institute grading) occurred in 14% of the cryotherapy group versus 74% of the saline group (P=0.0005). Narcotic and total parenteral nutrition use were statistically lower with cryotherapy (the abstract does not print those figures), patient-reported pain was significantly lower, and there were no differences in length of hospitalisation or weight loss.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 patients, and cryotherapy cannot be blinded — subjective secondary outcomes (pain, activity scores) are open to expectation effects, though the graded mucositis endpoint is less so. The comparator was saline rinsing, an active oral care ritual, not nothing.
cards.source: Lilleby K et al. A prospective, randomized study of cryotherapy during administration of high-dose melphalan to decrease the severity and duration of oral mucositis in patients with multiple myeloma undergoing autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplantation. Bone Marrow Transplant. 2006. PMID: 16633359. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Mahood 1991 (bolus 5-FU): cryotherapy significantly reduced stomatitis by physician (P=.0002) and patient (P=.0001) assessment — no rates printed
cards.summary: Mahood 1991 (bolus 5-FU): cryotherapy significantly reduced stomatitis by physician (P=.0002) and patient (P=.0001) assessment — no rates printed
cards.type: Randomised trial (first cycle of bolus fluorouracil plus leucovorin)
cards.people: 95 patients scheduled to receive their first cycle of fluorouracil plus leucovorin, randomised to oral cryotherapy during chemotherapy administration or control. The abstract does not print ages or the sex split.
cards.result: Subsequent mucositis was significantly reduced in the cryotherapy group as judged by the attending physicians (P=.0002) and by the patients themselves (P=.0001). The abstract prints no mucositis rates, grades or effect sizes, and none are supplied here; the authors state they adopted cryotherapy routinely for bolus 5-FU plus leucovorin on the basis of this result.
cards.watchOut: A significance-only record from 1991: the direction is clear, the magnitude is unknowable from this abstract. Bolus 5-FU schedules (the pharmacology that makes a 30-minute ice window work) are now less common, bounding transport to modern infusional regimens.
cards.source: Mahood DJ et al. Inhibition of fluorouracil-induced stomatitis by oral cryotherapy. J Clin Oncol. 1991. PMID: 1999715. cards.headline: Synthesis: ice chips during infusion reduce mucositis in both tested settings — POSSIBLE on small, partly rate-free trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: ice chips during infusion reduce mucositis in both tested settings — POSSIBLE on small, partly rate-free trials
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lilleby 2006 (40 melphalan transplant patients) and Mahood 1991 (95 bolus 5-FU patients) — 135 patients total.
cards.result: Oral cryotherapy during the infusion window reduced mucositis in both settings where it has been randomised — dramatically (74% to 14% severe mucositis) under high-dose melphalan, and significantly (magnitude unprinted) under bolus 5-FU. It is cheap and near-harmless; the evidence is positive but thin.

shelves.title: Oral versus intravenous antibiotics for low-risk febrile neutropenia
shelves.question: In low-risk patients with febrile neutropenia, is oral antibiotic therapy as effective as intravenous therapy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amoxicillin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Ceftazidime/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Ciprofloxacin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Clavulanic Acid/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Fever/drug therapy/etiology · Fever of Unknown Origin/drug therapy · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy · Neutropenia/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials published back-to-back in 1999 (one double-blind, one open-label equivalence trial) agree that, in carefully defined low-risk patients treated in hospital, oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate performs equivalently to intravenous regimens. Success without regimen modification was 71% versus 67% in the double-blind trial (difference 3%, 95% CI −8 to 15) and 86% versus 84% per-protocol in the equivalence trial, whose ≤10% equivalence margin was met. The trade-off is tolerability: oral therapy failed more often through intolerance (16% versus 1% in Freifeld) and intravenous therapy more often through regimen modification. There were no deaths in the double-blind trial. Both trials kept patients hospitalised until fever and neutropenia resolved — the outpatient step-down use this evidence is often cited for is an extrapolation beyond these records, stated plainly on the cards.

cards.headline: Freifeld 1999 (double-blind): oral therapy succeeded without modification in 71% of episodes versus 67% intravenous; no deaths
cards.summary: Freifeld 1999 (double-blind): oral therapy succeeded without modification in 71% of episodes versus 67% intravenous; no deaths
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (hospitalised low-risk febrile neutropenia)
cards.people: 232 febrile neutropenic episodes (116 per group; 84 patients oral, 79 intravenous), aged 5–74 years, with neutropenia expected to last no more than 10 days and no other underlying conditions; patients remained hospitalised until fever and neutropenia resolved. Oral therapy was ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate; intravenous therapy was ceftazidime.
cards.result: Treatment succeeded without modification in 71% of oral episodes versus 67% of intravenous episodes (difference 3%; 95% CI −8 to 15; P=0.48). Failure because modification was needed occurred in 13% versus 32% (P<0.001); failure because the patient could not tolerate the regimen in 16% versus 1% (P<0.001). There were no deaths. Intolerance of oral antibiotics was 16% versus 8% for placebo (P=0.07).
cards.watchOut: Episodes, not only patients, were the unit of analysis, and 'low-risk' was tightly defined (short expected neutropenia, no comorbidity). The 16% oral intolerance rate is the regimen's weak point — chiefly gastrointestinal — and is part of the result, not a footnote.
cards.source: Freifeld A et al. A double-blind comparison of empirical oral and intravenous antibiotic therapy for low-risk febrile patients with neutropenia during cancer chemotherapy. cards.headline: Kern 1999 (EORTC equivalence trial): per-protocol success 86% oral versus 84% intravenous; equivalence within the 10% margin demonstrated
cards.summary: Kern 1999 (EORTC equivalence trial): per-protocol success 86% oral versus 84% intravenous; equivalence within the 10% margin demonstrated
cards.type: Prospective, open-label, multicentre randomised equivalence trial (International Antimicrobial Therapy Cooperative Group, EORTC)
cards.people: 353 febrile patients with granulocytopenia expected to resolve within 10 days were enrolled; 312 treated per protocol were evaluable. Oral therapy was ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily plus amoxicillin-clavulanate; intravenous therapy was ceftriaxone plus amikacin. All patients were hospitalised until fever resolved.
cards.result: Equivalence (absolute difference in success ≤10%) was demonstrated at the second interim analysis and the trial stopped after 353 enrolments. Per-protocol success was 86% on oral therapy (95% CI 80–91) versus 84% intravenous (78–90) (P=0.02 for the equivalence comparison); intention-to-treat success was 80% versus 77% (P=0.03). Duration of fever, time to regimen change, duration of therapy and survival were similar; adverse-event types differed slightly but were similar in frequency (the abstract prints no survival figures, and none are supplied here).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and stopped early once equivalence was shown — appropriate for an equivalence design, but it means the trial's precision rests on its prespecified margin rather than on a large sample. Survival 'similarity' is asserted without figures in this record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oral antibiotics are equivalent to intravenous in hospitalised low-risk febrile neutropenia — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: oral antibiotics are equivalent to intravenous in hospitalised low-risk febrile neutropenia — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Freifeld 1999 (232 episodes, double-blind) and Kern 1999 (353 enrolled, open-label equivalence) — the two 1999 NEJM trials.
cards.result: For patients whose neutropenia is expected to be brief and who have no complicating conditions, oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate controls febrile neutropenia as reliably as intravenous therapy, with intolerance (not failure of infection control) as its main cost.
cards.watchOut: Both trials treated patients in hospital until resolution. Using them to justify fully outpatient or immediate-discharge pathways imports later evidence that is not on this shelf.

shelves.title: Levofloxacin prophylaxis in neutropenia (Bucaneve; Cullen)
shelves.question: In patients expected to have prolonged chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, does levofloxacin prophylaxis reduce febrile episodes and documented infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bacteremia/microbiology/mortality · Bacterial Infections/etiology/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fever of Unknown Origin/prevention & control · Humans · Levofloxacin · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Neutropenia/chemically induced/complications/drug therapy · Ofloxacin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Risk
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials (NEJM 2005) agree. In patients facing more than seven days of neutropenia, including acute leukaemia (Bucaneve, n=760), levofloxacin cut febrile episodes from 85% to 65% (relative risk 0.76; absolute difference −20 percentage points) and microbiologically documented infections by 17 points. In solid-tumour and lymphoma patients on cyclic chemotherapy (Cullen, n=1565), febrile episodes fell from 15.2% to 10.8% across the course (cycle 1: 7.9% to 3.5%) and infection-related hospitalisation from 21.6% to 15.7%. The populations differ — deep, prolonged neutropenia versus shorter cyclic neutropenia — and the question's 'prolonged' framing fits Bucaneve most directly; Cullen is carded as the same-intervention trial in the adjacent population, and the difference is disclosed rather than smoothed over. Neither trial showed a mortality benefit (mortality similar in Bucaneve; four infection-related deaths in each arm in Cullen), and no mortality claim is made. Both trials leave the resistance cost unmeasured — Bucaneve's authors state it explicitly — which is the standing caveat on this shelf.

cards.headline: Bucaneve 2005: fever during neutropenia in 65% on levofloxacin versus 85% on placebo (absolute difference −20 points)
cards.summary: Bucaneve 2005: fever during neutropenia in 65% on levofloxacin versus 85% on placebo (absolute difference −20 points)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (levofloxacin 500 mg daily from chemotherapy start to neutropenia resolution)
cards.people: 760 consecutive adults with cancer in whom chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (<1000 neutrophils/mm³) was expected for more than seven days, stratified by underlying disease (acute leukaemia versus solid tumour or lymphoma); the intention-to-treat fever analysis included 375 levofloxacin and 363 placebo patients.
cards.result: Fever during neutropenia occurred in 65% on levofloxacin versus 85% on placebo (relative risk 0.76; absolute difference −20 percentage points, 95% CI −26 to −14; P=0.001). Microbiologically documented infections were lower by 17 points (95% CI −24 to −10; P<0.001), bacteraemias by 16 points and single-agent gram-negative bacteraemias by 7 points. Mortality and tolerability were similar in the two groups (the abstract prints no mortality figures, and none are supplied here). Effects were similar in leukaemia and solid-tumour/lymphoma strata.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own closing caveat is part of this result: 'the long-term effect of this intervention on microbial resistance in the community is not known.' The trial measures episodes prevented in the treated patient, not the ecological price.
cards.source: Bucaneve G et al. Levofloxacin to prevent bacterial infection in patients with cancer and neutropenia. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID: 16148283. cards.headline: Cullen 2005: febrile episodes 10.8% on levofloxacin versus 15.2% on placebo across the chemotherapy course; hospitalisation 15.7% versus 21.6%
cards.summary: Cullen 2005: febrile episodes 10.8% on levofloxacin versus 15.2% on placebo across the chemotherapy course; hospitalisation 15.7% versus 21.6%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 7 days in each cycle's expected neutropenic window)
cards.people: 1565 patients receiving cyclic chemotherapy for solid tumours or lymphoma at risk of temporary severe neutropenia (<500/mm³) were randomised (781 levofloxacin, 784 placebo); tumours were mainly breast (35.4%), lung (22.5%), testicular (14.4%) and lymphoma (12.8%).
cards.result: During the first cycle, at least one febrile episode occurred in 3.5% on levofloxacin versus 7.9% on placebo (P<0.001); across the whole course, 10.8% versus 15.2% (P=0.01). Probable infection occurred in 34.2% versus 41.5% (P=0.004) and hospitalisation for infection in 15.7% versus 21.6% (P=0.004). Severe infection was 1.0% versus 2.0% (P=0.15), with four infection-related deaths in each group.
cards.watchOut: This population's neutropenia is briefer and shallower in aggregate than Bucaneve's — the absolute gains are correspondingly smaller. The trial did not systematically evaluate antibacterial resistance, so it cannot answer the ecological objection either.

cards.headline: Synthesis: levofloxacin prophylaxis prevents febrile episodes and infections in neutropenia — LIKELY; resistance unmeasured, mortality unchanged
cards.summary: Synthesis: levofloxacin prophylaxis prevents febrile episodes and infections in neutropenia — LIKELY; resistance unmeasured, mortality unchanged
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bucaneve 2005 (760 patients, prolonged neutropenia) and Cullen 2005 (1565 patients, cyclic chemotherapy) — 2,325 patients in two placebo-controlled trials.
cards.result: Prophylactic levofloxacin reliably reduces fever, documented infection and infection-related hospitalisation during chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, with the largest absolute gains where neutropenia is deepest and longest. It does not reduce mortality in these records.
cards.watchOut: The unpriced variable is resistance: neither trial measured it systematically, and community-level fluoroquinolone resistance can erode exactly the benefit carded here. Local resistance patterns govern whether this shelf's answer transports.

shelves.title: Direct oral anticoagulant prophylaxis in ambulatory cancer patients (AVERT; CASSINI)
shelves.question: In ambulatory patients with cancer starting chemotherapy at high venous-thromboembolism risk (Khorana score ≥2), does prophylaxis with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban or rivaroxaban) prevent VTE versus placebo, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Factor Xa Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Incidence · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy · Pyrazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyridones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Risk Factors · Venous Thromboembolism/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is a venous-thromboembolism event composite that includes death from VTE). Two placebo-controlled trials of factor Xa prophylaxis in Khorana score ≥2 ambulatory patients starting chemotherapy point the same way on treatment but differ over the full follow-up. AVERT (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, n=563 analysed) reduced VTE over 180 days from 10.2% to 4.2% (hazard ratio 0.41 in relative terms; P<0.001), with major bleeding higher on apixaban over the same window (3.5% versus 1.8%; HR 2.00). CASSINI (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily, n=841) missed its primary 180-day analysis (6.0% versus 8.8%; HR 0.66; P=0.10) but its prespecified on-treatment analysis was clearly positive (2.6% versus 6.4%; HR 0.40), with major bleeding 2.0% versus 1.0%. The question is widened from the topic file's apixaban-only framing to the class question the two trials jointly answer, and the widening is disclosed here. Net reading: prophylaxis prevents VTE while the drug is being taken, at roughly double the major-bleeding rate; no mortality benefit is shown or claimed — all-cause mortality is not an endpoint of either record, and the death component of the composites is death from VTE only. POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because one of the two primary analyses is null.

cards.headline: AVERT: VTE in 4.2% on apixaban versus 10.2% on placebo over 180 days (HR 0.41); major bleeding 3.5% versus 1.8%
cards.summary: AVERT: VTE in 4.2% on apixaban versus 10.2% on placebo over 180 days (HR 0.41); major bleeding 3.5% versus 1.8%
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily)
cards.people: 574 ambulatory patients with cancer at intermediate-to-high VTE risk (Khorana score ≥2) starting chemotherapy were randomised; 563 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (288 apixaban, 275 placebo). Follow-up was 180 days. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Objectively documented venous thromboembolism occurred in 12 of 288 patients (4.2%) on apixaban versus 28 of 275 (10.2%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.41 in relative terms, 95% CI 0.26–0.65; P<0.001). Major bleeding in the modified intention-to-treat analysis occurred in 10 patients (3.5%) versus 5 (1.8%) (HR 2.00, 95% CI 1.01–3.95; P=0.046); during the treatment period, major bleeding was 2.1% versus 1.1% (HR 1.89, 95% CI 0.39–9.24).
cards.watchOut: The efficacy and bleeding figures come from a modified intention-to-treat population (563 of 574 randomised). The bleeding hazard ratio's confidence interval only just excludes 1.0 in the full-window analysis and does not in the on-treatment window — quote the pair of analyses together.
cards.source: Carrier M et al. Apixaban to prevent venous thromboembolism in patients with cancer (AVERT). N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 30511879. cards.headline: CASSINI: 180-day primary analysis not significant (6.0% vs 8.8%; P=0.10), but on-treatment events were 2.6% versus 6.4% (HR 0.40)
cards.summary: CASSINI: 180-day primary analysis not significant (6.0% vs 8.8%; P=0.10), but on-treatment events were 2.6% versus 6.4% (HR 0.40)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for up to 180 days, with screening ultrasound every 8 weeks)
cards.people: 1080 ambulatory patients with cancer and Khorana score ≥2 were enrolled; 49 (4.5%) had thrombosis at screening and were not randomised, leaving 841 randomised (420 rivaroxaban, 421 placebo). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary efficacy composite (objectively confirmed proximal lower-limb DVT, pulmonary embolism, symptomatic upper-limb or distal DVT, and death from VTE) occurred by day 180 in 25 of 420 (6.0%) on rivaroxaban versus 37 of 421 (8.8%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.66 in relative terms, 95% CI 0.40–1.09; P=0.10 — not significant). In the prespecified intervention-period analysis, the composite occurred in 11 patients (2.6%) versus 27 (6.4%) (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.20–0.80). Major bleeding occurred in 8 of 405 (2.0%) versus 4 of 404 (1.0%) (HR 1.96, 95% CI 0.59–6.49).
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which analysis is quoted: the trial's own primary (to day 180, including time off drug) is null, and the positive on-treatment analysis — though prespecified — is the supportive one. Screening out patients with thrombosis at entry (4.5%) also means the randomised population was already partly depleted of imminent events.

shelves.title: Progressive resistance training in breast-cancer lymphoedema (PAL)
shelves.question: In breast-cancer survivors with stable arm lymphoedema, does progressive weight lifting worsen lymphoedema — or improve symptoms — versus no exercise?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms/complications/surgery · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lymphedema/etiology/therapy · Mastectomy · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength · Postoperative Complications/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Weight Lifting
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the large definitive trial (PAL, n=141) answered the safety question the field had feared: slowly progressive weight lifting did not increase arm swelling over one year (≥5% swelling increase in 11% versus 12%; cumulative incidence ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.88–1.13), and it reduced specialist-assessed exacerbations (14% versus 29%; P=0.04) and symptom severity while increasing strength. The earlier pilot (Ahmed 2006, n=45 — the topic file calls it 'the Schmitz pilot'; first author is Ahmed, with Schmitz a co-author, corrected here) points the same way. A condition of the PAL result belongs on the face of the shelf: participants wore a well-fitted compression garment while lifting, and progression was slow and supervised. The claim is 'does not worsen, and helps symptoms' — not that exercise treats lymphoedema as a decongestive therapy.

cards.headline: PAL trial: weight lifting did not increase arm swelling over 1 year (≥5% increase in 11% vs 12%) and halved exacerbations (14% vs 29%)
cards.summary: PAL trial: weight lifting did not increase arm swelling over 1 year (≥5% increase in 11% vs 12%) and halved exacerbations (14% vs 29%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (twice-weekly progressive weight lifting for 1 year)
cards.people: 141 breast-cancer survivors with stable arm lymphoedema were randomised to progressive weight lifting or control; all were required to wear a well-fitted compression garment while lifting. The primary outcome was change in arm and hand swelling at 1 year by water displacement. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: The proportion with an increase of 5% or more in limb swelling was 11% in the weight-lifting group versus 12% in controls (cumulative incidence ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.88–1.13). Weight lifting produced greater improvement in self-reported symptom severity (P=0.03), greater upper- and lower-body strength (P<0.001 for both), and a lower incidence of lymphoedema exacerbations as assessed by a certified lymphoedema specialist (14% versus 29%; P=0.04). There were no serious adverse events related to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Participants had stable lymphoedema and lifted with compression garments under a slowly progressive, supervised protocol; the trial does not license unsupervised heavy lifting or lifting during an active exacerbation. The exacerbation outcome, though specialist-assessed, is softer than the volumetric primary.
cards.source: Schmitz KH et al. Weight lifting in women with breast-cancer-related lymphedema. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19675330. shelves.title: Acupuncture for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain (SWOG S1200)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with aromatase-inhibitor-related arthralgia, does true acupuncture reduce joint pain versus sham acupuncture or waitlist control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Aromatase Inhibitors/adverse effects · Waiting Lists · Acupuncture Therapy/methods · Arthralgia/therapy/drug therapy · Breast Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a downgrade from the strength the topic file implies, for a reason printed on the trial's own card: SWOG S1200 (n=226) prespecified 2 points on the Brief Pain Inventory worst-pain scale as the clinically meaningful difference, and true acupuncture beat sham by 0.92 points at 6 weeks (P=.01) and by 1.08 points at 52 weeks — statistically significant, durable, and below the trial's own meaningfulness threshold, which the authors themselves flag ('uncertain clinical importance'). The smaller Crew 2010 trial (38 evaluable) showed a much larger separation (worst pain 3.0 versus 5.5 at 6 weeks), larger than the definitive trial supports. The 52-week report carded here is a follow-up report of S1200, not a second trial — the trial is counted once; Crew is the independent second trial. Real but small average benefit, honestly labelled: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SWOG S1200 (primary report, 2018): worst-pain scores 0.92 points lower with true versus sham acupuncture at 6 weeks — below the 2-point meaningfulness threshold
cards.summary: SWOG S1200 (primary report, 2018): worst-pain scores 0.92 points lower with true versus sham acupuncture at 6 weeks — below the 2-point meaningfulness threshold
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (11 US sites; true acupuncture versus sham versus waitlist, 2:1:1)
cards.people: 226 postmenopausal women with early-stage breast cancer taking an aromatase inhibitor, with Brief Pain Inventory worst pain (BPI-WP) of at least 3 (mean baseline 6.6, SD 1.5; mean age 60.7 years, SD 8.6; 88% white), randomised to true acupuncture (110), sham acupuncture (59) or waitlist control (57); 206 (91.1%) completed the trial. Treatment was 12 sessions over 6 weeks, then weekly for 6 weeks.
cards.result: From baseline to 6 weeks, mean BPI-WP fell by 2.05 points on true acupuncture, 1.07 on sham and 0.99 on waitlist. The adjusted difference for true versus sham was 0.92 points (95% CI 0.20–1.65; P=.01) and for true versus waitlist 0.96 points (0.24–1.67; P=.01) — both below the 2-point difference the trial had specified as clinically meaningful; the authors conclude the improvement was 'of uncertain clinical importance'. Grade 1 bruising was more common with true acupuncture (47% versus 25%; P=.01).
cards.watchOut: This 2018 paper is the trial's primary report; the topic file pinned the 2022 long-term report as the anchor. Both are carded, the primary first. A sham needle is not an inert placebo — skin stimulation at non-points may itself be active — which cuts both ways in interpreting the modest true-versus-sham gap.
