shelves.title: Venlafaxine for hot flashes (Loprinzi)
shelves.question: In women with bothersome hot flashes (including breast-cancer survivors), does venlafaxine reduce hot-flash scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents, Second-Generation/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms · Cyclohexanols/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Humans · Venlafaxine Hydrochloride
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one placebo-controlled randomised trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file claimed a second trial (venlafaxine against clonidine) as the shelf's second leg; no such record could be pinned in PubMed searches for this build, so the claim is treated as unverified and the shelf is built honestly on the single trial. In 221 women (191 evaluable) with a history of breast cancer or reluctance to use hormones, four weeks of venlafaxine reduced median hot-flash scores by 61% at both 75 mg and 150 mg daily versus 27% on placebo, with a dose gradient at 37.5 mg (37%). The cost is side effects — dry mouth, appetite loss, nausea and constipation were significantly more frequent at 75–150 mg. Four weeks is the whole of the evidence horizon. If the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or held until a second placebo-controlled trial is pinned.

cards.headline: Loprinzi 2000: hot-flash scores fell 61% on venlafaxine 75–150 mg versus 27% on placebo at 4 weeks
cards.summary: Loprinzi 2000: hot-flash scores fell 61% on venlafaxine 75–150 mg versus 27% on placebo at 4 weeks
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging randomised trial (4 weeks of treatment after a baseline week)
cards.people: 221 women with a history of breast cancer or reluctance to take hormonal treatment because of fear of breast cancer were randomised to placebo (56) or venlafaxine 37.5 mg (56), 75 mg (55) or 150 mg (54) daily; 191 provided data throughout (50, 49, 43 and 49 respectively) and form the analysis set.
cards.result: After week 4, median hot-flash scores (frequency combined with severity, from daily diaries) were reduced from baseline by 27% on placebo (95% CI 11–34), 37% on venlafaxine 37.5 mg (26–54), 61% on 75 mg (50–68) and 61% on 150 mg (48–75). Side effects — mouth dryness, decreased appetite, nausea and constipation — were significantly more frequent in the 75 mg and 150 mg groups than on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks of treatment, and the analysis rests on the 191 of 221 women with complete diaries. The placebo response (27%) is large, as hot-flash trials reliably show; the drug's added value is the ~34-point gap at 75 mg, not the 61% headline. The trial predates modern reporting standards and prints median percentage reductions rather than absolute flash counts.
cards.source: Loprinzi CL et al. Venlafaxine in management of hot flashes in survivors of breast cancer: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2000. PMID: 11145492. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Olanzapine for breakthrough chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (Navari)
shelves.question: In patients with breakthrough nausea and vomiting despite guideline prophylaxis, is olanzapine superior to metoclopramide?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antiemetics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aprepitant · Benzodiazepines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cisplatin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Isoquinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Metoclopramide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Morpholines/administration & dosage · Nausea/chemically induced/drug therapy/prevention & control · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Olanzapine · Palonosetron · Quinuclidines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Vomiting/chemically induced/drug therapy/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised double-blind trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. Scope boundary, stated on the face of the shelf: this is the BREAKTHROUGH-treatment question — patients already vomiting despite dexamethasone, palonosetron and fosaprepitant prophylaxis. Olanzapine PROPHYLAXIS is a different question, homed on Shelf #769; the topic file offered prophylaxis trials as this shelf's second leg, and they are not imported — evidence from a different question does not bulk out a shelf. In the breakthrough trial, 108 evaluable patients: no emesis over 72 hours in 70% on olanzapine versus 31% on metoclopramide, and no nausea in 68% versus 23% (both P<0.01), with no grade 3–4 toxicities. A single modest-sized trial with a large effect: POSSIBLE. If the developer rejects the exception, withdraw the shelf.

cards.headline: Navari 2013: for breakthrough CINV, no emesis in 70% on olanzapine versus 31% on metoclopramide over 72 hours
cards.summary: Navari 2013: for breakthrough CINV, no emesis in 70% on olanzapine versus 31% on metoclopramide over 72 hours
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised phase III trial (treatment of breakthrough CINV during highly emetogenic chemotherapy)
cards.people: 276 chemotherapy-naive patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy (cisplatin ≥70 mg/m², or doxorubicin ≥50 mg/m² plus cyclophosphamide ≥600 mg/m²) consented; all received prophylactic dexamethasone, palonosetron and fosaprepitant. 112 developed breakthrough emesis or nausea and were randomised to olanzapine 10 mg daily or metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for 3 days; 108 were evaluable (56 olanzapine, 52 metoclopramide). Median age of consenting patients was 62 years (range 38–79); 43% were women.
cards.result: During the 72-hour observation period, 39 of 56 patients (70%) on olanzapine had no emesis versus 16 of 52 (31%) on metoclopramide (P<0.01). No nausea (score 0 on a 0–10 scale) was reported by 68% (38/56) versus 23% (12/52) (P<0.01). There were no grade 3 or 4 toxicities in either group.
cards.watchOut: The randomised denominator is the 108 patients who actually broke through, not the 276 consented — the trial answers 'which rescue drug', not 'how often rescue is needed'. It is a single trial from one research group, and metoclopramide at 10 mg three times daily is a modest comparator dose.
cards.source: Navari RM et al. The use of olanzapine versus metoclopramide for the treatment of breakthrough chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Support Care Cancer. 2013. shelves.title: Megestrol acetate for cancer anorexia–cachexia
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer and anorexia/cachexia, does megestrol acetate improve appetite and weight versus placebo — and is there a dose–response?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anorexia/drug therapy · Appetite/drug effects · Cachexia/drug therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Megestrol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Megestrol Acetate · Middle Aged · Paraneoplastic Syndromes/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Surveys and Questionnaires · Survival Rate · Time Factors · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the two carded trials pull in different directions on the placebo question, and the balance shows both. The 1994 NCCTG dose-ranging trial (342 evaluable patients, no placebo arm) found a significant dose–response for appetite stimulation (P=0.02) across 160–1280 mg/day, with only a trend for nonfluid weight gain and 800 mg/day judged optimal. The one modern placebo-controlled trial pinned for this build (Currow 2021, n=190) missed its primary endpoint: day-7 appetite responders were 79.3% on megestrol 480 mg versus 58.5% on placebo (P=0.067), with no quality-of-life or performance differences. Older placebo-controlled trials exist — the dose trial's own abstract references them — but their records were not pinned in this build and they are not carded. The topic file's paediatric megestrol RCT is a different population and is not imported. Net: a real dose-related appetite signal that the best modern placebo test could not confirm at conventional significance, and no carded trial demonstrating significant weight gain with figures. POSSIBLE, and one of the weaker shelves in this batch.

The authors judge the optimal dose in this study to be 800 mg/day, with no further benefit at 1280 mg/day, while noting lower starting doses may be reasonable in practice given formulation, availability and cost.

cards.summary: Currow 2021 (placebo-controlled): appetite responders 79.3% on megestrol versus 58.5% on placebo — primary endpoint not significant (P=0.067)
cards.type: Multisite, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled phase III trial (megestrol versus dexamethasone versus placebo; up to 4 weeks)
cards.people: 190 people with advanced cancer and anorexia for at least 2 weeks (appetite score ≤4 on a 0–10 scale) were randomised to megestrol acetate 480 mg/day (61), dexamethasone 4 mg/day (67) or placebo (62). The primary outcome was at day 7; responders had at least 25% improvement in appetite score.
cards.result: At week 1, responders were 79.3% on megestrol, 65.5% on dexamethasone and 58.5% on placebo (P=0.067) — no significant difference between arms, and the authors conclude no benefit was seen over placebo, with anorexia improving in all arms. Treatment-emergent adverse events were frequent (90.4% of participants), including altered mood and insomnia; hyperglycaemia and deep vein thrombosis were more frequent on dexamethasone.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks maximum exposure, a day-7 primary endpoint and a high placebo response make this a hard test for any appetite drug — but it is the only modern placebo-controlled test carded here, and it did not confirm the benefit. shelves.title: Celecoxib to prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome
shelves.question: In patients receiving capecitabine, does celecoxib prevent grade ≥2 hand–foot syndrome versus capecitabine alone?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/drug therapy/pathology · Aged · Algorithms · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Capecitabine · Celecoxib · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Drug Combinations · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Hand-Foot Syndrome/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Prospective Studies · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage/pharmacology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, with two corrections to the topic file disclosed. First, the comparator: the record describes randomisation 'with or without celecoxib' — an open comparison against capecitabine alone, not the placebo control the file states; the question is corrected to match. Second, the record's abstract does not print the number of patients randomised at all, an unusual reporting gap flagged on the card. Within those limits, the trial (stage II–III colorectal cancer, single centre) found grade 2 hand–foot syndrome in 14.7% with celecoxib versus 29.6% without (P=0.035), grade 1 in 57.4% versus 74.6% (P=0.034), and hazard ratios in relative terms of 0.414 for grade ≥2 (P=0.005) and 0.556 for grade ≥1 (P=0.001), with celecoxib the only significant factor in the multivariable model. If the developer rejects the exception, withdraw the shelf.

cards.headline: Zhang 2012: grade 2 hand–foot syndrome in 14.7% with celecoxib versus 29.6% without (P=0.035); hazard ratio 0.414 in relative terms
cards.summary: Zhang 2012: grade 2 hand–foot syndrome in 14.7% with celecoxib versus 29.6% without (P=0.035); hazard ratio 0.414 in relative terms
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, randomised phase III trial (open comparison: capecitabine with versus without celecoxib)
cards.people: Patients with stage II–III colorectal cancer receiving capecitabine-based chemotherapy, enrolled August 2008 to December 2010. The abstract does not print the total number randomised, the arm sizes, mean age or the sex split — a reporting gap flagged here rather than filled.
cards.result: Grade 1 hand–foot syndrome occurred in 57.4% with celecoxib versus 74.6% without (P=0.034), and grade 2 in 14.7% versus 29.6% (P=0.035). In Cox models, celecoxib use was associated with hazard ratios in relative terms of 0.556 for grade ≥1 syndrome (P=0.001) and 0.414 for grade ≥2 (P=0.005), and was the only factor affecting grade ≥1 and ≥2 incidence in multivariable analysis; dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase level also affected incidence in univariable analyses. The authors conclude celecoxib can prevent capecitabine-related hand–foot syndrome effectively and safely; the abstract prints no comparative adverse-event figures beyond that conclusion, and none are supplied here.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, open-label (hand–foot grading is examiner-judged, so blinding matters), and an abstract that omits the sample size entirely. The relative hazard ratios look stronger than the absolute grade-2 difference (about 15 points) warrants on their own; quote the absolute rates first.

Celecoxib can prevent capecitabine-related hand-foot syndrome in stage II and III colorectal cancer patients: result of a single-center, prospective randomized phase III trial. Ann Oncol. 2012. shelves.title: Mometasone cream for acute radiation dermatitis
shelves.question: In women receiving breast radiotherapy, does prophylactic mometasone cream reduce acute radiation dermatitis versus placebo or emollient?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Breast Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Dermatologic Agents/administration & dosage · Dose Fractionation, Radiation · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Emollients/administration & dosage · Erythema/pathology/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Mometasone Furoate · Pregnadienediols/administration & dosage · Radiodermatitis/pathology/prevention & control · Sample Size · Skin Cream/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two double-blind randomised trials in different breast-radiotherapy settings, both positive on clinician-assessed dermatitis. The topic file pinned a single trial; a second (Ho 2018, postmastectomy) was pinned in this build and is carded. In breast-conserving radiotherapy (Hindley 2014), mometasone beat an emollient comparator on mean and maximum RTOG scores and erythema, with better dermatology quality-of-life scores — but that abstract prints neither its sample size nor any effect sizes, only P values, a gap flagged on its card. In postmastectomy radiotherapy (Ho 2018, n=124), moist desquamation occurred in 43.8% on mometasone versus 66.7% on control cream (P=.012), though patient-reported skin outcomes did not differ. The Ho trial's hard event rates carry the stamp; Hindley supports direction. LIKELY, with the reporting gaps on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: Hindley 2014: mometasone reduced mean and maximum RTOG dermatitis scores versus emollient (P=.046 and P=.018) — sample size and effect sizes not printed
cards.summary: Hindley 2014: mometasone reduced mean and maximum RTOG dermatitis scores versus emollient (P=.046 and P=.018) — sample size and effect sizes not printed
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial (daily mometasone furoate versus Diprobase emollient, from the start of radiotherapy for 5 weeks)
cards.people: Patients receiving breast radiotherapy of 40 Gy in 2.67-Gy fractions over 3 weeks. The abstract does not print the number of participants, mean age or other demographics — a reporting gap flagged here rather than filled.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, mean modified RTOG score, was significantly lower with mometasone than with the emollient (P=.046), as were maximum RTOG score (P=.018) and mean erythema score (P=.012). Dermatology Life Quality Index scores were significantly lower (better) with mometasone at weeks 4 and 5 after correction for anxiety and depression scores. The abstract reports P values without effect sizes or event rates, and none are supplied here. The authors note the trial was designed to confirm an earlier positive study (Boström 2001).
cards.watchOut: A P-value-only record: direction and significance are clear, magnitude is unknowable from this abstract. The comparator is an emollient cream used as control, not an inert placebo, which if anything biases against the steroid.

cards.summary: Ho 2018 (postmastectomy): moist desquamation in 43.8% on mometasone versus 66.7% on control cream (P=.012)
cards.type: Two-arm, double-blind randomised trial (mometasone furoate 0.1% versus Eucerin cream, twice daily from day 1 of radiotherapy to 14 days after)
cards.people: 124 patients receiving postmastectomy chest-wall radiotherapy (50 Gy, with or without nodal irradiation; daily bolus 3–10 mm in all patients) were enrolled between May 2013 and February 2016; 35% had stage III disease and 68% had undergone reconstruction.
cards.result: Moist desquamation — the core of the primary endpoint (grade ≥2 dermatitis with moist desquamation, or any grade ≥3) — occurred in 43.8% in the mometasone arm versus 66.7% in the control arm (P=.012); the whole-cohort rate was 54.8%. Postmastectomy chest-wall irradiation with bolus is a high-dermatitis setting; absolute gains will be smaller where baseline risk is lower.

shelves.title: Exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer (PACES pilot)
shelves.question: In patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer, does a supervised exercise programme during treatment improve fatigue and physical function versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Colonic Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy/physiopathology/therapy · Demography · Exercise · Fatigue/complications · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength · Patient Compliance · Physical Fitness · Pilot Projects · Quality of Life · Self Report · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this shelf rests on a pilot trial only, and it is flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file directed the builder to pin the full PACES results paper before building; searches for this build found only the 2018 pilot/feasibility report and the 2010 design paper — no full PACES effectiveness results could be pinned, and the shelf is therefore built honestly at pilot strength rather than borrowed from other exercise trials. The pilot randomised just 23 patients (of 63 referred), reported high compliance and no adverse events, and described maintained or improved fitness and fatigue levels without printing comparative effect estimates. That establishes feasibility, not efficacy: MAYBE (weak evidence) for the fatigue/function question. Scope boundary: the post-treatment exercise question is homed on Shelf #768 (CHALLENGE); this shelf covers exercise DURING adjuvant chemotherapy only. If the full PACES results are published and pinned, this shelf should be rebuilt; if the developer rejects the exception, withdraw it.

cards.headline: PACES pilot 2018: 23 of 63 referred patients randomised; exercise during chemotherapy was feasible and safe, with no comparative effect estimates reported
cards.summary: PACES pilot 2018: 23 of 63 referred patients randomised; exercise during chemotherapy was feasible and safe, with no comparative effect estimates reported
cards.type: Pilot randomised trial report (recruitment and feasibility, with descriptive outcomes) — Netherlands Trial Register NTR2159
cards.people: 63 patients with colon cancer undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy were referred; 23 agreed to participate and were randomised to a low-intensity home-based programme (Onco-Move), a moderate-to-high-intensity supervised resistance and aerobic programme (OnTrack), or usual care. The 40 non-participants all gave reasons; those who did not want to exercise had higher baseline fatigue and a more negative attitude toward exercise.
cards.result: Compliance with both programmes was high and no adverse events occurred. On average, participants maintained or improved physical fitness and maintained or decreased fatigue during chemotherapy and at 6-month follow-up — reported descriptively, without between-group effect estimates, confidence intervals or P values in the abstract, and none are supplied here. The authors conclude recruitment was difficult and that effectiveness needs to be established in a larger trial.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility report wearing a results question's clothes: with 23 participants across three arms it cannot detect plausible effects on fatigue or function, and it does not try to. Self-selection (participants were the less fatigued, more exercise-positive minority) further limits what even feasibility means here.
cards.source: van Waart H et al. Recruitment to and pilot results of the PACES randomized trial of physical exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer. Int J Colorectal Dis. 2018. shelves.title: Palonosetron for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
shelves.question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, is palonosetron superior to first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists for delayed-phase emesis control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antiemetics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Routes · Female · Humans · Isoquinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced/prevention & control · Ondansetron/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Palonosetron · Quinuclidines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two large phase III double-blind trials, with two corrections to the topic file disclosed. First, the comparator: the Aapro trial compared palonosetron with ONDANSETRON, not dolasetron as the file states; the second trial (Saito 2009) used granisetron — the question's 'first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists' framing covers both and is retained. Second, in Aapro the whole-population delayed-phase advantage was numerical, and the statistically significant delayed-phase superiority was demonstrated in the dexamethasone-pretreated stratum; Saito, in which everyone received dexamethasone, showed delayed-phase superiority outright (56.8% versus 44.5% complete response; P<0.0001) with acute-phase non-inferiority. The shelf's claim is therefore precise: with dexamethasone co-treatment, palonosetron is at least as good acutely and better in the delayed phase than a first-generation comparator. Doses differ between the trials (0.25 mg in Aapro's licensed-dose arm; 0.75 mg in Saito's Japanese programme) and are printed on the cards.

cards.headline: Aapro 2006: palonosetron matched ondansetron acutely; with dexamethasone, delayed complete response was 42.0% versus 28.6%
cards.summary: Aapro 2006: palonosetron matched ondansetron acutely; with dexamethasone, delayed complete response was 42.0% versus 28.6%
cards.type: Phase III, double-blind, randomised trial (single-dose palonosetron 0.25 mg or 0.75 mg versus ondansetron 32 mg, before highly emetogenic chemotherapy)
cards.people: 667 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy; dexamethasone pre-treatment was used at investigator discretion with stratification, and 447 patients (two-thirds) received it. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Acute-phase (first 24 hours) complete response was 59.2% on palonosetron 0.25 mg, 65.5% on 0.75 mg and 57.0% on ondansetron — palonosetron was at least as effective acutely. Complete-response rates were slightly higher with palonosetron in the delayed (24–120 h) and overall phases in the whole population (the abstract does not print those whole-population figures). Among dexamethasone-pretreated patients, palonosetron 0.25 mg plus dexamethasone beat ondansetron plus dexamethasone significantly in the delayed phase (42.0% versus 28.6%) and overall (40.7% versus 25.2%). Both drugs were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The licensed-dose superiority claim for the delayed phase rests on the dexamethasone stratum, not the full intention-to-treat population — quote it with the stratum attached. Dexamethasone use was discretionary (stratified, not randomised), so the stratum comparison is a subgroup of a randomised trial.

A phase III, double-blind, randomized trial of palonosetron compared with ondansetron in preventing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting following highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Ann Oncol. 2006. PMID: 16766588. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Saito 2009: delayed-phase complete response 56.8% on palonosetron versus 44.5% on granisetron (P<0.0001), both with dexamethasone
cards.summary: Saito 2009: delayed-phase complete response 56.8% on palonosetron versus 44.5% on granisetron (P<0.0001), both with dexamethasone
cards.type: Phase III, multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy randomised trial (75 institutions, Japan)
cards.people: 1143 patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy (cisplatin, or anthracycline plus cyclophosphamide) were recruited; 1114 were in the efficacy analyses (555 palonosetron 0.75 mg, 559 granisetron 40 µg/kg), all with dexamethasone. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Acute-phase complete response (no emesis, no rescue medication) was 75.3% on palonosetron versus 73.3% on granisetron (difference 2.9%, 95% CI −2.70 to 7.27), meeting the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin. Delayed-phase complete response was 56.8% versus 44.5% (P<0.0001), demonstrating superiority. Main treatment-related adverse events were constipation (17.4% versus 15.7%) and raised aminotransferases; no grade 4 main treatment-related events were reported.
cards.watchOut: The palonosetron dose (0.75 mg) is the Japanese licensed dose, higher than the 0.25 mg used in Aapro and in Western practice; whether the delayed-phase margin is dose-dependent cannot be settled from these two records. The population is entirely Japanese, a transport caveat for pharmacogenetically influenced emesis pathways.

shelves.title: Benzydamine for radiation-induced oral mucositis (Epstein)
shelves.question: In patients receiving radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, does benzydamine hydrochloride rinse prevent or reduce oral mucositis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Benzydamine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouth Mucosa · Mouthwashes · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Radiotherapy Dosage · Stomatitis/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. In patients receiving conventional fractionation to cumulative doses up to 5000 cGy, benzydamine 0.15% rinse reduced erythema and ulceration by about 30% in relative terms versus placebo (P=0.006), left more patients ulcer-free (>33% versus 18%; P=0.037) and delayed systemic analgesic use. The same trial's accelerated-fractionation subgroup — higher daily doses — showed no benefit, and that null is part of this shelf's answer, printed on the card. One trial from 2001, in pre-IMRT radiotherapy: POSSIBLE. If the developer rejects the exception, withdraw the shelf.

cards.headline: Epstein 2001: benzydamine cut erythema and ulceration by ~30% (relative) versus placebo in conventional radiotherapy — but not in accelerated fractionation
cards.summary: Epstein 2001: benzydamine cut erythema and ulceration by ~30% (relative) versus placebo in conventional radiotherapy — but not in accelerated fractionation
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (0.15% benzydamine rinse, 15 mL for 2 minutes, 4–8 times daily, before and during radiotherapy and for 2 weeks after)
cards.people: Patients with head and neck carcinoma receiving radiotherapy: 145 in the conventional-fractionation analysis (69 benzydamine, 76 placebo) and 20 receiving accelerated radiotherapy (≥220 cGy/day). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: During conventional radiotherapy up to cumulative doses of 5000 cGy, benzydamine significantly reduced erythema and ulceration by approximately 30% in relative terms compared with placebo (P=0.006); more than 33% of benzydamine patients remained ulcer-free versus 18% on placebo (P=0.037), and benzydamine significantly delayed the use of systemic analgesics (P<0.05). Benzydamine was not effective in the accelerated-radiotherapy subgroup. Adverse-event incidence was comparable between groups; early discontinuation for adverse events was 6% (benzydamine) versus 5% (placebo), and one death in the placebo group was related to the primary diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is bounded by dose intensity: at accelerated fractionation the rinse failed, in a small subgroup (n=20) — underpowered to prove futility, but the record gives no reason to expect benefit there. The '~30%' is the authors' relative summary of erythema/ulceration scores; the abstract does not print the underlying scores.
cards.source: Epstein JB et al. Benzydamine HCl for prophylaxis of radiation-induced oral mucositis: results from a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Cancer. 2001. PMID: 11550161. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Methylnaltrexone for opioid-induced constipation in advanced illness (Thomas)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced illness and opioid-induced constipation unresponsive to laxatives, does subcutaneous methylnaltrexone induce laxation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Constipation/chemically induced/drug therapy · Defecation/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Laxatives/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quaternary Ammonium Compounds/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Terminally Ill
shelves.balance: LIKELY — one fully reported phase III trial (Thomas 2008, n=133) plus the pooled responder analysis of both phase III trials, carded second and labelled post hoc. In Thomas, laxation within 4 hours of the first dose occurred in 48% on methylnaltrexone versus 15% on placebo, and after at least two of the first four doses in 52% versus 8% (P<0.001 for both co-primary outcomes), with no evidence of central opioid withdrawal or loss of analgesia. The pooled analysis of Studies 301 and 302 (the second trial is represented through this pooled report; its standalone primary report was not pinned in this build, and the structure is disclosed rather than hidden) found rescue-free bowel movements within 4 hours in more than 50% on methylnaltrexone versus 14.6% on placebo (P<0.0001). No mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf: post hoc survival analyses of these pooled data exist in the literature but are not randomised mortality evidence and are not carded.

cards.headline: Thomas 2008: laxation within 4 hours of the first dose in 48% on methylnaltrexone versus 15% on placebo
cards.summary: Thomas 2008: laxation within 4 hours of the first dose in 48% on methylnaltrexone versus 15% on placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial (Study 302; subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 0.15 mg/kg every other day for 2 weeks)
cards.people: 133 patients with advanced illness, on opioids for at least 2 weeks and on stable opioid and laxative doses for at least 3 days without relief of opioid-induced constipation. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Both co-primary outcomes favoured methylnaltrexone (P<0.001 for both): laxation within 4 hours after the first dose in 48% versus 15% on placebo, and laxation without rescue laxative within 4 hours after two or more of the first four doses in 52% versus 8%. Median time to laxation was significantly shorter on methylnaltrexone (the abstract does not print the medians). There was no evidence of centrally mediated opioid withdrawal or change in pain scores. Abdominal pain and flatulence were the most common adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A 3-month open-label extension followed the blinded phase; its maintained response rates are uncontrolled and are fenced here, not carded as evidence. The population is advanced illness (largely palliative); results do not automatically extend to chronic non-cancer pain, which has its own trials.

cards.headline: Pooled responder analysis of Studies 301 + 302 (post hoc): rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours in >50% on methylnaltrexone versus 14.6% on placebo
cards.summary: Pooled responder analysis of Studies 301 + 302 (post hoc): rescue-free bowel movement within 4 hours in >50% on methylnaltrexone versus 14.6% on placebo
cards.type: Post hoc pooled responder analysis of two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trials — labelled as pooled/post hoc, not a primary trial report
cards.people: Pooled data from Study 301 (NCT00401362) and Study 302 (NCT00402038, the Thomas trial above): 165 patients treated with methylnaltrexone 0.15 or 0.30 mg/kg and 123 with placebo, all with advanced illness and opioid-induced constipation.
cards.result: More than 50% of methylnaltrexone-treated patients (either dose) had a rescue-medication-free bowel movement within 4 hours of the first dose, versus 14.6% on placebo (P<0.0001 for both doses). Response was significantly greater than placebo in every subgroup examined (age, sex, primary diagnosis, baseline distress, morphine-equivalent dose). Common adverse events were abdominal pain (27.9% pooled methylnaltrexone versus 9.8% placebo), flatulence (13.3% versus 5.7%) and nausea (10.9% versus 4.9%).
cards.watchOut: This is a post hoc responder analysis, carded to document the second phase III trial's contribution; it is not independent confirmation beyond the two trials it pools, and the shelf counts the evidence as two trials, not three sources. Subgroup claims in post hoc analyses (for example, larger responses at 0.30 mg/kg in non-cancer diagnoses) are hypothesis-generating only.

shelves.title: Octreotide for malignant bowel obstruction
shelves.question: In patients with inoperable malignant bowel obstruction, does octreotide reduce vomiting versus placebo (with standard co-therapy)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/administration & dosage · Australia/epidemiology · Comorbidity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage · Humans · Intestinal Neoplasms/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Intestinal Obstruction/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Placebo Effect · Prevalence · Risk Factors · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced/diagnosis/mortality
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one randomised trial whose primary endpoint was null. The topic file anchored this shelf on the trial's quality-of-life secondary report and spoke of the parent trial as a separate source; there is one trial, reported twice, and it is counted once here, with the primary report (Currow 2015 — the file's 'Curley' attribution is also corrected) leading the shelf. On the primary outcome, days free of vomiting at 72 hours, octreotide did not beat placebo (17 versus 14 patients completely free of vomiting, P=0.67; mean days free 1.87 versus 1.69, P=0.47). An adjusted secondary analysis found fewer vomiting episodes on octreotide (incidence rate ratio 0.40 in relative terms, 95% CI 0.19–0.86; P=0.019), but octreotide patients were also twice as likely to receive hyoscine butylbromide (P=0.004), a confounder the authors themselves raise; and the quality-of-life report found no between-group difference. A null primary with a confounded adjusted secondary signal earns MAYBE (weak evidence) — enough to justify the further study the authors call for, not enough to claim benefit.

cards.headline: Currow 2015 (primary report): no reduction in days free of vomiting with octreotide (1.87 vs 1.69 days; P=0.47)
cards.summary: Currow 2015 (primary report): no reduction in days free of vomiting with octreotide (1.87 vs 1.69 days; P=0.47)
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial (12 Australian services; octreotide 600 µg/24 h by infusion plus standardised supportive therapy in both arms)
cards.people: People with advanced cancer and vomiting from inoperable bowel obstruction, recruited to the study's power calculation; 87 participants provided data at 72 hours (45 in the octreotide arm). The trial's companion quality-of-life report states 112 were randomised; this primary report's abstract does not print the total randomised, and the discrepancy is noted rather than resolved. Both arms received ranitidine infusion, dexamethasone and parenteral hydration.
cards.result: The primary outcome — patient-reported days free of vomiting at 72 hours — did not differ: 17 people on octreotide and 14 on placebo were completely free of vomiting (P=0.67), and mean days free of vomiting were 1.87 (SD 1.10) versus 1.69 (SD 1.15) (P=0.47). An adjusted multivariate analysis found fewer vomiting episodes on octreotide (incidence rate ratio 0.40 in relative terms, 95% CI 0.19–0.86; P=0.019); however, octreotide patients were 2.02 times more likely to be given hyoscine butylbromide (P=0.004), potentially reflecting increased colicky pain.
cards.watchOut: Read the two analyses together: the prespecified primary comparison is null, and the positive adjusted analysis is vulnerable to the differential rescue-medication use printed in the same abstract. The authors' own conclusion is that further study is warranted — not that octreotide works.
cards.source: Currow DC et al. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial of octreotide in malignant bowel obstruction. J Pain Symptom Manage. 2015. PMID: 25462210. cards.summary: Quality-of-life secondary report of the same trial: no between-group difference in health-related quality of life
cards.type: Secondary-outcome report of the Currow randomised trial — same trial as the card above, counted once
cards.people: 106 of the 112 randomised participants were analysed (52 octreotide, 54 placebo); 6 were excluded for major protocol violations. Baseline health-related quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C15-PAL) was low: mean 22.1 on octreotide and 31.5 on placebo.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant within-group improvement in mean quality-of-life scores in either arm (octreotide P=0.21; placebo P=0.78) and no significant between-group difference in change, although both groups reported reductions in mean nausea and vomiting (octreotide P<0.01; placebo P=0.02) and pain scores (octreotide P<0.01; placebo P=0.03). cards.watchOut: This is the report the topic file pinned as the shelf's anchor. It is a secondary analysis of the same single trial — it adds the quality-of-life null, but it is not a second trial and must never be counted as one. The within-group improvements in both arms underline how much standardised supportive care itself does in this setting.

shelves.title: Cannabis extract for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (Grimison)
shelves.question: In patients with refractory CINV despite guideline prophylaxis, does an oral THC:CBD cannabis extract improve complete response versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Vomiting/chemically induced/prevention & control · Nausea/chemically induced/prevention & control · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Dronabinol/adverse effects/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Antiemetics/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Aged · Cannabidiol/therapeutic use/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Administration, Oral · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Cannabis/adverse effects · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised placebo-controlled trial, flagged here as a two-trial-gate exception candidate. The topic file offered older dronabinol and nabilone trials as the second leg; those are different agents tested before modern prophylaxis existed — a different question — and they are not imported. In the carded trial, an oral THC:CBD extract (2.5 mg/2.5 mg three times daily) added to guideline-consistent prophylaxis raised complete response (no vomiting or retching and no rescue medication, hours 0–120) from 8% to 24% (absolute difference 16 points, 95% CI 4–28; P=.01) in patients whose nausea or vomiting was already refractory. Two qualifications belong on the face of the shelf: the trial recruited 147 evaluable patients against a planned 250, so it is smaller than designed; and the benefit came with more sedation (18% versus 7%), dizziness (10% versus 0%) and transient anxiety (4% versus 1%). If the developer rejects the exception, withdraw the shelf.

cards.headline: Grimison 2024: complete response 24% on THC:CBD extract versus 8% on placebo in refractory CINV (absolute difference 16 points; P=.01)
cards.summary: Grimison 2024: complete response 24% on THC:CBD extract versus 8% on placebo in refractory CINV (absolute difference 16 points; P=.01)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, two-stage phase II/III trial (combined prespecified analysis of the phase II and III components)
cards.people: 147 evaluable adults (of a planned 250) with refractory nausea and/or vomiting during moderately or highly emetogenic intravenous chemotherapy despite guideline-consistent prophylaxis; background prophylaxis included a corticosteroid and 5-HT3 antagonist in 97%, an NK1 antagonist in 80% and olanzapine in 10%. Treatment was THC 2.5 mg plus CBD 2.5 mg capsules or matching placebo, three times daily from day −1 to day 5, in addition to standard antiemetics. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Complete response (no vomiting or retching and no rescue medications during hours 0–120 of the first on-study cycle) was 24% on THC:CBD versus 8% on placebo (absolute difference 16%, 95% CI 4–28; P=.01), with similar-direction effects on absence of significant nausea, rescue-medication use, daily vomits and Functional Living Index-Emesis quality of life. Bothersome adverse events of special interest were more frequent on THC:CBD: sedation 18% versus 7%, dizziness 10% versus 0% and transient anxiety 4% versus 1%. No serious adverse events were attributed to THC:CBD.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment fell well short of plan (147 of 250), so the confidence interval is wide (4–28 points) and the result, while positive, is one under-recruited trial. The population is specifically refractory cases after modern prophylaxis — the low 8% placebo complete-response rate reflects that, and the finding does not transfer to first-line antiemetic use. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Grimison P et al. Oral cannabis extract for secondary prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: final results of a randomized, placebo-controlled, phase II/III trial. shelves.title: Perioperative and neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable NSCLC (CheckMate 816, KEYNOTE-671, AEGEAN)
shelves.question: In resectable stage II-III non-small-cell lung cancer, does adding PD-(L)1 blockade to platinum chemotherapy around surgery — neoadjuvant or perioperative — improve event-free survival versus chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy/surgery · Humans · Ipilimumab/adverse effects · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/surgery · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Nivolumab/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Platinum Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY for event-free survival — three large randomised trials with three different antibodies converge: event-free survival hazard ratios of 0.63 (CheckMate 816, neoadjuvant nivolumab), 0.58 (KEYNOTE-671, perioperative pembrolizumab) and 0.68 (AEGEAN, perioperative durvalumab), with pathological complete response rates roughly five-to-ten-fold higher than chemotherapy alone. The survival ledger is younger: in the reports carded here, overall survival had NOT reached significance in either trial that reported it (CheckMate 816 first interim HR 0.57, confidence interval crossing 1; KEYNOTE-671 24-month survival 80.9% versus 77.6%, P=0.02 against a stricter prespecified criterion) — so no mortality claim is made on this shelf, and the stamp covers event-free survival and pathological response. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): a class whose rationale is an eventual survival benefit. Later overall-survival reports should be swept and carded as updates to these trials, not as new shelves.

cards.headline: CheckMate 816: neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy — EFS 31.6 versus 20.8 months (HR 0.63); pCR 24.0% versus 2.2%; overall survival not significant at first interim
cards.summary: CheckMate 816: neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy — EFS 31.6 versus 20.8 months (HR 0.63); pCR 24.0% versus 2.2%; overall survival not significant at first interim
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, open-label trial (three cycles of nivolumab plus platinum chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone before resection; blinded independent review of endpoints)
cards.people: Patients with stage IB to IIIA resectable NSCLC. The record's abstract does not print the total number randomised, the mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Median event-free survival was 31.6 months (95% CI 30.2 to not reached) with nivolumab plus chemotherapy versus 20.8 months (95% CI 14.0 to 26.7) with chemotherapy alone (hazard ratio for progression, recurrence or death 0.63, 97.38% CI 0.43 to 0.91; P=0.005 — a relative measure; the medians are printed beside it). Pathological complete response occurred in 24.0% versus 2.2% (odds ratio 13.94, 99% CI 3.49 to 55.75; P<0.001). At the first prespecified interim analysis, the hazard ratio for death was 0.57 (99.67% CI 0.30 to 1.07), which did not meet the criterion for significance. Surgery took place in 83.2% of the nivolumab group and 75.4% of the chemotherapy group; grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 33.5% versus 36.9%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment. The survival data in this report are immature and formally non-significant; quote the EFS and pCR results as this trial's findings and treat any survival claim as pending later analyses. The abstract does not print the randomised N — a reporting gap in the record, flagged rather than filled.

cards.headline: KEYNOTE-671: perioperative pembrolizumab — 24-month EFS 62.4% versus 40.6% (HR 0.58); overall survival not significant at this analysis
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-671: perioperative pembrolizumab — 24-month EFS 62.4% versus 40.6% (HR 0.58); overall survival not significant at this analysis
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (neoadjuvant pembrolizumab or placebo with cisplatin-based chemotherapy for 4 cycles, surgery, then adjuvant pembrolizumab or placebo for up to 13 cycles)
cards.people: 797 patients with resectable stage II, IIIA or IIIB (N2) NSCLC were randomised (397 pembrolizumab, 400 placebo). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: At the first interim analysis (median follow-up 25.2 months), event-free survival at 24 months was 62.4% with pembrolizumab versus 40.6% with placebo (hazard ratio for progression, recurrence or death 0.58, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.72; P<0.001). Estimated 24-month overall survival was 80.9% versus 77.6% (P=0.02, which did not meet the prespecified significance criterion). Major pathological response occurred in 30.2% versus 11.0% (difference 19.2 points, 95% CI 13.9 to 24.7) and pathological complete response in 18.1% versus 4.0% (difference 14.2 points, 95% CI 10.1 to 18.7). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 44.9% versus 37.3%, including grade 5 events in 1.0% versus 0.8%.
cards.watchOut: This card reports the first interim analysis: overall survival was not statistically significant at this cutoff under the trial's multiplicity plan, despite the nominal P=0.02. Later survival analyses of KEYNOTE-671 exist in the literature but are not part of this verified record and no figures from them are carded; the shelf should be updated, not replaced, when they are pinned.

cards.summary: AEGEAN: perioperative durvalumab — EFS hazard ratio 0.68; pCR 17.2% versus 4.3%

cards.headline: Synthesis: perioperative immunotherapy transforms event-free survival in resectable NSCLC; survival proof is still maturing — LIKELY (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: perioperative immunotherapy transforms event-free survival in resectable NSCLC; survival proof is still maturing — LIKELY (Tier C)

cards.result: Adding immunotherapy to chemotherapy around surgery delays progression, recurrence or death by a consistent relative 32-42% and multiplies pathological complete responses several-fold, without preventing surgery or adding much high-grade toxicity. A fourth trial of the class (Neotorch, toripalimab) is named in the topic file but is not carded here. On the carded records, overall survival benefit is suggested but not yet formally demonstrated; that is the question the maturing follow-up will answer.
cards.watchOut: All three trials exclude or separately handle EGFR/ALK-driven disease, and their populations are surgical candidates with stage II-III tumours. The class stamp (LIKELY) grades event-free survival; the survival claim awaits the trials' later analyses and a re-sweep.

shelves.title: Adjuvant immunotherapy after resection and chemotherapy in NSCLC (IMpower010, KEYNOTE-091)
shelves.question: In completely resected stage IB-IIIA non-small-cell lung cancer, does one year of adjuvant PD-(L)1 blockade after resection (with adjuvant chemotherapy in most patients) improve disease-free survival versus observation or placebo — and does PD-L1 expression identify who benefits?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · B7-H1 Antigen/metabolism · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy/surgery · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY that adjuvant immunotherapy improves disease-free survival in the overall resected population: two large trials agree (IMpower010 DFS HR 0.81 in the intention-to-treat population; KEYNOTE-091 median DFS 53.6 versus 42.0 months, HR 0.76). MAYBE (weak evidence) for the claim that high PD-L1 expression identifies the beneficiaries — the two trials point in opposite directions: IMpower010's benefit was concentrated in PD-L1-positive tumours under its hierarchical testing, while KEYNOTE-091, positive overall, did NOT meet its dual primary endpoint in the PD-L1 TPS 50% or greater population (HR 0.82, p=0.14). Neither carded record reports overall survival, so no mortality claim is made or supported on this shelf. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): the topic was filed on an emerging overall-survival claim — a correction is recorded here, because the pinned IMpower010 record is its first (disease-free survival) report and contains no survival data; the survival question must be swept from later reports before any such claim is carded.

cards.headline: IMpower010: adjuvant atezolizumab improved disease-free survival, most in PD-L1-positive stage II-IIIA disease (HR 0.66); no survival data in this report
cards.summary: IMpower010: adjuvant atezolizumab improved disease-free survival, most in PD-L1-positive stage II-IIIA disease (HR 0.66); no survival data in this report
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, multicentre, open-label trial (atezolizumab 1200 mg every 21 days for 16 cycles versus best supportive care, after complete resection and adjuvant platinum chemotherapy)
cards.people: 1005 patients with resected stage IB (tumours 4 cm or larger) to IIIA NSCLC who had received adjuvant chemotherapy were randomised (507 atezolizumab, 498 best supportive care); 495 in each group received the assigned management. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Disease-free survival was tested hierarchically. In stage II-IIIA patients whose tumours expressed PD-L1 on at least 1% of tumour cells, the hazard ratio was 0.66 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; p=0.0039); in all stage II-IIIA patients, 0.79 (0.64 to 0.96; p=0.020); and in the full intention-to-treat population, 0.81 (0.67 to 0.99; p=0.040) — relative measures; this record prints no arm-level disease-free survival rates, so none are carded. Atezolizumab-related grade 3 and 4 adverse events occurred in 53 (11%) of 495 patients, and grade 5 events in 4 patients (1%). Overall survival is not reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with investigator-assessed disease-free survival as the endpoint — a design open to assessment bias, mitigated only partly by the hierarchical testing. The PD-L1 gradient comes from the testing hierarchy and subgroup structure, and KEYNOTE-091 (card below) did not reproduce a PD-L1-high advantage; the two records together justify the split stamp.

cards.summary: KEYNOTE-091: adjuvant pembrolizumab improved DFS overall (53.6 versus 42.0 months; HR 0.76) but NOT in the PD-L1 TPS 50%+ population (HR 0.82; p=0.14)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, triple-blind, placebo-controlled interim analysis (PEARLS/KEYNOTE-091; pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks for up to 18 cycles versus placebo after complete resection; adjuvant chemotherapy per local practice)
cards.people: 1177 patients with completely resected stage IB (tumours 4 cm or larger), II or IIIA NSCLC were randomised (590 pembrolizumab, 587 placebo), including 168 and 165 respectively with PD-L1 tumour proportion score of 50% or greater. Median follow-up at this interim analysis was 35.6 months. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: In the overall population, median disease-free survival was 53.6 months (95% CI 39.2 to not reached) on pembrolizumab versus 42.0 months (31.3 to not reached) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.91; p=0.0014). In the PD-L1 TPS 50% or greater population — a dual primary endpoint — median disease-free survival was not reached in either group and the hazard ratio was 0.82 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.18; p=0.14): not significant. Grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 34% versus 26%; serious adverse events in 24% versus 15%; treatment-related adverse events led to death in 4 participants (1%) on pembrolizumab and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis. The discordance between the overall result and the PD-L1-high subgroup is the trial's most important feature and is unexplained within this record — it may reflect subgroup size (about 330 patients), chance, or biology; what it cannot support is a claim that the highest PD-L1 expressors benefit most. Overall survival is not reported in this record.

cards.result: After resection of stage IB-IIIA NSCLC, a year of adjuvant PD-(L)1 blockade reduces the hazard of recurrence or death by roughly a fifth to a quarter across two large trials. But the biomarker story failed to cohere: atezolizumab's benefit looked PD-L1-driven, pembrolizumab's overall benefit came with a null result in its PD-L1-highest subgroup. Until the trials' overall-survival analyses mature, the honest shelf claim is delayed recurrence, not longer life.

shelves.question: In untreated EGFR-mutation-positive (exon 19 deletion or L858R) advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, does osimertinib improve overall survival versus first-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: Acrylamides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Aniline Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy/genetics/mortality · Double-Blind Method · ErbB Receptors/antagonists & inhibitors/genetics · Erlotinib Hydrochloride/therapeutic use · Female · Gefitinib/therapeutic use · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Proportional Hazards Models · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Indoles · Pyrimidines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. FLAURA is the single definitive double-blind trial, and it showed a survival benefit: median overall survival 38.6 versus 31.8 months (hazard ratio 0.80; P=0.046), on top of the progression-free survival advantage (HR 0.46) reported in the trial's primary analysis and restated in this record. The survival P value is close to the boundary and overall survival was a secondary endpoint, which is why the proposed stamp stays at POSSIBLE for the developer to rule on — under his standing rule (Nov 8, 2026) an outstanding single trial with a hard-endpoint result is a category he wants to see and may card on one trial, and this shelf is flagged accordingly rather than held back for a second trial that will never be run. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): an overall-survival benefit claim. Scope boundary: adjuvant osimertinib after resection (ADAURA) is a different question, homed on Shelf #763.

cards.headline: FLAURA: overall survival 38.6 versus 31.8 months on osimertinib versus gefitinib or erlotinib (HR 0.80; P=0.046)
cards.summary: FLAURA: overall survival 38.6 versus 31.8 months on osimertinib versus gefitinib or erlotinib (HR 0.80; P=0.046)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind trial (osimertinib 80 mg daily versus gefitinib 250 mg daily or erlotinib 150 mg daily as a combined comparator group; final analysis of overall survival, a secondary endpoint)
cards.people: 556 patients with previously untreated advanced NSCLC harbouring an EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation were randomised 1:1 (279 osimertinib, 277 comparator). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 38.6 months (95% CI 34.5 to 41.8) on osimertinib versus 31.8 months (95% CI 26.6 to 36.0) on the comparator EGFR inhibitors (hazard ratio for death 0.80, 95.05% CI 0.64 to 1.00; P=0.046 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute medians). At 3 years, 28% of the osimertinib group versus 9% of the comparator group were still receiving a trial regimen; median exposure was 20.7 versus 11.5 months. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were reported in 42% on osimertinib and 47% on the comparator. The record's background restates the trial's primary progression-free survival result (hazard ratio 0.46, from the earlier primary report).
cards.watchOut: Overall survival was a secondary endpoint and its confidence interval reaches 1.00 — a real but borderline-significant survival gain. Patients in the comparator group could receive osimertinib after progression in the trial's later phases of care outside this analysis; the record does not quantify crossover, so no adjusted estimate is carded.

shelves.question: In untreated ALK-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, does alectinib improve progression-free survival and CNS control versus crizotinib?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase · Animals · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carbazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy/mortality · Central Nervous System Neoplasms/drug therapy/secondary · Crizotinib · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyridines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Receptor Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/analysis/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised phase 3 trials (the global ALEX and the Asian ALESIA, run to test consistency) both found large progression-free survival advantages for alectinib over crizotinib (hazard ratios 0.47 and 0.22 by investigator assessment), with markedly fewer CNS progressions (12% versus 45% in ALEX; cause-specific HR 0.16) and fewer grade 3-5 adverse events despite longer treatment. Neither record reports mature overall survival, and no survival claim is made on this shelf. Both trials were open-label, with blinded independent review corroborating the investigator-assessed primary endpoint in each. PROPOSED: LIKELY.

cards.headline: ALEX: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.47; CNS progression in 12% on alectinib versus 45% on crizotinib
cards.summary: ALEX: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.47; CNS progression in 12% on alectinib versus 45% on crizotinib
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, open-label trial (alectinib 600 mg twice daily versus crizotinib 250 mg twice daily; primary endpoint investigator-assessed progression-free survival)
cards.people: 303 patients with previously untreated advanced ALK-positive NSCLC, including patients with asymptomatic CNS disease (152 alectinib, 151 crizotinib); median follow-up 17.6 months (crizotinib) and 18.6 months (alectinib). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Progression or death occurred in 41% on alectinib versus 68% on crizotinib; 12-month event-free survival was 68.4% (95% CI 61.0 to 75.9) versus 48.7% (40.4 to 56.9), hazard ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.65; P<0.001 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates); median progression-free survival on alectinib was not reached. CNS progression occurred in 12% versus 45% (cause-specific hazard ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.28; P<0.001). Response rates were 82.9% versus 75.5% (P=0.09). Grade 3 to 5 adverse events were less frequent on alectinib (41% versus 50%). Independent-review progression-free survival was consistent with the primary analysis.
cards.watchOut: Open-label; overall survival was a secondary endpoint and is not reported in this record — alectinib's claim here is progression and CNS control, not proven longer life. The record's MeSH list includes an 'Animals' heading, an artefact of the source record, reproduced as printed.

cards.people: 187 Asian patients with untreated ALK-positive NSCLC were randomised 2:1 (125 alectinib, 62 crizotinib); median follow-up 16.2 and 15.0 months. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Investigator-assessed progression-free survival favoured alectinib (hazard ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.38; p<0.0001; median not estimable versus 11.1 months), as did independent-review assessment (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.61; p<0.0001). shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. CheckMate 743 is the only phase 3 first-line immunotherapy trial in this disease and the first regimen in over a decade to improve survival: median overall survival 18.1 versus 14.1 months (hazard ratio 0.74; p=0.0020), with 2-year survival 41% versus 27% and a similar grade 3-4 adverse-event burden to chemotherapy. The trial was open-label. Under the developer's standing rule (Nov 8, 2026) an outstanding single randomised trial with a hard-endpoint result is a category he wants to see and may card on one trial; the shelf is flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE for his verdict rather than held for a second trial. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): an overall-survival benefit claim. The topic file noted the benefit was largest in non-epithelioid histology; the verified record's abstract prints no histology-subgroup figures, so no subgroup claim is carded.

cards.headline: CheckMate 743: overall survival 18.1 versus 14.1 months (HR 0.74; p=0.0020); 2-year survival 41% versus 27%
cards.summary: CheckMate 743: overall survival 18.1 versus 14.1 months (HR 0.74; p=0.0020); 2-year survival 41% versus 27%
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, open-label trial (103 hospitals in 21 countries; nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks plus ipilimumab 1 mg/kg every 6 weeks for up to 2 years versus platinum-pemetrexed chemotherapy for up to 6 cycles; primary endpoint overall survival)
cards.people: 605 patients with previously untreated, unresectable malignant pleural mesothelioma and performance status 0-1 were randomised (303 immunotherapy, 302 chemotherapy); 77% were male and the median age was 69 years (IQR 64 to 75). The prespecified interim analysis had a median follow-up of 29.7 months.
cards.result: Overall survival was longer with nivolumab plus ipilimumab: median 18.1 months (95% CI 16.8 to 21.4) versus 14.1 months (12.4 to 16.2) on chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.74, 96.6% CI 0.60 to 0.91; p=0.0020 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute medians). Two-year overall survival was 41% (95% CI 35.1 to 46.5) versus 27% (21.9 to 32.4). Grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 30% versus 32%. Treatment-related deaths occurred in 3 patients (1%) on immunotherapy (pneumonitis, encephalitis, heart failure) and 1 (<1%) on chemotherapy (myelosuppression).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and reported at a prespecified interim analysis — later follow-up can shift the estimates. No histology-subgroup results are printed in this record's abstract, so the often-quoted non-epithelioid advantage is not carded here. Mesothelioma's chemotherapy control arm is itself modest, which conditions what a 4-month median gain means.

shelves.title: Prophylactic cranial irradiation in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer: two eras, two answers
shelves.question: In extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer responding to chemotherapy, does prophylactic cranial irradiation improve overall survival — in the era before routine brain MRI, and in the era of MRI staging and surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Brain Neoplasms/epidemiology/prevention & control/secondary · Carcinoma, Small Cell/drug therapy/mortality/radiotherapy/secondary · Combined Modality Therapy · Cranial Irradiation · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology/radiotherapy · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Risk · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree because their worlds differ, and the balance is the shelf. The EORTC trial (Slotman 2007), conducted without baseline brain imaging or MRI surveillance, found prophylactic cranial irradiation cut symptomatic brain metastases (hazard ratio 0.27; 1-year cumulative incidence 14.6% versus 40.4%) and improved 1-year survival (27.1% versus 13.3%). The Japanese trial (Takahashi 2017), which required MRI-confirmed absence of brain metastases at entry and MRI surveillance every 3 months, found no survival benefit (hazard ratio 1.27, favouring observation numerically) and was stopped early for futility. The honest reading: where MRI surveillance is practised, Slotman's survival benefit has not been reproduced; where it is not, the older result may still hold. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): survival claims in both directions.

cards.headline: EORTC (Slotman 2007): PCI cut symptomatic brain metastases (HR 0.27) and raised 1-year survival from 13.3% to 27.1% — in the pre-MRI era
cards.summary: EORTC (Slotman 2007): PCI cut symptomatic brain metastases (HR 0.27) and raised 1-year survival from 13.3% to 27.1% — in the pre-MRI era
cards.type: Randomised trial (EORTC 08993-22993; prophylactic cranial irradiation versus no further therapy in patients aged 18 to 75 whose extensive-stage SCLC had responded to chemotherapy; brain imaging only when symptoms suggested metastases)
cards.people: 286 patients (143 per group) with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer and any response to chemotherapy. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, time to symptomatic brain metastases, favoured irradiation (hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.44; P<0.001); the cumulative 1-year incidence of brain metastases was 14.6% (95% CI 8.3 to 20.9) versus 40.4% (32.1 to 48.6). Median disease-free survival rose from 12.0 to 14.7 weeks and median overall survival from 5.4 to 6.7 months; 1-year survival was 27.1% (95% CI 19.4 to 35.5) versus 13.3% (8.1 to 19.9). Irradiation had side effects but no clinically significant effect on global health status.
cards.watchOut: No baseline brain imaging was required: some 'prophylactic' treatments were in fact treating occult metastases that modern MRI staging would have found, and the control group received no surveillance imaging — the trial answers the question as posed in 1999-2007 practice, not in an MRI-surveilled clinic. That is the whole tension with the trial below.

cards.headline: Takahashi 2017: with MRI staging and 3-monthly MRI surveillance, PCI did not improve survival (HR 1.27) and the trial stopped early for futility
cards.summary: Takahashi 2017: with MRI staging and 3-monthly MRI surveillance, PCI did not improve survival (HR 1.27) and the trial stopped early for futility
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, open-label trial (47 institutions in Japan; PCI 25 Gy in 10 fractions versus observation; all patients had MRI-confirmed absence of brain metastases after responding to platinum chemotherapy, and protocol MRI surveillance to 24 months)
cards.people: 224 patients with extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer were randomised (113 PCI, 111 observation). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The trial was terminated early after a planned interim analysis of the first 163 patients showed a Bayesian predictive probability of PCI superiority of 0.011%. In the final analysis, median overall survival was 11.6 months (95% CI 9.5 to 13.3) with PCI versus 13.7 months (10.2 to 16.4) with observation (hazard ratio 1.27, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.68; p=0.094 — a relative measure pointing, non-significantly, against PCI). Grade 3 or worse adverse events at 3 months were mostly anorexia (6% versus 2%), malaise (3% versus under 1%) and lower-limb weakness (under 1% versus 5%); there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Early termination for futility truncates information: the confidence interval (0.96 to 1.68) excludes the survival benefit Slotman reported but cannot exclude small effects in either direction. The control group's median survival (13.7 months) was more than double Slotman's control group — a different, MRI-selected population, which is precisely the point.

cards.headline: Synthesis: PCI's survival benefit belongs to the pre-MRI world; under MRI surveillance it has not been shown — SPLIT (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: PCI's survival benefit belongs to the pre-MRI world; under MRI surveillance it has not been shown — SPLIT (Tier C)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EORTC 08993-22993 (Slotman 2007), 286 patients, and Takahashi 2017, 224 patients.
cards.result: Prophylactic cranial irradiation plainly prevents brain metastases from becoming symptomatic. Whether it extends life depends on what the clinic does instead: Slotman's control patients were unimaged until symptoms, and irradiation bought survival; Takahashi's control patients were MRI-staged and MRI-watched, metastases were caught and treated as they appeared, and prophylaxis bought nothing. The two trials are both right, about different systems of care.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded (irradiation cannot be), and Takahashi stopped early. Practice patterned on MRI surveillance should follow Takahashi; settings without MRI access inherit Slotman's logic. If a third trial in an MRI-era Western population reports, this shelf must be re-ruled.

shelves.title: Consolidation durvalumab after chemoradiotherapy in limited-stage SCLC (ADRIATIC)
shelves.question: In limited-stage small-cell lung cancer without progression after concurrent chemoradiotherapy, does consolidation durvalumab improve overall survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology/therapy · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Small Cell Lung Carcinoma/drug therapy/mortality · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Chemoradiotherapy/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Progression-Free Survival · Adult · Neoplasm Staging · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects · Cranial Irradiation/adverse effects · Survival Analysis · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/therapeutic use/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. ADRIATIC is the first positive consolidation trial in limited-stage small-cell lung cancer in decades, and it is double-blind and placebo-controlled: median overall survival 55.9 versus 33.4 months (hazard ratio 0.73; P=0.01), with progression-free survival also improved (HR 0.76) and no excess of high-grade adverse events. The absolute survival separation is very large, which is both the finding and the reason for care — it comes from the trial's first planned interim analysis. Under the developer's standing rule (Nov 8, 2026), an outstanding single randomised blinded trial with a hard-endpoint result is a category he wants to see and may card on one trial; the shelf is flagged accordingly. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): an overall-survival benefit claim. The trial's third arm (durvalumab plus tremelimumab, 200 patients) remains blinded in this record and is not carded.

cards.headline: ADRIATIC: median overall survival 55.9 versus 33.4 months (HR 0.73; P=0.01); progression-free survival HR 0.76
cards.summary: ADRIATIC: median overall survival 55.9 versus 33.4 months (HR 0.73; P=0.01); progression-free survival HR 0.76
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (durvalumab 1500 mg every 4 weeks for up to 24 months versus placebo, after concurrent platinum chemoradiotherapy without progression; first planned interim analysis; randomisation stratified by stage and receipt of prophylactic cranial irradiation)
cards.people: 730 patients were randomised across three arms; the carded comparison is durvalumab alone (264 patients) versus placebo (266 patients). A third arm, durvalumab plus tremelimumab (200 patients), remains blinded in this report. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Overall survival was longer with durvalumab: median 55.9 months (95% CI 37.3 to not reached) versus 33.4 months (25.5 to 39.9) (hazard ratio for death 0.73, 98.321% CI 0.54 to 0.98; P=0.01 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute medians). Progression-free survival was also longer: median 16.6 months (95% CI 10.2 to 28.2) versus 9.2 months (7.4 to 12.9) (hazard ratio 0.76, 97.195% CI 0.59 to 0.98; P=0.02). Maximum grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 24.4% versus 24.2%; adverse events led to discontinuation in 16.4% versus 10.6% and to death in 2.7% versus 1.9%; grade 3 or 4 pneumonitis or radiation pneumonitis occurred in 3.1% versus 2.6%.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis: the placebo arm's median survival (33.4 months) is itself historically strong, and the medians' confidence intervals are wide (the durvalumab median's upper bound was not reached). The tremelimumab combination question is unanswered in this record. Both primary endpoints were tested against adjusted alpha levels, hence the unusual confidence levels printed.
cards.source: Cheng Y et al. Durvalumab after Chemoradiotherapy in Limited-Stage Small-Cell Lung Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 39268857. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03703297, from the record's databank fields. cards.result: For a disease whose post-chemoradiotherapy plateau lasted decades, consolidation durvalumab moved median survival from 33.4 to 55.9 months — a gain of nearly two years at the median — with a placebo-like high-grade toxicity profile apart from more discontinuations.
