shelves.title: One-week (26 Gy in 5 fractions) versus three-week radiotherapy after surgery for early breast cancer (FAST-Forward)
shelves.question: In early breast cancer after breast-conserving surgery, is 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week noninferior for local control and late toxicity versus 40 Gy in 15 fractions over 3 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Breast Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/radiotherapy/surgery · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Mastectomy/methods · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Grading · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/epidemiology · Neoplasm Staging · Radiation Dose Hypofractionation · Radiation Injuries/epidemiology/etiology · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects/methods · Risk Assessment/methods · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom/epidemiology
shelves.balance: One very large noninferiority trial settles the 26 Gy schedule, and separates it from the 27 Gy schedule that shares its card. In FAST-Forward (n=4,096 after breast conservation surgery or mastectomy), 5-year ipsilateral breast tumour relapse was 2.1% with the standard 40 Gy in 15 fractions; the five-fraction schedules were noninferior, with absolute differences of −0.7 percentage points for 26 Gy (HR 0.67) and −0.3 points for 27 Gy (HR 0.86) against a pre-set noninferiority margin of 1.6 points of excess relapse. Late normal-tissue effects split the two experimental arms: moderate or marked clinician-assessed effects at 5 years occurred in 9.9% (40 Gy), 11.9% (26 Gy — not significantly different across 1–5 years, odds ratio 1.12, p=0.20) and 15.4% (27 Gy — significantly worse, odds ratio 1.55, p<0.0001). So the one-week answer is specifically 26 Gy in 5 fractions: equal local control, equal late toxicity, one week instead of three. The wider fractionation family (the FAST and START trials) is concordant background, named here but not carded; this shelf stands on FAST-Forward, whose size and directness carry the stamp. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: FAST-Forward: 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week was noninferior to 40 Gy in 15 fractions for 5-year local control (relapse difference −0.7 points) with no excess late normal-tissue effects — while 27 Gy in 5 fractions caused significantly more
cards.summary: FAST-Forward: 26 Gy in 5 fractions over 1 week was noninferior to 40 Gy in 15 fractions for 5-year local control (relapse difference −0.7 points) with no excess late normal-tissue effects — while 27 Gy in 5 fractions caused significantly more
cards.people: 4,096 patients aged at least 18 years with invasive breast cancer (pT1–3, pN0–1, M0) after breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy at 97 UK centres; 1,361 assigned to 40 Gy in 15 fractions, 1,367 to 27 Gy in 5 fractions, and 1,368 to 26 Gy in 5 fractions; median follow-up 71.5 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, ipsilateral breast tumour relapse, occurred in 31 patients in the 40 Gy group, 27 in the 27 Gy group and 21 in the 26 Gy group; hazard ratios versus 40 Gy were 0.86 (95% CI 0.51–1.44) for 27 Gy and 0.67 (0.38–1.16) for 26 Gy. The 5-year incidence of relapse after 40 Gy was 2.1%; estimated absolute differences were −0.3 percentage points (27 Gy) and −0.7 points (26 Gy), both within the pre-defined noninferiority margin of no more than 1.6% excess. At 5 years, moderate or marked clinician-assessed normal-tissue effects in the breast or chest wall were reported in 9.9% of 40 Gy patients, 15.4% of 27 Gy patients and 11.9% of 26 Gy patients; across all assessments from 1–5 years, the odds ratios versus 40 Gy were 1.55 (95% CI 1.32–1.83; p<0.0001) for 27 Gy and 1.12 (0.94–1.34; p=0.20) for 26 Gy. Patient and photographic assessments agreed: higher normal-tissue-effect risk for 27 Gy, not for 26 Gy.
cards.watchOut: The two five-fraction arms are NOT interchangeable: 27 Gy met noninferiority for tumour control but was significantly more toxic to normal tissue, so the practice answer is the 26 Gy schedule alone. Five-year follow-up is early for late radiation effects; the trial's longer-term reports will refine the toxicity tail.
cards.source: Murray Brunt A et al. Hypofractionated Breast Radiotherapy for 1 Week Versus 3 Weeks (FAST-Forward): 5-Year Efficacy and Late Normal Tissue Effects Results From a Multicentre, Non-Inferiority, Randomised, Phase 3 Trial. The Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32580883. Registry ID: ISRCTN19906132, as printed in the record's abstract text (the record's databank fields are empty). shelves.title: Adjuvant capecitabine in HER2-negative/triple-negative breast cancer (CREATE-X; CIBOMA): benefit tracks the residual-disease population
shelves.question: In triple-negative (and HER2-negative) breast cancer with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, does adjuvant capecitabine improve disease-free and overall survival versus observation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/surgery · Capecitabine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects · Female · Hand-Foot Syndrome/etiology · Humans · Middle Aged · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Neoplasm Staging · Preoperative Care · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Survival Analysis · Triple Negative Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials of adjuvant capecitabine after standard chemotherapy point in different directions, and the population difference explains much of it. CREATE-X (n=910) enrolled the shelf's exact population — HER2-negative breast cancer with RESIDUAL invasive disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — and was stopped early at a pre-specified interim analysis that met its primary endpoint: 5-year disease-free survival 74.1% versus 67.6% (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.92) and overall survival 89.2% versus 83.6% (HR for death 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.90), with the triple-negative subgroup showing the largest gains (disease-free survival HR 0.58; overall survival HR 0.52) and hand-foot syndrome in 73.4% of capecitabine patients. CIBOMA (n=876) enrolled early triple-negative patients after standard neo-/adjuvant chemotherapy WITHOUT requiring residual disease, and its primary analysis was null: disease-free survival HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.63–1.06; P=.136). CIBOMA's pre-planned phenotype analysis suggested benefit confined to the nonbasal subgroup (disease-free survival HR 0.53 vs 0.94 in basal; overall-survival HR 0.42 vs 1.23; interaction P=.0052) — hypothesis-generating by the authors' own statement, and flagged as such here. Balance: adjuvant capecitabine improves disease-free and overall survival where the trial question was residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy; it is not supported as blanket extended therapy after standard chemotherapy in unselected early TNBC. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: CREATE-X: adjuvant capecitabine improved 5-year disease-free survival (74.1% vs 67.6%, HR 0.70) and overall survival (89.2% vs 83.6%, HR 0.59) in HER2-negative breast cancer with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
cards.summary: CREATE-X: adjuvant capecitabine improved 5-year disease-free survival (74.1% vs 67.6%, HR 0.70) and overall survival (89.2% vs 83.6%, HR 0.59) in HER2-negative breast cancer with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy
cards.type: Randomized trial (phase 3; stopped early at a pre-specified interim analysis)
cards.people: 910 patients with HER2-negative residual invasive breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy containing an anthracycline, a taxane, or both, randomised to standard postsurgical treatment with or without capecitabine. The abstract does not print the arm counts, mean age, or sex split.
cards.result: The trial was terminated early after a pre-specified interim analysis met the primary endpoint. In the final analysis, 5-year disease-free survival was 74.1% in the capecitabine group versus 67.6% in the control group (HR for recurrence, second cancer, or death 0.70; 95% CI 0.53–0.92; P=0.01), and 5-year overall survival was 89.2% versus 83.6% (HR for death 0.59; 95% CI 0.39–0.90; P=0.01). Among patients with triple-negative disease, disease-free survival was 69.8% versus 56.1% (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.39–0.87) and overall survival 78.8% versus 70.3% (HR 0.52; 95% CI 0.30–0.90). Hand-foot syndrome, the most common adverse reaction to capecitabine, occurred in 73.4% of capecitabine patients.
cards.watchOut: Early termination at an interim analysis tends to inflate effect sizes; the survival hazard ratios should be read with that in mind. The population is defined by residual invasive disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — the high-risk feature that CIBOMA did not require.
cards.source: Masuda N et al. Adjuvant Capecitabine for Breast Cancer After Preoperative Chemotherapy (CREATE-X). The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28564564. Registry ID: UMIN000000843, from the record's databank fields (UMIN Clinical Trials Registry). cards.headline: CIBOMA: extended adjuvant capecitabine after standard chemotherapy in early triple-negative breast cancer did NOT significantly improve disease-free survival (HR 0.82, P=.136); a nonbasal-subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating
cards.summary: CIBOMA: extended adjuvant capecitabine after standard chemotherapy in early triple-negative breast cancer did NOT significantly improve disease-free survival (HR 0.82, P=.136); a nonbasal-subgroup signal is hypothesis-generating
cards.people: 876 patients with operable early triple-negative breast cancer after anthracycline- and/or taxane-containing neo-/adjuvant chemotherapy, randomised to capecitabine (n=448) or observation (n=428); median age 49 years, 55.9% lymph-node-negative, 73.9% basal phenotype; median follow-up 7.3 years. Residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy was not an entry requirement.
cards.result: Disease-free survival was not significantly prolonged with capecitabine versus observation (HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.63–1.06; P=.136). In a pre-planned subgroup analysis, patients with a nonbasal phenotype seemed to derive benefit (disease-free survival HR 0.53, versus 0.94 in the basal phenotype; interaction P=.0694), with an overall-survival HR of 0.42 in nonbasal versus 1.23 in basal patients (interaction P=.0052); the authors state this will require additional validation. 75.2% of capecitabine patients completed the planned 8 cycles.
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis is null; the phenotype findings are subgroup results the authors themselves label as needing validation. An erratum to this report exists in the database (PMID 32135071) but its text is not reproduced in the record; the figures carded are as printed in the primary abstract. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields; none is printed on this card.

shelves.title: Tucatinib plus trastuzumab and capecitabine in previously treated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (HER2CLIMB)
shelves.question: In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1, does tucatinib plus trastuzumab and capecitabine improve progression-free and overall survival versus trastuzumab and capecitabine — including in patients with brain metastases?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Brain Neoplasms/secondary · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology · Capecitabine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Consolidation Chemotherapy · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Middle Aged · Oxazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Progression-Free Survival · Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Pyridines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quinazolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases/analysis/antagonists & inhibitors · Trastuzumab/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: One double-blind trial answers the question, including its brain-metastases clause. In HER2CLIMB (612 patients previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and T-DM1), adding tucatinib to trastuzumab plus capecitabine improved progression-free survival in the primary population (1-year PFS 33.1% vs 12.3%; HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42–0.71 — note the drafting topic file's 'PFS HR 0.66' is wrong; 0.66 is the overall-survival hazard ratio, and the record governs) and improved overall survival (2-year 44.9% vs 26.6%; HR for death 0.66, 95% CI 0.50–0.88, P=0.005; median 21.9 vs 17.4 months). Uniquely, the trial enrolled patients with brain metastases, in whom 1-year progression-free survival was 24.9% versus 0% (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34–0.69). Diarrhoea and grade ≥3 aminotransferase elevations were more common with tucatinib (the abstract does not print the percentages). The topic file called this shelf DOUBLE-A on the strength of HER2CLIMB-02, a trial of a DIFFERENT combination (tucatinib with T-DM1) that is not carded here; as built, the shelf rests on HER2CLIMB alone and is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects single-trial shelves it should be withdrawn or re-scoped, though the double-blind design, the survival benefit and the brain-metastases population make it a strong candidate for his OUTSTANDING-SINGLE pathway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: HER2CLIMB: adding tucatinib to trastuzumab plus capecitabine improved progression-free survival (HR 0.54) and overall survival (HR 0.66) in heavily pretreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, with benefit in brain metastases (HR 0.48)
cards.summary: HER2CLIMB: adding tucatinib to trastuzumab plus capecitabine improved progression-free survival (HR 0.54) and overall survival (HR 0.66) in heavily pretreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, with benefit in brain metastases (HR 0.48)
cards.people: 612 patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and trastuzumab emtansine, with or without brain metastases, assigned to tucatinib or placebo added to trastuzumab and capecitabine; the primary progression-free-survival population was the first 480 randomised patients. The abstract does not print the arm counts, mean age, or sex split.
cards.result: Progression-free survival at 1 year was 33.1% in the tucatinib-combination group versus 12.3% in the placebo-combination group (HR for progression or death 0.54; 95% CI 0.42–0.71; P<0.001), with median progression-free survival of 7.8 versus 5.6 months. Overall survival at 2 years was 44.9% versus 26.6% (HR for death 0.66; 95% CI 0.50–0.88; P=0.005), with median overall survival of 21.9 versus 17.4 months. Among patients with brain metastases, progression-free survival at 1 year was 24.9% versus 0% (HR 0.48; 95% CI 0.34–0.69; P<0.001) and median progression-free survival was 7.6 versus 5.4 months. Common adverse events in the tucatinib group included diarrhoea, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, nausea, fatigue and vomiting; diarrhoea and grade ≥3 elevations in aminotransferase levels were more common in the tucatinib-combination group (percentages not printed in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: A single trial as carded: the topic plan's second-trial support (HER2CLIMB-02) tests tucatinib with T-DM1, a different regimen, and is fenced by name rather than carded. The drafting topic file quoted the progression-free-survival hazard ratio as 0.66; the record's PFS hazard ratio is 0.54 (0.66 is the survival hazard ratio) — the record governs.

shelves.title: Adding abiraterone (± enzalutamide) to ADT in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer (STAMPEDE platform trials)
shelves.question: In high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer treated with ADT and radiotherapy, does adding abiraterone (± enzalutamide) for 2 years improve metastasis-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Abiraterone Acetate/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Benzamides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects/methods/statistics & numerical data · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Disease-Free Survival · Humans · Male · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Neoplasm Grading · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/epidemiology/prevention & control · Nitriles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Phenylthiohydantoin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Progression-Free Survival · Prostatectomy · Prostatic Neoplasms/diagnosis/mortality/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials within the STAMPEDE platform, pooled in a pre-planned meta-analysis of their primary results (the publication form is disclosed on the card), give a clear answer. Among 1,974 men with high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer on 3 years of ADT (radiotherapy mandated or encouraged; 85% planned to receive it), adding 2 years of abiraterone-based combination therapy improved metastasis-free survival (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.44–0.64; 6-year metastasis-free survival 82% vs 69%) and overall survival (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.48–0.73), with prostate-cancer-specific survival HR 0.49. Adding enzalutamide to abiraterone gave no additional metastasis-free-survival benefit (interaction HR 1.02, p=0.91) but substantially more grade ≥3 toxicity (58% vs 37% for the abiraterone-only combination in the respective trials), and all seven grade 5 adverse events occurred in the combination arms. The platform's design used a one-sided type-1 error of 1.25% for power calculations, flagged on the card. Balance: two years of abiraterone on top of ADT improves metastasis-free and overall survival in high-risk non-metastatic disease; the enzalutamide addition adds harm without benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: STAMPEDE (two platform trials pooled): adding abiraterone-based therapy to ADT improved metastasis-free survival (HR 0.53; 6-year 82% vs 69%) and overall survival (HR 0.60) in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer; enzalutamide added toxicity, not benefit
cards.summary: STAMPEDE (two platform trials pooled): adding abiraterone-based therapy to ADT improved metastasis-free survival (HR 0.53; 6-year 82% vs 69%) and overall survival (HR 0.60) in high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer; enzalutamide added toxicity, not benefit
cards.type: Pre-planned meta-analysis of two randomized phase 3 trials (platform protocol; publication form disclosed)
cards.people: 1,974 men with high-risk non-metastatic prostate cancer (node-positive, or node-negative with at least two of: stage T3/T4, Gleason 8–10, PSA ≥40 ng/mL) or high-risk relapse, treated at 113 UK and Swiss sites; the abiraterone trial allocated 455 to ADT alone and 459 to ADT plus abiraterone/prednisolone, and the second trial allocated 533 to ADT alone and 527 to ADT plus abiraterone/prednisolone and enzalutamide. Median age 68 years; median PSA 34 ng/mL; 39% were node-positive and 85% were planned to receive radiotherapy.
cards.result: With a median follow-up of 72 months, metastasis-free survival was significantly longer in the combination-therapy groups (HR 0.53; 95% CI 0.44–0.64; p<0.0001), with 6-year metastasis-free survival of 82% (95% CI 79–85) versus 69% (66–72) and 180 versus 306 metastasis-free-survival events. Overall survival also favoured combination therapy (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.73; p<0.0001), as did prostate-cancer-specific survival (HR 0.49; 0.37–0.65), biochemical failure-free survival (HR 0.39) and progression-free survival (HR 0.44). There was no evidence that adding enzalutamide to abiraterone improved metastasis-free survival further (interaction HR 1.02; p=0.91) and no between-trial heterogeneity. Grade ≥3 adverse events in the first 24 months were reported in 37% versus 29% (abiraterone trial) and 58% versus 32% (abiraterone-plus-enzalutamide trial); the most common excess events were hypertension and alanine transaminitis. Seven grade 5 adverse events were reported, all in the combination-therapy groups and none in the control groups.
cards.watchOut: This record is a meta-analysis BY DESIGN — the pre-planned pooled primary analysis of two randomised trials in one platform protocol (its PubMed publication type is Meta-Analysis), not two separate trial reports; the trials are counted as the two randomised comparisons they are. The platform's power calculation used a one-sided type-1 error rate of 1.25%, an unusually stringent but one-sided design choice, flagged here. Both trials were open-label.
cards.source: Attard G et al. Abiraterone Acetate and Prednisolone With or Without Enzalutamide for High-Risk Non-Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A Meta-Analysis of Primary Results From Two Randomised Controlled Phase 3 Trials of the STAMPEDE Platform Protocol. The Lancet. 2022. PMID: 34953525. Registry IDs: NCT00268476, from the record's databank fields, and ISRCTN78818544, as printed in the record's abstract text. shelves.title: Enzalutamide (± leuprolide) in high-risk biochemical recurrence after definitive therapy (EMBARK)
shelves.question: In high-risk biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy/radiotherapy without metastases on conventional imaging, does enzalutamide (with or without leuprolide) delay metastasis versus leuprolide alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Androgen Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Leuprolide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Nitriles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prostatic Neoplasms/blood/drug therapy/pathology · Quality of Life · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/blood/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Benzamides · Phenylthiohydantoin
shelves.balance: One phase 3 trial, on a surrogate primary endpoint, with survival data not yet in the record. In EMBARK (n=1,068 patients with high-risk biochemical recurrence — PSA doubling time ≤9 months — and no metastases on conventional imaging), 5-year metastasis-free survival was 87.3% with enzalutamide plus leuprolide versus 71.4% with leuprolide alone (HR for metastasis or death 0.42, 95% CI 0.30–0.61, P<0.001 — note the drafting topic file's hazard ratio of 0.58 does not appear in the record; 0.42 governs), and 80.0% with enzalutamide monotherapy (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46–0.87, P=0.005). No new safety signals were observed and quality-of-life measures showed no substantial between-group differences. The record reports NO overall-survival results, so no mortality claim is made or supported by this shelf: metastasis-free survival is a surrogate here, and whether delaying metastasis in a population defined by PSA kinetics translates into longer life is precisely what longer follow-up must show. The shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate for the developer (single trial, surrogate primary). PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: EMBARK: enzalutamide plus leuprolide improved 5-year metastasis-free survival to 87.3% versus 71.4% for leuprolide alone (HR 0.42) in high-risk biochemical recurrence; enzalutamide monotherapy also helped (HR 0.63)
cards.summary: EMBARK: enzalutamide plus leuprolide improved 5-year metastasis-free survival to 87.3% versus 71.4% for leuprolide alone (HR 0.42) in high-risk biochemical recurrence; enzalutamide monotherapy also helped (HR 0.63)
cards.people: 1,068 patients with prostate cancer and high-risk biochemical recurrence (PSA doubling time ≤9 months) after prostatectomy or radiotherapy, without metastases on conventional imaging; 355 assigned to enzalutamide plus leuprolide, 358 to placebo plus leuprolide, and 355 to enzalutamide monotherapy; median follow-up 60.7 months. The abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: At 5 years, metastasis-free survival (by blinded independent central review) was 87.3% (95% CI 83.0–90.6) in the combination group, 71.4% (65.7–76.3) in the leuprolide-alone group, and 80.0% (75.0–84.1) in the monotherapy group. Enzalutamide plus leuprolide was superior to leuprolide alone (HR for metastasis or death 0.42; 95% CI 0.30–0.61; P<0.001), and enzalutamide monotherapy was also superior (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.46–0.87; P=0.005). No new safety signals were observed, with no substantial between-group differences in quality-of-life measures. The record reports no overall-survival results.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is metastasis-free survival on conventional imaging in a PSA-defined population — a surrogate; the survival question is unanswered in this record and no mortality claim is carded. The drafting topic file quoted a combination hazard ratio of 0.58; the record prints 0.42, and the record governs.

shelves.title: 177Lu-PSMA-617 radioligand therapy in PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (VISION) — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
shelves.question: In PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after AR-pathway inhibition and taxane chemotherapy, does 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care improve overall survival versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Combined Modality Therapy · Dipeptides/therapeutic use · Heterocyclic Compounds, 1-Ring/therapeutic use · Humans · Kallikreins/antagonists & inhibitors · Lutetium/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Positron-Emission Tomography · Prostate/diagnostic imaging · Prostate-Specific Antigen/antagonists & inhibitors/therapeutic use · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/mortality/radiotherapy · Radioisotopes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial establishing a new drug class in this disease, with benefits on both of its alternate primary endpoints. In VISION (831 of 1,179 screened patients randomised, all with PSMA-positive scans after at least one AR-pathway inhibitor and one or two taxane regimens), adding 177Lu-PSMA-617 to protocol-permitted standard care prolonged imaging-based progression-free survival (median 8.7 vs 3.4 months; HR 0.40, 99.2% CI 0.29–0.57) and overall survival (median 15.3 vs 11.3 months; HR for death 0.62, 95% CI 0.52–0.74), with all key secondary endpoints also favouring the radioligand. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent with 177Lu-PSMA-617 (52.7% vs 38.0%), but quality of life was not adversely affected. Two scope notes: the standard-care control excluded chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radium-223 and investigational drugs by protocol, so the comparison is against a deliberately restricted standard; and the population is gated by PSMA-PET positivity (348 of the 1,179 screened patients were not randomised). The lutetium-PSMA question in neuroendocrine tumours is a different diagnosis, homed on Shelf #742, not here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: VISION: 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care improved overall survival (15.3 vs 11.3 months, HR 0.62) and imaging-based progression-free survival (8.7 vs 3.4 months, HR 0.40) in PSMA-positive mCRPC after AR-pathway inhibition and taxane therapy
cards.summary: VISION: 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care improved overall survival (15.3 vs 11.3 months, HR 0.62) and imaging-based progression-free survival (8.7 vs 3.4 months, HR 0.40) in PSMA-positive mCRPC after AR-pathway inhibition and taxane therapy
cards.people: 831 patients with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (of 1,179 screened) previously treated with at least one androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitor and one or two taxane regimens, randomised 2:1 to 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus protocol-permitted standard care or standard care alone; median follow-up 20.9 months. The abstract does not print the arm counts or a mean age.
cards.result: 177Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard care significantly prolonged both alternate primary endpoints versus standard care alone: imaging-based progression-free survival (median 8.7 vs 3.4 months; HR for progression or death 0.40; 99.2% CI 0.29–0.57; P<0.001) and overall survival (median 15.3 vs 11.3 months; HR for death 0.62; 95% CI 0.52–0.74; P<0.001). All key secondary endpoints significantly favoured 177Lu-PSMA-617. Adverse events of grade 3 or above occurred in 52.7% of the radioligand group versus 38.0% of controls, but quality of life was not adversely affected.
cards.watchOut: Protocol-permitted standard care excluded chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radium-223 and investigational drugs — a restricted comparator that flatters the relative benefit. Eligibility required a PSMA-positive PET scan; the result does not extend to PSMA-negative or unscanned disease. The earlier TheraP trial compared the same radioligand against cabazitaxel chemotherapy — a different question — and is fenced here by name, not carded.

shelves.title: PARP inhibition in HRR-altered metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (PROfound; TRITON3)
shelves.question: In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with homologous-recombination-repair gene alterations progressing on an AR-pathway inhibitor, does olaparib improve progression-free and overall survival versus physician's-choice AR switch?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androstenes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated Proteins/genetics · Benzamides · Genes, BRCA1 · Genes, BRCA2 · Humans · Loss of Function Mutation · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis/drug therapy · Nitriles · Phenylthiohydantoin/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Phthalazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Piperazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Progression-Free Survival · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant/drug therapy/genetics/mortality/pathology
shelves.balance: Two open-label phase 3 trials of PARP inhibition in biomarker-selected mCRPC agree on progression, and one shows a survival benefit despite heavy crossover. In PROfound (cohort A: 245 men with BRCA1, BRCA2 or ATM alterations progressing on a next-generation hormonal agent), olaparib improved imaging-based progression-free survival (median 7.4 vs 3.6 months; HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.25–0.47) versus physician's choice of the other AR agent, and the final analysis showed longer overall survival (median 19.1 vs 14.7 months; HR for death 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.97, P=0.02) even though 66% of control patients crossed over to olaparib (crossover-adjusted cohort A hazard ratio 0.42, with wide confidence intervals). In TRITON3, rucaparib improved imaging-based progression-free survival in the BRCA subgroup (11.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.36–0.69) and in the intention-to-treat population (HR 0.61) versus physician's choice of docetaxel or an AR switch; its record reports no overall-survival analysis. The honest caveat is ATM: PROfound's cohort A bundled ATM with BRCA1/2, while TRITON3's exploratory ATM analysis showed no progression benefit (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.59–1.52) — the class benefit is BRCA-driven, and ATM-only disease should not be assumed to share it. Anaemia and nausea were olaparib's main toxic effects; fatigue and nausea were rucaparib's most frequent. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: PROfound: olaparib improved progression-free survival in BRCA1/2/ATM-altered mCRPC (7.4 vs 3.6 months, HR 0.34) and, at final analysis, overall survival (19.1 vs 14.7 months, HR 0.69) despite 66% crossover
cards.summary: PROfound: olaparib improved progression-free survival in BRCA1/2/ATM-altered mCRPC (7.4 vs 3.6 months, HR 0.34) and, at final analysis, overall survival (19.1 vs 14.7 months, HR 0.69) despite 66% crossover
cards.type: Randomized trial (open-label, phase 3; primary progression report and final overall-survival report, one trial)
cards.people: Men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing on a new hormonal agent (enzalutamide or abiraterone), with centrally confirmed alterations in prespecified homologous-recombination-repair genes: cohort A, 245 patients with BRCA1, BRCA2 or ATM alterations; cohort B, 142 patients with alterations in 12 other genes; 256 patients were assigned to olaparib and 131 to physician's-choice control in total. The abstracts do not print a mean age.
cards.result: Primary report: in cohort A, imaging-based progression-free survival was significantly longer with olaparib (median 7.4 vs 3.6 months; HR for progression or death 0.34; 95% CI 0.25–0.47; P<0.001), with benefits also in confirmed response rate and time to pain progression; interim median overall survival in cohort A was 18.5 versus 15.1 months, with 81% of progressing control patients crossing over to olaparib at that report. Anaemia and nausea were the main toxic effects of olaparib. Final survival report: median overall survival in cohort A was 19.1 months with olaparib versus 14.7 months with control (HR for death 0.69; 95% CI 0.50–0.97; P=0.02); in cohort B it was 14.1 versus 11.5 months (no hazard ratio printed), and in the overall population 17.3 versus 14.0 months. Overall, 66% of control patients crossed over to olaparib; a crossover-adjusted sensitivity analysis gave hazard ratios for death of 0.42 (95% CI 0.19–0.91) in cohort A, 0.83 (0.11–5.98) in cohort B, and 0.55 (0.29–1.06) overall.
cards.watchOut: One trial counted once across two reports. Cohort A's headline bundles ATM with BRCA1/2; the trial does not isolate an ATM-only effect, and TRITON3's ATM analysis (next card) found none. The crossover-adjusted estimates are sensitivity analyses with wide intervals, not randomised comparisons.

Survival with Olaparib in Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32955174. Registry ID: NCT02987543, from both records' databank fields. cards.result: Imaging-based progression-free survival was significantly longer with rucaparib than control in the BRCA subgroup (median 11.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.36–0.69) and in the intention-to-treat population (median 10.2 vs 6.4 months; HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.47–0.80; P<0.001 for both comparisons). shelves.title: Adjuvant versus early-salvage radiotherapy after radical prostatectomy (RADICALS-RT; RAVES; GETUG-AFU 17)
shelves.question: After radical prostatectomy with adverse pathology or detectable PSA, does adjuvant radiotherapy improve outcomes versus observation with early-salvage radiotherapy at PSA recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/pathology/radiotherapy/surgery · Aged · Biomarkers, Tumor/blood · Disease-Free Survival · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Grading · Proportional Hazards Models · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostatectomy · Prostatic Neoplasms/pathology/radiotherapy/surgery · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Salvage Therapy · Survival Analysis · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials converge: irradiating everyone up front buys no biochemical-control advantage over watching PSA and irradiating early at recurrence — it only irradiates many men who never need it and adds urinary and sexual morbidity. In RADICALS-RT (n=1,396), 5-year biochemical progression-free survival was 85% with adjuvant radiotherapy versus 88% under an observation-with-salvage policy (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81–1.49, p=0.56), while only 33% of the salvage-policy group ever received radiotherapy by 8 years; grade 3–4 urethral stricture was 6% versus 4% and self-reported incontinence was worse at 1 year with adjuvant treatment. In RAVES (n=333), 5-year freedom from biochemical progression was 86% versus 87% (HR 1.12) — its formal noninferiority criterion was not met (p for noninferiority = 0.15), disclosed on the card, though control was near-identical and grade ≥2 genitourinary toxicity was lower with salvage (54% vs 70%). In GETUG-AFU 17 (n=424, all patients also receiving 6 months of hormonal therapy), 5-year event-free survival was 92% versus 90% (HR 0.81, p=0.42), with more late genitourinary toxicity and erectile dysfunction in the adjuvant arm. Two caveats are printed on the cards: RADICALS-RT's primary endpoint (10-year freedom from distant metastases) is not yet reported in its record, so the shelf's endpoints are biochemical; and GETUG-AFU 17's abstract prints two irreconcilable pairs of late genitourinary toxicity figures, flagged rather than repaired. Balance: an early-salvage policy is the standard these trials support. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference for adjuvant superiority).

cards.headline: RADICALS-RT: adjuvant radiotherapy did not improve 5-year biochemical progression-free survival versus an observation policy with early salvage (85% vs 88%, HR 1.10) — and only a third of the policy group ever needed radiation
cards.summary: RADICALS-RT: adjuvant radiotherapy did not improve 5-year biochemical progression-free survival versus an observation policy with early salvage (85% vs 88%, HR 1.10) — and only a third of the policy group ever needed radiation
cards.type: Randomized trial (phase 3; interim report — primary endpoint not yet reported)
cards.people: 1,396 patients with at least one risk factor for biochemical progression after radical prostatectomy (pT3/4, Gleason 7–10, positive margins, or preoperative PSA ≥10 ng/mL) in Canada, Denmark, Ireland and the UK; 697 assigned to adjuvant radiotherapy and 699 to observation with salvage radiotherapy at PSA progression; median age 65 years; median follow-up 4.9 years.
cards.result: Five-year biochemical progression-free survival was 85% in the adjuvant radiotherapy group and 88% in the salvage-policy group (HR 1.10; 95% CI 0.81–1.49; p=0.56). Freedom from non-protocol hormone therapy at 5 years was 93% versus 92% (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.58–1.33; p=0.53). In the adjuvant group, 93% received radiotherapy within 6 months; in the salvage-policy group, only 33% had received radiotherapy within 8 years. Self-reported urinary incontinence was worse at 1 year in the adjuvant group (mean score 4.8 vs 4.0; p=0.0023), and grade 3–4 urethral stricture within 2 years occurred in 6% versus 4% (p=0.020).
cards.watchOut: This record is an interim report: the trial's primary outcome — freedom from distant metastases at 10 years — is not yet reported in it, so the carded endpoints are biochemical progression and toxicity, not metastasis or survival. The authors' conclusion (observation with salvage should be the current standard) rests on those endpoints plus the sparing effect.

cards.people: 333 patients after radical prostatectomy with high-risk features (positive margins, extraprostatic extension, or seminal vesicle invasion) and postoperative PSA ≤0.10 ng/mL, at 32 Australian and New Zealand centres; 166 assigned to adjuvant radiotherapy and 167 to early-salvage radiotherapy triggered at PSA ≥0.20 ng/mL; median follow-up 6.1 years. The abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Five-year freedom from biochemical progression was 86% (95% CI 81–92) in the adjuvant group versus 87% (82–93) in the salvage group (stratified HR 1.12; 95% CI 0.65–1.90); the p value for noninferiority was 0.15, so the trial's pre-specified noninferiority criterion was NOT formally met, as the authors state. Half of the salvage group (50%) had radiotherapy triggered. The grade 2 or worse genitourinary toxicity rate was lower in the salvage group (54% [90 of 167]) than in the adjuvant group (70% [116 of 166]); grade 2 or worse gastrointestinal toxicity was 10% versus 14%. Enrolment was closed prematurely on data-monitoring advice because event rates were unexpectedly low.
cards.watchOut: Formally, this trial is noninferiority NOT PROVEN — the near-identical point estimates come with a wide confidence interval (HR up to 1.90) and early closure for low event rates. The shelf's confidence comes from the three trials' convergence, not from RAVES alone.

cards.people: 424 men after radical prostatectomy with pT3a, pT3b or pT4a disease, pNx or pN0, and positive surgical margins, at 46 French hospitals; 212 assigned to immediate adjuvant radiotherapy and 212 to salvage radiotherapy at biochemical relapse; ALL patients in both arms received 6 months of triptorelin. The abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Five-year event-free survival was 92% (95% CI 86–95) in the adjuvant group and 90% (85–94) in the salvage group (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.48–1.36; log-rank p=0.42). In the salvage group, 115 of 212 patients (54%) initiated radiotherapy after biochemical relapse. Acute grade ≥3 toxic effects occurred in 3% (adjuvant) versus 2% (salvage). Late erectile dysfunction of grade 2 or worse was reported in 28% of the adjuvant group versus 8% of the salvage group (p<0.0001). Enrolment was terminated early (424 of a planned 718 patients) because of unexpectedly low event rates, and the authors note the analysis lacked statistical power.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints TWO irreconcilable pairs for late grade ≥2 genitourinary toxicity — 59% versus 22% in one sentence and 27% versus 7% (p<0.0001) in the next, both labelled 'late'. The inconsistency is in the record itself; both pairs are reported here rather than silently choosing one, and the direction (more urinary harm with adjuvant treatment) is the same in both. Hormonal therapy in both arms distinguishes this trial from RADICALS-RT and RAVES.

shelves.title: Moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions) versus conventional fractionation in localised prostate cancer (CHHiP; PROFIT)
shelves.question: In localized prostate cancer, is moderately hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions) noninferior to conventional fractionation (74 Gy in 37 fractions) for biochemical/clinical failure?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · International Agencies · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Prostatic Neoplasms/pathology/radiotherapy · Radiation Dose Hypofractionation · Radiotherapy, Intensity-Modulated/methods · Risk Factors · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two large noninferiority trials say yes for the 60 Gy in 20 fractions schedule. In CHHiP (n=3,216, localised prostate cancer, most receiving 3–6 months of androgen suppression), the proportion free of biochemical or clinical failure at 5 years was 90.6% with 60 Gy in 20 fractions versus 88.3% with 74 Gy in 37 fractions — noninferior (HR 0.84, 90% CI 0.68–1.03; p for noninferiority = 0.0018 against a critical HR of 1.208) — with similar long-term side-effects and 5-year cumulative grade ≥2 bowel/bladder adverse events of 11.9%/11.7% (60 Gy) versus 13.7%/9.1% (74 Gy). CHHiP's more aggressive 57 Gy in 19 fractions schedule did NOT establish noninferiority (HR 1.20; pNI=0.48), a boundary printed on the card: the answer licenses 60/20, not every shorter schedule. In PROFIT (n=1,206, intermediate-risk disease, no androgen deprivation permitted, and a 78 Gy in 39 fractions control), 5-year biochemical-clinical failure-free survival was 85% in both arms (HR 0.96, 90% CI 0.77–1.2), again noninferior, with prostate-cancer deaths of 10 versus 12 and no significant difference in late grade ≥3 genitourinary or gastrointestinal toxicity. Balance: 60 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks is a standard-equivalent, more convenient schedule. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: CHHiP: 60 Gy in 20 fractions was noninferior to 74 Gy in 37 fractions for 5-year biochemical/clinical failure-free survival (90.6% vs 88.3%, HR 0.84) — but 57 Gy in 19 fractions could not claim noninferiority
cards.summary: CHHiP: 60 Gy in 20 fractions was noninferior to 74 Gy in 37 fractions for 5-year biochemical/clinical failure-free survival (90.6% vs 88.3%, HR 0.84) — but 57 Gy in 19 fractions could not claim noninferiority
cards.people: 3,216 men with localised prostate cancer (pT1b–T3a, N0, M0) at 71 centres, randomised 1:1:1 — 1,065 to 74 Gy in 37 fractions, 1,074 to 60 Gy in 20 fractions, and 1,077 to 57 Gy in 19 fractions, all with intensity-modulated technique; most patients received 3–6 months of neoadjuvant and concurrent androgen suppression. Median follow-up 62.4 months. The abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: The proportion free of biochemical or clinical failure at 5 years was 88.3% (95% CI 86.0–90.2) in the 74 Gy group, 90.6% (88.5–92.3) in the 60 Gy group, and 85.9% (83.4–88.0) in the 57 Gy group. The 60 Gy schedule was non-inferior to 74 Gy (HR 0.84; 90% CI 0.68–1.03; p for noninferiority = 0.0018, against a critical hazard ratio of 1.208), but noninferiority could not be claimed for 57 Gy (HR 1.20; 90% CI 0.99–1.46; pNI=0.48). The estimated cumulative 5-year incidence of RTOG grade 2 or worse bowel and bladder adverse events was 13.7% and 9.1% in the 74 Gy group, 11.9% and 11.7% in the 60 Gy group, and 11.3% and 6.6% in the 57 Gy group. No treatment-related deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is schedule-specific: the same trial failed to establish it for 57 Gy in 19 fractions, so this card supports 60 Gy in 20 fractions only. The registry ID appears in the record's abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty.
cards.source: Dearnaley D et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2016. PMID: 27339115. Registry ID: ISRCTN97182923, as printed in the record's abstract text (databank fields empty). cards.headline: PROFIT: 60 Gy in 20 fractions was not inferior to 78 Gy in 39 fractions in intermediate-risk prostate cancer (5-year failure-free survival 85% in both arms, HR 0.96) without added late toxicity
cards.summary: PROFIT: 60 Gy in 20 fractions was not inferior to 78 Gy in 39 fractions in intermediate-risk prostate cancer (5-year failure-free survival 85% in both arms, HR 0.96) without added late toxicity
cards.people: 1,206 men with intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer (T1–2a with Gleason ≤6 and PSA 10.1–20 ng/mL; T2b–2c with Gleason ≤6 and PSA ≤20 ng/mL; or T1–2 with Gleason 7 and PSA ≤20 ng/mL); 608 allocated to hypofractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks) and 598 to conventional radiotherapy (78 Gy in 39 fractions over 8 weeks). Androgen deprivation was not permitted. Median follow-up 6.0 years.
cards.result: Biochemical-clinical failure (PSA failure by nadir+2, hormonal intervention, clinical local or distant failure, or death from prostate cancer) occurred in 109 of 608 patients in the hypofractionated arm and 117 of 598 in the standard arm; 5-year failure-free survival was 85% in both arms (HR 0.96; 90% CI 0.77–1.2), meeting the pre-set noninferiority margin (hazard ratio below 1.32). Ten deaths from prostate cancer occurred in the hypofractionated arm and 12 in the standard arm. No significant differences were detected in grade ≥3 late genitourinary or gastrointestinal toxicity.
cards.watchOut: PROFIT's control was 78 Gy in 39 fractions (dose-escalated) rather than CHHiP's 74 Gy, its population was intermediate-risk only, and it prohibited androgen deprivation — a cleaner radiation-only comparison but a narrower one. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields or abstract; none is printed on this card.

shelves.title: Second-generation androgen-receptor inhibitors in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (SPARTAN; PROSPER; ARAMIS)
shelves.question: In non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with rapid PSA doubling, does adding apalutamide to ADT improve metastasis-free and overall survival versus ADT alone?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/drug therapy/secondary · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androgen Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Exanthema/chemically induced · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis/prevention & control · Proportional Hazards Models · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant/drug therapy/pathology · Thiohydantoins/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Three double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials — one per drug — answer the question for the class, with the apalutamide trial leading. In SPARTAN (n=1,207, PSA doubling time ≤10 months), apalutamide more than doubled median metastasis-free survival (40.5 vs 16.2 months; HR for metastasis or death 0.28, 95% CI 0.23–0.35) and, at the pre-specified final analysis (median follow-up 52 months), significantly improved overall survival (median 73.9 vs 59.9 months; HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64–0.96, p=0.016) despite 19% of placebo patients crossing over to apalutamide; its characteristic harms were rash (23.8% vs 5.5%), hypothyroidism (8.1% vs 2.0%) and fracture (11.7% vs 6.5%). PROSPER (enzalutamide, n=1,401) and ARAMIS (darolutamide, n=1,509) replicate the pattern: metastasis-free-survival hazard ratios of 0.29 and 0.41, and final overall-survival hazard ratios of 0.73 (median 67.0 vs 56.3 months) and 0.69 (3-year survival 83% vs 77%) respectively — each trial counted once across its two reports on its card. Darolutamide's adverse-event profile was closest to placebo (discontinuation 8.9% vs 8.7%). A provenance note for the developer: the drafting topic file pinned SPARTAN to a citation that proved to be a letter commenting on the trial; the carded anchor is the recovered primary report (Smith et al., NEJM 2018, PMID 29420164), as detailed in the first card's watch-out. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: SPARTAN: apalutamide improved metastasis-free survival (40.5 vs 16.2 months, HR 0.28) and overall survival (73.9 vs 59.9 months, HR 0.78) in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with rapid PSA doubling
cards.summary: SPARTAN: apalutamide improved metastasis-free survival (40.5 vs 16.2 months, HR 0.28) and overall survival (73.9 vs 59.9 months, HR 0.78) in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with rapid PSA doubling
cards.type: Randomized trial (double-blind, phase 3; primary report and pre-specified final overall-survival report, one trial)
cards.people: 1,207 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (by conventional imaging) and a PSA doubling time of 10 months or less, all continuing androgen-deprivation therapy; 806 assigned to apalutamide 240 mg daily and 401 to placebo. The abstracts do not print a mean age.
cards.result: Primary analysis (after 378 events): median metastasis-free survival was 40.5 months with apalutamide versus 16.2 months with placebo (HR for metastasis or death 0.28; 95% CI 0.23–0.35; P<0.001), and time to symptomatic progression was longer (HR 0.45; 95% CI 0.32–0.63; P<0.001). Adverse events leading to discontinuation occurred in 10.6% versus 7.0%; rash (23.8% vs 5.5%), hypothyroidism (8.1% vs 2.0%) and fracture (11.7% vs 6.5%) were more frequent with apalutamide. Final overall-survival analysis (median follow-up 52 months; 428 deaths): median overall survival was 73.9 versus 59.9 months (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.64–0.96; p=0.016), reaching pre-specified statistical significance, and time to cytotoxic chemotherapy was longer (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.49–0.81). After unblinding, 19% of patients still on placebo crossed over to apalutamide, and subsequent life-prolonging therapy was received by 46% of the apalutamide arm versus 84% of the placebo arm.
cards.watchOut: Anchor-recovery note: the citation originally pinned to this shelf in the drafting file (PMID 29952180) is a published letter commenting on SPARTAN, not the trial. The carded primary report was recovered through that letter's comment link (Smith et al., NEJM 2018, PMID 29420164); the letter is fenced and is not evidence. The final-survival record carries no databank fields; the registry ID is from the primary report.

Apalutamide and Overall Survival in Prostate Cancer. European Urology. 2021. PMID: 32907777. cards.headline: PROSPER: enzalutamide improved metastasis-free survival (36.6 vs 14.7 months, HR 0.29) and overall survival (67.0 vs 56.3 months, HR 0.73) in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
cards.summary: PROSPER: enzalutamide improved metastasis-free survival (36.6 vs 14.7 months, HR 0.29) and overall survival (67.0 vs 56.3 months, HR 0.73) in non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
cards.type: Randomized trial (double-blind, phase 3; primary report and final overall-survival report, one trial)
cards.people: 1,401 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and a PSA doubling time of 10 months or less (median 3.7 months) continuing androgen-deprivation therapy; 933 assigned to enzalutamide 160 mg daily and 468 to placebo. The abstracts do not print a mean age.
cards.result: Primary analysis: metastasis or death had occurred in 23% of the enzalutamide group versus 49% of the placebo group; median metastasis-free survival was 36.6 versus 14.7 months (HR for metastasis or death 0.29; 95% CI 0.24–0.35; P<0.001). At the first interim survival analysis 11% versus 13% had died. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 31% versus 23%. Final survival analysis (as of October 15, 2019): 288 of 933 patients (31%) in the enzalutamide group and 178 of 468 (38%) in the placebo group had died; median overall survival was 67.0 months (95% CI 64.0 to not reached) versus 56.3 months (54.4–63.0) (HR for death 0.73; 95% CI 0.61–0.89; P=0.001) — described in the report as a 27% lower relative risk of death; the absolute figures are the death proportions and medians printed here. The most frequently reported adverse events were fatigue and musculoskeletal events.
cards.watchOut: One trial counted once across its two reports. The '27% lower risk' phrasing in the report is a relative measure; this card leads with the absolute death proportions (31% vs 38%) and median survivals.

cards.headline: ARAMIS: darolutamide improved metastasis-free survival (40.4 vs 18.4 months, HR 0.41) and overall survival (3-year 83% vs 77%, HR 0.69) with an adverse-event profile close to placebo
cards.summary: ARAMIS: darolutamide improved metastasis-free survival (40.4 vs 18.4 months, HR 0.41) and overall survival (3-year 83% vs 77%, HR 0.69) with an adverse-event profile close to placebo
cards.type: Randomized trial (double-blind, phase 3; primary report and final overall-survival report, one trial)
cards.people: 1,509 men with nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and a PSA doubling time of 10 months or less continuing androgen-deprivation therapy; 955 assigned to darolutamide 600 mg twice daily and 554 to placebo. The abstracts do not print a mean age.
cards.result: Primary analysis (after 437 primary-endpoint events): median metastasis-free survival was 40.4 months with darolutamide versus 18.4 months with placebo (HR for metastasis or death 0.41; 95% CI 0.34–0.50; P<0.001), with benefits across secondary endpoints including overall survival. Discontinuation because of adverse events was 8.9% versus 8.7%, and darolutamide was not associated with a higher incidence of seizures, falls, fractures, cognitive disorder or hypertension than placebo; fatigue was the exception among frequent events. Final survival analysis (median follow-up 29.0 months; after unblinding, all 170 patients still receiving placebo crossed over to darolutamide): overall survival at 3 years was 83% (95% CI 80–86) versus 77% (72–81) (HR for death 0.69; 95% CI 0.53–0.88; P=0.003) — a 31% lower relative risk of death, with the absolute 3-year rates printed here. No new safety signals were observed.
cards.watchOut: One trial counted once across its two reports. The final survival analysis followed unblinding and crossover of the remaining placebo patients to darolutamide, which biases the survival comparison toward the null rather than inflating it.

shelves.title: Metastasis-directed therapy for oligometastatic prostate cancer recurrence (STOMP; ORIOLE)
shelves.question: In oligometastatic prostate cancer (≤3–5 lesions), does metastasis-directed SBRT delay progression and defer ADT versus surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Androgen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Biopsy · Disease Progression · Humans · Lymph Node Excision · Lymphatic Metastasis · Male · Metastasectomy · Middle Aged · Palliative Care · Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Prostate/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostatectomy · Prostatic Neoplasms/diagnosis/mortality/secondary/therapy · Radiosurgery · Radiotherapy · Testosterone/blood · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Burden · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: Two small randomised phase 2 trials give a consistent but fragile signal, and the fragility must be stated plainly. In STOMP (n=62 men with choline-PET-detected oligorecurrent prostate cancer, ≤3 extracranial lesions), metastasis-directed therapy (surgery or stereotactic radiotherapy to all lesions) lengthened median ADT-free survival from 13 to 21 months — but the comparison did NOT reach significance (HR 0.60 with an 80% confidence interval of 0.40–0.90; log-rank P=.11), a detail the drafting topic file omitted and this shelf restores: with 80% intervals and P=.11, STOMP is a hypothesis-raising result, not a demonstrated one. In ORIOLE (n=54 men with 1–3 metastases on conventional imaging), stereotactic ablative radiotherapy reduced progression at 6 months from 61% on observation to 19% (P=.005) and improved median progression-free survival (not reached vs 5.8 months; HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.11–0.81, P=.002), with no grade ≥3 toxicity; STOMP likewise saw no grade 2–5 toxicity. Neither trial reports overall survival, and both endpoints — ADT deferral and 6-month progression — are surrogates whose link to longer life is unproven. The shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate in spirit (two trials, but small phase 2s with surrogate endpoints). PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: STOMP: metastasis-directed therapy lengthened median ADT-free survival (21 vs 13 months) in oligorecurrent prostate cancer — but the difference was NOT significant (HR 0.60 on an 80% CI; log-rank P=.11)
cards.summary: STOMP: metastasis-directed therapy lengthened median ADT-free survival (21 vs 13 months) in oligorecurrent prostate cancer — but the difference was NOT significant (HR 0.60 on an 80% CI; log-rank P=.11)
cards.people: 62 men with asymptomatic biochemical recurrence after curative-intent primary treatment, three or fewer extracranial metastatic lesions on choline PET-CT, and serum testosterone above 50 ng/dL, randomised 1:1 to surveillance or metastasis-directed therapy (surgery or stereotactic body radiotherapy) of all detected lesions; median follow-up 3 years. The abstract does not print the arm counts or a mean age.
cards.result: Median ADT-free survival was 13 months (80% CI 12–17) in the surveillance group and 21 months (80% CI 14–29) in the metastasis-directed-therapy group (HR 0.60; 80% CI 0.40–0.90; log-rank P=.11) — a difference that did not reach statistical significance, reported with the trial's 80% confidence intervals as printed. Quality of life was similar between arms at baseline and remained comparable at 3 months and 1 year. Six patients in the MDT arm developed grade 1 toxicity; no grade 2 to 5 toxicity was observed.
cards.watchOut: This trial is routinely cited as 'positive'; its own numbers are not significant (P=.11) and its intervals are 80%, not 95%. The authors' conclusion is exploratory ('should be explored further in phase III trials'), and this card matches that register.

cards.summary: ORIOLE: stereotactic ablative radiotherapy cut 6-month progression from 61% to 19% versus observation in oligometastatic prostate cancer (P=.005), with no grade ≥3 toxicity
cards.people: 54 men with recurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer and 1 to 3 metastases detectable by conventional imaging, who had not received ADT within 6 months of enrolment or for more than 3 years in total, randomised 2:1 at three US centres — 36 to stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) and 18 to observation; median age 68 years in both arms.
cards.result: Progression at 6 months (a composite of PSA increase, progression on conventional imaging, symptomatic progression, ADT initiation, or death) occurred in 7 of 36 patients (19%) receiving SABR and 11 of 18 (61%) undergoing observation (P=.005). Median progression-free survival was not reached with SABR versus 5.8 months with observation (HR 0.30; 95% CI 0.11–0.81; P=.002). Total consolidation of PSMA-PET-avid disease was associated with fewer new lesions at 6 months (16% vs 63%; P=.006). No toxic effects of grade 3 or greater were observed.
cards.watchOut: A 54-patient phase 2 trial with a 6-month composite endpoint heavily weighted by PSA events; the trial shows delayed progression and deferred ADT, not longer survival, and its imaging standard (conventional imaging for eligibility, PSMA-PET analysed secondarily) differs from STOMP's choline-PET entry.

shelves.title: Triplet therapy in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer: an AR inhibitor added to ADT plus docetaxel (ARASENS; PEACE-1)
shelves.question: In metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel improve overall survival versus ADT plus docetaxel?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androgen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Androgen Receptor Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Docetaxel/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis/drug therapy · Neutropenia/chemically induced · Proportional Hazards Models · Prostatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant · Pyrazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: This shelf asks the TRIPLET question — an androgen-receptor agent added on top of ADT plus docetaxel — which is distinct from the doublet-intensification question (ADT plus docetaxel, or ADT plus an AR agent) homed on Shelf #767; the angle is named here so the two shelves do not duplicate. Two phase 3 trials support the triplet, with different agents. In ARASENS (n=1,306; 86.1% with de novo metastatic disease), adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel significantly reduced the risk of death (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.57–0.80, P<0.001 — described in the record as a 32.5% lower relative risk; the abstract prints no median survivals, so none are carded, and the drafting topic file's 'not reached vs 48.9 months' figures do not appear in the record), with grade 3/4 adverse events similar between arms (66.1% vs 63.5%; neutropenia 33.7% vs 34.2%). In PEACE-1 (n=1,172 analysed; 2×2 factorial, open-label), adding abiraterone to standard care improved overall survival in the pre-specified ADT-plus-docetaxel population (HR 0.75, 95.1% CI 0.59–0.95, p=0.017) and in the overall population (HR 0.82, 95.1% CI 0.69–0.98, p=0.030) — note the topic file attached the 0.82 figure to the docetaxel stratum; the record assigns 0.75 to that stratum and 0.82 overall, and the record governs. In PEACE-1's docetaxel population, grade ≥3 adverse events were 63% with abiraterone versus 52% without, driven mainly by hypertension (22% vs 13%), without increased neutropenia or febrile neutropenia. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: ARASENS: adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel significantly improved overall survival in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (HR 0.68, P<0.001) without increasing grade 3/4 adverse events
cards.summary: ARASENS: adding darolutamide to ADT plus docetaxel significantly improved overall survival in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (HR 0.68, P<0.001) without increasing grade 3/4 adverse events
cards.people: 1,306 patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer randomised 1:1 — 651 to darolutamide (600 mg twice daily) plus ADT and docetaxel and 655 to matching placebo plus ADT and docetaxel; 86.1% had disease that was metastatic at initial diagnosis. The abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: At the primary analysis, the risk of death was significantly lower in the darolutamide group than in the placebo group (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.57–0.80; P<0.001) — expressed in the record as a 32.5% lower risk, a relative measure; the abstract prints no median overall-survival values, so none are carded here. Darolutamide was also associated with consistent benefits across secondary endpoints and pre-specified subgroups. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 66.1% of the darolutamide group and 63.5% of the placebo group; neutropenia, the most common grade 3/4 event, occurred in 33.7% versus 34.2%, with event rates highest during the overlapping docetaxel period in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Any median-survival figures attached to ARASENS (the drafting file quoted 'not reached versus 48.9 months') do not appear in this record and are not carded. The trial is double-blind for darolutamide; docetaxel was open in both arms by design.

cards.headline: PEACE-1: adding abiraterone to ADT plus docetaxel improved overall survival (docetaxel-population HR 0.75; overall-population HR 0.82) in de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer
cards.summary: PEACE-1: adding abiraterone to ADT plus docetaxel improved overall survival (docetaxel-population HR 0.75; overall-population HR 0.82) in de novo metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer
cards.people: 1,173 men with de novo metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma enrolled at 77 hospitals in seven European countries (one later withdrew consent, leaving 1,172 analysed), randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to standard care (ADT alone or with docetaxel), standard care plus prostate radiotherapy, standard care plus abiraterone, or standard care plus radiotherapy and abiraterone; the pre-specified population of interest for the triplet question — patients whose standard care included ADT plus docetaxel — numbered 355 with abiraterone and 355 without. Median follow-up was 4.4 years for overall survival.
cards.result: With no interaction between abiraterone and radiotherapy, the pooled abiraterone comparison showed longer overall survival in the overall population (HR 0.82; 95.1% CI 0.69–0.98; p=0.030) and in the ADT-plus-docetaxel population (HR 0.75; 95.1% CI 0.59–0.95; p=0.017), with radiographic progression-free survival also improved (HR 0.50 in the docetaxel population; 99.9% CI 0.34–0.71; p<0.0001). In the docetaxel population, grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 63% of patients who received abiraterone and 52% of those who did not; hypertension showed the largest difference (22% vs 13%), and adding abiraterone did not increase neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, fatigue or neuropathy.
cards.watchOut: The drafting topic file assigned the HR of 0.82 to the docetaxel stratum; the record assigns 0.82 to the OVERALL population and 0.75 to the docetaxel population — the record governs, and this card prints both with their populations labelled. The trial's other factorial question (prostate radiotherapy) is a separate question and is not scored on this shelf.

cards.people: 2,478 analysed patients across ARASENS (darolutamide triplet, double-blind) and PEACE-1 (abiraterone triplet within a factorial design).

Toxicity of the triplet over the doublet was modest for darolutamide (grade 3/4 events 66.1% vs 63.5%) and greater for abiraterone in PEACE-1 (63% vs 52%, mainly hypertension). This shelf's distinct angle versus Shelf #767 is the triplet comparison: #767 homes the doublet-intensification question, and its results are not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled predominantly or exclusively de novo metastatic disease (ARASENS 86.1%; PEACE-1 by design); the triplet's value in metachronous low-volume relapse is less directly evidenced by these records.

shelves.title: Radium-223 in symptomatic bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (ALSYMPCA)
shelves.question: In symptomatic bone-predominant metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer without visceral disease, does radium-223 improve overall survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Neoplasms · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Isotopes · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Prostatic Neoplasms · Radium
shelves.balance: One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial answers this question, and it is an outstanding single: in ALSYMPCA, 921 men with castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases (post-docetaxel, ineligible, or declining) received six injections of radium-223 or placebo on top of best standard care, and overall survival improved (updated analysis: median 14.9 vs 11.3 months; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58–0.83), with low rates of myelosuppression and fewer adverse events than placebo. No second randomised trial asks the same question. The one combination trial is fenced as a warning: adding radium-223 to abiraterone/prednisone (ERA-223) gave no symptomatic-skeletal-event benefit and nearly tripled fractures (29% vs 11%), so the survival claim belongs to radium-223 as used in ALSYMPCA — bone-targeted therapy added to standard care, not layered onto abiraterone. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: ALSYMPCA: radium-223 improved overall survival in bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (median 14.9 vs 11.3 months; HR 0.70) — a double-blind placebo-controlled trial
cards.summary: ALSYMPCA: radium-223 improved overall survival in bone-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (median 14.9 vs 11.3 months; HR 0.70) — a double-blind placebo-controlled trial
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (single outstanding trial)
cards.people: 921 men with castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases who had received, were not eligible to receive, or had declined docetaxel, randomised 2:1 to six intravenous injections of radium-223 (50 kBq per kilogram, one every 4 weeks) or matching placebo; all patients also received the best standard of care. The primary end point was overall survival; the trial was terminated for efficacy at a prespecified interim analysis (314 deaths) and an updated analysis was performed at 528 deaths, before crossover.
cards.result: At the interim analysis, overall survival favoured radium-223 (median 14.0 vs 11.2 months; HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; P=0.002). The updated analysis confirmed the benefit (median 14.9 vs 11.3 months; HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.83; P<0.001) — a 30% relative reduction in the risk of death. All main secondary efficacy end points, including time to the first symptomatic skeletal event, also favoured radium-223. Radium-223 was associated with low rates of myelosuppression and fewer adverse events than placebo.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE): it is large, double-blind and placebo-controlled with a hard survival end point, but it has never been replicated. The enrolled population had bone metastases without the visceral-disease question being asked; the benefit should not be extrapolated to visceral-predominant disease. Because the trial stopped at an interim analysis for efficacy, the point estimate may sit slightly optimistic relative to a fully run trial.
cards.source: Parker C et al. Alpha emitter radium-223 and survival in metastatic prostate cancer. N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID: 23863050. Registry ID: NCT00699751, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ERA-223 (fenced warning): adding radium-223 to abiraterone/prednisone did not improve skeletal-event-free survival and increased fractures (29% vs 11%)
cards.summary: ERA-223 (fenced warning): adding radium-223 to abiraterone/prednisone did not improve skeletal-event-free survival and increased fractures (29% vs 11%)
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial — fenced: a different (combination) question, carded as a warning
cards.people: 806 chemotherapy-naive men with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases, randomised to up to six injections of radium-223 (55 kBq/kg) or placebo, all receiving abiraterone acetate plus prednisone or prednisolone. The primary end point was symptomatic skeletal event-free survival. The study was unblinded prematurely after more fractures and deaths were noted in the radium-223 group in an unplanned analysis (all patients had completed radium-223 or placebo by then).
cards.result: Symptomatic skeletal event-free survival was not improved by adding radium-223 (median 22.3 vs 26.0 months; HR 1.122; 95% CI 0.917 to 1.374; p=0.2636) — the treatment made no difference to the primary end point. Fractures (any grade) occurred in 112 of 392 patients (29%) in the radium-223 group and 45 of 394 (11%) in the placebo group; grade 3–4 fractures were 9% vs 3%. The investigators concluded the combination is not recommended.
cards.watchOut: This card fences the combination, not the drug: it does not contradict ALSYMPCA, where radium-223 was added to best standard care in a later-line, symptomatic population rather than layered concurrently onto abiraterone in chemotherapy-naive, asymptomatic men. Its lesson is that the ALSYMPCA survival claim cannot be assumed to transfer to combination use.

shelves.title: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy before cystectomy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (SWOG 8710; BA06 3081)
shelves.question: In muscle-invasive bladder cancer, does neoadjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy before radical cystectomy improve overall survival versus cystectomy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carcinoma, Transitional Cell · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Cisplatin · Cystectomy · Doxorubicin · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Invasiveness · Survival Analysis · Urinary Bladder Neoplasms · Vinblastine
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials of two different cisplatin triplets give the same answer. SWOG 8710 (307 eligible patients) found median survival of 77 months with three cycles of MVAC before cystectomy versus 46 months with cystectomy alone, and no residual cancer in the specimen in 38% vs 15% — though the survival comparison itself sat at P=0.06. The larger BA06 trial (976 patients, median follow-up 8 years) found a statistically significant 16% relative reduction in the risk of death with neoadjuvant CMV (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72–0.99), raising 10-year survival from 30% to 36%. Neither trial alone is overwhelming — one is large but modest in effect, the other striking in its medians but not conventionally significant — but they are independent, randomised, and concordant, and together they are the evidence base for the neoadjuvant standard. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: SWOG 8710: neoadjuvant MVAC before cystectomy — median survival 77 vs 46 months and no residual cancer in 38% vs 15% of specimens
cards.summary: SWOG 8710: neoadjuvant MVAC before cystectomy — median survival 77 vs 46 months and no residual cancer in 38% vs 15% of specimens
cards.people: 317 patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (stage T2 to T4a) planned for radical cystectomy were enrolled over 11 years; 307 were eligible, with 154 assigned to radical cystectomy alone and 153 to three cycles of methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin and cisplatin (MVAC) followed by radical cystectomy. The analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: Median survival was 77 months in the combination-therapy group versus 46 months in the cystectomy-alone group (P=0.06 by two-sided stratified log-rank test — a large difference that did not reach conventional significance in this trial alone). Significantly more patients in the chemotherapy group had no residual cancer in the cystectomy specimen (38% vs 15%, P<0.001), and in both groups the absence of residual disease was associated with improved survival.
cards.watchOut: The headline survival comparison is P=0.06: quoting the 77-versus-46-month medians without that caveat overstates what this trial proved on its own. The regimens of the era (MVAC) have since been joined by dose-dense MVAC and gemcitabine–cisplatin in practice; this shelf verifies the neoadjuvant principle and its size, not a choice between modern regimens. This trial predates trial registration; the record carries no registry ID, which is legitimate for its era.
cards.source: Grossman HB et al. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus cystectomy compared with cystectomy alone for locally advanced bladder cancer. N Engl J Med. 2003. PMID: 12944571. Registry ID: none — the trial predates registration and the record's databank fields are empty. cards.headline: BA06 3081: neoadjuvant CMV improved survival in 976 patients (HR 0.84; 10-year survival 36% vs 30%)
cards.summary: BA06 3081: neoadjuvant CMV improved survival in 976 patients (HR 0.84; 10-year survival 36% vs 30%)
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial, long-term report (pre-registration era)
cards.people: 976 patients with muscle-invasive urothelial cancer of the bladder treated by cystectomy and/or radiotherapy, recruited between 1989 and 1995 and randomised to no neoadjuvant chemotherapy or three cycles of cisplatin, methotrexate and vinblastine (CMV). Median follow-up at this report was 8.0 years.
cards.result: Neoadjuvant CMV produced a statistically significant 16% relative reduction in the risk of death (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.72 to 0.99; P=.037), corresponding to an increase in 10-year survival from 30% to 36% — an absolute gain of 6 percentage points at 10 years.
cards.watchOut: The local-therapy backbone was cystectomy and/or radiotherapy, so the trial supports neoadjuvant chemotherapy before definitive local therapy generally, not cystectomy alone specifically. The relative effect (HR 0.84) is more modest than SWOG 8710's median-survival gap suggests; the two trials are reconciled in the synthesis. The record's title prints the trial name as 'BA06 30894'; the trial is cited here by its standard name, BA06 3081. No registry ID appears in the record — the trial predates registration.
