shelves.title: Adjuvant atezolizumab + bevacizumab after resection or ablation of high-risk hepatocellular carcinoma (IMbrave050)
shelves.question: In hepatocellular carcinoma at high recurrence risk after curative resection or ablation, does adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improve recurrence-free survival versus active surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Bevacizumab · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular · Watchful Waiting · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Liver Neoplasms · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: One randomised phase 3 trial, read twice. At its prespecified interim analysis (median follow-up 17.4 months), IMbrave050 met its primary endpoint: adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved recurrence-free survival versus active surveillance (HR 0.72, adjusted 95% CI 0.53–0.98; p=0.012), at the cost of grade 3–4 adverse events in 41% versus 13%. In the trial's updated analysis, that benefit was not sustained — the recurrence-free-survival hazard ratio attenuated to 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.12) — and overall survival remained immature with a point estimate against the treatment (HR 1.26, 95% CI 0.85–1.87); the investigators concluded the benefit–risk profile does not support adjuvant use. The class warning stands behind it: adjuvant sorafenib (STORM) was also negative, and the first-line atezolizumab–bevacizumab question in advanced disease is homed on Shelf #850. Balance: an early recurrence delay that faded with follow-up; on the mature data, no sustained difference. Single trial — THIN. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: IMbrave050 (primary interim analysis): adjuvant atezolizumab + bevacizumab improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.72) in high-risk resected/ablated HCC — a benefit the updated analysis later showed was not sustained
cards.summary: IMbrave050 (primary interim analysis): adjuvant atezolizumab + bevacizumab improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.72) in high-risk resected/ablated HCC — a benefit the updated analysis later showed was not sustained
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (primary prespecified interim analysis)
cards.people: 668 adults with hepatocellular carcinoma at high risk of recurrence after curative-intent surgical resection or ablation, recruited at 134 hospitals and medical centres in 26 countries and randomly assigned 1:1 to atezolizumab 1200 mg plus bevacizumab 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks for 17 cycles (12 months; n=334) or to active surveillance (n=334). The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival by independent review facility assessment in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: At the prespecified interim analysis (Oct 21, 2022; median follow-up 17.4 months), recurrence-free survival was significantly improved with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (hazard ratio 0.72; adjusted 95% CI 0.53–0.98; p=0.012); median recurrence-free survival was not evaluable in either group. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 136 (41%) of 332 treated patients versus 44 (13%) of 330 in the surveillance group; grade 5 adverse events occurred in six patients (2%, two treatment-related) with the combination versus one (<1%) with surveillance, and 29 patients (9%) discontinued both drugs because of adverse events. Overall survival was immature. The authors noted this was the first phase 3 adjuvant trial in hepatocellular carcinoma to report positive results, while calling for longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: This card reports the PRIMARY interim analysis only; the same trial's updated analysis (carded next) reversed the conclusion, and any reading of this shelf must take the two together. The trial was open-label, though the primary endpoint was assessed by an independent review facility.

cards.type: Updated analysis of the same randomized phase 3 trial (post hoc RFS update; second interim OS analysis)
cards.people: The same 668 patients randomised in IMbrave050 (design as on the primary-analysis card). Patients in the surveillance group were eligible to cross over to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab after independent-review-assessed recurrence.
cards.result: In the updated analysis, the recurrence-free-survival hazard ratio was 0.90 (95% CI 0.72–1.12) — the initial benefit was not sustained. At the second interim analysis, overall survival data remained immature (hazard ratio 1.26; 95% CI 0.85–1.87). Results were consistent across clinically relevant subgroups, and updated safety was consistent with the primary analysis. The investigators concluded that the overall benefit–risk profile does not support atezolizumab plus bevacizumab as adjuvant therapy, while noting subgroup analyses suggesting possible benefit in select patients warrant prospective evaluation.

The overall-survival confidence interval (0.85–1.87) is wide and the data immature — the record supports 'no demonstrated benefit', not proof of harm.

shelves.title: Bevacizumab added to first-line chemotherapy in advanced ovarian cancer (GOG-0218; ICON7)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer, does adding bevacizumab to carboplatin–paclitaxel (with maintenance) improve progression-free survival, and in whom does it affect overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Angiogenesis Inhibitors · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bevacizumab · Carboplatin · Carcinoma, Ovarian Epithelial · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Neoplasms, Glandular and Epithelial · Ovarian Neoplasms · Paclitaxel · Quality of Life · Survival Analysis · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials agree on the shape of the effect. GOG-0218 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=1,873) found bevacizumab given throughout — during chemotherapy and as maintenance — prolonged median progression-free survival from 10.3 to 14.1 months (HR 0.717), while bevacizumab only during chemotherapy did not (HR 0.908); there was no overall-survival difference. ICON7 (open-label, n=1,528, half the bevacizumab dose) confirmed a smaller progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.81) that peaked while bevacizumab was being given and waned after it stopped, with an overall-survival difference confined to the subgroup at high risk of progression (median 36.6 vs 28.8 months). Toxicity is real but bounded: hypertension requiring treatment in 23% versus 7% (GOG-0218 throughout arm) and gastrointestinal-wall disruption in about 2.6% versus 1.2%. Balance: bevacizumab throughout first-line therapy delays progression by roughly 2–4 months with no overall survival gain; the only survival signal sits in ICON7's high-risk subgroup. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: GOG-0218: bevacizumab throughout (chemotherapy + maintenance) prolonged progression-free survival (14.1 vs 10.3 months; HR 0.717); bevacizumab only during chemotherapy did not; no overall-survival benefit
cards.summary: GOG-0218: bevacizumab throughout (chemotherapy + maintenance) prolonged progression-free survival (14.1 vs 10.3 months; HR 0.717); bevacizumab only during chemotherapy did not; no overall-survival benefit
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (double-blind, placebo-controlled, three arms)
cards.people: 1,873 women with newly diagnosed stage III (incompletely resectable) or stage IV epithelial ovarian cancer after debulking surgery. All received carboplatin (AUC 6) plus paclitaxel 175 mg/m² for cycles 1–6 with a study treatment in cycles 2–22: placebo throughout (control), bevacizumab 15 mg/kg in cycles 2–6 then placebo (bevacizumab-initiation), or bevacizumab in cycles 2–22 (bevacizumab-throughout). The primary endpoint was progression-free survival.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 10.3 months (control), 11.2 months (bevacizumab-initiation) and 14.1 months (bevacizumab-throughout). Versus control, the hazard ratio for progression or death was 0.908 (95% CI 0.795–1.040; P=0.16) for initiation and 0.717 (95% CI 0.625–0.824; P<0.001) for throughout. At the time of analysis 76.3% of patients were alive, with no significant differences in overall survival among the three groups. Hypertension requiring medical therapy occurred in 7.2% (control), 16.5% (initiation) and 22.9% (throughout); gastrointestinal-wall disruption requiring intervention occurred in 1.2%, 2.8% and 2.6% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The progression-free-survival gain requires bevacizumab to continue as maintenance — starting it and stopping with chemotherapy (the initiation arm) gave no significant benefit. Progression-free survival here is the benefit; the record shows no overall-survival difference, and this shelf claims none.
cards.source: Burger RA et al. Incorporation of bevacizumab in the primary treatment of ovarian cancer. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 22204724. Registry ID: NCT00262847, from the record. cards.headline: ICON7: bevacizumab (7.5 mg/kg) improved progression-free survival (HR 0.81) with the effect maximal on treatment; an overall-survival difference appeared only in the high-risk subgroup (median 36.6 vs 28.8 months)
cards.summary: ICON7: bevacizumab (7.5 mg/kg) improved progression-free survival (HR 0.81) with the effect maximal on treatment; an overall-survival difference appeared only in the high-risk subgroup (median 36.6 vs 28.8 months)
cards.people: 1,528 women with ovarian cancer (9% high-risk early-stage; 70% stage IIIC or IV; 30% at high risk for progression) randomly assigned to carboplatin (AUC 5 or 6) plus paclitaxel 175 mg/m² every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, with or without bevacizumab 7.5 mg/kg given concurrently for 5–6 cycles and continued for 12 additional cycles or until progression. Outcomes included progression-free survival (restricted mean) and interim/updated overall survival.
cards.result: Progression-free survival (restricted mean) at 36 months was 20.3 months with standard therapy versus 21.8 months with bevacizumab added (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.81; 95% CI 0.70–0.94; P=0.004). Non-proportional hazards were detected: the effect was maximal at 12 months, coinciding with the end of planned bevacizumab, and diminished by 24 months. In updated analyses at 42 months, progression-free survival (restricted mean) was 22.4 versus 24.1 months (P=0.04); in patients at high risk for progression the benefit was greater (14.5 vs 18.1 months), with respective median overall survival of 28.8 and 36.6 months. Bevacizumab was associated with more toxic effects, most often grade ≥2 hypertension (18% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: ICON7 used half the GOG-0218 dose (7.5 vs 15 mg/kg) and was open-label. shelves.title: Intraperitoneal chemotherapy after optimal debulking in stage III ovarian cancer (GOG-172; GOG-252)
shelves.question: In optimally debulked stage III ovarian cancer, does intraperitoneal cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve overall survival versus intravenous chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain · Adenocarcinoma · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carcinoma · Cisplatin · Combined Modality Therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Infusions, Parenteral · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Ovarian Neoplasms · Paclitaxel · Peritoneal Neoplasms · Quality of Life · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: The two eras of this question disagree, and the shelf's work is the disagreement. GOG-172 (2006, n=415 eligible) gave the largest survival gain of its era: adding intraperitoneal cisplatin and paclitaxel to intravenous paclitaxel extended median overall survival from 49.7 to 65.6 months (P=0.03) and progression-free survival from 18.3 to 23.8 months — but only 42% of patients completed six intraperitoneal cycles, grade 3–4 toxicity was substantially higher, and quality of life was worse during and shortly after treatment (though not at one year). GOG-252 (2019, n=1,560), run a generation later with dose-dense weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab in every arm, found no significant progression-free-survival advantage for either intraperitoneal regimen (medians 24.9 months intravenous carboplatin, 27.4 intraperitoneal carboplatin, 26.2 intraperitoneal cisplatin). Whether the difference is the modern backbone (weekly paclitaxel, bevacizumab), the lower intraperitoneal cisplatin dose in GOG-252, or the old result itself is unresolved. Balance: a real survival benefit in the trial that asked the question plainly, not reproduced when the regimen was modernised. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: GOG-172: intraperitoneal cisplatin + paclitaxel improved overall survival (median 65.6 vs 49.7 months) in optimally debulked stage III ovarian cancer — with heavy toxicity and only 42% completing six cycles
cards.summary: GOG-172: intraperitoneal cisplatin + paclitaxel improved overall survival (median 65.6 vs 49.7 months) in optimally debulked stage III ovarian cancer — with heavy toxicity and only 42% completing six cycles
cards.people: 429 patients randomised (415 eligible) with stage III ovarian or primary peritoneal carcinoma and no residual mass greater than 1.0 cm after debulking. The intravenous group received intravenous paclitaxel 135 mg/m² over 24 hours followed by intravenous cisplatin 75 mg/m² on day 2; the intraperitoneal group received the same intravenous paclitaxel followed by intraperitoneal cisplatin 100 mg/m² on day 2 and intraperitoneal paclitaxel 60 mg/m² on day 8, every 3 weeks for six cycles. Quality of life was assessed.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 18.3 months (intravenous) versus 23.8 months (intraperitoneal; P=0.05 by log-rank), and median overall survival was 49.7 versus 65.6 months (P=0.03). Grade 3 and 4 pain, fatigue, and haematologic, gastrointestinal, metabolic and neurologic toxic effects were more common in the intraperitoneal group (P≤0.001). Only 42% of patients in the intraperitoneal group completed six cycles of the assigned therapy. Quality of life was significantly worse in the intraperitoneal group before cycle 4 and 3–6 weeks after treatment, but not one year after treatment.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports medians and P values, not hazard ratios — no HR is printed on this card. The control arm (intravenous cisplatin with 24-hour paclitaxel) is not the modern carboplatin backbone, and the 42% completion rate means the survival result was achieved despite, not because of, deliverability. This is the trial the modern era failed to reproduce (next card).
cards.source: Armstrong DK et al. Intraperitoneal cisplatin and paclitaxel in ovarian cancer. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16394300. Registry ID: none in the record — the trial predates routine registration reporting in journal records. cards.headline: GOG-252: with dose-dense weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab in all arms, neither intraperitoneal regimen significantly improved progression-free survival (medians 27.4 and 26.2 vs 24.9 months)
cards.summary: GOG-252: with dose-dense weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab in all arms, neither intraperitoneal regimen significantly improved progression-free survival (medians 27.4 and 26.2 vs 24.9 months)
cards.people: 1,560 women with newly diagnosed advanced ovarian carcinoma randomly assigned to six cycles of: intravenous paclitaxel 80 mg/m² weekly with intravenous carboplatin AUC 6; weekly intravenous paclitaxel with intraperitoneal carboplatin AUC 6; or 3-weekly intravenous paclitaxel with intraperitoneal cisplatin 75 mg/m² (day 2) and intraperitoneal paclitaxel 60 mg/m² (day 8). All participants received bevacizumab 15 mg/kg in cycles 2–22. Median follow-up 84.8 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 24.9 months (intravenous carboplatin), 27.4 months (intraperitoneal carboplatin) and 26.2 months (intraperitoneal cisplatin); in the 1,380 patients with stage II/III disease and residual ≤1 cm, medians were 26.9, 28.7 and 27.8 months respectively. Median overall survival for all enrolled was 75.5, 78.9 and 72.9 months respectively. Patient-reported neurotoxicity scores were similar across arms, but quality-of-life (FACT-O Trial Outcome Index) scores during chemotherapy were statistically worse in the intraperitoneal cisplatin arm. The authors concluded that, combined with bevacizumab, neither intraperitoneal regimen significantly increased progression-free survival over the intravenous reference, and the intraperitoneal carboplatin regimen was better tolerated than intraperitoneal cisplatin.
cards.watchOut: GOG-252 is not a straight replication of GOG-172: every arm received weekly paclitaxel and bevacizumab, and the intraperitoneal cisplatin dose was 75 rather than 100 mg/m². Its null result therefore contests the modern value of the intraperitoneal route rather than directly refuting the 2006 finding — the era conflict is the finding.

shelves.title: HIPEC at interval cytoreductive surgery in stage III ovarian cancer (OVHIPEC; KOV-HIPEC-01)
shelves.question: In stage III ovarian cancer responding to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, does adding hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy to interval cytoreductive surgery improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus surgery alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carboplatin · Carcinoma, Ovarian Epithelial · Cisplatin · Combined Modality Therapy · Cytoreduction Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Hyperthermia, Induced · Intention to Treat Analysis · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Neoplasms, Glandular and Epithelial · Ovarian Neoplasms · Paclitaxel · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials converge on the interval-surgery setting and diverge outside it. OVHIPEC (n=245, all interval surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy) found hyperthermic intraperitoneal cisplatin improved recurrence-free survival (14.2 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.66) and overall survival (45.7 vs 33.9 months; HR 0.67), with grade 3–4 adverse events no higher than surgery alone (27% vs 25%). KOV-HIPEC-01 (n=184, mixed primary and interval surgery) was null on its primary population (progression-free survival P=0.43; overall survival P=0.52) — but in its prespecified interval-surgery subgroup the effects matched OVHIPEC (progression-free-survival HR 0.60; overall-survival HR 0.53), while its primary-surgery subgroup showed nothing. Balance: at interval cytoreduction after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, one dedicated trial plus a concordant subgroup support a survival benefit; at primary surgery, there is none. The single-trial flag (OUTSTANDING-SINGLE for the interval question's dedicated trial) is carried on the cards. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: OVHIPEC: HIPEC at interval cytoreductive surgery improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.66; 14.2 vs 10.7 months) and overall survival (HR 0.67; 45.7 vs 33.9 months) without added grade 3–4 toxicity
cards.summary: OVHIPEC: HIPEC at interval cytoreductive surgery improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.66; 14.2 vs 10.7 months) and overall survival (HR 0.67; 45.7 vs 33.9 months) without added grade 3–4 toxicity
cards.people: 245 patients with stage III epithelial ovarian cancer who had at least stable disease after three cycles of neoadjuvant carboplatin (AUC 5–6) and paclitaxel (175 mg/m²), randomly assigned at the time of interval cytoreductive surgery — where complete or optimal (≤10 mm residual) cytoreduction was deemed feasible — to surgery with or without hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy with cisplatin 100 mg/m². Three further cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel followed surgery. Primary endpoint: recurrence-free survival.
cards.result: Events of recurrence or death occurred in 110 of 123 patients (89%) in the surgery group and 99 of 122 (81%) in the surgery-plus-HIPEC group (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.50–0.87; P=0.003); median recurrence-free survival was 10.7 versus 14.2 months. At a median follow-up of 4.7 years, 76 patients (62%) in the surgery group and 61 (50%) in the HIPEC group had died (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.48–0.94; P=0.02); median overall survival was 33.9 versus 45.7 months. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were similar (25% surgery vs 27% surgery-plus-HIPEC; P=0.76).
cards.watchOut: A single dedicated trial for the interval-surgery question (open-label, Dutch-led, cisplatin 100 mg/m² at 40°C) — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE at drafting; its survival benefit is large for an added intraoperative step and awaits a second dedicated interval-surgery trial. The 10-year durability sometimes quoted for this trial is not in this record and is not claimed here.

cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (single-blind, two institutions, South Korea)
cards.people: 184 women with stage III or IV primary advanced ovarian cancer and residual tumour less than 1 cm after primary or interval maximal cytoreductive surgery, randomly assigned (1:1) to HIPEC (cisplatin 75 mg/m², 41.5°C, 90 minutes) or control. Primary endpoint: progression-free survival; overall survival and adverse events were key secondary endpoints. Median follow-up 69.4 months.
cards.result: In the whole population, median progression-free survival was 18.8 months (control) versus 19.8 months (HIPEC; P=0.43) and median overall survival 61.3 versus 69.5 months (P=0.52) — no significant benefit. In the subgroup undergoing interval cytoreductive surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, median progression-free survival was 15.4 versus 17.4 months (hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.37–0.99; P=0.04) and median overall survival 48.2 versus 61.8 months (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.29–0.96; P=0.04). In the primary-surgery subgroup, progression-free survival was 29.7 (control) versus 23.9 months (HIPEC) and overall survival was not reached in the control group versus 71.3 months with HIPEC — no benefit. The authors concluded HIPEC did not improve survival overall, while the interval-surgery subgroup results were concordant with benefit.
cards.watchOut: The interval-surgery result is a subgroup of a trial whose primary analysis was null — hypothesis-supporting, not confirmatory on its own; it gains weight only because OVHIPEC asked exactly that question in exactly that population and was positive. The trial mixed stage IV patients and used a lower cisplatin dose (75 vs 100 mg/m²) than OVHIPEC.

shelves.title: Dose-dense weekly paclitaxel in advanced ovarian cancer (JGOG 3016; GOG-262; MITO-7)
shelves.question: In advanced ovarian cancer, does dose-dense weekly paclitaxel with 3-weekly carboplatin improve progression-free and overall survival versus conventional 3-weekly therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carboplatin · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Ovarian Neoplasms · Paclitaxel · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: One positive Japanese trial and two Western trials that could not repeat it. JGOG 3016 (n=631 eligible) found dose-dense weekly paclitaxel with 3-weekly carboplatin improved progression-free survival (28.0 vs 17.2 months; HR 0.71) and 3-year overall survival (72.1% vs 65.1%; HR 0.75), with more early discontinuation for toxicity and much more grade 3–4 anaemia (69% vs 44%). GOG-262 (n=692, 84% receiving bevacizumab) found no overall progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.89; P=0.18), with a significant interaction: benefit in patients not receiving bevacizumab (HR 0.62) and none in those who did (HR 0.99). MITO-7 (n=810) tested a different weekly regimen (weekly carboplatin as well) and found no progression-free-survival difference (HR 0.96), though quality of life and several toxicities favoured the weekly schedule. Balance: the dose-dense advantage was real in the population and regimen in which it was discovered, and has not generalised — whether the gap is pharmacogenomic, regimen design, or the bevacizumab backbone remains unsettled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: JGOG 3016: dose-dense weekly paclitaxel improved progression-free survival (28.0 vs 17.2 months; HR 0.71) and 3-year overall survival (72.1% vs 65.1%; HR 0.75) in Japanese patients
cards.summary: JGOG 3016: dose-dense weekly paclitaxel improved progression-free survival (28.0 vs 17.2 months; HR 0.71) and 3-year overall survival (72.1% vs 65.1%; HR 0.75) in Japanese patients
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (open-label, 85 centres in Japan)
cards.people: 637 patients enrolled with stage II–IV epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer; 631 eligible for the intention-to-treat analysis. The conventional group (n=319) received paclitaxel 180 mg/m² plus carboplatin AUC 6 on day 1 of a 21-day cycle; the dose-dense group (n=312) received paclitaxel 80 mg/m² on days 1, 8 and 15 plus carboplatin AUC 6 on day 1, for six cycles. Primary endpoint: progression-free survival.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 28.0 months (95% CI 22.3–35.4) with dose-dense therapy versus 17.2 months (15.7–21.1) with conventional therapy (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.58–0.88; p=0.0015). Overall survival at 3 years was 72.1% versus 65.1% (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57–0.98; p=0.03). More dose-dense patients discontinued early (165 vs 117), with withdrawal for toxicity higher in the dose-dense group (113 vs 69). Neutropenia was near-universal in both groups (92% vs 88%); grade 3–4 anaemia was more frequent with dose-dense therapy (69% vs 44%; p<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: A single-population result: the trial was conducted entirely in Japan, and neither Western trial (next cards) reproduced the progression-free-survival advantage. The conventional arm's paclitaxel dose (180 mg/m²) and the population's pharmacogenomics differ from Western practice, which is one proposed explanation for the discordance — proposed, not established.

cards.summary: GOG-262: weekly paclitaxel did not prolong progression-free survival overall (HR 0.89; P=0.18) — benefit only in the subgroup not receiving bevacizumab (HR 0.62), with a significant interaction (P=0.047)
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (bevacizumab use by patient election, prospectively stratified)
cards.people: 692 patients with ovarian cancer, prospectively stratified by whether they elected to receive bevacizumab (84% did), then randomly assigned to paclitaxel 175 mg/m² every 3 weeks plus carboplatin AUC 6, or weekly paclitaxel 80 mg/m² plus carboplatin AUC 6, for six cycles. Primary endpoint: progression-free survival.
cards.result: Weekly paclitaxel was not associated with longer progression-free survival overall (14.7 vs 14.0 months; hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.74–1.06; P=0.18). Among patients not receiving bevacizumab, weekly paclitaxel prolonged progression-free survival by 3.9 months (14.2 vs 10.3 months; hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.40–0.95; P=0.03); among those receiving bevacizumab it did not (14.9 vs 14.7 months; hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.83–1.20; P=0.60), and the test for interaction was significant (P=0.047). Grade 3–4 anaemia was higher with weekly therapy (36% vs 16%), as was grade 2–4 sensory neuropathy (26% vs 18%), while grade 3–4 neutropenia was lower (72% vs 83%).
cards.watchOut: The non-bevacizumab subgroup was only 16% of the trial, and bevacizumab was elected, not randomised — the interaction is the trial's most interesting output, not a licence to claim a proven benefit in non-bevacizumab patients. The overall trial answer to the shelf question, on a largely bevacizumab-treated population, is no.
cards.source: Chan JK et al. Weekly vs. Every-3-Week Paclitaxel and Carboplatin for Ovarian Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26933849. Registry ID: NCT01167712, from the record. cards.headline: MITO-7: a weekly carboplatin–paclitaxel regimen (both drugs weekly) gave no progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.96) but better quality of life and less neuropathy than 3-weekly therapy
cards.summary: MITO-7: a weekly carboplatin–paclitaxel regimen (both drugs weekly) gave no progression-free-survival benefit (HR 0.96) but better quality of life and less neuropathy than 3-weekly therapy
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (open-label, multicentre, Italy and France)
cards.people: 810 eligible women with FIGO stage IC–IV ovarian cancer and no prior chemotherapy, randomly allocated to carboplatin AUC 6 plus paclitaxel 175 mg/m² every 3 weeks for six cycles, or carboplatin AUC 2 plus paclitaxel 60 mg/m² weekly for 18 weeks. Coprimary endpoints: progression-free survival and quality of life (FACT-O Trial Outcome Index). Median follow-up 22.3 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 17.3 months (3-weekly) versus 18.3 months (weekly) (hazard ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.80–1.16; p=0.66). Quality-of-life scores differed significantly between schedules (treatment-by-time interaction p<0.0001): scores worsened at every cycle with 3-weekly therapy, while with weekly therapy they remained stable after a transient week-1 worsening. Grade 3–4 neutropenia (42% vs 50%), febrile neutropenia (0.5% vs 3%), grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia (1% vs 7%) and grade ≥2 neuropathy (6% vs 17%) were all less frequent with the weekly regimen. Three deaths were attributed to chemotherapy (two 3-weekly, one weekly).
cards.watchOut: MITO-7's weekly regimen is not JGOG 3016's dose-dense regimen: carboplatin was also split weekly at a lower peak dose, so the trial tests a gentler weekly schedule, not dose density of paclitaxel against 3-weekly carboplatin. Its contribution to this shelf is the null efficacy result plus a genuine tolerability advantage — relevant to schedule choice, not to the survival question.

shelves.title: Mirvetuximab soravtansine in platinum-resistant, FRα-positive ovarian cancer (MIRASOL)
shelves.question: In folate-receptor-alpha-positive, platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, does mirvetuximab soravtansine improve progression-free and overall survival versus investigator-choice chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Carcinoma, Ovarian Epithelial · Immunoconjugates · Maytansine · Ovarian Neoplasms · Folate Receptor 1 · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Platinum Compounds
shelves.balance: A single randomised phase 3 trial, and the first to show an overall-survival benefit in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. In 453 patients with high folate-receptor-α expression (≥75% of tumour cells with ≥2+ staining) and one to three prior lines, mirvetuximab soravtansine beat investigator-choice chemotherapy on every endpoint: progression-free survival 5.62 versus 3.98 months, objective response 42.3% versus 15.9%, and overall survival 16.46 versus 12.75 months (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.50–0.89) — while causing fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (41.7% vs 54.1%), fewer serious adverse events and fewer discontinuations. The earlier SORAYA study was single-arm and cannot substitute for a second randomised trial, so the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stands: an open-label trial whose survival result is strong, internally consistent and unmatched by any comparator-era result in this disease, but unreplicated. Balance: for FRα-high platinum-resistant disease, this is the new reference treatment on one trial's evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: MIRASOL: mirvetuximab soravtansine improved progression-free survival (5.62 vs 3.98 months), response (42.3% vs 15.9%) and overall survival (16.46 vs 12.75 months; HR 0.67) versus chemotherapy in FRα-positive platinum-resistant ovarian cancer — with fewer grade ≥3 adverse events
cards.summary: MIRASOL: mirvetuximab soravtansine improved progression-free survival (5.62 vs 3.98 months), response (42.3% vs 15.9%) and overall survival (16.46 vs 12.75 months; HR 0.67) versus chemotherapy in FRα-positive platinum-resistant ovarian cancer — with fewer grade ≥3 adverse events
cards.people: 453 participants with platinum-resistant, high-grade serous ovarian cancer, previously treated with one to three lines of therapy, whose tumours had high folate receptor α expression (≥75% of cells with ≥2+ staining intensity). Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to mirvetuximab soravtansine 6 mg/kg of adjusted ideal body weight every 3 weeks (n=227) or investigator's-choice chemotherapy — paclitaxel, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, or topotecan (n=226). The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed progression-free survival; overall survival and objective response were key secondary endpoints.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 5.62 months (95% CI 4.34–5.95) with mirvetuximab versus 3.98 months (2.86–4.47) with chemotherapy (P<0.001). An objective response occurred in 42.3% versus 15.9% (odds ratio 3.81; 95% CI 2.44–5.94; P<0.001). Overall survival was significantly longer with mirvetuximab (median 16.46 vs 12.75 months; hazard ratio for death 0.67; 95% CI 0.50–0.89; P=0.005). During treatment, grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 41.7% versus 54.1%, serious adverse events in 23.9% versus 32.9%, and events leading to discontinuation in 9.2% versus 15.9%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with investigator-assessed progression-free survival as the primary endpoint — the overall-survival result (a key secondary endpoint, HR 0.67) is the finding least exposed to that design. Eligibility required high FRα expression by a specific immunohistochemistry threshold; the result does not extend to FRα-low tumours. Single randomised trial — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE; the supporting SORAYA study was single-arm and is not carded as randomised evidence.

shelves.title: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer (KEYNOTE-826; BEATcc)
shelves.question: In persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, does adding pembrolizumab to platinum chemotherapy (± bevacizumab) improve overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · Carcinoma · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Progression-Free Survival · Survival Analysis · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms
shelves.balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials, two different checkpoint inhibitors, the same answer. KEYNOTE-826 (double-blind, n=617) added pembrolizumab to platinum chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab: in PD-L1 CPS ≥1 disease, progression-free survival improved (10.4 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.62) and 24-month overall survival was 53.0% versus 41.7% (HR 0.64), with consistent effects in the intention-to-treat and CPS ≥10 populations. BEATcc (open-label, n=410) added atezolizumab to a fixed bevacizumab-plus-platinum backbone: progression-free survival 13.7 versus 10.4 months (HR 0.62) and interim overall survival 32.1 versus 22.8 months (HR 0.68). The regimens differ (pembrolizumab with optional bevacizumab versus atezolizumab with mandatory bevacizumab), so this is class replication rather than a duplicate trial — and it is why the stamp is LIKELY rather than a single-trial flag. Toxicity is additive but familiar: anaemia and neutropenia dominate in KEYNOTE-826; BEATcc's grade ≥3 rates were 79% versus 75%. The locally advanced (chemoradiation) setting is a different question, homed on Shelf #854. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: KEYNOTE-826: adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy (± bevacizumab) improved progression-free survival (HR 0.62 in CPS ≥1) and overall survival (24-month 53.0% vs 41.7%; HR 0.64) in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-826: adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy (± bevacizumab) improved progression-free survival (HR 0.62 in CPS ≥1) and overall survival (24-month 53.0% vs 41.7%; HR 0.64) in persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer
cards.people: 617 patients with persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer randomly assigned 1:1 to pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 35 cycles, plus platinum-based chemotherapy and, per investigator discretion, bevacizumab. The dual primary endpoints (progression-free and overall survival) were tested sequentially in the PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) ≥1 population (n=548), the intention-to-treat population (n=617) and the CPS ≥10 population (n=317). Results are from the protocol-specified first interim analysis.
cards.result: In CPS ≥1 patients, median progression-free survival was 10.4 versus 8.2 months (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.50–0.77; P<0.001); in the intention-to-treat population, 10.4 versus 8.2 months (HR 0.65; 0.53–0.79); in CPS ≥10, 10.4 versus 8.1 months (HR 0.58; 0.44–0.77). Overall survival at 24 months was 53.0% versus 41.7% (HR for death 0.64; 95% CI 0.50–0.81; P<0.001) in CPS ≥1, 50.4% versus 40.4% (HR 0.67; 0.54–0.84) in intention-to-treat, and 54.4% versus 44.6% (HR 0.61; 0.44–0.84) in CPS ≥10. The most common grade 3–5 adverse events were anaemia (30.3% vs 26.9%) and neutropenia (12.4% vs 9.7%).
cards.watchOut: Bevacizumab use was by investigator discretion (not randomised), so this trial isolates the pembrolizumab effect, not the bevacizumab one (that question is Shelf #1896). Results reported here are the first interim analysis; later analyses of this trial exist, and the direction and approximate size of the survival effect were maintained in them, but this pack cards the record fetched at drafting.

cards.people: 410 patients with metastatic (stage IVB), persistent or recurrent cervical cancer, previously untreated and not amenable to curative surgery or radiation, enrolled at 92 sites in Europe, Japan and the USA and randomly assigned 1:1 to standard therapy — cisplatin 50 mg/m² or carboplatin AUC 5, paclitaxel 175 mg/m² and bevacizumab 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks — with or without atezolizumab 1200 mg. Dual primary endpoints: investigator-assessed progression-free survival and overall survival in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 13.7 months (95% CI 12.3–16.6) with atezolizumab versus 10.4 months (9.7–11.7) with standard therapy (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.49–0.78; p<0.0001). At the interim overall-survival analysis, median overall survival was 32.1 months (25.3–36.8) versus 22.8 months (20.3–28.0) (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.52–0.88; p=0.0046). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 79% of the atezolizumab group and 75% of the standard group; grade 1–2 diarrhoea, arthralgia, pyrexia and rash were increased with atezolizumab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the overall-survival analysis carded here is the trial's interim analysis. Unlike KEYNOTE-826, bevacizumab was mandatory in both arms, so BEATcc tests checkpoint blockade added to the full GOG-240 backbone — concordant with, but not a rerun of, the pembrolizumab trial.

shelves.title: Bevacizumab added to chemotherapy in advanced cervical cancer (GOG-240)
shelves.question: In metastatic, persistent or recurrent cervical cancer, does adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy doublets improve overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bevacizumab · Cisplatin · Female · Humans · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Paclitaxel · Quality of Life · Survival Analysis · Topotecan · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms
shelves.balance: One randomised trial broke a decades-long survival plateau in this disease, and none has repeated the experiment. GOG-240 (n=452, 2×2 factorial) found that adding bevacizumab 15 mg/kg to chemotherapy doublets improved overall survival from 13.3 to 17.0 months (HR 0.71; 98% CI 0.54–0.95) and response rates from 36% to 48%; the trial's other question — topotecan–paclitaxel versus cisplatin–paclitaxel — was answered in the negative (HR for death 1.20). The harms are specific and must ride with the benefit: grade ≥2 hypertension 25% versus 2%, grade ≥3 thromboembolism 8% versus 1%, and grade ≥3 gastrointestinal fistula 3% versus 0% — in a population many of whose members had received prior pelvic radiation. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label). The bevacizumab backbone this trial established is the platform onto which checkpoint inhibitors were later added (Shelf #1895). PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: GOG-240: adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy improved overall survival (17.0 vs 13.3 months; HR 0.71) and response (48% vs 36%) in advanced cervical cancer — with more hypertension, thromboembolism and fistula
cards.summary: GOG-240: adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy improved overall survival (17.0 vs 13.3 months; HR 0.71) and response (48% vs 36%) in advanced cervical cancer — with more hypertension, thromboembolism and fistula
cards.people: 452 patients with recurrent, persistent or metastatic cervical cancer, most previously treated with cisplatin-based chemoradiation. Using a 2×2 factorial design, patients were randomly assigned to chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab 15 mg/kg; chemotherapy was cisplatin 50 mg/m² plus paclitaxel 135 or 175 mg/m², or topotecan 0.75 mg/m² on days 1–3 plus paclitaxel 175 mg/m² on day 1, in 21-day cycles until progression, unacceptable toxicity or complete response. The primary endpoint was overall survival; a 30% reduction in the hazard ratio for death was prespecified as clinically important.
cards.result: Topotecan–paclitaxel was not superior to cisplatin–paclitaxel (hazard ratio for death 1.20). Pooling the two chemotherapy regimens, adding bevacizumab increased overall survival (17.0 vs 13.3 months; hazard ratio for death 0.71; 98% CI 0.54–0.95; P=0.004 in a one-sided test) and response rates (48% vs 36%; P=0.008). Bevacizumab was associated with more grade ≥2 hypertension (25% vs 2%), grade ≥3 thromboembolic events (8% vs 1%) and grade ≥3 gastrointestinal fistulas (3% vs 0%).
cards.watchOut: Single trial, open-label, and its survival P value is reported from a one-sided test — the 98% confidence interval (0.54–0.95) is the honest summary. The fistula risk matters most in patients with prior pelvic irradiation and bowel involvement, and it is the reason this regimen's benefit cannot be quoted without its harms. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: no second randomised trial of bevacizumab in this setting exists.

shelves.title: Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone in high-risk endometrial cancer (PORTEC-3)
shelves.question: In high-risk endometrial cancer after surgery, does adjuvant chemoradiotherapy improve overall and failure-free survival versus radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Australia · Canada · Carboplatin · Carcinoma, Endometrioid · Chemoradiotherapy, Adjuvant · Cisplatin · Dose Fractionation, Radiation · Endometrial Neoplasms · Europe · Female · Gynecologic Surgical Procedures · Humans · Lymph Node Excision · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Grading · Neoplasm Staging · New Zealand · Paclitaxel · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large randomised trial with a split answer. In PORTEC-3's final analysis (n=660, median follow-up 60.2 months), adding chemotherapy during and after pelvic radiotherapy improved 5-year failure-free survival (75.5% vs 68.6%; HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.53–0.95; p=0.022) but did not significantly improve 5-year overall survival (81.8% vs 76.7%; adjusted HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.54–1.06; p=0.11). The cost was steep: grade ≥3 adverse events during treatment in 60% versus 12%, and grade ≥2 neuropathy persisting at 3 years in 8% versus 1%. Trial-level subgroup reporting (outside this record) suggests the benefit concentrates in stage III and serous/p53-abnormal disease, which is how the trial is usually applied — but on the carded record the population-level claim is a failure-free-survival benefit without a proven overall-survival benefit. THIN: single trial, survival claim subgroup-dependent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: PORTEC-3 (final results): chemoradiotherapy improved 5-year failure-free survival (75.5% vs 68.6%; HR 0.71) but not overall survival (81.8% vs 76.7%; adjusted HR 0.76, NS) — with grade ≥3 toxicity in 60% vs 12%
cards.summary: PORTEC-3 (final results): chemoradiotherapy improved 5-year failure-free survival (75.5% vs 68.6%; HR 0.71) but not overall survival (81.8% vs 76.7%; adjusted HR 0.76, NS) — with grade ≥3 toxicity in 60% vs 12%
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (open-label, international, Gynaecological Cancer Intergroup)
cards.people: 686 women enrolled (660 eligible in the final analysis) with high-risk endometrial cancer: FIGO 2009 stage I endometrioid grade 3 with deep myometrial invasion or lymphovascular space invasion, endometrioid stage II–III, or stage I–III serous or clear-cell histology. Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to pelvic radiotherapy alone (48.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions) or chemoradiotherapy — two cycles of cisplatin 50 mg/m² during radiotherapy, then four cycles of carboplatin AUC 5 plus paclitaxel 175 mg/m². Co-primary endpoints: overall survival and failure-free survival. Median follow-up 60.2 months.
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 81.8% (95% CI 77.5–86.2) with chemoradiotherapy versus 76.7% (72.1–81.6) with radiotherapy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.76; 95% CI 0.54–1.06; p=0.11) — not significant. Five-year failure-free survival was 75.5% (70.3–79.9) versus 68.6% (63.1–73.4) (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% CI 0.53–0.95; p=0.022). Grade ≥3 adverse events during treatment occurred in 198 (60%) of 330 patients receiving chemoradiotherapy versus 41 (12%) of 330 receiving radiotherapy (p<0.0001), and grade ≥2 neuropathy persisted significantly more often after chemoradiotherapy (8% vs 1% at 3 years; p<0.0001). The authors concluded adjuvant chemotherapy during and after radiotherapy did not improve 5-year overall survival although it increased failure-free survival, and that women should be individually counselled.
cards.watchOut: The overall-survival result in this final record is not significant (adjusted HR 0.76, CI crossing 1) — summaries quoting a stronger survival figure are drawing on subgroup analyses (stage III, serous histology) that are not in this abstract and are not carded here as trial-level claims. The trial predates routine molecular (p53/POLE/MMR) classification, so applying its average result to molecularly defined subgroups is extrapolation.

shelves.title: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced cervical cancer (OUTBACK)
shelves.question: In locally advanced cervical cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy, does additional adjuvant (outback) chemotherapy improve overall survival versus chemoradiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Carboplatin · Cisplatin · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms · Neoplasm Staging · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Chemoradiotherapy · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Paclitaxel
shelves.balance: A large, clean negative trial. OUTBACK (n=919 eligible, median follow-up 60 months) added four cycles of carboplatin–paclitaxel after standard cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy in locally advanced cervical cancer and found 5-year overall survival of 72% versus 71% (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.70–1.17; p=0.81) — no benefit, with more grade 3–4 toxicity (decreased neutrophils 20% vs 8%; anaemia 18% vs 8%) and more serious adverse events (30% vs 22%). The investigators' conclusion was unambiguous: adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy should not be given in this setting. Do not confuse the timing: chemotherapy given BEFORE chemoradiotherapy (induction, INTERLACE) is a different strategy with positive results, homed on Shelf #854. Balance: on a survival primary endpoint, in an adequately sized trial, additional post-chemoradiation chemotherapy made no difference and added harm. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: OUTBACK: adjuvant carboplatin–paclitaxel after chemoradiotherapy did not improve 5-year overall survival (72% vs 71%; HR 0.90) in locally advanced cervical cancer, and increased grade 3–4 toxicity
cards.summary: OUTBACK: adjuvant carboplatin–paclitaxel after chemoradiotherapy did not improve 5-year overall survival (72% vs 71%; HR 0.90) in locally advanced cervical cancer, and increased grade 3–4 toxicity
cards.people: 926 patients randomised (919 eligible) aged ≥18 with histologically confirmed squamous, adenosquamous or adenocarcinoma of the cervix — FIGO 2008 stage IB1 with nodal involvement, or stage IB2, II, IIIB or IVA — and ECOG performance status 0–2. All received standard cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin 40 mg/m² weekly × 5 weeks with 45.0–50.4 Gy external-beam radiotherapy plus brachytherapy); the adjuvant group then received four cycles of carboplatin AUC 5 plus paclitaxel 155 mg/m² every 21 days. Primary endpoint: overall survival at 5 years, intention-to-treat. Median follow-up 60 months.
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 72% (95% CI 67–76) in the adjuvant-chemotherapy group (105 deaths) and 71% (66–75) in the chemoradiotherapy-only group (116 deaths) (difference 1%; 95% CI −6 to 7; hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.70–1.17; p=0.81). The most common clinically significant grade 3–4 adverse events were decreased neutrophils (20% in the adjuvant group vs 8% in the control group) and anaemia (18% vs 8%). Serious adverse events occurred in 30% versus 22%, most commonly from infectious complications. There were no treatment-related deaths. The authors concluded adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy increased short-term toxicity, did not improve overall survival, and should not be given in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.70–1.17) excludes a large benefit but not a small one; the stamp rests on a point estimate near unity in a 919-patient trial with a survival primary endpoint. The result applies to unselected locally advanced disease after standard chemoradiotherapy — it does not address induction chemotherapy before chemoradiotherapy (INTERLACE; Shelf #854), which asks the opposite-timing question and was positive.

shelves.title: Carboplatin–paclitaxel versus cisplatin–paclitaxel–doxorubicin (TAP) in advanced endometrial cancer (GOG-0209)
shelves.question: In advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, is carboplatin–paclitaxel noninferior to cisplatin–paclitaxel–doxorubicin (TAP) for overall survival, with less toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carboplatin · Cisplatin · Endometrial Neoplasms · Female · Filgrastim · Humans · Middle Aged · Paclitaxel · Progression-Free Survival · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One very large noninferiority trial settled the practical question. GOG-0209 (n=1,381) compared carboplatin–paclitaxel (TC) with the three-drug TAP regimen and concluded noninferiority for overall survival (median 37 vs 41 months; HR 1.002; 90% CI 0.90–1.12) and progression-free survival (median 13 vs 14 months; HR 1.032; 90% CI 0.93–1.15). The median-survival gap favouring TAP is the nuance that belongs on the card face: the point estimates lean slightly toward the triplet, and noninferiority was established against the trial's prespecified margin, not by equality of medians. What tipped practice was deliverability and harm: TAP caused more grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia (23% vs 12%), vomiting (7% vs 4%), diarrhoea (6% vs 2%) and metabolic toxicity (14% vs 8%), while TC caused more neutropenia (80% vs 52%); febrile neutropenia was similar (6% vs 7%), grade >2 sensory neuropathy was recorded in 20% (TC) versus 26% (TAP), and small quality-of-life differences favoured TC. Balance: equivalent-enough survival with a simpler, better-tolerated doublet — the basis on which TC became the global first-line standard. THIN in form (a single trial carries an equivalence claim), large in size. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: GOG-0209: carboplatin–paclitaxel was noninferior to TAP for overall survival (median 37 vs 41 months; HR 1.002, 90% CI 0.90–1.12) and progression-free survival, with a more favourable toxicity profile overall
cards.summary: GOG-0209: carboplatin–paclitaxel was noninferior to TAP for overall survival (median 37 vs 41 months; HR 1.002, 90% CI 0.90–1.12) and progression-free survival, with a more favourable toxicity profile overall
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 noninferiority trial (open-label, NRG Oncology/GOG)
cards.people: 1,381 women enrolled (2003–2009) with stage III, stage IV or recurrent endometrial cancer, performance status 0–2 and adequate organ function; prior radiotherapy or hormonal therapy permitted, prior chemotherapy (including radiosensitising) not. Treatment was TAP — doxorubicin 45 mg/m² and cisplatin 50 mg/m² on day 1, paclitaxel 160 mg/m² on day 2 with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor — or TC: paclitaxel 175 mg/m² plus carboplatin AUC 6 on day 1, every 21 days for seven cycles. Primary endpoint: overall survival (modified intention-to-treat).
cards.result: Noninferiority of TC to TAP was concluded for overall survival (median 37 vs 41 months; hazard ratio 1.002; 90% CI 0.90–1.12) and for progression-free survival (median 13 vs 14 months; hazard ratio 1.032; 90% CI 0.93–1.15). Neutropenic fever occurred in 7% (TAP) and 6% (TC). Grade >2 sensory neuropathy was recorded in 26% of TAP patients and 20% of TC patients (P=0.40). More grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia (23% vs 12%), vomiting (7% vs 4%), diarrhoea (6% vs 2%) and metabolic toxicity (14% vs 8%) occurred with TAP; neutropenia was more common with TC (80% vs 52%). Small health-related quality-of-life differences favoured TC. The authors concluded that, with noninferiority demonstrated, TC is the global first-line standard for advanced endometrial cancer.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is a margin-relative claim: the median overall survival numerically favoured TAP by 4 months, and the confidence interval excludes neither a small TAP advantage nor a small TC one. The trial also predates immunotherapy combinations in this disease (Shelf #853 covers pembrolizumab/dostarlimab added to chemotherapy in advanced endometrial cancer), which have since moved the first-line question on from either arm of this trial.

J Clin Oncol. 2020. PMID: 33078978. Registry ID: NCT00063999, from the record. shelves.title: Neoadjuvant-plus-adjuvant versus adjuvant-only pembrolizumab in resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma (SWOG S1801)
shelves.question: In resectable stage IIIB–IV melanoma, does starting pembrolizumab before surgery (3 doses) and continuing afterwards improve event-free survival versus the same total therapy given entirely after surgery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Disease Progression · Melanoma · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Skin Neoplasms · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: One randomised trial asked a timing question, not a drug question — both arms received 18 doses of pembrolizumab; only the placement of the first three (before versus after surgery) differed. SWOG S1801 (phase 2, n=313) found event-free survival at 2 years of 72% with neoadjuvant-plus-adjuvant therapy versus 49% with adjuvant-only therapy (P=0.004 by log-rank), at a median follow-up of 14.7 months, with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events no higher in the neoadjuvant arm (12% vs 14%). The event-free-survival endpoint includes failure to reach or complete surgery, which is part of the strategy being tested, not a flaw in it. Overall survival was not yet reported — this shelf claims an event-free-survival benefit only. NADINA (neoadjuvant ipilimumab–nivolumab) answers the adjacent question with a different, more intense regimen and is fenced, not merged; adjuvant-only pembrolizumab and nivolumab are homed on Shelf #761. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: SWOG S1801: three neoadjuvant pembrolizumab doses before surgery (then adjuvant therapy) improved 2-year event-free survival (72% vs 49%; P=0.004) versus the same drug given entirely after surgery
cards.summary: SWOG S1801: three neoadjuvant pembrolizumab doses before surgery (then adjuvant therapy) improved 2-year event-free survival (72% vs 49%; P=0.004) versus the same drug given entirely after surgery
cards.people: 313 patients with clinically detectable, measurable stage IIIB–IVC melanoma amenable to surgical resection, randomly assigned to three doses of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by surgery and 15 adjuvant doses (neoadjuvant-adjuvant group, n=154), or to surgery followed by pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks for 18 doses over approximately 1 year (adjuvant-only group, n=159). The primary endpoint was event-free survival in the intention-to-treat population; events included progression or toxicity precluding surgery, inability to resect all gross disease, failure to start adjuvant therapy within 84 days of surgery, recurrence after surgery, or death.
cards.result: At a median follow-up of 14.7 months, event-free survival was significantly longer in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group (P=0.004 by the log-rank test). In a landmark analysis, 2-year event-free survival was 72% (95% CI 64–80) in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group and 49% (95% CI 41–59) in the adjuvant-only group. Treatment-related adverse events of grade ≥3 occurred in 12% and 14% of patients respectively. No new toxic effects were identified.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports event rates and the log-rank P value, not a hazard ratio — none is printed on this card. Follow-up was short (median 14.7 months) and overall survival was not a reported outcome of this record; the trial is a randomised phase 2, large for its design but a single study — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. The comparator is not 'no treatment': both arms received the same total pembrolizumab, so the result indicts timing, and says nothing about pembrolizumab versus none (see Shelf #761 for adjuvant therapy versus observation-era questions).

shelves.title: Adjuvant dabrafenib + trametinib in resected BRAF-mutated stage III melanoma (COMBI-AD)
shelves.question: In resected stage III BRAF V600-mutated melanoma, does 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib improve relapse-free survival versus placebo, and does it extend survival?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imidazoles · Male · Melanoma · Middle Aged · Mutation · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasm Staging · Oximes · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf · Pyridones · Pyrimidinones · Skin Neoplasms · Survival Analysis · Young Adult · Cutaneous Malignant Melanoma
shelves.balance: A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial whose two answers must not be fused. COMBI-AD (n=870) showed 12 months of adjuvant dabrafenib plus trametinib substantially improves relapse-free survival — 3-year 58% versus 39% at the primary analysis (HR 0.47) and HR 0.52 in the final analysis after nearly a decade of follow-up, with distant metastasis-free survival HR 0.56. But the final overall-survival analysis was not significant (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.62–1.01; P=0.06), despite an early interim estimate (HR 0.57) that had not crossed its prespecified boundary; the prespecified BRAF V600E subgroup showed HR 0.75 (0.58–0.96). The dissociation — durable relapse prevention without a proven survival extension — is the balance of this shelf, and any summary that sells the combination as life-extending overstates the record. The adjuvant alternatives (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) are homed on Shelf #761; no randomised trial compares the targeted and immune adjuvant strategies head-to-head. PROPOSED LIKELY (for relapse-free survival; no survival claim).

cards.people: 870 patients with completely resected stage III melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations, randomly assigned to oral dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg once daily (n=438) or matched placebos (n=432) for 12 months. Primary endpoint: relapse-free survival; secondary endpoints included overall survival, distant metastasis-free survival, freedom from relapse and safety. Median follow-up 2.8 years.
cards.result: The estimated 3-year relapse-free survival rate was 58% in the combination group versus 39% in the placebo group (hazard ratio for relapse or death 0.47; 95% CI 0.39–0.58; P<0.001). The 3-year overall survival rate was 86% versus 77% (hazard ratio for death 0.57; 95% CI 0.42–0.79; P=0.0006), but this did not cross the prespecified interim analysis boundary of P=0.000019, so it was not a demonstrated survival benefit. Distant metastasis-free survival and freedom from relapse also favoured the combination. The safety profile was consistent with that seen in metastatic melanoma, with no new toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: Read the survival line exactly as the record gives it: a nominally small P value that failed the trial's own interim boundary is not a positive survival result — and the final analysis (next card) confirmed that caution. Pyrexia and discontinuation for adverse events are the combination's familiar burdens from the metastatic setting.

cards.type: Final results of the same randomized phase 3 trial
cards.people: The same 870 patients randomised in COMBI-AD, followed for a median of 8.33 years in the dabrafenib-plus-trametinib group and 6.87 years in the placebo group. This report presents the trial's final results for overall survival, melanoma-specific survival, relapse-free survival and distant metastasis-free survival.
cards.result: Kaplan–Meier estimates for overall survival favoured dabrafenib plus trametinib, but the benefit was not significant (hazard ratio for death 0.80; 95% CI 0.62–1.01; P=0.06 by stratified log-rank test) — a 20% relative reduction in the risk of death that the data do not confirm. A consistent benefit was seen across prespecified subgroups, including the 792 patients with BRAF V600E melanoma (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.58–0.96). Relapse-free survival favoured the combination (hazard ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.43–0.63), as did distant metastasis-free survival (hazard ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.44–0.71). No new safety signals were reported.
cards.watchOut: The V600E subgroup's significant hazard ratio does not rescue the trial-level survival claim — the overall analysis is the claim, and it is negative by the trial's own test. Equally, 'not significant' is not 'no effect': the confidence interval (0.62–1.01) is compatible with a meaningful survival benefit, which is why this shelf stamps the relapse claim LIKELY and the survival claim unproven rather than disproven.

shelves.title: Combined BRAF + MEK inhibition versus BRAF inhibition alone in metastatic BRAF-mutated melanoma (COMBI-d; COMBI-v)
shelves.question: In untreated BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma, does dabrafenib plus trametinib improve overall survival versus BRAF inhibition alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fever · Humans · Imidazoles · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Melanoma · Middle Aged · Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinases · Mutation · Oximes · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf · Pyridones · Pyrimidinones
shelves.balance: Two randomised phase 3 trials, each against a different single-agent BRAF inhibitor, plus their pooled 5-year follow-up. COMBI-v (n=704, versus vemurafenib) crossed its prespecified interim stopping boundary for overall survival: 12-month survival 72% versus 65% (HR 0.69; P=0.005), with progression-free survival 11.4 versus 7.3 months (HR 0.56) and far fewer cutaneous squamous-cell cancers (1% vs 18%). COMBI-d (n=423, double-blind versus dabrafenib alone) improved progression-free survival (9.3 vs 8.8 months; HR 0.75) and response (67% vs 51%); its interim survival estimate favoured the combination (HR 0.63) without crossing its stringent stopping boundary. The pooled 5-year analysis of both trials (n=563 on the combination) gives the durable picture: overall survival 34% at 5 years, and 71% at 5 years among the 19% who achieved a complete response. Pyrexia is the combination's signature toxicity (51% vs 28% in COMBI-d). Balance: adding MEK inhibition to BRAF inhibition improves survival over BRAF inhibition alone — the question that defined an era of melanoma therapy, now largely superseded by immunotherapy-first sequencing (Shelf #1905) but not by any failure of these trials. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: COMBI-d: dabrafenib + trametinib versus dabrafenib alone improved progression-free survival (9.3 vs 8.8 months; HR 0.75) and response (67% vs 51%); interim overall survival favoured the combination (HR 0.63) without crossing the stopping boundary
cards.summary: COMBI-d: dabrafenib + trametinib versus dabrafenib alone improved progression-free survival (9.3 vs 8.8 months; HR 0.75) and response (67% vs 51%); interim overall survival favoured the combination (HR 0.63) without crossing the stopping boundary
cards.people: 423 previously untreated patients with unresectable stage IIIC or IV melanoma with a BRAF V600E or V600K mutation, randomly assigned to dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg once daily, or dabrafenib plus placebo. Primary endpoint: progression-free survival; a preplanned interim overall-survival analysis was conducted.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 9.3 months with the combination versus 8.8 months with dabrafenib alone (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57–0.99; P=0.03). The overall response rate was 67% versus 51% (P=0.002). At 6 months, the interim overall survival rate was 93% versus 85% (hazard ratio for death 0.63; 95% CI 0.42–0.94; P=0.02), but the specified efficacy-stopping boundary (two-sided P=0.00028) was not crossed. Adverse-event rates were similar overall, with more dose modifications in the combination group; cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma was less frequent with the combination (2% vs 9%), while pyrexia was more frequent (51% vs 28%) and more often grade 3 (6% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: This record is COMBI-d's primary report: its primary endpoint is progression-free survival and its survival analysis is an interim one that deliberately did not meet its own stopping rule. The survival claim of this shelf rests on COMBI-v (next card) and the pooled long-term analysis (third card). COMBI-d's comparator is dabrafenib alone, which is the comparison this shelf's question names; COMBI-v (next card) used vemurafenib as its comparator.

cards.people: 704 patients with metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation, randomly assigned to dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily plus trametinib 2 mg once daily, or vemurafenib 960 mg twice daily, as first-line therapy. Primary endpoint: overall survival. The preplanned interim overall-survival analysis was performed after 77% of expected events had occurred.
cards.result: The overall survival rate at 12 months was 72% (95% CI 67–77) with the combination versus 65% (59–70) with vemurafenib (hazard ratio for death 0.69; 95% CI 0.53–0.89; P=0.005); the prespecified interim stopping boundary was crossed and the study was stopped for efficacy in July 2014. Median progression-free survival was 11.4 versus 7.3 months (hazard ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.46–0.69; P<0.001), and the objective response rate was 64% versus 51% (P<0.001). Rates of severe adverse events and discontinuations were similar; cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma and keratoacanthoma occurred in 1% of the combination group versus 18% of the vemurafenib group.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is vemurafenib monotherapy, the weaker of the two single-agent BRAF inhibitors in tolerability; the survival result nonetheless answers the shelf's question for the class comparison (combination versus BRAF inhibition alone), and COMBI-d's dabrafenib-controlled data point the same way. Early stopping for efficacy can exaggerate effect sizes; the pooled 5-year analysis (next card) is the durability check.

cards.people: 563 patients randomly assigned to dabrafenib plus trametinib across COMBI-d (n=211) and COMBI-v (n=352), all previously untreated with BRAF V600E/K-mutated unresectable or metastatic melanoma. Median duration of follow-up was 22 months (range 0–76).
cards.result: Progression-free survival rates on the combination were 21% (95% CI 17–24) at 4 years and 19% (15–22) at 5 years; overall survival rates were 37% (33–42) at 4 years and 34% (30–38) at 5 years. Baseline performance status, age, sex, number of organ sites and lactate dehydrogenase level were significantly associated with both outcomes in multivariate analysis. A complete response occurred in 109 patients (19%) and was associated with an overall survival rate of 71% (95% CI 62–79) at 5 years. The authors concluded first-line dabrafenib plus trametinib led to long-term benefit in approximately one third of patients.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of the combination arms only — it describes durability on treatment, not the randomised comparison, which is carried by the two trial cards above. Its role on this shelf is to show the combination's benefit is not a transient interim artefact.

shelves.title: Tebentafusp in HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma
shelves.question: In HLA-A*02:01-positive metastatic uveal melanoma, does tebentafusp improve overall survival versus investigator-choice therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents · Cytokine Release Syndrome · Dacarbazine · Exanthema · Female · Humans · Ipilimumab · Male · Melanoma · Middle Aged · Recombinant Fusion Proteins · Survival Analysis · Uveal Neoplasms
shelves.balance: A single randomised phase 3 trial that produced the first overall-survival benefit ever shown in metastatic uveal melanoma — a disease where, as the trial record puts it, 1-year survival was approximately 50% and no systemic treatment had proven a survival benefit. In 378 previously untreated HLA-A*02:01-positive patients, tebentafusp (a bispecific gp100-targeting T-cell engager) improved 1-year overall survival to 73% versus 59% (HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.37–0.71) against investigator's choice of pembrolizumab, ipilimumab or dacarbazine, with progression-free survival also favouring tebentafusp (6-month 31% vs 19%; HR 0.73). The toxicity is front-loaded and mechanism-typical: rash 83%, pyrexia 76%, pruritus 69%, mostly in the first doses, with only 2% discontinuing for treatment-related events and no treatment-related deaths. Two fences: the benefit applies only to HLA-A*02:01-positive patients (roughly half of populations of European ancestry, fewer in others), and there is no second trial — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: Tebentafusp improved overall survival in metastatic uveal melanoma (1-year 73% vs 59%; HR 0.51) — the first survival benefit ever shown in this disease — in HLA-A*02:01-positive patients
cards.summary: Tebentafusp improved overall survival in metastatic uveal melanoma (1-year 73% vs 59%; HR 0.51) — the first survival benefit ever shown in this disease — in HLA-A*02:01-positive patients
cards.people: 378 previously untreated patients with metastatic uveal melanoma who were HLA-A*02:01-positive, randomly assigned 2:1 to tebentafusp (n=252) or investigator's choice of single-agent pembrolizumab, ipilimumab or dacarbazine (n=126), stratified by lactate dehydrogenase level. Tebentafusp is a bispecific protein — an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor targeting glycoprotein 100 fused to an anti-CD3 effector. Primary endpoint: overall survival.
cards.result: Overall survival at 1 year was 73% in the tebentafusp group versus 59% in the control group (hazard ratio for death 0.51; 95% CI 0.37–0.71; P<0.001). Progression-free survival was also higher with tebentafusp (31% vs 19% at 6 months; hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.58–0.94; P=0.01). The most common treatment-related adverse events were cytokine-mediated and skin-related events, including rash (83%), pyrexia (76%) and pruritus (69%); these decreased in incidence and severity after the first three or four doses, infrequently led to discontinuation (2%), and there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Eligibility required HLA-A*02:01 positivity — the result is silent on the HLA-negative half of this disease, for whom no survival-proven systemic therapy existed at this record. The control arm pooled three different single agents, so the trial answers 'tebentafusp versus the available choices', not versus any one of them. Single trial — flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label; first-in-disease landmark).
cards.source: Nathan P et al. Overall Survival Benefit with Tebentafusp in Metastatic Uveal Melanoma. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 34551229. shelves.title: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy versus ipilimumab in advanced melanoma
shelves.question: In advanced melanoma progressing on/after anti-PD-1 (mostly), does tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy improve progression-free survival versus ipilimumab?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cell- and Tissue-Based Therapy · Ipilimumab · Lymphocytes, Tumor-Infiltrating · Melanoma · Immunotherapy, Adoptive
shelves.balance: The first randomised trial of adoptive cell therapy in a solid tumour, and it won its primary endpoint. In 168 patients with unresectable stage IIIC/IV melanoma — 86% of them refractory to anti-PD-1 therapy — tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy after lymphodepleting chemotherapy, followed by high-dose interleukin-2, doubled median progression-free survival versus ipilimumab (7.2 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.35–0.72) and more than doubled the response rate (49% vs 21%). Median overall survival was numerically longer with TIL therapy (25.8 vs 18.9 months), but the record reports no hazard ratio and the trial was not powered to settle survival — this shelf claims the progression-free-survival result only. The price is the platform: grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 100% of TIL patients (mainly chemotherapy-related myelosuppression) versus 57% with ipilimumab, plus the manufacturing and centre requirements of a bespoke cell product. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label; landmark first randomised cell-therapy win). PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: TIL therapy versus ipilimumab: progression-free survival doubled (7.2 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50) and response rate 49% vs 21% in mostly anti-PD-1-refractory advanced melanoma — the first randomised cell-therapy trial in a solid tumour
cards.summary: TIL therapy versus ipilimumab: progression-free survival doubled (7.2 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50) and response rate 49% vs 21% in mostly anti-PD-1-refractory advanced melanoma — the first randomised cell-therapy trial in a solid tumour
cards.people: 168 patients with unresectable stage IIIC or IV melanoma, 86% with disease refractory to anti-PD-1 therapy, randomly assigned 1:1 to tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy (n=84) — infusion of at least 5×10⁹ TILs preceded by nonmyeloablative lymphodepleting chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide plus fludarabine) and followed by high-dose interleukin-2 — or ipilimumab 3 mg/kg (n=84). Primary endpoint: progression-free survival, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 7.2 months (95% CI 4.2–13.1) in the TIL group versus 3.1 months (3.0–4.3) with ipilimumab (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.50; 95% CI 0.35–0.72; P<0.001). An objective response occurred in 49% (95% CI 38–60) versus 21% (13–32). Median overall survival was 25.8 months (18.2 to not reached) versus 18.9 months (13.8–32.6); the record reports no hazard ratio for overall survival. Treatment-related adverse events of grade ≥3 occurred in all patients who received TILs and in 57% of those who received ipilimumab; in the TIL group these were mainly chemotherapy-related myelosuppression.
cards.watchOut: The comparator, single-agent ipilimumab, is a reasonable salvage standard for the era but a modest one; the trial does not compare TIL therapy with modern combination salvage regimens. Overall survival cannot be claimed from this record (no hazard ratio reported). Deliverability is part of the evidence: TIL therapy requires a resectable lesion for manufacture, weeks of production, lymphodepletion and high-dose IL-2 at an experienced centre — the intention-to-treat result already absorbs some of that attrition.
cards.source: Rohaan MW et al. Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocyte Therapy or Ipilimumab in Advanced Melanoma. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 36477031. Registry ID: NCT02278887, from the record.
