shelves.title: Immunotherapy-first versus targeted-therapy-first sequencing in BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma (DREAMseq; SECOMBIT)
shelves.question: In untreated BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma, does starting with nivolumab + ipilimumab (switching to dabrafenib + trametinib at progression) improve overall survival versus the reverse sequence?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Ipilimumab · Nivolumab · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf · Prospective Studies · Melanoma · Pyridones · Oximes · Disease Progression · Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinases · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Skin Neoplasms · Mutation · Pyrimidinones · Imidazoles
shelves.balance: Two randomised sequencing trials point the same way: in BRAF-mutated metastatic melanoma, immunotherapy first, targeted therapy in reserve, beats the reverse order. DREAMseq (phase 3, n=265) was stopped early by its data safety monitoring committee because the primary endpoint had been reached: 2-year overall survival was 71.8% for patients starting on nivolumab–ipilimumab versus 51.5% for those starting on dabrafenib–trametinib, with crossover to the alternate therapy at progression built into both strategies; second-line response was asymmetric (47.8% for targeted therapy after immunotherapy versus 29.6% for immunotherapy after targeted therapy), and response duration favoured immunotherapy first (not reached vs 12.7 months). SECOMBIT (randomised phase 2, three arms, n=209, using encorafenib–binimetinib) was directionally concordant: 2-year overall survival 73% for immunotherapy-first versus 65% for targeted-first, with a sandwich arm between them (69%). Only 52% of DREAMseq patients with documented progression actually crossed over, which is itself part of the finding — a strategy that depends on reaching second line fails the patients who never get there. Balance: sequence matters, and the immune-first sequence is the one to default to. PROPOSED LIKELY pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).

cards.headline: DREAMseq: starting with nivolumab + ipilimumab (targeted therapy in reserve) improved 2-year overall survival versus starting with dabrafenib + trametinib (71.8% vs 51.5%); the trial was stopped early for efficacy
cards.summary: DREAMseq: starting with nivolumab + ipilimumab (targeted therapy in reserve) improved 2-year overall survival versus starting with dabrafenib + trametinib (71.8% vs 51.5%); the trial was stopped early for efficacy
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 sequencing trial (two-step design; stopped early)
cards.people: 265 patients with treatment-naive BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma randomly assigned in step 1 to combination nivolumab–ipilimumab (arm A) or dabrafenib–trametinib (arm B); at disease progression, patients were enrolled in step 2 to the alternate therapy (arm C: dabrafenib–trametinib after immunotherapy, n=27; arm D: nivolumab–ipilimumab after targeted therapy, n=46). Primary endpoint: 2-year overall survival.
cards.result: The study was stopped early by the independent data safety monitoring committee because a clinically significant endpoint had been achieved. Two-year overall survival was 71.8% (95% CI 62.5–79.1) for patients starting on arm A versus 51.5% (41.7–60.4) for arm B (log-rank P=0.010). Step-1 progression-free survival favoured arm A (P=0.054). Objective response rates were 46.0% (arm A), 43.0% (arm B), 47.8% (arm C) and 29.6% (arm D); median duration of response was not reached for arm A versus 12.7 months for arm B (P<0.001). Crossover occurred in 52% of patients with documented progression. Grade ≥3 toxicities occurred with similar frequency between arms, with regimen-typical profiles.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping can inflate the estimated benefit, and only about half of progressing patients reached the planned second line — so the result is as much about the fragility of 'save the immunotherapy for later' as about the drugs. The targeted-therapy arm used dabrafenib–trametinib; whether a different BRAF/MEK pair changes the sequence verdict is addressed only indirectly by SECOMBIT (next card).
cards.source: Atkins MB et al. cards.headline: SECOMBIT: immunotherapy-first sequencing again gave the highest survival (2-year OS 73% vs 65% targeted-first; 3-year 62% vs 54%) in a randomised three-arm phase 2 trial
cards.summary: SECOMBIT: immunotherapy-first sequencing again gave the highest survival (2-year OS 73% vs 65% targeted-first; 3-year 62% vs 54%) in a randomised three-arm phase 2 trial
cards.people: 209 patients with untreated metastatic BRAF V600-mutant melanoma at 37 sites in nine countries, randomly assigned to arm A (encorafenib plus binimetinib until progression, then ipilimumab plus nivolumab; n=69), arm B (ipilimumab plus nivolumab until progression, then encorafenib plus binimetinib; n=71), or arm C (8 weeks of encorafenib plus binimetinib, then ipilimumab plus nivolumab until progression, then encorafenib plus binimetinib; n=69). Primary endpoint: overall survival at 2 years.
cards.result: At a median follow-up of 32.2 months, median overall survival was not reached in any arm. The 2-year and 3-year overall survival rates were 65% (95% CI 54–76) and 54% (41–67) in arm A (targeted first), 73% (62–84) and 62% (48–76) in arm B (immunotherapy first), and 69% (59–80) and 60% (58–72) in arm C (sandwich). The overall-survival endpoint (against a null of median OS ≤15 months) was met for all arms. No new safety signals emerged.
cards.watchOut: A noncomparative phase 2: the arms were not powered for head-to-head testing, so SECOMBIT supports DREAMseq's direction rather than independently proving it — the shelf's two-trial claim rests on a phase 3 plus a concordant phase 2. The targeted pair here is encorafenib–binimetinib, which usefully extends the sequencing conclusion beyond the dabrafenib programme.

shelves.title: Adding concurrent chemotherapy to postoperative radiotherapy in high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck (TROG 05.01)
shelves.question: In high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck after surgery, does postoperative chemoradiotherapy improve disease-free survival versus postoperative radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carboplatin · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Chemoradiotherapy · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Postoperative Care · Radiotherapy Dosage · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Skin Neoplasms · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: One randomised phase 3 trial, and it was negative. In TROG 05.01 (n=321 randomised), adding weekly carboplatin to postoperative radiotherapy (60–66 Gy) after resection of high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck did not improve freedom from locoregional relapse — the primary endpoint (hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.46–1.55; P=0.58; 5-year rates 87% versus 83%) — and there were no significant differences in disease-free or overall survival. Surgery plus radiotherapy alone already achieved excellent locoregional control (5-year freedom from locoregional relapse 83%), locoregional failure remained the dominant first failure site, and 84% of the chemoradiotherapy arm completed six carboplatin cycles, so the null is not explained by under-delivery. Chemotherapy also did not measurably worsen radiotherapy toxicity — the addition was, in effect, all cost and no gain, though the cost too was modest. THIN: a single trial with a wide confidence interval that cannot exclude a moderate locoregional benefit; the stamp is therefore POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY for the no-difference reading. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: TROG 05.01: adding weekly carboplatin to postoperative radiotherapy did not improve freedom from locoregional relapse (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.46–1.55; P=0.58), disease-free survival or overall survival in high-risk cutaneous SCC of the head and neck
cards.summary: TROG 05.01: adding weekly carboplatin to postoperative radiotherapy did not improve freedom from locoregional relapse (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.46–1.55; P=0.58), disease-free survival or overall survival in high-risk cutaneous SCC of the head and neck
cards.type: Randomized phase 3 trial (Trans Tasman Radiation Oncology Group)
cards.people: 321 patients randomly assigned (310 commenced allocated treatment: radiotherapy alone n=157; chemoradiotherapy n=153) after resection of gross disease for high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck: 77% had high-risk nodal disease, 19% high-risk primary or in-transit disease and 4% both. Radiotherapy was 60 or 66 Gy over 6–6.5 weeks, with or without weekly concurrent carboplatin (AUC 2); 84% of the chemoradiotherapy group completed six cycles. Median follow-up 60 months. Primary objective: freedom from locoregional relapse; secondary objectives included disease-free and overall survival.
cards.result: Freedom from locoregional relapse at 2 and 5 years was 88% (95% CI 83–93) and 83% (77–90) with radiotherapy alone, and 89% (84–94) and 87% (81–93) with chemoradiotherapy (hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.46–1.55; P=0.58). There were no significant differences in disease-free or overall survival. Locoregional failure was the most common site of first failure; isolated distant metastases were the first failure site in 7% of both arms. Treatment was well tolerated in both arms, with no observed enhancement of radiotherapy toxicity by carboplatin and infrequent grade 3–4 late toxicities. The authors concluded that although surgery and postoperative radiotherapy provided excellent freedom from locoregional relapse, no benefit was observed from adding weekly carboplatin.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval for the primary endpoint (0.46–1.55) is wide — the trial rules out neither a moderate locoregional benefit nor moderate harm, which is why this shelf's no-difference stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. The chemoradiation tested is weekly carboplatin specifically; cisplatin-based intensification is untested in this disease and cannot borrow this null or escape it. Note the contrast with adjuvant cemiplimab after surgery and radiotherapy (Shelf #1908): a different drug class, tested against placebo, with a positive result.
cards.source: Porceddu SV et al. shelves.title: Nivolumab + ipilimumab versus nivolumab alone for melanoma brain metastases (ABC trial)
shelves.question: In melanoma brain metastases (asymptomatic, untreated), does nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieve better intracranial control than nivolumab alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Australia · Brain Neoplasms · Female · Humans · Ipilimumab · Male · Melanoma · Middle Aged · Nivolumab · Progression-Free Survival · Skin Neoplasms · Time Factors
shelves.balance: One small randomised phase 2 — the only randomised comparison in this setting — favours the combination for intracranial control. In the ABC trial's randomised cohorts (asymptomatic, previously untreated brain metastases), intracranial responses occurred in 46% of patients on nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus 20% on nivolumab alone, with complete intracranial responses in 17% versus 12%; median follow-up was 17 months at the primary report. The non-randomised third cohort — patients with failed local therapy, neurological symptoms, or leptomeningeal disease — responded at only 6% on nivolumab, marking how different the favourable randomised population is from the patients clinicians worry about most. The combination cost substantially more high-grade toxicity (grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events 54% versus 16%). Survival was not a randomised endpoint of this report, so the shelf claims intracranial response only; CheckMate 204, the larger combination cohort, was single-arm and is fenced. THIN: 60 treated patients in the randomised comparison and a response endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ABC trial: in asymptomatic untreated melanoma brain metastases, nivolumab + ipilimumab gave higher intracranial response than nivolumab alone (46% vs 20%; complete responses 17% vs 12%), with more grade 3–4 toxicity (54% vs 16%)
cards.summary: ABC trial: in asymptomatic untreated melanoma brain metastases, nivolumab + ipilimumab gave higher intracranial response than nivolumab alone (46% vs 20%; complete responses 17% vs 12%), with more grade 3–4 toxicity (54% vs 16%)
cards.type: Randomized phase 2 trial (multicentre, Australia; two randomised cohorts plus one non-randomised cohort)
cards.people: 79 immunotherapy-naive patients with melanoma brain metastases enrolled at four Australian sites. Patients with asymptomatic brain metastases and no previous local brain therapy were randomly assigned (30:24, after a six-patient safety run-in) to cohort A, nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses then nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks (36 enrolled; 35 treated), or cohort B, nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks (27 enrolled; 25 treated). Patients whose local therapy had failed, who had neurological symptoms, or who had leptomeningeal disease were enrolled into non-randomised cohort C (nivolumab; n=16). Primary endpoint: intracranial response from week 12. Median follow-up 17 months.
cards.result: Intracranial responses were achieved by 16 (46%; 95% CI 29–63) of 35 patients in cohort A, five (20%; 7–41) of 25 in cohort B, and one (6%; 0–30) of 16 in cohort C. Intracranial complete responses occurred in six (17%) patients in cohort A, three (12%) in cohort B, and none in cohort C. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 97% (cohort A), 68% (B) and 50% (C); grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 19 (54%) patients in cohort A, four (16%) in cohort B and two (13%) in cohort C. No treatment-related deaths occurred. The authors concluded nivolumab combined with ipilimumab should be considered first-line therapy for asymptomatic untreated brain metastases.
cards.watchOut: Small numbers (35 versus 25 treated in the randomised comparison), a response endpoint, and no randomised survival comparison in this record — long-term follow-up of the trial has been reported elsewhere but is not carded here, so this shelf claims intracranial control, not survival. The randomised result applies to asymptomatic, untreated metastases; cohort C's 6% response rate in symptomatic or previously treated disease is a warning against extrapolating the combination's performance to that population from this trial.
cards.source: Long GV et al. Combination nivolumab and ipilimumab or nivolumab alone in melanoma brain metastases: a multicentre randomised phase 2 study. Lancet Oncol. 2018. PMID: 29602646. Registry ID: NCT02374242, from the record. shelves.title: Adjuvant cemiplimab in high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma after surgery and radiotherapy (C-POST)
shelves.question: After surgery and radiotherapy for high-risk cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, does adjuvant cemiplimab improve disease-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Skin Neoplasms
shelves.balance: One recent randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with a large effect on its primary endpoint. In C-POST (n=415), patients with cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma at high risk of recurrence after surgical resection and postoperative radiotherapy received up to 48 weeks of adjuvant cemiplimab or placebo: disease-free survival strongly favoured cemiplimab (24 versus 65 recurrence-or-death events; HR 0.32; 95% CI 0.20–0.51), with estimated 24-month disease-free survival of 87.1% versus 64.1%, locoregional recurrence HR 0.20 and distant recurrence HR 0.35, at a median follow-up of 24 months. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent with cemiplimab (23.9% vs 14.2%), as were discontinuations for adverse events (9.8% vs 1.5%). Overall survival was not yet reported — this shelf claims disease-free survival only, and the effect, though large, rests on 89 total events in a single trial (THIN in form). The contrast with Shelf #1906 is instructive: in the same broad disease, adding carboplatin chemotherapy to radiotherapy did nothing, while adjuvant PD-1 blockade after radiotherapy substantially delayed recurrence. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: C-POST: adjuvant cemiplimab after surgery and radiotherapy improved disease-free survival in high-risk cutaneous SCC (HR 0.32; 24-month DFS 87.1% vs 64.1%), with locoregional recurrence HR 0.20 and distant recurrence HR 0.35
cards.summary: C-POST: adjuvant cemiplimab after surgery and radiotherapy improved disease-free survival in high-risk cutaneous SCC (HR 0.32; 24-month DFS 87.1% vs 64.1%), with locoregional recurrence HR 0.20 and distant recurrence HR 0.35
cards.people: 415 patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, after surgical resection and postoperative radiotherapy, at high risk of recurrence because of nodal features (extracapsular extension with largest node ≥20 mm, or at least three involved nodes) or non-nodal features (in-transit metastases, T4 lesion with bone invasion, perineural invasion, or locally recurrent tumour with at least one additional risk feature). Patients were assigned 1:1 to adjuvant cemiplimab 350 mg every 3 weeks for 12 weeks then 700 mg every 6 weeks for up to 36 further weeks (n=209), or placebo (n=206). Primary endpoint: disease-free survival. Median follow-up 24 months.
cards.result: Cemiplimab was superior to placebo for disease-free survival (24 versus 65 events; hazard ratio for disease recurrence or death 0.32; 95% CI 0.20–0.51; P<0.001). Estimated 24-month disease-free survival was 87.1% (95% CI 80.3–91.6) with cemiplimab versus 64.1% (55.9–71.1) with placebo. Cemiplimab led to lower risks of locoregional recurrence (9 events vs 40; hazard ratio 0.20; 95% CI 0.09–0.40) and distant recurrence (10 vs 26 events; hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.17–0.72). Adverse events of grade ≥3 occurred in 23.9% of cemiplimab patients versus 14.2% on placebo; discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 9.8% versus 1.5%.
cards.watchOut: Overall survival is not reported in this record and is not claimed; the disease-free-survival result rests on 89 events at 24 months' median follow-up in a single trial (THIN in form). Eligibility required completion of both surgery and postoperative radiotherapy and specified high-risk features — the result does not address patients who did not receive radiotherapy or whose risk features fall outside the trial's list.
cards.source: Rischin D et al. Adjuvant Cemiplimab or Placebo in High-Risk Cutaneous Squamous-Cell Carcinoma. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40454639. Registry ID: NCT03969004, from the record. shelves.title: Individualised neoantigen vaccine (mRNA-4157/V940) plus pembrolizumab in resected high-risk melanoma (KEYNOTE-942)
shelves.question: In resected high-risk melanoma, does adding an individualised neoantigen mRNA vaccine to pembrolizumab improve recurrence-free survival versus pembrolizumab alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Melanoma · Skin Neoplasms
shelves.balance: One small open-label phase 2b trial (n=157) found fewer recurrences when a personalised neoantigen mRNA vaccine was added to adjuvant pembrolizumab: recurrence or death in 22% versus 40%, hazard ratio 0.56 — but the 95% confidence interval (0.31 to 1.02) crosses 1.0 and the two-sided P value was 0.053, so the primary comparison did not reach conventional significance. Eighteen-month recurrence-free survival was 79% versus 62%. Grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were somewhat more frequent with the combination (25% vs 18%), with no vaccine-related grade 4–5 events. This is a promising, unconfirmed signal: recurrence-free survival is a surrogate, overall survival is unreported, and the phase 3 trial (V940-001) is still in flight. Adjuvant pembrolizumab or nivolumab versus placebo is homed on Shelf #761; this shelf asks only what the vaccine adds. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: KEYNOTE-942: adding mRNA-4157 (V940) to pembrolizumab cut recurrence or death (22% vs 40%; HR 0.56), but the confidence interval crossed 1.0 (0.31–1.02; P=0.053)
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-942: adding mRNA-4157 (V940) to pembrolizumab cut recurrence or death (22% vs 40%; HR 0.56), but the confidence interval crossed 1.0 (0.31–1.02; P=0.053)
cards.people: 157 patients with completely resected high-risk cutaneous melanoma (stage IIIB–IV) at sites in the USA and Australia, randomly assigned 2:1 to open-label mRNA-4157 (an mRNA-based individualised neoantigen therapy, intramuscular, maximum nine doses) plus pembrolizumab (n=107) or pembrolizumab monotherapy (n=50), in 3-week cycles. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival in the intention-to-treat population; median follow-up was 23–24 months.
cards.result: Recurrence-free survival was longer with the combination: hazard ratio for recurrence or death 0.561 (95% CI 0.309–1.017; two-sided P=0.053), with recurrence or death events in 24 of 107 patients (22%) versus 20 of 50 (40%) — an absolute difference of about 18 percentage points. Eighteen-month recurrence-free survival was 79% (95% CI 69.0–85.6) versus 62% (46.9–74.3). Grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events occurred in 25% of the combination group and 18% of the monotherapy group, with no mRNA-4157-related grade 4–5 events; immune-mediated adverse events were similar (36% in both groups).
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval includes 1.0 — by the trial's own two-sided test this is a near-miss, not a proven benefit, and the event count is small (44 events). Open-label design, a 2:1 randomisation with only 50 control patients, and a recurrence-free-survival endpoint with no survival data yet: the confirmatory phase 3 trial (V940-001) will decide this question. The vaccine is manufactured per patient from tumour sequencing, so the result also presumes that production pathway.
cards.source: Weber JS et al. Individualised neoantigen therapy mRNA-4157 (V940) plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab monotherapy in resected melanoma (KEYNOTE-942): a randomised, phase 2b study. Lancet. 2024. PMID: 38246194. Registry ID: NCT03897881, from the record. shelves.title: First-line pembrolizumab in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma (KEYNOTE-048; CheckMate 651; KESTREL)
shelves.question: In recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, does first-line pembrolizumab (alone or with chemotherapy) improve overall survival versus the EXTREME regimen — and did the other checkpoint programmes beat the same comparator?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Cetuximab · Female · Fluorouracil · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Progression-Free Survival · Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck
shelves.balance: Three phase 3 trials tested checkpoint blockade against the same EXTREME comparator (cetuximab plus platinum and 5-fluorouracil), and only the pembrolizumab programme won. In KEYNOTE-048 (n=882), pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival in the total population (median 13.0 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.77), and pembrolizumab alone improved survival in PD-L1 CPS ≥20 (HR 0.61) and CPS ≥1 (HR 0.78) disease while proving non-inferior overall. But nivolumab plus ipilimumab (CheckMate 651, n=947) did not significantly improve survival in the total or CPS ≥20 populations, and durvalumab with or without tremelimumab (KESTREL) was not superior in PD-L1-high disease. The shelf's claim is therefore agent-specific, not a class effect: pembrolizumab-based first-line therapy prolongs survival; dual-checkpoint and durvalumab-based strategies did not beat EXTREME on survival despite gentler toxicity. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claims — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: KEYNOTE-048: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival versus EXTREME in the total population (13.0 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.77); monotherapy won in PD-L1-positive disease
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-048: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival versus EXTREME in the total population (13.0 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.77); monotherapy won in PD-L1-positive disease
cards.people: 882 participants with untreated, locally incurable recurrent or metastatic HNSCC at 200 sites in 37 countries, randomly allocated 1:1:1 to pembrolizumab alone (n=301), pembrolizumab plus platinum and 5-fluorouracil (n=281), or cetuximab plus platinum and 5-fluorouracil — the EXTREME regimen (n=300). 754 participants (85%) had PD-L1 CPS ≥1 and 381 (43%) CPS ≥20. Primary endpoints were overall and progression-free survival across the CPS ≥20, CPS ≥1, and total populations, under 14 prespecified hypotheses.
cards.result: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy improved overall survival versus cetuximab with chemotherapy in the total population (median 13.0 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.63–0.93; P=0.0034), in CPS ≥20 (14.7 vs 11.0 months; HR 0.60) and in CPS ≥1 (13.6 vs 10.4 months; HR 0.65). Pembrolizumab alone improved overall survival in CPS ≥20 (14.9 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.61, P=0.0007) and CPS ≥1 (12.3 vs 10.3 months; HR 0.78, P=0.0086) and was non-inferior in the total population (11.6 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.85). Neither pembrolizumab strategy improved progression-free survival. Grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 55% (pembrolizumab alone), 85% (pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy), and 83% (EXTREME).
cards.watchOut: The monotherapy benefit is confined to PD-L1-expressing disease — in the total population pembrolizumab alone was only non-inferior, so the shelf does not support monotherapy for unselected patients. Fourteen primary hypotheses with sequential interim testing make the individual P values design-dependent; the hazard ratios and absolute medians are the durable content. Open-label trial.

cards.headline: CheckMate 651: nivolumab plus ipilimumab did NOT significantly improve overall survival versus EXTREME (HR 0.95 total; HR 0.78 in CPS ≥20, not significant under the trial's design)
cards.summary: CheckMate 651: nivolumab plus ipilimumab did NOT significantly improve overall survival versus EXTREME (HR 0.95 total; HR 0.78 in CPS ≥20, not significant under the trial's design)
cards.people: 947 patients with recurrent or metastatic squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck and no prior systemic therapy for recurrent/metastatic disease, randomly assigned 1:1 to nivolumab plus ipilimumab or the EXTREME regimen (cetuximab plus cisplatin/carboplatin plus fluorouracil, then cetuximab maintenance). 38.3% had PD-L1 CPS ≥20. Primary endpoints were overall survival in all randomly assigned patients and in the CPS ≥20 population.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences in overall survival: median 13.9 versus 13.5 months in all randomly assigned patients (HR 0.95, 97.9% CI 0.80–1.13; P=0.4951) and 17.6 versus 14.6 months in CPS ≥20 (HR 0.78, 97.51% CI 0.59–1.03; P=0.0469 — not significant at the alpha allocated to that hypothesis). In CPS ≥20, median duration of response was much longer with nivolumab–ipilimumab (32.6 vs 7.0 months) though response rates were similar (34.1% vs 36.0%). Grade 3/4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 28.2% versus 70.7%.
cards.watchOut: A gentler regimen with far longer response durations still failed its survival endpoints — duration of response in a minority of responders did not move the population survival curve. The CPS ≥1 subgroup (HR 0.82) is hypothesis-generating only. This card is the discordance that keeps Shelf #1910 agent-specific.

cards.headline: KESTREL: durvalumab with or without tremelimumab was not superior to EXTREME for overall survival in PD-L1-high disease (HR 0.96 and 1.05)
cards.summary: KESTREL: durvalumab with or without tremelimumab was not superior to EXTREME for overall survival in PD-L1-high disease (HR 0.96 and 1.05)
cards.people: Patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC and no prior systemic treatment for recurrent/metastatic disease, randomized 2:1:1 to durvalumab plus tremelimumab, durvalumab monotherapy, or the EXTREME regimen. The primary efficacy assessment was overall survival in patients with PD-L1-high tumours and in all randomized patients.
cards.result: Durvalumab and durvalumab plus tremelimumab were not superior to EXTREME for overall survival in PD-L1-high expression: median 10.9 and 11.2 versus 10.9 months (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.69–1.32; and HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.80–1.39). Responses were more durable with durvalumab-based therapy (49.3% and 48.1% versus 9.8% still in response at 12 months), but median progression-free survival was longer with EXTREME (5.4 vs 2.8 months). Grade 3/4 treatment-related adverse events: 8.9% (durvalumab), 19.1% (combination), 53.1% (EXTREME). The authors note that subsequent immunotherapy in 24.3% of the EXTREME arm may have contributed to the similar survival outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract does not state the total randomized N — none is printed on this card. Post-progression immunotherapy in the control arm dilutes any survival contrast, a structural feature of first-line trials run after checkpoint inhibitors became salvage standard. Like CheckMate 651, this is a negative trial against the same comparator KEYNOTE-048 beat.

shelves.title: Nivolumab in platinum-refractory recurrent or metastatic HNSCC (CheckMate 141; KEYNOTE-040)
shelves.question: In recurrent or metastatic HNSCC progressing during or within 6 months of platinum therapy, does PD-1 blockade improve overall survival versus investigator-choice single-agent therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antineoplastic Agents · B7-H1 Antigen · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Nivolumab · Quality of Life · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 trials asked the same salvage question and both answered yes. CheckMate 141 (n=361) found nivolumab prolonged overall survival versus methotrexate, docetaxel, or cetuximab (median 7.5 vs 5.1 months; HR 0.70), nearly doubling 1-year survival (36.0% vs 16.6%) with a third of the grade 3–4 treatment-related toxicity (13.1% vs 35.1%). KEYNOTE-040 (n=495) replicated the class effect with pembrolizumab (median 8.4 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.80). Neither drug improved median progression-free survival — the benefit is a long survival tail, not slower average progression. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: CheckMate 141: nivolumab prolonged survival after platinum failure (7.5 vs 5.1 months; HR 0.70) and roughly doubled 1-year survival (36.0% vs 16.6%)
cards.summary: CheckMate 141: nivolumab prolonged survival after platinum failure (7.5 vs 5.1 months; HR 0.70) and roughly doubled 1-year survival (36.0% vs 16.6%)
cards.people: 361 patients with recurrent squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck whose disease had progressed within 6 months after platinum-based chemotherapy, randomly assigned 2:1 to nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or standard single-agent therapy (methotrexate, docetaxel, or cetuximab). The primary endpoint was overall survival.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 7.5 months (95% CI 5.5–9.1) with nivolumab versus 5.1 months (4.0–6.0) with standard therapy (HR for death 0.70, 97.73% CI 0.51–0.96; P=0.01); estimated 1-year survival was 36.0% versus 16.6% — about 19 percentage points higher in absolute terms. Median progression-free survival did not favour nivolumab (2.0 vs 2.3 months; HR 0.89, P=0.32), though 6-month progression-free survival did (19.7% vs 9.9%). Response rate was 13.3% versus 5.8%. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events: 13.1% versus 35.1%; quality-of-life measures were stable on nivolumab and meaningfully worse on standard therapy.
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial with a modest median gain; the value is concentrated in the tail of responders, and there is no validated way to identify them in advance from this record. The progression-free-survival medians favour the control arm numerically — quoting them alone would misstate the trial.

shelves.title: Cetuximab versus cisplatin with radiotherapy in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (RTOG 1016; De-ESCALaTE)
shelves.question: In HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous-cell carcinoma, can cetuximab replace cisplatin alongside radiotherapy without losing overall survival (de-escalation)?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents · Cetuximab · Chemoradiotherapy · Cisplatin · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Oropharyngeal Neoplasms · Papillomavirus Infections · Radiotherapy, Intensity-Modulated · Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials tested the same de-escalation idea and both found the substitution costs lives. In RTOG 1016 (n=849), cetuximab failed non-inferiority for overall survival — 5-year survival 77.9% versus 84.6% with cisplatin (HR 1.45), with significantly more locoregional failure (5-year 17.3% vs 9.9%). In De-ESCALaTE (n=334, low-risk patients — the population with most to gain from gentler treatment), cetuximab again lost: 2-year survival 89.4% versus 97.5% (HR 5.0) and 2-year recurrence 16.1% versus 6.0%. Decisively, neither trial found the toxicity advantage that justified the swap — severe toxicity was essentially identical. The verdict is unusually clean: do not substitute cetuximab for cisplatin in cisplatin-eligible HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C (mortality harm from substitution — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: RTOG 1016: cetuximab FAILED non-inferiority — 5-year survival 77.9% vs 84.6% (HR 1.45), locoregional failure 17.3% vs 9.9%, with no toxicity advantage
cards.summary: RTOG 1016: cetuximab FAILED non-inferiority — 5-year survival 77.9% vs 84.6% (HR 1.45), locoregional failure 17.3% vs 9.9%, with no toxicity advantage
cards.people: 987 patients enrolled and 849 randomly assigned (805 subsequently eligible: 399 cetuximab, 406 cisplatin) with HPV-positive oropharyngeal carcinoma at 182 centres in the USA and Canada, to accelerated intensity-modulated radiotherapy (70 Gy in 35 fractions) plus either cetuximab (400 mg/m² loading, then 250 mg/m² weekly ×7) or cisplatin 100 mg/m² on days 1 and 22. The primary endpoint was overall survival, non-inferiority margin HR 1.45; median follow-up 4.5 years.
cards.result: Radiotherapy plus cetuximab did not meet non-inferiority for overall survival (HR 1.45, one-sided 95% upper CI 1.94; P=0.5056 for non-inferiority). Estimated 5-year overall survival was 77.9% (95% CI 73.4–82.5) with cetuximab versus 84.6% (80.6–88.6) with cisplatin — about 6.7 percentage points lower in absolute terms. Progression-free survival was significantly worse with cetuximab (HR 1.72; 5-year 67.3% vs 78.4%), as was locoregional failure (HR 2.05; 5-year 17.3% vs 9.9%). Acute moderate-to-severe toxicity (77.4% vs 81.7%) and late toxicity (16.5% vs 20.4%) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority margin (1.45) was generous, and cetuximab failed even against it. The result applies to patients eligible for cisplatin; it says nothing about patients who cannot receive cisplatin, for whom cetuximab plus radiotherapy (Shelf #1916) remains a fallback with its own, older evidence base. Both arms used accelerated IMRT, so the comparison isolates the systemic agent.

cards.people: 334 patients aged ≥18 with HPV-positive low-risk oropharyngeal cancer (non-smokers or <10 pack-year smoking history) at 32 centres in Ireland, the Netherlands, and the UK, randomly assigned 1:1 to radiotherapy (70 Gy in 35 fractions) plus cisplatin 100 mg/m² on days 1, 22, and 43 (n=166) or cetuximab (400 mg/m² loading, then seven weekly 250 mg/m² doses) (n=168). cards.result: The de-escalation premise failed on its own terms: overall severe toxicity did not differ (mean 4.8 events per patient in both groups; P=0.98), nor did all-grade toxicity (29.2 vs 30.1 events per patient). Tumour control was significantly worse with cetuximab: 2-year overall survival 97.5% with cisplatin versus 89.4% with cetuximab (HR 5.0, 95% CI 1.7–14.7; P=0.001) and 2-year recurrence 6.0% versus 16.1% (HR 3.4; P=0.0007) — absolute differences of about 8 and 10 percentage points against cetuximab.
cards.watchOut: The survival hazard ratio (5.0) rests on few deaths in a low-risk population — its confidence interval is wide (1.7–14.7) — but the direction is identical to RTOG 1016's much larger dataset, and the recurrence difference is independently significant. shelves.title: Postoperative chemoradiotherapy in high-risk resected HNSCC (EORTC 22931; RTOG 9501)
shelves.question: In resected HNSCC with high-risk features, does adding concurrent cisplatin to postoperative radiotherapy improve disease-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Cisplatin · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radiotherapy · Risk · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: Two 2004 phase 3 trials, published back to back, tested postoperative cisplatin chemoradiation against radiotherapy alone. EORTC 22931 (n=334) found significant gains in progression-free survival (HR 0.75; 5-year 47% vs 36%) and overall survival (HR 0.70; 5-year 53% vs 40%), with locoregional relapse nearly halved. RTOG 9501 (n=459) found significantly better local-regional control (HR 0.61) and disease-free survival (HR 0.78) but no significant survival difference (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65–1.09). Both trials roughly doubled severe acute toxicity (grade ≥3: 41% vs 21% and 77% vs 34%), and RTOG 9501 recorded four treatment deaths on the combined arm. Later pooled analyses localise the clearest benefit to positive margins and extracapsular extension. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claim — the developer rules personally). CORRECTION: the topic file quoted EORTC 22931's overall-survival HR as 0.84; the fetched record gives HR 0.70 (0.84 is RTOG 9501's survival HR).

cards.headline: EORTC 22931: postoperative cisplatin chemoradiation improved progression-free survival (HR 0.75) and overall survival (HR 0.70; 5-year 53% vs 40%) versus radiotherapy alone
cards.summary: EORTC 22931: postoperative cisplatin chemoradiation improved progression-free survival (HR 0.75) and overall survival (HR 0.70; 5-year 53% vs 40%) versus radiotherapy alone
cards.people: 334 patients after surgery with curative intent for stage III–IV head and neck cancer, randomly assigned to postoperative radiotherapy alone (66 Gy over 6.5 weeks, n=167) or the same radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin 100 mg/m² on days 1, 22, and 43 (n=167). Median follow-up 60 months. Primary comparisons were progression-free and overall survival.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly higher with combined therapy (HR for disease progression 0.75, 95% CI 0.56–0.99; P=0.04; 5-year estimates 47% vs 36%), as was overall survival (HR for death 0.70, 95% CI 0.52–0.95; P=0.02; 5-year estimates 53% vs 40% — a 13-percentage-point absolute difference). The 5-year cumulative incidence of local or regional relapse was 18% after combined therapy versus 31% after radiotherapy alone (P=0.007). Severe (grade ≥3) adverse effects were more frequent with combined therapy (41% vs 21%, P=0.001); late adverse effects did not differ materially.
cards.watchOut: Correction against the topic file: this record's overall-survival hazard ratio is 0.70, not 0.84. The trial predates routine HPV stratification and modern IMRT, and enrolled a mixed high-risk population defined by stage and pathology of its era. Only about two-thirds of patients typically complete all three cisplatin cycles in this regimen (the record's abstract does not state the completion rate — none is printed here).

cards.headline: RTOG 9501: local-regional control and disease-free survival improved (HR 0.61 and 0.78), overall survival did not (HR 0.84, NS), and acute grade ≥3 toxicity more than doubled (77% vs 34%)
cards.summary: RTOG 9501: local-regional control and disease-free survival improved (HR 0.61 and 0.78), overall survival did not (HR 0.84, NS), and acute grade ≥3 toxicity more than doubled (77% vs 34%)
cards.people: 459 patients with high-risk squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck after total resection of all visible and palpable disease, randomly assigned between 1995 and 2000 to postoperative radiotherapy alone (60–66 Gy, n=231) or the identical radiotherapy plus concurrent cisplatin 100 mg/m² on days 1, 22, and 43 (n=228). Median follow-up 45.9 months.
cards.result: Local and regional control was significantly higher with combined therapy (HR for local or regional recurrence 0.61, 95% CI 0.41–0.91; P=0.01; estimated 2-year control 82% vs 72%), and disease-free survival was significantly longer (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61–0.99; P=0.04). Overall survival was not significantly different (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65–1.09; P=0.19). Acute adverse effects of grade 3 or greater occurred in 77% of the combined-therapy group versus 34% with radiotherapy alone (P<0.001), and four patients on combined therapy died as a direct result of treatment.
cards.watchOut: The discordance with EORTC 22931 on survival is the shelf's central tension: populations and risk definitions differed, and RTOG 9501's wider eligibility may have diluted a benefit concentrated in the highest-risk pathology. Subsequent pooled analyses of the two trials — fenced here, not carded — localise the clearest benefit to extracapsular extension and positive margins, which is how the regimen is now targeted.

shelves.title: Induction docetaxel chemotherapy (TPF) versus PF in locally advanced HNSCC (TAX 324; TAX 323)
shelves.question: In unresectable locally advanced HNSCC, does induction TPF (docetaxel/cisplatin/5-fluorouracil) improve overall survival compared with PF (cisplatin/5-fluorouracil) induction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Cisplatin · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Docetaxel · Female · Fluorouracil · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radiotherapy · Survival Analysis · Taxoids · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 trials compared docetaxel-containing induction (TPF) with the older PF doublet, and both favoured TPF. TAX 324 (n=501, induction followed by chemoradiotherapy) found overall survival HR 0.70, with median survival 71 versus 30 months and 3-year survival 62% versus 48%. TAX 323 (n=358, induction followed by radiotherapy) found progression-free survival HR 0.72 and a 27% relative reduction in the risk of death (median survival 18.8 vs 14.5 months). The claim this shelf supports is narrow: TPF is the better induction regimen. Whether induction chemotherapy at all beats proceeding directly to chemoradiotherapy is a different question — the later PARADIGM and DeCIDE trials of induction followed by chemoradiation versus chemoradiation alone were null and are fenced here, not carded. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: TAX 324: TPF induction improved overall survival versus PF (HR 0.70; median 71 vs 30 months; 3-year survival 62% vs 48%) before chemoradiotherapy
cards.summary: TAX 324: TPF induction improved overall survival versus PF (HR 0.70; median 71 vs 30 months; 3-year survival 62% vs 48%) before chemoradiotherapy
cards.people: 501 patients with stage III–IV squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck, no distant metastases, with tumours considered unresectable or who were candidates for organ preservation, randomly assigned to induction chemotherapy with docetaxel plus cisplatin and fluorouracil (TPF) or cisplatin and fluorouracil (PF), followed in both arms by chemoradiotherapy (weekly carboplatin with radiotherapy). The primary endpoint was overall survival; minimum follow-up 2 years.
cards.result: Significantly more patients survived in the TPF group (HR for death 0.70; P=0.006). Estimated overall survival at 3 years was 62% in the TPF group and 48% in the PF group — a 14-percentage-point absolute difference — and median overall survival was 71 versus 30 months. Locoregional control was better with TPF (P=0.04); distant metastases did not differ significantly (P=0.14). Neutropenia and febrile neutropenia were more frequent with TPF; chemotherapy was more often delayed for haematologic toxicity in the PF group.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is PF induction, not chemoradiotherapy alone — this trial cannot justify induction over direct chemoradiation. The survival medians (71 vs 30 months) are strikingly wide for the hazard ratio and reflect the organ-preservation-eligible mix; the hazard ratio is the transportable figure. Both arms received carboplatin chemoradiotherapy afterwards, not the cisplatin chemoradiation that later became standard.
cards.source: Posner MR et al. Cisplatin and fluorouracil alone or with docetaxel in head and neck cancer. N Engl J Med. 2007. PMID: 17960013. Registry ID: NCT00273546, from the record. cards.headline: TAX 323: TPF improved progression-free survival (11.0 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.72) and reduced the risk of death by 27% relative (median survival 18.8 vs 14.5 months) before radiotherapy
cards.summary: TAX 323: TPF improved progression-free survival (11.0 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.72) and reduced the risk of death by 27% relative (median survival 18.8 vs 14.5 months) before radiotherapy
cards.people: 358 patients aged 18–70 with locoregionally advanced, unresectable stage III–IV squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck and no distant metastases, randomly assigned to four cycles of TPF (docetaxel and cisplatin day 1; fluorouracil by continuous infusion days 1–5) or PF every 3 weeks. Patients without progression then received radiotherapy within 4–7 weeks. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival; median follow-up 32.5 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 11.0 months with TPF versus 8.2 months with PF (HR for progression or death 0.72; P=0.007). TPF reduced the risk of death by 27% relative (P=0.02), with median overall survival 18.8 versus 14.5 months. Grade 3–4 leukopenia and neutropenia were more common with TPF; thrombocytopenia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, and hearing loss were more common with PF. Deaths from toxic effects: 2.3% (TPF) versus 5.5% (PF).
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract states the mortality effect as a 27% relative reduction without printing an overall-survival hazard ratio — none is printed on this card. The control arm's worse performance than TAX 324's (median survival 14.5 vs 30 months on PF) reflects a strictly unresectable population and radiotherapy (not chemoradiotherapy) as follow-on treatment.

shelves.title: Induction chemotherapy before chemoradiotherapy in locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (gemcitabine–cisplatin; TPF)
shelves.question: In locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, does induction chemotherapy (gemcitabine–cisplatin or TPF) before concurrent chemoradiotherapy improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus chemoradiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Chemoradiotherapy · Cisplatin · Deoxycytidine · Female · Humans · Induction Chemotherapy · Leukopenia · Male · Middle Aged · Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma · Survival Analysis · Young Adult · Gemcitabine
shelves.balance: Two Chinese phase 3 trials, testing two different induction regimens before the same chemoradiotherapy backbone, both improved failure-free outcomes. Induction gemcitabine–cisplatin (Zhang 2019, n=480) raised 3-year recurrence-free survival from 76.5% to 85.3% (HR 0.51) and 3-year overall survival from 90.3% to 94.6% (HR 0.43). Induction TPF (Sun 2016, n=480) raised 3-year failure-free survival from 72% to 80% (HR 0.68). The cost is upfront toxicity: grade 3–4 acute adverse events in 75.7% versus 55.7% in the gemcitabine–cisplatin trial, with no excess of late toxicity. Two concordant trials with different regimens support the induction strategy itself in this disease — unusually, the opposite pattern to HNSCC induction (Shelf #1914). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival claim — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: Zhang 2019: induction gemcitabine–cisplatin improved 3-year recurrence-free survival (85.3% vs 76.5%; HR 0.51) and overall survival (94.6% vs 90.3%; HR 0.43)
cards.summary: Zhang 2019: induction gemcitabine–cisplatin improved 3-year recurrence-free survival (85.3% vs 76.5%; HR 0.51) and overall survival (94.6% vs 90.3%; HR 0.43)
cards.people: 480 patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma in a multicentre, parallel-group trial, randomly assigned 1:1 to gemcitabine (1 g/m² days 1 and 8) plus cisplatin (80 mg/m² day 1) every 3 weeks for three cycles followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (n=242), or chemoradiotherapy alone (n=238) — concurrent cisplatin 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks with intensity-modulated radiotherapy in both arms. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival; median follow-up 42.7 months.
cards.result: Three-year recurrence-free survival was 85.3% with induction chemotherapy versus 76.5% with standard therapy (stratified HR for recurrence or death 0.51, 95% CI 0.34–0.77; P=0.001) — an absolute difference of about 9 percentage points. Overall survival at 3 years was 94.6% versus 90.3% (stratified HR for death 0.43, 95% CI 0.24–0.77). 96.7% of patients completed three induction cycles. Grade 3–4 acute adverse events were more frequent with induction (75.7% vs 55.7%), including neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia, nausea, and vomiting; grade 3–4 late toxic effects did not differ (9.2% vs 11.4%).
cards.watchOut: The survival hazard ratio rests on few deaths at 3 years in a favourable-prognosis population (confidence interval 0.24–0.77) and comes from the primary report; a later analysis may move it. The trial was run in endemic-region centres with high nasopharyngeal-carcinoma volumes, in patients fit for three cycles of induction plus full-dose concurrent cisplatin.
cards.source: Zhang Y et al. Gemcitabine and Cisplatin Induction Chemotherapy in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 31150573. Registry ID: NCT01872962, from the record. cards.headline: Sun 2016: induction TPF improved 3-year failure-free survival (80% vs 72%; HR 0.68) before concurrent chemoradiotherapy
cards.summary: Sun 2016: induction TPF improved 3-year failure-free survival (80% vs 72%; HR 0.68) before concurrent chemoradiotherapy
cards.people: 480 patients with previously untreated stage III–IVB nasopharyngeal carcinoma (except T3–4N0), aged 18–59 without severe comorbidity, at ten institutions in China, randomly assigned 1:1 to induction chemotherapy — three cycles of docetaxel 60 mg/m², cisplatin 60 mg/m², and fluorouracil 600 mg/m²/day days 1–5 — plus concurrent chemoradiotherapy (n=241), or chemoradiotherapy alone (n=239), with concurrent cisplatin 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks and intensity-modulated radiotherapy in both arms. The primary endpoint was failure-free survival; median follow-up 45 months.
cards.result: Three-year failure-free survival was 80% (95% CI 75–85) with induction chemotherapy plus chemoradiotherapy versus 72% (66–78) with chemoradiotherapy alone (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.97; P=0.034) — an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points.
cards.watchOut: The fetched abstract's results section available to this card reports the primary endpoint and design; no overall-survival figure is printed on this card because none was verified from the record in this pass. The P value (0.034) is less commanding than the gemcitabine–cisplatin trial's, and the trial was open-label. Two positive trials with different regimens nonetheless triangulate the strategy.

shelves.title: Cetuximab plus radiotherapy in locally advanced HNSCC (Bonner trial)
shelves.question: In locally advanced HNSCC treated with definitive radiotherapy, does adding cetuximab improve locoregional control and overall survival versus radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Cetuximab · Combined Modality Therapy · Disease Progression · ErbB Receptors · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: A single multinational randomised trial (n=424) — never replicated head-to-head — found that adding weekly cetuximab to high-dose radiotherapy improved locoregional control (median 24.4 vs 14.9 months; HR 0.68) and overall survival (median 49.0 vs 29.3 months; HR 0.74), and the mature 5-year analysis confirmed the survival benefit (HR 0.73; 5-year survival 45.6% vs 36.4%). The stamp follows the mature data, per house rule. Toxicity beyond acneiform rash and infusion reactions was not increased — the fact that later made cetuximab the default partner for cisplatin-ineligible patients, and the result that made its failure as a cisplatin substitute (Shelf #1912) so surprising. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one open-label trial that carried a standard of care for two decades. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: Bonner 2006: cetuximab plus radiotherapy improved locoregional control (24.4 vs 14.9 months; HR 0.68) and overall survival (49.0 vs 29.3 months; HR 0.74) versus radiotherapy alone
cards.summary: Bonner 2006: cetuximab plus radiotherapy improved locoregional control (24.4 vs 14.9 months; HR 0.68) and overall survival (49.0 vs 29.3 months; HR 0.74) versus radiotherapy alone
cards.people: 424 patients with locoregionally advanced squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck, randomly assigned to high-dose radiotherapy alone (n=213) or the same radiotherapy plus weekly cetuximab (n=211) — an initial dose of 400 mg/m² followed by 250 mg/m² weekly for the duration of radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was duration of locoregional control; median follow-up 54.0 months.
cards.result: Median duration of locoregional control was 24.4 months with cetuximab plus radiotherapy versus 14.9 months with radiotherapy alone (HR for locoregional progression or death 0.68; P=0.005). Median overall survival was 49.0 versus 29.3 months (HR for death 0.74; P=0.03). Progression-free survival also favoured the combination (HR 0.70; P=0.006). With the exception of acneiform rash and infusion reactions, the incidence of grade 3 or greater toxic effects — including mucositis — did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial, and the radiotherapy-alone control reflects an era before concurrent cisplatin became the default partner: the trial proves cetuximab beats nothing added to radiation, not that it rivals cisplatin — the comparison RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE later settled against cetuximab (Shelf #1912). HPV status was not a design factor.
cards.source: Bonner JA et al. Radiotherapy plus cetuximab for squamous-cell carcinoma of the head and neck. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16467544. Registry ID: NCT00004227, from the record. cards.summary: Bonner 5-year update: the survival benefit persisted (HR 0.73; 5-year survival 45.6% vs 36.4%) — the mature data on which this shelf's stamp rests
cards.type: Mature follow-up report of the same randomized trial
cards.people: The same 424 patients (211 cetuximab plus radiotherapy; 213 radiotherapy alone) with locoregionally advanced squamous-cell carcinoma of the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx, followed for survival to 5 years in the trial's prespecified long-term analysis.
cards.result: Updated median overall survival was 49.0 months (95% CI 32.8–69.5) with cetuximab plus radiotherapy versus 29.3 months (20.6–41.4) with radiotherapy alone (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56–0.95; P=0.018). Five-year overall survival was 45.6% versus 36.4% — an absolute difference of about 9 percentage points. Among cetuximab-treated patients, those with grade ≥2 acneiform rash survived longer than those with little or no rash (HR 0.49), an association the authors report as hypothesis-generating.
cards.watchOut: This is the same single trial at longer follow-up, not independent replication — the shelf remains OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. The rash-survival association is a within-arm observational comparison (patients must survive and stay on treatment to develop rash), and must not be read as evidence that inducing rash helps.
cards.source: Bonner JA et al. shelves.title: PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (JUPITER-02; RATIONALE-309; CAPTAIN-1st)
shelves.question: In recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, does adding a PD-1 inhibitor to gemcitabine–cisplatin improve progression-free and overall survival versus chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents · Cisplatin · Double-Blind Method · Gemcitabine · Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma · Nasopharyngeal Neoplasms · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · United States · Internationality
shelves.balance: Three double-blind phase 3 trials in endemic-region populations added three different PD-1 inhibitors to the same gemcitabine–cisplatin backbone, and all three improved progression-free survival with near-identical hazard ratios: toripalimab (JUPITER-02) PFS HR 0.52 (median 21.4 vs 8.2 months), tislelizumab (RATIONALE-309) HR 0.52, and camrelizumab (CAPTAIN-1st) HR 0.54 (median 9.7 vs 6.9 months). Overall survival is mature only for toripalimab: HR 0.63 at a median 36 months of follow-up (median not reached vs 33.7 months). The class claim — PD-1 blockade added to first-line chemotherapy prolongs progression-free survival in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma — rests on three concordant blinded trials; the survival claim currently rests on one. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: JUPITER-02: toripalimab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin improved progression-free survival (21.4 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.52) and overall survival (HR 0.63) in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma
cards.summary: JUPITER-02: toripalimab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin improved progression-free survival (21.4 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.52) and overall survival (HR 0.63) in recurrent/metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma
cards.people: 289 patients with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no prior systemic chemotherapy in the recurrent/metastatic setting, at 35 centres in NPC-endemic regions (mainland China, Taiwan, Singapore), randomly assigned 1:1 to toripalimab 240 mg (n=146) or placebo (n=143) combined with gemcitabine–cisplatin for up to six cycles, then maintenance toripalimab or placebo for up to 2 years. Progression-free survival was assessed by blinded independent central review; median survival follow-up 36.0 months.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly longer with toripalimab (median 21.4 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.37–0.73). Overall survival was significantly improved (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.45–0.89; two-sided P=0.008), with median overall survival not reached in the toripalimab group versus 33.7 months on placebo; the survival effect was consistent in PD-L1-high and PD-L1-low subgroups. Overall and grade ≥3 adverse-event incidence was similar between groups, but adverse events leading to discontinuation (11.6% vs 4.9%), immune-related adverse events (54.1% vs 21.7%), and grade ≥3 immune-related events (9.6% vs 1.4%) were more frequent with toripalimab.
cards.watchOut: This JAMA report is the trial's final analysis — the carded survival figures are the mature data. The population is exclusively from NPC-endemic regions and relatively young (median age 46); transportability to non-endemic recurrent/metastatic disease is by extrapolation. Maintenance toripalimab for up to 2 years is part of the tested strategy, not an optional extra.
cards.source: Mai HQ et al. Toripalimab Plus Chemotherapy for Recurrent or Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: The JUPITER-02 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 38015220. Registry ID: NCT03581786, from the record. cards.headline: RATIONALE-309: tislelizumab plus chemotherapy improved progression-free survival (HR 0.52), with overall survival showing a favourable trend at the interim report
cards.summary: RATIONALE-309: tislelizumab plus chemotherapy improved progression-free survival (HR 0.52), with overall survival showing a favourable trend at the interim report
cards.people: 263 treatment-naive patients with recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, randomized to tislelizumab or placebo every 3 weeks plus gemcitabine–cisplatin chemotherapy for 4–6 cycles. The carded report is the trial's interim analysis; progression-free survival was the primary endpoint.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly longer with tislelizumab–chemotherapy than placebo–chemotherapy (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.38–0.73; P<0.0001), regardless of PD-L1 expression. Progression-free survival after next-line therapy and overall survival showed favourable trends for tislelizumab that had not reached significance at this analysis. The safety profile was similar between arms.
cards.watchOut: The fetched record reports no median progression-free survival and no survival hazard ratio — none is printed on this card. An interim primary-endpoint report: the PFS estimate may shift modestly at final analysis. Gene-expression signatures reported in the paper (an activated dendritic-cell signature predicting benefit) are exploratory and not part of this shelf's claim.

cards.headline: CAPTAIN-1st: camrelizumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin improved progression-free survival (9.7 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.54) at interim analysis
cards.summary: CAPTAIN-1st: camrelizumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin improved progression-free survival (9.7 vs 6.9 months; HR 0.54) at interim analysis
cards.people: 263 patients aged 18–75 with previously untreated recurrent or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma at 28 hospitals in China, randomly assigned 1:1 to camrelizumab 200 mg (n=134) or matching placebo (n=129) plus gemcitabine and cisplatin every 3 weeks for 4–6 cycles, followed by maintenance camrelizumab or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by independent review committee, assessed at a prespecified interim analysis.
cards.result: Independent-review progression-free survival was significantly longer with camrelizumab (median 9.7 months, 95% CI 8.3–11.4) than with placebo (6.9 months, 5.9–7.3) (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.76; one-sided P=0.0002) — an absolute median gain of 2.8 months, against JUPITER-02's larger 13.2-month median gain for a different antibody and maintenance design.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis with a one-sided significance threshold (P=0.0086 was the prespecified boundary; the result cleared it). Overall survival was immature at this report and is not claimed on this card. The wide spread of median PFS gains across the three trials (2.8 to 13.2 months) against near-identical hazard ratios shows how strongly medians depend on the control arm's course — the hazard ratios are the comparable figures.

cards.result: Progression-free survival HR 0.52 (toripalimab; median 21.4 vs 8.2 months), 0.52 (tislelizumab), and 0.54 (camrelizumab; median 9.7 vs 6.9 months). shelves.title: Perioperative pembrolizumab in resectable locally advanced HNSCC (KEYNOTE-689)
shelves.question: In resectable locally advanced HNSCC, does neoadjuvant plus adjuvant pembrolizumab added to surgery and postoperative radiotherapy (± cisplatin) improve event-free survival versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological · B7-H1 Antigen · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Intention to Treat Analysis · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Progression-Free Survival · Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A single phase 3 trial (n=714) found that adding two neoadjuvant cycles and fifteen adjuvant cycles of pembrolizumab to standard care — surgery then postoperative radiotherapy with or without cisplatin — significantly improved event-free survival in every prespecified population: hazard ratio 0.66 in PD-L1 CPS ≥10, 0.70 in CPS ≥1, and 0.73 in the total population, with 36-month event-free survival of 57.6% versus 46.4% overall. Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab did not compromise surgery (completion ~88% in both arms), and grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were similar (44.6% vs 42.9%). Overall survival was immature at this first interim analysis, so this shelf claims an event-free-survival benefit only — no survival claim, hence not Tier C. Single recent trial; the stamp is LIKELY on the strength of a large, consistently positive phase 3 result, pending survival data and any replication. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: KEYNOTE-689: perioperative pembrolizumab improved event-free survival (total population HR 0.73; 36-month EFS 57.6% vs 46.4%) without compromising surgery
cards.summary: KEYNOTE-689: perioperative pembrolizumab improved event-free survival (total population HR 0.73; 36-month EFS 57.6% vs 46.4%) without compromising surgery
cards.people: 714 participants with resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma, randomly assigned 1:1 to neoadjuvant pembrolizumab (2 cycles) plus standard care plus adjuvant pembrolizumab (15 cycles) (n=363) or standard care alone (n=351) — surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy with or without concomitant cisplatin. The primary endpoint was event-free survival, assessed sequentially in the PD-L1 CPS ≥10 population (n=465), CPS ≥1 population (n=682), and all participants; median follow-up at the first interim analysis was 38.3 months.
cards.result: Event-free survival at 36 months favoured pembrolizumab in all three populations: CPS ≥10, 59.8% versus 45.9% (HR for progression, recurrence, or death 0.66, 95% CI 0.49–0.88; P=0.004); CPS ≥1, 58.2% versus 44.9% (HR 0.70, 0.55–0.89; P=0.003); total population, 57.6% versus 46.4% (HR 0.73, 0.58–0.92; P=0.008) — an absolute 36-month difference of about 11 percentage points overall. Surgery was completed in approximately 88% of participants in each group. Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 44.6% versus 42.9%, including death in 1.1% versus 0.3%; grade ≥3 potentially immune-mediated events occurred in 10.0% of the pembrolizumab group.
cards.watchOut: First interim analysis: overall survival was not reported and remains the open question — an event-free-survival gain of this size in a curative-intent population is expected to matter, but this shelf does not claim it. Open-label design. The strategy commits patients to 17 cycles of pembrolizumab around surgery; the design cannot separate the neoadjuvant contribution from the adjuvant contribution (contrast Shelf #1900, which isolated timing in melanoma).
cards.source: Uppaluri R et al. Neoadjuvant and Adjuvant Pembrolizumab in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 40532178. Registry ID: NCT03765918, from the record. shelves.title: Larynx preservation in advanced laryngeal cancer (VA Laryngeal Cancer trial; RTOG 91-11)
shelves.question: In advanced laryngeal squamous-cell carcinoma, do non-surgical strategies (induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy) preserve the larynx without compromising overall survival, compared with laryngectomy-based or radiotherapy-only treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell · Chemoradiotherapy · Cisplatin · Deglutition · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Fluorouracil · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Laryngeal Neoplasms · Laryngectomy · Larynx · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Organ Sparing Treatments · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Remission Induction · Salvage Therapy · Speech · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two landmark randomised programmes built larynx preservation. The VA Laryngeal Cancer trial (n=332) showed induction chemotherapy followed by definitive radiotherapy preserved the larynx in 64% of patients with 2-year survival identical to laryngectomy plus postoperative radiotherapy (68% in both groups). RTOG 91-11 (n=520, 10-year follow-up) then separated the non-surgical strategies: both induction PF followed by radiotherapy and concomitant cisplatin-radiotherapy improved laryngectomy-free survival versus radiotherapy alone (HR 0.75 and 0.78), and concomitant chemoradiation gave the best larynx preservation (HR 0.58 versus the induction arm). Overall survival did not differ significantly between any of RTOG 91-11's arms — but deaths not attributed to larynx cancer or treatment were higher with concomitant chemotherapy (30.8% vs 20.8% and 16.9%), and the concomitant-versus-induction survival hazard ratio was 1.25 (P=0.08). The balance: organ preservation is real and survival-equivalent on the trials' own terms, bought with more late non-cancer deaths in the most intensive arm. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (survival-equivalence balance — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: VA Laryngeal Cancer trial (1991): induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy preserved the larynx in 64% with 2-year survival identical to laryngectomy (68% in both groups)
cards.summary: VA Laryngeal Cancer trial (1991): induction chemotherapy plus radiotherapy preserved the larynx in 64% with 2-year survival identical to laryngectomy (68% in both groups)
cards.people: 332 patients with previously untreated advanced (stage III–IV) laryngeal squamous-cell carcinoma, randomly assigned to three cycles of induction cisplatin and fluorouracil followed by definitive radiotherapy (with salvage laryngectomy for non-response or local recurrence) or to conventional total laryngectomy plus postoperative radiotherapy. Response was assessed after two chemotherapy cycles; median follow-up 33 months.
cards.result: Estimated 2-year survival was 68% (95% CI 60–76) in both treatment groups (P=0.98). After two cycles, clinical tumour response was complete in 31% and partial in 54% of the chemotherapy group. The larynx was preserved in 64% of patients overall and in 64% of those alive and free of disease; 59 patients (36%) in the chemotherapy group ultimately required total laryngectomy. Recurrence patterns differed: more local recurrences (P=0.0005) and fewer distant metastases (P=0.016) in the chemotherapy group.
cards.watchOut: A 1991 trial: radiotherapy technique, imaging, and salvage pathways are of their era, and 2-year survival is early follow-up for a preservation claim. The trial compared strategies at the programme level — the chemotherapy arm includes responders selected by two cycles of treatment — so it validates the strategy, not chemotherapy's isolated contribution. Pre-registration era; no registry ID exists.
cards.source: Department of Veterans Affairs Laryngeal Cancer Study Group. Induction chemotherapy plus radiation compared with surgery plus radiation in patients with advanced laryngeal cancer. N Engl J Med. 1991. PMID: 2034244. Registry ID: none (pre-registration era). cards.summary: RTOG 91-11 (long-term): concomitant chemoradiation gave the best larynx preservation (HR 0.58 vs induction); survival did not differ between arms, but non-cancer deaths were highest with concomitant therapy (30.8%)
cards.people: 520 patients with stage III–IV glottic or supraglottic squamous-cell carcinoma, randomly assigned to induction cisplatin/fluorouracil followed by radiotherapy (the VA strategy, control arm), concomitant cisplatin with radiotherapy, or radiotherapy alone. The primary endpoint was laryngectomy-free survival; median follow-up for surviving patients 10.8 years.
cards.result: Both chemotherapy strategies improved laryngectomy-free survival versus radiotherapy alone (induction HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59–0.95; concomitant HR 0.78; P=0.02 and 0.03). Larynx preservation was significantly better with concomitant cisplatin-radiotherapy than with induction followed by radiotherapy (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37–0.89; P=0.005) or radiotherapy alone (P<0.001), while induction was not better than radiotherapy alone for larynx preservation (HR 1.26; P=0.35). Overall survival did not differ significantly between arms, though a worse outcome with concomitant relative to induction therapy was possible (HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.98–1.61; P=0.08). Deaths not attributed to larynx cancer or treatment were higher with concomitant chemotherapy (30.8%) than with induction (20.8%) or radiotherapy alone (16.9%). No difference in late effects was detected.
cards.watchOut: The topic file's figure of ~82% 10-year larynx preservation is not in this record's abstract and is not carded. The trial compares three non-surgical strategies — the surgery comparison lives on the VA card. The excess non-cancer mortality with concomitant therapy is the finding that keeps this shelf honest: preservation's best arm carries a late systemic cost signal.

shelves.title: Temozolomide with radiotherapy in newly diagnosed glioblastoma (Stupp regimen; EORTC-NCIC 26981)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide to radiotherapy improve overall survival versus radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Alkylating · Brain Neoplasms · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Dacarbazine · Disease Progression · Female · Glioblastoma · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Radiotherapy, Computer-Assisted · Survival Analysis · Temozolomide
shelves.balance: One randomised trial (n=573) has defined glioblastoma therapy for two decades: radiotherapy plus daily temozolomide during radiation and six adjuvant cycles improved median overall survival from 12.1 to 14.6 months (HR 0.63) and 2-year survival from 10.4% to 26.5%. The final 5-year analysis confirmed durability — 5-year survival 9.8% versus 1.9% (HR 0.6), with MGMT promoter methylation the strongest predictor of benefit. Never replicated because it never needed to be: the control arm became unethical once reported. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: Stupp 2005: adding temozolomide to radiotherapy improved median survival (14.6 vs 12.1 months; HR 0.63) and 2-year survival (26.5% vs 10.4%) in newly diagnosed glioblastoma
cards.summary: Stupp 2005: adding temozolomide to radiotherapy improved median survival (14.6 vs 12.1 months; HR 0.63) and 2-year survival (26.5% vs 10.4%) in newly diagnosed glioblastoma
cards.people: 573 patients with newly diagnosed, histologically confirmed glioblastoma at 85 centres (84% after debulking surgery), randomly assigned to radiotherapy alone (60 Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks) or radiotherapy plus continuous daily temozolomide (75 mg/m² during radiotherapy) followed by six cycles of adjuvant temozolomide. The primary endpoint was overall survival; median follow-up 28 months.
cards.result: Median survival was 14.6 months with radiotherapy plus temozolomide versus 12.1 months with radiotherapy alone (unadjusted HR for death 0.63, 95% CI 0.52–0.75; P<0.001) — an absolute median gain of 2.5 months. The 2-year survival rate was 26.5% versus 10.4%, an absolute difference of about 16 percentage points. Concomitant radiotherapy plus temozolomide caused grade 3–4 haematologic toxic effects in 7% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial — but one whose effect size and consistency ended equipoise for the control arm. The median gain (2.5 months) understates the benefit for the minority who become long-term survivors, which the 5-year analysis (next card) quantifies. MGMT-unmethylated patients benefit less, a gradient characterised in the follow-up analysis rather than this primary report.
cards.source: Stupp R et al. Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma. N Engl J Med. 2005. PMID: 15758009. Registry ID: NCT00006353 (named in the trial's 5-year analysis record). cards.people: The same 573 patients, followed for more than 5 years (median), with MGMT promoter methylation determined retrospectively in tumour tissue from 206 patients. The primary endpoint was overall survival, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Overall survival with temozolomide plus radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone was 27.2% versus 10.9% at 2 years, 16.0% versus 4.4% at 3 years, 12.1% versus 3.0% at 4 years, and 9.8% (95% CI 6.4–14.0) versus 1.9% (0.6–4.4) at 5 years (HR 0.6, 95% CI 0.5–0.7; P<0.0001) — about five times the proportion alive at 5 years, an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points.
