shelves.title: Short-course radiotherapy plus temozolomide in elderly glioblastoma (NCIC CE.3)
shelves.question: In patients aged 65 or older with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding temozolomide to short-course radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 fractions) improve overall survival versus short-course radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Central Nervous System Neoplasms · Chemoradiotherapy · Dacarbazine · Disease Progression · Female · Glioblastoma · Humans · Male · Quality of Life · Radiotherapy · Survival Analysis · Temozolomide
shelves.balance: One randomised trial (n=562, median age 73) answered the elderly version of the Stupp question against the short-course radiation schedule older patients actually receive: adding concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide improved median overall survival from 7.6 to 9.3 months (HR 0.67) and progression-free survival from 3.9 to 5.3 months (HR 0.50), with similar quality of life. The benefit was largest in MGMT-methylated tumours (13.5 vs 7.7 months; HR 0.53) and smaller and formally non-significant in unmethylated tumours (10.0 vs 7.9 months; HR 0.75, P=0.055; interaction P=0.08). The elderly RT-schedule trials (Nordic, NOA-08) frame the population but answer different questions and are fenced. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: NCIC CE.3: in patients ≥65, adding temozolomide to short-course radiotherapy improved survival (9.3 vs 7.6 months; HR 0.67) — most in MGMT-methylated tumours (HR 0.53)
cards.summary: NCIC CE.3: in patients ≥65, adding temozolomide to short-course radiotherapy improved survival (9.3 vs 7.6 months; HR 0.67) — most in MGMT-methylated tumours (HR 0.53)
cards.people: 562 patients aged 65 or older (median 73, range 65–90) with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, randomly assigned 1:1 to short-course radiotherapy alone (40 Gy in 15 fractions) or the same radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide. MGMT status was determined in 354 patients (165 methylated, 189 unmethylated). The primary endpoint was overall survival.
cards.result: Median overall survival was longer with radiotherapy plus temozolomide (9.3 vs 7.6 months; HR for death 0.67, 95% CI 0.56–0.80; P<0.001), as was median progression-free survival (5.3 vs 3.9 months; HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.41–0.60). In MGMT-methylated tumours, median survival was 13.5 versus 7.7 months (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.38–0.73; P<0.001). In unmethylated tumours it was 10.0 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.56–1.01; P=0.055; P for interaction 0.08). Quality of life was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is short-course radiotherapy, the age-appropriate standard — not the 60 Gy Stupp schedule of Shelf #1920, so cross-shelf median comparisons mislead. The unmethylated subgroup result is formally non-significant with an interaction P of 0.08: the shelf records a gradient, not a rule to withhold treatment by MGMT status.

shelves.title: Tumour Treating Fields plus maintenance temozolomide in newly diagnosed glioblastoma (EF-14)
shelves.question: After chemoradiotherapy for newly diagnosed glioblastoma, does adding Tumour Treating Fields to maintenance temozolomide improve progression-free and overall survival versus temozolomide alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Alkylating · Chemoradiotherapy · Dacarbazine · Disease-Free Survival · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glioblastoma · Humans · Maintenance Chemotherapy · Male · Middle Aged · Mitosis · Survival Analysis · Temozolomide
shelves.balance: One open-label randomised trial (n=695) is the only survival advance in glioblastoma since temozolomide: adding Tumour Treating Fields — low-intensity alternating electric fields delivered at least 18 hours a day through scalp arrays — to maintenance temozolomide improved median progression-free survival from 4.0 to 6.7 months (HR 0.63) and median overall survival from 16.0 to 20.9 months (HR 0.63). Systemic adverse events were similar (48% vs 44%); the device's signature toxicity is mild-to-moderate skin injury under the arrays (52%). Two structural caveats ride the shelf: randomisation occurred after patients had completed chemoradiotherapy without progression, so survival is counted from a post-treatment landmark, not from diagnosis; and the trial is unblinded with no sham device. The recurrent-disease trial (EF-11) was not positive on survival and is fenced. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label device trial; hard-endpoint result). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: EF-14 (final analysis): TTFields plus temozolomide improved progression-free survival (6.7 vs 4.0 months; HR 0.63) and overall survival (20.9 vs 16.0 months; HR 0.63) after chemoradiotherapy
cards.summary: EF-14 (final analysis): TTFields plus temozolomide improved progression-free survival (6.7 vs 4.0 months; HR 0.63) and overall survival (20.9 vs 16.0 months; HR 0.63) after chemoradiotherapy
cards.people: 695 patients with glioblastoma whose tumour had been resected or biopsied and who had completed concomitant radiochemotherapy (median time from diagnosis to randomisation 3.8 months), enrolled at 83 centres and randomly assigned 2:1 to Tumour Treating Fields (200 kHz, at least 18 hours per day via four scalp transducer arrays) plus maintenance temozolomide (n=466) or temozolomide alone (n=229), for 6–12 cycles. This report is the trial's final analysis; the primary endpoint was progression-free survival and the key secondary endpoint overall survival, measured from randomisation.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival from randomisation was 6.7 months in the TTFields–temozolomide group versus 4.0 months with temozolomide alone (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.52–0.76; P<0.001). Median overall survival was 20.9 versus 16.0 months (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.53–0.76; P<0.001) — an absolute median gain of 4.9 months from the post-chemoradiation landmark. Systemic adverse-event frequency was 48% versus 44%. Mild-to-moderate skin toxicity beneath the transducer arrays occurred in 52% of TTFields patients and in no controls.
cards.watchOut: Randomisation after completed chemoradiotherapy means both arms are drawn from patients who reached that landmark without progression — the 20.9-month median cannot be compared with diagnosis-anchored medians such as the Stupp trial's 14.6 months (Shelf #1920). Open-label with no sham device, and benefit in such device trials can track adherence (patients are asked to wear the device at least 18 hours a day); the record's abstract does not report an adherence-stratified analysis — none is printed here.

shelves.title: Vorasidenib in IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma (INDIGO)
shelves.question: In residual or recurrent IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma treated with surgery only, does vorasidenib delay progression and time to next intervention versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Glioma · Isocitrate Dehydrogenase · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Pyridines · Antineoplastic Agents · Enzyme Inhibitors · Diamines
shelves.balance: One double-blind phase 3 trial (n=331) in patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma whose only prior treatment was surgery: the oral mutant-IDH inhibitor vorasidenib more than doubled median progression-free survival (27.7 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.39) and markedly delayed the time to next anticancer intervention (HR 0.26) — the endpoint that matters in a young population for whom delaying radiation and chemotherapy is the therapeutic goal. Grade ≥3 adverse events were more frequent on vorasidenib (22.8% vs 13.5%), driven by liver-enzyme elevation (grade ≥3 ALT increase 9.6% vs 0%). Follow-up was short (median 14.2 months), overall survival is immature, and placebo patients could cross over at progression — so this shelf claims delayed progression and deferred intervention, not longer life. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: INDIGO: vorasidenib improved progression-free survival (27.7 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.39) and time to next intervention (HR 0.26) in grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma
cards.summary: INDIGO: vorasidenib improved progression-free survival (27.7 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.39) and time to next intervention (HR 0.26) in grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma
cards.people: 331 patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH1- or IDH2-mutant glioma whose only previous treatment was surgery, randomly assigned to oral vorasidenib 40 mg once daily (n=168) or matched placebo (n=163) in 28-day cycles. The primary endpoint was imaging-based progression-free survival by blinded independent review; the key secondary endpoint was time to next anticancer intervention. Crossover to vorasidenib was permitted at confirmed progression; median follow-up 14.2 months, with 68.3% of patients still on assigned treatment at the analysis.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly improved with vorasidenib (median 27.7 vs 11.1 months; HR for progression or death 0.39, 95% CI 0.27–0.56; P<0.001), as was time to next intervention (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.15–0.43; P<0.001). Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 22.8% on vorasidenib versus 13.5% on placebo; an increased alanine aminotransferase level of grade 3 or higher occurred in 9.6% versus 0%.
cards.watchOut: A progression endpoint in a slow-growing tumour with a median follow-up (14.2 months) shorter than the treatment arm's median progression-free survival — the 27.7-month median is an early estimate. Overall survival is unreported and will be confounded by permitted crossover; the trial's rationale is deferring radiation and alkylating chemotherapy (and their late toxicities) in young patients, a benefit the time-to-next-intervention result captures directly. Hepatic monitoring is part of the treatment's real cost.

shelves.title: Pazopanib in pretreated non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma (PALETTE)
shelves.question: In advanced non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma after chemotherapy, does pazopanib improve progression-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents · Cross-Over Studies · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Indazoles · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines · Sarcoma · Soft Tissue Neoplasms · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=369) in metastatic non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma progressing after standard chemotherapy: pazopanib tripled median progression-free survival (4.6 vs 1.6 months; HR 0.31) without improving overall survival (12.5 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.86, P=0.25) — and with no crossover permitted, that survival null is a clean one. The price is a heavy low-grade toxicity load: fatigue 65%, diarrhoea 58%, nausea 54%, weight loss 48%, and hypertension 41% on pazopanib. This shelf claims a progression benefit only, with the survival result printed beside it so the two are never separated. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: PALETTE: pazopanib improved progression-free survival (4.6 vs 1.6 months; HR 0.31) but not overall survival (12.5 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.86, P=0.25) in pretreated non-adipocytic sarcoma
cards.summary: PALETTE: pazopanib improved progression-free survival (4.6 vs 1.6 months; HR 0.31) but not overall survival (12.5 vs 10.7 months; HR 0.86, P=0.25) in pretreated non-adipocytic sarcoma
cards.people: 369 patients with angiogenesis-inhibitor-naive metastatic non-adipocytic soft-tissue sarcoma progressing despite previous standard chemotherapy, at 72 institutions in 13 countries, randomly assigned 2:1 to pazopanib 800 mg once daily (n=246) or placebo (n=123), with patients, treating investigators, outcome assessors, and analysts all masked and no subsequent crossover. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival; efficacy analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 4.6 months (95% CI 3.7–4.8) on pazopanib versus 1.6 months (0.9–1.8) on placebo (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.24–0.40; P<0.0001) — an absolute median gain of 3.0 months. Overall survival was 12.5 months (10.6–14.8) versus 10.7 months (8.7–12.8) (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.67–1.11; P=0.25) — not significantly different. The most common adverse events on pazopanib were fatigue (65%), diarrhoea (58%), nausea (54%), weight loss (48%), and hypertension (41%); median relative dose intensity was 96%.
cards.watchOut: Adipocytic sarcoma (liposarcoma) was excluded — this shelf says nothing about it, and the exclusion is in the question itself. A progression-free gain of 3 months against this toxicity profile, with no survival benefit and no crossover to excuse the null, is a judgement call for the individual patient; the shelf reports both halves without resolving it.
cards.source: van der Graaf WT et al. Pazopanib for metastatic soft-tissue sarcoma (PALETTE): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22595799. shelves.title: Eribulin versus dacarbazine in pretreated liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma
shelves.question: In advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after at least two prior regimens, does eribulin improve overall survival versus dacarbazine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents · Antineoplastic Agents, Alkylating · Dacarbazine · Female · Furans · Humans · Ketones · Leiomyosarcoma · Liposarcoma · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Grading · Soft Tissue Neoplasms · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Polyether Polyketides
shelves.balance: One open-label phase 3 trial (n=452) against an active comparator found eribulin improved overall survival versus dacarbazine (median 13.5 vs 11.5 months; HR 0.77, P=0.0169) in patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after at least two prior regimens. The gain is modest — 2.0 months of median survival — and the harm side is not trivial: grade 3 or worse adverse events in 67% versus 56%, and deaths in 4% versus 1% (one death judged treatment-related, on eribulin). The trial pooled two histologies stratified at randomisation; the primary record reports the pooled result, and claims that the benefit is concentrated in liposarcoma rest on subgroup analyses not carded here. A single trial with a modest effect and a real toxicity increment carries POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: Schöffski 2016: eribulin improved overall survival versus dacarbazine (13.5 vs 11.5 months; HR 0.77) — with more grade ≥3 toxicity (67% vs 56%) and more deaths (4% vs 1%)
cards.summary: Schöffski 2016: eribulin improved overall survival versus dacarbazine (13.5 vs 11.5 months; HR 0.77) — with more grade ≥3 toxicity (67% vs 56%) and more deaths (4% vs 1%)
cards.people: 452 patients aged 18 or older with intermediate- or high-grade advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma who had received at least two previous systemic regimens for advanced disease (including an anthracycline), at 110 sites in 22 countries, randomly assigned 1:1 to eribulin mesilate 1.4 mg/m² on days 1 and 8 (n=228) or dacarbazine (n=224) every 21 days until progression. Randomisation was stratified by disease type, geographical region, and number of previous regimens. The primary endpoint was overall survival in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly improved with eribulin (median 13.5 months, 95% CI 10.9–15.6) versus dacarbazine (11.5 months, 9.6–13.0) (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.95; P=0.0169) — an absolute median gain of 2.0 months. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 99% versus 97% of treated patients; grade 3 or higher adverse events were more common with eribulin (67% vs 56%), as were deaths (4% vs 1%); one death, in the eribulin group, was considered treatment-related by the investigators.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial, and dacarbazine dosing varied by centre (850–1200 mg/m²), so the comparator was not perfectly uniform. The abstract reports the pooled liposarcoma-plus-leiomyosarcoma population only: the drafting process flagged that the benefit may be concentrated in the liposarcoma stratum, but no histology-specific figure was verified from this record and none is carded — a reader needing the subgroup answer must go to the stratified analyses. The mortality figures on this card cut both ways and both are printed: fewer cancer deaths (the HR) alongside more on-treatment deaths (4% vs 1%).
cards.source: Schöffski P et al. Eribulin versus dacarbazine in previously treated patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma: a randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 26874885. Registry ID: NCT01327885, from the record. shelves.title: Three years versus one year of adjuvant imatinib in high-risk GIST (SSGXVIII/AIO)
shelves.question: In resected high-risk gastrointestinal stromal tumour, does 3 years of adjuvant imatinib improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus 1 year?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents · Benzamides · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms · Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Piperazines · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-kit · Pyrimidines · Receptor, Platelet-Derived Growth Factor alpha · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One open-label randomised trial (n=400) settled GIST adjuvant duration: 36 months of imatinib 400 mg/day beat 12 months on recurrence-free survival (HR 0.46; 5-year 65.6% vs 47.9%) and overall survival (HR 0.45; 5-year 92.0% vs 81.7%) in patients at high risk of recurrence after resection. The cost of the longer course is attrition: 25.8% of the 36-month group discontinued imatinib for reasons other than recurrence, versus 12.6% of the 12-month group. ACOSOG Z9001 (1 year versus placebo) answers the prior question — whether any adjuvant imatinib helps — and is fenced, not merged. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (open-label; duration-defining survival benefit). PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C (overall-survival benefit — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: SSGXVIII/AIO: 3 years of adjuvant imatinib improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.46; 5-year 65.6% vs 47.9%) and overall survival (HR 0.45; 5-year 92.0% vs 81.7%) versus 1 year
cards.summary: SSGXVIII/AIO: 3 years of adjuvant imatinib improved recurrence-free survival (HR 0.46; 5-year 65.6% vs 47.9%) and overall survival (HR 0.45; 5-year 92.0% vs 81.7%) versus 1 year
cards.people: 400 patients with KIT-positive gastrointestinal stromal tumour removed at surgery and a high estimated risk of recurrence (modified NIH consensus criteria), entered at 24 hospitals in Finland, Germany, Norway, and Sweden between 2004 and 2008, randomly assigned to imatinib 400 mg/day orally for 12 months (n=200) or 36 months (n=200), started within 12 weeks of surgery. Diagnosis was centrally confirmed in 382 of 397 intention-to-treat patients; KIT or PDGFRA mutation was detected in 91% of tested tumours. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival; median follow-up 54 months.
cards.result: Patients assigned 36 months of imatinib had longer recurrence-free survival (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.32–0.65; P<0.001; 5-year recurrence-free survival 65.6% vs 47.9% — an absolute difference of about 18 percentage points) and longer overall survival (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.22–0.89; P=0.02; 5-year survival 92.0% vs 81.7% — about 10 percentage points). Imatinib was generally well tolerated, but discontinuation for a reason other than recurrence was twice as common with the longer course (25.8% vs 12.6%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial — but a duration question can only be answered by a duration trial, and this one's survival separation is large. The survival hazard ratio rests on relatively few deaths (confidence interval 0.22–0.89). Benefit beyond 3 years (still longer courses) is a different question this trial does not answer; nor does it address adjuvant imatinib in intermediate-risk disease or in PDGFRA-D842V-mutant tumours, which are imatinib-resistant.
cards.source: Joensuu H et al. One vs three years of adjuvant imatinib for operable gastrointestinal stromal tumor: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22453568. Registry ID: NCT00116935, from the record. shelves.title: Ripretinib in fourth-line advanced GIST (INVICTUS)
shelves.question: In advanced GIST progressing on or after imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib, does ripretinib improve progression-free survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms · Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds · Prognosis · Proto-Oncogene Mas · Pyridines · Survival Rate · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (n=129) in patients whose GIST had progressed on at least three prior kinase inhibitors: ripretinib, a switch-control KIT/PDGFRA inhibitor, improved median progression-free survival from 1.0 to 6.3 months (HR 0.15) — one of the largest progression effects recorded in a refractory solid tumour. Placebo patients were permitted to cross over to ripretinib at progression, which was ethically necessary and makes any survival comparison uninterpretable by design; this record's carded content claims the progression benefit only. The population is heavily pretreated with no remaining standard options, which is the context for the effect size. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: INVICTUS: ripretinib improved progression-free survival versus placebo in fourth-line GIST (6.3 vs 1.0 months; HR 0.15)
cards.summary: INVICTUS: ripretinib improved progression-free survival versus placebo in fourth-line GIST (6.3 vs 1.0 months; HR 0.15)
cards.people: 129 patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours that had progressed on (or who were intolerant of) at least imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib, with ECOG performance status 0–2, at 29 specialised hospitals in 12 countries, randomly assigned 2:1 to oral ripretinib 150 mg once daily (n=85) or placebo (n=44), with treatment masked until blinded central review showed progression; placebo patients could then cross over to ripretinib. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by blinded independent central review; median follow-up at the primary analysis was 6.3 months in the ripretinib group and 1.6 months in the placebo group.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 6.3 months (95% CI 4.6–6.9) with ripretinib versus 1.0 month (0.9–1.7) with placebo (HR 0.15, 95% CI 0.09–0.25; P<0.0001) — an absolute median gain of 5.3 months in a population whose disease had exhausted three prior lines. The most common grade 3–4 treatment-related events on ripretinib included lipase increase (5%), hypertension (4%), fatigue (2%), and hypophosphataemia.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival against placebo in a no-option population is the claim — nothing more. Crossover at progression was built into the design, so overall-survival comparisons between the randomised arms are confounded and none is carded. The placebo arm's 1.0-month median reflects the natural history of fourth-line GIST as much as the drug's effect; the hazard ratio (0.15) is the durable figure. Small trial (n=129), inevitable in this setting.
cards.source: Blay JY et al. Ripretinib in patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours (INVICTUS): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol. 2020. PMID: 32511981. Registry ID: NCT03353753, from the record. shelves.title: Interval-compressed chemotherapy in localized Ewing sarcoma (AEWS0031)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed localized Ewing sarcoma, does interval-compressed VDC/IE chemotherapy (every 2 weeks) improve event-free survival versus standard 3-weekly scheduling?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bone Neoplasms · Child · Child, Preschool · Cyclophosphamide · Doxorubicin · Drug Administration Schedule · Etoposide · Humans · Ifosfamide · Infant · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Sarcoma, Ewing · Vincristine · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One large cooperative-group randomised trial (n=568 eligible) in patients under 50 with newly diagnosed localized Ewing sarcoma: giving the same VDC/IE chemotherapy every 2 weeks instead of every 3 improved 5-year event-free survival from 65% to 73% (P=0.048), with similar toxicity — the gain bought purely by schedule compression, enabled by filgrastim support, with no new drug. The delivered compression was partial: median achieved cycle interval was 15 days (mean 17.3) versus 21 days (mean 22.5), because cycles waited on count recovery. The abstract reports event rates and the P value without a hazard ratio; none is printed on these cards. A single-trial result at P=0.048 is real but not lavish — the stamp reflects a large, well-run, practice-defining trial whose effect, while modest, costs no extra toxicity. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: AEWS0031: interval-compressed VDC/IE improved 5-year event-free survival in localized Ewing sarcoma (73% vs 65%; P=0.048) with similar toxicity
cards.summary: AEWS0031: interval-compressed VDC/IE improved 5-year event-free survival in localized Ewing sarcoma (73% vs 65%; P=0.048) with similar toxicity
cards.people: 587 patients younger than 50 years with newly diagnosed localized extradural Ewing sarcoma were enrolled and randomly assigned; 568 were eligible (284 per arm). Both arms received 14 cycles of alternating vincristine–doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide–etoposide with filgrastim support, scheduled every 21 days (standard) or every 14 days (interval-compressed), with cycles starting when neutrophil and platelet thresholds were met; primary-tumour treatment (surgery, radiation, or both) began at week 13. The primary endpoint was event-free survival, reported at a median of 5 years.
cards.result: Event-free survival at a median of 5 years was 73% in the interval-compressed arm versus 65% in the standard arm (P=0.048) — an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points, from schedule compression alone, with the same drugs and cumulative doses. The toxicity of the two regimens was similar. The achieved compression was incomplete: median cycle interval was 15 days (mean 17.3) in the compressed arm versus 21 days (mean 22.5) in the standard arm, because count recovery gated each cycle.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports no hazard ratio — none is printed on this card (figures circulating in summaries that quote one come from elsewhere in the paper). P=0.048 is a borderline significance level for a single trial; the stamp leans on the trial's size, the hard endpoint, and the zero added toxicity. The population includes children, adolescents, and adults to age 50 treated on a paediatric-style regimen; transportability to older adults is limited.

shelves.title: Nirogacestat in progressing desmoid tumours (DeFi)
shelves.question: In adults with progressing desmoid tumours, does nirogacestat improve progression-free survival and symptom burden versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Amyloid Precursor Protein Secretases · Antineoplastic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Desmoid Tumors · Gamma Secretase Inhibitors and Modulators · Progression-Free Survival · Quality of Life · Tetrahydronaphthalenes · Valine
shelves.balance: The DeFi trial is the first positive randomised trial in desmoid tumours — a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the γ-secretase inhibitor nirogacestat in 142 adults whose tumours were progressing. Progression-free survival strongly favoured the drug (hazard ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.55; P<0.001), with an estimated 76% versus 44% of patients event-free at 2 years — a 32-percentage-point absolute difference — and objective responses in 41% versus 8% (complete responses 7% versus 0%). Patient-reported pain, symptom burden, functioning and quality of life all improved significantly more on nirogacestat (P≤0.01). The price is real but mostly low-grade toxicity: diarrhoea in 84%, nausea 54%, fatigue 51%, hypophosphataemia 42% and rash 32%, with 95% of adverse events grade 1 or 2 — plus ovarian dysfunction in 27 of 36 (75%) women of childbearing potential, which resolved in 74% of those affected and must be counselled before treatment. There is no second trial and no survival claim; this shelf rests on progression and symptom endpoints in a rare tumour with no previously approved therapy. Flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: DeFi: nirogacestat more than tripled the chance of remaining progression-free at 2 years in progressing desmoid tumours (hazard ratio 0.29; 76% vs 44% event-free)
cards.summary: DeFi: nirogacestat more than tripled the chance of remaining progression-free at 2 years in progressing desmoid tumours (hazard ratio 0.29; 76% vs 44% event-free)
cards.people: 142 adults with desmoid tumours progressing by RECIST version 1.1, recruited internationally and assigned 1:1 to oral nirogacestat 150 mg twice daily (n=70) or placebo (n=72). The primary endpoint was progression-free survival; secondary endpoints included objective response and patient-reported pain, symptom burden, functioning and health-related quality of life.
cards.result: Nirogacestat significantly improved progression-free survival (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.29, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.55; P<0.001), consistently across prespecified subgroups; the likelihood of being event-free at 2 years was 76% with nirogacestat and 44% with placebo. Objective responses occurred in 41% versus 8% (P<0.001), with complete responses in 7% versus 0% and a median time to response of 5.6 versus 11.1 months. All patient-reported secondary outcomes favoured nirogacestat (P≤0.01).
cards.watchOut: Among women of childbearing potential receiving nirogacestat, 27 of 36 (75%) had adverse events consistent with ovarian dysfunction, resolving in 20 of the 27 (74%) — a fertility counselling obligation that belongs on the face of any recommendation. Other adverse events were frequent (diarrhoea 84%, nausea 54%, fatigue 51%, hypophosphataemia 42%, maculopapular rash 32%) though 95% were grade 1 or 2. Desmoid tumours can stabilise or regress spontaneously — the placebo arm's 44% event-free rate at 2 years is that natural history showing through — and there is no overall-survival outcome in this record.
cards.source: Gounder M et al. Nirogacestat, a γ-Secretase Inhibitor for Desmoid Tumors. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID: 36884323. Registry ID: NCT03785964, from the record. shelves.title: Screening by clinical breast examination in Mumbai (Mittra)
shelves.question: In women aged 35–64 in a low-resource setting without mammography, does screening by clinical breast examination every two years reduce breast cancer mortality over 20 years versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Breast Neoplasms · Cluster Analysis · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · India · Mammography · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Prospective Studies · Survival Rate · Time Factors
shelves.balance: One very large, very long cluster-randomised trial (151,538 women in Mumbai, 20 clusters, 20 years, four biennial rounds of clinical breast examination by trained primary health workers). Screening clearly downstaged disease: stage III/IV cancers were 37% of diagnoses in the screening arm versus 47% in controls (P=0.001), and cancers were detected about 1.3 years younger. The mortality result is split by age and by analysis: overall, breast cancer mortality was 15% lower in relative terms (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.71–1.01; P=0.07) — a confidence interval crossing 1.0, so the overall claim is not significant. In a post hoc subgroup of women aged 50 and over the relative reduction was nearly 30% (rate ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.54–0.94; P=0.02), while women under 50 showed none (0.93, CI 0.79–1.09). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme, a non-significant primary mortality result, and a significant subgroup that was post hoc; Tier C because the claim is about cancer mortality (the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: Mittra 2021: biennial clinical breast examination downstaged cancers (stage III/IV 37% vs 47%) but the overall mortality reduction was not significant (rate ratio 0.85, CI 0.71–1.01)
cards.summary: Mittra 2021: biennial clinical breast examination downstaged cancers (stage III/IV 37% vs 47%) but the overall mortality reduction was not significant (rate ratio 0.85, CI 0.71–1.01)
cards.people: 151,538 women aged 35–64 with no history of breast cancer, in 20 geographically distinct Mumbai clusters randomised 10:10 to screening or control. The screening arm (n=75,360) received four rounds of clinical breast examination by trained female primary health workers plus cancer awareness every two years, then five rounds of active surveillance; the control arm (n=76,178) received one round of cancer awareness then eight rounds of surveillance. Total trial duration was 20 years (recruitment from May 1998; database locked March 2019).
cards.result: Breast cancer was detected earlier in the screening arm (mean age 55.18 vs 56.50 years; P=0.01) and the proportion diagnosed at stage III or IV was significantly lower (37% vs 47%; P=0.001). Breast cancer mortality overall was 20.82 deaths per 100,000 person-years in the screening arm versus 24.62 in controls — a relative rate ratio of 0.85 (95% CI 0.71–1.01; P=0.07), i.e. a 15% relative reduction whose interval crosses 1.0 and is not statistically significant. All-cause mortality was 5% lower in relative terms (rate ratio 0.95, CI 0.81–1.10; P=0.49), also not significant.
cards.watchOut: The headline mortality claim fails its own significance test overall — the card leads with the downstaging (which is significant) and states the mortality result exactly as reported. The control arm received cancer awareness and active surveillance, not nothing, which compresses the contrast. Results come from a single programme in one city with trained dedicated health workers; performance elsewhere is an extrapolation.
cards.source: Mittra I et al. Effect of screening by clinical breast examination on breast cancer incidence and mortality after 20 years: prospective, cluster randomised controlled trial in Mumbai. BMJ. 2021. PMID: 33627312. Registry ID: NCT00632047 (also CTRI/2010/091/001205), from the record. shelves.title: Population mass H. pylori eradication on the Matsu Islands (Chiang)
shelves.question: In a high-incidence population, does mass Helicobacter pylori screening and eradication reduce gastric cancer incidence and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Disease Eradication · Female · Gastroscopy · Helicobacter Infections · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Incidence · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Stomach Neoplasms · Taiwan
shelves.balance: One long-running population programme in a genuinely high-incidence setting — but read its design before its numbers. Chiang 2021 reports the Matsu Islands (Taiwan) mass eradication programme: six screening rounds between 2004 and 2018 in residents aged 30+, 85.5% coverage of 7,616 eligible people, cut H. pylori prevalence from 64.2% to 15.0%, with reinfection under 1% per person-year. Against the programme's own historical control period (1995–2003, before eradication), gastric cancer incidence was 53% lower in relative terms (95% CI 30–69%; P<0.001), while gastric cancer mortality was 25% lower in relative terms with an interval crossing no effect (95% CI −14% to 51%; P=0.18) — not significant. Two corrections to the topic draft stand on this shelf: the design is a long-term cohort study with historical controls, not a randomised trial (so the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE framing does not apply), and the eligible population was about 7,600 residents, not the draft's larger figure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C (cancer mortality claimed — the developer rules personally). Individual-patient eradication evidence is homed on Shelves #219 and #322; this shelf is the population-programme question.

cards.headline: Chiang 2021: mass eradication cut H. pylori prevalence from 64% to 15%; gastric cancer incidence was 53% lower (relative) than the historical era, mortality 25% lower but not significant (P=0.18)
cards.summary: Chiang 2021: mass eradication cut H. pylori prevalence from 64% to 15%; gastric cancer incidence was 53% lower (relative) than the historical era, mortality 25% lower but not significant (P=0.18)
cards.type: Long-term cohort study with historical controls (population programme)
cards.people: Residents of the Matsu Islands, Taiwan — a high-incidence gastric cancer region — aged 30 or older, offered mass H. pylori screening and eradication in six rounds between 2004 and 2018. Of 7,616 eligible residents, 6,512 participated (85.5% coverage); 93.5% of those screening positive were referred for treatment. Effectiveness was assessed against cancer-registry and mortality outcomes from the pre-eradication period 1995–2003 in the same population, with follow-up to 31 December 2016 (incidence) and 31 December 2018 (mortality).
cards.result: H. pylori prevalence fell from 64.2% (95% CI 62.8–65.5%) in 2004 to 15.0% (13.7–16.3%) in 2018, with reinfection under 1% per person-year. Versus the historical control period, gastric cancer incidence was reduced by 53% in relative terms (95% CI 30–69%; P<0.001). Gastric cancer mortality was reduced by 25% in relative terms (95% CI −14% to 51%; P=0.18) — an interval that includes no effect, so the mortality result is not significant. The authors projected incidence would keep falling and estimated (a prediction, not an observation) that the mortality effect would become significant by 2025.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls are the weak point: gastric cancer incidence was falling across Taiwan for other reasons (refrigeration, diet, smoking) during the same decades, so part of the 53% relative incidence reduction may belong to the era, not the programme; the non-significant mortality result is the honest headline outcome. The topic draft's description of this as a randomised programme in a much larger screened population is corrected on this card — the record describes a cohort programme in 7,616 eligible residents. Absolute incidence and mortality rates are not given in the abstract, so the shelf quotes relative effects labelled as such.

shelves.title: Single low-dose CT screen for lung cancer in high-risk people (UKLS)
shelves.question: In high-risk ever-smokers aged 50–75 selected by a validated risk model, does a single low-dose CT screen reduce lung cancer mortality versus usual care?
shelves.balance: UKLS is the small, single-screen sibling of the repeated-screening trials. It randomised 4,055 people aged 50–75 at high risk by the LLPv2 model (5-year lung cancer risk ≥4.5%) to one low-dose CT screen or usual care, and followed them a median of 7.3 years. Lung cancers numbered 86 in the screened group versus 75 in controls; lung cancer deaths were 30 versus 46 — a relative rate of 0.65 (95% CI 0.41–1.02), an absolute difference of roughly 1.5% versus 2.3% of participants, with P=0.062: suggestive, not significant, in a trial the authors describe as underpowered alone. The same paper's meta-analysis of nine screening trials (NLST, NELSON, and others) found a pooled relative risk of lung cancer death of 0.84 (95% CI 0.76–0.92) for CT screening — so the modality works on the pooled evidence; what UKLS itself adds is that risk-model selection concentrates yield and that even one screen may carry much of the benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE for this shelf's single-screen question (the repeated-screening mortality claim lives on Shelf #164), Tier C (cancer mortality — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: UKLS meta-analysis 2021: across nine CT screening trials, lung cancer mortality was lower with screening (pooled relative risk 0.84, CI 0.76–0.92)
cards.summary: UKLS meta-analysis 2021: across nine CT screening trials, lung cancer mortality was lower with screening (pooled relative risk 0.84, CI 0.76–0.92)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials of low-dose CT screening for lung cancer, including the large repeated-screening trials (NLST, NELSON) and UKLS itself, pooled by the UKLS investigators in the same publication.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk of lung cancer death with CT screening versus control was 0.84 (95% CI 0.76–0.92) — a 16% relative reduction, statistically significant. UKLS's own point estimate (0.65) was more favourable than the pooled figure but far less precise, consistent with small-trial scatter around a real, more modest effect.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials mostly used repeated annual or biennial screens, so the meta-analysis supports CT screening as a modality; it does not by itself prove that a single screen suffices — that is UKLS's distinctive, still-unproven suggestion. For the repeated-screening mortality evidence and its harms (false positives, overdiagnosis), the library's home is Shelf #164; this shelf exists for the single-screen, risk-model-selected design.

shelves.title: Zoledronic acid versus pamidronate for hypercalcaemia of malignancy: higher, faster, longer responses
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy, is a single dose of zoledronic acid superior to pamidronate for complete response (normalised corrected calcium) by day 10 and duration of response?
shelves.mesh: Diphosphonates/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypercalcemia/drug therapy · Neoplasms/complications · Pamidronate · Zoledronic Acid
shelves.balance: Two identical randomised double-blind trials, pooled as the protocol specified, give a clear answer. In 275 patients evaluable for efficacy with moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy (corrected calcium ≥3.00 mmol/L), a single dose of zoledronic acid produced complete response (normalised corrected calcium) by day 10 in 88.4% at 4 mg and 86.7% at 8 mg, versus 69.7% on pamidronate 90 mg (P=.002 and P=.015) — absolute advantages of about 19 and 17 percentage points. Calcium normalised by day 4 in roughly 50% on zoledronic acid versus 33.3% on pamidronate, and complete responses lasted a median of 32 days (4 mg) and 43 days (8 mg) versus 18 days. The recommended initial dose from the trials is 4 mg. PROPOSED LIKELY — two concurrent identical double-blind trials with concordant, clinically large differences on the defining endpoint of the condition.

cards.headline: Major 2001 (pooled twin trials): complete response by day 10 in 88.4% (zoledronic acid 4 mg) and 86.7% (8 mg) vs 69.7% on pamidronate
cards.summary: Major 2001 (pooled twin trials): complete response by day 10 in 88.4% (zoledronic acid 4 mg) and 86.7% (8 mg) vs 69.7% on pamidronate
cards.type: Protocol-specified pooled analysis of two identical randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trials
cards.people: Patients with moderate-to-severe hypercalcaemia of malignancy (corrected serum calcium ≥3.00 mmol/L [12.0 mg/dL]) in two identical, concurrent, parallel, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trials: 287 patients randomised and evaluated for safety, 275 evaluated for efficacy. Treatment was a single dose of zoledronic acid 4 mg or 8 mg by 5-minute infusion, or pamidronate 90 mg by 2-hour infusion. Endpoints: complete response rate by day 10, response duration, and time to relapse.
cards.result: Complete response rates by day 10 were 88.4% for zoledronic acid 4 mg (P=.002 versus pamidronate), 86.7% for zoledronic acid 8 mg (P=.015), and 69.7% for pamidronate 90 mg. Normalisation of corrected calcium occurred by day 4 in approximately 50% of zoledronic-acid patients versus 33.3% on pamidronate. Median duration of complete response was 32 days (4 mg), 43 days (8 mg), and 18 days (pamidronate). The authors conclude zoledronic acid is superior, with 4 mg recommended for initial treatment and 8 mg for relapsed or refractory hypercalcaemia.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is biochemical — normalising calcium — in a condition where normalising calcium is itself the treatment goal; survival was not an endpoint and hypercalcaemia of malignancy remains a poor-prognosis state. The trials are from 2001, single-dose, and predate current infusion-time and renal-monitoring practice for zoledronic acid; the comparison dose of pamidronate (90 mg) was the standard of its era.

J Clin Oncol. 2001. PMID: 11208851. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). shelves.title: Tarlatamab in previously treated small-cell lung cancer: overall survival 13.6 vs 8.3 months (hazard ratio 0.60) in the phase 3 DeLLphi-304 trial
shelves.question: In extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer that has progressed on or after platinum chemotherapy, does tarlatamab improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Anthracyclines · *Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage/adverse effects · *Lung Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Progression-Free Survival · *Small Cell Lung Carcinoma/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Topotecan/administration & dosage/adverse effects · *Antibodies, Bispecific/administration & dosage/adverse effects · *Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dyspnea/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Cough/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Severity of Illness Index · Disease Progression · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Carbolines · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings
shelves.balance: Yes — tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager aimed at DLL3, is the first agent in years to move survival in this setting. In the phase 3 DeLLphi-304 trial (Mountzios 2025), 509 patients whose small-cell lung cancer had progressed on or after platinum chemotherapy lived a median of 13.6 months on tarlatamab versus 8.3 months on the investigator's choice of standard second-line chemotherapy (topotecan, lurbinectedin or amrubicin) — hazard ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.77; P < 0.001), a relative measure that here translates to 5.3 months of median survival — with fewer grade 3-or-worse adverse events than chemotherapy (54% versus 80%) and fewer discontinuations (5% versus 12%). The phase 2 DeLLphi-301 study (Ahn 2023) had set the stage with objective responses in 40% at the 10 mg dose (32% at 100 mg) in a heavily pretreated population, and the phase 1 study (Paz-Ares 2023) first showed the responses could last (median duration 12.3 months). The drug's signature toxicity is cytokine-release syndrome — about half of patients, mostly grade 1–2 and early — plus neurologic events, managed with step-up dosing and monitoring. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a positive phase 3 survival trial in a disease with almost no wins, consistent with its phase 2. Flagged for the developer's eye: the phase 3 result is a prespecified interim analysis, so the stamp leans on one randomised trial rather than two. A different question — tarlatamab with durvalumab as first-line maintenance (DeLLphi-305) — is not carded here.

cards.headline: Mountzios 2025 (DeLLphi-304): tarlatamab beat standard second-line chemotherapy on survival — 13.6 vs 8.3 months, hazard ratio 0.60 — with fewer severe adverse events
cards.summary: Mountzios 2025 (DeLLphi-304): tarlatamab beat standard second-line chemotherapy on survival — 13.6 vs 8.3 months, hazard ratio 0.60 — with fewer severe adverse events
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial, prespecified interim analysis (DeLLphi-304) (Mountzios 2025)
cards.people: 509 patients with small-cell lung cancer that had progressed during or after platinum-based chemotherapy were randomised to tarlatamab (a bispecific DLL3×CD3 T-cell engager) or the investigator's choice of standard care — topotecan, lurbinectedin or amrubicin. The primary endpoint was overall survival; this report is the trial's prespecified interim analysis.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 13.6 months (95% CI 11.1 to 16.1) on tarlatamab versus 8.3 months (7.0 to 10.2) on standard care: hazard ratio for death 0.60 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.77; P < 0.001) — a 40% relative reduction in the risk of death, alongside a 5.3-month absolute gain in median survival. Tarlatamab also significantly improved progression-free survival and cancer-related dyspnoea and cough. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 54% of tarlatamab patients versus 80% on chemotherapy; discontinuation for adverse events in 5% versus 12%.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis: the survival curves will mature further, and interim looks tend to flatter. Open-label treatment (unavoidable given cytokine-release monitoring) leaves the symptom endpoints open to bias, though overall survival — the primary endpoint — is not. The control arm's three-drug menu also means 'standard care' varied by country and investigator.

cards.headline: Ahn 2023 (DeLLphi-301): objective responses in 40% at the 10 mg dose and 32% at 100 mg in heavily pretreated small-cell lung cancer; cytokine-release syndrome in about half, mostly mild
cards.summary: Ahn 2023 (DeLLphi-301): objective responses in 40% at the 10 mg dose and 32% at 100 mg in heavily pretreated small-cell lung cancer; cytokine-release syndrome in about half, mostly mild
cards.people: 220 patients with previously treated small-cell lung cancer received tarlatamab 10 mg (99 patients) or 100 mg (87 patients) every 2 weeks; 34 further patients were excluded from the efficacy analysis after a protocol-specified interim analysis. The primary endpoint was objective response by blinded independent central review. Median follow-up was 10.6 months (10 mg) and 10.3 months (100 mg).
cards.result: Objective response occurred in 40% (97.5% CI 29 to 52) at 10 mg and 32% (97.5% CI 21 to 44) at 100 mg; among responders, a duration of response of at least 6 months was estimated in 59% in both groups. Median progression-free survival was 4.9 and 3.9 months, and 9-month overall survival 68% and 66%. Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 51% (10 mg) and 61% (100 mg), primarily during cycle 1 and mostly grade 1–2 (grade 3 in 1% and 6%); treatment discontinuation for adverse events was 3% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: No control arm: a 40% response rate in third-line small-cell lung cancer is far above historical chemotherapy, but response rate is not survival — which is why this card supports, and the phase 3 card carries, the shelf's claim. One indexing note: this record's PubMed MeSH includes '*Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy' for a small-cell lung cancer trial; the terms are copied verbatim from the record, and the error is PubMed's, not the trial's.

cards.headline: Paz-Ares 2023 (DeLLphi-300, phase 1): confirmed responses in 23.4% of pretreated patients, median duration of response 12.3 months — the durability signal that launched the programme
cards.summary: Paz-Ares 2023 (DeLLphi-300, phase 1): confirmed responses in 23.4% of pretreated patients, median duration of response 12.3 months — the durability signal that launched the programme
cards.people: 107 patients with relapsed or refractory small-cell lung cancer after at least one line of systemic therapy (median 2 previous lines; 36% with brain metastases (39 of 107)) received tarlatamab across target doses from 0.003 to 100 mg every 2 weeks, with step-up dosing in cycle 1 to blunt cytokine-release syndrome.
cards.result: Confirmed objective responses occurred in 23.4% of patients (25 of 107), with a median duration of response of 12.3 months and median overall survival of 13.2 months. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 90.7%; cytokine-release syndrome in 52% (grade 3 in 1%), neutropenia in 16% (grade 3–4 in 10%), and one grade 5 pneumonitis. Treatment discontinuation for treatment-related events was 3.7% (4 patients).
cards.watchOut: A first-in-human dose-ranging study with no comparator and doses mostly below the ones later used: its durable responses (median 12.3 months in responders) are hypothesis-grade evidence. It earns its card as the programme's origin and the first durability read, not as independent confirmation of benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: phase 1 durability, phase 2 responses, phase 3 survival — the full staircase, climbed in order — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: phase 1 durability, phase 2 responses, phase 3 survival — the full staircase, climbed in order — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (DeLLphi-304, 509 patients), one phase 2 dose-comparison trial (DeLLphi-301, 220 patients) and the phase 1 first-in-human study (DeLLphi-300, 107 patients), all in small-cell lung cancer progressing after platinum-based therapy.
cards.result: Overall survival 13.6 versus 8.3 months (hazard ratio 0.60) against real second-line chemotherapy in phase 3; objective responses of 40% (10 mg) in phase 2 and a median response duration of 12.3 months among phase 1 responders — response, durability and survival all pointing the same way, in a disease where second-line therapy has historically bought weeks. Cytokine-release syndrome affects about half of patients but is mostly low-grade and front-loaded; severe adverse events were less frequent than with chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: The LIKELY stamp rests on a single phase 3 trial read at a prespecified interim analysis — the developer's two-trial instinct should note that the second 'trial' here is an uncontrolled phase 2. If the mature survival data soften, this is the shelf to revisit first. First-line maintenance combinations (DeLLphi-305) ask a different question and are not carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mountzios G et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40454646); Ahn MJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37861218); Paz-Ares L et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2023 (PMID: 36689692).

shelves.title: Belzutifan in kidney cancer: progression-free survival advantage and 21.9% vs 3.5% response after immunotherapy in LITESPARK-005; 49% response in von Hippel–Lindau kidney tumours
shelves.question: In advanced clear-cell renal cell carcinoma after immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatment, does belzutifan (a HIF-2α inhibitor) help — and does it work in von Hippel–Lindau disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use/adverse effects · *Carcinoma, Renal Cell/drug therapy/mortality · *Everolimus/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · *Kidney Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Progression-Free Survival · *Indenes/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Administration, Oral · Basic Helix-Loop-Helix Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult · Treatment Outcome · Endothelial PAS Domain-Containing Protein 1
shelves.balance: For pretreated clear-cell kidney cancer, belzutifan beat everolimus on the measures that show a drug is active, but not yet on survival. In LITESPARK-005 (Choueiri 2024), 746 patients whose cancer had advanced after both checkpoint immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic therapy had identical median progression-free survival in the two arms (5.6 months each) yet clearly better progression-free rates at 18 months on belzutifan (24.0% versus 8.3%; P = 0.002) — the curves separate late, so the median hides the benefit — and a far higher objective response rate (21.9% versus 3.5%; P < 0.001). Overall survival was 21.4 versus 18.1 months (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07; P = 0.20 — not significant). Grade 3-or-worse adverse events were similar (61.8% versus 62.5%), with fewer discontinuations on belzutifan (5.9% versus 14.7%). In von Hippel–Lindau disease (Jonasch 2021), where HIF-2α accumulation is the disease mechanism itself, single-arm belzutifan produced responses in 49% of kidney tumours, 77% of pancreatic lesions and 30% of CNS haemangioblastomas, with every evaluable retinal eye improving; anaemia (90%) is the on-target cost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): progression and response gains without a survival win in the randomised trial, plus mechanism-perfect but uncontrolled evidence in VHL.

cards.headline: Choueiri 2024 (LITESPARK-005): belzutifan vs everolimus after immunotherapy — 18-month progression-free survival 24.0% vs 8.3% and responses 21.9% vs 3.5%, but overall survival not significantly different
cards.summary: Choueiri 2024 (LITESPARK-005): belzutifan vs everolimus after immunotherapy — 18-month progression-free survival 24.0% vs 8.3% and responses 21.9% vs 3.5%, but overall survival not significantly different
cards.people: 746 patients with advanced clear-cell renal cell carcinoma whose disease had progressed after immune checkpoint inhibitors and anti-angiogenic therapies were randomised 1:1 to belzutifan 120 mg daily or everolimus 10 mg daily. Primary endpoints were progression-free survival and overall survival; median follow-up for survival was 25.7 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 5.6 months in both groups, but at 18 months 24.0% of belzutifan patients versus 8.3% of everolimus patients were alive and progression-free (P = 0.002). Objective responses occurred in 21.9% (95% CI 18.3 to 25.8) versus 3.5% (1.9 to 5.9) (P < 0.001). Overall survival was 21.4 versus 18.1 months (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07; P = 0.20 — not significant). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 61.8% on belzutifan and 62.5% on everolimus; discontinuation for adverse events in 5.9% versus 14.7%.
cards.watchOut: The equal medians are the trap in this abstract: half of each group progressed early, and belzutifan's advantage lives in the tail of patients who stay controlled — a real benefit, but one that reaches only about a quarter of patients by 18 months. With survival not significant at this follow-up, the honest claim is 'delays progression and shrinks tumours in a minority', not 'extends life'.
cards.source: Choueiri TK et al. Belzutifan versus Everolimus for Advanced Renal-Cell Carcinoma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39167807. cards.headline: Jonasch 2021: belzutifan in von Hippel–Lindau disease — kidney tumour responses in 49%, pancreatic lesions 77%, CNS haemangioblastomas 30%; anaemia in 90%
cards.summary: Jonasch 2021: belzutifan in von Hippel–Lindau disease — kidney tumour responses in 49%, pancreatic lesions 77%, CNS haemangioblastomas 30%; anaemia in 90%
cards.people: 61 adults with von Hippel–Lindau disease and at least one measurable renal cell carcinoma (tumours no larger than 3 cm) received belzutifan 120 mg daily. The primary endpoint was the objective response rate in VHL-associated renal cell carcinoma; pancreatic lesions, CNS haemangioblastomas and retinal haemangioblastomas were also assessed.
cards.result: The objective response rate in renal cell carcinoma was 49% (95% CI 36 to 62), with responses also seen in pancreatic lesions (47 of 61 patients, 77%) and CNS haemangioblastomas (15 of 50 patients, 30%); all 16 evaluable eyes with retinal haemangioblastomas showed improvement. The most common adverse events were anaemia (90%) and fatigue (66%); one patient discontinued for grade 1 dizziness.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm in a disease whose tumours grow slowly and variably, so some 'responses' would be hard to attribute without a control — though shrinkage in three separate organ systems at once is difficult to explain away. Anaemia in 9 of 10 patients is the mechanism (HIF-2α drives erythropoietin) announcing itself; long-term dosing in a lifelong germline disease is the open question this 2021 report cannot answer.
cards.source: Jonasch E et al. Belzutifan for Renal Cell Carcinoma in von Hippel-Lindau Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34818478. cards.headline: Synthesis: an active drug with a late-separating benefit in sporadic kidney cancer, and a mechanism-matched one in VHL — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: an active drug with a late-separating benefit in sporadic kidney cancer, and a mechanism-matched one in VHL — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One phase 3 randomised trial in pretreated clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (746 patients) and one single-arm phase 2 trial in von Hippel–Lindau disease (61 patients).
cards.result: Against everolimus: progression-free survival advantage concentrated in the tail (24.0% vs 8.3% progression-free at 18 months; medians identical at 5.6 months), a six-fold response-rate advantage (21.9% vs 3.5%), no significant overall-survival difference yet (hazard ratio 0.88, P = 0.20), and tolerability at least as good. In VHL: responses across kidney (49%), pancreas (77%) and CNS (30%) from a drug that blocks the exact pathway the germline mutation unleashes — the cleanest mechanism-to-effect match in oncology, bought with near-universal anaemia.
cards.watchOut: The two halves of this shelf answer different clinical questions (a salvage therapy in common kidney cancer; a systemic therapy for a rare syndrome) and neither should borrow the other's strength: the randomised trial lacks a survival win, and the VHL trial lacks a control. Survival follow-up from LITESPARK-005 is the evidence that would move this stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of Choueiri TK et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 39167807); Jonasch E et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34818478).

shelves.title: Omitting radiotherapy in low-risk older breast cancer: local recurrence rises to 9.5% at 10 years, survival unchanged — a trade-off, not a free pass
shelves.question: In older women with low-risk, hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer treated with breast-conserving surgery and endocrine therapy, can radiotherapy be omitted without harming survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Breast/pathology · Breast Neoplasms*/metabolism, pathology, radiotherapy, surgery · Mastectomy, Segmental/adverse effects · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local*/mortality · Neoplasm Staging · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Withholding Treatment · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the trial evidence is strong, and what it shows is a trade-off, not a verdict. In PRIME II, 1,326 women aged 65 or older with hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative tumours up to 3 cm, clear margins and adjuvant endocrine therapy were randomised to whole-breast radiotherapy or none: at 10 years, local recurrence was 9.5% without radiotherapy versus 0.9% with it (HR 10.4), yet distant recurrence was not higher (1.6% vs 3.0%) and overall survival was identical (80.8% vs 80.7%) (Kunkler 2023, PMID: 36791159; 5-year report Kunkler 2015, PMID: 25637340, carded as a companion, not independent evidence). The LUMINA cohort shows biomarker selection can find women whose 5-year recurrence risk without radiotherapy is lower still (2.3% in Ki67-defined luminal A disease; Whelan 2023, PMID: 37585627) — with PRIME II's warning attached: recurrence without radiotherapy keeps accruing through year 10. So omission is a legitimate, evidence-framed choice for women who fit these criteria and accept roughly 9 extra local recurrences per 100 over a decade in exchange for avoiding radiotherapy; it is not evidence that radiotherapy does nothing. Tier C: the shelf turns on cancer recurrence and survival outcomes from essentially one randomised trial, flagged for the developer's personal verdict. Radiotherapy for DCIS is homed at shelf #943.

cards.headline: Kunkler 2023 (PRIME II, 10 years): omitting radiotherapy — local recurrence 9.5% vs 0.9%, but overall survival identical (80.8% vs 80.7%)
cards.summary: Kunkler 2023 (PRIME II, 10 years): omitting radiotherapy — local recurrence 9.5% vs 0.9%, but overall survival identical (80.8% vs 80.7%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 10-year report (Kunkler 2023, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: The 10-year report of the PRIME II phase 3 randomised trial: 1,326 women aged 65 years or older with hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative, T1 or T2 (≤3 cm) breast cancer, treated with breast-conserving surgery with clear margins and adjuvant endocrine therapy, randomised to whole-breast irradiation (658) or no irradiation (668). Median follow-up 9.1 years.
cards.result: Cumulative local recurrence within 10 years was 9.5% (95% CI 6.8 to 12.3) without radiotherapy versus 0.9% (95% CI 0.1 to 1.7) with it (hazard ratio 10.4, 95% CI 4.1 to 26.1; P < 0.001). Distant recurrence as the first event was not higher without radiotherapy (1.6% vs 3.0%), regional recurrence and breast-cancer-specific survival did not differ substantially, and 10-year overall survival was almost identical: 80.8% without radiotherapy versus 80.7% with it.
cards.watchOut: Local recurrence is not a soft outcome for the woman who experiences it — it usually means further surgery, sometimes mastectomy, and the radiotherapy she tried to avoid, a decade of endocrine therapy notwithstanding. The trial's women were selected low-risk and received endocrine therapy; the numbers do not transfer to higher-risk disease or to women who stop endocrine therapy.
cards.source: Kunkler IH et al. Breast-Conserving Surgery with or without Irradiation in Early Breast Cancer. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36791159. Registry ID: ISRCTN95889329. cards.headline: Kunkler 2015 (PRIME II, 5 years): ipsilateral recurrence 4.1% without radiotherapy vs 1.3% with it; 5-year survival 93.9% in both groups
cards.summary: Kunkler 2015 (PRIME II, 5 years): ipsilateral recurrence 4.1% without radiotherapy vs 1.3% with it; 5-year survival 93.9% in both groups
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 5-year report (Kunkler 2015, Lancet Oncology)
cards.people: The 5-year report of the same PRIME II trial (companion publication, not an independent trial): 1,326 women aged 65 years or older with low-risk early breast cancer (hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative, tumours up to 3 cm, clear margins; grade 3 histology or lymphovascular invasion permitted but not both) after breast-conserving surgery, all receiving adjuvant endocrine treatment, randomised to whole-breast radiotherapy (658) or no further treatment (668).
cards.result: After median follow-up of 5 years, ipsilateral breast tumour recurrence was 4.1% (n = 26) without radiotherapy versus 1.3% (n = 5) with it (p = 0.0002; hazard ratio for omission 5.19, 95% CI 1.99 to 13.52). There were no differences in regional recurrence, distant metastases or contralateral cancers, and 5-year overall survival was 93.9% in both groups (p = 0.34). Of 89 deaths, breast cancer caused 8 of 49 in the no-radiotherapy group and 4 of 40 in the radiotherapy group.
cards.watchOut: Carded so the shelf shows the recurrence gap widening over time (4.1% vs 1.3% at 5 years; 9.5% vs 0.9% at 10) — most recurrences without radiotherapy arrive late, which is exactly why short-horizon omission studies flatter omission. It is the same patients as the 10-year report and adds no independent weight.
cards.source: Kunkler IH et al. Breast-conserving surgery with or without irradiation in women aged 65 years or older with early breast cancer (PRIME II): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25637340. Registry ID: ISRCTN95889329. cards.headline: Whelan 2023 (LUMINA): in biomarker-selected luminal A patients who omitted radiotherapy, 5-year local recurrence was 2.3% — within the prespecified acceptable boundary
cards.summary: Whelan 2023 (LUMINA): in biomarker-selected luminal A patients who omitted radiotherapy, 5-year local recurrence was 2.3% — within the prespecified acceptable boundary
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Whelan 2023, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: Prospective cohort study (LUMINA): women aged at least 55 years with T1N0, grade 1 or 2, luminal A breast cancer (oestrogen-receptor positive, progesterone-receptor >20%, HER2-negative, Ki67 ≤13.25% on central testing) after breast-conserving surgery, all receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy, who did not receive radiotherapy. Of 740 registered patients, 500 eligible patients were enrolled. The prespecified acceptability boundary was an upper 90% confidence limit for 5-year local recurrence below 5%.
cards.result: At 5 years, local recurrence in the ipsilateral breast was 2.3% (90% CI 1.3 to 3.8; 95% CI 1.2 to 4.1), meeting the prespecified boundary. Contralateral breast cancer occurred in 1.9% and recurrence of any type in 2.7%.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm cohort: 2.3% at 5 years in biomarker-selected patients cannot be compared directly with PRIME II's randomised arms (different age floor, tumour size, biology selection and follow-up). Its contribution is showing that molecular selection can identify a group whose short-term recurrence risk without radiotherapy is low — with the PRIME II lesson in mind that recurrence keeps accruing to year 10.
cards.source: Whelan TJ et al. Omitting Radiotherapy after Breast-Conserving Surgery in Luminal A Breast Cancer. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37585627. cards.headline: Synthesis: omission trades a real, growing local-recurrence risk for no survival loss in selected low-risk women — a values decision the evidence frames but does not make
cards.summary: Synthesis: omission trades a real, growing local-recurrence risk for no survival loss in selected low-risk women — a values decision the evidence frames but does not make
cards.people: One randomised trial reported at 5 and 10 years (PRIME II, 1,326 women ≥65, hormone-receptor-positive, node-negative, ≤3 cm, clear margins, all on endocrine therapy) and one biomarker-selected prospective cohort (LUMINA, 500 women ≥55 with luminal A disease).
cards.result: With radiotherapy: local recurrence 0.9% at 10 years. Without: 9.5% at 10 years (HR 10.4) — about 9 extra local recurrences per 100 women over a decade, with no difference in distant recurrence, breast-cancer-specific survival or overall survival (80.8% vs 80.7%). In LUMINA's Ki67-selected cohort, 5-year local recurrence without radiotherapy was 2.3%. Radiotherapy also carries burden and late risks that these reports were not designed to quantify.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about invasive cancer in older, low-risk women on endocrine therapy. Radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery for DCIS is a different question, homed at shelf #943. Nothing here applies to younger women, larger or node-positive tumours, HER2-positive or triple-negative disease, or women not taking endocrine therapy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kunkler IH et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36791159); Kunkler IH et al. Lancet Oncology. 2015 (PMID: 25637340); Whelan TJ et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37585627).

shelves.title: A blood test for colorectal cancer screening: about four in five cancers found, but only one in eight advanced adenomas — a detection net, not a prevention tool
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults, how accurately does a blood-based cell-free DNA test detect colorectal cancer and advanced adenomas?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · *Cell-Free Nucleic Acids/blood · Colonoscopy · *Colorectal Neoplasms/blood/diagnosis · *Early Detection of Cancer/methods · *Precancerous Conditions/blood/diagnosis · *Mass Screening/methods · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: Two large prospective accuracy studies with colonoscopy as the reference standard point the same way. In ECLIPSE (Chung 2024, PMID: 38477985), a cell-free DNA blood test detected 83.1% of colorectal cancers (95% CI 72.2 to 90.3) with 89.6% specificity for advanced neoplasia — but only 13.2% of advanced precancerous lesions. In PREEMPT CRC (Shaukat 2025, PMID: 40455622), a second blood test in 27,010 evaluable adults detected 79.2% of cancers with 91.5% specificity, and its 12.5% sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions fell below the study's own prespecified acceptance criterion. So the honest answer is: a blood test finds about four in five cancers that are already present, at the price of a false-positive rate near 1 in 10 — but it is nearly blind to the advanced adenomas whose removal is what makes screening prevent cancer rather than merely detect it. Its plausible role is reaching the large minority who refuse every stool and endoscopic test; whether that trade reduces incidence or mortality is unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: two prospective accuracy studies, no outcomes trial). The multitarget stool DNA comparison is at shelf #2622.

cards.headline: Chung 2024 (ECLIPSE): a cell-free DNA blood test detected 83.1% of colorectal cancers but only 13.2% of advanced precancerous lesions; specificity for advanced neoplasia 89.6%
cards.summary: Chung 2024 (ECLIPSE): a cell-free DNA blood test detected 83.1% of colorectal cancers but only 13.2% of advanced precancerous lesions; specificity for advanced neoplasia 89.6%
cards.people: Prospective accuracy study in a US screening-eligible, average-risk population: 10,258 persons enrolled, 7,861 evaluable with both the blood test and screening colonoscopy as the reference standard.
cards.result: Sensitivity for colorectal cancer was 83.1% (95% CI 72.2 to 90.3) and 87.5% for stage I–III cancers; sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions was only 13.2% (11.3 to 15.3). Specificity was 89.6% (88.8 to 90.3) for advanced neoplasia and 89.9% against a completely negative colonoscopy — so about 1 in 10 people without advanced neoplasia tested positive. Funded by Guardant Health; the record names the funder but does not print a commercial product name.
cards.watchOut: A test that misses nearly 9 in 10 advanced adenomas cannot prevent cancer the way colonoscopy or stool-DNA testing can — it can only find cancers that already exist. The cancer-sensitivity estimate rests on the cancers found at the single study colonoscopy (wide confidence interval, 72–90%), and there are no mortality or interval-cancer data.
cards.source: Chung DC et al. A cell-free DNA blood-based test for colorectal cancer screening (ECLIPSE). N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38477985. Registry ID: NCT04136002. cards.headline: Shaukat 2025 (PREEMPT CRC): a second blood test, in 27,010 people — 79.2% sensitivity for cancer, 91.5% specificity, and 12.5% sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions, below its own prespecified target
cards.summary: Shaukat 2025 (PREEMPT CRC): a second blood test, in 27,010 people — 79.2% sensitivity for cancer, 91.5% specificity, and 12.5% sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions, below its own prespecified target
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic accuracy study (Shaukat 2025, PREEMPT CRC)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre cross-sectional study at 201 centres: 27,010 evaluable asymptomatic average-risk adults aged 45–85, all undergoing screening colonoscopy with histopathology as the reference; blood drawn before colonoscopy, both sides blinded.
cards.result: Sensitivity for colorectal cancer was 79.2% (57 of 72 cancers; 95% CI 68.4 to 86.9) and specificity for advanced colorectal neoplasia 91.5%. The positive predictive value for advanced neoplasia was 15.5% and the negative predictive value 90.8%. Sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions was 12.5% (321 of 2,567), which did not meet the prespecified acceptance criterion. The record describes an investigational test and names no commercial product.
cards.watchOut: Only 72 cancers in 27,010 people — the sensitivity estimate is statistically fragile, and the study answers an accuracy question only: whether offering a blood test actually gets unscreened people screened, and whether that reduces deaths, is untested here.
cards.source: Shaukat A et al. Clinical validation of a circulating tumor DNA-based blood test to screen for colorectal cancer (PREEMPT CRC). JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40455622. Registry ID: NCT04369053. cards.headline: Synthesis: two large prospective studies agree — about 4 in 5 cancers detected, about 9 in 10 without advanced neoplasia test negative, and only about 1 in 8 advanced adenomas found
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large prospective studies agree — about 4 in 5 cancers detected, about 9 in 10 without advanced neoplasia test negative, and only about 1 in 8 advanced adenomas found
cards.people: Two prospective accuracy studies with colonoscopy reference standards: ECLIPSE (7,861 evaluable) and PREEMPT CRC (27,010 evaluable), together roughly 35,000 average-risk screening-age adults.
cards.result: Cancer sensitivity 83.1% and 79.2%; specificity for advanced neoplasia 89.6% and 91.5%; advanced-precancerous-lesion sensitivity 13.2% and 12.5%. The consistent picture: a blood test is a reasonable cancer-detection net for people who will not take any other test, and a poor precancer-prevention tool, because the lesions screening exists to remove are the ones it cannot see.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is not outcome: no randomised trial has yet shown that blood-based screening reduces colorectal cancer incidence or mortality, and a positive blood test still requires the colonoscopy the patient was avoiding. Compare the stool-DNA balance at shelf #2622 and colonoscopy-based screening shelves before quoting these numbers as a screening recommendation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chung DC et al. N Engl J Med. 2024 (PMID: 38477985); Shaukat A et al. JAMA. 2025 (PMID: 40455622).
