shelves.title: Multitarget stool DNA versus FIT: about 93% of cancers and 43% of advanced adenomas detected, against FIT's 67–74% and 23% — paid for with roughly double the false positives
shelves.question: In screening-age adults, does multitarget stool DNA testing detect more cancers and advanced adenomas than FIT, and at what false-positive cost?
shelves.mesh: Actins/genetics · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Morphogenetic Protein 3/genetics · Chromosome Aberrations · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/epidemiology/genetics · *DNA Mutational Analysis · DNA, Neoplasm/analysis/genetics · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Feces/chemistry · Female · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Humans · Immunologic Techniques · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Middle Aged · Muscle Proteins/genetics · Mutation · Nerve Tissue Proteins/genetics · Occult Blood · Precancerous Conditions/diagnosis/epidemiology/genetics · Proto-Oncogene Proteins/genetics · Proto-Oncogene Proteins p21(ras) · ras Proteins/genetics
shelves.balance: Three prospective studies against a colonoscopy reference standard give a consistent exchange. The multitarget stool DNA test detects more disease than a single FIT: in DeeP-C (Imperiale 2014, PMID: 24645800), 92.3% of cancers versus 73.8% and 42.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 23.8%; in BLUE-C (Imperiale 2024, PMID: 38477986), the next-generation test detected 93.9% of cancers versus 67.3% and 43.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 23.3%. The same direction held in Alaska Native people (Redwood 2016, PMID: 26520415). The cost is specificity: 86.6% (first generation) and 90.6% (next generation) versus about 95% for FIT — in absolute terms roughly 9–13 false positives per 100 people without advanced neoplasia, against about 5, each buying a colonoscopy. What no study here shows is a programme outcome: FIT is meant to be repeated annually, stool DNA three-yearly, and neither mortality nor cumulative programme detection is measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective accuracy studies, two manufacturer-funded, no outcomes trial). The blood-based test comparison is at shelf #2621.

cards.headline: Imperiale 2014 (DeeP-C): multitarget stool DNA found 92.3% of cancers and 42.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 73.8% and 23.8% for FIT — with specificity 86.6% versus 94.9%
cards.summary: Imperiale 2014 (DeeP-C): multitarget stool DNA found 92.3% of cancers and 42.4% of advanced precancerous lesions versus 73.8% and 23.8% for FIT — with specificity 86.6% versus 94.9%
cards.people: 9,989 evaluable asymptomatic average-risk adults undergoing screening colonoscopy; the multitarget stool DNA test (KRAS mutations, NDRG4/BMP3 methylation, plus a haemoglobin immunoassay) and a commercial FIT were each compared against colonoscopy, processed independently of its findings.
cards.result: Sensitivity for colorectal cancer: 92.3% with stool DNA versus 73.8% with FIT (P = 0.002). Sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions: 42.4% versus 23.8% (P < 0.001); for polyps with high-grade dysplasia 69.2% versus 46.2%; for sessile serrated polyps ≥1 cm, 42.4% versus 5.1%. Specificity among participants with nonadvanced or negative findings was 86.6% versus 94.9% (P < 0.001) — roughly 13 versus 5 false positives per 100 people without advanced lesions. The numbers needed to screen to detect one cancer were 154 (colonoscopy), 166 (stool DNA) and 208 (FIT). Funded by Exact Sciences; the record names the funder but does not print a brand name for the test.
cards.watchOut: A single-test comparison at one point in time: FIT is designed to be repeated annually and stool DNA every three years, so cumulative programme sensitivity narrows the gap this head-to-head snapshot shows. The specificity deficit is real and recurring — each round sends roughly 1 in 8–10 lesion-free people to colonoscopy.
cards.source: Imperiale TF et al. Multitarget stool DNA testing for colorectal-cancer screening (DeeP-C). N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 24645800. Registry ID: NCT01397747. cards.headline: Imperiale 2024 (BLUE-C): the next-generation stool DNA test kept the pattern — cancer sensitivity 93.9% versus 67.3% for FIT, advanced-lesion sensitivity 43.4% versus 23.3%, specificity 90.6% versus 94.8%
cards.summary: Imperiale 2024 (BLUE-C): the next-generation stool DNA test kept the pattern — cancer sensitivity 93.9% versus 67.3% for FIT, advanced-lesion sensitivity 43.4% versus 23.3%, specificity 90.6% versus 94.8%
cards.people: 20,176 asymptomatic adults aged 40 or older undergoing screening colonoscopy: 98 with colorectal cancer, 2,144 with advanced precancerous lesions, 6,973 with nonadvanced adenomas and 10,961 with nonneoplastic findings or a negative colonoscopy.
cards.result: With the next-generation test, sensitivity for colorectal cancer was 93.9% (95% CI 87.1 to 97.7) and specificity for advanced neoplasia 90.6% (90.1 to 91.0); sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions was 43.4% (41.3 to 45.6). FIT in the same participants: 67.3% sensitivity for cancer, 23.3% for advanced precancerous lesions, 94.8% specificity for advanced neoplasia. All sensitivity comparisons favoured stool DNA (P < 0.001) and the specificity comparison favoured FIT (P < 0.001). Funded by Exact Sciences; the record names the funder but does not print a brand name for the test.
cards.watchOut: An industry-funded validation of the manufacturer's own successor product, with FIT as a one-off comparator rather than a repeated annual programme. The improved specificity (90.6% versus 86.6% for the first-generation test) still leaves about twice FIT's false-positive rate.
cards.source: Imperiale TF et al. Next-generation multitarget stool DNA test for colorectal cancer screening (BLUE-C). N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38477986. Registry ID: NCT04144738. cards.headline: Redwood 2016: in Alaska Native people — among the world's highest colorectal cancer rates — stool DNA detected 49% of screening-relevant neoplasia versus 28% for FIT, and all 10 cancers
cards.summary: Redwood 2016: in Alaska Native people — among the world's highest colorectal cancer rates — stool DNA detected 49% of screening-relevant neoplasia versus 28% for FIT, and all 10 cancers
cards.people: Prospective cross-sectional study of asymptomatic Alaska Native adults aged 40–85 undergoing screening or surveillance colonoscopy (868 enrolled, 661 completed), a population with limited access to endoscopy.
cards.result: Detection of screening-relevant neoplasia was 49% with multitarget stool DNA versus 28% with FIT (P < .001); in the screening subgroup, 50% versus 31% (P = .01). Detection of adenomas ≥2 cm was 62% versus 29% (P = .05), rising to 80% for lesions ≥3 cm. For the 10 cancers, detection was 100% versus 80% (P = .48). Specificity was 93% versus 96% (P = .03).
cards.watchOut: Small numbers where it matters most — 10 cancers — and a mixed screening/surveillance population, so the cancer figure (100% versus 80%) is compatible with almost any true difference. Its value is showing the same direction of effect in a high-incidence, low-access population, not in refining the estimates.
cards.source: Redwood DG et al. Stool DNA testing for screening detection of colorectal neoplasia in Alaska Native people. Mayo Clin Proc. 2016. PMID: 26520415. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: across three prospective studies, stool DNA detects roughly a fifth more cancers and twice the advanced adenomas of a single FIT — and roughly doubles the false-positive rate
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three prospective studies, stool DNA detects roughly a fifth more cancers and twice the advanced adenomas of a single FIT — and roughly doubles the false-positive rate
cards.people: Three prospective accuracy studies against colonoscopy: DeeP-C (9,989 participants), BLUE-C (20,176) and an Alaska Native cohort (661), spanning the first- and next-generation versions of the multitarget stool DNA test.
cards.result: Cancer sensitivity 92.3% and 93.9% for stool DNA versus 73.8% and 67.3% for FIT; advanced-precancerous-lesion sensitivity 42.4% and 43.4% versus 23.8% and 23.3%; specificity for advanced neoplasia 86.6% (first generation) and 90.6% (next generation) versus 94.9% and 94.8%. In absolute terms: of 100 people without advanced neoplasia, about 9–13 test positive on stool DNA versus about 5 on FIT — each a colonoscopy referral.
cards.watchOut: All three studies are single-round accuracy comparisons, two of them funded by the test's manufacturer; none measures what programmes deliver — mortality, or cumulative detection under annual FIT versus three-yearly stool DNA. The blood-test comparison is at shelf #2621.
cards.source: Synthesis of Imperiale TF et al. N Engl J Med. 2014 (PMID: 24645800); Imperiale TF et al. N Engl J Med. 2024 (PMID: 38477986); Redwood DG et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2016 (PMID: 26520415).

shelves.title: CT colonography versus colonoscopy: 90% of large lesions found, and in a randomised trial its higher uptake made the population yield equal — with a third of scanned patients still needing further investigation
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults invited to colorectal screening, does CT colonography find as many cancers and large polyps as colonoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Adenoma/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Aged · Colon/diagnostic imaging · Colonic Polyps/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging/pathology · *Colonography, Computed Tomographic · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Predictive Value of Tests · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: CT colonography finds most of what matters and trades accuracy for acceptability. Against colonoscopy in 2,531 asymptomatic adults (Johnson 2008, PMID: 18799557), it identified 90% of people with adenomas or cancers ≥10 mm, but only 78% of those with lesions ≥6 mm, with a positive predictive value of 0.23. In the randomised COCOS invitation trial (Stoop 2012, PMID: 22088831), participation was higher for CT colonography than colonoscopy (34% versus 22% relative; relative risk 1.56), which exactly offset colonoscopy's higher per-participant yield: advanced neoplasia found per 100 invitees was 2.1 versus 1.9. In symptomatic patients (Atkin 2013, PMID: 23414650 — a different population, flagged on its card), detection was equal at 11%, but 30.0% of the CT group needed further colonic investigation versus 8.2%. So: as a programme, CT colonography can find as many cancers and large polyps per person invited; as a test, it misses about 1 in 10 large lesions and sends a substantial minority on to colonoscopy anyway. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: two randomised trials plus a large accuracy study).

cards.headline: Johnson 2008 (ACRIN 6664): CT colonography identified 90% of people with adenomas or cancers ≥10 mm — and 78% of those with lesions ≥6 mm
cards.summary: Johnson 2008 (ACRIN 6664): CT colonography identified 90% of people with adenomas or cancers ≥10 mm — and 78% of those with lesions ≥6 mm
cards.people: 2,600 asymptomatic adults aged 50 or older at 15 US centres, each undergoing CT colonography followed by optical colonoscopy with histology as the reference standard; complete data for 2,531 (97%).
cards.result: Per-patient sensitivity for large (≥10 mm) adenomas and cancers was 0.90 (±0.03), specificity 0.86, positive predictive value 0.23 and negative predictive value 0.99; per-polyp sensitivity for large lesions was 0.84. For adenomas ≥6 mm, per-patient sensitivity fell to 0.78 — CT colonography missed about 1 in 10 people harbouring a large lesion and about 1 in 5 with a 6 mm lesion.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy in expert hands with tagged, prepared bowel and trained radiologists; the 0.23 positive predictive value means most positive scans do not correspond to a large lesion, and every positive still ends in the colonoscopy the patient was trying to avoid. Smaller (6–9 mm) lesions — the ones a surveillance strategy must handle — are where the test is weakest.
cards.source: Johnson CD et al. Accuracy of CT colonography for detection of large adenomas and cancers (ACRIN 6664). N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18799557. Registry ID: NCT00084929. cards.headline: Stoop 2012 (COCOS): in a randomised invitation trial, more people accepted CT colonography than colonoscopy (34% versus 22% relative) — and the yield of advanced neoplasia per 100 invitees came out the same
cards.summary: Stoop 2012 (COCOS): in a randomised invitation trial, more people accepted CT colonography than colonoscopy (34% versus 22% relative) — and the yield of advanced neoplasia per 100 invitees came out the same
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of screening invitation (Stoop 2012, COCOS)
cards.people: Population-based randomised trial in Amsterdam and Rotterdam: 5,924 people aged 50–75 invited to colonoscopy screening and 2,920 to non-cathartic CT colonography; CT-positive participants (lesions ≥10 mm) were offered colonoscopy, those with 6–9 mm lesions surveillance.
cards.result: Participation was 22% for colonoscopy versus 34% for CT colonography (relative risk 1.56, 95% CI 1.46 to 1.68). Per 100 participants, colonoscopy found more advanced neoplasia (8.7 versus 6.1; relative risk 1.46, 1.06 to 2.03), but per 100 invitees the yield was nearly identical — 1.9 versus 2.1 for all advanced neoplasia and 1.5 versus 2.0 for lesions ≥10 mm. Serious adverse events were two post-polypectomy bleeds after colonoscopy and three in the CT pathway.
cards.watchOut: A Dutch population with low baseline uptake of colonoscopy screening: where colonoscopy participation is already high, the uptake advantage shrinks and colonoscopy's per-participant yield advantage dominates. Non-cathartic preparation was used, which is not the protocol in the ACRIN accuracy study.
cards.source: Stoop EM et al. Participation and yield of colonoscopy versus non-cathartic CT colonography in population-based screening (COCOS). Lancet Oncol. 2012. PMID: 22088831. Registry ID: NTR1829 (Dutch Trial Register). cards.headline: Atkin 2013 (SIGGAR): in symptomatic patients, CT colonography and colonoscopy detected cancer or large polyps at the same rate (11%) — but 30.0% of the CT group needed further colonic investigation versus 8.2%
cards.summary: Atkin 2013 (SIGGAR): in symptomatic patients, CT colonography and colonoscopy detected cancer or large polyps at the same rate (11%) — but 30.0% of the CT group needed further colonic investigation versus 8.2%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, symptomatic patients (Atkin 2013, SIGGAR)
cards.people: Pragmatic multicentre randomised trial in 21 UK hospitals: 1,610 patients aged 55 or older with symptoms suggestive of colorectal cancer, assigned to colonoscopy (1,047 analysed) or CT colonography (533 analysed). A symptomatic, not a screening, population — included because it is the largest randomised head-to-head of the two tests.
cards.result: Detection rates of colorectal cancer or large (≥10 mm) polyps were 11% in both groups. Additional colonic investigation was required in 160 of 533 (30.0%) after CT colonography versus 86 of 1,047 (8.2%) after colonoscopy (relative risk 3.65, 95% CI 2.87 to 4.65); almost half the post-CT referrals were for small polyps or clinical uncertainty with low predictive value. CT colonography missed 1 of 29 colorectal cancers; colonoscopy missed none of 55. Serious adverse events were rare with both.
cards.watchOut: Symptomatic patients with an 11% prevalence of cancer or large polyps are not a screening population, and the referral-rate problem SIGGAR exposes — small polyps and uncertainty triggering colonoscopy anyway — is a protocol problem as much as a test problem: the authors themselves call for guidelines to cut it.
cards.source: Atkin W et al. Computed tomographic colonography versus colonoscopy for investigation of patients with symptoms suggestive of colorectal cancer (SIGGAR). Lancet. 2013. PMID: 23414650. Registry ID: ISRCTN95152621. cards.headline: Synthesis: CT colonography finds about 9 in 10 large lesions; in the one randomised programme test, easier uptake exactly offset its lower per-participant yield
cards.summary: Synthesis: CT colonography finds about 9 in 10 large lesions; in the one randomised programme test, easier uptake exactly offset its lower per-participant yield
cards.people: One large accuracy study in asymptomatic adults (ACRIN 6664, 2,531 complete datasets), one randomised invitation trial (COCOS, 8,844 invitees) and one randomised trial in symptomatic patients (SIGGAR, 1,580 analysed).
cards.result: Per-patient sensitivity 0.90 for lesions ≥10 mm and 0.78 for lesions ≥6 mm; population yield of advanced neoplasia per invitee 2.1 (CT colonography) versus 1.9 (colonoscopy) per 100, driven by participation of 34% versus 22% relative. The structural costs: about 30% of CT-examined patients in SIGGAR needed further colonic investigation, and positive scans carry a predictive value of only about 0.23 for a large lesion.
cards.watchOut: No trial here measures cancer mortality by test, and the accuracy and programme studies used different preparations and positivity thresholds, so the numbers are not interchangeable. Extracolonic findings on CT — a real source of downstream testing — are not quantified in these records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Johnson CD et al. N Engl J Med. 2008 (PMID: 18799557); Stoop EM et al. Lancet Oncol. 2012 (PMID: 22088831); Atkin W et al. Lancet. 2013 (PMID: 23414650).

shelves.title: MRI-based prostate screening: insignificant-cancer diagnoses roughly halved in two population trials, significant-cancer detection held or improved — the overdiagnosis half of the bargain, proven; the mortality half, not yet
shelves.question: In men invited to prostate screening, does an MRI-based pathway reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis versus PSA-only screening?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Early Detection of Cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · Follow-Up Studies · Image-Guided Biopsy/adverse effects/statistics & numerical data · *Magnetic Resonance Imaging/statistics & numerical data · Neoplasm Grading · *Prostate/pathology/diagnostic imaging · *Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · *Prostatic Neoplasms/blood/diagnosis/epidemiology/pathology
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence says the MRI pathway buys the trade screening has always wanted. In GÖTEBORG-2 (Hugosson 2024, PMID: 39321360), omitting biopsy after a negative MRI cut diagnoses of clinically insignificant cancer by more than half in relative terms (relative risk 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.57; overall detection 2.8% versus 4.5%), with no significant difference in significant-cancer detection (relative risk 0.84, 0.66 to 1.07) and fewer advanced cancers (15 versus 23). In STHLM3-MRI (Nordström 2021, PMID: 34391509), a risk-model-plus-MRI strategy detected more significant cancers (relative proportion 1.44) and fewer low-grade ones (0.46) than PSA plus systematic biopsy, with fewer biopsies and fewer biopsy infections. PROSTAGRAM (Eldred-Evans 2021, PMID: 33570542) points the same way in a paired comparison. What is not yet shown — anywhere — is a mortality benefit, and the significant-cancer estimate in GÖTEBORG-2 is compatible with a small loss. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: two population randomised trials plus a paired cohort, consistent direction). The MRI-first pathway in men already referred for suspected cancer is homed at shelf #801.

cards.headline: Hugosson 2024 (GÖTEBORG-2): MRI-targeted biopsy only — diagnoses of clinically insignificant cancer fell by more than half relative (RR 0.43), with no significant loss of significant-cancer detection
cards.summary: Hugosson 2024 (GÖTEBORG-2): MRI-targeted biopsy only — diagnoses of clinically insignificant cancer fell by more than half relative (RR 0.43), with no significant loss of significant-cancer detection
cards.people: Population-based Swedish trial: men aged 50–60 invited to PSA screening from 2015; those with PSA ≥3 ng/mL had prostate MRI and were randomised to systematic biopsy (plus targeted if MRI suspicious) or MRI-targeted biopsy only. 6,575 versus 6,578 men; median follow-up 3.9 years, including repeat screening rounds.
cards.result: Prostate cancer was detected in 2.8% of the MRI-targeted group versus 4.5% of the systematic-biopsy group. The relative risk of detecting clinically insignificant (ISUP grade 1) cancer was 0.43 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.57; P < 0.001), and lower still at repeat rounds (0.25) than the first (0.49). For clinically significant cancer (ISUP grade ≥2) the relative risk was 0.84 (0.66 to 1.07) — not statistically significant. Advanced or high-risk cancers numbered 15 versus 23 (relative risk 0.65, 0.34 to 1.24). Five severe adverse events occurred in total.
cards.watchOut: Four years is early: the trial shows the overdiagnosis half of the bargain clearly, but the significant-cancer relative risk of 0.84 has a confidence interval reaching 1.07, and no mortality result exists yet. Men with a negative MRI avoided biopsy entirely — the safety of that omission is supported by the low interval advanced-cancer count, not yet by long-term outcomes.
cards.source: Hugosson J et al. Results after four years of screening for prostate cancer with PSA and MRI (GÖTEBORG-2). N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 39321360. Registry ID: ISRCTN94604465. population-based randomised screening trial (hugosson 2024, göteborg-2) population-based swedish trial: men aged 50–60 invited to psa screening from 2015; those with psa ≥3 ng/ml had prostate mri and were randomised to systematic biopsy (plus targeted if mri suspicious) or mri-targeted biopsy only. 6,575 versus 6,578 men; median follow-up 3.9 years, including repeat screening rounds. prostate cancer was detected in 2.8% of the mri-targeted group versus 4.5% of the systematic-biopsy group. the relative risk of detecting clinically insignificant (isup grade 1) cancer was 0.43 (95% ci 0.32 to 0.57; p < 0.001), and lower still at repeat rounds (0.25) than the first (0.49). for clinically significant cancer (isup grade ≥2) the relative risk was 0.84 (0.66 to 1.07) — not statistically significant. advanced or high-risk cancers numbered 15 versus 23 (relative risk 0.65, 0.34 to 1.24). five severe adverse events occurred in total. four years is early: the trial shows the overdiagnosis half of the bargain clearly, but the significant-cancer relative risk of 0.84 has a confidence interval reaching 1.07, and no mortality result exists yet. men with a negative mri avoided biopsy entirely — the safety of that omission is supported by the low interval advanced-cancer count, not yet by long-term outcomes. hugosson j et al. results after four years of screening for prostate cancer with psa and mri (göteborg-2). n engl j med. 2024. pmid: 39321360. registry id: isrctn94604465. mesh: humans · male · middle aged · *early detection of cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · follow-up studies · image-guided biopsy/adverse effects/statistics & numerical data · *magnetic resonance imaging/statistics & numerical data · neoplasm grading · *prostate/pathology/diagnostic imaging · *prostate-specific antigen/blood · *prostatic neoplasms/blood/diagnosis/epidemiology/pathology

cards.headline: Nordström 2021 (STHLM3-MRI): a risk-prediction blood test plus MRI-targeted biopsy detected more significant cancers (relative proportion 1.44) and fewer low-grade cancers (0.46) than PSA plus systematic biopsy
cards.summary: Nordström 2021 (STHLM3-MRI): a risk-prediction blood test plus MRI-targeted biopsy detected more significant cancers (relative proportion 1.44) and fewer low-grade cancers (0.46) than PSA plus systematic biopsy
cards.people: Population-based randomised non-inferiority trial in Stockholm: 49,118 men aged 50–74 invited, 12,750 enrolled with blood samples, and 2,293 with elevated risk (PSA ≥3 ng/mL or Stockholm3 score ≥0.11) randomised to systematic biopsy or to biparametric MRI with targeted plus systematic biopsy if MRI-positive.
cards.result: Compared with PSA plus systematic biopsy, the Stockholm3-plus-MRI strategy detected clinically significant cancer in 3.0% versus 2.1% of men tested (relative proportion 1.44, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.81) and low-grade cancer in 0.7% versus 1.4% (0.46, 0.32 to 0.66), with fewer biopsy procedures overall. The Stockholm3 score discriminated better than PSA (area under the curve 0.76 versus 0.60). Antibiotic prescriptions for infection were fewer in the experimental group (1.8% versus 4.4%) as were hospital admissions (1.2% versus 3.4%).
cards.watchOut: A paired strategy comparison — risk model plus MRI — so the gain cannot be credited to MRI alone; the Stockholm3 test is a proprietary panel (the record names the test; the strategy's performance may not transfer to PSA-only triage). One screening round only: nothing here speaks to repeat rounds or mortality.
cards.source: Nordström T et al. Prostate cancer screening using a combination of risk-prediction, MRI, and targeted prostate biopsies (STHLM3-MRI). Lancet Oncol. 2021. PMID: 34391509. Registry ID: NCT03377881. cards.headline: Eldred-Evans 2021 (PROSTAGRAM): in 408 unscreened men given all three tests, a short MRI at a strict threshold flagged a similar share as PSA — and would have found 11 significant cancers to PSA's 7
cards.summary: Eldred-Evans 2021 (PROSTAGRAM): in 408 unscreened men given all three tests, a short MRI at a strict threshold flagged a similar share as PSA — and would have found 11 significant cancers to PSA's 7
cards.people: Prospective population-based cohort at UK primary care practices: 408 men aged 50–69 consented to PSA, short non-contrast MRI and ultrasonography, each read blinded; any positive test triggered systematic biopsy, with fusion-targeted biopsies added for imaging-positive men.
cards.result: Positive results: MRI score 3–5 in 17.7%, ultrasonography 23.7%, PSA ≥3 ng/mL in 9.9%. At the stricter MRI threshold (score 4–5), positivity was 10.6% — statistically indistinguishable from PSA's 9.9%. Clinically significant cancers detected: 7 by PSA, 14 by MRI at score 3–5, 11 by MRI at score 4–5, 9 and 4 by ultrasonography at the two thresholds. Clinically insignificant cancers: 6 by PSA, 5 by MRI at score 4–5, 13 by ultrasonography at score 3–5. There was no evidence ultrasonography outperformed PSA.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-round: 408 of 2,034 invited men attended (20%), so the volunteers may not represent a screening population, and cancer counts are in single figures. It compares tests head-to-head within men — a design that cannot show what a programme built on any one of them would do over time.
cards.source: Eldred-Evans D et al. Population-based prostate cancer screening with magnetic resonance imaging or ultrasonography: the IP1-PROSTAGRAM study. JAMA Oncol. 2021. PMID: 33570542. cards.headline: Synthesis: two population randomised trials converge — MRI-based pathways roughly halve insignificant-cancer diagnoses while holding or improving significant-cancer detection
cards.summary: Synthesis: two population randomised trials converge — MRI-based pathways roughly halve insignificant-cancer diagnoses while holding or improving significant-cancer detection
cards.people: GÖTEBORG-2 (13,153 randomised men, repeat rounds, 3.9 years), STHLM3-MRI (2,293 randomised after risk triage) and the PROSTAGRAM paired cohort (408 men).
cards.result: Insignificant cancer: relative risk 0.43 (GÖTEBORG-2) and relative proportion 0.46 for low-grade cancer (STHLM3-MRI). Significant cancer: relative risk 0.84 (0.66 to 1.07) when biopsy is omitted after a negative MRI, and relative proportion 1.44 (1.15 to 1.81) when a risk model triages to MRI-targeted biopsy. Advanced or high-risk cancers were fewer, not more, in the MRI arm of GÖTEBORG-2 (15 versus 23).
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint here is detection, not death: whether halving overdiagnosis while detecting significant cancers a little earlier converts into fewer prostate-cancer deaths is the unanswered question, and it is the question PSA screening itself took decades to answer. The MRI-first pathway for men already referred with suspected cancer is a different question, homed at shelf #801.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hugosson J et al. N Engl J Med. 2024 (PMID: 39321360); Nordström T et al. Lancet Oncol. 2021 (PMID: 34391509); Eldred-Evans D et al. JAMA Oncol. 2021 (PMID: 33570542).

shelves.title: Supplemental ultrasound after mammography: about 4 extra cancers per 1,000 screens, mostly small and node-negative, and interval cancers halved in the randomised trial — bought with a biopsy yield of only about 1 in 10
shelves.question: In women with dense breasts and a negative mammogram, does supplemental ultrasound screening find additional cancers?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Breast Neoplasms/diagnosis · Carcinoma, Ductal, Breast · Carcinoma, Lobular · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Female · Humans · Japan · *Mammography · Middle Aged · Sensitivity and Specificity · *Ultrasonography, Mammary
shelves.balance: Yes, it finds more cancers — the question is the exchange rate. In the J-START randomised trial (Ohuchi 2016, PMID: 26547101), adding ultrasound to mammography in women aged 40–49 raised sensitivity from 77.0% to 91.1%, detection from 0.32% to 0.50%, and halved interval cancers (0.05% versus 0.10%), while specificity fell from 91.4% to 87.7%. In ACRIN 6666 (Berg 2008, PMID: 18477782; Berg 2012, PMID: 22474203), in elevated-risk women with dense tissue, the supplemental yield was 4.2 cancers per 1,000 women at the first screen and 3.7 per 1,000 at incidence screens — mostly small, invasive, node-negative cancers — while the positive predictive value of an ultrasound-prompted biopsy was only about 9–16%. Neither study measures mortality, and J-START's extra stage 0 disease warns that some of the gain is overdiagnosis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: a large randomised trial plus a three-round prospective cohort). The MRI comparison for high-risk women is homed at shelf #800.

cards.headline: Ohuchi 2016 (J-START): adding ultrasound to mammography raised sensitivity from 77.0% to 91.1% and cut interval cancers from 0.10% to 0.05% — at a specificity cost (87.7% versus 91.4%)
cards.summary: Ohuchi 2016 (J-START): adding ultrasound to mammography raised sensitivity from 77.0% to 91.1% and cut interval cancers from 0.10% to 0.05% — at a specificity cost (87.7% versus 91.4%)
cards.people: Randomised trial at 42 Japanese sites: 72,998 asymptomatic women aged 40–49 assigned to mammography plus ultrasonography (36,859) or mammography alone (36,139), screened twice over 2 years; first-round results reported here. A general population of younger women rather than a density-selected one — in this age group dense breasts are the norm.
cards.result: Sensitivity was 91.1% (95% CI 87.2 to 95.0) with adjunctive ultrasound versus 77.0% (70.3 to 83.7) without (P = 0.0004); specificity was 87.7% versus 91.4% (P < 0.0001). More cancers were detected (0.50% versus 0.32%, P = 0.0003), more of them at stage 0 or I (71.3% versus 52.0% of those with staging, P = 0.0194), and interval cancers were fewer (0.05% versus 0.10%, P = 0.034).
cards.watchOut: Women in their forties, screened in a Japanese programme with its own recall thresholds: the absolute detection gain (0.18 percentage points) and the false-positive burden will differ in older or density-selected populations. Mortality was not an outcome — earlier stage and fewer interval cancers are surrogates, and some of the extra stage 0 disease is the overdiagnosis screening critics predict.
cards.source: Ohuchi N et al. Sensitivity and specificity of mammography and adjunctive ultrasonography to screen for breast cancer in the Japan Strategic Anti-cancer Randomized Trial (J-START). Lancet. 2016. PMID: 26547101. Registry ID: UMIN000000757. cards.headline: Berg 2008 (ACRIN 6666): in women at elevated risk with dense tissue, one supplemental ultrasound added 4.2 cancers per 1,000 women screened — and dropped the biopsy positive predictive value to 8.9%
cards.summary: Berg 2008 (ACRIN 6666): in women at elevated risk with dense tissue, one supplemental ultrasound added 4.2 cancers per 1,000 women screened — and dropped the biopsy positive predictive value to 8.9%
cards.people: Prospective paired study at 21 sites: 2,809 women at elevated breast-cancer risk, all with at least heterogeneously dense tissue in one quadrant, underwent mammography and physician-performed ultrasound in randomised order, each read masked to the other; reference standard available for 2,637.
cards.result: Diagnostic yield rose from 7.6 per 1,000 women (mammography alone) to 11.8 per 1,000 (combined) — a supplemental yield of 4.2 per 1,000 (95% CI 1.1 to 7.2). Of the 12 cancers found by ultrasound alone, 11 (92%) were invasive, median size 10 mm, and 8 of 9 with nodal data were node-negative. The price: the positive predictive value of a biopsy recommendation was 22.6% for mammography, 8.9% for ultrasound and 11.2% for the combination — most ultrasound-prompted biopsies found no cancer.
cards.watchOut: Elevated-risk women examined by physicians, not technologists, in a research network — yields and false-positive rates in routine practice, with less experienced operators, are unlikely to be better. A single screen: the incidence-round data (next card) show the supplemental yield persists but so does the false-positive accumulation.
cards.source: Berg WA et al. Combined screening with ultrasound and mammography vs mammography alone in women at elevated risk of breast cancer (ACRIN 6666). JAMA. 2008. PMID: 18477782. cards.headline: Berg 2012 (ACRIN 6666, three annual rounds): supplemental ultrasound kept finding 3.7 cancers per 1,000 incidence screens; combined sensitivity 0.76 versus 0.52 for mammography alone, specificity 0.84 versus 0.91
cards.summary: Berg 2012 (ACRIN 6666, three annual rounds): supplemental ultrasound kept finding 3.7 cancers per 1,000 incidence screens; combined sensitivity 0.76 versus 0.52 for mammography alone, specificity 0.84 versus 0.91
cards.type: Prospective paired diagnostic study, three annual rounds (Berg 2012, ACRIN 6666)
cards.people: The ACRIN 6666 cohort over three annual paired screens: 2,662 women completing 7,473 mammogram-plus-ultrasound screenings, with an MRI substudy in 612 women after the third round.
cards.result: Across the second and third (incidence) rounds, supplemental ultrasound identified 3.7 cancers per 1,000 screens (95% CI 2.1 to 5.8). Sensitivity was 0.76 for mammography plus ultrasound versus 0.52 for mammography alone; specificity 0.84 versus 0.91; biopsy positive predictive value 0.16 versus 0.38. Screens needed to detect one cancer: 127 for mammography, 234 for supplemental ultrasound. A single MRI after negative mammography and ultrasound found a further 14.7 cancers per 1,000 (3.5 to 25.9) at 0.65 specificity — the MRI comparison is homed at shelf #800.
cards.watchOut: The same cohort as the 2008 card, not independent confirmation — and the women were at elevated risk, so absolute yields overstate what an average-risk dense-breast population would see. Even so, the false-positive arithmetic compounds annually: a specificity of 0.84 means roughly 1 in 6 cancer-free women recalled or biopsied per round.
cards.source: Berg WA et al. Detection of breast cancer with addition of annual screening ultrasound or a single screening MRI to mammography in women with elevated breast cancer risk (ACRIN 6666). cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — supplemental ultrasound finds additional cancers, about 4 per 1,000 screens, mostly small invasive node-negative ones, and roughly doubles the false-positive burden
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — supplemental ultrasound finds additional cancers, about 4 per 1,000 screens, mostly small invasive node-negative ones, and roughly doubles the false-positive burden
cards.people: One randomised trial in women aged 40–49 (J-START, 72,998 women) and one prospective paired cohort at elevated risk with dense tissue (ACRIN 6666, 2,637–2,662 women, three rounds).
cards.result: Detection: +0.18 percentage points in J-START (0.50% versus 0.32%) and +4.2 per 1,000 in ACRIN's prevalence round, +3.7 per 1,000 in incidence rounds. Sensitivity: 91.1% versus 77.0% (J-START) and 0.76 versus 0.52 (ACRIN). Interval cancers halved in J-START (0.05% versus 0.10%). Specificity fell by 3.7 points in J-START and 7 points in ACRIN; the biopsy positive predictive value for ultrasound-prompted workup was about 9–16%.
cards.watchOut: Detection is not mortality: no study here shows fewer breast-cancer deaths, and J-START's stage shift includes more stage 0 disease. For women at high risk, MRI finds several times more cancers than ultrasound does — that comparison lives at shelf #800, and this shelf should not be quoted as settling the supplemental-imaging choice.

shelves.title: Lengthening lung screening intervals: two years after a negative round looks safe in the one randomised test — 2.5 years in NELSON let interval cancers and late stages climb
shelves.question: After a negative lung-cancer screening round, can screening intervals be safely lengthened beyond one year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cause of Death · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Female · Humans · Incidence · Italy/epidemiology · Lung Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/mortality/pathology/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · *Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: The evidence supports one careful step, not two. MILD randomised smokers with negative screens to annual or biennial low-dose CT (Pastorino 2019, PMID: 31336289): at 10 years, lung-cancer mortality on biennial screening was HR 1.10 versus annual — statistically indistinguishable, but with a confidence interval (0.59 to 2.05) too wide to prove equivalence — while saving 44% of follow-up scans in baseline-negative participants and showing no increase in interval or advanced-stage cancers. NELSON's experience warns against going further: after a 2.5-year interval, interval cancers rose (28, versus 5 and 19 after shorter gaps) and the advanced-stage share of screen-detected cancers rose to 17.3% from 6.8% (Yousaf-Khan 2017, PMID: 27364640), against a background sensitivity of 84.6% (Horeweg 2014, PMID: 25282284). So: lengthening to two years after a negative round is a reasonable, evidence-backed economy; beyond that, the one large dataset shows the benefit leaking away. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single small randomised interval comparison plus within-trial analyses). Whether screening itself reduces lung-cancer deaths is homed at shelf #164.

cards.headline: Pastorino 2019 (MILD): biennial screening after a negative baseline produced 10-year lung-cancer mortality statistically indistinguishable from annual screening (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.59 to 2.05) — and saved 44% of scans
cards.summary: Pastorino 2019 (MILD): biennial screening after a negative baseline produced 10-year lung-cancer mortality statistically indistinguishable from annual screening (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.59 to 2.05) — and saved 44% of scans
cards.people: Randomised comparison inside the Italian MILD trial: 2,376 screening-arm participants assigned to annual (1,190) or biennial (1,186) low-dose CT, median screening period 6.2 years, 23,083 person-years of follow-up.
cards.result: At 10 years, overall mortality in the biennial arm versus annual was HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.12) and lung-cancer-specific mortality HR 1.10 (0.59 to 2.05) — neither significantly different. Biennial screening saved 44% of follow-up scans in participants with a negative baseline examination and 38% overall, with no increase in stage II–IV or interval cancers. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval is the story: HR 1.10 with limits 0.59 to 2.05 cannot exclude a doubling of lung-cancer mortality on biennial screening. MILD was small, its screening arm was recruited over a long period, and 'no increase in interval cancers' is an underpowered observation — this card supports 'two years looks reasonable', not 'two years is proven equivalent'.

cards.headline: Yousaf-Khan 2017 (NELSON): after a 2.5-year interval, interval cancers jumped (28, versus 5 and 19 after shorter gaps) and screen-detected cancers were more often stage IIIb/IV (17.3% versus 6.8%)
cards.summary: Yousaf-Khan 2017 (NELSON): after a 2.5-year interval, interval cancers jumped (28, versus 5 and 19 after shorter gaps) and screen-detected cancers were more often stage IIIb/IV (17.3% versus 6.8%)
cards.people: Final (fourth) round analysis of the Dutch-Belgian NELSON trial: 7,915 people in the screening arm, screened at baseline, 1 year, 2 years and then after a 2.5-year interval, with nodule volumetry.
cards.result: In round 4, 46 cancers were screen-detected and 28 interval cancers had appeared since round 3 — more interval cancers than in the 1-year interval (5) or the 2-year interval (19). The share of stage IIIb/IV cancers among screen-detected cases was 17.3% after the 2.5-year gap versus 6.8% in the 1-year-interval round (P = 0.02) and 5.2% after the 2-year interval (P = 0.10). The authors conclude the 2.5-year interval reduced the effect of screening.
cards.watchOut: Not a randomised interval comparison — the 2.5-year gap came last, in an older cohort with more accumulated risk, and round-to-round comparisons are confounded by round order and nodule-protocol changes. It is a warning signal about stretching too far, not a precise estimate of the harm.

cards.headline: Horeweg 2014 (NELSON): across the first three rounds, screening sensitivity was 84.6% and specificity 98.6% — and the 35 interval cancers were far more advanced than screen-detected ones (83% versus 22% stage III–IV)
cards.summary: Horeweg 2014 (NELSON): across the first three rounds, screening sensitivity was 84.6% and specificity 98.6% — and the 35 interval cancers were far more advanced than screen-detected ones (83% versus 22% stage III–IV)
cards.people: Prespecified performance analysis of the NELSON screening arm: 7,155 participants attending at least one round, median follow-up 8.16 years, with registry follow-up for interval cancers over the first three rounds plus 2 years.
cards.result: Sensitivity was 84.6% (95% CI 79.6 to 89.2), specificity 98.6%, positive predictive value 40.4% and negative predictive value 99.8%. Thirty-four participants (under 1%) developed 35 interval cancers; 19 (56%) appeared in the first year after screening and 15 (44%) in the second. Interval cancers were diagnosed at stage III–IV in 83% of cases versus 22% of screen-detected cancers (P < 0.0001) and were more often small-cell carcinoma (20% versus 4%).
cards.watchOut: Interval cancers are biologically nastier — fast-growing tumours declare themselves between any pair of scans — so their advanced stage does not by itself prove the interval was too long. What it does show is the margin: with about 1 in 6 cancers already escaping a 1–2-year schedule, there is little slack for longer gaps in unselected smokers.
cards.source: Horeweg N et al. Detection of lung cancer through low-dose CT screening (NELSON): a prespecified analysis of screening test performance and interval cancers. Lancet Oncol. 2014. PMID: 25282284. Registry ID: ISRCTN63545820. cards.headline: Synthesis: two years after a negative round has one small randomised trial behind it; two and a half years has a stage-shift warning against it
cards.summary: Synthesis: two years after a negative round has one small randomised trial behind it; two and a half years has a stage-shift warning against it
cards.people: MILD's randomised annual-versus-biennial comparison (2,376 participants) and NELSON's within-trial interval analyses (7,155–7,915 screened participants) — the only direct evidence on lengthening intervals after negative rounds.
cards.result: Biennial versus annual (MILD): lung-cancer mortality HR 1.10 (0.59 to 2.05), 44% of follow-up scans saved in baseline-negative participants, no observed increase in interval or advanced cancers. A 2.5-year gap (NELSON): interval cancers rose to 28 from 5–19, and the advanced-stage share of screen-detected cancers rose to 17.3% from 6.8%. Baseline screening performance (NELSON): sensitivity 84.6%, specificity 98.6%.
cards.watchOut: Neither source tests risk-stratified intervals (longer gaps only for the lowest-risk negatives), which is where practice is heading; both predate current volumetric and AI-assisted protocols. The mortality case for screening itself is homed at shelf #164 — this shelf assumes screening is happening and asks only how often.

shelves.title: The EarlyCDT autoantibody test shifted lung cancers to earlier stages in one randomised trial — against no screening at all, not against the CT screening it is meant to triage
shelves.question: In smokers eligible for lung screening, does a blood autoantibody test triage who benefits from low-dose CT?
shelves.mesh: *Early Detection of Cancer · Hematologic Tests · Humans · *Lung Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Neoplasm Staging · Scotland/epidemiology
shelves.balance: One trial, carefully read, supports a narrower claim than its headline. In ECLS (Sullivan 2021, PMID: 32732334), 12,208 high-risk Scots were randomised to the EarlyCDT-Lung autoantibody test — with CT follow-up only if positive — or to standard care. At 2 years, cancers in the intervention arm were less often diagnosed at stage III/IV: 58.9% versus 73.2% (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.99). But mortality did not differ significantly, and the control arm received no CT screening at all — so the trial shows a test-plus-CT package beats symptomatic presentation, which was never in doubt, and says nothing about whether the blood test improves on the low-dose CT screening it would actually be triaging. The test-negative arm also went unimaged, a withholding whose cost is folded invisibly into the results. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: a single randomised trial, surrogate stage outcome, no mortality signal). The mortality evidence for low-dose CT itself is homed at shelf #164; screening intervals are at shelf #2626.

cards.headline: Sullivan 2021 (ECLS): test-positive patients sent to CT were diagnosed earlier — 58.9% at stage III/IV versus 73.2% under standard care (HR 0.64) — with no significant mortality difference at 2 years
cards.summary: Sullivan 2021 (ECLS): test-positive patients sent to CT were diagnosed earlier — 58.9% at stage III/IV versus 73.2% under standard care (HR 0.64) — with no significant mortality difference at 2 years
cards.people: Randomised trial in Scotland: 12,208 people at high risk of lung cancer assigned to the EarlyCDT-Lung autoantibody blood test (with 6-monthly low-dose CT for up to 2 years if test-positive) or to standard clinical care; outcomes from validated registry data at 2 years. The test is named in the publication as EarlyCDT-Lung; the record does not name its manufacturer.
cards.result: 127 lung cancers were diagnosed (1.0% of participants). In the intervention arm, 33 of 56 cancers (58.9%) presented at stage III/IV, versus 52 of 71 (73.2%) in the control arm — an absolute difference of about 14 percentage points; the hazard ratio for late-stage presentation was 0.64 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.99). Differences in lung-cancer and all-cause mortality at 2 years were not statistically significant.
cards.watchOut: The comparison that matters was never run: the control arm got standard care (symptomatic presentation), not low-dose CT screening, so ECLS cannot show the blood test adds anything to CT screening itself — the authors say so explicitly. A stage shift at 2 years, without a mortality difference, is a promissory note: stage shifts have failed to convert into mortality benefits before.
cards.source: Sullivan FM et al. Earlier diagnosis of lung cancer in a randomised trial of an autoantibody blood test followed by imaging (ECLS). Eur Respir J. 2021. PMID: 32732334. cards.people: The ECLS randomised trial (12,208 high-risk participants, 2-year outcomes) is the entire direct evidence base for autoantibody triage in lung screening.
cards.result: Late-stage presentation: 58.9% versus 73.2% (hazard ratio 0.64, 0.41 to 0.99). Lung-cancer and all-cause mortality: no significant difference at 2 years. Test-negative participants received no imaging, so the trial also implicitly tests withholding CT from test-negatives — the false-negative cost of that triage cannot be separated from the stage-shift benefit in these results.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote this shelf as evidence about screening efficacy: low-dose CT's mortality benefit is homed at shelf #164, and ECLS compared a test-plus-CT package against no screening at all. shelves.title: Pancreatic surveillance in high-risk people: most cancers found at stage I and a large survival gap against cancers found outside — with lead-time bias entitled to much of the credit, and the yield concentrated in CDKN2A carriers
shelves.question: In adults at high inherited or familial risk of pancreatic cancer, does regular MRI/EUS surveillance find cancer earlier and improve survival?
shelves.mesh: *Carcinoma, Pancreatic Ductal/genetics/pathology/surgery · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Humans · Pancreas/surgery · *Pancreatic Neoplasms/diagnosis/genetics/surgery
shelves.balance: Surveillance does find pancreatic cancer earlier — that much the cohorts establish. In CAPS5 (Dbouk 2022, PMID: 35704792), seven of nine cancers diagnosed during surveillance were stage I, and screen-detected patients had a median survival of 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers diagnosed outside surveillance (hazard ratio 0.13) — a contrast that lead-time and length bias guarantee is flattered, by an amount no observational design can remove. The European experience (Vasen 2016, PMID: 27114589) adds the crucial qualifier: the yield concentrates in CDKN2A mutation carriers (7.3% developed cancer; 75% resected; five-year survival 24%), while in familial kindreds without a known mutation only 0.9% developed a tumour and resections for ultimately low-risk precursor lesions outnumbered cancers found. There is no randomised trial and no unscreened control group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective cohorts only, survival comparisons bias-exposed).

cards.headline: Dbouk 2022 (CAPS5): of nine pancreatic cancers found during surveillance, seven (77.8%) were stage I — and screen-detected patients lived a median 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers found outside surveillance
cards.summary: Dbouk 2022 (CAPS5): of nine pancreatic cancers found during surveillance, seven (77.8%) were stage I — and screen-detected patients lived a median 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers found outside surveillance
cards.people: Prospective multicentre cohort (eight US centres, 2014–2021): 1,461 high-risk individuals enrolled in the Cancer of Pancreas Screening-5 study — 48.5% carrying a pathogenic variant in a pancreatic-cancer susceptibility gene, the rest from familial pancreatic cancer kindreds — under regular MRI/EUS surveillance; the analysis also updates the full CAPS1–5 cohort of 1,731.
cards.result: Ten participants were diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, one after dropping out of surveillance (metastatic). Of the nine diagnosed during surveillance, seven (77.8%) had stage I disease by surgical pathology, one stage II and one stage III; seven of the nine were alive after a median 2.6 years. Eight further patients were resected for worrisome lesions — three with high-grade and five with low-grade dysplasia. Across CAPS1–5, five-year survival for screen-detected pancreatic cancer is 73.3% to date, and median survival 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers diagnosed outside surveillance (hazard ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.50). The record carries no registry ID.
cards.watchOut: The survival contrast is exactly where lead-time and length bias live: surveillance finds cancers earlier by construction, and slow-growing cancers are over-represented among the screen-detected, so some — possibly much — of the 9.8-versus-1.5-year gap would exist even if early treatment changed nothing. There is no unscreened control group, and the comparison group (cancers found outside surveillance) is small and self-selected.
cards.source: Dbouk M et al. The Multicenter Cancer of Pancreas Screening Study: impact on stage and survival (CAPS5). J Clin Oncol. 2022. PMID: 35704792. Registry ID: none in the record. prospective surveillance cohort (dbouk 2022, caps5) prospective multicentre cohort (eight us centres, 2014–2021): 1,461 high-risk individuals enrolled in the cancer of pancreas screening-5 study — 48.5% carrying a pathogenic variant in a pancreatic-cancer susceptibility gene, the rest from familial pancreatic cancer kindreds — under regular mri/eus surveillance; the analysis also updates the full caps1–5 cohort of 1,731. ten participants were diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, one after dropping out of surveillance (metastatic). of the nine diagnosed during surveillance, seven (77.8%) had stage i disease by surgical pathology, one stage ii and one stage iii; seven of the nine were alive after a median 2.6 years. eight further patients were resected for worrisome lesions — three with high-grade and five with low-grade dysplasia. across caps1–5, five-year survival for screen-detected pancreatic cancer is 73.3% to date, and median survival 9.8 years versus 1.5 years for cancers diagnosed outside surveillance (hazard ratio 0.13, 95% ci 0.03 to 0.50). the record carries no registry id. the survival contrast is exactly where lead-time and length bias live: surveillance finds cancers earlier by construction, and slow-growing cancers are over-represented among the screen-detected, so some — possibly much — of the 9.8-versus-1.5-year gap would exist even if early treatment changed nothing. there is no unscreened control group, and the comparison group (cancers found outside surveillance) is small and self-selected. dbouk m et al. the multicenter cancer of pancreas screening study: impact on stage and survival (caps5). j clin oncol. 2022. pmid: 35704792. registry id: none in the record. mesh: *carcinoma, pancreatic ductal/genetics/pathology/surgery · early detection of cancer/methods · humans · pancreas/surgery · *pancreatic neoplasms/diagnosis/genetics/surgery

cards.headline: Vasen 2016 (European expert centres): surveillance worked where the risk was genetic — CDKN2A carriers had a 7.3% cancer yield and 75% resection rate — and barely at all in familial kindreds without a known mutation
cards.summary: Vasen 2016 (European expert centres): surveillance worked where the risk was genetic — CDKN2A carriers had a 7.3% cancer yield and 75% resection rate — and barely at all in familial kindreds without a known mutation
cards.people: Prospective surveillance (annual MRI/MRCP and/or endoscopic ultrasound) at three European expert centres: 411 asymptomatic high-risk individuals — 178 CDKN2A mutation carriers, 214 from familial pancreatic cancer kindreds, and 19 BRCA1/2 or PALB2 carriers.
cards.result: Pancreatic cancer was detected in 13 of 178 CDKN2A carriers (7.3%); the resection rate was 75% and five-year survival 24%. In the familial-kindred cohort, only 2 of 214 (0.9%) developed a pancreatic tumour — one advanced cancer and one early neuroendocrine tumour — while 13 (6.1%) underwent resection for a suspected precursor lesion and only 4 (1.9%) proved to have high-risk lesions. One BRCA2 carrier had pancreatic cancer. No serious complications resulted from the programme.
cards.watchOut: Even in the best subgroup, five-year survival after a screen-detected cancer was 24% — a reminder that 'resectable' pancreatic cancer is still usually lethal, and a check on the CAPS survival figures, which come from a later era and a different case mix. The familial-kindred numbers show the harm side of surveillance: six resections for suspected precursors for every two cancers found, most specimens low-risk.
cards.source: Vasen H et al. Benefit of surveillance for pancreatic cancer in high-risk individuals: outcome of long-term prospective follow-up studies from three European expert centers. J Clin Oncol. 2016. PMID: 27114589. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance clearly finds pancreatic cancer earlier in high-risk people; how much of the survival gap is the finding, and how much is bias, no study here can say
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance clearly finds pancreatic cancer earlier in high-risk people; how much of the survival gap is the finding, and how much is bias, no study here can say
cards.people: Two prospective surveillance cohorts with no unscreened randomised comparison: CAPS1–5 (1,731 high-risk individuals, US) and three European expert centres (411 individuals).
cards.result: Stage: 77.8% of in-surveillance cancers at stage I in CAPS5, versus 85.7% at stage IV among the few cancers arising outside surveillance. Survival: median 9.8 versus 1.5 years (hazard ratio 0.13, 0.03 to 0.50) in CAPS — an observational contrast exposed to lead-time and length bias. Yield is sharply subgroup-dependent: 7.3% of CDKN2A carriers developed cancer (75% resected, 24% five-year survival) versus 0.9% of familial-kindred members, among whom resections for ultimately low-risk lesions outnumbered cancers found.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here applies outside genuinely high-risk groups — surveillance of average-risk people would drown in false positives and futile resections. And the honest summary for counselling is: surveillance converts a usually-metastatic diagnosis into a usually-stage-I one; whether that conversion is worth its surgeries in people who would never have developed cancer is unmeasured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dbouk M et al. J Clin Oncol. 2022 (PMID: 35704792); Vasen H et al. J Clin Oncol. 2016 (PMID: 27114589).

shelves.title: Denosumab versus zoledronic acid for bone metastases: superior in breast and prostate cancer, noninferior in other tumours — with hypocalcaemia traded for renal harm
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer at risk of skeletal complications, does denosumab prevent skeletal-related events better than zoledronic acid?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/*therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Bone Density Conservation Agents/*therapeutic use · Bone Diseases/etiology, *prevention & control · Bone Neoplasms/complications, *drug therapy, secondary · Bone and Bones/drug effects · Breast Neoplasms/*pathology · Denosumab · Diphosphonates/*therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imidazoles/*therapeutic use · Middle Aged · RANK Ligand/*therapeutic use · Zoledronic Acid
shelves.balance: Three identically designed phase 3 trials — same doses (denosumab 120 mg subcutaneously versus zoledronic acid 4 mg intravenously, every four weeks), same primary endpoint (time to first skeletal-related event: fracture, radiation or surgery to bone, or spinal cord compression) — cover the solid-tumour spectrum. In breast cancer (2,046 patients), denosumab was superior: hazard ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.95) for first events and rate ratio 0.77 for first-and-subsequent events (Stopeck 2010, PMID: 21060033). In castration-resistant prostate cancer (1,904 patients), likewise superior: median time to first event 20.7 versus 17.1 months, hazard ratio 0.82 (0.71 to 0.95) (Fizazi 2011, PMID: 21353695). In other solid tumours and myeloma (1,776 patients), denosumab was noninferior (hazard ratio 0.84, 0.71 to 0.98) but superiority was not significant after multiplicity adjustment (Henry 2011, PMID: 21343556). Overall survival and disease progression never differed — this is complication prevention, not cancer treatment. The harm profiles trade places: hypocalcaemia is commoner on denosumab (13% versus 6% in the prostate trial), renal adverse events and acute-phase reactions commoner on zoledronic acid, and osteonecrosis of the jaw is infrequent and similar (about 1–2%) on both. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a consistent relative reduction of about a fifth in first skeletal events (labelled relative) — in the prostate trial that is a 3.6-month delay in the median time to a first event.

cards.headline: Stopeck 2010 (breast cancer): denosumab beat zoledronic acid on time to first skeletal event (HR 0.82) and on total events (rate ratio 0.77)
cards.summary: Stopeck 2010 (breast cancer): denosumab beat zoledronic acid on time to first skeletal event (HR 0.82) and on total events (rate ratio 0.77)
cards.people: 2,046 patients with advanced breast cancer and bone metastases randomised to subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg plus intravenous placebo (n = 1,026) or intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg (renally dose-adjusted) plus subcutaneous placebo (n = 1,020), every four weeks, with calcium and vitamin D recommended. Primary endpoint: time to first on-study skeletal-related event (pathologic fracture, radiation or surgery to bone, or spinal cord compression).
cards.result: Denosumab was superior for time to first skeletal-related event (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.95; P = .01 for superiority) and for time to first and subsequent events (rate ratio 0.77, 0.66 to 0.89; P = .001) — relative measures, as reported. Bone-turnover marker suppression was greater with denosumab. Overall survival, disease progression and overall adverse-event rates were similar. Renal adverse events and acute-phase reactions were commoner with zoledronic acid; hypocalcaemia was commoner with denosumab; osteonecrosis of the jaw occurred in 2.0% versus 1.4% (P = .39).
cards.watchOut: A relative reduction of about a fifth in event hazard (labelled relative) in a population whose absolute event risk depends on prognosis and prior events; the abstract does not report a single absolute risk difference for the primary endpoint. A sponsor-designed programme with the comparator dosed exactly as labelled — a fair fight, but the sponsor's fight.
cards.source: Stopeck AT et al.. Denosumab compared with zoledronic acid for the treatment of bone metastases in patients with advanced breast cancer: a randomized, double-blind study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010. PMID: 21060033. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00321464. cards.headline: Fizazi 2011 (prostate cancer): denosumab delayed the first skeletal event to a median 20.7 versus 17.1 months (HR 0.82); hypocalcaemia 13% versus 6%
cards.summary: Fizazi 2011 (prostate cancer): denosumab delayed the first skeletal event to a median 20.7 versus 17.1 months (HR 0.82); hypocalcaemia 13% versus 6%
cards.people: 1,904 men with castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases, no prior intravenous bisphosphonate, randomised at 342 centres to subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg plus intravenous placebo (950 in the efficacy analysis) or intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg plus subcutaneous placebo (951), every four weeks, with calcium and vitamin D strongly recommended. Primary endpoint: time to first on-study skeletal-related event, tested for noninferiority then superiority.
cards.result: Median time to first skeletal-related event: 20.7 months (95% CI 18.8 to 24.9) on denosumab versus 17.1 months (15.0 to 19.4) on zoledronic acid — hazard ratio 0.82 (0.71 to 0.95; P = 0.0002 for noninferiority, P = 0.008 for superiority). Adverse events (97% both groups) and serious adverse events (63% versus 60%) were similar. Hypocalcaemia occurred in 121 patients (13%) on denosumab versus 55 (6%) on zoledronic acid (P < 0.0001); osteonecrosis of the jaw in 22 (2%) versus 12 (1%) (P = 0.09).
cards.watchOut: The 3.6-month median delay is the honest absolute translation of the 0.82 hazard ratio — quote both. Hypocalcaemia at 13% is the price of the stronger antiresorptive, landing in men often also on androgen deprivation and chemotherapy; calcium and vitamin D supplementation was 'strongly recommended', not enforced.
cards.source: Fizazi K et al.. Denosumab versus zoledronic acid for treatment of bone metastases in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer: a randomised, double-blind study. The Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21353695. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00321620. cards.headline: Henry 2011 (other solid tumours and myeloma): denosumab noninferior (HR 0.84) but not proven superior — the programme's one trial where the claim stops at 'as good as'
cards.summary: Henry 2011 (other solid tumours and myeloma): denosumab noninferior (HR 0.84) but not proven superior — the programme's one trial where the claim stops at 'as good as'
cards.people: 1,776 patients with advanced cancer and bone metastases (excluding breast and prostate cancer) or multiple myeloma, randomised double-blind, double-dummy to monthly subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg (n = 886) or intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg, renally adjusted (n = 890), with daily calcium and vitamin D recommended. Primary endpoint: time to first on-study skeletal-related event.
cards.result: Denosumab was noninferior to zoledronic acid for time to first skeletal-related event (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.98; P = .0007 for noninferiority). Superiority was not established: P = .03 unadjusted but P = .06 after multiplicity adjustment, and first-and-subsequent events gave a rate ratio of 0.90 (0.77 to 1.04; P = .14). Overall survival and disease progression were similar. Hypocalcaemia was commoner with denosumab; acute-phase reactions, renal adverse events and creatinine rises were commoner with zoledronic acid; osteonecrosis of the jaw was similarly infrequent in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The mixed basket (lung, other solid tumours, myeloma) dilutes any single-tumour claim — this trial licenses 'not worse than zoledronic acid' for the group, not superiority for any member of it. The record carries no registry identifier. The comparison here is strictly denosumab versus zoledronic acid as antiresorptives.

cards.headline: Synthesis: across 5,726 randomised patients, denosumab delays skeletal events at least as well as zoledronic acid everywhere, and better in breast and prostate cancer — survival unchanged
cards.summary: Synthesis: across 5,726 randomised patients, denosumab delays skeletal events at least as well as zoledronic acid everywhere, and better in breast and prostate cancer — survival unchanged
cards.people: Three double-blind phase 3 trials with an identical design and endpoint: breast cancer (n = 2,046), castration-resistant prostate cancer (n = 1,904), and other solid tumours or myeloma (n = 1,776).
cards.result: Time to first skeletal-related event: HR 0.82 (superior) in breast, HR 0.82 (superior; median 20.7 vs 17.1 months) in prostate, HR 0.84 (noninferior only) in other tumours/myeloma — relative reductions of about a fifth where superiority held (labelled relative). Overall survival and disease progression: no difference in any trial. Harms trade: hypocalcaemia more with denosumab (13% vs 6% in prostate); renal events and acute-phase reactions more with zoledronic acid; jaw osteonecrosis 1–2% on both.
cards.watchOut: All three trials were sponsor-run with the same protocol — consistency across them is reassuring but not independent replication. Denosumab's practical advantages (subcutaneous dosing, no renal monitoring or dose adjustment) are convenience claims from the trial reports, not randomised outcomes; and stopping denosumab without follow-on antiresorptive cover carries the rebound risk addressed on the osteoporosis shelves, a consideration these cancer trials did not test.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stopeck AT et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 21060033); Fizazi K et al. The Lancet. 2011 (PMID: 21353695); Henry DH et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2011 (PMID: 21343556).

shelves.title: Cancer-related fatigue: exercise is the treatment that works — ginseng helped at 8 weeks in one trial; methylphenidate did not beat placebo
shelves.question: In cancer-related fatigue, do exercise programmes, ginseng or methylphenidate help?

shelves.balance: SPLIT: The three proposed remedies have three different answers. Exercise: in a meta-analysis of 113 randomised trials (11,525 unique participants), exercise improved cancer-related fatigue with a weighted effect size of 0.30 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.36), psychological interventions 0.27 and the two combined 0.26 — while pharmaceutical interventions as a class did not (0.09, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.19) (Mustian KM et al., PMID: 28253393). Ginseng: American (Wisconsin) ginseng 2000 mg/day missed its 4-week primary endpoint (P = .07) but separated at 8 weeks (change in fatigue score 20 vs 10.3 points; P = .003) in one 364-patient trial (Barton DL et al., PMID: 23853057). Methylphenidate: the 148-patient NCCTG trial of the long-acting preparation found no benefit on its primary endpoint (P = .35), with a hypothesis-generating signal only in the most fatigued, most advanced subgroup (Moraska AR et al., PMID: 20625123). Prescribe exercise first; the pills are, at best, adjuncts.

cards.headline: Mustian 2017: across 113 RCTs (11,525 patients), exercise improved cancer-related fatigue (weighted effect size 0.30) — pharmaceutical treatments did not (0.09)
cards.summary: Mustian 2017: across 113 RCTs (11,525 patients), exercise improved cancer-related fatigue (weighted effect size 0.30) — pharmaceutical treatments did not (0.09)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 113 unique randomised trial articles in adults with cancer (11,525 unique participants; 78% female; mean age 54), testing exercise, psychological, combined exercise and psychological, or pharmaceutical interventions with cancer-related fatigue severity as the outcome, during and after primary treatment. Study quality was assessed on a modified 12-item PEDro scale.
cards.result: Weighted effect sizes for reducing fatigue: exercise 0.30 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.36; P < .001), psychological interventions 0.27 (0.21 to 0.33; P < .001), exercise plus psychological 0.26 (0.13 to 0.38; P < .001), and pharmaceutical interventions 0.09 (0.00 to 0.19; P = .05) — not effective. Studies were of good quality on average (mean PEDro score 8.2, range 5 to 12) with no evidence of publication bias. The authors conclude that clinicians should prescribe exercise or psychological interventions as first-line treatments for cancer-related fatigue.
cards.watchOut: An effect size of 0.30 is small-to-moderate — real, but not transformative — and is pooled across many exercise types, cancer types and treatment phases. The pharmaceutical category lumps unlike drugs together (stimulants among them, including the methylphenidate carded separately below); the class average neither acquits nor convicts any single agent.
cards.source: Mustian KM et al. Comparison of Pharmaceutical, Psychological, and Exercise Treatments for Cancer-Related Fatigue: A Meta-analysis. JAMA Oncology. 2017. PMID: 28253393. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Barton 2013 (N07C2): Wisconsin ginseng 2000 mg/day missed its 4-week primary endpoint (P = .07) but improved fatigue at 8 weeks (change 20 vs 10.3 points; P = .003)
cards.summary: Barton 2013 (N07C2): Wisconsin ginseng 2000 mg/day missed its 4-week primary endpoint (P = .07) but improved fatigue at 8 weeks (change 20 vs 10.3 points; P = .003)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Barton 2013, NCCTG N07C2)
cards.people: 364 fatigued cancer patients and survivors enrolled from 40 institutions in a multisite double-blind trial of American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius, Wisconsin ginseng) 2000 mg/day versus placebo for 8 weeks. The primary endpoint was the general subscale of the Multidimensional Fatigue Symptom Inventory–Short Form (MFSI-SF) at 4 weeks, with changes at 4 and 8 weeks compared by two-sample t tests.
cards.result: Changes from baseline in the MFSI-SF general subscale at 4 weeks were 14.4 (SD 27.1) in the ginseng arm versus 8.2 (SD 24.8) in the placebo arm (P = .07). At 8 weeks the difference was statistically significant: a change score of 20 (SD 27) for the ginseng group versus 10.3 (SD 26.1) for placebo (P = .003). Greater benefit was reported in patients receiving active cancer treatment than in those who had completed treatment. Toxicities by self-report and clinician grading did not differ significantly between arms, and the authors report no discernible toxicities associated with the treatment.
cards.watchOut: A positive secondary timepoint after a missed primary endpoint is weaker evidence than P = .003 suggests on its own. The tested product was Wisconsin-grown American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) at 2000 mg/day; the record names no manufacturer or brand — and ginseng products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness. Eight weeks without discernible toxicity is reassuring but short.
cards.source: Barton DL et al. Wisconsin Ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) to improve cancer-related fatigue: a randomized, double-blind trial, N07C2. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2013. PMID: 23853057. Registry ID: none in the record (cooperative-group trial NCCTG N07C2). cards.headline: Moraska 2010 (N05C7): long-acting methylphenidate did not improve cancer-related fatigue versus placebo (P = .35) — a subgroup signal only
cards.summary: Moraska 2010 (N05C7): long-acting methylphenidate did not improve cancer-related fatigue versus placebo (P = .35) — a subgroup signal only
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Moraska 2010, NCCTG N05C7)
cards.people: 148 adults with cancer-related fatigue randomly assigned double-blind to long-acting methylphenidate (target dose 54 mg/day) or placebo for 4 weeks, in the North Central Cancer Treatment Group N05C7 trial. The primary outcome measure was the Brief Fatigue Inventory; secondary measures included quality-of-life and sleep instruments and a global impression of change.
cards.result: There was no evidence that methylphenidate improved the primary endpoint of cancer-related fatigue compared with placebo (P = .35). Comparisons of secondary endpoints, including clinically significant changes in quality-of-life variables and fatigue change from baseline, were similarly negative. A subset analysis suggested that patients with more severe fatigue and/or more advanced disease did have some improvement (in stage III or IV disease, mean improvement in usual fatigue was 19.7 with methylphenidate versus 2.1 with placebo; P = .02). Self-reported toxicities differed significantly, with increased nervousness and appetite loss in the methylphenidate arm. The authors conclude the trial could not support its prestudy hypothesis.
cards.watchOut: The stage III/IV subgroup finding is a subset of a negative trial — exactly the pattern that generates false leads — and it is the entire basis for the separate question of methylphenidate in advanced cancer fatigue; it needs a dedicated trial, not adoption. The regimen tested was the long-acting preparation at a 54 mg/day target for 4 weeks; other doses and immediate-release schedules were not tested.
cards.source: Moraska AR et al. Phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of long-acting methylphenidate for cancer-related fatigue: North Central Cancer Treatment Group NCCTG-N05C7 trial. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20625123. Registry ID: none in the record (cooperative-group trial NCCTG N05C7). cards.headline: Synthesis: exercise first (LIKELY benefit), ginseng a maybe (POSSIBLE), methylphenidate no (LIKELY no difference overall)
cards.summary: Synthesis: exercise first (LIKELY benefit), ginseng a maybe (POSSIBLE), methylphenidate no (LIKELY no difference overall)
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 113 RCTs (11,525 participants) plus the two largest agent-specific trials: ginseng (n = 364) and long-acting methylphenidate (n = 148).
cards.result: Exercise weighted effect size 0.30 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.36); pharmaceutical interventions as a class 0.09 (0.00 to 0.19). Ginseng: primary endpoint missed at 4 weeks (P = .07), positive at 8 weeks (P = .003), no excess toxicity. Methylphenidate: primary endpoint negative (P = .35), with a subgroup signal in advanced disease and more nervousness and appetite loss.
cards.watchOut: Fatigue trials are unusually vulnerable to placebo response and unblinding — exercise cannot be blinded at all. The ginseng and methylphenidate limbs each rest on a single trial; the exercise limb rests on 113. That asymmetry is the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mustian KM et al. JAMA Oncology. 2017 (PMID: 28253393); Barton DL et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2013 (PMID: 23853057); Moraska AR et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 20625123).
