shelves.title: One 8 Gy fraction relieves bone-metastasis pain as well as a multi-fraction course — the trade is a fourfold higher retreatment rate (25% vs 7%)
shelves.question: In metastatic cancer with bone pain, does single-fraction radiotherapy relieve pain as well as multi-fraction courses?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Neoplasms/mortality/radiotherapy/secondary* · Disease Progression · Dose Fractionation, Radiation* · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/complications/etiology · Pain Management · Palliative Care* · Quality of Life · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Radiotherapy Dosage · Surveys and Questionnaires · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The Dutch Bone Metastasis Study randomised 1,171 patients with painful bone metastases to a single 8 Gy fraction or 4 Gy in six fractions: a pain response — a decrease of at least two points on a 0–10 scale — occurred in 71% of patients at some time during the first year, the difference between the groups was not significant and stayed well within the 10% margin, and repeated-measures analysis confirmed the two schedules were equivalent in palliation; pain medication, quality of life and side effects also did not differ (Steenland E et al., PMID: 10577695). A cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies found that the meta-conclusion — single-fraction radiotherapy is equally efficacious — has remained consistent as trials accumulated (Chow R et al., PMID: 31445837). The honest caveats are retreatment (25% after the single fraction versus 7% after six fractions in the Dutch study, partly because doctors were more willing to retreat single-fraction patients) and more pathological fractures after the single fraction, though the absolute percentage was low. Treatment costs were €1,734 versus €2,305, the 25% saving narrowing to 8% once retreatment costs were included.

cards.headline: Steenland 1999 (Dutch Bone Metastasis Study): 8 Gy × 1 versus 4 Gy × 6 in 1,171 patients — equal pain response (71% overall), more retreatments after the single fraction (25% vs 7%)
cards.summary: Steenland 1999 (Dutch Bone Metastasis Study): 8 Gy × 1 versus 4 Gy × 6 in 1,171 patients — equal pain response (71% overall), more retreatments after the single fraction (25% vs 7%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Steenland 1999, Dutch Bone Metastasis Study)
cards.people: 1,171 patients with painful bone metastases randomised to receive either a single fraction of 8 Gy (n = 585) or six fractions of 4 Gy (n = 586). The primary tumour was breast in 39%, prostate in 23%, lung in 25% and other sites in 13%; metastases were in the spine (30%), pelvis (36%), femur (10%), ribs (8%), humerus (6%) and other sites (10%). Pain, analgesic consumption, quality of life and side effects were collected by mailed questionnaires; the main endpoint was pain on a 0–10 scale, response being a decrease of at least two points from the initial score. Median survival was 7 months and patients participated for an average of 4 months.
cards.result: Overall, 71% of patients experienced a response at some time during the first year; the difference in response between the two groups was not significant and stayed well within the margin of 10%, and an analysis of repeated measures confirmed the schedules were equivalent in palliation. No differences were found in pain medication, quality of life or side effects. Retreatment was much commoner after the single fraction: 147 patients (25%) versus 41 (7%) — with indications that doctors were more willing to retreat the single-fraction group, since time to retreatment was shorter and the preceding pain score lower there. Pathological fractures were unexpectedly more frequent in the single-fraction group, but the absolute percentage was low (the abstract gives no figure). Costs were calculated at €1,734 for the single fraction and €2,305 for six fractions; including retreatment costs reduced the 25% difference to 8%.
cards.watchOut: A 1999 trial with questionnaire follow-up and heavy attrition in a population with a median survival of 7 months; response 'at some time during the first year' is a generous endpoint. It enrolled painful, uncomplicated metastases — cord compression, impending fracture and neuropathic pain are different problems (surgery for cord compression is shelf #2725).
cards.source: Steenland E et al. The effect of a single fraction compared to multiple fractions on painful bone metastases: a global analysis of the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 1999. PMID: 10577695. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Chow 2019: cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies — the 'single fraction is equally effective' conclusion has not moved as trials accumulated
cards.summary: Chow 2019: cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies — the 'single fraction is equally effective' conclusion has not moved as trials accumulated
cards.people: Cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies of single-fraction versus multiple-fraction palliative radiation therapy for bone metastases, testing whether the pooled conclusion changed as studies were added over publication time. Study quality was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and the majority of included studies had a low risk of bias.
cards.result: All but one endpoint — overall response rates in assessable patients — maintained the same meta-conclusion over publication time: single-fraction radiotherapy is equally efficacious as multiple-fraction radiotherapy. Additional studies have simply confirmed the pre-existing conclusion and refined the point estimate. The authors conclude that future resources should not be used to repeat these trials and can be better allocated to other hypotheses.
cards.watchOut: A cumulative meta-analysis demonstrates the stability of a conclusion, not its size — this abstract reports no pooled response percentages, so none are printed here. The retreatment difference seen in the Dutch trial is the consistent qualification across this literature.
cards.source: Chow R et al. Single vs multiple fraction palliative radiation therapy for bone metastases: Cumulative meta-analysis. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 2019. PMID: 31445837. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: for uncomplicated painful bone metastases, one visit does the work of six — plan on retreating about one patient in four
cards.summary: Synthesis: for uncomplicated painful bone metastases, one visit does the work of six — plan on retreating about one patient in four
cards.people: The largest single trial (n = 1,171) and a cumulative meta-analysis of 29 randomised studies.
cards.result: Pain response 71% overall in the Dutch study, with no significant difference between 8 Gy × 1 and 4 Gy × 6, and equivalence confirmed on repeated measures; the meta-analytic conclusion of equal efficacy has been stable across decades of trials. Retreatment: 25% versus 7%. Costs modestly favour the single fraction even after retreatment is counted.
cards.watchOut: Both sources concern painful, uncomplicated bone metastases treated with conventional external-beam radiotherapy. They do not cover re-irradiation, stereotactic treatment, radiopharmaceuticals, or metastases threatening the spinal cord or a weight-bearing bone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steenland E et al. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 1999 (PMID: 10577695); Chow R et al. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 31445837).

shelves.question: In metastatic spinal cord compression, does decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy beat radiotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Decompression, Surgical* · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Spinal Cord Compression/etiology* · Spinal Neoplasms/complications/radiotherapy/secondary/surgery* · Spine/surgery · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the only randomised trial, 101 patients with spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer were assigned to direct decompressive surgical resection followed by radiotherapy (ten 3 Gy fractions) or to the same radiotherapy alone. Significantly more patients in the surgery group were able to walk after treatment (42 of 50, 84%, versus 29 of 51, 57%; odds ratio 6.2, 95% CI 2.0 to 19.8; P = 0.001); surgical patients retained the ability to walk much longer (median 122 versus 13 days; P = 0.003); and of the 32 patients who entered the study unable to walk, significantly more regained walking with surgery (10 of 16, 62%, versus 3 of 16, 19%; P = 0.01). The need for corticosteroids and opioid analgesics was significantly reduced in the surgical group (Patchell RA et al., PMID: 16112300). The trial was stopped early because a predetermined stopping rule was met at interim analysis — early stopping tends to exaggerate effect sizes — and its patients were selected for single-site compression and fitness for surgery, so the size of the advantage should be read down even though its direction has never been contradicted by a second trial. Tier C: a single trial, stopped early and non-blinded.

cards.headline: Patchell 2005: surgery + radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone — walking after treatment 84% (42/50) vs 57% (29/51) (OR 6.2; 95% CI 2.0 to 19.8; P = 0.001); walking retained a median of 122 vs 13 days
cards.summary: Patchell 2005: surgery + radiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone — walking after treatment 84% (42/50) vs 57% (29/51) (OR 6.2; 95% CI 2.0 to 19.8; P = 0.001); walking retained a median of 122 vs 13 days
cards.people: 101 patients with spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer, randomly assigned in a multi-institutional, non-blinded trial to direct decompressive surgical resection followed by radiotherapy (n = 50) or radiotherapy alone (n = 51); radiotherapy in both groups was ten fractions of 3 Gy. The primary endpoint was the ability to walk; secondary endpoints included urinary continence, muscle strength and functional status, the need for corticosteroids and opioid analgesics, and survival. After an interim analysis the study was stopped because a predetermined early-stopping criterion was met; 123 patients had been assessed for eligibility and 101 randomised. All analyses were by intention to treat.
cards.result: Significantly more patients in the surgery group (42 of 50, 84%) than in the radiotherapy group (29 of 51, 57%) were able to walk after treatment (odds ratio 6.2, 95% CI 2.0 to 19.8; P = 0.001). Patients treated with surgery retained the ability to walk significantly longer (median 122 days versus 13 days; P = 0.003). Of the 32 patients who entered the study unable to walk, 10 of 16 (62%) in the surgery group regained the ability to walk versus 3 of 16 (19%) in the radiation group (P = 0.01). The need for corticosteroids and opioid analgesics was significantly reduced in the surgical group.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for benefit — a design that reliably overstates effect size — and non-blinded, with a functional endpoint. Entry required compression suitable for direct decompressive surgery in patients fit for a major spinal operation; the result does not extend to multilevel disease, highly radiosensitive tumours, or patients too frail for surgery. The record carries no registry identifier; enrolment predates routine trial registration.
cards.source: Patchell RA et al. Direct decompressive surgical resection in the treatment of spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2005. PMID: 16112300. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for selected patients with metastatic cord compression, operate first — the one trial is strongly positive and structurally optimistic
cards.summary: Synthesis: for selected patients with metastatic cord compression, operate first — the one trial is strongly positive and structurally optimistic
cards.people: One randomised multi-institutional trial, 101 patients, stopped early at a pre-planned interim analysis.
cards.result: Walking after treatment 84% vs 57% (OR 6.2, 2.0 to 19.8); walking retained for a median of 122 vs 13 days; regained walking among those unable to walk at entry 62% vs 19%; corticosteroid and opioid needs significantly lower with surgery.
cards.watchOut: This remains the only randomised trial of surgery for metastatic cord compression — practice, and this shelf's LIKELY stamp, rest on a single early-stopped study in selected patients, interpreted alongside the observational literature rather than above it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Patchell RA et al. Lancet. 2005 (PMID: 16112300).

shelves.title: Brain metastases: hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy plus memantine delays cognitive failure versus conventional whole-brain treatment — with no survival cost
shelves.question: In brain metastases, does hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy plus memantine preserve cognition versus conventional whole-brain radiotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Antiparkinson Agents/therapeutic use · Brain Neoplasms/drug therapy/radiotherapy/secondary · Chemoradiotherapy · Cognition/radiation effects · Cognition Disorders/etiology/prevention & control · Female · Hippocampus/radiation effects · Humans · Male · Memantine/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Progression-Free Survival · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Radiation Injuries/etiology/prevention & control · Radiotherapy Planning, Computer-Assisted/methods · Radiotherapy, Intensity-Modulated/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials answer the two halves of this question. Adding memantine to conventional whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) delayed cognitive decline: in RTOG 0614 (554 patients accrued, 508 eligible), time to cognitive decline was longer on memantine (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.99; P = .01), and the probability of cognitive failure at 24 weeks was 53.8% versus 64.9% on placebo — although the trial's primary endpoint, delayed recall at 24 weeks, narrowly missed significance (P = .059) after heavy patient loss left only 149 analysable patients and 35% power (Brown PD et al., PMID: 23956241). Sparing the hippocampi on top of memantine helped further: in NRG Oncology CC001 (518 patients), hippocampal-avoidance WBRT plus memantine cut the risk of cognitive failure versus WBRT plus memantine (adjusted hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.95; P = .02), with less deterioration in executive function at 4 months (23.3% vs 40.4%) and in learning and memory at 6 months, and no difference in overall survival, intracranial progression-free survival or toxicity (Brown PD et al., PMID: 32058845). The combined package has never been randomised against plain WBRT without memantine, so its total advantage over the old standard is a two-step inference from two trials sharing an investigator group and a control-arm design — but each step is a properly powered randomised comparison in the same direction, and neither step cost survival or tumour control. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — not Tier C: two phase III randomised trials.

cards.headline: Brown 2020 (NRG Oncology CC001): hippocampal-avoidance WBRT plus memantine cut the risk of cognitive failure by about a quarter relative versus WBRT plus memantine (adjusted HR 0.74), with no difference in survival or intracranial control
cards.summary: Brown 2020 (NRG Oncology CC001): hippocampal-avoidance WBRT plus memantine cut the risk of cognitive failure by about a quarter relative versus WBRT plus memantine (adjusted HR 0.74), with no difference in survival or intracranial control
cards.type: Randomised phase III trial (NRG Oncology CC001)
cards.people: 518 adults with brain metastases randomised to hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy (HA-WBRT) plus memantine or conventional WBRT plus memantine, enrolled July 2015 to March 2018. Primary endpoint: time to cognitive function failure (decline by reliable change index on at least one cognitive test). Median follow-up for alive patients 7.9 months.
cards.result: Risk of cognitive failure was significantly lower after HA-WBRT plus memantine (adjusted hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.95; P = .02). The difference came from less deterioration in executive function at 4 months (23.3% vs 40.4%; P = .01) and in learning and memory at 6 months (11.5% vs 24.7% [P = .049] and 16.4% vs 33.3% [P = .02]). Overall survival, intracranial progression-free survival and toxicity did not differ between arms. At 6 months, HA-WBRT patients reported less fatigue, less difficulty remembering things and less difficulty speaking.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received memantine, so this trial isolates the hippocampal-avoidance component only — it cannot be quoted as the effect of the combined package versus old-style WBRT alone. Median follow-up under 8 months reflects the short survival of this population; the cognitive benefit is a delay in failure, measured while patients lived, not a permanent preservation.
cards.source: Brown PD et al. Hippocampal Avoidance During Whole-Brain Radiotherapy Plus Memantine for Patients With Brain Metastases: Phase III Trial NRG Oncology CC001. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32058845. Registry ID: NCT02360215. cards.headline: Brown 2013 (RTOG 0614): memantine added to WBRT delayed time to cognitive decline (HR 0.78) and cut 24-week cognitive failure from 64.9% to 53.8% — but the primary endpoint, delayed recall at 24 weeks, missed significance (P = .059) after most patients were lost
cards.summary: Brown 2013 (RTOG 0614): memantine added to WBRT delayed time to cognitive decline (HR 0.78) and cut 24-week cognitive failure from 64.9% to 53.8% — but the primary endpoint, delayed recall at 24 weeks, missed significance (P = .059) after most patients were lost
cards.people: 554 patients with brain metastases accrued (508 eligible), randomised within 3 days of starting WBRT to memantine 20 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks, with serial standardised cognitive testing. Only 149 patients were analysable at 24 weeks because of death and dropout.
cards.result: There was less decline in delayed recall at 24 weeks on memantine, but it was not statistically significant (P = .059), with only 35% statistical power at that timepoint. Time to cognitive decline was significantly longer on memantine (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.99; P = .01); the probability of cognitive function failure at 24 weeks was 53.8% on memantine versus 64.9% on placebo. Memantine was superior for executive function at 8 and 16 weeks and for processing speed and delayed recognition at 24 weeks. Grade 3–4 toxicities and compliance were similar in the two arms.
cards.watchOut: The headline most often quoted from this trial — 'memantine prevents cognitive decline' — rests on the secondary time-to-decline analysis; the pre-specified primary endpoint did not reach significance, largely because two-thirds of patients could not be tested at 24 weeks in a population with high early mortality. The drug was, however, essentially free of added toxicity.
cards.source: Brown PD et al. Memantine for the prevention of cognitive dysfunction in patients receiving whole-brain radiotherapy: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Neuro-Oncology. 2013. PMID: 23956241. Registry ID: NCT00566852. cards.headline: Synthesis: protect the hippocampi and add memantine — each randomised step preserves cognition, neither costs survival — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: protect the hippocampi and add memantine — each randomised step preserves cognition, neither costs survival — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Two phase III randomised trials in adults with brain metastases receiving whole-brain radiotherapy: RTOG 0614 (n = 554 accrued; memantine vs placebo on a WBRT backbone) and NRG CC001 (n = 518; hippocampal avoidance vs conventional fields, memantine in both arms).
cards.result: Memantine step: time to cognitive decline HR 0.78 (0.62–0.99); cognitive failure at 24 weeks 53.8% vs 64.9%. Hippocampal-avoidance step (on memantine): cognitive failure adjusted HR 0.74 (0.58–0.95); executive-function deterioration at 4 months 23.3% vs 40.4%. Neither trial showed any difference in overall survival, intracranial progression or serious toxicity. For a patient with brain metastases and good performance status who is to receive WBRT and has no metastases in the hippocampal-avoidance region, HA-WBRT plus memantine is the cognition-preserving standard these trials built.
cards.watchOut: The package-versus-plain-WBRT comparison is indirect: no trial randomised HA-WBRT plus memantine against WBRT alone, and both trials come from the same cooperative-group stable. The question of WBRT itself versus stereotactic radiosurgery for limited brain metastases is a different question and is not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brown PD et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2020 (PMID: 32058845); Brown PD et al. Neuro-Oncology. 2013 (PMID: 23956241).

shelves.title: Tumour lysis syndrome: rasburicase normalises uric acid far faster and deeper than allopurinol — but no study has shown fewer clinical tumour-lysis events, kidney failures or deaths
shelves.question: In patients at risk of tumour lysis syndrome, does rasburicase control uric acid better than allopurinol, and does it change clinical outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Allopurinol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Biomarkers/blood · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hematologic Neoplasms/drug therapy · Humans · Hyperuricemia/blood/drug therapy/etiology · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Lysis Syndrome/blood/drug therapy/etiology · United States · Urate Oxidase/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Uric Acid/blood · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the laboratory answer and the clinical answer point in different directions. On uric acid, rasburicase wins decisively in randomised trials: in children at high risk, uric-acid exposure over 96 hours was 2.6-fold lower on rasburicase than allopurinol (relative measure; AUC 128 vs 329 mg/dL·hour; P < .0001), with an 86% versus 12% fall in plasma uric acid within 4 hours of the first dose (Goldman SC et al., PMID: 11342423); in adults, uric-acid response rates were 87% on rasburicase versus 66% on allopurinol (P = .001), 90% versus 53% in patients already hyperuricaemic, with control reached in 4 hours versus 27 hours (Cortes J et al., PMID: 20713865). On clinical outcomes, there is no comparable win: the adult systematic review and meta-analysis (21 studies, 1,261 patients) found no statistically significant difference in clinical tumour-lysis development between rasburicase and control groups in the controlled trials, and concluded that evidence is lacking that rasburicase improves clinical outcomes compared with alternatives — at significant cost (Lopez-Olivo MA et al., PMID: 23684124). The trials were powered on a blood level, not on dialysis, kidney failure or death, and those events are uncommon enough that the observational literature cannot settle them either. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (faster, deeper uric-acid control) / LIKELY (no difference shown in clinical outcomes). Tier C: the clinical-outcome leg rests on observational and meta-analytic data, and the only adult randomised trial used a laboratory endpoint.

cards.headline: Cortes 2010: in adults at risk of tumour lysis, rasburicase controlled plasma uric acid in 87% versus 66% on allopurinol — and in 4 hours rather than 27 in patients already hyperuricaemic
cards.summary: Cortes 2010: in adults at risk of tumour lysis, rasburicase controlled plasma uric acid in 87% versus 66% on allopurinol — and in 4 hours rather than 27 in patients already hyperuricaemic
cards.people: 275 adults with haematologic malignancies at risk of hyperuricaemia and tumour lysis syndrome, randomised to rasburicase alone (0.20 mg/kg/day IV, days 1–5; n = 92), rasburicase followed by oral allopurinol (n = 92), or allopurinol alone (300 mg/day orally, days 1–5; n = 91). Primary endpoint: proportion achieving or maintaining plasma uric acid ≤ 7.5 mg/dL during days 3–7.
cards.result: Plasma uric acid response rate was 87% with rasburicase, 78% with rasburicase plus allopurinol, and 66% with allopurinol; rasburicase was significantly better than allopurinol (P = .001) overall, in patients at high risk of tumour lysis (89% vs 68%; P = .012), and in those with baseline hyperuricaemia (90% vs 53%; P = .015). Time to uric-acid control in hyperuricaemic patients was 4 hours for both rasburicase arms versus 27 hours for allopurinol. Rasburicase was well tolerated alone and in sequence with allopurinol.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a uric-acid threshold, not tumour lysis syndrome itself: the trial was not designed or powered to detect differences in clinical TLS, dialysis or death, and it should never be cited as showing that faster urate control saves kidneys or lives.
cards.source: Cortes J et al. Control of plasma uric acid in adults at risk for tumor Lysis syndrome: efficacy and safety of rasburicase alone and rasburicase followed by allopurinol compared with allopurinol alone--results of a multicenter phase III study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20713865. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Goldman 2001: in children with leukaemia or lymphoma at high risk of tumour lysis, rasburicase produced 2.6-fold less uric-acid exposure than allopurinol over 96 hours, with an 86% versus 12% fall within 4 hours
cards.summary: Goldman 2001: in children with leukaemia or lymphoma at high risk of tumour lysis, rasburicase produced 2.6-fold less uric-acid exposure than allopurinol over 96 hours, with an 86% versus 12% fall within 4 hours
cards.people: 52 children with leukaemia or lymphoma at high risk for tumour lysis, randomised at 6 centres to rasburicase or allopurinol for 5–7 days during induction chemotherapy. Primary endpoint: area under the serial plasma uric acid concentration curve over the first 96 hours (AUC 0–96).
cards.result: Mean uric acid AUC 0–96 was 128 ± 70 mg/dL·hour on rasburicase versus 329 ± 129 on allopurinol (P < .0001) — a 2.6-fold (95% CI 2.0 to 3.4) lower exposure to uric acid (relative measure). Four hours after the first dose, plasma uric acid had fallen by 86% on rasburicase versus 12% on allopurinol (P < .0001). No anti-rasburicase antibodies were detected at day 14, and the authors concluded rasburicase is a safe and effective alternative to allopurinol in this paediatric population.
cards.watchOut: A paediatric trial of 52 patients with a pharmacokinetic endpoint: it establishes the speed and depth of urate lowering in children, nothing about clinical tumour-lysis events. Rasburicase also carries a specific hazard this abstract predates in emphasis — haemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency — which is a screening issue, not something these efficacy data address.

cards.headline: Lopez-Olivo 2013 (meta-analysis): across 21 adult studies, rasburicase normalised uric acid in 93.4% — but controlled trials showed no significant difference in clinical tumour-lysis development, and the reviewers concluded clinical-outcome benefit is unproven
cards.summary: Lopez-Olivo 2013 (meta-analysis): across 21 adult studies, rasburicase normalised uric acid in 93.4% — but controlled trials showed no significant difference in clinical tumour-lysis development, and the reviewers concluded clinical-outcome benefit is unproven
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials and observational studies of rasburicase for tumour lysis syndrome in adults: 21 studies (24 publications), 1,261 patients, 768 of whom received rasburicase for treatment or prophylaxis; 4 controlled trials and 17 observational studies. Primary outcome: development of clinical TLS.
cards.result: No statistically significant differences in clinical TLS development were observed in the controlled trials between rasburicase and control groups, and heterogeneity prevented a pooled meta-analysis of the trials. In the observational studies, 7.4% of patients developed clinical TLS after rasburicase (95% CI 1.7% to 16.7%), 93.4% achieved normalised serum uric acid (95% CI 91.7% to 94.6%), 4.4% developed acute kidney injury (95% CI 3.0% to 6.0%), and 2.6% died (95% CI 0.95% to 5.0%). Mean uric-acid reductions ranged from 5.3 to 12.8 mg/dL. The authors concluded rasburicase is effective at lowering uric acid but, at significant cost, lacks evidence of improved clinical outcomes over alternatives, and may reasonably be limited to patients at high risk of TLS.
cards.watchOut: Mostly observational data with confounding by indication — the sickest, highest-risk patients receive rasburicase, which biases uncontrolled comparisons against it; equally, the absence of a demonstrated clinical benefit in the controlled trials is real and cannot be waved away. Both directions of uncertainty are why the stamp splits.
cards.source: Lopez-Olivo MA et al. Rasburicase in tumor lysis syndrome of the adult: a systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2013. PMID: 23684124. cards.headline: Synthesis: rasburicase is the better urate-lowering drug by a wide, randomised margin — and an unproven clinical treatment — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: rasburicase is the better urate-lowering drug by a wide, randomised margin — and an unproven clinical treatment — SPLIT
cards.people: One adult phase III trial (n = 275) and one paediatric randomised trial (n = 52) with laboratory endpoints, plus a systematic review of 21 adult studies (1,261 patients) addressing clinical outcomes.
cards.result: Uric acid: response 87% vs 66% in adults; control in 4 vs 27 hours; 2.6-fold lower urate exposure in children (relative). Clinical outcomes: no significant difference in clinical tumour-lysis development in controlled trials; observational event rates after rasburicase — clinical TLS 7.4%, acute kidney injury 4.4%, death 2.6% — with no valid comparator. The rational use the evidence supports is risk-stratified: rasburicase where urate burden is high or rising fast and the stakes of failure are greatest, allopurinol where risk is lower — a practice pattern, it should be admitted, that rests on the laboratory evidence plus judgement, not on outcome trials.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the size of the urate effect smuggle in an outcome claim: no card on this shelf shows rasburicase preventing dialysis, kidney failure or death. Equally, the shelf does not show rasburicase is clinically useless — the outcome trials that could show it have never been run at adequate size.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cortes J et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 20713865); Goldman SC et al. Blood. 2001 (PMID: 11342423); Lopez-Olivo MA et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2013 (PMID: 23684124).

shelves.title: Oxybutynin cools hot flushes: scores fell two to three times more than on placebo in six weeks — dry mouth included
shelves.question: In women with or without breast cancer who have bothersome hot flushes, does oxybutynin reduce hot-flush frequency and scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — oxybutynin, an anticholinergic bladder drug, reduced hot flushes more than placebo at both doses tested in the ACCRU SC-1603 trial (Leon-Ferre RA et al., PMID: 32337497): among 150 women with or without breast cancer who had at least 28 hot flushes per week and were not candidates for estrogen-based therapy, six weeks of oxybutynin cut the weekly hot-flush score by 16.9 points at 5 mg twice daily and 10.6 points at 2.5 mg twice daily versus 5.7 on placebo (P<.005 for both), and weekly frequency fell by 7.5 and 4.8 flushes versus 2.6 on placebo (P<.003 for both), with improvements in most daily-interference measures and overall quality of life. The price is the anticholinergic profile: more dry mouth, difficulty urinating, and abdominal pain than placebo, mostly grade 1 or 2, with no difference in discontinuation for adverse effects. Six weeks in 150 women establishes short-term efficacy, not long-term safety of daily anticholinergic exposure in this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): an effective nonhormonal option for bothersome hot flushes, with dose-dependent anticholinergic side effects and no long-term data.

cards.headline: Leon-Ferre 2020 (ACCRU SC-1603): oxybutynin cut hot-flush scores by 10.6–16.9 points versus 5.7 on placebo in six weeks — dry mouth and urinary difficulty were the cost
cards.summary: Leon-Ferre 2020 (ACCRU SC-1603): oxybutynin cut hot-flush scores by 10.6–16.9 points versus 5.7 on placebo in six weeks — dry mouth and urinary difficulty were the cost
cards.people: 150 women with or without breast cancer, with 28 or more hot flushes per week lasting longer than 30 days, who were not candidates for estrogen-based therapy, randomised double-blind to oral oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, or placebo for six weeks; mean age 57 (SD 8.2) years, and 65% were taking tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor.
cards.result: Both oxybutynin doses produced greater reductions in the weekly hot-flush score than placebo (5 mg twice daily: −16.9 [SD 15.6]; 2.5 mg twice daily: −10.6 [SD 7.7]; placebo: −5.7 [SD 10.2]; P<.005 for both doses versus placebo) and in weekly hot-flush frequency (5 mg twice daily: −7.5 [SD 6.6]; 2.5 mg twice daily: −4.8 [SD 3.2]; placebo: −2.6 [SD 4.3]; P<.003 for both). Most hot-flush-related daily interference measures and overall quality of life also improved. Patients on both oxybutynin arms reported more side effects than placebo, particularly dry mouth, difficulty urinating, and abdominal pain; most side effects were grade 1 or 2, and there were no differences in study discontinuation because of adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short for a symptom that can persist for years, and 150 women cannot characterise the long-term anticholinergic burden — cognitive effects in particular — of twice-daily oxybutynin, the concern that shadows this drug class in older women (see the anticholinergic-burden shelf #2760 for the wider context). The record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID, and its abstract gives score and frequency changes rather than responder proportions, so the share of women achieving a personally meaningful reduction cannot be stated from this record.
cards.source: Leon-Ferre RA et al. Oxybutynin vs Placebo for Hot Flashes in Women With or Without Breast Cancer: A Randomized, Double-Blind Clinical Trial (ACCRU SC-1603). JNCI cancer spectrum. 2020. PMID: 32337497. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, dose-ordered short-term effect on flush scores and frequency — an option where hormones are off the table, with anticholinergic strings attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, dose-ordered short-term effect on flush scores and frequency — an option where hormones are off the table, with anticholinergic strings attached
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 150 women (two-thirds on tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor), six weeks of treatment — the entire record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Weekly hot-flush score change: −16.9 (5 mg twice daily), −10.6 (2.5 mg twice daily), −5.7 (placebo); P<.005 for both doses versus placebo. Weekly frequency change: −7.5, −4.8, and −2.6 flushes respectively; P<.003 for both. Daily interference and overall quality of life: improved on most measures. Side effects: more dry mouth, difficulty urinating, and abdominal pain on oxybutynin, mostly grade 1–2; discontinuation for adverse effects no different. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not compare oxybutynin head-to-head with the other nonhormonal options shelved in this library (venlafaxine, gabapentin, fezolinetant), so it cannot rank them; choice among them turns on side-effect profiles and patient preference. The trial's population — women ineligible for estrogen therapy, most on endocrine therapy for breast cancer — is exactly where the question arises, which strengthens applicability, but durability beyond six weeks and long-term anticholinergic safety remain open. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single short trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leon-Ferre RA et al. JNCI cancer spectrum. 2020 (PMID: 32337497).

shelves.title: Ginger for chemo nausea: day-1 severity fell at every dose in a 576-patient trial — best at half a gram, and no brand was tested
shelves.question: In patients receiving chemotherapy, does ginger reduce acute chemotherapy-induced nausea versus placebo on top of standard antiemetics?
shelves.mesh: Antiemetics/administration & dosage/isolation & purification/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Zingiber officinale/chemistry · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced/prevention & control · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Phytotherapy* · Serotonin 5-HT3 Receptor Antagonists/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced/prevention & control · Vomiting, Anticipatory/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ginger added to a standard 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic reduced the severity of acute chemotherapy-induced nausea in the largest trial of the question (Ryan JL et al., PMID: 21818642): 744 patients were randomised to placebo or 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 1.5 g of ginger daily, and in the 576 analysed, all ginger doses significantly reduced acute nausea severity versus placebo on day 1 of chemotherapy (P=0.003), with the largest reductions at 0.5 g and 1.0 g (P=0.017 and P=0.036) — more ginger was not better. A systematic review and meta-analysis in breast cancer (Kim SD et al., PMID: 36232567) found the same direction across five randomised trials, for both acute and delayed nausea and vomiting severity, with no serious side effects. Two cautions discipline the claim: the Ryan record reports significance without a printed effect size on its 7-point nausea scale, so the size of the relief cannot be stated from the record, and the proven outcome is nausea severity on day 1 — not vomiting abolished, and not a substitute for guideline antiemetics, which every patient received. The trial report names no branded ginger product, so no specific commercial preparation is endorsed by this evidence, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest, inexpensive adjunct for acute nausea on top of standard antiemetics, at 0.5–1.0 g daily.

cards.headline: Ryan 2012 (URCC CCOP): all ginger doses cut day-1 acute nausea severity versus placebo (P=0.003) — 0.5 g and 1.0 g worked best, on top of a 5-HT3 antiemetic for everyone
cards.summary: Ryan 2012 (URCC CCOP): all ginger doses cut day-1 acute nausea severity versus placebo (P=0.003) — 0.5 g and 1.0 g worked best, on top of a 5-HT3 antiemetic for everyone
cards.people: 744 cancer patients randomised double-blind at multiple centres to placebo or ginger 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 1.5 g daily (three 250 mg capsules twice daily for six days starting three days before chemotherapy), with 576 patients in the final analysis (91% female, mean age 53); all patients received a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic on day 1 of every cycle, and nausea severity was rated on a 7-point scale for days 1–4 of each cycle. The trial report names no branded ginger product or company.
cards.result: Mixed-model analyses showed all doses of ginger significantly reduced acute nausea severity compared with placebo on day 1 of chemotherapy (P=0.003). The largest reduction in nausea intensity occurred with 0.5 g (P=0.017) and 1.0 g (P=0.036) of ginger; the 1.5 g dose did not outperform the lower doses. Anticipatory nausea was a key factor in acute chemotherapy-induced nausea (P<0.0001). The authors conclude that ginger at a daily dose of 0.5–1.0 g significantly aids in reducing the severity of acute chemotherapy-induced nausea in adult cancer patients. The record's abstract does not print the point differences on the 7-point nausea scale, so the magnitude of relief cannot be quantified from this record.
cards.watchOut: The headline outcome is nausea severity on a self-rated 7-point scale on day 1 — a real but subjective endpoint — and the abstract withholds the actual point differences, so 'significant' cannot be converted into 'noticeable' from this record. The trial report names no branded product or manufacturer: the tested preparation was trial-supplied ginger capsules, and current commercial ginger products may differ in safety and effectiveness. Of 744 randomised patients, 576 (77%) entered the final analysis, and the population was 91% female, which limits precision for men and for tumour types under-represented in community oncology accrual.
cards.source: Ryan JL et al. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) reduces acute chemotherapy-induced nausea: a URCC CCOP study of 576 patients. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2012. PMID: 21818642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kim 2022 meta-analysis: five breast-cancer trials point the same way — ginger reduced acute and delayed CINV severity, with no serious side effects
cards.summary: Kim 2022 meta-analysis: five breast-cancer trials point the same way — ginger reduced acute and delayed CINV severity, with no serious side effects
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials of ginger for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in breast cancer patients, identified from PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang to June 2022; outcomes included Rhodes Index scores and the severity and frequency of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, with subgroup analysis by acute versus delayed phase.
cards.result: Overall, ginger was associated with a reduction in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses found ginger efficient for managing the severity of acute chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in breast cancer patients, and statistically significant for managing delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as well. The authors conclude ginger may help lower both acute and delayed symptoms in breast cancer patients and, since there were no serious side effects, is thought to be safe. The record's abstract reports no pooled effect sizes, so the size of the pooled benefit cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials in one cancer type, pooled without effect sizes in the record — this card corroborates direction, not magnitude, and its inclusion of Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang) brings in trials whose reporting standards vary. cards.headline: Synthesis: ginger eases acute nausea severity on top of standard antiemetics — a small, safe adjunct, not an antiemetic replacement
cards.summary: Synthesis: ginger eases acute nausea severity on top of standard antiemetics — a small, safe adjunct, not an antiemetic replacement
cards.people: One 744-patient multicentre randomised trial (576 analysed) plus a five-trial meta-analysis in breast cancer — the record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Acute day-1 nausea severity: significantly reduced by all ginger doses versus placebo (P=0.003), best at 0.5 g (P=0.017) and 1.0 g (P=0.036) daily; effect size on the 7-point scale not printed in the record. Meta-analysis: acute and delayed symptom severity reduced in breast cancer trials; no serious side effects. Vomiting as a separate endpoint and any branded product: not established by either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Keep the claim in its lane: every Ryan patient received a modern 5-HT3 antagonist, so this is evidence about adding ginger to antiemetics, never about ginger instead of them; and because no branded product is named in the trial report, patients should be told plainly that current products may differ in safety and effectiveness from the trial preparation. Tier C is set because the flagship trial's record withholds its effect size and the supporting meta-analysis is small.

shelves.title: Laser light before the sores start: severe mucositis fell from 40.5% to 6.4% in head and neck chemoradiation
shelves.question: In patients receiving radiotherapy (with or without chemotherapy) for head and neck cancer, does low-level laser therapy / photobiomodulation prevent severe oral mucositis versus sham?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/therapy · Chemoradiotherapy/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/therapy · Humans · Low-Level Light Therapy* · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck · Stomatitis/prevention & control/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — preventive low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation) produced one of the largest supportive-care effects in this library: in the phase III trial (Antunes HS et al., PMID: 24044799), 94 patients receiving concurrent chemoradiation for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma had severe (grade 3–4) oral mucositis in 6.4% of the laser group versus 40.5% of the sham group — a relative risk of 0.158 (95% CI 0.050 to 0.498), an 84% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed here — alongside quality-of-life advantages in pain, swallowing, fatigue, and social eating. The MASCC/ISOO systematic review and guideline update (Zadik Y et al., PMID: 31286228) independently recommends photobiomodulation for prevention of oral mucositis in exactly these settings — head and neck radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, and stem-cell transplantation — provided the clinician adheres to all parameters of one of the validated protocols. The discipline in that proviso is the catch: effects are protocol-specific (wavelength, dose, schedule), the flagship trial is a single centre's 94 patients, and the guideline finds evidence inadequate for treating established mucositis or for chemotherapy-only settings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preventive photobiomodulation, delivered to a validated protocol, substantially reduces severe oral mucositis in head and neck chemoradiation.

cards.headline: Antunes 2013 phase III: severe oral mucositis in 6.4% with preventive laser versus 40.5% with sham — relative risk 0.158 alongside better pain and swallowing scores
cards.summary: Antunes 2013 phase III: severe oral mucositis in 6.4% with preventive laser versus 40.5% with sham — relative risk 0.158 alongside better pain and swallowing scores
cards.people: 94 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma receiving conventional radiotherapy plus concurrent cisplatin every three weeks, in a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial conducted from June 2007 to December 2010; the device was a diode InGaAlP laser (660 nm, 100 mW, 1 J, 4 J/cm²), and mucositis was scored on WHO and OMAS scales with quality of life by EORTC questionnaires.
cards.result: A six-fold decrease in the incidence of grade 3–4 oral mucositis was detected in the low-level laser therapy group compared with placebo: 6.4% versus 40.5%, a relative risk ratio of 0.158 (95% CI 0.050 to 0.498) — an 84% relative reduction, with the absolute rates 6.4% and 40.5% as printed. After treatment, EORTC QLQ-C30 scores favoured laser therapy for physical and emotional functioning, fatigue, and pain, and the QLQ-H&N35 showed improvements in the laser arm for pain, swallowing, and trouble with social eating.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-four patients at a single centre with an effect size this large invites the usual small-trial caution — the confidence interval (0.050 to 0.498) still spans a two-fold to twenty-fold relative effect. The result belongs to one specific laser protocol (660 nm InGaAlP, 4 J/cm²) delivered preventively through chemoradiation; it does not license other devices, doses, or after-the-fact treatment of established mucositis, and the record reports no long-term oncologic safety follow-up of irradiating the tumour field with a growth-modulating light therapy.
cards.source: Antunes HS et al. Phase III trial of low-level laser therapy to prevent oral mucositis in head and neck cancer patients treated with concurrent chemoradiation. Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology. 2013. PMID: 24044799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zadik 2019 (MASCC/ISOO): guideline-level recommendation for photobiomodulation to prevent oral mucositis — in defined settings, with strict protocol adherence
cards.summary: Zadik 2019 (MASCC/ISOO): guideline-level recommendation for photobiomodulation to prevent oral mucositis — in defined settings, with strict protocol adherence
cards.type: Systematic review and clinical practice guideline (Zadik 2019, MASCC/ISOO)
cards.people: Systematic review by the Mucositis Study Group of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer / International Society of Oral Oncology (MASCC/ISOO), searching PubMed and Web of Science, grading each intervention in each cancer-treatment setting by level of evidence and issuing a Recommendation, a Suggestion, or No Guideline Possible.
cards.result: Recommendations are made for prevention of oral mucositis and related pain with photobiomodulation in patients treated with haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, head and neck radiotherapy without chemotherapy, and head and neck radiotherapy with chemotherapy; for each modality one to two clinically effective protocols are recommended, and the clinician should adhere to all parameters of the protocol selected. Because of inadequate evidence, no guideline was possible for treatment of established oral mucositis or for management of chemotherapy-related oral mucositis. The authors note the reported clinical settings were extremely variable, limiting data integration.
cards.watchOut: A guideline recommendation built on heterogeneous small trials is only as portable as its protocols: the review itself stresses that settings varied extremely and that benefit attaches to specific parameter sets, so a centre improvising with different equipment is outside the evidence. The recommendation is for prevention in three defined settings — it pointedly does not extend to treating mucositis once established, where clinicians most often reach for it.
cards.source: Zadik Y et al. Systematic review of photobiomodulation for the management of oral mucositis in cancer patients and clinical practice guidelines. cards.summary: Synthesis: severe mucositis falls from about two in five patients to about one in sixteen with protocol-faithful preventive laser — prevention only, settings only
cards.people: One 94-patient phase III randomised trial in head and neck chemoradiation plus the MASCC/ISOO systematic review and guideline covering transplantation and head and neck radiotherapy settings.
cards.result: Grade 3–4 oral mucositis: 6.4% with preventive low-level laser versus 40.5% with sham (relative risk 0.158, 95% CI 0.050 to 0.498; absolute rates as printed). Guideline position: Recommendation for prevention in stem-cell transplantation and head and neck radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy, using one of the validated protocols in full; No Guideline Possible for treatment of established mucositis. cards.watchOut: The gap between the trial's spectacular relative effect and a POSSIBLE stamp is the replication gap: one centre, 94 patients, one device protocol. Services adopting photobiomodulation should adopt a published protocol whole — parameters, timing, and operator training — and audit their own severe-mucositis rates, because the evidence does not support improvisation. Tier C is set because the flagship evidence is a single small phase III trial, guideline endorsement notwithstanding.

shelves.title: A quarter-tablet appetite drug: 60% on low-dose olanzapine gained over 5% of their weight versus 9% on placebo
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer and chemotherapy-related anorexia, does low-dose olanzapine improve appetite and weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Middle Aged · Olanzapine/therapeutic use · Anorexia*/chemically induced/drug therapy/complications · Quality of Life · Lung Neoplasms*/drug therapy/complications · Double-Blind Method · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — low-dose olanzapine produced a strikingly large appetite and weight effect in a single randomised trial (Sandhya L et al., PMID: 36977285): among 124 patients with untreated locally advanced or metastatic gastric, hepatopancreaticobiliary, or lung cancer starting chemotherapy, 2.5 mg of olanzapine daily for 12 weeks gave weight gain of more than 5% in 60% of analysable patients (35 of 58) versus 9% on placebo (5 of 54; P<.001), appetite improvement on a visual analogue scale in 43% versus 13% (P<.001), and appetite improvement on the FAACT anorexia–cachexia subscale in 22% versus 4% (P=.004), with better quality of life and nutritional status, lesser chemotherapy toxicity, and minimal attributable side effects. The size of the effect is exactly why the stamp stops at POSSIBLE: one trial, 124 patients from a single programme, 80% metastatic disease across three tumour types, and 12 weeks of follow-up cannot establish durability, survival impact, or the longer-term metabolic and sedative profile of daily olanzapine in this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a simple, inexpensive, well-tolerated intervention that significantly improved appetite and weight in this trial — pending confirmation.

cards.headline: Sandhya 2023: olanzapine 2.5 mg daily — 60% gained more than 5% of body weight versus 9% on placebo, and appetite improved on both measures
cards.summary: Sandhya 2023: olanzapine 2.5 mg daily — 60% gained more than 5% of body weight versus 9% on placebo, and appetite improved on both measures
cards.people: 124 adults with untreated, locally advanced, or metastatic gastric, hepatopancreaticobiliary, or lung cancers randomised double-blind to olanzapine 2.5 mg once daily for 12 weeks or placebo, alongside chemotherapy; both groups received standard nutritional assessment and dietary advice. Median age was 55 years (range 18–78); 112 patients were analysable (58 olanzapine, 54 placebo), 80% had metastatic cancer, and tumour sites were gastric 55%, lung 35%, and hepatopancreaticobiliary 10%.
cards.result: The olanzapine arm had a greater proportion of patients with weight gain of more than 5% (35 of 58 [60%] versus 5 of 54 [9%]; P<.001) and improvement in appetite by visual analogue scale (25 of 58 [43%] versus 7 of 54 [13%]; P<.001) and by the FAACT anorexia–cachexia subscale (scores ≥37: 13 of 58 [22%] versus 2 of 54 [4%]; P=.004). Patients on olanzapine had better quality of life and nutritional status and lesser chemotherapy toxicity. Side effects attributable to olanzapine were minimal. The authors describe low-dose daily olanzapine as a simple, inexpensive, well-tolerated intervention that significantly improves appetite and weight gain in newly diagnosed patients on chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-programme trial of 124 patients with an unusually large effect (a 51-percentage-point difference in the primary weight outcome) is precisely the profile that replication tends to shrink; treat the direction as promising and the magnitude as provisional. Weight gain of >5% is not characterised by composition in this record — fat, fluid, and lean mass are not separated — and 12 weeks cannot speak to survival, function, or the cumulative metabolic and sedative effects of daily olanzapine. Twelve of 124 randomised patients were not analysable.
cards.source: Sandhya L et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, one very large appetite-and-weight signal at a genuinely low dose — worth offering, not yet worth generalising
cards.people: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 124 patients (112 analysable) with advanced gastric, lung, or hepatopancreaticobiliary cancers starting chemotherapy — the entire record carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Weight gain >5%: 60% on olanzapine versus 9% on placebo (P<.001). Appetite improvement: 43% versus 13% by visual analogue scale (P<.001); 22% versus 4% by FAACT anorexia–cachexia subscale (P=.004). Quality of life and nutritional status: better on olanzapine; chemotherapy toxicity: lesser; attributable side effects: minimal. Survival and weight composition: not reported. The population was newly diagnosed and starting first chemotherapy — the result should not be assumed for refractory cachexia late in the disease course, where anorexia is driven by tumour metabolism more than by treatment. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial.

shelves.title: Mirtazapine for cancer appetite: appetite rose in both arms of the one blinded trial — the placebo patients improved just as much
shelves.question: In patients with cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia, does mirtazapine improve appetite and weight versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anorexia/drug therapy/etiology · Cachexia*/drug therapy/etiology · Double-Blind Method · Hand Strength · Humans · Mirtazapine/therapeutic use · Neoplasms*/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the single double-blind trial behind this question (Hunter CN et al., PMID: 34051293) randomised 120 patients with incurable solid tumours, cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia to mirtazapine 15 mg at night or placebo for eight weeks. Appetite improved significantly in both arms (P < 0.0001 in each) and the improvement did not differ between arms in either the per-protocol (P = 0.472) or intention-to-treat (P = 0.462) analysis; weight, lean body mass, handgrip strength, quality of life, fatigue, inflammatory markers and survival likewise did not differ. Mirtazapine did blunt the rise in depressive symptoms and caused more somnolence — real drug effects, but not appetite effects. A placebo-arm improvement this large is itself the lesson: appetite in this setting fluctuates and responds to attention, so uncontrolled experience with mirtazapine will keep looking better than the drug is. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on the one randomised test, mirtazapine is no better than placebo for appetite in cancer-associated anorexia and cachexia.

cards.headline: Hunter 2021: appetite improved just as much on placebo as on mirtazapine (between-arm P = 0.472) — and weight, lean mass, strength and survival did not differ either
cards.summary: Hunter 2021: appetite improved just as much on placebo as on mirtazapine (between-arm P = 0.472) — and weight, lean mass, strength and survival did not differ either
cards.people: 120 patients with incurable solid tumours, anorexia (appetite loss ≥4 on a 0–10 scale) and cachexia (>5% body-weight loss over 6 months, or >2% with BMI <20), with low depression scores (≤3 on a 0–6 scale), randomised 1:1 to mirtazapine 15 mg daily at night for 8 weeks or placebo; 48 (80%) on mirtazapine and 52 (87%) on placebo were assessable for the primary endpoint of change in appetite at day 28.
cards.result: Appetite score increased significantly within both arms (P < 0.0001 for mirtazapine and for placebo), but the increase did not differ between arms in the per-protocol analysis (P = 0.472) or the intention-to-treat analysis (P = 0.462). Mirtazapine was associated with significantly less increase in depressive symptoms and a higher prevalence of somnolence. Changes in quality of life, fatigue, body weight, lean body mass, handgrip strength, inflammatory markers, adverse events and survival did not differ significantly between mirtazapine and placebo. The authors conclude mirtazapine 15 mg at night is no better than placebo for appetite in this population.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 120 patients with about a fifth not assessable for the primary endpoint — it can exclude a large appetite effect but not a small one, and eight weeks is short for weight or survival outcomes. Entry required low depression scores, so the result does not speak to patients whose appetite loss is entangled with depression, the group in whom mirtazapine's antidepressant and sedative effects might matter most.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one properly blinded trial, and the placebo arm did the improving — mirtazapine for cancer appetite is an unproven hope, not a treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: one properly blinded trial, and the placebo arm did the improving — mirtazapine for cancer appetite is an unproven hope, not a treatment
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, 120 patients with incurable solid tumours and cancer-associated anorexia–cachexia (Hunter 2021) — the entire randomised record for this question.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (appetite change at day 28): no between-arm difference (per-protocol P = 0.472; intention-to-treat P = 0.462) despite significant within-arm improvement in both groups (P < 0.0001 each). Secondary endpoints — weight, lean body mass, handgrip strength, quality of life, fatigue, inflammatory markers, survival: no significant differences. Tolerability signals: more somnolence on mirtazapine; less worsening of depressive symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A null in one 120-patient trial is not proof of zero effect in every cancer population — dose was fixed at 15 mg, follow-up was eight weeks, and patients with significant depression were excluded by design. But the burden of proof now sits with anyone prescribing mirtazapine for appetite: the only blinded test found the improvement belonged to the placebo arm as much as to the drug. Tier C is set because the evidence base is a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hunter CN et al. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2021 (PMID: 34051293).

shelves.title: Frozen gloves and socks against paclitaxel neuropathy: the cooled hand lost touch sensation a third as often — in a small trial where each patient was her own control
shelves.question: In patients receiving paclitaxel, does local cryotherapy (frozen gloves/socks during infusion) prevent or reduce peripheral neuropathy versus no cooling?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents, Phytogenic/adverse effects* · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy*/pathology · Cryotherapy/methods* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Japan/epidemiology · Middle Aged · Paclitaxel/adverse effects* · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/chemically induced/epidemiology/therapy* · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor trial (Hanai A et al., PMID: 29924336) used each patient as her own control: 36 women wore frozen gloves and socks on the dominant side during weekly paclitaxel, and objective tactile-sensitivity loss at a cumulative 960 mg/m² was 27.8% on the cooled hand versus 80.6% on the uncooled hand (odds ratio 20.00), with subjective neuropathy symptoms of 2.8% versus 41.7% and a hazard ratio of 0.13 for symptom onset; nobody dropped out for cold intolerance. The wider record points the same way: a meta-analysis of 9 trials and 2,250 patients (Jia J et al., PMID: 34912720) found grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy at a relative risk of 0.65 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.75) with cryotherapy — a 35% relative reduction — and fewer taxane dose reductions (RR 0.48). The evidence is promising rather than settled: the anchor is small, unblinded by nature and self-controlled, and the meta-analysis pools small heterogeneous trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cooling the hands and feet during paclitaxel probably reduces neuropathy, at the price of 90 minutes of cold discomfort per infusion.

cards.headline: Hanai 2018: on the cooled side, tactile-sensitivity loss was 27.8% versus 80.6% on the uncooled side — and patient-reported neuropathy was 2.8% versus 41.7% in the hand
cards.summary: Hanai 2018: on the cooled side, tactile-sensitivity loss was 27.8% versus 80.6% on the uncooled side — and patient-reported neuropathy was 2.8% versus 41.7% in the hand
cards.people: 40 women with breast cancer receiving weekly paclitaxel 80 mg/m² (1-hour infusion) in Japan, each wearing frozen gloves and socks on the dominant side for 90 minutes spanning the infusion, with the untreated non-dominant side as the within-patient control; 36 patients reached the cumulative dose of 960 mg/m² and were analysed (4 did not, for pneumonia, severe fatigue, severe liver dysfunction and macular oedema). No patient dropped out because of cold intolerance.
cards.result: At cumulative paclitaxel 960 mg/m², incidence on the intervention versus control side — hand tactile sensitivity loss 27.8% vs 80.6% (OR 20.00, 95% CI 3.20 to 828.96, P < .001); foot tactile loss 25.0% vs 63.9% (OR infinite, 95% CI 3.32 to infinite, P < .001); hand warm-sense deficit 8.8% vs 32.4% (OR 9.00, P = .02); foot warm-sense deficit 33.4% vs 57.6% (OR 5.00, P = .04). Patient Neuropathy Questionnaire symptoms: hand 2.8% vs 41.7% and foot 2.8% vs 36.1% (both P < .001), with hazard ratios for symptom onset of 0.13 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.34) in the hand and 0.13 (0.04 to 0.38) in the foot. Manipulative dexterity deteriorated less on the cooled side (mean delay −2.5 seconds, SD 12.0, vs +8.6 seconds, SD 25.8; P = .005).
cards.watchOut: The self-controlled design removes between-patient confounding but cannot be blinded — patients knew which side was cooled, which matters most for the subjective questionnaire outcomes (the objective monofilament and thermosensory results are less exposed to that bias). Only 36 patients, all women with breast cancer on one paclitaxel schedule at Japanese centres; the enormous odds ratios with very wide confidence intervals (one is literally infinite) are what tiny event counts look like, and the cooled side was always the dominant side.
cards.source: Hanai A et al. Effects of Cryotherapy on Objective and Subjective Symptoms of Paclitaxel-Induced Neuropathy: Prospective Self-Controlled Trial. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2018. PMID: 29924336. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jia 2021 meta-analysis (9 trials, 2,250 patients): grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy relative risk 0.65 with cryotherapy — a 35% relative reduction — and fewer dose reductions for neuropathy
cards.summary: Jia 2021 meta-analysis (9 trials, 2,250 patients): grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy relative risk 0.65 with cryotherapy — a 35% relative reduction — and fewer dose reductions for neuropathy
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 9 clinical trials totalling 2,250 patients receiving taxane chemotherapy, comparing cryotherapy (frozen gloves/socks or equivalent cooling) with no cooling, with neuropathy graded by CTCAE criteria and by the Patient Neuropathy Questionnaire (PNQ).
cards.result: By CTCAE grading, cryotherapy significantly reduced grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.75, P < 0.00001 — a 35% relative reduction) and grade ≥2 motor neuropathy (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.94, P = 0.04). By PNQ, sensory neuropathy was reduced (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.31, P < 0.0001) but motor neuropathy was not significantly reduced (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.88, P = 0.28). Cryotherapy was also associated with fewer taxane dose reductions due to neuropathy (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.95, P = 0.04). The authors conclude cryotherapy is likely to prevent taxane-induced peripheral neuropathy while calling for higher-quality evidence. All figures are relative risks; the review does not report a single pooled absolute incidence applicable across the differing trial populations.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and heterogeneous in cooling method, taxane and outcome scale, and several share the unblinded self-controlled design of the anchor trial, so the meta-analysis inherits rather than cures those biases; the motor-neuropathy estimate rests on very few events (CI 0.03 to 0.94). Publication bias toward positive small trials is a live concern in a literature this size.
cards.source: Jia J et al. Cryotherapy for Prevention of Taxane-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy: A Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in Oncology. 2021. PMID: 34912720. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a dramatic within-patient result in 36 women, backed by a concordant meta-analysis — benefit is plausible and consistent, certainty is not yet high
cards.summary: Synthesis: a dramatic within-patient result in 36 women, backed by a concordant meta-analysis — benefit is plausible and consistent, certainty is not yet high
cards.people: One prospective self-controlled trial of 36 analysable patients (Hanai 2018) plus a meta-analysis of 9 trials and 2,250 patients (Jia 2021) — the randomised and quasi-randomised record on cooling to prevent taxane neuropathy.
cards.result: Objective neuropathy signs: tactile loss 27.8% vs 80.6% (hand) in the anchor trial; pooled grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy RR 0.65 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.75), a 35% relative reduction, in the meta-analysis. Subjective symptoms: 2.8% vs 41.7% (anchor, hand PNQ); pooled PNQ sensory RR 0.11. Dose reductions for neuropathy: pooled RR 0.48. Tolerability in the anchor trial: no dropouts for cold intolerance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: What is missing is a large, conventionally randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment and long follow-up for persistent neuropathy and function — the outcome that matters is not numbness at the last infusion but neuropathy a year later. Frostbite risk, Raynaud phenomenon and cold intolerance in routine practice (outside a trial's selected volunteers) also deserve the caution the trials' zero-dropout figure may understate. Tier C is set because the anchor is a single small self-controlled trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hanai A et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2018 (PMID: 29924336); Jia J et al. Frontiers in Oncology. 2021 (PMID: 34912720).

shelves.title: Acetyl-L-carnitine backfired: the supplement taken to prevent taxane neuropathy significantly increased it by 24 weeks (SWOG S0715)
shelves.question: In women receiving taxane chemotherapy for breast cancer, does acetyl-L-carnitine prevent chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy — or worsen it?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcarnitine/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Adult · Aged · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy*/pathology/surgery · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Dietary Supplements · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Linear Models · Mastectomy/methods · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Nerve Regeneration/drug effects · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/chemically induced*/prevention & control* · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Sensitivity and Specificity · Severity of Illness Index · Taxoids/adverse effects*/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — this shelf exists because the answer reversed the expectation. Acetyl-L-carnitine was biologically plausible and supported by small earlier studies, so SWOG S0715 (Hershman DL et al., PMID: 23733756) randomised 409 women receiving adjuvant taxane chemotherapy to acetyl-L-carnitine 3,000 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks. At the 12-week primary endpoint there was no protection (neurotoxicity scores 0.9 points worse on acetyl-L-carnitine, 95% CI −2.2 to 0.4, P = .17), and by 24 weeks the supplement arm had significantly MORE neuropathy: scores 1.8 points worse (95% CI −3.2 to −0.4, P = .01), more patients with a >5-point deterioration (38% vs 28%, P = .05), worse functional status scores, and grade 3–4 neurotoxicity in eight patients versus one on placebo. The authors' conclusion is blunt — patients should be discouraged from using supplements without proven efficacy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): a supplement taken to prevent chemotherapy neuropathy made the neuropathy worse in the only large blinded test. Established-neuropathy treatment with duloxetine is a different question, shelved at #1456.

cards.headline: Hershman 2013 (SWOG S0715): no protection at 12 weeks, and by 24 weeks acetyl-L-carnitine had significantly worsened neuropathy — grade 3–4 neurotoxicity in 8 patients versus 1 on placebo
cards.summary: Hershman 2013 (SWOG S0715): no protection at 12 weeks, and by 24 weeks acetyl-L-carnitine had significantly worsened neuropathy — grade 3–4 neurotoxicity in 8 patients versus 1 on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, SWOG S0715 (Hershman 2013)
cards.people: 409 evaluable women undergoing adjuvant taxane-based chemotherapy for breast cancer (208 acetyl-L-carnitine, 201 placebo), randomised double-blind to acetyl-L-carnitine 3,000 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks; neuropathy measured by the 11-item neurotoxicity (NTX) component of the FACT-Taxane scale, with the primary endpoint at 12 weeks.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, NTX scores were 0.9 points lower (more neuropathy) with acetyl-L-carnitine than placebo (95% CI −2.2 to 0.4; P = .17) — no benefit. At 24 weeks, scores were 1.8 points lower with acetyl-L-carnitine (95% CI −3.2 to −0.4; P = .01), a statistically significant worsening. Patients on acetyl-L-carnitine were more likely to have a >5-point decrease in FACT-NTX scores (38% vs 28%; P = .05), FACT Trial Outcome Index scores were 3.5 points lower (P = .03), and grade 3–4 neurotoxicity was more frequent on acetyl-L-carnitine (eight patients vs one). No differences were seen in fatigue (FACIT-Fatigue) or other toxicities; serum carnitine levels rose on the supplement, confirming exposure. The authors state this is the first study showing a nutritional supplement increased chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
cards.watchOut: The harm signal rests on the 24-week secondary endpoint — the 12-week primary endpoint was null — so strictly this is one trial with a significant secondary-timepoint result and a small absolute count of severe events (8 vs 1). The population is women receiving adjuvant taxanes; whether the same applies to other neurotoxic regimens, or to acetyl-L-carnitine used for established rather than prevented neuropathy, is untested here. None of that softens the practical conclusion: the hypothesised benefit was absent at both timepoints.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the prevention hypothesis failed and the direction flipped to harm — the burden of proof for supplements in chemotherapy now runs the other way
cards.summary: Synthesis: the prevention hypothesis failed and the direction flipped to harm — the burden of proof for supplements in chemotherapy now runs the other way
cards.people: One large double-blind randomised trial, 409 women on adjuvant taxane chemotherapy (SWOG S0715, Hershman 2013) — the definitive randomised record for acetyl-L-carnitine as neuropathy prevention.
cards.result: Prevention at 12 weeks: none (difference 0.9 points in the wrong direction, P = .17). At 24 weeks: significantly worse neuropathy on acetyl-L-carnitine (1.8 points, 95% CI −3.2 to −0.4, P = .01); >5-point deterioration 38% vs 28% (P = .05); grade 3–4 neurotoxicity 8 vs 1 patients. Fatigue and other toxicities: no difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm).
cards.watchOut: Do not over-extend the verdict: this trial condemns prophylactic acetyl-L-carnitine during taxane therapy, not every use of the compound in every neuropathy. But within its question it is the whole evidence base, it was adequately powered and blinded, and both timepoints leaned the same way — which is why a single trial earns a harm stamp here rather than a shrug. Tier C is set because it remains a single trial whose significant result sits at a secondary timepoint.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hershman DL et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2013 (PMID: 23733756).
