shelves.title: Duloxetine for aromatase-inhibitor joint pain: a real but sub-one-point average advantage in SWOG S1202 — worth it for responders, not a transformation
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with early breast cancer and aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia, does duloxetine reduce joint pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Aromatase Inhibitors/adverse effects* · Arthralgia/chemically induced/diagnosis/prevention & control* · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy*/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Pain Measurement · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SWOG S1202 (Henry NL et al., PMID: 29136387) randomised 299 postmenopausal women with early-stage breast cancer whose aromatase-inhibitor joint pain scored at least 4 of 10 to duloxetine or placebo for 13 weeks. Average joint pain at 12 weeks was 0.82 points lower on duloxetine (95% CI −1.24 to −0.40, P = .0002), with the same direction for worst pain, stiffness, pain interference and functioning. Two cautions keep the stamp at POSSIBLE: the average advantage (0.82 points) is well under the 2-point drop the trial itself defined as clinically significant for an individual patient, so the benefit is real on average but modest per person; and low-grade adverse events were much commoner on duloxetine (78% vs 50% any grade, though grade 3 rates were similar). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): duloxetine eases aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia by a modest average amount, bought with frequent low-grade side effects. The acupuncture trial for the same syndrome (SWOG S1200) is shelved at #1787; duloxetine for established chemotherapy neuropathy is #1456.

cards.headline: Henry 2018 (SWOG S1202): average joint pain 0.82 points lower on duloxetine than placebo at 12 weeks (P = .0002) — statistically clear, individually modest, with any-grade adverse events in 78% vs 50%
cards.summary: Henry 2018 (SWOG S1202): average joint pain 0.82 points lower on duloxetine than placebo at 12 weeks (P = .0002) — statistically clear, individually modest, with any-grade adverse events in 78% vs 50%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, SWOG S1202 (Henry 2018)
cards.people: 299 postmenopausal women with early-stage breast cancer on aromatase-inhibitor therapy who had average joint pain of ≥4 out of 10 that developed or worsened after starting the inhibitor, randomised 1:1 to duloxetine or placebo for 13 weeks at multiple centres; 127 on duloxetine and 128 on placebo were evaluable for the primary analysis of average joint pain through 12 weeks.
cards.result: By 12 weeks the average joint pain score was 0.82 points lower with duloxetine than with placebo (95% CI −1.24 to −0.40; P = .0002), in models adjusted for baseline pain stratum and prior taxane use. Similar patterns favoured duloxetine for worst joint pain, joint stiffness, pain interference and functioning. A clinically significant change had been defined as a ≥2-point decrease from baseline — larger than the average between-group difference achieved. Adverse events of any grade were more frequent on duloxetine (78% vs 50%); rates of grade 3 adverse events were similar between arms.
cards.watchOut: About 15% of randomised patients were not evaluable for the primary analysis, follow-up was 12 weeks, and the trial does not show whether the pain relief translates into the outcome that ultimately matters — staying on aromatase-inhibitor therapy for the full planned course. The 0.82-point average difference also conceals distribution: some patients gain a clinically important ≥2-point relief and others none, and the abstract does not report the responder proportions.
cards.source: Henry NL et al. Randomized, Multicenter, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial of Duloxetine Versus Placebo for Aromatase Inhibitor-Associated Arthralgias in Early-Stage Breast Cancer: SWOG S1202. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2018. PMID: 29136387. Registry ID: NCT01598298. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run cooperative-group trial — a genuine but small average pain advantage, with side effects in most patients who take the drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run cooperative-group trial — a genuine but small average pain advantage, with side effects in most patients who take the drug
cards.people: One multicentre double-blind phase 3 trial, 299 randomised and 255 evaluable women with aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia (SWOG S1202, Henry 2018) — the entire placebo-controlled record for duloxetine in this syndrome.
cards.result: Average joint pain at 12 weeks: 0.82 points lower on duloxetine (95% CI −1.24 to −0.40, P = .0002); worst pain, stiffness, interference and functioning concordant. Any-grade adverse events 78% vs 50%; grade 3 events similar. Adherence to aromatase inhibitors and longer-term pain: not reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The honest framing for a patient is a trade: a roughly one-point average improvement on a ten-point pain scale, a good chance of nausea, dry mouth or somnolence-type low-grade effects (78% had some adverse event), against a chance of being one of the responders with a ≥2-point gain. A trial powered on aromatase-inhibitor persistence — the clinical prize — has not been done. Tier C is set because this is a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Henry NL et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2018 (PMID: 29136387).

shelves.title: NEPA versus palonosetron alone: one capsule containing both antiemetic pathways raised delayed complete response from 69.5% to 76.9%
shelves.question: In patients receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (anthracycline–cyclophosphamide), does the fixed combination netupitant–palonosetron (NEPA) improve complete response versus palonosetron alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiemetics/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects* · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Isoquinolines/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced/prevention & control* · Palonosetron · Pyridines/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Quinuclidines/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Vomiting/chemically induced/prevention & control* · Piperazines · Benzeneacetamides
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — in the phase 3 anchor trial (Aapro M et al., PMID: 24603643), 1,455 chemotherapy-naïve patients receiving anthracycline–cyclophosphamide chemotherapy (classified moderately emetogenic in the trial) took a single oral dose of the fixed netupitant 300 mg–palonosetron 0.50 mg combination (NEPA) or palonosetron 0.50 mg alone, each with day-1 dexamethasone. Complete response (no vomiting, no rescue medication) in the delayed phase (25–120 hours) — the primary endpoint — was 76.9% on NEPA versus 69.5% on palonosetron, an absolute gain of 7.4 percentage points (P = 0.001), with concordant gains overall (74.3% vs 66.6%) and in the acute phase (88.4% vs 85.0%), and a similar safety profile. A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (Luo WT et al., PMID: 39284781) found NEPA plus dexamethasone also beat aprepitant-based NK1 regimens on complete response (overall-phase relative risk 1.15, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.30), with the largest subgroup effect in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (RR 1.31). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding netupitant to palonosetron in one capsule genuinely improves complete response, most clearly in the delayed phase where patients suffer longest. Note the trial's dexamethasone doses differed between arms (12 mg with NEPA, 20 mg with palonosetron), which if anything handicapped the combination.

cards.headline: Aapro 2014: delayed-phase complete response 76.9% with NEPA versus 69.5% with palonosetron alone (P = 0.001) — an absolute gain of 7.4 points in 1,455 patients
cards.summary: Aapro 2014: delayed-phase complete response 76.9% with NEPA versus 69.5% with palonosetron alone (P = 0.001) — an absolute gain of 7.4 points in 1,455 patients
cards.people: 1,455 chemotherapy-naïve patients receiving moderately emetogenic anthracycline–cyclophosphamide chemotherapy in a multinational double-blind phase 3 trial, randomised to a single oral dose of NEPA (netupitant 300 mg + palonosetron 0.50 mg) or palonosetron 0.50 mg alone; all received oral dexamethasone on day 1 only (12 mg in the NEPA arm, 20 mg in the palonosetron arm). Primary endpoint: complete response (no emesis, no rescue medication) in the delayed phase (25–120 h) of cycle 1.
cards.result: Complete response was higher with NEPA than palonosetron in every phase: delayed 76.9% vs 69.5% (P = 0.001), overall (0–120 h) 74.3% vs 66.6% (P = 0.001), and acute (0–24 h) 88.4% vs 85.0% (P = 0.047). NEPA was also superior in the delayed and overall phases for no emesis, no significant nausea, and complete protection (complete response plus no significant nausea). NEPA was well tolerated with a safety profile similar to palonosetron alone.
cards.watchOut: One chemotherapy setting: anthracycline–cyclophosphamide, rated moderately emetogenic when the trial was run (modern classifications treat it as highly emetogenic, which is a labelling shift, not a data change). Dexamethasone dose differed between arms (12 vs 20 mg) — a design asymmetry, though it favoured the control arm. Results are for cycle 1; multi-cycle durability is outside this record, and the comparison is against palonosetron without any NK1 antagonist, not against a three-drug aprepitant regimen.
cards.source: Aapro M et al. A randomized phase III study evaluating the efficacy and safety of NEPA, a fixed-dose combination of netupitant and palonosetron, for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting following moderately emetogenic chemotherapy. Annals of Oncology. 2014. PMID: 24603643. Registry ID: NCT01339260. cards.headline: Luo 2025 meta-analysis (7 RCTs): NEPA plus dexamethasone beat even aprepitant-based NK1 regimens on complete response (overall relative risk 1.15), strongest in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (RR 1.31)
cards.summary: Luo 2025 meta-analysis (7 RCTs): NEPA plus dexamethasone beat even aprepitant-based NK1 regimens on complete response (overall relative risk 1.15), strongest in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (RR 1.31)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 RCTs (Luo WT 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised controlled trials comparing NEPA (netupitant–palonosetron) plus dexamethasone against other NK1-antagonist-based regimens (an NK1 antagonist plus a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone, largely aprepitant-based), with literature searched to December 2023.
cards.result: NEPA plus dexamethasone gave higher complete-response rates than aprepitant-based regimens in the overall phase (relative risk 1.15, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.30) and delayed phase (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.41); better nausea control (overall RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.36; delayed RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.40); and less rescue-therapy use (overall RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.95; delayed RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.78). Adverse-event rates were comparable (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.10). In subgroup analysis the complete-response advantage was largest in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.60). All effect measures are relative risks, as reported by the review.
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is aprepitant-based triple therapy, not palonosetron alone — so this card supports NEPA's standing among NK1 regimens rather than re-testing the anchor question, and its relative risks have confidence intervals that only just exclude 1.0 for the primary comparison (1.02 to 1.30). Seven trials is a thin base for subgroup claims such as the moderately-emetogenic advantage.
cards.source: Luo WT et al. Comparative effectiveness of netupitant-palonosetron plus dexamethasone versus aprepitant-based regimens in mitigating chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. The Oncologist. 2025. PMID: 39284781. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a 7.4-point absolute gain in delayed complete response in the pivotal trial, and a meta-analysis placing NEPA at least level with — probably ahead of — aprepitant-based prophylaxis
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 7.4-point absolute gain in delayed complete response in the pivotal trial, and a meta-analysis placing NEPA at least level with — probably ahead of — aprepitant-based prophylaxis
cards.people: One double-blind phase 3 trial of 1,455 patients (Aapro 2014) plus a meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials of NEPA against aprepitant-based regimens (Luo WT 2025).
cards.result: Against palonosetron alone: delayed complete response 76.9% vs 69.5% (absolute +7.4 points, P = 0.001); overall 74.3% vs 66.6%; acute 88.4% vs 85.0%. Against aprepitant-based regimens: complete response relative risk 1.15 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.30) overall, 1.20 delayed; adverse events comparable (RR 1.03). Safety in the pivotal trial was similar to palonosetron alone. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain over palonosetron alone is worthwhile but not dramatic — roughly one extra complete response for every 14 patients treated — and cost and formulary position, not efficacy, are what usually decide between NEPA and a generic aprepitant regimen in practice. Evidence is for anthracycline–cyclophosphamide-type regimens in cycle 1; extrapolation to every emetogenic regimen goes beyond these records. Tier C is set per the build slate, reflecting that the head-to-head record against palonosetron alone is a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aapro M et al. Annals of Oncology. 2014 (PMID: 24603643); Luo WT et al. The Oncologist. 2025 (PMID: 39284781).

shelves.title: Levofloxacin for the first 12 weeks of myeloma therapy (TEAMM): febrile episodes or death cut from 27% to 19%, with no resistance penalty detected
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma starting therapy, does levofloxacin prophylaxis for the first 12 weeks reduce febrile episodes and death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use* · Antibiotic Prophylaxis/methods* · Double-Blind Method · Febrile Neutropenia/prevention & control* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infections/drug therapy* · Levofloxacin/therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy*/pathology · Prognosis · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — TEAMM (Drayson MT et al., PMID: 31668592) is a large, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial: 977 patients with newly diagnosed myeloma in 93 UK hospitals received levofloxacin 500 mg daily or placebo for the first 12 weeks of anti-myeloma therapy. The primary outcome — first febrile episode or death within 12 weeks — occurred in 95 of 489 patients (19%) on levofloxacin versus 134 of 488 (27%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.86, P = 0.0018), an absolute difference of about 8 percentage points. Serious adverse events were similar between arms (the exception was five episodes of mostly reversible tendonitis on levofloxacin), and the trial found no increase in health-care-associated infections or resistant-organism carriage — the harms that usually argue against prophylaxis. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): twelve weeks of levofloxacin at myeloma diagnosis prevents roughly one febrile episode or death for every 12–13 patients treated. This shelf is distinct from shelf #1784, which covers levofloxacin prophylaxis during prolonged chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (Bucaneve; Cullen) — a different population and treatment phase.

cards.headline: Drayson 2019 (TEAMM): febrile episode or death within 12 weeks in 19% on levofloxacin versus 27% on placebo (HR 0.66, P = 0.0018) — with no rise in resistant-organism carriage or health-care-associated infection
cards.summary: Drayson 2019 (TEAMM): febrile episode or death within 12 weeks in 19% on levofloxacin versus 27% on placebo (HR 0.66, P = 0.0018) — with no rise in resistant-organism carriage or health-care-associated infection
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, TEAMM (Drayson 2019)
cards.people: 977 patients aged 21 years or older with newly diagnosed myeloma, enrolled within 14 days of starting active myeloma treatment at 93 UK hospitals, randomised 1:1 to levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily (489 patients) or placebo (488 patients) for 12 weeks, with dose reduction for reduced renal function; median follow-up 12 months.
cards.result: First febrile episodes or deaths within the first 12 weeks: 95 (19%) in the levofloxacin group versus 134 (27%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.86; P = 0.0018). By 16 weeks, 597 serious adverse events had been reported (308 in the levofloxacin group, 289 in the placebo group), similar between groups except for five episodes (1%) of mostly reversible tendonitis in the levofloxacin group. The investigators report the benefit was achieved without increasing health-care-associated infections, and the trial also investigated antibiotic-resistant organism carriage.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a composite of febrile episodes and death, and the abstract does not separate the two — most of the prevented events will have been febrile episodes rather than deaths, so the result should not be quoted as a mortality reduction. The trial predates several modern myeloma regimens and was run in the UK; fluoroquinolone resistance patterns and baseline infection risk differ by place and era. Tendonitis, though uncommon and mostly reversible here, is a real fluoroquinolone class harm.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one large, well-blinded trial with a clear composite benefit and no detected resistance penalty — prophylaxis at myeloma diagnosis earns its place, with the composite caveat attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large, well-blinded trial with a clear composite benefit and no detected resistance penalty — prophylaxis at myeloma diagnosis earns its place, with the composite caveat attached
cards.people: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 977 patients with newly diagnosed myeloma (TEAMM, Drayson 2019) — the entire randomised record for prophylaxis in this specific window.
cards.result: First febrile episode or death within 12 weeks: 19% (95/489) on levofloxacin vs 27% (134/488) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.66 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.86), absolute difference about 8 percentage points. Serious adverse events similar overall; tendonitis 5 episodes on levofloxacin. Health-care-associated infections and resistant carriage: no increase reported. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A single trial, however large, leaves open whether the benefit persists with contemporary quadruplet induction and routine growth-factor and antiviral prophylaxis, and whether population-level fluoroquinolone resistance erodes it over years of routine use — the trial's own carriage data cover its follow-up window, not a decade of practice. Whether death alone is reduced remains unanswered by the published composite. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial in one health system.
cards.source: Synthesis of Drayson MT et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 31668592).

shelves.title: Imetelstat in ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (IMerge): 40% freed from transfusions for at least 8 weeks versus 15% on placebo — with grade 3–4 cytopenias in most
shelves.question: In adults with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes relapsed or refractory to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, does imetelstat achieve red-cell transfusion independence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Adolescent · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Erythropoiesis · Myelodysplastic Syndromes*/drug therapy · Thrombocytopenia*/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Oligonucleotides*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — IMerge (Platzbecker U et al., PMID: 38048786) randomised 178 heavily transfused patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes who had relapsed on, were refractory to, or were ineligible for erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to imetelstat 7.5 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or placebo. The primary endpoint — at least 8 consecutive weeks free of red-cell transfusion — was reached by 40% on imetelstat versus 15% on placebo (rate difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 9.9 to 36.9, P = 0.0008), and the authors describe transfusion independence lasting approximately a year in responders, with disease-modifying activity. The price is myelosuppression: grade 3–4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91% on imetelstat versus 47% on placebo, driven by neutropenia (68% vs 3%) and thrombocytopenia (62% vs 8%), though no treatment-related deaths were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real, clinically meaningful chance of transfusion independence for patients with no ESA option left, bought with substantial cytopenias that need monitoring. The stamp stops at POSSIBLE because this is a single trial and the benefit is concentrated in a responder minority.

cards.headline: Platzbecker 2024 (IMerge): 8-week transfusion independence in 40% on imetelstat versus 15% on placebo (P = 0.0008) — against grade 3–4 neutropenia in 68% and thrombocytopenia in 62%
cards.summary: Platzbecker 2024 (IMerge): 8-week transfusion independence in 40% on imetelstat versus 15% on placebo (P = 0.0008) — against grade 3–4 neutropenia in 68% and thrombocytopenia in 62%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, IMerge (Platzbecker 2024)
cards.people: 178 adults with red-cell transfusion-dependent lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (low or intermediate-1 IPSS risk) who were ESA-relapsed, ESA-refractory or ESA-ineligible, at 118 sites in 17 countries, randomised 2:1 to imetelstat 7.5 mg/kg as a 2-hour intravenous infusion every 4 weeks (118 patients) or placebo (60 patients); median follow-up 19.5 months (imetelstat) and 17.5 months (placebo).
cards.result: Red-cell transfusion independence for at least 8 consecutive weeks: 47 of 118 patients (40%, 95% CI 30.9 to 49.3) on imetelstat versus 9 of 60 (15%, 95% CI 7.1 to 26.6) on placebo — rate difference 25% (95% CI 9.9 to 36.9; P = 0.0008). By data cutoff, 77% of the imetelstat group and 75% of the placebo group had discontinued treatment. Grade 3–4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 107 of 118 (91%) on imetelstat versus 28 of 59 (47%) on placebo; the commonest were neutropenia (80 patients [68%] vs 2 [3%]) and thrombocytopenia (73 [62%] vs 5 [8%]). No treatment-related deaths were reported. The authors report durable transfusion independence of approximately 1 year and disease-modifying activity.
cards.watchOut: Transfusion independence is a meaningful but surrogate-adjacent endpoint — the abstract does not report a survival or leukaemia-progression advantage, and three quarters of both arms had stopped treatment by data cutoff. The cytopenias are not incidental: in a population already transfusion-dependent, grade 3–4 neutropenia in two thirds of patients means infection risk and monitoring burden are part of the treatment, not an afterthought. Single trial; the 2:1 randomisation leaves a small (n = 60) placebo arm.
cards.source: Platzbecker U et al. Imetelstat in patients with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes who have relapsed or are refractory to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (IMerge): a multinational, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: a 25-point absolute gain in transfusion independence in a no-option population, paid for in cytopenias — benefit real, reach limited to responders
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 25-point absolute gain in transfusion independence in a no-option population, paid for in cytopenias — benefit real, reach limited to responders
cards.people: One multinational double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 178 patients with ESA-failed lower-risk MDS (IMerge, Platzbecker 2024) — the entire phase 3 record for imetelstat in this setting.
cards.result: ≥8-week transfusion independence: 40% vs 15% (rate difference 25%, 95% CI 9.9 to 36.9, P = 0.0008), with durability of approximately 1 year reported by the authors. Grade 3–4 adverse events: 91% vs 47%; neutropenia 68% vs 3%; thrombocytopenia 62% vs 8%; treatment-related deaths: none. Survival benefit: not reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: What would move this stamp: longer follow-up showing whether transfusion independence converts into fewer iron-overload complications, better quality of life or longer survival, and real-world rates of the cytopenias outside a trial's monitoring. Until then the honest summary is a trade — a 2-in-5 chance of a year or so without transfusions against a near-certainty of significant blood-count suppression. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single trial.

shelves.title: Deferasirox versus deferoxamine: the once-daily tablet matched the overnight infusion on liver iron where doses were adequate — and patients much preferred it
shelves.question: In patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia and iron overload, does the oral chelator deferasirox reduce liver iron concentration comparably to deferoxamine, with acceptable safety?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Benzoates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Child · Child, Preschool · Deferasirox · Deferoxamine/therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Iron/metabolism · Iron Chelating Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Liver/metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Safety · Triazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · beta-Thalassemia/drug therapy*/metabolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the pivotal phase 3 trial (Cappellini MD et al., PMID: 16352812) randomised 586 regularly transfused patients with beta-thalassaemia to once-daily oral deferasirox or deferoxamine, dosed according to baseline liver iron concentration (LIC). In patients with LIC ≥7 mg Fe/g dry weight, the two drugs produced significant and similar dose-dependent reductions in LIC and serum ferritin; the trial's primary endpoint (maintenance or reduction of LIC) was not met in the overall population, apparently because patients with LIC <7 received proportionally lower deferasirox doses relative to deferoxamine. The Cochrane review (Bollig C et al., PMID: 28809446; 16 studies, 1,807 participants) reaches the matching conclusion: similar efficacy is achievable depending on the dose ratio (about 1 mg deferasirox to 1.8–2 mg deferoxamine), pooled intermediate markers favoured deferoxamine at the ratios actually compared (LIC mean difference 2.37 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.07), patient satisfaction was clearly better with the oral drug (RR 2.20), and mortality and long-term safety data remain limited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deferasirox is a legitimate once-daily oral alternative that controls liver iron comparably when dosed adequately — its advantage is a life without nightly infusions, not superior iron removal.

cards.headline: Cappellini 2006: in patients with liver iron ≥7 mg Fe/g, deferasirox matched deferoxamine's iron reductions — but the overall primary endpoint was missed because the low-iron group was relatively underdosed
cards.summary: Cappellini 2006: in patients with liver iron ≥7 mg Fe/g, deferasirox matched deferoxamine's iron reductions — but the overall primary endpoint was missed because the low-iron group was relatively underdosed
cards.people: 586 regularly transfused patients with beta-thalassaemia aged 2 years or older, randomised to once-daily oral deferasirox (296 patients) or deferoxamine (290 patients), with the dose of each drug set by baseline liver iron concentration (LIC); primary endpoint was maintenance or reduction of LIC, with serum ferritin, net body iron balance, safety and tolerability as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: In both arms, patients with LIC values of 7 mg Fe/g dry weight or higher had significant and similar dose-dependent reductions in LIC and serum ferritin, and similar effects on net body iron balance. The primary endpoint was not met in the overall population, possibly because proportionally lower doses of deferasirox relative to deferoxamine were given to patients with LIC below 7 mg Fe/g dry weight. The most common adverse events on deferasirox were rash, gastrointestinal disturbances and mild, non-progressive increases in serum creatinine; no agranulocytosis, arthropathy or growth failure was associated with deferasirox.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority-style question answered with a missed overall primary endpoint and a post-hoc dose explanation — the 'comparable' claim is solid only for the higher-iron subgroup at adequate doses, and LIC is an intermediate marker: the trial does not show equivalent prevention of cardiac iron, organ damage or death, the outcomes chelation ultimately exists to prevent. The record reports no exact LIC change figures, so none are quoted here.
cards.source: Cappellini MD et al. A phase 3 study of deferasirox (ICL670), a once-daily oral iron chelator, in patients with beta-thalassemia. Blood. 2006. PMID: 16352812. cards.headline: Bollig 2017 (Cochrane, 16 studies, 1,807 participants): similar efficacy is achievable depending on the dose ratio — pooled liver-iron and ferritin markers favoured deferoxamine at the ratios compared, while satisfaction strongly favoured the oral drug (RR 2.20)
cards.summary: Bollig 2017 (Cochrane, 16 studies, 1,807 participants): similar efficacy is achievable depending on the dose ratio — pooled liver-iron and ferritin markers favoured deferoxamine at the ratios compared, while satisfaction strongly favoured the oral drug (RR 2.20)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 16 randomised studies involving 1,807 people with thalassaemia and iron overload; nine studies (1,251 participants) compared deferasirox with standard deferoxamine treatment, with further small comparisons against deferiprone, combinations, and placebo in non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.
cards.result: For deferasirox versus deferoxamine, pooled serum ferritin was higher on deferasirox (mean difference 454.42 ng/mL, 95% CI 337.13 to 571.71; moderate-quality evidence) and pooled LIC higher (mean difference 2.37 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.07; moderate quality), with a lower responder proportion for LIC 1 to <7 mg Fe/g dry weight (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.92) — heterogeneity the reviewers attribute to the differing dose ratios compared. In the phase 3 study, similar or superior efficacy was achieved in the highly iron-overloaded subgroup at a mean ratio of 1 mg deferasirox to 1.8 mg deferoxamine. Patient satisfaction was better with deferasirox among those previously on deferoxamine (RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.89 to 2.57; moderate quality); discontinuation rates were similar; mortality data were low quality and long-term safety data limited.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled outcomes are intermediate markers (ferritin, LIC) of moderate-quality evidence, with substantial heterogeneity explained — but not eliminated — by dose ratio; rare toxicities and mortality are precisely where the review finds the data thinnest. The review's search closed in 2016, so later long-term safety experience is outside this record.
cards.source: Bollig C et al. Deferasirox for managing iron overload in people with thalassaemia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28809446. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: comparable iron control at the right dose ratio, decisively better convenience — the case for deferasirox is adherence and quality of life, not stronger chelation
cards.summary: Synthesis: comparable iron control at the right dose ratio, decisively better convenience — the case for deferasirox is adherence and quality of life, not stronger chelation
cards.people: One phase 3 head-to-head trial of 586 patients (Cappellini 2006) and a Cochrane review of 16 randomised studies and 1,807 participants (Bollig 2017) in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia.
cards.result: Liver iron and ferritin: similar reductions in the LIC ≥7 subgroup of the phase 3 trial; pooled across dose ratios, markers modestly favoured deferoxamine (LIC mean difference 2.37 mg Fe/g dry weight, 95% CI 1.68 to 3.07). Satisfaction: RR 2.20 (95% CI 1.89 to 2.57) favouring deferasirox in prior deferoxamine users. Discontinuations: similar. Mortality and rare long-term harms: insufficient data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything here is surrogate-marker evidence: neither the trial nor the review can say the oral drug prevents cardiac siderosis or death as reliably as decades of deferoxamine experience suggest for the infusion. Dose ratio is the whole game — underdosed deferasirox is inferior deferasirox — and renal and hepatic monitoring accompany the convenience. Tier C is set because the anchor trial missed its overall primary endpoint.

shelves.title: Ruxolitinib for steroid-refractory acute GVHD (REACH2): response in 62% versus 39% on best available therapy — and responses lasted
shelves.question: In patients with glucocorticoid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, does ruxolitinib improve day-28 overall response versus best available therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Graft vs Host Disease/drug therapy* · Humans · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Pyrazoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Pyrimidines · Stem Cell Transplantation/adverse effects* · Thrombocytopenia/chemically induced · Transplantation, Homologous · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — REACH2 (Zeiser R et al., PMID: 32320566) randomised 309 patients aged 12 or older with glucocorticoid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation to ruxolitinib 10 mg twice daily or the investigator's choice from nine commonly used second-line therapies. Overall response at day 28 — the primary endpoint — was 62% on ruxolitinib versus 39% on control (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.22, P < 0.001), and responses were more durable: day-56 durable response 40% vs 22%, estimated loss of response by 6 months 10% vs 39%, and median failure-free survival 5.0 vs 1.0 months (HR 0.46). Overall survival leaned the same way without reaching significance (median 11.1 vs 6.5 months; HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.15). Thrombocytopenia was commoner on ruxolitinib (33% vs 18%), with anaemia and cytomegalovirus infection frequent in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ruxolitinib is the first second-line therapy for steroid-refractory acute GVHD to beat best available therapy in a randomised trial — held at POSSIBLE because the trial was open-label and the survival difference is unproven.

cards.headline: Zeiser 2020 (REACH2): day-28 overall response 62% on ruxolitinib versus 39% on investigator's-choice therapy (OR 2.64, P < 0.001), with failure-free survival of 5.0 versus 1.0 months
cards.summary: Zeiser 2020 (REACH2): day-28 overall response 62% on ruxolitinib versus 39% on investigator's-choice therapy (OR 2.64, P < 0.001), with failure-free survival of 5.0 versus 1.0 months
cards.people: 309 patients aged 12 years or older with glucocorticoid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, in a multicentre open-label phase 3 trial, randomised to oral ruxolitinib 10 mg twice daily (154 patients) or investigator's choice from a list of nine commonly used options (155 patients); primary endpoint overall response (complete or partial) at day 28, key secondary endpoint durable overall response at day 56.
cards.result: Overall response at day 28: 62% (96 patients) on ruxolitinib vs 39% (61) on control (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.22; P < 0.001). Durable overall response at day 56: 40% (61) vs 22% (34) (OR 2.38, 95% CI 1.43 to 3.94; P < 0.001). Estimated cumulative incidence of loss of response at 6 months: 10% vs 39%. Median failure-free survival: 5.0 vs 1.0 months (hazard ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.60). Median overall survival: 11.1 vs 6.5 months (HR for death 0.83, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.15). Commonest adverse events to day 28: thrombocytopenia (33% vs 18%), anaemia (30% vs 28%) and cytomegalovirus infection (26% vs 21%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label design with response assessed by treating teams, and a heterogeneous control arm (nine different therapies chosen by investigators) — both soften certainty even with a blinded-looking effect size this large. Overall survival, the outcome families ask about first, did not differ significantly (HR 0.83, CI 0.60 to 1.15). The population spans adolescents and adults with a disease whose prognosis varies sharply by grade and organ involvement, which the abstract-level numbers average over.
cards.source: Zeiser R et al. Ruxolitinib for Glucocorticoid-Refractory Acute Graft-versus-Host Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32320566. Registry ID: NCT02913261. cards.headline: Synthesis: response, durability and failure-free survival all favour ruxolitinib by wide margins — survival does not yet, and the trial could not be blinded
cards.summary: Synthesis: response, durability and failure-free survival all favour ruxolitinib by wide margins — survival does not yet, and the trial could not be blinded
cards.people: One randomised open-label phase 3 trial, 309 patients with glucocorticoid-refractory acute GVHD (REACH2, Zeiser 2020) — the entire randomised head-to-head record against best available therapy.
cards.result: Day-28 overall response 62% vs 39% (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.65 to 4.22); day-56 durable response 40% vs 22%; loss of response at 6 months 10% vs 39%; failure-free survival 5.0 vs 1.0 months (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.60); overall survival HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.15), not significant. Thrombocytopenia 33% vs 18%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial is the ceiling on certainty here: response endpoints in GVHD involve judgement, and judgement is exactly what blinding protects. The result is nonetheless the strongest randomised evidence any second-line acute-GVHD therapy has produced, and the consistency across response, durability and failure-free survival argues against pure assessment bias. Tier C is set because it is one trial with an unproven survival effect.

shelves.title: L-glutamine in sickle cell disease: one fewer pain crisis and one fewer hospitalisation at the median over 48 weeks — a modest gain from a pharmaceutical-grade powder
shelves.question: In patients with sickle cell disease, does oral L-glutamine reduce pain crises and hospitalisations versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Anemia, Sickle Cell/complications/drug therapy* · Antisickling Agents/therapeutic use* · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glutamine/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Humans · Hydroxyurea/therapeutic use* · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/etiology/prevention & control · Pain Management* · Young Adult · beta-Thalassemia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single phase 3 trial (Niihara Y et al., PMID: 30021096) randomised 230 patients aged 5 to 58 with sickle cell anaemia or sickle β0-thalassaemia and at least two pain crises in the previous year to pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine powder (0.3 g/kg twice daily, the tested product in this trial, funded by Emmaus Medical) or placebo for 48 weeks; about two thirds in both arms also took hydroxyurea. The glutamine group had fewer pain crises (median 3.0 vs 4.0, P = 0.005) and fewer hospitalisations (median 2.0 vs 3.0, P = 0.005). Low-grade nausea, non-cardiac chest pain, fatigue and musculoskeletal pain were commoner on glutamine. Two cautions define the stamp: the absolute gain is one fewer crisis and one fewer hospitalisation at the median over a year, and the result rests on medians from a single trial — the record does not report mean crisis rates or a rate ratio. Note also that the tested product was a pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine powder; the publication names no consumer supplement brand, and current supplement products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a modest, real reduction in crises for a disease with few oral options. Hydroxyurea is shelved at #669, transfusion at #670, and voxelotor/crizanlizumab (with their reversals) at #847.

cards.headline: Niihara 2018: median pain crises over 48 weeks were 3.0 on L-glutamine versus 4.0 on placebo (P = 0.005), and median hospitalisations 2.0 versus 3.0 (P = 0.005)
cards.summary: Niihara 2018: median pain crises over 48 weeks were 3.0 on L-glutamine versus 4.0 on placebo (P = 0.005), and median hospitalisations 2.0 versus 3.0 (P = 0.005)
cards.people: 230 patients aged 5 to 58 years (53.9% female) with sickle cell anaemia or sickle β0-thalassaemia and a history of two or more pain crises in the previous year, randomised 2:1 in a multicentre double-blind trial to pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine 0.3 g/kg per dose twice daily by mouth (152 patients) or placebo (78 patients) for 48 weeks; patients on a stable hydroxyurea dose for at least 3 months continued it (about two thirds of both groups). The tested product was a pharmaceutical-grade L-glutamine powder; the trial was funded by Emmaus Medical.
cards.result: Patients on L-glutamine had significantly fewer pain crises than those on placebo (P = 0.005), with a median of 3.0 crises in the L-glutamine group and 4.0 in the placebo group over 48 weeks. Hospitalisations were also fewer (P = 0.005), median 2.0 versus 3.0. Low-grade nausea, non-cardiac chest pain, fatigue and musculoskeletal pain occurred more frequently in the L-glutamine group than in the placebo group. The authors conclude the median number of pain crises over 48 weeks was lower with oral L-glutamine, alone or with hydroxyurea, than with placebo.
cards.watchOut: The published record reports medians, not means or a crisis rate ratio — with skewed crisis counts, a one-crisis median difference can overstate or understate the average patient's gain, and the abstract gives no confidence interval for the treatment effect. The trial also predates the withdrawal-era reassessment of other sickle-cell drugs shelved at #847; its own result has not been re-tested in a second trial. The tested preparation was a pharmaceutical-grade powder at a weight-based dose — not interchangeable by assumption with over-the-counter glutamine supplements, which may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Niihara Y et al. A Phase 3 Trial of l-Glutamine in Sickle Cell Disease. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30021096. Registry ID: NCT01179217. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, a consistent direction on crises and hospitalisations, and a modest absolute gain — enough for POSSIBLE, not for more
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, a consistent direction on crises and hospitalisations, and a modest absolute gain — enough for POSSIBLE, not for more
cards.people: One multicentre double-blind phase 3 trial, 230 children and adults with sickle cell disease (Niihara 2018) — the entire randomised record for L-glutamine in this disease.
cards.result: Pain crises over 48 weeks: median 3.0 vs 4.0 (P = 0.005). Hospitalisations: median 2.0 vs 3.0 (P = 0.005). Background hydroxyurea in about two thirds of both arms, so the effect is largely an add-on effect. Adverse events: more low-grade nausea, non-cardiac chest pain, fatigue and musculoskeletal pain on L-glutamine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Median-based results from a single trial are fragile evidence: a confirmatory trial with rate-based endpoints, and clarity on which patients (by baseline crisis frequency and hydroxyurea use) gain most, would either firm this up or shrink it. Families should also hear the product caveat plainly — the benefit, if real, belongs to the pharmaceutical-grade preparation at the studied dose. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Niihara Y et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30021096).

shelves.title: Argatroban for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: fewer deaths, amputations and new clots than historical controls — the only kind of evidence this question has
shelves.question: In patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, does argatroban anticoagulation prevent the composite of death, amputation and new thrombosis compared with historical controls?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Arginine/analogs & derivatives · Blood Coagulation/drug effects · Blood Coagulation Tests · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Exanthema/chemically induced · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Heparin/adverse effects* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/chemically induced · Pipecolic Acids/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Purpura/chemically induced · Sulfonamides · Thrombocytopenia/chemically induced/drug therapy* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — there is no randomised trial of argatroban in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and there is unlikely ever to be one: the anchor evidence (Lewis BE et al., PMID: 11294800) is a prospective multicentre study comparing 304 argatroban-treated patients with 193 historical controls. The composite of death, amputation or new thrombosis occurred in 25.6% of argatroban patients with isolated HIT versus 38.8% of historical controls (P = 0.014); in HIT with thrombosis syndrome the figures were 43.8% versus 56.5% (P = 0.13), with time-to-event analyses favouring argatroban in both groups (P = 0.010 and P = 0.014) and no increase in bleeding. Historical controls are the weakest comparator in routine use — supportive care, diagnosis speed and case mix all drift over time, and every one of those drifts tends to flatter the newer treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): argatroban is a reasonable, widely used anticoagulant for HIT on the strength of this historically controlled evidence and its pharmacology, but the size of its benefit over simply stopping heparin has never been measured against a concurrent control.

cards.headline: Lewis 2001: composite of death, amputation or new thrombosis in 25.6% on argatroban versus 38.8% in historical controls with isolated HIT (P = 0.014); in HIT with thrombosis, 43.8% versus 56.5% (P = 0.13)
cards.summary: Lewis 2001: composite of death, amputation or new thrombosis in 25.6% on argatroban versus 38.8% in historical controls with isolated HIT (P = 0.014); in HIT with thrombosis, 43.8% versus 56.5% (P = 0.13)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre study of 304 patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (isolated thrombocytopenia, n = 160) or HIT with thrombosis syndrome (HITTS, n = 144), treated with intravenous argatroban 2 µg/kg/min adjusted to an activated partial thromboplastin time 1.5–3.0 times baseline, for an average of 6 days; outcomes over 37 days were compared with 193 historical control patients (HIT n = 147, HITTS n = 46) who had not received a direct thrombin inhibitor.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (all-cause death, all-cause amputation or new thrombosis) occurred in 25.6% of argatroban patients vs 38.8% of controls in isolated HIT (P = 0.014), and in 43.8% vs 56.5% in HITTS (P = 0.13). Time-to-event analysis of the composite favoured argatroban in both HIT (P = 0.010) and HITTS (P = 0.014), and argatroban significantly reduced new thrombosis and death caused by thrombosis (P < 0.05). Therapeutic aPTT was generally reached within 4–5 hours, platelet counts rose significantly faster than in controls (P = 0.0001), and bleeding events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls are the central weakness: the control patients were treated earlier, plausibly with later HIT recognition and less standardised care, so some — potentially much — of the 13-point composite gap may belong to era rather than drug. The HITTS comparison, the sickest group, did not reach significance on the composite proportion (P = 0.13) with only 46 controls. No concurrent comparator, no blinding, and a composite that mixes death with new thrombosis.
cards.source: Lewis BE et al. Argatroban anticoagulant therapy in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Circulation. 2001. PMID: 11294800. Registry ID: none in the record. outcomes over 37 days were compared with 193 historical control patients (hit n = 147, hitts n = 46) who had not received a direct thrombin inhibitor. the primary composite endpoint (all-cause death, all-cause amputation or new thrombosis) occurred in 25.6% of argatroban patients vs 38.8% of controls in isolated hit (p = 0.014), and in 43.8% vs 56.5% in hitts (p = 0.13). time-to-event analysis of the composite favoured argatroban in both hit (p = 0.010) and hitts (p = 0.014), and argatroban significantly reduced new thrombosis and death caused by thrombosis (p < 0.05). therapeutic aptt was generally reached within 4–5 hours, platelet counts rose significantly faster than in controls (p = 0.0001), and bleeding events were similar between groups. historical controls are the central weakness: the control patients were treated earlier, plausibly with later hit recognition and less standardised care, so some — potentially much — of the 13-point composite gap may belong to era rather than drug. the hitts comparison, the sickest group, did not reach significance on the composite proportion (p = 0.13) with only 46 controls. no concurrent comparator, no blinding, and a composite that mixes death with new thrombosis. lewis be et al. argatroban anticoagulant therapy in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. circulation. 2001. pmid: 11294800. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · arginine/analogs & derivatives · blood coagulation/drug effects · blood coagulation tests · diarrhea/chemically induced · exanthema/chemically induced · female · hemorrhage/chemically induced · heparin/adverse effects* · humans · male · middle aged · pain/chemically induced · pipecolic acids/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · purpura/chemically induced · sulfonamides · thrombocytopenia/chemically induced/drug therapy* · treatment outcome

cards.summary: Synthesis: direction favourable, design weak — argatroban's HIT evidence is a historically controlled study, and the stamp prices that honestly
cards.people: One prospective multicentre study, 304 argatroban-treated patients versus 193 historical controls (Lewis 2001) — the pivotal evidence for argatroban in HIT; no randomised controlled trial exists in this record.
cards.result: Composite death/amputation/new thrombosis: HIT 25.6% vs 38.8% (P = 0.014); HITTS 43.8% vs 56.5% (P = 0.13), with time-to-event analyses significant in both groups. New thrombosis and thrombotic death: significantly reduced. Bleeding: similar to controls. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Clinicians reading this shelf should separate two questions: whether to anticoagulate HIT with a non-heparin agent (standard practice, supported by the natural history of untreated HIT) and how large argatroban's specific advantage is (unmeasured against any concurrent control). This shelf answers only the second, and weakly. Tier C is set because the design is historically controlled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lewis BE et al. Circulation. 2001 (PMID: 11294800).

shelves.title: Tranexamic acid to prevent bleeding in thrombocytopenic haematology patients: two blinded trials, two nulls — no routine role
shelves.question: In patients with haematological malignancies and severe thrombocytopenia, does prophylactic tranexamic acid prevent clinically significant bleeding versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antifibrinolytic Agents*/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hematologic Neoplasms*/complications/drug therapy · Hemorrhage/chemically induced/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Transfusion/adverse effects · Tranexamic Acid*/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two placebo-controlled randomised trials, in two countries and two eras, asked whether prophylactic tranexamic acid prevents bleeding in patients with haematological malignancies and severe thrombocytopenia, and both answered no. A-TREAT (Gernsheimer TB et al., PMID: 35667085) found WHO grade ≥2 bleeding in 50.3% on tranexamic acid versus 54.2% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.34, P = .44), with no difference in platelet transfusions. TREATT (TREATT Trial Investigators, PMID: 39642900), the larger trial with 616 randomised patients, found death or grade ≥2 bleeding in 31.7% versus 34.2% (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.27, P = 0.62), again with no difference in thrombotic events. Reassuringly, neither trial showed a thrombosis penalty — but a drug that neither helps nor measurably harms has no routine role. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic tranexamic acid should not be used routinely to prevent bleeding in thrombocytopenic haematology patients. Tranexamic acid's life-saving roles in trauma, postpartum and surgical bleeding are different questions, shelved elsewhere (e.g., #138, #1246).

cards.headline: Gernsheimer 2022 (A-TREAT): WHO grade ≥2 bleeding in 50.3% on tranexamic acid versus 54.2% on placebo (adjusted OR 0.83, P = .44) — and no saving in platelet transfusions
cards.summary: Gernsheimer 2022 (A-TREAT): WHO grade ≥2 bleeding in 50.3% on tranexamic acid versus 54.2% on placebo (adjusted OR 0.83, P = .44) — and no saving in platelet transfusions
cards.people: Randomised double-blind trial enrolling 337 adults (mean age 53.9; 41.8% women) undergoing treatment for haematological malignancies, assigned to tranexamic acid 1,300 mg orally or 1,000 mg intravenously three times daily (168 patients) or placebo (169 patients) for up to 30 days; treatment was activated in 330 patients when platelet counts fell below 30,000/µL, and 279 (83%) had complete outcome ascertainment.
cards.result: WHO grade ≥2 bleeding within 30 days of activation occurred in 50.3% (73/145) on tranexamic acid and 54.2% (78/144) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.34; P = .44). There was no significant difference in mean platelet transfusions (mean difference 0.1, 95% CI −1.9 to 2.0), mean days alive without grade ≥2 bleeding (mean difference 0.8, 95% CI −0.4 to 2.0), thrombotic events (3.7% [6/163] vs 5.5% [9/163]) or deaths due to serious bleeding. Common adverse events (diarrhoea, febrile neutropenia, fatigue, nausea) were frequent and similar in both arms, reflecting the underlying treatment.
cards.watchOut: Of 3,120 patients screened, only 356 were eligible and 337 randomised, and 17% lacked complete outcome ascertainment — the trial is smaller and leakier than its design promised, so it excludes a large benefit rather than a modest one. Prophylactic platelet transfusion practice continued in the background, which is the right design for the routine-use question but compresses any tranexamic acid effect.
cards.source: Gernsheimer TB et al. Prophylactic tranexamic acid in patients with hematologic malignancy: a placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial. Blood. 2022. PMID: 35667085. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: TREATT 2025: death or grade ≥2 bleeding in 31.7% on tranexamic acid versus 34.2% on placebo (HR 0.92, P = 0.62) in 616 randomised patients — the bigger trial confirms the null
cards.summary: TREATT 2025: death or grade ≥2 bleeding in 31.7% on tranexamic acid versus 34.2% on placebo (HR 0.92, P = 0.62) in 616 randomised patients — the bigger trial confirms the null
cards.people: International randomised double-blind phase 3 trial at 27 haematology centres in Australia and the UK, enrolling 616 adults receiving intensive chemotherapy or haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for a haematological malignancy whose platelet count was ≤10 × 10⁹/L for 5 days or longer; tranexamic acid (1 g intravenously or 1.5 g orally every 8 hours; 310 patients) or placebo (306 patients) started when platelets fell below 30 × 10⁹/L and continued to platelet recovery or day 30, with prophylactic platelet transfusion maintained as standard care. Modified intention-to-treat analysis: 300 vs 297 patients.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — death or WHO grade 2 or higher bleeding up to day 30 — occurred in 31.7% (90/298, 95% CI 26.6 to 37.4) on tranexamic acid versus 34.2% (98/295, 95% CI 29.0 to 40.0) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.27; P = 0.62). There were no differences in thrombotic events or veno-occlusive disease. Serious adverse events to day 60 numbered 94 in 77 participants on tranexamic acid and 103 in 82 participants on placebo. The investigators conclude there is insufficient evidence to support routine tranexamic acid use in this setting.
cards.watchOut: TREATT's confidence interval (HR 0.67 to 1.27) still admits a modest benefit, so 'no routine role' rather than 'proven useless in every subgroup' is the correct reading; patients with active bleeding (treatment, not prophylaxis) were not the question. Bleeding rates were lower than in A-TREAT, reflecting differing populations and transfusion practice — consistency of the null across both is the point.
cards.source: TREATT Trial Investigators et al. Tranexamic acid versus placebo to prevent bleeding in patients with haematological malignancies and severe thrombocytopenia (TREATT): a randomised, double-blind, parallel, phase 3 superiority trial. The Lancet Haematology. 2025. PMID: 39642900. Registry ID: NCT03136445. cards.headline: Synthesis: two blinded trials, two nulls, no thrombosis penalty — routine prophylactic tranexamic acid in thrombocytopenic haematology patients is a closed question
cards.summary: Synthesis: two blinded trials, two nulls, no thrombosis penalty — routine prophylactic tranexamic acid in thrombocytopenic haematology patients is a closed question
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials: A-TREAT, 337 patients (Gernsheimer 2022), and TREATT, 616 patients (2025) — together the complete placebo-controlled record for prophylactic tranexamic acid in haematological malignancy.
cards.result: Grade ≥2 bleeding: 50.3% vs 54.2% (adjusted OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.34) in A-TREAT; death or grade ≥2 bleeding 31.7% vs 34.2% (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.27) in TREATT. Platelet transfusions: no difference. Thrombotic events: no increase in either trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A prophylaxis null is not a treatment null: these trials do not address tranexamic acid given for established bleeding, nor its proven roles in trauma, surgery and postpartum haemorrhage covered by other shelves. Nor do they exclude benefit in narrower niches (for example patients refractory to platelet transfusion) that neither trial isolated. What they close is the routine-prophylaxis question they actually asked.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gernsheimer TB et al. Blood. 2022 (PMID: 35667085); TREATT Trial Investigators et al. The Lancet Haematology. 2025 (PMID: 39642900).

shelves.title: Avatrombopag for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia: 70% versus 73% met the endpoint — the placebo arm did just as well in a first-episode population
shelves.question: In patients with non-haematological malignancies and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, does avatrombopag raise platelet counts enough to avoid platelet transfusion and chemotherapy dose delays versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anemia*/drug therapy · Antineoplastic Agents*/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Neutropenia*/etiology · Thiazoles · Thiophenes · Thrombocytopenia*/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the phase 3 trial (Al-Samkari H et al., PMID: 35240074) randomised 122 patients with ovarian, bladder or lung cancer and platelet counts below 50 × 10⁹/L to oral avatrombopag 60 mg daily or placebo, given for 5 days before and after chemotherapy. The composite primary endpoint — avoiding platelet transfusion, a ≥15% chemotherapy dose reduction and a ≥4-day delay — was met by 70% (57/82) on avatrombopag and 73% (29/40) on placebo (difference −3.0%, 95% CI −21.6 to 15.6; P = 0.72), with the same picture per protocol (85% vs 84%). The investigators note the placebo group did surprisingly well: these were relatively chemotherapy-naïve patients (no previous chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, at most two prior lines), whose counts may recover spontaneously, leaving little room for any drug to show benefit. Safety was acceptable (serious adverse events 18% vs 20%; no treatment-related deaths), and the drug does raise platelet counts in other settings — so the authors argue for testing in more persistent thrombocytopenia rather than abandoning the approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this population, avatrombopag did not keep chemotherapy on schedule any better than placebo.

cards.headline: Al-Samkari 2022: primary endpoint met by 70% on avatrombopag versus 73% on placebo (difference −3.0%, P = 0.72) — a negative phase 3 trial in 122 patients
cards.summary: Al-Samkari 2022: primary endpoint met by 70% on avatrombopag versus 73% on placebo (difference −3.0%, P = 0.72) — a negative phase 3 trial in 122 patients
cards.people: 122 adults with ovarian, bladder or lung cancer receiving chemotherapy who had severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50 × 10⁹/L), at 71 hospitals and cancer centres in seven countries, randomised 2:1 to oral avatrombopag 60 mg once daily (82 patients) or placebo (40 patients), dosed 5 days before and 5 days after chemotherapy; eligibility required no more than two previous chemotherapy lines, ECOG performance status ≤2, and no previous history of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia. Median follow-up 31 days.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (no platelet transfusion, no ≥15% chemotherapy dose reduction and no ≥4-day chemotherapy delay due to thrombocytopenia, through the start of the next cycle) was reached by 57 of 82 patients (70%, 95% CI 58 to 79) on avatrombopag versus 29 of 40 (73%, 95% CI 56 to 85) on placebo — difference −3.0% (95% CI −21.6 to 15.6; P = 0.72). Per protocol: 51 of 60 (85%) vs 27 of 32 (84%); difference 0.6% (P = 0.96). Serious adverse events occurred in 15 (18%) on avatrombopag and 8 (20%) on placebo; common grade 3–4 events were the cytopenias of chemotherapy itself; most adverse events were judged unrelated to study drug and no treatment-related deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own eligibility criteria built in a high placebo response: patients with previous chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia were excluded, so many placebo patients' counts recovered without help — a design that tests the drug in the population least likely to need it. The confidence interval (−21.6 to +15.6 points) is wide: with 122 patients the trial cannot exclude a moderate benefit or harm on the composite. Results say nothing about patients with persistent, recurrent thrombocytopenia across cycles.
cards.source: Al-Samkari H et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one negative trial in a low-risk population — no demonstrated benefit on transfusion avoidance or chemotherapy scheduling, and the interesting population remains untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: one negative trial in a low-risk population — no demonstrated benefit on transfusion avoidance or chemotherapy scheduling, and the interesting population remains untested
cards.people: One international double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 122 patients with non-haematological malignancies and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (Al-Samkari 2022) — the entire randomised record for avatrombopag in this indication.
cards.result: Composite endpoint (no transfusion, dose reduction or delay): 70% vs 73% intention-to-treat (difference −3.0%, 95% CI −21.6 to 15.6, P = 0.72); 85% vs 84% per protocol. Serious adverse events 18% vs 20%; treatment-related deaths none. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Do not read this as proof that thrombopoietin agonists cannot help chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia: the trial selected patients whose thrombocytopenia was likely transient and first-time. The claim that survives is narrower — in relatively chemotherapy-naïve patients with a first severe platelet drop, adding avatrombopag around one cycle changed nothing measurable. Tier C is set because it is a single, small trial.

shelves.title: Intravenous iron for chemotherapy-induced anaemia: one transfusion spared for roughly every 20 patients treated instead of oral iron — a modest, clean effect
shelves.question: In patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia, does intravenous iron (alone or with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents) raise haemoglobin and reduce transfusion versus oral iron or no iron?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the evidence here is a systematic review and meta-analysis (Buchrits S et al., PMID: 35887920) of 8 randomised trials totalling 1,015 patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia, comparing intravenous iron with oral iron (271 patients) or no iron (191 patients), and excluding trials that used erythropoiesis-stimulating agents — so this shelf isolates iron's own effect. Intravenous iron reduced the proportion of patients needing a red-cell transfusion compared with oral iron (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95 — a 28% relative reduction — with a number needed to treat of 20, 95% CI 11 to 100) and increased the haematopoietic response, defined as a haemoglobin rise above 1 g/dL or above 11 g/dL (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.5, a relative measure). Adverse events overall (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.07) and severe adverse events (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.57) did not differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron spares roughly one transfusion for every 20 patients treated compared with oral iron, without a safety penalty in these trials — a useful, modest effect, held at POSSIBLE because the underlying trials are few, small and span three decades of changing practice. Intravenous iron in kidney disease and pregnancy are different questions, shelved at #294/#369 and #673.

cards.headline: Buchrits 2022 (8 RCTs, 1,015 patients): transfusion need fell with intravenous iron versus oral iron (RR 0.72 — a 28% relative reduction; NNT 20), and haematopoietic response rose (RR 1.23), with no excess adverse events
cards.summary: Buchrits 2022 (8 RCTs, 1,015 patients): transfusion need fell with intravenous iron versus oral iron (RR 0.72 — a 28% relative reduction; NNT 20), and haematopoietic response rose (RR 1.23), with no excess adverse events
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled trials published between January 1990 and July 2021, randomising 1,015 patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia: 553 to intravenous iron, 271 to oral iron and 191 to no iron. Trials using erythropoiesis-stimulating agents were excluded, isolating the effect of iron itself. Primary outcome: the percentage of patients requiring a red-blood-cell transfusion during the study period.
cards.result: Intravenous iron decreased the percentage of patients requiring a blood transfusion compared with oral iron (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.95 — a 28% relative reduction), with a number needed to treat of 20 (95% CI 11 to 100). Haematopoietic response (haemoglobin increase >1 g/dL or to above 11 g/dL) was increased (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.5, a relative measure). There was no difference in adverse events (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.07; 8 trials) or severe adverse events (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.57; 8 trials). The authors conclude intravenous iron for chemotherapy-induced anaemia should be considered in clinical practice.
cards.watchOut: Eight trials across 31 years (1990–2021) means heterogeneous iron preparations, doses, transfusion thresholds and chemotherapy eras pooled into single estimates; the transfusion comparison is specifically against oral iron, and the no-iron comparison (191 patients) is not separately quantified in the record for the primary outcome. The confidence interval for the number needed to treat (11 to 100) is wide, and no mortality or quality-of-life benefit is shown. The record carries no MeSH terms, so this card's source says so plainly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, modest transfusion-sparing effect from iron alone — worth using, not worth overselling
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, modest transfusion-sparing effect from iron alone — worth using, not worth overselling
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials and 1,015 patients with chemotherapy-induced anaemia (Buchrits 2022), excluding erythropoiesis-stimulating-agent trials — the randomised record for intravenous iron as sole therapy in this population.
cards.result: Transfusion requirement versus oral iron: RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.95), a 28% relative reduction; number needed to treat 20 (95% CI 11 to 100). Haematopoietic response: RR 1.23 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.5). Adverse events: RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.07); severe adverse events RR 1.09 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.57). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The clinically live questions sit outside this record: how intravenous iron performs alongside modern erythropoiesis-stimulating-agent use, which iron preparation and dose are best, and whether sparing transfusions improves how patients feel or function — none is answered by these eight trials. The effect is best framed to patients as 'about one transfusion avoided for every twenty patients given intravenous instead of oral iron', not as an anaemia cure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Buchrits S et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35887920).

shelves.title: FIT every year versus every two or three years: at the repeat round the detection of advanced neoplasia was the same whatever the interval — 1.9% overall, with no interval effect (p=0.62); mortality was never tested
shelves.question: In average-risk adults screened with faecal immunochemical testing, does annual testing detect more colorectal cancers and advanced adenomas than biennial testing, and does the interval change colorectal cancer mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/diagnosis · Aged · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Feces/chemistry · Follow-Up Studies · Hemoglobins/analysis · Humans · Immunochemistry · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Occult Blood · Sensitivity and Specificity · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for detection at the repeat round, within a 1–3-year range: in the Dutch randomised comparison of 7,501 invitees, second-round participation was 63.2% with a 1-year interval, 62.5% with 2 years and 64.0% with 3 years; positivity in the second round (6.0%, down from 8.4% in round one) did not depend on interval length (p=0.23), and neither did the detection rate of advanced neoplasia (1.9% in round two versus 3.3% in round one; interval comparison p=0.62). No trial has randomised the FIT interval and followed participants to colorectal cancer mortality, so that half of the question is unanswered by direct evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): annual testing finds no more advanced neoplasia at the repeat round than biennial or triennial testing; any mortality difference between intervals is untested, not disproven.

cards.headline: van Roon 2013: second-round advanced-neoplasia detection 1.9% overall and flat across 1-, 2- and 3-year intervals (p=0.62); participation 61–65% in every group
cards.summary: van Roon 2013: second-round advanced-neoplasia detection 1.9% overall and flat across 1-, 2- and 3-year intervals (p=0.62); participation 61–65% in every group
cards.people: 7,501 Dutch residents aged 50–74 randomly selected and invited for two rounds of one-sample FIT (cutoff 50 ng Hb/mL, 10 µg Hb/g faeces) separated by 1, 2 or 3 years.
cards.result: First-round participation was 64.7% (1-year group), 61.0% (2-year) and 62.0% (3-year); second-round participation was 63.2%, 62.5% and 64.0% respectively, with triennial screening drawing a higher second-round participation than annual (p=0.04). Second-round positivity was 6.0% versus 8.4% in round one (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.58–0.82) and did not depend on interval (p=0.23); advanced-neoplasia detection was 1.9% in round two versus 3.3% in round one (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43–0.76), likewise independent of interval (p=0.62). Positive predictive value was 41% versus 33% (p=0.07).
cards.watchOut: Only two rounds and a detection endpoint: the trial cannot speak to cumulative cancers found over a decade of annual versus biennial testing, interval cancers, or mortality — and its cutoff (10 µg/g) is lower than many programmes now use.
cards.source: van Roon AH et al. Random comparison of repeated faecal immunochemical testing at different intervals for population-based colorectal cancer screening. Gut. 2013. PMID: 22387523. cards.people: One randomised population trial (n=7,501) directly comparing FIT intervals on participation and detection.
cards.result: Advanced neoplasia at round two: 1.9% overall, no interval dependence (p=0.62). Participation: ~61–65% in all groups. Colorectal cancer mortality by interval: no randomised data. cards.watchOut: Programmes choosing annual testing are buying more rounds over a lifetime, not a better yield per round; modelling studies, not trials, are what support any long-term difference.

shelves.title: Endoscopic screening for gastric cancer: a large Chinese cluster trial cut upper-GI cancer deaths in high-risk areas (0.77% versus 0.99%), but the gastric-specific 12-year trial found 13.1 versus 13.5 deaths per 100,000 person-years — not significant
shelves.question: In high-incidence populations, does population endoscopic screening for gastric cancer reduce gastric cancer mortality versus no screening?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Early Detection of Cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · China/epidemiology · Aged · Adult · Risk Assessment · Esophageal Neoplasms/mortality/diagnostic imaging/diagnosis · Risk Factors · Stomach Neoplasms/mortality/diagnostic imaging · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms/mortality/diagnosis · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Mass Screening/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by population and by how specific the endpoint is. In the multicentre Chinese cluster-randomised trial (234,635 participants), an invitation to endoscopic screening reduced upper gastrointestinal cancer mortality in high-risk areas — adjusted cumulative risk 0.77% versus 0.99% over 7.5 years (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.66–0.91) — but not significantly in non-high-risk areas (0.26% versus 0.30%; risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65–1.13). The trial aimed squarely at non-cardia gastric cancer (Hua County, 33,847 residents, 12 years) found mortality of 13.1 versus 13.5 per 100,000 person-years (adjusted rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.49–1.50) — a non-significant 15% relative reduction, with per-protocol estimates (0.70) also non-significant. PROPOSED SPLIT: screening probably reduces upper-GI cancer deaths where incidence is high, but a gastric-cancer-specific mortality benefit is not yet statistically secured.

cards.headline: Xia 2025: upper-GI cancer mortality 0.77% versus 0.99% in high-risk areas (risk ratio 0.78) — 0.26% versus 0.30% and non-significant in non-high-risk areas
cards.summary: Xia 2025: upper-GI cancer mortality 0.77% versus 0.99% in high-risk areas (risk ratio 0.78) — 0.26% versus 0.30% and non-significant in non-high-risk areas
cards.people: 234,635 participants (median age 52) in high-risk and non-high-risk areas of China, randomised by cluster (2015–2017, follow-up to 2022) to invitation for endoscopic screening or usual care; in non-high-risk areas only risk-score-positive screening-group members were invited for endoscopy.
cards.result: In high-risk areas (64,836 screening versus 59,379 control), 480 screening-group participants (adjusted cumulative risk 0.77%) versus 545 controls (0.99%) died of upper gastrointestinal cancers within 7.5 years (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.66–0.91). In non-high-risk areas the adjusted risk was 0.26% (146 deaths) versus 0.30% (149 deaths) (risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65–1.13).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint combines oesophageal and gastric cancers, so the gastric-specific effect is diluted and cannot be read off directly; invitation-to-screen analysis also dilutes the effect of actually being scoped.
cards.source: Xia C et al. Effect of an Endoscopy Screening on Upper Gastrointestinal Cancer Mortality: A Community-Based Multicenter Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. Gastroenterology. 2025. cards.summary: Liu 2026 (Hua County, 12-year report): non-cardia gastric cancer mortality 13.1 versus 13.5 per 100,000 person-years — adjusted rate ratio 0.85, not significant
cards.people: 33,847 permanent residents aged 45–69 in 668 villages in rural Hua County, northern China, cluster-randomised to upper-GI endoscopic screening (17,104; 88.7% underwent endoscopy) or no screening (16,743), enrolled 2012–2016 with up to 12 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Non-cardia gastric cancer mortality was 13.1 per 100,000 person-years in the screening group versus 13.5 in controls; the intention-to-treat adjusted rate ratio was 0.85 (95% CI 0.49–1.50), a 15% relative reduction that was not statistically significant. cards.watchOut: Gastric cancer deaths were few, so the trial is underpowered for its own primary endpoint despite 12 years of follow-up; a single screening round in one rural county may not generalise to repeated-screening programmes such as Korea's.
