shelves.title: WISDOM: risk-based breast screening was non-inferior to annual mammography for stage ≥IIB cancers (30.0 versus 48.0 per 100,000 person-years) with far fewer mammograms — but biopsies were not reduced
shelves.question: In women invited to breast screening, does risk-based screening (interval and modality set by individual risk) detect cancer as safely as standard annual mammography, with fewer false positives?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Biopsy/statistics & numerical data · Breast/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Breast Neoplasms/diagnosis/epidemiology/genetics/prevention & control · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/diagnosis/epidemiology/genetics/prevention & control · Counseling/statistics & numerical data · Early Detection of Cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · Feasibility Studies · Follow-Up Studies · Genetic Risk Score · Genetic Testing/statistics & numerical data · Incidence · Magnetic Resonance Imaging/statistics & numerical data · Mammography/statistics & numerical data · Neoplasm Staging · Risk Assessment/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — safe on the cancer endpoint, unsuccessful on the biopsy endpoint. In WISDOM (28,372 women randomised), stage ≥IIB cancer rates were 30.0 per 100,000 person-years with risk-based screening versus 48.0 with annual screening (rate difference −18.0, 95% CI −40.2 to 4.1), meeting non-inferiority, and mammograms were far fewer (rate difference −3,835.9 per 100,000 person-years). But the co-primary hope of fewer biopsies failed: biopsy rates were not lower (rate difference +98.7 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI −17.9 to 215.3; 1,029 versus 943 biopsies). In the parallel observational cohort, 89% of women (15,980/18,031) chose risk-based screening when offered the choice. PROPOSED SPLIT: risk-based screening safely reallocates intensity — less screening for low-risk women, more for high-risk — without the promised reduction in biopsies.

cards.headline: WISDOM (Esserman 2025): stage ≥IIB cancers 30.0 versus 48.0 per 100,000 person-years (non-inferior); mammograms −3,835.9 per 100,000 person-years; biopsies 1,029 versus 943 — not reduced
cards.summary: WISDOM (Esserman 2025): stage ≥IIB cancers 30.0 versus 48.0 per 100,000 person-years (non-inferior); mammograms −3,835.9 per 100,000 person-years; biopsies 1,029 versus 943 — not reduced
cards.people: 28,372 women aged 40–74 without prior breast cancer or DCIS, recruited across all 50 US states (2016–2023, median follow-up 5.1 years), randomised to annual mammography or risk-based screening set by 9-gene sequencing, a polygenic risk score and the BCSC v2 model: highest risk — alternating mammography/MRI every 6 months; elevated — annual mammography; average — biennial; low risk (age 40–49, <1.3% 5-year risk) — no screening until age 50 or risk threshold.
cards.result: Stage ≥IIB cancer rate: 30.0 (95% CI 16.3–43.8) per 100,000 person-years risk-based versus 48.0 (30.1–65.5) annual (rate difference −18.0, 95% CI −40.2 to 4.1) — non-inferior. Biopsy rate difference: +98.7 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI −17.9 to 215.3), i.e. not lower (1,029 versus 943 biopsies). Mammogram rate difference: −3,835.9 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI −4,516.8 to −3,154.9). Cancer, biopsy, mammogram and MRI rates all rose with risk category, confirming the stratification worked.
cards.watchOut: Only 52 stage ≥IIB cancers in total drive the safety endpoint, adherence to assigned screening was incomplete (diluting the contrast), and participants were 77% non-Hispanic White and largely college-educated; five years is short for a screening-strategy trial.

shelves.title: HPV self-sampling: with PCR-based tests, a self-collected vaginal sample finds CIN2+ as accurately as a clinician's sample (pooled sensitivity ratio 0.99) — but signal-amplification tests lose accuracy (0.85), and specificity dips 2–4%
shelves.question: How accurately does HPV testing on a self-collected vaginal sample detect cervical precancer (CIN2+) compared with clinician-collected samples?
shelves.mesh: Colposcopy/methods · Early Detection of Cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Incidence · Intention to Treat Analysis/methods · Mass Screening/methods · Papillomaviridae/genetics/immunology · Papillomavirus Infections/complications/pathology/virology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sensitivity and Specificity · Specimen Handling/methods · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/epidemiology/pathology · Vagina/cytology/pathology · Vaginal Smears/methods · Uterine Cervical Dysplasia/epidemiology/pathology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by assay technology. The updated Arbyn meta-analyses (56 accuracy studies) found PCR-based high-risk HPV assays on self samples were as sensitive as on clinician samples for CIN2+ and CIN3+ (pooled sensitivity ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.97–1.02), whereas signal-amplification assays were less sensitive on self samples (ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.80–0.89); specificity to exclude CIN2+ was 2% (PCR) to 4% (signal amplification) lower on self samples. The earlier 2014 analysis (36 studies, 154,556 women) had found self-sample sensitivity lower overall (ratio 0.88 for CIN2+) because signal-based assays dominated. Mailing kits home also raised participation among underscreened women (relative participation 2.33, 95% CI 1.86–2.91 versus invitation letters). PROPOSED SPLIT: self-sampling is accurate enough with PCR-based assays and reaches women clinics miss; with older signal-based assays it is a second-best test.

cards.headline: Arbyn 2018 (updated meta-analyses): PCR assays on self samples match clinician samples (sensitivity ratio 0.99); signal-amplification assays do not (0.85); mailing kits doubled participation
cards.summary: Arbyn 2018 (updated meta-analyses): PCR assays on self samples match clinician samples (sensitivity ratio 0.99); signal-amplification assays do not (0.85); mailing kits doubled participation
cards.people: 56 diagnostic-accuracy studies comparing high-risk HPV assays on vaginal self samples versus clinician samples with colposcopy/biopsy verification of CIN2+, plus 25 participation trials in irregularly or never-screened women (minimum population 400).
cards.result: PCR-based assays: pooled sensitivity ratio for CIN2+/CIN3+ on self versus clinician samples 0.99 (95% CI 0.97–1.02). Signal-amplification assays: 0.85 (95% CI 0.80–0.89). Specificity to exclude CIN2+ was 2% lower (PCR) or 4% lower (signal amplification) on self samples. Mailed self-sampling kits produced higher participation than invitation/reminder letters (pooled relative participation 2.33, 95% CI 1.86–2.91); opt-in kit requests did not (1.22, 95% CI 0.93–1.61). Heterogeneity was substantial (I² >95%).
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is pooled across many assays, devices and settings with very high heterogeneity; a programme's result depends on the specific validated PCR assay and the follow-up pathway for positives, not on self-sampling in the abstract.
cards.source: Arbyn M et al. Detecting cervical precancer and reaching underscreened women by using HPV testing on self samples: updated meta-analyses. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2018. PMID: 30518635. cards.headline: Arbyn 2014: across 36 studies and 154,556 women, self samples were less sensitive overall (ratio 0.88 for CIN2+) — the deficit was concentrated in signal-based assays
cards.summary: Arbyn 2014: across 36 studies and 154,556 women, self samples were less sensitive overall (ratio 0.88 for CIN2+) — the deficit was concentrated in signal-based assays
cards.people: 36 studies enrolling 154,556 women in whom a self-collected sample was followed by a clinician-collected sample, with CIN2+ verified by colposcopy and biopsy in all women or in test-positive women.
cards.result: In screening settings, HPV testing on self samples detected on average 76% (95% CI 69–82) of CIN2+ and 84% (72–92) of CIN3+, with pooled specificity 86% to exclude CIN2+. Pooled relative sensitivity of self versus clinician samples was 0.88 (95% CI 0.85–0.91) for CIN2+ and 0.89 (0.83–0.96) for CIN3+; relative specificity was 0.96. Signal-based assays were less sensitive and specific on self samples, while some PCR-based tests showed similar sensitivity on both sample types.
cards.watchOut: This earlier pool predates widespread PCR-assay use, which is why its headline is more pessimistic than the 2018 update; read together, the two analyses isolate the assay — not the sampling — as the variable that matters.
cards.source: Arbyn M et al. Accuracy of human papillomavirus testing on self-collected versus clinician-collected samples: a meta-analysis. The Lancet. Oncology. 2014. PMID: 24433684. shelves.title: Liver-cancer surveillance in cirrhosis: cohort evidence links it to earlier detection and better survival (hazard ratio 0.67), but scanning every 3 months instead of 6 found no more small cancers in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In patients with cirrhosis, does regular ultrasound surveillance improve early-stage detection and survival from hepatocellular carcinoma, and is 6-monthly surveillance better than 3-monthly?
shelves.mesh: Belgium/epidemiology · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · France/epidemiology · Humans · Incidence · Liver Cirrhosis/complications/diagnostic imaging · Liver Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Ultrasonography · alpha-Fetoproteins/analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — surveillance itself versus surveillance intensity. For intensity, the randomised answer is clear: in Trinchet's trial of 1,278 patients with compensated cirrhosis, ultrasound every 3 months detected more tiny focal lesions (≤10 mm: 41% versus 28%, p=0.002) but no more hepatocellular carcinomas ≤30 mm (79% versus 70%, p=0.30) and no difference in HCC incidence (p=0.13) versus every 6 months. For surveillance versus none there is no cirrhosis randomised trial; the 2022 cohort meta-analysis (59 studies, 145,396 patients) associated surveillance with earlier-stage detection (risk ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.73–1.98), more curative treatment (risk ratio 1.83, 1.69–1.97) and better survival after lead-time adjustment (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.72), with physical harms from false positives in 8.8–27.5%. PROPOSED SPLIT: 6-monthly surveillance is the supported standard; 3-monthly adds false alarms, not curable cancers.

cards.headline: Trinchet 2011: ultrasound every 3 months found more sub-centimetre lesions (41% versus 28%) but no more small HCCs (79% versus 70% ≤30 mm, p=0.30)
cards.summary: Trinchet 2011: ultrasound every 3 months found more sub-centimetre lesions (41% versus 28%) but no more small HCCs (79% versus 70% ≤30 mm, p=0.30)
cards.people: 1,278 patients with histologically proven compensated cirrhosis (alcohol 39.2%, hepatitis C 44.1%, hepatitis B 12.5%) at 43 French and Belgian sites, randomised to ultrasound every 3 months or every 6 months, with standardised recall procedures for focal lesions.
cards.result: At least one focal lesion was detected in 358 patients (28%), but HCC was confirmed in only 123 (9.6%). Two-year focal-lesion incidence was 20.4% (3-monthly) versus 13.2% (6-monthly) (p=0.067), and lesions ≤10 mm were commoner with 3-monthly scans (41% versus 28%, p=0.002); however HCC incidence did not differ (p=0.13) and the prevalence of tumours ≤30 mm was 79% versus 70% (p=0.30).
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised interval, not surveillance itself, and predates modern antiviral therapy that has lowered HCC incidence; recall-procedure limits, not scan frequency, were the bottleneck the authors identified.
cards.source: Trinchet JC et al. Ultrasonographic surveillance of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis: a randomized trial comparing 3- and 6-month periodicities. Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.). 2011. cards.headline: Singal 2022 meta-analysis (59 cohort studies, 145,396 patients): surveillance associated with early detection (RR 1.86), curative treatment (RR 1.83) and survival (HR 0.67)
cards.summary: Singal 2022 meta-analysis (59 cohort studies, 145,396 patients): surveillance associated with early detection (RR 1.86), curative treatment (RR 1.83) and survival (HR 0.67)
cards.people: 59 studies including 145,396 patients with cirrhosis and HCC, of whom 41,052 (28.2%) had surveillance-detected cancer, comparing outcomes by whether HCC was detected under surveillance.
cards.result: Surveillance was associated with improved early-stage detection (risk ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.73–1.98), curative-treatment receipt (risk ratio 1.83, 95% CI 1.69–1.97) and overall survival after lead-time-bias adjustment (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.72), with high heterogeneity (I² 75–82%). Physical harms from false-positive or indeterminate results occurred in 8.8–27.5% across the four studies reporting them, mostly mild.
cards.watchOut: All component studies are observational: patients who attend surveillance differ from those who do not, and lead-time adjustment is modelling, not randomisation — hence Tier C and a SPLIT rather than a clean benefit stamp.
cards.source: Singal AG et al. HCC surveillance improves early detection, curative treatment receipt, and survival in patients with cirrhosis: A meta-analysis. Journal of hepatology. 2022. shelves.title: BEST3: offering a swallowable Cytosponge test in primary care found ten times more Barrett's oesophagus — 140 cases versus 13 — including 9 treatable dysplasias or stage I cancers versus none
shelves.question: In primary-care patients with chronic reflux symptoms, does a non-endoscopic Cytosponge-TFF3 test identify Barrett's oesophagus accurately enough to target endoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Barrett Esophagus/diagnosis/etiology/pathology · Biomarkers/analysis · Esophagoscopy/instrumentation · Female · Gastroesophageal Reflux/complications/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Trefoil Factor-3/isolation & purification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for detection, which is the outcome the trial measured: in BEST3 (13,514 patients randomised across 109 English general practices), offering Cytosponge-TFF3 to patients on long-term acid suppression produced 140 Barrett's diagnoses (2% of 6,834) versus 13 (<1% of 6,388) with usual care over 12 months (absolute difference 18.3 per 1,000 person-years; adjusted rate ratio 10.6, 95% CI 6.0–18.8, p<0.0001), including 9 cases of dysplastic Barrett's or stage I oesophago-gastric cancer versus none. Among those who swallowed the device successfully, 59% of endoscopies after a positive test confirmed Barrett's or cancer; harms were one device detachment requiring endoscopic removal and sore throat in 4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the offer of Cytosponge testing finds substantially more Barrett's — and a few early, treatable cancers — than usual care; whether that converts into fewer oesophageal cancer deaths is untested.

cards.headline: BEST3 (Fitzgerald 2020): Barrett's diagnosed in 140 (2%) offered Cytosponge versus 13 (<1%) usual care — rate ratio 10.6; dysplasia or stage I cancer 9 versus 0
cards.summary: BEST3 (Fitzgerald 2020): Barrett's diagnosed in 140 (2%) offered Cytosponge versus 13 (<1%) usual care — rate ratio 10.6; dysplasia or stage I cancer 9 versus 0
cards.people: 13,514 patients aged ≥50 who had taken acid-suppressants for reflux symptoms for over 6 months with no endoscopy in the past 5 years, in 109 English general practices (cluster and individual randomisation combined), allocated to usual care or usual care plus an offer of Cytosponge-TFF3 with endoscopy if TFF3-positive.
cards.result: Barrett's oesophagus was diagnosed in 140/6,834 (2%) in the intervention group versus 13/6,388 (<1%) in usual care (absolute difference 18.3 per 1,000 person-years, 95% CI 14.8–21.8; adjusted rate ratio 10.6, 95% CI 6.0–18.8, p<0.0001). Nine intervention participants (<1%) were diagnosed with dysplastic Barrett's (4) or stage I oesophago-gastric cancer (5) versus none in usual care. Of 6,834 in the intervention group, 2,679 (39%) expressed interest and 1,750 underwent the procedure; 1,654 (95%) swallowed it successfully; 221 of those tested positive and had endoscopy, of whom 131 (59% of those endoscoped) had Barrett's or cancer. One detachment required endoscopic removal; sore throat occurred in 63/1,654 (4%).
cards.watchOut: Only 39% of those offered testing took it up, so the population effect is an offer effect; the endpoint is detection of a precursor, not cancer mortality, and extra endoscopies with false positives are part of the package (41% of post-positive endoscopies found no Barrett's).

shelves.title: Skin-cancer screening and melanoma deaths: the Schleswig-Holstein pilot was followed by a halving of mortality — but nationwide German screening from 2008 produced no mortality decline, and the pilot region's rate climbed back to the national level
shelves.question: Does organised population skin-cancer screening reduce melanoma mortality, or mainly increase detection of thin and in-situ lesions?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Germany · Humans · Male · Melanoma/mortality · Skin Neoplasms/mortality · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pilot region and the national programme tell different stories. After the 2003–04 SCREEN pilot (360,288 people examined in Schleswig-Holstein), age-standardised melanoma mortality there fell 47% in men (1.9 to 1.0 per 100,000) and 49% in women (1.4 to 0.7) by 2008/09, while adjacent regions and Germany overall were stable. But when Germany rolled screening out nationally in 2008, incidence rose ~28% to 18.2 per 100,000 by 2010 with no downward mortality trend (2.3 deaths per 100,000 in 2013), and Schleswig-Holstein's mortality rose back to 2.4 per 100,000 — the same as Germany overall. PROPOSED SPLIT: an intensive one-off regional campaign coincided with a temporary mortality fall; routine nationwide screening has shown detection gains without a measurable mortality benefit — overdiagnosis is the demonstrated effect, mortality reduction is not.

cards.headline: Katalinic 2012 (SCREEN): melanoma mortality in Schleswig-Holstein fell from 1.9 to 1.0 (men) and 1.4 to 0.7 (women) per 100,000 after 360,288 people were screened — comparison regions flat
cards.summary: Katalinic 2012 (SCREEN): melanoma mortality in Schleswig-Holstein fell from 1.9 to 1.0 (men) and 1.4 to 0.7 (women) per 100,000 after 360,288 people were screened — comparison regions flat
cards.people: 360,288 residents aged ≥20 of Schleswig-Holstein, Germany, given whole-body skin examination in a one-year population screening project (July 2003–June 2004); melanoma mortality trends compared with adjacent regions (Denmark, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Hamburg, Lower Saxony) and Germany excluding Schleswig-Holstein.
cards.result: Age-standardised melanoma mortality in Schleswig-Holstein fell from 1.9 per 100,000 men and 1.4 per 100,000 women in 1998–99 to 1.0 and 0.7 by 2008/09 — declines of 47% and 49%. The annual percentage change over 2000–2009 was −7.5% (95% CI −14.0 to −0.5) in men and −7.1% (−10.5 to −2.9) in women, significantly different from all comparison areas, where rates were stable.
cards.watchOut: Ecological design: nobody was randomised, screened individuals were not linked to the deaths avoided, and a one-year campaign's effect appearing over a decade invites confounding by awareness, treatment and registration changes — the authors themselves call it strong evidence, not proof.
cards.source: Katalinic A et al. Does skin cancer screening save lives?: an observational study comparing trends in melanoma mortality in regions with and without screening. Cancer. 2012. cards.headline: Katalinic 2015 (nationwide Germany): incidence up ~28% after 2008 screening rollout, mortality flat at 2.3 per 100,000 — and Schleswig-Holstein back up to 2.4
cards.summary: Katalinic 2015 (nationwide Germany): incidence up ~28% after 2008 screening rollout, mortality flat at 2.3 per 100,000 — and Schleswig-Holstein back up to 2.4
cards.people: Population-based cancer-registry (GEKID) and cause-of-death data for all Germany, 2008–2013, after nationwide skin-cancer screening was introduced in 2008, compared with the Schleswig-Holstein pilot region.
cards.result: With nationwide screening, the age-standardised melanoma incidence rose by approximately 28% to 18.2 cases per 100,000 in 2010. For Germany overall there was no downward trend in melanoma mortality; the 2013 mortality rate was 2.3 deaths per 100,000 per year. In the pilot region, mortality had fallen to 1.0/100,000 by 2008 but then rose again, reaching 2.4/100,000 — once again the same as Germany overall.
cards.watchOut: The nationwide programme's examinations were less thorough than the pilot's (the authors' own explanation), so this card does not prove screening cannot work — it proves the programme as delivered did not reproduce the pilot's association.
cards.source: Katalinic A et al. Skin Cancer Screening in Germany. Documenting Melanoma Incidence and Mortality From 2008 to 2013. Deutsches Arzteblatt international. 2015. PMID: 26429634. cards.summary: Synthesis: detection reliably rises; mortality benefit appeared once, ecologically and temporarily, and vanished under routine delivery
cards.people: Two observational analyses of the same German experience — the SCREEN pilot region (360,288 screened) and the nationwide programme that followed it.
cards.result: Pilot region mortality: −47% (men), −49% (women) by 2008/09. Nationwide: incidence +28%, mortality unchanged (2.3/100,000, 2013); pilot region back to 2.4/100,000. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C because the mortality claim is observational and ecological.

shelves.title: Thyroid cancer screening: detection has risen 4.5% a year while mortality stands still — the USPSTF recommends against screening asymptomatic adults (grade D), judging harms at least moderate and benefits no greater than small
shelves.question: Does ultrasound screening for thyroid cancer in asymptomatic adults reduce thyroid cancer deaths, or only multiply diagnoses of indolent cancers?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Advisory Committees · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Asymptomatic Diseases · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Humans · Male · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Thyroid Neoplasms/diagnosis · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — net harm, in the USPSTF's bounded judgement: thyroid cancer detection in the US rose 4.5% per year over a decade to an incidence of 15.3 cases per 100,000 (2013) with no corresponding change in mortality, and overall 5-year survival is already 98.1%. The Task Force found inadequate direct evidence on screening benefits but bounded them as no greater than small — the cancer is rare, treated and monitored patients fare alike for the common types, and mass screening elsewhere changed incidence without changing mortality — while bounding harms as at least moderate, given proven treatment harms and substantial overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Its conclusion: the net benefit of screening asymptomatic adults is negative (grade D, recommend against). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): population thyroid ultrasound screening multiplies diagnoses of cancers that would never have caused harm, exposing people to surgery and lifelong treatment without a shown mortality gain.

cards.headline: USPSTF 2017: recommends against thyroid cancer screening in asymptomatic adults (grade D) — incidence 15.3 per 100,000, 5-year survival 98.1%, mortality flat as detection climbs
cards.summary: USPSTF 2017: recommends against thyroid cancer screening in asymptomatic adults (grade D) — incidence 15.3 per 100,000, 5-year survival 98.1%, mortality flat as detection climbs
cards.type: Evidence review and recommendation statement (Bibbins-Domingo 2017, USPSTF)
cards.people: Asymptomatic adults in the general population; the review covered screening (neck palpation and ultrasound) accuracy, treatment benefits and harms for screen-detected thyroid cancer, and population screening experience including the Korean programme.
cards.result: Detection incidence rose 4.5% per year over 10 years to 15.3 cases per 100,000 persons in the US in 2013, without a corresponding change in mortality; 5-year survival for thyroid cancer overall is 98.1%. The USPSTF bounded screening benefits as no greater than small (rare cancer; no outcome difference between treatment and monitoring for common tumour types; no mortality change after introduction of mass screening) and harms as at least moderate (adequate evidence of treatment harms; overdiagnosis and overtreatment likely substantial), concluding net benefit is negative — a grade D recommendation against screening.
cards.watchOut: This is a bounded judgement built from indirect evidence, not a screening trial — no randomised trial of thyroid screening exists. It addresses asymptomatic average-risk adults, not surveillance of nodules, radiation-exposed patients, or hereditary syndromes.
cards.source: Bibbins-Domingo K et al. Screening for Thyroid Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28492905. cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial, no mortality signal, a formal recommendation against — screening's measurable product is diagnoses
cards.people: The USPSTF evidence synthesis is the authoritative record for this question; the Korean ultrasound experience it draws on is the world's largest natural experiment in thyroid screening.
cards.result: Detection: +4.5% per year for a decade. Mortality: unchanged. Recommendation: grade D against screening. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C because the claim rests on observational and indirect evidence, which is all that exists.
cards.watchOut: Anyone citing rising thyroid cancer incidence as a reason to screen has the causality backwards on this evidence: the screening is the cause of the rise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bibbins-Domingo K et al. JAMA. 2017 (PMID: 28492905).

shelves.title: ANCHOR: treating anal precancer in people with HIV cut progression to anal cancer by 57% in relative terms — 173 versus 402 cases per 100,000 person-years
shelves.question: In people living with HIV aged 35 and over, does treating anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions prevent anal cancer versus active monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anus Neoplasms/etiology/pathology/prevention & control/therapy · Biopsy · Female · HIV Infections/complications · Homosexuality, Male · Humans · Male · Papillomavirus Infections/complications · Precancerous Conditions/etiology/pathology/therapy · Prospective Studies · Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions/etiology/pathology/therapy · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in ANCHOR, among 4,446 people living with HIV aged ≥35 with biopsy-proven anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, progression to anal cancer occurred at 173 per 100,000 person-years with treatment versus 402 per 100,000 person-years with active monitoring over a median 25.8 months — a 57% relative reduction (95% CI 6–80; p=0.03), on absolute counts of 9 versus 21 cancers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): treating anal HSIL prevents anal cancer in people with HIV; the absolute rates are low in both arms, so roughly 100 people need treatment and surveillance for about two years to prevent one cancer — and the trial does not extend to people without HIV.

cards.headline: ANCHOR (Palefsky 2022): 9 cancers on treatment versus 21 on monitoring — rate 173 versus 402 per 100,000 person-years (p=0.03)
cards.summary: ANCHOR (Palefsky 2022): 9 cancers on treatment versus 21 on monitoring — rate 173 versus 402 per 100,000 person-years (p=0.03)
cards.people: 4,459 people living with HIV aged ≥35 with biopsy-proven anal HSIL at 25 US sites (4,446 analysed), randomised to HSIL treatment (office ablation, ablation or excision under anaesthesia, or topical fluorouracil or imiquimod, repeated until resolution) or active monitoring without treatment; all had high-resolution anoscopy at least every 6 months.
cards.result: With median follow-up of 25.8 months, anal cancer was diagnosed in 9 participants in the treatment group (173 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI 90–332) versus 21 in the monitoring group (402 per 100,000 person-years, 95% CI 262–616) — a 57% lower rate in relative terms (95% CI 6–80; p=0.03 by log-rank).
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped with only 30 cancers, so the relative estimate is imprecise (the interval runs from 6% to 80%); treatment is a programme of repeated procedures under anoscopy surveillance, not a one-off intervention, and both arms received intensive monitoring that itself may catch cancers early.
cards.source: Palefsky JM et al. Treatment of Anal High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions to Prevent Anal Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 35704479. Registry ID: NCT02135419. shelves.title: Lynch syndrome colonoscopy intervals: 3-yearly surveillance in Finland produced no more colorectal cancer than 2-yearly-or-closer elsewhere — cumulative incidence by age 70 was 41%/36% (men/women) versus 58%/55%, and survival after cancer was 89–92% whatever the interval
shelves.question: In carriers of Lynch syndrome, how often should colonoscopic surveillance be performed — does a 1–2-year interval prevent more colorectal cancers than a 3-year interval?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for interval length, on prospective observational data: in the Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database, path_MLH1 carriers under 3-yearly colonoscopy in Finland (n=505) had cumulative colorectal cancer incidence by age 70 of 41% (men) and 36% (women), versus 58% and 55% under 2-yearly-or-more-frequent protocols elsewhere (n=439) — differences not significant (p>0.05), with mean time from last colonoscopy to cancer virtually identical (32.7 versus 31.0 months). In the companion survival analysis, 10-year survival after colon cancer was 89%, 90%, 90% and 92% whether the last colonoscopy was <1.5, 1.5–2.5, 2.5–3.5 or >3.5 years before diagnosis (p=0.91), while stage strongly predicted survival (93%, 94% and 82% for stages I–III, p<0.001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): shortening surveillance below a 3-year interval has not been shown to prevent more Lynch colorectal cancers or improve survival — surveillance itself is not in question here, only its frequency.

cards.headline: Seppälä 2017 (PLSD): cumulative CRC by age 70 in path_MLH1 carriers — 41%/36% under Finnish 3-yearly surveillance versus 58%/55% under ≤2-yearly protocols (p>0.05)
cards.summary: Seppälä 2017 (PLSD): cumulative CRC by age 70 in path_MLH1 carriers — 41%/36% under Finnish 3-yearly surveillance versus 58%/55% under ≤2-yearly protocols (p>0.05)
cards.people: 944 carriers of pathogenic MLH1 variants: 505 Finnish carriers enrolled in 3-yearly colonoscopy (4,625 observation years) and 439 carriers from other countries enrolled in colonoscopy 2-yearly or more frequently (3,299 observation years), all under surveillance with polypectomy.
cards.result: Cumulative colorectal cancer incidence at age 70 was 41% for men and 36% for women in the Finnish (3-yearly) series versus 58% and 55% in the non-Finnish (≤2-yearly) series (p>0.05). Mean time from last colonoscopy to cancer was 32.7 months (Finnish) versus 31.0 months (non-Finnish) (p>0.05). Ten-year overall survival after colorectal cancer was 88% versus 91% (p>0.05).
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: the Finnish and non-Finnish series differ in population background incidence and practice in ways adjustment cannot fully remove, and the point estimates actually favour the longer interval, which itself signals confounding rather than a true protective effect of waiting.
cards.source: Seppälä T et al. Colorectal cancer incidence in path_MLH1 carriers subjected to different follow-up protocols: a Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database report. Hereditary cancer in clinical practice. 2017. PMID: 29046738. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Dominguez-Valentin 2019 (PLSD): 10-year survival after colon cancer 89–92% across all intervals since last colonoscopy (p=0.91) — stage, not interval, predicted survival
cards.summary: Dominguez-Valentin 2019 (PLSD): 10-year survival after colon cancer 89–92% across all intervals since last colonoscopy (p=0.91) — stage, not interval, predicted survival
cards.people: 99 carriers of class 4/5 pathogenic mismatch-repair variants (77 MLH1, 17 MSH2, 2 MSH6 among those ≤65) who developed colon cancer after a first surveillance colonoscopy, grouped by time since the previous colonoscopy.
cards.result: Cancers were detected <1.5, 1.5–2.5, 2.5–3.5 and >3.5 years after the previous colonoscopy in 9, 43, 31 and 13 cases. Ten-year crude survival was 89%, 90%, 90% and 92% across those interval groups (p=0.91). By contrast, survival by stage was 93% (stage I), 94% (stage II) and 82% (stage III) (p<0.001); only one stage IV cancer occurred (in the 2.5–3.5-year group).
cards.watchOut: Only 99 cancers, so subgroup numbers are small; this analysis covers survival after cancer develops and cannot by itself rule out an incidence effect of shorter intervals — that is the companion report's job.
cards.source: Dominguez-Valentin M et al. Survival by colon cancer stage and screening interval in Lynch syndrome: a prospective Lynch syndrome database report. Hereditary cancer in clinical practice. 2019. PMID: 31636762. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: two prospective database reports, one message — below 3 years, more colonoscopies have not bought fewer cancers or better survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: two prospective database reports, one message — below 3 years, more colonoscopies have not bought fewer cancers or better survival
cards.people: Prospective Lynch Syndrome Database analyses totalling 944 path_MLH1 carriers for incidence and 99 subsequent colon cancers for survival.
cards.result: CRC incidence by 70: 41%/36% (3-yearly) versus 58%/55% (≤2-yearly), not significant. Survival by interval: 89–92%, p=0.91. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for interval shortening, Tier C because the evidence is observational.
cards.watchOut: These data concern MLH1 carriers chiefly; MSH6 and PMS2 carriers have lower penetrance and may warrant different intervals for other reasons, and no one should read this shelf as questioning surveillance itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Seppälä T et al. Hereditary Cancer in Clinical Practice. 2017 (PMID: 29046738); Dominguez-Valentin M et al. Hereditary Cancer in Clinical Practice. 2019 (PMID: 31636762).

shelves.title: IBIS-II: five years of anastrozole halved breast cancer in high-risk postmenopausal women — 85 versus 165 cases over a median 131 months (hazard ratio 0.51), and the protection persisted after treatment stopped
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women at increased risk of breast cancer, does anastrozole for 5 years prevent invasive breast cancer versus placebo, and do benefits persist after treatment stops?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anastrozole · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Aromatase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/prevention & control · Carcinoma, Ductal, Breast/prevention & control · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/prevention & control · Carcinoma, Lobular/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Middle Aged · Nitriles/therapeutic use · Postmenopause · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large and durable, from one trial reported twice: IBIS-II randomised 3,864 high-risk postmenopausal women to anastrozole 1 mg daily or placebo for 5 years. At the first report (median 5.0 years), breast cancer had developed in 40 women (2%) on anastrozole versus 85 (4%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.32–0.68). At the long-term report (median follow-up 131 months), cases were 85 versus 165 (hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.39–0.66) — a 49% relative reduction — with benefit continuing in the post-treatment period (hazard ratio 0.64 after year 5) and invasive oestrogen-receptor-positive cancer reduced by 54% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.46). Deaths did not differ (69 versus 70), and there was no excess of fractures or cardiovascular disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): anastrozole prevents breast cancer in high-risk postmenopausal women with protection outlasting the five treatment years; a mortality benefit has not been shown.

cards.headline: IBIS-II first report (Cuzick 2014): breast cancer in 40 (2%) on anastrozole versus 85 (4%) on placebo at median 5 years — hazard ratio 0.47
cards.summary: IBIS-II first report (Cuzick 2014): breast cancer in 40 (2%) on anastrozole versus 85 (4%) on placebo at median 5 years — hazard ratio 0.47
cards.people: 3,864 postmenopausal women aged 40–70 at increased risk of breast cancer, recruited in 18 countries (2003–2012), randomised to anastrozole 1 mg daily (n=1,920) or matching placebo (n=1,944) for 5 years; primary endpoint histologically confirmed breast cancer (invasive or DCIS).
cards.result: After median follow-up of 5.0 years, 40 women in the anastrozole group (2%) and 85 in the placebo group (4%) had developed breast cancer (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.32–0.68, p<0.0001). Predicted cumulative incidence at 7 years was 2.8% versus 5.6%. Deaths were 18 versus 17, with no cause more common in either group.
cards.watchOut: Five years is early for a prevention claim; the musculoskeletal and vasomotor side effects of oestrogen deprivation were largely — but the trial's framing matters — not significantly attributable to treatment in this report.
cards.source: Cuzick J et al. Anastrozole for prevention of breast cancer in high-risk postmenopausal women (IBIS-II): an international, double-blind, randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24333009. Registry ID: ISRCTN31488319. cards.headline: IBIS-II long-term report (Cuzick 2020): 85 versus 165 breast cancers at median 131 months (HR 0.51); benefit persisted after treatment (HR 0.64); deaths 69 versus 70
cards.summary: IBIS-II long-term report (Cuzick 2020): 85 versus 165 breast cancers at median 131 months (HR 0.51); benefit persisted after treatment (HR 0.64); deaths 69 versus 70
cards.people: The same 3,864 IBIS-II women, followed annually after the 5-year treatment period for breast cancer incidence, deaths, other cancers, fractures and cardiovascular events; median follow-up 131 months.
cards.result: Breast cancer occurred in 85 women on anastrozole versus 165 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.39–0.66, p<0.0001) — a 49% relative reduction; the effect was larger during treatment (hazard ratio 0.39) and remained significant after (0.64, 95% CI 0.45–0.91). Invasive ER-positive cancer: hazard ratio 0.46. DCIS: hazard ratio 0.41. Deaths overall (69 versus 70; hazard ratio 0.96) and from breast cancer (2 versus 3) did not differ. Non-breast cancers were fewer on anastrozole (147 versus 200; odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.91), driven by non-melanoma skin cancer; no excess fractures or cardiovascular disease emerged.
cards.watchOut: One trial, however large and long, is one trial — and the endpoint prevented is cancer diagnosis, not death; with 2 versus 3 breast-cancer deaths, any mortality effect is far beyond this sample size.
cards.source: Cuzick J et al. Use of anastrozole for breast cancer prevention (IBIS-II): long-term results of a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2020. PMID: 31839281. cards.headline: Synthesis: a halving of breast-cancer incidence that outlasts the pills — with mortality untouched and a single-trial base
cards.summary: Synthesis: a halving of breast-cancer incidence that outlasts the pills — with mortality untouched and a single-trial base
cards.people: IBIS-II (n=3,864), reported at 5 years and again at a median of 131 months.
cards.result: Breast cancer: 40 versus 85 cases at 5 years (HR 0.47); 85 versus 165 long-term (HR 0.51). Deaths: 69 versus 70. Fractures/cardiovascular excess: none. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C because one trial carries a benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: Uptake of preventive therapy is low in practice because of side-effect fears; these data quantify what is being declined — roughly one cancer prevented per 29 high-risk women treated over a decade (85 versus 165 per ~1,900).
cards.source: Synthesis of Cuzick J et al. The Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24333009); Cuzick J et al. The Lancet. 2020 (PMID: 31839281).

shelves.title: MAP.3: exemestane cut invasive breast cancer by 65% in relative terms in high-risk postmenopausal women — 11 cancers versus 32 over a median 35 months (0.19% versus 0.55% per year), with no serious toxicity signal
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women at increased risk, does exemestane prevent invasive breast cancer versus placebo, and at what cost in menopausal symptoms and bone health?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androstadienes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aromatase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/epidemiology/prevention & control · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/epidemiology/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Invasiveness · Postmenopause · Quality of Life · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from the single MAP.3 trial: 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk were randomised to exemestane or placebo; at a median 35 months, invasive breast cancer was detected in 11 women on exemestane versus 32 on placebo — annual incidence 0.19% versus 0.55%, a 65% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.70, p=0.002). Invasive plus non-invasive cancers: 0.35% versus 0.77% per year (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.27–0.79). Adverse events were slightly commoner on exemestane (88% versus 85%, p=0.003) but there were no significant differences in skeletal fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers or treatment-related deaths, and quality-of-life differences were minimal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): exemestane substantially reduces invasive breast cancer over three years in at-risk postmenopausal women, with symptom costs that were small in-trial; longer-term bone safety rests on the aromatase-inhibitor class record rather than this trial's 35 months.

cards.headline: MAP.3 (Goss 2011): invasive breast cancer 11 on exemestane versus 32 on placebo (HR 0.35); adverse events 88% versus 85%; fractures and cardiovascular events not different
cards.summary: MAP.3 (Goss 2011): invasive breast cancer 11 on exemestane versus 32 on placebo (HR 0.35); adverse events 88% versus 85%; fractures and cardiovascular events not different
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Goss 2011, NCIC CTG MAP.3)
cards.people: 4,560 postmenopausal women aged ≥35 with at least one risk factor (age ≥60, Gail 5-year risk >1.66%, prior atypical hyperplasia or LCIS, or DCIS with mastectomy); median age 62.5 years, median Gail score 2.3%; randomised to exemestane 25 mg daily or placebo, median follow-up 35 months.
cards.result: Invasive breast cancer: 11 cases on exemestane versus 32 on placebo (annual incidence 0.19% versus 0.55%; hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.70, p=0.002) — a 65% relative reduction. Invasive plus in-situ cancers: 0.35% versus 0.77% per year (hazard ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.27–0.79, p=0.004). Adverse events occurred in 88% versus 85% (p=0.003), with no significant between-group differences in skeletal fractures, cardiovascular events, other cancers or treatment-related deaths, and minimal quality-of-life differences.
cards.watchOut: Only 43 invasive cancers in total and a 35-month median follow-up: the trial shows incidence reduction, not mortality benefit, and cannot exclude the class's known bone-density cost emerging over the full five treatment years women are usually offered.
cards.source: Goss PE et al. Exemestane for breast-cancer prevention in postmenopausal women. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 21639806. Registry ID: NCT00083174. shelves.title: TAM-01: tamoxifen at a quarter of the standard dose (5 mg for 3 years) halved new breast events after intraepithelial neoplasia — 14 versus 28 events at 5 years, still 25 versus 41 at 10 years, without extra serious harm
shelves.question: In women with breast intraepithelial neoplasia (atypical hyperplasia, LCIS or DCIS), does low-dose tamoxifen 5 mg/day prevent recurrence and new breast events versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Biomarkers, Tumor/metabolism · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Placebos/adverse effects · Research Design · Tamoxifen/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in TAM-01, 500 women with hormone-sensitive or unknown breast intraepithelial neoplasia were randomised to tamoxifen 5 mg daily for 3 years or placebo. At median 5.1 years there were 14 neoplastic events on tamoxifen versus 28 on placebo (11.6 versus 23.9 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.26–0.92, p=0.02), with contralateral events reduced by 75% in relative terms (3 versus 12; hazard ratio 0.25) and a 5-year number needed to treat of 22. At the 10-year report (median 9.7 years), events were 25 versus 41 (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.35–0.95) and the NNT had improved to 14. Serious adverse events did not differ (12 versus 16 in the first report, including one deep-vein thrombosis and one stage I endometrial cancer on tamoxifen). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): low-dose tamoxifen prevents recurrence and new events after intraepithelial neoplasia with a durable effect and limited toxicity.

cards.summary: TAM-01 (DeCensi 2019): neoplastic events 14 on low-dose tamoxifen versus 28 on placebo (HR 0.48); contralateral events 3 versus 12; serious adverse events 12 versus 16
cards.people: 500 women aged ≤75 with hormone-sensitive or unknown breast intraepithelial neoplasia (atypical ductal hyperplasia, lobular or ductal carcinoma in situ) after surgery, randomised to tamoxifen 5 mg daily or placebo for 3 years; median follow-up 5.1 years.
cards.result: Neoplastic events (invasive cancer or DCIS): 14 on tamoxifen versus 28 on placebo (11.6 versus 23.9 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.26–0.92, p=0.02); 5-year number needed to treat 22. Contralateral events: 3 versus 12 (hazard ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.07–0.88). Patient-reported outcomes did not differ except slightly more frequent daily hot flashes on tamoxifen (p=0.02). Serious adverse events: 12 versus 16, including one deep-vein thrombosis and one stage I endometrial cancer on tamoxifen and one pulmonary embolism on placebo.

cards.people: The same 500 TAM-01 women (20% atypical ductal hyperplasia, 11% LCIS, 69% DCIS; mean age 54, 58% postmenopausal), followed to a median of 9.7 years after 3 years of tamoxifen 5 mg or placebo.
cards.result: Breast events (invasive cancer or DCIS) totalled 66: 25 on tamoxifen versus 41 on placebo (annual rate 11.3 versus 19.5 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.35–0.95, p=0.03); 77% were invasive and 59% ipsilateral. Contralateral cancer: 6 versus 16 (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.14–0.92). In the DCIS subgroup (70% of participants) recurrence fell by 50% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.28–0.91). cards.watchOut: Still the same single 500-woman trial; subgroup claims (DCIS driving the effect) rest on ~46 events, and women with hormone-receptor-negative neoplasia were not the studied population.

shelves.title: Metformin after polypectomy: one year of low-dose metformin (250 mg) cut adenoma recurrence to 30.6% versus 51.6% on placebo in non-diabetic patients — a small single-country trial of 133 completers
shelves.question: In patients without diabetes after polypectomy, does low-dose metformin for one year prevent metachronous colorectal adenomas and polyps versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/drug therapy/pathology · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chemoprevention · Colonic Polyps/drug therapy/pathology · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Japan · Male · Metformin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/pathology · Neoplasms, Second Primary/drug therapy/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promising but thin: in the Higurashi phase 3 trial, non-diabetic Japanese patients with resected adenomas were randomised to metformin 250 mg daily or placebo for one year, after which adenomas were found in 22/71 (30.6% as reported) on metformin versus 32/62 (51.6%) on placebo (risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.92, p=0.016), and total polyps in 38.0% versus 56.5% (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.97, p=0.034); median polyp count was 0 versus 1 (p=0.041). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one year of low-dose metformin reduced one-year adenoma recurrence in this trial — a single small study at an unusually low dose, awaiting replication before it can be called established.

cards.headline: Higurashi 2016: adenomas at 1 year in 30.6% on metformin 250 mg versus 51.6% on placebo (RR 0.60, p=0.016); total polyps 38.0% versus 56.5%
cards.summary: Higurashi 2016: adenomas at 1 year in 30.6% on metformin 250 mg versus 51.6% on placebo (RR 0.60, p=0.016); total polyps 38.0% versus 56.5%
cards.people: Non-diabetic adults in five Japanese hospitals who had single or multiple colorectal adenomas or polyps resected endoscopically; 151 randomised (79 metformin, 72 placebo) to metformin 250 mg daily or identical placebo for 1 year, with colonoscopy at one year; 133 underwent the follow-up colonoscopy (71 metformin, 62 placebo).
cards.result: Adenomas were present in 22/71 (30.6% as reported; 95% CI 19.9–41.2) on metformin versus 32/62 (51.6%; 39.2–64.1) on placebo (p=0.016; risk ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.92). Total polyps (hyperplastic plus adenomas): 27/71 (38.0%) versus 35/62 (56.5%) (p=0.034; risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.97). Median number of polyps: 0 (IQR 0–1) versus 1 (0–1) (p=0.041).
cards.watchOut: Very small (133 completers from 498 screened), one year, one country, and a metformin dose (250 mg) far below diabetes doses — all reasons the effect size may not replicate; adenoma recurrence at one year is also a surrogate for cancer prevention.
cards.source: Higurashi T et al. Metformin for chemoprevention of metachronous colorectal adenoma or polyps in post-polypectomy patients without diabetes: a multicentre double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2016. PMID: 26947328. shelves.title: Celecoxib prevents colorectal adenomas — recurrence 43.2% and 37.5% versus 60.7% over three years — at a cardiovascular price that rises with dose: event risk ratios 2.6 and 3.4 in the APC trial
shelves.question: In patients with a recently removed colorectal adenoma, does celecoxib prevent adenoma recurrence versus placebo, and at what cardiovascular cost?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma/drug therapy/prevention & control · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced/mortality · Celecoxib · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/prevention & control · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gastrointestinal Diseases/chemically induced · Humans · Kidney Diseases/chemically induced · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a real preventive effect bought with dose-related cardiovascular harm. In the APC trial (2,035 patients with removed adenomas), the cumulative incidence of one or more adenomas by year 3 was 60.7% on placebo versus 43.2% on celecoxib 200 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.77) and 37.5% on 400 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48–0.64). But adjudicated cardiovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, stroke or heart failure) rose with dose: risk ratio 2.6 (95% CI 1.1–6.1) at 200 mg twice daily and 3.4 (95% CI 1.5–7.9) at 400 mg twice daily in APC, with the pooled APC+PreSAP hazard ratio 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1) and dose-related systolic blood-pressure rises of up to 5.2 mm Hg at 3 years. Serious adverse events overall were 18.8% (placebo), 20.4% and 23.0%. PROPOSED SPLIT: celecoxib demonstrably prevents adenoma recurrence and demonstrably harms the cardiovascular system at these doses — which is why it is not routinely recommended for this indication.

cards.headline: APC (Bertagnolli 2006): adenomas by year 3 in 60.7% on placebo versus 43.2% (200 mg twice daily) and 37.5% (400 mg twice daily); cardiovascular risk ratios 2.6 and 3.4
cards.summary: APC (Bertagnolli 2006): adenomas by year 3 in 60.7% on placebo versus 43.2% (200 mg twice daily) and 37.5% (400 mg twice daily); cardiovascular risk ratios 2.6 and 3.4
cards.people: 2,035 patients with colorectal adenomas removed before entry (placebo 679, celecoxib 200 mg twice daily 685, 400 mg twice daily 671), stratified by low-dose aspirin use, with colonoscopies at years 1 and 3 (completed by 89.5% at year 1 and 75.7% at year 3).
cards.result: Cumulative incidence of one or more detected adenomas by year 3: 60.7% placebo versus 43.2% on 200 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.77, p<0.001) and 37.5% on 400 mg twice daily (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48–0.64, p<0.001). Serious adverse events: 18.8% versus 20.4% (risk ratio 1.1) and 23.0% (risk ratio 1.2). Cardiovascular events were increased on celecoxib (risk ratio 2.6, 95% CI 1.1–6.1, low dose; 3.4, 95% CI 1.5–7.9, high dose).
cards.watchOut: Adenoma recurrence is a surrogate — the trial was not powered for colorectal cancer itself — and a quarter of participants missed the year-3 colonoscopy; the population had sporadic adenomas, not familial polyposis (a separate evidence base).
cards.source: Bertagnolli MM et al. Celecoxib for the prevention of sporadic colorectal adenomas. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16943400. Registry ID: NCT00005094. cards.headline: Solomon 2006 (APC + PreSAP pooled safety): composite cardiovascular hazard ratio 1.9 overall — 2.6 and 3.4 at twice-daily doses, 1.3 at 400 mg once daily — with dose-related blood-pressure rises
cards.summary: Solomon 2006 (APC + PreSAP pooled safety): composite cardiovascular hazard ratio 1.9 overall — 2.6 and 3.4 at twice-daily doses, 1.3 at 400 mg once daily — with dose-related blood-pressure rises
cards.type: Pooled safety analysis of two randomised trials (Solomon 2006, APC and PreSAP)
cards.people: Individual-patient data from APC (celecoxib 200 or 400 mg twice daily) and PreSAP (400 mg once daily) — both placebo-controlled adenoma-prevention trials — with centrally adjudicated serious cardiovascular events and up to 37 months of follow-up.
cards.result: 83 patients across both trials experienced cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke or heart failure. Hazard ratios for the composite were 2.6 (95% CI 1.1–6.1) for 200 mg twice daily and 3.4 (95% CI 1.5–7.9) for 400 mg twice daily in APC, and 1.3 (95% CI 0.6–2.6) for 400 mg once daily in PreSAP; the overall hazard ratio was 1.9 (95% CI 1.1–3.1). Systolic blood pressure rose significantly at both twice-daily doses (up to +5.2 mm Hg at 3 years on 400 mg twice daily) but not on once-daily dosing.
cards.watchOut: Event counts are small (83 across two trials) and the once-daily estimate is compatible with meaningful harm (upper bound 2.6); the analysis cannot identify a dose proven safe, only doses proven harmful.
cards.source: Solomon SD et al. Effect of celecoxib on cardiovascular events and blood pressure in two trials for the prevention of colorectal adenomas. Circulation. 2006. PMID: 16943394. shelves.title: Taiwan's universal infant hepatitis B vaccination: childhood liver-cancer incidence fell from 0.70 to 0.36 per 100,000 within a decade, and vaccinated birth cohorts carried a relative risk of 0.31 into early adulthood
shelves.question: Did universal infant hepatitis B immunisation reduce the incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma in children and young adults?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Brain Neoplasms/epidemiology · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/epidemiology/virology · Carrier State · Child · Female · Hepatitis B/complications/prevention & control/transmission · Hepatitis B Surface Antigens/blood · Hepatitis B Vaccines/administration & dosage · Humans · Immunization Programs · Incidence · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical · Liver Neoplasms/epidemiology/virology · Male · Poisson Distribution · Registries · Regression Analysis · Taiwan/epidemiology · Vaccination
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — the first demonstration that a vaccine prevents a human cancer, from Taiwan's nationwide programme (launched July 1984) tracked through the national cancer registry: average annual hepatocellular carcinoma incidence in children aged 6–14 fell from 0.70 per 100,000 (1981–86) to 0.57 (1986–90) and 0.36 (1990–94) (p<0.01), and in children aged 6–9 from 0.52 per 100,000 in those born 1974–84 to 0.13 in those born 1984–86 (p<0.001), with mortality falling in parallel. The 20-year follow-up found the protection extended to age 29: 64 cancers in 37.7 million person-years among vaccinated cohorts versus 444 in 78.5 million among unvaccinated — an age- and sex-adjusted relative risk of 0.31 (p<0.001). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): universal infant hepatitis B immunisation prevents hepatocellular carcinoma from childhood into early adulthood; residual cases concentrate in children of highly infectious carrier mothers and in incomplete vaccination.

cards.headline: Chang 1997: after universal vaccination began in 1984, HCC incidence in 6–14-year-olds fell from 0.70 to 0.36 per 100,000; in 6–9-year-olds, from 0.52 (born 1974–84) to 0.13 (born 1984–86)
cards.summary: Chang 1997: after universal vaccination began in 1984, HCC incidence in 6–14-year-olds fell from 0.70 to 0.36 per 100,000; in 6–9-year-olds, from 0.52 (born 1974–84) to 0.13 (born 1984–86)
cards.type: National registry cohort analysis (Chang 1997, Taiwan Childhood Hepatoma Study Group)
cards.people: All children in Taiwan (population ~21 million) captured by the National Cancer Registry and 17 major medical centres, 1981–1994; the universal hepatitis B vaccination programme began July 1984 (initially infants of carrier mothers, then all neonates); primary analysis confined to liver cancers at age ≥6 to exclude hepatoblastoma.
cards.result: Average annual HCC incidence in children 6–14 years declined from 0.70 per 100,000 (1981–86) to 0.57 (1986–90) to 0.36 (1990–94) (p<0.01), and mortality from HCC fell correspondingly. In children 6–9 years, incidence declined from 0.52 per 100,000 for those born 1974–84 to 0.13 for those born 1984–86 (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Before-and-after national data without an unvaccinated concurrent control country; concurrent improvements in aflatoxin exposure or treatment could contribute, though the birth-cohort pattern (fall confined to post-1984 births) argues for the vaccine.
cards.source: Chang MH et al. Universal hepatitis B vaccination in Taiwan and the incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma in children. Taiwan Childhood Hepatoma Study Group. cards.headline: Chang 2009 (20-year follow-up): HCC relative risk 0.31 in vaccinated cohorts — 64 cancers in 37.7 million person-years versus 444 in 78.5 million; failures concentrated in incomplete vaccination (OR 4.32) and maternal carriage
cards.summary: Chang 2009 (20-year follow-up): HCC relative risk 0.31 in vaccinated cohorts — 64 cancers in 37.7 million person-years versus 444 in 78.5 million; failures concentrated in incomplete vaccination (OR 4.32) and maternal carriage
cards.people: 1,958 patients diagnosed with HCC at ages 6–29 in Taiwan between 1983 and 2004, from two national registries, comparing age- and sex-specific incidence between vaccinated and unvaccinated birth cohorts; immunisation records of the 64 vaccinated-cohort cases were examined for predictors.
cards.result: HCC incidence was significantly lower in vaccinated cohorts aged 6–19 (64 cancers among vaccinees in 37,709,304 person-years versus 444 in unvaccinated subjects in 78,496,406 person-years; adjusted relative risk 0.31, p<0.001). Among vaccinated cohorts, HCC risk was associated with incomplete vaccination (<3 doses: odds ratio 4.32, 95% CI 2.34–7.91), maternal HBsAg positivity (OR 29.50, 95% CI 13.98–62.60) and maternal HBeAg positivity (OR 5.13 with immunoglobulin at birth; 9.43 without).
cards.watchOut: Registry-based and observational — but the effect size (relative risk 0.31) clears the two-sided observational floor, the birth-cohort design is strong, and no competing explanation fits the timing; adult HCC prevention is extrapolated, since follow-up reaches only age 29.
cards.source: Chang MH et al. Decreased incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatitis B vaccinees: a 20-year follow-up study. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2009. PMID: 19759364. shelves.title: Quadrivalent HPV vaccine in women aged 24–45: 90.5% efficacy against vaccine-type infection and disease in women not already infected — but only 30.9% in the whole randomised population, because many were already exposed
shelves.question: In women aged 24–45, does quadrivalent HPV vaccination prevent vaccine-type HPV infection and disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Alphapapillomavirus · Colombia/epidemiology · Double-Blind Method · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Human Papillomavirus Recombinant Vaccine Quadrivalent, Types 6, 11, 16, 18 · Humans · Incidence · Middle Aged · Papillomavirus Infections/complications/epidemiology/prevention & control/virology · Papillomavirus Vaccines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/immunology · Philippines/epidemiology · Safety · Thailand/epidemiology · United States/epidemiology · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/epidemiology/prevention & control/virology · Vaccination/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sharply split by prior exposure: in the randomised trial of 3,819 women aged 24–45, per-protocol efficacy against the composite of persistent infection and disease from HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18 was 90.5% (95% CI 73.7–97.5; 4/1,615 cases on vaccine versus 41/1,607 on placebo), and 83.1% against types 16/18 endpoints (4/1,601 versus 23/1,579). But in the intention-to-treat population — everyone randomised, including women already infected at baseline — efficacy against the first endpoint was only 30.9% (95% CI 11.1–46.5; 108/1,886 versus 154/1,883) and 22.6% (95% CI −2.9 to 41.9) for types 16/18. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were recorded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the vaccine works in mid-adult women who have not yet met the vaccine types; its population yield at this age is limited by prior exposure, which is why programmes target adolescents.

cards.headline: Muñoz 2009: per-protocol efficacy 90.5% (4 versus 41 cases) in women naive to the relevant types; intention-to-treat efficacy 30.9% (108 versus 154) — no vaccine-related serious adverse events
cards.summary: Muñoz 2009: per-protocol efficacy 90.5% (4 versus 41 cases) in women naive to the relevant types; intention-to-treat efficacy 30.9% (108 versus 154) — no vaccine-related serious adverse events
cards.people: 3,819 women aged 24–45 with no history of genital warts or cervical disease, enrolled from community, academic and primary-care sites internationally, allocated to quadrivalent HPV vaccine (types 6, 11, 16, 18; n=1,911) or placebo (n=1,908) at day 1 and months 2 and 6; co-primary endpoints were ≥6-month infection and cervical/external genital disease from the four types, and from types 16/18 alone.
cards.result: Per-protocol efficacy: 90.5% (95% CI 73.7–97.5) against the four-type endpoint (4/1,615 vaccine versus 41/1,607 placebo cases) and 83.1% (95% CI 50.6–95.8) against the 16/18 endpoint (4/1,601 versus 23/1,579). Intention-to-treat efficacy: 30.9% (95% CI 11.1–46.5) against the four-type endpoint (108/1,886 versus 154/1,883) and 22.6% (95% CI −2.9 to 41.9) against 16/18, because infection and disease were already present at baseline. No vaccine-related serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The per-protocol population is selected for type-naivety, which is uncommon by the late thirties; endpoints are infection and early disease, not cancer; and the vaccine is prophylactic only — it does not clear established infection, which is the whole explanation of the ITT gap.
cards.source: Muñoz N et al. Safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of quadrivalent human papillomavirus (types 6, 11, 16, 18) recombinant vaccine in women aged 24-45 years: a randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19493565. Registry ID: NCT00090220. shelves.title: Quitting smoking after an early-stage lung cancer diagnosis: continuing smokers carried nearly triple the mortality hazard in non-small-cell cancer (HR 2.94) — modelled five-year survival 70% for quitters versus 33% for continuing smokers
shelves.question: In people diagnosed with early-stage lung cancer, does quitting smoking after diagnosis improve survival versus continuing to smoke?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/mortality · Female · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Lung Neoplasms/mortality · Male · Prognosis · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Small Cell Lung Carcinoma/mortality · Smoking Cessation/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational but with effects beyond the usual confounding range: Parsons' systematic review of longitudinal studies found continued smoking after diagnosis associated with significantly increased all-cause mortality in early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer (hazard ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.15–7.54) and recurrence (hazard ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.01–3.41), and in limited-stage small-cell cancer with increased mortality (hazard ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.33–2.59), second primary tumours (hazard ratio 4.31, 95% CI 1.09–16.98) and recurrence (hazard ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.06–1.50). Life-table modelling from these data estimated five-year survival for a 65-year-old with early-stage non-small-cell cancer at 70% if they quit versus 33% if they continued, and 63% versus 29% in limited-stage small-cell cancer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): quitting at diagnosis is associated with substantially better survival — the modelled gains exceed what fewer cardiorespiratory deaths would explain, implicating slower cancer progression.

cards.headline: Parsons 2010: continued smoking after diagnosis — mortality HR 2.94 in early NSCLC and 1.86 in limited-stage SCLC; modelled 5-year survival 70% versus 33% (NSCLC) for quitters versus continuing smokers
cards.summary: Parsons 2010: continued smoking after diagnosis — mortality HR 2.94 in early NSCLC and 1.86 in limited-stage SCLC; modelled 5-year survival 70% versus 33% (NSCLC) for quitters versus continuing smokers
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Parsons 2010)
cards.people: Longitudinal observational studies (10 included; 9/10 mostly early-stage tumours) measuring prognostic outcomes by smoking continuation versus cessation after a primary lung cancer diagnosis, searched to December 2008 across Medline, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and CENTRAL.
cards.result: Continued smoking was associated with increased all-cause mortality in early-stage non-small-cell lung cancer (hazard ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.15–7.54) and recurrence (1.86, 95% CI 1.01–3.41); in limited-stage small-cell cancer, with all-cause mortality (1.86, 95% CI 1.33–2.59), second primary tumours (4.31, 95% CI 1.09–16.98) and recurrence (1.26, 95% CI 1.06–1.50). Life-table modelling estimated 5-year survival at 70% (quitters) versus 33% (continuing smokers) for a 65-year-old with early-stage NSCLC, and 63% versus 29% in limited-stage SCLC. No study reported cancer-specific mortality for NSCLC.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial exists or is likely; quitters may differ from continuing smokers in performance status, treatment tolerance and comorbidity, and the NSCLC mortality interval is wide (1.15–7.54) — hence POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, despite the large point estimates.
cards.source: Parsons A et al. Influence of smoking cessation after diagnosis of early stage lung cancer on prognosis: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2010. PMID: 20093278. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for menopause-related quality of life only, in a trial where women chose their own operation. In the Dutch TUBA study (Steenbeek MP et al., PMID: 34081085), 577 BRCA1/2 carriers chose risk-reducing salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy or immediate salpingo-oophorectomy; over the first year the rise in climacteric symptoms on the Greene Climacteric Scale was 6.7 points (95% CI 5.0–8.4) greater after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone therapy than after salpingectomy alone, and 3.6 points (2.3–4.8) greater even when hormone therapy followed salpingo-oophorectomy. Cancer worry, tracked in the same cohort (van Bommel MHD et al., PMID: 34997316), was high before surgery in 57% of women and fell after surgery in 54%, with only 6% persistently highly worried — and it fell after either operation. The decisive unknown is stated plainly by the trialists: whether delaying oophorectomy is oncologically safe is being tested in a separate international follow-up study and is not answered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy preserves menopause-related quality of life better than immediate salpingo-oophorectomy, on nonrandomised evidence, with cancer safety unproven.

cards.headline: Steenbeek 2021 (TUBA): climacteric symptoms rose 6.7 points more after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone therapy — and 3.6 points more with it — than after salpingectomy alone
cards.summary: Steenbeek 2021 (TUBA): climacteric symptoms rose 6.7 points more after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone therapy — and 3.6 points more with it — than after salpingectomy alone
cards.people: 577 premenopausal BRCA1/2 pathogenic-variant carriers in the Netherlands (mean age 37.2 years; 51.5% BRCA1) who had completed childbearing and chose either risk-reducing salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy (394 operated at analysis) or standard risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy at the recommended age (154 operated), with hormone replacement recommended after salpingo-oophorectomy when not contraindicated; follow-up 3 and 12 months after surgery.
cards.result: The adjusted mean increase from baseline in Greene Climacteric Scale score (range 0–63, higher = more symptoms) over 1 year was 6.7 points (95% CI 5.0–8.4; P<.001) higher after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone replacement therapy than after salpingectomy, and 3.6 points (95% CI 2.3–4.8; P<.001) higher after salpingo-oophorectomy with hormone replacement therapy than after salpingectomy. Secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, sexual functioning and distress, cancer worry, decisional regret, and surgical outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Women chose their own strategy, so the groups may differ in ways adjustment cannot remove — this is preference-trial, not randomised, evidence. Follow-up is only 1 year, and the trial answers the menopause question only: whether leaving the ovaries in place longer costs cancers is explicitly deferred to a separate international study, so the benefit is real but the safety half of the question is open.
cards.source: Steenbeek MP et al. Association of Salpingectomy With Delayed Oophorectomy Versus Salpingo-oophorectomy With Quality of Life in BRCA1/2 Pathogenic Variant Carriers: A Nonrandomized Controlled Trial. JAMA Oncology. 2021. PMID: 34081085. Registry ID: NCT02321228. cards.headline: van Bommel 2022 (TUBA cohort): cancer worry was high before surgery in 57% and fell in 54% by 12 months — 6% stayed persistently highly worried after either operation
cards.summary: van Bommel 2022 (TUBA cohort): cancer worry was high before surgery in 57% and fell in 54% by 12 months — 6% stayed persistently highly worried after either operation
cards.type: Prospective cohort analysis within the TUBA study (van Bommel 2022)
cards.people: The same 577 BRCA1/2 carriers in TUBA (NCT02321228), choosing salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy or salpingo-oophorectomy, with the Cancer Worry Scale measured before surgery and 3 and 12 months after.
cards.result: Of all carriers, 320 (57%) had high cancer worry (score ≥14) before surgery, and 54% had lower worry 12 months after surgery than before. Latent-class analysis found three patterns: persistently low worry (56%), persistently high worry (6%), and fluctuating, mostly declining, worry (37%). Persistently high worry was associated with younger age (below 35 for BRCA1 or 40 for BRCA2), unemployment, previous breast cancer, lower education, and a more recent BRCA1/2 diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: Cancer worry is a psychological secondary outcome from the same nonrandomised cohort — it shows worry settles for most women whichever operation they choose, but it is not evidence about cancer incidence, and the persistently worried 6% are identified by association, not by a tested intervention.
cards.source: van Bommel MHD et al. Cancer worry among BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant carriers choosing surgery to prevent tubal/ovarian cancer: course over time and associated factors. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2022. PMID: 34997316. Registry ID: NCT02321228. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real quality-of-life advantage for the staged operation, bought with an unanswered safety question
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real quality-of-life advantage for the staged operation, bought with an unanswered safety question
cards.people: One multicentre nonrandomised preference trial (TUBA, n=577) and its prospective cancer-worry analysis, in premenopausal BRCA1/2 carriers choosing between salpingectomy with delayed oophorectomy and immediate salpingo-oophorectomy.
cards.result: Menopause symptoms: Greene Climacteric Scale rise 6.7 points greater after salpingo-oophorectomy without hormone therapy and 3.6 points greater with hormone therapy than after salpingectomy alone over 1 year. Cancer worry: high in 57% before surgery, lower at 12 months in 54%, persistently high in 6%. Cancer outcomes: not reported — oncologic safety of delayed oophorectomy is under study elsewhere. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: nonrandomised evidence and an open safety question are exactly what the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: The shelf must not be read as "the staged operation is safe" — it shows women feel better after it for the first year. Any carrier choosing it is accepting an unquantified interval cancer risk in exchange for a measured quality-of-life gain.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steenbeek MP et al. JAMA Oncology. 2021 (PMID: 34081085); van Bommel MHD et al. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2022 (PMID: 34997316).

shelves.title: Oral contraceptives in BRCA1/2 carriers: ovarian cancer risk roughly halved in two meta-analyses — the breast cancer signal splits by measure, hazard ratio 1.55 versus odds ratio 1.06
shelves.question: In carriers of BRCA1/2 mutations, do oral contraceptives reduce ovarian cancer risk, and is there an offsetting increase in breast cancer risk?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · BRCA1 Protein/genetics · Breast Neoplasms/epidemiology/genetics · Contraceptive Agents · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Mutation · Ovarian Neoplasms · Reproducibility of Results · BRCA2 Protein
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the ovarian side of the ledger is consistent, the breast side is not. The 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (van Bommel MHD et al., PMID: 36383189) found ovarian cancer risk lower in oral contraceptive users (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.52–0.74; odds ratio 0.49, 0.38–0.63), with the protection vanishing after stopping; for breast cancer the same review found a hazard ratio of 1.55 (1.36–1.76) in seven studies yet an odds ratio of 1.06 (0.90–1.25) in four others. The earlier meta-analysis (Iodice S et al., PMID: 20537530) agrees on the ovary — summary relative risk 0.50 (0.33–0.75), with a further 36% relative reduction per additional 10 years of use — and found no significant breast cancer association overall (summary relative risk 1.13, 0.88–1.45), except for formulations used before 1975 (1.47, 1.06–2.04). All of this is observational evidence graded low or very low quality, in women whose baseline risks are very high. PROPOSED SPLIT: ovarian protection is the consistent finding; a breast cancer increase is possible but unproven for modern formulations.

cards.headline: van Bommel 2023: ovarian risk down (HR 0.62, OR 0.49) but breast hazard ratio 1.55 against an odds ratio of 1.06 — and ovarian protection vanishes after stopping
cards.summary: van Bommel 2023: ovarian risk down (HR 0.62, OR 0.49) but breast hazard ratio 1.55 against an odds ratio of 1.06 — and ovarian protection vanishes after stopping
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (van Bommel 2023)
cards.people: BRCA1/2 pathogenic-variant carriers in studies indexed to June 2021: breast cancer analyses pooled 7 studies with 7,525 women (hazard-ratio set) and 4 studies with 9,106 women (odds-ratio set); ovarian analyses pooled 2 studies with 10,981 women (hazard-ratio set) and 8 studies with 10,390 women (odds-ratio set). No differences were observed between BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers.
cards.result: Breast cancer risk with oral contraceptive use: hazard ratio 1.55 (95% CI 1.36–1.76; I² 0%) but odds ratio 1.06 (95% CI 0.90–1.25; I² 52%), and risk was still increased in ever-users more than 10 years after last use in the hazard-ratio set. Ovarian cancer risk: hazard ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.52–0.74; I² 0%) and odds ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.38–0.63; I² 64%), with the protective effect vanishing after cessation. Tubal ligation also protected against ovarian cancer (hazard ratio 0.44, 0.26–0.74, in one study). The quality of evidence was rated low or very low.
cards.watchOut: The breast answer literally depends on which pooled measure you read, and every included study is observational — women who choose the pill differ from women who do not. Hazard and odds sets draw on different study collections, so the split is a property of the literature, not a precision problem that more of the same studies will fix.
cards.source: van Bommel MHD et al. Contraceptives and cancer risks in BRCA1/2 pathogenic variant carriers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Human Reproduction Update. 2023. PMID: 36383189. MeSH: Female · Humans · BRCA1 Protein/genetics · Breast Neoplasms/epidemiology/genetics · Contraceptive Agents · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Mutation · Ovarian Neoplasms · Reproducibility of Results · BRCA2 Protein
