cards.headline: Iodice 2010: ovarian summary relative risk 0.50, falling a further 36% per 10 years of use; breast summary relative risk 1.13 and not significant — except pre-1975 formulations (1.47)
cards.summary: Iodice 2010: ovarian summary relative risk 0.50, falling a further 36% per 10 years of use; breast summary relative risk 1.13 and not significant — except pre-1975 formulations (1.47)
cards.people: 18 studies of ascertained BRCA1/2 mutation carriers, including 2,855 breast cancer cases and 1,503 ovarian cancer cases, with literature searched to March 2010; analyses covered ever use, duration of use, and time since stopping.
cards.result: Ever oral contraceptive use was associated with a significantly reduced ovarian cancer risk (summary relative risk 0.50; 95% CI 0.33–0.75), with a significant 36% relative risk reduction for each additional 10 years of use (summary relative risk 0.64; 95% CI 0.53–0.78; P for trend <0.01). For breast cancer there was no significant association overall (summary relative risk 1.13; 95% CI 0.88–1.45) and none with duration of use; formulations used before 1975 were associated with increased breast cancer risk (summary relative risk 1.47; 95% CI 1.06–2.04), while more recent formulations were not (1.17; 0.74–1.86).
cards.watchOut: A 2010 literature base: most exposure in these cohorts is to older, higher-dose formulations, and case-control designs in carrier families carry survival and recall biases. The duration-response for ovarian protection is the strongest causal hint in either meta-analysis, but it remains an association.
cards.source: Iodice S et al. Oral contraceptive use and breast or ovarian cancer risk in BRCA1/2 carriers: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Cancer. 2010. PMID: 20537530. cards.headline: Synthesis: halve the ovarian risk on paper, argue about the breast — the split is the honest answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: halve the ovarian risk on paper, argue about the breast — the split is the honest answer
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of observational studies in BRCA1/2 carriers (2010: 18 studies, 2,855 breast and 1,503 ovarian cases; 2023: up to 10,981 women per analysis), with no randomised data existing or likely.
cards.result: Ovarian cancer: relative measures 0.49–0.62 across both reviews, with a duration gradient (summary relative risk 0.64 per extra 10 years) and loss of protection after stopping. Breast cancer: summary relative risk 1.13 (not significant), odds ratio 1.06 (not significant), hazard ratio 1.55 (significant) — the signal depends on study set and measure; pre-1975 formulations carried a significant 1.47. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: observational evidence throughout, graded low to very low quality by the 2023 reviewers.
cards.watchOut: Absolute stakes differ by gene and age: a relative halving of a very high ovarian risk is a large absolute gain, while even a real relative breast increase applies to a risk many carriers are already managing with surveillance or surgery. Counselling has to be individual — the shelf reports the split, it does not resolve it.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Bommel MHD et al. Human Reproduction Update. 2023 (PMID: 36383189); Iodice S et al. European Journal of Cancer. 2010 (PMID: 20537530).

shelves.title: Simple hysterectomy in low-risk cervical cancer: pelvic recurrence 2.52% versus 2.17% at 3 years — noninferior, with far less urinary retention and better sexual health
shelves.question: In low-risk early-stage cervical cancer, is simple hysterectomy non-inferior to radical hysterectomy for pelvic recurrence, with fewer bladder and bowel complications?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Canada · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/pathology/surgery · Hysterectomy/adverse effects/methods · Lymph Nodes/pathology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/epidemiology · Neoplasm Staging · Prognosis · Retrospective Studies · Urinary Incontinence/etiology · Urinary Retention/etiology · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/pathology/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — less surgery, the same pelvic control, and measurably less harm, in the one randomised trial that asked. In SHAPE (Plante M et al., PMID: 38416430), 700 women with low-risk cervical cancer (lesions ≤2 cm with limited stromal invasion) were randomised to simple or radical hysterectomy, both with lymph-node assessment: pelvic recurrence at 3 years was 2.52% after simple and 2.17% after radical hysterectomy (absolute difference 0.35 percentage points; 90% CI −1.62 to 2.32), inside the prespecified 4-point noninferiority margin. The harm gradient ran the other way: urinary retention beyond 4 weeks in 0.6% versus 9.9%, incontinence beyond 4 weeks in 4.7% versus 11.0%. The trial’s sexual-health and quality-of-life analysis (Ferguson SE et al., PMID: 39353164) favoured simple hysterectomy on desire, arousal, pain, lubrication, sexual-vaginal functioning, body image, and global health status at 36 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): de-escalation to simple hysterectomy in strictly low-risk disease, resting on a single trial.

cards.headline: Plante 2024 (SHAPE): pelvic recurrence 2.52% versus 2.17% at 3 years (difference 0.35 points, inside the 4-point margin) — urinary retention beyond 4 weeks 0.6% versus 9.9%
cards.summary: Plante 2024 (SHAPE): pelvic recurrence 2.52% versus 2.17% at 3 years (difference 0.35 points, inside the 4-point margin) — urinary retention beyond 4 weeks 0.6% versus 9.9%
cards.people: 700 women (350 per group) with low-risk cervical cancer — lesions ≤2 cm with limited stromal invasion; 91.7% FIGO 2009 stage IB1, 61.7% squamous histology, 59.3% grade 1–2 — randomised to radical hysterectomy or simple hysterectomy, both including lymph-node assessment; median follow-up 4.5 years.
cards.result: Pelvic recurrence at 3 years was 2.52% in the simple hysterectomy group and 2.17% in the radical hysterectomy group (absolute difference 0.35 percentage points; 90% CI −1.62 to 2.32), meeting the prespecified 4-percentage-point noninferiority margin; per-protocol results were similar. Urinary incontinence was lower with simple hysterectomy within 4 weeks (2.4% vs 5.5%; P=0.048) and beyond 4 weeks (4.7% vs 11.0%; P=0.003), as was urinary retention within 4 weeks (0.6% vs 11.0%; P<0.001) and beyond 4 weeks (0.6% vs 9.9%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is defined by the 4-point margin the investigators chose — the confidence interval still allows up to about 2.3 extra pelvic recurrences per 100 women at 3 years. The result applies only to the trial’s strict low-risk definition (≤2 cm, limited stromal invasion); it licenses no de-escalation beyond it, and bowel outcomes were not the differentiator the urinary outcomes were.
cards.source: Plante M et al. Simple versus Radical Hysterectomy in Women with Low-Risk Cervical Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38416430. Registry ID: NCT01658930. randomised phase 3 noninferiority trial (plante 2024, shape) 700 women (350 per group) with low-risk cervical cancer — lesions ≤2 cm with limited stromal invasion; 91.7% figo 2009 stage ib1, 61.7% squamous histology, 59.3% grade 1–2 — randomised to radical hysterectomy or simple hysterectomy, both including lymph-node assessment; median follow-up 4.5 years. pelvic recurrence at 3 years was 2.52% in the simple hysterectomy group and 2.17% in the radical hysterectomy group (absolute difference 0.35 percentage points; 90% ci −1.62 to 2.32), meeting the prespecified 4-percentage-point noninferiority margin; per-protocol results were similar. urinary incontinence was lower with simple hysterectomy within 4 weeks (2.4% vs 5.5%; p=0.048) and beyond 4 weeks (4.7% vs 11.0%; p=0.003), as was urinary retention within 4 weeks (0.6% vs 11.0%; p<0.001) and beyond 4 weeks (0.6% vs 9.9%; p<0.001). noninferiority is defined by the 4-point margin the investigators chose — the confidence interval still allows up to about 2.3 extra pelvic recurrences per 100 women at 3 years. the result applies only to the trial’s strict low-risk definition (≤2 cm, limited stromal invasion); it licenses no de-escalation beyond it, and bowel outcomes were not the differentiator the urinary outcomes were. plante m et al. simple versus radical hysterectomy in women with low-risk cervical cancer. the new england journal of medicine. 2024. pmid: 38416430. registry id: nct01658930. mesh: female · humans · canada · carcinoma, squamous cell/pathology/surgery · hysterectomy/adverse effects/methods · lymph nodes/pathology · neoplasm recurrence, local/epidemiology · neoplasm staging · prognosis · retrospective studies · urinary incontinence/etiology · urinary retention/etiology · uterine cervical neoplasms/pathology/surgery

cards.headline: Ferguson 2025 (SHAPE secondary analysis): sexual dysfunction cutoffs met only in the radical group at 6 months; sexual-vaginal functioning better to 24 months and global health better at 36 months after simple hysterectomy
cards.summary: Ferguson 2025 (SHAPE secondary analysis): sexual dysfunction cutoffs met only in the radical group at 6 months; sexual-vaginal functioning better to 24 months and global health better at 36 months after simple hysterectomy
cards.type: Randomised trial secondary analysis — sexual health and quality of life (Ferguson 2025, SHAPE)
cards.people: SHAPE participants with at least one postoperative quality-of-life measure, assessed to 36 months with the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), Female Sexual Distress Scale-Revised, and the EORTC QLQ-C30 and cervical-cancer module QLQ-CX24; baseline scores were balanced between groups.
cards.result: FSFI total scores met the cutoff for sexual dysfunction up to 6 months in the radical hysterectomy group (P=.02). Group differences favoured simple hysterectomy for desire and arousal at 3 months (P≤.001), pain and lubrication up to 12 months (P≤.018), symptom experience up to 24 months (P=.031), body image at 3, 24, and 36 months (P≤.01), sexual-vaginal functioning up to 24 months (P≤.022), sexual activity up to 36 months (P=.024), and global health status at 36 months (P=.025). Sexual distress was higher in the radical group at 3 months (P=.018).
cards.watchOut: This is a secondary analysis of the same single trial, not independent confirmation — questionnaire outcomes in an unblinded surgical trial are vulnerable to expectation effects, and the many subscale comparisons invite multiplicity. It strengthens the harm side of SHAPE’s ledger; it does not add oncologic evidence.
cards.source: Ferguson SE et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, a clean noninferiority result, and a one-directional harm gradient
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, a clean noninferiority result, and a one-directional harm gradient
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 noninferiority trial (SHAPE, n=700, low-risk cervical cancer) plus its prespecified-style sexual-health and quality-of-life secondary analysis.
cards.result: Pelvic recurrence at 3 years: 2.52% (simple) versus 2.17% (radical), difference 0.35 points (90% CI −1.62 to 2.32), within the 4-point margin. Harms: urinary retention beyond 4 weeks 0.6% versus 9.9%; incontinence beyond 4 weeks 4.7% versus 11.0%; sexual dysfunction, body image, and global health all favouring simple hysterectomy out to 36 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim, so the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: De-escalation evidence is only as wide as its entry criteria. Tumours larger than 2 cm or with deeper stromal invasion were not studied, and 3-year pelvic recurrence is not lifetime cure — the margin for late divergence is what longer follow-up must close.
cards.source: Synthesis of Plante M et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38416430); Ferguson SE et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2025 (PMID: 39353164).

shelves.title: Minimally invasive radical hysterectomy harms survival: disease-free survival 86.0% versus 96.5% at 4.5 years in LACC, and 4-year mortality 9.1% versus 5.3% in the companion cohort
shelves.question: In early-stage cervical cancer, does minimally invasive radical hysterectomy worsen recurrence and survival versus open abdominal radical hysterectomy?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/mortality/surgery · Adult · Carcinoma, Adenosquamous/mortality/surgery · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/mortality/surgery · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Hysterectomy/methods · Middle Aged · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasm Staging · Prospective Studies · Survival Rate · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the randomised trial and the population data point the same way, and the effect is large. In LACC (Ramirez PT et al., PMID: 30380365), 631 women with early-stage cervical cancer were randomised to minimally invasive or open radical hysterectomy: disease-free survival at 4.5 years was 86.0% versus 96.5% (difference −10.6 percentage points; 95% CI −16.4 to −4.7), with a hazard ratio for recurrence or death from cervical cancer of 3.74 (1.63–8.58) and for death from any cause of 6.00 (1.77–20.30). The companion epidemiologic study (Melamed A et al., PMID: 30379613) found 4-year mortality of 9.1% after minimally invasive versus 5.3% after open surgery (hazard ratio 1.65; 1.22–2.22) in 2,461 US women, and a survival decline that began exactly when minimally invasive surgery was adopted. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): open radical hysterectomy is the safer operation for early-stage cervical cancer.

cards.headline: Ramirez 2018 (LACC): disease-free survival 86.0% versus 96.5% at 4.5 years — recurrence hazard ratio 3.74 and death hazard ratio 6.00 against minimally invasive surgery
cards.summary: Ramirez 2018 (LACC): disease-free survival 86.0% versus 96.5% at 4.5 years — recurrence hazard ratio 3.74 and death hazard ratio 6.00 against minimally invasive surgery
cards.people: 631 women (319 minimally invasive, 312 open) with stage IA1 with lymphovascular invasion, IA2, or IB1 cervical cancer (91.9% IB1; squamous, adenocarcinoma, or adenosquamous histology; mean age 46.0 years); minimally invasive surgery was laparoscopic in 84.4% and robot-assisted in 15.6%. Groups were balanced for histology, lymphovascular invasion, parametrial and nodal involvement, tumour size and grade, and adjuvant therapy use.
cards.result: Disease-free survival at 4.5 years was 86.0% with minimally invasive versus 96.5% with open surgery (difference −10.6 percentage points; 95% CI −16.4 to −4.7), far outside the −7.2-point noninferiority boundary. Three-year disease-free survival was 91.2% versus 97.1% (hazard ratio for disease recurrence or death from cervical cancer 3.74; 95% CI 1.63–8.58), and 3-year overall survival was 93.8% versus 99.0% (hazard ratio for death from any cause 6.00; 95% CI 1.77–20.30). The differences persisted after adjustment for age, body-mass index, stage, lymphovascular invasion, and nodal involvement.
cards.watchOut: The trial closed early and the death hazard ratio rests on few events, hence its wide interval (1.77–20.30) — but the recurrence signal is the primary endpoint, is large, and survived adjustment. Surgeon experience and tumour-handling technique (manipulators, intracorporeal colpotomy) are candidate mechanisms the trial itself cannot separate.
cards.source: Ramirez PT et al. Minimally Invasive versus Abdominal Radical Hysterectomy for Cervical Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30380365. Registry ID: NCT00614211. cards.headline: Melamed 2018: 4-year mortality 9.1% versus 5.3% (hazard ratio 1.65) in 2,461 US women — and population survival began falling the year minimally invasive surgery took off
cards.summary: Melamed 2018: 4-year mortality 9.1% versus 5.3% (hazard ratio 1.65) in 2,461 US women — and population survival began falling the year minimally invasive surgery took off
cards.type: Epidemiologic cohort study with interrupted time-series analysis (Melamed 2018)
cards.people: 2,461 women undergoing radical hysterectomy for stage IA2 or IB1 cervical cancer at Commission on Cancer-accredited US hospitals, 2010–2013 (49.8% minimally invasive), analysed with inverse-probability propensity weighting; plus a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results interrupted time-series of radical hysterectomy outcomes, 2000–2010. Median follow-up 45 months.
cards.result: Four-year mortality was 9.1% among women who underwent minimally invasive surgery and 5.3% among those who underwent open surgery (hazard ratio 1.65; 95% CI 1.22–2.22; P=0.002). Before minimally invasive adoption (2000–2006), the 4-year relative survival rate was stable (annual percentage change 0.3%; 95% CI −0.1 to 0.6); after 2006 it declined by 0.8% (0.3–1.4) per year (P=0.01 for change of trend). Women receiving minimally invasive surgery had smaller, lower-grade tumours — features that should have favoured them.
cards.watchOut: Observational data cannot fully exclude confounding — but here the confounding by tumour features runs in the protective direction, and the time-series break coincides with adoption of the technique. Its role on this shelf is corroboration of the randomised result, not the primary evidence.
cards.source: Melamed A et al. Survival after Minimally Invasive Radical Hysterectomy for Early-Stage Cervical Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30379613. cards.headline: Synthesis: a randomised harm signal with a population-level echo — the direction of practice reversed on this evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a randomised harm signal with a population-level echo — the direction of practice reversed on this evidence
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (LACC, n=631) and one national cohort with time-series analysis (n=2,461), both in early-stage cervical cancer treated with radical hysterectomy.
cards.result: Disease-free survival at 4.5 years 86.0% versus 96.5%; hazard ratio for recurrence or cervical-cancer death 3.74; hazard ratio for death 6.00 (trial) and 1.65 for 4-year mortality (cohort: 9.1% versus 5.3%). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C: harm claims go to the developer personally, however concordant the evidence.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about radical hysterectomy for cancer — it does not indict minimally invasive hysterectomy for benign disease or the simple hysterectomy studied in SHAPE, and later technique modifications (tumour containment) remain untested against these results in randomised trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ramirez PT et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30380365); Melamed A et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30379613).

shelves.title: Sentinel-node mapping in endometrial cancer: sensitivity 97.2% and negative predictive value 99.6% in FIRES, with a 97% per-patient negative predictive value in SENTI-ENDO
shelves.question: In women with apparent early-stage endometrial cancer, does sentinel-lymph-node mapping stage the cancer as accurately as full lymphadenectomy?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma, Clear Cell/diagnostic imaging/pathology/surgery · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Carcinosarcoma/diagnostic imaging/pathology/surgery · Coloring Agents · Cystadenocarcinoma, Serous/diagnostic imaging/pathology/surgery · Endometrial Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging/pathology/surgery · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Indocyanine Green · Lymph Node Excision/methods · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Grading · Neoplasm Staging · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Sentinel Lymph Node/diagnostic imaging/pathology/surgery · Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for staging accuracy, from two prospective diagnostic cohorts checked against the full dissection they would replace. In FIRES (Rossi EC et al., PMID: 28159465), 340 women with clinical stage 1 endometrial cancer had indocyanine-green sentinel-node mapping followed by complete pelvic lymphadenectomy: of 36 node-positive patients with successful mapping, the sentinel node caught 35 — sensitivity 97.2% (95% CI 85.0–100) and negative predictive value 99.6% (97.9–100). In SENTI-ENDO (Ballester M et al., PMID: 21489874), dual-label mapping in 111 women gave a per-patient negative predictive value of 97% (91–99) and sensitivity of 84% (62–95), with all three false negatives in type 2 cancers; ultrastaging found metastases conventional histology missed in 47% of node-positive patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mapping stages accurately enough to spare most women a full lymphadenectomy, on prospective cohort — not randomised — evidence.

cards.headline: Rossi 2017 (FIRES): sentinel nodes caught 35 of 36 node-positive patients — sensitivity 97.2%, negative predictive value 99.6%, mapping succeeded in 86%
cards.summary: Rossi 2017 (FIRES): sentinel nodes caught 35 of 36 node-positive patients — sensitivity 97.2%, negative predictive value 99.6%, mapping succeeded in 86%
cards.type: Prospective multicentre diagnostic-accuracy cohort study (Rossi 2017, FIRES)
cards.people: 385 women enrolled (340 analysed) with clinical stage 1 endometrial cancer of all histologies and grades undergoing robotic staging at 10 US centres: cervical indocyanine-green injection and sentinel-node mapping, then complete pelvic lymphadenectomy (para-aortic in 58%); negative sentinel nodes were ultrastaged with cytokeratin immunohistochemistry.
cards.result: Successful mapping of at least one sentinel node in 293 of 340 patients (86%). Forty-one patients (12%) had positive nodes; among the 36 node-positive patients with successful mapping, sentinel nodes identified metastases in 35 (97%) — sensitivity 97.2% (95% CI 85.0–100) and negative predictive value 99.6% (97.9–100). The commonest grade 3–4 events were postoperative neurological disorders (4 patients) and respiratory distress or failure (4 patients); 22 patients had serious adverse events, one (a ureteral injury during sentinel-node dissection) related to the study intervention.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic-accuracy study, not a treatment trial: it shows mapping finds the metastases, not that omitting lymphadenectomy leaves survival unchanged — the 3% of node-positive patients missed are the honest price printed on the record. Mapping failed entirely in 14% of patients, who still need a backup plan.
cards.source: Rossi EC et al. A comparison of sentinel lymph node biopsy to lymphadenectomy for endometrial cancer staging (FIRES trial): a multicentre, prospective, cohort study. The Lancet Oncology. 2017. PMID: 28159465. Registry ID: NCT01673022. cards.headline: Ballester 2011 (SENTI-ENDO): per-hemipelvis negative predictive value 100%, but per-patient sensitivity 84% — all three false negatives were type 2 cancers
cards.summary: Ballester 2011 (SENTI-ENDO): per-hemipelvis negative predictive value 100%, but per-patient sensitivity 84% — all three false negatives were type 2 cancers
cards.type: Prospective multicentre diagnostic-accuracy cohort study (Ballester 2011, SENTI-ENDO)
cards.people: 133 women with FIGO stage I–II endometrial cancer at nine French centres: cervical dual injection (technetium colloid and patent blue) for pelvic sentinel-node assessment, then systematic pelvic-node dissection, with serial sectioning and immunohistochemistry of sentinel nodes.
cards.result: At least one sentinel node was detected in 111 of 125 eligible patients; 19 of 111 (17%) had pelvic-node metastases. Per hemipelvis, negative predictive value was 100% (95% CI 95–100) and sensitivity 100% (63–100). Per patient, three false negatives (two contralateral pelvic, one para-aortic) gave a negative predictive value of 97% (95% CI 91–99) and sensitivity of 84% (62–95) — all three in type 2 endometrial cancer. Immunohistochemistry and serial sectioning detected metastases missed by conventional histology in 9 of 111 patients (8%), representing 9 of the 19 (47%) with metastases; sentinel biopsy upstaged 10% of low-risk and 15% of intermediate-risk patients. No injection complications or anaphylactic reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: The older dual-label technique and the per-patient framing give the less flattering numbers, and the type 2 concentration of false negatives matters: mapping accuracy is histology-dependent. Like FIRES, this is accuracy against dissection, not a survival comparison.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two prospective cohorts agree mapping finds nearly all nodal disease — the residual miss rate and type 2 caveat ride along
cards.summary: Synthesis: two prospective cohorts agree mapping finds nearly all nodal disease — the residual miss rate and type 2 caveat ride along
cards.people: Two prospective multicentre diagnostic cohorts (FIRES n=340 with indocyanine green; SENTI-ENDO n=111 analysed with dual labelling), each verifying sentinel-node results against systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy.
cards.result: Sensitivity 97.2% and negative predictive value 99.6% (FIRES, per protocol); per-patient sensitivity 84% and negative predictive value 97% (SENTI-ENDO), with ultrastaging adding metastases in about half of node-positive patients in SENTI-ENDO. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: diagnostic cohort evidence without a randomised survival comparison is developer-review material.
cards.watchOut: Neither study randomises women to mapping versus dissection and follows survival — the inference that spared lymphadenectomies cost nothing oncologically rests on the very low false-negative rates, and FIRES’ own framing (a 3% miss among node-positive patients) is the number to quote, not zero.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rossi EC et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2017 (PMID: 28159465); Ballester M et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2011 (PMID: 21489874).

shelves.title: Chemotherapy first in advanced ovarian cancer: survival noninferior in two trials (hazard ratios 0.98 and 0.87) — with far fewer postoperative deaths and severe complications
shelves.question: In advanced ovarian cancer, does neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval debulking give survival as good as primary debulking surgery, with less perioperative morbidity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Neoplasm Staging · Ovarian Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/surgery · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — survival is a draw in both randomised trials; the perioperative harm is not. In EORTC 55971 (Vergote I et al., PMID: 20818904), the hazard ratio for death with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and interval debulking versus primary surgery was 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13; P=0.01 for noninferiority), and residual tumour ≤1 cm was achieved in 80.6% after interval versus 41.6% after primary debulking. In CHORUS (Kehoe S et al., PMID: 26002111), median overall survival was 24.1 versus 22.6 months (hazard ratio 0.87; 95% CI 0.72–1.05), while grade 3–4 postoperative adverse events occurred in 14% versus 24% and deaths within 28 days of surgery in under 1% versus 6%. In both trials, complete resection of all macroscopic disease — whenever achieved — was the strongest predictor of survival. PROPOSED SPLIT: chemotherapy-first is a legitimate, gentler route to the same survival in bulky stage IIIC/IV disease, not a better one.

cards.headline: Vergote 2010 (EORTC 55971): hazard ratio for death 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13) — interval debulking left residual ≤1 cm in 80.6% versus 41.6% after primary surgery
cards.summary: Vergote 2010 (EORTC 55971): hazard ratio for death 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13) — interval debulking left residual ≤1 cm in 80.6% versus 41.6% after primary surgery
cards.people: 670 patients randomised (632 eligible and treated) with stage IIIC or IV epithelial ovarian, fallopian-tube, or primary peritoneal carcinoma — 74.5% had metastatic lesions larger than 5 cm and 61.6% larger than 10 cm — assigned to primary debulking surgery followed by platinum-based chemotherapy, or neoadjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery.
cards.result: The hazard ratio for death (intention-to-treat) with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking versus primary debulking was 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13; P=0.01 for noninferiority), and the hazard ratio for progressive disease was 1.01 (90% CI 0.89–1.15). The largest residual tumour was ≤1 cm in 41.6% of patients after primary debulking and 80.6% after interval debulking. Postoperative adverse effects and mortality tended to be higher after primary debulking. Complete resection of all macroscopic disease, at either operation, was the strongest independent predictor of overall survival.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority here means "not worse by the trial’s margin" in a population with very bulky disease treated in an earlier surgical era; critics note the low complete-resection rates at primary surgery. The trial does not show chemotherapy-first is better — it shows the order can be swapped without a survival penalty in patients like these.
cards.source: Vergote I et al. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy or primary surgery in stage IIIC or IV ovarian cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20818904. Registry ID: NCT00003636. cards.headline: Kehoe 2015 (CHORUS): median survival 24.1 versus 22.6 months (HR 0.87) — grade 3–4 postoperative events 14% versus 24%, deaths within 28 days under 1% versus 6%
cards.summary: Kehoe 2015 (CHORUS): median survival 24.1 versus 22.6 months (HR 0.87) — grade 3–4 postoperative events 14% versus 24%, deaths within 28 days under 1% versus 6%
cards.people: 552 women with suspected stage III or IV ovarian cancer at 87 hospitals in the UK and New Zealand, randomised to primary surgery followed by six cycles of chemotherapy, or three cycles of primary (carboplatin-based) chemotherapy, then surgery, then three more cycles; 550 eligible women analysed intention-to-treat, with 451 deaths by May 2014.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 22.6 months in the primary-surgery group versus 24.1 months in the primary-chemotherapy group; the hazard ratio for death was 0.87 in favour of primary chemotherapy (one-sided 90% CI upper bound 0.98; 95% CI 0.72–1.05), meeting the noninferiority criterion (upper bound <1.18). Grade 3–4 postoperative adverse events occurred in 24% (60/252) of the primary-surgery group versus 14% (30/209) of the primary-chemotherapy group (P=0.0007), and deaths within 28 days after surgery in 6% (14 women) versus under 1% (1 woman) (P=0.001). Grade 3–4 chemotherapy toxicity was similar (49% vs 40%; P=0.0654), mostly uncomplicated neutropenia.
cards.watchOut: CHORUS enrolled women with suspected (not all confirmed) advanced cancer and its surgical outcomes have been debated; the survival point estimate favouring chemotherapy-first should not be read as superiority — the trial was designed and powered for noninferiority, and its confidence interval includes no difference.
cards.source: Kehoe S et al. Primary chemotherapy versus primary surgery for newly diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer (CHORUS): an open-label, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one verdict — the sequence can be reversed without losing survival, and the operation gets safer
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one verdict — the sequence can be reversed without losing survival, and the operation gets safer
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 noninferiority trials totalling over 1,180 women with bulky stage III/IV ovarian cancer (EORTC 55971, international; CHORUS, UK/New Zealand), each comparing primary debulking surgery with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and interval debulking.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for death: 0.98 (90% CI 0.84–1.13) and 0.87 (95% CI 0.72–1.05) — both noninferior. Perioperative harm (CHORUS): grade 3–4 postoperative events 14% versus 24%; death within 28 days of surgery under 1% versus 6%. Complete macroscopic resection remained the strongest survival predictor in EORTC 55971. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: The split framing matters: patients or centres that can achieve high complete-resection rates up front are not shown to gain from delay, and neither trial tested modern maintenance therapy eras. What is settled is narrower — chemotherapy-first is an acceptable standard, per CHORUS’ own conclusion, not a compromise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vergote I et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20818904); Kehoe S et al. Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 26002111).

shelves.title: Lenvatinib versus sorafenib in unresectable liver cancer: survival noninferior (13.6 versus 12.3 months) — different toxicities, and slower deterioration of fatigue, pain and diarrhoea
shelves.question: In unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, is lenvatinib non-inferior to sorafenib for overall survival as first-line therapy, and how do toxicity and quality of life compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/drug therapy/mortality · Female · Humans · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Niacinamide/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Phenylurea Compounds/therapeutic use · Quinolines/therapeutic use · Sorafenib · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — survival is statistically a tie, the side-effect profiles are genuinely different, and patient-reported deterioration comes later on some symptom scales with lenvatinib. In REFLECT (Kudo M et al., PMID: 29433850), median overall survival was 13.6 months on lenvatinib versus 12.3 months on sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.79–1.06), meeting the 1.08 noninferiority margin. The commonest adverse events diverged by drug: hypertension 42%, diarrhoea 39%, decreased appetite 34% and weight loss 31% on lenvatinib, versus hand–foot syndrome 52%, diarrhoea 46%, hypertension 30% and decreased appetite 27% on sorafenib. The trial’s patient-reported-outcomes analysis (Vogel A et al., PMID: 34087115) found nominally significant delays in definitive deterioration with lenvatinib for fatigue (hazard ratio 0.83), pain (0.80) and diarrhoea (0.52), but not for global health status (0.89). PROPOSED SPLIT: an equal-survival choice between two different toxicity and quality-of-life profiles, from a single trial.

cards.headline: Kudo 2018 (REFLECT): median survival 13.6 versus 12.3 months (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.06) — noninferiority met; hypertension 42% on lenvatinib, hand–foot syndrome 52% on sorafenib
cards.summary: Kudo 2018 (REFLECT): median survival 13.6 versus 12.3 months (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.06) — noninferiority met; hypertension 42% on lenvatinib, hand–foot syndrome 52% on sorafenib
cards.people: 954 eligible patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and no prior treatment for advanced disease, at 154 sites in 20 countries, randomised to oral lenvatinib (12 mg/day if ≥60 kg, 8 mg/day if <60 kg; n=478) or sorafenib 400 mg twice daily (n=476) in 28-day cycles.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 13.6 months (95% CI 12.1–14.9) with lenvatinib versus 12.3 months (10.4–13.9) with sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.79–1.06), meeting the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.08. The most common any-grade adverse events were hypertension (42%), diarrhoea (39%), decreased appetite (34%), and decreased weight (31%) for lenvatinib, and palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia (52%), diarrhoea (46%), hypertension (30%), and decreased appetite (27%) for sorafenib.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single trial, and noninferiority is not superiority: the confidence interval includes sorafenib being modestly better. The abstract reports any-grade adverse-event rates without a comparative grade ≥3 breakdown, so "different toxicity" is better supported than "less toxicity" in either direction.
cards.source: Kudo M et al. Lenvatinib versus sorafenib in first-line treatment of patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2018. cards.headline: Vogel 2021 (REFLECT patient-reported outcomes): time to definitive deterioration delayed with lenvatinib for fatigue (HR 0.83), pain (0.80) and diarrhoea (0.52) — global quality of life not different (0.89)
cards.summary: Vogel 2021 (REFLECT patient-reported outcomes): time to definitive deterioration delayed with lenvatinib for fatigue (HR 0.83), pain (0.80) and diarrhoea (0.52) — global quality of life not different (0.89)
cards.people: 931 of the 954 REFLECT patients (468 lenvatinib, 463 sorafenib) with a baseline patient-reported-outcome assessment; EORTC QLQ-C30 and hepatocellular-carcinoma-specific QLQ-HCC18 scales collected at baseline, each cycle, and end of treatment, analysed post hoc as secondary and exploratory endpoints.
cards.result: Overall mean change-from-baseline differences on most scales favoured lenvatinib but were not nominally statistically or clinically significant. Time to definitive, meaningful deterioration was nominally significantly delayed with lenvatinib on the QLQ-C30 fatigue (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.69–0.99), pain (0.80; 0.66–0.96), and diarrhoea (0.52; 0.42–0.65) domains, but not on other domains and not for global health status/quality of life (0.89; 0.73–1.09). Across scales, responders to treatment deteriorated later than non-responders by 4.8 to 14.6 months of median time.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc analyses of an open-label trial: patients knew which drug they were taking, several nominally significant domains sit among many tested, and "delayed deterioration" on three symptom scales is a softer claim than better overall quality of life — which was not shown.

cards.headline: Synthesis: equal survival, unlike side effects — the choice is which burden a patient would rather carry
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal survival, unlike side effects — the choice is which burden a patient would rather carry
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 noninferiority trial (REFLECT, n=954) and its patient-reported-outcomes analysis (n=931), in first-line unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma.
cards.result: Overall survival 13.6 versus 12.3 months (hazard ratio 0.92; noninferiority margin 1.08 met). Toxicity signatures: hypertension-led for lenvatinib, hand–foot-syndrome-led for sorafenib. Quality of life: deterioration delayed for fatigue, pain, and diarrhoea with lenvatinib; global health status not significantly different. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the shelf rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: First-line hepatocellular carcinoma has since moved toward immunotherapy combinations for eligible patients; this shelf answers the lenvatinib-versus-sorafenib question as asked, for patients in whom that remains the choice, and should not be read as a ranking against regimens it never faced.

shelves.title: NALIRIFOX in metastatic pancreatic cancer: survival 11.1 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.83) — a real but modest gain, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 87%
shelves.question: In metastatic pancreatic cancer, does NALIRIFOX improve overall survival versus gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line therapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Gemcitabine · Paclitaxel · Pancreatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Albumins · Adenocarcinoma/drug therapy · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a statistically real survival gain of about two months in the median, at full chemotherapy cost. In NAPOLI-3 (Wainberg ZA et al., PMID: 37708904), 770 patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma were randomised to NALIRIFOX or nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine: median overall survival was 11.1 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.70–0.99; p=0.036). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 87% on NALIRIFOX and 86% on the comparator, with treatment-related deaths in 2% of each group. A pooled individual-patient-data meta-analysis (Nichetti F et al., PMID: 38190183) places the result in context: NALIRIFOX and FOLFIRINOX produced near-identical survival (11.1 versus 11.7 months; hazard ratio 1.06), both ahead of gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel — so NAPOLI-3 establishes a new reference regimen, not a uniquely effective one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): first-line NALIRIFOX extends survival versus gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel, on a single phase 3 trial.

cards.headline: Wainberg 2023 (NAPOLI-3): median overall survival 11.1 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.83; p=0.036) — grade ≥3 events in 87% versus 86%
cards.summary: Wainberg 2023 (NAPOLI-3): median overall survival 11.1 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.83; p=0.036) — grade ≥3 events in 87% versus 86%
cards.people: 770 patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and ECOG performance status 0–1, at 187 sites in 18 countries, randomised to NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan 50 mg/m², oxaliplatin 60 mg/m², leucovorin 400 mg/m², fluorouracil 2400 mg/m² over 46 h, days 1 and 15 of a 28-day cycle; n=383) or nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m² plus gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² on days 1, 8, and 15 (n=387); median follow-up 16.1 months.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 11.1 months (95% CI 10.0–12.1) with NALIRIFOX versus 9.2 months (8.3–10.6) with nab-paclitaxel–gemcitabine (hazard ratio 0.83; 95% CI 0.70–0.99; p=0.036). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 322 of 370 (87%) patients receiving NALIRIFOX and 326 of 379 (86%) receiving the comparator; treatment-related deaths occurred in 6 (2%) and 8 (2%) patients respectively.
cards.watchOut: The p-value (0.036) and the confidence interval’s upper bound (0.99) sit close to no effect — this is a genuine but fragile single-trial result, in patients fit enough (ECOG 0–1) for a four-drug regimen. The trial does not compare NALIRIFOX with FOLFIRINOX, the other four-drug standard it most resembles.

cards.headline: Nichetti 2024 (pooled analysis of 7 trials, 2,581 patients): NALIRIFOX and FOLFIRINOX statistically indistinguishable (OS HR 1.06); both beat gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel
cards.summary: Nichetti 2024 (pooled analysis of 7 trials, 2,581 patients): NALIRIFOX and FOLFIRINOX statistically indistinguishable (OS HR 1.06); both beat gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with reconstructed individual patient data (Nichetti 2024)
cards.people: Seven phase 3 trials (2011–2023) of first-line therapy for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, totalling 2,581 patients: 383 treated with NALIRIFOX, 433 with FOLFIRINOX, and 1,756 with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel; survival curves were reconstructed from published Kaplan–Meier plots and validated by network meta-analysis.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 7.4 months with NALIRIFOX and 7.3 months with FOLFIRINOX versus 5.7 months with gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel. Median overall survival was 11.1 months with NALIRIFOX, 11.7 months with FOLFIRINOX (hazard ratio versus NALIRIFOX 1.06; 95% CI 0.81–1.39; P=.65), and 10.4 months with gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel (hazard ratio versus NALIRIFOX 1.18; 95% CI 1.00–1.39; P=.05). Objective response rates did not differ significantly (41.8%, 31.6%, and 35.0%). NALIRIFOX had lower grade ≥3 haematological toxicity (e.g., decreased platelets 1.6% vs 11.8% with FOLFIRINOX and 10.8% with gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel) but more severe diarrhoea than gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel (20.3% vs 15.7%).
cards.watchOut: Indirect comparison built from reconstructed curves, not a head-to-head trial — cross-trial differences in era and patient selection can manufacture or erase differences of this size. Its honest use here is context: NAPOLI-3’s comparator was the weaker of the two established standards.
cards.source: Nichetti F et al. NALIRIFOX, FOLFIRINOX, and Gemcitabine With Nab-Paclitaxel as First-Line Chemotherapy for Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Network Open. 2024. PMID: 38190183. cards.headline: Synthesis: a new reference regimen by two months of median survival — and no evidence it beats its closest cousin
cards.summary: Synthesis: a new reference regimen by two months of median survival — and no evidence it beats its closest cousin
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (NAPOLI-3, n=770) plus a pooled reconstructed-data meta-analysis of seven first-line phase 3 trials (n=2,581) in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
cards.result: Overall survival: 11.1 versus 9.2 months against gemcitabine–nab-paclitaxel (hazard ratio 0.83); versus FOLFIRINOX, no significant difference (hazard ratio 1.06). Grade ≥3 adverse events: 87% on NALIRIFOX. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial mortality benefit claim goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: Median gains of this size in pancreatic cancer are averages over a wide spread — some patients benefit substantially, most briefly. The shelf supports NALIRIFOX as a first-line option for fit patients; it does not support choosing it over FOLFIRINOX on survival grounds.

shelves.title: BTK-inhibitor regimens beat chemoimmunotherapy in untreated CLL: 3-year progression-free survival 89.4% versus 72.9% in E1912 and 42-month 74.6% versus 24.8% in GLOW
shelves.question: In previously untreated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, do BTK-inhibitor-based regimens improve progression-free survival versus chemoimmunotherapy, and in whom?
shelves.mesh: Adenine/analogs & derivatives · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Immunotherapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines · Progression-Free Survival · Pyrazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Rituximab/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Vidarabine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials in two different age-and-fitness populations, both decisively positive. In E1912 (Shanafelt TD et al., PMID: 31365801), patients aged 70 or younger received ibrutinib–rituximab or fludarabine–cyclophosphamide–rituximab: progression-free survival at 3 years was 89.4% versus 72.9% (hazard ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.22–0.56), and overall survival at 3 years was 98.8% versus 91.5% (hazard ratio 0.17; 0.05–0.54) at a planned interim analysis, with grade ≥3 infections in 10.5% versus 20.3%. In GLOW (Niemann CU et al., PMID: 37944541), older or comorbid patients received fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax or chlorambucil–obinutuzumab: at 46 months the progression-free-survival hazard ratio was 0.214 (0.138–0.334), with 42-month rates of 74.6% versus 24.8%, and 15 versus 30 deaths. The benefit in E1912 was clearest without IGHV mutation (90.7% vs 62.5% at 3 years); with mutated IGHV the 3-year rates were nearly identical (87.7% vs 88.0%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): BTK-based first-line therapy is superior to chemoimmunotherapy for progression-free survival across both populations.

cards.headline: Shanafelt 2019 (E1912): 3-year progression-free survival 89.4% versus 72.9% (HR 0.35) and overall survival 98.8% versus 91.5% (HR 0.17) for ibrutinib–rituximab over FCR in patients ≤70
cards.summary: Shanafelt 2019 (E1912): 3-year progression-free survival 89.4% versus 72.9% (HR 0.35) and overall survival 98.8% versus 91.5% (HR 0.17) for ibrutinib–rituximab over FCR in patients ≤70
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, planned interim analysis (Shanafelt 2019, ECOG-ACRIN E1912)
cards.people: 529 patients aged 70 years or younger with previously untreated CLL, randomised 2:1 to ibrutinib plus rituximab (six cycles after one cycle of ibrutinib alone, then ibrutinib until progression; n=354) or six cycles of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab (n=175); median follow-up 33.6 months.
cards.result: Progression-free survival favoured ibrutinib–rituximab (89.4% vs 72.9% at 3 years; hazard ratio for progression or death 0.35; 95% CI 0.22–0.56; P<0.001), as did overall survival (98.8% vs 91.5% at 3 years; hazard ratio for death 0.17; 95% CI 0.05–0.54; P<0.001). In patients without IGHV mutation, 3-year progression-free survival was 90.7% versus 62.5% (hazard ratio 0.26; 0.14–0.50); with IGHV mutation it was 87.7% versus 88.0% (hazard ratio 0.44; 0.14–1.36). Grade ≥3 adverse events overall were similar (80.1% vs 79.7%), but grade ≥3 infectious complications were less common with ibrutinib–rituximab (10.5% vs 20.3%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Interim analysis: the striking overall-survival hazard ratio (0.17) rests on few deaths and an early look, and ibrutinib was continued indefinitely in this design — the trial does not answer fixed-duration questions, and its comparator (FCR) is the regimen fittest young patients would otherwise receive, which is precisely the point but limits generalisation to frailer patients.
cards.source: Shanafelt TD et al. Ibrutinib-Rituximab or Chemoimmunotherapy for Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31365801. Registry ID: NCT02048813. cards.headline: Niemann 2023 (GLOW, 4-year follow-up): progression-free survival HR 0.214 for fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax versus chlorambucil–obinutuzumab in older or comorbid patients — deaths 15 versus 30
cards.summary: Niemann 2023 (GLOW, 4-year follow-up): progression-free survival HR 0.214 for fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax versus chlorambucil–obinutuzumab in older or comorbid patients — deaths 15 versus 30
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, updated 46-month analysis (Niemann 2023, GLOW)
cards.people: 211 patients with previously untreated CLL who were aged 65 or older, or 18–64 with comorbidity (Cumulative Illness Rating Scale >6 or creatinine clearance <70 mL/min), at 67 centres in 14 countries, randomised to fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax (3 cycles ibrutinib lead-in, then 12 cycles of the combination; n=106) or six cycles of chlorambucil–obinutuzumab (n=105); median follow-up 46 months.
cards.result: Progression-free survival remained superior for ibrutinib–venetoclax (hazard ratio 0.214; 95% CI 0.138–0.334; p<0.0001), with 42-month progression-free survival rates of 74.6% (95% CI 65.0–82.0) versus 24.8% (16.5–34.1). There were 15 deaths in the ibrutinib–venetoclax group (three from post-treatment infections) and 30 in the chlorambucil–obinutuzumab group (ten from post-treatment infections). Treatment-related deaths were reported in one patient in each group.
cards.watchOut: This card is the trial’s 4-year follow-up report rather than its primary publication, and the comparator — chlorambucil–obinutuzumab — is the gentlest chemoimmunotherapy, appropriate for this older, comorbid population but a lower bar than FCR. Overall survival by group is given as death counts (15 versus 30), not a hazard ratio, in this record.
cards.source: Niemann CU et al. Fixed-duration ibrutinib-venetoclax versus chlorambucil-obinutuzumab in previously untreated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (GLOW): 4-year follow-up from a multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial. The Lancet Oncology. 2023. PMID: 37944541. Registry ID: NCT03462719. cards.headline: Synthesis: in younger fit patients and in older comorbid patients alike, BTK-based therapy wins on progression-free survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: in younger fit patients and in older comorbid patients alike, BTK-based therapy wins on progression-free survival
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 trials in previously untreated CLL: E1912 (n=529, age ≤70, ibrutinib–rituximab versus FCR) and GLOW (n=211, older/comorbid, fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax versus chlorambucil–obinutuzumab, 46-month follow-up).
cards.result: Progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.35 (E1912; 3-year rates 89.4% versus 72.9%) and 0.214 (GLOW; 42-month rates 74.6% versus 24.8%). Overall survival: E1912 interim hazard ratio 0.17 (98.8% versus 91.5% at 3 years); GLOW deaths 15 versus 30. Subgroup note: E1912’s advantage was concentrated in IGHV-unmutated disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C: the shelf carries a mortality benefit claim, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: RESONATE-2 (ibrutinib versus chlorambucil in older patients) is not carded here because it already lives on live shelf #676; this shelf was built on E1912 and GLOW so the one-home rule holds. Continuous ibrutinib (E1912 design) and fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax (GLOW design) are different commitments — the shelf establishes the class’s superiority to chemoimmunotherapy, not which BTK strategy is best.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shanafelt TD et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31365801); Niemann CU et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2023 (PMID: 37944541).

shelves.title: Bendamustine–rituximab over R-CHOP in indolent lymphoma: progression-free survival 69.5 versus 31.2 months in StiL, complete response noninferior in BRIGHT — with less alopecia, neuropathy and infection
shelves.question: In indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma, does bendamustine plus rituximab improve progression-free survival versus R-CHOP as first-line therapy, with less toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bendamustine Hydrochloride · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Disease-Free Survival · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Lymphoma, Mantle-Cell/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Nitrogen Mustard Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Prednisone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Rituximab · Treatment Outcome · Vincristine/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large progression-free-survival advantage and a kinder toxicity profile in one trial, response noninferiority in the other. In StiL NHL1-2003 (Rummel MJ et al., PMID: 23433739), median progression-free survival was 69.5 months on bendamustine–rituximab versus 31.2 months on R-CHOP (hazard ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.44–0.74; p<0.0001), with haematological toxicity in 30% versus 68%, infections in 37% versus 50%, peripheral neuropathy in 7% versus 29%, and alopecia in 0% versus 100% of patients receiving at least three cycles. In BRIGHT (Flinn IW et al., PMID: 24591201), complete response was 31% on bendamustine–rituximab versus 25% on R-CHOP/R-CVP (noninferiority met), with overall response 97% versus 91% (P=.0102). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): bendamustine–rituximab is at least as effective as R-CHOP-class therapy first-line in indolent lymphoma, with a longer progression-free survival in StiL and fewer of the toxicities patients notice most.

cards.headline: Rummel 2013 (StiL NHL1-2003): median progression-free survival 69.5 versus 31.2 months (HR 0.58) — haematological toxicity 30% versus 68%, neuropathy 7% versus 29%, alopecia 0% versus 100%
cards.summary: Rummel 2013 (StiL NHL1-2003): median progression-free survival 69.5 versus 31.2 months (HR 0.58) — haematological toxicity 30% versus 68%, neuropathy 7% versus 29%, alopecia 0% versus 100%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 noninferiority trial (Rummel 2013, StiL NHL1-2003)
cards.people: 549 patients with newly diagnosed stage III–IV indolent or mantle-cell lymphoma at 81 German centres (274 assigned bendamustine–rituximab, 275 R-CHOP; 261 and 253 assessed per protocol), treated with up to six cycles of bendamustine 90 mg/m² days 1–2 plus rituximab, or standard CHOP plus rituximab; median follow-up 45 months. Patients and physicians were not masked.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was significantly longer with bendamustine–rituximab (69.5 months vs 31.2 months; hazard ratio 0.58; 95% CI 0.44–0.74; p<0.0001). Bendamustine–rituximab was better tolerated: alopecia 0 versus 245 of 245 patients (100%) receiving ≥3 cycles of R-CHOP (p<0.0001), haematological toxicity 30% versus 68% (p<0.0001), infections 37% versus 50% (p=0.0025), peripheral neuropathy 7% versus 29% (p<0.0001), and stomatitis 6% versus 19% (p<0.0001). Erythematous skin reactions were more common with bendamustine–rituximab (16% vs 9%; p=0.024).
cards.watchOut: The primary analysis was per-protocol in an open-label trial designed for noninferiority, and the population mixes indolent subtypes with mantle-cell lymphoma — the headline hazard ratio is an average across histologies with different natural histories. Overall survival is not reported in this record; the claim is progression-free survival and tolerability.

cards.headline: Flinn 2014 (BRIGHT): complete response 31% versus 25% — noninferior to R-CHOP/R-CVP, with overall response 97% versus 91%
cards.summary: Flinn 2014 (BRIGHT): complete response 31% versus 25% — noninferior to R-CHOP/R-CVP, with overall response 97% versus 91%
cards.people: 447 treatment-naive patients with indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma or mantle-cell lymphoma worldwide, randomised to bendamustine–rituximab (n=224) or investigator-preselected standard rituximab-chemotherapy (R-CHOP or R-CVP; n=223) for six cycles (two additional permitted); response assessed by a blinded independent review committee.
cards.result: Complete response was 31% with bendamustine–rituximab versus 25% with R-CHOP/R-CVP (P=.0225 for noninferiority at the 0.88 margin), and overall response rates were 97% versus 91% (P=.0102). Vomiting and drug-hypersensitivity reactions were significantly more frequent with bendamustine–rituximab, while peripheral neuropathy/paresthesia and alopecia were significantly more frequent with the standard regimens (all P<.05).
cards.watchOut: BRIGHT’s primary endpoint is response, not progression-free or overall survival, and its control arm mixes R-CHOP and R-CVP by investigator choice. It corroborates that bendamustine–rituximab is not a weaker regimen; the duration-of-benefit claim rests on StiL.
cards.source: Flinn IW et al. Randomized trial of bendamustine-rituximab or R-CHOP/R-CVP in first-line treatment of indolent NHL or MCL: the BRIGHT study. Blood. 2014. PMID: 24591201. cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised trials converge — bendamustine–rituximab is a preferred first-line backbone for indolent lymphoma
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised trials converge — bendamustine–rituximab is a preferred first-line backbone for indolent lymphoma
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 noninferiority trials (StiL NHL1-2003, n=549 assessed 514 per protocol; BRIGHT, n=447) comparing bendamustine–rituximab with R-CHOP-class therapy in untreated indolent and mantle-cell lymphomas.
cards.result: Progression-free survival (StiL): median 69.5 versus 31.2 months, hazard ratio 0.58. Complete response (BRIGHT): 31% versus 25%, noninferior; overall response 97% versus 91%. Toxicity: consistently less alopecia, neuropathy, and haematological toxicity with bendamustine–rituximab; more skin reactions (StiL) and vomiting/hypersensitivity (BRIGHT). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither record reports an overall-survival advantage, and both trials predate routine use of maintenance and targeted agents that have since reshaped indolent-lymphoma care. The comparison settled here is bendamustine–rituximab versus R-CHOP as the opening move.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rummel MJ et al. Lancet. 2013 (PMID: 23433739); Flinn IW et al. Blood. 2014 (PMID: 24591201).

shelves.title: Adding daratumumab to VRd in transplant-eligible myeloma: 48-month progression-free survival 84.3% versus 67.7% in PERSEUS, MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4% in GRIFFIN
shelves.question: In transplant-eligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, does adding daratumumab to VRd induction and consolidation improve progression-free survival versus VRd alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bortezomib/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Lenalidomide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy · Membrane Glycoproteins · ADP-ribosyl Cyclase 1
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large phase 3 trial and a randomised phase 2 trial agree that the four-drug regimen deepens responses and delays progression. In PERSEUS (Sonneveld P et al., PMID: 38084760), 709 transplant-eligible patients received daratumumab plus VRd or VRd alone, both with lenalidomide maintenance: estimated progression-free survival at 48 months was 84.3% versus 67.7% (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.42; 95% CI 0.30–0.59; P<0.001), complete response or better in 87.9% versus 70.1%, and MRD-negative status in 75.2% versus 47.5%; deaths numbered 34 versus 44. In GRIFFIN (Voorhees PM et al., PMID: 32325490), stringent complete response after consolidation was 42.4% versus 32.0%, deepening with follow-up (62.6% vs 45.4%), with MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4% and 24-month progression-free survival 95.8% versus 89.8%. The price is haematological: grade 3–4 neutropenia 62.1% versus 51.0% in PERSEUS, and serious adverse events 57.0% versus 49.3%. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): daratumumab-VRd is the stronger induction for transplant-eligible patients.

cards.headline: Sonneveld 2024 (PERSEUS): progression-free survival at 48 months 84.3% versus 67.7% (HR 0.42) — complete response or better 87.9% versus 70.1%, MRD-negative 75.2% versus 47.5%
cards.summary: Sonneveld 2024 (PERSEUS): progression-free survival at 48 months 84.3% versus 67.7% (HR 0.42) — complete response or better 87.9% versus 70.1%, MRD-negative 75.2% versus 47.5%
cards.people: 709 transplant-eligible patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, randomised to subcutaneous daratumumab plus VRd (bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone) induction and consolidation with lenalidomide maintenance, or VRd induction and consolidation with lenalidomide maintenance alone; median follow-up 47.5 months.
cards.result: The risk of disease progression or death was lower with daratumumab-VRd: estimated progression-free survival at 48 months was 84.3% versus 67.7% (hazard ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.30–0.59; P<0.001, crossing the prespecified stopping boundary). Complete response or better occurred in 87.9% versus 70.1% (P<0.001) and MRD-negative status in 75.2% versus 47.5% (P<0.001). Death occurred in 34 patients in the daratumumab group and 44 in the VRd group. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in most patients in both groups, most commonly neutropenia (62.1% vs 51.0%) and thrombocytopenia (29.1% vs 17.3%); serious adverse events occurred in 57.0% versus 49.3%.
cards.watchOut: Overall survival is immature in this record — deaths are reported as counts (34 versus 44), not a tested difference. The daratumumab group also received daratumumab with maintenance, so PERSEUS tests a whole strategy, not induction alone; and subcutaneous daratumumab in both induction and maintenance is a resource-intensive regimen whose absolute benefit shrinks in lower-risk disease.
cards.source: Sonneveld P et al. Daratumumab, Bortezomib, Lenalidomide, and Dexamethasone for Multiple Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38084760. Registry ID: NCT03710603. cards.headline: Voorhees 2020 (GRIFFIN): stringent complete response 42.4% versus 32.0% after consolidation, deepening to 62.6% versus 45.4% — MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4%
cards.summary: Voorhees 2020 (GRIFFIN): stringent complete response 42.4% versus 32.0% after consolidation, deepening to 62.6% versus 45.4% — MRD negativity 51.0% versus 20.4%
cards.people: 207 transplant-eligible patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, randomised 1:1 to daratumumab-RVd or RVd induction (four cycles), autologous transplant, consolidation (two cycles), and maintenance (lenalidomide with or without daratumumab, 26 cycles); median follow-up 22.1 months for the updated response analysis.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, stringent complete response by the end of post-transplant consolidation, favoured daratumumab-RVd (42.4% vs 32.0%; odds ratio 1.57; 95% CI 0.87–2.82; one-sided P=.068, meeting the prespecified one-sided α of 0.10). With longer follow-up, stringent complete response improved to 62.6% versus 45.4% (P=.0177) and MRD negativity (10⁻⁵ threshold) to 51.0% versus 20.4% (P<.0001). Progression occurred in 4 patients (3.8%) on daratumumab-RVd and 7 (6.8%) on RVd; 24-month progression-free survival rates were 95.8% and 89.8%. Grade 3/4 haematologic adverse events and infections were more common with daratumumab-RVd, though grade 3/4 infection rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial with a generous one-sided α (0.10) and a response-depth primary endpoint — supportive, not standalone, evidence. Its value on this shelf is that its direction and magnitude match PERSEUS on MRD and response depth in an independently randomised population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the four-drug strategy deepens every measurable layer of response and delays progression by a wide margin
cards.summary: Synthesis: the four-drug strategy deepens every measurable layer of response and delays progression by a wide margin
cards.people: One phase 3 trial (PERSEUS, n=709) and one randomised phase 2 trial (GRIFFIN, n=207) of daratumumab added to VRd/RVd induction, consolidation, and maintenance in transplant-eligible newly diagnosed myeloma.
cards.result: Progression-free survival at 48 months 84.3% versus 67.7% (hazard ratio 0.42, PERSEUS). MRD negativity 75.2% versus 47.5% (PERSEUS) and 51.0% versus 20.4% (GRIFFIN, 10⁻⁵). Harms: more grade 3–4 neutropenia (62.1% vs 51.0%) and serious adverse events (57.0% vs 49.3%) in PERSEUS. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Overall survival remains unproven in these records — the case for D-VRd is built on progression-free survival and response depth, with MRD as a surrogate whose survival translation is still being confirmed. Cost and treatment burden are real and unmeasured in either abstract.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sonneveld P et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38084760); Voorhees PM et al. Blood. 2020 (PMID: 32325490).

shelves.title: Early transplant in myeloma buys progression-free survival, not life: 67.5 versus 46.2 months in DETERMINATION and 50 versus 36 months in IFM 2009 — overall survival identical in both
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, does early autologous stem-cell transplantation added to RVd improve progression-free and overall survival versus RVd alone with transplant reserved for relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bortezomib/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Disease-Free Survival · Humans · Lenalidomide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Maintenance Chemotherapy/methods · Melphalan/administration & dosage · Multiple Myeloma/diagnosis/drug therapy/surgery · Stem Cell Transplantation · Transplantation, Autologous
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the same split in two large trials on two continents: transplant first delays progression by roughly a year and a half to two years, and does not extend life. In DETERMINATION (Richardson PG et al., PMID: 35660812), median progression-free survival was 67.5 months with RVd plus transplant versus 46.2 months with RVd alone (hazard ratio for progression or death in the RVd-alone group 1.53; 95% CI 1.23–1.91), while 5-year survival was 80.7% versus 79.2% (hazard ratio for death 1.10; 0.73–1.65), with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 94.2% versus 78.2%. In IFM 2009 (Attal M et al., PMID: 28379796), median progression-free survival was 50 versus 36 months (adjusted hazard ratio 0.65; P<0.001), complete response 59% versus 48%, MRD undetectable 79% versus 65% — and 4-year overall survival 81% versus 82%. PROPOSED SPLIT: early transplant is a progression-delaying choice with a real toxicity price, not a life-extending one.

cards.headline: Richardson 2022 (DETERMINATION): median progression-free survival 67.5 versus 46.2 months — 5-year survival 80.7% versus 79.2% (HR for death 1.10); grade ≥3 events 94.2% versus 78.2%
cards.summary: Richardson 2022 (DETERMINATION): median progression-free survival 67.5 versus 46.2 months — 5-year survival 80.7% versus 79.2% (HR for death 1.10); grade ≥3 events 94.2% versus 78.2%
cards.people: 722 adults aged 18–65 with symptomatic newly diagnosed myeloma in the United States: after one RVd cycle, randomised to two more RVd cycles plus mobilisation then five further RVd cycles (RVD-alone, n=357), or high-dose melphalan plus autologous transplant followed by two RVd cycles (transplantation, n=365); both groups received lenalidomide maintenance until progression or unacceptable toxicity. Median follow-up 76.0 months.
cards.result: Disease progression or death occurred in 328 patients; the risk was 53% relatively higher in the RVd-alone group (hazard ratio 1.53; 95% CI 1.23–1.91; P<0.001), with median progression-free survival 46.2 versus 67.5 months. Partial response or better: 95.0% versus 97.5% (P=0.55); complete response or better: 42.0% versus 46.8% (P=0.99). Treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 78.2% (RVd alone) and 94.2% (transplantation). Five-year survival was 79.2% versus 80.7% (hazard ratio for death 1.10; 95% CI 0.73–1.65) — no overall survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: The RVd-alone strategy in this trial meant transplant deferred, not abandoned — many patients could still receive it at relapse, which is exactly why overall survival can equalise. Maintenance until progression in both arms also differs from the one-year maintenance in IFM 2009, yet the survival answer came out the same.
cards.source: Richardson PG et al. Triplet Therapy, Transplantation, and Maintenance until Progression in Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35660812. Registry ID: NCT01208662. cards.headline: Attal 2017 (IFM 2009): median progression-free survival 50 versus 36 months (adjusted HR 0.65) — 4-year survival 81% versus 82%; grade 3–4 neutropenia 92% versus 47%
cards.summary: Attal 2017 (IFM 2009): median progression-free survival 50 versus 36 months (adjusted HR 0.65) — 4-year survival 81% versus 82%; grade 3–4 neutropenia 92% versus 47%
cards.people: 700 patients with newly diagnosed myeloma in France, randomised after three RVD induction cycles to consolidation with five further RVD cycles (n=350) or high-dose melphalan plus autologous transplant followed by two RVD cycles (n=350); both groups received one year of lenalidomide maintenance.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 50 months in the transplantation group versus 36 months in the RVD-alone group (adjusted hazard ratio for progression or death 0.65; P<0.001), consistent across subgroups including stage and cytogenetic risk. Complete response was higher with transplantation (59% vs 48%; P=0.03), as was undetectable MRD (79% vs 65%; P<0.001). Overall survival at 4 years did not differ (81% transplantation vs 82% RVD alone). Grade 3–4 neutropenia was more frequent with transplantation (92% vs 47%), as were grade 3–4 gastrointestinal disorders (28% vs 7%) and infections (20% vs 9%); treatment-related deaths, second primary cancers, thromboembolism, and neuropathy did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Four-year survival follow-up is shorter than DETERMINATION’s, and one year of maintenance is no longer the common standard — but as a replication of the progression-free-survival gain and the survival null in an independent health system, it is exactly what a two-trial shelf needs.
cards.source: Attal M et al. Lenalidomide, Bortezomib, and Dexamethasone with Transplantation for Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28379796. Registry ID: NCT01191060. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, one trade — about 14–21 extra months before progression, bought with transplant toxicity, at no measured survival gain
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one trade — about 14–21 extra months before progression, bought with transplant toxicity, at no measured survival gain
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 trials totalling 1,422 patients with newly diagnosed myeloma (DETERMINATION, US, maintenance until progression; IFM 2009, France, one year of maintenance), each comparing RVd/RVD plus early autologous transplant versus RVd/RVD alone with transplant deferred.
cards.result: Progression-free survival: medians 67.5 versus 46.2 months and 50 versus 36 months, both highly significant. Overall survival: 5-year 80.7% versus 79.2% and 4-year 81% versus 82% — no difference in either. Toxicity: grade ≥3 events 94.2% versus 78.2% (DETERMINATION); grade 3–4 neutropenia 92% versus 47% (IFM 2009). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: The honest framing for patients is timing, not outcome: transplant now or transplant later produced the same survival in these trials, so the decision turns on how a patient values years without progression against the transplant’s upfront burden — and on preserving stem-cell options, which both trials protected by collecting cells early.
cards.source: Synthesis of Richardson PG et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35660812); Attal M et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28379796).

shelves.title: Intensive follow-up after colorectal cancer surgery finds more curable recurrences but saves no lives: 5-year mortality 13.0% versus 14.1% in COLOFOL, deaths 18.2% versus 15.9% in FACS
shelves.question: In patients with stage II–III colorectal cancer, does high-frequency follow-up testing (CEA and CT) improve overall survival versus less frequent follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aftercare/methods · Aged · Carcinoembryonic Antigen/blood · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/mortality/surgery · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/diagnosis · Neoplasm Staging · Proportional Hazards Models · Survival Rate · Time Factors · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — to survival, which is what patients are usually told the scans are for. In COLOFOL (Wille-Jørgensen P et al., PMID: 29800179), 2,509 patients with stage II–III colorectal cancer were randomised to CT and CEA testing at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months versus at 12 and 36 months only: 5-year overall mortality was 13.0% versus 14.1% (risk difference 1.1%; 95% CI −1.6 to 3.8; P=.43), colorectal-cancer-specific mortality 10.6% versus 11.4% (P=.52), and recurrence 21.6% versus 19.4% (P=.15). In FACS (Primrose JN et al., PMID: 24430319), intensive CEA, CT, or combined follow-up did triple the rate of curative-intent surgery for recurrence (6.6–8.0% versus 2.3% with minimum follow-up) — yet deaths were 18.2% in the combined intensive groups versus 15.9% with minimum follow-up, not significantly different. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): intensive surveillance detects more treatable recurrences without a demonstrated survival benefit.

cards.headline: Wille-Jørgensen 2018 (COLOFOL): 5-year overall mortality 13.0% versus 14.1% (P=.43) and cancer-specific mortality 10.6% versus 11.4% (P=.52) for five-test versus two-test follow-up
cards.summary: Wille-Jørgensen 2018 (COLOFOL): 5-year overall mortality 13.0% versus 14.1% (P=.43) and cancer-specific mortality 10.6% versus 11.4% (P=.52) for five-test versus two-test follow-up
cards.people: 2,509 patients with stage II or III colorectal cancer after curative surgery at 24 centres in Sweden, Denmark, and Uruguay (mean age 63.5 years; 45% women), randomised to CT of thorax and abdomen plus serum CEA at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 36 months (n=1,253) or at 12 and 36 months only (n=1,256), and followed for 5 years; 94.3% completed the trial. The trial was unblinded.
cards.result: Five-year overall mortality was 13.0% (161/1,253) in the high-frequency group versus 14.1% (174/1,256) in the low-frequency group (risk difference 1.1%; 95% CI −1.6% to 3.8%; P=.43). Five-year colorectal-cancer-specific mortality was 10.6% (128/1,248) versus 11.4% (137/1,250) (risk difference 0.8%; 95% CI −1.7% to 3.3%; P=.52). The colorectal-cancer-specific recurrence rate was 21.6% (265/1,248) versus 19.4% (238/1,250) (risk difference 2.2%; 95% CI −1.0% to 5.4%; P=.15). Intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses agreed.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval for overall mortality (−1.6% to 3.8%) excludes a large benefit but not a small one; and both arms received scheduled testing — COLOFOL compares more versus less surveillance, not surveillance versus none. Recurrence was, if anything, detected slightly more often with high-frequency testing, without a mortality translation.
cards.source: Wille-Jørgensen P et al. Effect of More vs Less Frequent Follow-up Testing on Overall and Colorectal Cancer-Specific Mortality in Patients With Stage II or III Colorectal Cancer: The COLOFOL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29800179. Registry ID: NCT00225641. cards.headline: Primrose 2014 (FACS): curative-intent surgery for recurrence 6.7% (CEA), 8% (CT) and 6.6% (both) versus 2.3% with minimum follow-up — deaths 18.2% versus 15.9%, not significant
cards.summary: Primrose 2014 (FACS): curative-intent surgery for recurrence 6.7% (CEA), 8% (CT) and 6.6% (both) versus 2.3% with minimum follow-up — deaths 18.2% versus 15.9%, not significant
cards.people: 1,202 UK patients after curative surgery for primary colorectal cancer (including adjuvant therapy if indicated, no residual disease), randomised to CEA only (n=300), CT only (n=299), CEA plus CT (n=302), or minimum follow-up with investigation only if symptoms occurred (n=301). CEA was measured every 3 months for 2 years then 6-monthly for 3 years; CT was 6-monthly for 2 years then annually for 3 years. Mean observation 4.4 years.
cards.result: Recurrence was detected in 199 participants (16.6%); 71 (5.9%) were treated for recurrence with curative intent. Surgical treatment of recurrence with curative intent was 2.3% (7/301) with minimum follow-up, 6.7% (20/300) with CEA (absolute difference 4.4%; adjusted odds ratio 3.00; 95% CI 1.23–7.33), 8% (24/299) with CT (difference 5.7%; adjusted odds ratio 3.63; 1.51–8.69), and 6.6% (20/302) with CEA plus CT (difference 4.3%; adjusted odds ratio 3.10; 1.10–8.71) — combining CEA and CT added nothing. Deaths did not differ significantly: 18.2% (164/901) across the intensive groups versus 15.9% (48/301) with minimum follow-up (difference 2.3%; 95% CI −2.6% to 7.1%). The authors conclude that if a survival advantage exists for any strategy, it is likely to be small.
cards.watchOut: FACS shows the mechanism works — intensive follow-up genuinely gets more recurrences to curative surgery — and still cannot show a mortality benefit, which is the more uncomfortable finding for surveillance programmes. Its minimum-follow-up arm is the closest either trial comes to a no-routine-testing control.
cards.source: Primrose JN et al. Effect of 3 to 5 years of scheduled CEA and CT follow-up to detect recurrence of colorectal cancer: the FACS randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 24430319.
