cards.headline: Synthesis: surveillance delivers exactly what it promises — earlier, more operable recurrences — except the longer life it is sold on
cards.summary: Synthesis: surveillance delivers exactly what it promises — earlier, more operable recurrences — except the longer life it is sold on
cards.people: Two randomised trials of follow-up intensity after curative colorectal cancer surgery (COLOFOL n=2,509, frequency comparison; FACS n=1,202, modality comparison against minimum follow-up).
cards.result: Mortality: COLOFOL 5-year overall 13.0% versus 14.1% (P=.43), cancer-specific 10.6% versus 11.4% (P=.52); FACS deaths 18.2% (intensive combined) versus 15.9% (minimum), not significant. Process: curative-intent recurrence surgery roughly tripled with intensive follow-up in FACS (6.6–8.0% versus 2.3%). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for survival, Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial proves follow-up is worthless — reassurance, trial-of-treatment planning, and the small subgroup whose recurrences are cured all sit outside the mortality endpoint. But a patient told "these scans will help you live longer" is being told something two randomised trials could not find.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wille-Jørgensen P et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 29800179); Primrose JN et al. JAMA. 2014 (PMID: 24430319).
cards.search: synthesis: surveillance delivers exactly what it promises — earlier, more operable recurrences — except the longer life it is sold on synthesis: surveillance delivers exactly what it promises — earlier, more operable recurrences — except the longer life it is sold on in patients with stage ii–iii colorectal cancer, does high-frequency follow-up testing (cea and ct) improve overall survival versus less frequent follow-up? synthesis two randomised trials of follow-up intensity after curative colorectal cancer surgery (colofol n=2,509, frequency comparison; facs n=1,202, modality comparison against minimum follow-up). mortality: colofol 5-year overall 13.0% versus 14.1% (p=.43), cancer-specific 10.6% versus 11.4% (p=.52); facs deaths 18.2% (intensive combined) versus 15.9% (minimum), not significant. process: curative-intent recurrence surgery roughly tripled with intensive follow-up in facs (6.6–8.0% versus 2.3%). proposed likely (the treatment made no difference) for survival, tier c not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf. neither trial proves follow-up is worthless — reassurance, trial-of-treatment planning, and the small subgroup whose recurrences are cured all sit outside the mortality endpoint. but a patient told "these scans will help you live longer" is being told something two randomised trials could not find. synthesis of wille-jørgensen p et al. jama. 2018 (pmid: 29800179); primrose jn et al. jama. 2014 (pmid: 24430319).

shelves.title: Stopping imatinib in deep molecular remission: about half stay treatment-free — 41% in persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months in STIM, 50% molecular relapse-free survival at 24 months in EURO-SKI
shelves.question: In chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia with a sustained deep molecular response, can imatinib be stopped safely — how many patients stay in treatment-free remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Benzamides · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · France · Fusion Proteins, bcr-abl/antagonists & inhibitors/genetics · Gene Expression Regulation, Leukemic · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Myelogenous, Chronic, BCR-ABL Positive/drug therapy/enzymology/genetics/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-abl/antagonists & inhibitors/genetics · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction · Survival Rate · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — roughly half of carefully selected patients stay off treatment, relapses come early and are recaptured, and nobody in these studies progressed. In STIM (Mahon FX et al., PMID: 20965785), imatinib was stopped in 100 patients in complete molecular remission for at least 2 years: among 69 patients with at least 12 months of follow-up, 42 (61%) relapsed molecularly — 40 of them within 6 months — leaving a 41% probability (95% CI 29–52) of persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months; every relapsing patient responded to imatinib reintroduction, 26 regaining sustained complete molecular remission. In EURO-SKI (Saussele S et al., PMID: 29735299), 755 evaluable patients stopping any tyrosine kinase inhibitor after at least 3 years of therapy and at least 1 year of deep molecular response had molecular relapse-free survival of 61% (57–64) at 6 months and 50% (46–54) at 24 months, with estimated savings of €22 million and no serious adverse events from stopping. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): discontinuation is a realistic, monitored option for sustained deep responders — about a coin-flip of staying treatment-free.

cards.headline: Mahon 2010 (STIM): 42 of 69 patients (61%) relapsed after stopping imatinib — 40 within 6 months — and all responded again on reintroduction; 41% stayed in complete molecular remission at 12 months
cards.summary: Mahon 2010 (STIM): 42 of 69 patients (61%) relapsed after stopping imatinib — 40 within 6 months — and all responded again on reintroduction; 41% stayed in complete molecular remission at 12 months
cards.type: Prospective multicentre non-randomised discontinuation study (Mahon 2010, STIM)
cards.people: 100 patients in France with chronic myeloid leukaemia in complete molecular remission (greater than 5-log reduction, undetectable transcripts) on imatinib for more than 2 years, who stopped imatinib and were monitored by quantitative RT-PCR; this interim analysis covers the 69 patients with at least 12 months of follow-up (median 24 months). Patients with prior immunomodulatory therapy (other than interferon α), other malignancies, or allogeneic transplant were excluded.
cards.result: Of the 69 patients, 42 (61%) had molecular relapse — 40 before 6 months, one at month 7, and one at month 19. The probability of persistent complete molecular remission at 12 months was 41% (95% CI 29–52). All patients who relapsed responded to reintroduction of imatinib: 16 of 42 showed decreases in BCR-ABL levels, and 26 achieved complete molecular remission that was sustained after rechallenge.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm interim analysis with a strict complete-molecular-remission entry bar (undetectable transcripts, not merely deep response) — its 41% persistence figure is therefore not directly comparable to studies using major-molecular-response loss as the relapse trigger. "Safely" here means relapses were molecular, early, and recaptured; it required intensive PCR monitoring.
cards.source: Mahon FX et al. Discontinuation of imatinib in patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia who have maintained complete molecular remission for at least 2 years: the prospective, multicentre Stop Imatinib (STIM) trial. The Lancet Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20965785. Registry ID: NCT00478985. cards.headline: Saussele 2018 (EURO-SKI): molecular relapse-free survival 61% at 6 months and 50% at 24 months in 755 patients — longer treatment and longer deep response predicted success; €22 million saved
cards.summary: Saussele 2018 (EURO-SKI): molecular relapse-free survival 61% at 6 months and 50% at 24 months in 755 patients — longer treatment and longer deep response predicted success; €22 million saved
cards.type: Prospective multicentre non-randomised discontinuation trial (Saussele 2018, EURO-SKI)
cards.people: 758 patients enrolled at 61 European centres in 11 countries with chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia, treated with any tyrosine kinase inhibitor for at least 3 years without treatment failure and in confirmed deep molecular response for at least 1 year; 755 were evaluable for molecular response, with median follow-up of 27 months. Relapse was defined as loss of major molecular response (MMR).
cards.result: Molecular relapse-free survival was 61% (95% CI 57–64) at 6 months and 50% (46–54) at 24 months. Of 755 patients, 371 (49%) lost MMR, 13 (2%) restarted therapy while in MMR, and four (1%) died in MMR of causes unrelated to leukaemia; no serious adverse events (loss of haematological response, progression to accelerated phase or blast crisis) were reported. In the imatinib first-line learning sample (n=405), longer treatment duration (odds ratio per year 1.14; 95% CI 1.05–1.23) and longer deep-molecular-response duration (1.13 per year; 1.04–1.23) predicted MMR maintenance at 6 months. Stopping was associated with an estimated €22 million in cost savings.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised and interim (the analysis was prespecified after 200 patients had 6-month status): patients who reach sustained deep responses are a selected, favourable group, so the 50% figure describes them, not all patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia. The two studies on this shelf also use different relapse definitions (loss of complete versus major molecular response), which is why their percentages are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Saussele S et al. Discontinuation of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in chronic myeloid leukaemia (EURO-SKI): a prespecified interim analysis of a prospective, multicentre, non-randomised, trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping works for about half of deep responders, fails early when it fails, and has not cost anyone their response in these cohorts
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping works for about half of deep responders, fails early when it fails, and has not cost anyone their response in these cohorts
cards.people: Two prospective multicentre discontinuation studies (STIM, n=100 imatinib patients in complete molecular remission; EURO-SKI, n=755 evaluable patients stopping any TKI after sustained deep molecular response), neither randomised.
cards.result: Treatment-free persistence: 41% in complete molecular remission at 12 months (STIM, strict definition) and 50% molecular relapse-free survival at 24 months (EURO-SKI, MMR definition). Relapses cluster in the first 6 months; STIM relapsers all responded to reintroduction; EURO-SKI reported no progressions as serious adverse events and €22 million saved. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: non-randomised single-arm evidence is developer-review material.
cards.watchOut: Both studies are as much about the monitoring as the stopping: monthly molecular testing early on is the safety net that makes a 50% relapse rate acceptable. Outside a structured programme with rapid restart, these results do not apply.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mahon FX et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 20965785); Saussele S et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2018 (PMID: 29735299).

shelves.title: Adjuvant capecitabine after biliary tract cancer resection: median survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months — but the primary intention-to-treat analysis missed significance (p=0.097)
shelves.question: After resection of biliary tract cancer, does adjuvant capecitabine improve overall survival versus observation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/therapy · Biliary Tract Surgical Procedures/adverse effects/mortality · Capecitabine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Progression-Free Survival · Time Factors · United Kingdom · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a clinically large survival difference whose primary analysis fell just short of significance, with every prespecified sensitivity analysis pointing the same way. In BILCAP (Primrose JN et al., PMID: 30922733), 447 patients with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer were randomised to eight cycles of capecitabine or observation: median overall survival was 51.1 versus 36.4 months, but the intention-to-treat hazard ratio was 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04; p=0.097); the protocol-specified adjusted sensitivity analysis gave 0.71 (0.55–0.92; p=0.010) and the per-protocol analysis 0.75 (0.58–0.97; p=0.028), with median recurrence-free survival 24.4 versus 17.5 months. The long-term analysis (Bridgewater J et al., PMID: 35316080), at a median follow-up of 106 months, found median survival 49.6 versus 36.1 months with the same pattern (intention-to-treat hazard ratio 0.84, 0.67–1.06; adjusted 0.74, 0.59–0.94). Grade 3 toxicity affected 44% of capecitabine patients, led by hand–foot syndrome in 20%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjuvant capecitabine probably extends survival after biliary tract resection — adopted as standard of care on evidence that is suggestive rather than decisive.

cards.headline: Primrose 2019 (BILCAP): median survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months — ITT HR 0.81 (p=0.097, primary endpoint missed); adjusted HR 0.71 (p=0.010), per-protocol HR 0.75 (p=0.028)
cards.summary: Primrose 2019 (BILCAP): median survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months — ITT HR 0.81 (p=0.097, primary endpoint missed); adjusted HR 0.71 (p=0.010), per-protocol HR 0.75 (p=0.028)
cards.people: 447 patients (223 capecitabine, 224 observation) aged 18 or older with histologically confirmed cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer after macroscopically complete curative-intent resection, ECOG performance status under 2, at 44 UK specialist centres; capecitabine 1250 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 of a 21-day cycle for eight cycles, starting within 16 weeks of surgery. Median follow-up 60 months. Treatment was open-label.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, median overall survival was 51.1 months (95% CI 34.6–59.1) with capecitabine versus 36.4 months (29.7–44.5) with observation (adjusted hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.63–1.04; p=0.097) — the primary endpoint was not met. A protocol-specified sensitivity analysis adjusting for minimisation factors, nodal status, grade, and gender gave a hazard ratio of 0.71 (0.55–0.92; p=0.010); the prespecified per-protocol analysis (210 vs 220 patients) gave median survival 53 versus 36 months (adjusted hazard ratio 0.75; 0.58–0.97; p=0.028). Median recurrence-free survival was 24.4 versus 17.5 months (intention-to-treat). Among 213 patients receiving at least one cycle, 44% had at least one grade 3 toxicity (hand–foot syndrome 20%, diarrhoea 8%, fatigue 8%); serious adverse events occurred in 21% versus 10%; no deaths were deemed treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The honest headline is the missed primary endpoint: the trial did not prove a survival benefit by its own prespecified test, and the significant analyses are adjusted and per-protocol companions. Recruitment took eight years across a mixed group of biliary cancers, and the field adopted capecitabine anyway — a judgment this shelf reports rather than launders into certainty.
cards.source: Primrose JN et al. Capecitabine compared with observation in resected biliary tract cancer (BILCAP): a randomised, controlled, multicentre, phase 3 study. The Lancet Oncology. 2019. cards.headline: Bridgewater 2022 (BILCAP long-term): at 106 months of follow-up, median survival 49.6 versus 36.1 months — ITT HR 0.84, adjusted HR 0.74; the pattern did not change with time
cards.summary: Bridgewater 2022 (BILCAP long-term): at 106 months of follow-up, median survival 49.6 versus 36.1 months — ITT HR 0.84, adjusted HR 0.74; the pattern did not change with time
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, long-term follow-up analysis (Bridgewater 2022, BILCAP)
cards.people: The same 447 BILCAP patients (223 capecitabine, 224 observation) with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer, followed to a data cutoff of January 21, 2021 — median follow-up 106 months — with exploratory subgroup analyses by resection status, grade, nodal status, and sex.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 49.6 months (95% CI 35.1–59.1) in the capecitabine group versus 36.1 months (29.7–44.2) in the observation group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.67–1.06) in the intention-to-treat analysis; the protocol-specified sensitivity analysis adjusting for minimisation factors, nodal status, grade, and sex gave a hazard ratio of 0.74 (0.59–0.94). The authors conclude the long-term analysis supports the original finding and that capecitabine should be considered the standard of care after resection.
cards.watchOut: A second report of the same single trial — it adds maturity, not independence. The intention-to-treat analysis remains non-significant at long-term follow-up too, so the shelf’s stamp stays POSSIBLE however consistent the direction.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, a 15-month median survival gap, and a primary endpoint that missed — suggestive enough to become standard, not strong enough to call proven
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, a 15-month median survival gap, and a primary endpoint that missed — suggestive enough to become standard, not strong enough to call proven
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (BILCAP, n=447) reported twice: primary analysis at 60 months median follow-up and long-term analysis at 106 months, in resected biliary tract cancer.
cards.result: Median overall survival ~50 versus ~36 months at both cuts. Hazard ratios: intention-to-treat 0.81 (p=0.097) and 0.84 (long-term), neither significant; adjusted sensitivity 0.71 and 0.74, both significant; per-protocol 0.75. Grade 3 toxicity in 44% on capecitabine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial mortality claim with a missed primary endpoint is precisely the developer’s personal-review category.
cards.watchOut: Clinicians reading this shelf should hold both facts at once: BILCAP is the best randomised evidence adjuvant therapy has in this disease, and it did not meet its primary endpoint. Presenting capecitabine as "proven to extend life" overstates the record; presenting it as useless understates it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Primrose JN et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 30922733); Bridgewater J et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2022 (PMID: 35316080).
cards.search: synthesis: one trial, a 15-month median survival gap, and a primary endpoint that missed — suggestive enough to become standard, not strong enough to call proven synthesis: one trial, a 15-month median survival gap, and a primary endpoint that missed — suggestive enough to become standard, not strong enough to call proven after resection of biliary tract cancer, does adjuvant capecitabine improve overall survival versus observation? synthesis one randomised phase 3 trial (bilcap, n=447) reported twice: primary analysis at 60 months median follow-up and long-term analysis at 106 months, in resected biliary tract cancer. median overall survival ~50 versus ~36 months at both cuts. hazard ratios: intention-to-treat 0.81 (p=0.097) and 0.84 (long-term), neither significant; adjusted sensitivity 0.71 and 0.74, both significant; per-protocol 0.75. grade 3 toxicity in 44% on capecitabine. proposed possible (benefit), tier c: a single-trial mortality claim with a missed primary endpoint is precisely the developer’s personal-review category. clinicians reading this shelf should hold both facts at once: bilcap is the best randomised evidence adjuvant therapy has in this disease, and it did not meet its primary endpoint. presenting capecitabine as "proven to extend life" overstates the record; presenting it as useless understates it. synthesis of primrose jn et al. the lancet oncology. 2019 (pmid: 30922733); bridgewater j et al. journal of clinical oncology. 2022 (pmid: 35316080).

shelves.title: Bevacizumab plus capecitabine in older patients with metastatic colorectal cancer: progression-free survival 9.1 versus 5.1 months in AVEX, pooled survival hazard ratio 0.79 in meta-analysis
shelves.question: In older or frail patients with advanced colorectal cancer, does capecitabine plus bevacizumab improve progression-free survival versus capecitabine alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Bevacizumab · Capecitabine · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/secondary · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/secondary · Male · Neoplasm Staging · Prognosis · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — progression delayed by four months in the one randomised trial in this population, with a pooled survival signal behind it. In AVEX (Cunningham D et al., PMID: 24028813), 280 patients aged 70 or older (median 76) who were not candidates for oxaliplatin- or irinotecan-based therapy received capecitabine with or without bevacizumab: median progression-free survival was 9.1 versus 5.1 months (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p<0.0001), with grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events in 40% versus 22% and haemorrhage in 25% versus 7%. A systematic review and meta-analysis of bevacizumab plus fluoropyrimidine monotherapy in unfit or older patients (Pinto C et al., PMID: 27687553) pooled 782 patients and found hazard ratios of 0.52 (0.43–0.64) for progression-free survival and 0.79 (0.64–0.98) for overall survival, with more hypertension, bleeding, thromboembolism, and proteinuria on bevacizumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the combination is an effective gentler-intent regimen for older patients, on one randomised trial plus a mixed-design meta-analysis.

cards.headline: Cunningham 2013 (AVEX): median progression-free survival 9.1 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.53; p<0.0001) in patients ≥70 — grade ≥3 treatment-related events 40% versus 22%
cards.summary: Cunningham 2013 (AVEX): median progression-free survival 9.1 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.53; p<0.0001) in patients ≥70 — grade ≥3 treatment-related events 40% versus 22%
cards.people: 280 patients aged 70 years or older (median 76, range 70–87) with previously untreated, unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer who were not deemed candidates for oxaliplatin- or irinotecan-based regimens, at 40 sites in ten countries, randomised to capecitabine 1000 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 alone (n=140) or with bevacizumab 7.5 mg/kg on day 1 (n=140), every 3 weeks until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly longer with bevacizumab plus capecitabine (median 9.1 months; 95% CI 7.3–11.4) than with capecitabine alone (5.1 months; 4.2–6.3) (hazard ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.41–0.69; p<0.0001). Treatment-related grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 40% (53 patients) versus 22% (30), and treatment-related serious adverse events in 14% versus 8%. The commonest grade ≥3 events of special interest were hand–foot syndrome (16% vs 7%), diarrhoea (7% vs 7%), and venous thromboembolic events (8% vs 4%); haemorrhage of any grade occurred in 25% versus 7%. Treatment-related deaths occurred in five patients on the combination and four on capecitabine alone.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is progression-free survival in an open-label trial; overall survival by arm is not reported in this record, so the survival claim on this shelf comes from the meta-analysis below, not from AVEX itself. The population — older patients judged unfit for doublet chemotherapy — is exactly the group in whom bevacizumab’s bleeding and thrombotic risks bite hardest.
cards.source: Cunningham D et al. Bevacizumab plus capecitabine versus capecitabine alone in elderly patients with previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer (AVEX): an open-label, randomised phase 3 trial. cards.headline: Pinto 2017 (meta-analysis, 782 patients): adding bevacizumab to fluoropyrimidine monotherapy — PFS HR 0.52 and OS HR 0.79, with hypertension 27% versus 4.9% and bleeding 24% versus 6.4%
cards.summary: Pinto 2017 (meta-analysis, 782 patients): adding bevacizumab to fluoropyrimidine monotherapy — PFS HR 0.52 and OS HR 0.79, with hypertension 27% versus 4.9% and bleeding 24% versus 6.4%
cards.people: Eight studies (three randomised trials, four single-arm phase II trials, one prospective cohort) totalling 782 unfit or older patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (median age 75 years; 87.7% ECOG 0–1); monotherapy was capecitabine in 531 patients and 5-fluorouracil in 251, and 500 patients also received bevacizumab. Literature searched to May 31, 2016.
cards.result: Adding bevacizumab improved progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.43–0.64; P<.00001; I²=0%) and overall survival (hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.64–0.98; P=.03; I²=0%). All-grade adverse events were more frequent with bevacizumab: hypertension 27% versus 4.9%, bleeding 24% versus 6.4%, thromboembolic events 10% versus 5%, and proteinuria 25.6% versus 8.2%.
cards.watchOut: Only three of the eight pooled studies are randomised — the overall-survival hazard ratio leans partly on single-arm and cohort data in a selected population, which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE and Tier C rather than stronger. The zero heterogeneity (I²=0%) is reassuring for consistency, not for freedom from bias.
cards.source: Pinto C et al. Efficacy and Safety of Bevacizumab Combined With Fluoropyrimidine Monotherapy for Unfit or Older Patients With Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clinical Colorectal Cancer. 2017. PMID: 27687553. cards.headline: Synthesis: four extra months before progression for older patients, with a consistent pooled survival signal and a clear toxicity bill
cards.summary: Synthesis: four extra months before progression for older patients, with a consistent pooled survival signal and a clear toxicity bill
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (AVEX, n=280, age ≥70) plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies (n=782) of bevacizumab added to fluoropyrimidine monotherapy in unfit or older patients with metastatic colorectal cancer.
cards.result: Progression-free survival: median 9.1 versus 5.1 months (AVEX, hazard ratio 0.53); pooled hazard ratio 0.52. Overall survival: pooled hazard ratio 0.79. Harms: grade ≥3 treatment-related events 40% versus 22% (AVEX); pooled all-grade hypertension 27% versus 4.9% and bleeding 24% versus 6.4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the mortality signal rests substantially on non-randomised data within the meta-analysis.
cards.watchOut: AVEX’s population was chosen for frailty — patients "not deemed candidates" for doublet chemotherapy — so the result should not be generalised to fit older patients, for whom stronger regimens remain the comparator that matters.

shelves.title: Maintenance capecitabine–bevacizumab after CAPOX-B induction: time to second progression 11.7 versus 8.5 months — benefit in every mutational subgroup, quality of life preserved
shelves.question: In metastatic colorectal cancer responding to induction chemotherapy, does maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab improve progression-free survival versus observation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bevacizumab · Capecitabine · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neoplasm Staging · Organoplatinum Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Oxaliplatin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — maintenance delays the endpoint that matters in this design, second progression after re-induction, in the one phase 3 trial that tested it. In CAIRO3 (Simkens LH et al., PMID: 25862517), 558 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer who had stable disease or better after six cycles of CAPOX-B were randomised to maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab or observation, with CAPOX-B reintroduced at first progression in both groups: median time to second progression (PFS2) was 11.7 months on maintenance versus 8.5 months on observation (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.56–0.81; p<0.0001), hand–foot syndrome occurred in 23% during maintenance, and global quality of life did not deteriorate or differ between groups. The updated analysis (Goey KKH et al., PMID: 28911067), at a median follow-up of 87 months, found the PFS2 benefit in every molecular subgroup — hazard ratios 0.57 in RAS/BRAF wild-type, 0.74 in RAS-mutant, and 0.28 in BRAF-mutant tumours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): maintenance capecitabine–bevacizumab after CAPOX-B induction, resting on a single trial.

cards.headline: Simkens 2015 (CAIRO3): median PFS2 11.7 versus 8.5 months (HR 0.67; p<0.0001) — hand–foot syndrome in 23% on maintenance, quality of life unchanged
cards.summary: Simkens 2015 (CAIRO3): median PFS2 11.7 versus 8.5 months (HR 0.67; p<0.0001) — hand–foot syndrome in 23% on maintenance, quality of life unchanged
cards.people: 558 patients older than 18 years with previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer and stable disease or better after six 3-weekly cycles of capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab (CAPOX-B), WHO performance status 0–1, at 64 Dutch hospitals, randomised to maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab (n=279) or observation (n=279); on first progression both groups were to receive CAPOX-B again until second progression (PFS2, the primary endpoint). Median follow-up 48 months. Open-label.
cards.result: Median PFS2 was 11.7 months in the maintenance group versus 8.5 months in the observation group (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.56–0.81; p<0.0001), and the difference remained significant when any treatment after first progression was considered. Maintenance was well tolerated, although hand–foot skin reaction occurred in 64 patients (23%) during maintenance. Global quality of life did not deteriorate during maintenance and was clinically not different between groups.
cards.watchOut: PFS2 is a strategy endpoint — it credits maintenance partly because the observation group’s clock keeps running through re-induction — and overall survival is not reported in this record, so the shelf claims delayed progression, not longer life. Only patients who had already responded to or stabilised on CAPOX-B were randomised, a favourable subset of metastatic colorectal cancer.
cards.source: Simkens LH et al. Maintenance treatment with capecitabine and bevacizumab in metastatic colorectal cancer (CAIRO3): a phase 3 randomised controlled trial of the Dutch Colorectal Cancer Group. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25862517. Registry ID: NCT00442637. cards.headline: Goey 2017 (CAIRO3 updated analysis): at 87 months, PFS2 benefit in all subgroups — HR 0.57 (RAS/BRAF wild-type), 0.74 (RAS-mutant), 0.28 (BRAF-mutant); overall-survival benefit absent in the RAS-mutant subgroup
cards.summary: Goey 2017 (CAIRO3 updated analysis): at 87 months, PFS2 benefit in all subgroups — HR 0.57 (RAS/BRAF wild-type), 0.74 (RAS-mutant), 0.28 (BRAF-mutant); overall-survival benefit absent in the RAS-mutant subgroup
cards.type: Randomised trial updated subgroup analysis (Goey 2017, CAIRO3)
cards.people: The same 558 CAIRO3 patients (279 maintenance, 279 observation), with centrally assessed RAS/BRAF mutation status (available in 420 and 381 patients) and mismatch-repair status, at a median follow-up of 87 months; post hoc analyses adjusted for baseline covariables and primary-tumour sidedness.
cards.result: All mutational subgroups showed significant improvement from maintenance for the primary endpoint PFS2: RAS/BRAF wild-type hazard ratio 0.57 (95% CI 0.39–0.84), RAS-mutant 0.74 (0.55–0.98), and V600E BRAF-mutant 0.28 (0.12–0.64). Secondary endpoints also favoured maintenance except overall survival in the RAS-mutant subgroup. Right-sided tumours carried an inferior prognosis, but patients with right- and left-sided tumours both benefited significantly from maintenance. RAS mutations were found in 58% (240/420), BRAF mutations in 9% (36/381), and mismatch-repair deficiency in 1% (4/279) of assessed patients.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc subgroup analysis of the same single trial — it answers "in whom does the CAIRO3 result hold?" (answer: broadly) rather than adding independent evidence, and the RAS-mutant overall-survival exception is a reminder that the progression benefit does not convert uniformly into survival.

cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-designed strategy trial — maintenance wins time before second progression across subgroups, with survival conversion unproven
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (CAIRO3, n=558) and its updated molecular-subgroup analysis at 87 months, in metastatic colorectal cancer responding to CAPOX-B induction.
cards.result: Primary endpoint PFS2: median 11.7 versus 8.5 months (hazard ratio 0.67); subgroup hazard ratios 0.28–0.74, all significant. shelves.title: Nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil after gemcitabine: survival 6.1 versus 4.2 months in NAPOLI-1, maintained at final analysis (6.2 versus 4.2) — the liposomal drug alone did nothing
shelves.question: In metastatic pancreatic cancer progressing on gemcitabine-based therapy, does nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil improve overall survival versus fluorouracil alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Camptothecin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Carcinoma, Pancreatic Ductal/drug therapy/mortality · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Fatigue/chemically induced · Female · Fluorouracil/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Irinotecan · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leucovorin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Liposomes · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neutropenia/chemically induced · Pancreatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced · Gemcitabine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a two-month median survival gain in a disease with almost no second-line options, from a single trial whose internal control arm usefully isolates the active ingredient. In NAPOLI-1 (Wang-Gillam A et al., PMID: 26615328), 417 patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer previously treated with gemcitabine-based therapy were randomised to nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil and folinic acid, nanoliposomal irinotecan alone, or fluorouracil and folinic acid: median overall survival was 6.1 months on the combination versus 4.2 months on fluorouracil alone (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.49–0.92; p=0.012), while the monotherapy arm did no better than control (4.9 versus 4.2 months; hazard ratio 0.99). The final analysis (Wang-Gillam A et al., PMID: 30654298) confirmed the combination’s advantage (6.2 versus 4.2 months; hazard ratio 0.75; 0.57–0.99), with estimated 1-year survival of 26% versus 16%. Grade 3–4 neutropenia (27%), diarrhoea (13%), vomiting (11%), and fatigue (14%) were the commonest severe toxicities of the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil extends survival after gemcitabine — as a combination, not as a single agent.

cards.headline: Wang-Gillam 2016 (NAPOLI-1): median survival 6.1 versus 4.2 months (HR 0.67; p=0.012) for the combination — monotherapy 4.9 months (HR 0.99); grade 3–4 neutropenia 27%, diarrhoea 13%
cards.summary: Wang-Gillam 2016 (NAPOLI-1): median survival 6.1 versus 4.2 months (HR 0.67; p=0.012) for the combination — monotherapy 4.9 months (HR 0.99); grade 3–4 neutropenia 27%, diarrhoea 13%
cards.people: 417 patients with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma previously treated with gemcitabine-based therapy, at 76 sites in 14 countries, randomised to nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil and folinic acid (n=117), nanoliposomal irinotecan monotherapy (n=151), or fluorouracil and folinic acid (n=149); the combination arm was added by protocol amendment, changing randomisation to 1:1:1. Primary analysis after 313 events. Open-label.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 6.1 months (95% CI 4.8–8.9) with nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil and folinic acid versus 4.2 months (3.3–5.3) with fluorouracil and folinic acid (hazard ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.49–0.92; p=0.012). Nanoliposomal irinotecan monotherapy did not differ from control (4.9 months [4.2–5.6] versus 4.2 months [3.6–4.9]; hazard ratio 0.99; 0.77–1.28; p=0.94). The grade 3–4 adverse events most frequent on the combination were neutropenia (27%), diarrhoea (13%), vomiting (11%), and fatigue (14%).
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial with a mid-course protocol amendment that added the winning arm — the design is defensible and the monotherapy arm’s null is reassuring against bias, but the survival claim still rests on one study in patients fit enough for second-line combination therapy after gemcitabine.
cards.source: Wang-Gillam A et al. cards.headline: Wang-Gillam 2019 (NAPOLI-1 final analysis): survival advantage maintained (6.2 versus 4.2 months; HR 0.75) — 1-year survival 26% versus 16%; long-term survivors had better performance status and lower CA19-9
cards.summary: Wang-Gillam 2019 (NAPOLI-1 final analysis): survival advantage maintained (6.2 versus 4.2 months; HR 0.75) — 1-year survival 26% versus 16%; long-term survivors had better performance status and lower CA19-9
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, final overall-survival analysis (Wang-Gillam 2019, NAPOLI-1)
cards.people: The same 417 NAPOLI-1 patients (combination n=117, monotherapy n=151, fluorouracil–folinic acid n=149), followed to November 16, 2015, by which time 382 overall-survival events had occurred; the analysis also characterised patients surviving at least one year.
cards.result: The overall-survival advantage of nanoliposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil–leucovorin over fluorouracil–leucovorin was maintained (median 6.2 versus 4.2 months; hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.57–0.99). Progression-free survival, objective response rate, and disease control rate also favoured the combination. Estimated 1-year overall survival was 26% with the combination versus 16% with control. Baseline features associated with survival of at least one year on the combination were Karnofsky performance status ≥90, age ≤65 years, lower CA19-9, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio ≤5, and no liver metastases. No new safety concerns were detected.
cards.watchOut: A confirmatory re-analysis of the same trial at greater maturity — the hazard ratio attenuated from 0.67 to 0.75 as events accrued, which is normal but worth printing. The long-term-survivor profile describes prognosis, not a way to select patients the drug will help.
cards.source: Wang-Gillam A et al. NAPOLI-1 phase 3 study of liposomal irinotecan in metastatic pancreatic cancer: Final overall survival analysis and characteristics of long-term survivors. European Journal of Cancer. 2019. PMID: 30654298. Registry ID: NCT01494506. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, internally coherent — the combination works modestly, the single agent does not, and the effect survived final analysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, internally coherent — the combination works modestly, the single agent does not, and the effect survived final analysis
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (NAPOLI-1, n=417) in gemcitabine-pretreated metastatic pancreatic cancer, reported at primary (313 events) and final (382 events) analyses.
cards.result: Overall survival: 6.1 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio 0.67) at primary analysis; 6.2 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio 0.75) at final analysis; 1-year survival 26% versus 16%. Monotherapy hazard ratio 0.99 — no effect. Grade 3–4 neutropenia 27% and diarrhoea 13% on the combination. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial mortality benefit claim.
cards.watchOut: Two months of median survival is the honest scale of this advance — meaningful in a disease where second-line medians are measured in single months, and no basis for presenting the regimen as transformative. Performance status at entry gates who can receive it at all.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang-Gillam A et al. Lancet. 2016 (PMID: 26615328); Wang-Gillam A et al. European Journal of Cancer. 2019 (PMID: 30654298).

shelves.title: Adding an NK1 antagonist to standard antiemetics in cisplatin chemotherapy: complete response 72.7% versus 52.3% and 62.7% versus 43.3% in two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding an NK1 receptor antagonist (aprepitant/fosaprepitant) to a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone improve complete response versus standard dual prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antiemetics/administration & dosage · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Aprepitant · Cisplatin/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines/administration & dosage · Nausea/chemically induced/prevention & control · Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Neurokinin-1 Receptor Antagonists · Ondansetron/administration & dosage · Placebos · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large double-blind phase 3 trials, run on different continents, land within a point of each other on a twenty-point absolute gain. In the first (Hesketh PJ et al., PMID: 14559886), patients receiving cisplatin ≥70 mg/m² for the first time had a complete response (no emesis and no rescue therapy, days 1–5) in 72.7% on the aprepitant regimen versus 52.3% on standard ondansetron–dexamethasone (P<.001), with the advantage largest on days 2–5. In the second (Poli-Bigelli S et al., PMID: 12784346), complete response was 62.7% (163/260) versus 43.3% (114/263) (P<0.001), with day-1 rates of 82.8% versus 68.4% and days 2–5 rates of 67.7% versus 46.8%. Tolerability was indistinguishable: overall adverse events 72.8% versus 72.6% in Poli-Bigelli, with similar serious events, discontinuations, and deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding aprepitant to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone prevents chemotherapy-induced vomiting in about one extra patient in five receiving high-dose cisplatin.

cards.headline: Hesketh 2003 (Aprepitant Protocol 052): complete response days 1–5 in 72.7% versus 52.3% (P<.001) — the advantage concentrated in the delayed phase, days 2–5
cards.summary: Hesketh 2003 (Aprepitant Protocol 052): complete response days 1–5 in 72.7% versus 52.3% (P<.001) — the advantage concentrated in the delayed phase, days 2–5
cards.people: Patients receiving cisplatin ≥70 mg/m² for the first time, randomised to standard therapy (ondansetron and dexamethasone on day 1; dexamethasone on days 2–4) or an aprepitant regimen (aprepitant plus ondansetron and dexamethasone on day 1; aprepitant and dexamethasone on days 2–3; dexamethasone on day 4); 260 patients per group in the efficacy analysis, with nausea and vomiting recorded in patient diaries. Primary endpoint: complete response (no emesis and no rescue therapy) on days 1–5, analysed by modified intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Complete response on days 1–5 was 72.7% in the aprepitant group versus 52.3% in the standard-therapy group (P<.001), as were the percentages on day 1 and especially on days 2–5 (P<.001 for all three comparisons). Addition of aprepitant was generally well tolerated, with tolerability assessed by reported adverse events and physical and laboratory assessments.
cards.watchOut: The setting is first-ever high-dose cisplatin with 2003-era dual prophylaxis as the comparator — the trial proves the NK1 contribution, not aprepitant’s value on top of modern multi-drug regimens that may already include other agents. The record reports percentages without the day-by-day breakdown beyond the P values.
cards.source: Hesketh PJ et al. The oral neurokinin-1 antagonist aprepitant for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in patients receiving high-dose cisplatin--the Aprepitant Protocol 052 Study Group. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2003. PMID: 14559886. cards.headline: Poli-Bigelli 2003: complete response 62.7% (163/260) versus 43.3% (114/263) (P<0.001) — adverse events 72.8% versus 72.6%, serious events and deaths similar
cards.summary: Poli-Bigelli 2003: complete response 62.7% (163/260) versus 43.3% (114/263) (P<0.001) — adverse events 72.8% versus 72.6%, serious events and deaths similar
cards.people: Patients with cancer scheduled for high-dose cisplatin chemotherapy in Latin America, randomised to standard therapy (intravenous ondansetron 32 mg and oral dexamethasone 20 mg on day 1; dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily on days 2–4) or the aprepitant regimen (aprepitant 125 mg, ondansetron, and dexamethasone 12 mg on day 1; aprepitant 80 mg and dexamethasone 8 mg on days 2–3; dexamethasone 8 mg on day 4). Efficacy was evaluated in 523 patients and safety in 568, using diaries of emesis, rescue therapy, and nausea severity.
cards.result: Complete response over the 5 days after chemotherapy was 62.7% (163/260) in the aprepitant group versus 43.3% (114/263) in the standard group (P<0.001). Day-1 complete response was 82.8% versus 68.4% (P<0.001), and days 2–5 complete response 67.7% versus 46.8% (P<0.001). The overall incidence of adverse events was similar (72.8% [206/283] versus 72.6% [207/285]), as were rates of serious adverse events, discontinuations due to adverse events, and deaths.
cards.watchOut: A near-replica of the Hesketh trial by design — that is its strength (independent confirmation) and its limit (same sponsor programme, same cisplatin setting, same endpoint). Complete response counts vomiting and rescue use, not nausea itself, which NK1 antagonists affect less.
cards.source: Poli-Bigelli S et al. Addition of the neurokinin 1 receptor antagonist aprepitant to standard antiemetic therapy improves control of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Latin America. Cancer. 2003. PMID: 12784346. cards.headline: Synthesis: the cleanest kind of antiemetic evidence — two blinded trials, one endpoint, a consistent twenty-point gain, no toxicity price
cards.summary: Synthesis: the cleanest kind of antiemetic evidence — two blinded trials, one endpoint, a consistent twenty-point gain, no toxicity price
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (n=520 and n=523 in efficacy analyses) of aprepitant added to ondansetron plus dexamethasone in patients receiving high-dose cisplatin.
cards.result: Complete response (days 1–5): 72.7% versus 52.3% and 62.7% versus 43.3% — absolute gains of about 20 and 19 percentage points. Tolerability: adverse-event incidence essentially identical (72.8% versus 72.6% in the trial reporting it fully). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C not set: two concordant randomised blinded trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate current guideline prophylaxis, which has absorbed this result — triple therapy including an NK1 antagonist is now the standard these trials created. The shelf is the evidence record for that standard, in the cisplatin setting where it was proven.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hesketh PJ et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2003 (PMID: 14559886); Poli-Bigelli S et al. Cancer. 2003 (PMID: 12784346).

shelves.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for severe post-cancer fatigue: clinically significant improvement in 54% versus 4% on a waiting list — pooled data name CBT the strongest psychosocial strategy
shelves.question: In patients with severe cancer-related fatigue during or after chemotherapy, does cognitive behavioural therapy reduce fatigue versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Fatigue/etiology/psychology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications · Survivors/psychology · Treatment Outcome · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking result in the one dedicated randomised trial, backed by pooled individual-patient data across the psychosocial literature. In Gielissen’s trial (Gielissen MF et al., PMID: 17050873), 112 disease-free cancer survivors with somatically unexplained severe fatigue received CBT designed for fatigue or waited: fatigue severity fell 13.3 points more (95% CI 8.6–18.1) and functional impairment 383.2 points more (197.1–569.2) with CBT, and clinically significant improvement occurred in 54% versus 4% for fatigue and 50% versus 18% for function. The POLARIS individual-patient-data meta-analyses (Abrahams HJG et al., PMID: 33448521), pooling 14 randomised trials in 1,091 women with breast cancer and 1,008 men with prostate cancer, found small overall effects of psychosocial interventions on fatigue (β −0.19 and −0.11), with the largest effects for CBT as the strategy (β −0.27), for fatigue-specific interventions (β −0.48), and for interventions targeting only clinically fatigued patients (β −0.85). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fatigue-focused CBT reduces severe post-treatment fatigue — the trial evidence is strong in effect size but narrow in provenance.

cards.headline: Gielissen 2006: fatigue severity fell 13.3 points more with CBT than waiting (95% CI 8.6–18.1) — clinically significant improvement 54% versus 4% for fatigue, 50% versus 18% for function
cards.summary: Gielissen 2006: fatigue severity fell 13.3 points more with CBT than waiting (95% CI 8.6–18.1) — clinically significant improvement 54% versus 4% for fatigue, 50% versus 18% for function
cards.people: 112 disease-free cancer survivors with somatically unexplained persistent fatigue (a long-term effect reported by 30–40% of cured patients), randomised to immediate cognitive behaviour therapy designed specifically for post-cancer fatigue or a waiting-list condition; outcomes at baseline and 6 months, analysed intention-to-treat in 50 intervention and 48 waiting-list patients. Primary outcomes: fatigue severity (Checklist Individual Strength) and functional impairment (Sickness Impact Profile).
cards.result: Patients receiving CBT reported a significantly greater decrease in fatigue severity than the waiting-list group (difference 13.3; 95% CI 8.6 to 18.1) and in functional impairment (difference 383.2; 95% CI 197.1 to 569.2). Clinically significant improvement was seen in 54% versus 4% of patients for fatigue severity and 50% versus 18% for functional impairment. The authors conclude CBT has a clinically relevant effect in reducing fatigue and functional impairment in cancer survivors.
cards.watchOut: A waiting-list comparator cannot blind anyone and inflates effects relative to attention-matched controls — patients know they are being treated, and fatigue is self-reported. The trial is also from a single research programme in survivors after treatment; the candidate question’s "during chemotherapy" half is not what this trial studied.

cards.headline: Abrahams 2020 (POLARIS individual-patient-data meta-analyses): overall psychosocial effect small (β −0.19 breast, −0.11 prostate) — but CBT β −0.27, fatigue-specific β −0.48, and fatigue-targeted β −0.85
cards.summary: Abrahams 2020 (POLARIS individual-patient-data meta-analyses): overall psychosocial effect small (β −0.19 breast, −0.11 prostate) — but CBT β −0.27, fatigue-specific β −0.48, and fatigue-targeted β −0.85
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analyses of randomised trials (Abrahams 2020, POLARIS consortium)
cards.people: Pooled individual patient data from 14 randomised controlled trials of psychosocial interventions for cancer-related fatigue in patients with non-metastatic cancer, analysed separately in 1,091 women with breast cancer and 1,008 men with prostate cancer, testing sociodemographic, clinical, symptom-baseline, and intervention-related moderators with mixed-effects interaction models.
cards.result: Statistically significant, small overall effects on fatigue were found (breast cancer: β −0.19; 95% CI −0.30 to −0.08; prostate cancer: β −0.11; 95% CI −0.21 to −0.00). Effects did not differ by sociodemographic or clinical characteristics or by baseline fatigue or pain. Among women with breast cancer, significantly larger effects were found for cognitive behavioral therapy as the intervention strategy (β −0.27; 95% CI −0.40 to −0.15), for fatigue-specific interventions (β −0.48; −0.79 to −0.18), and for interventions targeting only patients with clinically relevant fatigue (β −0.85; −1.40 to −0.30).
cards.watchOut: This pools all psychosocial interventions, not CBT alone — the CBT figure is a moderator subgroup, hypothesis-shaping rather than a standalone pooled CBT estimate. Its role here is to show the Gielissen result is not an isolated anomaly: across 14 trials, the closer an intervention is to fatigue-specific CBT in fatigued patients, the bigger the effect.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the effect is real and large where it has been tested properly — and tested properly in remarkably few places
cards.summary: Synthesis: the effect is real and large where it has been tested properly — and tested properly in remarkably few places
cards.people: One dedicated randomised trial of fatigue-specific CBT in severely fatigued disease-free survivors (n=112, waiting-list control) plus individual-patient-data meta-analyses of 14 randomised psychosocial-intervention trials (n=2,099) in breast and prostate cancer.
cards.result: Fatigue severity difference 13.3 points and clinically significant improvement 54% versus 4% (dedicated trial). Pooled effects: β −0.19 (breast) and −0.11 (prostate) overall; β −0.27 for CBT strategy and −0.85 for interventions restricted to clinically fatigued patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the benefit claim rests mainly on one research group’s randomised trial against a waiting list.
cards.watchOut: Usual care in the candidate question is weaker than even a waiting list in one respect — nobody is promised treatment later — so real-world effects may differ. What the evidence does not support is generic counselling for unselected patients: the pooled data say target the severely fatigued, with a fatigue-specific protocol.

shelves.title: CBT for insomnia in breast-cancer survivors: benefits maintained to 12 months in Savard 2005 — and professional delivery beat video delivery, remission 71.3% versus 44.3%, in 2014
shelves.question: In breast-cancer survivors with insomnia, does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep versus control, and do gains persist?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Breast Neoplasms/complications/psychology · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Depression · Fatigue · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/etiology/psychology/therapy · Stress, Psychological · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same programme, a decade apart, showing the therapy works in person and still works, less well, by video. In the first (Savard J et al., PMID: 16135475), 57 women with insomnia caused or aggravated by breast cancer received eight weekly group CBT sessions or waited: subjective sleep indices (sleep diary and Insomnia Severity Index) improved significantly, medicated nights fell, depression and anxiety decreased, and global quality of life rose — with effects generally clinically significant and maintained at 3, 6, and 12 months, though polysomnographic results were more equivocal. In the second (Savard J et al., PMID: 25083010), 242 women were randomised to professionally administered CBT-I, video-based CBT-I, or no treatment: both active formats beat no treatment on subjective sleep, but professional delivery was superior on insomnia severity and remission (Insomnia Severity Index <8 in 71.3% versus 44.3%; P<0.005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CBT-I improves insomnia in breast-cancer survivors, durably to at least 12 months, with face-to-face delivery the stronger format.

cards.headline: Savard 2005: CBT beat waiting list on diary and Insomnia Severity Index outcomes, cut medicated nights, and held its gains at 3, 6 and 12 months — polysomnography equivocal
cards.summary: Savard 2005: CBT beat waiting list on diary and Insomnia Severity Index outcomes, cut medicated nights, and held its gains at 3, 6 and 12 months — polysomnography equivocal
cards.people: 57 women with insomnia caused or aggravated by breast cancer, randomly assigned to CBT (n=27) or a waiting-list control (n=30). Treatment was eight weekly group sessions combining stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, sleep hygiene, and fatigue management. Sleep was assessed subjectively (daily diary, Insomnia Severity Index) and objectively (polysomnography), plus hypnotic use, psychological distress, and quality of life, with follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 months.
cards.result: Participants who received CBT had significantly better subjective sleep indices, a lower frequency of medicated nights, lower levels of depression and anxiety, and greater global quality of life at post-treatment than waiting-list controls after their waiting period. Results were more equivocal on polysomnographic indices. Therapeutic effects were well maintained up to 12 months after the intervention and were generally clinically significant.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (n=57) against a waiting list, with the headline outcomes self-reported by unblinded patients — expectation can move diary sleep more than polysomnography, and here it apparently did. The abstract reports significance and durability rather than effect sizes, so the shelf grades the direction, not a magnitude.
cards.source: Savard J et al. Randomized study on the efficacy of cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia secondary to breast cancer, part I: Sleep and psychological effects. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2005. PMID: 16135475. cards.headline: Savard 2014: professional CBT-I and video CBT-I both beat no treatment — but remission was 71.3% with professional versus 44.3% with video delivery (P<0.005)
cards.summary: Savard 2014: professional CBT-I and video CBT-I both beat no treatment — but remission was 71.3% with professional versus 44.3% with video delivery (P<0.005)
cards.people: 242 women with breast cancer who had received radiation therapy in the past 18 months and had insomnia symptoms or were using hypnotic medication, randomised to professionally administered CBT-I (six weekly individual ~50-minute sessions; n=81), video-based CBT-I (a 60-minute animated video plus six booklets; n=80), or no treatment (n=81). Outcomes: Insomnia Severity Index and sleep parameters from daily diaries and actigraphy, before and after treatment.
cards.result: Both CBT-I formats were associated with significantly greater subjective sleep improvements than no treatment. Professional delivery was associated with significantly greater improvements than video delivery in insomnia severity, early morning awakenings, depression, fatigue, and dysfunctional beliefs about sleep. Insomnia remission (Insomnia Severity Index <8) was significantly greater with professional than video CBT-I (71.3% versus 44.3%; P<0.005). The authors frame video CBT-I as a valuable entry level within a stepped-care model, with face-to-face sessions the optimal format.
cards.watchOut: Short-term (post-treatment) endpoints only in this record — the durability claim on this shelf comes from the 2005 trial. Both trials are from one research group in one health system, and actigraphy, like polysomnography before it, is not the source of the headline effects.
cards.source: Savard J et al. Is a video-based cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as efficacious as a professionally administered treatment in breast cancer? cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT-I works in this population, lasts at least a year, and works best delivered by a person
cards.summary: Synthesis: CBT-I works in this population, lasts at least a year, and works best delivered by a person
cards.people: Two randomised trials from the Savard programme in women with breast-cancer-related insomnia (2005: n=57, group CBT-I versus waiting list, 12-month follow-up; 2014: n=242, professional versus video versus no treatment).
cards.result: Subjective sleep, insomnia severity, hypnotic use, distress, and quality of life all improved with CBT-I; gains maintained to 12 months (2005). Remission 71.3% (professional) versus 44.3% (video) in 2014, both formats superior to no treatment. Objective sleep measures were equivocal in 2005. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: The single-programme provenance is the residual caution — independent replication in other centres and in non-breast cancers is thinner than the two-trial count suggests. The stepped-care reading (video first, professional for non-remitters) is the authors’ own and is the most defensible implementation claim.

shelves.title: Acupuncture for chronic pain in cancer survivors: electroacupuncture cut pain by 1.9 points and auricular by 1.6 versus usual care in PEACE — but auricular treatment caused more dropouts
shelves.question: In cancer survivors with chronic musculoskeletal pain, do electroacupuncture or auricular acupuncture reduce pain versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture, Ear · Adult · Cancer Survivors · Chronic Pain/therapy · Electroacupuncture/adverse effects/methods · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Musculoskeletal Pain/etiology/therapy · Neoplasms/complications/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a well-run three-arm trial with a clinically meaningful margin over usual care, set against a wider literature that is positive but heterogeneous. In PEACE (Mao JJ et al., PMID: 33734288), 360 cancer survivors with chronic musculoskeletal pain received ten weekly sessions of electroacupuncture or auricular acupuncture, or usual care: pain severity on the Brief Pain Inventory fell 1.9 points more with electroacupuncture (97.5% CI 1.4–2.4; P<.001) and 1.6 points more with auricular acupuncture (1.0–2.1; P<.001) than with usual care by week 12; auricular treatment was not shown noninferior to electroacupuncture, and 10.5% of the auricular group versus 0.7% of the electroacupuncture group stopped because of adverse events (P<.001). A systematic review and meta-analysis of acupuncture and acupressure for cancer pain (He Y et al., PMID: 31855257) found real acupuncture beat sham by a mean difference of −1.38 points across seven high-quality sham-controlled trials, with substantial heterogeneity (I²=81%) and a moderate evidence grade. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acupuncture reduces chronic musculoskeletal pain in cancer survivors versus usual care, on one large trial plus a supportive but heterogeneous meta-analysis.

cards.headline: Mao 2021 (PEACE): pain fell 1.9 points with electroacupuncture and 1.6 with auricular versus usual care (both P<.001) — auricular noninferiority not shown; dropouts for adverse events 10.5% versus 0.7%
cards.summary: Mao 2021 (PEACE): pain fell 1.9 points with electroacupuncture and 1.6 with auricular versus usual care (both P<.001) — auricular noninferiority not shown; dropouts for adverse events 10.5% versus 0.7%
cards.people: 360 adults with a prior cancer diagnosis, no current evidence of disease, musculoskeletal pain for at least 3 months, and baseline Brief Pain Inventory pain intensity of at least moderate level (mean 5.2 of 10), at an urban academic cancer centre and five suburban sites in New York and New Jersey, randomised 2:2:1 to electroacupuncture (n=145), auricular acupuncture (n=143), or usual care (n=72); intervention groups received ten weekly sessions, and usual-care patients were offered ten sessions after week 12. Primary outcome: change in average pain severity at week 12; 94.4% completed the primary endpoint. Study statisticians were blinded.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, electroacupuncture reduced pain severity by 1.9 points (97.5% CI 1.4–2.4; P<.001) and auricular acupuncture by 1.6 points (97.5% CI 1.0–2.1; P<.001) from baseline to week 12. Noninferiority of auricular acupuncture to electroacupuncture was not demonstrated. Adverse events were mild, but 15 of 143 patients (10.5%) receiving auricular acupuncture and 1 of 145 (0.7%) receiving electroacupuncture discontinued treatment because of adverse events (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Usual care is not a sham control — patients knew they were receiving acupuncture, so expectation and attention effects are inside the 1.9-point estimate, and the trial’s own sham-controlled literature (next card) suggests a smaller specific effect. Follow-up for the primary endpoint is 12 weeks; durability beyond the treatment course is not what this record shows.
cards.source: Mao JJ et al. Effectiveness of Electroacupuncture or Auricular Acupuncture vs Usual Care for Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain Among Cancer Survivors: The PEACE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Oncology. 2021. PMID: 33734288. Registry ID: NCT02979574. cards.headline: He 2020 (meta-analysis, 17 RCTs, 1,111 patients): real versus sham acupuncture mean difference −1.38 points — heterogeneity I²=81%, evidence graded moderate
cards.summary: He 2020 (meta-analysis, 17 RCTs, 1,111 patients): real versus sham acupuncture mean difference −1.38 points — heterogeneity I²=81%, evidence graded moderate
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (He 2020)
cards.people: Seventeen randomised trials (1,111 patients) comparing acupuncture or acupressure with sham control, analgesic therapy, or usual care for cancer pain, from English- and Chinese-language databases to March 31, 2019; 14 trials (920 patients) entered the meta-analysis. Primary outcome: pain intensity on the Brief Pain Inventory, Numerical Rating Scale, Visual Analog Scale, or Verbal Rating Scale.
cards.result: Seven sham-controlled trials judged at low risk of bias across all domains showed real acupuncture associated with reduced pain intensity versus sham (mean difference −1.38 points; 95% CI −2.13 to −0.64; I²=81%). Acupuncture or acupressure combined with analgesic therapy reduced pain intensity in six trials (mean difference −1.44; −1.98 to −0.89; I²=92%) and reduced opioid dose in two trials (mean difference −30.00 mg morphine-equivalent daily dose; −37.5 to −22.5). The overall evidence grade was moderate because of substantial heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: This literature is mostly pain during active cancer care, not chronic musculoskeletal pain in survivors — it corroborates a specific effect beyond sham but in a neighbouring population, and heterogeneity above 80% means the pooled number is an average of disagreeing trials. Publication bias in this field is a standing concern the moderate grade partly reflects.
cards.source: He Y et al. Clinical Evidence for Association of Acupuncture and Acupressure With Improved Cancer Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Oncology. 2020. PMID: 31855257. cards.headline: Synthesis: better than usual care in a rigorous trial, better than sham in the pooled literature — a real, moderate-sized effect with an expectation component nobody has removed
cards.summary: Synthesis: better than usual care in a rigorous trial, better than sham in the pooled literature — a real, moderate-sized effect with an expectation component nobody has removed
cards.people: One large three-arm randomised trial in cancer survivors (PEACE, n=360) plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (n=1,111) of acupuncture and acupressure for cancer pain.
cards.result: Versus usual care: −1.9 points (electroacupuncture) and −1.6 points (auricular) on a 0–10 pain scale at 12 weeks. Versus sham (meta-analysis): −1.38 points, I²=81%, moderate-grade evidence. Harms: mild; auricular discontinuation for adverse events 10.5% versus 0.7% for electroacupuncture. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim for the survivor population.
cards.watchOut: For a survivor choosing today, the practical read is: expect roughly a 1.5–2-point pain reduction over doing nothing extra, prefer electroacupuncture over auricular on tolerability, and know that how much of the effect is needling-specific remains genuinely unsettled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mao JJ et al. JAMA Oncology. 2021 (PMID: 33734288); He Y et al. JAMA Oncology. 2020 (PMID: 31855257).

shelves.title: Gabapentin 900 mg for hot flushes in breast cancer: severity scores fell 49% versus 21% on placebo at 4 weeks — the 300 mg dose failed, and pooled trials show more dizziness and dropouts
shelves.question: In women with hot flushes during breast-cancer treatment, does gabapentin reduce hot-flush frequency and scores versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/complications · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gabapentin · Hot Flashes/complications/drug therapy · Humans · Menopause · Middle Aged · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, clean, dose-split trial, supported in direction and shadowed on harms by the pooled literature. In the 420-woman trial (Pandya KJ et al., PMID: 16139656), hot-flush severity scores fell by 49% at 4 weeks and 46% at 8 weeks on gabapentin 900 mg/day, versus 21% and 15% on placebo (P=0.0001 and P=0.007 for overall treatment effect), while gabapentin 300 mg/day (33% and 31%) was not significantly different from placebo — only the higher dose worked, on both frequency and severity. The systematic review and meta-analysis of gabapentin for hot flashes (Toulis KA et al., PMID: 19302896) pooled four randomised trials and found greater percentage reductions in frequency (weighted mean difference 23.72%; 95% CI 16.46–30.97) and composite score (27.26%; 21.24–33.29) with gabapentin, but with extreme heterogeneity (I²=97.8% and 95.6%) and more dropouts for adverse events (relative risk 2.09; 1.13–3.85), dizziness or unsteadiness (relative risk 6.94; 3.19–15.13), and fatigue or somnolence (4.78; 2.23–10.25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): gabapentin 900 mg/day reduces hot flushes in women with breast cancer, at a real cost in dizziness and sedation.

cards.headline: Pandya 2005: severity-score falls of 49% (900 mg) versus 21% (placebo) at 4 weeks and 46% versus 15% at 8 weeks — 300 mg (33%, 31%) not significantly different from placebo
cards.summary: Pandya 2005: severity-score falls of 49% (900 mg) versus 21% (placebo) at 4 weeks and 46% versus 15% at 8 weeks — 300 mg (33%, 31%) not significantly different from placebo
cards.people: 420 women with breast cancer having at least two hot flashes per day, at multiple institutions, randomly assigned to placebo, gabapentin 300 mg/day, or gabapentin 900 mg/day in three divided doses for 8 weeks; patients kept a one-week self-report diary of hot-flash frequency, severity, and duration at baseline and during weeks 4 and 8. Analyses were by intention to treat; evaluable data were available for 371 participants at 4 weeks and 347 at 8 weeks.
cards.result: Percentage decreases in hot-flash severity score from baseline at weeks 4 and 8 were 21% (95% CI 12–30) and 15% (1–29) on placebo, 33% (23–43) and 31% (16–46) on gabapentin 300 mg, and 49% (42–56) and 46% (34–58) on gabapentin 900 mg. Group differences were significant (P=0.0001 at 4 weeks and P=0.007 at 8 weeks by ANCOVA adjusted for baseline values); only the 900 mg dose was associated with significant decreases in both hot-flash frequency and severity.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is short for a symptom that runs for years on endocrine therapy, and diary-based flush scores in a trial of a sedating drug carry an unblinding risk — patients who feel dizzy may guess their allocation. The dose split is the trial’s most useful feature: it disciplines prescribing to the dose that was actually shown to work.
cards.source: Pandya KJ et al. Gabapentin for hot flashes in 420 women with breast cancer: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2005. PMID: 16139656. cards.headline: Toulis 2009 (meta-analysis of 4 RCTs): frequency reduction advantage 23.72% and composite-score advantage 27.26% for gabapentin — heterogeneity I²≈96–98%, dropout relative risk 2.09, dizziness 6.94
cards.summary: Toulis 2009 (meta-analysis of 4 RCTs): frequency reduction advantage 23.72% and composite-score advantage 27.26% for gabapentin — heterogeneity I²≈96–98%, dropout relative risk 2.09, dizziness 6.94
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Toulis 2009)
cards.people: Seven trials (901 patients, 2002–2008, all in North America) of gabapentin for hot flashes in women with natural or tamoxifen-induced menopause — four enrolling women with a history of breast cancer and three postmenopausal women — with four placebo-controlled randomised trials (total daily doses 900–2400 mg) entering the meta-analysis; outcomes were percentage reduction in hot-flash frequency and composite severity score, dropouts, and adverse events.
cards.result: Women assigned gabapentin reported significantly greater percentage reductions in hot-flash frequency (weighted mean difference 23.72%; 95% CI 16.46–30.97; P<0.001) and composite score (27.26%; 21.24–33.29; P<0.001), with significant between-study heterogeneity (I²=97.8% and 95.6%). Dropouts due to adverse events were more frequent on gabapentin (relative risk 2.09; 95% CI 1.13–3.85; P=0.02), as were dizziness or unsteadiness (relative risk 6.94; 3.19–15.13; P<0.001) and fatigue or somnolence (4.78; 2.23–10.25; P<0.001). The reviewers estimate reductions of 20–30% in frequency and severity, while cautioning the data were too heterogeneous for a reliable summary effect.
cards.watchOut: The heterogeneity is the story: with I² near 98%, the pooled percentages should be read as "consistently positive, magnitude uncertain," and the included trials mix breast-cancer and natural-menopause populations at doses up to 2400 mg. The harm relative risks, by contrast, are consistent (I²=0% for dropouts and fatigue) and deserve equal billing.
cards.source: Toulis KA et al. Gabapentin for the treatment of hot flashes in women with natural or tamoxifen-induced menopause: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009. PMID: 19302896. cards.headline: Synthesis: effective at the tested dose, sedating at the same dose — benefit and harm arrive together
cards.summary: Synthesis: effective at the tested dose, sedating at the same dose — benefit and harm arrive together
cards.people: One large randomised double-blind trial (n=420, women with breast cancer) with an internal dose comparison, plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomised trials in menopausal hot flashes (seven trials, 901 patients reviewed).
cards.result: Hot-flush severity score at 4 weeks: −49% on gabapentin 900 mg versus −21% on placebo; the 300 mg dose was not significantly effective. Pooled frequency advantage 23.72% and composite-score advantage 27.26%, with I²≈96–98%. Harms (pooled): dropout relative risk 2.09, dizziness/unsteadiness 6.94, fatigue/somnolence 4.78. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the shelf’s benefit claim rests on a single large trial, with the meta-analysis too heterogeneous to upgrade it.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here supports low-dose gabapentin for flushes, and nothing addresses use beyond eight weeks or in women whose flushes arise from natural menopause alone in the breast-cancer-specific trial. Non-hormonal alternatives exist; this shelf answers only the gabapentin question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pandya KJ et al. Lancet. 2005 (PMID: 16139656); Toulis KA et al. Clinical Therapeutics. 2009 (PMID: 19302896).
