shelves.title: Exercise during androgen deprivation: three randomised trials agree fatigue falls and fitness rises — fat gain is blunted when training starts with treatment, but weight and bone are unmoved
shelves.question: In men receiving androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer, does structured exercise improve fatigue, body composition and physical function versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Androgen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Exercise Therapy · Fatigue/etiology/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal · Physical Fitness · Prostatic Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Weight Lifting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for fatigue, fitness and body composition, not for weight or bone. Three randomised trials in men on androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) point the same way. Segal RJ et al. (PMID: 12721238) randomised 155 men to 12 weeks of resistance exercise: fatigue interfered less with daily activities (P=.002), quality of life was higher (P=.001) and upper- and lower-body muscular fitness improved, but body composition did not change. Cormie P et al. (PMID: 24467669) started supervised aerobic plus resistance exercise within 10 days of the first ADT injection in 63 men: over 3 months lean mass was preserved (P=.019) and whole-body fat gain was prevented (between-group difference -1.4 kg, P=.001; percentage fat -1.3%, P<.001), with better fatigue scores (difference 3.1, P=.042). Taaffe DR et al. (PMID: 28249801) followed 163 men for 12 months: fatigue fell by about 5 points with impact-loading plus resistance training at 6 and 12 months (p=0.005), with comparable gains from aerobic plus resistance training by 12 months, and the most fatigued men improved most. No trial showed a survival, fracture or falls outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): structured exercise during ADT reduces fatigue and improves fitness and quality of life across three concordant randomised trials, and blunts fat gain when started at ADT initiation; effects on weight, bone and hard outcomes are unshown.

cards.headline: Segal 2003: 12 weeks of resistance exercise — fatigue interfered less with daily life (P=.002) and quality of life rose (P=.001); body composition unchanged
cards.summary: Segal 2003: 12 weeks of resistance exercise — fatigue interfered less with daily life (P=.002) and quality of life rose (P=.001); body composition unchanged
cards.people: 155 men with prostate cancer at two Canadian sites, scheduled to receive ADT for at least 3 months, randomised to a resistance exercise programme three times weekly for 12 weeks (n=82) or a waiting-list control group (n=73). Primary outcomes were fatigue and disease-specific quality of life by questionnaire at 12 weeks.
cards.result: Men assigned to resistance exercise had less interference from fatigue on activities of daily living (P=.002) and higher quality of life (P=.001) than controls, and higher upper-body (P=.009) and lower-body (P<.001) muscular fitness. The intervention did not improve body composition: no significant change in body weight, body-mass index, waist circumference or subcutaneous skinfolds.
cards.watchOut: A waiting-list control cannot be blinded, and both primary outcomes are self-reported — expectation effects are plausible. Twelve weeks is short, and the trial predates modern ADT intensification with androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors.
cards.source: Segal RJ et al. Resistance exercise in men receiving androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2003. PMID: 12721238. cards.headline: Cormie 2015: exercise started with the first ADT injection preserved lean mass and prevented fat gain (-1.4 kg, P=.001) over 3 months
cards.summary: Cormie 2015: exercise started with the first ADT injection preserved lean mass and prevented fat gain (-1.4 kg, P=.001) over 3 months
cards.people: 63 men in Australia scheduled to receive ADT, randomised within 10 days of their first ADT injection to a 3-month supervised programme of aerobic and resistance exercise (n=32) or usual care (n=31). The primary outcome was body composition (lean and fat mass); secondary outcomes included bone density, physical function, fatigue and quality of life.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, exercise preserved appendicular lean mass (P=.019) and prevented gains in whole-body fat mass (difference -1.4 kg, P=.001), trunk fat mass (-0.9 kg, P=.008) and percentage fat (-1.3%, P<.001). Cardiovascular fitness (peak oxygen consumption +1.1 mL/kg/min, P=.004), muscular strength, lower-body function, fatigue (difference 3.1, P=.042) and psychological distress all favoured exercise. No significant group differences were seen for bone mineral density or other remaining outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=63) and short (3 months): it shows toxicity can be prevented at initiation, not that benefits persist or that fractures and falls fall. Supervised clinic-based exercise is more intensive than what most services can offer.
cards.source: Cormie P et al. Can supervised exercise prevent treatment toxicity in patients with prostate cancer initiating androgen-deprivation therapy: a randomised controlled trial. randomised controlled trial (cormie 2015) 63 men in australia scheduled to receive adt, randomised within 10 days of their first adt injection to a 3-month supervised programme of aerobic and resistance exercise (n=32) or usual care (n=31). the primary outcome was body composition (lean and fat mass); secondary outcomes included bone density, physical function, fatigue and quality of life. compared with usual care, exercise preserved appendicular lean mass (p=.019) and prevented gains in whole-body fat mass (difference -1.4 kg, p=.001), trunk fat mass (-0.9 kg, p=.008) and percentage fat (-1.3%, p<.001). cardiovascular fitness (peak oxygen consumption +1.1 ml/kg/min, p=.004), muscular strength, lower-body function, fatigue (difference 3.1, p=.042) and psychological distress all favoured exercise. no significant group differences were seen for bone mineral density or other remaining outcomes. small (n=63) and short (3 months): it shows toxicity can be prevented at initiation, not that benefits persist or that fractures and falls fall. supervised clinic-based exercise is more intensive than what most services can offer. cormie p et al. can supervised exercise prevent treatment toxicity in patients with prostate cancer initiating androgen-deprivation therapy: a randomised controlled trial. bju international. 2015. pmid: 24467669. registry id: actrn12610000691044. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · androgen antagonists/administration & dosage,*adverse effects · antineoplastic agents, hormonal/administration & dosage,*adverse effects · blood pressure · body composition* · bone density · exercise therapy*/methods · fatigue/chemically induced,prevention & control · humans · male · middle aged · muscle strength* · physical fitness · prostatic neoplasms/*drug therapy,physiopathology · quality of life · stress, psychological · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Taaffe 2017: over 12 months, both exercise modes cut fatigue by about 5 points — the most fatigued men gained most
cards.summary: Taaffe 2017: over 12 months, both exercise modes cut fatigue by about 5 points — the most fatigued men gained most
cards.people: 163 men aged 43–90 years on ADT in Australia, randomised to impact-loading plus resistance training (n=58), aerobic plus resistance training (n=54), or usual care/delayed exercise (n=51) for 12 months. Fatigue was measured with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and vitality with the SF-36.
cards.result: Fatigue was reduced (p=0.005) in the impact-loading plus resistance group at 6 and 12 months (about 5 points) and in the aerobic plus resistance (p=0.005) and delayed-exercise (p=0.022) groups at 12 months. Vitality increased for all groups at 12 months (about 4 points, p≤0.001). Men with the highest baseline fatigue and lowest vitality improved the most (ptrend<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The delayed-exercise control group also exercised in the second 6 months, which dilutes the 12-month contrast; participants were mostly well-functioning volunteers. Fatigue is a questionnaire outcome in an unblinded trial.
cards.source: Taaffe DR et al. Effects of Different Exercise Modalities on Fatigue in Prostate Cancer Patients Undergoing Androgen Deprivation Therapy: A Year-long Randomised Controlled Trial. European Urology. 2017. PMID: 28249801. Registry ID: ACTRN12609000200280. cards.headline: Synthesis: fatigue, fitness and quality of life improve in every trial; fat gain is prevented only when training starts with ADT; hard outcomes untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: fatigue, fitness and quality of life improve in every trial; fat gain is prevented only when training starts with ADT; hard outcomes untested
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 381 men receiving ADT for prostate cancer (Segal 2003, Canada, resistance training 12 weeks; Cormie 2015, Australia, supervised aerobic plus resistance from ADT initiation, 3 months; Taaffe 2017, Australia, two exercise modes, 12 months).
cards.result: Fatigue: improved in all three trials (Segal P=.002 for fatigue interference; Cormie difference 3.1, P=.042; Taaffe about 5 points, p=0.005). Body composition: unchanged in Segal's 12-week trial in men already facing ADT, but fat gain prevented and lean mass preserved when exercise began with the first injection (Cormie: -1.4 kg fat-mass difference). Fitness and strength: improved wherever measured. Survival, fractures and falls: not reported in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — moderate, concordant evidence on patient-reported and functional outcomes; Tier C is not set because three randomised trials concur.
cards.watchOut: All outcomes are surrogates or self-reports from unblinded trials in motivated volunteers; the shelf cannot support claims about survival, bone health or cardiovascular events, and the optimal mode, dose and durability beyond 12 months are unsettled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Segal RJ et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2003 (PMID: 12721238); Cormie P et al. BJU International. 2015 (PMID: 24467669); Taaffe DR et al. European Urology. 2017 (PMID: 28249801).

shelves.title: Bioimpedance surveillance with early compression (PREVENT): progression to chronic lymphoedema 7.9% versus 19.2% after a triggered intervention — one trial, reported twice
shelves.question: In women at risk after breast-cancer surgery, does prospective bioimpedance surveillance with early compression prevent progression to chronic lymphoedema versus tape-measure surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anthropometry/instrumentation · Arm/pathology · Breast Cancer Lymphedema/diagnosis/etiology/prevention & control · Breast Neoplasms/complications · Cancer Survivors/statistics & numerical data · Dielectric Spectroscopy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Middle Aged · Prognosis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from a single large randomised trial, reported at interim and at final analysis. In PREVENT, women after breast-cancer surgery were randomised to surveillance by bioimpedance spectroscopy (BIS) or tape measurement (TM), with a 4-week compression sleeve and gauntlet triggered by subclinical change. In the final report (Ridner SH et al., PMID: 35099283), 879 women were analysed: BIS triggered intervention less often (20.1% vs 27.5%, p=0.011) and later (median 9.7 vs 3.9 months), and among women who triggered, progression to chronic lymphoedema needing complex decongestive physiotherapy was 7.9% with BIS versus 19.2% with TM (relative risk 0.41; absolute reduction 11.3 percentage points, 95% CI 2.3 to 20.3; p=0.016). The earlier interim analysis (Ridner SH et al., PMID: 31054038) pointed the same way but was not significant for progression (4.9% vs 14.7%, p=0.130). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BIS-triggered early compression reduced progression to chronic lymphoedema in the one trial that has tested it; the comparison is against tape-measure surveillance with the same compression trigger, not against no surveillance.

cards.headline: Ridner 2022 (PREVENT, final): progression to chronic lymphoedema 7.9% (BIS) versus 19.2% (tape) after triggered compression — relative risk 0.41, p=0.016
cards.summary: Ridner 2022 (PREVENT, final): progression to chronic lymphoedema 7.9% (BIS) versus 19.2% (tape) after triggered compression — relative risk 0.41, p=0.016
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, final report (Ridner 2022, PREVENT)
cards.people: 1,200 women with new breast cancer enrolled internationally (2014–2018); 963 randomised and 879 analysed (BIS n=442; tape measure n=437) after mastectomy or partial mastectomy with axillary treatment, radiotherapy or taxane chemotherapy. Subclinical lymphoedema triggered a 4-week, 12-hour-per-day compression sleeve and gauntlet in both arms. Median follow-up 32.9 months; the primary outcome was progression to chronic lymphoedema (≥10% arm-volume change) requiring complex decongestive physiotherapy (CDP) among the 209 women who triggered intervention.
cards.result: BIS patients triggered intervention less often (20.1%, 89/442, vs 27.5%, 120/437; p=0.011) and later (median 9.7 vs 3.9 months, p=0.001). Overall 14.4% (30/209) of triggered patients progressed to CDP, with a lower likelihood in the BIS arm: 7.9% (7/89) versus 19.2% (23/120); relative risk 0.41 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.81); absolute reduction 11.3 percentage points (95% CI 2.3 to 20.3); p=0.016.
cards.watchOut: The headline percentages are among the minority who triggered an intervention (209 of 879), not among all women surveilled — the absolute benefit per woman screened is much smaller. The trial was sponsored within a surveillance-device ecosystem and cannot separate the device from the earlier-trigger threshold it creates; there is no no-surveillance arm.
cards.source: Ridner SH et al. A Comparison of Bioimpedance Spectroscopy or Tape Measure Triggered Compression Intervention in Chronic Breast Cancer Lymphedema Prevention. Lymphatic Research and Biology. 2022. PMID: 35099283. Registry ID: NCT02167659. cards.headline: Ridner 2019 (PREVENT, interim): same direction, not yet significant — progression 4.9% versus 14.7% among triggered patients (p=0.130)
cards.summary: Ridner 2019 (PREVENT, interim): same direction, not yet significant — progression 4.9% versus 14.7% among triggered patients (p=0.130)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, prespecified interim analysis (Ridner 2019, PREVENT)
cards.people: The first 508 PREVENT participants with at least 12 months of follow-up, randomised to BIS or tape-measure surveillance with the same 4-week compression intervention on triggering; progression was defined as tape-measure volume change ≥10% above the presurgical baseline requiring CDP.
cards.result: 109 patients (21.9%) triggered intervention: fewer with BIS than tape (15.8% vs 28.5%, p<0.001), and later (9.5 vs 2.8 months, p=0.002). Twelve triggering patients progressed to CDP — 2 in the BIS group (4.9%) and 10 in the tape group (14.7%) — a 67% relative reduction and 9.8% absolute reduction that was not statistically significant (p=0.130).
cards.watchOut: An interim look at the same trial as the 2022 final report — it is not independent confirmation. Event counts were small (12 progressions), which is why the final analysis was needed.
cards.source: Ridner SH et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, two reports — BIS triggers less, later, and with fewer progressions; no second trial and no untreated comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, two reports — BIS triggers less, later, and with fewer progressions; no second trial and no untreated comparator
cards.people: One international randomised trial (PREVENT, NCT02167659): 879 analysed women at risk of breast-cancer-related lymphoedema, BIS versus tape-measure surveillance, both with compression triggered by subclinical change, followed a median of 32.9 months.
cards.result: Trigger rate 20.1% (BIS) versus 27.5% (tape); progression to chronic lymphoedema among triggered patients 7.9% versus 19.2% (relative risk 0.41; absolute reduction 11.3 percentage points). Interim and final analyses agree in direction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged Tier C: the shelf rests on a single trial for a benefit claim, so it goes to the developer personally.
cards.watchOut: Both cards report the same trial — the evidence base is one study, however large. Whether BIS surveillance beats symptom-based care, and whether the benefit justifies device costs across health systems, remain untested randomised questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ridner SH et al. Lymphatic Research and Biology. 2022 (PMID: 35099283); Ridner SH et al. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 31054038) — interim and final reports of the single PREVENT trial.

shelves.title: Urea cream prevents sorafenib hand–foot skin reactions (any grade 56.0% versus 73.6%) but did not prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome (56% versus 62.4%)
shelves.question: In patients receiving sorafenib or capecitabine, does prophylactic urea-based cream prevent hand–foot skin reactions versus control?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/complications/drug therapy · China · Emulsions/administration & dosage · Female · Hand-Foot Syndrome/drug therapy/prevention & control · Humans · Incidence · Liver Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Niacinamide/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Odds Ratio · Phenylurea Compounds/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Skin/drug effects · Sorafenib · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Urea/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by drug. For sorafenib, one large open-label randomised trial (Ren Z et al., PMID: 25667293) in 871 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma found 10% urea-based cream three times daily cut any-grade hand–foot skin reaction over 12 weeks from 73.6% to 56.0% (odds ratio 0.457, 95% CI 0.344 to 0.608) and grade ≥2 reactions from 29.2% to 20.7% (odds ratio 0.635), delaying first occurrence (median 84 vs 34 days). For capecitabine, a smaller double-blind-era trial (Wongkraisri C et al., PMID: 39962445) in 216 patients found no prevention: any-grade hand–foot syndrome 56% with urea cream versus 62.4% with usual care (p=0.36), grade 3 in 41.1% versus 47.7% (p=0.34), and no delay in onset. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylactic urea cream reduces sorafenib-associated hand–foot skin reactions in a single open-label trial; it does not prevent capecitabine-associated hand–foot syndrome.

cards.headline: Ren 2015: urea cream cut sorafenib hand–foot skin reactions — any grade 56.0% versus 73.6% (OR 0.457), grade ≥2 20.7% versus 29.2%
cards.summary: Ren 2015: urea cream cut sorafenib hand–foot skin reactions — any grade 56.0% versus 73.6% (OR 0.457), grade ≥2 20.7% versus 29.2%
cards.people: 871 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma at centres across China starting sorafenib, randomised to 10% urea-based cream three times daily plus best supportive care (n=439) or best supportive care alone, excluding all creams (n=432), for up to 12 weeks; reactions assessed every 2 weeks.
cards.result: The 12-week incidence of any-grade hand–foot skin reaction was 56.0% with urea cream versus 73.6% with supportive care alone (odds ratio 0.457, 95% CI 0.344 to 0.608; P<.001), and grade ≥2 reactions 20.7% versus 29.2% (odds ratio 0.635, 95% CI 0.466 to 0.866; P=.004). Median time to first reaction was 84 versus 34 days (hazard ratio 0.658, 95% CI 0.541 to 0.799). Sorafenib dose reductions/interruptions (9.1% vs 11.8%), response rate and disease control did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a no-cream control: patients applying cream three times daily knew their allocation, and grading of a visible skin reaction is hard to blind — the authors themselves called for blinded, placebo-controlled trials. Single-country, single-tumour population.
cards.source: Ren Z et al. Randomized controlled trial of the prophylactic effect of urea-based cream on sorafenib-associated hand-foot skin reactions in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25667293. cards.headline: Wongkraisri 2025: urea cream did not prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome — any grade 56% versus 62.4% (p=0.36)
cards.summary: Wongkraisri 2025: urea cream did not prevent capecitabine hand–foot syndrome — any grade 56% versus 62.4% (p=0.36)
cards.people: 216 patients with cancer receiving capecitabine, randomised 1:1 to usual care alone (n=109) or usual care plus urea-based cream (n=107), assessed each cycle over a median of six capecitabine cycles. Primary endpoint: proportion with any-grade hand–foot syndrome.
cards.result: Any-grade hand–foot syndrome occurred in 56% (60/107) with urea cream versus 62.4% (68/109) with usual care (p=0.36). Grade 3 syndrome occurred in 41.1% (44/107) versus 47.7% (52/109) (p=0.34); capecitabine modification for hand–foot syndrome in 15.9% versus 18.3% (p=0.89); onset timing was similar. The authors noted a tendency to lesser severity in later cycles only.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than the sorafenib trial and in a different drug injury: capecitabine hand–foot syndrome is a cumulative palmoplantar toxicity, not the focal hyperkeratotic reaction of sorafenib — a null here does not erase the sorafenib result, nor vice versa.
cards.source: Wongkraisri C et al. Randomized controlled trial on the efficacy of topical urea-based cream in preventing capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome. BMC Cancer. 2025. PMID: 39962445. shelves.title: Neutropenic diet does not reduce infections: pooled relative risk 1.02 for major infections across 15 studies and 4,320 patients — with one bacteremia signal in transplant trials
shelves.question: In patients receiving chemotherapy or stem-cell transplantation, does a neutropenic diet reduce infection versus a regular/liberalised diet?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for infection prevention in the populations studied. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Jamal F et al., PMID: 42721418) pooled 15 comparative studies with 4,320 patients with cancer: the neutropenic diet was not associated with fewer major infections (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.18), bacteremia/fungemia (0.97, 0.78 to 1.22), pneumonia (0.98) or deaths (0.94, 0.77 to 1.15), and results restricted to randomised trials were consistent. An earlier systematic review (Matteucci S et al., PMID: 37513590) found the same null for infection and mortality across 12 studies, with worse quality of life on the restricted diet. One subgroup cuts the other way: in randomised trials limited to haematologic malignancy/HSCT patients (6 studies, 855 patients), the neutropenic diet was associated with lower bacteremia/fungemia (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.95) — hypothesis-generating, not practice-settling. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine neutropenic diets do not reduce infections or mortality versus a liberalised diet; a possible bacteremia benefit in prolonged-neutropenia transplant patients is the open exception.

cards.headline: Jamal 2026: major infections RR 1.02 (0.88–1.18), mortality RR 0.94 — no outcome favoured the neutropenic diet overall
cards.summary: Jamal 2026: major infections RR 1.02 (0.88–1.18), mortality RR 0.94 — no outcome favoured the neutropenic diet overall
cards.people: 15 comparative studies including 4,320 adults or children with cancer (chemotherapy or HSCT), comparing a neutropenic diet with a liberalised diet; literature searched through January 2026. Primary outcomes were major infections and bacteremia/fungemia; secondary outcomes pneumonia, diarrhea and mortality, pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: Neutropenic diet versus liberalised diet: major infections relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.88 to 1.18; P=.795); bacteremia/fungemia 0.97 (0.78 to 1.22); pneumonia 0.98 (0.59 to 1.63); diarrhea 1.12 (0.96 to 1.31); mortality 0.94 (0.77 to 1.15). Sensitivity analyses restricted to randomised trials were consistent. In the 9 haematologic malignancy/HSCT studies (1,769 patients) no outcome differed; but in the 6 randomised trials in those patients (855 patients) the neutropenic diet was associated with lower bacteremia/fungemia (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.95; P=.023), with no differences in other outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled studies are not randomised, diets labelled 'neutropenic' vary widely, and the one positive finding is a subgroup of a subgroup (randomised, transplant/haematologic, one outcome) — exactly the pattern that generates false positives. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Jamal F et al. Neutropenic Diet Versus Liberalized Diet in Patients With Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JCO Oncology Practice. 2026. PMID: 42721418. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Matteucci 2023: 12 studies — no reduction in infection or mortality on a low-bacterial diet, and quality of life was worse
cards.summary: Matteucci 2023: 12 studies — no reduction in infection or mortality on a low-bacterial diet, and quality of life was worse
cards.people: 12 studies of a low-bacterial (neutropenic) diet in neutropenic patients with cancer, identified from 1,985 records across Cochrane Library, PubMed, CINAHL and EMBASE, with dual-reviewer screening and risk-of-bias assessment.
cards.result: The low-bacterial diet did not demonstrate a reduction in infection or mortality rates compared with a free diet. Definitions, composition and start timing of the diet were heterogeneous across studies. The diet showed a negative correlation with quality of life, attributed to reduced palatability and limited food variety, with a negative impact on nutritional status.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without pooled effect sizes — it corroborates the direction of the 2026 meta-analysis but cannot quantify anything. Quality-of-life harm is reported qualitatively, not as a pooled estimate.
cards.source: Matteucci S et al. Low-Bacterial Diet in Cancer Patients: A Systematic Review. Nutrients. 2023. PMID: 37513590. MeSH: Humans · Quality of Life · Diet · Neoplasms/complications

cards.headline: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer for most patients — restriction does not prevent infection; the transplant bacteremia subgroup is the live question
cards.summary: Synthesis: two reviews, one answer for most patients — restriction does not prevent infection; the transplant bacteremia subgroup is the live question
cards.people: Jamal 2026 meta-analysis (15 studies, 4,320 patients) and Matteucci 2023 systematic review (12 studies), covering chemotherapy and HSCT populations, adults and children.
cards.result: Major infections RR 1.02 (0.88–1.18); bacteremia/fungemia RR 0.97; mortality RR 0.94 — all null overall, consistent in randomised-only analyses. Exception: randomised HSCT/haematologic trials, bacteremia/fungemia RR 0.67 (0.47–0.95). Quality of life: worse on the restricted diet (qualitative). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for routine use, with the HSCT subgroup declared on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: A null pooled across mostly non-randomised studies is weaker than a null from trials; the reviews agree, which is why this is POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE (weak evidence). Centres caring for prolonged-neutropenia transplant patients may reasonably await a definitive trial before liberalising.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jamal F et al. JCO Oncology Practice. 2026 (PMID: 42721418); Matteucci S et al. Nutrients. 2023 (PMID: 37513590).

shelves.title: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in cancer: transfusions fall by a third, but on-study mortality rises (HR 1.17) and thromboembolism rises by half (RR 1.52)
shelves.question: In chemotherapy-induced anaemia, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents increase mortality and thromboembolism even as they reduce transfusions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anemia/drug therapy/etiology · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Effect Modifier, Epidemiologic · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Erythropoietin/adverse effects · Female · Hematinics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Proportional Hazards Models · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recombinant Proteins · Research Design · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — on mortality and clots, with a real transfusion benefit on the other side of the scale. Bohlius J et al. (PMID: 19410717) pooled individual data from 53 randomised trials with 13,933 patients with cancer: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) increased mortality during the active study period (combined hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.30) and worsened overall survival (1.06, 1.00 to 1.12), with little heterogeneity. The updated Cochrane review (Tonia T et al., PMID: 23235597), covering 91 trials and 20,102 participants, found the same mortality signal (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.29), more thromboembolic complications (risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.34 to 1.74), and — the benefit — fewer red-cell transfusions (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.68; on average one unit of blood less per patient). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): in patients with cancer, ESAs increase deaths during treatment and thromboembolism while reducing transfusion need by about a third; the harm claim is why this shelf is Tier C for the developer's personal review.

cards.headline: Bohlius 2009: on-study mortality HR 1.17 (1.06–1.30) across 53 trials and 13,933 patients — little heterogeneity
cards.summary: Bohlius 2009: on-study mortality HR 1.17 (1.06–1.30) across 53 trials and 13,933 patients — little heterogeneity
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials, individual patient data (Bohlius 2009)
cards.people: 13,933 patients with cancer in 53 randomised trials comparing ESAs (epoetin alfa, epoetin beta or darbepoetin alfa) plus transfusions as needed versus transfusion alone, for prophylaxis or treatment of anaemia, irrespective of anticancer treatment; 10,441 patients on chemotherapy in 38 trials analysed separately. 1,530 patients died during the active study period and 4,993 overall.
cards.result: ESAs increased mortality during the active study period (combined hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.30) and worsened overall survival (1.06, 1.00 to 1.12), with little heterogeneity (I² 0% for on-study mortality). In patients on chemotherapy, the on-study mortality hazard ratio was 1.10 (0.98 to 1.24) and overall survival 1.04 (0.97 to 1.11). There was little evidence that effects differed by anticancer treatment type (p for interaction 0.42).
cards.watchOut: The chemotherapy-only subgroup estimates cross 1.0 — the mortality signal is strongest in the all-comers pool, which includes radiotherapy and no-treatment settings and older trials using higher haemoglobin targets than modern practice. Absolute excess deaths are not stated as rates in the record.
cards.source: Bohlius J et al. Recombinant human erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and mortality in patients with cancer: a meta-analysis of randomised trials. The Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19410717. cards.headline: Tonia 2012 (Cochrane): transfusions RR 0.65 — but mortality HR 1.17 and thromboembolism RR 1.52 across 91 trials
cards.summary: Tonia 2012 (Cochrane): transfusions RR 0.65 — but mortality HR 1.17 and thromboembolism RR 1.52 across 91 trials
cards.people: 91 randomised trials with 20,102 participants with cancer, receiving or not receiving anticancer therapy, comparing ESAs (plus transfusion if needed) with no ESA; searches to November 2011. Outcomes included transfusion need, haematological response, mortality, survival, thromboembolism and quality of life.
cards.result: ESAs reduced red-cell transfusions (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.68; 70 trials, 16,093 participants; on average one unit of blood less, mean difference -0.98 units). But ESAs increased mortality during the active study period (hazard ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.29; 70 trials, 15,935 participants), decreased overall survival (hazard ratio 1.05, 1.00 to 1.11; 78 trials, 19,003 participants), and increased thromboembolic complications (risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.34 to 1.74; 57 trials, 15,498 participants). Evidence for a quality-of-life benefit was only suggestive, and an effect on tumour response was not supported (risk ratio 1.02, 0.98 to 1.06).
cards.watchOut: The review's haemoglobin-response figure is internally inconsistent in the record and is not quoted here. Trials span eras and haemoglobin targets; effects at today's restricted targets and thresholds may be smaller in both directions, but no later pooled analysis has reversed the direction of harm.
cards.source: Tonia T et al. Erythropoietin or darbepoetin for patients with cancer. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 23235597. cards.headline: Synthesis: the trade is explicit — about one unit of blood saved per patient, bought with more clots and more deaths on treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: the trade is explicit — about one unit of blood saved per patient, bought with more clots and more deaths on treatment
cards.people: Two independent pooled analyses of the randomised ESA literature in cancer: Bohlius 2009 (53 trials, 13,933 patients, individual data) and the Cochrane update, Tonia 2012 (91 trials, 20,102 participants).
cards.result: Transfusion risk ratio 0.65 (0.62–0.68); on-study mortality hazard ratio 1.17 in both analyses (1.06–1.30 and 1.06–1.29); overall survival hazard ratio 1.05–1.06; thromboembolism risk ratio 1.52 (1.34–1.74). PROPOSED LIKELY (harm), Tier C because the shelf carries a harm claim on mortality — the developer reviews it personally.
cards.watchOut: Neither analysis can fully separate the drug from the haemoglobin targets of its era, and neither gives a clean absolute excess-death rate; the stamp rests on the consistency, size and low heterogeneity of the relative harm signals across two pools.

shelves.title: Subcutaneous ketamine for refractory cancer pain: response 31% versus 27% on placebo in the one phase 3 trial — with twice the adverse events and a number-needed-to-harm of 6
shelves.question: In refractory cancer pain, does subcutaneous ketamine added to opioids improve pain control versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Ketamine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Logistic Models · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications/pathology · Pain Measurement · Intractable Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Palliative Care/methods · Prognosis · Proportional Hazards Models · Queensland · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the only adequately sized trial, with harm on the face. Hardy J et al. (PMID: 22965960) randomised 185 patients with chronic uncontrolled cancer pain on opioids and standard co-analgesics to dose-escalated subcutaneous ketamine or placebo over 3 to 5 days: positive responses were 31% (29/93) on ketamine versus 27% (25/92) on placebo (difference 0.04, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.18; P=.55), a number needed to treat of 25, while adverse events worse than baseline occurred at almost twice the rate (incidence rate ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.61) and the number needed to harm through toxicity-related withdrawal was 6. The Cochrane review (Bell RF et al., PMID: 28657160) found only two other eligible trials (20 and 10 participants, crossover, intrathecal and intravenous routes) and judged the overall evidence very low quality — insufficient to assess benefit or harm for ketamine as an opioid adjuvant in refractory cancer pain generally. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for subcutaneous dose-escalated ketamine the phase 3 answer is no net benefit; for other routes and regimens the honest answer is that the evidence is too thin to tell. Tier C: a single trial carries the null, and the shelf carries a harm signal.

cards.headline: Hardy 2012: response 31% ketamine versus 27% placebo (P=.55); adverse events IRR 1.95; NNT 25, NNH 6
cards.summary: Hardy 2012: response 31% ketamine versus 27% placebo (P=.55); adverse events IRR 1.95; NNT 25, NNH 6
cards.people: 185 participants with chronic uncontrolled cancer pain receiving opioids and standard adjuvant therapy, at multiple Australian sites; subcutaneous ketamine or placebo, dose-escalated over 3 to 5 days. A positive outcome required clinically relevant pain improvement with limited breakthrough analgesia and acceptable toxicity.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in positive outcomes between arms (difference 0.04, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.18; P=.55): response rates 31% (29 of 93) on ketamine and 27% (25 of 92) on placebo. Pain type (nociceptive versus neuropathic) did not predict response. Adverse events worse than baseline occurred at almost twice the incidence on ketamine after day 1 (incidence rate ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.61; P<.001), and patients on ketamine were more likely to have a more severe grade of adverse event per day (odds ratio 1.09, 1.00 to 1.18). Number needed to treat for one additional positive outcome: 25; number needed to harm (toxicity-related withdrawal): 6.
cards.watchOut: One regimen only — rapid subcutaneous escalation to high dose (up to 500 mg) over days. The result does not directly answer low-dose, slower, or intravenous regimens used in some palliative units, which remain untested at this standard.

cards.headline: Bell 2017 (Cochrane): three trials total, evidence rated very low quality — insufficient to assess ketamine as an opioid adjuvant
cards.summary: Bell 2017 (Cochrane): three trials total, evidence rated very low quality — insufficient to assess ketamine as an opioid adjuvant
cards.people: Three randomised trials of ketamine added to opioids for refractory cancer pain in adults: the Hardy 2012 subcutaneous trial (185 participants) plus two small crossover studies (20 participants, intrathecal ketamine added to intrathecal morphine; 10 participants, intravenous ketamine bolus added to morphine). Searches to December 2016/January 2017; evidence graded with GRADE.
cards.result: Pooling was not appropriate because of clinical heterogeneity. The two small crossover studies reported reduced pain intensity and morphine requirements with ketamine; the large parallel-group subcutaneous study found no difference in patient-reported pain intensity, almost twice the adverse-event incidence (needle-site irritation and cognitive disturbance most common), and two serious adverse events thought related to ketamine (bradyarrhythmia and cardiac arrest). The intravenous study reported hallucinations in 4 of 10 participants. Overall risk of bias was unclear in all three studies and the quality of evidence was judged very low.
cards.watchOut: A very-low-quality rating means the review is a map of ignorance, not a verdict: it neither confirms Hardy's null for other regimens nor rescues the small positive crossover studies, whose designs (tiny, crossover, carryover-prone) are the weakest in the set.
cards.source: Bell RF et al. Ketamine as an adjuvant to opioids for cancer pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28657160. cards.headline: Synthesis: the regimen that was properly tested failed; the regimens that reported benefit were barely tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: the regimen that was properly tested failed; the regimens that reported benefit were barely tested
cards.people: Hardy 2012 phase 3 trial (n=185, subcutaneous dose-escalated ketamine versus placebo, both on opioids) read alongside the Cochrane review of all randomised evidence to 2017 (3 trials, 215 participants).
cards.result: Subcutaneous ketamine: response 31% versus 27% (P=.55), adverse events IRR 1.95, NNH 6 versus NNT 25. All other randomised evidence: two crossover studies of 20 and 10 patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the tested subcutaneous regimen; Tier C because a single trial carries the shelf and a harm claim is on its face.
cards.watchOut: Clinicians using low-dose ketamine infusions will not find their regimen in this evidence — the shelf should be read as 'no net benefit where tested, untested where commonly improvised', not as proof that no ketamine regimen can help any patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hardy J et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2012 (PMID: 22965960); Bell RF et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28657160).

shelves.title: GnRH agonist during chemotherapy: ovarian failure 8% versus 22% (POEMS) and early menopause 8.9% versus 25.9% (PROMISE) — with 12-year safety data now reassuring
shelves.question: In premenopausal women receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, does a GnRH agonist protect ovarian function and future fertility versus chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/surgery · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/agonists · Goserelin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Middle Aged · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Premenopause · Primary Ovarian Insufficiency/chemically induced/prevention & control · Regression Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials agree on ovarian protection, and the long-term follow-up answers the safety worry. In POEMS (Moore HC et al., PMID: 25738668), 257 premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer were randomised to chemotherapy with or without goserelin: ovarian failure at 2 years was 8% versus 22% (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.97; P=.04), and pregnancies occurred in 21% versus 11% (P=.03). In PROMISE-GIM6 (Del Mastro L et al., PMID: 21771987), 281 women randomised to chemotherapy with or without triptorelin had early-menopause rates of 8.9% versus 25.9% at 12 months (absolute difference -17 percentage points; odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.59). At a median 12.4 years (Lambertini M et al., PMID: 34850043), PROMISE showed no difference in disease-free survival (65.7% vs 69.2%; HR 1.16) or overall survival (81.2% vs 81.3%; HR 1.17), including in hormone-receptor-positive disease, with 9 versus 4 post-treatment pregnancies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a GnRH agonist during chemotherapy roughly halves-to-thirds chemotherapy-induced ovarian failure across two trials, with more pregnancies and no survival penalty at 12 years; POEMS' missing primary-endpoint data keep this at POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Moore 2015 (POEMS): ovarian failure at 2 years 8% with goserelin versus 22% without (OR 0.30); pregnancies 21% versus 11%
cards.summary: Moore 2015 (POEMS): ovarian failure at 2 years 8% with goserelin versus 22% without (OR 0.30); pregnancies 21% versus 11%
cards.people: 257 premenopausal women with operable hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer randomised to standard chemotherapy with the GnRH agonist goserelin or chemotherapy alone; 218 were eligible and evaluable, and 135 had complete primary-endpoint data. Ovarian failure was defined as no menses in the preceding 6 months with postmenopausal FSH at 2 years.
cards.result: Ovarian failure occurred in 8% of the goserelin group versus 22% of the chemotherapy-alone group (odds ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.97; two-sided P=.04); sensitivity analyses for missing data were consistent. Among the 218 evaluable patients, pregnancy occurred in more women with goserelin (21% vs 11%, P=.03), and disease-free survival (P=.04) and overall survival (P=.05) also favoured the goserelin group.
cards.watchOut: Only 135 of 257 randomised women had complete primary-endpoint data — the authors themselves state that missing data weaken interpretation. The survival differences were secondary endpoints in a trial not powered for them and should not be quoted as a cancer benefit. Participants had hormone-receptor-negative disease, so POEMS alone does not answer the hormone-receptor-positive question.
cards.source: Moore HC et al. Goserelin for ovarian protection during breast-cancer adjuvant chemotherapy. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25738668. Registry ID: NCT00068601. cards.headline: Del Mastro 2011 (PROMISE-GIM6): early menopause 8.9% with triptorelin versus 25.9% without — absolute difference -17 points (OR 0.28)
cards.summary: Del Mastro 2011 (PROMISE-GIM6): early menopause 8.9% with triptorelin versus 25.9% without — absolute difference -17 points (OR 0.28)
cards.people: 281 premenopausal women with stage I–III breast cancer at 16 Italian centres (2003–2008) receiving adjuvant or neoadjuvant chemotherapy, randomised to chemotherapy alone (n=133) or chemotherapy plus triptorelin 3.75 mg intramuscularly every 4 weeks during chemotherapy (n=148). Early menopause was assessed 12 months after the last chemotherapy cycle.
cards.result: Early menopause occurred in 25.9% of the chemotherapy-alone group versus 8.9% of the chemotherapy-plus-triptorelin group — an absolute difference of -17 percentage points (95% CI -26 to -7.9; P<.001); odds ratio 0.28 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.59; P<.001), in an intention-to-treat analysis with imputed values for missing data.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the endpoint is resumption of menses with hormone levels at 12 months — a surrogate for fertility, not pregnancies or live births. Most participants had hormone-receptor-positive disease and many received tamoxifen, which itself disturbs menses.
cards.source: Del Mastro L et al. Effect of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogue triptorelin on the occurrence of chemotherapy-induced early menopause in premenopausal women with breast cancer: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21771987. Registry ID: NCT00311636. cards.headline: Lambertini 2022 (PROMISE, 12 years): no survival cost — DFS 65.7% versus 69.2%, OS 81.2% versus 81.3%; pregnancies 9 versus 4
cards.summary: Lambertini 2022 (PROMISE, 12 years): no survival cost — DFS 65.7% versus 69.2%, OS 81.2% versus 81.3%; pregnancies 9 versus 4
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, long-term follow-up report (Lambertini 2022, PROMISE-GIM6)
cards.people: The 281 PROMISE-GIM6 participants (80.4% hormone-receptor-positive), followed for a median of 12.4 years (interquartile range 11.3–13.2). Post hoc endpoints: disease-free survival, overall survival and post-treatment pregnancies.
cards.result: No differences in 12-year disease-free survival (65.7% [95% CI 57.0 to 73.1] with GnRH agonist vs 69.2% [60.3 to 76.5] without; HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.77) or overall survival (81.2% [73.6 to 86.8] vs 81.3% [73.1 to 87.2]; HR 1.17, 0.67 to 2.03). In hormone-receptor-positive disease the hazard ratios were 1.02 for DFS and 1.12 for OS. Post-treatment pregnancies: 9 in the GnRH-agonist arm versus 4 in the control arm (HR 2.14, 95% CI 0.66 to 6.92).
cards.watchOut: Survival was a post hoc endpoint and the confidence intervals are wide — 'no difference seen' in 281 women is reassurance, not proof of equivalence. Pregnancy counts are small and not significant; the fertility claim rests on the ovarian-function endpoints of the two primary reports.
cards.source: Lambertini M et al. Long-Term Outcomes With Pharmacological Ovarian Suppression During Chemotherapy in Premenopausal Early Breast Cancer Patients. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2022. PMID: 34850043. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two agonists, one effect size — ovarian failure cut by about two-thirds, pregnancies up, survival unchanged at 12 years
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two agonists, one effect size — ovarian failure cut by about two-thirds, pregnancies up, survival unchanged at 12 years
cards.people: POEMS (Moore 2015; goserelin; hormone-receptor-negative disease; ovarian failure at 2 years) and PROMISE-GIM6 (Del Mastro 2011 with Lambertini 2022 long-term follow-up; triptorelin; mostly hormone-receptor-positive disease; early menopause at 12 months, survival at 12 years). Combined randomised population 538 women.
cards.result: Ovarian failure/early menopause: 8% versus 22% (OR 0.30) and 8.9% versus 25.9% (OR 0.28). Pregnancies: 21% versus 11% (POEMS); 9 versus 4 (PROMISE). Survival at 12 years: no difference (OS HR 1.17, CI crossing 1 widely). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — concordant randomised evidence, held below LIKELY by POEMS' missing endpoint data and the surrogate nature of the primary endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was designed around live birth, the outcome patients care most about; menstrual resumption overstates fertility. GnRH agonists are an addition to — not a substitute for — embryo/oocyte cryopreservation where that is feasible.

shelves.title: Pilocarpine for radiation dry mouth: salivary flow and global relief improve in two placebo-controlled trials totalling 369 patients — sweating is the price, and 5 mg three times daily was the sweet spot
shelves.question: In patients with xerostomia after radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, does pilocarpine improve salivary flow and dry-mouth symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Double-Blind Method · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pilocarpine/administration & dosage · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Saliva/metabolism · Xerostomia/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — old but properly blinded evidence. LeVeque FG et al. (PMID: 8501499) randomised 162 patients with significant xerostomia after at least 40 Gy to dose-titrated oral pilocarpine or placebo for 12 weeks: pilocarpine produced significant improvement in overall global assessment (P=.035), significantly reduced use of oral comfort agents such as artificial saliva (P=.020), improved dryness nearly significantly (P=.057), and significantly increased whole and parotid salivary flow after dosing. The integrated analysis of both placebo-controlled trials (Rieke JW et al., PMID: 7852133; 369 patients) confirmed significant improvements in salivary flow and global condition in both studies, with the fixed-dose study also showing significant gains in dryness, mouth comfort and speaking; adverse effects were those of a cholinergic agonist — sweating commonest — rising with dose, and 5.0 mg three times daily gave the best balance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pilocarpine improves salivary flow and gives clinically significant symptomatic relief of postradiation xerostomia, with dose-related cholinergic side effects; the trials are from the pre-IMRT era, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: LeVeque 1993: global improvement significant (P=.035), comfort-agent use down (P=.020), salivary flow up — in 162 irradiated patients
cards.summary: LeVeque 1993: global improvement significant (P=.035), comfort-agent use down (P=.020), salivary flow up — in 162 irradiated patients
cards.people: 162 patients with head and neck cancer who had received at least 40 Gy (117 had received >60 Gy) with clinically significant xerostomia, in a multicentre dose-titration study: pilocarpine 2.5 mg three times daily for 4 weeks, then 5.0 mg, then 10.0 mg, with down-titration allowed for side effects, versus matching placebo over 12 weeks. Outcomes were questionnaires, visual analogue scales and sialometry.
cards.result: Pilocarpine produced a significant improvement in overall global assessments compared with placebo (P=.035) and a statistically significant decrease in use of oral comfort agents such as artificial saliva, hard candy and water (P=.020). Improvement in dryness approached significance (P=.057). Post-dose whole and parotid salivary flow improved significantly in the pilocarpine groups. Adverse experiences were primarily sweating (mild to moderate, the commonest), rhinitis, headache, nausea and urinary frequency; no serious drug-related adverse experiences occurred.
cards.watchOut: Subjective endpoints dominate and several comparisons were made — the dryness result itself missed significance (P=.057). Patients had residual salivary function after older radiation techniques; pilocarpine cannot stimulate glands that no longer function.
cards.source: LeVeque FG et al. A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-titration study of oral pilocarpine for treatment of radiation-induced xerostomia in head and neck cancer patients. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (leveque 1993) 162 patients with head and neck cancer who had received at least 40 gy (117 had received >60 gy) with clinically significant xerostomia, in a multicentre dose-titration study: pilocarpine 2.5 mg three times daily for 4 weeks, then 5.0 mg, then 10.0 mg, with down-titration allowed for side effects, versus matching placebo over 12 weeks. outcomes were questionnaires, visual analogue scales and sialometry. pilocarpine produced a significant improvement in overall global assessments compared with placebo (p=.035) and a statistically significant decrease in use of oral comfort agents such as artificial saliva, hard candy and water (p=.020). improvement in dryness approached significance (p=.057). post-dose whole and parotid salivary flow improved significantly in the pilocarpine groups. adverse experiences were primarily sweating (mild to moderate, the commonest), rhinitis, headache, nausea and urinary frequency; no serious drug-related adverse experiences occurred. subjective endpoints dominate and several comparisons were made — the dryness result itself missed significance (p=.057). patients had residual salivary function after older radiation techniques; pilocarpine cannot stimulate glands that no longer function. leveque fg et al. a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-titration study of oral pilocarpine for treatment of radiation-induced xerostomia in head and neck cancer patients. journal of clinical oncology. 1993. pmid: 8501499. mesh: administration, oral · double-blind method · female · head and neck neoplasms/radiotherapy · humans · male · middle aged · pilocarpine/administration & dosage · radiotherapy/adverse effects · saliva/metabolism · xerostomia/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology

cards.headline: Rieke 1995: integrated analysis of both trials (369 patients) — flow and global relief significant in both; 5 mg three times daily balanced benefit and side effects
cards.summary: Rieke 1995: integrated analysis of both trials (369 patients) — flow and global relief significant in both; 5 mg three times daily balanced benefit and side effects
cards.type: Integrated analysis of two randomised double-blind trials (Rieke 1995)
cards.people: 369 patients with clinically significant xerostomia after at least 40 Gy to the head and neck, pooled from the dose-titration study (162 patients) and a fixed-dose study (207 patients receiving placebo, pilocarpine 5.0 mg or 10.0 mg three times daily), each treated for 12 weeks with questionnaire, visual-analogue and sialometry assessments at baseline and weeks 4, 8 and 12.
cards.result: Statistically significant improvements in salivary flow in pilocarpine groups versus placebo, and a significant improvement in the overall 'global' condition of xerostomia, were seen in both studies. In the fixed-dose study there were also significant improvements in oral dryness, mouth comfort, ability to speak and reduced use of oral comfort agents; in the dose-titration study, dryness approached significance (p=0.057) and comfort-agent use fell (p=0.045). All doses (2.5, 5.0 and 10.0 mg three times daily) were judged safe; adverse events were cholinergic, sweating commonest, increasing with dose. The authors concluded 5.0 mg three times daily produced the best clinical results when efficacy and side effects were weighed together, and that best results may require more than 8 weeks of continuous treatment.
cards.watchOut: An integrated report by the trials' own investigators, pooling one trial whose card appears separately on this shelf (LeVeque 1993) — it is corroboration of analysis, not a third independent trial. Both trials predate intensity-modulated radiotherapy, which spares parotid tissue and changes the population.
cards.source: Rieke JW et al. Oral pilocarpine for radiation-induced xerostomia: integrated efficacy and safety results from two prospective randomized clinical trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real symptomatic benefit in patients with residual gland function — modest, dose-limited by sweating, and tested before modern radiotherapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real symptomatic benefit in patients with residual gland function — modest, dose-limited by sweating, and tested before modern radiotherapy
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (dose-titration, n=162; fixed-dose, n=207) in postradiation xerostomia, reported individually (LeVeque 1993) and integrated (Rieke 1995).
cards.result: Global relief: significant in both reports (P=.035 in the titration trial). Salivary flow: significantly improved post-dose in both studies. Comfort-agent use: significantly reduced (P=.020/.045). Dryness scores: significant in the fixed-dose study, borderline (p=0.057) in the titration study. Harm: dose-related cholinergic effects, sweating predominating; no serious drug-related events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No trial measured dental outcomes, nutrition or long-term adherence, and none enrolled the post-IMRT population now typical. Benefit requires functioning residual gland tissue — an eligibility filter the trials applied implicitly through their entry criteria.

shelves.title: Whole-brain radiotherapy for lung-cancer brain metastases (QUARTZ): no survival or quality-of-life gain over supportive care alone — HR 1.06 for death, and more drowsiness, hair loss and nausea
shelves.question: In non-small-cell lung cancer with brain metastases and poor prognosis, does whole-brain radiotherapy improve survival or quality of life versus best supportive care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Brain Neoplasms/radiotherapy/secondary/therapy · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/radiotherapy/secondary/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/pathology · Middle Aged · Palliative Care · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — from the one phase 3 trial that asked. QUARTZ (Mulvenna P et al., PMID: 27604504) randomised 538 patients with brain metastases from non-small-cell lung cancer, unsuitable for resection or stereotactic radiotherapy, to optimal supportive care including dexamethasone with or without whole-brain radiotherapy (20 Gy in five fractions). There was no difference in overall survival (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.26), overall quality of life, or dexamethasone use. The primary outcome, quality-adjusted life-years, differed by 4.7 days (46.4 QALY days with WBRT versus 41.7 without; two-sided 90% CI -12.7 to 3.3) — a difference whose confidence interval includes the prespecified 7-day non-inferiority margin, so formal non-inferiority was not cleanly established even though no outcome favoured WBRT. Patients receiving WBRT reported significantly more drowsiness, hair loss, nausea and dry or itchy scalp, with no difference in serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this poor-prognosis population WBRT added toxicity without demonstrable survival or quality-of-life benefit. Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.

cards.headline: Mulvenna 2016 (QUARTZ): survival HR 1.06 (0.90–1.26); QALYs 46.4 versus 41.7 days; no quality-of-life or dexamethasone difference
cards.summary: Mulvenna 2016 (QUARTZ): survival HR 1.06 (0.90–1.26); QALYs 46.4 versus 41.7 days; no quality-of-life or dexamethasone difference
cards.people: 538 patients (median age 66 years, range 38–85) with brain metastases from non-small-cell lung cancer unsuitable for surgical resection or stereotactic radiotherapy, at 69 UK and 3 Australian centres (2007–2014), randomised to optimal supportive care (including dexamethasone) plus whole-brain radiotherapy 20 Gy in five daily fractions (n=269) or supportive care alone (n=269). Primary outcome: quality-adjusted life-years from survival and weekly EQ-5D.
cards.result: No evidence of a difference in overall survival (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.26), overall quality of life, or dexamethasone use. Mean QALYs were 46.4 days with WBRT versus 41.7 days without — a difference of 4.7 days whose two-sided 90% CI (-12.7 to 3.3) includes the prespecified 7-day non-inferiority margin. Significantly more episodes of drowsiness, hair loss, nausea and dry or itchy scalp were reported during WBRT; serious adverse event rates did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority trial whose confidence interval did not exclude the margin — strictly, omitting WBRT was not proven non-inferior on QALYs; the null rests on the totality (no survival, quality-of-life or steroid-sparing signal in WBRT's favour). Patients were selected as unsuitable for surgery or stereotactic treatment, so the result does not extend to patients eligible for focal therapy, or to other primary tumours.
cards.source: Mulvenna P et al. Dexamethasone and supportive care with or without whole brain radiotherapy in treating patients with non-small cell lung cancer with brain metastases unsuitable for resection or stereotactic radiotherapy (QUARTZ): results from a phase 3, non-inferiority, randomised trial. The Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27604504. Registry ID: ISRCTN3826061. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, no favourable outcome for WBRT — supportive care with dexamethasone is a defensible default in this population
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, no favourable outcome for WBRT — supportive care with dexamethasone is a defensible default in this population
cards.people: QUARTZ (n=538) is the only randomised trial of whole-brain radiotherapy versus supportive care alone in NSCLC brain metastases unsuitable for focal therapy.
cards.result: Overall survival HR 1.06 (0.90–1.26); QALY difference 4.7 days (90% CI -12.7 to 3.3) against a 7-day non-inferiority margin; quality of life and dexamethasone use unchanged; symptomatic toxicity (drowsiness, hair loss, nausea, scalp symptoms) higher with WBRT. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C for single-trial status.
cards.watchOut: The trial predates routine CNS-penetrant systemic therapy and hippocampal-avoidance techniques; its population — poor prognosis, focal therapy unsuitable — is exactly the one in which a small QALY effect would be hardest to detect and least likely to change management.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mulvenna P et al. The Lancet. 2016 (PMID: 27604504).

shelves.title: Conquer Fear: a structured psychological intervention cuts fear of recurrence versus relaxation control — face-to-face in 2017, and again online in groups in 2023 (effect size 0.47)
shelves.question: In cancer survivors with clinically significant fear of recurrence, does a structured psychological intervention (Conquer Fear) reduce fear versus relaxation control?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms/psychology/therapy · Colorectal Neoplasms/psychology/therapy · Fear/psychology · Female · Humans · Male · Melanoma/psychology/therapy · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/psychology · Neoplasms/psychology/therapy · Psychotherapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials of the same programme family, eight years and two delivery modes apart. Butow PN et al. (PMID: 29095681) randomised 222 survivors of curable breast or colorectal cancer or melanoma with above-cutoff fear of recurrence to five face-to-face ConquerFear sessions or a relaxation attention control: Fear of Cancer Recurrence Inventory (FCRI) total scores improved significantly more with ConquerFear immediately post-therapy (P<.001), and the advantage was maintained at 3 months (P=.017) and 6 months (P=.018), with parallel gains in cancer-specific distress. Tauber NM et al. (PMID: 37489745) randomised 85 breast-cancer survivors to online group ConquerFear-Group or online group relaxation: fear fell more with the intervention (Cohen's d=0.47, p=0.001; severity d=0.57, p<0.001), with effects stable over 6 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Conquer Fear reduces fear of recurrence versus an active relaxation control in survivors screened for clinically significant fear; effects are moderate and measured on the programme's own target scale.

cards.headline: Butow 2017 (ConquerFear): FCRI total improved versus relaxation control (P<.001) and stayed better at 3 and 6 months
cards.summary: Butow 2017 (ConquerFear): FCRI total improved versus relaxation control (P<.001) and stayed better at 3 and 6 months
cards.people: 222 survivors (of 704 potentially eligible; 121 intervention, 101 control) of curable breast or colorectal cancer or melanoma, 2 months to 5 years after completing treatment (endocrine therapy excepted), scoring above the clinical cutoff on the FCRI severity subscale, at 17 Australian sites. Intervention: five face-to-face ConquerFear sessions (attention training, metacognition, acceptance/mindfulness, screening behaviour, values-based goal setting). Control: Taking-it-Easy relaxation therapy, matched for attention.
cards.result: ConquerFear participants had clinically and statistically greater improvements in FCRI total score from baseline to post-therapy (P<.001) and FCRI severity (P=.001), maintained at 3 months (P=.017 and P=.023) and, for total score, at 6 months (P=.018). Three FCRI subscales (coping, psychological distress, triggers), general anxiety, cancer-specific distress, mental quality of life and metacognitions also improved more at post-therapy; psychological distress and cancer-specific distress differences persisted at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Only 42% of contactable eligible survivors consented, and outcomes are self-reported by participants who knew their allocation — an attention control reduces but cannot remove expectation effects. Effect sizes in points are not stated in the record, only significance levels.
cards.source: Butow PN et al. Randomized Trial of ConquerFear: A Novel, Theoretically Based Psychosocial Intervention for Fear of Cancer Recurrence. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2017. PMID: 29095681. cards.headline: Tauber 2023 (ConquerFear-Group, online): fear reduction d=0.47 (p=0.001), severity d=0.57 — maintained over 6 months in 85 survivors
cards.summary: Tauber 2023 (ConquerFear-Group, online): fear reduction d=0.47 (p=0.001), severity d=0.57 — maintained over 6 months in 85 survivors
cards.people: 85 breast-cancer survivors (of 866 eligible; 475 screened, 18% randomised) who had completed primary treatment 3 months to 5 years earlier and scored ≥22 on the Fear of Cancer Recurrence Inventory–Short Form, randomised to online group-based ConquerFear-Group (metacognitive strategies, values clarification, follow-up education) or online group relaxation training (active control), in 12 groups total. Outcomes at baseline, 1 week post-intervention, and 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: Compared with relaxation control, ConquerFear-Group produced larger reductions in fear of recurrence (FCRI total: Cohen's d=0.47, p=0.001) and FCR severity (d=0.57, p<0.001), plus greater gains in mindfulness and decentering, sustained from baseline through the 6-month follow-up; emotion regulation, worry and rumination improved at some time points.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=85) and breast-cancer only, with heavy screening attrition (866 eligible to 85 randomised) — the women who enrol in online group therapy trials are a selected subset. A replication of the delivery format, not of the exact face-to-face intervention.
cards.source: Tauber NM et al. ConquerFear-Group: A randomized controlled trial of an online-delivered group-based psychological intervention for fear of cancer recurrence in breast cancer survivors. Psycho-Oncology. 2023. PMID: 37489745. cards.summary: Synthesis: the programme works against an active control in two formats — moderate effects, self-reported outcomes, screened populations
cards.people: Two randomised trials of Conquer Fear-family interventions versus relaxation attention controls: Butow 2017 (n=222, face-to-face, mixed cancers) and Tauber 2023 (n=85, online group, breast cancer), both enrolling only survivors above a clinical fear cutoff and following patients to 6 months.
cards.result: FCRI total: significantly greater reduction in both trials (P<.001 and d=0.47, p=0.001), maintained at 6 months in both. Cancer-specific distress also improved and persisted (Butow). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials keep this out of Tier C; unblinded self-report outcomes keep it below LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: No trial compares Conquer Fear with usual care alone, generic CBT, or no treatment, and none reports effects beyond 6 months or on healthcare use; the eligible population is the minority of survivors with clinically significant fear who volunteer for therapy trials.

shelves.title: GP-led follow-up after breast cancer: recurrence confirmed in 22 versus 21 days (1996) and serious clinical events 3.5% versus 3.7% (2006) — two randomised trials, no safety signal
shelves.question: After treatment for early breast cancer, is GP-led follow-up as safe as hospital specialist follow-up for recurrence detection, quality of life and satisfaction?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare · Anxiety/etiology · Breast Neoplasms/therapy · Depression/etiology · Family Practice · Fatigue/etiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitalization · Humans · Medical Records · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Quality of Life · Referral and Consultation · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on every outcome the trials measured, across a decade of replication. Grunfeld E et al. (PMID: 8811760) randomised 296 women with breast cancer in remission to routine follow-up in general practice or hospital: median time from presentation to hospital confirmation of recurrence was 22 days in the GP group versus 21 days in the hospital group, most recurrences (18/26, 69%) presented as interval events between scheduled visits, and quality-of-life differences were small. Grunfeld E et al. (PMID: 16418496) randomised 968 women with early-stage breast cancer to family-physician or cancer-centre follow-up: recurrence-related serious clinical events occurred in 3.5% versus 3.7% (difference 0.19 percentage points, 95% CI -2.26 to 2.65), recurrences in 11.2% versus 13.2% and deaths in 6.0% versus 6.2%, with no significant differences on any quality-of-life questionnaire. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): GP-led follow-up detected recurrence as promptly and as safely as specialist follow-up in two randomised trials; satisfaction was the question's third limb and the trials' quality-of-life instruments showed no penalty for GP care.

cards.headline: Grunfeld 1996: time to confirmation of recurrence 22 days (GP) versus 21 days (hospital); 69% of recurrences were interval events
cards.summary: Grunfeld 1996: time to confirmation of recurrence 22 days (GP) versus 21 days (hospital); 69% of recurrences were interval events
cards.people: 296 women with breast cancer in remission receiving regular follow-up at district general hospitals in England, randomised to routine follow-up transferred to general practice or continued hospital follow-up, followed for 18 months. Outcomes: time from first presentation of symptoms to confirmation of recurrence, and quality of life (SF-36 dimensions, EORTC symptom scale, hospital anxiety and depression scale).
cards.result: Most recurrences (18 of 26, 69%) presented as interval events, and almost half of recurrences in the hospital group (7 of 16, 44%) presented first to general practice anyway. Median time to hospital confirmation was 21 days (range 1–376) in the hospital group and 22 days (range 4–64) in the general-practice group. Between-group differences in change in SF-36 scores were small (social functioning -1.8, 95% CI -7.2 to 3.5; mental health 0.5, -4.1 to 5.1; general health perception 0.6, -3.6 to 4.8). Depression scores rose slightly more in the GP group at mid-trial (difference 0.6, 0.1 to 1.2), with no significant difference in anxiety or EORTC scales.
cards.watchOut: Only 26 recurrences — the trial can exclude large delays, not small ones, and the hospital group's range (to 376 days) shows where delay actually lived. Conducted in 1990s England, before modern imaging, tumour markers and rapid-access pathways.
cards.source: Grunfeld E et al. Routine follow up of breast cancer in primary care: randomised trial. BMJ. 1996. PMID: 8811760. cards.headline: Grunfeld 2006: serious clinical events 3.5% (family physician) versus 3.7% (cancer centre) in 968 women — difference 0.19 points
cards.summary: Grunfeld 2006: serious clinical events 3.5% (family physician) versus 3.7% (cancer centre) in 968 women — difference 0.19 points
cards.people: 968 women with early-stage breast cancer in Canada who had completed adjuvant treatment, were disease-free and were 9–15 months from diagnosis (adjuvant hormonal therapy could continue), randomised to follow-up by their own family physician or at the cancer centre per usual practice. Primary outcome: recurrence-related serious clinical events (SCEs); secondary outcome: health-related quality of life.
cards.result: In the family-physician group there were 54 recurrences (11.2%) and 29 deaths (6.0%); in the cancer-centre group 64 recurrences (13.2%) and 30 deaths (6.2%). SCEs occurred in 17 family-physician patients (3.5%) versus 18 cancer-centre patients (3.7%) — a difference of 0.19 percentage points (95% CI -2.26 to 2.65). No statistically significant differences were detected on any quality-of-life questionnaire.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval around the SCE difference (-2.26 to +2.65 points) still allows a small absolute excess in either direction, and event rates were low because participants were selected disease-free survivors. Family physicians received guideline support within a trial — unsupported real-world transfer may perform worse.
cards.source: Grunfeld E et al. Randomized trial of long-term follow-up for early-stage breast cancer: a comparison of family physician versus specialist care. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2006. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two countries, two decades — GP follow-up matched specialist follow-up on detection speed, events and quality of life
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two countries, two decades — GP follow-up matched specialist follow-up on detection speed, events and quality of life
cards.people: Grunfeld 1996 (n=296, England, women in remission, 18 months) and Grunfeld 2006 (n=968, Canada, early-stage disease-free survivors), both randomised comparisons of primary-care-led versus specialist-led routine follow-up after breast cancer.
cards.result: Time to recurrence confirmation: 22 versus 21 days median. Serious clinical events: 3.5% versus 3.7% (difference 0.19 points, 95% CI -2.26 to 2.65). Recurrences and deaths: numerically similar in both trials. Quality of life: no significant difference on any instrument in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a concordant null from two randomised trials; Tier C is not set.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate contemporary surveillance imaging and biomarker follow-up, and neither was powered as a formal non-inferiority trial for rare catastrophic delays. The finding licenses GP-led follow-up with a safety-net pathway, not abandonment of follow-up.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grunfeld E et al. BMJ. 1996 (PMID: 8811760); Grunfeld E et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2006 (PMID: 16418496).
