shelves.title: Daily aspirin during vascular-prevention trials: cancers on aspirin metastasised less (HR 0.64) — a post hoc analysis of trials that were never designed to treat cancer
shelves.question: Does daily aspirin during randomised trials reduce distant metastasis of incident cancers?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/epidemiology/prevention & control · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Neoplasm Metastasis/prevention & control · Neoplasms/epidemiology/prevention & control · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a striking signal from analyses that were not the trials' purpose. Rothwell PM et al. (PMID: 22440947) reviewed every incident cancer arising in five large UK randomised trials of daily aspirin (≥75 mg) versus control for vascular prevention (17,285 participants; 987 new solid cancers over a mean 6.5 years): allocation to aspirin reduced the risk of cancer with distant metastasis (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.84, p=0.001), driven by adenocarcinoma (HR 0.54, 0.38 to 0.77) rather than other solid cancers (HR 0.82, 0.53 to 1.28). Aspirin reduced metastasis present at diagnosis (HR 0.69), metastasis appearing later in initially localised cancers (HR 0.45), and fatal adenocarcinoma overall (HR 0.65, 0.53 to 0.82). The companion individual-patient analysis (Rothwell PM et al., PMID: 21144578) found aspirin reduced cancer death across eight trials (odds ratio 0.79, 0.68 to 0.92), with benefit emerging after 5 years and a 20-year risk of death from solid cancer still lower on aspirin (HR 0.80, 0.72 to 0.88). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): daily aspirin taken during these trials was associated with substantially less distant metastasis of incident adenocarcinomas; Tier C, because this is a mortality/metastasis benefit claim resting on post hoc analysis of trials randomised for another purpose — the developer reviews it personally.

cards.headline: Rothwell 2012: metastasis HR 0.64 overall, 0.54 for adenocarcinoma — among 987 cancers arising in 17,285 trial participants
cards.summary: Rothwell 2012: metastasis HR 0.64 overall, 0.54 for adenocarcinoma — among 987 cancers arising in 17,285 trial participants
cards.type: Analysis of incident cancers within randomised trials (Rothwell 2012)
cards.people: All five large UK randomised trials of daily aspirin (≥75 mg daily) versus control for prevention of vascular events: 17,285 participants, of whom 987 developed a new solid cancer during a mean in-trial follow-up of 6.5 years. Electronic and paper records were reviewed for every incident cancer; effects on metastasis at presentation or during follow-up (including post-trial follow-up) were stratified by histology.
cards.result: Allocation to aspirin reduced the risk of cancer with distant metastasis (all cancers: hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.84, p=0.001; adenocarcinoma: HR 0.54, 0.38 to 0.77, p=0.0007; other solid cancers: HR 0.82, 0.53 to 1.28, p=0.39), mainly by reducing the proportion of adenocarcinomas presenting with metastatic rather than local disease (odds ratio 0.52, 0.35 to 0.75). Aspirin also reduced adenocarcinoma metastatic at initial diagnosis (HR 0.69, 0.50 to 0.95) and metastasis on later follow-up in patients initially non-metastatic (HR 0.45, 0.28 to 0.72; colorectal cancer HR 0.26, 0.11 to 0.57), and death from adenocarcinoma in patients without metastasis at diagnosis (HR 0.50, 0.34 to 0.74). Overall risk of fatal adenocarcinoma fell (HR 0.65, 0.53 to 0.82) but risk of other fatal cancers did not (HR 1.06, 0.84 to 1.32). A low-dose slow-release platelet-targeted formulation was as effective as higher doses.
cards.watchOut: Cancer and metastasis were not the randomised trials' endpoints: staging and follow-up were assembled retrospectively from records, histology-specific cuts are multiple, and participants were vascular-risk patients — mostly men — not patients with diagnosed cancer. Nothing here tests aspirin as a treatment after a cancer diagnosis; that question required (and later received) dedicated adjuvant trials.
cards.source: Rothwell PM et al. Effect of daily aspirin on risk of cancer metastasis: a study of incident cancers during randomised controlled trials. The Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22440947. cards.headline: Rothwell 2011: cancer death OR 0.79 across eight trials; 20-year solid-cancer death HR 0.80 — benefit only after 5 years
cards.summary: Rothwell 2011: cancer death OR 0.79 across eight trials; 20-year solid-cancer death HR 0.80 — benefit only after 5 years
cards.people: Eight randomised trials of daily aspirin versus no aspirin with mean scheduled treatment of at least 4 years (25,570 patients, 674 cancer deaths); individual patient data available from seven trials (23,535 patients, 657 cancer deaths); 20-year follow-up from death certificates and cancer registries in three large UK trials (12,659 patients, 1,634 cancer deaths).
cards.result: Allocation to aspirin reduced death due to cancer (pooled odds ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.92, p=0.003). On individual-patient analysis, benefit was apparent only after 5 years (all cancers HR 0.66, 0.50 to 0.87; gastrointestinal cancers HR 0.46, 0.27 to 0.77). The 20-year risk of cancer death remained lower on aspirin (all solid cancers HR 0.80, 0.72 to 0.88; gastrointestinal cancers HR 0.65, 0.54 to 0.78; adenocarcinomas HR 0.66, 0.56 to 0.77), increasing with scheduled treatment duration (≥7.5 years: solid cancers HR 0.69). The absolute reduction in 20-year cancer-death risk reached 7.08% (95% CI 2.42 to 11.74) at age 65 years and older. Benefit was unrelated to dose (75 mg upwards) or sex.
cards.watchOut: A latency of about 5 years (longer for stomach, colorectal and prostate cancers) means this is a prevention-timescale effect, not evidence of benefit for a patient with cancer today. Bleeding harms of long-term aspirin — the reason these analyses never translated directly into blanket recommendations — are outside this card's numbers and are covered elsewhere in the library.
cards.source: Rothwell PM et al. Effect of daily aspirin on long-term risk of death due to cancer: analysis of individual patient data from randomised trials. The Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21144578. cards.headline: Synthesis: randomised allocation, post hoc endpoints — less metastasis and fewer cancer deaths on aspirin, on a 5-to-20-year clock
cards.summary: Synthesis: randomised allocation, post hoc endpoints — less metastasis and fewer cancer deaths on aspirin, on a 5-to-20-year clock
cards.people: Two pooled analyses of the UK-led randomised trials of daily aspirin versus control for vascular prevention: Rothwell 2012 (5 trials, 17,285 participants, 987 incident cancers, metastasis outcomes) and Rothwell 2011 (8 trials, 25,570 patients, cancer-death outcomes with follow-up to 20 years).
cards.result: Distant metastasis: HR 0.64 (0.48–0.84); adenocarcinoma metastasis HR 0.54. Cancer death: OR 0.79 (0.68–0.92); 20-year solid-cancer death HR 0.80 (0.72–0.88). Non-adenocarcinoma cancers: no metastasis or fatal-cancer benefit (HR 0.82 and 1.06). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a cancer-mortality benefit claim built on secondary analyses, however large and randomised the parent trials.
cards.watchOut: These analyses cannot distinguish preventing metastasis from preventing the cancers that metastasise, and they predate the dedicated adjuvant-aspirin trials in diagnosed cancer. The shelf answers the question as asked — what happened during the randomised trials — and must not be read as a treatment recommendation for established cancer.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rothwell PM et al. The Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 22440947); Rothwell PM et al. The Lancet. 2011 (PMID: 21144578).

shelves.title: Barrett's surveillance (BOSS): 2-yearly endoscopy did not improve survival over 12.8 years — deaths 333 versus 356 (HR 0.95), and surveillance cost $115,563 per QALY
shelves.question: In people with Barrett's oesophagus without dysplasia, does regular endoscopic surveillance detect earlier cancer and improve survival versus no surveillance?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Barrett Esophagus/mortality/pathology/diagnosis/therapy · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Esophageal Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/diagnosis · Aged · Adenocarcinoma/pathology/mortality/diagnosis · Esophagoscopy/adverse effects · United Kingdom · Disease Progression · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Time Factors · Precancerous Conditions/pathology/mortality/diagnosis · Neoplasm Staging
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — on survival, in the first randomised trial of the practice. BOSS (Old O et al., PMID: 40180292) randomised 3,453 patients with Barrett's oesophagus at 109 UK centres to 2-yearly surveillance endoscopy or endoscopy only when symptoms required it, with a minimum of 10 years of follow-up (median 12.8 years). Overall survival did not differ: 333 deaths among 1,733 surveillance patients versus 356 among 1,719 at-need patients (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10). Cancer-specific survival did not differ (108 versus 106 cancer deaths; HR 1.01), nor did time to oesophageal adenocarcinoma diagnosis (40 versus 31 diagnoses; HR 1.32, CI crossing 1) or cancer stage at diagnosis; serious adverse events were similar (0.46% versus 0.41%). The alongside economic evaluation (Deidda M et al., PMID: 40383306) found surveillance cost more ($5,309 versus $3,182) for a negligible QALY gain (8.647 versus 8.629) — $115,563 per QALY gained over a modelled 22.8-year horizon. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): regular 2-yearly surveillance did not improve overall or cancer-specific survival in BOSS and is unlikely to be cost-effective at that interval. Tier C: a single trial carrying a mortality null — for the developer's personal review.

cards.headline: Old 2025 (BOSS): overall survival HR 0.95 (0.82–1.10); cancer deaths 108 versus 106; adenocarcinoma diagnoses 40 versus 31
cards.summary: Old 2025 (BOSS): overall survival HR 0.95 (0.82–1.10); cancer deaths 108 versus 106; adenocarcinoma diagnoses 40 versus 31
cards.people: 3,453 patients with Barrett's oesophagus at 109 UK centres, randomised to 2-yearly surveillance endoscopy (n=1,733) or 'at-need' endoscopy offered for symptoms only (n=1,719). Minimum follow-up 10 years; median follow-up for the primary outcome (overall survival, intention-to-treat) was 12.8 years.
cards.result: There was no evidence of a difference in overall survival (333 deaths in the surveillance arm versus 356 in the at-need arm; hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.10; P=.503), cancer-specific survival (108 versus 106 deaths from any cancer; HR 1.01, 0.77 to 1.33), time to diagnosis of oesophageal adenocarcinoma (40 versus 31 patients diagnosed; HR 1.32, 0.82 to 2.11), or cancer stage at diagnosis. Serious adverse events related to interventions were reported by 8 surveillance patients (0.46%) and 7 at-need patients (0.41%). The authors concluded at-need endoscopy may be a safe alternative for low-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Adenocarcinoma was rare (71 diagnoses in 3,453 patients over ~13 years), so the trial is powered for overall survival, not for small cancer-specific effects in higher-risk subgroups (long-segment Barrett's, dysplasia at entry) — BOSS enrolled a largely non-dysplastic, lower-risk population and its null should not be stretched to dysplastic Barrett's, where surveillance and ablation rest on different evidence.
cards.source: Old O et al. Barrett's Oesophagus Surveillance Versus Endoscopy at Need Study (BOSS): A Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 40180292. Registry ID: NCT00987857. randomised controlled trial (old 2025, boss) 3,453 patients with barrett's oesophagus at 109 uk centres, randomised to 2-yearly surveillance endoscopy (n=1,733) or 'at-need' endoscopy offered for symptoms only (n=1,719). minimum follow-up 10 years; median follow-up for the primary outcome (overall survival, intention-to-treat) was 12.8 years. there was no evidence of a difference in overall survival (333 deaths in the surveillance arm versus 356 in the at-need arm; hazard ratio 0.95, 95% ci 0.82 to 1.10; p=.503), cancer-specific survival (108 versus 106 deaths from any cancer; hr 1.01, 0.77 to 1.33), time to diagnosis of oesophageal adenocarcinoma (40 versus 31 patients diagnosed; hr 1.32, 0.82 to 2.11), or cancer stage at diagnosis. serious adverse events related to interventions were reported by 8 surveillance patients (0.46%) and 7 at-need patients (0.41%). the authors concluded at-need endoscopy may be a safe alternative for low-risk patients. adenocarcinoma was rare (71 diagnoses in 3,453 patients over ~13 years), so the trial is powered for overall survival, not for small cancer-specific effects in higher-risk subgroups (long-segment barrett's, dysplasia at entry) — boss enrolled a largely non-dysplastic, lower-risk population and its null should not be stretched to dysplastic barrett's, where surveillance and ablation rest on different evidence. old o et al. barrett's oesophagus surveillance versus endoscopy at need study (boss): a randomized controlled trial. gastroenterology. 2025. pmid: 40180292. registry id: nct00987857. mesh: humans · barrett esophagus/mortality/pathology/diagnosis/therapy · male · female · middle aged · esophageal neoplasms/mortality/pathology/diagnosis · aged · adenocarcinoma/pathology/mortality/diagnosis · esophagoscopy/adverse effects · united kingdom · disease progression · early detection of cancer/methods · time factors · precancerous conditions/pathology/mortality/diagnosis · neoplasm staging

cards.headline: Deidda 2025 (BOSS economic evaluation): surveillance $5,309 versus $3,182 per patient, QALYs 8.647 versus 8.629 — $115,563 per QALY
cards.summary: Deidda 2025 (BOSS economic evaluation): surveillance $5,309 versus $3,182 per patient, QALYs 8.647 versus 8.629 — $115,563 per QALY
cards.type: Economic evaluation alongside a randomised trial (Deidda 2025)
cards.people: The BOSS trial population (3,453 patients), with costs and quality-of-life outcomes from the trial and a decision-tree/Markov model extrapolating a further 10 years beyond the trial (22.8-year horizon). The surveillance arm did identify more high-grade dysplasia over the trial's median 12.8 years of follow-up.
cards.result: Total costs were $5,309 with 2-yearly surveillance versus $3,182 with at-need endoscopy; total QALYs were 8.647 versus 8.629. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for 2-yearly surveillance was $115,563 per QALY gained; sensitivity analyses on the proportion of undetected high-grade dysplasia in the at-need arm gave $94,513 per QALY (best case) to $146,272 per QALY (worst case). The authors concluded surveillance every 2 to 3 years is unlikely to be cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: An economic model built on a trial whose cancer endpoints were null: the QALY difference (0.018) is far inside modelling uncertainty, and the result depends on assumptions about undetected high-grade dysplasia in the at-need arm. It corroborates the trial's clinical null in cost terms; it is not independent clinical evidence.
cards.source: Deidda M et al. Cost-Effectiveness of Regular Surveillance Versus Endoscopy at Need for Patients With Barrett's Esophagus: Economic Evaluation Alongside the Barrett's Oesophagus Surveillance Study (BOSS) Randomized Controlled Trial. Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 40383306. cards.headline: Synthesis: the first randomised test of Barrett's surveillance found no survival benefit to buy — and a six-figure price per QALY for trying
cards.summary: Synthesis: the first randomised test of Barrett's surveillance found no survival benefit to buy — and a six-figure price per QALY for trying
cards.people: BOSS (Old 2025): 3,453 patients with Barrett's oesophagus, 2-yearly surveillance versus symptom-triggered endoscopy, median 12.8 years of follow-up; with its alongside economic evaluation (Deidda 2025).
cards.result: Overall survival HR 0.95 (0.82–1.10); cancer-specific survival HR 1.01; adenocarcinoma diagnoses 40 versus 31 (HR 1.32, not significant); stage at diagnosis unchanged; surveillance cost $115,563 per QALY gained. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the strongest null the evidence allows, from a single very large long trial; Tier C for personal review because the claim is a mortality null resting on one trial.
cards.watchOut: Observational literature long suggested surveillance finds earlier-stage cancer; BOSS shows stage shift did not occur and survival did not move in its population. Patients with dysplasia or long-segment disease were not the trial's centre of gravity — do not apply this shelf to them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Old O et al. Gastroenterology. 2025 (PMID: 40180292); Deidda M et al. Gastroenterology. 2025 (PMID: 40383306).

shelves.title: Oxybutynin for hot flushes on androgen deprivation (Alliance A222001): flushes per day fell by 6.89 on 5 mg versus 2.15 on placebo — one small 6-week trial
shelves.question: In men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy for prostate cancer who have hot flushes, does oxybutynin reduce flush frequency versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Androgen Antagonists/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Hot Flashes/chemically induced/drug therapy · Mandelic Acids/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Muscarinic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Prostatic Neoplasms/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small, short, well-blinded trial with a clear dose response. Alliance A222001 (Stish BJ et al., PMID: 41587370) randomised 88 men on a stable androgen-deprivation regimen with at least 28 hot flushes per week to oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, or placebo for 6 weeks; 81 were analysed. Hot flushes per day fell by 2.15 on placebo, 4.77 on 2.5 mg (P=.02) and 6.89 on 5 mg (P<.001) from a baseline average of 10.1 flushes per day; daily hot-flush scores fell by 4.85, 9.94 (P=.07) and 13.95 points (P=.002) respectively. Interference with daily life (HFRDIS) improved by 14.2 points on 2.5 mg (P=.042) and 20.7 points on 5 mg (P<.01) versus 3.1 on placebo. No treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): oxybutynin reduces hot-flush frequency and interference in men on ADT over 6 weeks, with a dose gradient favouring 5 mg twice daily; Tier C because a single small trial carries the benefit claim.

cards.headline: Stish 2026 (Alliance A222001): hot flushes per day -6.89 (5 mg), -4.77 (2.5 mg), -2.15 (placebo); no grade 3+ treatment-related adverse events
cards.summary: Stish 2026 (Alliance A222001): hot flushes per day -6.89 (5 mg), -4.77 (2.5 mg), -2.15 (placebo); no grade 3+ treatment-related adverse events
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Stish 2026, Alliance A222001)
cards.people: 88 men with prostate cancer on a stable androgen-deprivation regimen reporting at least 28 hot flushes per week, randomised to oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, or matching placebo for 6 weeks; 81 participants were eligible for the final analysis, reporting an average of 10.1 (SD 5.55) hot flushes per day and a mean daily hot-flush score of 18.2 (SD 13.5) at baseline. Primary endpoint: change in patient-reported hot-flush score at 6 weeks.
cards.result: Reductions in hot flushes per day were 2.15 on placebo, 4.77 on oxybutynin 2.5 mg (P=.02 versus placebo) and 6.89 on 5 mg (P<.001). Daily hot-flush scores fell by 4.85, 9.94 (P=.07) and 13.95 points (P=.002) respectively. Hot Flash-Related Daily Interference Scale total scores improved by 14.2 points on 2.5 mg (P=.042) and 20.7 points on 5 mg (P<.01) versus 3.1 points on placebo. No treatment-related grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, 81 analysed patients, and a symptom-diary endpoint: the placebo arm itself improved by 2.15 flushes per day, and anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary effects, cognition in older men) cannot be judged on 6 weeks of exposure in a trial this size. Longer-term benefit and safety in the typically elderly ADT population are unknown.
cards.source: Stish BJ et al. Alliance A222001: Oxybutynin Versus Placebo for the Treatment of Hot Flashes in Patients Receiving Androgen-Deprivation Therapy for Prostate Cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026. PMID: 41587370. Registry ID: NCT04600336. cards.headline: Synthesis: a dose-responsive win in one small trial — enough for POSSIBLE, not for a settled recommendation
cards.summary: Synthesis: a dose-responsive win in one small trial — enough for POSSIBLE, not for a settled recommendation
cards.people: Alliance A222001 (Stish 2026) is the only randomised trial of oxybutynin for ADT-associated hot flushes: 88 randomised, 81 analysed, three arms, 6 weeks.
cards.result: Hot flushes/day: -6.89 (5 mg twice daily) and -4.77 (2.5 mg) versus -2.15 (placebo). Hot-flush score: -13.95 versus -4.85 (P=.002) at 5 mg. Daily-life interference: +20.7-point improvement versus 3.1 on placebo. No grade 3+ treatment-related adverse events in 6 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single-trial benefit claim for the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Hot flushes wane and fluctuate naturally, and diary endpoints are expectation-sensitive despite blinding (anticholinergic dry mouth can unblind). Replication and longer follow-up — particularly cognitive safety in older men — are the missing pieces.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stish BJ et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026 (PMID: 41587370).

shelves.title: Brentuximab vedotin plus AVD in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma (ECHELON-1): 6-year survival 93.9% versus 89.4% on ABVD (HR 0.59) — bought with more neutropenia and neuropathy, less lung toxicity
shelves.question: In adults with advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma, does brentuximab vedotin plus AVD chemotherapy improve progression-free and overall survival versus ABVD?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bleomycin/administration & dosage · Brentuximab Vedotin · Dacarbazine/administration & dosage · Disease-Free Survival · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hodgkin Disease/drug therapy/mortality · Humans · Immunoconjugates/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Immunologic Factors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Neutropenia/chemically induced · Survival Rate · Vinblastine/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large phase 3 trial whose survival advantage grew with follow-up. ECHELON-1 randomised 1,334 patients with previously untreated stage III or IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma to brentuximab vedotin plus AVD (A+AVD) or ABVD. At the primary report (Connors JM et al., PMID: 29224502), 2-year modified progression-free survival was 82.1% versus 77.2% (difference 4.9 percentage points; HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98; P=.04), with interim deaths 28 versus 39. At a median of 73 months (Ansell SM et al., PMID: 35830649), 39 patients on A+AVD and 64 on ABVD had died (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.88; P=.009); 6-year overall survival was 93.9% versus 89.4%, and progression-free survival HR was 0.68. The costs: neutropenia in 58% versus 45% (febrile neutropenia reduced by primary G-CSF prophylaxis, 11% versus 21% without it in early experience) and peripheral neuropathy in 67% versus 43%, mostly resolving; against that, grade ≥3 pulmonary toxicity was under 1% with A+AVD versus 3% with ABVD, and fewer A+AVD patients needed subsequent therapy or developed second cancers (23 versus 32). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): A+AVD improves progression-free and overall survival over ABVD in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma. Tier C: a mortality benefit resting on a single trial goes to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Connors 2018 (ECHELON-1, primary): 2-year modified PFS 82.1% versus 77.2% (HR 0.77); neutropenia 58% versus 45%, neuropathy 67% versus 43%
cards.summary: Connors 2018 (ECHELON-1, primary): 2-year modified PFS 82.1% versus 77.2% (HR 0.77); neutropenia 58% versus 45%, neuropathy 67% versus 43%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, primary report (Connors 2018, ECHELON-1)
cards.people: 1,334 patients with previously untreated stage III or IV classic Hodgkin lymphoma, randomised to brentuximab vedotin, doxorubicin, vinblastine and dacarbazine (A+AVD, n=664) or doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine (ABVD, n=670), for up to six cycles. Primary endpoint: modified progression-free survival (progression, death, or non-complete response with subsequent therapy) by independent review; median follow-up 24.6 months.
cards.result: Two-year modified progression-free survival was 82.1% (95% CI 78.8 to 85.0) on A+AVD versus 77.2% (73.7 to 80.4) on ABVD — a difference of 4.9 percentage points (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98; P=.04). Deaths were 28 versus 39 (interim overall survival HR 0.73, 0.45 to 1.18; P=.20). Neutropenia occurred in 58% versus 45%; febrile neutropenia on A+AVD was 11% in the 83 patients receiving primary G-CSF prophylaxis versus 21% in those not receiving it. Peripheral neuropathy occurred in 67% versus 43% (67% of affected A+AVD patients had resolution or improvement by last follow-up). Grade ≥3 pulmonary toxicity: under 1% versus 3%. Of on-treatment deaths, 7 of 9 on A+AVD were associated with neutropenia and 11 of 13 on ABVD with pulmonary toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the primary endpoint is a modified PFS that counts starting subsequent therapy as an event — a softer composite than standard PFS, chosen by the sponsor; the unmodified survival question needed the 2022 report. Neuropathy and neutropenia burdens are real and front-loaded.
cards.source: Connors JM et al. Brentuximab Vedotin with Chemotherapy for Stage III or IV Hodgkin's Lymphoma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29224502. Registry ID: NCT01712490. cards.headline: Ansell 2022 (ECHELON-1, 6 years): deaths 39 versus 64 (HR 0.59, P=.009); 6-year survival 93.9% versus 89.4%; PFS HR 0.68
cards.summary: Ansell 2022 (ECHELON-1, 6 years): deaths 39 versus 64 (HR 0.59, P=.009); 6-year survival 93.9% versus 89.4%; PFS HR 0.68
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, overall-survival report (Ansell 2022, ECHELON-1)
cards.people: The same 1,334 ECHELON-1 participants (A+AVD n=664; ABVD n=670), followed for a median of 73.0 months. Key secondary endpoint: overall survival in the intention-to-treat population; progression-free survival and subsequent therapy, second cancers and safety also assessed.
cards.result: Deaths numbered 39 on A+AVD versus 64 on ABVD (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.88; P=.009). Six-year overall survival estimates were 93.9% (95% CI 91.6 to 95.5) versus 89.4% (86.6 to 91.7) — an absolute difference of 4.5 percentage points. Progression-free survival favoured A+AVD (HR 0.68, 0.53 to 0.86). Fewer A+AVD patients received subsequent therapy including transplantation, and fewer second cancers were reported (23 versus 32 patients). Peripheral neuropathy remained more frequent with A+AVD but had resolved or ameliorated in most patients in both groups by last follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, however large: overall survival was a secondary endpoint tested after a non-significant interim look, and subsequent-therapy differences (including transplant access) can mediate survival in an open-label trial. Results apply to stage III/IV disease treated with six cycles and G-CSF support, not to early-stage or PET-adapted strategies tested elsewhere.
cards.source: Ansell SM et al. Overall Survival with Brentuximab Vedotin in Stage III or IV Hodgkin's Lymphoma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35830649. Registry ID: NCT01712490. shelves.title: Acalabrutinib versus ibrutinib in relapsed CLL (ELEVATE-RR): identical progression-free survival (38.4 months both arms, HR 1.00) with less atrial fibrillation (9.4% versus 16.0%)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does acalabrutinib match ibrutinib for progression-free survival with less atrial fibrillation and hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Adenine/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Benzamides/administration & dosage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines/administration & dosage · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Pyrazines/administration & dosage · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: SPLIT — equal efficacy, unequal tolerability, in the first head-to-head randomised trial of BTK inhibitors. ELEVATE-RR (Byrd JC et al., PMID: 34310172) randomised 533 patients with previously treated CLL harbouring del(17p) or del(11q) to acalabrutinib 100 mg twice daily or ibrutinib 420 mg once daily. At a median follow-up of 40.9 months, acalabrutinib was noninferior for progression-free survival: median 38.4 months in both arms (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.27). All-grade atrial fibrillation/flutter was significantly less frequent with acalabrutinib (9.4% versus 16.0%, P=.02), and fewer patients stopped acalabrutinib for adverse events (14.7% versus 21.3%). Grade ≥3 infections were comparable (30.8% versus 30.0%), Richter transformation similar (3.8% versus 4.9%), and median overall survival was not reached in either arm (HR 0.82, 0.59 to 1.15; deaths 23.5% versus 27.5%). PROPOSED SPLIT: acalabrutinib matches ibrutinib on progression-free survival in high-risk relapsed CLL and wins on atrial fibrillation and treatment discontinuation; the trial record does not report the hypertension comparison the question also asks about. Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.

cards.headline: Byrd 2021 (ELEVATE-RR): PFS noninferior (HR 1.00); atrial fibrillation 9.4% versus 16.0% (P=.02); discontinuation for adverse events 14.7% versus 21.3%
cards.summary: Byrd 2021 (ELEVATE-RR): PFS noninferior (HR 1.00); atrial fibrillation 9.4% versus 16.0% (P=.02); discontinuation for adverse events 14.7% versus 21.3%
cards.people: 533 patients with previously treated chronic lymphocytic leukaemia with centrally confirmed del(17)(p13.1) or del(11)(q22.3), randomised to oral acalabrutinib 100 mg twice daily (n=268) or ibrutinib 420 mg once daily (n=265) until progression or unacceptable toxicity. Primary endpoint: independent-review-assessed noninferiority of progression-free survival. Median follow-up 40.9 months; 46.3% of acalabrutinib and 41.1% of ibrutinib patients remained on treatment at data cutoff.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 38.4 months in both arms (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.27) — noninferiority met. All-grade atrial fibrillation/flutter occurred in 9.4% on acalabrutinib versus 16.0% on ibrutinib (P=.02). Grade ≥3 infections were comparable (30.8% vs 30.0%), as was Richter transformation (3.8% vs 4.9%). Median overall survival was not reached in either arm (HR 0.82, 0.59 to 1.15), with 63 deaths (23.5%) on acalabrutinib and 73 (27.5%) on ibrutinib. Discontinuations for adverse events: 14.7% versus 21.3%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in a genomically high-risk relapsed population (all patients had del(17p) or del(11q)) — the tolerability gap may differ in unselected or treatment-naive patients. The abstract record does not report hypertension rates, so the hypertension half of the candidate question cannot be answered from the carded record and is flagged rather than filled in. Noninferiority on PFS is not equivalence on survival: the OS confidence interval (0.59 to 1.15) is wide.
cards.source: Byrd JC et al. Acalabrutinib Versus Ibrutinib in Previously Treated Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: Results of the First Randomized Phase III Trial. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2021. cards.people: ELEVATE-RR (Byrd 2021) is the only randomised head-to-head trial of acalabrutinib versus ibrutinib: 533 patients with previously treated, cytogenetically high-risk CLL, median follow-up 40.9 months.

shelves.title: After high-risk adenomas: starting surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years was noninferior to 3 years for colorectal cancer at 5 years in EPoS II — an interim read of a 10-year trial
shelves.question: In patients who have had high-risk adenomas removed, can the first surveillance colonoscopy wait until 5 years instead of the currently recommended 3 years without increasing colorectal cancer incidence?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Adenoma/pathology/surgery · Colonic Polyps/pathology/surgery · Colonoscopy/methods/statistics & numerical data · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/epidemiology/pathology/prevention & control · Early Detection of Cancer/methods/statistics & numerical data · Follow-Up Studies · Incidence · Time Factors · Neoplasm Staging · Europe/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the interim evidence, waiting longer found no more cancer. EPoS II randomised 10,799 patients with high-risk adenomas in eight European countries to a first surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years or at 3 years (Jover R et al., PMID: 42748427). At the 5.5-year interim analysis, the 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence was 0.77% with 5-year surveillance and 0.82% with 3-year surveillance (difference -0.05 percentage points; upper boundary of the 99.12% CI 0.68, inside the prespecified 0.7-point noninferiority margin), with 5 colorectal cancer deaths in total (3 vs 2). The supporting UK cohort of 21,318 post-polypectomy patients (Cross AJ et al., PMID: 33674342) shows why the question matters: without surveillance, high-risk patients' cancer incidence ran above the general population's (SIR 1.30), so surveillance itself is not being questioned — only its timing. This is a single trial, reported at interim, with the definitive 10-year analysis still to come, and noninferiority margins are a judgement, not a fact. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): at 5 years, a 5-year first interval performed no worse than 3 years in high-risk adenomas — Tier C because it rests on one interim trial report bearing on a cancer endpoint.

cards.headline: EPoS II (Jover 2026, interim): cancer in 0.77% (5-year interval) versus 0.82% (3-year interval) — noninferiority met at 5.5 years in 10,799 high-risk patients
cards.summary: EPoS II (Jover 2026, interim): cancer in 0.77% (5-year interval) versus 0.82% (3-year interval) — noninferiority met at 5.5 years in 10,799 high-risk patients
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial, interim analysis (Jover 2026, EPoS II)
cards.people: 10,799 patients in eight European countries with high-risk adenomas (at least one adenoma ≥10 mm, high-grade dysplasia, or villous growth, or 3 to 10 adenomas) after complete polyp removal, randomised to first surveillance colonoscopy at 5 years (5,398) or at 3 years (5,401, who also had colonoscopy at 5 years). Primary endpoint: cumulative colorectal cancer incidence at 10 years; prespecified noninferiority margin 0.7 percentage points.
cards.result: At the interim analysis after 5.5 years of follow-up, 5-year cumulative colorectal cancer incidence was 0.77% in the 5-year group and 0.82% in the 3-year group (difference -0.05 percentage points); the upper boundary of the one-sided 99.12% confidence interval was 0.68, meeting the noninferiority criterion. Cancer stage distribution did not appear to differ substantially. Five patients died of colorectal cancer: 3 (0.06%) in the 5-year group and 2 (0.04%) in the 3-year group.
cards.watchOut: Interim, not final: the trial's own primary endpoint is at 10 years, and cancers seeded but not yet detectable at year 5 could still separate the strategies. Noninferiority was judged against a 0.7-percentage-point margin chosen by the investigators; a reader who wants a tighter guarantee should wait for the 10-year analysis. Inverse probability weighting was needed for missed surveillance colonoscopies.
cards.source: Jover R et al. Colonoscopy Intervals and Colorectal Cancer Incidence after Adenoma Removal. The New England journal of medicine. 2026. PMID: 42748427. Registry ID: NCT02319928. cards.headline: Cross 2021: without surveillance, high-risk patients ran a higher cancer incidence than the general population (SIR 1.30) — the risk EPoS II is timing against
cards.summary: Cross 2021: without surveillance, high-risk patients ran a higher cancer incidence than the general population (SIR 1.30) — the risk EPoS II is timing against
cards.people: 21,318 patients who underwent colonoscopy and polypectomy at 17 UK hospitals, mostly between 2000 and 2010, followed through 2017 (median 10.1 years; 368 colorectal cancers). The 2020 UK guideline definition classifies 29% as high-risk.
cards.result: Compared with the general population, colorectal cancer incidence without surveillance was higher in patients with high-grade dysplasia (SIR 1.74, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.42) and in high-risk patients overall (SIR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.62); for high-risk patients after a first surveillance colonoscopy the SIR was 1.22 (0.91 to 1.60). Low-risk patients without surveillance ran below population incidence (SIR 0.75, 0.63 to 0.88).
cards.watchOut: Observational and retrospective: who received surveillance was not randomised, and standardised incidence ratios compare against the general population, not against a randomised alternative interval. This card supplies the risk context for EPoS II; it does not itself compare 3- against 5-year intervals, and its ratios sit in the range that cannot carry a shelf on their own.

shelves.title: One round of cervical screening in rural India: HPV testing cut cervical cancer deaths by about half (HR 0.52); visual inspection worked in one trial (HR 0.65) and not in the other
shelves.question: In low-resource settings without organised cytology programmes, does a single round of screening — HPV testing, cytology, or visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) — reduce cervical cancer incidence and death?
shelves.mesh: Acetic Acid · Adult · Biopsy · Colposcopy · Cytological Techniques · Female · Humans · Incidence · India · Mass Screening/methods · Middle Aged · Papillomaviridae/isolation & purification · Papillomavirus Infections/diagnosis · Predictive Value of Tests · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/diagnosis/epidemiology/mortality/virology · Uterine Cervical Dysplasia/diagnosis/epidemiology/virology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the test. In the Osmanabad cluster-randomised trial of 131,746 women aged 30–59 (Sankaranarayanan R et al., PMID: 19339719), a single round of HPV testing produced 34 cervical cancer deaths versus 64 in the control group (hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.83) and fewer advanced cancers (HR 0.47); neither cytology nor VIA significantly reduced advanced cancers or deaths in that trial. In the Dindigul cluster trial of about 80,000 women (Sankaranarayanan R et al., PMID: 17679017), one round of nurse-delivered VIA did reduce mortality (83 vs 92 deaths; HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.89) and incidence (HR 0.75). The difference between the VIA results plausibly reflects training and quality assurance, which the Dindigul team emphasise. Both trials are single-round, single-region, and two decades old; organised repeat HPV screening is a different, stronger intervention. PROPOSED SPLIT: HPV testing — benefit shown on deaths in one very large trial; VIA — benefit in one of two trials, contingent on programme quality. Tier C because mortality benefit claims rest substantially on single trials.

cards.headline: Osmanabad (Sankaranarayanan 2009): one round of HPV testing — 34 vs 64 cervical cancer deaths (HR 0.52); cytology and VIA arms showed no significant reduction
cards.summary: Osmanabad (Sankaranarayanan 2009): one round of HPV testing — 34 vs 64 cervical cancer deaths (HR 0.52); cytology and VIA arms showed no significant reduction
cards.people: 52 village clusters with 131,746 healthy women aged 30–59 in Osmanabad district, India, randomised to screening by HPV testing (34,126 women), cytologic testing (32,058), VIA (34,074) or standard care (31,488). Screen-positive women received colposcopy, biopsy and treatment of precancerous lesions or cancer.
cards.result: Cervical cancer was diagnosed in 127 women in the HPV group (39 at stage II or higher) versus 118 in controls (82 advanced): hazard ratio for advanced cancer 0.47 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.69). Deaths from cervical cancer: 34 in the HPV group versus 64 in controls (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.83). No significant reductions in advanced cancers or deaths were observed in the cytology or VIA groups. Mild adverse events were reported in 0.1% of screened women.
cards.watchOut: One round of screening, one district, follow-up through the first decade of the 2000s. The mortality result is a single trial's — large and randomised, but unreplicated for HPV screening at the time — and it tests a whole pathway (test, colposcopy, treatment), not the test alone.

cards.headline: Dindigul (Sankaranarayanan 2007): one round of nurse-delivered VIA — mortality HR 0.65 and incidence HR 0.75, contradicting Osmanabad's VIA arm
cards.summary: Dindigul (Sankaranarayanan 2007): one round of nurse-delivered VIA — mortality HR 0.65 and incidence HR 0.75, contradicting Osmanabad's VIA arm
cards.people: 114 clusters in Dindigul district, India: 49,311 eligible women aged 30–59 in the intervention group (31,343 screened, 63.6%) and 30,958 women receiving standard care. VIA was performed by trained nurses, with colposcopy, biopsy and cryotherapy at the same visit where appropriate.
cards.result: Over 2000–2006, the intervention group accrued 167 cervical cancer cases and 83 deaths versus 158 cases and 92 deaths in controls: incidence hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.95) and mortality hazard ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.89). Of 1,874 women found with precancerous lesions, 72% received treatment.
cards.watchOut: Only 63.6% of eligible women were screened, and person-years differed markedly between arms (274,430 vs 178,781) — the hazard ratios carry the comparison, but the trial's VIA success came with intensive training and sustained quality assurance that the authors themselves name as the condition for the effect.

cards.summary: Synthesis: screening can prevent cervical cancer deaths in low-resource settings — HPV testing on the strongest single-trial evidence, VIA only where quality is assured
cards.people: Two cluster-randomised trials in rural India totalling over 210,000 women, each testing a single round of screening against standard care.
cards.result: HPV testing: deaths 34 vs 64 (HR 0.52). VIA: deaths HR 0.65 in Dindigul, no significant effect in Osmanabad. Cytology: no significant effect in Osmanabad. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the mortality claims are single-trial claims, and the two VIA trials disagree.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial answers the modern programme question — repeated HPV screening at 5-year intervals with self-sampling and thermal ablation — and both predate HPV vaccination cohorts reaching screening age. shelves.title: Elacestrant in pretreated ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.70 overall and 0.55 in ESR1-mutated tumours — one open-label phase 3 trial, nausea in 35%
shelves.question: In patients with metastatic hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer and ESR1 mutations after endocrine therapy, does elacestrant improve progression-free survival compared with standard endocrine therapy?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/metabolism · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4 · Estrogen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases/metabolism · Receptors, Estrogen/metabolism · Tetrahydronaphthalenes
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In EMERALD (Bidard FC et al., PMID: 35584336), 477 patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after one to two lines of endocrine therapy (all pretreated with a CDK4/6 inhibitor) were randomised to elacestrant or standard endocrine monotherapy: progression-free survival hazard ratio was 0.70 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; P=.002) in all patients and 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.77; P=.0005) in the 47.8% with detectable ESR1 mutations — the subgroup this question asks about, where the benefit was largest. Treatment-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 7.2% on elacestrant versus 3.1% on standard care, and nausea of any grade in 35.0% versus 18.8%. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): elacestrant prolonged progression-free survival in one phase 3 trial, most clearly in ESR1-mutated disease; no survival result is reported in this record.

cards.headline: Bidard 2022 (EMERALD): PFS HR 0.70 (P=.002) in all patients and 0.55 (P=.0005) in ESR1-mutated disease — treatment-related grade 3/4 events 7.2% versus 3.1%, nausea 35.0% versus 18.8%
cards.summary: Bidard 2022 (EMERALD): PFS HR 0.70 (P=.002) in all patients and 0.55 (P=.0005) in ESR1-mutated disease — treatment-related grade 3/4 events 7.2% versus 3.1%, nausea 35.0% versus 18.8%
cards.people: 477 patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer who had received one to two lines of endocrine therapy, required pretreatment with a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and at most one line of chemotherapy, randomised to elacestrant 400 mg orally once daily (n=239) or standard-of-care endocrine monotherapy (n=238). ESR1 mutation was detected in 47.8% of patients; 43.4% had received two prior endocrine therapies.
cards.result: Progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was prolonged with elacestrant in all patients (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.88; P=.002) and in patients with ESR1 mutation (hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.77; P=.0005). Treatment-related grade 3/4 adverse events occurred in 7.2% on elacestrant and 3.1% on standard care; treatment-related events leading to discontinuation in 3.4% versus 0.9%. Nausea of any grade occurred in 35.0% versus 18.8% (grade 3/4 in 2.5% and 0.9%).
cards.watchOut: Single open-label trial — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. The endpoint is progression-free survival; this record reports no overall-survival benefit, and the ESR1-mutated result is a prespecified primary-endpoint population but still a biomarker subgroup of one trial.

shelves.title: Tisotumab vedotin in recurrent cervical cancer after chemotherapy: median survival 11.5 versus 9.5 months (HR 0.70) and response 17.8% versus 5.2% — one open-label phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer previously treated with chemotherapy, does tisotumab vedotin improve survival compared with investigator-choice chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Progression-Free Survival · Survival Analysis · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Oligopeptides/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In innovaTV 301 (Vergote I et al., PMID: 38959480), 502 patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer were randomised to tisotumab vedotin or investigator's-choice chemotherapy as second- or third-line therapy: median overall survival was 11.5 months (95% CI 9.8 to 14.9) versus 9.5 months (95% CI 7.9 to 10.7) — a hazard ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; P=0.004), a 30% relative reduction in the risk of death — median progression-free survival 4.2 versus 2.9 months (HR 0.67), and confirmed response 17.8% versus 5.2%. Grade 3 or greater adverse events occurred in 52.0% on tisotumab vedotin versus 62.3% on chemotherapy, and 14.8% stopped tisotumab vedotin because of toxic effects. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tisotumab vedotin extended survival by a median 2.0 months in one phase 3 trial in a setting with few options.

cards.headline: Vergote 2024 (innovaTV 301): median survival 11.5 versus 9.5 months (HR 0.70, P=0.004); PFS 4.2 versus 2.9 months; response 17.8% versus 5.2% — grade ≥3 events 52.0% versus 62.3%
cards.summary: Vergote 2024 (innovaTV 301): median survival 11.5 versus 9.5 months (HR 0.70, P=0.004); PFS 4.2 versus 2.9 months; response 17.8% versus 5.2% — grade ≥3 events 52.0% versus 62.3%
cards.people: 502 patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer randomised 1:1 to tisotumab vedotin monotherapy 2.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks (n=253) or investigator's choice of chemotherapy (n=249; topotecan, vinorelbine, gemcitabine, irinotecan, or pemetrexed) as second- or third-line therapy.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 11.5 months (95% CI 9.8 to 14.9) on tisotumab vedotin versus 9.5 months (95% CI 7.9 to 10.7) on chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; P=0.004) — a 30% relative reduction in the risk of death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Median progression-free survival was 4.2 versus 2.9 months (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82; P<0.001). Confirmed objective response was 17.8% versus 5.2% (odds ratio 4.0; 95% CI 2.1 to 7.6; P<0.001). At least one treatment-period adverse event occurred in 98.4% versus 99.2%; grade 3 or greater events in 52.0% versus 62.3%; 14.8% stopped tisotumab vedotin because of toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: Single open-label trial — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. The absolute survival gain is a median 2.0 months against a mixed investigator-choice comparator basket, not against one standard regimen.
cards.source: Vergote I et al. Tisotumab Vedotin as Second- or Third-Line Therapy for Recurrent Cervical Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38959480. Registry ID: NCT04697628. shelves.title: Idecabtagene vicleucel in triple-class-exposed relapsed myeloma: median progression-free survival 13.3 versus 4.4 months (HR 0.49) and complete response 39% versus 5% — one open-label phase 3 trial, cytokine release syndrome in 88%
shelves.question: In patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does idecabtagene vicleucel improve progression-free survival compared with standard regimens?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Immunotherapy, Adoptive/adverse effects/methods · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy/therapy · Progression-Free Survival · Receptors, Chimeric Antigen/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In KarMMa-3 (Rodriguez-Otero P et al., PMID: 36762851), 386 patients with relapsed and refractory myeloma after two to four prior regimens (66% triple-class-refractory, 95% daratumumab-refractory) were randomised 2:1 to idecabtagene vicleucel or one of five standard regimens: at median follow-up 18.6 months, median progression-free survival was 13.3 versus 4.4 months (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.65; P<0.001), response 71% versus 42%, and complete response 39% versus 5%; overall-survival data were immature. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 93% versus 75%; among 225 patients who received ide-cel, cytokine release syndrome occurred in 88% (grade ≥3 in 5%) and neurotoxic effects in 15% (grade ≥3 in 3%). Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ide-cel roughly tripled median progression-free survival in one phase 3 trial, with survival benefit not yet shown and substantial CAR T toxicity.

cards.headline: Rodriguez-Otero 2023 (KarMMa-3): median PFS 13.3 versus 4.4 months (HR 0.49, P<0.001); response 71% versus 42%, complete response 39% versus 5% — grade 3–4 events 93% versus 75%
cards.summary: Rodriguez-Otero 2023 (KarMMa-3): median PFS 13.3 versus 4.4 months (HR 0.49, P<0.001); response 71% versus 42%, complete response 39% versus 5% — grade 3–4 events 93% versus 75%
cards.people: 386 adults with relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma after two to four prior regimens including an immunomodulatory agent, a proteasome inhibitor and daratumumab, refractory to the last regimen, randomised 2:1 to idecabtagene vicleucel (150×10⁶ to 450×10⁶ CAR-positive T cells; n=254) or one of five standard regimens (n=132). 66% had triple-class-refractory disease and 95% daratumumab-refractory disease; median follow-up 18.6 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 13.3 months on ide-cel versus 4.4 months on standard regimens (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.49; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.65; P<0.001). A response occurred in 71% versus 42% (P<0.001) and a complete response in 39% versus 5%. Overall-survival data were immature. Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 93% versus 75%. Among the 225 patients who received ide-cel, cytokine release syndrome occurred in 88% (grade ≥3 in 5%) and investigator-identified neurotoxic effects in 15% (grade ≥3 in 3%).
cards.watchOut: Single open-label trial — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. shelves.title: Axicabtagene ciloleucel as second-line therapy for early relapsed large B-cell lymphoma: median event-free survival 8.3 versus 2.0 months (HR 0.40) and 24-month event-free survival 41% versus 16% — one phase 3 trial, grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21%
shelves.question: In patients with early relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, does axicabtagene ciloleucel improve event-free survival compared with standard second-line care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Biological Products/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Female · Humans · Immunotherapy, Adoptive · Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Progression-Free Survival · Receptors, Chimeric Antigen/antagonists & inhibitors · Stem Cell Transplantation · Transplantation, Autologous
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In ZUMA-7 (Locke FL et al., PMID: 34891224), 359 patients whose large B-cell lymphoma was refractory to or had relapsed within 12 months of first-line chemoimmunotherapy were randomised to axicabtagene ciloleucel or standard care (salvage chemoimmunotherapy, then high-dose therapy with autologous transplant in responders): at median follow-up 24.9 months, median event-free survival was 8.3 versus 2.0 months and 24-month event-free survival 41% versus 16% (hazard ratio for event or death 0.40; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.51; P<0.001), response 83% versus 50% with complete response 65% versus 32%, and estimated 2-year overall survival 61% versus 52% at interim analysis. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 91% versus 83%; among axi-cel recipients, grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome occurred in 6% and grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21%, with no deaths from either. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): axi-cel markedly improved event-free survival in one phase 3 trial, with high-grade toxicity on both arms.

cards.people: 359 patients with large B-cell lymphoma refractory to or relapsed no more than 12 months after first-line chemoimmunotherapy, randomised 1:1 to axicabtagene ciloleucel (n=180) or standard care (n=179; two or three cycles of investigator-selected protocol-defined chemoimmunotherapy, followed by high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell transplantation in patients with a response). A response occurred in 83% versus 50%, with complete response in 65% versus 32%. In an interim analysis, estimated overall survival at 2 years was 61% versus 52%. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 91% versus 83%. Among patients who received axi-cel, grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome occurred in 6% and grade ≥3 neurologic events in 21%; no deaths related to cytokine release syndrome or neurologic events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Single trial for this product and question — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. shelves.title: Fixed-duration ibrutinib plus venetoclax in untreated CLL in older or comorbid patients: progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.216 versus chlorambucil–obinutuzumab, undetectable MRD in marrow 55.7% versus 21.0% — one phase 3 trial (GLOW)
shelves.question: In patients with treatment-naive chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does fixed-duration ibrutinib plus venetoclax improve progression-free survival compared with chemoimmunotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy/mortality · Aged · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adenine/analogs & derivatives · Piperidines/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Adult · Comorbidity · Aged, 80 and over · Pyrimidines/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Young Adult · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In GLOW (Kater AP et al., PMID: 38319255), 211 previously untreated patients with CLL who were 65 or older or had comorbidities were randomised to fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax (3 cycles of ibrutinib lead-in, then 12 cycles of the combination) or 6 cycles of chlorambucil–obinutuzumab: at median follow-up 27.7 months there were 22 progression-free-survival events versus 67 (hazard ratio 0.216; 95% CI 0.131 to 0.357; P<0.001), best undetectable minimal residual disease in bone marrow was 55.7% versus 21.0% (P<0.001), and only 4 versus 27 patients had required subsequent therapy. Grade 3 or greater adverse events occurred in 75.5% versus 69.5%, with neutropenia most common in both arms (34.9% versus 49.5%); all-cause deaths were 10.4% versus 11.4% at this report. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fixed-duration ibrutinib–venetoclax gave a large progression-free-survival advantage in one trial in older or comorbid patients; a survival advantage was not shown at this follow-up.

cards.headline: Kater 2022 (GLOW): 22 versus 67 PFS events (HR 0.216, P<0.001); marrow undetectable MRD 55.7% versus 21.0%; subsequent therapy needed by 4 versus 27 patients — grade ≥3 events 75.5% versus 69.5%
cards.summary: Kater 2022 (GLOW): 22 versus 67 PFS events (HR 0.216, P<0.001); marrow undetectable MRD 55.7% versus 21.0%; subsequent therapy needed by 4 versus 27 patients — grade ≥3 events 75.5% versus 69.5%
cards.people: 211 patients with previously untreated CLL aged 65 or older, or aged 18–64 with a Cumulative Illness Rating Scale score above 6 or creatinine clearance below 70 mL/min, randomised 1:1 to ibrutinib–venetoclax (n=106; 3 cycles of ibrutinib lead-in then 12 cycles of ibrutinib plus venetoclax) or chlorambucil–obinutuzumab (n=105; 6 cycles). Median follow-up 27.7 months.
cards.result: Progression-free survival by independent review was significantly longer with ibrutinib–venetoclax: 22 versus 67 events (hazard ratio 0.216; 95% CI 0.131 to 0.357; P<0.001), consistent across predefined subgroups. Best undetectable minimal residual disease in bone marrow by next-generation sequencing was 55.7% versus 21.0% (P<0.001); sustained undetectable MRD in peripheral blood from 3 to 12 months after treatment ended was 84.5% versus 29.3%. Four versus 27 patients required subsequent therapy (HR 0.143; 95% CI 0.050 to 0.410). Grade 3 or greater adverse events occurred in 75.5% versus 69.5%, neutropenia being most common in both arms (34.9% versus 49.5%). All-cause deaths were 11 (10.4%) versus 12 (11.4%).
cards.watchOut: Single open-label trial — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. The comparator, chlorambucil–obinutuzumab, is the gentler chemoimmunotherapy used in older or comorbid patients, not the strongest modern alternative; deaths did not differ at 27.7 months, and the trial population excludes younger, fit patients.
cards.source: Kater AP et al. Fixed-Duration Ibrutinib-Venetoclax in Patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia and Comorbidities. NEJM Evidence. 2022. PMID: 38319255. Registry ID: NCT03462719. shelves.title: Sunitinib in advanced GIST after imatinib failure: median time to tumour progression 27.3 versus 6.4 weeks (HR 0.33) — one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, unblinded early at interim analysis
shelves.question: In patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour progressing on imatinib, does sunitinib improve time to tumour progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzamides · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors/drug therapy/mortality/pathology · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate · Indoles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrimidines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyrroles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sunitinib · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on a single randomised trial. In the pivotal trial (Demetri GD et al., PMID: 17046465), 312 patients with advanced GIST resistant to or intolerant of imatinib were randomised 2:1 to sunitinib 50 mg daily (4 weeks on, 2 weeks off) or placebo: median time to tumour progression was 27.3 weeks (95% CI 16.0 to 32.1) versus 6.4 weeks (95% CI 4.4 to 10.0), hazard ratio 0.33 (P<0.0001) — a 67% relative reduction in the hazard of progression, with the absolute medians printed alongside. The trial was unblinded early after a planned interim analysis showed the difference. The most common treatment-related adverse events were fatigue, diarrhoea, skin discolouration and nausea. Single-trial flag under the relaxed beyond-4,000 intake tier; sunitinib is mentioned as prior therapy on other GIST shelves but this trial had no card-home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): sunitinib quadrupled median time to progression after imatinib failure in one double-blind trial stopped early at interim analysis.

cards.headline: Demetri 2006: median time to tumour progression 27.3 versus 6.4 weeks (HR 0.33, P<0.0001) — trial unblinded early at planned interim analysis; commonest harms fatigue, diarrhoea, skin discolouration, nausea
cards.summary: Demetri 2006: median time to tumour progression 27.3 versus 6.4 weeks (HR 0.33, P<0.0001) — trial unblinded early at planned interim analysis; commonest harms fatigue, diarrhoea, skin discolouration, nausea
cards.people: 312 patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumour resistant to or intolerant of previous imatinib, randomised 2:1 to sunitinib (n=207) or placebo (n=105), given orally once daily at a 50 mg starting dose in 6-week cycles of 4 weeks on and 2 weeks off treatment, in a multicentre international trial.
cards.result: Median time to tumour progression was 27.3 weeks (95% CI 16.0 to 32.1) on sunitinib versus 6.4 weeks (95% CI 4.4 to 10.0) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.33; P<0.0001) — a 67% relative reduction in the hazard of progression, with the absolute medians printed alongside. The trial was unblinded early when a planned interim analysis showed significantly longer time to progression with sunitinib. Therapy was reasonably well tolerated; the most common treatment-related adverse events were fatigue, diarrhoea, skin discolouration and nausea. The record states significant clinical benefit including disease control and superior survival with sunitinib, without printing the survival figures in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: Single trial — carried under the relaxed intake tier and flagged single-trial. Early unblinding at interim analysis can exaggerate the effect size, the primary endpoint is time to progression rather than survival, and the abstract does not print the survival numbers behind its survival claim, so none are carded here.

shelves.title: Denosumab on androgen deprivation: new vertebral fractures 1.5% versus 3.9% at 36 months in one large trial — bone density up at every site, adverse events no higher
shelves.question: In men receiving androgen deprivation therapy for non-metastatic prostate cancer, does denosumab reduce fractures compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androgen Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Denosumab · Double-Blind Method · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology/prevention & control · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/agonists · Humans · Incidence · Injections, Subcutaneous · Lumbar Vertebrae/drug effects/injuries/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Orchiectomy · Osteoporosis/chemically induced/drug therapy · Prostatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/physiopathology/surgery · RANK Ligand/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large double-blind trial, a fracture endpoint actually won. In HALT (Smith MR et al., PMID: 19671656), 1,468 men on androgen-deprivation therapy for nonmetastatic prostate cancer received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months or placebo. New vertebral fractures at 36 months occurred in 1.5% on denosumab versus 3.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.38; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.78; P=0.006) — a 62% relative reduction, 2.4 percentage points absolute. Lumbar-spine bone mineral density at 24 months rose 5.6% on denosumab versus a 1.0% loss on placebo (P<0.001), with gains at hip, femoral neck and radius. Rates of adverse events were similar between groups. The catch is scope: the fracture win is vertebral fractures in a single trial; non-vertebral and hip fracture rates are not reported as won in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab reduces new vertebral fractures and raises bone density in men on androgen deprivation, on the strength of one trial.

New vertebral fractures at 36 months: 1.5% on denosumab versus 3.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.38; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.78; P=0.006) — a 62% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed alongside. shelves.title: Trabectedin versus dacarbazine in pretreated liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma: progression-free survival 4.2 versus 1.5 months — overall survival a draw (12.4 versus 12.9 months)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after anthracycline therapy, does trabectedin improve progression-free survival compared with dacarbazine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Alkylating/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dacarbazine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Dioxoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Disease-Free Survival · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Leiomyosarcoma/drug therapy · Liposarcoma/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Rate · Tetrahydroisoquinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Trabectedin · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for disease control, not for survival. In the single phase 3 trial (Demetri GD et al., PMID: 26371143), 518 patients with metastatic liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after an anthracycline and at least one further regimen were randomised 2:1 to trabectedin or dacarbazine. Median progression-free survival was 4.2 versus 1.5 months (hazard ratio 0.55; P<.001) — a 45% relative reduction in the risk of progression or death. Overall survival, the trial's primary endpoint, did not differ: median 12.4 versus 12.9 months (hazard ratio 0.87; P=.37) at an interim analysis with 64% of patients censored. The commonest grade 3–4 adverse effects on trabectedin were myelosuppression and transient transaminase elevations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): trabectedin delays progression versus dacarbazine in heavily pretreated L-sarcomas; a survival benefit was not shown.

cards.headline: Demetri 2016: median PFS 4.2 versus 1.5 months (HR 0.55, P<.001) — median OS 12.4 versus 12.9 months (HR 0.87, P=.37)
cards.summary: Demetri 2016: median PFS 4.2 versus 1.5 months (HR 0.55, P<.001) — median OS 12.4 versus 12.9 months (HR 0.87, P=.37)
cards.people: 518 patients with advanced liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma after prior anthracycline therapy and at least one additional systemic regimen, randomised 2:1 to trabectedin (n=345) or dacarbazine (n=173) intravenously every 3 weeks.
cards.result: Final progression-free survival analysis: median PFS 4.2 months on trabectedin versus 1.5 months on dacarbazine (hazard ratio 0.55; P<.001), a 45% relative reduction in the risk of disease progression or death, with benefit across all preplanned subgroups. Interim overall survival (the primary endpoint; 64% censored): median 12.4 versus 12.9 months (hazard ratio 0.87; P=.37). Most common grade 3–4 adverse effects on trabectedin were myelosuppression and transient elevation of transaminases, consistent with both agents' known toxicities.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged), and the trial's own primary endpoint — overall survival — was null at interim analysis; the shelf's claim is disease control only. The trial was open-label in design as reported in this record (no blinding is stated), so progression assessment carries more weight than it would in a blinded trial.

shelves.title: Regorafenib after sorafenib in liver cancer (RESORCE): median survival 10.6 versus 7.8 months — the first second-line survival win, paid for in hypertension and hand-foot reactions
shelves.question: In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma progressing on sorafenib, does regorafenib improve survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Niacinamide/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Phenylurea Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyridines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sorafenib · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real survival gain in one double-blind trial. In RESORCE (Bruix J et al., PMID: 27932229), 573 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma who had tolerated and progressed on sorafenib, with Child-Pugh A liver function, were randomised 2:1 to regorafenib 160 mg (weeks 1–3 of each 4-week cycle) plus best supportive care or placebo. Median overall survival was 10.6 months versus 7.8 months (hazard ratio 0.63; 95% CI 0.50–0.79; one-sided p<0.0001) — a 37% relative reduction in the risk of death, 2.8 months at the median. The price: grade 3–4 hypertension in 15% versus 5%, hand-foot skin reaction in 13% versus 1%, fatigue in 9% versus 5%; adverse events occurred in 100% of regorafenib recipients versus 93% on placebo, though deaths attributed to study drug were 2% versus 1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): regorafenib extends survival after sorafenib in patients fit enough to have tolerated sorafenib, with substantial symptomatic toxicity.

cards.headline: Bruix 2017 (RESORCE): median OS 10.6 versus 7.8 months (HR 0.63) — grade 3–4 hypertension 15% versus 5%, hand-foot reaction 13% versus 1%
cards.summary: Bruix 2017 (RESORCE): median OS 10.6 versus 7.8 months (HR 0.63) — grade 3–4 hypertension 15% versus 5%, hand-foot reaction 13% versus 1%
cards.people: 573 adults with hepatocellular carcinoma who tolerated sorafenib (at least 400 mg/day for at least 20 of the last 28 days), progressed on it, and had Child-Pugh A liver function, at 152 sites in 21 countries, randomised 2:1 to regorafenib 160 mg daily on weeks 1–3 of each 4-week cycle (n=379) or placebo (n=194), both with best supportive care.
cards.result: Overall survival: hazard ratio 0.63 (95% CI 0.50–0.79; one-sided p<0.0001), a 37% relative reduction in the risk of death; median survival 10.6 months (95% CI 9.1–12.1) versus 7.8 months (6.3–8.8). Adverse events in 100% (374/374 treated) versus 93% (179/193). Commonest clinically relevant grade 3–4 treatment-emergent events: hypertension 15% versus 5%, hand-foot skin reaction 13% versus 1%, fatigue 9% versus 5%, diarrhoea 3% versus 0%. Of 88 deaths during the study (13% regorafenib, 20% placebo), seven (2%) on regorafenib and two (1%) on placebo were judged drug-related.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged). Entry required having tolerated sorafenib and Child-Pugh A function — a selected, fitter slice of post-sorafenib patients; the survival figure does not transfer to patients who stopped sorafenib for intolerance or who have worse liver function.

shelves.title: Cabozantinib in previously treated liver cancer (CELESTIAL): median survival 10.2 versus 8.0 months — high-grade adverse events roughly double (68% versus 36%)
shelves.question: In patients with previously treated advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, does cabozantinib improve survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anilides/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/drug therapy · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Receptor Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a survival gain in one double-blind trial, with a heavy toxicity bill. In CELESTIAL (Abou-Alfa GK et al., PMID: 29972759), 707 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma previously treated with sorafenib (up to two prior systemic regimens) were randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib 60 mg daily or placebo. Median overall survival was 10.2 versus 8.0 months (hazard ratio for death 0.76; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.92; P=0.005) — a 24% relative reduction in the risk of death. Median progression-free survival was 5.2 versus 1.9 months (HR 0.44; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.52), and objective response rates were 4% versus less than 1% (P=0.009). Grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 68% versus 36% — palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia 17% versus 0%, hypertension 16% versus 2%, raised aspartate aminotransferase 12% versus 7%, fatigue 10% versus 4%, diarrhoea 10% versus 2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cabozantinib extends survival after sorafenib, at roughly double the high-grade adverse-event rate.

shelves.title: Ramucirumab in liver cancer with alpha-fetoprotein ≥400 ng/mL (REACH-2): median survival 8.5 versus 7.3 months — the first biomarker-selected win in this disease
shelves.question: In patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and elevated alpha-fetoprotein after sorafenib, does ramucirumab improve survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/blood/drug therapy/pathology · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Liver Neoplasms/blood/drug therapy/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Staging · Sorafenib/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · alpha-Fetoproteins/analysis · Ramucirumab
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest survival gain in one double-blind trial, in a biomarker-defined subgroup. In REACH-2 (Zhu AX et al., PMID: 30665869), 292 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A, and alpha-fetoprotein of at least 400 ng/mL after first-line sorafenib were randomised 2:1 to ramucirumab 8 mg/kg every 2 weeks or placebo, both with best supportive care. Median overall survival was 8.5 versus 7.3 months (hazard ratio 0.710; 95% CI 0.531–0.949; p=0.0199) — a 29% relative reduction in the risk of death, 1.2 months at the median. Median progression-free survival was 2.8 versus 1.6 months (HR 0.452; p<0.0001); objective response did not differ significantly (5% versus 1%; p=0.1697), and neither time to symptom deterioration nor time to performance-status deterioration differed. Grade 3 or worse hypertension occurred in 13% versus 5% and hyponatraemia in 6% versus 0%; serious adverse events in 35% versus 29%, with three treatment-related deaths on ramucirumab. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ramucirumab extends survival modestly in AFP-high hepatocellular carcinoma after sorafenib.

cards.headline: Zhu 2019 (REACH-2): median OS 8.5 versus 7.3 months (HR 0.710, p=0.0199); PFS 2.8 versus 1.6 months (HR 0.452); response 5% versus 1% (not significant)
cards.summary: Zhu 2019 (REACH-2): median OS 8.5 versus 7.3 months (HR 0.710, p=0.0199); PFS 2.8 versus 1.6 months (HR 0.452); response 5% versus 1% (not significant)
cards.people: 292 patients aged 18 or older with hepatocellular carcinoma (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer stage B or C, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1) and alpha-fetoprotein ≥400 ng/mL, previously treated with first-line sorafenib, at 92 centres in 20 countries, randomised 2:1 to intravenous ramucirumab 8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (n=197) or placebo (n=95), both with best supportive care. Median follow-up 7.6 months.
cards.result: Median overall survival 8.5 months (95% CI 7.0–10.6) versus 7.3 months (5.4–9.1) (hazard ratio 0.710; 95% CI 0.531–0.949; p=0.0199) — a 29% relative reduction in the risk of death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Median progression-free survival 2.8 versus 1.6 months (HR 0.452; 95% CI 0.339–0.603; p<0.0001). Objective response nine (5%) of 197 versus one (1%) of 95 (p=0.1697, not significant). Time to deterioration in FHSI-8 symptom scores (3.7 versus 2.8 months; HR 0.799; p=0.238) and ECOG performance status (HR 1.082; p=0.77) did not differ. Grade ≥3 events in at least 5%: hypertension 13% versus 5%, hyponatraemia 6% versus 0%, increased AST 3% versus 5%. Serious adverse events 35% versus 29%; three ramucirumab patients died of treatment-related events (acute kidney injury, hepatorenal syndrome, renal failure).
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged), in a biomarker-selected population defined by the earlier REACH trial's subgroup — the AFP ≥400 ng/mL threshold is the whole claim, and the median survival gain (1.2 months) is the smallest of the post-sorafenib wins. Symptom and performance-status deterioration were not delayed.
