shelves.title: Fruquintinib in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer: two trials, one answer — median survival 9.3 versus 6.6 months (FRESCO) and 7.4 versus 4.8 months (FRESCO-2)
shelves.question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer after standard therapies, does fruquintinib improve overall survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzofurans/administration & dosage/adverse effects · China · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality/pathology/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Quinazolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Survival Analysis · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A/antagonists & inhibitors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant double-blind trials, one in China and one global. In FRESCO (Li J et al., PMID: 29946728), 416 Chinese patients whose metastatic colorectal cancer had progressed after at least two chemotherapy lines (no prior VEGFR inhibitor) were randomised 2:1 to fruquintinib 5 mg (21 days on, 7 off) or placebo: median overall survival 9.3 versus 6.6 months (hazard ratio 0.65; 95% CI 0.51–0.83; P<.001) and median progression-free survival 3.7 versus 1.8 months (HR 0.26). In FRESCO-2 (Dasari A et al., PMID: 37331369), 691 heavily pretreated patients across 14 countries (median four prior lines; all had received standard therapies and progressed on or were intolerant to trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib or both): median overall survival 7.4 versus 4.8 months (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.55–0.80; p<0.0001). Grade 3–4 treatment-emergent events occurred in 61.2% versus 19.7% in FRESCO; grade 3 or worse events in 63% versus 50% in FRESCO-2, hypertension the commonest (14% on fruquintinib in FRESCO-2). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fruquintinib extends survival by roughly 2.6–2.7 months at the median in refractory metastatic colorectal cancer, with substantial toxicity.

cards.headline: Li 2018 (FRESCO): median OS 9.3 versus 6.6 months (HR 0.65, P<.001); PFS 3.7 versus 1.8 months (HR 0.26); grade 3–4 events 61.2% versus 19.7%
cards.summary: Li 2018 (FRESCO): median OS 9.3 versus 6.6 months (HR 0.65, P<.001); PFS 3.7 versus 1.8 months (HR 0.26); grade 3–4 events 61.2% versus 19.7%
cards.people: 416 patients aged 18–75 (mean age 54.6 years; 38.7% women) at 28 hospitals in China, with metastatic colorectal cancer progressed after at least two lines of chemotherapy and no prior VEGFR-inhibitor therapy, randomised 2:1 to fruquintinib 5 mg daily (n=278) or placebo (n=138), 21 days on and 7 days off in 28-day cycles, until progression, intolerable toxicity or withdrawal.
cards.result: Median overall survival 9.3 months (95% CI 8.2–10.5) on fruquintinib versus 6.6 months (5.9–8.1) on placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.65; 95% CI 0.51–0.83; P<.001) — a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Median progression-free survival 3.7 versus 1.8 months (HR 0.26; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.34; P<.001). Grade 3–4 treatment-emergent adverse events 61.2% (170 patients) versus 19.7% (27); serious adverse events 15.5% versus 5.8%; hospitalisation 14.4% versus 5.1%.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (China) trial in patients who had never received a VEGFR inhibitor — the cleaner of the two settings, and the reason the global FRESCO-2 trial matters as the second leg. Toxicity is not incidental: three in five recipients had a grade 3–4 event.

cards.headline: Dasari 2023 (FRESCO-2): median OS 7.4 versus 4.8 months (HR 0.66, p<0.0001) in patients pretreated with trifluridine-tipiracil and/or regorafenib
cards.summary: Dasari 2023 (FRESCO-2): median OS 7.4 versus 4.8 months (HR 0.66, p<0.0001) in patients pretreated with trifluridine-tipiracil and/or regorafenib
cards.people: 691 patients with metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma at 124 centres in 14 countries, all having received every current standard cytotoxic and targeted therapy and progressed on or intolerant to trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib or both (median four prior lines; 73% had more than three), randomised 2:1 to fruquintinib 5 mg (n=461) or placebo (n=230) on days 1–21 of 28-day cycles, plus best supportive care.
cards.result: Median overall survival 7.4 months (95% CI 6.7–8.2) on fruquintinib versus 4.8 months (4.0–5.8) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.55–0.80; p<0.0001) — a 34% relative reduction in the risk of death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Grade 3 or worse adverse events in 286 (63%) of 456 fruquintinib patients versus 116 (50%) of 230 on placebo; commonest on fruquintinib were hypertension (14%), asthenia (8%) and hand-foot syndrome (6%). One treatment-related death in each group (intestinal perforation on fruquintinib; cardiac arrest on placebo).
cards.watchOut: The placebo group's 50% grade ≥3 event rate shows how sick this population is — the drug's added toxicity sits on top of a very high background. Quality-of-life analyses were still ongoing in this record, so the survival gain cannot yet be set against how patients felt.

shelves.question: In patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, does perioperative durvalumab added to neoadjuvant chemotherapy improve event-free and overall survival compared with chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/adverse effects/methods · Cisplatin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cystectomy · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives · Gemcitabine · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Neoadjuvant Therapy/adverse effects/methods · Progression-Free Survival · Survival Analysis · Urinary Bladder Neoplasms/mortality/pathology/therapy · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — event-free and overall survival both improved in one large open-label trial. In NIAGARA (Powles T et al., PMID: 39282910), 1,063 cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer were randomised to neoadjuvant durvalumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin for four cycles, then radical cystectomy and eight cycles of adjuvant durvalumab, or to neoadjuvant gemcitabine–cisplatin then cystectomy alone. Estimated event-free survival at 24 months was 67.8% versus 59.8% (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82; P<0.001) — a 32% relative reduction in the risk of progression, recurrence, not undergoing cystectomy, or death. Estimated overall survival at 24 months was 82.2% versus 75.2% (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.93; P=0.01) — a 25% relative reduction in the risk of death, 7.0 percentage points absolute. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were 40.6% versus 40.9%, treatment-related deaths 0.6% in each group, and cystectomy was performed in 88.0% versus 83.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): perioperative durvalumab improves event-free and overall survival around cystectomy without measurably adding high-grade toxicity.

cards.headline: Powles 2024 (NIAGARA): 24-month EFS 67.8% versus 59.8% (HR 0.68, P<0.001); 24-month OS 82.2% versus 75.2% (HR 0.75, P=0.01); grade 3–4 treatment-related events 40.6% versus 40.9%
cards.summary: Powles 2024 (NIAGARA): 24-month EFS 67.8% versus 59.8% (HR 0.68, P<0.001); 24-month OS 82.2% versus 75.2% (HR 0.75, P=0.01); grade 3–4 treatment-related events 40.6% versus 40.9%
cards.people: 1,063 cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, randomised 1:1 to neoadjuvant durvalumab plus gemcitabine–cisplatin every 3 weeks for four cycles, followed by radical cystectomy and adjuvant durvalumab every 4 weeks for eight cycles (n=533), or neoadjuvant gemcitabine–cisplatin followed by cystectomy alone (n=530). Open-label design.
cards.result: Event-free survival at 24 months (estimated): 67.8% (95% CI 63.6 to 71.7) in the durvalumab group versus 59.8% (55.4 to 64.0) in the comparison group (hazard ratio for progression, recurrence, not undergoing radical cystectomy, or death 0.68; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82; P<0.001) — a 32% relative reduction, 8.0 percentage points absolute. Overall survival at 24 months (estimated): 82.2% (78.7 to 85.2) versus 75.2% (71.3 to 78.8) (HR for death 0.75; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.93; P=0.01) — a 25% relative reduction, 7.0 percentage points absolute. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events 40.6% versus 40.9%; treatment-related deaths 0.6% in each group; radical cystectomy performed in 88.0% versus 83.2%.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged), and open-label: patients and investigators knew the assignment, which can colour event ascertainment and post-recurrence care, though overall survival is harder to bias. The design bundles neoadjuvant plus adjuvant durvalumab, so neither phase's separate contribution can be read off this trial. Survival figures are 24-month estimates, not mature medians.
cards.source: Powles T et al. Perioperative Durvalumab with Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy in Operable Bladder Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39282910. Registry ID: NCT03732677. shelves.title: Tivozanib versus sorafenib as third- or fourth-line therapy in kidney cancer (TIVO-3): progression-free survival 5.6 versus 3.9 months in an open-label trial — survival not the endpoint won
shelves.question: In patients with relapsed or refractory advanced renal cell carcinoma, does tivozanib improve progression-free survival compared with sorafenib?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Renal Cell/drug therapy/pathology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kidney Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds/administration & dosage · Prognosis · Quinolines/administration & dosage · Research Design · Sorafenib/administration & dosage · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a progression-free survival gain in one open-label trial. In TIVO-3 (Rini BI et al., PMID: 31810797), 350 patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma who had received at least two previous systemic treatments (including at least one VEGFR inhibitor) were randomised to tivozanib 1.5 mg daily in 4-week cycles or sorafenib 400 mg twice daily. Median progression-free survival by independent review was 5.6 versus 3.9 months (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.56–0.94; p=0.016) — a 27% relative reduction in the risk of progression or death, 1.7 months at the median, at a median follow-up of 19.0 months. The commonest grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse event was hypertension: 20% on tivozanib versus 14% on sorafenib. Serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in 11% versus 10%, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors report tivozanib was better tolerated overall than sorafenib. Overall survival was not the endpoint this record reports as won. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tivozanib delays progression versus sorafenib as third- or fourth-line therapy; a survival benefit is not shown in this record.

cards.headline: Rini 2020 (TIVO-3): median PFS 5.6 versus 3.9 months (HR 0.73, p=0.016) — grade 3–4 hypertension 20% versus 14%, no treatment-related deaths
cards.summary: Rini 2020 (TIVO-3): median PFS 5.6 versus 3.9 months (HR 0.73, p=0.016) — grade 3–4 hypertension 20% versus 14%, no treatment-related deaths
cards.people: 350 patients older than 18 years with histologically or cytologically confirmed metastatic renal cell carcinoma, at least two previous systemic treatments including at least one VEGFR inhibitor, ECOG performance status 0–1, and no previous tivozanib or sorafenib, at 120 academic hospitals in 12 countries, randomised 1:1 to tivozanib 1.5 mg orally once daily in 4-week cycles (n=175) or sorafenib 400 mg orally twice daily continuously (n=175). Median follow-up 19.0 months.
cards.result: Primary endpoint, progression-free survival by independent review: median 5.6 months (95% CI 5.29–7.33) on tivozanib versus 3.9 months (3.71–5.55) on sorafenib (hazard ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.56–0.94; p=0.016) — a 27% relative reduction in the risk of progression or death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Most common grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse event was hypertension: 35 (20%) of 173 tivozanib patients versus 23 (14%) of 170 sorafenib patients. Serious treatment-related adverse events in 19 (11%) versus 17 (10%); no treatment-related deaths in either group.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf (flagged), open-label (investigators and patients unmasked), with progression-free survival — assessed by independent review, which mitigates but does not remove the concern — as the won endpoint; this record reports no overall-survival advantage. The population mixes post-VEGFR-inhibitor and post-checkpoint-inhibitor patients from a treatment era that has since moved on.
cards.source: Rini BI et al. Tivozanib versus sorafenib in patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma (TIVO-3): a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label study. The Lancet Oncology. 2020. PMID: 31810797. Registry ID: NCT02627963. shelves.title: D2 versus D1 gastrectomy in the West: fewer cancer deaths and recurrences at 15 years in the Dutch trial (cancer death 37% versus 48%) — paid for with double the operative mortality (10% versus 4%) and no overall survival win
shelves.question: In patients with gastric cancer having gastrectomy, does D2 lymphadenectomy improve survival compared with D1 in Western populations?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/pathology/surgery · Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrectomy · Humans · Lymph Node Excision/methods · Male · Prospective Studies · Stomach Neoplasms/pathology/surgery · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — D2 dissection buys cancer control and charges operative lives for it, and in the Western randomised record the two roughly cancel. At 15 years in the Dutch trial, gastric-cancer death was 37% after D2 versus 48% after D1, local recurrence 12% versus 22% and regional recurrence 13% versus 19% — but overall 15-year survival was 29% versus 21% (P=.34, not significant), because D2 operative mortality was 10% versus 4% (P=.004), complications 43% versus 25% and reoperations 18% versus 8% (Songun I et al., PMID: 20409751). The British MRC trial showed the same price up front: hospital mortality 13% versus 6.5% (P=.04) and morbidity 46% versus 28%, with the excess accounted for by the pancreaticosplenectomy then bundled into D2 (Cuschieri A et al., PMID: 8606613). PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE (benefit) for cancer-specific death and locoregional recurrence at long follow-up; POSSIBLE (harm) for operative mortality and morbidity with the era's technique — modern spleen- and pancreas-preserving D2 was not what these trials tested.

cards.headline: Songun 2010 (Dutch D1D2, 15-year follow-up): cancer death 37% (D2) versus 48% (D1); local recurrence 12% versus 22% — but operative mortality 10% versus 4% and overall survival 29% versus 21% (P=.34)
cards.summary: Songun 2010 (Dutch D1D2, 15-year follow-up): cancer death 37% (D2) versus 48% (D1); local recurrence 12% versus 22% — but operative mortality 10% versus 4% and overall survival 29% versus 21% (P=.34)
cards.type: Randomised nationwide trial, 15-year follow-up (Songun 2010, Dutch D1D2 trial)
cards.people: 711 patients with resectable gastric adenocarcinoma treated with curative intent (380 D1, 331 D2) across 80 Dutch hospitals, randomised 1989–1993 and followed for a median of 15.2 years.
cards.result: Overall 15-year survival: 29% (D2) versus 21% (D1), P=.34. Gastric-cancer-related death: 37% (123/331) versus 48% (182/380). Local recurrence 12% versus 22%; regional recurrence 13% versus 19%. Operative mortality: 10% (32) versus 4% (15), P=.004. Complications: 43% (142) versus 25% (94), P<.0001. Reoperations: 18% (59) versus 8% (30), P=.00016.
cards.watchOut: A 1989–1993 surgical era in which D2 routinely included distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy — the operative-mortality penalty belongs substantially to those resections, and the trial's own authors recommend modern spleen-preserving D2 in high-volume centres rather than the operation actually tested.
cards.source: Songun I et al. Surgical treatment of gastric cancer: 15-year follow-up results of the randomised nationwide Dutch D1D2 trial. The Lancet Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20409751. cards.headline: Cuschieri 1996 (MRC trial): D2 hospital mortality 13% versus 6.5% (P=.04), morbidity 46% versus 28% — the excess traced to pancreatico-splenic resection
cards.summary: Cuschieri 1996 (MRC trial): D2 hospital mortality 13% versus 6.5% (P=.04), morbidity 46% versus 28% — the excess traced to pancreatico-splenic resection
cards.type: Randomised controlled surgical trial, preliminary report (Cuschieri 1996, MRC)
cards.people: 400 patients with potentially curable gastric cancer (200 D1, 200 D2) randomised after staging laparotomy across European centres involving 32 surgeons.
cards.result: Postoperative hospital mortality: 13% (D2) versus 6.5% (D1), P=.04. Overall postoperative morbidity: 46% versus 28% (P<.001), with longer postoperative stay after D2. The excess morbidity and mortality were accounted for by distal pancreaticosplenectomy and splenectomy; survival beyond 3 years was 30% in patients whose gastrectomy included en-bloc pancreatico-splenic resection versus 50% in the remainder.
cards.watchOut: A preliminary (1996) report of short-term outcomes — it prices the operation but cannot judge its long-term cancer control; that judgement comes from the Dutch 15-year record. Both trials predate pancreas-preserving D2 technique and modern perioperative care.
cards.source: Cuschieri A et al. Postoperative morbidity and mortality after D1 and D2 resections for gastric cancer: preliminary results of the MRC randomised controlled surgical trial. Lancet. 1996. PMID: 8606613. cards.headline: Synthesis: cancer control up, operative deaths up — the Western trials net out near zero on overall survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: cancer control up, operative deaths up — the Western trials net out near zero on overall survival
cards.people: Two Western randomised trials: Dutch D1D2 (711 curative-intent patients, 15-year follow-up) and the MRC trial (400 patients, short-term report).
cards.result: Gastric-cancer death 37% versus 48% and local recurrence 12% versus 22% favouring D2 (Dutch, 15 years); operative mortality 10% versus 4% (Dutch) and 13% versus 6.5% (MRC) against D2; overall survival 29% versus 21%, not significant. PROPOSED SPLIT, as on the face of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both trials tested D2 with routine splenopancreatectomy. Whether modern spleen- and pancreas-preserving D2 in high-volume Western centres keeps the cancer benefit without the operative price is asserted by guidelines but not randomised in the West. Tier C.

shelves.title: Stent as a bridge to surgery for obstructing left-sided colon cancer: stomas fall (47.5% versus 67.9% in CReST) and complications fall in the pooled trials — mortality, recurrence and survival do not move
shelves.question: In patients with obstructing left-sided colon cancer, does a self-expanding metal stent as a bridge to surgery improve outcomes compared with emergency surgery?
shelves.mesh: Carcinoma · Colorectal Neoplasms/complications · Humans · Intestinal Obstruction/etiology/surgery · Quality of Life · Stents/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a stoma and morbidity benefit, honestly bounded: no survival advantage has been shown. In CReST, the largest trial (245 patients), stenting relieved obstruction in 82.4% of attempts; among curative-intent patients, stoma formation was 47.5% with stent-then-elective-surgery versus 67.9% with emergency surgery (P=.003), while 30-day mortality (3.6% versus 5.6%), hospital stay, perioperative morbidity, quality of life, 3-year recurrence and mortality did not differ (CReST Collaborative Group, PMID: 35986684). Pooling seven randomised trials (448 patients), postoperative complications were 37.8% after stent-bridge versus 54.9% after emergency surgery (P=.02), stoma rates 28.8% versus 46.0% and wound infection 8.1% versus 15.5%, with no mortality difference (Allievi N et al., PMID: 28761765). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer stomas and fewer complications, bought with a roughly one-in-five stent failure rate and no demonstrated oncological gain or loss.

cards.headline: CReST 2022: stoma in 47.5% (stent bridge) versus 67.9% (emergency surgery) in curative-intent patients (P=.003); 30-day mortality 3.6% versus 5.6% and 3-year recurrence and mortality not different
cards.summary: CReST 2022: stoma in 47.5% (stent bridge) versus 67.9% (emergency surgery) in curative-intent patients (P=.003); 30-day mortality 3.6% versus 5.6% and 3-year recurrence and mortality not different
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (CReST Collaborative Group 2022, CReST)
cards.people: 245 patients with left-sided colonic obstruction and radiological features of carcinoma at 39 UK hospitals, randomised to endoluminal stenting followed by elective surgery 1–4 weeks later (n=123 allocated; stenting attempted in 119) or emergency surgical decompression with or without tumour resection.
cards.result: Stenting relieved obstruction in 98 of 119 attempts (82.4%). In the 89% treated with curative intent: 30-day postoperative mortality 3.6% (4/110) versus 5.6% (6/107), P=.48; median hospital stay 19 versus 18 days, P=.94. Stoma formation: 47.5% (47/99) versus 67.9% (72/106), P=.003. No significant differences in perioperative morbidity, critical-care use, quality of life, 3-year recurrence or mortality.
cards.watchOut: One in six stent attempts failed to relieve obstruction, returning those patients to emergency surgery anyway; the trial ran 2009–2014 and its neutral oncological results, while reassuring, come with wide confidence intervals for recurrence.
cards.source: CReST Collaborative Group et al. Colorectal Endoscopic Stenting Trial (CReST) for obstructing left-sided colorectal cancer: randomized clinical trial. British Journal of Surgery. 2022. PMID: 35986684. Registry ID: ISRCTN13846816 (in the abstract text). cards.headline: Allievi 2017 meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 448 patients): complications 37.8% versus 54.9% (P=.02), stoma 28.8% versus 46.0%, wound infection 8.1% versus 15.5% — mortality not different
cards.summary: Allievi 2017 meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 448 patients): complications 37.8% versus 54.9% (P=.02), stoma 28.8% versus 46.0%, wound infection 8.1% versus 15.5% — mortality not different
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials totalling 448 patients with left-sided malignant colorectal obstruction, comparing stenting as a bridge to surgery with emergency resection.
cards.result: Postoperative complication rate: 37.84% (stent bridge) versus 54.87% (emergency surgery), P=.02. Stoma rate: 28.8% versus 46.02%, P<.0001. Wound infection: 8.11% versus 15.49%, P=.01. Mortality rate: no difference between groups.
cards.watchOut: The component trials are small and span different eras and stent generations; complication definitions vary. The pooled complication advantage is consistent with CReST's stoma result but CReST itself found no significant perioperative-morbidity difference, so the morbidity claim is softer than the stoma claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the stent buys a planned operation and often a stoma-free one — it does not buy survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: the stent buys a planned operation and often a stoma-free one — it does not buy survival
cards.people: CReST (n=245) plus seven pooled randomised trials (n=448) in obstructing left-sided colorectal cancer.
cards.result: Stoma formation 47.5% versus 67.9% (CReST curative-intent) and 28.8% versus 46.0% (pooled); complications 37.8% versus 54.9% (pooled); mortality, recurrence and survival not significantly different in either record. Stent technical success 82.4% in CReST. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Anagrelide versus hydroxyurea in high-risk essential thrombocythaemia: SPLIT — PT1 found more arterial thrombosis, bleeding and myelofibrosis transformation on anagrelide, ANAHYDRET found it non-inferior in WHO-defined disease
shelves.question: In patients with essential thrombocythaemia at high risk, does anagrelide match hydroxyurea for thrombosis prevention (PT1, ANAHYDRET)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aspirin/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemorrhage/etiology,mortality · Humans · Hydroxyurea/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/etiology · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Platelet Count · Primary Myelofibrosis/etiology,prevention & control · Quinazolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Thrombocythemia, Essential/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Thrombosis/etiology,mortality
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and the split tracks how the disease was defined. In PT1 (809 high-risk patients, older diagnostic criteria, median follow-up 39 months, both drugs with low-dose aspirin), anagrelide was worse on the composite of arterial/venous thrombosis, serious haemorrhage or related death (odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04–2.37; P=0.03), with more arterial thrombosis (P=0.004), serious haemorrhage (P=0.008) and transformation to myelofibrosis (P=0.01), but less venous thromboembolism (P=0.006). In ANAHYDRET (259 previously untreated patients diagnosed by strict WHO criteria), anagrelide was non-inferior for platelet, haemoglobin and leukocyte control and ET-related events over 36 months (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.57–1.46), with no significant difference in major arterial (7 versus 8) or venous (2 versus 6) thrombosis. Platelet-count control itself was equivalent in both trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: hydroxyurea remains the safer default on PT1's hard-event data; anagrelide matched it in the WHO-defined, previously untreated ANAHYDRET population — the diagnosis definition, not the platelet number, decides which trial applies.

cards.headline: PT1 (Harrison 2005): anagrelide plus aspirin worse than hydroxyurea plus aspirin — composite OR 1.57, more arterial events, bleeding and myelofibrosis transformation, fewer venous events
cards.summary: PT1 (Harrison 2005): anagrelide plus aspirin worse than hydroxyurea plus aspirin — composite OR 1.57, more arterial events, bleeding and myelofibrosis transformation, fewer venous events
cards.people: 809 patients with essential thrombocythemia at high risk for vascular events, randomised to low-dose aspirin plus either anagrelide or hydroxyurea; median follow-up 39 months; primary endpoint the actuarial risk of arterial thrombosis, venous thrombosis, serious haemorrhage, or death from thrombotic or haemorrhagic causes.
cards.result: Patients on anagrelide were significantly more likely to reach the primary endpoint (odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.37; P=0.03). Anagrelide plus aspirin was associated with increased rates of arterial thrombosis (P=0.004), serious hemorrhage (P=0.008), and transformation to myelofibrosis (P=0.01), but a decreased rate of venous thromboembolism (P=0.006). Withdrawal from assigned treatment was more likely on anagrelide (P<0.001). Long-term platelet-count control was equivalent in both groups. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.watchOut: PT1 used pre-WHO diagnostic criteria, so some enrolled patients would now be classified as early myelofibrosis — the very subgroup in whom anagrelide looked worst; that misclassification is the leading explanation for the clash with ANAHYDRET, and it cuts both ways: PT1's harm signal may not apply to strictly WHO-defined essential thrombocythaemia.
cards.source: Harrison CN et al. Hydroxyurea compared with anagrelide in high-risk essential thrombocythemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16000354. cards.headline: ANAHYDRET (Gisslinger 2013): anagrelide non-inferior to hydroxyurea in WHO-classified essential thrombocythemia — event HR 0.92 at 36 months, no significant thrombosis or bleeding difference
cards.summary: ANAHYDRET (Gisslinger 2013): anagrelide non-inferior to hydroxyurea in WHO-classified essential thrombocythemia — event HR 0.92 at 36 months, no significant thrombosis or bleeding difference
cards.people: 259 previously untreated, high-risk patients with essential thrombocythemia diagnosed according to WHO classification, randomised to anagrelide or hydroxyurea in a prospective non-inferiority phase 3 study; total observation 730 patient-years.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of anagrelide was confirmed at 6 months on the primary endpoint criteria and at 12 and 36 months for platelet counts, haemoglobin and leukocyte counts (P<.001) and ET-related events (hazard ratios 1.19 [95% CI 0.61–2.30], 1.03 [0.57–1.81] and 0.92 [0.57–1.46]). Over the whole observation there was no significant difference in major arterial thrombosis (7 versus 8), major venous thrombosis (2 versus 6), severe bleeding (5 versus 2), minor arterial (24 versus 20) or venous (3 versus 3) thrombosis, minor bleeding (18 versus 15), or discontinuation (adverse events 12 versus 15).
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority trial of 259 patients cannot exclude the event differences PT1 (809 patients) detected — its confidence interval for ET-related events at 36 months (0.57–1.46) still includes meaningful harm; single-blind design per the record's MeSH. The honest reading is compatibility in WHO-defined disease, not proof of equality.
cards.source: Gisslinger H et al. Anagrelide compared with hydroxyurea in WHO-classified essential thrombocythemia: the ANAHYDRET Study, a randomized controlled trial. Blood. 2013. PMID: 23315161. cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 1,068 patients with high-risk essential thrombocythaemia: PT1 (809, older criteria, aspirin co-therapy) and ANAHYDRET (259, WHO criteria, previously untreated).
cards.result: Platelet control: equivalent in both. Hard events: PT1 composite OR 1.57 (1.04–2.37) against anagrelide; ANAHYDRET ET-related events HR 0.92 (0.57–1.46) at 36 months. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C for the developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Mitapivat in thalassaemia: transfusion reduction response 30% versus 13% in transfusion-dependent disease (ENERGIZE-T) and haemoglobin response 42% versus 2% in non-transfusion-dependent disease (ENERGIZE) — two double-blind trials
shelves.question: In patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia, does mitapivat improve haemoglobin and reduce transfusion burden compared with placebo (ENERGIZE-T), and in non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (ENERGIZE)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · alpha-Thalassemia/drug therapy,therapy · beta-Thalassemia/drug therapy,therapy · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Piperazines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quinolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of the oral pyruvate kinase activator mitapivat 100 mg twice daily agree in direction across the thalassaemia spectrum. In transfusion-dependent α- or β-thalassaemia (ENERGIZE-T, 258 patients, 48 weeks), a transfusion reduction response (≥50% fewer red-cell units, by ≥2 units, in any consecutive 12 weeks to week 48) occurred in 30% (52/171) versus 13% (11/87) on placebo (adjusted difference 18 percentage points, 95% CI 8–27; p=0.0003). In non-transfusion-dependent α- or β-thalassaemia (ENERGIZE, 194 patients, 24 weeks), a haemoglobin response (≥1.0 g/dL mean rise, weeks 12–24) occurred in 42% (55/130) versus 2% (1/64) (difference 41 points, 95% CI 32–50; p<0.0001). Headache, initial insomnia, nausea and upper respiratory infection were the commonest events on mitapivat; no deaths were reported in either trial. The candidate asked about transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia: both trials enrolled α-thalassaemia as well as β-thalassaemia, and ENERGIZE-T's endpoint is transfusion reduction rather than haemoglobin — declared here rather than silently widened. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): mitapivat reduces transfusion burden in dependent disease and raises haemoglobin in non-dependent disease, on two concordant trials.

cards.headline: ENERGIZE-T (Cappellini 2026): transfusion reduction response 30% on mitapivat versus 13% on placebo over 48 weeks in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (p=0.0003)
cards.summary: ENERGIZE-T (Cappellini 2026): transfusion reduction response 30% on mitapivat versus 13% on placebo over 48 weeks in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (p=0.0003)
cards.people: 258 adults (median age 33.5 years; 53% female) with transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia across 19 countries, randomised 2:1 to mitapivat 100 mg twice daily (171 in the full analysis set) or placebo (87) for 48 weeks; primary endpoint transfusion reduction response (≥50% reduction in transfused red-cell units with a reduction of ≥2 units in any consecutive 12-week period to week 48 versus baseline).
cards.result: Transfusion reduction responses occurred in 30% (52/171) on mitapivat versus 13% (11/87) on placebo (adjusted difference 18 percentage points, 95% CI 8–27; two-sided p=0.0003). Adverse events were reported in 90% on mitapivat versus 84% on placebo (safety sets 172 and 85), most commonly headache, upper respiratory tract infection, initial insomnia, diarrhoea and fatigue; serious adverse events in 11% versus 15%; discontinuation for adverse events in 6% versus 1%. No deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: A 30% response rate means most transfusion-dependent patients did not halve their transfusion burden; the endpoint is a burden reduction, not transfusion independence, and the trial mixed α- and β-thalassaemia genotypes — genotype-specific rates are not in this record. The record's journal year is 2026 (published ahead of the print issue); figures are taken from the fetched record as published.

randomised double-blind phase 3 trial (cappellini 2026, energize-t) 258 adults (median age 33.5 years; 53% female) with transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia across 19 countries, randomised 2:1 to mitapivat 100 mg twice daily (171 in the full analysis set) or placebo (87) for 48 weeks; primary endpoint transfusion reduction response (≥50% reduction in transfused red-cell units with a reduction of ≥2 units in any consecutive 12-week period to week 48 versus baseline). transfusion reduction responses occurred in 30% (52/171) on mitapivat versus 13% (11/87) on placebo (adjusted difference 18 percentage points, 95% ci 8–27; two-sided p=0.0003). adverse events were reported in 90% on mitapivat versus 84% on placebo (safety sets 172 and 85), most commonly headache, upper respiratory tract infection, initial insomnia, diarrhoea and fatigue; serious adverse events in 11% versus 15%; discontinuation for adverse events in 6% versus 1%. no deaths were reported. a 30% response rate means most transfusion-dependent patients did not halve their transfusion burden; the endpoint is a burden reduction, not transfusion independence, and the trial mixed α- and β-thalassaemia genotypes — genotype-specific rates are not in this record. the record's journal year is 2026 (published ahead of the print issue); figures are taken from the fetched record as published. cappellini md et al. efficacy and safety of mitapivat in adults with transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia (energize-t): a double-blind, randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. lancet (london, england). 2026. pmid: 42721980. registry id: nct04770779. mesh: adult · female · humans · male · alpha-thalassemia/drug therapy,therapy · beta-thalassemia/drug therapy,therapy · double-blind method · treatment outcome · piperazines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · quinolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use

cards.headline: ENERGIZE (Taher 2025): haemoglobin response 42% on mitapivat versus 2% on placebo at weeks 12–24 in non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: ENERGIZE (Taher 2025): haemoglobin response 42% on mitapivat versus 2% on placebo at weeks 12–24 in non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (p<0.0001)
cards.people: 194 adults with non-transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia and haemoglobin ≤10 g/dL at 70 hospitals in 18 countries, randomised 2:1 to mitapivat 100 mg twice daily (130) or placebo (64) for 24 weeks; primary endpoint haemoglobin response (≥1.0 g/dL increase from baseline in mean haemoglobin from week 12 through week 24). 63% of enrolled patients were female.
cards.result: Haemoglobin response occurred in 42% (55/130) on mitapivat versus 2% (1/64) on placebo (least-squares mean difference 41%, 95% CI 32–50; two-sided p<0.0001). Adverse events were reported in 83% (107/129 treated) on mitapivat versus 79% (50/63) on placebo; most common with mitapivat were headache (22% versus 10%), initial insomnia (14% versus 5%), nausea (12% versus 8%) and upper respiratory tract infection (11% versus 6%). No deaths were reported. The trialists also report improved fatigue with mitapivat.
cards.watchOut: Haemoglobin rise is a laboratory endpoint in a 24-week trial; whether it converts into fewer long-term complications of non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia is not shown in this record. As with ENERGIZE-T, α- and β-thalassaemia are pooled.
cards.source: Taher AT et al. shelves.title: BEACON: encorafenib plus cetuximab (with or without binimetinib) roughly doubles survival in previously treated BRAF V600E metastatic colorectal cancer — 9.3 versus 5.9 months on updated analysis
shelves.question: In patients with metastatic colorectal cancer and BRAF V600E mutation, does encorafenib plus cetuximab improve survival compared with chemotherapy (BEACON)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzimidazoles/administration & dosage · Carbamates/administration & dosage · Cetuximab/administration & dosage · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/mortality · Disease Progression · Electrocorticography · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Irinotecan/therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf/genetics · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large randomised trial, reported twice, with a survival gain in a poor-prognosis niche. In BEACON (665 patients, PMID: 31566309), median overall survival was 9.0 months on encorafenib–binimetinib–cetuximab (triplet) and 8.4 months on encorafenib–cetuximab (doublet) versus 5.4 months on cetuximab–chemotherapy control (hazard ratios 0.52 and 0.60); response was 26% on triplet versus 2% on control. On the updated analysis (Tabernero, PMID: 33503393), median survival was 9.3 months for both triplet and doublet versus 5.9 months for control (hazard ratios 0.60 and 0.61), with grade ≥3 adverse events in 65.8%, 57.4% and 64.2% respectively — so the doublet matched the triplet on survival with fewer severe events, and the doublet is the regimen the update names a new standard of care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit of about 3.4–3.9 months in previously treated BRAF V600E disease, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.

cards.headline: Kopetz 2019 (BEACON, primary interim): median survival 9.0 months triplet and 8.4 months doublet versus 5.4 months control (HR 0.52 and 0.60); response 26% versus 2%
cards.summary: Kopetz 2019 (BEACON, primary interim): median survival 9.0 months triplet and 8.4 months doublet versus 5.4 months control (HR 0.52 and 0.60); response 26% versus 2%
cards.people: 665 patients with BRAF V600E-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer progressed after one or two previous regimens, randomised 1:1:1 to encorafenib + binimetinib + cetuximab (triplet), encorafenib + cetuximab (doublet), or investigator's choice of cetuximab + irinotecan or cetuximab + FOLFIRI (control); open-label.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 9.0 months in the triplet group and 5.4 months in the control group (hazard ratio for death 0.52; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.70; P<0.001), a 48% relative reduction in the hazard of death. Confirmed response rate was 26% (95% CI 18 to 35) on triplet versus 2% (95% CI 0 to 7) on control (P<0.001). Median survival in the doublet group was 8.4 months (hazard ratio versus control 0.60; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.79; P<0.001). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 58% (triplet), 50% (doublet) and 61% (control).
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial and a prespecified interim analysis; the control arm's 5.4-month median survival reflects how poor the prognosis is after prior therapy, so the absolute gain (about 3–3.6 months at this analysis) is the honest scale of the benefit. Single-trial shelf: no second randomised trial of this regimen exists in the record set.
cards.source: Kopetz S et al. Encorafenib, Binimetinib, and Cetuximab in BRAF V600E-Mutated Colorectal Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31566309. cards.headline: Tabernero 2021 (BEACON, updated): median survival 9.3 months for both triplet and doublet versus 5.9 months control (HR 0.60 and 0.61); grade ≥3 events 65.8%, 57.4% and 64.2%
cards.summary: Tabernero 2021 (BEACON, updated): median survival 9.3 months for both triplet and doublet versus 5.9 months control (HR 0.60 and 0.61); grade ≥3 events 65.8%, 57.4% and 64.2%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — updated analysis (Tabernero 2021, BEACON CRC)
cards.people: The same 665 BEACON patients (triplet n=224, doublet n=220, control n=221) with 6 months of additional follow-up; objective response assessed for all randomised patients.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 9.3 months (95% CI 8.2 to 10.8) for triplet versus 5.9 months (95% CI 5.1 to 7.1) for control (hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.75), and 9.3 months (95% CI 8.0 to 11.3) for doublet (hazard ratio versus control 0.61; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.77). Confirmed response rates were 26.8% (triplet), 19.5% (doublet) and 1.8% (control). Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 65.8%, 57.4% and 64.2% respectively. The authors conclude encorafenib plus cetuximab is a new standard of care in this setting.
cards.watchOut: An update of the same single trial, not independent confirmation; with longer follow-up the triplet's survival advantage over the doublet disappeared (both 9.3 months), while its severe-event rate stayed highest — the update supports the doublet, not the triplet, as the default regimen.
cards.source: Tabernero J et al. Encorafenib Plus Cetuximab as a New Standard of Care for Previously Treated BRAF V600E-Mutant Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: Updated Survival Results and Subgroup Analyses from the BEACON Study. shelves.title: CLEAR: lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab more than doubles progression-free survival versus sunitinib in first-line advanced kidney cancer (23.9 versus 9.2 months) — the survival edge narrows at final analysis (HR 0.79)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma, does lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab beat sunitinib for progression-free survival (CLEAR)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Renal Cell/drug therapy/mortality · Everolimus/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Kidney Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Programmed Cell Death 1 Receptor/antagonists & inhibitors · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Quinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Sunitinib/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large phase 3 trial with a very large progression-free-survival effect and a survival effect that shrank as data matured. In CLEAR (Motzer, PMID: 33616314), median progression-free survival was 23.9 months on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 9.2 months on sunitinib (hazard ratio 0.39), and overall survival initially favoured the combination (hazard ratio 0.66; P=0.005). At the final prespecified survival analysis (Motzer, PMID: 38227898), the survival hazard ratio was 0.79 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.99), median survival was 53.7 versus 54.3 months, 36-month survival was 66.4% versus 60.2%, progression-free survival stayed 23.9 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.47), response was 71.3% versus 36.7%, and grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent events occurred in 82.4% on the combination versus 71.8% on sunitinib in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial first-line benefit driven by progression-free survival and response, with a modest mature survival edge and more severe toxicity.

cards.headline: Motzer 2021 (CLEAR, primary): PFS 23.9 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.39), survival HR 0.66 — grade ≥3 events 82.4% versus 71.8% on sunitinib
cards.summary: Motzer 2021 (CLEAR, primary): PFS 23.9 versus 9.2 months (HR 0.39), survival HR 0.66 — grade ≥3 events 82.4% versus 71.8% on sunitinib
cards.people: 1,069 patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma and no previous systemic therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to lenvatinib 20 mg daily + pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=355), lenvatinib 18 mg + everolimus 5 mg (n=357), or sunitinib 50 mg daily 4 weeks on/2 weeks off (n=357); open-label, primary endpoint progression-free survival by independent review.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was longer with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab than with sunitinib (median 23.9 vs 9.2 months; hazard ratio for progression or death 0.39; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.49; P<0.001) — a 61% relative reduction in the hazard — and longer with lenvatinib plus everolimus (14.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65). Overall survival was longer with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio for death 0.66; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.88; P=0.005) but not with lenvatinib plus everolimus (hazard ratio 1.15; P=0.30). Grade ≥3 adverse events: 82.4% (lenvatinib–pembrolizumab), 83.1% (lenvatinib–everolimus), 71.8% (sunitinib).
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial; the survival result at this report was immature, and the lenvatinib–everolimus arm shows the lenvatinib backbone alone does not explain the combination's survival signal. The question on this shelf is the pembrolizumab combination only.
cards.source: Motzer R et al. Lenvatinib plus Pembrolizumab or Everolimus for Advanced Renal Cell Carcinoma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33616314. Registry ID: NCT02811861. cards.headline: Motzer 2024 (CLEAR, final survival analysis): OS HR 0.79, median 53.7 versus 54.3 months, 36-month survival 66.4% versus 60.2%; PFS HR 0.47; response 71.3% versus 36.7%
cards.summary: Motzer 2024 (CLEAR, final survival analysis): OS HR 0.79, median 53.7 versus 54.3 months, 36-month survival 66.4% versus 60.2%; PFS HR 0.47; response 71.3% versus 36.7%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — final prespecified overall survival analysis (Motzer 2024, CLEAR)
cards.people: The lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus sunitinib comparison from CLEAR (treatment-naive advanced renal cell carcinoma), with 23 additional months of follow-up from the primary analysis; data cutoff July 31, 2022.
cards.result: Overall survival hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.99); median overall survival 53.7 months (95% CI 48.7 to not estimable) on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 54.3 months (95% CI 40.9 to not estimable) on sunitinib; 36-month survival 66.4% (95% CI 61.1 to 71.2) versus 60.2% (95% CI 54.6 to 65.2). Median progression-free survival 23.9 (95% CI 20.8 to 27.7) versus 9.2 months (95% CI 6.0 to 11.0; hazard ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.38 to 0.57). Objective response 71.3% versus 36.7% (relative risk 1.94; 95% CI 1.67 to 2.26). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in over 90% of patients on either treatment.
cards.watchOut: The mature survival picture is more equivocal than the primary report: medians are essentially identical (53.7 versus 54.3 months) and the hazard ratio (0.79) rests on the curve shape and later separation, in an era when sunitinib-arm patients could receive effective later-line immunotherapy. Single-trial shelf.

shelves.title: KEYNOTE-775: lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab extends survival in previously treated advanced endometrial cancer — 17.4 versus 12.0 months in mismatch-repair-proficient disease, at an 88.9% grade ≥3 event rate
shelves.question: In patients with advanced endometrial cancer, does lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab improve survival after prior therapy (KEYNOTE-775)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Endometrial Neoplasms/drug therapy/mortality · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quinolines/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial, confirmed at its final analysis, with a survival gain and a heavy toxicity price. In Study 309/KEYNOTE-775 (Makker, PMID: 35045221), median overall survival in mismatch-repair-proficient (pMMR) disease was 17.4 months on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 12.0 months on physician's-choice chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.68), and 18.3 versus 11.4 months overall (hazard ratio 0.62); progression-free survival was 6.6 versus 3.8 months in pMMR disease (hazard ratio 0.60). At the final prespecified analysis (Makker, PMID: 37058687) the effects held: survival hazard ratios 0.70 (pMMR) and 0.65 (all-comers), response 32.4% versus 15.1% in pMMR disease. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 88.9% on the combination versus 72.7% on chemotherapy in the primary report. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit after platinum therapy, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.

cards.headline: Makker 2022 (KEYNOTE-775, primary): OS 17.4 versus 12.0 months in pMMR (HR 0.68) and 18.3 versus 11.4 overall (HR 0.62); PFS 6.6 versus 3.8 months in pMMR (HR 0.60)
cards.summary: Makker 2022 (KEYNOTE-775, primary): OS 17.4 versus 12.0 months in pMMR (HR 0.68) and 18.3 versus 11.4 overall (HR 0.62); PFS 6.6 versus 3.8 months in pMMR (HR 0.60)
cards.people: 827 patients with advanced endometrial cancer previously treated with at least one platinum-based regimen (697 mismatch-repair-proficient, 130 mismatch-repair-deficient), randomised 1:1 to lenvatinib 20 mg daily + pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (n=411) or physician's-choice chemotherapy — doxorubicin or weekly paclitaxel (n=416); open-label.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was longer with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab (pMMR: 6.6 vs 3.8 months; hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.72; P<0.001; overall: 7.2 vs 3.8 months; hazard ratio 0.56). Median overall survival was longer (pMMR: 17.4 vs 12.0 months; hazard ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.84; P<0.001; overall: 18.3 vs 11.4 months; hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.51 to 0.75; P<0.001) — about a 32–38% relative reduction in the hazard of death, with the absolute medians printed alongside. Grade ≥3 adverse events: 88.9% versus 72.7%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, against a weak comparator (single-agent doxorubicin or weekly paclitaxel after platinum), and nearly 9 in 10 combination patients had a grade ≥3 event — the survival gain is bought with substantial toxicity. Single-trial shelf.
cards.source: Makker V et al. Lenvatinib plus Pembrolizumab for Advanced Endometrial Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35045221. Registry ID: NCT03517449. cards.headline: Makker 2023 (KEYNOTE-775, final analysis): OS HR 0.70 in pMMR and 0.65 in all-comers; response 32.4% versus 15.1% in pMMR; no new safety signals
cards.summary: Makker 2023 (KEYNOTE-775, final analysis): OS HR 0.70 in pMMR and 0.65 in all-comers; response 32.4% versus 15.1% in pMMR; no new safety signals
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — final prespecified overall survival analysis (Makker 2023, Study 309/KEYNOTE-775)
cards.people: The same 827 patients with advanced, recurrent or metastatic endometrial cancer (lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab n=411; physician's-choice chemotherapy n=416), final prespecified survival analysis with updated progression-free survival, response and safety.
cards.result: Lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab continued to show benefit in overall survival (pMMR hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.83; all-comer hazard ratio 0.65; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.77), progression-free survival (pMMR hazard ratio 0.60; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.72; all-comer 0.56; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.66) and objective response (pMMR 32.4% vs 15.1%; all-comers 33.8% vs 14.7%), with benefit in all subgroups of interest and no new safety signals.
cards.watchOut: An update of the same single trial, not independent confirmation; this record reports hazard ratios and response rates without updated absolute survival medians, so the absolute scale of benefit still rests on the primary report. First-line immunotherapy–chemotherapy questions in this disease are homed separately (live shelf #853, RUBY/NRG GY018); this shelf is the after-platinum setting only.

shelves.title: KEYNOTE-716: adjuvant pembrolizumab cuts recurrence in resected stage IIB/C melanoma — 36-month recurrence-free survival 76.2% versus 63.4%, distant-metastasis-free survival 84.4% versus 74.7%; overall survival not yet shown
shelves.question: In patients with resected stage IIB/C melanoma, does adjuvant pembrolizumab reduce recurrence (KEYNOTE-716)?
shelves.mesh: Child · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · COVID-19 · Double-Blind Method · Melanoma/drug therapy/surgery · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Aged · Adolescent
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, consistent across its reports, on recurrence endpoints rather than survival. In KEYNOTE-716 (Luke, PMID: 35367007), first recurrence or death at the second interim analysis had occurred in 15% on pembrolizumab versus 24% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.61). At the final distant-metastasis-free-survival analysis (Luke, PMID: 38452313; median follow-up 39.4 months), 36-month distant-metastasis-free survival was 84.4% versus 74.7% (hazard ratio 0.59) and 36-month recurrence-free survival was 76.2% versus 63.4% (hazard ratio 0.62). Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 16% versus 4% at the first interim analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial reduction in recurrence and distant metastasis after resection of stage IIB/C disease, with no overall-survival result in these records.

cards.headline: Luke 2022 (KEYNOTE-716, interim analyses): recurrence or death 15% versus 24% at second interim (HR 0.61); grade 3–4 treatment-related events 16% versus 4%
cards.summary: Luke 2022 (KEYNOTE-716, interim analyses): recurrence or death 15% versus 24% at second interim (HR 0.61); grade 3–4 treatment-related events 16% versus 4%
cards.people: 976 patients aged 12 years or older with newly diagnosed, completely resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma (negative sentinel node biopsy) at 160 centres in 16 countries, randomised 1:1 to pembrolizumab 200 mg (2 mg/kg if paediatric) or placebo every 3 weeks for 17 cycles (487 versus 489).
cards.result: At the first interim analysis (median follow-up about 14.4 months), 54 (11%) of 487 pembrolizumab patients and 82 (17%) of 489 placebo patients had a first recurrence or died (hazard ratio 0.65; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.92; p=0.0066). At the second interim analysis (median follow-up 20.9 months), 72 (15%) versus 115 (24%) had recurred or died (hazard ratio 0.61; 95% CI 0.45 to 0.82). Median recurrence-free survival was not reached in either group. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events at first interim: 78 (16%) of 483 versus 21 (4%) of 486. No deaths were due to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: Interim analyses with median recurrence-free survival not reached in either arm — the benefit is a relative reduction in events so far, in a population where about three-quarters of placebo patients had not recurred; overall survival is not an endpoint reported here. Single-trial shelf.

cards.headline: Luke 2024 (KEYNOTE-716, final DMFS analysis): 36-month distant-metastasis-free survival 84.4% versus 74.7% (HR 0.59); recurrence-free survival 76.2% versus 63.4% (HR 0.62)
cards.summary: Luke 2024 (KEYNOTE-716, final DMFS analysis): 36-month distant-metastasis-free survival 84.4% versus 74.7% (HR 0.59); recurrence-free survival 76.2% versus 63.4% (HR 0.62)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 3 trial — final distant-metastasis-free-survival analysis (Luke 2024, KEYNOTE-716)
cards.people: The same 976 patients with resected stage IIB or IIC melanoma (pembrolizumab n=487; placebo n=489); median follow-up 39.4 months (range 26.0–51.4) at the January 4, 2023 cutoff.
cards.result: Median distant-metastasis-free survival was not reached in either group; estimated 36-month distant-metastasis-free survival was 84.4% on pembrolizumab versus 74.7% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.79) — an absolute difference of 9.7 percentage points. Estimated 36-month recurrence-free survival was 76.2% versus 63.4% (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.79), an absolute difference of 12.8 percentage points, consistent across most subgroups including stage IIB and IIC. The safety profile was manageable and consistent with previous reports.
cards.watchOut: Still no overall-survival result in this record, and medians for both endpoints remain unreached — roughly 1 in 4 pembrolizumab patients had still recurred by 36 months, and about 37% of placebo patients had not. Adjuvant stage III melanoma immunotherapy is a different, already-homed question (live shelf #761); this shelf is stage IIB/C only.

shelves.title: FLAURA2: adding chemotherapy to first-line osimertinib extends survival in EGFR-mutated lung cancer — median 47.5 versus 37.6 months at final analysis, with grade ≥3 events doubled (70% versus 34%)
shelves.question: In patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC, does osimertinib plus chemotherapy beat osimertinib alone in first line (FLAURA2)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aniline Compounds/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy/genetics · ErbB Receptors/genetics · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics · Mutation · Pemetrexed/adverse effects · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Acrylamides · Indoles · Pyrimidines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one phase 3 trial whose progression-free-survival win matured into a survival win. In FLAURA2 (Planchard, PMID: 37937763), progression-free survival favoured osimertinib plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over osimertinib alone (hazard ratio 0.62), with 57% versus 41% alive and progression-free at 24 months and response in 83% versus 76%. At the planned final survival analysis (Jänne, PMID: 41104938), median overall survival was 47.5 months on the combination versus 37.6 months on osimertinib alone (hazard ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.96; P=0.02) — a median gain of 9.9 months — while grade ≥3 adverse events of any cause occurred in 70% versus 34%, and osimertinib discontinuation for adverse events in 12% versus 7%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single-trial survival benefit bought with roughly double the severe-toxicity rate, capped at POSSIBLE in this band.

cards.headline: Planchard 2023 (FLAURA2, primary): PFS HR 0.62; 57% versus 41% progression-free at 24 months; response 83% versus 76%; response duration 24.0 versus 15.3 months
cards.summary: Planchard 2023 (FLAURA2, primary): PFS HR 0.62; 57% versus 41% progression-free at 24 months; response 83% versus 76%; response duration 24.0 versus 15.3 months
cards.people: 557 patients with untreated EGFR-mutated (exon 19 deletion or L858R) advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, randomised 1:1 to osimertinib 80 mg daily plus chemotherapy (pemetrexed 500 mg/m² plus cisplatin 75 mg/m² or carboplatin) or osimertinib 80 mg daily alone; open-label, primary endpoint investigator-assessed progression-free survival.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was significantly longer with osimertinib–chemotherapy (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.62; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.79; P<0.001), a 38% relative reduction in the hazard; blinded central review agreed (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.80). At 24 months, 57% (95% CI 50 to 63) versus 41% (95% CI 35 to 47) were alive and progression-free. Objective response: 83% versus 76%; median response duration 24.0 (95% CI 20.9 to 27.8) versus 15.3 months (95% CI 12.7 to 19.4). Grade ≥3 adverse events from any cause were more frequent with the combination, driven by chemotherapy-related events (rates quantified in the final-analysis card).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with an investigator-assessed primary endpoint (central review concordant); the record's abstract does not print the median progression-free-survival values or a combination grade ≥3 percentage, so neither is stated here. Single-trial shelf; osimertinib versus first-generation inhibitors (FLAURA) is a different, already-homed question at live shelf #1832.
cards.source: Planchard D et al. Osimertinib with or without Chemotherapy in EGFR-Mutated Advanced NSCLC. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37937763. Registry ID: NCT04035486. cards.headline: Jänne 2026 (FLAURA2, final survival analysis): median OS 47.5 versus 37.6 months (HR 0.77; P=0.02); grade ≥3 events 70% versus 34%
cards.summary: Jänne 2026 (FLAURA2, final survival analysis): median OS 47.5 versus 37.6 months (HR 0.77; P=0.02); grade ≥3 events 70% versus 34%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — planned final overall survival analysis (Jänne 2026, FLAURA2)
cards.people: The same 557 patients with untreated EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC (osimertinib plus platinum–pemetrexed n=279; osimertinib alone n=278), final analysis of the key secondary endpoint, overall survival.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 47.5 months with osimertinib plus platinum–pemetrexed versus 37.6 months with osimertinib monotherapy (hazard ratio for death 0.77; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.96; P=0.02) — a 23% relative reduction in the hazard of death and a 9.9-month absolute median gain. Grade ≥3 adverse events of any cause: 70% versus 34%; adverse events leading to osimertinib discontinuation: 12% versus 7%. The authors describe the added severe events as increased but reversible.
cards.watchOut: An update of the same single trial, not independent confirmation; the survival gain comes with chemotherapy's toxicity burden up front for every patient, including the substantial minority who would have done well for years on osimertinib alone — the trial cannot identify them in advance.

shelves.title: Hairy cell leukaemia: the purine analogues work — cladribine gave 91% complete responses in 349 evaluable patients in the pivotal single-arm series, and pentostatin beat interferon in the one randomised trial (complete remission 76% versus 11%)
shelves.question: 'My father has hairy cell leukaemia — is there treatment, how well does it work?' — In classic hairy cell leukaemia, what response rates and durability do the purine analogues cladribine and pentostatin achieve, and how do they compare with each other and with the older interferon treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Antineoplastic Agents/therapeutic use · Cladribine/adverse effects · Cladribine/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Interferons/therapeutic use · Leukemia, Hairy Cell/complications · Leukemia, Hairy Cell/drug therapy · Leukemia, Hairy Cell/mortality · Leukemia, Hairy Cell/pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasms, Second Primary/chemically induced · Pentostatin/therapeutic use · Remission Induction · Splenectomy · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: Yes — hairy cell leukaemia is one of the most treatment-responsive leukaemias, and the purine analogues cladribine and pentostatin are the reason. The one randomised trial in the record compared pentostatin with the older interferon alfa-2a in 313 eligible previously untreated patients: confirmed complete remission 76% on pentostatin versus 11% on interferon, complete plus partial remission 79% versus 38%, both response and relapse-free survival favouring pentostatin at P<.0001 (Grever 1995, PMID: 7707126). Cladribine's pivotal evidence is single-arm and is labelled as such on its card: in the Scripps series of 349 evaluable patients, a single 7-day course gave 91% complete and 7% partial responses, with overall survival of 96% at 48 months — though 26% relapsed at a median of 29 months (Saven 1998, PMID: 9731048). The long retrospective comparisons find the two purine analogues equivalent: complete remission about 81–82% for either as first-line treatment, median disease-free survival 15 years (pentostatin) and 11+ years (first-line cladribine) at 12.5 years of follow-up (Else 2005, PMID: 16245328), and at 16 years a median relapse-free survival of 16 years with only 8 of 233 patients dying of hairy-cell-leukaemia-related causes (Else 2009, PMID: 19344416). The honest limit in the same records: remissions are long but the disease-free curve shows no plateau — relapse continues for decades, second courses work again (69% complete remission second-line), and cure remains elusive. PROPOSED LIKELY: first-line purine analogue therapy very likely produces a complete remission lasting many years; it is control measured in decades, not guaranteed cure.

cards.headline: Grever 1995 (the one randomised trial): pentostatin beat interferon decisively — complete remission 76% versus 11%, complete plus partial 79% versus 38%
cards.summary: Grever 1995 (the one randomised trial): pentostatin beat interferon decisively — complete remission 76% versus 11%, complete plus partial 79% versus 38%
cards.type: Randomised controlled intergroup trial, pentostatin versus interferon alfa-2a (Grever 1995)
cards.people: 356 previously untreated patients with hairy cell leukaemia entered on an intergroup randomised trial, of whom 313 were eligible: 159 assigned to interferon alfa-2a (3 million units subcutaneously three times weekly) and 154 to pentostatin (4 mg/m2 intravenously every 2 weeks). Median follow-up was 57 months (range 19–82).
cards.result: Confirmed complete remission was achieved by 17 of 159 patients on interferon (11%) versus 117 of 154 on pentostatin (76%); complete plus partial remission was 60 of 159 (38%) versus 121 of 154 (79%). Both the response rate and relapse-free survival significantly favoured pentostatin (P<.0001 for both). Myelosuppression was more frequent with pentostatin (P=.013). This trial is why interferon — the previous standard — was displaced by the purine analogues.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is against interferon, a treatment nobody would now choose first — the trial proves pentostatin's superiority over the old standard, not over cladribine (that comparison was never randomised; see the retrospective cards). Response assessment predates modern minimal-residual-disease methods, and the trial belongs to the pre-registration era, hence no registry ID.
cards.source: Grever M, Kopecky K, Foucar MK, Head D, Bennett JM, Hutchison RE, Corbett WE, Cassileth PA, Habermann T, Golomb H. Randomized comparison of pentostatin versus interferon alfa-2a in previously untreated patients with hairy cell leukemia: an intergroup study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 1995. PMID: 7707126. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era intergroup trial). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Saven 1998 (single-arm, labelled as such): one 7-day course of cladribine gave 91% complete responses in 349 evaluable patients; 26% later relapsed, and a second course worked again
cards.summary: Saven 1998 (single-arm, labelled as such): one 7-day course of cladribine gave 91% complete responses in 349 evaluable patients; 26% later relapsed, and a second course worked again
cards.type: Single-arm case series of cladribine, no comparison group (Saven 1998)
cards.people: 358 patients with hairy cell leukaemia treated at a single centre (Scripps) with cladribine at 0.087 or 0.1 mg/kg/day by continuous intravenous infusion for 7 days; 349 were evaluable for response. There was no control or comparison group.
cards.result: Complete response in 319 patients (91%) and partial response in 22 (7%) — an overall response rate of 98% after a single course. At a median response follow-up of 52 months, 90 patients (26%) had relapsed, at a median of 29 months; the treatment-failure rate at 48 months was 19% among responders (16% of complete responders, 54% of partial responders). A second course at first relapse (53 evaluable patients) again produced complete response in 33 (62%) and partial response in 14 (26%). Overall survival was 96% at 48 months. Second neoplasms occurred in 27 patients (8%), an observed-to-expected ratio of 1.88 (95% CI 1.24–2.74).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm evidence, labelled as such: with no comparator, the 91% complete-response figure cannot be set against what another treatment would have done in the same patients — though spontaneous remission in hairy cell leukaemia is rare enough that a 91% complete-response rate after one course is not plausibly natural history. The second-neoplasm signal (observed/expected 1.88) is part of this card's record and part of long-term follow-up planning; whether it reflects the drug, the disease, or surveillance is unresolved in the abstract.
cards.source: Saven A, Burian C, Koziol JA, Piro LD. Long-term follow-up of patients with hairy cell leukemia after cladribine treatment. Blood. 1998. PMID: 9731048. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era single-arm series). cards.headline: Else 2005: at 12.5 years, pentostatin and first-line cladribine looked equivalent — complete remission 81% versus 82%, median disease-free survival 15 versus 11+ years — but relapses never stopped
cards.summary: Else 2005: at 12.5 years, pentostatin and first-line cladribine looked equivalent — complete remission 81% versus 82%, median disease-free survival 15 versus 11+ years — but relapses never stopped
cards.type: Retrospective comparison of pentostatin versus cladribine, median follow-up 12.5 years (Else 2005)
cards.people: 219 patients with hairy cell leukaemia treated with purine analogues and followed retrospectively for a median of 12.5 years: 185 received pentostatin and 34 received cladribine as first-line therapy.
cards.result: Overall response was 96% with pentostatin and 100% with first-line cladribine; complete remission 81% versus 82%; median disease-free survival 15 years versus 11+ years. Relapse had occurred by 5 and 10 years in 24% and 42% of pentostatin patients and 33% and 48% of cladribine patients; 10-year survival was 96% versus 100%. Complete-remission rates fell with each successive relapse (69% to 45%; P≤0.001), achieving complete remission after first-line therapy predicted longer disease-free survival (P=0.00007), and the disease-free survival curve showed no plateau — the authors' conclusion: cure remains elusive, but purine analogues achieve long-term survival with good quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and unbalanced (185 versus 34 patients) — treatment choice was by era and clinician, not randomisation, so 'equivalence' here means no large difference was seen, not that equivalence was proven. The cladribine group's shorter median disease-free survival (11+ years, still accruing events) partly reflects its follow-up structure. The durable message is the shared one: a fifth to a half of patients relapse by 10 years depending on the series, yet survival remains above 95%.
cards.source: Else M, Dearden CE, Matutes E et al. Long remissions in hairy cell leukemia with purine analogs: a report of 219 patients with a median follow-up of 12.5 years. Cancer. 2005. PMID: 16245328. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective comparison). cards.headline: Else 2009: at 16 years, median relapse-free survival was 16 years, only 8 of 233 patients died of hairy cell leukaemia, and complete responders could expect a normal lifespan
cards.summary: Else 2009: at 16 years, median relapse-free survival was 16 years, only 8 of 233 patients died of hairy cell leukaemia, and complete responders could expect a normal lifespan
cards.type: Retrospective long-term follow-up series, median 16 years (Else 2009)
cards.people: 233 patients with hairy cell leukaemia treated initially with pentostatin (n=188) or cladribine (n=45) and followed retrospectively for a median of 16 years from diagnosis.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in outcome between pentostatin and cladribine. Overall complete remission was 80% and median relapse-free survival 16 years. After relapse (79 patients) or non-response (5), second-line treatment again gave 69% complete remission with a median relapse-free survival of 11 years; third-line treatment (23 patients) gave 50% complete remission and 6.5 years. Patients still in complete remission at 5 years retained a 25% risk of relapse by 15 years. Only 8 patients died of hairy-cell-leukaemia-related causes, and the authors concluded that patients who achieve complete remission can expect a normal lifespan.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective single-programme series spanning treatment eras; survival this good partly reflects the disease's indolence and modern supportive care, not the drugs alone. 'Normal lifespan' applies to complete responders — partial responders and the multiply relapsed do worse (treatment failure at 48 months was 54% for partial responders in Saven 1998). Later relapses respond less well each time (complete remission 69% second-line, 50% third-line), so long follow-up is not optional.

cards.headline: Synthesis: purine analogues transformed hairy cell leukaemia — complete remission in roughly 4 of 5 to 9 of 10 patients, remissions measured in decades, retreatment effective — but relapse continues and cure is not claimed
cards.summary: Synthesis: purine analogues transformed hairy cell leukaemia — complete remission in roughly 4 of 5 to 9 of 10 patients, remissions measured in decades, retreatment effective — but relapse continues and cure is not claimed
cards.people: Four sources: the one randomised trial (Grever 1995 — 313 eligible patients, pentostatin versus interferon), the pivotal single-arm cladribine series (Saven 1998 — 349 evaluable patients), and two long retrospective comparisons from one programme (Else 2005 — 219 patients, 12.5 years; Else 2009 — 233 patients, 16 years).
cards.result: Response: complete remission 76% for pentostatin against 11% for interferon in the randomised trial (P<.0001); 91% complete response for a single 7-day cladribine course in single-arm data; about 80–82% complete remission for either purine analogue as first-line therapy in the long series. Durability: median disease-free/relapse-free survival of 11–16 years; 10-year survival 96–100%; only 8 of 233 patients died of the disease over 16 years in Else 2009. Limits: relapse in 24–48% by 10 years depending on agent and series, no plateau in the disease-free curve, diminishing complete-remission rates with each retreatment (69% second-line, 50% third-line), and a second-neoplasm signal in the cladribine series (observed/expected 1.88). PROPOSED LIKELY: a father diagnosed with classic hairy cell leukaemia today can expect first-line cladribine or pentostatin to put him into a complete remission that will likely last many years — among the best outcomes in leukaemia — with effective retreatment if it returns.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: these records concern classic hairy cell leukaemia treated with purine analogues. They do not cover hairy cell leukaemia variant (which responds differently), modern additions such as rituximab combinations or BRAF inhibitors for relapsed/refractory disease, or treatment during active infection — all outside the fetched record. The cladribine evidence is single-arm by historical accident (the drug worked too visibly to randomise against placebo); the stamp rests on the randomised pentostatin trial plus concordant large series, not on a cladribine RCT, because none exists.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grever M et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 1995 (PMID: 7707126); Saven A et al. Blood. 1998 (PMID: 9731048); Else M et al. Cancer. 2005 (PMID: 16245328); Else M et al. British Journal of Haematology. 2009 (PMID: 19344416).
