shelves.title: Bile duct cancer (advanced biliary tract cancer): gemcitabine + cisplatin beats gemcitabine alone — median survival 11.7 vs 8.1 months in the ABC-02 trial — and adding a third chemotherapy drug did not help
shelves.question: How is bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) treated? If the cancer cannot be removed by surgery, which chemotherapy actually helps people live longer? Clinical question underneath: in adults with locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer (cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder or ampullary cancer), does first-line gemcitabine plus cisplatin improve overall survival compared with gemcitabine alone, and does intensifying the regimen further add benefit?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/drug therapy · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/mortality · Cisplatin/therapeutic use · Deoxycytidine/analogs & derivatives · Gemcitabine · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for the chemotherapy backbone — two randomised trials point the same way. The phase 3 ABC-02 trial (Valle 2010, PMID: 20375404; 410 patients) found median overall survival of 11.7 months on cisplatin plus gemcitabine versus 8.1 months on gemcitabine alone (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.80, P<0.001 — a relative reduction in the risk of death of about a third, alongside the absolute 3.6-month median gain), with progression-free survival 8.0 vs 5.0 months and tumour control 81.4% vs 71.8% (P=0.049); neutropenia was more common on the combination but neutropenia-associated infections were similar. The smaller Japanese randomised study (Okusaka 2010, PMID: 20628385; 84 patients) was consistent: 1-year survival 39.0% vs 31.0%, median survival 11.2 vs 7.7 months. Intensifying further did not help: in SWOG S1815 (Shroff 2025, PMID: 39671534; 452 randomised), adding nab-paclitaxel to gemcitabine-cisplatin gave median survival 14.0 vs 13.6 months (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72-1.14, P=.41) with more toxicity. BOUNDARY: the modern immunotherapy additions are homed elsewhere and are NOT re-carded here — durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) and pembrolizumab added to this same backbone are on Shelf #858; second-line FOLFOX (ABC-06) is on Shelf #1885; adjuvant capecitabine after surgery is on Shelf #3415. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): gemcitabine plus cisplatin is the proven first-line chemotherapy backbone for advanced biliary tract cancer.

cards.headline: ABC-02 (Valle 2010, phase 3, n=410): cisplatin + gemcitabine extended median survival to 11.7 months vs 8.1 on gemcitabine alone (HR 0.64, P<0.001)
cards.summary: ABC-02 (Valle 2010, phase 3, n=410): cisplatin + gemcitabine extended median survival to 11.7 months vs 8.1 on gemcitabine alone (HR 0.64, P<0.001)
cards.people: 410 patients with locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer or ampullary cancer, randomised to cisplatin (25 mg/m²) followed by gemcitabine (1000 mg/m² on days 1 and 8, every 3 weeks for eight cycles; n=204) or gemcitabine alone (1000 mg/m² on days 1, 8 and 15, every 4 weeks for six cycles; n=206), for up to 24 weeks. Primary endpoint overall survival; median follow-up 8.2 months, 327 deaths. The trial grew out of an earlier randomised phase 2 study of 86 patients by the same group.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 11.7 months with cisplatin-gemcitabine versus 8.1 months with gemcitabine alone (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.80, P<0.001) — a relative reduction in the hazard of death of 36%, corresponding to the absolute median gain of 3.6 months printed beside it. Median progression-free survival was 8.0 versus 5.0 months (P<0.001), and the rate of tumour control was higher on the combination (81.4% vs 71.8%, P=0.049). Adverse events were similar except for more neutropenia with the combination; neutropenia-associated infections were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The population mixes three related cancers (bile duct, gallbladder, ampullary), so the estimate is for advanced biliary tract cancer as a group, not cholangiocarcinoma alone. Survival gains are real but measured in months, and this 2010 trial predates the immunotherapy combinations now layered on this backbone (homed on Shelf #858).
cards.source: Valle J et al. Cisplatin plus gemcitabine versus gemcitabine for biliary tract cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20375404. Registry ID: NCT00262769. cards.headline: BT22 (Okusaka 2010, randomised, n=84): the Japanese study agreed — 1-year survival 39.0% vs 31.0%, median survival 11.2 vs 7.7 months, for the combination
cards.summary: BT22 (Okusaka 2010, randomised, n=84): the Japanese study agreed — 1-year survival 39.0% vs 31.0%, median survival 11.2 vs 7.7 months, for the combination
cards.people: 84 patients with advanced biliary tract cancer in Japan, randomised to cisplatin 25 mg/m² plus gemcitabine 1000 mg/m² on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle, or gemcitabine alone 1000 mg/m² on days 1, 8 and 15 of a 28-day cycle, for at least 12 weeks and up to 48 weeks; 83 patients were analysed.
cards.result: For the combination versus gemcitabine alone: 1-year survival rate 39.0% vs 31.0%, median survival time 11.2 vs 7.7 months, median progression-free survival 5.8 vs 3.7 months, and overall response rate 19.5% vs 11.9%. The most common grade 3 or 4 toxicities (combination/single-agent) were neutropenia (56.1%/38.1%), thrombocytopenia (39.0%/7.1%), leukopenia (29.3%/19.0%), haemoglobin decrease (36.6%/16.7%) and gamma-GTP increase (29.3%/35.7%).
cards.watchOut: A small phase 2-sized randomised study (84 patients) without the statistical power of ABC-02; its value is consistency — an independent population showing the same direction and similar medians — not stand-alone proof. Blood-count toxicity, especially low platelets, was substantially more frequent on the combination.
cards.source: Okusaka T et al. Gemcitabine alone or in combination with cisplatin in patients with biliary tract cancer: a comparative multicentre study in Japan. British Journal of Cancer. 2010. PMID: 20628385. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SWOG S1815 (Shroff 2025, phase 3, n=452): adding nab-paclitaxel to gemcitabine-cisplatin did NOT improve survival (14.0 vs 13.6 months; HR 0.91, P=.41) and added toxicity
cards.summary: SWOG S1815 (Shroff 2025, phase 3, n=452): adding nab-paclitaxel to gemcitabine-cisplatin did NOT improve survival (14.0 vs 13.6 months; HR 0.91, P=.41) and added toxicity
cards.people: 452 patients with newly diagnosed locally advanced unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer (67% intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, 16% gallbladder, 17% extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma among the 441 eligible and analysable), randomised 2:1 to gemcitabine + cisplatin + nab-paclitaxel (GAP) or gemcitabine + cisplatin (GC). Primary outcome overall survival.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in overall survival: median 14.0 months (95% CI 12.4 to 16.1) on GAP versus 13.6 months (95% CI 9.7 to 16.6) on GC (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.14, P=.41). Median progression-free survival was 7.5 months (95% CI 6.4 to 8.5) versus 6.3 months (95% CI 4.4 to 8.2) (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.12, P=.32). Exploratory subsets suggested larger progression-free benefits in gallbladder cancer and locally advanced disease, but these were not statistically established for survival. More toxicity was encountered with GAP.
cards.watchOut: A well-powered negative trial: it closes the door on simply adding a third cytotoxic drug for unselected patients. The subset signals (gallbladder, locally advanced) are exploratory interaction findings, not a basis for choosing the triplet. Note the control arm's 13.6-month median exceeds ABC-02's 11.7 — cross-trial comparisons reflect different eras and case mix, not a better backbone.

randomised phase 3 trial (swog s1815; shroff 2025) 452 patients with newly diagnosed locally advanced unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer (67% intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, 16% gallbladder, 17% extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma among the 441 eligible and analysable), randomised 2:1 to gemcitabine + cisplatin + nab-paclitaxel (gap) or gemcitabine + cisplatin (gc). primary outcome overall survival. there was no significant difference in overall survival: median 14.0 months (95% ci 12.4 to 16.1) on gap versus 13.6 months (95% ci 9.7 to 16.6) on gc (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% ci 0.72 to 1.14, p=.41). median progression-free survival was 7.5 months (95% ci 6.4 to 8.5) versus 6.3 months (95% ci 4.4 to 8.2) (hr 0.89, 95% ci 0.71 to 1.12, p=.32). exploratory subsets suggested larger progression-free benefits in gallbladder cancer and locally advanced disease, but these were not statistically established for survival. more toxicity was encountered with gap. a well-powered negative trial: it closes the door on simply adding a third cytotoxic drug for unselected patients. the subset signals (gallbladder, locally advanced) are exploratory interaction findings, not a basis for choosing the triplet. note the control arm's 13.6-month median exceeds abc-02's 11.7 — cross-trial comparisons reflect different eras and case mix, not a better backbone. shroff rt et al. swog s1815: a phase iii randomized trial of gemcitabine, cisplatin, and nab-paclitaxel versus gemcitabine and cisplatin in newly diagnosed, advanced biliary tract cancers. journal of clinical oncology. 2025. pmid: 39671534. registry id: nct03768414. mesh: albumins/administration & dosage · antineoplastic combined chemotherapy protocols/therapeutic use* · biliary tract neoplasms/drug therapy* · biliary tract neoplasms/mortality · cisplatin/administration & dosage · deoxycytidine/analogs & derivatives · gemcitabine · humans · paclitaxel/administration & dosage

cards.headline: Synthesis: gemcitabine + cisplatin is the proven first-line backbone (two randomised trials agree); a third cytotoxic drug adds toxicity, not survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: gemcitabine + cisplatin is the proven first-line backbone (two randomised trials agree); a third cytotoxic drug adds toxicity, not survival
cards.people: Three randomised trials in advanced biliary tract cancer: ABC-02 (410 patients; Valle 2010), the Japanese BT22 study (84 patients; Okusaka 2010) and SWOG S1815 (452 randomised, 441 analysable; Shroff 2025).
cards.result: Gemcitabine plus cisplatin versus gemcitabine alone: median survival 11.7 vs 8.1 months (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.80) in the phase 3 trial, with a consistent smaller trial (11.2 vs 7.7 months; 1-year survival 39.0% vs 31.0%). Adding nab-paclitaxel to the doublet: no survival benefit (HR 0.91, P=.41), more toxicity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for gemcitabine-cisplatin as the first-line chemotherapy backbone.
cards.watchOut: Boundaries (one-home rule): adding durvalumab (TOPAZ-1) or pembrolizumab to this backbone is homed on Shelf #858; second-line FOLFOX after progression (ABC-06) is on Shelf #1885; capecitabine after curative surgery is on Shelf #3415. Those questions are deliberately not re-carded here. Tier C.

shelves.title: Breast cancer in men: no randomised trials exist in men — registry data say tamoxifen, not an aromatase inhibitor, is the endocrine treatment with the survival record (deaths 17.9% vs 32.0% in 257 men)
shelves.question: How is breast cancer in men treated? Do the hormone treatments proven in women work the same in men? Clinical question underneath: in men with hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, what male-specific evidence exists for surgery and adjuvant endocrine therapy — in particular tamoxifen versus aromatase inhibitors — given that the randomised trials were done in women and men were excluded?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Aromatase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms, Male/drug therapy · Breast Neoplasms, Male/mortality · Humans · Male · Tamoxifen/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped, because every scrap of male-specific evidence is observational: there are no randomised trials of breast cancer treatment in men, and standard care is extrapolated from trials in women. That extrapolation fails at one tested point. In 257 men with hormone-receptor-positive disease from German registries (Eggemann 2013, PMID: 23224235), 37 of 207 men on tamoxifen died (17.9%) versus 16 of 50 on an aromatase inhibitor (32.0%) over a median 42.2 months (log-rank p=0.007); after adjustment, aromatase inhibitor treatment carried a higher mortality risk (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.13-2.13) — the reverse of the female-trial ordering. In a prospectively enrolled cohort of 448 men (Eggemann 2020, PMID: 32367072), men who did not receive tamoxifen had significantly worse disease-free survival (P=0.002); the reported recurrence-and-mortality figure was 18.2% without tamoxifen versus 11.2% with it, and adjusted analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.32 (95% CI 0.14-0.74) for recurrence with tamoxifen — a 68% relative reduction. The descriptive picture comes from Portugal's national registry (Montenegro 2025, PMID: 40079376; 620 men, 2001-2021): median age 68; 60.3% localised, 24.5% locally advanced, 15.2% metastatic; oestrogen-receptor-positive in 96.6%; mastectomy the primary surgery and tamoxifen the most-used adjuvant endocrine therapy; median survival 86 months (localised), 70 (locally advanced) and 41 (metastatic). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in men, tamoxifen is the endocrine therapy with male-specific outcome data behind it; aromatase inhibitors alone performed worse in the male registry data, contrary to what female trials would predict.

cards.headline: Eggemann 2013 (German registries, 257 men): deaths 17.9% on tamoxifen vs 32.0% on aromatase inhibitors (adjusted HR 1.55 for AI, p=0.007)
cards.summary: Eggemann 2013 (German registries, 257 men): deaths 17.9% on tamoxifen vs 32.0% on aromatase inhibitors (adjusted HR 1.55 for AI, p=0.007)
cards.people: 257 men with hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer from numerous German population-based cancer registries, treated with adjuvant tamoxifen (n=207) or an aromatase inhibitor (n=50). Median age at diagnosis 68 years (range 36-91); median follow-up 42.2 months (range 2-115).
cards.result: 37 patients treated with tamoxifen (17.9%) and 16 treated with an aromatase inhibitor (32.0%) died (log-rank p=0.007). After adjustment for age, tumour size, node status and tumour grading, aromatase inhibitor treatment was linked to a higher risk of mortality compared with tamoxifen (hazard ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.13-2.13, p=0.007). The authors concluded overall survival in male breast cancer was significantly better after adjuvant tamoxifen than after an aromatase inhibitor, and that tamoxifen should be considered the treatment of choice for hormone-receptor-positive male breast cancer.
cards.watchOut: Observational and lopsided (207 vs 50 men): doctors chose the drug, so the aromatase-inhibitor group may have differed in ways adjustment could not capture — but the direction is the opposite of the female randomised evidence, which is exactly why male-specific data matter here. Follow-up (median 42.2 months) is short for a hormone-sensitive cancer.
cards.source: Eggemann H et al. Adjuvant therapy with tamoxifen compared to aromatase inhibitors for 257 male breast cancer patients. Breast Cancer Research and Treatment. 2013. PMID: 23224235. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Eggemann 2020 (prospective cohort, 448 men): men who did not receive tamoxifen had worse disease-free survival (P=0.002); adjusted recurrence hazard ratio 0.32 with tamoxifen
cards.summary: Eggemann 2020 (prospective cohort, 448 men): men who did not receive tamoxifen had worse disease-free survival (P=0.002); adjusted recurrence hazard ratio 0.32 with tamoxifen
cards.people: 448 men with breast cancer treated between May 2009 and June 2018 in a prospectively enrolled German cohort (registered DRKS00009536). Median age at diagnosis 69 years (range 27-96); median follow-up 39 months (range 3-89). Almost half (43.5%) had positive axillary lymph nodes, and hormone-receptor positivity was observed in 98.4% of patients. Primary endpoint: disease-free survival.
cards.result: Disease-free survival among men who did not receive tamoxifen was significantly reduced compared with those who underwent tamoxifen therapy (P=0.002). The recurrence rate and mortality, as reported in the paper, were 18.2% in the group without tamoxifen treatment and 11.2% in the group with it. After adjustment for prognostic factors, tamoxifen was associated with a 68% relative reduction in the recurrence rate (hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.14-0.74). The most common site of metastases was bone.
cards.watchOut: Still not randomised — the comparison is between men who did and did not receive tamoxifen in routine care, and the reasons some men went untreated (frailty, refusal, contraindications) themselves predict worse outcomes. The paper's own framing states the problem plainly: treatment of male breast cancer rests on retrospective analyses or extrapolation from female studies because prospective male data were lacking.
cards.source: Eggemann H et al. Survival benefit of tamoxifen in male breast cancer: prospective cohort analysis. British Journal of Cancer. 2020. PMID: 32367072. Registry ID: DRKS00009536. cards.headline: Montenegro 2025 (Portugal national registry, 620 men, 2001-2021): 96.6% oestrogen-receptor-positive; mastectomy the main surgery, tamoxifen the commonest adjuvant hormone therapy; median survival 86 months if localised, 41 if metastatic
cards.summary: Montenegro 2025 (Portugal national registry, 620 men, 2001-2021): 96.6% oestrogen-receptor-positive; mastectomy the main surgery, tamoxifen the commonest adjuvant hormone therapy; median survival 86 months if localised, 41 if metastatic
cards.people: 620 men with breast cancer recorded in the Portuguese National Oncology registry from 2001 to 2021. Median age at diagnosis 68 years (interquartile range 60-77). Disease was localised in 60.3%, locally advanced in 24.5% and metastatic in 15.2%. Most tumours were invasive carcinoma of no special type (86%); oestrogen receptor was positive in 96.6% and progesterone receptor in 85.6%; triple-negative disease accounted for 1.6%.
cards.result: Mastectomy was the primary surgical intervention, and tamoxifen was the most widely used adjuvant endocrine therapy; endocrine therapy was also the most prescribed first-line therapy in advanced disease. Median overall survival was 86 months for localised disease, 70 months for locally advanced disease and 41 months for metastatic disease. The authors concluded that male breast cancer care is marked by later-stage diagnosis and reliance on female-derived protocols, and called for male-specific clinical trials.
cards.watchOut: Descriptive, with no treatment comparison: it shows what was done and how long men lived by stage, not which treatment caused what. Survival by stage spans two decades of changing practice (2001-2021), so the medians blend eras. Its value on this shelf is the denominator — how male breast cancer actually presents and is treated in a whole country.
cards.source: Montenegro MA et al. Male Breast Cancer in Portugal: A Descriptive Analysis of a 20-Year Cohort. European Journal of Breast Health. 2025. PMID: 40079376. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in men, the only treatment comparison with male outcome data favours tamoxifen — everything else is borrowed from women's trials, and one borrowed assumption already failed
cards.summary: Synthesis: in men, the only treatment comparison with male outcome data favours tamoxifen — everything else is borrowed from women's trials, and one borrowed assumption already failed
cards.people: Three male-specific observational datasets: 257 men in German registries comparing tamoxifen with aromatase inhibitors (Eggemann 2013), 448 men in a prospectively enrolled cohort comparing tamoxifen with no tamoxifen (Eggemann 2020), and 620 men in Portugal's national registry describing presentation, treatment and survival (Montenegro 2025). No randomised trial in men exists for any card on this shelf.
cards.result: Tamoxifen vs aromatase inhibitor: deaths 17.9% vs 32.0%, adjusted HR 1.55 (95% CI 1.13-2.13) against the inhibitor. Tamoxifen vs none: adjusted recurrence HR 0.32 (95% CI 0.14-0.74); disease-free survival significantly worse without tamoxifen (P=0.002). Practice and outcomes at national scale: mastectomy and tamoxifen predominate; median survival 86/70/41 months by stage. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for tamoxifen as the male endocrine standard — observational data only, so the stamp is capped.
cards.watchOut: The extrapolation problem is the shelf's central warning: chemotherapy, HER2-directed therapy, CDK4/6 inhibitors, radiotherapy and endocrine duration in men are all prescribed from trials that excluded or barely included men, and the one place male data exist (aromatase inhibitors) they contradict the female-trial ordering — a standing reason to distrust untested extrapolation in either direction. Tier C.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eggemann H et al. Breast Cancer Research and Treatment. 2013 (PMID: 23224235); Eggemann H et al. British Journal of Cancer. 2020 (PMID: 32367072); Montenegro MA et al. European Journal of Breast Health. 2025 (PMID: 40079376).

shelves.title: Eye cancer (uveal melanoma): plaque brachytherapy versus removing the eye — the COMS randomised trial of 1,317 patients found no survival difference at 5 years (81% vs 82%) or 12 years, but vision in the radiated eye usually deteriorated
shelves.question: I have been told I have an eye cancer (uveal melanoma, a medium choroidal melanoma) — should I have the eye removed, or can a radiation plaque save the eye without shortening my life? How do survival and vision compare after iodine-125 plaque brachytherapy versus enucleation?
shelves.mesh: Brachytherapy · Choroid Neoplasms/mortality · Choroid Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Choroid Neoplasms/surgery · Eye Enucleation · Iodine Radioisotopes/therapeutic use · Melanoma/mortality · Melanoma/radiotherapy · Melanoma/surgery · Prognosis · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference in survival) — this shelf is scoped to MEDIUM choroidal melanoma, the tumour size the Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) randomised. In the trial's initial mortality report (Diener-West 2001, PMID: 11448319; 1,317 patients: 660 enucleation, 657 iodine-125 brachytherapy), deaths were 188 of 660 (28%) after enucleation versus 176 of 657 (27%) after brachytherapy; 5-year survival was 81% versus 82% (P=.48), the adjusted relative risk of death was 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22), and 5-year death with confirmed melanoma metastasis was 11% versus 9% (adjusted relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.66–1.24); the trial was powered to exclude a ±25% relative difference. At 12 years (COMS Group 2006, PMID: 17159027; NCT00000124), 471 of 1,317 patients had died, cumulative all-cause mortality was 43% after brachytherapy versus 41% after enucleation, and death with confirmed metastasis at 5, 10 and 12 years was 10%, 18% and 21% after brachytherapy versus 11%, 17% and 17% after enucleation. What brachytherapy buys is the eye, not sight: among 623 brachytherapy patients analysed for vision (Melia 2001, PMID: 11158813), median visual acuity fell from 20/32 at baseline to 20/125 at 3 years, the proportion at 20/40 or better fell from 70% to 34%, and 45% were at 20/200 or worse by 3 years. BOUNDARY: small and large choroidal melanomas were studied in separate COMS arms and are not carded here; metastatic uveal melanoma treatment (tebentafusp) is homed on Shelf #1903 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference in survival): removing the eye did not make patients live longer in the only randomised test, so the choice turns on keeping the eye against its expected visual decline.

cards.headline: COMS Report No. 18 (Diener-West 2001): 5-year survival 81% after enucleation versus 82% after brachytherapy (P=.48); adjusted relative risk of death 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22)
cards.summary: COMS Report No. 18 (Diener-West 2001): 5-year survival 81% after enucleation versus 82% after brachytherapy (P=.48); adjusted relative risk of death 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — initial mortality findings (COMS Report No. 18, Diener-West 2001)
cards.people: 1,317 patients with medium choroidal melanoma randomised at COMS centres to enucleation (660) or iodine-125 brachytherapy (657); the trial was designed with power to exclude a ±25% relative difference in mortality between the treatments.
cards.result: By the initial mortality report, 188 of 660 patients (28%) assigned to enucleation and 176 of 657 (27%) assigned to brachytherapy had died. Five-year survival was 81% after enucleation versus 82% after brachytherapy (P=.48), and the adjusted relative risk of death (brachytherapy versus enucleation) was 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22). Death with confirmed melanoma metastasis at 5 years was 11% after enucleation versus 9% after brachytherapy (adjusted relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.66–1.24). No survival advantage for removing the eye was found.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.80–1.22) cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm of either treatment — the trial rules out large differences (it was powered around ±25% relative), not small ones. The population is medium tumours only: nothing here answers for small melanomas that might be observed, or large ones where enucleation remains usual.
cards.source: Diener-West M, Earle JD, Fine SL, et al. The COMS randomized trial of iodine 125 brachytherapy for choroidal melanoma: III. Initial mortality findings. COMS Report No. 18. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2001. PMID: 11448319. Registry ID: none in the record (this report predates the trial's registry listing; the 12-year report below carries NCT00000124). how do survival and vision compare after iodine-125 plaque brachytherapy versus enucleation? randomised controlled trial — initial mortality findings (coms report no. 18, diener-west 2001) 1,317 patients with medium choroidal melanoma randomised at coms centres to enucleation (660) or iodine-125 brachytherapy (657); the trial was designed with power to exclude a ±25% relative difference in mortality between the treatments. by the initial mortality report, 188 of 660 patients (28%) assigned to enucleation and 176 of 657 (27%) assigned to brachytherapy had died. five-year survival was 81% after enucleation versus 82% after brachytherapy (p=.48), and the adjusted relative risk of death (brachytherapy versus enucleation) was 0.99 (95% ci 0.80–1.22). death with confirmed melanoma metastasis at 5 years was 11% after enucleation versus 9% after brachytherapy (adjusted relative risk 0.91, 95% ci 0.66–1.24). no survival advantage for removing the eye was found. the confidence interval (0.80–1.22) cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm of either treatment — the trial rules out large differences (it was powered around ±25% relative), not small ones. the population is medium tumours only: nothing here answers for small melanomas that might be observed, or large ones where enucleation remains usual. diener-west m, earle jd, fine sl, et al. the coms randomized trial of iodine 125 brachytherapy for choroidal melanoma: iii. initial mortality findings. coms report no. 18. archives of ophthalmology. 2001. pmid: 11448319. registry id: none in the record (this report predates the trial's registry listing; the 12-year report below carries nct00000124). mesh: brachytherapy · choroid neoplasms/mortality · eye enucleation · iodine radioisotopes/therapeutic use · melanoma/mortality · survival rate

cards.headline: COMS Report No. 28 (2006): at 12 years, cumulative mortality 43% after brachytherapy versus 41% after enucleation — still no survival difference; older age and larger tumour diameter predicted death
cards.summary: COMS Report No. 28 (2006): at 12 years, cumulative mortality 43% after brachytherapy versus 41% after enucleation — still no survival difference; older age and larger tumour diameter predicted death
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — 12-year mortality and prognostic factors (COMS Report No. 28, COMS Group 2006)
cards.people: The same 1,317 randomised patients (660 enucleation, 657 brachytherapy) followed for up to 12 years; 471 of the 1,317 had died within 12 years of enrolment.
cards.result: Twelve-year cumulative all-cause mortality was 43% in the brachytherapy group versus 41% in the enucleation group. Death with histopathologically confirmed melanoma metastasis was 10%, 18% and 21% at 5, 10 and 12 years after brachytherapy, versus 11%, 17% and 17% after enucleation. The main baseline predictors of death were older age and larger basal tumour diameter, not the treatment assigned. The authors' finding stands: through 12 years, survival after eye-preserving plaque radiotherapy and after removal of the eye did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The small late divergence in confirmed-metastasis deaths (21% versus 17% at 12 years) sits inside wide uncertainty and beside an all-cause mortality comparison that runs the other way (43% versus 41%); the report does not claim a significant difference on either. Follow-up beyond 12 years is thinner, and uveal melanoma can metastasise late, so 'no difference shown by 12 years' is the accurate claim.
cards.source: Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study Group. The COMS randomized trial of iodine 125 brachytherapy for choroidal melanoma: V. Twelve-year mortality rates and prognostic factors: COMS report No. 28. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2006. PMID: 17159027. Registry ID: NCT00000124. cards.headline: COMS Report No. 16 (Melia 2001): the kept eye usually loses vision — median acuity 20/125 at 3 years, 34% still 20/40 or better, 45% at 20/200 or worse
cards.summary: COMS Report No. 16 (Melia 2001): the kept eye usually loses vision — median acuity 20/125 at 3 years, 34% still 20/40 or better, 45% at 20/200 or worse
cards.type: Randomised trial cohort analysis — visual acuity after brachytherapy (COMS Report No. 16, Melia 2001)
cards.people: 623 patients from the brachytherapy arm of the COMS medium-tumour trial with visual acuity analysed over 3 years after iodine-125 plaque treatment; at baseline their median visual acuity was 20/32 and 70% had acuity of 20/40 or better.
cards.result: By 3 years, median visual acuity in the treated eye was 20/125; 34% retained acuity of 20/40 or better and 45% had fallen to 20/200 or worse. The proportion who had lost six or more lines of acuity was 18% by 1 year, 34% by 2 years and 49% by 3 years; the proportion falling to 20/200 or worse was 17%, 33% and 43% at 1, 2 and 3 years. Radiation preserves the globe, but progressive visual loss in that eye is the expected course, not a complication outlier.
cards.watchOut: This card describes only the brachytherapy arm — enucleation removes vision in the eye entirely and immediately, so there is no like-for-like visual comparison; the real trade the trial offers is certain immediate loss of the eye versus a kept eye whose sight fades in most patients over 3 years. Vision outcomes vary with tumour size and position relative to the fovea and optic disc, which this pooled summary does not split out.
cards.source: Melia BM, Abramson DH, Albert DM, et al. Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study (COMS) randomized trial of I-125 brachytherapy for medium choroidal melanoma. I. Visual acuity after 3 years: COMS report No. 16. Ophthalmology. 2001. PMID: 11158813. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era report of the COMS trial). cards.headline: Synthesis: survival is the same either way in the randomised record; the decision is the eye itself versus its fading sight
cards.summary: Synthesis: survival is the same either way in the randomised record; the decision is the eye itself versus its fading sight
cards.people: One randomised trial of 1,317 patients with medium choroidal melanoma (COMS), reported at 5 years (Diener-West 2001), 12 years (COMS Group 2006, NCT00000124), and for visual acuity in the brachytherapy arm (Melia 2001, 623 patients).
cards.result: Mortality: 5-year survival 81% (enucleation) versus 82% (brachytherapy), adjusted relative risk of death 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22); 12-year all-cause mortality 41% versus 43%; confirmed-metastasis deaths at 12 years 17% versus 21%. Vision after brachytherapy: median 20/125 at 3 years, 34% at 20/40 or better, 45% at 20/200 or worse. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference in survival) — enucleation has never been shown to extend life for medium choroidal melanoma; plaque brachytherapy is an eye-preserving alternative whose cost is progressive visual loss in the treated eye.
cards.watchOut: Scoped strictly to medium choroidal melanoma as COMS defined and randomised it. Large-tumour and small-tumour management, proton-beam and other plaque isotopes, and treatment of metastatic disease (Shelf #1903) are outside this shelf. Tier C: developer's personal verdict on a single large randomised programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Diener-West M et al. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2001 (PMID: 11448319); Collaborative Ocular Melanoma Study Group. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2006 (PMID: 17159027); Melia BM et al. Ophthalmology. 2001 (PMID: 11158813).

shelves.title: Gallbladder cancer after surgery: adjuvant chemotherapy — BILCAP's main analysis just missed significance (HR 0.81, p=0.097) while Japan's ASCOT trial showed 5-year survival of 64% versus 52% with S-1
shelves.question: My gallbladder cancer has been removed by surgery — should I have chemotherapy afterwards to stop it coming back? What do the adjuvant trials (capecitabine, S-1) show?
shelves.mesh: Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/drug therapy · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/mortality · Biliary Tract Neoplasms/therapy · Capecitabine/administration & dosage · Chemoradiotherapy, Adjuvant · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Gallbladder Neoplasms/drug therapy · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped to ADJUVANT treatment after surgical resection of biliary tract cancers, which include gallbladder cancer; chemotherapy for ADVANCED biliary tract cancer is homed on Shelf #5314 (and immunotherapy combinations on #858, second-line FOLFOX on #1885) and is not re-carded here. No randomised trial has enrolled gallbladder cancer alone, so every estimate below is from mixed biliary-tract populations. In BILCAP (Primrose 2019, PMID: 30922733; 447 patients — 223 capecitabine, 224 observation — with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer), the primary intention-to-treat analysis did not reach significance: median overall survival 51.1 months (95% CI 34.6–59.1) versus 36.4 months (29.7–44.5), adjusted hazard ratio 0.81 (0.63–1.04), p=0.097; the pre-specified sensitivity analysis gave HR 0.71 (0.55–0.92), p=0.010, and the per-protocol analysis (210 vs 220 patients) median survival 53 versus 36 months, HR 0.75 (0.58–0.97), p=0.028; median recurrence-free survival was 24.4 versus 17.5 months, and grade 3 or worse toxicity occurred in 44% of treated patients. In Japan's ASCOT trial (Ikeda 2026 five-year report, PMID: 42777180; 440 patients — 218 S-1, 222 observation), adjuvant S-1 improved survival clearly: 5-year overall survival 64% versus 52% (an absolute difference of 12 percentage points), hazard ratio 0.72 (0.55–0.95), one-sided P=.01; median survival 8.2 versus 5.9 years; median recurrence-free survival 6.1 versus 3.5 years; the original 3-year figures were 77.1% versus 67.6%. A single-arm phase II study of chemoradiation after resection (SWOG S0809; Ben-Josef 2015, PMID: 25964250; 79 patients, 32% gallbladder) reported 2-year survival of 65% with no control group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjuvant fluoropyrimidine after resection probably extends survival, on one formally negative-but-supportive trial and one positive trial, with gallbladder-specific benefit unmeasured.

cards.headline: BILCAP (Primrose 2019): median survival 51.1 vs 36.4 months with adjuvant capecitabine — but the primary analysis missed significance (adjusted HR 0.81, p=0.097); sensitivity and per-protocol analyses were positive
cards.summary: BILCAP (Primrose 2019): median survival 51.1 vs 36.4 months with adjuvant capecitabine — but the primary analysis missed significance (adjusted HR 0.81, p=0.097); sensitivity and per-protocol analyses were positive
cards.people: 447 patients at 44 UK centres with resected cholangiocarcinoma or muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer, randomised to capecitabine 1250 mg/m² twice daily on days 1–14 of a 21-day cycle for 8 cycles (223) or observation (224); 213 patients received at least one capecitabine dose for the safety set.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat median overall survival was 51.1 months (95% CI 34.6–59.1) on capecitabine versus 36.4 months (29.7–44.5) on observation — an absolute median difference of 14.7 months — but the adjusted hazard ratio was 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04) with p=0.097, so the primary endpoint was not met. The pre-specified sensitivity analysis gave HR 0.71 (0.55–0.92), p=0.010, and in the per-protocol population (210 capecitabine, 220 observation) median survival was 53 versus 36 months (HR 0.75, 0.58–0.97; p=0.028). Median recurrence-free survival (ITT) was 24.4 versus 17.5 months. Grade 3 or worse toxicity occurred in 44% of treated patients (hand-foot syndrome 20%, diarrhoea 8%, fatigue 8%), and serious adverse events in 21% versus 10%.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions belong on the face. First, the trial's own primary analysis is negative (p=0.097) — the supportive numbers come from sensitivity and per-protocol analyses, which is why this shelf's stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Second, the abstract does not report a gallbladder-cancer-only subgroup: BILCAP mixed intrahepatic, hilar and distal cholangiocarcinoma with gallbladder cancer, and no gallbladder-specific effect can be quoted from this record.
cards.source: Primrose JN, Fox RP, Palmer DH, et al. Capecitabine compared with observation in resected biliary tract cancer (BILCAP): a randomised, controlled, multicentre, phase 3 study. The Lancet Oncology. 2019. PMID: 30922733. Registry ID: EudraCT 2005-003318-13. cards.headline: ASCOT / JCOG1202 (Ikeda 2026, 5-year report): adjuvant S-1 raised 5-year survival to 64% versus 52% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.95) after resection
cards.summary: ASCOT / JCOG1202 (Ikeda 2026, 5-year report): adjuvant S-1 raised 5-year survival to 64% versus 52% (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.95) after resection
cards.type: Randomised phase III trial — 5-year follow-up (ASCOT / JCOG1202, Ikeda 2026)
cards.people: 440 patients in Japan with resected biliary tract cancer, randomised to adjuvant S-1 40 mg/m² twice daily, 4 weeks on and 2 weeks off for 4 cycles (218), or observation (222).
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 64% with S-1 versus 52% with observation — an absolute difference of 12 percentage points — with a hazard ratio of 0.72 (95% CI 0.55–0.95) and one-sided P=.01. Median overall survival was 8.2 versus 5.9 years, and median recurrence-free survival 6.1 versus 3.5 years. The trial's original primary report had shown 3-year overall survival of 77.1% versus 67.6%; the five-year follow-up confirms the benefit persists.
cards.watchOut: A Japanese population and a drug (S-1, a tegafur combination) whose dosing and tolerability differ in Western patients because of pharmacogenetic differences in fluoropyrimidine metabolism — the direction of benefit supports the drug class, but the exact regimen does not transfer automatically. Like BILCAP, ASCOT enrolled all biliary tract sites; a gallbladder-only estimate is not in this record. The one-sided P value is as the trial pre-specified it.
cards.source: Ikeda M, et al. Adjuvant S-1 versus observation after resection of biliary tract cancer (ASCOT / JCOG1202): five-year follow-up report. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026. PMID: 42777180. Registry ID: UMIN000011688. cards.headline: SWOG S0809 (Ben-Josef 2015): after gemcitabine-capecitabine and chemoradiation, 2-year survival was 65% — with no comparison group
cards.summary: SWOG S0809 (Ben-Josef 2015): after gemcitabine-capecitabine and chemoradiation, 2-year survival was 65% — with no comparison group
cards.type: Single-arm phase II trial (SWOG S0809, Ben-Josef 2015)
cards.people: 79 eligible patients with resected extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (68%) or gallbladder cancer (32%, about 25 patients); 54 had R0 and 25 R1 resections. Treatment was gemcitabine plus capecitabine for 4 cycles followed by capecitabine with radiotherapy (45 Gy to lymphatics, 54–59.4 Gy to the tumour bed); 86% completed the protocol.
cards.result: Two-year overall survival was 65% (95% CI 53–74%) overall, 67% after R0 resection and 60% after R1 resection; median overall survival was 35 months. Grade 3 adverse events occurred in 52% and grade 4 in 11%, with one treatment-related death from gastrointestinal haemorrhage. The authors concluded the regimen was deliverable and the survival figures promising enough to justify further study.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 65% two-year survival has no untreated comparator, and patients fit enough to complete a trimodality protocol are a selected group — this card shows feasibility and a survival figure consistent with benefit, not evidence of benefit. Only about 25 of the 79 patients had gallbladder cancer. It is carded because it is the main adjuvant chemoradiation record and includes the largest gallbladder contingent of the three cards.
cards.source: Ben-Josef E, Guthrie KA, El-Khoueiry AB, et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: adjuvant fluoropyrimidine probably helps after resection; no trial has answered for gallbladder cancer alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: adjuvant fluoropyrimidine probably helps after resection; no trial has answered for gallbladder cancer alone
cards.people: Two randomised trials in resected biliary tract cancer (BILCAP, 447 patients, capecitabine; ASCOT, 440 patients, S-1) and one single-arm chemoradiation study (SWOG S0809, 79 patients, 32% gallbladder).
cards.result: BILCAP: median survival 51.1 vs 36.4 months, primary HR 0.81 (p=0.097, not significant), sensitivity HR 0.71 and per-protocol HR 0.75 (both significant). ASCOT: 5-year survival 64% vs 52% (absolute +12 points), HR 0.72 (0.55–0.95). S0809 (uncontrolled): 2-year survival 65%. Grade 3+ toxicity affected 44% on BILCAP's capecitabine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the class effect across two randomised trials favours treatment, one trial formally missed its primary endpoint, and gallbladder-specific randomised numbers do not exist.
cards.watchOut: Boundary: this shelf is adjuvant therapy after resection only. First-line treatment of advanced biliary tract cancer (gemcitabine-cisplatin and successors) is Shelf #5314, immunotherapy combinations are Shelf #858, and second-line FOLFOX is Shelf #1885 — none re-carded here. Every patient number on this shelf comes from mixed biliary-tract populations; presenting any figure as a gallbladder-cancer result would overstate the record. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of Primrose JN et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 30922733); Ikeda M et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026 (PMID: 42777180); Ben-Josef E et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2015 (PMID: 25964250).

shelves.title: Nasal and sinus cancer: endoscopic surgery matched or beat open surgery on margins and local control in cohort data (clear margins 85% versus 64%; 5-year local control 90% versus 82%), and 5-year survival after endoscopic resection plus tailored radiotherapy was 71.4% in intestinal-type adenocarcinoma
shelves.question: In people with cancer of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses (sinonasal cancer), how do surgery-based treatments perform — in particular endoscopic resection versus open approaches — for margin clearance, local control and survival?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: There are no randomised trials in sinonasal cancer; all evidence is retrospective and endoscopic cases are selected to be more favourable. Kobayashi 2026 (PMID: 42367673; Registry ID: none in the record), 110 patients at 10 Japanese centres, found negative margins in 85% with endoscopic surgery versus 64% with the open craniofacial approach, and 5-year local control of 90% versus 82% — but endoscopy was used in earlier-stage cases. Chen 2022 (PMID: 36132140; Registry ID: none in the record), 303 patients over 18 years, found 5-year overall survival of 61.0%, better survival with surgery than with radiotherapy/chemotherapy alone, better survival with the endoscopic than the open approach (p<0.05), and a clear benefit from margin-negative (R0) resection (p<0.001). Parys 2025 (PMID: 40224179; Registry ID: none in the record), 200 intestinal-type adenocarcinoma patients treated with endoscopic resection and tailored radiotherapy over 30 years, found 5-year overall survival 71.4% and disease-specific survival 85.1%, with local recurrence in 34.0%. Observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for endoscopic surgery-based treatment in selected patients (observational evidence only).

cards.headline: Kobayashi 2026: endoscopic surgery achieved clear margins in 85% versus 64% for open surgery, with 5-year local control 90% versus 82%
cards.summary: Kobayashi 2026: endoscopic surgery achieved clear margins in 85% versus 64% for open surgery, with 5-year local control 90% versus 82%
cards.people: Patients with nasoethmoidal malignancies having first surgical treatment at 10 Japanese tertiary hospitals, 2014-2016; n=110, median follow-up 69 months
cards.result: Negative-margin resection was achieved in 85% of endoscopic endonasal approach (EEA) cases, 78% of combined EEA-plus-craniofacial cases and 64% of craniofacial approach (CA) cases. Postoperative radiotherapy was given in 50%, 56% and 36% respectively. Five-year local control rates were 90% (EEA), 78% (combined) and 82% (CA). Squamous cell carcinoma (29%) and olfactory neuroblastoma (24%) were the commonest types.
cards.watchOut: Strong selection bias: EEA was performed in early-stage cases and the combined approach in advanced cases, so the margin and control differences partly reflect tumour stage, not technique.
cards.source: Kobayashi M, Hanazawa T, Nakagawa T, Otori N, Fujimoto Y, Kodama S, Sanuki T, Tanaka S, Ariizumi Y, Nibu KI, et al. Endoscopic Endonasal Approach for Surgical Treatment of Nasal and Ethmoidal Malignancies: A Retrospective Multicenter Study. Ther Adv Allergy Rhinol. 2026. PMID: 42367673. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Chen 2022: 5-year survival 61.0% across 303 sinonasal cancers; surgery beat non-surgical treatment and endoscopic beat open surgery
cards.summary: Chen 2022: 5-year survival 61.0% across 303 sinonasal cancers; surgery beat non-surgical treatment and endoscopic beat open surgery
cards.people: Patients with sinonasal malignancies treated with curative intent at one Chinese tertiary centre, 2000-2018; n=303
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 61.0% (95% CI 55.4% to 67.1%) and event-free survival 46.2% (95% CI 40.4% to 52.7%). Patients who received surgery had better overall survival than those who received only radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy, endoscopic surgery had better overall survival than the open approach (p<0.05), and margin-negative (R0) resection significantly benefited overall and event-free survival (p<0.001). Numbers in this card were taken from the article's abstract as published by the journal (Frontiers in Oncology) and indexed in PubMed Central this session.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective single-centre series spanning 18 years of changing technique; approach comparisons are confounded by stage and histology (melanoma had the worst and adenocarcinoma the best survival).
cards.source: Chen MY, Wen X, Wei Y, Chen L, Huang ZX, Lu T, Zheng NZ, Li J, Wen WP, Wen YH. Oncologic outcome of multimodality treatment for sinonasal malignancies: An 18-year experience. Front Oncol. 2022. PMID: 36132140. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Parys 2025: after endoscopic resection and tailored radiotherapy, 5-year survival was 71.4% and disease-specific survival 85.1% in intestinal-type adenocarcinoma
cards.summary: Parys 2025: after endoscopic resection and tailored radiotherapy, 5-year survival was 71.4% and disease-specific survival 85.1% in intestinal-type adenocarcinoma
cards.people: Patients primarily treated for sinonasal intestinal-type adenocarcinoma at one Belgian tertiary centre, 1992-2022; n=200
cards.result: Five-year overall survival was 71.4%, disease-specific survival 85.1% and local recurrence-free survival 55.2%; at 10 years these were 48.2%, 76.2% and 32.2%. Local recurrence occurred in 34.0% of patients. Poorly differentiated tumours had worse disease-specific survival than well-differentiated tumours (hazard ratio 3.38, 95% CI 1.20 to 9.51), and positive margins worsened disease-specific survival (hazard ratio 2.95, 95% CI 1.29 to 6.74). Numbers in this card were taken from the article's abstract as published by the journal (Frontiers in Oncology) this session.
cards.watchOut: One histology only (intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, often wood-dust related) and one expert centre over 30 years; there is no non-endoscopic comparator group in this study.
cards.source: Parys QA, De Witte M, Hauben E, Clement PM, Hermans R, Decramer T, van Loon J, Nuyts S, Jorissen M, Vander Poorten V, Van Gerven L. Long-term outcomes of endoscopic resection and tailored adjuvant radiotherapy for sinonasal intestinal-type adenocarcinoma: a historical single-center cohort study in 200 patients. Front Oncol. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery is the backbone of sinonasal cancer treatment, and endoscopic resection performs at least as well as open surgery in the patients selected for it
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery is the backbone of sinonasal cancer treatment, and endoscopic resection performs at least as well as open surgery in the patients selected for it
cards.people: All carded evidence: three retrospective cohorts, n=110, n=303 and n=200 patients
cards.result: Clear margins were commoner with endoscopic surgery (85% versus 64%; Kobayashi 2026), margin-negative resection predicted better survival (Chen 2022), and long-term survival after endoscopic resection plus radiotherapy was 71.4% at 5 years for intestinal-type adenocarcinoma (Parys 2025). No randomised comparison exists.
cards.watchOut: Every comparison is confounded by selection — endoscopy is chosen for smaller, earlier tumours — so these data support endoscopic surgery as a valid option in selected patients, not as proven superiority.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kobayashi 2026 (PMID: 42367673), Chen 2022 (PMID: 36132140) and Parys 2025 (PMID: 40224179).

shelves.title: Swollen arm after breast cancer treatment: compression shrinks the swelling by about a quarter — but hands-on lymphatic drainage added nothing in the two best trials (0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus placebo drainage in 194 women)
shelves.question: In women with a swollen arm and hand from breast cancer-related lymphoedema, does decongestive therapy — and specifically its manual lymphatic drainage component — reduce arm volume compared with compression garments alone or placebo drainage?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Scoped to breast cancer-related arm lymphoedema — the cause of swollen arms and hands with randomised treatment evidence; prevention (Shelf #3427) and resistance exercise (Shelf #1786) are homed separately. Compression-based therapy reduces swelling in every trial arm: garments alone cut excess arm volume by 22.6% (Dayes 2013), and decongestive therapy arms fell by about a fifth to a quarter in relative terms over 3 weeks (EFforT-BCRL). The contested add-on is manual lymphatic drainage (MLD). Cochrane (Ezzo 2015, PMID: 25994425) pooled two small trials (83 participants) showing bandaging alone reducing swelling 30–38.6% with a further 7.11% from MLD — but the two best trials found no added effect: Dayes 2013 (103 women) gave 29.0% versus 22.6% for full decongestive therapy versus garments alone (difference 6.4%, 95% CI −6.8 to 20.5; P = .34), and the blinded EFforT-BCRL trial (De Vrieze 2022, PMID: 35428594; NCT02609724; 194 women) found differences of 0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus traditional and placebo drainage. PROPOSED: SPLIT (compression-based therapy effective; added MLD: the treatment made no difference in the two best trials).

cards.headline: Ezzo 2015 (Cochrane): compression bandaging alone cut arm lymphoedema swelling by 30–38.6%; adding manual lymphatic drainage added a further 7.11% (95% CI 1.75–12.47) across 2 small trials (83 participants)
cards.summary: Ezzo 2015 (Cochrane): compression bandaging alone cut arm lymphoedema swelling by 30–38.6%; adding manual lymphatic drainage added a further 7.11% (95% CI 1.75–12.47) across 2 small trials (83 participants)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Ezzo 2015)
cards.people: Six randomised or quasi-randomised trials, 208 participants in total, of women with breast cancer-related lymphoedema (arm swelling after breast cancer surgery and/or radiotherapy), testing manual lymphatic drainage (MLD) alone or added to compression, physiotherapy or a sleeve.
cards.result: MLD plus compression bandaging versus bandaging alone (2 trials, 83 participants): bandaging alone produced significant percent reductions of 30% to 38.6%, and MLD added a mean difference of 7.11% (95% CI 1.75% to 12.47%); the corresponding volume reduction was borderline significant (P = 0.06). MLD plus standard physiotherapy versus physiotherapy alone (1 trial) improved both groups with no significant between-group difference. MLD was safe and well tolerated in all trials. The reviewers concluded those with mild-to-moderate lymphoedema may be the ones who benefit from adding MLD — a finding needing confirmation — with function results contradictory and quality-of-life results inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: Trials of 24–45 participants each, searched to May 2013, with unblinded assessors in four of six trials: the 7.11% added reduction rests on 83 participants and predates the two large sham-controlled trials carded below, which found no added effect at all. The 'mild-to-moderate benefit' subgroup was a data-driven split the reviewers themselves flagged as unconfirmed.
cards.source: Ezzo J, Manheimer E, McNeely ML, Howell DM, Weiss R, Johansson KI, Bao T, Bily L, Tuppo CM, Williams AF, Karadibak D. Manual lymphatic drainage for lymphedema following breast cancer treatment. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 25994425. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Dayes 2013: full decongestive therapy (daily manual lymphatic drainage and bandaging, then garments) did NOT significantly beat compression garments alone — excess arm volume fell 29.0% versus 22.6% (difference 6.4%, 95% CI −6.8 to 20.5; P = .34)
cards.summary: Dayes 2013: full decongestive therapy (daily manual lymphatic drainage and bandaging, then garments) did NOT significantly beat compression garments alone — excess arm volume fell 29.0% versus 22.6% (difference 6.4%, 95% CI −6.8 to 20.5; P = .34)
cards.people: 103 women with breast cancer-related arm lymphoedema (at least 10% volume difference between arms) at six institutions, randomised to compression garments alone or daily manual lymphatic drainage and bandaging followed by compression garments; 95 were evaluable at 6 weeks.
cards.result: Mean reduction in excess arm volume was 29.0% in the decongestive therapy group versus 22.6% in the garment-only group (difference 6.4%; 95% CI −6.8% to 20.5%; P = .34). Absolute volume loss was 250 mL versus 143 mL (difference 107 mL; 95% CI 13 to 203 mL; P = .03). There was no difference in the proportion losing at least 50% of excess volume, and quality of life (SF-36) and arm function did not differ. The authors concluded the trial was unable to demonstrate a significant improvement from decongestive therapy over the conservative approach, possibly because of its size.
cards.watchOut: The one significant result (absolute mL lost, P = .03) is the secondary expression of the same data whose primary percent measure was null (P = .34) — larger arms lose more millilitres for the same percentage. Six weeks is also short for a lifelong condition; the trial cannot speak to maintenance, where garments are the constant in both arms.
cards.source: Dayes IS, Whelan TJ, Julian JA, et al. Randomized Trial of Decongestive Lymphatic Therapy for the Treatment of Lymphedema in Women With Breast Cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2013. PMID: not captured this session (DOI 10.1200/JCO.2012.45.7192). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: De Vrieze 2022 (EFforT-BCRL): in 194 women, adding real manual lymphatic drainage — traditional or fluoroscopy-guided — to decongestive therapy changed excess volume by 0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus placebo drainage: no added benefit
cards.summary: De Vrieze 2022 (EFforT-BCRL): in 194 women, adding real manual lymphatic drainage — traditional or fluoroscopy-guided — to decongestive therapy changed excess volume by 0.0 and −0.2 percentage points versus placebo drainage: no added benefit
cards.type: Multicentre three-arm double-blind randomised trial (De Vrieze 2022)
cards.people: 194 participants with unilateral chronic breast cancer-related lymphoedema at five Belgian hospitals, all receiving decongestive lymphatic therapy (education, skin care, compression therapy, exercises), randomised to additional fluoroscopy-guided MLD (n = 65), traditional MLD (n = 64) or placebo MLD (n = 65); assessor- and participant-blinded, 3 weeks of intensive treatment.
cards.result: Excess lymphoedema volume fell in every group: by 5.3 percentage points of percent excess volume (a 23.3% relative reduction) with fluoroscopy-guided MLD, 5.2 points (20.9% relative) with traditional MLD and 5.4 points (24.8% relative) with placebo MLD. Between-group differences were 0.0 percentage points (95% CI −2.0 to 2.1) for fluoroscopy-guided versus traditional MLD and −0.2 points (95% CI −2.1 to 1.8) versus placebo MLD. The authors concluded MLD did not provide clinically important additional benefit when added to the other components of decongestive therapy.
cards.watchOut: The strongest design in this literature — and a null. Its population is chronic, established lymphoedema; it does not test MLD started immediately after surgery (a prevention question), nor MLD for the trunk, breast or head and neck, where compression is hard to apply and drainage remains the pragmatic option.
cards.source: De Vrieze T, et al. Manual lymphatic drainage with or without fluoroscopy guidance did not substantially improve the effect of decongestive lymphatic therapy in people with breast cancer-related lymphoedema (EFforT-BCRL trial): a multicentre randomised trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: compression-based therapy shrinks the swollen arm by roughly a quarter to a third; the hands-on drainage component adds little or nothing in the trials big enough to tell
cards.summary: Synthesis: compression-based therapy shrinks the swollen arm by roughly a quarter to a third; the hands-on drainage component adds little or nothing in the trials big enough to tell
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: a Cochrane review (6 trials, 208 participants) and two multicentre randomised trials (103 and 194 participants), all in breast cancer-related arm lymphoedema.
cards.result: The base treatment works in every arm of every trial: compression-based care reduced excess arm volume by 22.6% (garments alone, Dayes 2013) and by about 21–25% relative over 3 weeks (all EFforT-BCRL arms), with bandaging alone reaching 30–38.6% in the small older trials. The contested component is manual lymphatic drainage: +7.11% in two small unblinded trials pooled by Cochrane, but a 6.4-point non-significant difference in Dayes 2013 and an exact null against placebo drainage in the blinded EFforT-BCRL trial. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (compression/decongestive therapy: effective base treatment · added manual lymphatic drainage: the treatment made no difference in the two best trials).
cards.watchOut: Scope: the carded evidence is arm lymphoedema after breast cancer treatment — the population in which this question has been trialled. Swollen arms and hands from other causes (venous thrombosis, infection, heart failure, drug effects) need their own diagnosis and treatment; exercise and resistance training for this population are homed separately on Shelf #1786, and prevention by early compression on Shelf #3427.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ezzo 2015 (PMID: 25994425), Dayes 2013 (PMID not captured this session) and De Vrieze 2022 (PMID: 35428594), carded above.

shelves.title: Testicular cancer: less treatment, same cure — 3 cycles of BEP matched 4 in good-prognosis disease (2-year progression-free survival 90.4% vs 89.4%), and one adjuvant BEP course prevented more recurrences than major lymph-node surgery in stage I disease (2 vs 15)
shelves.question: In men with testicular germ cell cancer, how much treatment is enough — three versus four cycles of BEP for good-prognosis metastatic disease, and adjuvant chemotherapy versus retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (or surveillance) for stage I nonseminoma?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Scoped to the randomised treatment choices in germ cell tumours; adjuvant treatment of stage I seminoma (carboplatin versus radiotherapy) is already homed on Shelf #1876 and is not re-carded. In good-prognosis metastatic disease, three cycles of BEP were equivalent to four (2-year progression-free survival 90.4% vs 89.4%; difference −1.0%, 80% confidence limits −3.8 to +1.8), and a 3-day schedule matched 5 days for efficacy (de Wit 2001, EORTC 30941/MRC TE20; 812 patients; PMID not captured this session, DOI 10.1200/JCO.2001.19.6.1629) — though the nested quality-of-life study (Fosså 2003, PMID: 12637478; 666 patients) found the 3-day schedule cost more gastrointestinal toxicity and tinnitus, so 5 days is preferred if four cycles are planned. In clinical stage I nonseminoma after orchidectomy, one course of adjuvant BEP prevented more recurrences than retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (2 vs 15 recurrences; 2-year recurrence-free survival 99.46% vs 91.87%; Albers 2008, PMID: 18458040; 382 patients). PROPOSED: SPLIT (de-escalation wins on both questions — fewer cycles for metastatic good-prognosis disease, one chemo course over big surgery for stage I nonseminoma).

cards.headline: de Wit 2001 (EORTC 30941 / MRC TE20): three cycles of BEP were equivalent to four in good-prognosis germ cell cancer — 2-year progression-free survival 90.4% versus 89.4% — and giving each cycle over 3 days matched 5 days
cards.summary: de Wit 2001 (EORTC 30941 / MRC TE20): three cycles of BEP were equivalent to four in good-prognosis germ cell cancer — 2-year progression-free survival 90.4% versus 89.4% — and giving each cycle over 3 days matched 5 days
cards.people: 812 patients with good-prognosis germ cell cancer randomised to three or four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin (BEP); 681 of them were also randomised to a 5-day or 3-day schedule per cycle (etoposide 500 mg/m2 per cycle).
cards.result: Projected 2-year progression-free survival was 90.4% on three cycles and 89.4% on four cycles (difference −1.0%; 80% confidence limits −3.8% to +1.8%), meeting the study's equivalence criterion (both bounds within 5%). For schedule, 2-year progression-free survival was 88.8% (5-day) versus 89.7% (3-day) (difference −0.9%; 80% confidence limits −4.1% to +2.2%), also equivalent. The authors concluded three cycles of BEP is sufficient therapy in good-prognosis germ cell cancer and the 3-day schedule has no detrimental effect.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence was judged on 80% confidence limits against a 5% margin — a looser standard than a modern 95% non-inferiority analysis, in a good-prognosis population whose ~90% progression-free survival leaves little room to detect harm. The result licenses three cycles in good-prognosis disease only; intermediate- and poor-prognosis patients were not in this trial.
cards.source: de Wit R, Roberts JT, Wilkinson PM, et al. cards.headline: Albers 2008 (AUO AH 01/94): one course of adjuvant BEP beat retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for preventing recurrence in stage I nonseminoma — 2 recurrences versus 15 (2-year recurrence-free survival 99.46% versus 91.87%)
cards.summary: Albers 2008 (AUO AH 01/94): one course of adjuvant BEP beat retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for preventing recurrence in stage I nonseminoma — 2 recurrences versus 15 (2-year recurrence-free survival 99.46% versus 91.87%)
cards.people: 382 patients with clinical stage I nonseminomatous germ cell tumours after orchidectomy, randomised to retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND, n = 191) or one course of BEP chemotherapy (n = 191), 1996–2005; median follow-up 4.7 years.
cards.result: Two recurrences occurred with chemotherapy versus 15 with surgery (P = .0011). The 2-year recurrence-free survival difference was 7.59% (95% CI 3.13% to 12.05%) in favour of chemotherapy (99.46% [95% CI 96.20–99.92%] versus 91.87% [95% CI 86.87–95.02%]). The hazard ratio for recurrence with surgery as opposed to chemotherapy was 7.937 (95% CI 1.808 to 34.48) — a relative measure; the absolute recurrence counts were 15 of 191 versus 2 of 191. The authors concluded one course of BEP was superior to community-standard RPLND for preventing recurrence.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is against RPLND 'performed according to community standards' across many centres, not expert-centre nerve-sparing surgery, and the trial predates modern risk-adapted surveillance: most stage I patients cured by orchidectomy alone receive adjuvant treatment they never needed under either strategy, and recurrences in both arms were salvageable — recurrence, not survival, is what differed.
cards.source: Albers P, Siener R, Krege S, et al.; German Testicular Cancer Study Group. Randomized phase III trial comparing retroperitoneal lymph node dissection with one course of bleomycin and etoposide plus cisplatin chemotherapy in the adjuvant treatment of clinical stage I nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumors: AUO trial AH 01/94. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2008. PMID: 18458040. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Fosså 2003: within the same TE20 trial, the 3-day BEP schedule cost more early gastrointestinal toxicity and more tinnitus at 2 years — so 5 days is preferred if four cycles are planned, 3 days acceptable for three
cards.summary: Fosså 2003: within the same TE20 trial, the 3-day BEP schedule cost more early gastrointestinal toxicity and more tinnitus at 2 years — so 5 days is preferred if four cycles are planned, 3 days acceptable for three
cards.type: Prospective quality-of-life study within a randomised trial (Fosså 2003)
cards.people: 666 patients with metastatic testicular cancer in EORTC 30941 / MRC TE20 (four versus three cycles of BEP, over 5 versus 3 days) with prospectively collected EORTC QLQ-C30 quality-of-life data.
cards.result: Two years after chemotherapy, 36% of patients had improved global quality of life versus baseline and 13% had deteriorated. At 3 months, the 3-day regimen caused more gastrointestinal toxicity than the 5-day regimen, reaching clinical relevance (≥10-point change) when four cycles were given. The 3-day schedule also increased the 2-year risk of tinnitus, clinically relevant after four cycles. The authors recommended the 5-day regimen if four cycles of BEP are planned, and judged the 3-day regimen acceptable when only three cycles are given, despite more nausea/vomiting at 3 months.
cards.watchOut: Quality of life is the soft half of the TE20 evidence: unblinded patients reporting symptoms on schedules they could feel differing. The tinnitus signal matters because cisplatin ototoxicity is permanent and this population is young with decades of survivorship — but exact tinnitus rates were not captured from the record this session, so none are printed.
cards.source: Fosså SD, de Wit R, Roberts JT, et al.; EORTC Genitourinary Group / MRC Testicular Cancer Study Group. Quality of life in good prognosis patients with metastatic germ cell cancer: a prospective study of the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Genitourinary Group/Medical Research Council Testicular Cancer Study Group (30941/TE20). cards.headline: Synthesis: testicular germ cell cancer treatment is a de-escalation success — three BEP cycles cure good-prognosis disease as well as four, and one adjuvant course prevents more recurrences than big surgery in stage I nonseminoma
cards.summary: Synthesis: testicular germ cell cancer treatment is a de-escalation success — three BEP cycles cure good-prognosis disease as well as four, and one adjuvant course prevents more recurrences than big surgery in stage I nonseminoma
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: two randomised trials (812 and 382 patients) and the quality-of-life study (666 patients) nested in the larger trial. Stage I seminoma adjuvant treatment (carboplatin versus radiotherapy) is homed on Shelf #1876 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Cure rates are high enough that the randomised questions are about doing less, safely. Three cycles of BEP matched four on 2-year progression-free survival (90.4% vs 89.4%) in good-prognosis metastatic disease, with the 3-day schedule equivalent in efficacy but worse for gut toxicity and tinnitus when four cycles are used. In stage I nonseminoma after orchidectomy, one course of BEP prevented more recurrences than retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (2 vs 15 recurrences). PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (3 cycles BEP: equivalent for good-prognosis metastatic disease · 1 adjuvant BEP course: fewer recurrences than RPLND in stage I nonseminoma · surveillance and seminoma adjuvant choices sit on other shelves).
cards.watchOut: Everything carded here is germ cell tumour treatment in trial populations of young men; none of it covers salvage therapy after relapse, poor-prognosis intensification, or late effects (cardiovascular disease, second cancers, infertility), which drive survivorship care. Treatment belongs in specialist centres — outcomes in these trials come from protocol care.
cards.source: Synthesis of de Wit 2001 (PMID not captured this session), Albers 2008 (PMID: 18458040) and Fosså 2003 (PMID: 12637478), carded above.

shelves.title: Group therapy in metastatic breast cancer: mood and pain improved in the 235-woman BEST trial, but survival was not prolonged (median 17.9 vs 17.6 months) — the 1989 survival claim failed both randomised replications
shelves.question: Does supportive-expressive group therapy prolong survival in metastatic breast cancer — the claim and its randomised refutation?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: The survival claim does not survive its randomised tests in metastatic disease. Spiegel 1989 (PMID: 2571815; 86 women) reported mean survival of 36.6 versus 18.9 months with weekly supportive group therapy plus self-hypnosis. The larger multicentre BEST trial, Goodwin 2001 (PMID: 11742045; 235 women), found median survival of 17.9 versus 17.6 months (hazard ratio for death 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45) — the treatment made no difference to survival — while mood and pain perception improved, particularly in women who were initially more distressed. Spiegel's own replication attempt in 2007 (PMID: 17647221; NCT00226928; 125 women) again found no survival effect (median 30.7 versus 33.3 months). One positive outlier exists outside metastatic disease: Andersen 2008 (PMID: 19016270; 227 women with regional breast cancer) reported lower recurrence and breast-cancer death with a psychologist-led group intervention over a median 11 years, a different population and intervention that has not overturned the two metastatic trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for mood and pain only, with no survival benefit.

cards.headline: Spiegel 1989: women with metastatic breast cancer randomised to a year of weekly supportive group therapy with self-hypnosis lived a mean of 36.6 months versus 18.9 months with routine oncological care alone
cards.summary: Spiegel 1989: women with metastatic breast cancer randomised to a year of weekly supportive group therapy with self-hypnosis lived a mean of 36.6 months versus 18.9 months with routine oncological care alone
cards.people: 86 patients with metastatic breast cancer; the intervention group (n = 50) received a 1-year intervention of weekly supportive group therapy with self-hypnosis for pain, and the control group (n = 36) received routine oncological care; both groups had routine oncological care.
cards.result: Survival from randomisation was a mean of 36.6 (SD 37.6) months in the intervention group compared with 18.9 (SD 10.8) months in the control group, a significant difference. At 10-year follow-up only 3 of the patients were alive and death records were obtained for the other 83. Survival plots indicated that divergence in survival began at 20 months after entry, or 8 months after the intervention ended.
cards.watchOut: A small single-centre trial (86 women) whose survival finding the two later, larger randomised tests in metastatic disease — Goodwin 2001 and Spiegel 2007, both carded on this shelf — did not reproduce; the very large standard deviation in the intervention group (37.6 months around a 36.6-month mean) signals a few long survivors driving the mean.
cards.source: Spiegel D, Bloom JR, Kraemer HC, Gottheil E. Effect of psychosocial treatment on survival of patients with metastatic breast cancer. Lancet. 1989. PMID: 2571815. cards.headline: Goodwin 2001 (BEST trial): in 235 women with metastatic breast cancer, weekly supportive-expressive group therapy improved mood and pain perception but did not prolong survival — median 17.9 versus 17.6 months, hazard ratio for death 1.06
cards.summary: Goodwin 2001 (BEST trial): in 235 women with metastatic breast cancer, weekly supportive-expressive group therapy improved mood and pain perception but did not prolong survival — median 17.9 versus 17.6 months, hazard ratio for death 1.06
cards.people: 235 women with metastatic breast cancer expected to survive at least three months, randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to weekly supportive-expressive group therapy (158 women) or to a control group receiving no such intervention (77 women); all women received educational materials and any medical or psychosocial care deemed necessary.
cards.result: The psychological intervention did not prolong survival: median survival was 17.9 months in the intervention group and 17.6 months in the control group (hazard ratio for death 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45, univariate; 1.23, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.72, multivariate) — the treatment made no difference to survival. Women assigned to supportive-expressive therapy had greater improvement in psychological symptoms and reported less pain (P = 0.04) than controls, with a significant interaction by baseline psychological score: women who were more distressed benefited, whereas those who were less distressed did not.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest and most rigorous test of the exact intervention Spiegel reported on, and its survival result is null; the mood and pain gains were concentrated in the subgroup who were more distressed at baseline, so they should not be promised to every patient.
cards.source: Goodwin PJ, Leszcz M, Ennis M, Koopmans J, Vincent L, Guther H, et al. The effect of group psychosocial support on survival in metastatic breast cancer. cards.headline: Spiegel 2007 replication: in a second randomised trial of 125 women with metastatic breast cancer, supportive-expressive group therapy again made no difference to survival — median 30.7 versus 33.3 months
cards.summary: Spiegel 2007 replication: in a second randomised trial of 125 women with metastatic breast cancer, supportive-expressive group therapy again made no difference to survival — median 30.7 versus 33.3 months
cards.people: 125 women with confirmed metastatic (n = 122) or locally recurrent (n = 3) breast cancer, randomly assigned to supportive-expressive group therapy plus educational materials (n = 64) or educational materials only (n = 61), for a minimum of 1 year; therapy was 90 minutes once a week.
cards.result: Overall mortality after 14 years was 86% and median survival time was 32.8 months. No overall statistically significant effect of treatment on survival was found: median survival was 30.7 months in the treatment group compared with 33.3 months in controls. The trial was designed explicitly to replicate the group's own 1989 finding and did not reproduce it.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports a statistically significant intervention site-by-condition interaction, so results were not uniform across sites; the headline finding, however, is no overall survival effect, and the control group's median survival was numerically the longer of the two.

cards.headline: Andersen 2008: in 227 women with regional (non-metastatic) breast cancer, a psychologist-led group intervention was followed by lower recurrence (hazard ratio 0.55) and lower breast-cancer death (hazard ratio 0.44) over a median of 11 years
cards.summary: Andersen 2008: in 227 women with regional (non-metastatic) breast cancer, a psychologist-led group intervention was followed by lower recurrence (hazard ratio 0.55) and lower breast-cancer death (hazard ratio 0.44) over a median of 11 years
cards.people: 227 patients surgically treated for regional breast cancer, randomised before adjuvant therapy to a psychologist-led small-group intervention (strategies to reduce stress, improve mood, alter health behaviours and maintain adherence to cancer treatment) plus assessment, or to assessment only.
cards.result: After a median of 11 years of follow-up, disease recurrence was reported in 62 of 212 (29%) women and death in 54 of 227 (24%) women. Compared with the assessment-only arm, the intervention arm had a reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence (hazard ratio 0.55; P = .034), of death from breast cancer (hazard ratio 0.44; P = .016) and of death from all causes (hazard ratio 0.51; P = .028). These hazard ratios are relative measures; the absolute event rates were 29% for recurrence and 24% for death across the cohort as reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A different question from the metastatic trials: earlier-stage disease, a psychologist-led intervention with health-behaviour and adherence components, and a single-centre programme. It keeps the survival hypothesis alive for early disease but does not rehabilitate the metastatic claim tested by Goodwin 2001 and Spiegel 2007.
