cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised trials in metastatic breast cancer found no survival prolongation from supportive-expressive group therapy, while mood and pain improved in the largest trial; the one positive survival trial was in earlier-stage disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised trials in metastatic breast cancer found no survival prolongation from supportive-expressive group therapy, while mood and pain improved in the largest trial; the one positive survival trial was in earlier-stage disease
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials in metastatic breast cancer (86, 235 and 125 women) and one randomised trial in regional breast cancer (227 women).
cards.result: Spiegel 1989 reported mean survival of 36.6 versus 18.9 months (PMID: 2571815). Goodwin 2001 found median survival of 17.9 versus 17.6 months (hazard ratio for death 1.06) — the treatment made no difference to survival — with improved mood and less pain, mainly in initially distressed women (PMID: 11742045). Spiegel 2007, the originators' own replication, found median survival of 30.7 versus 33.3 months (PMID: 17647221). Andersen 2008, in regional rather than metastatic disease, reported hazard ratios of 0.55 for recurrence and 0.44 for breast-cancer death (PMID: 19016270). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for mood and pain only, with no survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 1989 survival doubling without its two failed replications: on the full record, group therapy in metastatic breast cancer is a symptom intervention, not a life-prolonging one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Spiegel D et al. Lancet. 1989 (PMID: 2571815); Goodwin PJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11742045); Spiegel D et al. Cancer. 2007 (PMID: 17647221; NCT00226928); Andersen BL et al. Cancer. 2008 (PMID: 19016270).

shelves.title: Stretching surveillance after low-risk adenomas: Norwegian low-risk patients offered no surveillance died of colorectal cancer less often than the general population (SMR 0.75, still ≤0.90 at 13 years), and UK low-risk patients without surveillance matched population incidence — observational evidence only
shelves.question: After removal of colorectal adenomas, can colonoscopic surveillance be safely stretched to 5–10 years in low-risk patients instead of 3-yearly surveillance, without missing interval cancers?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Adenoma · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Colorectal Neoplasms · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Norway · Registries · Risk
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for stretching surveillance in low-risk patients — observational evidence only, printed on the face. Three large registry/cohort datasets point the same way. In Norway, where guidelines recommended NO routine surveillance after low-risk adenomas, colorectal-cancer mortality in 40,826 post-adenoma patients was lower in the low-risk group than in the general population (SMR 0.75), and with follow-up extended to a median 13 years the low-risk SMR stayed at or below 1.0 in both sexes (women 0.90, men 0.70). In a 33,011-patient UK cohort, low-risk patients who had NO surveillance had a colorectal-cancer incidence statistically indistinguishable from the general population (SIR 0.86), although a single surveillance visit was associated with lower incidence (HR 0.56) in every risk group — the tension that keeps this at POSSIBLE rather than higher. No randomised trial of surveillance intervals in low-risk patients is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Løberg 2014: in Norway's no-surveillance-for-low-risk system, patients whose low-risk adenomas were removed died of colorectal cancer LESS often than the general population (SMR 0.75)
cards.summary: Løberg 2014: in Norway's no-surveillance-for-low-risk system, patients whose low-risk adenomas were removed died of colorectal cancer LESS often than the general population (SMR 0.75)
cards.people: 40,826 Norwegian patients who had colorectal adenomas removed between 1993 and 2007, followed through 2011 (median 7.7 years, maximum 19.0) through the Cancer Registry and Cause of Death Registry of Norway. Contemporary Norwegian guidelines recommended colonoscopy after 10 years for high-risk adenomas, after 5 years for patients with three or more adenomas, and no surveillance for low-risk adenomas; high-risk was defined here as multiple adenomas or adenomas with a villous component or high-grade dysplasia.
cards.result: 1,273 patients were diagnosed with colorectal cancer and 383 colorectal-cancer deaths were observed against 398 expected (overall SMR 0.96, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.06). Colorectal-cancer mortality was increased in the high-risk group (242 observed vs 209 expected; SMR 1.16, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.31) but reduced in the low-risk group (141 observed vs 189 expected; SMR 0.75, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.88) — under a policy that offered low-risk patients no surveillance colonoscopy at all.
cards.watchOut: Polyp size and exact polyp number were not available in the registry, so the low-risk/high-risk split is cruder than a modern endoscopy report; and a mortality comparison against the general population is not a comparison against 3-yearly surveillance — it shows no-surveillance was not catastrophic, not that it equals intensive surveillance.
cards.source: Løberg M et al. Long-term colorectal-cancer mortality after adenoma removal. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25162886. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cross 2020: UK low-risk patients with no surveillance had colorectal-cancer incidence no higher than the general population (SIR 0.86) — yet one surveillance visit was associated with about half the incidence in every risk group
cards.summary: Cross 2020: UK low-risk patients with no surveillance had colorectal-cancer incidence no higher than the general population (SIR 0.86) — yet one surveillance visit was associated with about half the incidence in every risk group
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre cohort of 33,011 patients who had colonoscopy with adenoma removal at 17 UK hospitals (87% between 2000 and 2010), followed through 2016; after exclusions 28,972 were analysed — 14,401 (50%) low-risk, 11,852 (41%) intermediate-risk and 2,719 (9%) high-risk under the 2002 UK guidelines. Median follow-up 9.3 years.
cards.result: Colorectal-cancer incidence per 100,000 person-years was 140 (95% CI 122 to 162) in the low-risk group, 221 (195 to 251) in the intermediate-risk group and 366 (295 to 453) in the high-risk group. A single surveillance visit was associated with 40–50% relative lower incidence than none: hazard ratios 0.56 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.80) low-risk, 0.59 (0.43 to 0.81) intermediate-risk and 0.49 (0.29 to 0.82) high-risk. But compared with the general population, incidence WITHOUT surveillance was similar in low-risk patients (SIR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.02) and intermediate-risk patients (1.16, 0.97 to 1.37), and higher only in high-risk patients (1.91, 1.39 to 2.56). The authors conclude some low-risk and intermediate-risk patients could be managed by screening rather than surveillance.
cards.watchOut: The surveillance hazard ratios come from an observational comparison — patients who attend surveillance differ from those who do not, and surveillance also removes new adenomas, so the HR 0.56 cannot be read as pure interval effect. The two halves of this card genuinely pull in opposite directions, which is why the shelf stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Cross AJ et al. Long-term colorectal cancer incidence after adenoma removal and the effects of surveillance on incidence: a multicentre, retrospective, cohort study. Gut. 2020. PMID: 31953252. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jodal 2022: with follow-up extended to a median 13 years, low-risk adenoma patients still showed no excess colorectal-cancer death (women SMR 0.90, men SMR 0.70)
cards.summary: Jodal 2022: with follow-up extended to a median 13 years, low-risk adenoma patients still showed no excess colorectal-cancer death (women SMR 0.90, men SMR 0.70)
cards.people: 40,293 Norwegian individuals who had adenomas removed from 1993 to 2007, followed through 2018 (median follow-up 13.0 years); standardised incidence and mortality ratios calculated against the sex-matched general population. High-risk adenomas were defined as two or more adenomas, a villous component, or high-grade dysplasia. This is the same Norwegian cohort as Løberg 2014 with longer follow-up — not an independent population.
cards.result: Over follow-up, 1,079 women (5.5%) and 866 men (4.2%) developed colorectal cancer, and 328 women (1.7%) and 275 men (1.3%) died of it. Colorectal-cancer mortality was increased in women overall (SMR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.26) and reduced in men (SMR 0.79, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.89). By risk group: women with high-risk adenomas had increased colorectal-cancer death (SMR 1.37, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.57), while women with low-risk adenomas had a similar risk to the general population (SMR 0.90, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.07), men with high-risk adenomas were similar (SMR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.04), and men with low-risk adenomas had reduced risk (SMR 0.70, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.84). The authors suggest sex-specific surveillance recommendations should be considered.
cards.watchOut: Same underlying Norwegian population as the Løberg 2014 card — count this as durability of the same evidence over a longer horizon, not as a second confirmation. The women's overall SMR of 1.13 is a reminder that 'post-adenoma' is not uniformly low risk; the reassuring numbers belong to the low-risk subgroup specifically.
cards.source: Jodal HC et al. Long-term colorectal cancer incidence and mortality after adenoma removal in women and men. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2022. PMID: 34716941. cards.headline: Synthesis: low-risk adenoma patients managed with little or no surveillance fare no worse than the general population on colorectal cancer — stretching their interval looks safe, on observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: low-risk adenoma patients managed with little or no surveillance fare no worse than the general population on colorectal cancer — stretching their interval looks safe, on observational evidence only
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Norwegian national cohort reported at median 7.7 years (40,826 patients) and again at median 13.0 years (40,293 patients — the same population, longer follow-up), and one UK multicentre cohort (28,972 analysed, 14,401 low-risk). No randomised surveillance-interval trial in low-risk patients is carded.
cards.result: Under Norway's no-surveillance policy for low-risk adenomas, low-risk colorectal-cancer mortality was below the general population at 7.7 years (SMR 0.75; Løberg 2014) and remained at or below population rates at 13 years in both sexes (SMR 0.90 women, 0.70 men; Jodal 2022). UK data agree that low-risk patients without surveillance match general-population incidence (SIR 0.86; Cross 2020), while also showing an association between one surveillance visit and lower incidence (HR 0.56) that prevents a stronger stamp. High-risk patients are a different question — their risk is elevated (SMR 1.16–1.37) and this shelf says nothing about stretching their surveillance; the high-risk 5-versus-3-year question is homed elsewhere (live shelf #4128, EPoS II). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Every card compares against the general population or against non-attenders, never randomly against a 3-yearly programme; and baseline colonoscopy quality (complete excision, bowel preparation) has improved since these 1993–2010 cohorts, which could shift absolute risks in either direction for today's low-risk patient.

synthesis the carded evidence: one norwegian national cohort reported at median 7.7 years (40,826 patients) and again at median 13.0 years (40,293 patients — the same population, longer follow-up), and one uk multicentre cohort (28,972 analysed, 14,401 low-risk). no randomised surveillance-interval trial in low-risk patients is carded. under norway's no-surveillance policy for low-risk adenomas, low-risk colorectal-cancer mortality was below the general population at 7.7 years (smr 0.75; løberg 2014) and remained at or below population rates at 13 years in both sexes (smr 0.90 women, 0.70 men; jodal 2022). uk data agree that low-risk patients without surveillance match general-population incidence (sir 0.86; cross 2020), while also showing an association between one surveillance visit and lower incidence (hr 0.56) that prevents a stronger stamp. high-risk patients are a different question — their risk is elevated (smr 1.16–1.37) and this shelf says nothing about stretching their surveillance; the high-risk 5-versus-3-year question is homed elsewhere (live shelf #4128, epos ii). proposed possible (benefit) — observational only. every card compares against the general population or against non-attenders, never randomly against a 3-yearly programme; and baseline colonoscopy quality (complete excision, bowel preparation) has improved since these 1993–2010 cohorts, which could shift absolute risks in either direction for today's low-risk patient. synthesis of løberg m et al. the new england journal of medicine. 2014 (pmid: 25162886); cross aj et al. gut. 2020 (pmid: 31953252); jodal hc et al. alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2022 (pmid: 34716941).

shelves.title: Lung cancer screening eligibility: 20 pack-years (not 30) at ages 50–80 is the modelling-supported line, the 15-year quit window is contested by the ACS, and risk-based selection beats pack-year rules in simulation
shelves.question: In adults at high risk for lung cancer, what pack-year and quit-time criteria best define eligibility for low-dose CT screening?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Early Detection of Cancer · Humans · Lung · Lung Neoplasms · Middle Aged · Risk Assessment · Sensitivity and Specificity · Smoking · Smoking Cessation · Tomography, X-Ray Computed
shelves.balance: The criteria question has a modelling answer, not a trial answer: the screening trials themselves used fixed entry rules (the National Lung Screening Trial's 30 pack-years and quit within 15 years — its mortality result is homed on live shelf #164 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here). The comparative work is simulation and cohort analysis. The CISNET modelling for the USPSTF (Meza 2021) found annual strategies starting at age 50–55 with a minimum of 20 pack-years were efficient and beat the 2013 criteria (30 pack-years, ages 55–80): eligibility 20.6%–23.6% vs 14.1% of the population, lung cancer deaths averted 469–558 vs 381 per 100,000, at the cost of more false positives and overdiagnosis. The USPSTF's 2021 recommendation adopted exactly that: ages 50–80, at least 20 pack-years, quit within 15 years. The American Cancer Society's 2023 update kept 20 pack-years and ages 50–80 but dropped the quit-time limit altogether, judging years since quitting should not start or stop screening. Risk-model selection does better still on paper (Katki 2016: screening the same 9.0 million highest-risk ever-smokers was estimated to avert 20% more deaths, 55,717 vs 46,488, with a number needed to screen of 162 vs 194), and the 20 pack-year threshold specifically repairs a racial eligibility gap (Aldrich 2019). PROPOSED LIKELY (criteria as modelled): at least 20 pack-years with a quit window of 15 years (USPSTF) — with the quit-time limit itself contested by the ACS and risk-based selection estimated to outperform any pack-year rule.

cards.headline: Krist 2021 (USPSTF recommendation): the current US criteria are ages 50–80, at least 20 pack-years, currently smoking or quit within the past 15 years — replacing the 2013 rule of 30 pack-years from age 55
cards.summary: Krist 2021 (USPSTF recommendation): the current US criteria are ages 50–80, at least 20 pack-years, currently smoking or quit within the past 15 years — replacing the 2013 rule of 30 pack-years from age 55
cards.people: Recommendation statement of the US Preventive Services Task Force (B recommendation), applying to adults aged 50 to 80 years with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years; based on a commissioned systematic review and a commissioned collaborative modelling study.
cards.result: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that annual low-dose CT screening has a moderate net benefit in persons at high risk based on age, cumulative tobacco exposure and years since quitting, and recommends annual screening in adults aged 50 to 80 years with at least a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years; screening should stop once a person has not smoked for 15 years or has a health problem substantially limiting life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative lung surgery. This replaces the 2013 statement (ages 55 to 80, 30 pack-years, quit within 15 years). The statement gives the criteria and their rationale; the effect sizes behind them are in the modelling and evidence-report cards on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A recommendation statement is a judgement built on the evidence, not itself evidence: its 20 pack-year / 15-year numbers inherit the assumptions of the modelling study carded next, including full uptake and adherence.

cards.headline: Meza 2021 (CISNET modelling for the USPSTF): annual screening from age 50–55 with a 20 pack-year minimum was efficient and beat the 2013 criteria — 469–558 vs 381 lung cancer deaths averted per 100,000
cards.summary: Meza 2021 (CISNET modelling for the USPSTF): annual screening from age 50–55 with a 20 pack-year minimum was efficient and beat the 2013 criteria — 469–558 vs 381 lung cancer deaths averted per 100,000
cards.people: Comparative simulation modelling with four lung cancer natural history models, following the 1950 and 1960 US birth cohorts from age 45 to 90; 1,092 low-dose CT screening strategies were modelled, varying starting and stopping ages, frequency, and eligibility by age/pack-years/years since quitting or by individual risk-model thresholds, assuming full uptake and adherence.
cards.result: Most efficient risk-factor-based strategies started screening at age 50 or 55 and stopped at 80; the 2013 USPSTF criteria were not among the efficient strategies for the 1960 birth cohort. Annual strategies with a minimum of 20 pack-years, compared with the 2013 criteria, were estimated to increase eligibility (20.6%–23.6% vs 14.1% of the population ever eligible), lung cancer deaths averted (469–558 vs 381 per 100,000) and life-years gained (6,018–7,596 vs 4,882 per 100,000) — but also false-positive results (1.9–2.5 vs 1.9 per person screened), overdiagnosed cases (83–94 vs 69 per 100,000) and radiation-related lung cancer deaths (29.0–42.5 vs 20.6 per 100,000). Risk-model-based strategies were estimated to give more benefits and fewer radiation deaths than risk-factor-based ones, but more overdiagnosed cases.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this card is a model estimate under full uptake and adherence, not an observed outcome: real programmes screen a fraction of eligible people, and the harms columns grow with the same eligibility expansion that grows the benefits.
cards.source: Meza R et al. Evaluation of the Benefits and Harms of Lung Cancer Screening With Low-Dose Computed Tomography: Modeling Study for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2021. cards.headline: Wolf 2024 (American Cancer Society 2023 guideline): same 20 pack-years and ages 50–80 — but years since quitting should NOT be an eligibility criterion at all
cards.summary: Wolf 2024 (American Cancer Society 2023 guideline): same 20 pack-years and ages 50–80 — but years since quitting should NOT be an eligibility criterion at all
cards.people: Guideline update of the American Cancer Society, developed from the USPSTF-commissioned systematic review, a second systematic review of lung cancer risk by years since quitting smoking, literature since 2021, two CISNET-validated lung cancer models, and an epidemiologic/modelling analysis of the effect of years since quitting and ageing on risk; the panel judged the overall evidence moderate and sufficient for a strong recommendation.
cards.result: The ACS recommends annual low-dose CT screening for asymptomatic individuals aged 50–80 years who currently smoke or formerly smoked and have at least a 20 pack-year history (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). For former smokers, the number of years since quitting is not an eligibility criterion to begin or to stop screening — a direct departure from the USPSTF's 15-year quit window. People who currently smoke should receive cessation counselling and connection to resources, and people with comorbid conditions substantially limiting life expectancy should not be screened.
cards.watchOut: Two major US guidelines now disagree on the quit-time half of this shelf's question: USPSTF keeps 15 years, ACS drops it. The ACS position rests on risk-by-years-since-quitting analyses and modelling, not on a trial of screening long-quit former smokers.
cards.source: Wolf AMD et al. Screening for lung cancer: 2023 guideline update from the American Cancer Society. CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians. 2024. PMID: 37909877. cards.headline: Katki 2016: selecting by individual risk instead of pack-year rules was estimated to avert 20% more deaths (55,717 vs 46,488) in the same 9.0 million people, with a number needed to screen of 162 vs 194
cards.summary: Katki 2016: selecting by individual risk instead of pack-year rules was estimated to avert 20% more deaths (55,717 vs 46,488) in the same 9.0 million people, with a number needed to screen of 162 vs 194
cards.type: Risk-model development, validation and modelled comparison (Katki 2016)
cards.people: Development and validation of empirical lung cancer incidence and death risk models in ever-smokers from the PLCO trial control group, validated in the PLCO and National Lung Screening Trial chest-radiography/screening groups and in the National Health Interview Survey; models were applied to US ever-smokers aged 50 to 80 years (NHIS 2010–2012), assuming screening yields the mortality reduction observed in the National Lung Screening Trial (whose own record is homed on live shelf #164).
cards.result: The lung cancer death model calibrated and discriminated well in US ever-smokers (estimated/observed 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.05; AUC 0.78, 95% CI 0.76–0.80). Under the then-current USPSTF criteria, an estimated 9.0 million ever-smokers qualified and 46,488 lung cancer deaths (95% CI 43,924–49,053) were estimated screen-avertable over 5 years (estimated number needed to screen 194, 95% CI 187–201). Risk-based selection of the same 9.0 million people at highest 5-year risk (at least 1.9%) was estimated to avert 20% more deaths (55,717, 95% CI 53,033–58,400) and to reduce the number needed to screen by 17% (162, 95% CI 157–166).
cards.watchOut: A modelled comparison, not a randomised comparison of selection strategies — and it assumes the National Lung Screening Trial's treatment effect transports unchanged to a differently selected population. It shows what pack-year rules leave on the table, not what a risk-based programme has achieved in practice.
cards.source: Katki HA et al. Development and Validation of Risk Models to Select Ever-Smokers for CT Lung Cancer Screening. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27179989. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aldrich 2019: under the old 30 pack-year rule only 32% of African American smokers who developed lung cancer had been eligible, versus 56% of white smokers — lowering the threshold to 20 pack-years made performance equitable
cards.summary: Aldrich 2019: under the old 30 pack-year rule only 32% of African American smokers who developed lung cancer had been eligible, versus 56% of white smokers — lowering the threshold to 20 pack-years made performance equitable
cards.type: Cohort diagnostic-accuracy evaluation of eligibility criteria (Aldrich 2019)
cards.people: Diagnostic-accuracy evaluation of USPSTF eligibility criteria in the Southern Community Cohort Study: 48,364 ever-smokers (32,463 African American, 15,901 white) aged 40 to 79 enrolled through community health centres in 12 southern US states (2002–2009) and followed for cancer incidence through 2014, with 1,269 incident lung cancers.
cards.result: Among all participants, 17% of African American smokers versus 31% of white smokers were eligible for screening under the criteria then in force (P < .001). Among people actually diagnosed with lung cancer, 32% of African American smokers (255 of 791) versus 56% of white smokers (270 of 478) had been eligible (P < .001) — mainly because African American smokers had fewer pack-years (median 25.8, IQR 16.9–42.0, vs 48.0, IQR 30.2–70.5). Lowering the minimum to 20 pack-years increased eligibility among African American smokers and produced equitable sensitivity and specificity across all ages (for a 55-year-old current African American smoker, sensitivity rose from 32.2% to 49.0% vs 56.5% for a white smoker, while specificity fell from 83.0% to 71.6% vs 69.4%).
cards.watchOut: One regional, predominantly low-income cohort: it demonstrates how a pack-year threshold interacts with different smoking patterns, but eligibility equity is not the same endpoint as deaths averted, and its numbers describe the pre-2021 criteria.
cards.source: Aldrich MC et al. Evaluation of USPSTF Lung Cancer Screening Guidelines Among African American Adult Smokers. JAMA Oncology. 2019. PMID: 31246249. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: the best-supported pack-year line is 20 (not 30), ages 50–80; the quit-time line is genuinely contested — 15 years in the USPSTF rule, no limit in the ACS rule — and risk models outperform both on paper
cards.summary: Synthesis: the best-supported pack-year line is 20 (not 30), ages 50–80; the quit-time line is genuinely contested — 15 years in the USPSTF rule, no limit in the ACS rule — and risk models outperform both on paper
cards.people: The carded evidence: two guideline statements (USPSTF 2021; ACS 2023), the CISNET modelling study behind the USPSTF change (1,092 strategies), a risk-model comparison applied to 9.0 million US ever-smokers, and a 48,364-person cohort evaluation of eligibility equity. These are modelling and guideline records, not trial enrolments, so participant totals are not summed and no small-N labelling applies. The screening trials' own mortality results are homed on live shelf #164 and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded.
cards.result: Moving from 30 to 20 pack-years was estimated to raise deaths averted from 381 to 469–558 per 100,000 (Meza 2021) and to close a racial eligibility gap (32% vs 56% of eventual cases eligible under the old rule; Aldrich 2019). Risk-based selection at a 5-year risk of at least 1.9% was estimated to avert a further 20% more deaths than categorical criteria (Katki 2016). On quit time, the two current US guidelines split: within 15 years (USPSTF) versus no quit-time criterion (ACS). PROPOSED LIKELY (criteria as modelled): at least 20 pack-years, ages 50–80, quit within 15 years — with the quit window flagged as contested.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial has ever compared eligibility criteria against each other — every 'best criteria' claim on this shelf is a model or a cohort re-analysis, and the models assume full uptake that real programmes do not achieve.

CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians. 2024 (PMID: 37909877); Katki HA et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27179989); Aldrich MC et al. JAMA Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 31246249). shelves.title: Methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain (observational only): specialist-supervised rotation or low-dose add-on relieved pain in about half to two-thirds of patients in small series — no randomised trial exists for this indication
shelves.question: Is methadone effective for refractory cancer-related neuropathic pain under specialist supervision?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid · Humans · Methadone · Middle Aged · Morphine · Neoplasms · Pain · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial tests methadone specifically for refractory neuropathic cancer pain. The Cochrane review (Nicholson 2017, PMID: 28177515) found only 6 trials with 388 participants in cancer pain generally — too heterogeneous to pool, low-quality evidence — with methadone similar to morphine for pain relief and an explicit warning that methadone should be initiated only by experienced practitioners because of titration difficulty and potentially fatal arrhythmias. The refractory-neuropathic evidence is observational: in a prospective cohort of 48 palliative inpatients rotated to methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain, 47% gained at least 20 mm on a visual analogue scale by day 28 (Fawoubo 2023, PMID: 34620692); in 19 rotation patients, pain scores fell 4 points by day 7 and the neuropathic DN4 screen turned negative in 65% (Rhondali 2013, PMID: 24116946); and adding low-dose methadone to ongoing opioids produced a response (at least 33% pain reduction) in 68.4% of 19 patients with uncontrolled pain (Hasegawa 2025, PMID: 40674591). All three series are small, uncontrolled, and run in specialist palliative units — exactly the supervised setting the question specifies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: under specialist supervision, rotation to or addition of methadone relieves refractory neuropathic cancer pain in a substantial share of patients, on small uncontrolled series; the randomised evidence base does not address this indication.

cards.headline: Nicholson 2017 (Cochrane): only 6 trials and 388 participants exist for methadone in cancer pain at all — methadone matched morphine where measured, evidence quality low, and initiation is for experienced practitioners only
cards.summary: Nicholson 2017 (Cochrane): only 6 trials and 388 participants exist for methadone in cancer pain at all — methadone matched morphine where measured, evidence quality low, and initiation is for experienced practitioners only
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised controlled trials comparing methadone (any formulation, any route) with active or placebo comparators in adults and children with cancer pain: 6 studies with 388 participants; no studies in children were identified. The included studies differed so much in methods and comparisons that no meta-analysis was feasible; evidence was assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Only one study (103 participants) reported the proportion achieving a given level of pain relief — a reduction of at least 20%, similar in the methadone and morphine groups. Using an outcome of 'no worse than mild pain', methadone was similar to morphine in effectiveness, and most participants who could tolerate methadone achieved that level. Adverse-event withdrawals with methadone were uncommon (12 of 202) and similar in other groups; somnolence was more common with methadone than morphine, dry mouth more common with morphine. The reviewers judged the quality of evidence low and state methadone should be initiated only by experienced practitioners, given dose-titration challenges and potentially fatal arrhythmias in some patients. No included trial addressed refractory neuropathic pain specifically.
cards.watchOut: General cancer pain, mostly first-line comparisons with morphine — not the refractory, neuropathic, post-rotation population of this shelf; its role here is to mark the ceiling of the randomised evidence and the supervision warning.
cards.source: Nicholson AB et al. Methadone for cancer pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28177515. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fawoubo 2023: in 48 palliative inpatients rotated to methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain, 47% gained at least 20 mm of pain relief and 53% reached a pain score under 4 by day 28
cards.summary: Fawoubo 2023: in 48 palliative inpatients rotated to methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain, 47% gained at least 20 mm of pain relief and 53% reached a pain score under 4 by day 28
cards.people: Prospective observational cohort of palliative care inpatients rotated to methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain: 48 patients included, of whom 17 completed the 28-day follow-up; pain intensity was assessed weekly for 28 days with a visual analogue scale and the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI). Study N = 48 (17 completers).
cards.result: Visual analogue pain rating decreased by at least 20 mm in 47% of patients, and pain intensity was significantly lower at day 28, with 53% of patients scoring below 4 (P < 0.001). The pressure/squeezing NPSI component decreased by more than 2 points in 50% of patients, and linear regression showed allodynia and pressure/squeezing accounted for the largest part of the overall pain alleviation (P = 0.01). The authors conclude methadone could significantly improve neuropathic pain through a targeted effect on allodynia and its pressure/squeezing component.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, and only 17 of 48 patients completed 28 days — in a palliative inpatient population, attrition is largely death and deterioration, so the completer results flatter the treatment; there is no comparison group to separate methadone's effect from concurrent care.
cards.source: Fawoubo A et al. Methadone and neuropathic cancer pain subcomponents: a prospective cohort pilot study. BMJ supportive & palliative care. 2023. PMID: 34620692. cards.headline: Rhondali 2013: rotation to methadone in 19 patients with refractory cancer pain cut pain scores by 4 points in a week, with the neuropathic screen turning negative in 65% (small series, N on the face)
cards.summary: Rhondali 2013: rotation to methadone in 19 patients with refractory cancer pain cut pain scores by 4 points in a week, with the neuropathic screen turning negative in 65% (small series, N on the face)
cards.people: Retrospective observational study of all patients undergoing opioid rotation to methadone from 2008 to 2011 in two French palliative care units (Lyon and Nice): 19 patients (7 female; median age 55 years), most with gastrointestinal cancer; 17 had mixed pain syndromes; the median morphine-equivalent daily dose before switching was 480 mg, and 13 patients had already undergone at least two non-methadone opioid rotations. Study N = 19.
cards.result: Between day 0 and day 7 the visual analogue pain score decreased by 4 points (P < 0.001). The DN4 neuropathic-pain score became negative on day 7 for 11 of 17 patients (65%). On day 7, 16 of 18 patients (89%) expressed moderate to greater-than-moderate pain relief. Methadone was discontinued in one patient on day 7 as ineffective, and after day 14 in 8 patients unable to take oral drugs. The authors conclude methadone rotation appears effective and well tolerated for refractory cancer pain.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients, no control group, and rotation itself (a fresh opioid, inpatient titration, intensified care) can relieve pain regardless of which drug is chosen; the series supports feasibility under supervision, not methadone-specific superiority.
cards.source: Rhondali W et al. Methadone rotation for cancer patients with refractory pain in a palliative care unit: an observational study. Journal of palliative medicine. 2013. PMID: 24116946. cards.headline: Hasegawa 2025: adding low-dose methadone to ongoing opioids produced a pain response in 68.4% of 19 patients with uncontrolled cancer pain, most with neuropathic pain (small single-arm study, N on the face)
cards.summary: Hasegawa 2025: adding low-dose methadone to ongoing opioids produced a pain response in 68.4% of 19 patients with uncontrolled cancer pain, most with neuropathic pain (small single-arm study, N on the face)
cards.people: Prospective, open-label, single-arm study of patients with uncontrolled cancer pain despite opioid dose titration, given low-dose methadone (starting dose 5 or 10 mg/day) combined with their ongoing opioid therapy: 19 patients participated, 11 (57.9%) with neuropathic pain; mean daily oral morphine-equivalent dose before combination was 112.6 mg. Study N = 19.
cards.result: The primary outcome — at least a 33% reduction in average pain intensity on a numerical rating scale by day 15 — occurred in 13 of 19 patients (68.4%, 95% CI 43.4 to 87.4). Mean average pain fell from 5.9 at baseline to 4.2 on day 8 and 3.3 on day 15 (P < 0.001). New or worsened nausea, vomiting and somnolence were each reported in 26.3%, constipation in 5.3%, and delirium occurred in one patient.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients, no control arm, 15 days: regression to the mean and concurrent care changes can produce exactly this picture; the wide confidence interval (43.4%–87.4%) is printed with the response rate for that reason.
cards.source: Hasegawa T et al. Efficacy and safety of combining low-dose methadone with ongoing opioid treatment for uncontrolled cancer pain: an open-label single-arm study. The oncologist. 2025. PMID: 40674591. Registry ID: UMIN000038924 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: specialist-supervised methadone rotation or add-on relieved refractory neuropathic cancer pain in roughly half to two-thirds of patients across three small uncontrolled series — with no randomised trial for this indication
cards.summary: Synthesis: specialist-supervised methadone rotation or add-on relieved refractory neuropathic cancer pain in roughly half to two-thirds of patients across three small uncontrolled series — with no randomised trial for this indication
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of methadone in cancer pain generally (6 trials, 388 participants, none for refractory neuropathic pain) and three uncontrolled specialist-unit series in refractory pain (48, 19 and 19 patients; the two N = 19 series are printed on their faces). Total participants across all cards are under 500 and the indication-specific evidence is 86 observational patients, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE with 'observational only' printed, per the standing rule.
cards.result: Rotation cohorts report at least 20 mm visual-analogue improvement in 47% (Fawoubo 2023), a 4-point score fall with neuropathic-screen reversal in 65% (Rhondali 2013), and a 33%-or-better response in 68.4% with low-dose add-on methadone (Hasegawa 2025). The Cochrane review finds methadone comparable to morphine in ordinary cancer pain on low-quality evidence and restricts initiation to experienced practitioners (Nicholson 2017). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Methadone's long, variable half-life, drug interactions and QT prolongation are why every source here is a specialist unit: the supervision in the question is part of the intervention, and these results do not transfer to unsupervised initiation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nicholson AB et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28177515); Fawoubo A et al. BMJ supportive & palliative care. 2023 (PMID: 34620692); Rhondali W et al. Journal of palliative medicine. 2013 (PMID: 24116946); Hasegawa T et al. The oncologist. 2025 (PMID: 40674591).

shelves.title: Adding a corticosteroid for opioid-resistant cancer pain: SPLIT — meta-analyses find a small one-week pain reduction, the dedicated randomised trial found none; benefit, if any, is small, brief and likeliest in inflammatory pain
shelves.question: For cancer pain that does not respond to opioids alone, does adding a corticosteroid help?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adult · Dexamethasone · Humans · Neoplasms · Pain · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pooled trials and the dedicated trial point different ways, and the split is named in the stamp. Pooling six studies with one-week data, the Cochrane review (Haywood 2015, PMID: 25908299; 15 studies, 1,926 participants overall) found corticosteroids reduced pain by a mean of 0.84 points on a 0–10 scale at one week (95% CI 1.38 to 0.30 lower) — a small effect on low-quality evidence, with the reviewers calling the overall evidence for efficacy weak. A 2025 adjuvant meta-analysis (Zhang 2025, PMID: 41074978) likewise found a dexamethasone pain-score reduction (MD −1.43). But the one randomised trial designed exactly around this question — dexamethasone 8 mg daily added to opioids in 76 advanced-cancer patients (Mercadante 2007, PMID: 17347500) — found no differences in pain intensity, opioid consumption or opioid escalation (the treatment made no difference to pain), though gastrointestinal symptoms eased and well-being improved for some weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: adding a corticosteroid may buy a small, short-lived pain reduction on pooled low-quality data, but the dedicated adjuvant trial found none; any benefit is most plausible for inflammation-driven pain (bone, nerve compression, capsular stretch) over days to a few weeks, weighed against steroid harms in advanced disease.

cards.headline: Haywood 2015 (Cochrane): corticosteroids lowered pain by 0.84 points at one week across six pooled studies — a small effect, on evidence the reviewers themselves call weak
cards.summary: Haywood 2015 (Cochrane): corticosteroids lowered pain by 0.84 points at one week across six pooled studies — a small effect, on evidence the reviewers themselves call weak
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised or prospective controlled trials of corticosteroids versus placebo, usual treatment or supportive care in adults over 18 with cancer-related pain: 15 studies enrolling 1,926 participants (trial sizes 20 to 598); most studies tested dexamethasone against standard therapy. Six studies contributed one-week pain data to the meta-analysis.
cards.result: Corticosteroid therapy resulted in less pain at one week (mean difference 0.84 lower on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI 1.38 to 0.30 lower; low-quality evidence). Adverse events were poorly documented. Analysis was limited by non-standardised pain measurement, different agents, doses and routes, risk of bias, small samples and attrition. The reviewers conclude the evidence for the efficacy of corticosteroids for pain control in cancer patients is weak, that significant relief in some studies lasted only a short period, and that further larger trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: A 0.84-point average on a 10-point scale sits below the roughly 2-point change patients usually notice, the follow-up is one week, and the pooled trials mix pain mechanisms — inflammatory pain plausibly responds while other cancer pain may not.
cards.source: Haywood A et al. Corticosteroids for the management of cancer-related pain in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25908299. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mercadante 2007: the dedicated randomised adjuvant trial — dexamethasone 8 mg added to opioids made no difference to pain intensity or opioid use in 76 advanced-cancer patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Mercadante 2007: the dedicated randomised adjuvant trial — dexamethasone 8 mg added to opioids made no difference to pain intensity or opioid use in 76 advanced-cancer patients (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Randomised controlled study in 76 advanced-cancer patients with pain requiring strong opioids: conventional opioid treatment alone (group O) versus dexamethasone 8 mg orally daily plus conventional treatment (group OS); pain and symptom intensity, well-being, opioid escalation index and distress were recorded weekly until death; 66 patients survived the 33–37-day analysis window.
cards.result: No differences in pain intensity, opioid consumption or opioid escalation index were found between the groups (the treatment made no difference to pain). Corticosteroids persistently decreased opioid-related gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with limited survival and improved the sense of well-being for some weeks, and corticosteroid-related toxicity was minimal. The authors call for larger studies to detect any minimal analgesic difference.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-six patients cannot exclude a small analgesic effect of the size the Cochrane pooling suggests, and a single 8-mg dexamethasone regimen in unselected advanced-cancer pain may dilute a real effect in inflammation-driven pain subtypes.
cards.source: Mercadante SL et al. A prospective randomized study of corticosteroids as adjuvant drugs to opioids in advanced cancer patients. The American journal of hospice & palliative care. 2007. PMID: 17347500. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2025: adjuvant-drug meta-analysis — dexamethasone improved pain scores (MD −1.43) within a combined-adjuvant analysis where NSAIDs and anticonvulsants carried most outcomes
cards.summary: Zhang 2025: adjuvant-drug meta-analysis — dexamethasone improved pain scores (MD −1.43) within a combined-adjuvant analysis where NSAIDs and anticonvulsants carried most outcomes
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of adjunctive medications added to opioids for cancer-related pain in adults, searching to June 2024: 13 studies (10 RCTs, n = 711; 3 retrospective studies, n = 314) evaluating NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antidepressants and corticosteroids; the record does not state how many of the included studies tested corticosteroids specifically.
cards.result: Combination therapy significantly reduced daily opioid consumption versus monotherapy (mean difference −18.84 mg; 95% CI −28.19 to −9.52; P < 0.0001), with significant reductions for NSAIDs and anticonvulsants. Pain scores improved with NSAIDs (MD −0.79), dexamethasone (MD −1.43; 95% CI −2.23 to −0.63; P = 0.0004) and anticonvulsants (MD −0.23). No significant increase in serious adverse events was observed with combination therapy versus opioid monotherapy (nausea/vomiting OR 0.80, P = 0.19; constipation OR 0.73, P = 0.53).
cards.watchOut: The dexamethasone figure is one subgroup inside a multi-adjuvant pooling whose study count for corticosteroids is not stated in the record; it corroborates the direction of the Cochrane estimate but cannot outweigh the dedicated null trial on its own.
cards.source: Zhang X et al. The role of combined adjuvant therapeutic drugs in modulating opioid dosage and pain status in cancer patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2025. PMID: 41074978. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled data say a small, short pain reduction (about 0.8–1.4 points at one week); the one trial built to test adjuvant dexamethasone says none — a genuine split on low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled data say a small, short pain reduction (about 0.8–1.4 points at one week); the one trial built to test adjuvant dexamethasone says none — a genuine split on low-quality evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review (15 studies, 1,926 participants; 6 studies pooled at one week), one dedicated randomised adjuvant trial (76 patients), and one multi-adjuvant meta-analysis (13 studies, 1,025 participants, overlapping with the Cochrane set). Total unique participants are roughly 2,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled corticosteroid pain reduction at one week: mean difference 0.84 points, low-quality evidence (Haywood 2015); dexamethasone subgroup reduction 1.43 points in a second meta-analysis (Zhang 2025). The dedicated randomised trial found no difference in pain intensity, opioid consumption or escalation index with dexamethasone 8 mg daily (the treatment made no difference), with better gastrointestinal symptoms and well-being instead (Mercadante 2007). PROPOSED SPLIT — pooled trials: small short-term benefit; dedicated trial: no added analgesia.
cards.watchOut: Steroid harms in advanced cancer — hyperglycaemia, insomnia, agitation, proximal weakness, infection — accrue with duration, while every benefit signal here is at about one week; the evidence supports a short, reviewed trial for inflammatory pain, not open-ended continuation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haywood A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (PMID: 25908299); Mercadante SL et al. The American journal of hospice & palliative care. 2007 (PMID: 17347500); Zhang X et al. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2025 (PMID: 41074978).

shelves.title: Acupuncture for chemotherapy-induced nausea: a modest adjunct benefit — complete protection rose from 34.5% to 52.9% when electroacupuncture was added to triple antiemetics, though vomiting itself barely changed and certainty is low
shelves.question: Does acupuncture help chemotherapy-induced nausea in adults with cancer?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Points · Antiemetics · Antineoplastic Agents · Electroacupuncture · Humans · Nausea · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vomiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as an adjunct to standard antiemetics, never instead of them. The Cochrane review (Ezzo 2006, PMID: 16625560; 11 trials, 1,247 patients, all receiving pharmacological antiemetics) found acupuncture-point stimulation reduced acute vomiting (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.69–0.99) but did not reduce acute or delayed nausea severity. A 2023 meta-analysis (Yan 2023, PMID: 37226372; 38 RCTs, 2,503 patients) found acupuncture added to usual care increased complete control of acute vomiting (RR 1.13) and delayed vomiting (RR 1.47), with certainty rated low or very low. The strongest single trial — a 239-patient sham-controlled study adding electroacupuncture to standard triple antiemetic therapy in breast-cancer patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy (Shen 2024, PMID: 39241208) — raised complete protection from 34.5% to 52.9% (an absolute gain of about 18 percentage points), driven by nausea outcomes: no-vomiting rates themselves were similar (76.7% versus 73.9%). A second sham-controlled trial (Li 2020, PMID: 32514290; 134 patients) found no significant difference in complete response, only modestly reduced severity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): acupuncture, mainly electroacupuncture at the P6 point, modestly improves nausea control on top of modern antiemetics; the vomiting effect is small and the evidence certainty is low.

cards.headline: Ezzo 2006 (Cochrane): acupuncture-point stimulation reduced acute vomiting (relative risk 0.82) across 11 trials and 1,247 patients — but did not reduce nausea severity
cards.summary: Ezzo 2006 (Cochrane): acupuncture-point stimulation reduced acute vomiting (relative risk 0.82) across 11 trials and 1,247 patients — but did not reduce nausea severity
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of acupuncture-point stimulation by any method (needles, electrical stimulation, magnets, acupressure) for acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in cancer patients: 11 trials, N = 1,247, pooled with a fixed-effect model. All trials used concomitant pharmacological antiemetics.
cards.result: Acupuncture-point stimulation of all methods combined reduced the incidence of acute vomiting (RR 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.69 to 0.99, P = 0.04) — an 18% relative reduction; the record gives no absolute vomiting rates. It did not reduce acute or delayed nausea severity. By modality, needle stimulation reduced acute vomiting (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.94) and electroacupuncture reduced acute vomiting (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.97), manual acupuncture did not, and noninvasive electrostimulation showed no benefit for any outcome. Acupressure reduced mean acute nausea severity slightly (standardised mean difference −0.19, 95% CI −0.37 to −0.01).
cards.watchOut: Most pooled trials predate modern triple antiemetic prophylaxis, and the headline outcome is vomiting — the symptom antiemetics already control best — while nausea, the symptom patients report as worst, did not improve in this analysis.
cards.source: Ezzo JM et al. Acupuncture-point stimulation for chemotherapy-induced nausea or vomiting. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006. PMID: 16625560. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Acupuncture Points · Antiemetics · Antineoplastic Agents · Electroacupuncture · Humans · Nausea · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Vomiting

cards.headline: Yan 2023: 38 trials and 2,503 patients — acupuncture added to usual care increased complete control of acute vomiting (RR 1.13) and delayed vomiting (RR 1.47), with certainty low to very low
cards.summary: Yan 2023: 38 trials and 2,503 patients — acupuncture added to usual care increased complete control of acute vomiting (RR 1.13) and delayed vomiting (RR 1.47), with certainty low to very low
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture or usual care for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: 38 RCTs with a total of 2,503 patients; the main outcome was complete control (no vomiting episodes and/or no more than mild nausea); evidence certainty was rated with GRADE.
cards.result: Acupuncture in addition to usual care may increase complete control of acute vomiting (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.25; 10 studies) and delayed vomiting (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.00; 10 studies) compared with usual care alone — both relative measures; the record gives no absolute control rates. No effects were found for all other review outcomes. The certainty of evidence was generally low or very low, and an exploratory analysis suggested adequate reporting of planned rescue antiemetics might shrink the acute-vomiting effect (P = 0.035).
cards.watchOut: Many included trials are small, single-centre and at unclear risk of bias, and the delayed-vomiting estimate rests on 10 studies with a wide interval (1.07–2.00); low-to-very-low certainty caps this shelf's stamp.
cards.source: Yan Y et al. Acupuncture for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in cancer patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Cancer medicine. 2023. PMID: 37226372. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Antineoplastic Agents · Vomiting · Nausea · Antiemetics · Neoplasms · Acupuncture Therapy

cards.headline: Shen 2024: sham-controlled trial in 239 patients — adding electroacupuncture to triple antiemetics raised complete protection from 34.5% to 52.9%, driven by nausea, not vomiting
cards.summary: Shen 2024: sham-controlled trial in 239 patients — adding electroacupuncture to triple antiemetics raised complete protection from 34.5% to 52.9%, driven by nausea, not vomiting
cards.people: Randomised, blinded, sham-controlled trial across six Chinese hospitals (March 2022 to December 2023) in patients with breast cancer undergoing highly emetogenic chemotherapy: true electroacupuncture (n = 120) versus sham electroacupuncture (n = 119), both groups receiving standard triple antiemetic therapy; 235 patients (98.3%) completed the trial. The primary endpoint was complete protection (no vomiting, no rescue treatment, no significant nausea) within 120 hours of chemotherapy.
cards.result: Complete protection was 52.9% with true electroacupuncture versus 34.5% with sham (P = .004) — an absolute difference of about 18 percentage points. True electroacupuncture also improved total control (13.4% versus 4.3%, P = .014), no significant nausea (58.8% versus 37.9%, P = .001) and no nausea (13.4% versus 4.3%, P = .014). However, no vomiting in the overall phase was similar in both groups (73.9% versus 76.7%, P = .622), and a post hoc analysis located the complete-protection advantage in the delayed phase, with no significant acute-phase difference.
cards.watchOut: One cancer type (breast), one country, and a composite endpoint whose movement came from nausea scores while vomiting — the hardest outcome — did not differ; blinding of acupuncture is inherently imperfect even with sham needles.
cards.source: Shen G et al. Effect of Adding Electroacupuncture to Standard Triple Antiemetic Therapy on Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2024. PMID: 39241208. Registry ID: NCT05275569. cards.headline: Li 2020: second sham-controlled trial (134 patients with advanced cancer) — complete response did not differ, though nausea and vomiting severity from day 3–4 onward was modestly lower with true acupuncture
cards.summary: Li 2020: second sham-controlled trial (134 patients with advanced cancer) — complete response did not differ, though nausea and vomiting severity from day 3–4 onward was modestly lower with true acupuncture
cards.people: Multi-centre, single-blind, randomised, sham-controlled trial in patients with advanced cancer receiving chemotherapy: true acupuncture (n = 68) versus sham acupuncture (n = 66); sessions twice on day 1 of chemotherapy and once daily on the following 4 days; the primary outcome was chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting graded by Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events.
cards.result: The true acupuncture group did not show significant improvement in complete response rates of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (all P > 0.05) — for complete response, the treatment made no difference. It modestly reduced the severity of nausea (from day 3 to day 21, P < 0.05) and vomiting (from day 4 to day 21, P < 0.05) compared with sham, and nutritional-appetite scores were higher on day 14 (21.82 versus 20.12, P = 0.003) and day 21 (22.39 versus 20.43, P = 0.001). No adverse events occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: The record reports severity differences without effect sizes, so the size of the severity benefit cannot be stated; the null on the primary complete-response outcome is the firmer finding and tempers the positive JCO trial.
cards.source: Li QW et al. Efficacy of acupuncture in the prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in patients with advanced cancer: a multi-center, single-blind, randomized, sham-controlled clinical research. Chinese medicine. 2020. PMID: 32514290. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: acupuncture on top of antiemetics modestly improves nausea control — complete protection up about 18 points in the best trial, vomiting barely moved, certainty low
cards.summary: Synthesis: acupuncture on top of antiemetics modestly improves nausea control — complete protection up about 18 points in the best trial, vomiting barely moved, certainty low
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews (11 trials/1,247 patients and 38 trials/2,503 patients, overlapping trial sets) and two sham-controlled trials (239 and 134 patients). Unique participants across the reviews and trials are in the low thousands, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled stimulation reduced acute vomiting relatively (RR 0.82; Ezzo 2006) and raised complete control of acute (RR 1.13) and delayed (RR 1.47) vomiting on low-to-very-low certainty (Yan 2023). The largest modern sham-controlled trial found complete protection 52.9% versus 34.5% with no difference in vomiting itself (Shen 2024); the other sham trial found no complete-response difference, only milder severity (Li 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) as an adjunct to standard antiemetic therapy.
cards.watchOut: Every positive result is adjunctive — no trial supports acupuncture instead of guideline antiemetics — and sham-controlled acupuncture trials cannot fully blind practitioners, so expectation effects remain a live alternative explanation for the nausea findings.

shelves.title: Stopping cervical cancer screening at 65 — safe only with documented adequate prior screening and no high-risk history: a negative HPV exit test leaves a modelled lifetime risk of 1 in 6,525, versus 1 in 588 when the history is unknown
shelves.question: In women aged 65 and older, when can cervical cancer screening be safely stopped?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cervix Uteri · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Humans · Mass Screening · Middle Aged · Papillomaviridae · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms · Vaginal Smears · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only (there is no randomised trial of stopping screening, and the stamp is capped accordingly). The convergent answer: screening can be stopped after age 65 in a woman who has had adequate prior screening and is not otherwise at high risk. The USPSTF (2018) recommends against screening women older than 65 who have had adequate prior screening and are not at high risk (D recommendation), and against screening after hysterectomy with removal of the cervix for non-cancer indications. The modelling evidence quantifies why an exit test matters: in Malagón 2018, a 70-year-old whose history was unknown had a remaining lifetime risk of 1 in 588 if she stopped, falling to 1 in 1,206 after a negative cytology exit test, 1 in 6,525 after a negative HPV test and 1 in 9,550 after a negative co-test — while a never-screened woman's lifetime risk was 1 in 45. The cautionary cohort (Sheu 2021) shows the flip side of the condition: among 296 women who met exit criteria but kept screening, no cervical cancer was found. The condition that does the work is documented adequate prior screening; where the history is inadequate or unknown, the evidence supports continuing (or an HPV exit test) rather than stopping on age alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only: stop at 65 when adequate prior screening is documented and the woman is not at high risk; do not stop on age alone when the screening history is inadequate or unknown.

cards.headline: USPSTF 2018: recommends against cervical cancer screening in women older than 65 who have had adequate prior screening and are not otherwise at high risk (D recommendation)
cards.summary: USPSTF 2018: recommends against cervical cancer screening in women older than 65 who have had adequate prior screening and are not otherwise at high risk (D recommendation)
cards.people: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement applying to women with a cervix; the Task Force reviewed clinical trials and cohort studies of cytology, high-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing and co-testing, and commissioned a decision analysis on the age to begin and end screening. The statement does not give a participant N.
cards.result: The USPSTF recommends screening women aged 21 to 65 years (every 3 years with cytology alone at 21–29; at 30–65, cytology every 3 years, hrHPV testing alone every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years — A recommendations). It recommends against screening women older than 65 years who have had adequate prior screening and are not otherwise at high risk for cervical cancer (D recommendation), against screening women younger than 21 (D), and against screening women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix for indications other than a high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer (D). It concludes with moderate to high certainty that screening in the over-65 adequately screened group does not result in a positive net benefit; deaths from cervical cancer in the US had declined from 2.8 to 2.3 per 100,000 women from 2000 to 2015.
cards.watchOut: The recommendation turns entirely on the qualifiers — 'adequate prior screening' and 'not otherwise at high risk'. The statement itself does not itemise the adequacy definition in the record; women with a history of high-grade lesions, in utero diethylstilbestrol exposure or immunocompromise sit outside this stopping rule.
cards.source: Curry SJ et al. Screening for Cervical Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30140884. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Malagón 2018: modelling — a negative HPV exit test at 70 cuts remaining lifetime cervical cancer risk from 1 in 588 (history unknown) to 1 in 6,525; a negative co-test to 1 in 9,550
cards.people: Markov natural-history and screening model calibrated to Canadian provincial registries and survey data, simulating cohorts of women aged 10–100 years; women with total hysterectomy were excluded. Outcomes are modelled remaining lifetime risks for older, unvaccinated women stopping screening at different ages with different exit tests — not observed trial outcomes.
cards.result: Women who were never screened had a modelled lifetime cervical cancer risk of 1 in 45; perfect adherence to cytology every 3 years from age 25 to 69 reduced it to 1 in 532. A 70-year-old woman whose screening history was unknown had an average remaining lifetime risk of 1 in 588 if she stopped screening; this fell to 1 in 1,206 with a negative cytology exit test (2.0-times reduction), 1 in 6,525 with a negative HPV test (12.9-times reduction) and 1 in 9,550 with a negative co-test (18.1-times reduction). Screening with cytology up to age 75 achieved further risk reductions, but with diminishing returns.
cards.watchOut: Modelled, not observed: the risk figures depend on the model's natural-history assumptions and Canadian calibration, and they describe unvaccinated women. They quantify the value of a documented negative exit test; they are not a substitute for a woman's actual screening history.
cards.source: Malagón T et al. Age at last screening and remaining lifetime risk of cervical cancer in older, unvaccinated, HPV-negative women: a modelling study. The Lancet. Oncology. 2018. PMID: 30392810. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sheu 2021: among 296 women who met exit criteria but kept screening past 65, continued testing found abnormalities but no cervical cancer (small cohort N on the face)
cards.summary: Sheu 2021: among 296 women who met exit criteria but kept screening past 65, continued testing found abnormalities but no cervical cancer (small cohort N on the face)
cards.people: 296 patients at a single urban hospital-based clinic (records 2008–2019) who met American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology exit criteria yet continued screening; the additional surveillance period ranged from 1 to 15 years (mean 3.98 years). N = 296.
cards.result: 39 individuals had abnormalities during the additional surveillance: 25 high-risk HPV positive only with negative cytology, 8 atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, 3 low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, 2 atypical glandular cells of undetermined significance, and 1 high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. No cases of cervical cancer were detected. The total abnormality rate including HPV-positive-only results was 332.20 per 10,000 person-years, and the cytologic abnormality rate was 119.25 per 10,000 person-years. The authors conclude the data suggest screening cessation may be appropriate with an adequate negative screening history.
cards.watchOut: A single-clinic retrospective series of 296 women: zero cancers in 296 women over about 4 extra years is reassuring but cannot by itself bound a rare outcome tightly, and most positives were HPV-positive-only results, which trigger follow-up burden without cancer yield.
cards.source: Sheu J et al. Prevalence of Positive Cervical Cancer Screening Tests Past the Age of 65 Years With Prior Adequate Negative Screening. Journal of lower genital tract disease. 2021. PMID: 34542083. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Coldman 2020 (HPV FOCAL exit round): among women HPV-negative at the 48-month exit, co-testing found almost no CIN2+ (0.3 per 1,000) — exit HPV negativity marks very low short-term risk
cards.summary: Coldman 2020 (HPV FOCAL exit round): among women HPV-negative at the 48-month exit, co-testing found almost no CIN2+ (0.3 per 1,000) — exit HPV negativity marks very low short-term risk
cards.type: Randomised screening trial, exit-round analysis (HPV FOCAL, Coldman 2020)
cards.people: HPV FOCAL randomised screening trial, women aged 25–65 in British Columbia: 9,457 randomised to control (cytology) and 9,552 to intervention (HPV testing); at the 48-month exit round, 7,448 control and 8,281 intervention participants were per-protocol eligible and screened with HPV plus cytology co-testing.
cards.result: Exit co-test results were similar by arm (P = 0.11); the relative rate of CIN2+ for intervention versus control was RR 0.83 relative (95% CI 0.56 to 1.23). Comparing intervention women who were HPV-negative at baseline with control women cytology-negative at baseline and 24 months, the RR for CIN2+ was 0.68 relative (95% CI 0.43 to 1.06). Among per-protocol women who were HPV-negative at exit, cytology co-testing identified little additional CIN2+ (rate 0.3 per 1,000, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.7). The authors conclude 4-year-interval HPV screening is as safe as 2-year-interval cytology in this analysis.
cards.watchOut: Participants were aged 25–65 and the exit round came after protocol screening and follow-up within a trial — it demonstrates what a negative HPV test at exit signifies, not the safety of stopping at 65 in an unscreened or underscreened population.
cards.source: Coldman AJ et al. Disease detection at the 48-month exit round of the HPV FOCAL cervical cancer screening trial in women per-protocol eligible for routine screening. International journal of cancer. 2020. PMID: 31245842. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: stop at 65 only on documented adequate prior screening (or a negative exit test) and no high-risk history — age alone, with an inadequate or unknown history, is not a safe stopping rule on this evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: stop at 65 only on documented adequate prior screening (or a negative exit test) and no high-risk history — age alone, with an inadequate or unknown history, is not a safe stopping rule on this evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: one national guideline synthesising trials, cohorts and a decision analysis; one calibrated modelling study; one retrospective cohort of 296 women screened past exit criteria; and one randomised screening trial's exit-round analysis (19,009 randomised). No randomised trial has randomised women to stop versus continue screening, so the evidence is observational and modelled, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.result: The USPSTF recommends against screening after 65 with adequate prior screening and no high-risk features (D recommendation). Modelling puts a 70-year-old's remaining lifetime risk at 1 in 588 with an unknown history, 1 in 1,206 after a negative cytology exit test, 1 in 6,525 after a negative HPV test and 1 in 9,550 after a negative co-test. Continued screening past exit criteria in 296 women found no cancer, and an HPV-negative exit in FOCAL carried a CIN2+ rate of 0.3 per 1,000 on co-testing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational and modelling evidence only: stop at 65 when adequate prior screening is documented and the woman is not at high risk; do not stop on age alone when the screening history is inadequate or unknown.
cards.watchOut: 'Adequate prior screening' is the load-bearing condition on every card. A woman of 65+ who was never screened, was underscreened, or has a high-grade lesion history is not in the population these data reassure about.
cards.source: Synthesis of Curry SJ et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 30140884); Malagón T et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2018 (PMID: 30392810); Sheu J et al. Journal of lower genital tract disease. 2021 (PMID: 34542083); Coldman AJ et al. International journal of cancer. 2020 (PMID: 31245842).

shelves.title: Survivorship mammography after breast cancer: annual mammography is the schedule the evidence was built on — observational data link each additional surveillance mammogram to lower breast cancer mortality, and no trial supports stretching the interval
shelves.question: In women who have completed breast cancer treatment, how often should mammography be done for survivorship screening?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms · Female · Follow-Up Studies · General Practice · Humans · Mammography · Medical Oncology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasm Staging · Physical Examination · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the mortality association, printed on the face. No randomised trial has compared annual with less frequent surveillance mammography after breast cancer treatment. What the trials do show is that follow-up built on regular examination and yearly mammography is as effective as more intensive follow-up (Cochrane, Moschetti 2016: overall survival HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.15, in 2,563 women — the more intensive approach made no difference). The mortality case for surveillance itself is observational: each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with a 0.69-fold decrease in the odds of breast cancer mortality in older survivors (Lash 2007), and the association persisted, weaker and non-significant, beyond five years (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19; Buist 2013). A modelling study estimates mammography's preclinical detectable phase at 35 months (Aarts 2019), which is why longer intervals are discussed — but the authors themselves say studies are needed before a longer interval can be recommended. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: annual mammography is the survivorship schedule the evidence was built on; a longer interval is a hypothesis, not a tested alternative.

cards.headline: Moschetti 2016 (Cochrane): follow-up built on regular physical examination and yearly mammography was as effective as more intensive follow-up — overall survival HR 0.98 (the treatment made no difference) — in 2,563 women
cards.summary: Moschetti 2016 (Cochrane): follow-up built on regular physical examination and yearly mammography was as effective as more intensive follow-up — overall survival HR 0.98 (the treatment made no difference) — in 2,563 women
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Moschetti 2016)
cards.people: Five randomised trials involving 4,023 women treated for stage I, II or III breast cancer; the pooled comparison of follow-up schemes covered two trials with 2,563 women comparing follow-up based on clinical visits and mammography with a more intensive scheme including radiological and laboratory tests.
cards.result: After pooling, no significant differences in overall survival (hazard ratio (HR) 0.98, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84 to 1.15, two studies, 2,563 participants, high-quality evidence) or disease-free survival (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.00, low-quality evidence) emerged between mammography-and-examination follow-up and more intensive follow-up. The review concludes that follow-up programmes based on regular physical examinations and yearly mammography alone are as effective as more intensive approaches for timeliness of recurrence detection, overall survival and quality of life. No trial in the review tested yearly mammography against a longer interval.
cards.watchOut: These trials compare more versus less intensive follow-up packages, not annual versus biennial mammography: they establish yearly mammography as a sufficient backbone, not that a longer interval would be worse.
cards.source: Moschetti I et al. Follow-up strategies for women treated for early breast cancer. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27230946. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lash 2007: each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with a 0.69-fold decrease in the odds of breast cancer mortality in 1,846 older survivors — observational, not randomised
cards.summary: Lash 2007: each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with a 0.69-fold decrease in the odds of breast cancer mortality in 1,846 older survivors — observational, not randomised
cards.type: Nested case-control study within a cohort (Lash 2007)
cards.people: 1,846 women aged at least 65 years with stage I or II breast cancer enrolled at six integrated health care delivery systems, with complete ascertainment of surveillance mammograms; 178 women died of breast cancer during 5 years of follow-up, and four controls were matched to each decedent.
cards.result: Each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with a 0.69-fold decrease in the odds of breast cancer mortality (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92). The protective association was strongest among women with stage I disease, those who received mastectomy, and those in the oldest age group. The authors note that trials comparing surveillance with no surveillance are unlikely, so this observational estimate is the main mortality evidence for surveillance itself.
cards.watchOut: Women who attend surveillance differ from women who do not — in health, engagement and treatment — so part of the 0.69 association may be healthy-attender bias rather than an effect of the mammograms themselves.
cards.source: Lash TL et al. Mammography surveillance and mortality in older breast cancer survivors. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2007. PMID: 17548838. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Buist 2013: beyond 5 years after diagnosis, a surveillance mammogram in the preceding year was associated with a modest, non-significant reduction in breast cancer mortality (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19) in 1,235 long-term survivors
cards.summary: Buist 2013: beyond 5 years after diagnosis, a surveillance mammogram in the preceding year was associated with a modest, non-significant reduction in breast cancer mortality (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19) in 1,235 long-term survivors
cards.people: 1,235 women aged 65 years or older diagnosed in 1990–1994 with early stage breast cancer who survived disease-free for at least 5 years, followed from year 6 through death, disenrollment, or 15 years after diagnosis; 85% received at least one surveillance mammogram in years 5–9 and 82% in years 10–14; 120 women died of breast cancer and 393 of other causes.
cards.result: Multivariable models suggested a modest reduction in breast cancer-specific mortality with surveillance mammogram receipt in the preceding year (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19, p = 0.29 — not statistically significant); the association with other-cause mortality was 0.95 (95% CI 0.78–1.17, p = 0.64). The record itself states that annual surveillance mammograms in older long-term survivors are recommended on little evidence, with no guidelines on when to stop.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval includes no effect: this study is consistent with continued benefit beyond year 5 but does not prove it, and it cannot separate annual from less frequent schedules.
cards.source: Buist DS et al. Long-term surveillance mammography and mortality in older women with a history of early stage invasive breast cancer. Breast cancer research and treatment. 2013. PMID: 24113745. Registry ID: none in the record.
