cards.headline: Aarts 2019: mammography detects contralateral second cancers with 91% sensitivity and an estimated 35-month preclinical detectable phase — longer than the recommended 12-month interval, a modelling result the authors say needs testing
cards.summary: Aarts 2019: mammography detects contralateral second cancers with 91% sensitivity and an estimated 35-month preclinical detectable phase — longer than the recommended 12-month interval, a modelling result the authors say needs testing
cards.type: Modelling study of test sensitivity and preclinical detectable phase (Aarts 2019)
cards.people: 589 women with a contralateral second breast cancer diagnosed in Florence between 1980 and 2005; test sensitivity and the duration of the preclinical detectable phase (PCDP) were estimated with an exponential model, stratified by follow-up period and age.
cards.result: For clinical breast examination, test sensitivity was 55% and the PCDP 16 months. For mammography, sensitivity was 91% and the PCDP 35 months — considerably longer than the recommended follow-up interval of 12 months. The authors conclude mammography can detect contralateral cancers early, and that future studies are needed to determine whether a longer follow-up interval is appropriate.
cards.watchOut: A modelled detectable phase is not an outcome trial: a 35-month window does not show that biennial mammography gives the same mortality results as annual mammography, only that the question is worth testing.
cards.source: Aarts AMWM et al. Towards evidence-based follow-up intervals for breast cancer survivors: Estimates of the preclinical detectable phase of contralateral second breast cancer. Breast (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2019. PMID: 30884341. Registry ID: none in the record. modelling study of test sensitivity and preclinical detectable phase (aarts 2019) 589 women with a contralateral second breast cancer diagnosed in florence between 1980 and 2005; test sensitivity and the duration of the preclinical detectable phase (pcdp) were estimated with an exponential model, stratified by follow-up period and age. for clinical breast examination, test sensitivity was 55% and the pcdp 16 months. for mammography, sensitivity was 91% and the pcdp 35 months — considerably longer than the recommended follow-up interval of 12 months. the authors conclude mammography can detect contralateral cancers early, and that future studies are needed to determine whether a longer follow-up interval is appropriate. a modelled detectable phase is not an outcome trial: a 35-month window does not show that biennial mammography gives the same mortality results as annual mammography, only that the question is worth testing. aarts amwm et al. towards evidence-based follow-up intervals for breast cancer survivors: estimates of the preclinical detectable phase of contralateral second breast cancer. breast (edinburgh, scotland). 2019. pmid: 30884341. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aftercare · aged · breast neoplasms · cancer survivors · early detection of cancer · evidence-based medicine · female · humans · mammography · middle aged · neoplasms, second primary · retrospective studies · sensitivity and specificity · time factors

cards.headline: Synthesis: annual mammography is the evidence-based default after breast cancer treatment — trials used yearly mammography as the sufficient backbone, cohorts link more surveillance mammograms to lower breast cancer mortality, and the case for a longer interval rests on modelling alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: annual mammography is the evidence-based default after breast cancer treatment — trials used yearly mammography as the sufficient backbone, cohorts link more surveillance mammograms to lower breast cancer mortality, and the case for a longer interval rests on modelling alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of five randomised follow-up trials (4,023 women; pooled scheme comparison 2,563 women) built on yearly mammography; a nested case-control study of 1,846 older survivors; a cohort of 1,235 long-term survivors followed beyond year 5; and a modelling study of 589 contralateral second cancers. Total carded participants exceed 7,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design — no randomised comparison of intervals — and it is printed here.
cards.result: Yearly-mammography follow-up was as effective as more intensive follow-up for survival (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.15; Moschetti 2016). Each additional surveillance mammogram was associated with lower odds of breast cancer mortality (0.69-fold; 95% CI 0.52 to 0.92; Lash 2007), and a mammogram in the preceding year remained associated with a modest, non-significant mortality reduction beyond year 5 (IRR 0.82, 95% CI 0.56–1.19; Buist 2013). Mammography's modelled preclinical detectable phase (35 months; Aarts 2019) raises — but does not answer — the question of a longer interval. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the mortality association: annual surveillance mammography is the schedule the evidence supports; less frequent schedules are untested in trials.
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomised women to annual versus less frequent mammography, so this shelf supports the annual default without being able to quantify what, if anything, is lost by stretching the interval.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moschetti I et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016 (PMID: 27230946); Lash TL et al. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2007 (PMID: 17548838); Buist DS et al. Breast cancer research and treatment. 2013 (PMID: 24113745); Aarts AMWM et al. Breast (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2019 (PMID: 30884341).

shelves.title: When to stop mammography screening: routine biennial screening is recommended to age 74 — beyond 75 there are no trial data, mixed observational results, and consistent evidence of rising overdiagnosis
shelves.question: At what age should average-risk women stop routine mammography screening?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Breast Neoplasms · Female · Mammography · Early Detection of Cancer · Middle Aged · Aged · Adult · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Age Factors · Ultrasonography, Mammary · United States · Mass Screening
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — because the question's honest answer is a boundary, not a tested age. The trial evidence for screening mammography runs to about age 69–74: the 2009 USPSTF review found mortality reduction for ages 39 to 69 with data lacking at 70 and older (Nelson 2009), and the 2024 USPSTF statement recommends biennial screening for women aged 40 to 74 while issuing an I statement — evidence insufficient — for women 75 and older (USPSTF 2024). Beyond 75, the dedicated systematic review found mixed mortality results, mixed false-positive findings, and consistently increased overdiagnosis across 36 studies (Mathieu 2024); modelling studies price continuation to 75 or 80 at $34,000–$88,000 per life-year gained but captured none of the harms fully (Mandelblatt 2003). So routine screening stopping at 74/75 is where the evidence stops; continuing beyond it is an individual judgement for women in good health, not an evidence-based default. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — for stopping at 74/75: no trial evidence establishes benefit beyond 74, and the balance at older ages is undetermined.

cards.headline: USPSTF 2024: biennial screening mammography is recommended for women aged 40 to 74 years (B recommendation) — and the evidence is insufficient to assess benefits and harms at 75 years or older (I statement)
cards.summary: USPSTF 2024: biennial screening mammography is recommended for women aged 40 to 74 years (B recommendation) — and the evidence is insufficient to assess benefits and harms at 75 years or older (I statement)
cards.type: Recommendation statement with commissioned systematic review (USPSTF 2024)
cards.people: Cisgender women and all other persons assigned female at birth aged 40 years or older at average risk of breast cancer; the statement rests on a commissioned systematic review of mammography screening strategies plus collaborative modelling studies.
cards.result: The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that biennial screening mammography in women aged 40 to 74 years has a moderate net benefit, and recommends it (B recommendation). For women 75 years or older it concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening mammography (I statement). The record reports no effect size for the 75-and-older group, because the underlying trial evidence does not extend there — printed plainly, as the record gives it.
cards.watchOut: An I statement is not a recommendation to stop: it is a statement that the evidence runs out at 74/75, which is exactly the boundary this shelf's question asks about — individual decisions beyond it rest on health status and life expectancy, not trial data.
cards.source: Nicholson WK et al. Screening for Breast Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38687503. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mathieu 2024: across 36 studies in women 75 and older, mortality results were mixed (some benefit, some none), false positives rose in some studies, and overdiagnosis consistently increased — a systematic review that could support no recommendation for or against continuing
cards.summary: Mathieu 2024: across 36 studies in women 75 and older, mortality results were mixed (some benefit, some none), false positives rose in some studies, and overdiagnosis consistently increased — a systematic review that could support no recommendation for or against continuing
cards.type: Systematic review of observational and modelling studies (Mathieu 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review of mammography screening studies in women aged 75 years and over: 36 studies, of which 27 were observational and 9 were modelling studies; the review was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42020203131).
cards.result: There was mixed evidence about the benefits and harms of continuing mammography screening beyond age 75: some studies showed a beneficial effect on breast cancer mortality and others showed no effect. Harms evidence was also mixed for false positives and recalls, but there was consistent evidence of increased overdiagnosis in older age groups. The authors conclude there is limited evidence to make a recommendation for or against continuing breast screening beyond 75, and that future studies should estimate overdiagnosis given competing causes of death. The record reports no pooled effect size for mortality.
cards.watchOut: Many included studies used no or uninformative comparison groups, biasing results toward screening's benefit — yet even with that tilt, the mortality evidence stayed mixed, which strengthens the 'insufficient evidence' reading rather than weakening it.
cards.source: Mathieu E et al. Health benefits and harms of mammography screening in older women (75+ years)-a systematic review. British journal of cancer. 2024. PMID: 38030747. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Female · Humans · Age Factors · Breast · Breast Neoplasms · Mammography · Mass Screening

cards.headline: Nelson 2009: mammography screening reduced breast cancer mortality by 15% (relative) at ages 39–49 and the trial data supported benefit to age 69 — with data lacking for women aged 70 and older
cards.summary: Nelson 2009: mammography screening reduced breast cancer mortality by 15% (relative) at ages 39–49 and the trial data supported benefit to age 69 — with data lacking for women aged 70 and older
cards.people: Systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force of randomised trials with breast cancer mortality outcomes, plus harms data from multiple sources; trials covered average-risk women aged 39 to 69 years in the analysable data.
cards.result: Mammography screening reduced breast cancer mortality by 15% for women aged 39 to 49 years (relative risk 0.85, 95% credible interval 0.75 to 0.96; 8 trials) — a relative measure; the review's conclusion is that screening reduces mortality for women aged 39 to 69 years and that data are insufficient for older women. Estimates of overdiagnosis varied from 1% to 10%. The review states plainly: data are lacking for women aged 70 years or older.
cards.watchOut: This 2009 review predates the 2024 statement's extension of the recommended range to 74 (which leans on modelling as well as trials); carded together, the two records show the stopping boundary is set by where trial data end plus modelling, not by a trial that tested stopping.
cards.source: Nelson HD et al. Screening for breast cancer: an update for the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. Annals of internal medicine. 2009. PMID: 19920273. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mandelblatt 2003: modelling studies estimated that extending biennial screening to age 75 or 80 cost $34,000 to $88,000 per life-year gained (2002 US dollars) versus stopping at 65 — with no study fully capturing harms such as overdiagnosis
cards.summary: Mandelblatt 2003: modelling studies estimated that extending biennial screening to age 75 or 80 cost $34,000 to $88,000 per life-year gained (2002 US dollars) versus stopping at 65 — with no study fully capturing harms such as overdiagnosis
cards.type: Systematic review of cost-effectiveness modelling studies (Mandelblatt 2003)
cards.people: Systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force of cost-effectiveness analyses of screening after age 65: 115 studies identified, 10 met inclusion criteria; analyses were conducted from a societal or government perspective.
cards.result: On average, extending biennial screening to age 75 or 80 years was estimated to cost 34,000 to 88,000 dollars (2002 US dollars) per life-year gained compared with stopping screening at age 65. Two studies suggested it was more cost-effective to target healthy women than those with several competing risks for death. No study fully captured the potential harms of screening, including anxiety from false-positive results and overdiagnosis. The authors conclude that biennial screening after 65 reduces mortality at reasonable costs for women without clinically significant comorbid conditions, on modelled — not trial — evidence.
cards.watchOut: Cost-effectiveness models assume the mortality benefit they are asked to value: they can price continuation but cannot prove it works, and by the review's own account they omitted the harms that matter most at older ages.
cards.source: Mandelblatt J et al. The cost-effectiveness of screening mammography beyond age 65 years: a systematic review for the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. Annals of internal medicine. 2003. PMID: 14623621. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the evidence boundary is 74 — routine screening is recommended through 74, no trial establishes benefit beyond it, observational mortality results at 75+ are mixed, and overdiagnosis rises with age, so 'stop at 75' is where the evidence stops, not a proven optimum
cards.summary: Synthesis: the evidence boundary is 74 — routine screening is recommended through 74, no trial establishes benefit beyond it, observational mortality results at 75+ are mixed, and overdiagnosis rises with age, so 'stop at 75' is where the evidence stops, not a proven optimum
cards.people: The carded evidence: the 2024 USPSTF statement and its commissioned review, a 36-study systematic review in women 75 and older (27 observational, 9 modelling), the 2009 USPSTF trial review, and a review of 10 cost-effectiveness models. No carded randomised trial enrolled average-risk women beyond their early 70s, so no participant total can cure the gap; the limitation is the age range of the evidence itself.
cards.result: Recommended range: biennial screening to age 74 with moderate certainty of moderate net benefit; insufficient evidence at 75+ (USPSTF 2024). Trial data support mortality reduction to age 69 and are lacking beyond 70 (Nelson 2009). At 75+, mortality findings split between benefit and no effect while overdiagnosis consistently increased (Mathieu 2024); models price extension to 75–80 at $34,000–$88,000 per life-year gained without capturing harms (Mandelblatt 2003). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): average-risk women can reasonably stop routine mammography at 75 — the age where recommendations end because evidence ends — with continuation an individual decision for healthy women with long life expectancy.
cards.watchOut: This shelf cannot name a biologically 'correct' stopping age, because none has been tested: anyone presenting 74/75 as proven rather than as the evidence boundary would be overstating every card on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nicholson WK et al. JAMA. 2024 (PMID: 38687503); Mathieu E et al. British journal of cancer. 2024 (PMID: 38030747); Nelson HD et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19920273); Mandelblatt J et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2003 (PMID: 14623621).

shelves.title: Barrett's surveillance interval (no trial fixes it): longer-than-guideline intervals showed no curability or mortality penalty in a 726-patient prospective cohort — the frequency question is answered only by observational data
shelves.question: How often should adults with non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus have surveillance endoscopy?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Disease Progression · Barrett Esophagus · Prospective Studies · Precancerous Conditions · Humans · Esophageal Neoplasms
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3441, which covers surveillance versus endoscopy at need (the BOSS comparison); this shelf covers the uncovered slice — how often surveillance should be done. No randomised trial has compared one surveillance interval against another in non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus. The best interval evidence is observational: in a multicentre prospective cohort of 726 patients (3,802 endoscopies), only 16% of non-dysplastic surveillance was adherent to the recommended interval, yet longer intervals than recommended showed no evidence of affecting endoscopic curability of adenocarcinoma or cause-specific mortality (Roumans 2023). A structured programme cohort detected high-grade dysplasia or T1 cancer at a combined rate of 1 per 77.6 endoscopy-years of follow-up (Bright 2009), and a Veterans Affairs cohort found most surveillance was non-adherent to the 3-year guideline interval with no difference in biopsy-positive endoscopies between adherent and non-adherent patients (Dalal 2018). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: no trial fixes the right interval; the observational record does not show that stretching beyond guideline intervals worsens curability or mortality, and does not show that shorter intervals help.

cards.headline: Roumans 2023: in 726 Barrett's patients, longer surveillance intervals than recommended showed no evidence of harming endoscopic curability of cancer or cause-specific mortality — the closest direct evidence on interval length
cards.summary: Roumans 2023: in 726 Barrett's patients, longer surveillance intervals than recommended showed no evidence of harming endoscopic curability of cancer or cause-specific mortality — the closest direct evidence on interval length
cards.people: Multicentre prospective cohort of 726 Barrett's esophagus surveillance patients in the Netherlands, with 3,802 endoscopies performed by 167 endoscopists; adherence to the recommended surveillance interval was 16% for non-dysplastic Barrett's, 55% for low-grade dysplasia, and 54% of endoscopies followed the Seattle biopsy protocol.
cards.result: There was no evidence to support the statements that longer surveillance intervals or fewer biopsies than recommended affect endoscopic curability of esophageal adenocarcinoma or cause-specific mortality (P > 0.20 for all, as printed in the record). Insufficient biopsies did not affect the probability of non-dysplastic Barrett's (OR 1.0) or low-grade dysplasia (OR 2.3) being misclassified as high-grade dysplasia or cancer (P > 0.05). The authors conclude the clinical consequences of nonadherence appeared limited and that surveillance recommendations should be optimised to minimise the burden of endoscopies.
cards.watchOut: Nonadherence was not randomised: patients scoped late differ from patients scoped on time, and 'no evidence of an effect' in 726 patients is not proof that interval length never matters — rare cancer outcomes leave wide uncertainty.
cards.source: Roumans CAM et al. Clinical consequences of nonadherence to Barrett's esophagus surveillance recommendations: a Multicenter prospective cohort study. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2023. PMID: 36579763. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adenocarcinoma · Disease Progression · Barrett Esophagus · Prospective Studies · Precancerous Conditions · Humans · Esophageal Neoplasms

cards.headline: Bright 2009: a structured surveillance programme (interval set by prior findings) found high-grade dysplasia or T1 cancer in 10 of 405 patients — a combined incidence of 1 per 77.6 endoscopy-years of follow-up
cards.summary: Bright 2009: a structured surveillance programme (interval set by prior findings) found high-grade dysplasia or T1 cancer in 10 of 405 patients — a combined incidence of 1 per 77.6 endoscopy-years of follow-up
cards.people: 405 patients enrolled in a structured Barrett's oesophagus surveillance programme begun in 2004, contributing 776 patient-years of endoscopy follow-up; the protocol specified the surveillance interval and biopsy number according to previous endoscopy and biopsy findings, and 93.7% of patients were scoped at the appropriate interval.
cards.result: In four patients, T1 stage oesophageal adenocarcinoma was identified, and in six patients high-grade dysplasia was identified (combined incidence of adenocarcinoma/high-grade dysplasia 1 per 77.6 endoscopy years of follow-up). Formalising surveillance lengthened the modal surveillance interval from 1 year to 2 years and increased the mean number of biopsies per endoscopy from 5.9 to 7. The authors conclude structured surveillance detects malignant progression at an early stage.
cards.watchOut: A single programme with no comparison interval: it shows what one protocolised schedule yields, not whether a longer or shorter interval would yield more or less — and most detected lesions were dysplasia, not cancer.
cards.source: Bright T et al. Outcome of endoscopy surveillance for Barrett's oesophagus. ANZ Journal of Surgery. 2009. PMID: 20078532. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dalal 2018: against a 3-year guideline interval, only 30% of 110 veterans with non-dysplastic Barrett's were guideline-adherent — and biopsy-positive endoscopies did not differ between adherent and non-adherent patients
cards.summary: Dalal 2018: against a 3-year guideline interval, only 30% of 110 veterans with non-dysplastic Barrett's were guideline-adherent — and biopsy-positive endoscopies did not differ between adherent and non-adherent patients
cards.people: 110 patients (96.4% male, 93.6% white, mean age 58.9 years) with incident biopsy-confirmed non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus at a single Veterans Affairs centre, identified 2006–2008 and followed for a median of 6.7 years; patients aged 76 and above and those developing dysplasia or cancer were excluded.
cards.result: Thirty-three cases (30.0%) were guideline adherent to the 3-year interval and 77 (70.0%) were nonadherent, including 25 (22.7%) with no surveillance at all. Biopsy-positive surveillance endoscopies did not differ between adherent and nonadherent cases (75.8% vs 76.6%, P = 0.92), and adherent cases were significantly older (61.5 vs 57.9 years, P = 0.04). The record reports no cancer or mortality outcomes by interval.
cards.watchOut: This card measures practice patterns, not interval efficacy: it excludes patients who developed dysplasia or cancer, so it cannot say whether the 3-year interval itself is right — it shows only that real-world timing is usually looser than the guideline.
cards.source: Dalal KS et al. Adherence to Surveillance Guidelines in Nondysplastic Barrett's Esophagus. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 27984402. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial compares surveillance intervals in non-dysplastic Barrett's; the observational record finds no curability or mortality penalty for longer-than-recommended intervals, at a detection yield of about 1 high-grade lesion per 78 endoscopy-years
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial compares surveillance intervals in non-dysplastic Barrett's; the observational record finds no curability or mortality penalty for longer-than-recommended intervals, at a detection yield of about 1 high-grade lesion per 78 endoscopy-years
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre prospective cohort on interval nonadherence and clinical consequences (726 patients, 3,802 endoscopies), one structured programme cohort (405 patients, 776 patient-years), and one single-centre adherence cohort (110 patients). Total carded participants = 1,241, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design, not size — all of it is observational.
cards.result: Longer surveillance intervals than recommended showed no evidence of affecting endoscopic curability of adenocarcinoma or cause-specific mortality (Roumans 2023). A protocolised programme detected T1 cancer or high-grade dysplasia at 1 per 77.6 endoscopy-years (Bright 2009), and guideline adherence to a 3-year interval was only 30% in practice, with no difference in biopsy-positive endoscopies by adherence (Dalal 2018). No carded record compares two named intervals head-to-head. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is the absence of any randomised interval comparison: guideline intervals rest on progression-rate modelling and convention, and the observational 'no harm from longer intervals' signal is confounded by who gets scoped late.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roumans CAM et al. Diseases of the Esophagus. 2023 (PMID: 36579763); Bright T et al. ANZ Journal of Surgery. 2009 (PMID: 20078532); Dalal KS et al. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 2018 (PMID: 27984402).

shelves.title: Adding AFP to ultrasound surveillance in cirrhosis (partial completion of #3387): the combination detects far more early liver cancers — early-stage sensitivity 63-74% versus 45-52% for ultrasound alone — at the price of more false positives
shelves.question: Should adults with cirrhosis be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma every 6 months with ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Humans · Liver Cirrhosis · Liver Neoplasms · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Sensitivity and Specificity · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Ultrasonography · alpha-Fetoproteins
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3387 covers ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis, including the 6-monthly interval and its survival evidence; this shelf answers only the part #3387 does not — what adding alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) to ultrasound buys. The diagnostic evidence is consistent in direction: ultrasound alone detects early-stage HCC poorly (47% sensitivity in Tzartzeva 2018; 63% with AFP added versus 45% without in the head-to-head studies, P=.002), and the Cochrane diagnostic review found the combination reached 96% sensitivity versus 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons, at the cost of more false positives (specificity 85% versus 93%). A 2022 network meta-analysis puts the same trade at 74.1% versus 51.6% early-stage sensitivity, with specificity falling from 87.9% to 83.9%. No carded study here is a randomised trial of the combined strategy against mortality — the case for adding AFP is a detection case, resting on the survival logic already weighed on #3387. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding AFP to 6-monthly ultrasound materially improves early HCC detection in cirrhosis, with a real false-positive cost; the mortality benefit of the combination itself is inferred, not trialled.

cards.headline: Tzartzeva 2018: ultrasound alone detected early-stage HCC with only 47% sensitivity; adding AFP raised early detection to 63% versus 45% without it (P=.002), at a small specificity cost
cards.summary: Tzartzeva 2018: ultrasound alone detected early-stage HCC with only 47% sensitivity; adding AFP raised early detection to 63% versus 45% without it (P=.002), at a small specificity cost
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 32 studies comprising 13,367 patients with cirrhosis, characterising the sensitivity and specificity of surveillance imaging with or without AFP measurement for overall and early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (literature searched January 1990 to August 2016).
cards.result: Ultrasound detected any-stage HCC with 84% sensitivity (95% CI 76%-92%) but early-stage HCC with only 47% sensitivity (95% CI 33%-61%). In studies comparing ultrasound with versus without AFP, ultrasound alone had lower sensitivity than ultrasound plus AFP for any-stage HCC (relative risk 0.88; 95% CI 0.83-0.93) and for early-stage HCC (relative risk 0.81; 95% CI 0.71-0.93), but higher specificity (relative risk 1.08; 95% CI 1.05-1.09). Early-stage sensitivity was 63% (95% CI 48%-75%) with AFP versus 45% (95% CI 30%-62%) without (P=.002). The authors conclude that adding AFP to ultrasound significantly increases sensitivity of early HCC detection in clinical practice.
cards.watchOut: These are detection (sensitivity/specificity) outcomes, not survival: finding more early cancers only helps if the earlier treatment changes outcomes, which is the separate question weighed on live shelf #3387.
cards.source: Tzartzeva K et al. Surveillance Imaging and Alpha Fetoprotein for Early Detection of Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Patients With Cirrhosis: A Meta-analysis. Gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29425931. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Colli 2021 (Cochrane): the AFP-plus-ultrasound combination had 96% sensitivity for HCC versus 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons — and about 15% false positives
cards.summary: Colli 2021 (Cochrane): the AFP-plus-ultrasound combination had 96% sensitivity for HCC versus 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons — and about 15% false positives
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy (Colli 2021, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane diagnostic-test-accuracy review of 373 studies in adults with chronic liver disease: AFP in 326 studies (144,570 participants), ultrasound in 39 studies (18,792 participants), and the combination of AFP and ultrasound in eight studies (5,454 participants); almost all studies were judged at high risk of bias.
cards.result: At a cut-off of 20 ng/mL, AFP alone had 60% sensitivity (95% CI 58%-62%) and 84% specificity for HCC; ultrasound alone had 72% sensitivity (95% CI 63%-79%) and 94% specificity. The combination of AFP (20 ng/mL cut-off) and ultrasound had 96% sensitivity (95% CI 88%-98%) and 85% specificity (95% CI 73%-93%). In a direct comparison of six studies (5,044 participants), the combination had higher sensitivity than ultrasound alone (96%, 95% CI 88%-98%, versus 76%, 95% CI 56%-89%) with specificity 85% versus 93%. The authors conclude that with the combination, less than 5% of HCC occurrences would be missed, with about 15% false-positive results, while cautioning that poor study quality and heterogeneity limit confidence.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were at high risk of bias, many AFP studies used case-control designs that flatter accuracy, and many participants were in clinical rather than surveillance settings — the 96% figure is a best-case pooled estimate, not a guarantee in a real surveillance programme.
cards.source: Colli A et al. Abdominal ultrasound and alpha-foetoprotein for the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma in adults with chronic liver disease. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33855699. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Singal 2022: in a network meta-analysis, adding AFP lifted early-stage sensitivity from 51.6% to 74.1%, while specificity fell from 87.9% to 83.9%
cards.summary: Singal 2022: in a network meta-analysis, adding AFP lifted early-stage sensitivity from 51.6% to 74.1%, while specificity fell from 87.9% to 83.9%
cards.people: Network meta-analysis of 41 studies comprising 62,517 patients with cirrhosis (literature searched January 1990 to December 2020), comparing a multitarget HCC blood test against ultrasound with or without AFP for early HCC detection, with sensitivity estimated at a fixed specificity using Bayesian models.
cards.result: Ultrasound-alone sensitivity for early-stage HCC was 51.6% (95% credible interval 43.3%-60.5%), which increased with the addition of AFP to 74.1% (95% credible interval 62.6%-82.4%); specificity fell from 87.9% to 83.9%. The multitarget blood test's sensitivity was similar to ultrasound with AFP (difference -3.3%; 95% credible interval -22.3% to 17.4% at 90% fixed specificity). The authors conclude the blood test could be a comparable alternative to ultrasound and AFP, which implicitly confirms the combined ultrasound-plus-AFP strategy as the benchmark the new test had to match.
cards.watchOut: This is an indirect, model-based comparison built to evaluate a commercial blood test, and several authors' comparisons rest on a single clinical validation study for that test; its ultrasound-plus-AFP estimates are nonetheless concordant with the two direct meta-analyses carded here.
cards.source: Singal AG et al. Comparison of a multitarget blood test to ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance: Results of a network meta-analysis. Hepatology communications. 2022. PMID: 35945907. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: adding AFP to ultrasound consistently raises early-HCC sensitivity by roughly a fifth to a quarter, and consistently costs specificity — the detection case is strong, the mortality case for the combination is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: adding AFP to ultrasound consistently raises early-HCC sensitivity by roughly a fifth to a quarter, and consistently costs specificity — the detection case is strong, the mortality case for the combination is untested
cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses of diagnostic accuracy in cirrhosis/chronic liver disease — 32 studies/13,367 patients (Tzartzeva 2018), 373 studies including eight combination studies/5,454 participants (Colli 2021, Cochrane), and 41 studies/62,517 patients (Singal 2022). Total participants across the reviews far exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the reviews overlap in their primary studies and their Ns must not be added as if independent.
cards.result: Early-stage sensitivity rises from 45%-52% on ultrasound alone to 63%-74% with AFP added (Tzartzeva 2018; Singal 2022), and overall sensitivity reaches 96% for the combination versus 76% for ultrasound alone in direct comparisons (Colli 2021). Specificity falls by roughly 4-8 points in each analysis, meaning more false-positive work-ups. No carded record randomised patients to ultrasound-plus-AFP versus ultrasound alone with survival as the outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the AFP addition, as a partial completion of live shelf #3387.
cards.watchOut: Sensitivity is a surrogate: this shelf does not show that the extra early cancers found by AFP translate into longer life — that inference borrows the surveillance-survival evidence homed on live shelf #3387.

shelves.title: Colonoscopy after 3-4 small adenomas (partial completion of #5549): risk is low when every adenoma is under 10 mm — the evidence supports a longer interval than the traditional 3 years
shelves.question: How soon should colonoscopy be repeated after removal of 3 to 4 small adenomas?
shelves.mesh: Adenoma · Aged · Colonic Polyps · Colonoscopy · Colorectal Neoplasms · Early Detection of Cancer · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: pack #5549 covers safely stretching surveillance to 5-10 years in low-risk patients (1-2 small adenomas and the registry cohorts behind that question); this shelf answers only the group #5549 does not isolate — patients with 3 to 4 small (under 10 mm) adenomas, historically labelled intermediate-risk and scoped at 3 years. The carded cohorts say that label overstates their risk when every adenoma is small: in a Spanish screening cohort, patients with 3-4 small adenomas had a 5.07% advanced-lesion rate at first follow-up versus 16.67% when one adenoma was 10-20 mm, and small adenomas alone were not significantly associated with advanced lesions (Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles 2016); in a Korean multicentre cohort the 3-4-adenoma group's 3-year advanced-neoplasia risk was 2.1% (Park 2017). Size still matters within 'small': adenomas of 6-9 mm carried higher metachronous risk than 1-5 mm adenomas in every count group, including 3-4 (odds ratio 4.91 in screening examinations; Hartstein 2020). The British guideline carded here reserves its 3-year surveillance for higher-risk findings (five or more polyps, or two or more including an advanced polyp) — criteria that 3-4 small adenomas alone do not meet. All of this is observational; no trial has randomised this group to different intervals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: the evidence supports repeating colonoscopy later than the traditional 3 years after 3-4 small adenomas, on the low-risk timetable weighed on #5549, rather than at 3 years — with the caveat that a 6-9 mm adenoma in the set argues for the shorter end of that range.

cards.headline: Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles 2016: patients with 3-4 small adenomas had only a 5.07% advanced-lesion rate at follow-up versus 16.67% when an adenoma was 10-20 mm — the authors say the interval should be lengthened
cards.summary: Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles 2016: patients with 3-4 small adenomas had only a 5.07% advanced-lesion rate at follow-up versus 16.67% when an adenoma was 10-20 mm — the authors say the interval should be lengthened
cards.people: Cohort of 561 intermediate-risk patients (63.3% men, mean age 59.01 ± 6.16 years) recruited at baseline screening colonoscopy (2006-2011) in a colorectal cancer screening programme, all of whom had index and first follow-up colonoscopy; low- and high-risk patients were excluded. The main outcome was advanced colorectal neoplasia (invasive carcinoma or advanced adenoma) at the first follow-up colonoscopy.
cards.result: Advanced lesions were detected in 7.66% of patients overall. Having 3-4 adenomas (odds ratio 3.613, 95% CI 1.661-7.859, P=0.001) and adenoma size 10 to under 20 mm (odds ratio 3.374, 95% CI 1.618-7.034, P=0.001) were independent factors associated with advanced neoplasia. But the subgroup with 3-4 adenomas plus at least one 10-20 mm adenoma (n=132) had a much higher advanced-lesion rate than patients with 3-4 small adenomas under 10 mm (16.67% vs 5.07%, P<0.001), and small adenomas alone (n=217) were not significantly associated with advanced lesions (odds ratio 0.521, 95% CI 0.257-1.056, P=0.066). The authors conclude that patients with 3-4 small adenomas achieved a very low advanced-lesion rate and should be considered low risk, with a lengthened surveillance interval.
cards.watchOut: A single-programme cohort of intermediate-risk patients: the 5.07% figure is the observed yield at whatever follow-up interval the programme used, not the result of comparing a 3-year against a longer interval head-to-head.
cards.source: Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles E et al. Intermediate-risk patients with three to four small adenomas should be considered low risk for colorectal cancer screening. prospective screening-programme cohort (pérez-cuadrado-robles 2016) cohort of 561 intermediate-risk patients (63.3% men, mean age 59.01 ± 6.16 years) recruited at baseline screening colonoscopy (2006-2011) in a colorectal cancer screening programme, all of whom had index and first follow-up colonoscopy; low- and high-risk patients were excluded. the main outcome was advanced colorectal neoplasia (invasive carcinoma or advanced adenoma) at the first follow-up colonoscopy. advanced lesions were detected in 7.66% of patients overall. having 3-4 adenomas (odds ratio 3.613, 95% ci 1.661-7.859, p=0.001) and adenoma size 10 to under 20 mm (odds ratio 3.374, 95% ci 1.618-7.034, p=0.001) were independent factors associated with advanced neoplasia. but the subgroup with 3-4 adenomas plus at least one 10-20 mm adenoma (n=132) had a much higher advanced-lesion rate than patients with 3-4 small adenomas under 10 mm (16.67% vs 5.07%, p<0.001), and small adenomas alone (n=217) were not significantly associated with advanced lesions (odds ratio 0.521, 95% ci 0.257-1.056, p=0.066). the authors conclude that patients with 3-4 small adenomas achieved a very low advanced-lesion rate and should be considered low risk, with a lengthened surveillance interval. a single-programme cohort of intermediate-risk patients: the 5.07% figure is the observed yield at whatever follow-up interval the programme used, not the result of comparing a 3-year against a longer interval head-to-head. pérez-cuadrado-robles e et al. intermediate-risk patients with three to four small adenomas should be considered low risk for colorectal cancer screening. digestive endoscopy : official journal of the japan gastroenterological endoscopy society. 2016. pmid: 26538148. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adenoma · aged · colonic polyps · colonoscopy · colorectal neoplasms · early detection of cancer · female · follow-up studies · humans · male · middle aged · risk factors

cards.headline: Park 2017: in 1,394 patients with 3 or more adenomas, the 3-4-adenoma group's advanced-neoplasia risk was 2.1% at 3 years and 14.4% at 5 years, versus 3.2% and 23.3% for 5 or more adenomas
cards.summary: Park 2017: in 1,394 patients with 3 or more adenomas, the 3-4-adenoma group's advanced-neoplasia risk was 2.1% at 3 years and 14.4% at 5 years, versus 3.2% and 23.3% for 5 or more adenomas
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre study at 10 university hospitals in Korea of 1,394 patients with 3 or more adenomas at index colonoscopy, comparing an intermediate-risk group (3-4 small adenomas, or at least one adenoma 10 mm or larger) with a high-risk group (5 or more small adenomas, or 3 or more with at least one 10 mm or larger). Mean follow-up was 4.0 years from baseline colonoscopy.
cards.result: Overall, 164 patients (11.8%) developed advanced colorectal neoplasia. The 3-year and 5-year risks of advanced neoplasia were 2.1% (95% CI 2.09-2.11) and 14.4% (95% CI 14.36-14.44) in the intermediate-risk group and 3.2% (95% CI 3.19-3.21) and 23.3% (95% CI 19.15-19.25) in the high-risk group (P=0.01). Having 5 or more adenomas was a significant risk factor (odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.11-2.23, P=0.01). The authors suggest a 3-year interval might be appropriate even for 5-10 adenomas and call for prospective studies of whether more intensive surveillance is needed — which frames the 3-4 group, at still lower risk, as not needing anything shorter.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, and its 'intermediate' group mixes 3-4 small adenomas with patients who had a large adenoma, so the 2.1% 3-year figure is an upper-bound blend for the purely-small-adenoma patient this shelf asks about.
cards.source: Park SK et al. Do surveillance intervals in patients with more than five adenomas at index colonoscopy be shorter than those in patients with three to four adenomas? cards.headline: Hartstein 2020: within 'small', size matters — patients whose adenomas included a 6-9 mm lesion had higher metachronous risk in every count group, including 3-4 adenomas (odds ratio 4.91 in screening examinations)
cards.summary: Hartstein 2020: within 'small', size matters — patients whose adenomas included a 6-9 mm lesion had higher metachronous risk in every count group, including 3-4 adenomas (odds ratio 4.91 in screening examinations)
cards.people: Retrospective review of a colonoscopy database at a single US academic centre: 2,477 qualifying baseline colonoscopies showing tubular adenomas 1-9 mm with low-grade dysplasia and no advanced adenomas, with follow-up colonoscopy at least 200 days later assessed for incident advanced neoplasia (cancer, high-grade dysplasia, adenoma 10 mm or larger, or villous elements).
cards.result: The absolute risk of metachronous advanced neoplasia rose from 3.6% in patients with 1-5 mm adenomas to 6.9% in patients with at least one adenoma of 6-9 mm (P=.001), and was highest (10.4%, P=.006) in patients with 5 or more adenomas of which one was 6-9 mm. Considering only screening colonoscopies, all baseline count groups (1-2, 3-4, and 5 or more adenomas) with adenomas 6-9 mm in size had increased risk of metachronous advanced neoplasia (odds ratios 4.07, 95% CI 1.50-11.04; 4.91, 95% CI 1.44-16.75; and 4.71, 95% CI 1.30-17.05, respectively). The authors conclude post-polypectomy guidelines should stratify by small (6-9 mm) versus diminutive (1-5 mm) size.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and retrospective, with wide confidence intervals in the 3-4 subgroup; it argues for caution at the 6-9 mm end of 'small', not for returning the whole 3-4-small-adenoma group to 3-yearly scopes.
cards.source: Hartstein JD et al. The predictive value of small versus diminutive adenomas for subsequent advanced neoplasia. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2020. PMID: 31525360. cards.headline: Rutter 2020 (BSG guideline): the 3-year surveillance group is defined by five or more polyps, or two or more including an advanced polyp — 3-4 small adenomas alone do not meet the high-risk criteria
cards.summary: Rutter 2020 (BSG guideline): the 3-year surveillance group is defined by five or more polyps, or two or more including an advanced polyp — 3-4 small adenomas alone do not meet the high-risk criteria
cards.people: British Society of Gastroenterology / Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland / Public Health England post-polypectomy surveillance guideline for people aged 18 years and over, developed with the AGREE II framework under the BSG's NICE-accredited process, incorporating national bowel cancer screening.
cards.result: The guideline's high-risk criteria for future colorectal cancer after polypectomy are: two or more premalignant polyps including at least one advanced colorectal polyp (a serrated polyp 10 mm or larger or with any dysplasia, or an adenoma 10 mm or larger or with high-grade dysplasia), or five or more premalignant polyps. This cohort should undergo a one-off surveillance colonoscopy at 3 years. A patient whose only findings are 3-4 adenomas all under 10 mm without high-grade dysplasia meets neither criterion, so the guideline framework does not place them in the 3-year group. The record reports no effect sizes — it is a guideline, carded for its risk criteria, not as outcome evidence.
cards.watchOut: A guideline is a synthesis, not new evidence: it is carded because its explicit high-risk criteria answer where 3-4 small adenomas fall, but the outcome data behind interval choice are the cohort cards above and the registry evidence on pack #5549.

cards.headline: Synthesis: after 3-4 small adenomas, observed advanced-neoplasia risk is low (about 2% at 3 years; 5.07% at first follow-up when all adenomas are under 10 mm) — the traditional 3-year recall is more intensive than the risk requires
cards.summary: Synthesis: after 3-4 small adenomas, observed advanced-neoplasia risk is low (about 2% at 3 years; 5.07% at first follow-up when all adenomas are under 10 mm) — the traditional 3-year recall is more intensive than the risk requires
cards.people: The carded evidence: two cohorts isolating the 3-4-adenoma group (561 intermediate-risk screening patients; 1,394 Korean patients with 3 or more adenomas), one size-stratified cohort (2,477 baseline colonoscopies), and one national guideline's risk criteria. Total participants across the cohorts exceed 4,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; all outcome evidence is observational.
cards.result: Advanced neoplasia followed 3-4 small adenomas in 5.07% of patients at first follow-up when every adenoma was under 10 mm, versus 16.67% when one adenoma was 10-20 mm (Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles 2016); the 3-year cumulative risk in the 3-4 group was 2.1% (Park 2017); risk within the group concentrates in patients with a 6-9 mm adenoma (odds ratio 4.91 for the 3-4 screening subgroup; Hartstein 2020); and the BSG high-risk criteria for 3-year surveillance exclude 3-4 small adenomas alone (Rutter 2020). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, as a partial completion of pack #5549.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial has compared intervals in this exact group; every interval recommendation is an inference from observed risk, and a patient with high-grade dysplasia, a serrated lesion, or a strong family history is outside this shelf's population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pérez-Cuadrado-Robles E et al. Digestive endoscopy : official journal of the Japan Gastroenterological Endoscopy Society. 2016 (PMID: 26538148); Park SK et al. Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology. 2017 (PMID: 27862272); Hartstein JD et al. Gastrointestinal endoscopy. 2020 (PMID: 31525360); Rutter MD et al. Gut. 2020 (PMID: 31776230).

shelves.title: ESAs in lower-risk MDS anaemia (PARTIAL completion of pack #4869's comparator question): epoetin alfa and darbepoetin alfa both beat placebo — transfusion incidence 36.1% versus 59.2% with darbepoetin, erythroid response 31.8% versus 4.4% with epoetin
shelves.question: In adults with myelodysplastic syndrome and anemia, do erythropoiesis-stimulating agents reduce transfusion needs?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anemia · Blood Transfusion · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Epoetin Alfa · Erythropoietin · Female · Hematinics · Hemoglobins · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myelodysplastic Syndromes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for transfusion reduction in lower-risk MDS. Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials point the same way: epoetin alfa raised erythroid response to 31.8% versus 4.4% on placebo (45.9% after blinded review-committee re-assessment) and reduced red-cell transfusions (Fenaux 2018), and darbepoetin alfa lowered transfusion incidence from weeks 5-24 to 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo (Platzbecker 2017) — an absolute difference of 23.1 percentage points. A meta-analysis of 30 studies (1,314 patients) found pooled erythroid response rates of 57.6% for epoetin alfa and 59.4% for darbepoetin alfa in studies using standardised criteria (Moyo 2008). PARTIAL completion: pack #4869 covers epoetin alfa only as the comparator arm against luspatercept in ESA-naive lower-risk MDS (COMMANDS); this shelf answers the prior question that pack presupposes — ESA versus placebo/control for transfusion needs — without re-carding the COMMANDS record. The evidence is in low- or intermediate-1-risk MDS with haemoglobin at or below 10 g/dL and low transfusion burden, and does not extend to higher-risk MDS. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Fenaux 2018: epoetin alfa beat placebo on erythroid response, 31.8% versus 4.4% (45.9% after blinded review), and reduced red-cell transfusions in 130 patients with low-risk MDS
cards.summary: Fenaux 2018: epoetin alfa beat placebo on erythroid response, 31.8% versus 4.4% (45.9% after blinded review), and reduced red-cell transfusions in 130 patients with low-risk MDS
cards.people: 130 patients with IPSS low- or intermediate-1-risk (low-risk) MDS, haemoglobin at or below 10.0 g/dL, and no or moderate red-cell transfusion dependence (at most 4 units per 8 weeks), randomised 2:1 to epoetin alfa 450 IU/kg/week (n = 85) or placebo (n = 45) for 24 weeks, with extension treatment for responders.
cards.result: Erythroid response by IWG-2006 criteria through week 24 was 31.8% on epoetin alfa versus 4.4% on placebo (P < 0.001); after blinded Response Review Committee review the rates were 45.9% versus 4.4% (P < 0.001). Epoetin alfa reduced red-cell transfusions and increased the time to first transfusion compared with placebo — the record states this direction without printing transfusion counts or rates, and no numbers are invented here.
cards.watchOut: The headline outcome is erythroid response, a haemoglobin-based measure; the transfusion benefit is reported in the record as a direction (fewer transfusions, longer time to first transfusion) without the underlying rates, so this card cannot quantify how many transfusions are avoided.
cards.source: Fenaux P et al. A phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled study assessing the efficacy and safety of epoetin-α in anemic patients with low-risk MDS. Leukemia. 2018. PMID: 29895954. cards.headline: Platzbecker 2017: darbepoetin alfa cut transfusion incidence to 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo over weeks 5-24 in 147 patients with lower-risk MDS
cards.summary: Platzbecker 2017: darbepoetin alfa cut transfusion incidence to 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo over weeks 5-24 in 147 patients with lower-risk MDS
cards.people: 147 patients with low/intermediate-1-risk MDS, haemoglobin at or below 10 g/dL, low transfusion burden and serum erythropoietin at or below 500 mU/mL, randomised 2:1 to subcutaneous darbepoetin alfa 500 µg every 3 weeks or placebo for 24 weeks, followed by 48 weeks of open-label darbepoetin alfa; median haemoglobin 9.3 g/dL and median serum erythropoietin 69 mU/mL.
cards.result: Transfusion incidence from weeks 5-24 was 36.1% (35/97) on darbepoetin alfa versus 59.2% (29/49) on placebo (P = 0.008) — an absolute difference of 23.1 percentage points. Erythroid response was 14.7% (11/75 evaluable) versus 0% (0/35 evaluable) (P = 0.016). In the open-label period, dose frequency increased to every 2 weeks in 81% (102/126), with a haematologic improvement-erythroid response rate of 34.7% (34/98); safety was consistent with the earlier phase 2 trial, with no new safety signals in the record.
cards.watchOut: Enrolment required a low transfusion burden and serum erythropoietin at or below 500 mU/mL — the patients most likely to respond. The result does not answer for transfusion-heavy or high-erythropoietin MDS, and the response rate depends heavily on which criteria and evaluable set are used (14.7% here versus 31.8-45.9% in the epoetin trial).
cards.source: Platzbecker U et al. A phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trial of darbepoetin alfa in patients with anemia and lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes. Leukemia. 2017. PMID: 28626220. cards.headline: Moyo 2008: across 30 studies and 1,314 patients, pooled erythroid response was 57.6% with epoetin alfa and 59.4% with darbepoetin alfa in standardised-criteria studies, with no significant difference between the agents
cards.summary: Moyo 2008: across 30 studies and 1,314 patients, pooled erythroid response was 57.6% with epoetin alfa and 59.4% with darbepoetin alfa in standardised-criteria studies, with no significant difference between the agents
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 30 studies from 1990-2006 in MDS patients treated with epoetin alfa (22 studies, 925 patients) or darbepoetin alfa (8 studies, 389 patients) — 1,314 patients in total.
cards.result: The pooled erythroid response rate was significantly higher in epoetin alfa studies using International Working Group criteria (57.6%) than in non-criteria studies (31.6%; P < 0.001). Predictors of higher response included a higher proportion of RA/RARS patients, lower mean baseline serum erythropoietin, and fixed dosing. There was no significant difference in pooled response between epoetin alfa (57.6%) and darbepoetin alfa (59.4%; P = 0.828).
cards.watchOut: Most pooled studies predate the two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials and many were uncontrolled series, so the pooled response rates describe what happens on treatment, not the advantage over placebo — the randomised cards above carry the causal claim on this shelf.
cards.source: Moyo V et al. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in the treatment of anemia in myelodysplastic syndromes: a meta-analysis. Annals of Hematology. 2008. PMID: 18351340. cards.headline: Synthesis: in lower-risk MDS with anaemia, ESAs reduce transfusion needs — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials and a 30-study meta-analysis agree
cards.summary: Synthesis: in lower-risk MDS with anaemia, ESAs reduce transfusion needs — two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials and a 30-study meta-analysis agree
cards.people: The carded evidence: two phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trials (epoetin alfa, 130 patients; darbepoetin alfa, 147 patients) and one meta-analysis of 30 studies (1,314 patients). Total carded participants exceed 1,500, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Darbepoetin alfa lowered transfusion incidence to 36.1% versus 59.2% on placebo (Platzbecker 2017); epoetin alfa raised erythroid response to 31.8-45.9% versus 4.4% and reduced transfusions (Fenaux 2018); pooled response rates were about 58-59% for either agent under standardised criteria (Moyo 2008). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The trials enrolled lower-risk, low-transfusion-burden patients — the slice where ESAs work. Nothing on this shelf answers for higher-risk MDS, heavy transfusion dependence, or high endogenous erythropoietin levels.

shelves.title: Scalp cooling beyond breast cancer (PARTIAL completion of live #1780): cooling reduced substantial alopecia by 43% relative in randomised trials and kept about half of 7,424 registry patients out of a head cover — with success set by regimen, from 95% on paclitaxel to 8% on TAC
shelves.question: For chemotherapy-induced hair loss, does scalp cooling reduce alopecia?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alopecia · Antineoplastic Agents · Female · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Patient Satisfaction · Prognosis · Registries · Scalp · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) beyond breast cancer. The randomised evidence pooled by Rugo 2018 (10 trials, 654 patients with solid tumours) found scalp cooling reduced the relative risk of more-than-50% alopecia by 43% (RR 0.57) — but 66% of those patients had breast cancer, so the randomised base is still breast-dominated. The broader-population evidence is the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry: in 1,411 cooled patients across regimens, 50% needed no head cover at their last session, with success ranging from 8% satisfaction after TAC to 95% after paclitaxel (van den Hurk 2012); in the expanded registry of 7,424 patients, 56% needed no head cover and 53% reported minimal hair loss, with results determined by drug and dose rather than by patient characteristics, and no gender effect in non-gender-specific cancers (Brook 2024). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1780 covers women with breast cancer on taxane/anthracycline regimens (the SCALP trial and its companion cohort, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the broader chemotherapy population, where the honest summary is that cooling works for most regimens but fails for some, and the non-breast evidence is registry-based rather than randomised. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: van den Hurk 2012: in the Dutch registry of 1,411 scalp-cooled patients across chemotherapy regimens, 50% needed no head cover — but results ranged from 8% satisfaction after TAC to 95% after paclitaxel
cards.summary: van den Hurk 2012: in the Dutch registry of 1,411 scalp-cooled patients across chemotherapy regimens, 50% needed no head cover — but results ranged from 8% satisfaction after TAC to 95% after paclitaxel
cards.type: Multicentre registry cohort (Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry, van den Hurk 2012)
cards.people: 1,411 scalp-cooled patients in 28 Dutch hospitals in the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry, treated with currently used chemotherapies for a range of cancers; nurses and patients completed questionnaires on patient, chemotherapy and cooling characteristics.
cards.result: Overall, 50% of the 1,411 scalp-cooled patients did not wear a head cover during their last chemotherapy session. Patients were satisfied with the results in 8% of cases after TAC chemotherapy and up to 95% after paclitaxel treatment. Besides type of chemotherapy, higher dose and shorter infusion time, older age, female gender and non-West-European hair type significantly increased head-cover use; hair length, quantity and chemical manipulation did not influence the result.
cards.watchOut: A registry of patients who chose cooling, with no uncooled comparison group: the 50% head-cover figure shows what cooling achieves in practice by regimen, not how much cooling adds over no cooling for each regimen — that comparison comes from the randomised meta-analysis card.
cards.source: van den Hurk CJ et al. Scalp cooling for hair preservation and associated characteristics in 1411 chemotherapy patients - results of the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry. Acta Oncologica. 2012. PMID: 22304489. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brook 2024: in 7,424 registry patients, 56% needed no head cover and 53% reported minimal hair loss; efficacy was set by drug and dose, not by patient characteristics, and gender did not matter in non-gender-specific cancers
cards.summary: Brook 2024: in 7,424 registry patients, 56% needed no head cover and 53% reported minimal hair loss; efficacy was set by drug and dose, not by patient characteristics, and gender did not matter in non-gender-specific cancers
cards.type: Multicentre registry cohort (Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry, Brook 2024)
cards.people: 7,424 scalp-cooled patients in 68 Dutch hospitals in the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry, across multiple chemotherapy regimens and cancer types; outcomes were head-cover use and WHO alopecia score (0 = no hair loss to 3 = total alopecia) reported at the start of the final cooling session (WHO score available for 7,183).
cards.result: Over half of patients (n = 4,191, 56%) did not wear a head cover, and 53% (3,784/7,183) reported minimal hair loss (WHO score 0/1) at the start of their final treatment. Outcomes were drug- and dose-dependent. No patient characteristic or lifestyle factor was a generic determinant of success, and for non-gender-specific cancers gender played no statistically significant role in head-cover use or WHO score.
cards.watchOut: Same registry, later and larger cut — the two registry cards are one data source at two time points, not two independent confirmations, and neither has an uncooled control arm.
cards.source: Brook TS et al. Results of the Dutch scalp cooling registry in 7424 patients: analysis of determinants for scalp cooling efficacy. The Oncologist. 2024. PMID: 38869252. cards.headline: Rugo 2018: pooling 10 randomised trials in 654 patients with solid tumours, scalp cooling reduced the relative risk of substantial alopecia by 43% (RR 0.57) — but two-thirds of the patients had breast cancer
cards.summary: Rugo 2018: pooling 10 randomised trials in 654 patients with solid tumours, scalp cooling reduced the relative risk of substantial alopecia by 43% (RR 0.57) — but two-thirds of the patients had breast cancer
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Rugo 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of scalp cooling during chemotherapy, searched to February 2017: 10 studies, 654 patients, most with breast cancer (432 patients, 66%), mainly receiving anthracyclines.
cards.result: For the binary outcome of under-50% versus over-50% alopecia, scalp cooling reduced the relative risk of alopecia by 43% (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.45-0.72; I² = 11%; P < .00001). For ordinal alopecia (scale 0-3), cooling significantly reduced alopecia (mean difference -0.80, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.41; I² = 0%). The quality of the evidence was graded moderate. The authors conclude the analysis supports scalp cooling to prevent alopecia in patients with solid tumours undergoing chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: The pooled relative effect is real but its population is two-thirds breast cancer on anthracyclines: applying RR 0.57 to a man on a non-breast regimen is an extrapolation the registry cards, not this meta-analysis, have to carry.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Scalp Hypothermia for Preventing Alopecia During Chemotherapy. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Clinical Breast Cancer. 2018. PMID: 28939291. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: scalp cooling reduces alopecia across the broader chemotherapy population, with success set mainly by regimen — randomised proof is still breast-heavy, registry data carry the rest
cards.summary: Synthesis: scalp cooling reduces alopecia across the broader chemotherapy population, with success set mainly by regimen — randomised proof is still breast-heavy, registry data carry the rest
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials (654 patients, 66% breast cancer) and the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry at two time points (1,411 and 7,424 cooled patients across regimens and cancer types). Total carded participants exceed 8,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cooling reduced the relative risk of substantial alopecia by 43% in randomised trials (RR 0.57; Rugo 2018). In unselected registry practice, about half to 56% of cooled patients needed no head cover, with regimen-dependent extremes from 8% satisfaction (TAC) to 95% (paclitaxel) (van den Hurk 2012; Brook 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Regimen is destiny on this shelf: a patient facing TAC-type chemotherapy should not be quoted the pooled average, and a patient on paclitaxel should not be quoted it either — in the opposite direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of van den Hurk CJ et al. Acta Oncologica. 2012 (PMID: 22304489); Brook TS et al. The Oncologist. 2024 (PMID: 38869252); Rugo HS et al. Clinical Breast Cancer. 2018 (PMID: 28939291).

shelves.title: Exercise during chemotherapy in breast cancer (PARTIAL completion of live #1793's colon-cancer question): supervised exercise reduced physical fatigue in PACES, and pooled randomised trials give a fatigue SMD of -0.38 during chemotherapy
shelves.question: Does exercise during chemotherapy reduce treatment-related fatigue in breast cancer?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Drug Administration Schedule · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Fatigue · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Status · Humans · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Muscle Strength · Nausea · Pain · Physical Fitness · Quality of Life · Self Report · Trastuzumab · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). In the PACES randomised trial of 230 women on adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, the supervised moderate-to-high-intensity programme (OnTrack) significantly reduced physical fatigue versus usual care (P < .001), and both exercise programmes preserved cardiorespiratory fitness and physical functioning (van Waart 2015). In the OptiTrain randomised trial (240 women), a mechanistic analysis of 86 participants found the resistance-plus-interval programme blunted the chemotherapy-driven rise in interleukin-6, and that change mediated about 32% of the exercise effect on general fatigue and about 28% on physical fatigue (Hiensch 2021). A meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials (1,793 participants) found exercise reduced fatigue overall (SMD -0.46), with the chemotherapy-period subgroup at SMD -0.38 and supervised combined resistance-plus-aerobic training the most effective format (SMD -1.13) (Medeiros Torres 2022). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1793 covers exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy for fatigue in colon cancer (the PACES pilot report in colon patients); this shelf covers breast cancer, the population in which the full PACES and OptiTrain trials were run. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: van Waart 2015 (PACES): in 230 women on adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, supervised moderate-to-high-intensity exercise significantly reduced physical fatigue versus usual care, and fewer patients needed chemotherapy dose adjustments
cards.summary: van Waart 2015 (PACES): in 230 women on adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, supervised moderate-to-high-intensity exercise significantly reduced physical fatigue versus usual care, and fewer patients needed chemotherapy dose adjustments
cards.people: 230 patients scheduled for adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer, randomised to a low-intensity home-based physical activity programme (Onco-Move), a moderate-to-high-intensity supervised combined resistance and aerobic programme (OnTrack), or usual care; outcomes assessed before randomisation, at the end of chemotherapy, and at 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: Onco-Move and OnTrack both produced less decline in cardiorespiratory fitness (P < .001), better physical functioning (P ≤ .001), less nausea and vomiting and less pain than usual care. OnTrack additionally gave better muscle strength (P = .002) and less physical fatigue (P < .001). A smaller percentage of OnTrack participants required chemotherapy dose adjustments (P = .002), and both intervention groups returned to work earlier and for more hours per week. By the 6-month follow-up most outcomes had returned to baseline levels in all three groups. The record reports fatigue as P values without printing the fatigue scale scores, and no scores are invented here.
cards.watchOut: The fatigue benefit was clearest for the supervised higher-intensity programme and for physical fatigue specifically; the home-based low-intensity programme's clearest wins were fitness and functioning, and most group differences had faded by 6 months after chemotherapy ended.
cards.source: van Waart H et al. Effect of Low-Intensity Physical Activity and Moderate- to High-Intensity Physical Exercise During Adjuvant Chemotherapy on Physical Fitness, Fatigue, and Chemotherapy Completion Rates: Results of the PACES Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25918291. Registry ID: NTR2159. cards.headline: Hiensch 2021 (OptiTrain): in a mechanistic analysis of 86 women from a 240-woman randomised trial, resistance-plus-interval training blunted the rise in interleukin-6, which mediated about a third of its fatigue benefit
cards.summary: Hiensch 2021 (OptiTrain): in a mechanistic analysis of 86 women from a 240-woman randomised trial, resistance-plus-interval training blunted the rise in interleukin-6, which mediated about a third of its fatigue benefit
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, mechanistic mediation analysis (OptiTrain, Hiensch 2021)
cards.people: The OptiTrain randomised trial assigned 240 women scheduled for chemotherapy for breast cancer to 16 weeks of resistance plus high-intensity interval training (RT-HIIT), moderate aerobic plus interval training (AT-HIIT), or usual care. This mechanistic analysis included participants with over 60% attendance plus a random selection of controls: 30 RT-HIIT, 27 AT-HIIT, 29 usual care (86 analysed; subgroup N on the face).
cards.result: Chemotherapy increased inflammation overall. The increases in interleukin-6 (-0.47, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.07) and CD8a (-0.28, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.004) were significantly less pronounced after RT-HIIT than usual care. Changes in IL-6 and CD8a significantly mediated the exercise effects on general fatigue (by 32.0% and 31.2%) and physical fatigue (by 27.7% and 26.4%). cards.headline: Medeiros Torres 2022: across 20 randomised trials and 1,793 women, exercise during adjuvant treatment reduced fatigue (SMD -0.46), with the during-chemotherapy subgroup at SMD -0.38 and supervised combined resistance-plus-aerobic training most effective
cards.summary: Medeiros Torres 2022: across 20 randomised trials and 1,793 women, exercise during adjuvant treatment reduced fatigue (SMD -0.46), with the during-chemotherapy subgroup at SMD -0.38 and supervised combined resistance-plus-aerobic training most effective
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Medeiros Torres 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials of physical exercise in women over 18 with stage I-IV breast cancer during adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, with fatigue measured on validated questionnaires: 20 trials, 1,793 participants.
cards.result: Exercise was statistically effective in reducing fatigue (SMD -0.46, 95% CI -0.66 to -0.27). Subgroup analysis suggested supervised combined resistance plus aerobic training was the most effective format (SMD -1.13, 95% CI -2.09 to -0.17); supervised resistance training alone (SMD -0.30, 95% CI -0.46 to -0.15) beat supervised aerobic training or mind-body techniques. During chemotherapy specifically, intervention groups showed a significant fatigue reduction (SMD -0.38, 95% CI -0.55 to -0.20).
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes chemotherapy-period and radiotherapy-period trials; the chemotherapy-only subgroup (SMD -0.38) is the figure that answers this shelf's question, and the largest subgroup estimate (combined training, SMD -1.13) rests on few trials with a wide interval.

shelves.title: Sunscreen and melanoma specifically (PARTIAL completion of live #221): the observational literature splits by study design
shelves.question: Does daily sunscreen use prevent melanoma in adults at average risk?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Cross-Sectional Studies · Geography, Medical · Humans · Melanoma · Observational Studies as Topic · Odds Ratio · Skin Neoplasms · Sunscreening Agents
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the carded observational literature disagrees with itself by study design: hospital-based case-control studies and one large cohort comparison of high- versus low-SPF use suggest protection, while population-based case-control studies show no association and cohort studies pooled in Rueegg 2019 show a positive association (hazard ratio 1.27) — the signature of confounding by indication, because sunscreen users are the people who burn, holiday in the sun and use tanning devices. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: the only randomised daily-use evidence (the Nambour trial and its melanoma follow-up) is homed on live shelf #221 and is NOT re-carded here; this shelf cards the wider sunscreen–melanoma literature for average-risk adults, all of it observational and therefore capped at POSSIBLE-grade reasoning. On this evidence, a protective effect of sunscreen on melanoma is unproven in average-risk adults — and so is any harmful effect.

cards.headline: Silva 2018 meta-analysis: sunscreen use was not associated with melanoma (pooled odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.92–1.33) across 25 studies and 9,813 cases
cards.summary: Silva 2018 meta-analysis: sunscreen use was not associated with melanoma (pooled odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.92–1.33) across 25 studies and 9,813 cases
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Silva 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 observational studies and one controlled trial (313,717 participants, 10,670 skin-cancer cases); the melanoma analysis pooled 25 studies with 9,813 melanoma cases, comparing sunscreen users with non-users in general populations.
cards.result: The overall meta-analysis found no significant association between sunscreen use and skin cancer (odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.91–1.28; I² = 89.4%); for melanoma specifically the pooled odds ratio was 1.10 (95% CI 0.92–1.33) — no association — and for non-melanoma skin cancer 0.99 (95% CI 0.62–1.57). A cumulative analysis showed a strong positive association before the 1980s (cumulative odds ratio 2.35) that weakened decade by decade and was no longer significant from the early 1990s. The authors conclude the review does not confirm the expected protective benefit of sunscreen against skin cancer in the general population.
cards.watchOut: Observational pooling with very high heterogeneity (I² = 89.4%): 'sunscreen use' ranges from ever-use to regular use across studies, and users differ from non-users in sun exposure and phenotype — the null pooled estimate cannot distinguish 'sunscreen does nothing' from 'sunscreen offsets the extra sun its users get'.
cards.source: Silva ESD et al. Use of sunscreen and risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European journal of dermatology : EJD. 2018. PMID: 29620003. cards.headline: Rueegg 2019: the sunscreen–melanoma association flips sign by study design — protective in hospital case-control studies (OR 0.57), null in population case-control studies (OR 1.17), positive in cohorts (HR 1.27)
cards.summary: Rueegg 2019: the sunscreen–melanoma association flips sign by study design — protective in hospital case-control studies (OR 0.57), null in population case-control studies (OR 1.17), positive in cohorts (HR 1.27)
cards.people: Systematic review and stratified meta-analysis of 28 studies published 1979–2018 with 21,069 melanoma cases: 23 case-control studies, 1 ecological study, 3 cohort studies and 1 randomised controlled trial, examining ever- versus never-use of sunscreen.
cards.result: Ever-use of sunscreen was inversely associated with melanoma in hospital-based case-control studies (adjusted odds ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.37–0.87) and the ecological study (rate ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35–0.66), not associated in population-based case-control studies (odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.90–1.51), and positively associated in the cohort studies (hazard ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.07–1.51); adjustment for sun exposure, sunburns and phenotype systematically moved estimates toward protection. The authors conclude the observational evidence is weak and heterogeneous, consistent with confounding by indication; the single randomised trial in the set (the Nambour trial, homed on live shelf #221) showed a protective point estimate (hazard ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.24–1.01).
cards.watchOut: The randomised-trial hazard ratio quoted inside this review is the Nambour trial already homed on live shelf #221 — it is reported here as part of this review's own results and is not a new card of that trial; the observational strata are the new evidence on this shelf, and they conflict.
