cards.headline: Ghiasvand 2016 (Norwegian Women and Cancer cohort): SPF ≥15 use was associated with lower melanoma risk than SPF <15 use (hazard ratio 0.67) — in women who also reported more sunburns and sun holidays
cards.summary: Ghiasvand 2016 (Norwegian Women and Cancer cohort): SPF ≥15 use was associated with lower melanoma risk than SPF <15 use (hazard ratio 0.67) — in women who also reported more sunburns and sun holidays
cards.people: Prospective population-based cohort of 143,844 Norwegian women aged 40–75 at inclusion, with 1,532,247 person-years of follow-up and 722 melanoma cases; sunscreen use was categorised as never, SPF <15, or SPF ≥15, analysed with multivariable Cox regression.
cards.result: Use of SPF ≥15 sunscreen was associated with significantly decreased melanoma risk compared with SPF <15 use (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.53–0.83), and the authors estimated that general use of SPF ≥15 sunscreens could reduce melanoma incidence in this age group by 18% (population attributable fraction, 95% CI 4%–30%). Sunscreen users, however, reported significantly more sunburns and sunbathing vacations and were more likely to use indoor tanning devices than non-users.
cards.watchOut: Observational: the comparison is high-SPF versus low-SPF use (not use versus non-use), in women only, and the exposure groups differ sharply in sun behaviour — residual confounding by indication is the central threat, as the Rueegg card shows the same literature producing a positive association in other cohorts.
cards.source: Ghiasvand R et al. Sunscreen Use and Subsequent Melanoma Risk: A Population-Based Cohort Study. cards.headline: Synthesis: for melanoma specifically, the non-randomised evidence splits by design — no observational consensus that sunscreen prevents melanoma in average-risk adults
cards.summary: Synthesis: for melanoma specifically, the non-randomised evidence splits by design — no observational consensus that sunscreen prevents melanoma in average-risk adults
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews/meta-analyses of the observational literature (Silva 2018, 25 melanoma studies; Rueegg 2019, 28 studies, 21,069 cases) and one large prospective cohort (Ghiasvand 2016, 143,844 women). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled ever-use of sunscreen was not associated with melanoma in Silva 2018 (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.92–1.33); Rueegg 2019 found the estimate protective, null or positive depending on study design (odds ratio 0.57 hospital case-control; 1.17 population case-control; hazard ratio 1.27 cohorts); and the Norwegian cohort found high-SPF use associated with lower risk than low-SPF use (hazard ratio 0.67). The randomised daily-use evidence is homed on live shelf #221 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: observational designs disagree, so sunscreen's effect on melanoma in average-risk adults is unproven outside the single homed trial.
cards.watchOut: None of the carded studies randomised daily sunscreen use; anyone quoting this shelf as 'sunscreen does not prevent melanoma' overstates it — the accurate statement is that the observational record is split and confounded, and the one randomised test lives on #221.

shelves.title: Total body skin examination screening and melanoma deaths in average-risk adults (PARTIAL completion of live #3389): no mortality benefit shown
shelves.question: In adults at average risk, does screening for skin cancer with total body examination reduce melanoma deaths?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Humans · Early Detection of Cancer · Mass Screening · Melanoma · Physical Examination · Skin Neoplasms
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no study has shown that screening average-risk adults with a total body (whole-body/visual) skin examination reduces melanoma deaths. There are no randomised trials; the direct programme evidence is nonrandomised and, in the 2023 USPSTF evidence report, suggested no melanoma mortality benefit at population level over 4–10 years. The best supporting signal is a surrogate: in the Queensland case-control study, a whole-body examination in the prior 3 years was associated with fewer thick melanomas (odds ratio 0.86) — alongside 38% more thin melanomas, the overdiagnosis signature. All carded evidence is observational, which caps the stamp. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3389 homes the German population-screening mortality story (the Schleswig-Holstein pilot and the nationwide programme); this shelf asks the narrower question — the clinician total body examination itself, in average-risk asymptomatic adults — and does not re-card the German programme studies.

cards.headline: Henrikson 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): nonrandomised analyses of two population screening programmes suggested no melanoma mortality benefit from visual skin examination screening over 4–10 years
cards.summary: Henrikson 2023 (USPSTF evidence report): nonrandomised analyses of two population screening programmes suggested no melanoma mortality benefit from visual skin examination screening over 4–10 years
cards.type: Systematic review / evidence report for the USPSTF (Henrikson 2023)
cards.people: Updated systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force: 20 studies in 29 articles (N = 6,053,411) in asymptomatic populations aged 15 or older; the direct screening-effectiveness evidence came from 3 nonrandomized analyses of 2 population-based skin cancer screening programmes in Germany (n = 1,791,615).
cards.result: The nonrandomized programme analyses suggested no melanoma mortality benefit at the population level over 4 to 10 years of follow-up. Compared with usual care, routine clinician skin examination was not associated with increased detection of skin cancer or precursor lesions (5 studies) or with stage at melanoma detection (3 studies), and evidence on lesion thickness at detection was inconsistent (6 studies, n = 2,935,513). Nine studies (n = 1,326,051) did confirm that more advanced stage at detection carries higher melanoma and all-cause mortality — the rationale for screening — but the examination itself was not shown to shift stage or deaths. Harms in 2 studies (n = 232) showed little to no persistent cosmetic or psychosocial harm.
cards.watchOut: The underlying programme analyses are the German screening experience also covered at programme level on live shelf #3389 — this card takes the review's examination-level conclusions (no mortality benefit, no stage shift), not a re-card of the German studies themselves.

cards.headline: Aitken 2010 (Queensland case-control): whole-body skin examination in the prior 3 years was associated with 14% lower odds of thick melanoma (OR 0.86) — and 38% higher odds of thin melanoma (OR 1.38)
cards.summary: Aitken 2010 (Queensland case-control): whole-body skin examination in the prior 3 years was associated with 14% lower odds of thick melanoma (OR 0.86) — and 38% higher odds of thin melanoma (OR 1.38)
cards.people: Population-based case-control study of Queensland residents aged 20–75 with a histologically confirmed first primary invasive cutaneous melanoma diagnosed 2000–2003: 3,762 cases (78.0% of eligibles) and 3,824 controls, interviewed about clinical whole-body skin examination in the three years before diagnosis (cases) or an equivalent period (controls).
cards.result: Whole-body clinical skin examination in the prior three years was associated with a 14% lower risk (relative measure) of being diagnosed with a thick melanoma (> 0.75 mm) (odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.98), with a gradient by thickness: odds ratio 0.93 for 0.76–1.49 mm, 0.83 for 1.50–2.99 mm, and 0.60 (95% CI 0.43–0.83) for melanomas ≥ 3 mm. Screening was simultaneously associated with a 38% higher risk of being diagnosed with a thin invasive melanoma (≤ 0.75 mm) (odds ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.22–1.56). The authors argue that because survival tracks thickness, screening would be expected to reduce mortality — an inference, not a measured mortality outcome.
cards.watchOut: Observational and self-reported examination history: people who seek skin checks differ from those who do not, thickness is a surrogate for death, and the 38% excess of thin melanomas is the pattern expected if examination also detects lesions that would never have killed (overdiagnosis).
cards.source: Aitken JF et al. Clinical whole-body skin examination reduces the incidence of thick melanomas. International journal of cancer. 2010. PMID: 19609948. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wernli 2016 (earlier USPSTF evidence report): no randomised trials of skin screening existed; a physician skin examination's sensitivity for melanoma was 40.2% in primary care and 49.0% with dermatologists
cards.summary: Wernli 2016 (earlier USPSTF evidence report): no randomised trials of skin screening existed; a physician skin examination's sensitivity for melanoma was 40.2% in primary care and 49.0% with dermatologists
cards.type: Systematic review / evidence report for the USPSTF (Wernli 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review for the US Preventive Services Task Force of clinical skin cancer screening among asymptomatic adults aged 15 or older at general (average) risk, searching studies from 1995 to 2015 with surveillance to February 2016.
cards.result: No randomized clinical trials of screening were identified, and evidence linking screening to mortality was limited to a single German ecologic study (the pilot programme homed on live shelf #3389). Diagnostic performance was modest: sensitivity to detect melanoma was 40.2% with specificity 86.1% for primary care physicians (n = 16,383) and sensitivity 49.0% with specificity 97.6% for dermatologists (n = 7,436). The number of excisions needed to detect one skin cancer from clinical visual examination ranged from 22 (women 65 or older) to 41 (women aged 20–34). Eight cohort studies (n = 236,485) confirmed thicker tumours and late stage predict higher melanoma mortality.
cards.watchOut: This 2016 review is superseded in scope by Henrikson 2023 on the first card; it is carded here for the examination's diagnostic accuracy and excision burden in average-risk adults, which the update does not re-report — and its one mortality citation is the German pilot already homed on #3389.
cards.source: Wernli KJ et al. Screening for Skin Cancer in Adults: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27458949. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: total body examination screening has never been shown to reduce melanoma deaths in average-risk adults — MAYBE (weak evidence), on observational data with a surrogate-only benefit signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: total body examination screening has never been shown to reduce melanoma deaths in average-risk adults — MAYBE (weak evidence), on observational data with a surrogate-only benefit signal
cards.people: The carded evidence: two USPSTF evidence reports (Wernli 2016; Henrikson 2023, 20 studies, N = 6,053,411) and one population-based case-control study of whole-body examination (Aitken 2010; 3,762 cases, 3,824 controls). Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: No randomised trial of screening exists. Nonrandomised programme analyses suggested no melanoma mortality benefit over 4–10 years (Henrikson 2023); the examination misses roughly half of melanomas in diagnostic-accuracy studies (sensitivity 40.2–49.0%) and requires 22–41 excisions per cancer found (Wernli 2016); and the strongest pro-screening signal is fewer thick melanomas after whole-body examination (odds ratio 0.86), offset by more thin melanomas (odds ratio 1.38) (Aitken 2010). Programme-level mortality history is homed on live shelf #3389 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a mortality benefit of total body examination screening in average-risk adults is unproven.
cards.watchOut: 'Unproven' is not 'disproven': no trial has tested the question, follow-up in programme analyses may be short for mortality, and higher-risk adults (many naevi, family history, prior skin cancer) are outside this shelf's average-risk question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Henrikson NB et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37071090); Aitken JF et al. International journal of cancer. 2010 (PMID: 19609948); Wernli KJ et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27458949).

shelves.title: When should the PSA discussion start? (PARTIAL completion of live #212): the mortality trials screened men from 50, proved benefit at 55–69, and a PSA at 60 sorts who benefits
shelves.question: In men, at what age should PSA screening be discussed for prostate cancer detection?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Europe · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Prostatic Neoplasms
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #212 already answers whether PSA screening reduces prostate-cancer deaths (ERSPC 2009 and PLCO, homed there and not re-carded here; the developer's verdict there is MAYBE (weak evidence)). This shelf asks the question #212 does not: at what age should the discussion happen? The trials' own designs bracket the answer. ERSPC pre-specified its core age group as 55–69 and showed its mortality benefit there (rate ratio 0.79 at 13 years). The Göteborg trial began inviting men at 50–64 and, screening to about age 69, halved prostate-cancer mortality (rate ratio 0.56) — evidence that a programme starting at 50 sits inside the tested range. Two observational analyses then refine the discussion by PSA level rather than birthday alone: a single PSA at 60 separated men who benefit from continued screening (≥2 ng/mL; 23 men screened per death averted) from those who do not (<1 ng/mL, where the authors recommend no further screening), and PSA measured at 45–55 identified the small high-risk group (top decile) in whom 44% of later prostate-cancer deaths occurred, supporting a baseline test in the late 40s with long intervals for the low-risk majority. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: discuss from about age 50, expect benefit mainly at 55–69, and let the age-60 PSA steer continuation — the age-specific evidence beyond the two big trials is observational and is labelled as such on its cards.

cards.headline: ERSPC at 13 years: the trial pre-specified ages 55–69 as its core group — and that is where its mortality benefit (rate ratio 0.79) was demonstrated
cards.summary: ERSPC at 13 years: the trial pre-specified ages 55–69 as its core group — and that is where its mortality benefit (rate ratio 0.79) was demonstrated
cards.people: Men aged 50–74 identified from population registries in eight European countries and randomised to PSA screening or no intervention; the trial's predefined core age group for the primary mortality analysis was 55–69 years. By 13 years of follow-up, 7,408 prostate cancers had been diagnosed in the intervention group and 6,107 in the control group.
cards.result: In the core age group, the rate ratio of prostate-cancer mortality was 0.85 after 9 years, 0.78 after 11 years and 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.91) at 13 years — a 21% relative reduction — equivalent to one prostate-cancer death averted per 781 men invited (95% CI 490–1929) or per 27 additional cancers detected. After adjustment for non-participation, the rate ratio in men actually screened was 0.73 (95% CI 0.61–0.88).
cards.watchOut: ERSPC randomised men from age 50, but its headline mortality analysis is the 55–69 core group; the trial does not by itself prove benefit from starting at 50 or continuing past 69 — those edges come from the other cards. This 13-year report is a later follow-up of the trial whose 9-year report is homed on live shelf #212; it is carded here for its age-group analysis, not to re-argue the mortality verdict.
cards.source: Schröder FH et al. Screening and prostate cancer mortality: results of the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC) at 13 years of follow-up. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 25108889. Registry ID: ISRCTN49127736. MeSH: Aged · Europe · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Prostatic Neoplasms

cards.headline: Göteborg 2010: inviting men from age 50 (screening to about 69) halved prostate-cancer mortality over 14 years — rate ratio 0.56, with 293 men invited per death prevented
cards.summary: Göteborg 2010: inviting men from age 50 (screening to about 69) halved prostate-cancer mortality over 14 years — rate ratio 0.56, with 293 men invited per death prevented
cards.people: 20,000 men born 1930–1944 (aged 50–64 at randomisation in December 1994) sampled from the Göteborg population register, randomised to invitation for PSA testing every 2 years up to an upper age limit of about 69 (n = 10,000) or no invitation (n = 10,000); 76% of the screening group attended at least once.
cards.result: Over a median follow-up of 14 years, prostate cancer was diagnosed in 12.7% of the screening group versus 8.2% of controls (hazard ratio 1.64). Prostate-cancer mortality was 0.50% versus 0.90% — an absolute reduction of 0.40% (95% CI 0.17–0.64) and a rate ratio of 0.56 (95% CI 0.39–0.82; p=0.002); among attendees the rate ratio was 0.44 (95% CI 0.28–0.68). Overall, 293 men (95% CI 177–799) needed to be invited and 12 diagnosed to prevent one prostate-cancer death.
cards.watchOut: Göteborg is one ERSPC centre reported separately, and its men entered at 50–64 as a single cohort — it shows a programme beginning at 50 can work, not that age 50 is provably a better start than 55.
cards.source: Hugosson J et al. Mortality results from the Göteborg randomised population-based prostate-cancer screening trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20598634. Registry ID: ISRCTN54449243. cards.headline: Carlsson 2014: a PSA at age 60 sorts the discussion — at ≥2 ng/mL screening prevented one death per 23 men screened; below 1 ng/mL the authors recommend no further screening
cards.summary: Carlsson 2014: a PSA at age 60 sorts the discussion — at ≥2 ng/mL screening prevented one death per 23 men screened; below 1 ng/mL the authors recommend no further screening
cards.people: Population-based cohort combining 1,756 men aged 57.5–62.5 in the screening arm of the Göteborg randomised trial with 1,162 unscreened men from the Malmö Preventive Project whose PSA at about age 60 was measured retrospectively in stored blood; 71.7% of men with a baseline level had PSA below 2 ng/mL.
cards.result: Benefit and harm at age 60 split sharply by PSA level. In men with PSA <2 ng/mL, screening raised incidence by 767 cases per 10,000 without decreasing prostate-cancer mortality. In men with PSA ≥2 ng/mL, the mortality reduction was large — only 23 men needed screening and 6 diagnosis to avoid one prostate-cancer death by 15 years. The authors conclude: no further screening for men with PSA <1 ng/mL at age 60; continuing to screen men with PSA above 2 ng/mL is beneficial; and a level of 1–2 ng/mL is an individual decision to be based on a discussion between patient and doctor.
cards.watchOut: Observational: the screened and unscreened cohorts come from different Swedish studies and eras, so the age-60 thresholds are well-supported guidance, not randomised proof.
cards.source: Carlsson S et al. Influence of blood prostate specific antigen levels at age 60 on benefits and harms of prostate cancer screening: population based cohort study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2014. PMID: 24682399. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vickers 2013: a PSA in the late 40s already flags the high-risk few — the top tenth at age 45–49 (≥1.6 µg/L) accounted for 44% of later prostate-cancer deaths
cards.summary: Vickers 2013: a PSA in the late 40s already flags the high-risk few — the top tenth at age 45–49 (≥1.6 µg/L) accounted for 44% of later prostate-cancer deaths
cards.people: Case-control study nested in the Malmö Preventive Project: 21,277 Swedish men aged 27–52 who provided blood at baseline in 1974–84 in a population where PSA testing remained extremely rare, followed for a median 27 years for prostate-cancer metastasis and death, with matched controls.
cards.result: Risk of death from prostate cancer tracked the early PSA: 44% (95% CI 34–53%) of deaths occurred in men whose PSA at age 45–49 was in the highest tenth of the distribution (≥1.6 µg/L), with a similar proportion (44%, 95% CI 32–56%) for the highest tenth at age 51–55 (≥2.4 µg/L). Below the median PSA (0.68 µg/L at 45–49; 0.85 µg/L at 51–55), the 15-year risk of metastasis remained low (0.09% and 0.28%), although a 25–30-year risk could not be ruled out. The authors suggest three lifetime PSA tests — mid-to-late 40s, early 50s, and age 60 — are probably sufficient for at least half of men.
cards.watchOut: Observational and from an unscreened era: it shows a late-40s PSA predicts risk decades ahead, which supports using it to plan the discussion — it does not show that screening from age 45 saves lives.
cards.source: Vickers AJ et al. Strategy for detection of prostate cancer based on relation between prostate specific antigen at age 40-55 and long term risk of metastasis: case-control study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013. PMID: 23596126. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the tested window is roughly 50–69 — start the discussion at about 50, and let PSA level, especially at 60, steer what happens next
cards.summary: Synthesis: the tested window is roughly 50–69 — start the discussion at about 50, and let PSA level, especially at 60, steer what happens next
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised screening trials reporting by age (the ERSPC 13-year report; Göteborg, 20,000 men) and two observational analyses of PSA level by age (Carlsson 2014; Vickers 2013). Participant numbers are large throughout, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: The tested window for PSA screening is roughly 50–69: Göteborg began inviting at 50 and halved prostate-cancer mortality, while ERSPC's pre-specified core group of 55–69 carries its demonstrated benefit (rate ratio 0.79 at 13 years). Within that window, PSA level refines the plan — a baseline in the late 40s identifies the small group accounting for nearly half of later prostate-cancer deaths (Vickers), and the age-60 PSA separates men who gain greatly from continued screening (≥2 ng/mL) from those the authors say need no further screening (<1 ng/mL) (Carlsson). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: open the discussion at about age 50, individualise it with a baseline PSA, and re-decide at 60 by level. Whether screening itself reduces mortality is homed on live shelf #212 and is not re-argued here.
cards.watchOut: No trial randomised men to different starting ages; the age answer is assembled from trial entry ages, a pre-specified core age group, and observational PSA-by-age analyses — strong enough to time a discussion, not to mandate a birthday.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schröder FH et al. Lancet (London, England). 2014 (PMID: 25108889); Hugosson J et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 20598634); Carlsson S et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2014 (PMID: 24682399); Vickers AJ et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2013 (PMID: 23596126).

shelves.title: Anamorelin in cancer cachexia: lean body mass rises in every trial — handgrip strength and walking do not (built on the non-ROMANA reports; the ROMANA programme is homed on live #12)
shelves.question: In adults with cancer cachexia, does anamorelin increase lean body mass versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anabolic Agents · Analysis of Variance · Appetite Stimulants · Body Composition · Cachexia · Clinical Trials, Phase II as Topic · Female · Humans · Hydrazines · Least-Squares Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength · Neoplasms · Oligopeptides · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United States · Weight Gain · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face, with two flags stated plainly. FLAG 1 (one-home / precedent call): the flagship ROMANA 1 and ROMANA 2 phase 3 trials (Temel 2016) are already carded with their figures on live shelf #12, the library's cancer-cachexia deposit shelf, so under the one-home rule their PMID is NOT carded here and none of their numbers are re-used on this shelf's cards. This dedicated anamorelin shelf is built instead on the three independent, gate-free trial reports — the pooled phase 2 analysis (Garcia 2015), the Japanese phase 2 trial (Takayama 2016) and the Japanese phase 3 trial ONO-7643-04 (Katakami 2018) — which answer the same question in the same direction. FLAG 2 (population): every carded trial is in non-small-cell lung cancer cachexia, so the shelf's evidence is narrower than its question's wording. The pattern is unusually consistent: lean body mass rose by about 1.4–2.1 kg relative to placebo over 12 weeks in all three reports, appetite and weight improved, and the functional co-endpoints — handgrip strength in all three, 6-minute walk in Katakami — did not improve in any (function made no difference). That mass-without-function pattern is also what live #12's ROMANA card shows. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: anamorelin increases lean body mass in cancer (NSCLC) cachexia; whether added mass that does not strengthen grip or walking helps patients is unproven.

cards.headline: Garcia 2015: pooled analysis of two phase 2 trials — anamorelin increased lean body mass by 1.89 kg while placebo lost 0.20 kg over 12 weeks (difference 2.09 kg)
cards.summary: Garcia 2015: pooled analysis of two phase 2 trials — anamorelin increased lean body mass by 1.89 kg while placebo lost 0.20 kg over 12 weeks (difference 2.09 kg)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two phase 2 randomised trials (Garcia 2015)
cards.people: A priori pooled analysis of two completed phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials in patients with advanced or incurable cancer and weight loss of 5% or more (mixed tumour types); 82 patients were enrolled (44 anamorelin hydrochloride 50 mg once daily, 38 placebo) and 74 were eligible for the efficacy analysis of lean body mass by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Lean body mass increased on anamorelin by a least-squares mean of 1.89 kg (95% CI 0.84–2.95) and fell on placebo by 0.20 kg (95% CI −1.23 to 0.83), a difference of 2.09 kg (95% CI 0.94–3.25, P = 0.0006). Adverse events occurred in 42 of 44 anamorelin patients (95%) and 33 of 38 placebo patients (87%); the most common grade 3–4 events on anamorelin were fatigue, asthenia, atrial fibrillation and dyspnoea (two patients, 5%, each). The authors conclude anamorelin had a favourable response profile supporting further investigation.
cards.watchOut: Small phase 2 numbers (74 analysed) and a 50-mg dose — half the dose used in later trials — mean this card establishes direction, not the size of the effect at the marketed dose; the pooled analysis was planned a priori, which strengthens it, but the trials' sponsor is the drug's developer.
cards.source: Garcia JM et al. Anamorelin for patients with cancer cachexia: an integrated analysis of two phase 2, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials. The Lancet. Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25524795. Registry ID: NCT00219817; NCT00267358. cards.headline: Takayama 2016: Japanese phase 2 trial (181 patients) — anamorelin 100 mg increased lean body mass (1.15 kg vs 0.55 kg on placebo) but handgrip strength did not improve
cards.summary: Takayama 2016: Japanese phase 2 trial (181 patients) — anamorelin 100 mg increased lean body mass (1.15 kg vs 0.55 kg on placebo) but handgrip strength did not improve
cards.people: 181 Japanese patients with non-small-cell lung cancer and cachexia (≥5% weight loss in the previous 6 months) randomised double-blind to anamorelin 50 mg, anamorelin 100 mg or placebo orally daily for 12 weeks; co-primary endpoints were change in lean body mass and handgrip strength over 12 weeks, with body weight, quality of life and performance status as secondaries.
cards.result: Lean body mass changed by 1.15 kg on anamorelin 100 mg versus 0.55 kg on placebo over 12 weeks, while efficacy on handgrip strength was not detected — function made no difference. Body weight changed by −0.93 kg (placebo), +0.54 kg (50 mg) and +1.77 kg (100 mg); anamorelin 100 mg significantly improved performance status and quality-of-life scores versus placebo, and 12 weeks of treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Placebo patients also gained lean body mass here (0.55 kg), unlike the other trials — the between-group lean-mass gap (0.60 kg) is the honest figure for this trial, and it is the smallest of the three reports carded.
cards.source: Takayama K et al. Anamorelin (ONO-7643) in Japanese patients with non-small cell lung cancer and cachexia: results of a randomized phase 2 trial. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2016. PMID: 27005463. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Katakami 2018 (ONO-7643-04): Japanese phase 3 trial (174 patients) — lean body mass rose 1.38 kg on anamorelin versus −0.17 kg on placebo, with no change in handgrip strength or 6-minute walk
cards.summary: Katakami 2018 (ONO-7643-04): Japanese phase 3 trial (174 patients) — lean body mass rose 1.38 kg on anamorelin versus −0.17 kg on placebo, with no change in handgrip strength or 6-minute walk
cards.people: 174 patients with unresectable stage III/IV non-small-cell lung cancer and cachexia in Japan, randomised double-blind to anamorelin 100 mg or placebo daily for 12 weeks; the primary endpoint was change in lean body mass by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, with appetite, body weight, quality of life, handgrip strength and 6-minute walk test as secondaries.
cards.result: The least-squares mean change in lean body mass over 12 weeks was 1.38 ± 0.18 kg on anamorelin versus −0.17 ± 0.17 kg on placebo (P < .0001). Body weight and anorexia symptoms also differed significantly at all time points, and prealbumin rose at weeks 3 and 9. No changes in handgrip strength or 6-minute walk test were detected between the groups — function made no difference. Twelve weeks of anamorelin was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A single-country trial in one tumour type; its regulatory context also differs (anamorelin is approved for cachexia in Japan but was refused in Europe and is not approved in the US, where regulators weighted the failed functional endpoints) — the lean-mass result is solid, its clinical meaning is the contested part.
cards.source: Katakami N et al. Anamorelin (ONO-7643) for the treatment of patients with non-small cell lung cancer and cachexia: Results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study of Japanese patients (ONO-7643-04). Cancer. 2018. PMID: 29205286. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: anamorelin reliably adds lean body mass and reliably fails to add function — and the largest programme's card lives on live #12
cards.summary: Synthesis: anamorelin reliably adds lean body mass and reliably fails to add function — and the largest programme's card lives on live #12
cards.people: The carded evidence: three independent trial reports totalling about 437 randomised patients (Garcia 2015 pooled phase 2, 82; Takayama 2016, 181; Katakami 2018, 174), all 12-week placebo comparisons. The ROMANA 1 and ROMANA 2 phase 3 trials are deliberately not carded here: they are already carded with their figures on live shelf #12 (cancer cachexia), and the one-home rule keeps them there; their published pattern — lean body mass up, handgrip unchanged — is the same as every card on this shelf.
cards.result: Lean body mass increased versus placebo in all three reports (differences of about 2.09 kg, 0.60 kg at the 100-mg dose, and 1.55 kg), appetite and weight improved, and no report found an improvement in handgrip strength or walking. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: anamorelin increases lean body mass in cancer cachexia (trial evidence in non-small-cell lung cancer); a functional or survival benefit has never been shown.
cards.watchOut: Lean body mass by DXA includes water and organ mass, not just contractile muscle — the field's own critique of this programme — so even the positive endpoint overstates what 'more muscle' would mean; judge this drug on the function column, which is empty.
cards.source: Synthesis of Garcia JM et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2015 (PMID: 25524795); Takayama K et al. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2016 (PMID: 27005463); Katakami N et al. Cancer. 2018 (PMID: 29205286).

shelves.title: Prophylactic gastrostomy vs reactive feeding in head and neck radiotherapy: short-term weight and quality of life favour prophylaxis in trial and pooled evidence; the largest matched cohort favours reactive feeding — split
shelves.question: In adults with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy, does prophylactic gastrostomy feeding preserve weight better than reactive nasogastric feeding?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Enteral Nutrition · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrostomy · Head and Neck Neoplasms · Humans · Length of Stay · Malnutrition · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (time horizon and study design) — printed on the face. The randomised and pooled evidence favours prophylactic gastrostomy for short-term weight and quality of life: Silander 2012 (134 patients randomised to prophylactic PEG or clinical practice) found significantly less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months with prophylactic PEG, and a systematic review of 5 studies (298 patients) found prophylactic PEG associated with less short-term critical weight loss (>10%) and better short-term quality of life, with no effect on other outcomes. Against that, the largest comparison — a propensity-matched analysis of 526 patients with oral cavity cancer receiving adjuvant radiotherapy (Ghosh Laskar 2023) — found median weight loss at 6 weeks was greater in the prophylactic cohort (5 kg vs 3 kg, P=0.002) and lower in the reactive cohort at every later timepoint to 1 year, and its authors recommend the reactive approach. The only direct PEG-versus-nasogastric randomised trial in the Cochrane review enrolled just 33 patients before stopping early. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylactic gastrostomy preserves weight and quality of life better in the first months in the trial and pooled evidence, but the largest matched cohort found the reactive strategy equal or better — the question is not settled.

cards.headline: Silander 2012: in 134 randomised patients, prophylactic PEG gave significantly less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months than clinical practice, with about 10% fewer malnourished patients through the first year
cards.summary: Silander 2012: in 134 randomised patients, prophylactic PEG gave significantly less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months than clinical practice, with about 10% fewer malnourished patients through the first year
cards.people: 134 patients with advanced head and neck cancer randomised to prophylactic percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) for enteral nutrition (study group) or clinical praxis (control group, in which feeding support was given reactively as needed); weight, body mass index, hospitalisation and health-related quality of life were recorded at 7 occasions over 2 years during and after radiotherapy-based treatment.
cards.result: No difference in hospital stay was found. After 6 months, health-related quality of life was significantly better and weight loss was significantly less in the prophylactic-PEG group. The number of malnourished patients was consistently about 10% lower in the study group during the first study year. The study group started enteral feeding significantly earlier and used it for significantly longer (P<.0001). The record reports significance levels without the absolute weight-loss figures for the 6-month comparison.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is 'clinical praxis' — reactive support of mixed kinds — not a protocolised reactive nasogastric strategy, and the trial predates modern chemoradiotherapy intensity for many patients; it supports prophylactic placement, but it is one centre's 134 patients.
cards.source: Silander E et al. Impact of prophylactic percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy on malnutrition and quality of life in patients with head and neck cancer: a randomized study. Head & neck. 2012. PMID: 21374756. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mellors 2021: across 5 studies (298 patients), prophylactic PEG was associated with less short-term critical weight loss (>10%) and better short-term quality of life than reactive enteral nutrition — and no effect on other outcomes
cards.summary: Mellors 2021: across 5 studies (298 patients), prophylactic PEG was associated with less short-term critical weight loss (>10%) and better short-term quality of life than reactive enteral nutrition — and no effect on other outcomes
cards.type: Systematic review of 5 studies including 3 randomised trials (Mellors 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials and comparative studies (5 studies, 3 of them randomised trials; 298 patients aged ≥18) with head and neck cancer undergoing curative-intent radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, comparing prophylactic percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy placement/feeding with reactive enteral nutrition; certainty assessed with GRADE.
cards.result: Prophylactic PEG was associated with a clinically important reduction in short-term critical weight loss (>10% weight loss) and significantly improved short-term quality of life. The timing of nutrition support commencement had no effect on all other outcomes examined (nutritional status, body mass index, treatment interruptions, disease-free and overall survival). Overall certainty of evidence was 'moderate' for nutritional status, treatment interruptions, short-term quality of life and disease-free survival, and 'low' for all other outcomes. Definitions of prophylactic PEG and reactive enteral nutrition were heterogeneous across studies.
cards.watchOut: Only 298 patients in total and mixed study designs, with the benefit confined to short-term weight and quality of life; this review cannot answer whether prophylactic tubes help or harm swallowing function or survival in the long run.
cards.source: Mellors K et al. Comparison of prophylactic percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy with reactive enteral nutrition in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy: A systematic review. Clinical nutrition ESPEN. 2021. PMID: 34857252. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ghosh Laskar 2023: in 526 propensity-matched patients, weight loss was greater with the prophylactic approach at 6 weeks (median 5 kg vs 3 kg, P=0.002) and lower with the reactive approach at every timepoint to 1 year
cards.summary: Ghosh Laskar 2023: in 526 propensity-matched patients, weight loss was greater with the prophylactic approach at 6 weeks (median 5 kg vs 3 kg, P=0.002) and lower with the reactive approach at every timepoint to 1 year
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of patients with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma enrolled in a randomised adjuvant-strategy trial who received adjuvant radiotherapy: a prophylactic feeding approach was used for all patients until 2010 and a reactive feeding approach from January 2011; after propensity-score matching, 268 patients in each cohort (526 total) were analysed for weight loss to 1 year.
cards.result: At 6 weeks after completing radiotherapy, median weight loss was 5 kg in the prophylactic cohort vs 3 kg in the reactive cohort (P=0.002). At all other time points until 1 year, median weight loss was lesser in the reactive than in the prophylactic cohort. The authors conclude a reactive feeding-tube approach should be preferred for oral cavity cancer patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: This is an era comparison (prophylactic before 2011, reactive after) inside one centre, so changes in radiotherapy technique and supportive care over time can masquerade as a feeding-strategy effect — but at 526 matched patients it is four times the size of the randomised trial and cannot be waved away.
cards.source: Ghosh Laskar S et al. Prophylactic versus reactive feeding approach in patients undergoing adjuvant radiation therapy for oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma: A propensity score matched-pair analysis. Head & neck. 2023. PMID: 36912016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2013: the only randomised trial of PEG versus nasogastric feeding enrolled 33 patients and stopped early — weight loss favoured PEG at 6 weeks (P=0.001) but not at 6 months
cards.summary: Cochrane 2013: the only randomised trial of PEG versus nasogastric feeding enrolled 33 patients and stopped early — weight loss favoured PEG at 6 weeks (P=0.001) but not at 6 months
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Nugent 2013; one included trial, 33 patients)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials comparing enteral feeding methods (nasogastric versus percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy feeding) in adults with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy and/or chemoradiotherapy; searches to 13 February 2012 found one eligible trial, in patients treated with chemoradiotherapy, terminated early for poor accrual with 33 patients eligible for analysis and a high degree of bias identified.
cards.result: Weight loss was greater for the nasogastric group at six weeks post-treatment than for the PEG group (P=0.001); at six months post-treatment there was no significant difference in weight loss between the groups. Triceps skin fold thickness at six weeks was lower in the nasogastric group (P=0.03). No statistically significant difference was found in complication rates or patient satisfaction, and the duration of PEG feeding was significantly longer than nasogastric feeding (P=0.0006). The review concludes the optimal enteral feeding method has yet to be established.
cards.watchOut: A 33-patient trial stopped early is hypothesis-generating at best; its value here is showing how thin the direct PEG-versus-nasogastric randomised evidence is underneath a question that is usually argued from cohorts.
cards.source: Nugent B et al. Enteral feeding methods for nutritional management in patients with head and neck cancers being treated with radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23440820. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: short-term weight and quality of life favour prophylactic gastrostomy in the trial and pooled evidence; the largest matched cohort favours the reactive approach — a genuine split
cards.summary: Synthesis: short-term weight and quality of life favour prophylactic gastrostomy in the trial and pooled evidence; the largest matched cohort favours the reactive approach — a genuine split
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of prophylactic PEG vs clinical practice (Silander 2012, 134 patients), one systematic review of 5 studies (Mellors 2021, 298 patients), one propensity-matched cohort (Ghosh Laskar 2023, 526 patients), and one Cochrane review whose only direct PEG-vs-nasogastric trial enrolled 33 patients. Total carded participants exceed 900, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Silander found significantly less weight loss and better quality of life at 6 months with prophylactic PEG; Mellors found less short-term critical weight loss (>10%) and better short-term quality of life, with no effect on treatment interruptions or survival; Ghosh Laskar found greater weight loss with prophylaxis at 6 weeks (median 5 vs 3 kg) and less weight loss with the reactive approach at every later point to 1 year; the Cochrane direct comparison (33 patients) favoured PEG at 6 weeks but not 6 months. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylactic gastrostomy preserves weight better in the first months on the trial/pooled evidence, but the largest comparison found the reactive strategy equal or better — neither strategy is proven superior overall.
cards.watchOut: Populations differ across the carded reports — advanced mixed head-and-neck sites on radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy versus oral-cavity-only adjuvant radiotherapy — so part of the split may be population and era, not the feeding strategy itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of Silander E et al. Head & neck. 2012 (PMID: 21374756); Mellors K et al. Clinical nutrition ESPEN. 2021 (PMID: 34857252); Ghosh Laskar S et al. Head & neck. 2023 (PMID: 36912016); Nugent B et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23440820).

shelves.title: Early oral feeding after esophagectomy: no complication penalty and faster bowel recovery in three randomised trials, but the largest trial found no faster functional recovery (7 vs 8 days)
shelves.question: In adults after esophagectomy, does early oral feeding improve recovery compared with tube feeding?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anastomotic Leak · Enteral Nutrition · Esophageal Neoplasms · Esophagectomy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Postoperative Care · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow) — printed on the face, with the largest trial's null primary outcome printed beside it. In NUTRIENT II (Berkelmans 2020, 132 patients after minimally invasive esophagectomy), starting oral feeding directly did not speed functional recovery — 7 days vs 8 days (P=0.436; the treatment made no difference) — and did not increase anastomotic leakage (18.5% vs 16.4%) or pneumonia (24.6% vs 34.3%). The larger Chinese non-inferiority trial (Sun 2018, 280 patients) found oral feeding on day 1 non-inferior for cardiorespiratory and gastrointestinal complications (30.0% vs 32.9%), with faster return of flatus (median 2 vs 3 days) and bowel movement (3 vs 4 days) and better quality of life at 2 weeks. A small randomised trial (Liao 2020, 41 patients) found shorter hospital stay and lower C-reactive protein with early oral feeding, with no difference in complications or mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow): early oral feeding after esophagectomy appears safe — no increase in leak or pneumonia in any carded trial — and speeds bowel recovery and short-term quality of life, but the best trial found no faster overall functional recovery, so 'improves recovery' is supported only in that narrower sense.

cards.headline: NUTRIENT II 2020: direct oral feeding after minimally invasive esophagectomy did not speed functional recovery — 7 vs 8 days (the treatment made no difference) — and did not increase leakage (18.5% vs 16.4%) or pneumonia (24.6% vs 34.3%)
cards.summary: NUTRIENT II 2020: direct oral feeding after minimally invasive esophagectomy did not speed functional recovery — 7 vs 8 days (the treatment made no difference) — and did not increase leakage (18.5% vs 16.4%) or pneumonia (24.6% vs 34.3%)
cards.people: 132 patients in an international multicentre open-label randomised trial after minimally invasive esophagectomy with intrathoracic anastomosis, randomised to direct start of oral feeding (intervention, n=65) or nil-by-mouth with tube feeding for 5 days (control, n=67). Primary outcome was time to functional recovery; secondary outcomes included anastomotic leakage, pneumonia and other complications by predefined definitions.
cards.result: Functional recovery was 7 days with direct oral feeding vs 8 days in the control group (P=0.436) — the treatment made no difference to the primary outcome. Anastomotic leakage did not differ (18.5% intervention vs 16.4% control, P=0.757). Pneumonia rates were comparable (24.6% vs 34.3%, P=0.221). Other morbidity was similar, except chyle leakage, which was more prevalent in the standard-of-care group (P=0.032). The authors conclude direct oral feeding does not affect functional recovery and did not increase the incidence or severity of postoperative complications.
cards.watchOut: This is the most rigorous test of the question and its primary outcome is null — any claim that early oral feeding 'speeds recovery' after esophagectomy has to reckon with 7 vs 8 days, P=0.436, in this trial; its contribution is safety (no leak or pneumonia penalty), not speed.
cards.source: Berkelmans GHK et al. Direct Oral Feeding Following Minimally Invasive Esophagectomy (NUTRIENT II trial): An International, Multicenter, Open-label Randomized Controlled Trial. Annals of surgery. 2020. PMID: 31090563. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sun 2018: oral feeding on day 1 was non-inferior to 7 days of tube feeding for complications in 280 patients (30.0% vs 32.9%), with faster bowel recovery and better quality of life at 2 weeks
cards.summary: Sun 2018: oral feeding on day 1 was non-inferior to 7 days of tube feeding for complications in 280 patients (30.0% vs 32.9%), with faster bowel recovery and better quality of life at 2 weeks
cards.people: 280 patients after McKeown minimally invasive esophagectomy for esophageal cancer, enrolled February 2014 to October 2015 and randomly allocated to early oral feeding on the first postoperative day (n=140) or late oral feeding 7 days after surgery with enteral tube feeding meanwhile (n=140). Primary endpoint was postoperative cardiac, respiratory and gastrointestinal complications; secondary outcomes included bowel function recovery and short-term quality of life.
cards.result: Early oral feeding was non-inferior to late feeding for cardiac, respiratory and gastrointestinal complications (30.0% vs 32.9%; 95% CI of the difference −13.8% to 8.0%). Compared with late feeding, the early group had significantly shorter time to first flatus (median 2 vs 3 days, P=0.001) and bowel movement (median 3 vs 4 days, P<0.001). Two weeks after the operation, the early group reported higher global quality-of-life and function scores and lower symptom scores.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-country, using the McKeown (cervical anastomosis) operation rather than NUTRIENT II's intrathoracic anastomosis; the quality-of-life advantage at 2 weeks is real in this trial but early and unblinded, so expectation effects cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Sun HB et al. Early Oral Feeding Following McKeown Minimally Invasive Esophagectomy: An Open-label, Randomized, Controlled, Noninferiority Trial. Annals of surgery. 2018. PMID: 28549015. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Liao 2020: in 41 randomised patients, early oral feeding shortened hospital stay and lowered C-reactive protein, with no difference in complications or mortality versus tube feeding
cards.summary: Liao 2020: in 41 randomised patients, early oral feeding shortened hospital stay and lowered C-reactive protein, with no difference in complications or mortality versus tube feeding
cards.people: 41 consecutive patients with esophageal carcinoma (stages I–III) after minimally invasive Ivor-Lewis surgery, enrolled October 2013 to January 2016 and randomly arranged to early oral feeding (n=21; tube-fed enteral nutrition plus oral 5% glucose in saline for the first 4 days, then liquid diet) or simple tube feeding (n=20; tube-fed for 7 days before liquid diet). The nutritional goal in both groups was 25 kcal/(kg·day). Outcomes included hospital stay, complications, mortality, albumin, prealbumin, transferrin and C-reactive protein.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in the incidence of postoperative complications or overall mortality between the groups, but the duration of hospital stay, interval until first liquid food, and time of ambulation were lower in the early oral feeding group (P<0.05). Early oral feeding patients also showed significantly lower C-reactive protein levels than the tube feeding group (P<0.05). The record reports significance levels without the absolute stay durations.
cards.watchOut: Only 41 patients — this trial can support the direction of the larger trials but cannot stand as safety evidence on its own; a leak-rate difference of clinical importance would be invisible at this size.
cards.source: Liao M et al. Early enteral feeding on esophageal cancer patients after esophageal resection and reconstruction. Annals of palliative medicine. 2020. PMID: 32312065. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Enteral Nutrition · Esophageal Neoplasms · Esophagectomy · Humans · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications

cards.headline: Synthesis: early oral feeding after esophagectomy is safe on the carded trials and speeds bowel recovery and early quality of life — but the best trial found no faster overall functional recovery
cards.summary: Synthesis: early oral feeding after esophagectomy is safe on the carded trials and speeds bowel recovery and early quality of life — but the best trial found no faster overall functional recovery
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials — NUTRIENT II (132 patients, intrathoracic anastomosis), Sun 2018 (280 patients, McKeown operation) and Liao 2020 (41 patients, Ivor-Lewis operation). Total carded participants are 453, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: No trial found more anastomotic leakage or pneumonia with early oral feeding (NUTRIENT II: leak 18.5% vs 16.4%, pneumonia 24.6% vs 34.3%). Functional recovery in NUTRIENT II was 7 vs 8 days (the treatment made no difference, P=0.436). Sun found complications non-inferior (30.0% vs 32.9%) with flatus a day earlier, bowel movement a day earlier and better 2-week quality of life; Liao found shorter stay and lower C-reactive protein. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, narrow): early oral feeding improves bowel recovery and short-term quality of life without a complication penalty, but has not been shown to speed overall functional recovery.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are in minimally invasive esophagectomy in selected patients; they do not license day-1 oral feeding after open surgery, in malnourished patients, or where the anastomosis is in doubt — NUTRIENT II itself excluded patients unable to take oral intake.
cards.source: Synthesis of Berkelmans GHK et al. Annals of surgery. 2020 (PMID: 31090563); Sun HB et al. Annals of surgery. 2018 (PMID: 28549015); Liao M et al. Annals of palliative medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32312065).

shelves.title: G-CSF primary prophylaxis at intermediate febrile-neutropenia risk (PARTIAL completion of live #370): untreated risk about 9% per course, observational benefit modest and concentrated in patients with added risk factors
shelves.question: In adults receiving chemotherapy at intermediate risk of febrile neutropenia, does primary G-CSF prophylaxis reduce febrile neutropenia compared with no prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Neoplasms · Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor · Medical Oncology · Febrile Neutropenia · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, observational evidence) — printed on the face: there is no randomised trial confined to the intermediate-risk (10–20%) band, so this slice rests on cohorts and claims data and is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #370 homes primary G-CSF prophylaxis inside the ≥20%-risk fence, where meta-analyses show febrile neutropenia roughly halved in relative terms (relative risk about 0.51–0.54); that relative effect is not re-carded here. What the intermediate-risk evidence adds is the baseline: without prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed at least one febrile-neutropenia episode over a course of chemotherapy in the prospective MASCC cohort (364 patients), concentrated in cycle 1 — so even a halving in relative terms buys only a few percentage points absolutely. In US claims data (13,937 intermediate-risk patients), 98% had at least one clinical risk factor yet only 35% received primary prophylaxis, and febrile-neutropenia risk rose with the number of risk factors; in a longitudinal claims cohort (142,730 patients on intermediate/high-risk regimens), first-cycle febrile neutropenia ran slightly lower with prophylaxis (2.6% across quarters) than without (2.7–3.7%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): primary G-CSF prophylaxis probably reduces febrile neutropenia at intermediate risk too, but the absolute gain is small on average and concentrated in patients with added risk factors — which is why guidelines recommend it selectively in this band rather than routinely.

cards.headline: MASCC 2023: without G-CSF prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed febrile neutropenia over a chemotherapy course — 5% in cycle 1 alone — in a prospective multinational cohort of 364 patients
cards.summary: MASCC 2023: without G-CSF prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed febrile neutropenia over a chemotherapy course — 5% in cycle 1 alone — in a prospective multinational cohort of 364 patients
cards.people: 364 patients (median age 56 years) with solid tumours or Hodgkin/non-Hodgkin lymphoma receiving chemotherapy regimens with an intermediate (10–20%) risk of febrile neutropenia, without G-CSF primary prophylaxis, in a prospective real-world multinational multicentre observational study (December 2016–October 2019), observed for up to 6 cycles and 30 days after the last administration; 1,601 cycles were analysed.
cards.result: The incidence of febrile neutropenia was 5% in cycle 1, 3% in cycles 2–3 and 1% in cycles 4–6. The rate of patients with at least one episode of febrile neutropenia was 9%, and 59% of febrile-neutropenia events were reported during cycle 1. Grade 4 neutropenia occurred in 11% in cycle 1, and 15% of patients experienced at least one episode of grade 4 neutropenia. The authors conclude the overall incidence was low, highest in cycle 1, and that prophylactic G-CSF in intermediate-risk patients could be considered at the clinician's judgement.
cards.watchOut: This cohort has no prophylaxis arm — it measures the untreated baseline risk that any prophylaxis benefit must be subtracted from, and at 9% per course it shows why a relative halving (the effect size homed on live #370) is worth only a few absolute percentage points in this band.
cards.source: Leon Rapoport B et al. A prospective, real-world, multinational study of febrile neutropenia (FN) occurrence in oncology patients receiving chemotherapy with intermediate risk of FN: a MASCC Neutropenia, Infection, and Myelosuppression Study Group initiative. cards.search: mascc 2023: without g-csf prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed febrile neutropenia over a chemotherapy course — 5% in cycle 1 alone — in a prospective multinational cohort of 364 patients mascc 2023: without g-csf prophylaxis, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed febrile neutropenia over a chemotherapy course — 5% in cycle 1 alone — in a prospective multinational cohort of 364 patients in adults receiving chemotherapy at intermediate risk of febrile neutropenia, does primary g-csf prophylaxis reduce febrile neutropenia compared with no prophylaxis? prospective observational cohort (mascc, leon rapoport 2023) 364 patients (median age 56 years) with solid tumours or hodgkin/non-hodgkin lymphoma receiving chemotherapy regimens with an intermediate (10–20%) risk of febrile neutropenia, without g-csf primary prophylaxis, in a prospective real-world multinational multicentre observational study (december 2016–october 2019), observed for up to 6 cycles and 30 days after the last administration; 1,601 cycles were analysed. the incidence of febrile neutropenia was 5% in cycle 1, 3% in cycles 2–3 and 1% in cycles 4–6. the rate of patients with at least one episode of febrile neutropenia was 9%, and 59% of febrile-neutropenia events were reported during cycle 1. grade 4 neutropenia occurred in 11% in cycle 1, and 15% of patients experienced at least one episode of grade 4 neutropenia. the authors conclude the overall incidence was low, highest in cycle 1, and that prophylactic g-csf in intermediate-risk patients could be considered at the clinician's judgement. this cohort has no prophylaxis arm — it measures the untreated baseline risk that any prophylaxis benefit must be subtracted from, and at 9% per course it shows why a relative halving (the effect size homed on live #370) is worth only a few absolute percentage points in this band. leon rapoport b et al. a prospective, real-world, multinational study of febrile neutropenia (fn) occurrence in oncology patients receiving chemotherapy with intermediate risk of fn: a mascc neutropenia, infection, and myelosuppression study group initiative. supportive care in cancer : official journal of the multinational association of supportive care in cancer. 2023. pmid: 37828258. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · middle aged · prospective studies · neoplasms · granulocyte colony-stimulating factor · medical oncology · febrile neutropenia · antineoplastic combined chemotherapy protocols

cards.headline: Aslam 2023: among 13,937 intermediate-risk patients, 98% had at least one risk factor but only 35% received primary G-CSF prophylaxis — and febrile-neutropenia risk rose with each added risk factor
cards.summary: Aslam 2023: among 13,937 intermediate-risk patients, 98% had at least one risk factor but only 35% received primary G-CSF prophylaxis — and febrile-neutropenia risk rose with each added risk factor
cards.people: 13,937 patients (mean age 67 years, 55% female) with nonmyeloid cancer treated with intermediate-risk chemotherapy regimens in US commercial and Medicare Advantage claims (1 January 2009 to 31 March 2020), analysed descriptively by receipt of primary G-CSF, secondary G-CSF, or no prophylaxis, with multivariable Cox regression for the association between number of risk factors and cumulative febrile-neutropenia risk.
cards.result: Patients had a mean of 2.3 risk factors (most commonly recent surgery, age ≥65 years, and baseline liver or renal dysfunction) and 98% had one or more; yet only 35% received primary prophylaxis and 12% secondary prophylaxis, and more than 54% received no prophylaxis regardless of risk-factor count. The hazard of incident febrile neutropenia was higher with increasing number of risk factors. Prophylaxis use varied more by regimen than by risk-factor count (76% primary prophylaxis with R-CHOP vs 22% with carboplatin/paclitaxel). Among patients with a first-line febrile-neutropenia event, 78% had an inpatient stay; cycle-1 febrile-neutropenia-related costs per patient per month were $13,886 with primary prophylaxis vs $18,233 with none.
cards.watchOut: Claims data cannot show that prophylaxis caused the cost difference — patients given prophylaxis differ from those not given it — and this study's direct febrile-neutropenia comparison by prophylaxis receipt is descriptive; its firm findings are the risk-factor gradient and the implementation gap.
cards.source: Aslam S et al. Risk of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia in intermediate-risk regimens: Clinical and economic outcomes of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor prophylaxis. Journal of managed care & specialty pharmacy. 2023. PMID: 36705281. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Weycker 2019: across 142,730 patients on intermediate/high-risk regimens, first-cycle febrile neutropenia was 2.6% with primary CSF prophylaxis vs 2.7–3.7% without, quarter by quarter
cards.summary: Weycker 2019: across 142,730 patients on intermediate/high-risk regimens, first-cycle febrile neutropenia was 2.6% with primary CSF prophylaxis vs 2.7–3.7% without, quarter by quarter
cards.people: 142,730 patients with non-metastatic breast (61%), colorectal (14%), ovarian (10%) or lung (5%) cancer or non-Hodgkin lymphoma (11%) receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy regimens with intermediate/high febrile-neutropenia risk in two US healthcare claims repositories, 2010–2016; the first cycle of the first course was characterised for primary prophylactic colony-stimulating factor (PP-CSF) use and febrile-neutropenia episodes, with multivariable-adjusted quarter-specific probabilities.
cards.result: PP-CSF use increased from 52% in the first quarter of 2010 to 58% in the last quarter of 2016; pegfilgrastim was the agent in over 96% of use. Adjusted incidence proportions for febrile neutropenia in the first cycle ranged from 2.7% (95% CI 2.3–3.0) to 3.7% (95% CI 3.1–4.3) among patients who did not receive PP-CSF, and were 2.6% (95% CI 2.5–2.7) across quarters among those who did. The authors conclude patients receiving PP-CSF appear to have a lower risk of febrile neutropenia during the first cycle, while underuse in intermediate/high-risk regimens may persist.
cards.watchOut: This cohort mixes intermediate- and high-risk regimens, so its small absolute gap (about 0.1–1.1 percentage points in cycle 1) cannot be read as the intermediate-risk effect alone; confounding by indication runs in both directions in claims data — higher-risk patients are both likelier to receive prophylaxis and likelier to develop febrile neutropenia.
cards.source: Weycker D et al. Use of colony-stimulating factor primary prophylaxis and incidence of febrile neutropenia from 2010 to 2016: a longitudinal assessment. Current medical research and opinion. 2019. PMID: 30550346. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: at intermediate risk the untreated febrile-neutropenia rate is about 9% per course, prophylaxis is associated with modestly lower rates in observational data, and the absolute benefit concentrates in patients with added risk factors
cards.summary: Synthesis: at intermediate risk the untreated febrile-neutropenia rate is about 9% per course, prophylaxis is associated with modestly lower rates in observational data, and the absolute benefit concentrates in patients with added risk factors
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective cohort without prophylaxis (MASCC 2023, 364 patients), and two US claims cohorts (Aslam 2023, 13,937 intermediate-risk patients; Weycker 2019, 142,730 patients on intermediate/high-risk regimens). Total carded participants exceed 150,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. All evidence for this slice is observational; the randomised/meta-analytic class effect at ≥20% risk is homed on live shelf #370 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Untreated, 9% of intermediate-risk patients developed febrile neutropenia over a course (5% in cycle 1). With prophylaxis, first-cycle rates in claims data were 2.6% vs 2.7–3.7% without. Risk rose with the number of clinical risk factors, yet most intermediate-risk patients received no prophylaxis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): primary G-CSF prophylaxis probably reduces febrile neutropenia at intermediate (10–20%) risk, with a small average absolute benefit that is largest in patients carrying additional risk factors.
cards.watchOut: No carded report randomises intermediate-risk patients to prophylaxis or none; the benefit claim is an extrapolation from the ≥20%-risk class effect (live #370) disciplined by the low untreated baseline measured here — if the baseline is 9%, even a true relative halving prevents roughly 4–5 events per 100 patients treated.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leon Rapoport B et al. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2023 (PMID: 37828258); Aslam S et al. Journal of managed care & specialty pharmacy. 2023 (PMID: 36705281); Weycker D et al. Current medical research and opinion. 2019 (PMID: 30550346).

shelves.title: Same-day vs next-day pegfilgrastim: same-day administration is associated with more febrile neutropenia in every carded cohort — not as effective (observational evidence)
shelves.question: In adults receiving chemotherapy, is pegfilgrastim given on the same day as chemotherapy as effective as next-day pegfilgrastim for preventing febrile neutropenia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Chemotherapy-Induced Febrile Neutropenia · Cohort Studies · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Filgrastim · Humans · Incidence · Lymphoma, Non-Hodgkin · Male · Medicare · Polyethylene Glycols · Retrospective Studies · Risk Adjustment · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm signal, observational evidence) — printed on the face: the evidence is entirely observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled observational — and it points one way: same-day pegfilgrastim is associated with MORE febrile neutropenia, not equal protection. In the largest study (Weycker 2018, Medicare claims; 65,003 patients, 261,184 cycles), cycle-1 febrile neutropenia was 11.4% in same-day cycles vs 8.4% in day 1–3 cycles (adjusted odds ratio 1.4 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates), and 7.7% vs 6.0% across all cycles (adjusted odds ratio 1.3). In breast-cancer patients on dose-dense doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide (Hobbs 2023, 360 patients), febrile neutropenia occurred in 24.6% with same-day vs 11.7% with next-day administration (P=0.002), with more grade ≥3 neutropenia (38.4% vs 13.6%), dose reductions and antibiotic use. In lymphoma patients on CHOP with or without rituximab (Cheng 2014, 141 patients, 655 cycles), febrile neutropenia was 9.4% in same-day cycles vs 5.1% in next-day cycles (P=0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (same-day administration is less effective, observational): on all carded evidence, pegfilgrastim given on the day of chemotherapy prevents febrile neutropenia less well than next-day administration — the convenience of a single visit is bought with a higher febrile-neutropenia rate.

cards.headline: Weycker 2018: in 261,184 Medicare cycles, febrile neutropenia was 11.4% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 8.4% with day 1–3 administration in cycle 1 (adjusted odds ratio 1.4)
cards.summary: Weycker 2018: in 261,184 Medicare cycles, febrile neutropenia was 11.4% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 8.4% with day 1–3 administration in cycle 1 (adjusted odds ratio 1.4)
cards.people: 65,003 patients aged ≥65 years with breast cancer or non-Hodgkin lymphoma in Medicare claims (January 2008–September 2015) who received chemotherapy with intermediate/high febrile-neutropenia risk and pegfilgrastim prophylaxis in at least one cycle; 261,184 cycles were stratified by administration day — same day ('Day 0', 5% of cycles) vs 1–3 days after chemotherapy ('Days 1–3') — with adjusted odds ratios for febrile neutropenia during the cycle.
cards.result: The incidence proportion for febrile neutropenia in cycle 1 was 11.4% for Day 0 vs 8.4% for Days 1–3 (adjusted odds ratio 1.4, P<.001 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). Across all cycles, incidence was 7.7% for Day 0 vs 6.0% for Days 1–3 (adjusted odds ratio 1.3, P<.001); results were similar for inpatient-only episodes (odds ratio 1.3) and a narrow febrile-neutropenia definition (odds ratio 1.5). The authors conclude the findings support guidelines that pegfilgrastim be administered the day after chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Same-day cycles were only 5% of the total and were not assigned at random — practices and patients choosing same-day dosing may differ — but the association survives adjustment and matches the direction of both smaller cohorts carded here.
cards.source: Weycker D et al. Risk of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia with same-day versus next-day pegfilgrastim prophylaxis among patients aged ≥65 years: a retrospective evaluation using Medicare claims. Current medical research and opinion. 2018. PMID: 29962268. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hobbs 2023: in 360 breast-cancer patients on dose-dense AC, febrile neutropenia was 24.6% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 11.7% with next-day (P=0.002), with more dose reductions and antibiotic use
cards.summary: Hobbs 2023: in 360 breast-cancer patients on dose-dense AC, febrile neutropenia was 24.6% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 11.7% with next-day (P=0.002), with more dose reductions and antibiotic use
cards.people: 360 patients aged ≥18 years with breast cancer receiving dose-dense doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide (ddAC) with pegfilgrastim between June 2016 and May 2020 in a multi-site retrospective cohort: pegfilgrastim was given on the same day as chemotherapy at one site (146 patients) and the day after at two other sites (214 patients). The primary endpoint was the incidence of febrile neutropenia by administration timing.
cards.result: Febrile neutropenia developed in 36 patients (24.6%) in the same-day group vs 25 (11.7%) in the next-day group (P=0.002). Same-day administration also significantly increased additional acute-care visits (11.6% vs 2.8%, P=0.0016), grade ≥3 neutropenia (38.4% vs 13.6%, P<0.0001), chemotherapy dose reductions (21.2% vs 6.1%, P<0.0001) and antibiotic use (26.7% vs 12.6%, P=0.001). Hospitalisation (15% vs 11.2%, P=0.36) and delay of the next cycle by ≥1 day (8.2% vs 6.1%, P=0.57) did not differ significantly. The authors conclude pegfilgrastim should be given the day after chemotherapy in ddAC.
cards.watchOut: Timing was determined by site, not by randomisation, so site-level practice differences are entangled with the timing effect; even so, a doubling of febrile neutropenia (24.6% vs 11.7%) on the most neutropenia-intensive common regimen is the strongest practical warning in this shelf.
cards.source: Hobbs J et al. Efficacy of same-day versus next-day administration of pegfilgrastim for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia in breast cancer patients receiving dose-dense doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide: A retrospective multi-site analysis. cards.headline: Cheng 2014: in 655 CHOP cycles, febrile neutropenia was 9.4% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 5.1% with next-day (P=0.03)
cards.summary: Cheng 2014: in 655 CHOP cycles, febrile neutropenia was 9.4% with same-day pegfilgrastim vs 5.1% with next-day (P=0.03)
cards.people: 141 adults with non-Hodgkin lymphoma receiving CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) with or without rituximab every 3 weeks, in a retrospective single-centre cohort; 655 chemotherapy cycles were evaluable — 320 cycles with pegfilgrastim 6 mg subcutaneously on day 1 (same day) and 335 cycles on day 2 or beyond (next day). Outcomes were febrile neutropenia and grade 4 neutropenia.
cards.result: Across all cycles, the incidence of febrile neutropenia was 9.4% in the same-day group vs 5.1% in the next-day group (P=0.03). Febrile neutropenia was highest after the first cycle in the same-day group (19.4% vs 11.1%, P=0.27). There were three deaths among patients who developed febrile neutropenia (two in the next-day group, one in the same-day group). The authors conclude their findings support the need for a randomised phase III study of administration timing.
cards.watchOut: Cycles, not patients, are the unit of analysis, and the same patient could contribute cycles to the count; the first-cycle difference (19.4% vs 11.1%) did not reach significance at this size. Direction, again, is the same as the other two cohorts.
cards.source: Cheng C et al. Rates of febrile neutropenia with pegfilgrastim on same day versus next day of CHOP with or without rituximab. Anti-cancer drugs. 2014. PMID: 24743519. Registry ID: none in the record. retrospective cohort (cheng 2014) 141 adults with non-hodgkin lymphoma receiving chop (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) with or without rituximab every 3 weeks, in a retrospective single-centre cohort; 655 chemotherapy cycles were evaluable — 320 cycles with pegfilgrastim 6 mg subcutaneously on day 1 (same day) and 335 cycles on day 2 or beyond (next day). outcomes were febrile neutropenia and grade 4 neutropenia. across all cycles, the incidence of febrile neutropenia was 9.4% in the same-day group vs 5.1% in the next-day group (p=0.03). febrile neutropenia was highest after the first cycle in the same-day group (19.4% vs 11.1%, p=0.27). there were three deaths among patients who developed febrile neutropenia (two in the next-day group, one in the same-day group). the authors conclude their findings support the need for a randomised phase iii study of administration timing. cycles, not patients, are the unit of analysis, and the same patient could contribute cycles to the count; the first-cycle difference (19.4% vs 11.1%) did not reach significance at this size. direction, again, is the same as the other two cohorts. cheng c et al. rates of febrile neutropenia with pegfilgrastim on same day versus next day of chop with or without rituximab. anti-cancer drugs. 2014. pmid: 24743519. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antibodies, monoclonal, murine-derived · antineoplastic combined chemotherapy protocols · chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia · cyclophosphamide · doxorubicin · filgrastim · granulocyte colony-stimulating factor · humans · incidence · lymphoma, large b-cell, diffuse · middle aged · polyethylene glycols · prednisolone · recombinant proteins · retrospective studies · rituximab · vincristine · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: every carded comparison finds more febrile neutropenia with same-day pegfilgrastim — it is not as effective as next-day administration on the observational evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: every carded comparison finds more febrile neutropenia with same-day pegfilgrastim — it is not as effective as next-day administration on the observational evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: three retrospective cohorts — Weycker 2018 (65,003 patients, 261,184 cycles, Medicare), Hobbs 2023 (360 breast-cancer patients on dose-dense AC) and Cheng 2014 (141 lymphoma patients, 655 CHOP cycles). Total carded participants exceed 65,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. No randomised timing trial was found; all evidence is observational.
cards.result: Febrile neutropenia was higher with same-day administration in all three: 11.4% vs 8.4% in cycle 1 (adjusted odds ratio 1.4), 24.6% vs 11.7% on dose-dense AC (P=0.002), and 9.4% vs 5.1% of CHOP cycles (P=0.03) — absolute gaps of 3 to 13 percentage points, always in the same direction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (same-day is less effective, observational): pegfilgrastim on the day of chemotherapy does not prevent febrile neutropenia as well as next-day pegfilgrastim.
cards.watchOut: Observational timing comparisons can be confounded — but here the confounding would have to run the same way in Medicare claims, a site-level breast-cancer comparison and a single-centre lymphoma cohort to manufacture the consistent gap; the burden of proof now sits with same-day dosing.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weycker D et al. Current medical research and opinion. 2018 (PMID: 29962268); Hobbs J et al. Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners. 2023 (PMID: 36579812); Cheng C et al. Anti-cancer drugs. 2014 (PMID: 24743519).
