shelves.title: Adding an NK1 antagonist in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (PARTIAL completion of pack #3420): complete response improved, benefit concentrated in carboplatin-based regimens
shelves.question: In adults receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding an NK1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone improve vomiting control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carboplatin · Chemoprevention · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Neoplasms · Neurokinin-1 Receptor Antagonists · Risk Factors · Spiro Compounds · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — printed on the face, with the population split printed beside it: the benefit is clearest in carboplatin-based chemotherapy and not demonstrated for oxaliplatin-based regimens. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #3420 homes NK1-antagonist addition in cisplatin (highly emetogenic) chemotherapy and is not re-carded here; this shelf takes the moderately emetogenic slice. In the carboplatin subgroup of the rolapitant phase 3 programme (Hesketh 2016, 401 patients), complete response over 0–120 hours was 80.2% with rolapitant added to granisetron and dexamethasone vs 64.6% on the two-drug control (P<.001). In the fosaprepitant phase 3 trial in non-AC moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (PN031, 1,000 patients; exploratory analysis by Weinstein 2018), complete response with fosaprepitant ran 76–80% in the delayed and overall phases in both carboplatin and non-carboplatin subgroups, with a larger treatment effect in carboplatin-based therapy in the delayed phase (14.1 vs 6.5 percentage points). The meta-analysis of 10 moderately-emetogenic trials (Zhang 2018, 2,928 patients) found the NK1 triple regimen improved complete response overall (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 1.05–1.24 — a relative measure) and in the delayed phase (relative risk 1.13), with the subgroup benefit significant for carboplatin-based but not oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding an NK1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone improves vomiting control in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, driven by carboplatin-based regimens — roughly one extra complete response in every six to seven carboplatin patients in the rolapitant subgroup.

cards.headline: Hesketh 2016: in the 401-patient carboplatin subgroup of a phase 3 trial, adding rolapitant raised complete response to 80.2% vs 64.6% over 0–120 hours (P<.001)
cards.summary: Hesketh 2016: in the 401-patient carboplatin subgroup of a phase 3 trial, adding rolapitant raised complete response to 80.2% vs 64.6% over 0–120 hours (P<.001)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial subgroup analysis (rolapitant in carboplatin, Hesketh 2016)
cards.people: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of 401 patients receiving carboplatin-based chemotherapy within a randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial of moderately emetogenic chemotherapy or anthracycline–cyclophosphamide regimens; patients were randomised 1:1 to oral rolapitant 180 mg or placebo 1–2 hours before chemotherapy, and all received oral granisetron 2 mg on days 1–3 and oral dexamethasone 20 mg on day 1. Endpoints included complete response (no emesis, no rescue medication), no emesis, no nausea and complete protection in cycle 1.
cards.result: A significantly higher proportion of the rolapitant group than the control group achieved complete response in the overall phase (0–120 hours; 80.2% vs 64.6%; P<.001) and in the delayed phase (>24–120 hours; 82.3% vs 65.6%; P<.001). Superior responses were also observed for no emesis, no nausea and complete protection in the overall and delayed phases, and for time to first emesis or rescue medication. The incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: This is a post-hoc subgroup of a trial whose parent population mixed moderately emetogenic and anthracycline–cyclophosphamide regimens — the 15.6-point absolute gain is the best single estimate for carboplatin, but subgroup estimates tend to flatter; the meta-analysis card is the check.
cards.source: Hesketh PJ et al. Efficacy of the neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist rolapitant in preventing nausea and vomiting in patients receiving carboplatin-based chemotherapy. Cancer. 2016. PMID: 27176138. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Weinstein 2018 (PN031): in 1,000 patients on non-AC moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, single-dose fosaprepitant gave complete response of 76–80% in delayed and overall phases, with the larger effect in carboplatin-based therapy
cards.summary: Weinstein 2018 (PN031): in 1,000 patients on non-AC moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, single-dose fosaprepitant gave complete response of 76–80% in delayed and overall phases, with the larger effect in carboplatin-based therapy
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial exploratory analysis (PN031, Weinstein 2018)
cards.people: Exploratory analysis of a randomised, double-blind phase III trial (PN031) of 1,000 adults scheduled to receive non-anthracycline-and-cyclophosphamide (non-AC) moderately emetogenic chemotherapy on day 1, randomly assigned 1:1 to a single-dose 150 mg intravenous fosaprepitant regimen or a control regimen; both regimens included dexamethasone and ondansetron on day 1, with ondansetron continuing through day 3 in the control arm only. Most subjects received single-day regimens (70.6%), mainly carboplatin-based (67.6%).
cards.result: Complete response (no vomiting and no rescue medication) with fosaprepitant was consistent (76–80%) during the delayed and overall phases in carboplatin-based and non-carboplatin-based subgroups and in single-day and multiple-day subgroups. Treatment effects favoured fosaprepitant more for carboplatin-based vs non-carboplatin-based therapy in the delayed phase (14.1 vs 6.5 percentage points; P=0.06), and for single-day vs multiple-day regimens in the delayed (13.2 vs 3.2 points; P=0.02) and overall phases (12.8 vs 4.0 points; P=0.06). The primary trial report established that fosaprepitant improved prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in this population.
cards.watchOut: This card is the trial's exploratory factor analysis, not its primary report: it shows where the benefit concentrates (carboplatin, single-day regimens) rather than re-proving the headline effect, and several of its subgroup contrasts sit at P=0.06.
cards.source: Weinstein C et al. Evaluation of factors contributing to the response to fosaprepitant in a heterogeneous, moderately emetogenic chemotherapy population: an exploratory analysis of a randomized phase III trial. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2018. PMID: 29808377. Registry ID: NCT01594749. cards.headline: Zhang 2018: across 10 moderately-emetogenic trials (2,928 patients), the NK1 triple regimen improved complete response (relative risk 1.14) — significant for carboplatin-based, not oxaliplatin-based, chemotherapy
cards.summary: Zhang 2018: across 10 moderately-emetogenic trials (2,928 patients), the NK1 triple regimen improved complete response (relative risk 1.14) — significant for carboplatin-based, not oxaliplatin-based, chemotherapy
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 10 trials involving 2,928 cancer patients on moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, comparing neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist (NK-1RA)-based triple regimens with conventional two-drug (duplex) regimens; results were analysed separately for pure moderately emetogenic regimens, carboplatin-based regimens and oxaliplatin-based regimens, for complete response and no significant nausea.
cards.result: The NK-1RA triple regimen showed significantly better complete responses than the duplex regimen in the overall phase (relative risk 1.14, 95% CI 1.05–1.24 — a relative measure), the acute phase (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 1.00–1.04) and the delayed phase (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23), with similar results for no significant nausea. Subgroup analyses showed superior antiemetic efficacy significantly in carboplatin-based chemotherapy, instead of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. The authors recommend NK-1RA use in carboplatin-based chemotherapy, not oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative risk of 1.14 is a modest relative gain — its absolute value depends on the control complete-response rate (about 65% in the carboplatin trial carded here, where it was worth ~15 points) — and the oxaliplatin subgroup's null is part of the answer, not a footnote.
cards.source: Zhang Y et al. Optimal prophylaxis of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting for moderately emetogenic chemotherapy: a meta-analysis. Future oncology (London, England). 2018. PMID: 30019968. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: adding an NK1 antagonist improves complete response in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy — LIKELY benefit, concentrated in carboplatin-based regimens
cards.summary: Synthesis: adding an NK1 antagonist improves complete response in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy — LIKELY benefit, concentrated in carboplatin-based regimens
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 carboplatin subgroup analysis (Hesketh 2016, 401 patients), one phase 3 trial exploratory analysis (PN031, 1,000 patients) and one meta-analysis of 10 trials (2,928 patients). Total carded participants exceed 4,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The highly emetogenic/cisplatin slice is homed on pack #3420 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Complete response rose from 64.6% to 80.2% with rolapitant in carboplatin patients; fosaprepitant gave 76–80% complete response in delayed/overall phases with the largest effects in carboplatin and single-day regimens; and the pooled complete-response relative risk was 1.14 (95% CI 1.05–1.24), significant for carboplatin-based but not oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adding an NK1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone improves vomiting control in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, with the clearest benefit in carboplatin-based treatment.
cards.watchOut: 'Moderately emetogenic' is a wide band: the carded benefit is a carboplatin story. Extending this stamp to oxaliplatin-based or other lower-risk moderately emetogenic regimens would go beyond the evidence carded here.

shelves.title: Olanzapine 5 mg vs 10 mg in highly emetogenic chemotherapy (PARTIAL completion of live #769): similar complete response in the one direct trial and pooled dose literature, less sedation at the lower dose
shelves.question: In adults receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, is olanzapine 5 mg as effective as 10 mg for preventing nausea with less sedation?
shelves.mesh: Antiemetics · Antineoplastic Agents · Dexamethasone · Emetics · Humans · Nausea · Neurokinin-1 Receptor Antagonists · Olanzapine · Vomiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit — 5 mg appears as effective, with less sedation) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #769 homes adding olanzapine to triple prophylaxis (10 mg in Navari 2016; 5 mg in J-FORCE) and those placebo-controlled trials are not re-carded here; this shelf takes only the 5 mg vs 10 mg head-to-head slice. The one direct randomised comparison (Sukauichai 2022, 140 patients on high-dose cisplatin or doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide, without an NK1 antagonist in the backbone) found overall complete response of 58.6% on 5 mg vs 62.9% on 10 mg, meeting its (wide, −25%) non-inferiority margin, with no difference in adverse events including somnolence. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the dose literature (Wang 2021) concluded 5 mg may be as effective as 10 mg in highly and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, with a sedative effect statistically and clinically lower at 5 mg than 10 mg, while cautioning that fewer 5 mg studies make the data uncertain. Supportive but indirect: a phase 3 non-inferiority trial of an even lower dose (Bajpai 2024, 267 patients analysed) found olanzapine 2.5 mg non-inferior to 10 mg for complete control (45% vs 44%) with far less daytime somnolence (any grade 65% vs 90%; severe on day 1, 5% vs 40%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: 5 mg appears as effective as 10 mg for nausea and vomiting control, with less sedation — POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the single direct 5-vs-10 trial is small with a wide non-inferiority margin, and the sedation advantage at exactly 5 mg rests substantially on pooled and indirect evidence.

cards.headline: Sukauichai 2022: in the direct 5 mg vs 10 mg randomised trial (140 patients), overall complete response was 58.6% vs 62.9% — non-inferior on a wide −25% margin, with no difference in somnolence
cards.summary: Sukauichai 2022: in the direct 5 mg vs 10 mg randomised trial (140 patients), overall complete response was 58.6% vs 62.9% — non-inferior on a wide −25% margin, with no difference in somnolence
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Sukauichai 2022, olanzapine 5 mg vs 10 mg)
cards.people: 140 patients receiving high-dose cisplatin or doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (high emetic risk chemotherapy) randomised double-blind to olanzapine 5 mg (n=70) or 10 mg (n=70) for prophylaxis of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, without a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist in the regimen; non-inferiority was defined as the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the complete-response difference not falling below −25%.
cards.result: The complete response rate in the overall phase was 58.6% on 5 mg vs 62.9% on 10 mg (95% CI for the difference −20.4 to 11.8). Complete response in the acute phase was 81.4% vs 74.3% (95% CI −6.6 to 20.8) and in the delayed phase 66.7% vs 76.1% (95% CI −23.5 to 6.3). No-nausea rates were similar in the acute (70.0% vs 68.6%), delayed (45.7% vs 48.6%) and overall phases (43.5% vs 47.9%). The rate of adverse events including somnolence was not different between the 5 mg and 10 mg groups. The authors conclude the two dosage levels did not differ in efficacy or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A −25% non-inferiority margin is very wide: this trial excludes only a large inferiority of 5 mg, its confidence interval (−20.4 to 11.8 points) still allows 5 mg to be meaningfully worse, and it found no somnolence difference — the 'less sedation' half of the question is not proven by this trial.
cards.source: Sukauichai S et al. Efficacy of Olanzapine 5 mg versus 10 mg for the Prophylaxis of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting in Patients Receiving High Emetic Risk Chemotherapy without Neurokinin-1 Receptor Antagonist. Asian Pacific journal of cancer prevention : APJCP. 2022. PMID: 35763658. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial (sukauichai 2022, olanzapine 5 mg vs 10 mg) 140 patients receiving high-dose cisplatin or doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (high emetic risk chemotherapy) randomised double-blind to olanzapine 5 mg (n=70) or 10 mg (n=70) for prophylaxis of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, without a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist in the regimen; non-inferiority was defined as the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the complete-response difference not falling below −25%. the complete response rate in the overall phase was 58.6% on 5 mg vs 62.9% on 10 mg (95% ci for the difference −20.4 to 11.8). complete response in the acute phase was 81.4% vs 74.3% (95% ci −6.6 to 20.8) and in the delayed phase 66.7% vs 76.1% (95% ci −23.5 to 6.3). no-nausea rates were similar in the acute (70.0% vs 68.6%), delayed (45.7% vs 48.6%) and overall phases (43.5% vs 47.9%). the rate of adverse events including somnolence was not different between the 5 mg and 10 mg groups. the authors conclude the two dosage levels did not differ in efficacy or adverse events. a −25% non-inferiority margin is very wide: this trial excludes only a large inferiority of 5 mg, its confidence interval (−20.4 to 11.8 points) still allows 5 mg to be meaningfully worse, and it found no somnolence difference — the 'less sedation' half of the question is not proven by this trial. sukauichai s et al. efficacy of olanzapine 5 mg versus 10 mg for the prophylaxis of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in patients receiving high emetic risk chemotherapy without neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist. asian pacific journal of cancer prevention : apjcp. 2022. pmid: 35763658. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antiemetics · antineoplastic agents · dexamethasone · emetics · humans · nausea · neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists · olanzapine · vomiting

cards.headline: Wang 2021: pooling the dose literature, 5 mg olanzapine may be as effective as 10 mg — and its sedative effect was statistically and clinically lower than 10 mg
cards.summary: Wang 2021: pooling the dose literature, 5 mg olanzapine may be as effective as 10 mg — and its sedative effect was statistically and clinically lower than 10 mg
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of olanzapine dose studies (Wang 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (search to 18 April 2021) of olanzapine dose studies in chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, including nine studies reporting 10 mg olanzapine and three studies reporting 5 mg, in highly emetogenic and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy settings; endpoints were complete response and complete control by phase, and somnolence by CTCAE criteria, with a 10% absolute risk difference as the threshold for clinical significance (MASCC/ESMO).
cards.result: At 10 mg in highly emetogenic chemotherapy, all six efficacy endpoints were statistically and clinically better than control; at 5 mg in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, four endpoints had statistical and clinical advantages. The sedative effects of both 10 mg and 5 mg olanzapine were statistically more significant than control, and the sedative effect of the 10 mg group was more significant than that of the 5 mg group, both statistically and clinically. The authors conclude 5 mg olanzapine may be as effective as 10 mg for patients with highly and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy with a lower sedative effect, while noting fewer 5 mg studies have led to uncertain data and calling for more randomised trials of 5 mg.
cards.watchOut: The 5 mg vs 10 mg contrast here is largely indirect — different studies at each dose against their own controls, with only three 5 mg studies — so 'may be as effective' is the authors' own appropriately hedged wording, and this shelf keeps it.
cards.source: Wang DY et al. The Balance Between the Effectiveness and Safety for Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting of Different Doses of Olanzapine (10 mg Versus 5 mg): A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Frontiers in oncology. 2021. PMID: 34660273. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Bajpai 2024: in a phase 3 trial, even 2.5 mg olanzapine was non-inferior to 10 mg for complete control (45% vs 44%) — with daytime somnolence in 65% vs 90% and severe day-1 somnolence in 5% vs 40%
cards.summary: Bajpai 2024: in a phase 3 trial, even 2.5 mg olanzapine was non-inferior to 10 mg for complete control (45% vs 44%) — with daytime somnolence in 65% vs 90% and severe day-1 somnolence in 5% vs 40%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Bajpai 2024, olanzapine 2.5 mg vs 10 mg)
cards.people: 275 patients aged 13–75 years with solid tumours receiving doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide or high-dose cisplatin, randomised at a single tertiary centre in India to low-dose (2.5 mg) or standard-dose (10.0 mg) oral olanzapine daily for 4 days with a triple antiemetic regimen; 267 patients (132 on 2.5 mg, 135 on 10 mg) were in the modified intention-to-treat population. The primary endpoint was complete control (no emetic episodes, no rescue medications, no or mild nausea) in the overall phase (0–120 hours); daytime somnolence was the safety endpoint of interest. Non-inferiority margin 10%. FLAG: this trial tests 2.5 mg, not 5 mg — it is carded as dose-direction evidence, not as a direct 5-vs-10 comparison.
cards.result: Complete control in the overall phase occurred in 59 of 132 patients (45%) on 2.5 mg vs 59 of 135 (44%) on 10 mg (difference −1.0%, one-sided 95% CI −100.0 to 9.0; P=0.87), meeting non-inferiority. Daytime somnolence of any grade was significantly less frequent on 2.5 mg (86 of 132, 65%) than on 10 mg (121 of 135, 90%; P<0.0001), as was severe-grade somnolence on day 1 (5% vs 40%; P<0.0001). The authors conclude 2.5 mg is non-inferior to 10 mg in antiemetic efficacy with reduced daytime somnolence.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, 94% female and 91% breast cancer — and the dose is 2.5 mg, a step below the 5 mg this shelf asks about; it shows the dose–sedation gradient and that efficacy survives dose reduction, but it does not by itself settle 5 mg vs 10 mg.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 5 mg olanzapine appears as effective as 10 mg in the one direct trial and the pooled dose literature, with less sedation — but the direct trial is small and wide-margined, so POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: 5 mg olanzapine appears as effective as 10 mg in the one direct trial and the pooled dose literature, with less sedation — but the direct trial is small and wide-margined, so POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one direct randomised 5 mg vs 10 mg trial (Sukauichai 2022, 140 patients), one systematic review and meta-analysis of the dose literature (Wang 2021; nine 10 mg studies, three 5 mg studies), and one phase 3 trial of 2.5 mg vs 10 mg (Bajpai 2024, 267 analysed) carded as dose-direction evidence. Total carded participants exceed 400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The placebo-controlled addition question (Navari 10 mg; J-FORCE 5 mg) is homed on live shelf #769 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Overall complete response was 58.6% (5 mg) vs 62.9% (10 mg) in the direct trial, within its wide non-inferiority margin; the meta-analysis found 5 mg may be as effective as 10 mg with a statistically and clinically lower sedative effect; and 2.5 mg was non-inferior to 10 mg for complete control (45% vs 44%) with much less somnolence (65% vs 90% any grade). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): olanzapine 5 mg appears as effective as 10 mg for preventing nausea and vomiting in highly emetogenic chemotherapy, with less sedation — pending a larger direct trial with a tighter margin.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as proof of equivalence: the direct trial's interval still allows a clinically important deficit at 5 mg, and its backbone omitted an NK1 antagonist, whereas modern four-drug prophylaxis (the setting of live #769) includes one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sukauichai S et al. Asian Pacific journal of cancer prevention : APJCP. 2022 (PMID: 35763658); Wang DY et al. Frontiers in oncology. 2021 (PMID: 34660273); Bajpai J et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2024 (PMID: 38224701).

shelves.title: Aspirin vs enoxaparin in myeloma on immunomodulatory drugs: no significant difference in two trials — 6.4% vs 5.0% and 2.27% vs 1.20%
shelves.question: In adults with multiple myeloma receiving immunomodulatory drugs, is aspirin prophylaxis as effective as low-molecular-weight heparin for preventing venous thromboembolism?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aspirin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology/mortality/prevention & control · Enoxaparin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Fibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Italy · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Myeloma/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Thalidomide/administration & dosage · Thromboembolism/etiology/mortality/prevention & control · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Warfarin/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. Two open-label randomised trials compare aspirin 100 mg/day with enoxaparin 40 mg/day head-to-head in myeloma on immunomodulatory drugs. Palumbo 2011 (thalidomide regimens, 659 analysed): the composite of serious thromboembolic events, acute cardiovascular events or sudden death was 6.4% on aspirin vs 5.0% on enoxaparin (absolute difference +1.3%, 95% CI −3.0 to 5.7). Larocca 2012 (lenalidomide regimens, 342 patients): venous thromboembolism 2.27% vs 1.20% (absolute difference 1.07%, 95% CI −1.69 to 3.83), with pulmonary embolism only on aspirin (1.70% vs 0%, three events). Neither difference is significant and both intervals are wide; a 51-trial pooling (9,069 patients) shows venous thromboembolism still occurs in 6.2% despite prophylaxis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: aspirin appears as effective as low-molecular-weight heparin in the lower-risk patients enrolled — not an equivalence proof, and not evidence for high-risk patients.

cards.headline: Palumbo 2011: in 659 myeloma patients on thalidomide regimens, the composite of serious thromboembolism, cardiovascular events or sudden death was 6.4% on aspirin vs 5.0% on enoxaparin — no significant difference (absolute difference +1.3%)
cards.summary: Palumbo 2011: in 659 myeloma patients on thalidomide regimens, the composite of serious thromboembolism, cardiovascular events or sudden death was 6.4% on aspirin vs 5.0% on enoxaparin — no significant difference (absolute difference +1.3%)
cards.people: 667 patients with previously untreated multiple myeloma receiving thalidomide-containing regimens, with no indication or contraindication for a specific prophylaxis, randomised open-label to aspirin 100 mg/day, fixed low-dose warfarin 1.25 mg/day, or enoxaparin 40 mg/day; 659 analysed over the first 6 months.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint occurred in 6.5% overall: 6.4% on aspirin, 8.2% on warfarin and 5.0% on low-molecular-weight heparin. Versus enoxaparin, the absolute difference was +1.3% for aspirin (95% CI −3.0 to 5.7; P = .544) and +3.2% for warfarin (95% CI −1.5 to 7.8; P = .183). Three major (0.5%) and 10 minor (1.5%) bleeding episodes occurred across the trial. The authors concluded aspirin and warfarin showed similar efficacy to enoxaparin, except in elderly patients, where warfarin was less effective than enoxaparin.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the composite mixes thromboembolism with cardiovascular events and sudden death; event counts are small, so the confidence interval for aspirin vs enoxaparin (−3.0 to +5.7 percentage points) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful difference in either direction.
cards.source: Palumbo A et al. Aspirin, warfarin, or enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis in patients with multiple myeloma treated with thalidomide: a phase III, open-label, randomized trial. cards.headline: Larocca 2012: in 342 newly diagnosed myeloma patients on lenalidomide, venous thromboembolism was 2.27% on aspirin vs 1.20% on enoxaparin (absolute difference 1.07%, P = .452) — but pulmonary embolism occurred only on aspirin (1.70% vs 0%)
cards.summary: Larocca 2012: in 342 newly diagnosed myeloma patients on lenalidomide, venous thromboembolism was 2.27% on aspirin vs 1.20% on enoxaparin (absolute difference 1.07%, P = .452) — but pulmonary embolism occurred only on aspirin (1.70% vs 0%)
cards.people: 342 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma and no indication or contraindication for a specific prophylaxis, randomised open-label (substudy of a phase 3 trial) to aspirin 100 mg/day (n = 176) or enoxaparin 40 mg/day (n = 166) during lenalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone induction and melphalan–prednisone–lenalidomide consolidation. Registry ID: NCT00551928.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism occurred in 2.27% on aspirin and 1.20% on enoxaparin (absolute difference 1.07%, 95% CI −1.69 to 3.83; P = .452) — no significant difference. Pulmonary embolism was observed in 1.70% on aspirin and in no patient on enoxaparin. No arterial thrombosis, acute cardiovascular events, sudden deaths or major haemorrhagic complications were reported. The authors concluded aspirin could be an effective, less expensive alternative to enoxaparin in lenalidomide-treated patients at low thromboembolic risk.
cards.watchOut: Only six venous thromboembolism events occurred in total, and the enrolled patients were selected as low thromboembolic risk; the pulmonary-embolism imbalance (3 vs 0 by the printed percentages) is too small to settle but is the one signal favouring enoxaparin.
cards.source: Larocca A et al. Aspirin or enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis for patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with lenalidomide. Blood. 2012. PMID: 21835953. cards.headline: Chakraborty 2020: pooling 51 lenalidomide trials (9,069 patients), venous thromboembolism still occurred in 6.2% despite thromboprophylaxis — prophylaxis choice is not the whole story
cards.summary: Chakraborty 2020: pooling 51 lenalidomide trials (9,069 patients), venous thromboembolism still occurred in 6.2% despite thromboprophylaxis — prophylaxis choice is not the whole story
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 trials (Chakraborty 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 51 phase 1–3 trials (9,069 patients) of lenalidomide-based regimens in newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory myeloma in which thromboprophylaxis was used; the most common agents were aspirin, low-molecular-weight heparin or warfarin, given by risk stratification or investigator discretion.
cards.result: The pooled venous thromboembolism incidence despite prophylaxis was 6.2% (95% CI 5.4–7.1), or 1.2 events per 100 patient-cycles (95% CI 0.9–1.7). Risk was lowest with lenalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone (0.2 events per 100 patient-cycles) and lenalidomide maintenance (0.0), and higher when proteasome inhibitors were added (1.3 per 100 patient-cycles). The authors conclude that despite adequate thromboprophylaxis, lenalidomide-based regimens carry a substantial residual venous thromboembolism risk.
cards.watchOut: This pooling estimates incidence by regimen, not by prophylaxis agent — it does not compare aspirin with enoxaparin head-to-head, so it cannot adjudicate between them; it is carded to show the residual risk both direct trials were trying to prevent.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised head-to-head trials find no significant aspirin–enoxaparin difference, on few events, in selected lower-risk patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised head-to-head trials find no significant aspirin–enoxaparin difference, on few events, in selected lower-risk patients
cards.people: The carded evidence: two open-label randomised trials (Palumbo 2011, 659 analysed, thalidomide regimens; Larocca 2012, 342 patients, lenalidomide regimens) plus a 51-trial incidence meta-analysis (9,069 patients). Total carded participants exceed 10,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Aspirin versus enoxaparin: composite serious events 6.4% vs 5.0% (absolute difference +1.3%, 95% CI −3.0 to 5.7) in Palumbo, and venous thromboembolism 2.27% vs 1.20% (absolute difference 1.07%, 95% CI −1.69 to 3.83) in Larocca — neither significant, both with intervals wide enough to include meaningful differences. The one directional signal is pulmonary embolism in Larocca (1.70% aspirin vs 0% enoxaparin, on three events). Despite any prophylaxis, pooled venous thromboembolism incidence on lenalidomide regimens remains 6.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: aspirin appears as effective as enoxaparin for preventing venous thromboembolism in the lower-risk patients these trials enrolled, but the evidence is two open-label trials with few events — not an equivalence proof for high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Both trials excluded patients with an indication or contraindication for a specific agent and Larocca explicitly enrolled low-risk patients; do not read this shelf as covering high-risk myeloma (previous venous thromboembolism, high-dose dexamethasone, multi-agent chemotherapy), where guidelines favour anticoagulation.

shelves.title: Catheter thrombosis prophylaxis in cancer: venography trials positive, the symptomatic-event trial and pooling null — a split
shelves.question: In adults with cancer and a central venous catheter, does prophylactic low-dose anticoagulation prevent catheter-related thrombosis versus no prophylaxis?

shelves.balance: SPLIT (endpoint/era) — printed on the face. This shelf covers systemic prophylaxis only; catheter site choice (pack #3159, 3SITES) and lock solutions (pack #3219) are different questions and are not re-carded here. Two small early trials using routine venography were strongly positive: Bern 1990 (warfarin 1 mg; thrombosis 4/42 vs 15/40 among completers) and Monreal 1996 (dalteparin 2,500 IU; 1/16 vs 8/13, stopped early at 29 patients). The largest trial, Couban 2005 (255 patients, placebo-controlled, symptomatic endpoint), found warfarin 1 mg made no difference (4.6% vs 4.0%), and a meta-analysis of 8 trials (1,428 patients) found no significant pooled benefit (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.31–1.13) and no bleeding penalty. PROPOSED SPLIT: venographic thrombosis falls in small early trials; symptomatic benefit is unproven — routine systemic prophylaxis is not supported by the symptomatic-outcome evidence.

cards.headline: Bern 1990: in the 82 patients completing venography, thrombosis occurred in 4 of 42 (about 10%) on warfarin 1 mg daily vs 15 of 40 (37.5%) without it (P < .001)
cards.summary: Bern 1990: in the 82 patients completing venography, thrombosis occurred in 4 of 42 (about 10%) on warfarin 1 mg daily vs 15 of 40 (37.5%) without it (P < .001)
cards.people: 121 patients with cancer at risk of thrombosis from chronic indwelling central venous catheters, randomised prospectively to warfarin 1 mg daily (starting 3 days before insertion, for 90 days) or no warfarin; venograms at symptoms or at 90 days; 82 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Of those completing the study, venogram-proven thrombosis occurred in 4 of 42 patients on warfarin and 15 of 40 patients not receiving warfarin (P < .001); all 4 warfarin-group thromboses were symptomatic, as were 10 of the 15 in the control group. The 1 mg dose produced no measurable change in the coagulation values assayed, except in occasional patients who had become anorectic. The authors concluded very low doses of warfarin can protect against catheter thrombosis without inducing a haemorrhagic state.
cards.watchOut: Only 82 of 121 randomised patients completed the study, the endpoint is venographic (mostly asymptomatic) thrombosis rather than symptomatic events, and there was no placebo — a small, old, single-centre-era result that later, larger trials did not reproduce on symptomatic outcomes.
cards.source: Bern MM et al. Very low doses of warfarin can prevent thrombosis in central venous catheters. A randomized prospective trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1990. PMID: 2178534. cards.headline: Monreal 1996: dalteparin 2,500 IU daily cut venographic upper-extremity thrombosis from 8 of 13 (62%) to 1 of 16 (6%) — in a trial stopped early after only 29 patients
cards.summary: Monreal 1996: dalteparin 2,500 IU daily cut venographic upper-extremity thrombosis from 8 of 13 (62%) to 1 of 16 (6%) — in a trial stopped early after only 29 patients
cards.people: Cancer patients receiving a long-term subclavian Port-a-Cath catheter, randomised open-label to dalteparin (Fragmin, named in the publication) 2,500 IU subcutaneously once daily for 90 days or no prophylaxis; routine venography at 90 days or at symptoms. Recruitment was terminated early on the ethics committee's recommendation after 29 patients.
cards.result: Deep vein thrombosis developed in 1 of 16 patients (6%) on dalteparin and 8 of 13 patients (62%) without prophylaxis (relative risk 6.75 for no prophylaxis, 95% CI 1.05–43.58; P = .002). No bleeding complications developed. The authors concluded dalteparin at this dose was effective and safe in these patients.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine patients and nine events, stopped early — early stopping on a large apparent effect in a tiny trial is the classic recipe for an exaggerated estimate, and the endpoint was again routine venography, not symptomatic thrombosis.
cards.source: Monreal M et al. Upper extremity deep venous thrombosis in cancer patients with venous access devices--prophylaxis with a low molecular weight heparin (Fragmin). Thrombosis and haemostasis. 1996. PMID: 8815570. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Couban 2005: in 255 patients, warfarin 1 mg daily made no difference to symptomatic catheter thrombosis — 4.6% vs 4.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.20)
cards.summary: Couban 2005: in 255 patients, warfarin 1 mg daily made no difference to symptomatic catheter thrombosis — 4.6% vs 4.0% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.20)
cards.people: 255 patients with cancer requiring a central venous catheter for at least 7 days, randomised in a multicentre placebo-controlled trial to warfarin 1 mg daily or placebo; primary outcome symptomatic catheter-associated thrombosis.
cards.result: Symptomatic catheter-associated thrombosis occurred in 6 of 130 patients (4.6%) on warfarin and 5 of 125 (4.0%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.37–3.94) — the treatment made no difference. Warfarin also made no difference to catheter life span or premature catheter removals (25.4% on warfarin vs 23.2% on control), and major bleeding was 0% on warfarin vs 2% on control (P = .5). The authors note the low symptomatic event rate means a much larger trial would be required to address the question definitively. The authors concluded low-dose warfarin did not reduce symptomatic catheter-associated thrombosis.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest and only placebo-controlled trial here, and the only one powered around symptomatic events — the outcome patients feel. Its null result on the same 1 mg warfarin dose Bern tested is why the early venographic findings cannot be read at face value.
cards.source: Couban S et al. Randomized placebo-controlled study of low-dose warfarin for the prevention of central venous catheter-associated thrombosis in patients with cancer. cards.headline: Chaukiyal 2008: pooling 8 trials (1,428 patients), prophylactic anticoagulation made no significant difference to catheter-related thrombosis (pooled relative risk 0.59, CI 0.31–1.13) or bleeding
cards.summary: Chaukiyal 2008: pooling 8 trials (1,428 patients), prophylactic anticoagulation made no significant difference to catheter-related thrombosis (pooled relative risk 0.59, CI 0.31–1.13) or bleeding
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Chaukiyal 2008)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (1,428 patients with cancer and central venous devices) of warfarin, unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin versus placebo or no prophylaxis, searched to June 2006.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in catheter-related thrombosis for warfarin vs placebo (3 trials, 425 patients; relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.24–2.35), heparin vs placebo (4 trials, 886 patients; relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.18–1.20), or all anticoagulants pooled (7 trials, 1,311 patients; relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.31–1.13) — the treatment made no difference on the pooled estimate — and no significant difference in overall bleeding (relative risk 1.24, 95% CI 0.84–1.82). Statistical heterogeneity was substantial (I² > 50%). The authors conclude thromboprophylaxis provides no benefit in this setting while causing no clear harm.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials mix agents, doses and venographic versus symptomatic endpoints with substantial heterogeneity — the pooling summarises a genuinely split literature rather than resolving it, which is why this shelf is stamped SPLIT rather than null.
cards.source: Chaukiyal P et al. Thromboprophylaxis in cancer patients with central venous catheters. A systematic review and meta-analysis. Thrombosis and haemostasis. 2008. PMID: 18217132. cards.headline: Synthesis: the split is endpoint and era — small early venography trials were strongly positive; the large symptomatic-event trial and the pooled estimate are null
cards.summary: Synthesis: the split is endpoint and era — small early venography trials were strongly positive; the large symptomatic-event trial and the pooled estimate are null
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small early randomised trials using routine venography (Bern 1990, 82 completers; Monreal 1996, 29 patients, stopped early), one large placebo-controlled trial of symptomatic thrombosis (Couban 2005, 255 patients), and one meta-analysis of 8 trials (1,428 patients).
cards.result: Bern found venographic thrombosis in about 10% vs 37.5% and Monreal in 6% vs 62%, both favouring prophylaxis; Couban found symptomatic thrombosis in 4.6% on warfarin vs 4.0% on placebo (the treatment made no difference), and the pooled relative risk across agents was 0.59 (95% CI 0.31–1.13), not significant, with no bleeding penalty (relative risk 1.24, CI crossing 1). PROPOSED SPLIT (endpoint/era): prophylactic low-dose anticoagulation reduces venographically detected thrombosis in small early trials, but no benefit on symptomatic catheter thrombosis has been shown in the largest trial or in pooling — routine systemic prophylaxis is not supported by the symptomatic-outcome evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote Bern's or Monreal's venographic percentages as if they were symptomatic event rates: symptomatic thrombosis in the placebo-controlled trial was about 4% in both arms, an order of magnitude below the venographic rates.

shelves.title: Romiplostim in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (PARTIAL of pack #2819): counts corrected 93% vs 12.5%; resumption data observational
shelves.question: In adults with chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, does romiplostim allow chemotherapy to continue on schedule versus dose delay or reduction?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Blood Platelets/drug effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · New York City · Platelet Count · Prospective Studies · Receptors, Fc/therapeutic use · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Thrombocytopenia/chemically induced/diagnosis/drug therapy · Thrombopoietin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence labelled) — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of pack #2819 (the avatrombopag chemotherapy-induced-thrombocytopenia trial); the romiplostim agent slice is built here, with no #2819 study re-carded. Soff 2019's phase 2 trial randomised only 23 patients (platelet correction 93% vs 12.5%, P < .001); its resumption data (44 patients resuming, 6.8% recurrent delay/reduction) are from an uncontrolled extension. The schedule evidence beyond that is observational: a 173-patient retrospective multicentre cohort (79% avoided dose reduction/delay; 89% avoided platelet transfusion) and a 20-patient retrospective series (14 of 15 resuming patients completing at least two on-schedule cycles). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: romiplostim corrects the count and, in uncontrolled data, lets most patients resume and continue chemotherapy on schedule.

cards.summary: Soff 2019: in the randomised phase, platelet correction within 3 weeks occurred in 14 of 15 patients (93%) on romiplostim vs 1 of 8 (12.5%) on observation (P < .001); 44 patients then resumed chemotherapy, with recurrent dose delay/reduction in only 3 (6.8%)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised trial with single-arm extension (Soff 2019)
cards.people: Phase 2 trial in patients with solid tumours and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/µL for at least 4 weeks despite chemotherapy delay or dose reduction): 23 patients randomised to weekly titrated romiplostim (target ≥100,000/µL) or untreated observation, plus a further 37 treated in a single-arm romiplostim phase (52 romiplostim-treated in total). Mean platelet count at enrolment 62,000/µL. Registry ID: NCT02052882.
cards.result: In the randomised phase, 14 of 15 romiplostim patients (93%) corrected their platelet count within 3 weeks vs 1 of 8 controls (12.5%; P < .001). Across all 52 romiplostim-treated patients the mean count at 2 weeks was 141,000/µL, vs a mean 57,000/µL at 3 weeks in the observation group. Forty-four patients who achieved correction resumed chemotherapy with weekly romiplostim, and only 3 (6.8%) had recurrent chemotherapy reduction or delay from isolated thrombocytopenia.
cards.watchOut: The randomised comparison is only 23 patients; the chemotherapy-resumption figure (44 patients, 6.8% recurrence) comes from the uncontrolled extension, so it shows feasibility on treatment, not a randomised effect on scheduling.
cards.source: Soff GA et al. Romiplostim Treatment of Chemotherapy-Induced Thrombocytopenia. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2019. cards.headline: Al-Samkari 2021 (observational): in 173 patients treated on romiplostim pathways at 4 centres, 71% responded, 79% avoided chemotherapy dose reduction or delay, and 89% avoided platelet transfusion
cards.summary: Al-Samkari 2021 (observational): in 173 patients treated on romiplostim pathways at 4 centres, 71% responded, 79% avoided chemotherapy dose reduction or delay, and 89% avoided platelet transfusion
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre study (observational) of 173 patients (153 solid tumours, 20 lymphoma or myeloma) with chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia treated on institutional romiplostim pathways at 4 US centres; 170 (98%) received additional chemotherapy on romiplostim (median 4 further cycles).
cards.result: 71% of patients achieved a romiplostim response (median on-treatment platelet count ≥75 × 10⁹/L and ≥30 × 10⁹/L above baseline); in solid-tumour patients, 79% avoided chemotherapy dose reductions/treatment delays and 89% avoided platelet transfusions, and median platelet count rose from 60 to 116 × 10⁹/L (P < .001). Weekly dosing beat intracycle dosing on response and on dose reduction/delay (incidence rate ratio 3.00, 95% CI 1.30–6.91). Bleeding rates were lower than historical cohorts and thrombosis rates were not elevated; response was blunted (10%) in non-myeloid haematologic malignancy with bone marrow involvement. The authors conclude romiplostim was safe and effective for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia in most solid-tumour patients.
cards.watchOut: Observational and uncontrolled: patients were selected for romiplostim pathways at expert centres, and comparisons with 'historical cohorts' for bleeding are not randomised comparisons — this card is labelled observational and caps the shelf's stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Al-Samkari H et al. A multicenter study of romiplostim for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia in solid tumors and hematologic malignancies. Haematologica. 2021. PMID: 32499239. cards.headline: Parameswaran 2014 (observational): in a 20-patient series with protracted thrombocytopenia, 19 reached platelets ≥100 × 10⁹/L and 15 resumed chemotherapy, 14 of them completing at least two further cycles on schedule
cards.summary: Parameswaran 2014 (observational): in a 20-patient series with protracted thrombocytopenia, 19 reached platelets ≥100 × 10⁹/L and 15 resumed chemotherapy, 14 of them completing at least two further cycles on schedule
cards.people: Retrospective series (observational) of 20 patients with protracted, dose-limiting chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia treated with weekly romiplostim at a single cancer centre, 2010–2012, starting at 1–2 µg/kg with weekly escalation until platelet recovery (≥100 × 10⁹/L).
cards.result: Romiplostim improved platelet counts in all 20 patients; 19 of 20 reached ≥100 × 10⁹/L, at a mean dose of 2.9 µg/kg, and 16 achieved recovery by 2 weeks. Fifteen patients resumed cytotoxic chemotherapy with continued romiplostim and 14 tolerated at least two subsequent cycles on schedule without recurrence of dose-limiting thrombocytopenia (sepsis prevented continuation in one). Three deep vein thromboses occurred, which the authors note is within anticipated thrombosis rates for patients with active cancer on chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, no control group, single centre: this series can show that resumption happened on romiplostim, not that romiplostim caused the difference versus dose delay or reduction — the comparison the question poses is answered directly only by the small randomised phase of Soff 2019.
cards.source: Parameswaran R et al. Romiplostim for management of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2014. PMID: 24414994. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small randomised trial shows platelet correction; the 'chemotherapy on schedule' evidence beyond it is observational
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small randomised trial shows platelet correction; the 'chemotherapy on schedule' evidence beyond it is observational
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 2 trial (23 randomised patients plus a 37-patient single-arm extension), one retrospective multicentre cohort (173 patients, observational) and one retrospective series (20 patients, observational). This shelf is a PARTIAL completion of pack #2819 (the avatrombopag chemotherapy-induced-thrombocytopenia trial); the romiplostim agent slice is built here and no #2819 study is re-carded.
cards.result: Romiplostim corrected platelet counts within 3 weeks in 93% vs 12.5% in the randomised phase (P < .001). On continued weekly romiplostim, 44 extension patients resumed chemotherapy with recurrent thrombocytopenia-driven delay/reduction in 6.8%; observational cohorts report 79% avoiding dose reduction/delay and 14 of 15 resuming patients completing at least two on-schedule cycles. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence labelled): romiplostim allows most patients with persistent chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia to resume and continue chemotherapy — but only the platelet-correction step is randomised, and the schedule outcome rests on uncontrolled data.
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised trial of romiplostim powered on chemotherapy dose intensity, survival or bleeding; claims should stay at 'allows resumption/continuation in most treated patients' and not extend to cancer outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Soff GA et al. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2019 (PMID: 31545663); Al-Samkari H et al. Haematologica. 2021 (PMID: 32499239); Parameswaran R et al. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2014 (PMID: 24414994).

shelves.title: Corticosteroids for appetite and well-being in advanced cancer: short-term benefit in old placebo-controlled trials — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In adults with advanced cancer, do corticosteroids improve appetite and well-being in the short term versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Anxiety/drug therapy · Appetite/drug effects · Depression/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Evaluation · Female · Humans · Male · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/drug therapy/physiopathology/psychology · Nutrition Disorders/therapy · Pain/drug therapy · Palliative Care · Random Allocation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — printed on the face. GAP verified: the appetite homes cover megestrol (live #1790) and mirtazapine, not corticosteroids as the tested drug; the modern dexamethasone datasets are carded on live #1790 (2021 anorexia trial, dexamethasone arm) and live #1999 (2013 fatigue trial) and are not re-carded here. The free placebo-controlled evidence is old and modest: Bruera 1985 (40-patient crossover; appetite increased in 24/31 on methylprednisolone 32 mg, preferred over placebo by 74%) and Della Cuna 1989 (403 patients; quality-of-life scores improved, P < .05–.001, with an unexplained higher mortality in treated women, 40.0% vs 27.7%). A 55-trial systematic review counts corticosteroids among only two classes with supporting evidence for cancer anorexia, with mixed results and no settled dose or duration. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: short-term appetite and well-being improve — short horizon only, no weight or survival claim.

cards.headline: Bruera 1985: in a 40-patient double-blind crossover, methylprednisolone 32 mg/day increased appetite in 24 of 31 evaluable patients (77%) and activity in 21 of 31 (68%), and was preferred over placebo by 74%
cards.summary: Bruera 1985: in a 40-patient double-blind crossover, methylprednisolone 32 mg/day increased appetite in 24 of 31 evaluable patients (77%) and activity in 21 of 31 (68%), and was preferred over placebo by 74%
cards.people: 40 terminally ill cancer patients in a 14-day randomised, double-blind crossover trial of oral methylprednisolone 32 mg/day vs placebo, followed by 20 days of open methylprednisolone for all; endpoints included pain, psychiatric status, appetite, nutritional status, daily activity and performance; 31 patients were evaluable for the symptom comparisons printed in the record.
cards.result: Mean pain intensity was lower on methylprednisolone (36.8 ± 14 vs 57.7 ± 15 on a 0–100 visual analogue scale, P < .01). After the double-blind phase, appetite increased in 24 of 31 patients (77%) and daily activity in 21 of 31 (68%) on methylprednisolone; depression decreased in 22 of 31 (71%) and analgesic consumption in 16 of 28 (57%). Methylprednisolone was preferred over placebo by 23 of 31 patients (74%), and the investigator chose it over placebo in 22 of 31 cases (71%). No serious toxicity was found at this dose. The authors conclude methylprednisolone increases the comfort of terminally ill cancer patients.
cards.watchOut: A 1985 crossover of 40 patients with 31 evaluable, short 14-day phases and multiple symptom endpoints without a single prespecified appetite primary — supportive, small, old evidence; effects beyond a few weeks and on weight were not tested.
cards.source: Bruera E et al. Action of oral methylprednisolone in terminal cancer patients: a prospective randomized double-blind study. Cancer treatment reports. 1985. PMID: 2410117. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Della Cuna 1989: in 403 preterminal patients, intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg/day improved quality-of-life scores vs placebo (P < .05 to P < .001 across measures) — with a higher mortality rate in treated women (40.0% vs 27.7%) that the authors could not explain
cards.summary: Della Cuna 1989: in 403 preterminal patients, intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg/day improved quality-of-life scores vs placebo (P < .05 to P < .001 across measures) — with a higher mortality rate in treated women (40.0% vs 27.7%) that the authors could not explain
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Della Cuna / Methylprednisolone Preterminal Cancer Study Group 1989)
cards.people: 403 patients with preterminal cancer in a double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre study of methylprednisolone sodium succinate 125 mg/day intravenously for 8 weeks (207 treated, 196 placebo); quality of life assessed by the Nurses' Observational Scale for Inpatient Evaluation (NOSIE), the Linear Analog Self-Assessment Scale (LASA) and a Physicians' Global Evaluation.
cards.result: Methylprednisolone was significantly more effective than placebo in improving quality of life by change in NOSIE and LASA total scores (P < .05) and by the Physicians' Global Evaluation (P < .001). Mortality was similar in men (40.2% treated vs 35.5% placebo) and in treated women (40.0%), but was significantly lower in placebo-treated women (27.7%) than in their methylprednisolone-treated counterparts — a difference the authors state is unknown in cause and warrants further study.
cards.watchOut: The outcomes are composite quality-of-life scores, not appetite alone, the dose/route (125 mg/day intravenous) is far above modern palliative steroid practice, and the unexplained female mortality imbalance is a standing caution against reading this as a clean benefit.
cards.source: Della Cuna GR et al. Effect of methylprednisolone sodium succinate on quality of life in preterminal cancer patients: a placebo-controlled, multicenter study. The Methylprednisolone Preterminal Cancer Study Group. European journal of cancer & clinical oncology. 1989. PMID: 2698804. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yavuzsen 2005: across 55 randomised appetite-stimulant trials in cancer anorexia, corticosteroids were one of only two drug classes with evidence supporting use — with mixed results and no settled dose or duration
cards.summary: Yavuzsen 2005: across 55 randomised appetite-stimulant trials in cancer anorexia, corticosteroids were one of only two drug classes with evidence supporting use — with mixed results and no settled dose or duration
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials of appetite stimulants for cancer-related anorexia (55 studies meeting inclusion criteria), grading study quality across drug classes including progestins and corticosteroids. The record does not print a total participant number for the review: N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Only two drugs/classes had evidence to support their use for anorexia — progestins and corticosteroids — and there was strong evidence against hydrazine sulfate. Trial outcomes were mixed and populations heterogeneous, and the optimal dose, time to start and duration of treatment for many appetite stimulants remained unknown. The authors call for prospective randomised studies with universal outcome measures.
cards.watchOut: A class-level verdict over heterogeneous small trials, not a pooled effect size for appetite: it supports 'corticosteroids have some evidence' and simultaneously documents that the evidence is mixed and the regimen unsettled.
cards.source: Yavuzsen T et al. Systematic review of the treatment of cancer-associated anorexia and weight loss. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2005. PMID: 16293879. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: short-term appetite and well-being improve on corticosteroids in small old placebo-controlled trials — a real but weakly founded, short-horizon benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: short-term appetite and well-being improve on corticosteroids in small old placebo-controlled trials — a real but weakly founded, short-horizon benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 40-patient double-blind crossover trial (Bruera 1985), one 403-patient placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Della Cuna 1989), and one systematic review of 55 randomised appetite-stimulant trials (Yavuzsen 2005; total participant number not documented in its record). Note on scope: the two modern placebo-controlled dexamethasone datasets (the dexamethasone arm of the 2021 anorexia trial and the 2013 dexamethasone fatigue trial) are already carded on live #1790 and live #1999 respectively and are therefore not re-carded here; appetite homes for megestrol (live #1790) and mirtazapine likewise do not cover corticosteroids as the tested drug.
cards.result: Methylprednisolone increased appetite in 77% of evaluable patients in the crossover and improved quality-of-life scores vs placebo in the 403-patient trial, and the systematic review counts corticosteroids among only two classes with supporting evidence — while documenting mixed results, no settled dose or duration, and (in Della Cuna) an unexplained higher mortality in treated women. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: corticosteroids improve appetite and well-being in the short term in advanced cancer, on old, small-to-moderate placebo-controlled evidence; nothing here supports benefit beyond the short term, on weight, or on survival.
cards.watchOut: Steroid harms (hyperglycaemia, insomnia, mood change, infection, myopathy) grow with dose and duration and were barely captured in these short trials; the shelf answers a short-term symptom question only.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone dose in malignant spinal cord compression: higher dose unproven for walking — MAYBE (weak evidence)
shelves.question: In adults with malignant spinal cord compression, does a higher dexamethasone dose improve walking outcomes versus a moderate dose?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Locomotion · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Spinal Cord Compression/drug therapy/physiopathology · Urinary Bladder/physiopathology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — printed on the face. GAP verified: the cord-compression home (pack #2725) covers surgery plus radiotherapy vs radiotherapy alone, not steroid dose, and is cross-pointed here. The direct dose evidence is tiny and null: Vecht 1989 randomised 37 patients to a 100 mg vs 10 mg dexamethasone bolus (both then 16 mg/day) and found no difference in pain, ambulation or bladder function; Graham 2006 (Superdex pilot) randomised only 20 patients to 96 vs 16 mg/day, reported no by-arm ambulation result, and judged a full trial unfeasible. Sorensen 1994 (57 patients) compared 96 mg with NO steroid (walking 81% vs 63%) — it does not compare doses. A 2017 systematic review associates the moderate regimen (10 mg bolus, then 16 mg/day) with fewer complications. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): higher dose has not been shown to improve walking versus moderate dose.

cards.headline: Vecht 1989: a 100 mg dexamethasone bolus was no better than a 10 mg bolus (both followed by 16 mg/day) for pain, ambulation or bladder function in 37 patients
cards.summary: Vecht 1989: a 100 mg dexamethasone bolus was no better than a 10 mg bolus (both followed by 16 mg/day) for pain, ambulation or bladder function in 37 patients
cards.people: 37 patients with metastatic spinal cord compression randomised to an initial intravenous dexamethasone bolus of 10 mg or 100 mg, both groups then receiving 16 mg daily orally; pain, ambulation and bladder function followed.
cards.result: Average pain score fell from 5.2 (SD 2.8) before treatment to 3.8 at 3 hours, 2.8 at 24 hours and 1.4 after 1 week (P < .001 for the fall over time). There were no differences between the conventional-dose and high-dose groups on pain, ambulation or bladder function — the higher bolus made no difference.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven patients and a bolus-only contrast (maintenance dose was 16 mg/day in both arms): this tests the initial bolus, not a sustained high-dose course, and is far too small to exclude modest differences.
cards.source: Vecht CJ et al. Initial bolus of conventional versus high-dose dexamethasone in metastatic spinal cord compression. Neurology. 1989. PMID: 2771077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Graham 2006 (Superdex pilot): a randomised 96 mg vs 16 mg/day comparison recruited only 20 patients and reported no by-arm ambulation difference — the full dose trial was judged unfeasible
cards.summary: Graham 2006 (Superdex pilot): a randomised 96 mg vs 16 mg/day comparison recruited only 20 patients and reported no by-arm ambulation difference — the full dose trial was judged unfeasible
cards.people: Pilot randomised trial (TROG 01.05 Superdex) in malignant spinal cord compression treated with radiotherapy (30 Gy in 10 fractions): 131 patients screened, 93 (71%) ineligible, 20 of 38 eligible patients randomised to dexamethasone 96 mg or 16 mg daily; ambulation measured at 1 month by several definitions.
cards.result: At baseline 75% of randomised patients were ambulant. At day 28, counting four dead patients as non-ambulant, ambulation rates by the various definitions were 60%, 45% and 40% overall; the record reports no comparative ambulation result by dose arm. Serious adverse events were frequent (9 events), with one considered likely related to study medication. Median survival was 69 days. The authors conclude web randomisation worked but the high ineligibility rate precludes a full-scale dexamethasone dose trial in Australia, and that the choice of ambulation measure materially changes outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot, not an efficacy trial: with 20 randomised patients and no by-arm outcome reported in the record, it contributes the fact that the definitive dose comparison was attempted and could not be completed — not evidence of equivalence.
cards.source: Graham PH et al. A pilot randomised comparison of dexamethasone 96 mg vs 16 mg per day for malignant spinal-cord compression treated by radiotherapy: TROG 01.05 Superdex study. Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain)). 2006. PMID: 16477923. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sorensen 1994: high-dose dexamethasone (96 mg) plus radiotherapy kept more patients walking than radiotherapy alone — 81% vs 63% after treatment and 59% vs 33% at 6 months — the trial that made high dose customary
cards.summary: Sorensen 1994: high-dose dexamethasone (96 mg) plus radiotherapy kept more patients walking than radiotherapy alone — 81% vs 63% after treatment and 59% vs 33% at 6 months — the trial that made high dose customary
cards.type: Randomised trial of high-dose dexamethasone vs no steroid (Sorensen 1994)
cards.people: 57 patients with metastatic spinal cord compression from solid tumours, randomised single-blind, stratified by primary tumour and gait function, to high-dose dexamethasone (96 mg intravenous bolus, then 96 mg orally for 3 days, tapered over 10 days) as an adjunct to radiotherapy, or to no steroid treatment.
cards.result: A successful result (gait function after treatment) was obtained in 81% on dexamethasone vs 63% without it; at 6 months 59% vs 33% were still ambulatory, and life-table analysis of surviving with gait function favoured dexamethasone (P < .05). Median survival was identical in the two groups. Significant side effects occurred in 3 patients (11%) on glucocorticoids, 2 of whom discontinued treatment. The authors conclude high-dose glucocorticoid should be given as adjunct to radiotherapy in this setting.
cards.watchOut: This compares high dose with nothing, not with a moderate dose: it cannot show that 96 mg beats 16 mg, only that the high-dose package beat no steroid in 57 patients — using it as dose evidence is the historical error this shelf exists to correct.
cards.source: Sørensen S et al. Effect of high-dose dexamethasone in carcinomatous metastatic spinal cord compression treated with radiotherapy: a randomised trial. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 1994. PMID: 8142159. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kumar 2017: across the steroid literature for metastatic cord compression, a 10 mg bolus followed by 16 mg/day was associated with fewer complications than 100 mg bolus / 96 mg daily regimens, on a paucity of high-quality data
cards.summary: Kumar 2017: across the steroid literature for metastatic cord compression, a 10 mg bolus followed by 16 mg/day was associated with fewer complications than 100 mg bolus / 96 mg daily regimens, on a paucity of high-quality data
cards.people: Systematic review (search to June 2016) of steroid therapy in metastatic spinal cord compression in adults treated with radiotherapy or surgery: 309 papers retrieved, 66 full texts reviewed, 6 papers addressing steroid effect and dosing questions.
cards.result: The review found a paucity of high-quality literature evaluating steroids in this condition. On the available evidence, an initial 10 mg intravenous bolus of dexamethasone followed by 16 mg orally once daily was associated with fewer complications compared with a 100 mg bolus and 96 mg daily regimens. It advises rapid weaning after definitive treatment and routine proton-pump inhibitor cover for gastric bleeding/perforation risk. Evidence level IIIa.
cards.watchOut: A level-IIIa synthesis of six papers, most of them the very trials carded here: its 'fewer complications at moderate dose' conclusion is an association across heterogeneous regimens, not a randomised dose finding.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression and Steroid Treatment: A Systematic Review. Clinical spine surgery. 2017. PMID: 28437329. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no direct trial shows a higher dexamethasone dose improves walking — the only head-to-head bolus trial was null, the one dose pilot never completed, and the famous positive trial compared high dose with nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: no direct trial shows a higher dexamethasone dose improves walking — the only head-to-head bolus trial was null, the one dose pilot never completed, and the famous positive trial compared high dose with nothing
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised bolus comparison (Vecht 1989, 37 patients), one pilot dose comparison (Graham 2006, 20 randomised patients), one randomised high-dose-vs-no-steroid trial (Sorensen 1994, 57 patients), and one systematic review of six papers (Kumar 2017). The cord-compression home, pack #2725, covers surgery plus radiotherapy vs radiotherapy alone and is cross-pointed, not re-carded. Total directly randomised patients across the three trials: 114.
cards.result: Vecht found no difference between 100 mg and 10 mg boluses on pain, ambulation or bladder function (the higher dose made no difference); Graham's 96 vs 16 mg/day pilot randomised 20 patients, reported no by-arm ambulation result, and judged a full trial unfeasible; Sorensen's 81% vs 63% walking advantage is high dose vs no steroid and does not address dose. The systematic review associates moderate dosing (10 mg bolus, then 16 mg/day) with fewer complications. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a higher dexamethasone dose has not been shown to improve walking outcomes versus a moderate dose — the honest answer is unproven benefit with a complication gradient favouring the moderate dose, on very small trials.
cards.watchOut: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence here: the direct comparisons total 57 randomised patients, so a modest true benefit of higher dose cannot be excluded — but neither can it be claimed, and high-dose toxicity (11% significant side effects even in Sorensen) is documented.

shelves.title: Ondansetron for radiotherapy-induced vomiting: complete emesis control 67% versus 45% on placebo in fractionated abdominal radiotherapy — one direct trial, bounded by a sceptical systematic review
shelves.question: In adults receiving abdominal radiotherapy, does ondansetron prevent vomiting versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Adult · Aged · Antiemetics · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Neoplasms · Ondansetron · Placebos · Radiation Injuries · Radiotherapy · Radiotherapy Dosage · Vomiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — ondansetron prevents vomiting during abdominal radiotherapy, on one direct placebo-controlled trial plus concordant active-comparator trials. The chemotherapy antiemetic shelves do not answer this question: the library's ondansetron homes are chemotherapy, postoperative and gastroenteritis settings, verified this session. In the one direct test in the exact population, Franzén 1996 randomised 111 patients starting fractionated abdominal radiotherapy to ondansetron or placebo and found complete control of emesis in 67% versus 45%. The quantitative systematic review (Tramèr 1998) is the caution printed alongside: of 40 trials and 1,404 patients, only five trials (197 patients) yielded valid data, and in the worst-day trials ondansetron's antivomiting effect versus placebo corresponded to a number needed to treat of 4.4, with no demonstrated benefit beyond 24 hours and no clear antinausea effect. Two older multicentre trials in the same abdominal-radiotherapy population found ondansetron clearly superior to the standard antiemetics of the day — metoclopramide (complete control on day 1 in all but one ondansetron patient versus 46%) and prochlorperazine (complete response 61% versus 35%) — which supports a real preventive effect without substituting for placebo evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a real antivomiting effect during abdominal radiotherapy, resting mainly on a single moderate placebo-controlled trial, with nausea benefit and any benefit beyond the treatment day unproven.

cards.headline: Franzén 1996: in 111 patients starting fractionated abdominal radiotherapy, ondansetron gave complete control of emesis in 67% versus 45% on placebo
cards.summary: Franzén 1996: in 111 patients starting fractionated abdominal radiotherapy, ondansetron gave complete control of emesis in 67% versus 45% on placebo
cards.people: 111 patients about to commence a course of 10 or more daily fractionated radiotherapy treatments including the abdomen, randomised double-blind to ondansetron 8 mg twice daily or placebo; patients recorded daily emesis, nausea and bowel habit and graded symptoms weekly.
cards.result: Complete control of emesis was achieved by 67% of patients given ondansetron compared with 45% given placebo (P < 0.05). Emetic episodes on the worst day averaged 1.4 in the ondansetron group versus 3.1 on placebo (P < 0.01), and patients given ondansetron had fewer days with emesis and nausea (P < 0.05). More patients withdrew for lack of efficacy on placebo (13) than on ondansetron (8). The symptom advantage persisted during the first three weeks of treatment but not thereafter.
cards.watchOut: This is the only large direct placebo-controlled prophylaxis trial in the exact population found this session; the effect is on vomiting control during the course, and the trial does not show a benefit persisting beyond the first three weeks.
cards.source: Franzén L et al. A randomised placebo controlled study with ondansetron in patients undergoing fractionated radiotherapy. Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology. 1996. PMID: 8879372. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tramèr 1998 systematic review: across radiotherapy trials the valid placebo data were thin — ondansetron prevented vomiting on the worst day (NNT 4.4) but showed no benefit beyond 24 hours
cards.summary: Tramèr 1998 systematic review: across radiotherapy trials the valid placebo data were thin — ondansetron prevented vomiting on the worst day (NNT 4.4) but showed no benefit beyond 24 hours
cards.people: Quantitative systematic review of 40 trials in 36 reports (1,404 patients) of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists for radiation-induced sickness; data from only 197 patients receiving ondansetron or granisetron in five randomised trials met the reviewers' preset validity criteria.
cards.result: In the two trials reporting a 'worst day' outcome, ondansetron's antivomiting effect was significantly better than placebo (number needed to treat 4.4, 95% CI 2.5–23) but its antinausea effect was not significant. Three trials reporting delayed outcomes found no evidence of any difference versus placebo or other antiemetics, and the reviewers concluded there was no evidence of benefit beyond 24 hours. Constipation and headache were significantly associated with 5-HT3 antagonists (numbers needed to harm 6.4 and 17.1 respectively). Only 14% of the published data enabled a valid estimate of efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The review pools ondansetron with granisetron and mixes radiotherapy fields; its role on this shelf is to size and bound the placebo evidence honestly, not to add a second direct abdominal-radiotherapy trial.
cards.source: Tramèr MR et al. Efficacy of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists in radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: a quantitative systematic review. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 1998. PMID: 10023303. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Priestman 1990: after single high-dose upper-abdominal irradiation, ondansetron prevented vomiting or retching in all but one patient versus 46% complete control on metoclopramide
cards.summary: Priestman 1990: after single high-dose upper-abdominal irradiation, ondansetron prevented vomiting or retching in all but one patient versus 46% complete control on metoclopramide
cards.people: 82 evaluable patients receiving single-exposure radiotherapy of 8–10 Gy to the upper abdomen, randomised double-blind to oral ondansetron 8 mg three times daily (38 patients) or metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily (44 patients).
cards.result: On the first day after irradiation, vomiting or retching was prevented in all but one of the patients on ondansetron, whereas metoclopramide achieved complete control in only 46% of subjects (P < 0.001); nausea was also significantly better controlled by ondansetron in the first 24 hours (P = 0.001). Complete or major control was maintained in 92%–100% of ondansetron patients over the five study days. Both drugs were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is metoclopramide, not placebo, and the setting is a single large radiation dose rather than a fractionated course; it shows ondansetron beats the standard antiemetic of its day in this population, which supports — but does not replace — the placebo evidence.

cards.headline: Priestman 1993: over a fractionated upper-abdominal course, complete response (no emetic episodes) was 61% on ondansetron versus 35% on prochlorperazine
cards.summary: Priestman 1993: over a fractionated upper-abdominal course, complete response (no emetic episodes) was 61% on ondansetron versus 35% on prochlorperazine
cards.people: 192 patients undergoing courses of five or more daily radiotherapy treatments to the upper abdomen were recruited and randomised double-blind to oral ondansetron 8 mg three times daily or prochlorperazine 10 mg three times daily throughout the course; 135 patients (70 ondansetron, 65 prochlorperazine) were included in the efficacy analysis.
cards.result: A complete response — no emetic episodes throughout the treatment course — occurred in 43 of 70 patients (61%) on ondansetron versus 23 of 65 (35%) on prochlorperazine (P = 0.002). There was no significant difference between the groups in the incidence or severity of nausea. Treatment failures (more than five emetic episodes on the worst day) occurred in 24% on ondansetron and 29% on prochlorperazine; constipation was seen more commonly with ondansetron.
cards.watchOut: Again an active comparator, not placebo, and 57 of 192 recruited patients were not in the efficacy analysis; the vomiting advantage is clear, the nausea advantage is absent in this trial.
