cards.headline: Synthesis: ondansetron prevents vomiting during abdominal radiotherapy — one direct placebo trial, one bounding systematic review, and two concordant active-comparator trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: ondansetron prevents vomiting during abdominal radiotherapy — one direct placebo trial, one bounding systematic review, and two concordant active-comparator trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: one placebo-controlled trial in fractionated abdominal radiotherapy (Franzén, 111 patients), one quantitative systematic review of the radiotherapy antiemetic literature (Tramèr, 40 trials / 1,404 patients, only 197 patients in valid trials), and two double-blind active-comparator trials in upper-abdominal radiotherapy (Priestman 1990, 82 evaluable; Priestman 1993, 135 in the efficacy analysis).
cards.result: Complete emesis control on ondansetron versus placebo was 67% versus 45% in the direct trial; the systematic review put the worst-day antivomiting number needed to treat at 4.4 versus placebo, found no benefit beyond 24 hours, and warned that most published data were not validly estimable. Against metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, ondansetron's complete-control rates were markedly higher (all but one patient versus 46% on day 1; 61% versus 35% over a course). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: ondansetron prevents vomiting in abdominal radiotherapy; the nausea benefit is inconsistent and any delayed benefit is unproven.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the active-comparator wins as placebo evidence: the placebo case rests on Franzén and on the small valid subset Tramèr could pool, which is why this shelf is capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Franzén L et al. Annals of oncology. 1996 (PMID: 8879372); Tramèr MR et al. European journal of cancer. 1998 (PMID: 10023303); Priestman TJ et al. Clinical oncology. 1990 (PMID: 1702012); Priestman TJ et al. Clinical oncology. 1993 (PMID: 8305355).

shelves.title: Transmucosal fentanyl for cancer breakthrough pain: faster, stronger relief than placebo and than oral morphine in enriched titration trials of opioid-tolerant patients
shelves.question: In cancer breakthrough pain, do transmucosal fentanyl formulations relieve pain faster than oral morphine or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fentanyl/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mouth Mucosa · Neoplasms/complications · Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three double-blind randomised trials, using the era's standard enriched design (dose titration first; only patients who found an effective dose were randomised to sequences of active and placebo units), point the same way. Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (OTFC lozenge) beat placebo on pain intensity and pain relief at every time point from 15 minutes (Farrar 1998; rescue medication needed for 15% of OTFC episodes vs 34% of placebo episodes). Head-to-head, OTFC — the record names the product as Actiq — beat oral morphine sulfate immediate release on pain intensity, pain-intensity difference and pain relief at all time points, including the 15-minute primary measure (Coluzzi 2001). The fentanyl buccal tablet likewise beat placebo, with a summed pain-intensity difference at 30 minutes of 3.0 versus 1.8 (Portenoy 2006); the buccal-tablet record does not give a brand name. All three trials enrolled opioid-tolerant patients on around-the-clock opioids, and roughly a third of patients never found a successful dose in titration and so never entered the randomised phase — the benefit is proven in titration responders, which is also how these products are prescribed. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): faster and greater relief than placebo and than oral morphine, in the population and design in which these formulations are actually used.

cards.headline: Farrar 1998: oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate beat placebo at every time point from 15 minutes; rescue medication was needed for 15% of fentanyl episodes versus 34% of placebo episodes
cards.summary: Farrar 1998: oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate beat placebo at every time point from 15 minutes; rescue medication was needed for 15% of fentanyl episodes versus 34% of placebo episodes
cards.people: Patients aged 18 or older with cancer on at least 60 mg/day oral morphine equivalents (or at least 50 µg/hour transdermal fentanyl) for chronic pain, with at least one breakthrough-pain episode daily; after open titration to an effective dose, 92 patients received randomised treatment and 89 were assessable, each treating episodes with 10 randomly ordered lozenge units (7 oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate, 3 placebo). The record describes the formulation as a lozenge and does not give a brand name.
cards.result: Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate produced significantly larger changes in pain intensity and better pain relief than placebo at all time points over 60 minutes (two-sided P<0.0001). Episodes treated with placebo required rescue medication more often than episodes treated with fentanyl (34% versus 15%; relative risk 2.27, 95% confidence interval 1.51–3.26; P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: An enriched design: only patients who first titrated to an effective lozenge dose entered the randomised phase, and each patient contributed multiple episodes, so the result describes titration responders treating repeated episodes — not a first prescription given to an unselected patient.
cards.source: Farrar JT et al. Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate: randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial for treatment of breakthrough pain in cancer patients. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 1998. PMID: 9554444. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Coluzzi 2001: oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (Actiq, as named in the record) beat oral immediate-release morphine on pain measures at all time points, including 15 minutes
cards.summary: Coluzzi 2001: oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (Actiq, as named in the record) beat oral immediate-release morphine on pain measures at all time points, including 15 minutes
cards.people: 134 adult ambulatory cancer patients at 19 US centres, on fixed scheduled opioids equivalent to 60–1,000 mg/day oral morphine (or 50–300 µg/hour transdermal fentanyl), with a previously successful immediate-release morphine dose (15–60 mg) and 1–4 breakthrough episodes daily; in the double-blind phase, successfully titrated patients treated episodes with 10 randomised sets pairing their successful OTFC dose (200–1,600 µg) with placebo capsules, or placebo OTFC with their morphine dose in capsules.
cards.result: 69% of patients (93 of 134) found a successful OTFC dose. OTFC yielded pain intensity, pain-intensity difference and pain relief outcomes at all time points that were significantly better than morphine sulfate immediate release; the primary variable was the 15-minute pain-intensity difference. Global performance scores also favoured OTFC, and more patients opted to continue OTFC than morphine after the study. The most common drug-associated side effects were somnolence, nausea, constipation and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is stacked by design in one respect: every randomised patient had already proven they could titrate OTFC successfully, while their morphine dose was their pre-study usual dose; 31% of enrolled patients never reached the randomised phase at all.
cards.source: Coluzzi PH et al. Breakthrough cancer pain: a randomized trial comparing oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (OTFC) and morphine sulfate immediate release (MSIR). Pain. 2001. cards.headline: Portenoy 2006: fentanyl buccal tablet beat placebo on summed pain-intensity difference at 30 minutes (3.0 vs 1.8; P<0.0001) in opioid-treated cancer patients
cards.summary: Portenoy 2006: fentanyl buccal tablet beat placebo on summed pain-intensity difference at 30 minutes (3.0 vs 1.8; P<0.0001) in opioid-treated cancer patients
cards.people: Opioid-treated patients with cancer-related breakthrough pain; 123 entered open-label titration to an effective fentanyl buccal tablet dose, 80 (65%) were titrated successfully, and 77 were randomly assigned to prespecified sequences of 10 tablets (7 fentanyl buccal tablet, 3 placebo), treating breakthrough episodes with pain recorded from 15 to 60 minutes. The record does not give a brand name for the buccal tablet.
cards.result: The primary outcome, summed pain-intensity difference at 30 minutes, was 3.0 ± 0.12 on fentanyl buccal tablet versus 1.8 ± 0.18 on placebo (P<0.0001). Pain relief, pain-intensity differences, summed measures and global performance ratings all significantly favoured the buccal tablet at all time points. Adverse events were typical of opioid drugs; poor oral tolerability was noted in 2 patients.
cards.watchOut: Same enriched structure as the lozenge trials: 35% of patients entering titration never randomised, so the proven benefit applies to patients who can find an effective buccal-tablet dose; the trial measures episode relief over 60 minutes, not any longer-term outcome.
cards.source: Portenoy RK et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled study of fentanyl buccal tablet for breakthrough pain in opioid-treated patients with cancer. The Clinical journal of pain. 2006. cards.headline: Synthesis: three enriched double-blind trials agree — transmucosal fentanyl relieves breakthrough episodes faster and more than placebo, and more than oral morphine
cards.summary: Synthesis: three enriched double-blind trials agree — transmucosal fentanyl relieves breakthrough episodes faster and more than placebo, and more than oral morphine
cards.people: The carded evidence: two placebo-controlled trials (OTFC lozenge, 89 assessable patients; fentanyl buccal tablet, 77 randomised patients) and one head-to-head crossover trial against oral immediate-release morphine (134 enrolled, 93 titrated), all in opioid-tolerant cancer patients.
cards.result: Fentanyl formulations separated from placebo at the first measured time point (15 minutes) in both placebo-controlled trials (P<0.0001), halved rescue-medication use versus placebo (15% vs 34% of episodes), and beat oral morphine on every pain measure at every time point in the head-to-head trial. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — concordant randomised evidence for faster, greater episode relief, within the titration-responder populations the trials enrolled.
cards.watchOut: Every carded trial used titration enrichment and episode-level crossover measurement, and all enrolled opioid-tolerant patients on substantial background opioids; nothing here speaks to opioid-naive patients, non-cancer breakthrough pain, or safety beyond typical opioid effects in these short trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Farrar JT et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 1998 (PMID: 9554444); Coluzzi PH et al. Pain. 2001 (PMID: 11240084); Portenoy RK et al. The Clinical journal of pain. 2006 (PMID: 17057563).

shelves.title: Adjuvant mitotane after resection of low-to-intermediate-risk adrenocortical carcinoma: ADIUVO found no significant benefit (79% vs 75% recurrence-free at 5 years)
shelves.question: In patients with resected adrenocortical carcinoma at low-to-intermediate recurrence risk, does adjuvant mitotane, compared with surveillance alone, prolong recurrence-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Mitotane/therapeutic use · Adrenocortical Carcinoma/drug therapy,surgery · Disease-Free Survival · Adrenal Cortex Neoplasms/drug therapy,surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The direct randomised evidence (ADIUVO, n=91, stopped early for slow recruitment) found 5-year recurrence-free survival of 79% on adjuvant mitotane versus 75% on surveillance (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85), with adverse events in all treated patients and 19% discontinuing. The retrospective literature behind the practice splits: Terzolo 2007 (n=177, broader risk) found median recurrence-free survival of 42 versus 10/25 months favouring mitotane, while the US 13-institution series (n=207) found no independent association after adjustment. ADIUVO's wide interval means benefit is not excluded — it is undemonstrated in this risk group.

cards.headline: ADIUVO 2023 (the randomised trial in this risk group): 5-year recurrence-free survival was 79% on adjuvant mitotane versus 75% on surveillance (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85) — no significant difference, in a trial stopped early for slow recruitment
cards.summary: ADIUVO 2023 (the randomised trial in this risk group): 5-year recurrence-free survival was 79% on adjuvant mitotane versus 75% on surveillance (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85) — no significant difference, in a trial stopped early for slow recruitment
cards.people: 91 patients with resected adrenocortical carcinoma at low-to-intermediate recurrence risk (complete R0 resection, stage I–III, Ki67 at most 10%), randomised at 23 centres in seven countries to adjuvant oral mitotane for 2 years (dose adjusted to plasma concentrations of 14–20 mg/L; n=45) or surveillance alone (n=46). The trial was discontinued prematurely because of slow recruitment, so 5-year outcomes are reported instead of the protocol-defined analysis.
cards.result: 5-year recurrence-free survival was 79% (95% CI 67–94) in the mitotane group and 75% (63–90) in the surveillance group (hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.30–1.85 — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 4 percentage points). Two patients in the mitotane group and five in the surveillance group died; 5-year overall survival was 95% (89–100) versus 86% (74–100), not significantly different. All 42 patients who received mitotane had adverse events and eight (19%) discontinued treatment; there were no grade 4 adverse events or treatment-related deaths. The authors conclude adjuvant mitotane might not be indicated in low-grade, localised disease given the good prognosis and the toxicity, while noting the premature stop means an efficacy cannot be ruled out.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early at 91 of the planned sample: the confidence interval (0.30–1.85) is wide enough to include both a large benefit and harm, so this is 'no difference demonstrated', not proof of no effect. The same publication's parallel observational cohort is not carded separately — it is the same programme and the fetched record prints no separate numbers for it.

cards.headline: Terzolo 2007 (retrospective, broader risk): median recurrence-free survival was 42 months with adjuvant mitotane versus 10 and 25 months in two untreated control groups — the study that made adjuvant mitotane standard practice
cards.summary: Terzolo 2007 (retrospective, broader risk): median recurrence-free survival was 42 months with adjuvant mitotane versus 10 and 25 months in two untreated control groups — the study that made adjuvant mitotane standard practice
cards.people: 177 patients with radically resected adrenocortical carcinoma in Italy and Germany, 1985–2005: 47 Italian patients given adjuvant mitotane, 55 Italian patients untreated (control group 1) and 75 German patients untreated (control group 2). Retrospective and not restricted to low-to-intermediate risk — the population is broader than this shelf's question, flagged on the face.
cards.result: Recurrence-free survival was significantly longer in the mitotane group: median 42 months versus 10 months in Italian controls and 25 months in German controls. Hazard ratios for recurrence in the control groups relative to the mitotane group were 2.91 (95% CI 1.77–4.78) and 1.97 (1.21–3.20) — relative measures; multivariable analysis also favoured mitotane. Adverse events were mainly grade 1–2, with temporary dose reduction in 13% of treated patients.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, with treatment allocated by centre practice rather than at random, and controls drawn from different countries and eras — exactly the design the ADIUVO trial was run to test, in a higher-risk mix of patients. Its large apparent benefit did not reproduce under randomisation in low-to-intermediate-risk disease.
cards.source: Retrospective comparative cohort study | Terzolo M et al. N Engl J Med. 2007. PMID: 17554118. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era retrospective study). cards.headline: Postlewait 2016 (US Adrenocortical Carcinoma Group, 13 institutions): adjuvant mitotane was associated with shorter crude recurrence-free and overall survival, and with no association at all after multivariable adjustment
cards.summary: Postlewait 2016 (US Adrenocortical Carcinoma Group, 13 institutions): adjuvant mitotane was associated with shorter crude recurrence-free and overall survival, and with no association at all after multivariable adjustment
cards.people: 207 patients who underwent resection of adrenocortical carcinoma at 13 US academic institutions, 1993–2014; 88 (43%) received adjuvant mitotane. Retrospective. Mitotane recipients had more adverse features — more hormonal secretion, more stage IV disease, and far more adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation — flagged on the face.
cards.result: Crude median recurrence-free survival was 10.0 months with mitotane versus 27.9 months without (P=0.007) and crude overall survival 31.7 versus 58.9 months (P=0.006) — comparisons confounded by the treated group's worse prognosis. On multivariable analysis, mitotane was not independently associated with recurrence-free or overall survival, and stage-specific analyses in both the full cohort and the no-chemotherapy cohort likewise showed no association with improved recurrence-free or overall survival. The authors conclude that, accounting for stage and adverse factors, adjuvant mitotane is not associated with improved outcomes, and that guidelines should be revisited.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs against mitotane here (it was given to higher-risk patients), just as centre/era effects may have favoured it in the 2007 series — the two retrospective cards are kept side by side precisely so neither is read alone.
cards.source: Retrospective multicentre cohort study | Postlewait LM et al. J Am Coll Surg. 2016. PMID: 26775162. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Synthesis: for low-to-intermediate-risk resected adrenocortical carcinoma, the one randomised trial found no significant benefit from adjuvant mitotane and surveillance patients did well (75% recurrence-free at 5 years) — while the older retrospective literature splits in both directions
cards.summary: Synthesis: for low-to-intermediate-risk resected adrenocortical carcinoma, the one randomised trial found no significant benefit from adjuvant mitotane and surveillance patients did well (75% recurrence-free at 5 years) — while the older retrospective literature splits in both directions
cards.people: Synthesis of ADIUVO (Terzolo 2023, randomised, n=91, this shelf's exact population), Terzolo 2007 (retrospective, n=177, broader risk) and Postlewait 2016 (retrospective, n=207, broader risk). No mitotane or ADIUVO home exists in the library — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: The direct evidence answers the question as posed: in low-to-intermediate-risk disease, adjuvant mitotane made no significant difference to recurrence-free survival (79% versus 75% at 5 years; hazard ratio 0.74 with a wide confidence interval), every treated patient had adverse events, and 19% stopped treatment — against a surveillance prognosis that was already good. The retrospective record that built the practice splits: the 2007 Italian/German series found much longer recurrence-free survival with mitotane (median 42 versus 10/25 months), while the US 13-institution series found no independent association after adjustment. Because ADIUVO stopped early, a real benefit in this risk group is not excluded — but none has been demonstrated, and the burden of proof now sits with treatment.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: SPLIT names a real split — randomised evidence in the target risk group is null (underpowered), and the two large retrospective series point in opposite directions in broader-risk patients. Nothing carded here addresses high-risk disease (positive margins, rupture, Ki67 above 10%), where ADIUVO does not apply.
cards.source: Synthesis of Terzolo M et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2023 (PMID: 37619579; NCT00777244); Terzolo M et al. N Engl J Med. 2007 (PMID: 17554118); Postlewait LM et al. J Am Coll Surg. 2016 (PMID: 26775162).

shelves.title: EMERALD-1: adding durvalumab plus bevacizumab to TACE lengthened progression-free survival (median 15.0 vs 8.2 months; HR 0.77) — one trial, survival data immature, so POSSIBLE
shelves.question: In adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma amenable to embolisation, does adding durvalumab plus bevacizumab to transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) prolong progression-free survival compared with TACE alone? (EMERALD-1.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Bevacizumab/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/therapy,mortality,drug therapy · Male · Liver Neoplasms/therapy,mortality,drug therapy · Female · Middle Aged · Aged · Chemoembolization, Therapeutic/methods · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Progression-Free Survival · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Adult
shelves.balance: A single phase 3 trial answers this exact question, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE (single programme). In EMERALD-1 (616 patients randomised 1:1:1), TACE plus durvalumab plus bevacizumab gave a median progression-free survival of 15.0 months versus 8.2 months with TACE plus placebo (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98; p=0.032) — a relative measure, with an absolute median gain of about 6.8 months. Durvalumab without bevacizumab did not significantly improve progression-free survival (10.0 months; HR 0.94, 0.75–1.19) — the bevacizumab component appears necessary. Overall survival was immature at the report and is not claimed on this shelf. The parallel phase 3 trial of a different combination, LEAP-012 (lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab plus TACE, 480 patients), points the same way (median PFS 14.6 vs 10.0 months; HR 0.66), which supports the strategy class but is a different regimen and cannot substitute for replication of EMERALD-1 itself. A 17-study meta-analysis of TACE plus tyrosine-kinase inhibitor plus checkpoint inhibitor versus TACE plus TKI (mostly non-randomised) is carded only as low-grade supportive context. First-line systemic therapy for unresectable HCC is homed on live shelf #850 and adjuvant therapy on pack #1889; TACE versus no TACE is pack #6335.

cards.headline: EMERALD-1 (Sangro 2025; 616 randomised): durvalumab plus bevacizumab with TACE gave median progression-free survival of 15.0 versus 8.2 months against TACE plus placebo (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98; p=0.032); durvalumab without bevacizumab did not (HR 0.94)
cards.summary: EMERALD-1 (Sangro 2025; 616 randomised): durvalumab plus bevacizumab with TACE gave median progression-free survival of 15.0 versus 8.2 months against TACE plus placebo (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.98; p=0.032); durvalumab without bevacizumab did not (HR 0.94)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (EMERALD-1) — 616 randomised
cards.people: Multiregional, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study at 157 sites in 18 countries: 616 adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma amenable to embolisation, ECOG performance status 0–1 and at least one measurable intrahepatic lesion, assigned 1:1:1 to TACE plus durvalumab plus bevacizumab (n=204), TACE plus durvalumab plus placebo (n=207), or TACE plus placebo alone (n=205). Median age 65.0 years; 78% male; 61% Asian. Primary endpoint: progression-free survival by blinded independent central review (RECIST 1.1).
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 15.0 months (95% CI 11.1–18.9) with durvalumab plus bevacizumab, 10.0 months (9.0–12.7) with durvalumab alone, and 8.2 months (6.9–11.1) with placebo. The hazard ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.61–0.98; two-sided p=0.032) for durvalumab plus bevacizumab versus placebo — a relative measure; the absolute median gain was about 6.8 months — and 0.94 (0.75–1.19; p=0.64) for durvalumab plus placebo versus placebo (the treatment made no significant difference without bevacizumab). The most common grade 3–4 adverse event with the combination was hypertension (6% of treated patients). Overall survival follow-up was continuing and is not reported in this publication.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one regimen, progression-free survival only: the confidence interval (0.61–0.98) only just excludes 1.0, and no overall-survival benefit is shown in this report. Safety denominators differ from the randomised numbers because not all assigned patients received the full combination (the treated sets printed on the record are smaller), so adverse-event percentages should be read against the treated populations.

cards.headline: LEAP-012 (Kudo 2025; 480 randomised, parallel phase 3 of a different combination): lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab with TACE gave median progression-free survival of 14.6 versus 10.0 months (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.84) — class support, not replication of EMERALD-1
cards.summary: LEAP-012 (Kudo 2025; 480 randomised, parallel phase 3 of a different combination): lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab with TACE gave median progression-free survival of 14.6 versus 10.0 months (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.84) — class support, not replication of EMERALD-1
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind phase 3 trial (LEAP-012) — 480 randomised; different regimen, carded as context
cards.people: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind phase 3 study at 137 sites in 33 countries: 480 adults with unresectable, non-metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma amenable to TACE, ECOG 0–1 and Child-Pugh class A, assigned to TACE plus lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab (n=237) or TACE plus dual placebo (n=243). Median age 66 years; 83% male. First interim analysis (final for progression-free survival).
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 14.6 months (95% CI 12.6–16.7) with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus 10.0 months (8.1–12.2) with placebo (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.84; one-sided p=0.0002) — a relative measure with an absolute median gain of about 4.6 months. Overall survival was not significant at this analysis (24-month survival 75% vs 69%; HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.57–1.11; p=0.087).
cards.watchOut: A different drug combination (a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor plus a PD-1 inhibitor, no bevacizumab) in a non-metastatic population. It corroborates the 'add systemic therapy to TACE' strategy; it does not replicate durvalumab plus bevacizumab, and cross-trial PFS comparisons between EMERALD-1 and LEAP-012 are not valid.
cards.source: Kudo M et al. Transarterial chemoembolisation combined with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab versus dual placebo for unresectable, non-metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (LEAP-012): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, phase 3 study. cards.type: Meta-analysis of 17 studies (Zeng 2025) — mostly non-randomised, carded as context only
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (searched to 1 November 2024) of 17 studies in hepatocellular carcinoma comparing TACE plus tyrosine-kinase inhibitor plus immune checkpoint inhibitor against TACE plus tyrosine-kinase inhibitor alone; outcomes included response rate, disease control, overall and progression-free survival and adverse events.
cards.result: The triple combination was associated with higher objective response (relative rate 1.57, 95% CI 1.36–1.80), higher disease control (relative rate 1.13, 1.06–1.20), and lower hazards of progression (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.36–0.53) and death (HR 0.37, 0.29–0.48), with no detected difference in adverse events. All are relative measures from a pooled, largely non-randomised literature.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes this large (OS HR 0.37) from predominantly retrospective comparisons are the signature of selection bias; this card is context for the strategy's popularity, not evidence for the EMERALD-1 regimen, which contains no tyrosine-kinase inhibitor.

shelves.title: TACE versus supportive care in unresectable HCC: two 2002 randomised trials and their meta-analysis agree — chemoembolisation improves survival in stringently selected patients (2-year survival about 63% and 31% versus 27% and 11%)
shelves.question: In adults with intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma, does transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) improve survival compared with best supportive care or systemic therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/mortality,pathology,therapy · Cause of Death · Chemoembolization, Therapeutic/methods · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Liver Neoplasms/mortality,pathology,therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from 2002, in different populations with different regimens, point the same way, and the systematic review of the era confirms the pooled result. Llovet 2002 (112 stringently selected patients, Child-Pugh A or B, Okuda I–II) was stopped early because chemoembolisation (gelatin sponge plus doxorubicin) beat conservative treatment (hazard ratio of death 0.47, 95% CI 0.25–0.91; 2-year survival 63% versus 27%); the embolisation-alone arm sat between (50% at 2 years). Lo 2002 (80 Asian patients, cisplatin in lipiodol) found actuarial survival of 57%, 31% and 26% at 1, 2 and 3 years versus 32%, 11% and 3% with symptomatic treatment (p=.002; adjusted relative risk of death 0.49, 0.29–0.81). Llovet & Bruix 2003 pooled 7 arterial-embolisation trials (545 patients): embolisation improved 2-year survival (odds ratio 0.53, 0.32–0.89), with the benefit carried by chemoembolisation with cisplatin or doxorubicin (OR 0.42) and not by embolisation alone (OR 0.59, not significant). The caveats are selection (both trials enrolled preserved-liver-function patients; Llovet screened 903 to randomise 112) and era (the comparator was symptomatic care, not modern systemic therapy — no trial compares TACE head-to-head with contemporary systemic regimens in intermediate-stage disease). Adding systemic/immune therapy to TACE is pack #6334; first-line systemic therapy is live shelf #850.

cards.headline: Llovet 2002 (112 randomised, stopped early): chemoembolisation versus conservative treatment — hazard ratio of death 0.47 (95% CI 0.25–0.91); 2-year survival 63% versus 27%
cards.summary: Llovet 2002 (112 randomised, stopped early): chemoembolisation versus conservative treatment — hazard ratio of death 0.47 (95% CI 0.25–0.91); 2-year survival 63% versus 27%
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in Spain: 903 patients assessed, 112 (12%) with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma unsuitable for curative treatment, Child-Pugh class A or B and Okuda stage I or II, randomised to regularly repeated arterial embolisation (gelatin sponge; n=37), chemoembolisation (gelatin sponge plus doxorubicin; n=40), or conservative treatment (n=35). Primary endpoint survival; intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: The trial was stopped at the ninth sequential inspection because chemoembolisation showed a survival benefit over conservative treatment (hazard ratio of death 0.47, 95% CI 0.25–0.91; p=0.025) — a relative measure; in absolute terms, survival at 1 and 2 years was 82% and 63% with chemoembolisation versus 63% and 27% with conservative treatment (p=0.009), with embolisation alone intermediate (75% and 50%). Deaths were 21 of 40 (chemoembolisation), 25 of 37 (embolisation) and 25 of 35 (control). Chemoembolisation produced objective responses sustained at least 6 months in 35% and a lower rate of portal-vein invasion; treatment allocation was the only variable independently related to survival (OR 0.45, 0.25–0.81).
cards.watchOut: Early stopping inflates effect sizes, and the selection was extreme — 903 screened for 112 randomised, all with preserved liver function and no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread by the era's criteria. The result licenses TACE for that selected phenotype, not for unselected intermediate-stage disease.
cards.source: Llovet JM et al. Arterial embolisation or chemoembolisation versus symptomatic treatment in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2002. PMID: 12049862. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lo 2002 (80 randomised): transarterial lipiodol chemoembolisation versus symptomatic treatment — survival 57%/31%/26% at 1/2/3 years versus 32%/11%/3% (p=.002); adjusted relative risk of death 0.49 (95% CI 0.29–0.81)
cards.summary: Lo 2002 (80 randomised): transarterial lipiodol chemoembolisation versus symptomatic treatment — survival 57%/31%/26% at 1/2/3 years versus 32%/11%/3% (p=.002); adjusted relative risk of death 0.49 (95% CI 0.29–0.81)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in Hong Kong (March 1996–October 1997): 80 Asian patients with newly diagnosed unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (of 279 assessed) assigned to chemoembolisation with cisplatin in lipiodol plus gelatin sponge (n=40; median 4.5 courses, range 1–15, repeated every 2–3 months) or symptomatic treatment (n=40; one control patient later excluded for unrecognised systemic metastasis). Main endpoint survival.
cards.result: Actuarial survival was significantly better with chemoembolisation — 1 year 57%, 2 years 31%, 3 years 26% — than with symptomatic treatment — 32%, 11% and 3% (p=.002), absolute gains of about 25, 20 and 23 percentage points. After adjustment for prognostic baseline variables the survival benefit remained significant (relative risk of death 0.49, 95% CI 0.29–0.81; p=.006). Death from liver failure was more frequent in the chemoembolisation group, though survivors' liver function did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A cisplatin–lipiodol regimen in an entirely Asian, largely hepatitis-B population — regimen and population both differ from the doxorubicin-based European trial, yet the survival conclusion agrees, which is the strength of the pair. The excess of liver-failure deaths on treatment is the standing harm signal: chemoembolisation spends liver reserve.

cards.headline: Llovet & Bruix 2003 systematic review (7 embolisation trials, 545 patients): arterial embolisation improved 2-year survival (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32–0.89) — driven by chemoembolisation (OR 0.42), not embolisation alone (OR 0.59, not significant)

cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Llovet & Bruix 2003) — 7 embolisation trials, 545 patients
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of primary treatments for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma published as full papers (1978–May 2002): 61 trials identified, 14 meeting criteria for meta-analysis — 7 of arterial embolisation (545 patients) and 7 of tamoxifen (898 patients). Random-effects estimates; sensitivity analysis by methodological quality.
cards.result: Arterial embolisation improved 2-year survival compared with control (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32–0.89; p=.017) — a relative (odds) measure. Sensitivity analysis showed a significant benefit for chemoembolisation with cisplatin or doxorubicin (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20–0.88) but none for embolisation alone (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.29–1.20). Objective responses occurred in 35% of treated patients (range 16–61%). Tamoxifen showed no survival benefit (OR 0.64, 0.36–1.13).
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, old and heterogeneous in regimen and selection; the review's own split — chemoembolisation yes, bland embolisation not shown — is the part most often lost when this literature is cited as 'TACE works'.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two small, selected, era-bound trials agree, and the pooled analysis agrees with them — TACE's survival benefit over supportive care is LIKELY, its standing against modern systemic therapy is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small, selected, era-bound trials agree, and the pooled analysis agrees with them — TACE's survival benefit over supportive care is LIKELY, its standing against modern systemic therapy is untested
cards.people: The carded evidence: Llovet 2002 (112 randomised, doxorubicin chemoembolisation, European), Lo 2002 (80 randomised, cisplatin–lipiodol, Hong Kong), and Llovet & Bruix 2003 (7 trials, 545 patients). TACE-plus-systemic combinations are pack #6334; first-line systemic therapy for unresectable HCC is live shelf #850.
cards.result: Absolute 2-year survival gains were about 36 points (63% vs 27%, Llovet) and 20 points (31% vs 11%, Lo) against symptomatic care, with relative risks of death around 0.47–0.49 in both trials. Concordance across regimens and continents, plus a significant pooled estimate, supports LIKELY for the supportive-care comparison in patients resembling those enrolled (preserved liver function, liver-confined disease). Neither trial — nor any carded trial — compares TACE with a modern systemic regimen, so the 'or systemic therapy' half of the question has no randomised answer on this record.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate sorafenib, let alone immunotherapy combinations; using them to rank TACE against today's systemic options would be an era error. Their durable content is narrower: in selected patients, treating the liver tumour beats not treating it.

shelves.title: Capivasertib plus fulvestrant in AKT-pathway-altered advanced breast cancer: progression-free survival roughly doubled in the phase 3 trial (7.3 vs 3.1 months in altered tumours, HR 0.50) — overall survival not yet reported in the fetched records
shelves.question: In adults with PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN-altered hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after endocrine therapy, does capivasertib plus fulvestrant improve progression-free and overall survival versus fulvestrant alone?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Fulvestrant · Humans · Progression-Free Survival · Proto-Oncogene Proteins c-akt · Pyrimidines · Pyrroles · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases
shelves.balance: One drug programme, two concordant randomised trials. The phase 3 CAPItello-291 trial (708 patients whose disease had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor, 69.1% after a CDK4/6 inhibitor) doubled median progression-free survival overall (7.2 vs 3.6 months; HR 0.60) and in the AKT-pathway-altered population the question asks about (7.3 vs 3.1 months; HR 0.50, a 50% relative reduction, with the absolute medians printed beside it). The earlier phase 2 FAKTION trial pointed the same way (10.3 vs 4.8 months; HR 0.58) in an unselected aromatase-inhibitor-resistant population, and a prespecified Chinese-cohort report of CAPItello-291 reproduced the benefit (altered tumours: HR 0.41). The harms are real and characteristic: grade 3 or higher rash 12.1% vs 0.3% and diarrhoea 9.3% vs 0.3% in the phase 3 trial, with 13.0% vs 2.3% discontinuing for adverse events. No overall-survival result appears in any fetched record, so the shelf claims progression-free survival only. A single programme, however concordant, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CAPItello-291 phase 3: progression-free survival doubled — 7.3 vs 3.1 months in AKT-pathway-altered tumours (HR 0.50); 7.2 vs 3.6 months overall (HR 0.60)
cards.summary: CAPItello-291 phase 3: progression-free survival doubled — 7.3 vs 3.1 months in AKT-pathway-altered tumours (HR 0.50); 7.2 vs 3.6 months overall (HR 0.60)
cards.people: 708 pre-, peri- and postmenopausal women and men with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer relapsing or progressing during or after an aromatase inhibitor, with or without prior CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy (69.1% had received one); 289 patients (40.8%) had AKT-pathway-altered (PIK3CA, AKT1 or PTEN) tumours; randomised 1:1 to capivasertib plus fulvestrant or placebo plus fulvestrant.
cards.result: In the overall population, median progression-free survival was 7.2 months with capivasertib–fulvestrant vs 3.6 months with placebo–fulvestrant (HR for progression or death 0.60; 95% CI 0.51–0.71; P < 0.001 — a 40% relative reduction, absolute medians beside it). In the AKT pathway-altered population, median progression-free survival was 7.3 vs 3.1 months (HR 0.50; 95% CI 0.38–0.65; P < 0.001 — a 50% relative reduction). The most frequent grade 3 or higher adverse events on capivasertib were rash (12.1% vs 0.3%) and diarrhoea (9.3% vs 0.3%); adverse events led to discontinuation in 13.0% vs 2.3%.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival is the proven endpoint; no overall-survival result is reported in this record, and the shelf does not borrow one. The trial's dual primary endpoints were the overall and altered populations — both positive — but the licensed population is the altered one, which is why the question is framed on it.

cards.headline: FAKTION phase 2: the same combination, earlier and unselected — median progression-free survival 10.3 vs 4.8 months (HR 0.58)
cards.summary: FAKTION phase 2: the same combination, earlier and unselected — median progression-free survival 10.3 vs 4.8 months (HR 0.58)
cards.people: 140 postmenopausal women with oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic or locally advanced inoperable breast cancer relapsed or progressed on an aromatase inhibitor, at 19 UK hospitals; fulvestrant with capivasertib 400 mg twice daily (4 days on, 3 days off) or placebo.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 10.3 months (95% CI 5.0–13.2) with capivasertib vs 4.8 months (3.1–7.7) with placebo (unadjusted HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.39–0.84; two-sided P = 0.0044 — a 42% relative reduction, absolute medians beside it). The most common grade 3–4 adverse events on capivasertib were hypertension (32% vs 24%), rash (20% vs 0) and diarrhoea (14% vs 4%). One death from atypical pulmonary infection was assessed as possibly related to capivasertib.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial run with a one-sided alpha of 0.20 by design and an intermittent dosing schedule; it is supportive evidence for the phase 3 result, not a second pivotal trial, and its population was not selected for AKT-pathway alteration.

cards.headline: CAPItello-291 Chinese cohort: the benefit reproduced in an independently reported cohort — altered tumours HR 0.41 (n = 134)
cards.summary: CAPItello-291 Chinese cohort: the benefit reproduced in an independently reported cohort — altered tumours HR 0.41 (n = 134)
cards.type: Prespecified cohort report of the phase 3 trial with a same-protocol extension (CAPItello-291)
cards.people: A prespecified exploratory Chinese cohort of CAPItello-291 (n = 24) plus an extended study run under the same protocol (n = 110) — 134 patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing during or after aromatase inhibitor treatment; 46 had PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN-altered tumours.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival favoured capivasertib–fulvestrant overall (6.9 vs 2.8 months; HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.34–0.76), in altered tumours (5.7 vs 1.9 months; HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.19–0.85) and, exploratorily, in non-altered tumours with confirmed sequencing (9.2 vs 2.7 months; HR 0.38). The most frequent adverse events on the combination were diarrhoea (60.6% vs 11.3%) and hyperglycaemia (57.7% vs 17.7%); 11.3% vs 3.2% discontinued for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial programme reported in a regional cohort plus an extension — a consistency check, not independent replication, and the non-altered-tumour signal is exploratory and hypothesis-generating only.

cards.headline: Synthesis: capivasertib plus fulvestrant prolongs progression-free survival in AKT-pathway-altered advanced breast cancer; survival benefit unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: capivasertib plus fulvestrant prolongs progression-free survival in AKT-pathway-altered advanced breast cancer; survival benefit unproven
cards.people: 982 patients across the three reports carded (708 phase 3 + 140 phase 2 + 134 Chinese cohort/extension; the cohort overlaps the phase 3 programme and is not additive evidence).
cards.result: Progression-free-survival hazard ratios were 0.50 in the altered population of the phase 3 trial, 0.58 in the phase 2 trial, and 0.41 in the altered Chinese cohort — concordant, with absolute median gains of about 4–5 months. Rash, diarrhoea and hyperglycaemia are the characteristic costs. No fetched record reports an overall-survival result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single trial programme) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: One sponsor programme: two randomised trials plus a cohort report of the larger one. If the eventual overall-survival analysis is neutral, this stamp should fall; the shelf is written so that it can.

shelves.title: INAVO120: adding inavolisib to palbociclib–fulvestrant more than doubled progression-free survival (15.0 vs 7.3 months, HR 0.43) and extended overall survival (34.0 vs 27.0 months, HR 0.67) in endocrine-resistant PIK3CA-mutated disease
shelves.question: In adults with PIK3CA-mutated hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does first-line inavolisib plus palbociclib and fulvestrant improve progression-free and overall survival versus palbociclib and fulvestrant alone?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Class I Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinases · Fulvestrant · Humans · Mutation · Phosphoinositide-3 Kinase Inhibitors · Piperazines · Progression-Free Survival · Pyridines
shelves.balance: A single phase 3 trial, but a complete one: INAVO120 randomised 325 patients with PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer who had relapsed during or within 12 months of completing adjuvant endocrine therapy — the endocrine-resistant first-line population. Adding inavolisib to palbociclib–fulvestrant more than doubled median progression-free survival (15.0 vs 7.3 months; HR 0.43, a 57% relative reduction with the absolute medians beside it) and, at the final survival analysis, extended median overall survival by 7 months (34.0 vs 27.0 months; HR 0.67; P = 0.02). Responses more than doubled (62.7% vs 28.0% at the final analysis). The added toxicity is the PI3K-class ledger — hyperglycaemia, stomatitis, diarrhoea and ocular effects on top of palbociclib's neutropenia (grade 3–4 neutropenia ~80% in both arms) — and the dedicated safety analysis shows it was managed mainly with dose interruption and supportive medicines, with only 6.8% discontinuing inavolisib. One trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean its results.

cards.headline: INAVO120 primary: progression-free survival 15.0 vs 7.3 months (HR 0.43); responses 58.4% vs 25.0%
cards.summary: INAVO120 primary: progression-free survival 15.0 vs 7.3 months (HR 0.43); responses 58.4% vs 25.0%
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial (INAVO120) — primary progression-free-survival report
cards.people: 325 patients (161 inavolisib, 164 placebo) with PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer who had relapsed during or within 12 months after completing adjuvant endocrine therapy; inavolisib 9 mg daily or placebo, each with palbociclib and fulvestrant; median follow-up ~21 months in both arms.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 15.0 months (95% CI 11.3–20.5) with inavolisib vs 7.3 months (5.6–9.3) with placebo (HR for progression or death 0.43; 95% CI 0.32–0.59; P < 0.001 — a 57% relative reduction, absolute medians beside it). An objective response occurred in 58.4% vs 25.0%. Grade 3–4 neutropenia was 80.2% vs 78.4%; grade 3–4 hyperglycaemia 5.6% vs 0%, stomatitis or mucosal inflammation 5.6% vs 0%, and diarrhoea 3.7% vs 0%. Discontinuation of any trial agent for adverse events: 6.8% vs 0.6%.
cards.watchOut: The population is specifically endocrine-resistant (relapse on or within 12 months of adjuvant endocrine therapy) — the result should not be read onto endocrine-sensitive first-line disease, where this triplet has not been tested in a fetched record.
cards.source: Turner NC et al. Inavolisib-Based Therapy in PIK3CA-Mutated Advanced Breast Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2024 (journal year as in the record). PMID: 39476340. Registry ID: NCT04191499, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: INAVO120 final survival analysis: overall survival 34.0 vs 27.0 months (HR 0.67, P = 0.02); updated progression-free HR 0.42
cards.summary: INAVO120 final survival analysis: overall survival 34.0 vs 27.0 months (HR 0.67, P = 0.02); updated progression-free HR 0.42
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial (INAVO120) — final overall-survival analysis
cards.people: The same 325 patients (161 inavolisib, 164 placebo), at a median follow-up of 34.2 and 32.3 months respectively — the trial's final overall-survival analysis.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 34.0 months (95% CI 28.4–44.8) with inavolisib vs 27.0 months (22.8–38.7) with placebo (HR for death 0.67; 95% CI 0.48–0.94; P = 0.02 against a prespecified significance boundary of P < 0.0469 — a 33% relative reduction in the hazard of death, absolute medians beside it). An objective response occurred in 62.7% vs 28.0% (P < 0.001). The updated hazard ratio for progression or death was 0.42 (95% CI 0.32–0.55). Hyperglycaemia, stomatitis or mucosal inflammation, gastrointestinal and ocular toxic effects remained more frequent with inavolisib; 6.8% discontinued inavolisib for adverse events vs 0.6% for placebo.
cards.watchOut: The same trial counted once: this card updates, and does not add to, Reference 1's population. A survival benefit from one trial in one biomarker-defined population is exactly the POSSIBLE pattern — strong, and unreplicated.

cards.headline: INAVO120 safety analysis: the added toxicities were managed mainly by interruption and supportive medicines — hyperglycaemia interrupted dosing in 27.2%, discontinued it in 0.6%
cards.summary: INAVO120 safety analysis: the added toxicities were managed mainly by interruption and supportive medicines — hyperglycaemia interrupted dosing in 27.2%, discontinued it in 0.6%
cards.type: Prespecified safety analysis of the phase 3 trial (INAVO120)
cards.people: The INAVO120 safety population (325 randomised patients; data cut-off 29 September 2023; median follow-up 21.3 months inavolisib, 21.5 months placebo), with prespecified analyses of hyperglycaemia, stomatitis/mucosal inflammation, rash and diarrhoea and their management.
cards.result: Hyperglycaemia led to inavolisib dose interruption in 27.2%, reduction in 2.5% and discontinuation in 0.6% (median onset 7.0 days; metformin the most-used antihyperglycaemic; no prediabetic patient discontinued for hyperglycaemia). Stomatitis/mucosal inflammation: interruption 9.9%, reduction 3.7%, discontinuation 0.6% (dexamethasone mouthwash most used). Rash: interruption 1.2%, discontinuation 0%. Diarrhoea: interruption 6.8%, discontinuation 0% (loperamide most used). The authors conclude the profile was generally consistent, manageable and tolerable, with events generally reversible.
cards.watchOut: Management success inside a protocol — with scheduled monitoring, mouthwash and metformin at hand — may exceed what routine practice achieves; the interruption rates (over a quarter for hyperglycaemia) are the honest workload figure.
cards.source: Im SA et al. Safety analyses of the INAVO120 randomised phase III trial of inavolisib or placebo with palbociclib-fulvestrant in patients with PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative, endocrine-resistant advanced breast cancer. shelves.title: TROPION-Breast01: datopotamab deruxtecan improved progression-free survival versus chemotherapy (HR 0.63) with fewer severe treatment-related events — but final overall survival was neutral (HR 1.01; the treatment made no difference to survival)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does datopotamab deruxtecan improve progression-free survival and response versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Breast Neoplasms · Camptothecin · Humans · Immunoconjugates · Progression-Free Survival · Receptors, Estrogen · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Trastuzumab
shelves.balance: One large phase 3 trial with a split answer, and the shelf keeps both halves. TROPION-Breast01 randomised 732 patients with endocrine-pretreated HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after 1–2 lines of chemotherapy: datopotamab deruxtecan significantly reduced the risk of progression or death versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy (HR 0.63, a 37% relative reduction; the primary record does not print the median progression-free survivals, so none are carded) and caused fewer grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (20.8% vs 44.7%). But at the final analysis, overall survival was neutral — HR 1.01 (the treatment made no difference to survival) — with a caveat the authors themselves raise: subsequent antibody-drug conjugate therapy was imbalanced (12.3% of the datopotamab arm vs 24.0% of the chemotherapy arm received one later), which may have diluted a survival difference. The detailed safety and patient-reported-outcome report adds the drug's signature costs — stomatitis in 57.2% and ocular surface events in 43.9%, mostly low grade, with rare interstitial lung disease including one grade 5 event — alongside delayed deterioration in quality of life, pain and physical functioning versus chemotherapy. A progression-free-survival win with a neutral survival result and a tolerability advantage: POSSIBLE, with the null printed in the title line where it belongs.

cards.headline: TROPION-Breast01 primary: progression-free survival HR 0.63 versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy; grade ≥3 treatment-related events 20.8% vs 44.7%
cards.summary: TROPION-Breast01 primary: progression-free survival HR 0.63 versus investigator's-choice chemotherapy; grade ≥3 treatment-related events 20.8% vs 44.7%
cards.type: Randomized, open-label phase 3 trial (TROPION-Breast01) — primary results
cards.people: 732 adults with inoperable/metastatic hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer who had progressed on endocrine therapy, for whom endocrine therapy was unsuitable, and who had received 1–2 prior lines of chemotherapy in the metastatic setting; randomised 1:1 to datopotamab deruxtecan 6 mg/kg every 3 weeks (n = 365) or investigator's-choice chemotherapy (n = 367; eribulin, vinorelbine, capecitabine or gemcitabine).
cards.result: Datopotamab deruxtecan significantly reduced the risk of progression or death versus chemotherapy (progression-free survival by blinded central review HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.52–0.76; P < 0.0001 — a 37% relative reduction; the record does not print median progression-free survivals, so none are stated). Overall survival was immature, with a trend favouring datopotamab deruxtecan (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.62–1.14 — superseded by Reference 2's final analysis). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were 20.8% vs 44.7%. The most common events on datopotamab deruxtecan were nausea (51.1%; grade ≥3 1.4%) and stomatitis (50%; grade ≥3 6.4%); on chemotherapy, neutropenia (42.5%; grade ≥3 30.8%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label (the progression endpoint was protected by blinded central review). The survival trend in this report is an interim look — Reference 2's final analysis is the survival answer, and it is neutral.

cards.headline: TROPION-Breast01 final survival analysis: overall survival HR 1.01 — the treatment made no difference to survival (P = 0.9445)
cards.summary: TROPION-Breast01 final survival analysis: overall survival HR 1.01 — the treatment made no difference to survival (P = 0.9445)
cards.type: Randomized, open-label phase 3 trial (TROPION-Breast01) — final overall-survival analysis
cards.people: The same 732 randomised patients, at a median follow-up of 22.8 months — the trial's final overall-survival analysis, a dual primary endpoint.
cards.result: Overall survival did not differ significantly between datopotamab deruxtecan and investigator's-choice chemotherapy (HR 1.01; 95% CI 0.83–1.22; P = 0.9445 — the treatment made no difference to survival). Use of antibody-drug conjugates (trastuzumab deruxtecan and sacituzumab govitecan) as subsequent therapy was imbalanced: 12.3% in the datopotamab arm vs 24.0% in the chemotherapy arm, which the authors note may have affected the survival results. Secondary endpoints (investigator-assessed progression-free survival, response rate, duration of response, time to subsequent therapy) continued to favour datopotamab deruxtecan, and no new safety signals emerged.
cards.watchOut: The subsequent-therapy imbalance is a real interpretive caveat, not a rescue: with HR 1.01 and a confidence interval spanning 0.83–1.22, the fetched record supports 'no demonstrated survival difference', and the shelf states it that way.

cards.headline: TROPION-Breast01 safety and patient-reported outcomes: stomatitis 57.2% and ocular events 43.9% (mostly low grade), rare lung disease — and slower deterioration in quality of life than chemotherapy
cards.summary: TROPION-Breast01 safety and patient-reported outcomes: stomatitis 57.2% and ocular events 43.9% (mostly low grade), rare lung disease — and slower deterioration in quality of life than chemotherapy
cards.type: Safety and patient-reported-outcome analysis of the phase 3 trial (TROPION-Breast01)
cards.people: The trial's safety populations (datopotamab deruxtecan n = 360; chemotherapy n = 351) at the final analysis, with protocol-advised steroid mouthwash and ophthalmologic assessments, and EORTC QLQ-C30 patient-reported outcomes as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: On datopotamab deruxtecan, nausea was the most common treatment-related event (51.9%; grade ≥3 1.4%); treatment-related oral mucositis/stomatitis occurred in 57.2% (grade ≥3 7.2%) and ocular surface events in 43.9% (grade ≥3 1.9%). Adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis occurred in 3.9% (grade ≥3 0.8%), including one grade 5 event. Most patients received anti-emetics (76.7%), prophylactic mouthwash (77.2%) or artificial tears (71.7%). Haematologic toxicity dominated the chemotherapy profile. Time to deterioration in global health status/quality of life, pain and physical functioning was delayed with datopotamab deruxtecan versus chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: The tolerability advantage was achieved inside a protocol that pushed prophylactic mouthwash, anti-emetics and eye care; without that scaffolding, the stomatitis and ocular rates in practice may be worse. Quality-of-life deterioration was delayed, not improved in absolute terms.

shelves.title: ExteNET: 1 year of extended adjuvant neratinib reduced invasive recurrence (2-year iDFS HR 0.67; 5-year HR 0.73) — at the cost of grade 3 diarrhoea in 40% without prophylaxis; benefit largest in hormone receptor-positive disease started within a year of trastuzumab
shelves.question: In adults with HER2-positive early breast cancer after locoregional treatment and neoadjuvant/adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy, does 1 year of extended adjuvant neratinib reduce invasive recurrence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Quinolines · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Trastuzumab
shelves.balance: One large trial followed for a decade, and its answer has stayed consistent while narrowing. ExteNET randomised 2,840 women with HER2-positive early breast cancer after trastuzumab-based therapy to 1 year of neratinib or placebo: invasive disease-free survival was better at 2 years (93.9% vs 91.6%; HR 0.67, a 33% relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it) and at 5 years (90.2% vs 87.7%; HR 0.73). The prespecified hormone receptor-positive analysis shows where the benefit concentrates: in women who started neratinib within a year of finishing trastuzumab, the 5-year absolute invasive disease-free survival benefit was 5.1% (HR 0.58), with an 8-year overall-survival difference that was numerical only (absolute 2.1%; HR 0.79; confidence interval crossing 1) — no fetched record shows a significant overall-survival benefit in the whole population. The cost is front-loaded and gastrointestinal: without diarrhoea prophylaxis, grade 3 diarrhoea affected 40% on neratinib vs 2% on placebo in both the 2- and 5-year reports. A real recurrence benefit in one trial, an unproven survival benefit, and a substantial tolerability price: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ExteNET primary (2 years): invasive disease-free survival 93.9% vs 91.6% (HR 0.67) — and grade 3 diarrhoea in 40% vs 2%
cards.summary: ExteNET primary (2 years): invasive disease-free survival 93.9% vs 91.6% (HR 0.67) — and grade 3 diarrhoea in 40% vs 2%
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ExteNET) — primary 2-year analysis
cards.people: 2,840 women (1,420 per arm) aged ≥18 years with stage 1–3 HER2-positive breast cancer (amended in 2010 to stage 2–3) who had completed neoadjuvant/adjuvant trastuzumab-based therapy up to 2 years (later 1 year) before randomisation, at 495 centres; oral neratinib 240 mg/day or placebo for 1 year; median follow-up 24 months.
cards.result: At 2 years, 70 invasive disease-free survival events had occurred on neratinib vs 109 on placebo (stratified HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.50–0.91; P = 0.0091 — a 33% relative reduction); the 2-year invasive disease-free survival rate was 93.9% (95% CI 92.4–95.2) vs 91.6% (90.0–93.0), an absolute difference of 2.3 percentage points. The most common grade 3–4 adverse events on neratinib were diarrhoea (grade 3 in 40%, grade 4 in <1%, vs grade 3 in 2% on placebo), vomiting (grade 3, 3% vs <1%) and nausea (grade 3, 2% vs <1%). Serious adverse events occurred in 7% vs 6%; seven deaths unrelated to disease progression occurred after study-drug discontinuation, none attributed to treatment.
cards.watchOut: The trial predates routine antidiarrhoeal prophylaxis and dose-escalation strategies, so the 40% grade 3 diarrhoea rate is the unmitigated figure; it also predates adjuvant T-DM1 and pertuzumab-era baselines, which matters when transporting the absolute benefit to current practice.
cards.source: Chan A et al. Neratinib after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy in patients with HER2-positive breast cancer (ExteNET): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol. 2016. PMID: 26874901. Registry ID: NCT00878709, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ExteNET 5-year analysis: the benefit persists — invasive disease-free survival 90.2% vs 87.7% (HR 0.73), no new long-term toxicity signal
cards.summary: ExteNET 5-year analysis: the benefit persists — invasive disease-free survival 90.2% vs 87.7% (HR 0.73), no new long-term toxicity signal
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ExteNET) — 5-year analysis
cards.people: The same 2,840 women, at a median follow-up of 5.2 years — a protocol-defined 5-year sensitivity analysis of invasive disease-free survival, by intention to treat.
cards.result: Patients on neratinib had significantly fewer invasive disease-free survival events than those on placebo (116 vs 163 events; stratified HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.57–0.92; P = 0.0083 — a 27% relative reduction); 5-year invasive disease-free survival was 90.2% (95% CI 88.3–91.8) vs 87.7% (85.7–89.4), an absolute difference of 2.5 percentage points. Without diarrhoea prophylaxis, grade 3–4 events on neratinib remained dominated by diarrhoea (40% grade 3, <1% grade 4, vs 2% on placebo). No evidence of increased long-term toxicity or of long-term adverse consequences of neratinib-associated diarrhoea was identified. An overall-survival analysis was planned after 248 events and is not reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: The same trial counted once, at a later cut: the absolute benefit at 5 years (2.5 points) is barely larger than at 2 years (2.3 points) in the whole population — the growth in benefit is in the hormone receptor-positive subgroup on Reference 3, not overall.

cards.headline: ExteNET hormone receptor-positive final analysis: started within a year of trastuzumab, the 5-year absolute benefit was 5.1% (HR 0.58); 8-year survival difference numerical only (HR 0.79)
cards.summary: ExteNET hormone receptor-positive final analysis: started within a year of trastuzumab, the 5-year absolute benefit was 5.1% (HR 0.58); 8-year survival difference numerical only (HR 0.79)
cards.type: Prespecified-subgroup descriptive analysis of the phase 3 trial (ExteNET) — hormone receptor-positive population
cards.people: Descriptive analyses in the trial's hormone receptor-positive population: 1,334 patients who initiated treatment ≤1 year after trastuzumab (670 neratinib, 664 placebo) and 297 who initiated >1 year after (146 vs 151); of the ≤1-year group, 354 had received neoadjuvant therapy and 295 of those had residual disease.
cards.result: In the hormone receptor-positive/≤1-year population, the absolute invasive disease-free survival benefit at 5 years was 5.1% (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.41–0.82), versus 1.3% (HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.29–1.84) in the >1-year group. Overall survival at 8 years in the ≤1-year group showed a numerical improvement only (absolute benefit 2.1%; HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.55–1.13 — not significant). In patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy, absolute benefits were 7.4% for 5-year invasive disease-free survival (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.33–1.07) and 9.1% for 8-year overall survival (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.23–0.92). Fewer central nervous system events occurred with neratinib.
cards.watchOut: Descriptive subgroup analyses, not powered comparisons: the ≤1-year and residual-disease figures identify where benefit concentrates, but their confidence intervals are wide and the 8-year survival signal in the residual-disease subgroup rests on few events.
cards.source: Chan A et al. Final Efficacy Results of Neratinib in HER2-positive Hormone Receptor-positive Early-stage Breast Cancer From the Phase III ExteNET Trial. Clin Breast Cancer. 2021. PMID: 33183970. Registry ID: NCT00878709, as the trial of References 1–2; none in this record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: extended adjuvant neratinib prevents invasive recurrences, most clearly in hormone receptor-positive disease started promptly — survival benefit unproven, diarrhoea the price
cards.summary: Synthesis: extended adjuvant neratinib prevents invasive recurrences, most clearly in hormone receptor-positive disease started promptly — survival benefit unproven, diarrhoea the price
cards.people: 2,840 women in the single ExteNET trial, reported across the three cards.
cards.result: Invasive disease-free survival HR 0.67 at 2 years and 0.73 at 5 years (absolute gains 2.3 and 2.5 percentage points overall; 5.1 points at 5 years in hormone receptor-positive disease started ≤1 year after trastuzumab). No fetched record demonstrates a significant overall-survival benefit. Grade 3 diarrhoea affected 40% without prophylaxis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single trial) pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: One trial, conducted before several current adjuvant standards existed. The stamp reflects a genuine, durable recurrence benefit that has never been independently replicated and never converted into a demonstrated survival benefit.

shelves.title: Quizartinib added to intensive chemotherapy in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML (QuANTUM-First): median survival 31.9 versus 15.1 months in the one phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive acute myeloid leukaemia fit for intensive chemotherapy, does adding quizartinib to induction and consolidation chemotherapy and as continuation therapy improve overall survival versus chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Benzothiazoles/therapeutic use* · Cytarabine · Double-Blind Method · fms-Like Tyrosine Kinase 3/antagonists & inhibitors/genetics · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy/genetics* · Phenylurea Compounds/therapeutic use* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one strong trial, honestly capped. In QuANTUM-First (Erba 2023, PMID: 37116523), 539 adults aged 18–75 with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML were randomised to quizartinib or placebo added to standard induction and consolidation (with or without allogeneic transplant) and continued as single-agent therapy for up to 3 years. Median overall survival was 31.9 months on quizartinib versus 15.1 months on placebo (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it). Post-hoc analyses of the same trial point the same way: the quizartinib association persisted when transplant in first remission was modelled as a time-dependent variable (Schlenk 2025, PMID: 40079105), and quizartinib produced deeper FLT3-ITD MRD-negative remissions, with end-of-induction MRD tracking relapse and survival (Levis 2026, PMID: 41052406). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were near-universal in both arms (92% versus 90%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp, and the confidence interval (to 0.98) leaves the true effect compatible with modest.

cards.headline: Erba 2023 (QuANTUM-First): median overall survival 31.9 months on quizartinib versus 15.1 months on placebo (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032)
cards.summary: Erba 2023 (QuANTUM-First): median overall survival 31.9 months on quizartinib versus 15.1 months on placebo (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Erba 2023, QuANTUM-First)
cards.people: 539 adults aged 18–75 years with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML at 193 hospitals in 26 countries, randomly assigned to quizartinib (n=268) or placebo (n=271) added to standard 7+3 induction and high-dose cytarabine consolidation, with or without allogeneic transplant, followed by single-agent continuation for up to 3 years. Median age 56 years; median follow-up 39.2 months.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 31.9 months (95% CI 21.0 to not estimable) with quizartinib versus 15.1 months (13.2 to 26.2) with placebo — hazard ratio 0.78 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.98; p=0.032), a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 92% on quizartinib and 90% on placebo; the most common were febrile neutropenia, hypokalaemia and pneumonia in both groups, plus neutropenia in the quizartinib group.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. The survival hazard ratio's confidence interval reaches 0.98 — the benefit, while significant, is compatible with a small effect — and the regimen tested is the whole package (induction, consolidation and up to 3 years of continuation), so this record cannot separate which phase contributes what.
cards.source: Erba HP et al. Quizartinib plus chemotherapy in newly diagnosed patients with FLT3-internal-tandem-duplication-positive acute myeloid leukaemia (QuANTUM-First): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 37116523. Registry ID: NCT02668653. cards.headline: Schlenk 2025 (QuANTUM-First, post-hoc transplant analysis): quizartinib and transplant in first remission each independently predicted longer survival (HR 0.55 and 0.53 in the CR1 analysis)
cards.summary: Schlenk 2025 (QuANTUM-First, post-hoc transplant analysis): quizartinib and transplant in first remission each independently predicted longer survival (HR 0.55 and 0.53 in the CR1 analysis)
cards.type: Post-hoc multivariable analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Schlenk 2025, QuANTUM-First)
cards.people: Post-hoc multivariable analysis of QuANTUM-First patients who achieved complete remission by end of induction (n=297; quizartinib 147, placebo 150), of whom 157 (52.9%) underwent allogeneic transplant in first remission; a parallel composite-remission analysis covered 368 patients, 196 transplanted.
cards.result: In the complete-remission analysis, both quizartinib treatment (HR 0.553, 95% CI 0.383 to 0.798; P=0.0015) and transplant in first remission (HR 0.527, 95% CI 0.349 to 0.796; P=0.0023) were significant predictors of longer overall survival — relative (hazard) measures from a post-hoc model with transplant as a time-dependent variable. The composite-remission analysis gave the same pattern (quizartinib HR 0.645; transplant HR 0.557). No new safety signals; post-transplant complications were mostly grade 2 or higher graft-versus-host disease, as expected.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and not randomised by transplant: patients who reach transplant in first remission are selected for fitness and response, so the transplant hazard ratio is not a randomised treatment effect. Its narrower use here is that the quizartinib association persisted with transplant accounted for as a time-dependent variable.

Haematologica. 2025. PMID: 40079105. Registry ID: NCT02668653. cards.headline: Levis 2026 (QuANTUM-First MRD analysis): quizartinib produced deeper FLT3-ITD MRD-negative remissions than placebo, and end-of-induction MRD level tracked relapse and survival
cards.summary: Levis 2026 (QuANTUM-First MRD analysis): quizartinib produced deeper FLT3-ITD MRD-negative remissions than placebo, and end-of-induction MRD level tracked relapse and survival
cards.type: Post-hoc MRD/biomarker analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Levis 2026, QuANTUM-First)
cards.people: Post-hoc measurable-residual-disease analysis of QuANTUM-First using an amplicon-based next-generation sequencing assay for FLT3-ITD, with samples collected throughout therapy; the record reports no single analysis N in its abstract.
cards.result: Quizartinib induced deeper remissions than placebo on FLT3-ITD MRD; the amount of MRD at completion of induction correlated with relapse and survival. Longer FLT3-ITD insertion mutations correlated with worse outcome, but quizartinib was beneficial irrespective of insertion length, and quizartinib increased MRD-negativity rates at end of induction versus placebo regardless of NPM1 comutation status. The assay was more sensitive in bone marrow than peripheral blood.
cards.watchOut: MRD is a depth-of-remission marker, not a patient outcome: this card supports the mechanism of the survival result but adds no independent survival evidence, and the analysis is post hoc. N for the MRD analysis is not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.source: Levis MJ et al. FLT3-ITD measurable residual disease from the QuANTUM-First trial. Blood Advances. 2026. PMID: 41052406. Registry ID: NCT02668653. cards.people: One randomised programme: QuANTUM-First, 539 adults aged 18–75 with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD-positive AML fit for intensive chemotherapy (Erba 2023), with post-hoc transplant (Schlenk 2025) and MRD (Levis 2026) analyses of the same trial.

Scope: FLT3-ITD-positive disease only, in patients fit for intensive chemotherapy; this says nothing about FLT3-TKD-only disease, older/unfit patients, or quizartinib as monotherapy. The two supporting cards are analyses of the same 539 patients, not independent confirmation.

shelves.title: Gilteritinib versus salvage chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML (ADMIRAL): median survival 9.3 versus 5.6 months in the one phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated acute myeloid leukaemia, does gilteritinib monotherapy improve overall survival versus salvage chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aniline Compounds/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy/genetics/mortality · Liver/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation* · Pyrazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Salvage Therapy* · Survival Analysis · fms-Like Tyrosine Kinase 3/genetics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one decisive trial, honestly capped. In ADMIRAL (Perl 2019, PMID: 31665578), 371 adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML were randomised 2:1 to gilteritinib 120 mg daily or salvage chemotherapy: median overall survival 9.3 versus 5.6 months (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it), and complete remission with full or partial haematologic recovery in 34.0% versus 15.3%. The 2-year follow-up held the line — survival 20.6% versus 14.2%, HR 0.665 (Perl 2022, PMID: 35081255) — and the transplant analysis shows the mechanism of durability: gilteritinib got more patients to transplant (26% versus 15%), and the relapse-free long-term survivors were concentrated there (Perl 2023, PMID: 36526260). Absolute survival remains short in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Perl 2019 (ADMIRAL): median overall survival 9.3 months on gilteritinib versus 5.6 months on salvage chemotherapy (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Perl 2019 (ADMIRAL): median overall survival 9.3 months on gilteritinib versus 5.6 months on salvage chemotherapy (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001)
cards.people: 371 adults with relapsed or refractory FLT3-mutated AML randomly assigned 2:1 to gilteritinib 120 mg daily (n=247) or salvage chemotherapy (n=124) in a phase 3 trial.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 9.3 months on gilteritinib versus 5.6 months on chemotherapy (hazard ratio for death 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.83; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it). Complete remission with full or partial haematologic recovery: 34.0% versus 15.3% (risk difference 18.6 percentage points, 95% CI 9.8 to 27.4); complete remission alone 21.1% versus 10.5%. Median event-free survival 2.8 versus 0.7 months. Adjusted for treatment duration, grade 3 or higher and serious adverse events occurred less frequently on gilteritinib; its most common grade 3 or higher events were febrile neutropenia (45.9%), anaemia (40.7%) and thrombocytopenia (22.8%).
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. Absolute survival remains short in both arms — the gain is a median of 3.7 months in a relapsed/refractory population — and the comparator is a preselected mix of high- and low-intensity salvage regimens, not one standard regimen.
cards.source: Perl AE et al. Gilteritinib or Chemotherapy for Relapsed or Refractory FLT3-Mutated AML. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31665578. Registry ID: NCT02421939.
