cards.headline: Perl 2022 (ADMIRAL 2-year follow-up): survival advantage maintained — 2-year survival 20.6% on gilteritinib versus 14.2% on chemotherapy (HR 0.665)
cards.summary: Perl 2022 (ADMIRAL 2-year follow-up): survival advantage maintained — 2-year survival 20.6% on gilteritinib versus 14.2% on chemotherapy (HR 0.665)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of a randomised phase 3 trial (Perl 2022, ADMIRAL)
cards.people: The same 371 ADMIRAL patients (gilteritinib n=247; salvage chemotherapy n=124) followed to a median survival follow-up of 37.1 months; deaths in 203 of 247 and 97 of 124 patients respectively, with 16 gilteritinib patients still on treatment.
cards.result: Median overall survival remained 9.3 versus 5.6 months (HR 0.665, 95% CI 0.518 to 0.853; two-sided P=0.0013 — a relative measure). Estimated 2-year survival was 20.6% (95% CI 15.8 to 26.0) versus 14.2% (95% CI 8.3 to 21.6). In the gilteritinib arm the 2-year cumulative incidence of relapse after composite complete remission was 75.7%, with few relapses after 18 months; 26 gilteritinib patients were alive at 2 years or more without relapse, 18 of whom had undergone transplantation and 16 of whom restarted gilteritinib as post-transplant maintenance. The commonest adverse events of interest in years 1–2 were raised liver transaminases, with incidence falling in year 2.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the same randomised patients, not a second trial: it shows the early survival difference did not evaporate, but most gilteritinib patients still relapsed (2-year relapse incidence 75.7% after composite remission) — durability is concentrated in the minority who reached transplant and maintenance.

cards.headline: Perl 2023 (ADMIRAL transplant analysis): gilteritinib got more patients to transplant (26% versus 15%); post-transplant survival was similar in both arms
cards.summary: Perl 2023 (ADMIRAL transplant analysis): gilteritinib got more patients to transplant (26% versus 15%); post-transplant survival was similar in both arms
cards.type: Transplant-outcomes analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Perl 2023, ADMIRAL)
cards.people: ADMIRAL patients who underwent haematopoietic stem cell transplantation during the trial: 64 of 247 (26%) in the gilteritinib arm and 19 of 124 (15%) in the chemotherapy arm; gilteritinib-arm patients could restart gilteritinib as post-transplant maintenance.
cards.result: For all transplant recipients, 12- and 24-month overall survival rates were 68% and 47%. Post-transplant survival was comparable between arms despite a trend favouring pre-transplant composite remission. Patients who resumed gilteritinib after transplant had low relapse rates after pre-transplant composite complete remission (20%) or complete remission (0%). The commonest adverse events on post-transplant gilteritinib were raised alanine aminotransferase (45%), pyrexia (43%) and diarrhoea (40%), with grade 3 or higher events mainly myelosuppression; grade III or higher acute graft-versus-host disease and related mortality were low.
cards.watchOut: Transplant was not randomised: who reached transplant reflects response and fitness, so the similar post-transplant survival across arms cannot be read as the drugs being equivalent after transplant — the gilteritinib advantage in this analysis is the higher remission rate that got more patients to transplant at all.
cards.source: Perl AE et al. Outcomes in Patients with FLT3-Mutated Relapsed/Refractory Acute Myelogenous Leukemia Who Underwent Transplantation in the Phase 3 ADMIRAL Trial of Gilteritinib versus Salvage Chemotherapy. Transplantation and Cellular Therapy. 2023. PMID: 36526260. Registry ID: none in the record (the parent trial is ADMIRAL, NCT02421939, as named in the primary report). cards.people: One randomised programme: ADMIRAL, 371 adults with relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML (Perl 2019), its 2-year follow-up (Perl 2022) and its transplant analysis (Perl 2023).

shelves.title: Ivosidenib plus azacitidine in unfit IDH1-mutated AML (AGILE): median survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months, confirmed at long-term follow-up
shelves.question: In older or unfit adults with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukaemia, does ivosidenib plus azacitidine improve event-free and overall survival versus azacitidine alone?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Azacitidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Febrile Neutropenia/chemically induced · Glycine/analogs & derivatives · Humans · Isocitrate Dehydrogenase/genetics · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/drug therapy/genetics* · Leukopenia/chemically induced · Pyridines/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small but decisive trial, honestly capped. In AGILE (Montesinos 2022, PMID: 35443108), 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive chemotherapy were randomised to ivosidenib plus azacitidine or placebo plus azacitidine: event-free survival HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.69) and median overall survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.73 — relative measures, absolute medians beside them). The long-term report at 28.6 months' median follow-up held the result (median survival 29.3 versus 7.9 months, HR 0.42; transfusion independence 53.8% versus 17.1%) (Montesinos 2025, PMID: 40706052). The combination began in a 23-patient phase 1b study with a 60.9% complete remission rate (DiNardo 2021, PMID: 33119479). Infections were less frequent on the combination; neutropenia and bleeding more frequent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Montesinos 2022 (AGILE): event-free survival HR 0.33 and median overall survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.44) for ivosidenib plus azacitidine versus azacitidine alone
cards.summary: Montesinos 2022 (AGILE): event-free survival HR 0.33 and median overall survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.44) for ivosidenib plus azacitidine versus azacitidine alone
cards.people: 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy, randomly assigned to oral ivosidenib 500 mg daily plus azacitidine (n=72) or placebo plus azacitidine (n=74); median follow-up 12.4 months.
cards.result: Event-free survival was significantly longer with ivosidenib-azacitidine (HR for treatment failure, relapse or death 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.69; P=0.002 — a relative measure); the estimated probability of remaining event-free at 12 months was 37% versus 12%. Median overall survival was 24.0 versus 7.9 months (HR for death 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.73; P=0.001). Grade 3 or higher febrile neutropenia occurred in 28% versus 34% and neutropenia in 27% versus 16%; bleeding of any grade in 41% versus 29%; infection of any grade was less frequent with ivosidenib (28% versus 49%); differentiation syndrome of any grade occurred in 14% versus 8%.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. The trial is small for a phase 3 (146 patients) and the event-free-survival definition counts failure to reach complete remission by week 24 as an event — a definition that favours the arm producing more remissions; the overall-survival result is the harder outcome and it agrees.
cards.source: Montesinos P et al. Ivosidenib and Azacitidine in IDH1-Mutated Acute Myeloid Leukemia. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35443108. Registry ID: NCT03173248. cards.headline: Montesinos 2025 (AGILE long-term): at 28.6 months' median follow-up, median overall survival 29.3 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.42), with transfusion independence in 53.8% versus 17.1%
cards.summary: Montesinos 2025 (AGILE long-term): at 28.6 months' median follow-up, median overall survival 29.3 versus 7.9 months (HR 0.42), with transfusion independence in 53.8% versus 17.1%
cards.type: Long-term post-hoc analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Montesinos 2025, AGILE)
cards.people: 148 patients randomised in AGILE as reported in this long-term post-hoc analysis (ivosidenib-azacitidine n=73; placebo-azacitidine n=75), median follow-up 28.6 months. (The primary report analysed 146 patients in its intention-to-treat population; each card uses its own record's numbers.)
cards.result: Median overall survival was 29.3 months (95% CI 13.2 to not reached) with ivosidenib-azacitidine versus 7.9 months (95% CI 4.1 to 11.3) with placebo-azacitidine (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.65; P<0.0001 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it). Haematologic recovery was faster and more durable on ivosidenib, and conversion to transfusion independence was more common (53.8% versus 17.1%; P=0.0004). Of 33 ivosidenib-treated patients evaluable for molecular MRD, 10 converted to MRD negativity; MRD-negative responders had numerically longer survival. The previously reported safety profile was maintained.
cards.watchOut: A longer look at the same small trial, not independent confirmation — and it is labelled post hoc. The randomised denominators differ slightly between the two reports (146 versus 148) as printed in their own records; the survival conclusion is the same in both.
cards.source: Montesinos P et al. Long-term results from the AGILE study of azacitidine plus ivosidenib vs placebo in newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML. Blood Advances. 2025. PMID: 40706052. cards.headline: DiNardo 2021 (phase 1b): the combination first showed a 78.3% overall response rate and 60.9% complete remission rate in 23 unfit patients
cards.summary: DiNardo 2021 (phase 1b): the combination first showed a 78.3% overall response rate and 60.9% complete remission rate in 23 unfit patients
cards.people: 23 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive induction (median age 76 years, range 61–88) treated open-label with ivosidenib 500 mg daily plus azacitidine 75 mg/m² on days 1–7 of 28-day cycles in a phase 1b dose-finding and expansion study.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 78.3% (18 of 23; 95% CI 56.3 to 92.5) and complete remission rate 60.9% (14 of 23; 95% CI 38.5 to 80.3). Median duration of response had not been reached at a median follow-up of 16 months, and the 12-month survival estimate was 82.0% (95% CI 58.8 to 92.8). IDH1 mutation clearance in marrow was seen in 10 of 14 complete responders. Treatment-related grade 3 or higher events in over 10% were neutropenia (22%), anaemia (13%), thrombocytopenia (13%) and QT prolongation (13%); differentiation syndrome of any grade occurred in 17%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and small (23 patients): response rates without a comparator cannot show benefit — this card is the programme's origin, and the randomised AGILE cards above carry the verdict. Its confidence intervals are wide (complete remission 38.5% to 80.3%).
cards.source: DiNardo CD et al. Mutant Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1 Inhibitor Ivosidenib in Combination With Azacitidine for Newly Diagnosed Acute Myeloid Leukemia. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2021. PMID: 33119479. Registry ID: NCT02677922. cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial, matured — survival roughly tripled at the median in unfit IDH1-mutated AML
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial, matured — survival roughly tripled at the median in unfit IDH1-mutated AML
cards.people: One randomised programme: AGILE, 146 patients in the primary analysis (Montesinos 2022) and 148 as randomised in the long-term report (Montesinos 2025), preceded by a 23-patient phase 1b study of the same combination (DiNardo 2021).
cards.result: Event-free survival HR 0.33 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.69); median overall survival 24.0 versus 7.9 months at primary analysis (HR 0.44) and 29.3 versus 7.9 months at 28.6 months' follow-up (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.65). Transfusion independence 53.8% versus 17.1%. Infections of any grade were less frequent on the combination (28% versus 49%); neutropenia and bleeding were more frequent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML in patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy. Nothing here covers IDH2-mutated disease, fit patients, or ivosidenib monotherapy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Montesinos P et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35443108); Montesinos P et al. Blood Advances. 2025 (PMID: 40706052); DiNardo CD et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2021 (PMID: 33119479).

shelves.title: Inotuzumab ozogamicin in relapsed/refractory B-ALL (INO-VATE): remissions 73.8% versus 30.9% and more transplants, with a modest survival gain and a 13–14% sinusoidal obstruction risk
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, does inotuzumab ozogamicin improve remission and overall survival versus standard chemotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Inotuzumab Ozogamicin · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Precursor Cell Lymphoblastic Leukemia-Lymphoma/drug therapy/mortality · Remission Induction · Sialic Acid Binding Ig-like Lectin 2/antagonists & inhibitors · Survival Analysis · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large remission effect, a modest survival effect, one trial. In INO-VATE (Kantarjian 2016, PMID: 27292104), inotuzumab ozogamicin produced complete remission in 80.7% versus 29.4% in the primary first-218 analysis, with MRD negativity in 78.4% versus 28.1% of remitters; the survival hazard ratio at that point (0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.03) crossed 1.0. The final report (Kantarjian 2019, PMID: 30920645) put full-population remission at 73.8% versus 30.9%, median survival at 7.7 versus 6.2 months and 2-year survival at 22.8% versus 10.0% (HR 0.75, 97.5% CI 0.57 to 0.99), with direct bridging to transplant in 39.6% versus 10.5%. The price is hepatic: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome in about 13–14% on inotuzumab versus about 1–2% on standard care (Kantarjian 2017, PMID: 28687420). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Kantarjian 2016 (INO-VATE): complete remission 80.7% versus 29.4% (P<0.001); median overall survival 7.7 versus 6.7 months (HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.03)
cards.summary: Kantarjian 2016 (INO-VATE): complete remission 80.7% versus 29.4% (P<0.001); median overall survival 7.7 versus 6.7 months (HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.03)
cards.people: 326 adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell ALL randomly assigned to inotuzumab ozogamicin or standard intensive chemotherapy; the primary remission analysis covered the first 218 patients (109 per group) and the survival analysis all 326.
cards.result: Complete remission (including with incomplete haematologic recovery) was 80.7% (95% CI 72.1 to 87.7) on inotuzumab versus 29.4% (95% CI 21.0 to 38.8) on standard therapy (P<0.001). Among remitters, MRD below the 0.01% threshold was achieved by 78.4% versus 28.1% (P<0.001), and duration of remission was longer (median 4.6 versus 3.1 months; HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.96). Progression-free survival was longer (median 5.0 versus 1.8 months; HR 0.45, 97.5% CI 0.34 to 0.61; P<0.001). Median overall survival was 7.7 versus 6.7 months (HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.03; P=0.04 — a relative measure whose interval crosses 1.0). Veno-occlusive liver disease of any grade occurred in 15 patients (11%) on inotuzumab versus 1 (1%) on standard therapy.
cards.watchOut: The remission result is overwhelming; the survival result is not: the hazard ratio's 97.5% confidence interval crosses 1.0 (0.58 to 1.03) at the primary analysis, so the honest claim is a large remission and progression-free benefit with a survival difference that was borderline at first report. One trial carries this shelf, capping the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Kantarjian HM et al. Inotuzumab Ozogamicin versus Standard Therapy for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. New England Journal of Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27292104. Registry ID: NCT01564784. cards.headline: Kantarjian 2019 (INO-VATE final report): remission 73.8% versus 30.9% in the full population; 2-year survival 22.8% versus 10.0% (HR 0.75); far more patients bridged to transplant (39.6% versus 10.5%)
cards.summary: Kantarjian 2019 (INO-VATE final report): remission 73.8% versus 30.9% in the full population; 2-year survival 22.8% versus 10.0% (HR 0.75); far more patients bridged to transplant (39.6% versus 10.5%)
cards.type: Final report of a randomised phase 3 trial (Kantarjian 2019, INO-VATE)
cards.people: All 326 randomised adults with relapsed/refractory B-cell precursor ALL (inotuzumab n=164; standard care n=162), with at least 2 years of follow-up; 307 received at least one dose.
cards.result: Complete remission/CR with incomplete recovery was 73.8% on inotuzumab versus 30.9% on standard care (1-sided P<0.0001), consistent across subgroups. Median overall survival was 7.7 versus 6.2 months, with 2-year survival rates of 22.8% versus 10.0% (overall HR 0.75, 97.5% CI 0.57 to 0.99; 1-sided P=0.0105 — a relative measure, absolutes beside it). More inotuzumab patients proceeded directly to transplant after remission (39.6% versus 10.5%; 1-sided P<0.0001). Veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome was more frequent on inotuzumab (23 of 164, 14.0%, versus 3 of 143, 2.1%).
cards.watchOut: The full-population remission rate (73.8%) is lower than the first-218 headline (80.7%) — both are printed, from their own records. The survival hazard ratio now excludes 1.0, but the absolute median gain is about 1.5 months; the larger practical effect is the 2-year survival tail and the bridge to transplant.
cards.source: Kantarjian HM et al. Inotuzumab ozogamicin versus standard of care in relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia: Final report and long-term survival follow-up from the randomized, phase 3 INO-VATE study. Cancer. 2019. PMID: 30920645. Registry ID: NCT01564784. cards.headline: Kantarjian 2017 (INO-VATE hepatic analysis): hepatotoxicity in 51% versus 34%, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome in 13% versus under 1% — the drug's defining harm
cards.summary: Kantarjian 2017 (INO-VATE hepatic analysis): hepatotoxicity in 51% versus 34%, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome in 13% versus under 1% — the drug's defining harm
cards.type: Prespecified safety analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Kantarjian 2017, INO-VATE)
cards.people: Prespecified safety analysis of the 307 INO-VATE patients who received at least one dose (inotuzumab n=164; standard care n=143), covering treatment-emergent hepatotoxicity during therapy, in follow-up without transplant, and after subsequent transplant, to a March 8, 2016 cutoff.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent hepatotoxicities of all grades were more frequent on inotuzumab (83 of 164, 51%) than standard care (49 of 143, 34%). Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome events — during treatment or follow-up without transplant, and after treatment plus subsequent transplant — were higher on inotuzumab (22 patients, 13%; 18 of the 22, 82%, grade 3 or worse) than standard care (1 patient, under 1%). During therapy or follow-up without transplant, 5 patients (3%) in the inotuzumab group developed sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.
cards.watchOut: This is a harm card from the same trial, not independent evidence: it quantifies the price of the remission benefit. The risk concentrates around transplant after inotuzumab, which is exactly the pathway the drug is used to enable — the two facts have to be held together.
cards.source: Kantarjian HM et al. Hepatic adverse event profile of inotuzumab ozogamicin in adult patients with relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: results from the open-label, randomised, phase 3 INO-VATE study. Lancet Haematology. 2017. PMID: 28687420. Registry ID: NCT01564784. shelves.title: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel in lenalidomide-refractory myeloma (CARTITUDE-4): progression-free HR 0.26, overall-survival HR 0.55 at the update
shelves.question: In adults with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior lines, does a single ciltacabtagene autoleucel infusion improve progression-free and overall survival versus standard regimens?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Lenalidomide/adverse effects · Multiple Myeloma/drug therapy/mortality* · Neurotoxicity Syndromes · Progression-Free Survival · B-Cell Maturation Antigen/immunology* · Immunotherapy, Adoptive/methods* · Antineoplastic Agents, Immunological/therapeutic use* · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one trial with unusually large effects, honestly capped. In CARTITUDE-4 (San-Miguel 2023, PMID: 37272512), 419 patients with lenalidomide-refractory myeloma after 1–3 prior lines were randomised to a single ciltacabtagene autoleucel infusion or physician's-choice standard care: progression-free survival HR 0.26 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.38), complete response or better in 73.1% versus 21.8%, and MRD absence in 60.6% versus 15.6%. Overall survival had not separated at the primary analysis (HR 0.78, interval crossing 1.0) but did at the prespecified update — HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79; p=0.0009) at 33.6 months (Einsele 2026, PMID: 41519141) — and patient-reported outcomes favoured cilta-cel (Mina 2025, PMID: 39756844). Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 76.1% of infused patients but was grade 3 or 4 in only 1.1%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single trial programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: San-Miguel 2023 (CARTITUDE-4): progression-free survival HR 0.26 — median not reached versus 11.8 months; complete response or better 73.1% versus 21.8%
cards.summary: San-Miguel 2023 (CARTITUDE-4): progression-free survival HR 0.26 — median not reached versus 11.8 months; complete response or better 73.1% versus 21.8%
cards.people: 419 patients with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma after 1–3 prior lines, randomly assigned to a single ciltacabtagene autoleucel infusion (n=208) or physician's-choice standard care (n=211); median follow-up 15.9 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was not reached with cilta-cel versus 11.8 months with standard care (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.38; P<0.001 — a relative measure); 12-month progression-free survival was 75.9% versus 48.6%. Overall response 84.6% versus 67.3%; complete response or better 73.1% versus 21.8%; MRD absence 60.6% versus 15.6%. Deaths from any cause: 39 versus 46 (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2 — not significant at this analysis). Among 176 patients who received cilta-cel, cytokine release syndrome occurred in 76.1% (grade 3 or 4 in 1.1%, no grade 5), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity in 4.5% (all grade 1 or 2), cranial nerve palsy in 9.1%, and CAR-T-related peripheral neuropathy in 2.8%.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. At the primary analysis overall survival had not separated (HR 0.78 with an interval crossing 1.0) — the claim then was progression-free survival and depth of response; the survival claim rests on the update below.
cards.source: San-Miguel J et al. Cilta-cel or Standard Care in Lenalidomide-Refractory Multiple Myeloma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37272512. Registry ID: NCT04181827. cards.headline: Einsele 2026 (CARTITUDE-4 updated analysis): overall survival HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79; p=0.0009) at 33.6 months' median follow-up; progression-free HR 0.29
cards.summary: Einsele 2026 (CARTITUDE-4 updated analysis): overall survival HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79; p=0.0009) at 33.6 months' median follow-up; progression-free HR 0.29
cards.type: Updated prespecified interim analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Einsele 2026, CARTITUDE-4)
cards.people: The same 419 randomised patients (cilta-cel n=208; standard care n=211) at 81 sites, in a prespecified second interim overall-survival analysis at a median follow-up of 33.6 months. Standard care was pomalidomide-bortezomib-dexamethasone or daratumumab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival remained not reached with cilta-cel (95% CI 34.5 months to not evaluable) versus 11.8 months (9.7 to 14.0) with standard care (HR 0.29, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.39). Median overall survival was not reached in either group as printed, and the hazard ratio for death was 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79; p=0.0009 — a relative measure; the record's abstract does not print the two arms' absolute survival percentages at a landmark). Maximum grade 3 treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 14% of the cilta-cel group and 37% of the standard-care group as printed in the record, most commonly anaemia (35%) with cilta-cel and neutropenia (28%) with standard care.
cards.watchOut: An update of the same trial, not a second trial — and still an interim survival analysis with median survival not reached in either arm, so the size of the eventual absolute survival gain is not yet measurable from this record. Open-label design: progression assessment and subsequent therapy choices were unblinded.
cards.source: Einsele H et al. Cilta-cel in lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma (CARTITUDE-4): an updated analysis including overall survival from an open-label, multicentre, randomised, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncology. 2026. cards.headline: Mina 2025 (CARTITUDE-4 patient-reported outcomes): symptom worsening delayed (median 23.7 versus 18.9 months; HR 0.42) and quality-of-life scores improved on cilta-cel while flat on standard care
cards.summary: Mina 2025 (CARTITUDE-4 patient-reported outcomes): symptom worsening delayed (median 23.7 versus 18.9 months; HR 0.42) and quality-of-life scores improved on cilta-cel while flat on standard care
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Mina 2025, CARTITUDE-4)
cards.people: The 419 CARTITUDE-4 patients; 191 of 208 (92%) in the cilta-cel group and 190 of 209 evaluable (91%) in the standard-care group completed baseline patient-reported assessments, with post-baseline compliance of 70–81% and 79–89% respectively.
cards.result: Median time to sustained worsening on the myeloma symptom scale was 23.7 months with cilta-cel versus 18.9 months with standard care (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.68 — a relative measure). At 12 months, mean change in EORTC global health status was +10.1 points (95% CI 7.0 to 13.1) with cilta-cel versus −1.5 (95% CI −5.3 to 2.3) with standard care, and on the EQ-5D-5L visual analogue scale +8.0 versus +1.4 points. Rates of clinically meaningful improvement in both scores were higher with cilta-cel.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial: patients knew whether they had received a one-time cell therapy or continuing chemotherapy, which can move self-reported scores independently of disease control. Post-baseline questionnaire compliance was incomplete (70–89%), so these are supporting, not primary, results.
cards.source: Mina R et al. Patient-reported outcomes following ciltacabtagene autoleucel or standard of care in patients with lenalidomide-refractory multiple myeloma (CARTITUDE-4). Lancet Haematology. 2025. PMID: 39756844. Registry ID: NCT04181827. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, matured — a very large progression-free effect, a survival effect at the update, and better patient-reported outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, matured — a very large progression-free effect, a survival effect at the update, and better patient-reported outcomes
cards.people: One randomised programme: CARTITUDE-4, 419 patients with lenalidomide-refractory myeloma after 1–3 prior lines — primary report (San-Miguel 2023), overall-survival update (Einsele 2026) and patient-reported outcomes (Mina 2025).
cards.result: Progression-free survival HR 0.26 at primary analysis and 0.29 at the update (median not reached versus 11.8 months); complete response or better 73.1% versus 21.8%; MRD absence 60.6% versus 15.6%. Overall survival HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.79) at 33.6 months. Cytokine release syndrome in 76.1% of infused patients was almost all low grade (grade 3 or 4, 1.1%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single trial programme caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: lenalidomide-refractory disease after 1–3 prior lines including a proteasome inhibitor and an immunomodulatory drug, in patients fit for CAR T-cell therapy. The triple-class-exposed, later-line cilta-cel evidence (CARTITUDE-1) and idecabtagene vicleucel are different questions — ide-cel in triple-class-exposed disease is homed on Shelf #4478.

shelves.title: Teclistamab in triple-class-exposed myeloma (MajesTEC-1, single-arm): responses in 63% lasting a median 18.4 months — infections in 76.4% in the trial, 44.8% of them grade 3 or 4
shelves.question: In adults with triple-class-exposed relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, does teclistamab produce durable responses, and at what infection cost?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable single-arm responses, a heavy infection cost, no comparator. In MajesTEC-1 (Moreau 2022, PMID: 35661166), weekly teclistamab produced responses in 63.0% of 165 triple-class-exposed patients (median five prior lines), complete response or better in 39.4%, with a median response duration of 18.4 months — and infections in 76.4%, grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%. The pattern repeats: 52.5% response and 70.0% infection incidence (10% grade 5) in the 40-patient post-BCMA cohort (Touzeau 2024, PMID: 39172760); 62% response in a 110-patient real-world cohort, where intravenous immunoglobulin prophylaxis was associated with lower infection risk (Mohan 2024, PMID: 38443345); and a pooled infection incidence of 56.5% any grade and 27.6% grade 3 or higher across 714 patients (Huang 2026, PMID: 42148087). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm pivotal evidence, labelled as such, caps the stamp — response durability is shown, comparative benefit is not.

cards.headline: Moreau 2022 (MajesTEC-1, single-arm): overall response 63.0% and complete response or better 39.4% in 165 triple-class-exposed patients — with infections in 76.4% (grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%)
cards.summary: Moreau 2022 (MajesTEC-1, single-arm): overall response 63.0% and complete response or better 39.4% in 165 triple-class-exposed patients — with infections in 76.4% (grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%)
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1–2 study (Moreau 2022, MajesTEC-1) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: 165 patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma after at least three therapy lines including triple-class exposure (immunomodulatory drug, proteasome inhibitor, anti-CD38 antibody); 77.6% had triple-class refractory disease and the median was five prior lines. Weekly subcutaneous teclistamab 1.5 mg/kg after step-up doses; median follow-up 14.1 months. Single-arm — no comparator.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 63.0%, with complete response or better in 39.4% and MRD negativity in 26.7% of all patients (46% of complete responders). Median duration of response was 18.4 months (95% CI 14.9 to not estimable) and median progression-free survival 11.3 months (95% CI 8.8 to 17.1). Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 72.1% (grade 3 in 0.6%, no grade 4); neutropenia in 70.9% (grade 3 or 4 in 64.2%); infections in 76.4% of patients, grade 3 or 4 in 44.8%. Neurotoxic events occurred in 14.5%, including immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity in 3.0% (all grade 1 or 2).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm evidence, labelled as such: response rates in a no-comparator study show the drug can shrink myeloma in heavily pretreated patients, but cannot show it beats any alternative or extends life — there is no survival comparison in this record. The infection figures are the other half of the question and they are large.
cards.source: Moreau P et al. Teclistamab in Relapsed or Refractory Multiple Myeloma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35661166. Registry ID: NCT03145181 and NCT04557098. cards.headline: Touzeau 2024 (MajesTEC-1 cohort C, single-arm): after prior BCMA-targeted therapy, response 52.5% in 40 patients — infections in 70.0%, grade 5 in 10%
cards.summary: Touzeau 2024 (MajesTEC-1 cohort C, single-arm): after prior BCMA-targeted therapy, response 52.5% in 40 patients — infections in 70.0%, grade 5 in 10%
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1–2 cohort (Touzeau 2024, MajesTEC-1 cohort C) — no comparator
cards.people: 40 MajesTEC-1 patients who had already received BCMA-targeted therapy (antibody-drug conjugate in 29, CAR T-cell therapy in 15, both in 4), median six prior lines (range 3–14), treated with weekly subcutaneous teclistamab 1.5 mg/kg; median follow-up 28.0 months. Single-arm cohort.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 52.5%, with very good partial response or better in 47.5% and complete response or better in 30.0%. Median duration of response was 14.8 months, median progression-free survival 4.5 months and median overall survival 15.5 months. The commonest treatment-emergent events were neutropenia, infections, cytokine release syndrome and anaemia. Infections occurred in 28 patients (70.0%), were grade 3 or 4 in 13 (32.5%) and grade 5 in 4 (10%).
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient single-arm cohort in an even more pretreated population: the lower progression-free survival (4.5 months) beside a similar response rate is the pattern of responses that do not last as long after prior BCMA therapy. The 10% grade 5 infection figure is four patients — small numbers, but it is the direction of the drug's known cost.
cards.source: Touzeau C et al. Efficacy and safety of teclistamab in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma after BCMA-targeting therapies. Blood. 2024. PMID: 39172760. Registry ID: NCT03145181 and NCT04557098. cards.headline: Mohan 2024 (real-world, 110 patients): response 62% outside trials — 78 infections in 44 patients; intravenous immunoglobulin prophylaxis was associated with lower infection risk (HR 0.33)
cards.summary: Mohan 2024 (real-world, 110 patients): response 62% outside trials — 78 infections in 44 patients; intravenous immunoglobulin prophylaxis was associated with lower infection risk (HR 0.33)
cards.people: Retrospective multi-institutional cohort of 110 consecutive patients who received at least one standard-of-care teclistamab dose up to August 2023; 86% had triple-class refractory disease, 76% penta-refractory disease and 35% prior BCMA-targeted therapy. Median follow-up 3.5 months.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 62%, with very good partial response or better in 51%; response was 54% with prior BCMA therapy versus 67% without (p=0.23). Estimated progression-free survival was 57% at 3 months and 52% at 6 months. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 56% and neurotoxicity syndrome in 11% (grade 3 or higher in 3.5% and 4.6%). Seventy-eight unique infections were diagnosed in 44 patients — all-grade infection incidence 40% and grade 3 or higher 26% at this short follow-up. Primary prophylaxis with intravenous immunoglobulin was associated with significantly lower infection risk on multivariable analysis (HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.64; p=0.001 — a relative, observational association).
cards.watchOut: Observational and short (median follow-up 3.5 months): the lower infection incidence than MajesTEC-1 (40% versus 76.4%) is at least partly a follow-up artefact — infections accumulate with time on drug. The immunoglobulin association is confounded by who receives prophylaxis and cannot be read as proof it works.
cards.source: Mohan M et al. Teclistamab in relapsed refractory multiple myeloma: multi-institutional real-world study. Blood Cancer Journal. 2024. PMID: 38443345. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective cohort). cards.headline: Huang 2026 (infection meta-analysis, 714 patients): pooled infection incidence 56.5% any grade and 27.6% grade 3 or higher; higher in the trial (76.4% / 44.8%) than in real-world cohorts (45.4% / 22.8%)
cards.summary: Huang 2026 (infection meta-analysis, 714 patients): pooled infection incidence 56.5% any grade and 27.6% grade 3 or higher; higher in the trial (76.4% / 44.8%) than in real-world cohorts (45.4% / 22.8%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of single-arm and cohort evidence (Huang 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies encompassing 714 patients treated with teclistamab for relapsed/refractory myeloma, pooling clinical-trial and real-world evidence, with a subgroup contrast between MajesTEC-1 and multi-institutional real-world cohorts.
cards.result: Pooled incidence of infection was 56.5% (95% CI 43.1 to 69.9) for any grade and 27.6% (95% CI 21.0 to 34.3) for grade 3 or higher. The trial subgroup was significantly higher than real-world cohorts (any grade 76.4% versus 45.4%; grade 3 or higher 44.8% versus 22.8%; both p<0.01). Infection-related mortality was reported in all cohorts, ranging from 0.9% to 7.3%, with COVID-19 and opportunistic pathogens such as Pneumocystis jirovecii prevalent. Heterogeneity was driven by follow-up duration and intravenous immunoglobulin prophylaxis rates (41.8% to 81.3%).
cards.watchOut: Five studies only, with wide intervals (any-grade infection 43.1% to 69.9%) and heterogeneity the authors attribute to follow-up length and prophylaxis practice — read the pooled figures as 'roughly half or more, accumulating over time', not as a precise rate. The trial-versus-real-world gap most likely reflects longer trial follow-up rather than safer real-world use.
cards.source: Huang ZY et al. Infection risk associated with teclistamab in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trial and real-world evidence. Frontiers in Immunology. 2026. PMID: 42148087. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD420261297645 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm pivotal evidence — deep, durable responses in about two-thirds, paid for with an infection burden in roughly half or more of patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm pivotal evidence — deep, durable responses in about two-thirds, paid for with an infection burden in roughly half or more of patients
cards.people: MajesTEC-1 single-arm programme (165 patients, Moreau 2022; 40-patient post-BCMA cohort, Touzeau 2024), a 110-patient real-world cohort (Mohan 2024) and a 714-patient infection meta-analysis (Huang 2026). No randomised evidence is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: Response 63.0% with complete response or better in 39.4% and median response duration 18.4 months in the pivotal cohort; 52.5% response after prior BCMA therapy; 62% response in real-world use. Infections: 76.4% any grade (44.8% grade 3 or 4) in the trial, 70.0% in the post-BCMA cohort with 10% grade 5, and a pooled 56.5% any grade / 27.6% grade 3 or higher across 714 patients; infection-related mortality 0.9% to 7.3% across cohorts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm and observational evidence, labelled as such, caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: triple-class-exposed relapsed/refractory myeloma, the MajesTEC-1 population. Without a randomised comparator, nothing here ranks teclistamab against CAR T-cell therapy or other bispecifics, and no survival benefit over alternatives can be claimed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moreau P et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35661166); Touzeau C et al. Blood. 2024 (PMID: 39172760); Mohan M et al. Blood Cancer Journal. 2024 (PMID: 38443345); Huang ZY et al. Frontiers in Immunology. 2026 (PMID: 42148087).

shelves.title: CD20×CD3 bispecifics in DLBCL after at least two lines (single-arm pivotal evidence): complete responses in about 4 in 10 with both glofitamab and epcoritamab, durable for years in responders
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after at least two prior lines, do CD20×CD3 bispecific antibodies (glofitamab, given for a fixed duration, and epcoritamab, given until progression) produce durable complete responses?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cytokine Release Syndrome/chemically induced/prevention & control · Lymphoma, Large B-Cell, Diffuse/drug therapy/immunology* · Lymphoma, Non-Hodgkin/drug therapy/immunology · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy · Antibodies, Bispecific/adverse effects/immunology/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — durable complete responses in a minority, from single-arm evidence only. Glofitamab (Dickinson 2022, PMID: 36507690) produced complete responses in 39% of 155 patients after at least two lines, 78% of them still ongoing at 12 months, on a fixed 12-cycle course. Epcoritamab (Thieblemont 2023, PMID: 36548927) produced complete responses in 38.9% of 157 patients, given until progression; at the 3-year update the complete-response rate was 41% with a median complete-response duration of 36.1 months — but median progression-free survival for all patients was only 4.2 months (Karimi 2026, PMID: 41634395). In 245 real-world patients treated with either drug, response rates were similar (51% and 53%) and survival lower than in the trials (Brooks 2025, PMID: 40663785). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm pivotal evidence, labelled as such, caps the stamp; nothing carded ranks the two drugs against each other.

cards.headline: Dickinson 2022 (glofitamab pivotal, single-arm): complete response 39% after at least two prior lines; 78% of complete responses still ongoing at 12 months
cards.summary: Dickinson 2022 (glofitamab pivotal, single-arm): complete response 39% after at least two prior lines; 78% of complete responses still ongoing at 12 months
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 pivotal study (Dickinson 2022, NP30179) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: 155 patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL after at least two prior therapy lines enrolled in the phase 2 part of a phase 1–2 study (154 received at least one dose); fixed-duration glofitamab for 12 cycles after obinutuzumab pretreatment. Median follow-up 12.6 months. Single-arm — no comparator. 52 patients had previously received CAR T-cell therapy.
cards.result: Complete response by independent review was 39% (95% CI 32 to 48); among the 52 post-CAR-T patients, 35% had a complete response. Median time to complete response was 42 days, and 78% of complete responses were ongoing at 12 months. Twelve-month progression-free survival was 37% (95% CI 28 to 46). Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 63% (grade 3 or higher in 4%); adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 62% overall, with grade 3 or higher neurologic events in 3%; 9% discontinued glofitamab for adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm evidence, labelled as such: a 39% complete-response rate in patients with no standard option is clinically meaningful, but without a comparator it cannot show a survival benefit, and the 12-month follow-up in this report is short for a durability claim — durability rests on responses ongoing at 12 months, not on a mature duration-of-response median.
cards.source: Dickinson MJ et al. Glofitamab for Relapsed or Refractory Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36507690. Registry ID: NCT03075696. cards.headline: Thieblemont 2023 (epcoritamab pivotal, single-arm): overall response 63.1% and complete response 38.9% in 157 patients; median duration of response 12.0 months, not reached in complete responders
cards.summary: Thieblemont 2023 (epcoritamab pivotal, single-arm): overall response 63.1% and complete response 38.9% in 157 patients; median duration of response 12.0 months, not reached in complete responders
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1/2 pivotal study (Thieblemont 2023, EPCORE NHL-1) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: 157 adults with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma after at least two prior lines including anti-CD20 therapy (median three prior lines; 61.1% primary refractory; 38.9% prior CAR T-cell therapy), treated with subcutaneous epcoritamab until progression in the phase 1/2 dose-expansion cohort; median follow-up 10.7 months. Single-arm — no comparator.
cards.result: Overall response rate was 63.1% (95% CI 55.0 to 70.6) and complete response rate 38.9% (95% CI 31.2 to 46.9), similar across prespecified subgroups including prior CAR T-cell exposure. Median duration of response was 12.0 months overall and not reached among complete responders. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 49.7% (grade 3 in 2.5%); pyrexia in 23.6% and fatigue in 22.9%. Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity occurred in 6.4%, with one fatal event.
cards.watchOut: The population is large B-cell lymphoma, broader than DLBCL alone, and treatment continued until progression — so its duration figures are not comparable head-to-head with glofitamab's fixed 12 cycles. Cross-trial comparison of the two drugs' percentages is not a randomised comparison and this pack does not make one.

cards.headline: Karimi 2026 (EPCORE NHL-1, 3-year update): complete response 41%; median duration of complete response 36.1 months — but median progression-free survival for all patients was 4.2 months
cards.summary: Karimi 2026 (EPCORE NHL-1, 3-year update): complete response 41%; median duration of complete response 36.1 months — but median progression-free survival for all patients was 4.2 months
cards.type: Single-arm trial 3-year update (Karimi 2026, EPCORE NHL-1) — no comparator
cards.people: The EPCORE NHL-1 population at a median follow-up of 37.1 months (data cutoff May 3, 2024): adults with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma on epcoritamab until progression; 39% had prior CAR T-cell therapy and 75% were refractory to at least two consecutive lines. The record's abstract does not restate the total N (157 in the primary report). Single-arm.
cards.result: Overall response was 59% and complete response 41% by investigator assessment. Median duration of response was 20.8 months (95% CI 13.0 to 32.0) and median duration of complete response 36.1 months (95% CI 20.2 to not reached), with the longest ongoing complete response beyond 43 months. Against that, median progression-free survival was 4.2 months (95% CI 2.8 to 5.5) in all patients versus 37.3 months in complete responders, and median overall survival 18.5 months (95% CI 11.7 to 27.7) in all patients and not reached in complete responders. Of 119 MRD-evaluable patients, 45% were MRD-negative at some point. Cytokine release syndrome occurred in 51%; grade 3 infections in 24%.
cards.watchOut: The two halves of this card are the honest picture of the whole class: complete responders do very well for years, while the median patient progresses at about 4 months — the average is a mixture of a durable-responder minority and early progression in the rest. Quoting only the 36.1-month complete-response duration would mislead.
cards.source: Karimi YH et al. Efficacy and safety of epcoritamab in relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma: 3-year update from the EPCORE NHL-1 trial. Annals of Hematology. 2026. cards.headline: Brooks 2025 (real-world, 245 patients, both drugs): response 51% on epcoritamab and 53% on glofitamab, but median progression-free survival 2.6 months and overall survival 7.8 months — lower than the trials
cards.summary: Brooks 2025 (real-world, 245 patients, both drugs): response 51% on epcoritamab and 53% on glofitamab, but median progression-free survival 2.6 months and overall survival 7.8 months — lower than the trials
cards.type: Retrospective multi-institutional real-world cohort (Brooks 2025) — observational, both drugs
cards.people: Retrospective cohort from 21 US institutions of 245 patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL treated commercially with epcoritamab (n=156) or glofitamab (n=89) between January 2023 and October 2024; 147 had prior CAR T-cell therapy and 174 would have been ineligible for the registrational trials.
cards.result: Overall response was 51% (complete response 23%) for epcoritamab and 53% (complete response 30%) for glofitamab. For the combined cohort, median progression-free survival was 2.6 months (95% CI 2.0 to 3.8) and median overall survival 7.8 months (95% CI 6.2 to 11.0); 6-month progression-free survival was 36% and 6-month overall survival 60%. Trial ineligibility and undetectable CD20 before treatment were associated with shorter progression-free and overall survival; among 17 patients with paired biopsies, 15 (88.2%) had lost CD20 expression after bispecific treatment.
cards.watchOut: Observational, and the population was sicker than the trials' (most would have been trial-ineligible, 60% post-CAR-T): the lower survival figures describe who gets these drugs in practice as much as how the drugs perform. It is the only carded source that reports both drugs from the same dataset, and it shows similar response rates for the two — not a randomised comparison.
cards.source: Brooks TR et al. Real-world outcomes of patients with aggressive B-cell lymphoma treated with epcoritamab or glofitamab. Blood. 2025. PMID: 40663785. cards.headline: Synthesis: two single-arm pivotal programmes — complete responses in about 4 in 10, durable for years in responders, with early progression in the median patient and lower real-world survival
cards.summary: Synthesis: two single-arm pivotal programmes — complete responses in about 4 in 10, durable for years in responders, with early progression in the median patient and lower real-world survival
cards.people: Glofitamab pivotal study, 155 patients (Dickinson 2022); epcoritamab pivotal study, 157 patients (Thieblemont 2023) with its 3-year update (Karimi 2026); and a 245-patient real-world cohort covering both drugs (Brooks 2025). All pivotal evidence is single-arm, labelled as such on every card.
cards.result: Complete response: 39% (glofitamab, fixed-duration) and 38.9% rising to 41% at 3 years (epcoritamab, until progression). Durability in responders is real — 78% of glofitamab complete responses ongoing at 12 months; epcoritamab median complete-response duration 36.1 months — while the all-patient medians are short (epcoritamab progression-free survival 4.2 months at 3 years; real-world combined median progression-free survival 2.6 months and overall survival 7.8 months). Cytokine release syndrome occurred in about half to two-thirds, mostly low grade. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm pivotal evidence caps the stamp, and no carded evidence ranks one drug over the other.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: relapsed/refractory DLBCL/large B-cell lymphoma after at least two lines. One pack honestly covers both drugs because the question, population and evidence shape are the same and no head-to-head trial exists in the records fetched; their schedules differ (glofitamab fixed 12 cycles, epcoritamab until progression) and that difference is stated, not smoothed over. Randomised glofitamab-combination evidence (STARGLO) answers a different question and is not carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dickinson MJ et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36507690); Thieblemont C et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2023 (PMID: 36548927); Karimi YH et al. Annals of Hematology. 2026 (PMID: 41634395); Brooks TR et al. Blood. 2025 (PMID: 40663785).

shelves.title: Rusfertide in polycythaemia vera (VERIFY phase 3; REVIVE phase 2): clinical response 77% versus 33% and mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8 versus placebo
shelves.question: In adults with polycythaemia vera needing cytoreduction or frequent phlebotomy, does rusfertide reduce phlebotomy dependence and control haematocrit versus placebo on top of standard care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hematocrit · Hepcidins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Iron · Polycythemia/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Polycythemia Vera/drug therapy/complications/diagnosis* · Peptides/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Injections · Double-Blind Method · Hematologic Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant randomised trials on control endpoints, no hard-outcome data yet. In VERIFY (Kuykendall 2026, PMID: 42868322), 293 phlebotomy-dependent patients were randomised to rusfertide or placebo on top of standard care: clinical response in 77% versus 33% (P<0.0001), mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8, and haematocrit below 45% maintained in 63% versus 14%, with better fatigue and symptom scores and no deaths reported. REVIVE's randomised-withdrawal period points the same way — response 60% on continued rusfertide versus 17% after switching to placebo (Kremyanskaya 2024, PMID: 38381675) — and a 20-patient open-label study shows haematocrit falling below 45% within about 5 weeks (PMID: 41175501). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the endpoints are haematocrit control and phlebotomy avoidance over weeks; neither trial shows fewer thromboses.

cards.headline: Kuykendall 2026 (VERIFY phase 3): clinical response 77% on rusfertide versus 33% on placebo (P<0.0001); mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8 over 32 weeks
cards.summary: Kuykendall 2026 (VERIFY phase 3): clinical response 77% on rusfertide versus 33% on placebo (P<0.0001); mean phlebotomies 0.5 versus 1.8 over 32 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Kuykendall 2026, VERIFY)
cards.people: 293 phlebotomy-dependent patients with polycythaemia vera and poorly controlled haematocrit, randomly assigned 1:1 double-blind to subcutaneous rusfertide (n=147) or placebo (n=146), with or without cytoreductive therapy, in Part 1a (32 weeks) of the phase 3 VERIFY trial.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — clinical response, defined as absence of phlebotomy eligibility during weeks 20–32 — was achieved by 113 patients (77%) on rusfertide versus 48 (33%) on placebo (P<0.0001). Mean number of phlebotomies was 0.5 (SD 1.2) versus 1.8 (SD 1.5) (P<0.0001), and haematocrit below 45% was maintained by 92 patients (63%) versus 21 (14%) (P<0.0001). Patient-reported fatigue and symptom scores improved significantly versus placebo (PROMIS Fatigue P=0.0252; MFSAF total symptom score P=0.0240). The commonest adverse events were injection-site reactions, anaemia and fatigue; no deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The endpoints are haematocrit control and phlebotomy avoidance over 32 weeks — the trial does not show fewer thromboses, the outcome phlebotomy is ultimately meant to prevent, and 32 weeks is short for a lifelong disease. A third of placebo patients also met the response definition, so the absolute gain is the 77% versus 33% contrast, not 77% alone.
cards.source: Kuykendall AT et al. VERIFY: A Phase III Trial of Rusfertide Versus Placebo in Phlebotomy-Dependent Patients With Polycythemia Vera Receiving Standard-of-Care Therapy. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026. PMID: 42868322. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kremyanskaya 2024 (REVIVE phase 2, randomised withdrawal): response 60% on continued rusfertide versus 17% on placebo (P=0.002) after open-label dose-finding
cards.summary: Kremyanskaya 2024 (REVIVE phase 2, randomised withdrawal): response 60% on continued rusfertide versus 17% on placebo (P=0.002) after open-label dose-finding
cards.type: Phase 2 trial with a double-blind randomised-withdrawal period (Kremyanskaya 2024, REVIVE)
cards.people: 70 patients with phlebotomy-dependent polycythaemia vera enrolled in part 1 (28-week open-label dose-finding); 59 responders/participants were then randomly assigned in part 2 to continue rusfertide (n=30) or switch to placebo (n=29) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: During part 1, the estimated mean number of phlebotomies per year fell from 8.7 (SD 2.9) in the 28 weeks before rusfertide to 0.6 (SD 1.0), and mean maximum haematocrit was 44.5% (SD 2.2) versus 50.0% (SD 5.8) before treatment. In the randomised withdrawal (part 2), a response — haematocrit control, absence of phlebotomy and completion of the regimen — occurred in 60% on rusfertide versus 17% on placebo (P=0.002). Symptom scores on the modified MPN-SAF diary improved during part 1.
cards.watchOut: A randomised-withdrawal design answers 'does stopping lose control?' in patients who already tolerated and responded to the drug — it enriches for responders and cannot estimate the effect in an unselected patient. The randomised period is small (59 patients, 12 weeks).
cards.source: Kremyanskaya M et al. Rusfertide, a Hepcidin Mimetic, for Control of Erythrocytosis in Polycythemia Vera. New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38381675. cards.headline: Chew 2025 (open-label phase 2, suboptimally controlled PV): haematocrit below 45% in 85% by week 8, and no phlebotomies at all during treatment, in 20 patients
cards.summary: Chew 2025 (open-label phase 2, suboptimally controlled PV): haematocrit below 45% in 85% by week 8, and no phlebotomies at all during treatment, in 20 patients
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 2 study (Chew 2025) — no comparator
cards.people: 20 patients with polycythaemia vera and baseline haematocrit above 48% treated open-label with rusfertide 40 mg subcutaneously twice weekly until haematocrit fell below 45%, then weekly; 15 (75%) completed 24 weeks and 13 (65%) completed 52 weeks. Single-arm — no comparator.
cards.result: By week 8, 17 patients (85%) had achieved haematocrit below 45% and 19 (95%) had achieved an absolute reduction of at least 5 percentage points from a mean baseline of 51.6%; median time to first haematocrit below 45% was 4.9 weeks, and mean haematocrit stayed below 45% from week 4 onward. No patient received phlebotomy during rusfertide treatment. Erythrocyte count fell from 5.98 to 4.79 ×10¹²/L (nominal p=0.0036) and iron-deficiency markers improved. Seventeen patients (85%) had treatment-emergent adverse events, most grade 1 or 2.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, single-arm, with 35% not completing a year: it shows speed of haematocrit fall, nothing comparative.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised trials agree — rusfertide holds haematocrit below 45% and cuts phlebotomy need versus placebo on top of standard care

shelves.title: Cabazitaxel vs switching androgen-receptor inhibitor in mCRPC (CARD): survival 13.6 vs 11.0 months and imaging progression-free survival 8.0 vs 3.7 months
shelves.question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing on an androgen-receptor inhibitor, does cabazitaxel improve survival versus switching to the alternative androgen-receptor inhibitor?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Androgen Antagonists/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Androstenes/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects, therapeutic use · Benzamides · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Phenylthiohydantoin/administration & dosage, adverse effects, analogs & derivatives · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Progression-Free Survival · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant/drug therapy, mortality · Taxoids/administration & dosage, adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single strong randomised trial, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. In CARD (de Wit 2019, PMID: 31566937; 255 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer previously treated with docetaxel and progressing within 12 months on abiraterone or enzalutamide), cabazitaxel doubled median imaging-based progression-free survival (8.0 vs 3.7 months; hazard ratio 0.54) and lengthened median overall survival (13.6 vs 11.0 months; HR for death 0.64, p=0.008) versus switching to the alternative androgen-receptor inhibitor, with grade 3 or higher adverse events in 56.3% vs 52.4%. CARD's quality-of-life analysis (Fizazi 2020, PMID: 32926841 — same patients) found pain response in 46% vs 19%. A Japanese real-world CARD-like analysis (Matsuyama 2023, PMID: 37308888 — observational, labelled) points the same way on time to treatment failure.

cards.headline: de Wit 2019 (CARD): cabazitaxel beat switching androgen-receptor inhibitor — imaging progression-free survival 8.0 vs 3.7 months (hazard ratio 0.54) and overall survival 13.6 vs 11.0 months (HR for death 0.64, p=0.008)
cards.summary: de Wit 2019 (CARD): cabazitaxel beat switching androgen-receptor inhibitor — imaging progression-free survival 8.0 vs 3.7 months (hazard ratio 0.54) and overall survival 13.6 vs 11.0 months (HR for death 0.64, p=0.008)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label phase 4 trial (de Wit 2019, CARD)
cards.people: 255 patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer previously treated with docetaxel who had progressed within 12 months on abiraterone or enzalutamide, randomised to cabazitaxel 25 mg/m² intravenously every 3 weeks plus prednisone and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (n=129) or the alternative androgen-signalling-targeted inhibitor — abiraterone or enzalutamide (n=126). Median follow-up 9.2 months.
cards.result: Imaging-based progression or death occurred in 95 of 129 (73.6%) on cabazitaxel vs 101 of 126 (80.2%) on the alternative inhibitor (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.73; P<0.001); median imaging-based progression-free survival was 8.0 vs 3.7 months. Median overall survival was 13.6 vs 11.0 months (HR for death 0.64, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.89; P=0.008). Median (any) progression-free survival was 4.4 vs 2.7 months (HR 0.52); PSA response occurred in 35.7% vs 13.5% (P<0.001) and tumour response in 36.5% vs 11.5% (P=0.004). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 56.3% vs 52.4%; no new safety signals were observed. Hazard ratios are relative measures; the absolute median gains are 4.3 months (imaging PFS) and 2.6 months (survival).
cards.watchOut: CARD enrolled a selected group — men who had already had docetaxel and had progressed quickly (within 12 months) on their first androgen-receptor inhibitor. The result does not cover men who responded to the first inhibitor for longer, or men who have not had docetaxel.
cards.source: de Wit R et al. Cabazitaxel versus Abiraterone or Enzalutamide in Metastatic Prostate Cancer. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31566937. Registry ID: NCT02485691. cards.headline: Fizazi 2020 (CARD quality-of-life analysis, same 255 patients): pain response 46% on cabazitaxel vs 19% on the alternative inhibitor (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: Fizazi 2020 (CARD quality-of-life analysis, same 255 patients): pain response 46% on cabazitaxel vs 19% on the alternative inhibitor (p<0.0001)
cards.type: Preplanned quality-of-life and pain analysis of the CARD randomised trial (Fizazi 2020) — same patients as Card 1
cards.people: The CARD randomised population (255 patients; pain response analysed in 111 cabazitaxel and 109 control patients with baseline and at least one post-baseline pain assessment). This is the same trial as the first card, not independent confirmation.
cards.result: Pain response was observed in 51 (46%) of 111 patients on cabazitaxel vs 21 (19%) of 109 on abiraterone or enzalutamide (p<0.0001). Median time to pain progression was not estimable on cabazitaxel vs 8.5 months on the alternative inhibitor (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.97; p=0.035), and median time to symptomatic skeletal events was not estimable (lower CI bound 20.0 months) vs 16.7 months (HR 0.59, 0.35 to 1.01; p=0.050). Time to FACT-P total-score deterioration was 14.8 vs 8.9 months (HR 0.72, p=0.21, not significant); the EQ-5D-5L utility index change significantly favoured cabazitaxel (p=0.030).
cards.watchOut: Open-label treatment with patient-reported outcomes invites expectation bias, and 'not estimable' medians reflect short follow-up (9.2 months) rather than permanent freedom from pain progression.
cards.source: Fizazi K et al. Quality of life in patients with metastatic prostate cancer following treatment with cabazitaxel versus abiraterone or enzalutamide (CARD): an analysis of a randomised, multicentre, open-label, phase 4 study. The Lancet Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32926841. Registry ID: NCT02485691. cards.headline: Matsuyama 2023 (Japanese post-marketing surveillance, CARD-like, observational): time to treatment failure 109 days on third-line cabazitaxel vs 58 days on a second alternative androgen-receptor therapy (hazard ratio 0.339)
cards.summary: Matsuyama 2023 (Japanese post-marketing surveillance, CARD-like, observational): time to treatment failure 109 days on third-line cabazitaxel vs 58 days on a second alternative androgen-receptor therapy (hazard ratio 0.339)
cards.type: Observational post-marketing surveillance analysis with propensity matching (Matsuyama 2023) — not randomised
cards.people: 535 real-world patients in a nationwide Japanese post-marketing surveillance (2014–2015) who, after docetaxel and within-1-year progression on an androgen-receptor-axis therapy, received third-line cabazitaxel (n=247) or the alternative agent (n=288; 91.3% abiraterone, 8.7% enzalutamide). Observational — no randomisation; labelled as such.
cards.result: Median time to treatment failure was 109 days (95% CI 94 to 128) on cabazitaxel vs 58 days (57 to 66) on the alternative agent (hazard ratio 0.339, 95% CI 0.279 to 0.413, a relative measure); after 1:1 propensity-score matching the HR was 0.323 (0.258 to 0.402). The authors note this population had more advanced disease than CARD's, and 61.9% of cabazitaxel patients started at 20 mg/m² or less, below the CARD dose.
cards.watchOut: Time to treatment failure is not survival, and despite propensity matching, doctors chose who got chemotherapy — fitter patients are likelier to be chosen, which biases observational comparisons in cabazitaxel's favour. This card supports consistency with CARD; it cannot confirm it.
cards.source: Matsuyama H et al. Real-world effectiveness of third-line cabazitaxel in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer: CARD-like analysis of data from a post-marketing surveillance in Japan. BMC Cancer. 2023. PMID: 37308888. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: after docetaxel and rapid progression on one androgen-receptor inhibitor, cabazitaxel — not a switch to the other inhibitor — is the treatment with randomised survival evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: after docetaxel and rapid progression on one androgen-receptor inhibitor, cabazitaxel — not a switch to the other inhibitor — is the treatment with randomised survival evidence
cards.people: CARD randomised trial, 255 patients (de Wit 2019), with its quality-of-life analysis (Fizazi 2020, same patients), plus a 535-patient Japanese real-world CARD-like cohort (Matsuyama 2023, observational).
cards.result: Median overall survival 13.6 vs 11.0 months (HR for death 0.64, p=0.008); median imaging-based progression-free survival 8.0 vs 3.7 months (HR 0.54); PSA response 35.7% vs 13.5%; pain response 46% vs 19%; grade ≥3 adverse events 56.3% vs 52.4%. The observational cohort's time-to-treatment-failure result (HR 0.339) is directionally consistent. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped at POSSIBLE because the randomised evidence is a single trial programme (CARD), however clean its result.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: the CARD population — docetaxel-pretreated, progressing within 12 months on abiraterone or enzalutamide. Sequencing questions outside that population (cabazitaxel before docetaxel, or after a long first-inhibitor response) are not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of de Wit R et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31566937); Fizazi K et al. Lancet Oncology. 2020 (PMID: 32926841); Matsuyama H et al. BMC Cancer. 2023 (PMID: 37308888).

shelves.title: Vismodegib in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma unsuitable for surgery/radiotherapy (ERIVANCE; STEVIE — single-arm): response 43% by independent review, median response duration 26.2 months at final update, 36% stopping for adverse events
shelves.question: In adults with locally advanced basal cell carcinoma unsuitable for surgery or radiotherapy, does vismodegib produce durable tumour responses? (ERIVANCE, STEVIE — single-arm; label as such.)
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence throughout, labelled as such; there is no randomised or untreated comparator in this programme. In the pivotal ERIVANCE study, independently assessed response was 43% in locally advanced basal cell carcinoma (21% complete) and 30% in metastatic disease, with a median duration of response of 7.6 months at the primary analysis (Sekulic 2012, PMID: 22670903); the final update put investigator-assessed response at 60.3% in locally advanced disease with a median duration of response of 26.2 months (Sekulic 2017, PMID: 28511673). The STEVIE practice-setting study found investigator-assessed response in 66.7% of locally advanced patients, with treatment stopped for adverse events in 36% (Basset-Seguin 2015, PMID: 25981813). Muscle spasms, hair loss, taste disturbance, weight loss and fatigue are the standing costs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): responses are real and sometimes durable, but single-arm data cannot separate drug effect from selection, and tolerability limits how long many patients stay on treatment.

cards.headline: Sekulic 2012 (ERIVANCE, single-arm, 96 patients in the efficacy cohorts): independently assessed response 43% in locally advanced BCC (21% complete) and 30% in metastatic BCC; median duration of response 7.6 months
cards.summary: Sekulic 2012 (ERIVANCE, single-arm, 96 patients in the efficacy cohorts): independently assessed response 43% in locally advanced BCC (21% complete) and 30% in metastatic BCC; median duration of response 7.6 months
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 pivotal study (ERIVANCE, Sekulic 2012) — no comparator
cards.people: Patients with metastatic basal cell carcinoma (33) or locally advanced basal cell carcinoma (63) that was inoperable or for whom surgery was inappropriate (multiple recurrences with low likelihood of surgical cure, or substantial anticipated disfigurement), in a multicentre international two-cohort non-randomised study; all received oral vismodegib 150 mg daily.
cards.result: The independently assessed objective response rate was 30% in metastatic disease (95% CI 16-48; P=0.001) and 43% in locally advanced disease (95% CI 31-56; P<0.001), with complete responses in 13 locally advanced patients (21%). Median duration of response was 7.6 months in both cohorts. Adverse events in more than 30% of patients were muscle spasms, alopecia, dysgeusia, weight loss and fatigue; serious adverse events were reported in 25% of patients and seven deaths due to adverse events were noted.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: response rates are judged against fixed thresholds (20% locally advanced, 10% metastatic), not against any control group, and the 7.6-month median duration of response at this analysis is the early, immature figure — the final update below is longer.
cards.source: Sekulic A et al. Efficacy and safety of vismodegib in advanced basal-cell carcinoma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22670903. Registry ID: NCT00833417. cards.headline: Basset-Seguin 2015 (STEVIE interim, single-arm, 499 patients): investigator-assessed response 66.7% in locally advanced BCC; 80% discontinued treatment, 36% for adverse events; adverse events in 98%
cards.summary: Basset-Seguin 2015 (STEVIE interim, single-arm, 499 patients): investigator-assessed response 66.7% in locally advanced BCC; 80% discontinued treatment, 36% for adverse events; adverse events in 98%
cards.type: Single-arm open-label safety study, pre-planned interim analysis (STEVIE, Basset-Seguin 2015) — no comparator
cards.people: 499 patients (468 locally advanced, 31 metastatic basal cell carcinoma) who had received oral vismodegib 150 mg daily and could be followed for 12 months or more, within 1,227 enrolled in an international open-label practice-setting safety study; locally advanced patients had been deemed ineligible for surgery.
cards.result: Median vismodegib exposure was 36.4 weeks. Treatment was discontinued in 400 patients (80%): 180 (36%) for adverse events, 70 (14%) for progressive disease and 51 (10%) at patient request. Adverse events occurred in 491 patients (98%) — most commonly muscle spasms (64%), alopecia (62%), dysgeusia (54%), weight loss (33%) and asthenia (28%) — and were mostly grade 1-2; serious adverse events occurred in 108 patients (22%), and of 31 deaths, 21 resulted from adverse events. Investigator-assessed overall response was 66.7% (302 of 453) in locally advanced disease (153 complete, 149 partial) and 37.9% (11 of 29) in metastatic disease.
cards.watchOut: An interim safety analysis: responses are investigator-assessed (typically higher than independent review, as ERIVANCE shows), and the 36% adverse-event discontinuation rate is the practical limit on how much of the response benefit patients can stay on treatment to collect.
cards.source: Basset-Seguin N et al. Vismodegib in patients with advanced basal cell carcinoma (STEVIE): a pre-planned interim analysis of an international, open-label trial. Lancet Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25981813. Registry ID: NCT01367665. cards.headline: Sekulic 2017 (ERIVANCE final update, 104 patients, 39 months after accrual): investigator-assessed response 60.3% in locally advanced BCC with median duration of response 26.2 months; median overall survival 33.4 months in metastatic disease
cards.summary: Sekulic 2017 (ERIVANCE final update, 104 patients, 39 months after accrual): investigator-assessed response 60.3% in locally advanced BCC with median duration of response 26.2 months; median overall survival 33.4 months in metastatic disease
cards.type: Single-arm pivotal study, long-term final update (ERIVANCE, Sekulic 2017) — no comparator
cards.people: 104 patients with measurable advanced basal cell carcinoma (locally advanced or metastatic) who received oral vismodegib 150 mg once daily until disease progression or intolerable toxicity in the ERIVANCE study; at data cutoff, 8 patients remained on study drug and 69 were in survival follow-up.
cards.result: Investigator-assessed objective response was 48.5% in metastatic disease (all partial responses) and 60.3% in locally advanced disease (20 complete and 18 partial responses), comparable across subgroups including aggressive histological subtypes. Median duration of response was 14.8 months (metastatic) and 26.2 months (locally advanced). Median overall survival was 33.4 months in the metastatic cohort and not estimable in the locally advanced cohort. Thirty-three deaths (31.7%) were reported, none related to vismodegib, and the adverse-event profile was consistent with earlier reports.
cards.watchOut: Investigator-assessed responses (60.3%) run higher than the independent-review figure from the same study (43%); durability (26.2 months median duration of response) is described only among responders, and with no control arm, survival figures cannot be attributed to the drug.
cards.source: Sekulic A et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of vismodegib in patients with advanced basal cell carcinoma: final update of the pivotal ERIVANCE BCC study. BMC Cancer. 2017. PMID: 28511673. Registry ID: NCT00833417. cards.headline: Synthesis: vismodegib produces responses in roughly 4-6 of 10 patients with locally advanced BCC, sometimes lasting over 2 years — but all evidence is single-arm and tolerability stops treatment in about a third (POSSIBLE)
cards.summary: Synthesis: vismodegib produces responses in roughly 4-6 of 10 patients with locally advanced BCC, sometimes lasting over 2 years — but all evidence is single-arm and tolerability stops treatment in about a third (POSSIBLE)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: the ERIVANCE pivotal cohort (96-104 patients, primary and final reports) and the STEVIE practice-setting interim cohort (499 patients). No randomised or controlled evidence exists in this set.
cards.result: The consistent picture: objective responses in locally advanced disease of 43% by independent review and 60-67% by investigator assessment, complete responses in about a fifth to a third, and a median response duration that matured to 26.2 months. The counterweight is tolerability — near-universal low-grade adverse events and discontinuation for adverse events in 36% in routine-practice conditions. Single-arm evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit), with the single-arm label carried on the face.
cards.watchOut: Without a comparator, neither the survival numbers nor the true drug-attributable response rate can be known; patients unsuitable for surgery or radiotherapy have few alternatives, which is the context in which this single-arm evidence is used.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sekulic A et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22670903; Basset-Seguin N et al. Lancet Oncology. 2015. PMID: 25981813; Sekulic A et al. BMC Cancer. 2017. PMID: 28511673. Registry IDs as on the cards above.
