shelves.title: Antiproliferative somatostatin analogues in GEP-NETs: lanreotide and octreotide LAR both delayed progression versus placebo (hazard ratios 0.47 and 0.34, relative) with no overall-survival difference shown
shelves.question: In patients with well-differentiated gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, do somatostatin analogues (lanreotide, octreotide LAR), compared with placebo, delay tumour progression (antiproliferative effect, separate from symptom control)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Diarrhea/etiology · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuroendocrine Tumors/drug therapy/mortality/secondary · Pancreatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology · Peptides, Cyclic/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Somatostatin/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: ⚠ PARTIAL row — flagged prominently: the stated home, live shelf #742, was verified against its own ask-index entry before building: #742 cards peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy (NETTER-1) and everolimus (RADIANT-4) only, and none of its PMIDs is re-carded here. This pack homes only the uncovered slice — the placebo-controlled antiproliferative somatostatin-analogue trials. Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree: CLARINET (lanreotide, N = 204) found median progression-free survival not reached versus 18.0 months on placebo, hazard ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.73) — a relative measure, with absolute 24-month progression-free survival of 65.1% versus 33.0%; PROMID (octreotide LAR, N = 85) found median time to progression 14.3 versus 6.0 months, hazard ratio 0.34 (0.20 to 0.59), also relative. A meta-analysis of exactly these two trials (289 patients) gives a pooled hazard ratio of 0.41 (0.29 to 0.58). Neither trial showed an overall-survival difference, and CLARINET showed no quality-of-life difference — the benefit is delayed progression, not longer life. The tested lanreotide product is named in the record as lanreotide Autogel (Depot in the United States), Ipsen.

cards.headline: CLARINET 2014: lanreotide prolonged progression-free survival — median not reached versus 18.0 months on placebo; 24-month progression-free survival 65.1% versus 33.0%
cards.summary: CLARINET 2014: lanreotide prolonged progression-free survival — median not reached versus 18.0 months on placebo; 24-month progression-free survival 65.1% versus 33.0%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (CLARINET), N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 204 patients with advanced, well- or moderately differentiated, nonfunctioning, somatostatin-receptor-positive enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (grade 1 or 2, Ki-67 <10%), randomised to lanreotide Autogel 120 mg (101) or placebo (103) every 28 days for 96 weeks; 96% had no tumour progression in the 3 to 6 months before randomisation and 33% had hepatic tumour volumes >25%.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was not reached on lanreotide versus 18.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.47, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.73 — a relative measure; P<0.001). Estimated progression-free survival at 24 months was 65.1% (54.0 to 74.1) versus 33.0% (23.0 to 43.3), an absolute difference of about 32 percentage points. There were no significant between-group differences in quality of life or overall survival (the treatment made no difference to those outcomes in this trial). The most common treatment-related adverse event was diarrhoea, in 26% on lanreotide versus 9% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Most patients had indolent, non-progressing tumours at entry, so absolute gains in faster-progressing disease are less certain; the hazard ratio is a relative measure and is printed with its absolute 24-month rates.
cards.source: Caplin ME et al. Lanreotide in metastatic enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 25014687. Registry ID: NCT00353496, EudraCT 2005-004904-35, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: PROMID 2009: octreotide LAR lengthened median time to tumour progression to 14.3 months versus 6.0 months on placebo
cards.summary: PROMID 2009: octreotide LAR lengthened median time to tumour progression to 14.3 months versus 6.0 months on placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3B trial (PROMID), J Clin Oncol 2009
cards.people: 85 treatment-naive patients with well-differentiated metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumours, randomised to octreotide LAR 30 mg intramuscularly monthly or placebo until progression or death; this report is the planned interim analysis, based on 67 tumour progressions and 16 deaths.
cards.result: Median time to tumour progression was 14.3 months on octreotide LAR versus 6.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.59 — a relative measure; P=.000072). After 6 months, stable disease was seen in 66.7% on octreotide LAR versus 37.2% on placebo. The effect was most favourable in patients with low hepatic tumour load and a resected primary tumour, and was similar in functionally active and inactive tumours. Deaths were 7 versus 9; the hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.81 (0.30 to 2.18), which the trialists state was not confirmatory because so few deaths had occurred.
cards.watchOut: Small (85 patients) and reported at a planned interim analysis; the survival comparison rests on only 16 deaths and shows no established difference.
cards.source: Rinke A et al. Placebo-controlled, double-blind, prospective, randomized study on the effect of octreotide LAR in the control of tumor growth in patients with metastatic neuroendocrine midgut tumors: a report from the PROMID Study Group. cards.headline: CLARINET open-label extension 2016: median progression-free survival of 32.8 months counted from core-study randomisation in the original lanreotide group (open-label, uncontrolled)
cards.summary: CLARINET open-label extension 2016: median progression-free survival of 32.8 months counted from core-study randomisation in the original lanreotide group (open-label, uncontrolled)
cards.type: Open-label extension study (uncontrolled) of the CLARINET trial, Endocr Relat Cancer 2016
cards.people: 88 patients from CLARINET (41 previously on lanreotide, 47 previously on placebo) who had stable disease at the end of the core study, or progression on placebo, continued or switched to open-label lanreotide Autogel 120 mg; 38% had pancreatic, 39% midgut and 23% other/unknown primary tumours.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival for the original lanreotide group (n = 101, counted from core-study randomisation through the extension) was 32.8 months (95% CI 30.9 to 68.0); a sensitivity analysis allowing for selection bias gave 30.8 months. In patients who switched from placebo to lanreotide after progression (n = 32), median time to further progression was 14.0 months. Patients continuing lanreotide reported fewer adverse events during the extension than in the core study.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, and extension entrants are selected survivors with stable or slower disease — these figures describe duration of control on continued treatment, not a randomised comparison, and overlap the CLARINET population rather than adding new patients.
cards.source: Caplin ME et al. Anti-tumour effects of lanreotide for pancreatic and intestinal neuroendocrine tumours: the CLARINET open-label extension study. Endocrine-related cancer. 2016. cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the two randomised placebo-controlled trials of somatostatin analogues in advanced gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours — 289 patients in total (143 on a somatostatin analogue, 146 on placebo), i.e. CLARINET and PROMID.
cards.result: Disease control favoured somatostatin analogues: hazard ratio for disease progression 0.41 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.58 — a relative measure; P<0.01), with response (disease-control) rates of 58.0% versus 32.2%. The only adverse event differing significantly from placebo was biliary stones (risk ratio 3.79, 1.28 to 11.17 — a relative measure).

shelves.title: Telotristat ethyl for carcinoid syndrome diarrhoea: about 0.7–0.8 fewer bowel movements per day than placebo in TELESTAR, with responders 42–44% versus 20%, and large urinary 5-HIAA falls in TELECAST
shelves.question: In patients with carcinoid syndrome diarrhoea inadequately controlled on somatostatin analogues, does telotristat ethyl, compared with placebo, reduce bowel-movement frequency and urinary 5-HIAA?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/therapeutic use · Defecation/drug effects · Diarrhea/drug therapy/etiology/urine · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Hydroxyindoleacetic Acid/urine · Male · Malignant Carcinoid Syndrome/complications/drug therapy/urine · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Peptides, Cyclic/therapeutic use · Phenylalanine/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Pyrimidines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Somatostatin/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Tryptophan Hydroxylase/antagonists & inhibitors · gamma-Glutamyltransferase/blood
shelves.balance: One development programme, two companion placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. In TELESTAR (N = 135, patients with ≥4 bowel movements/day despite stable somatostatin-analogue therapy), telotristat ethyl 250 mg and 500 mg three times daily reduced bowel-movement frequency by an estimated 0.81 and 0.69 movements/day more than placebo averaged over 12 weeks; durable responders (≥30% reduction for at least half the period) were 44% and 42% versus 20% on placebo, and urinary 5-HIAA fell significantly versus placebo at week 12. In TELECAST (N = 76, a broader carcinoid-syndrome population with <4 bowel movements/day on analogues), the primary biochemical endpoint fell sharply: median urinary 5-HIAA treatment differences from placebo of −54.0% (250 mg) and −89.7% (500 mg) at week 12. A prespecified pooled analysis found sustained ≥30% bowel-movement improvement in 69% of telotristat patients, reached significantly faster than on placebo in both trials. Long-term open-label follow-up (TELEPATH, N = 124) found no new safety signals. The bowel-movement gain is real but modest in absolute terms — under one movement per day on average — which, with the single-programme base, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Syndrome symptom control only; antitumour therapy for NETs is homed elsewhere (live shelf #742).

cards.summary: TELESTAR 2017: telotristat ethyl cut bowel-movement frequency by 0.81 (250 mg) and 0.69 (500 mg) movements/day more than placebo; responders 44% and 42% versus 20%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (TELESTAR), J Clin Oncol 2017
cards.people: 135 patients with carcinoid syndrome experiencing ≥4 bowel movements per day despite stable-dose somatostatin-analogue therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, telotristat ethyl 250 mg, or telotristat ethyl 500 mg three times daily for a 12-week double-blind period; 115 patients continued into an open-label extension on 500 mg.
cards.result: Estimated differences in bowel-movement frequency versus placebo, averaged over 12 weeks, were −0.81/day for 250 mg and −0.69/day for 500 mg (both P<.001). At week 12, mean reductions were −1.7 and −2.1 movements/day on telotristat versus −0.9 on placebo. Durable responses (≥30% reduction for ≥50% of the double-blind period) occurred in 44% (250 mg) and 42% (500 mg) versus 20% on placebo. Both doses significantly reduced mean urinary 5-HIAA versus placebo at week 12 (P<.001; the abstract reports no percentage figures). Mild nausea and asymptomatic gamma-glutamyltransferase increases were seen in some telotristat patients.
cards.watchOut: The average absolute gain over placebo is under one bowel movement per day, and there was no dose advantage of 500 mg over 250 mg on the primary endpoint; the trial's own record carries no registry ID in its databank fields.
cards.source: Kulke MH et al. Telotristat Ethyl, a Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor for the Treatment of Carcinoid Syndrome. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2017. PMID: 27918724. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: TELECAST 2018: urinary 5-HIAA fell by median treatment differences of −54.0% (250 mg) and −89.7% (500 mg) versus placebo at week 12
cards.summary: TELECAST 2018: urinary 5-HIAA fell by median treatment differences of −54.0% (250 mg) and −89.7% (500 mg) versus placebo at week 12
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (TELECAST), Endocr Relat Cancer 2018
cards.people: 76 patients with carcinoid syndrome (diarrhoea, flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, or elevated urinary 5-HIAA) who had <4 bowel movements/day on somatostatin analogues (or ≥1 symptom, or ≥4 bowel movements/day if not on analogues), randomised 1:1:1 to placebo or telotristat ethyl 250 mg or 500 mg three times daily for 12 weeks, followed by a 36-week open-label extension (67 patients).
cards.result: The primary endpoints were safety and percent change in 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA at week 12. Hodges–Lehmann median treatment differences from placebo were −54.0% (95% confidence limits −85.0% to −25.1%) for 250 mg and −89.7% (−113.1% to −63.9%) for 500 mg (both P<0.001) — relative percent changes in a biochemical marker. Through week 12, treatment-emergent adverse events were generally mild to moderate; serious events occurred in 5 (placebo), 1 (250 mg) and 3 (500 mg) patients, and open-label event rates were comparable.
cards.watchOut: TELECAST enrolled a milder-diarrhoea population than TELESTAR and its headline endpoint is biochemical (urinary 5-HIAA), not bowel-movement frequency — the two trials answer related but not identical questions.
cards.source: Pavel M et al. Telotristat ethyl in carcinoid syndrome: safety and efficacy in the TELECAST phase 3 trial. Endocrine-related cancer. 2018. PMID: 29330194. Registry ID: NCT02063659, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pooled TELESTAR/TELECAST analysis 2021: 69% of telotristat patients reached a sustained ≥30% bowel-movement improvement, significantly faster than on placebo in both trials
cards.summary: Pooled TELESTAR/TELECAST analysis 2021: 69% of telotristat patients reached a sustained ≥30% bowel-movement improvement, significantly faster than on placebo in both trials
cards.type: Prespecified pooled analysis of two phase 3 RCTs, J Gastrointest Cancer 2021
cards.people: Prespecified pooled analysis of the two phase 3 trials carded above (TELESTAR, N = 135, and TELECAST, N = 76), examining time to the first of 2 consecutive weeks with a mean bowel-movement improvement of ≥30% from baseline during the 12-week double-blind periods.
cards.result: A majority (69%) of telotristat-treated patients experienced a sustained ≥30% improvement. Median time to sustained improvement was significantly shorter on telotristat than placebo in TELESTAR (hazard ratio 2.3 [95% CI 1.3 to 4.1] for 250 mg and 2.2 [1.2 to 3.9] for 500 mg — relative measures) and in TELECAST (3.9 [1.6 to 11.1] and 4.2 [1.7 to 11.7]). In TELECAST, sustained worsening occurred in 42% on placebo versus 20% on telotristat; no significant difference in worsening was seen in TELESTAR.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-analysis of the same two trials — it adds timing information, not new patients, and its hazard ratios are relative measures of speed of response.
cards.source: Dillon JS et al. Time to Sustained Improvement in Bowel Movement Frequency with Telotristat Ethyl: Analyses of Phase III Studies in Carcinoid Syndrome. Journal of gastrointestinal cancer. 2021. PMID: 32146619. Registry ID: NCT01677910, NCT02063659, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: TELEPATH 2022 (open-label, uncontrolled): long-term telotristat exposure (mean 102.6 weeks in 124 patients) showed no new safety signals and stable quality of life
cards.summary: TELEPATH 2022 (open-label, uncontrolled): long-term telotristat exposure (mean 102.6 weeks in 124 patients) showed no new safety signals and stable quality of life
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension study (uncontrolled, TELEPATH), Neuroendocrinology 2022
cards.people: 124 patients who had taken part in phase 2 or 3 telotristat trials and continued their existing dose (250 or 500 mg three times daily) for 84 weeks in a nonrandomised, open-label long-term extension; the primary endpoint was safety and tolerability.
cards.result: Adverse-event type and frequency were consistent with the earlier trials, most events were mild to moderate, adverse events of special interest (liver-related, depression, gastrointestinal) were not related to dose or duration, and no deaths were related to telotristat. Quality-of-life scores remained stable and most patients reported adequate symptom relief throughout.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled, in patients who had already tolerated telotristat in earlier trials — a selected population; it supports long-term tolerability, not efficacy.
cards.source: Hörsch D et al. Long-Term Treatment with Telotristat Ethyl in Patients with Carcinoid Syndrome Symptoms: Results from the TELEPATH Study. Neuroendocrinology. 2022. PMID: 33940581. Registry ID: NCT02026063, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: telotristat ethyl reduces bowel movements and urinary 5-HIAA versus placebo as an add-on to somatostatin analogues — a modest average gain from one programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf.
cards.result: TELESTAR showed 0.69–0.81 fewer bowel movements/day than placebo with durable responders of 42–44% versus 20%; TELECAST showed median urinary 5-HIAA differences of −54.0% and −89.7% versus placebo; pooled analysis showed faster sustained improvement in both trials, and TELEPATH found no new long-term safety signals. shelves.title: FIRM-ACT: EDP-mitotane beat streptozocin-mitotane on response (23.2% versus 9.2%) and progression-free survival (5.0 versus 2.1 months), but overall survival was 14.8 versus 12.0 months — no significant difference
shelves.question: In advanced adrenocortical carcinoma, does first-line etoposide + doxorubicin + cisplatin with mitotane (EDP-M), compared with streptozocin + mitotane, improve progression-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Neoplasms/drug therapy · Adrenocortical Carcinoma/drug therapy · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cisplatin/administration & dosage · Disease-Free Survival · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage · Etoposide/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Mitotane/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Streptozocin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: A single randomised trial answers this question, supported by two earlier single-arm phase 2 studies of the winning regimen. In FIRM-ACT (N = 304), first-line EDP-mitotane gave a response rate of 23.2% versus 9.2% on streptozocin-mitotane and median progression-free survival of 5.0 versus 2.1 months (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians). Overall survival was 14.8 versus 12.0 months (hazard ratio 0.79, 0.61 to 1.02; P=0.07) — not significantly different: on survival, the treatment made no difference that this trial could establish, and crossover to the alternative regimen at progression (185 patients) blurs any survival contrast. Serious adverse-event rates did not differ significantly. The phase 2 studies that led to FIRM-ACT reported higher response rates for EDP-mitotane (48.6% in 72 patients, 2005; 53.5% in 28 patients, 1998) than the randomised trial itself found — a familiar pattern when a regimen meets a control arm. One trial, in a rare cancer, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Adjuvant mitotane after resection is a different question, homed on pack #6280.

cards.headline: FIRM-ACT 2012: response 23.2% versus 9.2% and median progression-free survival 5.0 versus 2.1 months for EDP-mitotane over streptozocin-mitotane; overall survival 14.8 versus 12.0 months, not significant
cards.summary: FIRM-ACT 2012: response 23.2% versus 9.2% and median progression-free survival 5.0 versus 2.1 months for EDP-mitotane over streptozocin-mitotane; overall survival 14.8 versus 12.0 months, not significant
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (FIRM-ACT), N Engl J Med 2012
cards.people: 304 patients with advanced adrenocortical carcinoma randomised to mitotane plus EDP (etoposide 100 mg/m² on days 2–4, doxorubicin 40 mg/m² on day 1, cisplatin 40 mg/m² on days 3 and 4, every 4 weeks) or mitotane plus streptozocin (1 g on days 1–5 in cycle 1, then 2 g on day 1, every 3 weeks); patients with progression crossed to the alternative regimen as second-line therapy. The primary endpoint was overall survival.
cards.result: For first-line therapy, response rate was 23.2% on EDP-mitotane versus 9.2% on streptozocin-mitotane (P<0.001) and median progression-free survival was 5.0 versus 2.1 months (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69 — a relative measure; P<0.001). Overall survival was 14.8 versus 12.0 months (hazard ratio 0.79, 0.61 to 1.02; P=0.07) — no significant difference (the treatment made no difference to overall survival that this trial could establish). Among the 185 patients who crossed over, second-line median progression-free survival was 5.6 months in the group receiving EDP-mitotane second and 2.2 months in the group receiving streptozocin-mitotane second. Rates of serious adverse events did not differ significantly between treatments.
cards.watchOut: The trial's primary endpoint — overall survival — was not met, and planned crossover at progression means the survival comparison is not a pure first-line contrast; the established gains are response and progression-free survival.
cards.source: Fassnacht M et al. Combination chemotherapy in advanced adrenocortical carcinoma. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22551107. Registry ID: NCT00094497, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Berruti 2005 (single-arm phase 2): EDP plus mitotane produced responses in 48.6% of 72 patients with advanced adrenocortical carcinoma
cards.summary: Berruti 2005 (single-arm phase 2): EDP plus mitotane produced responses in 48.6% of 72 patients with advanced adrenocortical carcinoma
cards.type: Prospective single-arm phase 2 trial, Endocr Relat Cancer 2005
cards.people: 72 patients with measurable advanced adrenocortical carcinoma not amenable to radical surgery, treated prospectively at multiple centres with EDP (etoposide 100 mg/m² on days 5–7, doxorubicin 20 mg/m² on days 1 and 8, cisplatin 40 mg/m² on days 1 and 9, every 4 weeks) plus oral mitotane up to 4 g/day. Uncontrolled.
cards.result: Five complete and 30 partial responses gave an overall response rate of 48.6% (95% CI 37.1 to 60.3). Median time to progression in responding patients was 18 months. Leukopenia was the dose-limiting toxicity and one treatment-related death from septic shock occurred. Ten patients had radical resection of residual disease after chemotherapy, and patients attaining disease-free status survived significantly longer than partial responders or non-responders (P<0.002).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator, and its dosing schedule differs from FIRM-ACT (split doxorubicin/cisplatin days); its 48.6% response rate was not reproduced under randomised conditions (23.2%).
cards.source: Berruti A et al. Etoposide, doxorubicin and cisplatin plus mitotane in the treatment of advanced adrenocortical carcinoma: a large prospective phase II trial. Endocrine-related cancer. 2005. PMID: 16172198. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Berruti 1998 (single-arm phase 2, Italian Group): EDP plus mitotane produced responses in 53.5% of 28 patients
cards.summary: Berruti 1998 (single-arm phase 2, Italian Group): EDP plus mitotane produced responses in 53.5% of 28 patients
cards.people: 28 patients (18 women, 10 men; median age 47 years) with measurable advanced, inoperable adrenocortical carcinoma, 18 with evidence of steroid hypersecretion, treated with the same split-schedule EDP regimen plus oral mitotane up to 4 g/day or the maximum tolerated dose. Uncontrolled.
cards.result: Two complete and 13 partial responses gave an overall response rate of 53.5% (95% CI 35 to 72); stable disease in 8 and progressive disease in 5. Time to progression in responders was 24.4 months. Only 9 of the patients regularly took the planned mitotane dose of 4 g/day — mitotane added neurologic and gastrointestinal toxicity and raised cholesterol and triglycerides — and 3 patients discontinued chemotherapy early because of toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Very small (28 patients) and uncontrolled; it establishes that the regimen has activity, not that it beats any alternative — that comparison exists only in FIRM-ACT.
cards.source: Berruti A et al. Mitotane associated with etoposide, doxorubicin, and cisplatin in the treatment of advanced adrenocortical carcinoma. Italian Group for the Study of Adrenal Cancer. Cancer. 1998. PMID: 9827725. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: EDP-mitotane is the more active first-line regimen on response and progression-free survival; a survival advantage has not been shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: EDP-mitotane is the more active first-line regimen on response and progression-free survival; a survival advantage has not been shown
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf.
cards.result: FIRM-ACT, the only randomised comparison, found response rates of 23.2% versus 9.2% and median progression-free survival of 5.0 versus 2.1 months favouring EDP-mitotane, with overall survival of 14.8 versus 12.0 months not significantly different. Two earlier single-arm phase 2 studies (N = 72 and N = 28) reported higher uncontrolled response rates of 48.6% and 53.5%. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for response and progression-free survival; on overall survival the treatment made no difference that the trial could establish.
cards.watchOut: This is a synthesis card, not a separate study; it adds no patients to the evidence base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fassnacht M et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22551107); Berruti A et al. Endocrine-related cancer. 2005 (PMID: 16172198); Berruti A et al. Cancer. 1998 (PMID: 9827725).

shelves.title: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab in first-line unresectable HCC (CheckMate 9DW): median survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months, with early curve crossing
shelves.question: In adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and no prior systemic therapy, does nivolumab plus ipilimumab improve overall survival versus lenvatinib or sorafenib?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Quinolines/administration & dosage,therapeutic use,adverse effects* · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/drug therapy,mortality* · Nivolumab/administration & dosage,therapeutic use,adverse effects* · Phenylurea Compounds/administration & dosage,therapeutic use,adverse effects* · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy,mortality* · Middle Aged · Sorafenib/administration & dosage,therapeutic use,adverse effects* · Aged · Ipilimumab/administration & dosage,therapeutic use,adverse effects* · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage* · Adult · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one first-line randomised trial caps the stamp. In CheckMate 9DW (Yau 2025, PMID: 40349714), 668 patients with previously untreated unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma were randomised to nivolumab plus ipilimumab or investigator's choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib: median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.96; p=0.018 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it), with 36-month survival 38% versus 24%. The curves crossed early — more deaths in the first 6 months on the combination (HR 1.65) before a sustained later separation (HR 0.61) — and treatment-related deaths were 12 versus 3. The same combination in sorafenib-pretreated patients (CheckMate 040) gave durable responses (objective response 32% in the regimen arm later used first-line; 5-year survival 29% in that arm), supporting the drug pair's activity but in a different, second-line population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single first-line trial programme caps the stamp.

cards.headline: Yau 2025 (CheckMate 9DW): median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months (HR 0.79) for nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus lenvatinib or sorafenib in first-line unresectable HCC
cards.summary: Yau 2025 (CheckMate 9DW): median overall survival 23.7 versus 20.6 months (HR 0.79) for nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus lenvatinib or sorafenib in first-line unresectable HCC
cards.people: 668 adults with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma and no previous systemic therapy (Child-Pugh 5 or 6, ECOG 0 or 1), randomised to nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks for up to four doses then nivolumab 480 mg every 4 weeks (n=335), or investigator's choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib (n=333); median follow-up 35.2 months. Open-label, randomised phase 3 trial.
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly improved with nivolumab plus ipilimumab (median 23.7 months, 95% CI 18.8 to 29.4, versus 20.6 months, 17.5 to 22.5; HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.96; p=0.018 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it). Survival rates were 49% versus 39% at 24 months and 38% versus 24% at 36 months. The survival curves crossed early: HR 1.65 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.43) for deaths in the first 6 months, then HR 0.61 (0.48 to 0.77) thereafter. Grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 41% versus 42%; 12 deaths were attributed to treatment with the combination and 3 with lenvatinib or sorafenib.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries the first-line question, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE. The early excess deaths on the combination (first-6-months HR 1.65) mean the average HR understates early harm and later benefit; patients at risk of early decompensation may not live long enough to reach the favourable part of the curve.
cards.source: Yau T et al. Nivolumab plus ipilimumab versus lenvatinib or sorafenib as first-line treatment for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (CheckMate 9DW): an open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2025. PMID: 40349714. Registry ID: NCT04039607. cards.headline: Yau 2020 (CheckMate 040): in sorafenib-pretreated HCC, the same combination gave a 32% objective response rate in the arm using the first-line regimen — a different (second-line) population
cards.summary: Yau 2020 (CheckMate 040): in sorafenib-pretreated HCC, the same combination gave a 32% objective response rate in the arm using the first-line regimen — a different (second-line) population
cards.people: 148 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma previously treated with sorafenib, randomised between three nivolumab-plus-ipilimumab dosing arms (50, 49 and 49 patients); median follow-up 30.7 months. Open-label phase 1/2 randomised cohort — second-line, not the first-line population of this shelf's question.
cards.result: Investigator-assessed objective response rate was 32% (95% CI 20 to 47) in arm A (nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses, then nivolumab — the regimen later used in CheckMate 9DW), 27% in arm B and 29% in arm C. Median duration of response was not reached in arm A (range 8.3 to 33.7+ months). Any-grade treatment-related adverse events occurred in 94%, 71% and 79% of arms A, B and C, with one treatment-related death (grade 5 pneumonitis, arm A).
cards.watchOut: This card supports the combination's antitumour activity only — its patients had already received sorafenib, so it cannot confirm the first-line survival result, and response rate is not survival.
cards.source: Yau T et al. Efficacy and Safety of Nivolumab Plus Ipilimumab in Patients With Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma Previously Treated With Sorafenib: The CheckMate 040 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Oncology. 2020. PMID: 33001135. Registry ID: NCT01658878. cards.headline: Melero 2024 (CheckMate 040, 5-year): responses in arm A proved durable — median duration of response 51.2 months and 60-month survival 29%
cards.summary: Melero 2024 (CheckMate 040, 5-year): responses in arm A proved durable — median duration of response 51.2 months and 60-month survival 29%
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised phase 1/2 cohort (Melero 2024, CheckMate 040)
cards.people: The same 148 sorafenib-pretreated patients as the Yau 2020 card, re-reported at a minimum 60 months of follow-up (median 62.6 months).
cards.result: Objective response rate was 34% in arm A, 27% in arm B and 29% in arm C. Median duration of response was 51.2 months in arm A (95% CI 12.6 to not estimable), 15.2 months in arm B and 21.7 months in arm C. Median overall survival was 22.2 months in arm A, 12.5 in arm B and 12.7 in arm C; 60-month survival rates were 29%, 19% and 21%. No new safety signals and no new discontinuations for immune-mediated adverse events appeared with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A longer look at the same second-line cohort, not independent confirmation of the first-line result. Durability in responders is the signal here; most patients still did not respond.
cards.source: Melero I et al. Nivolumab plus ipilimumab combination therapy in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma previously treated with sorafenib: 5-year results from CheckMate 040. Annals of Oncology. 2024. PMID: 38844309. Registry ID: not captured from the record this session. cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive first-line phase 3 trial, with an early-harm caveat, backed by durable second-line responses
cards.people: First-line evidence: CheckMate 9DW, 668 randomised patients (Yau 2025). Supporting programme evidence: CheckMate 040, 148 sorafenib-pretreated patients (Yau 2020; Melero 2024).

shelves.title: FGFR inhibitors in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma: response rates 35.5–42% in two single-arm phase 2 trials (FIGHT-202, FOENIX-CCA2)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated cholangiocarcinoma harbouring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, what response rates and durability do FGFR inhibitors (pemigatinib, futibatinib) achieve?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cholangiocarcinoma/drug therapy,genetics,pathology · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/classification,pathology · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factors/genetics · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Morpholines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Neoplasm Metastasis · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/drug therapy,genetics,pathology · Oncogene Proteins, Fusion/genetics · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pyrroles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Receptor, Fibroblast Growth Factor, Type 2/genetics · Receptors, Fibroblast Growth Factor/genetics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm evidence only, printed on the face of every card: neither trial had a randomised comparator, so response rates cannot prove a survival benefit. In FIGHT-202 (Abou-Alfa 2020, PMID: 32203698; final analysis Vogel 2024, PMID: 38838500), pemigatinib gave an objective response in 35.5% of 107 patients with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements (37.0% of 108 at final analysis), median duration of response 9.1 months and median overall survival 17.5 months. In FOENIX-CCA2 (Goyal 2023, PMID: 36652354), futibatinib gave a response in 42% of 103 patients, median duration 9.7 months. Hyperphosphataemia is the class harm (grade 3 in 30% on futibatinib). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm phase 2 evidence never rises above POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Abou-Alfa 2020 (FIGHT-202): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — pemigatinib response rate 35.5% in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma
cards.summary: Abou-Alfa 2020 (FIGHT-202): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — pemigatinib response rate 35.5% in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial (Abou-Alfa 2020, FIGHT-202) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM, open-label phase 2 design — no control group. 146 patients with previously treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma enrolled in three cohorts; this card reports the 107 patients with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements who received oral pemigatinib 13.5 mg daily (2 weeks on, 1 week off); median follow-up 17.8 months.
cards.result: Objective response occurred in 38 of 107 patients (35.5%, 95% CI 26.5 to 45.4) — 3 complete and 35 partial responses. Hyperphosphataemia was the most common all-grade adverse event (60%); 64% of all 146 patients had a grade 3 or worse adverse event (hypophosphataemia 12% the most frequent) and 45% a serious adverse event. No deaths were deemed treatment-related. Without a comparator, these figures show antitumour activity, not a proven survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm design printed on the face: a 35.5% response rate in a selected, biomarker-defined population cannot be compared with what chemotherapy or no treatment would have done in the same patients.

cards.headline: Vogel 2024 (FIGHT-202 final): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — response rate 37.0%, median survival 17.5 months at 45.4 months' follow-up
cards.summary: Vogel 2024 (FIGHT-202 final): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — response rate 37.0%, median survival 17.5 months at 45.4 months' follow-up
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial, final analysis (Vogel 2024, FIGHT-202) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM, open-label phase 2 design — no control group. Final analysis of FIGHT-202: 147 patients enrolled; cohort A (FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements) numbered 108 patients; median follow-up 45.4 months.
cards.result: In cohort A the objective response rate was 37.0% (95% CI 27.9 to 46.9; 3 complete and 37 partial responses), median duration of response 9.1 months, median progression-free survival 7.0 months and median overall survival 17.5 months (95% CI 14.4 to 22.9). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were hyperphosphataemia (58.5%), alopecia (49.7%) and diarrhoea (47.6%); 10.2% discontinued for adverse events. The survival figure has no comparator arm and cannot be read as a treatment effect.
cards.watchOut: The same single-arm trial as the Abou-Alfa 2020 card, matured — not independent confirmation. Cohort A grew from 107 to 108 patients between reports as printed in their own records.

cards.headline: Goyal 2023 (FOENIX-CCA2): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — futibatinib response rate 42% in FGFR2-rearranged intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
cards.summary: Goyal 2023 (FOENIX-CCA2): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — futibatinib response rate 42% in FGFR2-rearranged intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial (Goyal 2023, FOENIX-CCA2) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM, open-label, single-group phase 2 design — no control group. 103 patients with unresectable or metastatic FGFR2 fusion- or rearrangement-positive intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, progressed after one or more previous systemic lines (no previous FGFR inhibitor), treated with oral futibatinib 20 mg once daily; median follow-up 17.1 months.
cards.result: A response occurred in 43 of 103 patients (42%, 95% CI 32 to 52), median duration of response 9.7 months, median progression-free survival 9.0 months and median overall survival 21.7 months — all without a comparator. Common treatment-related grade 3 adverse events were hyperphosphataemia (30%), increased aspartate aminotransferase (7%), stomatitis (6%) and fatigue (6%); 2% discontinued permanently for treatment-related events and there were no treatment-related deaths. Quality of life was maintained.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm design printed on the face. The 42% response rate and 21.7-month median survival describe what happened on futibatinib; they do not estimate what futibatinib adds over any alternative.
cards.source: Goyal L et al. Futibatinib for FGFR2-Rearranged Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36652354. Registry ID: NCT02052778. cards.headline: Synthesis: two single-arm phase 2 trials, response rates 35.5–42%, no randomised evidence — POSSIBLE at most
cards.summary: Synthesis: two single-arm phase 2 trials, response rates 35.5–42%, no randomised evidence — POSSIBLE at most
cards.people: FIGHT-202 (pemigatinib): 107–108 patients with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements. FOENIX-CCA2 (futibatinib): 103 patients. Both single-arm, both in previously treated disease.
cards.result: Objective response 35.5% (primary report) to 37.0% (final analysis) for pemigatinib and 42% for futibatinib, with median response durations of 9.1 and 9.7 months. shelves.title: Ivosidenib in IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (ClarIDHy): progression-free survival HR 0.37; survival benefit only after crossover adjustment
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma, does ivosidenib improve progression-free and overall survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bile Duct Neoplasms/drug therapy,enzymology,genetics,pathology · Cholangiocarcinoma/drug therapy,enzymology,genetics,pathology · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm* · Enzyme Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Europe · Female · Glycine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Humans · Isocitrate Dehydrogenase/antagonists & inhibitors,genetics,metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Mutation* · Progression-Free Survival · Pyridines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Republic of Korea · Time Factors · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised trial programme caps the stamp. In ClarIDHy (Abou-Alfa 2020, PMID: 32416072), 185 patients with previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma were randomised to ivosidenib or placebo: progression-free survival improved clearly (median 2.7 versus 1.4 months; HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.54 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it). Final overall survival (Zhu 2021, PMID: 34554208) was 10.3 versus 7.5 months unadjusted (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.12; not significant), becoming 10.3 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.49) only after adjusting for the 43 placebo patients who crossed over to ivosidenib. The phase 1 cohort (Lowery 2019, PMID: 31300360) had shown a 5% response rate with prolonged stable disease. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the progression-free result is randomised and strong; the survival claim rests on a crossover adjustment.

cards.headline: Abou-Alfa 2020 (ClarIDHy): progression-free survival HR 0.37 for ivosidenib versus placebo in IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (median 2.7 versus 1.4 months)
cards.summary: Abou-Alfa 2020 (ClarIDHy): progression-free survival HR 0.37 for ivosidenib versus placebo in IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (median 2.7 versus 1.4 months)
cards.people: 185 patients with advanced, previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma (up to two previous regimens, ECOG 0 or 1), randomised 2:1 to oral ivosidenib 500 mg daily (n=124) or placebo (n=61); median follow-up for progression-free survival 6.9 months. Double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial; crossover to ivosidenib was allowed at progression.
cards.result: Progression-free survival by independent central review was significantly improved with ivosidenib (median 2.7 months, 95% CI 1.6 to 4.2, versus 1.4 months, 1.4 to 1.6; HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.54; one-sided p<0.0001 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it). The most common grade 3 or worse adverse event in both groups was ascites (7% in each). Serious adverse events occurred in 30% on ivosidenib and 22% on placebo; there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: The relative effect is large but the absolute gain is small (median 2.7 versus 1.4 months) — read both numbers together. Crossover at progression dilutes the later overall-survival comparison.
cards.source: Abou-Alfa GK et al. Ivosidenib in IDH1-mutant, chemotherapy-refractory cholangiocarcinoma (ClarIDHy): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 study. Lancet Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32416072. Registry ID: NCT02989857. cards.headline: Zhu 2021 (ClarIDHy final survival): median overall survival 10.3 versus 7.5 months unadjusted (HR 0.79, not significant); 10.3 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.49) after crossover adjustment
cards.summary: Zhu 2021 (ClarIDHy final survival): median overall survival 10.3 versus 7.5 months unadjusted (HR 0.79, not significant); 10.3 versus 5.1 months (HR 0.49) after crossover adjustment
cards.type: Final overall-survival report of a randomised phase 3 trial (Zhu 2021, ClarIDHy)
cards.people: 187 patients as randomised in this final report (ivosidenib n=126, placebo n=61; the primary report analysed 185), of whom 43 crossed over from placebo to ivosidenib at progression. Same ClarIDHy trial as the Abou-Alfa 2020 card.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 10.3 months (95% CI 7.8 to 12.4) with ivosidenib versus 7.5 months (4.8 to 11.1) with placebo (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.12; 1-sided P=.09 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it; not statistically significant). Adjusted for crossover, median survival on placebo was 5.1 months (3.8 to 7.6), giving HR 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.70; 1-sided P<.001). The most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent event was ascites (9% versus 7%); there were no treatment-related deaths, and quality of life did not apparently decline on ivosidenib.
cards.watchOut: The headline survival benefit depends on a statistical adjustment for crossover — the unadjusted randomised comparison did not reach significance. The randomised denominators differ slightly between reports (185 versus 187) as printed in their own records.
cards.source: Zhu AX et al. Final Overall Survival Efficacy Results of Ivosidenib for Patients With Advanced Cholangiocarcinoma With IDH1 Mutation: The Phase 3 Randomized Clinical ClarIDHy Trial. JAMA Oncology. 2021. PMID: 34554208. Registry ID: NCT02989857. cards.headline: Lowery 2019 (phase 1): ivosidenib in 73 patients with IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma — 5% partial responses, median progression-free survival 3.8 months
cards.summary: Lowery 2019 (phase 1): ivosidenib in 73 patients with IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma — 5% partial responses, median progression-free survival 3.8 months
cards.people: 73 patients with IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma, previously treated, in a phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study of ivosidenib monotherapy (500 mg daily selected for expansion). Single-arm, no comparator.
cards.result: Four patients (5%, 95% CI 1.5 to 13.4) had a partial response. Median progression-free survival was 3.8 months (95% CI 3.6 to 7.3), with 6-month progression-free survival 40.1%; median overall survival was 13.8 months with data censored for 66% of patients. Common adverse events were fatigue (42%), nausea (34%) and diarrhoea (32%); the only treatment-related grade 3 or worse event in more than one patient was fatigue (3%). No dose-limiting toxicities were seen.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and hypothesis-generating: its low response rate with prolonged stable disease is the pattern ClarIDHy later confirmed as delayed progression rather than tumour shrinkage.
cards.source: Lowery MA et al. Safety and activity of ivosidenib in patients with IDH1-mutant advanced cholangiocarcinoma: a phase 1 study. Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 2019. PMID: 31300360. cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial — clear progression-free benefit, survival benefit only after crossover adjustment
cards.people: One randomised programme: ClarIDHy, 185–187 patients (Abou-Alfa 2020; Zhu 2021), preceded by a 73-patient phase 1 cohort (Lowery 2019).
cards.result: Progression-free survival HR 0.37 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.54; median 2.7 versus 1.4 months). Overall survival 10.3 versus 7.5 months unadjusted (HR 0.79, not significant) and HR 0.49 after crossover adjustment. Objective responses were uncommon (5% in phase 1). shelves.title: KRAS G12C inhibitors in pancreatic cancer: response rates 21% (sotorasib, 38 patients) and 33.3% (adagrasib, 21 patients) in single-arm cohorts
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutant pancreatic cancer, what response rates do sotorasib and adagrasib achieve?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy · Mutation · Pancreatic Neoplasms/drug therapy,genetics,secondary* · Proto-Oncogene Proteins p21(ras)/genetics · Pyridines · Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors/administration & dosage,therapeutic use* · Administration, Oral · Treatment Outcome · Piperazines · Pyrimidines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-arm phase 1/2 cohorts only, printed on the face of every card: no randomised comparator exists for either drug in pancreatic cancer. In CodeBreaK 100 (Strickler 2023, PMID: 36546651), sotorasib gave a centrally confirmed response in 8 of 38 previously treated patients (21%), median progression-free survival 4.0 months and median overall survival 6.9 months. In KRYSTAL-1 (Bekaii-Saab 2023, PMID: 37099736), adagrasib gave responses in 7 of 21 patients with pancreatic cancer (33.3%) within a 57-patient measurable-disease solid-tumour cohort. KRAS G12C occurs in only about 1–2% of pancreatic cancers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): single-arm evidence never rises above POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Strickler 2023 (CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort): SINGLE-ARM phase 1/2, no randomised comparator — sotorasib response rate 21% in 38 patients
cards.summary: Strickler 2023 (CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort): SINGLE-ARM phase 1/2, no randomised comparator — sotorasib response rate 21% in 38 patients
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1/2 cohort (Strickler 2023, CodeBreaK 100) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM, single-group phase 1/2 design — no control group. 38 patients with KRAS p.G12C-mutated advanced pancreatic cancer, all metastatic, previously treated with a median of 2 lines of therapy, given sotorasib 960 mg orally once daily (pooled phase 1 and 2 population).
cards.result: A centrally confirmed objective response occurred in 8 of 38 patients (21%, 95% CI 10 to 37). Median progression-free survival was 4.0 months (95% CI 2.8 to 5.6) and median overall survival 6.9 months (5.0 to 9.1) — neither has a comparator. Treatment-related adverse events of any grade occurred in 42% of patients and grade 3 events in 16%; none were fatal or led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm design printed on the face, and small (38 patients): the 21% response rate's confidence interval runs from 10% to 37%, and the survival figures describe this selected cohort only.
cards.source: Strickler JH et al. Sotorasib in KRAS p.G12C-Mutated Advanced Pancreatic Cancer. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36546651. Registry ID: NCT03600883. cards.headline: Bekaii-Saab 2023 (KRYSTAL-1 pancreatic cohort): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — adagrasib responses in 7 of 21 patients with pancreatic cancer (33.3%)
cards.summary: Bekaii-Saab 2023 (KRYSTAL-1 pancreatic cohort): SINGLE-ARM phase 2, no randomised comparator — adagrasib responses in 7 of 21 patients with pancreatic cancer (33.3%)
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 cohort (Bekaii-Saab 2023, KRYSTAL-1) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM phase 2 cohort — no control group. KRYSTAL-1 enrolled patients with KRAS G12C-mutated advanced solid tumours other than lung and colorectal cancer: 64 enrolled, 63 treated with adagrasib 600 mg twice daily, 57 with measurable disease, including 21 with pancreatic cancer; median follow-up 16.8 months; median of 2 previous therapy lines.
cards.result: Among the 21 patients with pancreatic cancer, 7 (33.3%) had an objective response (all partial responses in the cohort as a whole). Across all 57 measurable-disease patients the response rate was 35.1%, median duration of response 5.3 months and median progression-free survival 7.4 months. Treatment-related adverse events of any grade occurred in 96.8% of treated patients and grade 3–4 in 27.0%; there were no grade 5 treatment-related events and none led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm design printed on the face. The pancreatic slice is 21 patients inside a mixed-tumour cohort; the cohort-wide duration-of-response and progression-free figures are not pancreatic-specific and must not be read as pancreatic results.
cards.source: Bekaii-Saab TS et al. Adagrasib in Advanced Solid Tumors Harboring a KRASG12C Mutation. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2023. PMID: 37099736. Registry ID: NCT03785249. cards.headline: Hong 2020 (CodeBreaK 100 phase 1): SINGLE-ARM first-in-human study — responses seen in pancreatic cancer, but the pancreatic N is not documented in the record
cards.summary: Hong 2020 (CodeBreaK 100 phase 1): SINGLE-ARM first-in-human study — responses seen in pancreatic cancer, but the pancreatic N is not documented in the record
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1 trial (Hong 2020, CodeBreaK 100) — no randomised comparator
cards.people: SINGLE-ARM phase 1 design — no control group. 129 patients with KRAS p.G12C-mutated advanced solid tumours (59 lung, 42 colorectal, 28 other tumours including pancreatic), heavily pretreated (median 3 previous lines), given sotorasib once daily in dose-escalation and expansion cohorts. The number of pancreatic patients in this record is N not documented.
cards.result: No dose-limiting toxic effects or treatment-related deaths were observed. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 56.6% of patients, grade 3 or 4 in 11.6%. Confirmed responses occurred in 32.2% of the lung subgroup and 7.1% of the colorectal subgroup, and responses were also observed in patients with pancreatic, endometrial and appendiceal cancers and melanoma — the record does not give a pancreatic-specific response count, so none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Programme-origin card only: it establishes tolerability and that pancreatic responses occurred, nothing more. Pancreatic N not documented in the record — labelled as such rather than estimated.
cards.source: Hong DS et al. KRASG12C Inhibition with Sotorasib in Advanced Solid Tumors. New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32955176. Registry ID: NCT03600883. shelves.title: Delayed sodium thiosulfate to prevent cisplatin hearing loss in children and adolescents
shelves.question: In children and adolescents receiving cisplatin for solid tumours, does delayed intravenous sodium thiosulfate (given 6 hours after each cisplatin dose) reduce cisplatin-induced hearing loss versus cisplatin alone, without compromising tumour control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Cisplatin/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Doxorubicin/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Hearing Loss/chemically induced,prevention & control · Hepatoblastoma/drug therapy,mortality · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Liver Neoplasms/drug therapy,mortality · Male · Single-Blind Method · Survival Analysis · Thiosulfates/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Antioxidants/adverse effects · Cisplatin/adverse effects · Hearing Loss/chemically induced,epidemiology · Neoplasm Staging · Neoplasms/drug therapy,pathology · Prognosis · Survival Rate · Thiosulfates/adverse effects · United States/epidemiology · Acetylcysteine/therapeutic use · Amifostine/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Chelating Agents/therapeutic use · Cytoprotection · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Disulfiram/therapeutic use · Ditiocarb/therapeutic use · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Ototoxicity/etiology,prevention & control · Thiosulfates/therapeutic use · Hearing Loss/chemically induced,prevention & control,epidemiology · Ototoxicity/prevention & control,etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for hearing protection; the tumour-control caveat is on the face of this shelf, not buried. Two independent randomised phase 3 trials point the same way on hearing: in SIOPEL 6 (standard-risk hepatoblastoma, n=109), grade 1 or worse hearing loss occurred in 33% with delayed sodium thiosulfate versus 63% with cisplatin alone (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.81 — a 48% relative reduction, 30 percentage points absolute); in ACCL0431 (mixed solid tumours, n=125 randomised, 104 assessable), hearing loss occurred in 28.6% versus 56.4% (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.73 — 27.8 percentage points absolute). On tumour control the trials differ in what they can say: SIOPEL 6, in localised hepatoblastoma only, showed no survival detriment (3-year overall survival 98% versus 92%; event-free survival 82% versus 79%). ACCL0431 was not powered for survival, and a post-hoc analysis reported in the Freyer 2019 review found significantly worse overall survival with sodium thiosulfate among patients with disseminated disease, but not among those with localised disease. The hearing benefit is LIKELY; use in disseminated disease carries an unresolved tumour-protection concern that families and oncologists must weigh explicitly. Product naming: both trials published the intervention simply as sodium thiosulfate and named no brand or manufacturer; the paediatric formulation later approved for this use is marketed as Pedmark (Fennec Pharmaceuticals) — that brand name does not appear in the trial records carded here, and current marketed product may differ from the trial material.

cards.headline: SIOPEL 6: hearing loss in 33% with delayed sodium thiosulfate versus 63% with cisplatin alone, with no survival detriment at 3 years
cards.summary: SIOPEL 6: hearing loss in 33% with delayed sodium thiosulfate versus 63% with cisplatin alone, with no survival detriment at 3 years
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (SIOPEL 6; cisplatin with or without sodium thiosulfate 20 g/m2 given 6 hours after cisplatin)
cards.people: 109 children older than 1 month and younger than 18 years with standard-risk hepatoblastoma (no metastatic disease) randomised to cisplatin alone (52) or cisplatin plus sodium thiosulfate (57); hearing assessed in 101 children by pure-tone audiometry at a minimum age of 3.5 years.
cards.result: Hearing loss of Brock grade 1 or higher occurred in 18 of 55 children (33%) in the sodium thiosulfate group versus 29 of 46 (63%) in the cisplatin-alone group (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.81; P=0.002) — a 48% relative reduction and 30 percentage points absolute. At a median 52 months of follow-up, 3-year event-free survival was 82% (95% CI 69 to 90) versus 79% (95% CI 65 to 88) and 3-year overall survival was 98% (95% CI 88 to 100) versus 92% (95% CI 81 to 97). Sodium thiosulfate was associated with few high-grade toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: A single-disease trial in localised hepatoblastoma only: it cannot answer the tumour-protection question in disseminated or non-hepatoblastoma disease, which is exactly where the ACCL0431 signal appeared (see the Freyer 2019 card).
cards.source: Brock PR et al. Sodium Thiosulfate for Protection from Cisplatin-Induced Hearing Loss. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 29924955. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00652132. cards.headline: ACCL0431: hearing loss in 28.6% with sodium thiosulfate versus 56.4% with observation across mixed childhood solid tumours
cards.summary: ACCL0431: hearing loss in 28.6% with sodium thiosulfate versus 56.4% with observation across mixed childhood solid tumours
cards.type: Randomised, open-label phase 3 trial (Children's Oncology Group ACCL0431; sodium thiosulfate 16 g/m2 given 6 hours after each cisplatin dose versus observation)
cards.people: 125 children and adolescents aged 1–18 years with newly diagnosed cancer and normal audiometry at 38 Children's Oncology Group hospitals in the USA and Canada, randomised to sodium thiosulfate (61) or observation (64); 104 were assessable for the primary endpoint of hearing loss 4 weeks after the final cisplatin dose.
cards.result: Hearing loss was identified in 14 of 49 participants (28.6%; 95% CI 16.6 to 43.3) in the sodium thiosulfate group versus 31 of 55 (56.4%; 95% CI 42.3 to 69.7) in the control group (P=0.00022); adjusted odds ratio 0.31 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.73; P=0.0036) — 27.8 percentage points absolute. No serious adverse event was deemed probably or definitely related to sodium thiosulfate; the most common grade 3–4 events were neutropenia in both groups and hypokalaemia.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (audiologists were masked, participants and clinicians were not), a lower dose (16 g/m2) than SIOPEL 6, and — critically — the trial was designed and powered for hearing, not survival; its post-hoc disseminated-disease survival signal is carried on the Freyer 2019 card and in the balance, not hidden.
cards.source: Freyer DR et al. cards.headline: Freyer 2019 review: sodium thiosulfate is the only systemic agent with paediatric hearing efficacy — and the ACCL0431 post-hoc analysis showed worse survival in disseminated disease
cards.summary: Freyer 2019 review: sodium thiosulfate is the only systemic agent with paediatric hearing efficacy — and the ACCL0431 post-hoc analysis showed worse survival in disseminated disease
cards.type: Narrative review of randomised otoprotection trials in children and adolescents with cancer
cards.people: Review of the paediatric randomised literature, including SIOPEL 6 (localised hepatoblastoma) and ACCL0431 (heterogeneous tumours, localised and disseminated).
cards.result: Amifostine, sodium diethyldithiocarbamate and disulfiram showed no hearing preservation; sodium thiosulfate showed efficacy in both paediatric trials. In SIOPEL 6 no effects on survival were shown. In ACCL0431, a post-hoc analysis showed significantly worse overall survival among patients with disseminated disease receiving sodium thiosulfate than among controls, but not among those with localised disease. The review concludes future studies must build disease outcomes into their design and harmonise ototoxicity endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The disseminated-disease survival finding is post-hoc and from a trial not powered for survival — it is a warning signal, not proof of harm; equally, it cannot be dismissed, and it is the reason this shelf does not extend its LIKELY stamp beyond hearing protection.

cards.headline: ACCL0431 subgroup report 2025: hearing loss in 22.4% with sodium thiosulfate versus 54.0% with observation; protection was largest in children under 5 and in neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma or medulloblastoma
cards.summary: ACCL0431 subgroup report 2025: hearing loss in 22.4% with sodium thiosulfate versus 54.0% with observation; protection was largest in children under 5 and in neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma or medulloblastoma
cards.type: Secondary subgroup analysis of the ACCL0431 randomised trial (SIOP Ototoxicity Scale outcomes at 4 weeks and 12 months)
cards.people: 121 evaluable ACCL0431 participants aged 1–18 years randomised to sodium thiosulfate or observation, analysed by age, sex, race/ethnicity, cancer diagnosis and cisplatin infusion duration.
cards.result: Cumulative incidence of grade 1 or worse hearing loss was 22.4% with sodium thiosulfate versus 54.0% with observation. Odds of hearing loss were greatest in children younger than 5 years versus older (adjusted odds ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.30 to 7.14) and in neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma or medulloblastoma versus germ cell tumour or osteosarcoma (odds ratio 11.26, 95% CI 3.08 to 47.35). The protective effect was also largest in those highest-risk groups (under 5 years: odds ratio 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.32; high-risk diagnoses: odds ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.45).
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same single trial — it refines who benefits most, it is not independent confirmation, and subgroup odds ratios rest on small numbers with wide confidence intervals.
cards.source: Ohlsen TJD et al. Otoprotective Effects of Sodium Thiosulfate by Demographic and Clinical Characteristics: A Report From Children's Oncology Group Study ACCL0431. Pediatric blood & cancer. 2025. PMID: 39654065. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: delayed sodium thiosulfate roughly halves cisplatin hearing loss in two randomised trials — LIKELY for hearing; disseminated-disease tumour control remains an open, on-the-face concern
cards.summary: Synthesis: delayed sodium thiosulfate roughly halves cisplatin hearing loss in two randomised trials — LIKELY for hearing; disseminated-disease tumour control remains an open, on-the-face concern
cards.people: Synthesis of two randomised phase 3 trials (SIOPEL 6, n=109; ACCL0431, n=125), a review of the paediatric otoprotection literature, and an ACCL0431 subgroup re-analysis.
cards.result: Hearing loss fell from 63% to 33% (SIOPEL 6) and from 56.4% to 28.6% (ACCL0431) with sodium thiosulfate given 6 hours after cisplatin — concordant, large, randomised effects, re-confirmed on the modern SIOP scale and largest in the youngest and highest-risk children. Survival was unharmed in localised hepatoblastoma; a post-hoc disseminated-disease survival detriment in ACCL0431 is unresolved. LIKELY for hearing protection, with the disseminated-disease caveat stated wherever this shelf is summarised.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial named a branded product or manufacturer; the approved paediatric formulation (Pedmark) post-dates the trials and is named in the balance as context, not as trial material.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brock PR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29924955); Freyer DR et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2017 (PMID: 27914822); Freyer DR et al. The Lancet. shelves.title: PICC versus implantable port for chemotherapy access
shelves.question: In adults with cancer needing long-term central venous access for chemotherapy, does a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) cause more catheter-related complications (thrombosis, infection, occlusion, unplanned removal) than a totally implantable port, and at what cost and quality-of-life difference?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage · Catheterization, Central Venous/adverse effects,methods · Catheterization, Peripheral/adverse effects,methods · Catheters, Indwelling/adverse effects · Central Venous Catheters/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Risk Factors · Venous Thrombosis/etiology · Young Adult · Catheterization, Peripheral/economics,statistics & numerical data · Catheters, Indwelling/economics,statistics & numerical data · Central Venous Catheters/economics,statistics & numerical data · Cost-Benefit Analysis/economics,methods,statistics & numerical data · Health Care Costs/statistics & numerical data · Neoplasms/economics · Catheterization, Central Venous/adverse effects · Catheterization, Peripheral/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Thrombosis/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — an implantable port causes fewer complications than a PICC for chemotherapy access. The PICCPORT randomised trial (399 patients with mainly breast and colorectal cancer) found catheter-related deep venous thrombosis in 8% with a PICC versus 1% with a port (hazard ratio 10.2, 95% CI 2.3 to 44.6) and more composite adverse events overall (hazard ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.6 to 4.6). The RCT-based meta-analysis (6 reports, 1,127 patients) and the network meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (2,585 patients) point the same way: ports had lower odds of overall complications (odds ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69), thrombotic and mechanical complications, and removal for complications. Ports cost more per device inserted but less per catheter day in the PICCPORT health-economic analysis (3.01 versus 6.58 EUR/day), driven by the cost of managing PICC adverse events; quality of life was similar, with a smaller post-implantation decline in global health status in the port group of the RCT meta-analysis. A PICC remains quicker to place and avoids a surgical pocket — the stamp is about complications, cost per day and durability, not about which device fits an individual patient's veins, treatment length or preference.

cards.headline: PICCPORT: catheter-related deep venous thrombosis in 8% with a PICC versus 1% with a port (hazard ratio 10.2)
cards.summary: PICCPORT: catheter-related deep venous thrombosis in 8% with a PICC versus 1% with a port (hazard ratio 10.2)
cards.type: Open-label randomised two-centre trial (PICCPORT; single-lumen PICC versus totally implanted port)
cards.people: 399 adults with non-haematological cancer (mainly breast and colorectal) at two Swedish oncology centres, randomised to PICC (201) or port (198) and followed for up to 1 year.
cards.result: PICCs were associated with 16 deep venous thromboses (8%) compared with 2 (1%) in the port group (hazard ratio 10.2; 95% CI 2.3 to 44.6; P=0.002). The composite of insertion complication, thrombosis, occlusion, infection and mechanical problems was also higher with a PICC (hazard ratio 2.7; 95% CI 1.6 to 4.6; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in solid tumours only, and the thrombosis hazard ratio rests on 18 events — its confidence interval (2.3 to 44.6) is wide even though the direction is consistent with every synthesis on this shelf.
cards.source: Taxbro K et al. Clinical impact of peripherally inserted central catheters vs implanted port catheters in patients with cancer: an open-label, randomised, two-centre trial. British journal of anaesthesia. 2019. PMID: 31005243. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01971021. cards.headline: PICCPORT cost analysis: a PICC cost more overall (824.58 versus 662.34 EUR per device) and about twice as much per catheter day (6.58 versus 3.01 EUR/day)
cards.summary: PICCPORT cost analysis: a PICC cost more overall (824.58 versus 662.34 EUR per device) and about twice as much per catheter day (6.58 versus 3.01 EUR/day)
cards.type: Health-economic evaluation of the PICCPORT randomised trial (healthcare perspective)
cards.people: The same 399 randomised PICCPORT patients with cancer; costs modelled across insertion, maintenance and adverse-event management categories.
cards.result: Combining all cost categories, the price per inserted device was 824.58 EUR for a PICC and 662.34 EUR for a port; adjusted for total catheter dwell time, the price was 6.58 EUR/day for a PICC versus 3.01 EUR/day for a port. The difference in catheter-related deep venous thrombosis was the main contributor to the cost difference.
cards.watchOut: Swedish healthcare costs from one trial's process model — absolute figures will not transfer to other health systems, though the driver (paying to manage PICC complications) is the trial's own clinical result.
cards.source: Taxbro K et al. cards.headline: RCT-based meta-analysis (1,127 patients): PICCs had more total complications, thrombosis, implantation failure and unplanned removal; ports cost more per device but similarly per catheter day
cards.summary: RCT-based meta-analysis (1,127 patients): PICCs had more total complications, thrombosis, implantation failure and unplanned removal; ports cost more per device but similarly per catheter day
cards.type: Meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials of implantable port versus PICC for chemotherapy
cards.people: Six studies based on five randomised trials, totalling 1,127 patients with cancer requiring chemotherapy; complications were the primary endpoint, with cost, chemotherapy impact and quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30) as secondary endpoints.
cards.result: The PICC group experienced a higher incidence of total complications, thrombosis, deep vein thrombosis, implantation failure, unplanned catheter removal and local reactions; the port group had more pocket/exit-site infection without septicaemia and more pain. Complication-free survival was better with a port. Total cost was higher for ports while cost per catheter day was similar. Global health status did not differ during or after treatment, though the port group had a smaller decline after implantation.
cards.watchOut: Five randomised trials is a thin base and this 2025 record carries no MeSH terms in its PubMed record (noted on its source line); the complication pattern nonetheless matches PICCPORT and the network meta-analysis.
cards.source: Qiu J et al. Implantable Port Catheters versus Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters for Cancer Patients Requiring Chemotherapy: An RCT-Based Meta-Analysis. Journal of Cancer. 2025. cards.headline: Network meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (2,585 patients): ports had lower odds of overall, thrombotic and mechanical complications and of removal for complications than PICCs
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (2,585 patients): ports had lower odds of overall, thrombotic and mechanical complications and of removal for complications than PICCs
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of central venous access devices for chemotherapy
cards.people: 11 randomised trials totalling 2,585 patients comparing non-tunnelled central catheters, PICCs, totally implantable ports and tunnelled catheters for chemotherapy delivery (search to August 2021).
cards.result: Ports were associated with lower odds than PICCs of overall complications (odds ratio 0.54; 95% CI 0.43 to 0.69), device removal due to complications (odds ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.26 to 0.93), thrombotic complications (odds ratio 0.37; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.62) and mechanical complications (odds ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.95). Ranking analyses placed ports lowest for overall, removal and thrombotic complications, and the authors judged ports superior on complications and quality of life without compromising cost-effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: A network analysis — some comparisons are indirect — and device generations and insertion practice across trials spanning decades vary; the direct PICCPORT result remains the anchor.
cards.source: Yeow M et al. A systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on choice of central venous access device for delivery of chemotherapy. Journal of vascular surgery. Venous and lymphatic disorders. 2022. PMID: 35367407. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: ports beat PICCs on thrombosis, overall complications and cost per day across one randomised trial and two randomised-evidence syntheses — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: ports beat PICCs on thrombosis, overall complications and cost per day across one randomised trial and two randomised-evidence syntheses — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the PICCPORT randomised trial and its cost analysis (399 patients), an RCT-only meta-analysis (1,127 patients) and a network meta-analysis of randomised trials (2,585 patients).
cards.result: Every randomised source points the same way: fewer thromboses (8% versus 1% in PICCPORT), fewer complications and removals overall, similar quality of life, and lower cost per catheter day once complication management is counted. LIKELY that an implantable port is the lower-complication choice for longer chemotherapy courses; short courses, difficult anatomy and patient preference can still favour a PICC.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial here was blinded (device trials cannot be), and haematological malignancy and very short treatment courses are under-represented.

shelves.question: In adults receiving an EGFR inhibitor (panitumumab or cetuximab), does a pre-emptive skin-toxicity regimen (moisturiser, sunscreen, topical steroid and oral tetracycline-class antibiotic started with treatment) reduce grade 2 or worse skin toxicity versus reactive treatment started after the rash appears?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one randomised trial supports the full pre-emptive bundle; a second randomised trial of its antibiotic component alone was null on its primary endpoint. In STEPP (95 patients on panitumumab), protocol-specified grade 2 or worse skin toxicities during the 6-week treatment period occurred in 29% with pre-emptive treatment (moisturisers, sunscreen, topical steroid and doxycycline started with therapy) versus 62% with reactive treatment — an absolute reduction of 33 percentage points — and quality-of-life impairment was smaller (mean Dermatology Life Quality Index change 1.3 versus 4.2 points at week 3). But the only other randomised card, the placebo-controlled N03CB trial of prophylactic tetracycline alone (61 patients on various EGFR inhibitors), found rash incidence did not differ (the treatment made no difference: 70% versus 76%, P=.61), with only a severity signal at week 4 (grade 2 rash 17% versus 55%, P=.04) amid high dropout. A systematic review of anti-EGFR dermatologic toxicity likewise reports several studies finding pre-emptive treatment more effective than reactive treatment, without a pooled randomised estimate. A single positive phase 2 trial of the bundle caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: STEPP: grade 2 or worse skin toxicity in 29% with pre-emptive treatment versus 62% with reactive treatment over 6 weeks
cards.summary: STEPP: grade 2 or worse skin toxicity in 29% with pre-emptive treatment versus 62% with reactive treatment over 6 weeks
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label randomised trial (STEPP; pre-emptive versus reactive skin treatment with panitumumab-containing therapy)
cards.people: 95 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer receiving panitumumab-containing therapy, randomised to pre-emptive treatment (48) or reactive treatment started after skin toxicity developed (47).
cards.result: The incidence of protocol-specified grade 2 or worse skin toxicities during the 6-week skin treatment period was 29% in the pre-emptive group and 62% in the reactive group — the pre-emptive regimen more than halved the incidence (a relative reduction of over 50%, 33 percentage points absolute). Mean Dermatology Life Quality Index change from baseline to week 3 was 1.3 points pre-emptive versus 4.2 points reactive, and the pre-emptive regimen was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A single open-label phase 2 trial of 95 patients with a 6-week endpoint — the entire positive case for the bundle rests on this one study, which is why the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Lacouture ME et al. Skin toxicity evaluation protocol with panitumumab (STEPP), a phase II, open-label, randomized trial evaluating the impact of a pre-Emptive Skin treatment regimen on skin toxicities and quality of life in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2010. PMID: 20142600. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.
