cards.headline: N03CB: prophylactic tetracycline alone did not reduce rash incidence (70% versus 76% — the treatment made no difference), though grade 2 rash at week 4 was less frequent
cards.summary: N03CB: prophylactic tetracycline alone did not reduce rash incidence (70% versus 76% — the treatment made no difference), though grade 2 rash at week 4 was less frequent
cards.type: Placebo-controlled double-blind randomised trial (North Central Cancer Treatment Group N03CB; tetracycline 500 mg twice daily for 28 days versus placebo)
cards.people: 61 evaluable patients starting an EGFR inhibitor (including cetuximab and gefitinib) with no rash at enrolment, monitored for 4 weeks on treatment and 4 further weeks.
cards.result: Rash incidence was comparable across arms: physicians reported rash in 16 tetracycline patients (70%) and 22 placebo patients (76%) (P=.61) — the treatment made no difference to whether a rash occurred. By week 4, physician-reported grade 2 rash occurred in 17% on tetracycline (4 patients) versus 55% on placebo (16 patients) (P=.04), and tetracycline patients reported better skin-related quality-of-life scores.
cards.watchOut: High dropout rates invite caution on the severity finding, and this trial tested the antibiotic alone, without the moisturiser, sunscreen and topical steroid of the STEPP bundle — a null for one component is not a null for the bundle, but it removes any claim that the antibiotic alone explains STEPP.
cards.source: Jatoi A et al. Tetracycline to prevent epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor-induced skin rashes: results of a placebo-controlled trial from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group (N03CB). Cancer. 2008. PMID: 18543329. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Systematic review of anti-EGFR dermatologic toxicity: grade 3/4 toxicity in about 10–20% of patients, and several studies found pre-emptive treatment more effective than reactive treatment
cards.summary: Systematic review of anti-EGFR dermatologic toxicity: grade 3/4 toxicity in about 10–20% of patients, and several studies found pre-emptive treatment more effective than reactive treatment
cards.type: Systematic review of dermatologic toxicity during anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer (269 reports)
cards.people: Reports from 2009–2016 covering panitumumab and cetuximab in metastatic colorectal cancer: 31 randomised trials, 120 non-randomised trials, 15 retrospective studies and 39 reviews, graded by level of evidence.
cards.result: Dermatologic toxicity of any grade occurs in most patients receiving anti-EGFR therapy, with grade 3/4 toxicity in approximately 10% to 20%; the commonest problems are papulopustular rash, xerosis and pruritus. Management guidance centres on emollients, sun avoidance and irritant avoidance, and several studies found pre-emptive treatment was more effective than reactive treatment at limiting the incidence and severity of skin toxicity. The review gives no pooled randomised effect estimate for pre-emption.
cards.watchOut: A broad toxicity review, not a meta-analysis of the pre-emptive question — it supports the direction of STEPP but cannot raise the stamp above what the single randomised bundle trial earns.
cards.source: Lacouture ME et al. Dermatologic Toxicity Occurring During Anti-EGFR Monoclonal Inhibitor Therapy in Patients With Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review. Clinical colorectal cancer. 2018. PMID: 29576427. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the pre-emptive bundle halved grade 2+ toxicity in its one randomised trial, while tetracycline alone did not prevent rash — POSSIBLE, single-trial bundle
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pre-emptive bundle halved grade 2+ toxicity in its one randomised trial, while tetracycline alone did not prevent rash — POSSIBLE, single-trial bundle
cards.people: Synthesis of the STEPP randomised trial (95 patients), the N03CB placebo-controlled tetracycline trial (61 patients) and a systematic review of anti-EGFR dermatologic toxicity (269 reports).
cards.result: Pre-emptive care as a bundle (skin care, sunscreen, topical steroid, oral doxycycline) reduced grade 2 or worse toxicity from 62% to 29% in STEPP with less quality-of-life impairment; the antibiotic component alone did not change rash incidence in N03CB. POSSIBLE — promising and low-risk, but carried by one small open-label trial.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of pre-emption with cetuximab as a bundle was found this session; STEPP used panitumumab, and extrapolation across EGFR antibodies is an assumption, stated here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lacouture ME et al. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2010 (PMID: 20142600); Jatoi A et al. Cancer. 2008 (PMID: 18543329); Lacouture ME et al. Clinical colorectal cancer. 2018 (PMID: 29576427).

shelves.title: Dexamethasone sparing after day 1 in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy
shelves.question: In adults receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy on a palonosetron- or NK1-antagonist-based antiemetic backbone, can dexamethasone be safely spared after day 1 (single-day versus multi-day dexamethasone) without losing complete-response rates — and does the answer differ by regimen?

shelves.balance: LIKELY — for the palonosetron doublet regimens actually tested; the NK1-triplet carboplatin regimen is carded separately and is less settled, so this shelf does not pool them into one claim. Regimen 1 — palonosetron plus dexamethasone with anthracycline/cyclophosphamide or other moderately emetogenic chemotherapy: an individual-patient meta-analysis of two phase 3 trials (405 women) found overall complete response of about 55% on the 1-day regimen versus about 51–59% on the 3-day regimen with no significant loss, and the five-trial individual-patient meta-analysis (1,194 patients) found the 1-day regimen non-inferior (pooled risk difference in complete response −1.5%, 95% CI −7.1 to 4.0, against a −8% margin). Regimen 2 — palonosetron plus dexamethasone with carboplatin/paclitaxel in gynaecological cancer: two small phase 2 trials were less reassuring (delayed complete response 69.8% versus 76.9% in one; overall complete response 60.7% versus 67.9% in the other, neither significant, one warning that reduced efficacy in women could not be refuted). Regimen 3 — NK1-antagonist triplet with carboplatin: a network meta-analysis estimated delayed complete response of 73.5% with 1-day versus 82.5% with 3-day dexamethasone (absolute difference 9.0%, 95% CI −2.3 to 21.1, not significant) and advised care with sparing in carboplatin triplet prophylaxis. Sparing after day 1 is LIKELY safe on a palonosetron doublet; on a carboplatin NK1 triplet the honest position is POSSIBLE, pending a direct trial.

cards.headline: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, anthracycline/cyclophosphamide: 1-day dexamethasone matched 3-day on complete response (about 55% versus 51–59% by age group)
cards.summary: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, anthracycline/cyclophosphamide: 1-day dexamethasone matched 3-day on complete response (about 55% versus 51–59% by age group)
cards.type: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials (palonosetron 0.25 mg plus dexamethasone 8 mg on day 1, with or without oral dexamethasone 8 mg on days 2–3)
cards.people: 405 chemotherapy-naive women with breast cancer receiving anthracycline and/or cyclophosphamide chemotherapy (94% received the anthracycline/cyclophosphamide combination): 200 on the 1-day regimen, 205 on the 3-day regimen.
cards.result: There were no between-treatment differences in complete response (no vomiting and no rescue antiemetics over 5 days) in either age group: in the 1-day group, overall complete response was 55.2% in younger and 54% in older patients; in the 3-day group, 51.5% in younger and 58.7% in older patients. Adjusted for age, the risk difference was −3.1% (95% CI −13.0 to 6.7; P=0.533) — no significant loss of antiemetic protection with sparing.
cards.watchOut: Women with breast cancer on one chemotherapy family only, analysed post hoc by age — supportive of sparing, but the wider five-trial analysis on the next card is the stronger statement.
cards.source: Celio L et al. Palonosetron plus single-dose dexamethasone for the prevention of nausea and vomiting in women receiving anthracycline/cyclophosphamide-containing chemotherapy: meta-analysis of individual patient data examining the effect of age on outcome in two phase III trials. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2013. PMID: 22869054. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, pooled moderately emetogenic and anthracycline chemotherapy: 1-day dexamethasone was non-inferior (risk difference −1.5%, 95% CI −7.1 to 4.0)
cards.summary: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, pooled moderately emetogenic and anthracycline chemotherapy: 1-day dexamethasone was non-inferior (risk difference −1.5%, 95% CI −7.1 to 4.0)
cards.type: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis of five randomised trials (non-inferiority margin −8%)
cards.people: 1,194 chemotherapy-naive adults undergoing moderately emetogenic chemotherapy or anthracycline/cyclophosphamide chemotherapy, comparing palonosetron plus 1-day dexamethasone against the same regimen plus dexamethasone on days 2–3.
cards.result: In the overall 5-day period the 1-day arm was non-inferior for complete response (pooled risk difference −1.5%, 95% CI −7.1 to 4.0; I2=0%) and for complete control (risk difference −2.4%, 95% CI −7.7 to 2.9). There was no significant interaction with type of chemotherapy, sex, age or alcohol consumption.
cards.watchOut: All five trials used a palonosetron backbone without an NK1 antagonist — this non-inferiority result does not automatically transfer to NEPA or aprepitant triplets, which are carded separately below.
cards.source: Okada Y et al. One-Day Versus Three-Day Dexamethasone in Combination with Palonosetron for the Prevention of Chemotherapy-Induced Nausea and Vomiting: A Systematic Review and Individual Patient Data-Based Meta-Analysis. The oncologist. 2019. PMID: 31217343. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, carboplatin/paclitaxel (gynaecological): delayed complete response 69.8% with 1-day versus 76.9% with 3-day dexamethasone (not significant)
cards.summary: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, carboplatin/paclitaxel (gynaecological): delayed complete response 69.8% with 1-day versus 76.9% with 3-day dexamethasone (not significant)
cards.type: Randomised phase 2 trial (palonosetron 0.75 mg plus dexamethasone 20 mg on day 1, with or without oral dexamethasone 8 mg on days 2–3)
cards.people: 82 evaluable patients with gynaecological cancer receiving paclitaxel plus carboplatin: 43 on the 1-day regimen and 39 on the 3-day regimen; the primary endpoint was complete response in the delayed phase.
cards.result: Delayed-phase complete response was 69.8% (30 of 43) with 1-day dexamethasone versus 76.9% (30 of 39) with 3-day dexamethasone (P=0.4652) — a 7.1 percentage point gap that was not statistically significant. Constipation and insomnia frequencies were similar and no serious adverse events occurred. The authors called for phase 3 evaluation.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 82 patients cannot establish non-inferiority — its confidence interval is compatible with a clinically meaningful loss, which is why the carboplatin doublet is stated more cautiously than the pooled doublet result.
cards.source: Furukawa N et al. Palonosetron in combination with 1-day versus 3-day dexamethasone to prevent nausea and vomiting in patients receiving paclitaxel and carboplatin. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2015. PMID: 25947257. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, carboplatin/paclitaxel (second trial): overall complete response 60.7% with 1-day versus 67.9% with 3-day dexamethasone; the authors could not refute reduced efficacy in women
cards.summary: Regimen — palonosetron doublet, carboplatin/paclitaxel (second trial): overall complete response 60.7% with 1-day versus 67.9% with 3-day dexamethasone; the authors could not refute reduced efficacy in women
cards.type: Randomised multicentre phase 2 trial (palonosetron plus 1-day versus 3-day dexamethasone)
cards.people: 116 women with cervical, endometrial or ovarian cancer at 12 hospitals in Hokkaido, Japan, receiving conventional or dose-dense carboplatin plus paclitaxel, randomised to 1-day or 3-day dexamethasone with palonosetron.
cards.result: Overall complete response was 60.7% (95% CI 46.8 to 73.5) in the 1-day arm versus 67.9% (95% CI 53.7 to 80.1) in the 3-day arm. Complete response was significantly lower in the 1-day arm among patients with pre-existing motion sickness (P=0.0370), and tended to be lower in the severe hyperemesis gravidarum cohort. The authors concluded the 1-day regimen was effective overall but that reduced efficacy in women on this regimen could not be refuted.
cards.watchOut: Again phase 2 and women-only; two concordant small trials both numerically favouring 3-day dexamethasone for carboplatin/paclitaxel is a pattern to respect, not to pool away.
cards.source: Matsuura M et al. Palonosetron in combination with 1-day versus 3-day dexamethasone for prevention of nausea and vomiting following paclitaxel and carboplatin in patients with gynecologic cancers: A randomized, multicenter, phase-II trial. cards.headline: Regimen — NK1-antagonist triplet, carboplatin and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy: delayed complete response estimated at 73.5% with 1-day versus 82.5% with 3-day dexamethasone (difference not significant; authors advise care)
cards.summary: Regimen — NK1-antagonist triplet, carboplatin and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy: delayed complete response estimated at 73.5% with 1-day versus 82.5% with 3-day dexamethasone (difference not significant; authors advise care)
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (4,534 patients) of dexamethasone duration with NK1-antagonist triplet prophylaxis
cards.people: 17 randomised trials involving 4,534 patients receiving carboplatin-based or other moderately emetogenic chemotherapy with an NK1 receptor antagonist plus a serotonin antagonist plus dexamethasone for 1 or 3 days.
cards.result: Delayed-phase complete response was 82.5% (95% credible interval 73.9 to 88.6) with 3-day dexamethasone plus NK1 antagonist versus 73.5% (95% CI 62.8 to 80.9) with 1-day — an absolute risk difference of 9.0% (95% CI −2.3 to 21.1), not statistically significant, with a similar trend for no nausea (difference 24.7%, 95% CI −14.9 to 54.6). In carboplatin-based chemotherapy the difference was 12.3% (95% CI −3.2 to 30.7). The authors concluded care is needed when sparing dexamethasone in NK1-triplet prophylaxis for carboplatin and non-carboplatin moderately emetogenic chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates are indirect and imprecise — the credible intervals include no difference — but this is the one regimen family where the point estimates consistently favour multi-day dexamethasone, so this shelf does not extend the doublet's LIKELY to triplets.
cards.source: Watanabe D et al. One-Day Versus Three-Day Dexamethasone with NK1RA for Patients Receiving Carboplatin and Moderate Emetogenic Chemotherapy: A Network Meta-analysis. The oncologist. 2022. PMID: 35427418. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: dexamethasone sparing after day 1 is non-inferior on palonosetron doublets (LIKELY) — carboplatin doublets are numerically weaker and NK1 triplets remain unsettled, carded per-regimen, not pooled
cards.summary: Synthesis: dexamethasone sparing after day 1 is non-inferior on palonosetron doublets (LIKELY) — carboplatin doublets are numerically weaker and NK1 triplets remain unsettled, carded per-regimen, not pooled
cards.people: Synthesis of two individual-patient meta-analyses (405 and 1,194 patients), two carboplatin/paclitaxel phase 2 trials (82 and 116 patients) and an NK1-triplet network meta-analysis (17 trials, 4,534 patients) — deliberately not pooled into a single claim, because backbone, schedule and emetogenicity differ across trials.
cards.result: On a palonosetron doublet for moderately emetogenic or anthracycline/cyclophosphamide chemotherapy, sparing dexamethasone after day 1 loses no measurable complete response (risk difference −1.5% against a −8% non-inferiority margin). For carboplatin/paclitaxel doublets the small trials lean the other way without significance, and for NK1 triplets in carboplatin the network point estimate favours 3-day dexamethasone by about 9–12 percentage points, also without significance. LIKELY for the doublet; POSSIBLE for the triplet.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial tested a NEPA (netupitant/palonosetron) backbone directly for dexamethasone duration this session — the triplet card is NK1-antagonist class evidence, and that gap is stated rather than filled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Celio L et al. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2013 (PMID: 22869054); Okada Y et al. The journal of obstetrics and gynaecology research. 2015 (PMID: 26199182); Watanabe D et al. The oncologist. 2022 (PMID: 35427418).

shelves.title: Prophylactic swallowing exercises in head-and-neck chemoradiotherapy
shelves.question: In adults receiving chemoradiotherapy for head and neck cancer, do prophylactic swallowing exercises (started before or during treatment) preserve swallowing function and reduce long-term feeding-tube dependence versus usual care with exercises only after dysfunction appears?
shelves.mesh: Chemoradiotherapy/adverse effects · Deglutition/physiology · Deglutition Disorders/etiology,prevention & control · Diet · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/therapy · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Muscles/physiology · Myofunctional Therapy/methods · Organ Size · Salivation/physiology · Smell/physiology · Taste/physiology · Tongue Habits · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/drug therapy,radiotherapy,rehabilitation · Deglutition · Deglutition Disorders/etiology,prevention & control,therapy · Disease Progression · Exercise Therapy · Feasibility Studies · Head and Neck Neoplasms/drug therapy,radiotherapy,rehabilitation · Muscle Stretching Exercises · Pain Measurement · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Statistics, Nonparametric · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Trismus · Cisplatin/administration & dosage · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis,prevention & control,rehabilitation · Exercise Therapy/methods · Fluoroscopy · Follow-Up Studies · Neoplasm Staging · Otorhinolaryngologic Neoplasms/pathology,therapy · Prospective Studies · Radiotherapy, Intensity-Modulated · Video Recording · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Oropharyngeal Neoplasms/radiotherapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the randomised trials are small, use different exercise programmes and comparators, and show preserved muscle structure and some functional measures rather than a proven reduction in feeding-tube dependence. In Pharyngocise (58 patients), the swallowing musculature deteriorated less and functional swallowing, mouth opening, chemosensory acuity and salivation deteriorated less with active exercises than with usual care or sham. In the Dutch Preventief trial (49 patients), both preventive programmes (standard exercises and a TheraBite device programme) were feasible with satisfactory compliance, and fewer patients remained tube-dependent than in the institute's historical comparisons — but the trial's own randomised contrast was between two active programmes, not against no exercises, and at 2 years (29 patients) the programmes did not differ except for weight gain. The PRESTO adherence trial (148 patients) shows the binding constraint: adherence falls during radiotherapy in every delivery mode and is highest with therapist support. No carded trial demonstrates a statistically significant reduction in long-term feeding-tube dependence against a no-exercise control — POSSIBLE, with benefit most plausible for muscle preservation and function when patients actually do the exercises.

cards.headline: Pharyngocise: swallowing muscle structure and functional swallowing deteriorated less with active exercises than with usual care or sham during chemoradiotherapy
cards.summary: Pharyngocise: swallowing muscle structure and functional swallowing deteriorated less with active exercises than with usual care or sham during chemoradiotherapy
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Pharyngocise; usual care versus sham swallowing intervention versus active swallowing exercises, treated daily during chemoradiotherapy)
cards.people: 58 patients with head and neck cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy, randomised across the three arms; primary outcome was swallowing muscle size and composition on T2-weighted MRI, with functional swallowing, dietary intake, chemosensory function, salivation, nutritional status and dysphagia complications as secondary outcomes. The abstract does not print the per-arm numbers.
cards.result: The swallowing musculature (genioglossus, hyoglossus and mylohyoid) demonstrated less structural deterioration in the active treatment arm, and functional swallowing, mouth opening, chemosensory acuity and salivation rate deteriorated less in the Pharyngocise group than in the comparison arms. The abstract reports these effects qualitatively, without effect sizes or P values.
cards.watchOut: A 58-patient trial whose abstract gives direction without numbers — the muscle-preservation signal is real as reported, but its size, and any effect on feeding-tube dependence, cannot be quantified from this record.
cards.source: Carnaby-Mann G et al. "Pharyngocise": randomized controlled trial of preventative exercises to maintain muscle structure and swallowing function during head-and-neck chemoradiotherapy. International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics. 2012. PMID: 22014959. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Preventief trial: preventive rehabilitation was feasible with satisfactory compliance, and fewer patients were tube-dependent than in historical comparisons — but both randomised arms exercised
cards.summary: Preventief trial: preventive rehabilitation was feasible with satisfactory compliance, and fewer patients were tube-dependent than in historical comparisons — but both randomised arms exercised
cards.type: Randomised preventive rehabilitation trial (standard preventive exercises versus experimental TheraBite-based programme, both starting with chemoradiotherapy)
cards.people: 49 patients with advanced oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx or nasopharynx cancer treated with concomitant chemoradiotherapy, randomised to a standard or an experimental preventive rehabilitation arm and assessed before and 10 weeks after treatment.
cards.result: Feasibility was good (all patients could execute the exercises within a week) and compliance satisfactory (mean 4 practice days per week). Mouth opening, oral intake and weight nevertheless decreased significantly in both arms. Compared with similar chemoradiotherapy studies at the same institute, fewer patients were still tube-dependent after treatment, and some functional outcomes seemed less affected than in published studies without rehabilitation. The experimental arm practised significantly fewer days yet obtained comparable results to the standard arm.
cards.watchOut: There is no no-exercise control arm — the tube-dependence comparison is against historical and literature controls, so this trial shows feasibility and a favourable pattern, not proof that prophylaxis caused the difference.
cards.source: van der Molen L et al. A randomized preventive rehabilitation trial in advanced head and neck cancer patients treated with chemoradiotherapy: feasibility, compliance, and short-term effects. Dysphagia. 2011. PMID: 20623305. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Preventief 2-year follow-up (29 patients): functional problems were limited at 1 and 2 years and the two exercise programmes did not differ, except greater weight gain with the TheraBite programme
cards.summary: Preventief 2-year follow-up (29 patients): functional problems were limited at 1 and 2 years and the two exercise programmes did not differ, except greater weight gain with the TheraBite programme
cards.type: Two-year follow-up report of the Preventief randomised trial (standard swallowing exercises versus TheraBite-based exercises)
cards.people: 29 patients from the Preventief cohort (14 standard, 15 experimental) assessed before treatment and at 10 weeks, 1 year and 2 years after chemoradiation for advanced head and neck cancer.
cards.result: By 1 year most initial tumour- and treatment-related problems had diminished significantly, except xerostomia (59%). The only additional improvement at 2 years was further significant weight increase (P=0.000), without regaining baseline; in subgroup analysis this was significant in the experimental (TheraBite) group only (P=0.002). Both programmes were feasible with good compliance despite chemoradiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the same small cohort, not an independent trial — it speaks to durability and programme equivalence, not to whether prophylaxis beats no prophylaxis.
cards.source: van der Molen L et al. Two-year results of a prospective preventive swallowing rehabilitation trial in patients treated with chemoradiation for advanced head and neck cancer. European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. 2014. cards.headline: PRESTO trial (148 patients): adherence to prophylactic swallowing exercises fell during radiotherapy in every delivery mode and was highest with therapist support
cards.summary: PRESTO trial (148 patients): adherence to prophylactic swallowing exercises fell during radiotherapy in every delivery mode and was highest with therapist support
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial of service-delivery modes for the same prophylactic exercise programme (paper diary versus app versus therapist support)
cards.people: 148 patients with oropharyngeal cancer treated with primary (chemo)radiotherapy, randomised to a 4-week prophylactic swallowing exercise programme supported by paper diary (49), app (49) or therapist (50), practising 5 days per week.
cards.result: Adherence and its evolution over time differed significantly between groups (P<.001), and adherence decreased in all three groups during the 4 training weeks (P<.001). The therapist-supported group achieved the highest adherence rates in all 4 weeks and the app group the lowest; the authors conclude that face-to-face therapist contact can overcome the well-known low adherence to prophylactic exercises in this population.
cards.watchOut: An adherence trial, not an efficacy trial — it does not show exercises work; it shows that how they are delivered decides whether patients do them, which conditions every efficacy claim on this shelf.
cards.source: Baudelet M et al. Increasing Adherence to Prophylactic Swallowing Exercises During Head and Neck Radiotherapy: The Multicenter, Randomized Controlled PRESTO-Trial. Dysphagia. 2023. PMID: 36121560. Registry ID: ISRCTN: ISRCTN98243550. shelves.title: Tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter versus repeated paracentesis in recurrent malignant ascites
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent malignant ascites needing repeated drainage, does a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter improve symptom control, days out of hospital and quality of life versus repeated large-volume paracentesis? (Observational evidence only.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ascites/therapy · Catheters, Indwelling · Female · Humans · Infusions, Parenteral · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Ascites/etiology,therapy · Catheters, Indwelling/adverse effects · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Genital Neoplasms, Female/complications,therapy · Paracentesis/adverse effects · Ascites/etiology,mortality,therapy · Bacterial Infections/etiology · Carcinoma, Hepatocellular/complications · Denmark · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Liver Cirrhosis/complications · Peritonitis/etiology · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only, labelled as such. Comparative floor, verified before building: exactly one genuine head-to-head comparative report in malignant ascites was found — a retrospective single-institution cohort with cost-effectiveness modelling in gynaecological malignancy (Wu 2022), which found no significant difference in ascites-related hospital days (P=0.21) or emergency department visits (P=0.69) between tunnelled catheter and repeated paracentesis, with the catheter the more cost-effective strategy on lower cost and essentially equal modelled quality-adjusted survival. The rest of the base is single-arm: a systematic overview of 221 published patients plus a 19-patient chart review (Fleming 2009) found peritonitis in a median 5.9% of published cases and judged indwelling catheters a safe, effective palliative strategy without overwhelming infection rates; a small prospective observational study (Riedel 2018) included 14 patients with malignant ascites treated with a PleurX catheter alongside paracentesis-treated controls and found no significant differences in adverse events or mortality comparisons it was far too small to settle. No randomised trial in malignant ascites was found. Premise correction: the two Macken reports a title search suggests (a feasibility-trial protocol and a systematic review) concern refractory ascites in end-stage liver disease, not malignancy, and were therefore NOT carded here. POSSIBLE, observational — symptom and hospital-use benefit is plausible and unproven.

cards.headline: Wu 2022 (the one genuine comparative report): no significant difference in hospital days or emergency visits versus repeated paracentesis; the tunnelled catheter was the more cost-effective strategy
cards.summary: Wu 2022 (the one genuine comparative report): no significant difference in hospital days or emergency visits versus repeated paracentesis; the tunnelled catheter was the more cost-effective strategy
cards.type: Retrospective comparative cohort with Markov cost-effectiveness modelling (tunnelled peritoneal catheter versus repeated large-volume paracentesis)
cards.people: Patients with recurrent ascites from gynaecological malignancies at a single institution, 2016–2019, treated with either a tunnelled peritoneal catheter or repeated large-volume paracentesis. The abstract does not print the cohort size — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the cohorts in average hospital days (P=0.21) or emergency department visits (P=0.69) related to ascites — on those outcomes the catheter made no demonstrated difference. Palliative care was more often involved in catheter patients' care. In the base case the catheter strategy cost less (3,043 versus 3,868 US dollars) with a negligibly lower modelled health benefit (0.22980 versus 0.22982 quality-adjusted life-years), and it was the more cost-effective strategy in 8,028 of 10,000 probabilistic simulations.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-institution, gynaecological cancers only, with cohort size not documented in the record and palliative-care involvement differing between groups — confounding by who gets offered a catheter is likely and unmeasured.
cards.source: Wu X et al. Cost-effectiveness of tunneled peritoneal catheters versus repeat paracenteses for recurrent ascites in gynecologic malignancies. Gynecologic oncology. 2022. PMID: 35086684. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Fleming 2009 overview: 221 published patients with refractory malignant ascites; peritonitis in a median 5.9% of cases, with untunnelled catheters most often associated with infection
cards.summary: Fleming 2009 overview: 221 published patients with refractory malignant ascites; peritonitis in a median 5.9% of cases, with untunnelled catheters most often associated with infection
cards.type: Systematic literature overview of indwelling intraperitoneal catheters plus a retrospective chart review (single-arm series only — no paracentesis comparator)
cards.people: 15 publications representing 221 patients with refractory malignant ascites treated with Tenckhoff, PleurX or other peritoneal catheters or intraperitoneal ports, plus 19 chart-review patients from two academic institutions (median age 60 years; 89% female; 73% gynaecological malignancies). Product naming: the overview names the Tenckhoff catheter (Quinton Instrument Company) and the PleurX catheter (Denver Biomedical Inc.) as published.
cards.result: A median 5.9% of published cases (range 2.5% to 34%) had documented peritonitis. In the chart review, 2 of 19 catheters (11%) had documented infections, 7 (37%) became occluded and 2 (11%) leaked; median time from catheter placement to death was 36 days (range 4 to 660), and 47% were admitted to hospice. The authors concluded indwelling intraperitoneal catheters appear to be a safe and effective palliative strategy without overwhelming infection rates.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm data: symptom relief and hospital avoidance are asserted from series without a comparator, survival after placement is measured in weeks, and the wide peritonitis range (2.5% to 34%) shows how much technique and reporting vary.
cards.source: Fleming ND et al. Indwelling catheters for the management of refractory malignant ascites: a systematic literature overview and retrospective chart review. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2009. PMID: 19328648. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Riedel 2018: 14 patients with malignant ascites received a PleurX catheter alongside paracentesis-treated controls; no significant differences in adverse events were found in a study far too small to settle the comparison
cards.summary: Riedel 2018: 14 patients with malignant ascites received a PleurX catheter alongside paracentesis-treated controls; no significant differences in adverse events were found in a study far too small to settle the comparison
cards.type: Prospective observational study with matched control groups (PleurX catheter versus large-volume paracentesis)
cards.people: 42 prospectively registered patients with refractory ascites (25 cirrhosis-related, 17 malignant) treated at one Danish department, 2015–2016; 14 of the malignant-ascites patients received a PleurX catheter, with cirrhotic paracentesis-treated patients as one control group. Product naming: the device is named as published — the PleurX catheter.
cards.result: Maximum follow-up was 480 days in the PleurX group and 366 days in the paracentesis group (median 84 and 173 days). There was no difference in mortality in the reported comparisons (hazard ratios 3.0 and 1.0; P=.23 and P=.96), mortality was higher in malignant ascites overall (P=.01), and no significant differences were found in adverse events (including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) or in plasma albumin, creatinine or sodium between groups.
cards.watchOut: The malignant subgroup is 14 catheter patients inside a study designed mainly around cirrhotic ascites — it contributes safety reassurance, not a usable estimate of symptom or hospital-use benefit in malignancy.
cards.source: Riedel AN et al. Prognosis of patients with ascites after PleurX insertion: an observational study. Scandinavian journal of gastroenterology. 2018. PMID: 29411667. cards.headline: Synthesis: one retrospective comparative cohort, one single-arm overview and one tiny prospective study — POSSIBLE, observational only, with no randomised evidence in malignant ascites
cards.summary: Synthesis: one retrospective comparative cohort, one single-arm overview and one tiny prospective study — POSSIBLE, observational only, with no randomised evidence in malignant ascites
cards.people: Synthesis of the Wu 2022 retrospective comparative cohort in gynaecological malignancy (cohort size N not documented in its record), the Fleming 2009 systematic overview (221 published patients plus 19 chart-review patients) and the Riedel 2018 prospective observational study (14 malignant-ascites catheter patients).
cards.result: Tunnelled catheters drain ascites at home with peritonitis in roughly 6% of published cases, and the single comparative cohort found hospital use no different from repeated paracentesis (the treatment made no demonstrated difference on hospital days or emergency visits) at lower modelled cost. Whether symptoms, days at home or quality of life are actually better is untested by any randomised or adequately sized comparative study. POSSIBLE — observational, labelled.
cards.watchOut: The cirrhosis long-term-drain literature (including a feasibility randomised trial protocol) asks a different disease question and was deliberately excluded; do not borrow its numbers for malignant ascites.

shelves.title: Endovascular stenting versus radiotherapy for malignant superior vena cava obstruction
shelves.question: In adults with malignant superior vena cava obstruction, does endovascular stenting relieve symptoms faster and more durably than radiotherapy (with chemotherapy where appropriate)? (Observational evidence only; symptom-relief speed is the honest endpoint.)
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Carcinoma/complications · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/complications · Male · Middle Aged · Radiotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stents · Superior Vena Cava Syndrome/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Palliative Care · Retrospective Studies · Steel · Stents/adverse effects · Superior Vena Cava Syndrome/diagnostic imaging,surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational evidence only, labelled as such; there is no randomised trial of stenting versus radiotherapy for malignant superior vena cava obstruction, and the honest endpoint is speed and completeness of symptom relief, not survival. The Rowell & Gleeson systematic review (44 non-randomised studies meeting inclusion) found chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy relieved obstruction in 77% of small-cell and 60% of non-small-cell lung cancer patients, with recurrence in 17–19%, while stent insertion relieved obstruction in 95%, with further obstruction in 11% but recanalisation possible in most, giving long-term patency of 92% — and the reviewers note stenting may provide relief in a higher proportion and more rapidly. A later pooled review of retrospective stenting series found clinical effectiveness of 90.5%, primary patency 86.2% and secondary patency 94.1%, with fatal complications in 1.46%. A 54-patient retrospective stent cohort reported 94.4% procedural success and 25% overall survival at 10 months, a reminder that prognosis is set by the cancer, not the stent. POSSIBLE: stenting probably relieves symptoms in more patients and faster than radiotherapy, on non-randomised comparisons vulnerable to selection bias; it does not treat the tumour, and radiotherapy or chemotherapy remains the disease-directed treatment where appropriate.

cards.headline: Rowell & Gleeson systematic review: stenting relieved obstruction in 95% versus 77% (small-cell) and 60% (non-small-cell) for chemotherapy/radiotherapy, with 92% long-term patency after recanalisation
cards.summary: Rowell & Gleeson systematic review: stenting relieved obstruction in 95% versus 77% (small-cell) and 60% (non-small-cell) for chemotherapy/radiotherapy, with 92% long-term patency after recanalisation
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies of steroids, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and stents for superior vena caval obstruction in carcinoma of the bronchus (Cochrane programme review published in Clinical Oncology)
cards.people: Two randomised and 44 non-randomised studies met inclusion, in patients with small-cell and non-small-cell lung cancer and superior vena caval obstruction (present at diagnosis in 10.0% of small-cell and 1.7% of non-small-cell cases). Neither randomised trial compared stenting with radiotherapy.
cards.result: In small-cell lung cancer, chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy relieved obstruction in 77%, with recurrence in 17%; in non-small-cell, 60% had relief, with recurrence in 19%. Stent insertion relieved obstruction in 95%; 11% had further obstruction but recanalisation was possible in the majority, resulting in a long-term patency rate of 92%. Morbidity after stenting was greater if thrombolytics were administered. The reviewers concluded stenting may provide relief in a higher proportion and more rapidly, while steroid effectiveness and optimal stent timing remain uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The stent-versus-radiotherapy contrast is entirely non-randomised: patients offered stents differ from those offered radiotherapy, so the 95% versus 60–77% gap overstates any causal difference by an unknown amount. A later Cochrane update record (2015) is marked WITHDRAWN in PubMed and was deliberately not carded.
cards.source: Rowell NP et al. Steroids, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and stents for superior vena caval obstruction in carcinoma of the bronchus: a systematic review. Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain)). 2002. PMID: 12555872. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pooled review of retrospective stenting series: clinical effectiveness 90.5%, primary patency 86.2%, fatal complications 1.46%
cards.summary: Pooled review of retrospective stenting series: clinical effectiveness 90.5%, primary patency 86.2%, fatal complications 1.46%
cards.type: Literature review with pooled rates from retrospective studies of percutaneous stenting for malignant superior vena cava syndrome
cards.people: Retrospective stenting series in malignant superior vena cava syndrome, pooled overall and by stent type (Wallstent, nitinol, steel and stent graft). The abstract does not print the total patient number — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Pooled clinical effectiveness was 90.50% (95% CI 88.86 to 91.97), primary patency 86.18% (95% CI 84.06 to 88.12) and secondary patency 94.05% (95% CI 91.82 to 95.82). Fatal complications occurred in 1.46% (95% CI 0.91 to 2.23) and non-fatal complications in 8.28% (95% CI 6.91 to 9.83). Primary patency was higher for nitinol stents (94.87%) and stent grafts (96.10%) than for Wallstent (83.38%). The authors report more than 90% of patients experiencing immediate relief of symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm pooling: 'clinical effectiveness' is symptom relief after stenting with no radiotherapy comparator, and series that publish are likelier to be series that worked.
cards.source: Léon D et al. Literature Review of Percutaneous Stenting for Palliative Treatment of Malignant Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS). Academic radiology. 2022. PMID: 34602363. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Retrospective stent cohort (54 patients): procedural success 94.4%, but overall survival at 10 months was 25% — prognosis is set by the cancer, not the stent
cards.summary: Retrospective stent cohort (54 patients): procedural success 94.4%, but overall survival at 10 months was 25% — prognosis is set by the cancer, not the stent
cards.type: Analytical retrospective cohort of endovascular stenting for malignant superior vena cava syndrome (single national cancer institute)
cards.people: 54 patients who underwent endovascular management for malignant superior vena cava syndrome at the National Cancer Institute of Colombia, 2016–2021.
cards.result: The successful procedure rate was 94.4%. Overall survival of the whole cohort at 10 months was 25%. Worse survival was associated with breast or lung cancer (P=0.031), unsuccessful procedure (P=0.011) and shorter symptom duration before the procedure (P=0.027); on multivariate analysis lung cancer (hazard ratio 2.55, 95% CI 1.21 to 5.36) and left-sided distal stent attachment (hazard ratio 3.27, 95% CI 1.31 to 8.15) were independent factors for worse survival.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre retrospective cohort with no radiotherapy arm — it quantifies how sick this population is and why survival must not be used as the endpoint for judging stenting.
cards.source: Guerrero-Macías S et al. Outcomes in patients managed with endovascular stent for malignant superior vena cava syndrome. Surgery open science. 2023. PMID: 37744312. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: stenting relieves malignant SVC obstruction in about 90–95% of patients, probably faster and more often than radiotherapy — POSSIBLE, observational only, symptom relief is the endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: stenting relieves malignant SVC obstruction in about 90–95% of patients, probably faster and more often than radiotherapy — POSSIBLE, observational only, symptom relief is the endpoint
cards.people: Synthesis of the Rowell & Gleeson systematic review (44 non-randomised studies), a pooled review of retrospective stenting series (total N not documented in its record) and a 54-patient retrospective stent cohort. No randomised comparison of stenting versus radiotherapy exists in this evidence base.
cards.result: Stent series consistently report immediate symptom relief in over 90% of patients with patency around 86–94% and fatal complications around 1.5%, against 60–77% relief for chemotherapy/radiotherapy in the review's non-randomised studies. Selection bias inflates the contrast by an unknown amount, and survival (25% at 10 months in the cohort) reflects the underlying cancer. POSSIBLE — observational, labelled.
cards.watchOut: The withdrawn 2015 Cochrane record on this question was excluded on its publication status; the carded review is the 2002 published version.

shelves.title: Intrathecal drug-delivery system for refractory cancer pain (single randomised trial)
shelves.question: In adults with refractory cancer pain despite systemic opioids, does an implantable intrathecal drug-delivery system improve pain control and reduce drug toxicity versus comprehensive medical management alone? (Single-trial shelf: one randomised trial carries this question.)
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage · Female · Humans · Infusion Pumps, Implantable · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications · Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Statistics, Nonparametric · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Cohort Studies · Longitudinal Studies · Neoplasms/complications,physiopathology · Intractable Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Palliative Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single-trial shelf, labelled as such: one randomised trial (Smith 2002, 202 patients enrolled) carries this question, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however positive its result. In that trial, clinical success (at least 20% pain reduction, or equal pain with at least 20% less toxicity) at 4 weeks was achieved by 84.5% of intrathecal drug-delivery patients versus 70.8% on comprehensive medical management alone (P=.05); success on both pain and toxicity together was 57.7% versus 37.5% (P=.02). Toxicity scores fell 50% with the device versus 17% without (P=.004), driven by fatigue and depressed consciousness, and 6-month survival was 53.9% versus 37.2% (P=.06) — a non-significant difference in a trial not powered for survival, reported here as the authors reported it, not as a survival claim. A planned crossover analysis (30 patients whose medical management had failed) found pain down 27% and toxicity down 51% after implant, consistent with the randomised result but uncontrolled. No second randomised trial exists in this evidence base; device harms, cost and the need for surgical implantation and refills sit outside the trial's 4-week primary endpoint.

cards.headline: Smith 2002 (the single randomised trial): clinical success in 84.5% with intrathecal delivery versus 70.8% with medical management; toxicity scores halved with the device
cards.summary: Smith 2002 (the single randomised trial): clinical success in 84.5% with intrathecal delivery versus 70.8% with medical management; toxicity scores halved with the device
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (implantable intrathecal drug-delivery system plus comprehensive medical management versus comprehensive medical management alone)
cards.people: 202 patients with refractory cancer pain (visual analogue pain scores of 5 or more on a 0–10 scale despite systemic therapy) enrolled; the 4-week primary analysis covers 71 device and 72 medical-management patients. Entry required unrelieved pain despite comprehensive medical management.
cards.result: Clinical success (at least 20% reduction in pain score, or equal score with at least 20% reduction in toxicity) was achieved by 60 of 71 device patients (84.5%) versus 51 of 72 medical patients (70.8%) (P=.05); at least 20% reduction in both pain and toxicity occurred in 57.7% versus 37.5% (P=.02). Mean pain scores fell 52% with the device (7.57 to 3.67) versus 39% without (7.81 to 4.76) (P=.055); mean toxicity scores fell 50% (7.22 to 3.59) versus 17% (6.36 to 5.27) (P=.004), with significant reductions in fatigue and depressed level of consciousness. Six-month survival was 53.9% versus 37.2% (P=.06).
cards.watchOut: One trial, unblinded by necessity, with a borderline primary P value (.05), substantial attrition by 4 weeks (143 of 202 analysed) in a population with advanced cancer, and a survival difference that did not reach significance — the result is genuinely positive and genuinely single.
cards.source: Smith TJ et al. Randomized clinical trial of an implantable drug delivery system compared with comprehensive medical management for refractory cancer pain: impact on pain, drug-related toxicity, and survival. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2002. PMID: 12351602. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Crossover analysis: in 30 patients whose expert medical management had failed, pain fell 27% and toxicity 51% after crossing over to intrathecal delivery
cards.summary: Crossover analysis: in 30 patients whose expert medical management had failed, pain fell 27% and toxicity 51% after crossing over to intrathecal delivery
cards.type: Planned prospective longitudinal analysis within the Smith randomised trial (patients crossing from medical management to device by 6 months)
cards.people: 30 of 99 medical-management patients (30%) for whom comprehensive medical management failed — pain scores of 5 or more despite a month of opioids at 320 mg or more morphine-equivalent plus adjunct drugs — who crossed over to an implantable intrathecal programmable pump with opioids and local anaesthetics.
cards.result: Clinical success was achieved after crossover, with pain scores significantly reduced by 27% (P=0.011) and drug toxicity scores by 51% (P<.0001). Median survival after implant was 103 days, similar to patients implanted as part of the initial randomisation; the authors note a 3-month survival may be long enough for the implant to be cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled before–after data in the most refractory subgroup — regression to the mean and survivor selection both favour the device, so this card supports consistency, not proof.
cards.source: Smith TJ et al. Implantable drug delivery systems (IDDS) after failure of comprehensive medical management (CMM) can palliate symptoms in the most refractory cancer pain patients. Journal of palliative medicine. 2005. PMID: 16128647. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Smith & Coyne evidence review: the randomised trial is the only controlled evidence; the 1980–2003 cohort literature showed pain relief without standardised assessment or control groups
cards.summary: Smith & Coyne evidence review: the randomised trial is the only controlled evidence; the 1980–2003 cohort literature showed pain relief without standardised assessment or control groups
cards.type: Evidence review of implantable drug-delivery systems for refractory cancer pain (cohort reports 1980–2003 plus the randomised trial)
cards.people: Published cohort reports from 1980 through 2003 and the 202-patient randomised trial population with unrelieved pain (scores of 5 or more) despite conventional management. This record carries no MeSH terms in PubMed (noted on its source line).
cards.result: The non-randomised trials all showed pain relief with acceptable complication rates but often lacked standardised assessment, control groups and multi-institution design. In the randomised trial, clinical success was 84.5% with the device versus 70.5% with medical management (P<.05), pain scores fell 52% versus 39% (P=0.057) and toxicity scores fell 52% versus 19% (P=0.01) by the review's figures, with all individual toxicities improved more by the device, especially fatigue and depressed consciousness.
cards.watchOut: A review co-authored by the trial's lead investigator — it organises the evidence honestly (including the weakness of the cohort base) but is not an independent appraisal, and its slightly different percentages reflect its own rounding of the trial data.
cards.source: Smith TJ et al. What is the evidence for implantable drug delivery systems for refractory cancer pain? Supportive cancer therapy. 2004. PMID: 18628140. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial shows better pain-plus-toxicity success with intrathecal delivery — POSSIBLE, single-trial shelf, exactly as labelled
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial shows better pain-plus-toxicity success with intrathecal delivery — POSSIBLE, single-trial shelf, exactly as labelled
cards.people: Synthesis of the Smith 2002 randomised trial (202 enrolled, 143 in the 4-week primary analysis), its planned crossover analysis (30 patients) and an evidence review of the 1980–2003 cohort literature.
cards.result: The randomised comparison favours the device on the combined pain-and-toxicity endpoint (84.5% versus 70.8%), on toxicity reduction (50% versus 17%) and on achieving both pain and toxicity success (57.7% versus 37.5%); the crossover experience is consistent. With one trial and no replication, the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf is labelled single-trial wherever it is summarised.

shelves.title: YOCAS yoga programme for sleep in cancer survivors
shelves.question: In cancer survivors with sleep disturbance after treatment, does the structured Yoga for Cancer Survivors (YOCAS) programme improve sleep quality versus standard care? (Programme named as published, per the non-drug-programme naming rule.)
shelves.mesh: Breathing Exercises · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Meditation/psychology · Middle Aged · Mind-Body Therapies · Neoplasm Staging · Neoplasms/psychology,therapy · Patient Education as Topic · Prognosis · Quality of Life · Sleep Wake Disorders/psychology,therapy · Survival Rate · Survivors/psychology · Cancer Survivors/psychology · Fatigue/etiology,psychology · Neoplasms/complications,psychology · Sleep/physiology · Sleep Wake Disorders/psychology · Yoga/psychology · Yoga · Breast Neoplasms/psychology,therapy · Sleep Quality · Adult · Exercise/psychology · COVID-19/psychology · Aged · Surveys and Questionnaires · Sleep
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial of one named programme carries this question, and a single programme trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The tested programme is the Yoga for Cancer Survivors (YOCAS) programme, named as published: pranayama breathing exercises, 16 gentle Hatha and restorative yoga postures, and meditation, in two 75-minute sessions per week for 4 weeks. In the Mustian 2013 multicentre trial (410 survivors with moderate or greater sleep disruption, 96% female, 75% breast cancer), YOCAS produced greater improvements than standard care in global sleep quality and, secondarily, in subjective sleep quality, daytime dysfunction, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and sleep-medication use (all P≤.05, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and actigraphy). A mediation analysis of the same trial found improvements in sleep quality and daytime dysfunction accounted for 22% and 37% respectively of the programme's fatigue benefit — supportive of a real sleep effect, but the same trial, not independent confirmation. A separate randomised trial of a different, online yoga programme in breast cancer (173 patients) also improved PSQI sleep quality, which supports yoga generally but does not replicate YOCAS itself.

cards.headline: Mustian 2013 (the YOCAS trial): the Yoga for Cancer Survivors programme improved global sleep quality, sleep efficiency and medication use versus standard care in 410 survivors
cards.summary: Mustian 2013 (the YOCAS trial): the Yoga for Cancer Survivors programme improved global sleep quality, sleep efficiency and medication use versus standard care in 410 survivors
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (standard care versus standard care plus the 4-week YOCAS programme: breathing exercises, 16 gentle Hatha and restorative postures, and meditation, two 75-minute sessions weekly)
cards.people: 410 cancer survivors (96% female; mean age 54 years; 75% breast cancer) with moderate or greater sleep disruption 2–24 months after surgery, chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy; sleep assessed by Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and actigraphy before and after the intervention. Programme naming: the tested programme is the Yoga for Cancer Survivors (YOCAS) programme, named exactly as published.
cards.result: Yoga participants demonstrated greater improvements in global sleep quality (the primary outcome) and, secondarily, in subjective sleep quality, daytime dysfunction, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and medication use at post-intervention (all P≤.05) compared with standard care. The abstract reports significance without printing the group means or effect sizes for these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded (a yoga trial cannot be blinded), self-reported primary outcome, and effect sizes not printed in the abstract — direction and significance are clear, magnitude is not quantifiable from this record.
cards.source: Mustian KM et al. Multicenter, randomized controlled trial of yoga for sleep quality among cancer survivors. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2013. PMID: 23940231. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00397930. cards.headline: Same-trial mediation analysis: sleep-quality and daytime-dysfunction improvements mediated 22% and 37% of the YOCAS fatigue benefit
cards.summary: Same-trial mediation analysis: sleep-quality and daytime-dysfunction improvements mediated 22% and 37% of the YOCAS fatigue benefit
cards.type: Mediation (path) analysis of the Mustian YOCAS randomised trial (same 410 survivors; fatigue by Multidimensional Fatigue Symptom Inventory, sleep by Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index)
cards.people: The same 410 survivors from the nationwide multicentre phase 3 YOCAS trial, comparing the YOCAS programme with standard survivorship care — a secondary analysis, not a new sample.
cards.result: YOCAS participants showed significantly greater improvements in cancer-related fatigue than standard-care participants (P<.01). Improvements in overall sleep quality and reductions in daytime dysfunction resulting from yoga significantly mediated the effect of yoga on fatigue (22% and 37% respectively, both P<.01).
cards.watchOut: Mediation within one trial cannot substitute for a second trial: it strengthens the interpretation that sleep genuinely improved (rather than only fatigue ratings shifting), but every number here descends from the same 410 patients.
cards.source: Lin PJ et al. cards.headline: A different programme, supportive only: 6 weeks of online yoga improved PSQI sleep quality versus waiting control in 173 women with breast cancer
cards.summary: A different programme, supportive only: 6 weeks of online yoga improved PSQI sleep quality versus waiting control in 173 women with breast cancer
cards.type: Randomised trial of an online yoga programme (twice-weekly 45-minute sessions for 6 weeks) versus waiting control — NOT the YOCAS programme
cards.people: 173 women with breast cancer or a history of breast cancer, randomised to online yoga or waiting control; sleep quality by Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and quality of life by EORTC questionnaires. This trial did not test YOCAS and is carded as class support only.
cards.result: The online yoga group showed improved sleep quality in the PSQI score and improved dyspnoea and physical-activity subitems of quality of life; the abstract does not print the PSQI values. The authors judged online yoga a safe, cost-effective remote supportive option.
cards.watchOut: Waiting-list control (expectation effects unconstrained), a different programme, dose and delivery mode — it supports 'yoga can improve reported sleep in survivors', not 'YOCAS works', and is labelled accordingly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the named YOCAS programme improved sleep quality in one large randomised trial, with same-trial mediation support — POSSIBLE, single-programme shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: the named YOCAS programme improved sleep quality in one large randomised trial, with same-trial mediation support — POSSIBLE, single-programme shelf
cards.people: Synthesis of the Mustian 2013 YOCAS randomised trial (410 survivors), its mediation analysis, and one randomised trial of a different online yoga programme (173 patients) carded as class support only.
cards.result: Four weeks of YOCAS (two 75-minute sessions weekly) improved global sleep quality, sleep efficiency and sleep-medication use versus standard care, and the sleep improvement statistically carried part of the fatigue benefit. One programme, one trial, no independent YOCAS replication found this session: POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Survivors in the YOCAS trial were 96% female and 75% breast cancer, 2–24 months post-treatment — men, other cancers and patients on active treatment are barely represented.

shelves.title: Barrier film and gel for radiation dermatitis in breast radiotherapy (physical-barrier slice)
shelves.question: In women receiving breast radiotherapy, does a physical barrier — a polyurethane film dressing (Mepitel Film) or a film-forming barrier gel (StrataXRT) — prevent moderate-to-severe radiation dermatitis versus standard skin care or sorbolene? (The barrier slice only; the topical-steroid slice is homed separately — see balance.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Breast Neoplasms/radiotherapy,surgery,complications · Mastectomy/adverse effects · Radiodermatitis/etiology,prevention & control · Silicones · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Administration, Topical · Adult · Breast Neoplasms/pathology,radiotherapy · Follow-Up Studies · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Prognosis · Radiodermatitis/etiology,pathology,prevention & control · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Silicone Gels/therapeutic use · Young Adult · Aged · Bandages · Gels · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Male · Radiodermatitis/drug therapy,prevention & control · Silicones/administration & dosage · Single-Blind Method · Breast Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Radiodermatitis/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for Mepitel Film in breast radiotherapy, on one large phase 3 trial supported by meta-analysis; the gel evidence is thinner and is stated separately. Scope: this shelf is only the physical-barrier slice of the radiation-dermatitis question — prophylactic mometasone cream is a different intervention with its own home at live shelf #1792, which is cross-pointed here in prose and not re-carded. Mepitel Film (named as published; a silicone polyurethane film): in the Behroozian phase 3 trial (376 patients at higher dermatitis risk), grade 2–3 dermatitis occurred in 15.5% with the film versus 45.6% with standard care (odds ratio 0.20 — an 80% relative reduction in odds, 30.1 percentage points absolute), grade 3 dermatitis in 2.8% versus 13.6% (odds ratio 0.19) and moist desquamation in 8.0% versus 19.2% (odds ratio 0.36); three patients removed the film for rash or itching. StrataXRT (named as published; a silicone-based film-forming gel): the breast evidence is a 56-patient pilot (lower erythema and melanin indices) and a meta-analysis of three small randomised trials (189 patients) with a strong grade 3 signal (odds ratio 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.22) but no significant difference for grade 2–3 combined (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.18 — the treatment's effect on that combined endpoint is unproven); its largest randomised trial (197 patients) is in head-and-neck radiotherapy, carded here as supportive evidence from a different site. LIKELY for the film in breast radiotherapy; POSSIBLE for the gel in breast radiotherapy.

cards.headline: Behroozian phase 3: grade 2–3 dermatitis in 15.5% with Mepitel Film versus 45.6% with standard care (odds ratio 0.20)
cards.summary: Behroozian phase 3: grade 2–3 dermatitis in 15.5% with Mepitel Film versus 45.6% with standard care (odds ratio 0.20)
cards.type: Randomised multicentre open-label phase 3 trial (Mepitel Film versus standard care, 2:1 randomisation) — product named as published: Mepitel Film
cards.people: 376 patients at higher risk of radiation dermatitis — large breasts after lumpectomy (bra size 36 inches or more, or cup size C or more) or after mastectomy — treated January 2020 to May 2022, in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (251 film, 125 standard care).
cards.result: Grade 2 or 3 dermatitis (CTCAE v5.0) occurred in 39 of 251 film patients (15.5%; 95% CI 11.3 to 20.6) versus 57 of 125 standard-care patients (45.6%; 95% CI 36.7 to 54.8) (odds ratio 0.20; P<.0001) — 30.1 percentage points absolute. Grade 3 dermatitis occurred in 2.8% versus 13.6% (odds ratio 0.19) and moist desquamation in 8.0% versus 19.2% (odds ratio 0.36). Combined patient- and clinician-reported Radiation-Induced Skin Reaction Assessment Scale scores were significantly lower with the film (P<.0001), as were blistering/peeling, erythema, pigmentation and oedema. Three patients removed the film prematurely (rash in 2, excessive pruritus in 1).
cards.watchOut: Open-label (a film cannot be blinded) and restricted to higher-risk patients — large-breasted or postmastectomy — so the absolute benefit in lower-risk patients will be smaller; the odds ratios are relative measures and are printed here beside the absolute rates, as this library requires.
cards.source: Behroozian T et al. Mepitel Film for the Prevention of Acute Radiation Dermatitis in Breast Cancer: A Randomized Multicenter Open-Label Phase III Trial. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2023. PMID: 36493331. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04166799. cards.headline: StrataXRT breast pilot (56 patients): erythema and melanin indices rose less with the film-forming silicone gel than with moisturising cream
cards.summary: StrataXRT breast pilot (56 patients): erythema and melanin indices rose less with the film-forming silicone gel than with moisturising cream
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial (StrataXRT film-forming silicone gel versus X-derm moisturising cream) — product named as published: StrataXRT
cards.people: 56 patients with breast cancer receiving whole-breast radiotherapy, randomised to StrataXRT or moisturising cream, assessed by physiological skin parameters, clinician visual scales and patient-reported symptoms to 4 weeks after radiotherapy.
cards.result: Two-way repeated-measures analysis showed different change patterns for erythema index (F=3.609, P=0.008) and melanin index (F=3.475, P=0.015), with significantly lower erythema and melanin indices in the StrataXRT group on post hoc analysis. The authors present the study as feasibility support for a larger trial; no grade-based dermatitis rates are printed in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: A 56-patient pilot with instrument-measured surrogate endpoints and no clinical grade rates in its record — it shows the gel does something measurable to skin physiology, not yet that it prevents grade 2–3 dermatitis in breast radiotherapy.
cards.source: Ahn S et al. Reducing Radiation Dermatitis Using a Film-forming Silicone Gel During Breast Radiotherapy: A Pilot Randomized-controlled Trial. In vivo (Athens, Greece). 2020. PMID: 31882508. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: StrataXRT's large trial is head-and-neck, not breast: grade 3 skin toxicity 28% with StrataXRT versus 45% with sorbolene at end of treatment (197 patients)
cards.summary: StrataXRT's large trial is head-and-neck, not breast: grade 3 skin toxicity 28% with StrataXRT versus 45% with sorbolene at end of treatment (197 patients)
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled superiority trial (StrataXRT versus 10% glycerine sorbolene cream) in head-and-neck radiotherapy — different anatomical site, carded as supportive evidence and labelled as such
cards.people: 197 patients with head and neck cancer receiving radical radiotherapy (50 Gy or more) with or without chemotherapy or biotherapy, randomised to StrataXRT or sorbolene usual care, followed to 4 weeks after treatment.
cards.result: Mean skin toxicity was lower with StrataXRT at end of treatment (P=0.002). Grade 2 toxicity was present in 80% on StrataXRT versus 91% on sorbolene and grade 3 in 28% versus 45%; after adjustment for cetuximab, risk of grade 2 toxicity was 12% relatively lower (relative risk 0.876, 95% CI 0.778 to 0.987) and of grade 3 toxicity 36% relatively lower (relative risk 0.648, 95% CI 0.442 to 0.947). There were no differences in patient-reported outcomes and no treatment interruptions or product-related adverse events in either arm.
cards.watchOut: Head-and-neck skin, dose and concurrent systemic therapy differ from breast radiotherapy — this card supports the gel's barrier effect as a class, and must not be quoted as breast evidence.
cards.source: Chan RJ et al. A single-blind, randomised controlled trial of StrataXRT® - A silicone-based film-forming gel dressing for prophylaxis and management of radiation dermatitis in patients with head and neck cancer. Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology. 2019. PMID: 31445838. Registry ID: ANZCTR: ACTRN12616000511437. cards.headline: StrataXRT breast meta-analysis (3 randomised trials, 189 patients): grade 3 dermatitis odds ratio 0.05, but grade 2–3 combined was not significant (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.18)
cards.summary: StrataXRT breast meta-analysis (3 randomised trials, 189 patients): grade 3 dermatitis odds ratio 0.05, but grade 2–3 combined was not significant (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.18)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of StrataXRT in breast radiotherapy
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 189 patients receiving adjuvant radiotherapy to breast or chest wall (per-protocol analysis): two compared StrataXRT with standard care and one compared it with Mepitel Film, reported separately.
cards.result: Against standard care, the odds ratio for acute grade 3 dermatitis favoured StrataXRT at 0.05 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.22; P<0.0001), while the odds ratio for grade 2–3 dermatitis combined was 0.32 (95% CI 0.03 to 3.18; P=0.33) — not significant. The head-to-head trial against Mepitel Film showed no significant difference on either endpoint. One trial reported significantly lower erythema (P=0.008) and melanin (P=0.015) indices with StrataXRT, and no additional safety concerns were raised. The authors call for larger high-quality studies.
cards.watchOut: Three small trials and 189 patients, per-protocol — the striking grade 3 odds ratio rests on few events, and the non-significant combined endpoint is the honest summary of the gel's breast evidence so far.
cards.source: Lee SF et al. StrataXRT for the prevention of acute radiation dermatitis in breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: Mepitel Film prevents grade 2–3 dermatitis in breast radiotherapy (LIKELY); StrataXRT gel is promising but thin in breast (POSSIBLE) — barrier slice only, steroid slice homed at live #1792
cards.summary: Synthesis: Mepitel Film prevents grade 2–3 dermatitis in breast radiotherapy (LIKELY); StrataXRT gel is promising but thin in breast (POSSIBLE) — barrier slice only, steroid slice homed at live #1792
cards.people: Synthesis of the Behroozian Mepitel Film phase 3 trial (376 patients), the StrataXRT breast pilot (56 patients), the StrataXRT head-and-neck trial (197 patients, supportive only) and the StrataXRT breast meta-analysis (3 trials, 189 patients). No reference from the mometasone shelf (live #1792) is carded here; that shelf is the home of the steroid slice and is cross-pointed in the balance only.
cards.result: A physical film barrier cut grade 2–3 dermatitis from 45.6% to 15.5% in a phase 3 breast trial, with concordant patient- and clinician-reported outcomes. The gel shows a strong grade 3 signal in a small meta-analysis, a positive physiological pilot in breast and a positive large trial at a different site. LIKELY for Mepitel Film in higher-risk breast radiotherapy; POSSIBLE for StrataXRT in breast radiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: All barrier trials are open-label or single-blind by necessity, and the phase 3 film population was selected for high dermatitis risk — absolute benefits in unselected patients will be smaller than 30 percentage points.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline + tocopherol (PENTO/PENTOCLO) for osteoradionecrosis of the jaw: complete healing in the Delanian phase II cohorts — but no completed randomised trial exists
shelves.question: In patients with osteoradionecrosis of the jaw after head-and-neck radiotherapy, does pentoxifylline plus tocopherol (with or without clodronate — the PENTO/PENTOCLO regimens) heal or stabilise lesions versus conservative care or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antimetabolites/administration & dosage · Antioxidants/administration & dosage* · Clodronic Acid/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Humans · Male · Mandibular Diseases/diagnostic imaging, drug therapy*, etiology · Middle Aged · Osteoradionecrosis/diagnostic imaging, drug therapy*, etiology · Pentoxifylline/administration & dosage* · Radiation-Protective Agents/administration & dosage* · Radiography · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Tocopherols/administration & dosage* · Wound Healing/drug effects
shelves.balance: GAP-E evidence, capped at POSSIBLE. The Delanian programme reports remarkable results without a control group: in the 2005 phase II cohort, 16 of 18 patients with refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis achieved complete recovery on pentoxifylline 800 mg + tocopherol 1000 IU daily (the worst 8 also received clodronate); in the 2011 PENTOCLO phase II cohort, all 54 eligible patients recovered completely, median 9 months, on the five-drug rotating regimen. A meta-analysis of 7 studies (211 patients) found 126 recovered fully or improved significantly, with progression in 15; an 11-study review found complete mucosal coverage ranging from 16.6% to 100%. PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate row: no completed randomised trial of PENTO/PENTOCLO for jaw osteoradionecrosis was found in this session's PubMed fetch — the Delanian reports are phase II single-arm trials, and the RAPTOR protocol (Shaw et al., PMID: 40708048, ISRCTN34217298; protocol only, not carded) itself describes RAPTOR as the first randomised controlled trial of PENTOCLO in this setting, still recruiting. The one completed Delanian placebo-controlled randomised trial of the same drug combination (PMID: 31987975, not carded) treated radiation-induced plexopathy, a different condition, and was negative. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the uncontrolled healing rates justify the ongoing trial, not a settled claim.

cards.headline: Delanian 2005 (phase II, 18 patients): pentoxifylline + tocopherol, with clodronate in the worst cases — 16 of 18 achieved complete recovery of refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis
cards.summary: Delanian 2005 (phase II, 18 patients): pentoxifylline + tocopherol, with clodronate in the worst cases — 16 of 18 achieved complete recovery of refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis
cards.people: 18 consecutive patients previously irradiated for head and neck cancer with exteriorised mandibular osteoradionecrosis (mean exposed bone length 13.4 ± 8 mm, mean SOMA score 12.6 ± 4.9), treated 1995–2002 with daily oral pentoxifylline 800 mg + vitamin E (tocopherol) 1000 IU for 6–24 months; the last 8 patients, the worst cases, also received clodronate 1600 mg/day 5 days a week. No control group.
cards.result: All patients improved at 6 months, with a mean 84% reduction in exposed bone length and a 67% reduction in SOMA score. Sixteen of 18 patients (89%) achieved complete recovery, 14 of them in 5 ± 2.6 months; the remaining two showed a 75% response at 6 months. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, 18 patients, no comparator — spontaneous sequestration and concurrent care cannot be separated from drug effect, and the sickest patients also got clodronate, so the PENTO-only contribution is not isolated. This is a phase II cohort, not the randomised trial it is sometimes described as.
cards.source: Delanian S et al. Major healing of refractory mandible osteoradionecrosis after treatment combining pentoxifylline and tocopherol: a phase II trial. Head & neck. 2005. PMID: 15641107. Registry ID: none in the record.
