cards.headline: Delanian 2011 (phase II PENTOCLO, 54 eligible patients): prolonged pentoxifylline–tocopherol–clodronate — all patients recovered completely, median 9 months
cards.summary: Delanian 2011 (phase II PENTOCLO, 54 eligible patients): prolonged pentoxifylline–tocopherol–clodronate — all patients recovered completely, median 9 months
cards.people: 54 eligible patients (of 72 treated) previously irradiated for head and neck cancer a mean 5 years earlier, with exteriorised refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis present for 1.4 ± 1.8 years, mainly after local surgery and hyperbaric oxygen had failed; mean exposed bone 17 ± 8 mm, mean SOMA score 16 ± 4. Daily oral PENTOCLO: pentoxifylline 800 mg, vitamin E 1000 IU and clodronate 1600 mg 5 days/week, alternating with prednisone 20 mg and ciprofloxacin 1000 mg 2 days/week, continued until healing (16 ± 9 months). No control group.
cards.result: All patients improved, with progressive significant reductions in exposed bone: −42% at 2 months, −62% at 4, −77% at 6, −92% at 12 and −96% at 18 months (p < 0.0001), with spontaneous sequestrectomies in 36 patients. All patients experienced complete recovery in a median of 9 months; SOMA score fell 64% by 6 months and 96% by 30 months. Treatment was reported safe and well tolerated. The authors state the findings will need to be confirmed in a randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Again uncontrolled: a refractory, heavily pre-treated population, a five-drug rotating regimen (steroid and antibiotic days included), and treatment continued until healing — so time itself is a competing explanation. Eighteen of 72 treated patients were not eligible for the analysis, and the record does not account for their outcomes here.
cards.source: Delanian S et al. Complete restoration of refractory mandibular osteoradionecrosis by prolonged treatment with a pentoxifylline-tocopherol-clodronate combination (PENTOCLO): a phase II trial. International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics. 2011. PMID: 20638190. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kolokythas 2019 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 studies, 211 patients): 126 of 211 recovered fully or improved significantly on pentoxifylline–tocopherol
cards.summary: Kolokythas 2019 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 studies, 211 patients): 126 of 211 recovered fully or improved significantly on pentoxifylline–tocopherol
cards.people: Seven studies meeting inclusion criteria, totalling 211 patients treated with pentoxifylline–tocopherol (PENTO) for osteoradionecrosis of the jaws; outcome was the proportion with full recovery or significant improvement not requiring further intervention, combined by maximum-likelihood estimation.
cards.result: Of 211 patients, 126 recovered fully or improved significantly without further intervention, 60 remained the same, 10 were lost to follow-up, and the disease progressed in 15. The authors conclude the current literature supports the use of PENTO for osteoradionecrosis of the jaws, while calling for additional well-designed prospective studies to validate the regimen.
cards.watchOut: A pooled proportion from mostly uncontrolled series is not a treatment effect — there is no untreated comparison rate, so the 126/211 figure cannot show how many would have healed or stabilised anyway. Publication bias toward positive series is likely in a literature this small.
cards.source: Kolokythas A et al. Management of osteoradionecrosis of the jaws with pentoxifylline-tocopherol: a systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis. International journal of oral and maxillofacial surgery. 2019. PMID: 30205911. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arqueros-Lemus 2023 (systematic review, 11 studies): complete mucosal coverage ranged from 16.6% to 100% across studies — no standardised protocol, good-quality trials still needed
cards.summary: Arqueros-Lemus 2023 (systematic review, 11 studies): complete mucosal coverage ranged from 16.6% to 100% across studies — no standardised protocol, good-quality trials still needed
cards.people: Eleven articles (cohort, case series, randomised or non-randomised clinical studies in humans) of pentoxifylline + tocopherol (PENTO) treatment for osteoradionecrosis of the jaws, identified through PubMed, Cochrane Library, Scopus and Web of Science under PRISMA.
cards.result: All studies reported some patients achieving complete mucosal coverage with no exposed bone after PENTO, ranging from 16.6% to 100% depending on the study. Clinical improvement or disease stabilisation was reported in 7.6% to 66.6% of patients, while disease progression was seen in five studies in 7.6% to 32% of patients. There is no standardised protocol for doses or duration, or for adding antibiotics and clodronate. The authors conclude good-quality clinical trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: The 16.6%–100% spread in complete-coverage rates across 11 small studies is itself the finding: case mix, lesion severity, dose and follow-up differ so much that no single healing rate can be quoted for PENTO.
cards.source: Arqueros-Lemus M et al. Pentoxifylline and tocopherol for the treatment of osteoradionecrosis of the jaws. A systematic review. Medicina oral, patologia oral y cirugia bucal. 2023. PMID: 36641743. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: striking healing rates in uncontrolled Delanian cohorts, no completed randomised trial — a promising regimen, not a proven one
cards.summary: Synthesis: striking healing rates in uncontrolled Delanian cohorts, no completed randomised trial — a promising regimen, not a proven one
cards.people: Two single-arm Delanian phase II cohorts (18 and 54 eligible patients), a 7-study meta-analysis of proportions (211 patients) and an 11-study systematic review — all uncontrolled; the first randomised trial (RAPTOR) is still running.
cards.result: Phase II results: 16/18 complete recovery (2005) and all 54 eligible patients recovered, median 9 months (2011). Pooled series: 126/211 recovered fully or improved significantly, 15 progressed. Review range for complete mucosal coverage: 16.6%–100%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), graded as GAP-E evidence.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf comes from patients who all received the drugs. Until a randomised comparison reports, 'heals refractory osteoradionecrosis' is a hypothesis with encouraging uncontrolled data behind it — not a settled benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Delanian S et al. Head & Neck. 2005 (PMID: 15641107); Delanian S et al. shelves.title: Flap fixation with quilting sutures after mastectomy: seroma roughly halved or better in every design — 22.5% versus 80.5% in the founding study, a pooled relative risk of 0.37 across 11 RCTs, and a better textbook outcome in the QUILT stepped-wedge RCT
shelves.question: In women having mastectomy (with or without immediate reconstruction), does flap fixation with quilting sutures reduce seroma formation and aspirations versus standard closure with drains?
shelves.mesh: Axilla · Breast Neoplasms/surgery* · Drainage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Lymph Node Excision* · Mammaplasty · Mastectomy* · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Seroma/etiology, prevention & control* · Surgical Flaps* · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control* · Suture Techniques · Time Factors · Tissue Adhesives/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: Concordant at every level of evidence. The founding ten Wolde study (2014) was a retrospective comparison of consecutive groups (176 patients) — PREMISE CORRECTION to the slate row, which described it as a randomised trial — finding seroma in 22.5% quilted versus 80.5% conventional, with fewer aspirations and fewer infections (11.2% vs 31.0%). The randomised evidence arrived later: the QUILT stepped-wedge cluster RCT (251 patients, 12 Dutch hospitals, NCT05272904) found textbook outcome in 65.7% versus 41.3% and wound complications including clinically significant seroma in 24.0% versus 55.6%, and the Eliav meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (2,009 patients) pooled a seroma relative risk of 0.367 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.539) — a 63% relative risk reduction, with the absolute rates from the comparative studies printed on the cards. No pain, shoulder-function or satisfaction penalty was found. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: ten Wolde 2014 (retrospective consecutive-groups comparison, 176 patients): quilting cut seroma from 80.5% to 22.5%, aspirations from 4.86 to 2.40, and surgical site infection from 31.0% to 11.2%
cards.summary: ten Wolde 2014 (retrospective consecutive-groups comparison, 176 patients): quilting cut seroma from 80.5% to 22.5%, aspirations from 4.86 to 2.40, and surgical site infection from 31.0% to 11.2%
cards.people: 176 patients after mastectomy and/or axillary lymph node dissection in two consecutive groups — quilted (n = 89), in which skin flaps were fixed to the underlying muscle, versus conventional closure (n = 87) — compared retrospectively for seroma incidence, number and volume of aspirations, and surgical site infection.
cards.result: The quilted group scored significantly better on all endpoints: seroma incidence fell from 80.5% to 22.5% (p < 0.01), mean number of aspirations from 4.86 to 2.40 (p = 0.015), aspiration volume from 1660 mL to 611 mL (p = 0.05), and surgical site infections from 31.0% to 11.2% (p < 0.01). Increasing age and lymph node dissection were risk factors for seroma; quilting was a protective factor.
cards.watchOut: PREMISE CORRECTION: this founding ten Wolde study is a retrospective comparison of consecutive groups, not the randomised trial it is sometimes described as — era effects and surgeon learning are uncontrolled. The randomised evidence for quilting comes from the later trials carded below.
cards.source: ten Wolde B et al. Quilting prevents seroma formation following breast cancer surgery: closing the dead space by quilting prevents seroma following axillary lymph node dissection and mastectomy. Annals of surgical oncology. 2014. PMID: 24217790. Registry ID: none in the record. retrospective comparative study (ten wolde 2014) 176 patients after mastectomy and/or axillary lymph node dissection in two consecutive groups — quilted (n = 89), in which skin flaps were fixed to the underlying muscle, versus conventional closure (n = 87) — compared retrospectively for seroma incidence, number and volume of aspirations, and surgical site infection. the quilted group scored significantly better on all endpoints: seroma incidence fell from 80.5% to 22.5% (p < 0.01), mean number of aspirations from 4.86 to 2.40 (p = 0.015), aspiration volume from 1660 ml to 611 ml (p = 0.05), and surgical site infections from 31.0% to 11.2% (p < 0.01). increasing age and lymph node dissection were risk factors for seroma; quilting was a protective factor. premise correction: this founding ten wolde study is a retrospective comparison of consecutive groups, not the randomised trial it is sometimes described as — era effects and surgeon learning are uncontrolled. the randomised evidence for quilting comes from the later trials carded below. ten wolde b et al. quilting prevents seroma formation following breast cancer surgery: closing the dead space by quilting prevents seroma following axillary lymph node dissection and mastectomy. annals of surgical oncology. 2014. pmid: 24217790. registry id: none in the record. mesh: axilla · breast neoplasms/surgery* · drainage · female · follow-up studies · humans · incidence · lymph node excision* · mammaplasty · mastectomy* · middle aged · prognosis · retrospective studies · risk factors · seroma/etiology, prevention & control* · surgical flaps* · surgical wound infection/prevention & control* · suture techniques · time factors · tissue adhesives/therapeutic use*

cards.headline: van Zeelst 2022 (combined prospective/retrospective study, 254 patients): clinically significant seroma in 12.9% quilted versus 62.3% non-quilted, with less healthcare use and no shoulder or pain penalty
cards.summary: van Zeelst 2022 (combined prospective/retrospective study, 254 patients): clinically significant seroma in 12.9% quilted versus 62.3% non-quilted, with less healthcare use and no shoulder or pain penalty
cards.type: Combined prospective and retrospective comparative study (van Zeelst 2022)
cards.people: 254 patients undergoing mastectomy and/or axillary lymph node dissection, receiving quilting sutures or conventional closure, in a combined prospective and retrospective study; primary outcome was clinically significant seroma, with shoulder function and analgesic use observed in the prospectively included patients.
cards.result: Clinically significant seroma occurred in 12.9% of the quilted cohort versus 62.3% of the non-quilted cohort (p < 0.001). Surgical site infections were significantly less frequent with quilting, hospital stay was shorter and outpatient visits fewer; the quilting procedure required 10 additional minutes of operating time. No significant differences were observed in postoperative shoulder function or analgesic use.
cards.watchOut: Part retrospective, so the same selection and era caveats apply as for the 2014 study, and the non-quilted seroma rate (62.3%) is at the high end of reported rates — the absolute gap will be smaller where conventional-closure seroma rates are lower.
cards.source: van Zeelst LJ et al. Quilting following mastectomy reduces seroma, associated complications and health care consumption without impairing patient comfort. Journal of surgical oncology. 2022. PMID: 34786726. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van Zeelst 2025 (QUILT stepped-wedge cluster RCT, 251 patients, 12 hospitals): textbook outcome in 65.7% quilted versus 41.3% conventional; wound complications including clinically significant seroma 24.0% versus 55.6%
cards.summary: van Zeelst 2025 (QUILT stepped-wedge cluster RCT, 251 patients, 12 hospitals): textbook outcome in 65.7% quilted versus 41.3% conventional; wound complications including clinically significant seroma 24.0% versus 55.6%
cards.type: Stepped-wedge randomised cluster trial — QUILT (van Zeelst 2025)
cards.people: 251 patients who underwent mastectomy in 12 Dutch hospitals in a stepped-wedge randomised cluster trial of the quilt technique versus conventional closure; primary outcome was textbook outcome at 6 months — absence of wound complications, readmissions, reoperations or unscheduled outpatient visits, and no increase in pain medication use versus before surgery. Registered as NCT05272904.
cards.result: Textbook outcome was higher with quilting (94/143, 65.7% vs 26/63, 41.3%; P = 0.003). Wound complications, including clinically significant seroma, occurred in 24.0% of quilted versus 55.6% of non-quilted patients (P < 0.001), and unscheduled outpatient visits in 30.2% versus 44.4% (P = 0.048). No significant differences were observed in postoperative pain, shoulder function, satisfaction, physical well-being of the chest, or cosmetic outcome.
cards.watchOut: A stepped-wedge implementation design compares periods before and after each hospital adopted quilting, so secular trends are partly confounded with the technique; the analysed groups are unequal (143 vs 63) because most cluster-periods fell after implementation. The 2023 QUILT publication (PMID: 37460983) is the study description, not separate results, and is not carded separately.
cards.source: Zeelst LJV et al. Quilt technique after mastectomy: stepped-wedge randomized cluster trial showing superior textbook outcome and reduced healthcare utilization. The British journal of surgery. 2025. PMID: 41026907. Registry ID: NCT05272904 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank list). cards.headline: Eliav 2021 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 2,009 patients): quilting reduced seroma incidence with a relative risk of 0.367 and shortened drainage duration
cards.summary: Eliav 2021 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 2,009 patients): quilting reduced seroma incidence with a relative risk of 0.367 and shortened drainage duration
cards.people: Eleven randomised controlled trials with 2,009 patients comparing quilting sutures with conventional closure after mastectomy, identified from five databases; primary outcome was seroma incidence, with drainage volume and duration as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: Quilting greatly reduced seroma formation compared with conventional closure (p < 0.001; relative risk 0.367, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.539; I² = 63.56%) — a 63% relative risk reduction; for absolute rates, the comparative studies on this shelf found seroma in 22.5% quilted versus 80.5% conventional (ten Wolde) and clinically significant seroma in 12.9% versus 62.3% (van Zeelst 2022). Quilting also shortened drainage duration (p = 0.015; SMD −1.657, 95% CI −2.991 to −0.324; 8 studies, n = 1,578; I² = 98.98%) but did not significantly affect drainage volume.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is substantial (I² = 64% for seroma, 99% for drainage duration), the component RCTs are small, and seroma definitions vary — the relative risk is a pooled average across unlike trials, which is why this card prints it as relative with the absolute rates from the comparative studies beside it.
cards.source: Eliav T et al. Effect of quilting on seroma formation in mastectomies: A meta-analysis. Surgical oncology. 2021. PMID: 34563996. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: concordant benefit at every level — retrospective, prospective, stepped-wedge randomised and pooled RCT evidence all favour quilting
cards.summary: Synthesis: concordant benefit at every level — retrospective, prospective, stepped-wedge randomised and pooled RCT evidence all favour quilting
cards.people: One retrospective comparison (176 patients), one combined prospective/retrospective study (254), one stepped-wedge randomised cluster trial (251 patients, 12 hospitals) and an 11-RCT meta-analysis (2,009 patients).
cards.result: Seroma: 80.5% → 22.5% (ten Wolde), clinically significant seroma 62.3% → 12.9% (van Zeelst 2022), wound complications 55.6% → 24.0% with better textbook outcome in the QUILT RCT, and a pooled relative risk of 0.367 across 11 RCTs (Eliav). No shoulder-function, pain or satisfaction penalty was found where measured. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The consistency is real, but absolute benefit depends on the local conventional-closure seroma rate — centres starting from 80% have far more to gain than centres starting from 30%. Quilting in these studies was generally paired with drain omission or early removal protocols, so the isolated suture effect and the package effect are not fully separable.
cards.source: Synthesis of ten Wolde B et al. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2014 (PMID: 24217790); van Zeelst LJ et al. Journal of Surgical Oncology. 2022 (PMID: 34786726); van Zeelst LJ et al. British Journal of Surgery. 2025 (PMID: 41026907); Eliav T et al. Surgical Oncology. 2021 (PMID: 34563996).

shelves.title: Cabozantinib in previously treated advanced NETs (CABINET): median PFS 8.4 vs 3.9 months in extra-pancreatic NET (HR 0.38, relative) and 13.8 vs 4.4 months in pancreatic NET (HR 0.23, relative)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated, progressive advanced pancreatic or extra-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, does cabozantinib, compared with placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
shelves.balance: One phase 3 trial (CABINET, Alliance A021602; NCT03375320) with two independently randomised cohorts is the evidence base, carded here as its two cohorts plus a grade 3 subgroup report. In extra-pancreatic NET (n = 203), median progression-free survival was 8.4 months on cabozantinib 60 mg daily versus 3.9 months on placebo (stratified hazard ratio 0.38 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians); in pancreatic NET (n = 95), 13.8 versus 4.4 months (hazard ratio 0.23, relative). Confirmed objective response was 5% (extra-pancreatic) and 19% (pancreatic) versus 0% on placebo in both cohorts. The grade 3 subgroup (24 patients pooled across cohorts) showed the same direction (median PFS 7.9 vs 3.0 months; hazard ratio 0.15, relative) but rests on very small numbers. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 62–65% on cabozantinib versus 23–27% on placebo, most commonly hypertension, fatigue, diarrhoea and thromboembolic events. The end point is progression-free survival; overall survival was a secondary end point and is immature/not reported as a benefit in these records — no survival claim is made. US approval for this indication followed in March 2025, per the slate record.

cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, extra-pancreatic cohort (CABINET), N Engl J Med 2025
cards.people: Extra-pancreatic cohort of the phase 3 CABINET trial (Alliance A021602, NCT03375320): 203 patients with previously treated, progressive advanced extra-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (prior peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy or targeted therapy or both), randomised 2:1 to cabozantinib 60 mg daily or placebo. This card and the next are the two explicitly labelled independent cohorts of the one trial report (PMID: 39282913).
cards.result: Median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 8.4 months on cabozantinib versus 3.9 months on placebo (stratified hazard ratio for progression or death 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.59; P < 0.001 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute medians). Confirmed objective response was 5% on cabozantinib versus 0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival, not survival: overall survival is immature in this report, and the response rate (5%) shows most of the benefit is disease stabilisation rather than shrinkage.
cards.source: Chan JA et al. Phase 3 Trial of Cabozantinib to Treat Advanced Neuroendocrine Tumors. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39282913. cards.headline: Grade 3 subgroup report (n = 24 pooled across cohorts): median PFS 7.9 vs 3.0 months (hazard ratio 0.15, relative); response 25% vs 0%
cards.summary: Grade 3 subgroup report (n = 24 pooled across cohorts): median PFS 7.9 vs 3.0 months (hazard ratio 0.15, relative); response 25% vs 0%
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of the CABINET phase 3 trial, Endocr Relat Cancer 2026
cards.people: Subgroup report of CABINET (NCT03375320): the 24 patients with well-differentiated grade 3 NETs (Ki-67 >20%) pooled from both cohorts because of small numbers — 16 randomised to cabozantinib and 8 to placebo; primary sites were pancreas (12), gastrointestinal tract (7), unknown (3) and lung/thymus (2). These patients are a subset of the two cohorts above, not additional patients.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival in grade 3 NETs was 7.9 months on cabozantinib versus 3.0 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.57 — a relative measure on very small numbers). Confirmed overall radiographic response was 25% (4/16) versus 0% (0/8). Safety was consistent with the trial as a whole.
cards.watchOut: Only 24 patients (8 on placebo): the hazard ratio's confidence interval (0.04 to 0.57) is very wide, and pooling two cohorts was a post-randomisation analytic choice made necessary by small numbers.
cards.source: Strosberg JR et al. Cabozantinib for advanced grade 3 neuroendocrine tumors: subgroup analysis of the phase 3 CABINET trial (Alliance A021602). Endocrine-related cancer. 2026. cards.summary: Synthesis: cabozantinib delays progression in both CABINET cohorts, at the cost of substantial grade ≥3 toxicity; survival benefit not shown
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf: the CABINET phase 3 trial's extra-pancreatic (203) and pancreatic (95) cohorts, plus its grade 3 subgroup report (24 patients, a subset).

shelves.title: Zanidatamab (Ziihera) in previously treated HER2-positive biliary tract cancer: a 41.3% response rate in a single-arm trial (HERIZON-BTC-01) — accelerated approval, confirmatory trial still owed
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated HER2-positive (IHC 3+) unresectable or metastatic biliary tract cancer, does zanidatamab, compared with historical or standard second-line outcomes, produce durable tumour responses?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — SINGLE-ARM evidence, capped at POSSIBLE by rule, and the regulatory status must be read with it. HERIZON-BTC-01 (87 patients with HER2-amplified, previously treated biliary tract cancer) found confirmed responses by independent review in 33 of 80 patients in the HER2-positive cohort 1 — an objective response rate of 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8) — with grade 3 treatment-related adverse events in 18% (diarrhoea 5% and decreased ejection fraction 3% the most common) and no grade 4 treatment-related events or treatment-related deaths. There is no randomised comparator: 41.3% is a rate in a selected, centrally tested population, not an effect against chemotherapy. The drug is zanidatamab, marketed as Ziihera (Jazz Pharmaceuticals) — named per the clarification exception, exactly as the approval record gives it. Its November 2024 FDA approval was ACCELERATED and is contingent on the ongoing confirmatory first-line trial (HERIZON-BTC-302); if that trial fails, the approval can be withdrawn, and this stamp must be revisited. Supporting context: the first-in-human phase 1 programme included a 22-patient biliary tract cancer expansion cohort at the 20 mg/kg every-2-weeks dose, and a 2025 systematic review of anti-HER2 agents in biliary tract cancer (368 patients, eight publications, several different agents) pooled a 34% response rate — class-level support, not zanidatamab-specific proof. Final results of HERIZON-BTC-01 were published in JAMA Oncology in 2026; the PubMed record carries no abstract, so no numbers beyond the primary report are carded from it.

cards.headline: HERIZON-BTC-01 primary report (single-arm, 87 patients): confirmed response rate 41.3% (33/80) in the HER2-positive cohort; grade 3 treatment-related events in 18%, no grade 4 or treatment-related deaths
cards.summary: HERIZON-BTC-01 primary report (single-arm, 87 patients): confirmed response rate 41.3% (33/80) in the HER2-positive cohort; grade 3 treatment-related events in 18%, no grade 4 or treatment-related deaths
cards.people: 87 patients at 32 sites in nine countries with HER2-amplified, unresectable locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer progressing on previous gemcitabine-based therapy (enrolled September 2020 to March 2022): cohort 1 (n=80), HER2 immunohistochemistry 2+ or 3+ (HER2-positive; 56% female, 65% Asian, median age 64 years); cohort 2 (n=7), IHC 0 or 1+. All received zanidatamab 20 mg/kg intravenously every 2 weeks. HER2 amplification was confirmed by in-situ hybridisation on central testing; ECOG performance status 0-1 required.
cards.result: Confirmed objective responses by independent central review in cohort 1: 33/80 (41.3%; 95% CI 30.4-52.8). At the October 2022 data cutoff (median follow-up 12.4 months), 18 (21%) patients remained on treatment and 69 (79%) had discontinued, 64 of them for radiographic progression. Sixteen patients (18%) had grade 3 treatment-related adverse events — most commonly diarrhoea (4 patients, 5%) and decreased ejection fraction (3 patients, 3%). There were no grade 4 treatment-related adverse events and no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: there is no internal estimate of what these patients would have done on second-line chemotherapy, and response rate in a biomarker-selected, centrally confirmed population cannot be compared naively with unselected historical series. Cohort 2 (IHC 0/1+, n=7) is too small to support any claim in HER2-low disease. The FDA-cited figure for the IHC 3+ subgroup is higher than 41.3%, but it is not in this fetched record and is therefore not carded here.
cards.source: Harding JJ et al. Zanidatamab for HER2-amplified, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer (HERIZON-BTC-01): a multicentre, single-arm, phase 2b study. cards.summary: Phase 1 programme (Meric-Bernstam 2022): the 20 mg/kg every-2-weeks dose came from a first-in-human study whose expansion phase included 22 patients with biliary tract cancer
cards.people: Patients with locally advanced or metastatic HER2-expressing or HER2-amplified solid tumours who had received all available approved therapies: part 1 dose escalation, n=46; part 2 expansion at the recommended dose of 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks, n=86 — comprising biliary tract cancer (n=22), colorectal cancer (n=28) and other HER2-expressing cancers (n=36).
cards.result: No dose-limiting toxicities were detected in part 1 and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached; the recommended part 2 dose was 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks — the dose and schedule used in HERIZON-BTC-01. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events were diarrhoea (52% in part 1; 43% in part 2, all grade 1-2 except one patient) and infusion reactions (43% in part 1, all grade 1-2).
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study across mixed tumour types: its biliary cohort (n=22) establishes feasibility and the dose, not efficacy in biliary tract cancer. Efficacy claims on this shelf rest on HERIZON-BTC-01 alone.

cards.headline: Systematic review of anti-HER2 therapy in biliary tract cancer (2025; 368 patients, 8 publications): pooled response rate 34% across several different agents — class-level context, not zanidatamab proof
cards.summary: Systematic review of anti-HER2 therapy in biliary tract cancer (2025; 368 patients, 8 publications): pooled response rate 34% across several different agents — class-level context, not zanidatamab proof
cards.people: 368 patients with locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer in eight publications (January 2019 to March 2024) of phase 1-3 trials of anti-HER2 agents: zanidatamab, pertuzumab plus trastuzumab, tucatinib plus trastuzumab, trastuzumab deruxtecan, trastuzumab-based chemotherapy combinations and neratinib.
cards.result: Across agents, the pooled objective response rate was 34% (95% CI 24-44) and disease control rate 64% (51-77); pooled weighted progression-free survival was 4.8 months and median overall survival 9.4 months; pooled duration of response was 5.0 months. Any adverse event occurred in 82.6% of patients and grade 3-4 events in 32.1%; 5.7% discontinued for treatment-related adverse events. The authors conclude anti-HER2 therapies are viable options in HER2-expressing biliary tract cancer, particularly in the second-line setting.
cards.watchOut: Pooled across different drugs, combinations and HER2 definitions — it supports the target, not this drug. Its pooled survival figures mix single-arm studies and must not be attributed to zanidatamab; HERIZON-BTC-01 is itself one of the included publications, so this review is not independent of the shelf's anchor trial.

shelves.title: Zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy in CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/GEJ cancer: two phase 3 trials agree (PFS HR 0.75 and 0.69; OS HR 0.75 and 0.77) — with a heavy nausea and vomiting burden and an absolute dependence on the CLDN18.2 test
shelves.question: In adults with untreated CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, does zolbetuximab plus chemotherapy, compared with chemotherapy alone, improve survival?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two large, concordant, double-blind phase 3 trials, the standard this library requires for LIKELY. SPOTLIGHT (zolbetuximab + mFOLFOX6; n=565): median progression-free survival 10.61 vs 8.67 months (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.94 — a relative measure) and overall survival HR 0.75 (0.60-0.94). GLOW (zolbetuximab + CAPOX; n=507): median PFS 8.21 vs 6.80 months (HR 0.687, 0.544-0.866) and median OS 14.39 vs 12.16 months (HR 0.771, 0.615-0.965). Three qualifications belong on the face. First, the benefit is concentrated in HIGH CLDN18.2 expression: both phase 3 trials required at least 75% of tumour cells to show moderate-to-strong membranous CLDN18 staining, and the earlier phase 2 FAST trial (which enrolled at a 40% threshold) found its clearest benefit in the 70%-and-over subgroup (PFS HR 0.38) — so the tested population is the high-expression population, defined by a COMPANION DIAGNOSTIC: no test, or a lower-expression tumour, means no evidence. Second, the gastrointestinal burden is substantial: in SPOTLIGHT the most common grade 3-or-worse adverse events were nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite, with grade 3-or-worse events overall in 87% vs 78%; in GLOW grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent events were 72.8% vs 69.9%. Third, the absolute gains are modest — about 2 months of median PFS and, in GLOW, 2.2 months of median OS — against hazard ratios that sound larger; both are printed so the relative and absolute stories can be read together. The SPOTLIGHT and GLOW citations were not re-verified at slate mining; both were verified from fetched PubMed records at build (PMIDs 37068504 and 37524953).

cards.headline: SPOTLIGHT (zolbetuximab + mFOLFOX6; n=565): median PFS 10.61 vs 8.67 months (HR 0.75) and OS HR 0.75 — grade 3+ events in 87% vs 78%, led by nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite
cards.summary: SPOTLIGHT (zolbetuximab + mFOLFOX6; n=565): median PFS 10.61 vs 8.67 months (HR 0.75) and OS HR 0.75 — grade 3+ events in 87% vs 78%, led by nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial (SPOTLIGHT, Shitara 2023)
cards.people: 565 adults at 215 centres in 20 countries with previously untreated, locally advanced unresectable or metastatic gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma that was CLDN18.2-positive — defined as at least 75% of tumour cells showing moderate-to-strong membranous CLDN18 staining — and HER2-negative, ECOG performance status 0-1; randomised 1:1 to zolbetuximab (800 mg/m2 loading, then 600 mg/m2 every 3 weeks) plus mFOLFOX6 (n=283) or placebo plus mFOLFOX6 (n=282).
cards.result: Progression-free survival (primary endpoint, independent review): median 10.61 months (95% CI 8.90-12.48) vs 8.67 months (8.21-10.28); HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.94; p=0.0066) — a relative measure, with an absolute median gain of about 1.9 months. Overall survival: HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.94; p=0.0053). Grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 242/279 (87%) on zolbetuximab vs 216/278 (78%) on placebo; the most common were nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite. Treatment-related deaths: 5 (2%) vs 4 (1%). Funded by Astellas Pharma.
cards.watchOut: The 75%-of-tumour-cells staining threshold is an eligibility wall, not a detail: SPOTLIGHT says nothing about tumours below it, and treatment is impossible to target without the CLDN18.2 companion test. The identical PFS and OS hazard ratios (both 0.75) are a coincidence of rounding in the report — do not read extra precision into them.

cards.headline: GLOW (zolbetuximab + CAPOX; n=507): median PFS 8.21 vs 6.80 months (HR 0.687) and median OS 14.39 vs 12.16 months (HR 0.771); grade 3+ treatment-emergent events 72.8% vs 69.9%
cards.summary: GLOW (zolbetuximab + CAPOX; n=507): median PFS 8.21 vs 6.80 months (HR 0.687) and median OS 14.39 vs 12.16 months (HR 0.771); grade 3+ treatment-emergent events 72.8% vs 69.9%
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial (GLOW, Shah 2023)
cards.people: 507 adults with previously untreated, CLDN18.2-positive, HER2-negative, locally advanced unresectable or metastatic gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, randomised 1:1 to zolbetuximab plus CAPOX (capecitabine and oxaliplatin) or placebo plus CAPOX. CLDN18.2 positivity used the same high-expression definition as SPOTLIGHT (at least 75% of tumour cells with moderate-to-strong membranous staining).
cards.result: Progression-free survival (primary endpoint): median 8.21 vs 6.80 months; HR 0.687 (95% CI 0.544-0.866; P=0.0007) — a relative measure; absolute median gain about 1.4 months. Overall survival: median 14.39 vs 12.16 months; HR 0.771 (95% CI 0.615-0.965; P=0.0118) — an absolute median gain of about 2.2 months. Grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between arms (72.8% zolbetuximab vs 69.9% placebo).
cards.watchOut: GLOW's abstract does not break out the nausea/vomiting rates that dominate SPOTLIGHT's safety profile; the class burden should be assumed from SPOTLIGHT and the phase 2 data rather than read as absent here. Two different chemotherapy backbones (CAPOX here, mFOLFOX6 in SPOTLIGHT) showing the same direction is what makes the pair concordant rather than duplicative.

cards.headline: FAST phase 2 (zolbetuximab + EOX; n=246 across three arms): PFS HR 0.44 and OS HR 0.55 overall — and the clearest benefit sat in the ≥70% CLDN18.2-expression subgroup (PFS HR 0.38), foreshadowing the phase 3 threshold
cards.summary: FAST phase 2 (zolbetuximab + EOX; n=246 across three arms): PFS HR 0.44 and OS HR 0.55 overall — and the clearest benefit sat in the ≥70% CLDN18.2-expression subgroup (PFS HR 0.38), foreshadowing the phase 3 threshold
cards.people: Adults with advanced gastric, gastro-oesophageal junction or oesophageal adenocarcinoma with moderate-to-strong CLDN18.2 expression in at least 40% of tumour cells, receiving first-line EOX (epirubicin, oxaliplatin, capecitabine): arm 1, EOX alone (n=84); arm 2, zolbetuximab 800/600 mg/m2 plus EOX (n=77); arm 3 (exploratory, added after enrolment began), zolbetuximab 1,000 mg/m2 plus EOX (n=85).
cards.result: Arm 2 vs arm 1: progression-free survival HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.29-0.67; P<0.0005) and overall survival HR 0.55 (0.39-0.77; P<0.0005) — relative measures. In patients with moderate-to-strong CLDN18.2 expression in at least 70% of tumour cells, the PFS benefit was retained and larger (HR 0.38; 0.23-0.62). Arm 3 showed a PFS benefit overall (HR 0.58) but not in high expressors, and no significant OS improvement. Most zolbetuximab-related adverse events (nausea, vomiting, neutropenia, anaemia) were grade 1-2, with no substantial overall increase in grade 3-or-worse events.
cards.watchOut: FAST's 40% entry threshold is lower than the phase 3 trials' 75%: its overall-population result mixes expression levels the phase 3 programme deliberately excluded, and the subgroup gradient (stronger effect at higher expression) is the finding that matters for practice — benefit is concentrated in high CLDN18.2 expression. EOX is also no longer a standard backbone; FAST is dose- and biomarker-finding evidence, with SPOTLIGHT and GLOW carrying the clinical claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, two backbones, one direction — a real survival benefit confined to CLDN18.2-high tumours and bought with gastrointestinal toxicity
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, two backbones, one direction — a real survival benefit confined to CLDN18.2-high tumours and bought with gastrointestinal toxicity
cards.people: SPOTLIGHT (n=565, mFOLFOX6 backbone) and GLOW (n=507, CAPOX backbone), both double-blind and placebo-controlled in CLDN18.2-positive (at least 75% of tumour cells, moderate-to-strong staining), HER2-negative, untreated advanced gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma; supported by the FAST phase 2 trial (n=246).
cards.result: PFS: HR 0.75 (median +1.9 months) and HR 0.687 (median +1.4 months). OS: HR 0.75 and HR 0.771 (GLOW median +2.2 months). Grade 3-or-worse events: 87% vs 78% (SPOTLIGHT, nausea/vomiting/appetite-led) and 72.8% vs 69.9% (GLOW). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — strong concordant evidence from two independent phase 3 trials.
cards.watchOut: Companion-diagnostic dependence is absolute: without a validated CLDN18.2 test showing high expression, none of these numbers applies, and the FAST gradient warns against extrapolating to moderate expressors. Hazard ratios are relative measures; the absolute median gains (roughly 1.4-1.9 months PFS, 2.2 months OS where reported) are the numbers to set against the nausea and vomiting burden in shared decision-making.

shelves.title: Perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT in resectable gastric/GEJ cancer (MATTERHORN): 2-year event-free survival 67.4% vs 58.5% (HR 0.71), and the final analysis confirms an overall-survival benefit (HR 0.78)
shelves.question: In adults with resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, does perioperative durvalumab added to FLOT chemotherapy, compared with FLOT alone, improve event-free and overall survival?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single large trial, capped at POSSIBLE by the single-programme rule, but a complete one: MATTERHORN (n=948, double-blind, placebo-controlled) met its primary endpoint and its key secondary endpoint in two separate journal reports of the same trial, each labelled as such on this shelf. Event-free survival: 2-year EFS 67.4% with perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT vs 58.5% with FLOT alone (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58-0.86 — a relative measure; absolute difference 8.9 percentage points at 2 years). Overall survival: the interim analysis at the primary report had NOT met its stringent significance threshold (P=0.03 against a threshold of P<0.0001), but the final OS analysis — presented at ESMO 2025 when the slate was mined and now verified from its journal report (Lancet 2026) — shows HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021, against a threshold of p<0.0499). Pathological complete response was 19.2% vs 7.2% (relative risk 2.69): pCR is a SURROGATE, and it is not the basis of the survival claim — the claim rests on the EFS and OS analyses above. Grade 3-4 adverse events were near-identical (71.6% vs 71.2%), and surgery was not materially delayed (10.1% vs 10.8%). A 2025 meta-analysis of phase 3 perioperative checkpoint trials supports the FLOT-plus-immunotherapy strategy at class level (EFS HR 0.732 vs FLOT alone) while noting discordance across agents and backbones. NAME-COLLISION NOTE: this MATTERHORN is the gastric-cancer trial (NCT04592913); pack #4169 homes an unrelated mitral-valve trial of the same name — the two share nothing but the acronym and must not be cross-contaminated.

cards.headline: MATTERHORN primary report (NEJM 2025; n=948): 2-year event-free survival 67.4% vs 58.5% (HR 0.71); pCR 19.2% vs 7.2%; interim OS had not crossed its significance threshold
cards.summary: MATTERHORN primary report (NEJM 2025; n=948): 2-year event-free survival 67.4% vs 58.5% (HR 0.71); pCR 19.2% vs 7.2%; interim OS had not crossed its significance threshold
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, double-blind, randomised trial — primary report (MATTERHORN, Janjigian 2025)
cards.people: 948 adults with resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, randomised 1:1 (474 per arm) to durvalumab 1,500 mg or placebo every 4 weeks plus FLOT for 4 cycles (2 neoadjuvant, 2 adjuvant), followed by durvalumab or placebo every 4 weeks for 10 cycles. Median follow-up 31.5 months. Funded by AstraZeneca.
cards.result: Event-free survival (primary endpoint): 2-year Kaplan-Meier estimate 67.4% on durvalumab plus FLOT vs 58.5% on placebo plus FLOT (HR for event or death 0.71; 95% CI 0.58-0.86; P<0.001) — a relative measure; the absolute 2-year difference is 8.9 percentage points. Overall survival at this interim analysis: 2-year OS 75.7% vs 70.4%, with a piecewise HR of 0.99 (0.70-1.39) for months 0-12 and 0.67 (0.50-0.90) from month 12 onward; P=0.03 by stratified log-rank, which did NOT meet the pre-set significance threshold of P<0.0001 — OS was not yet proven at this report. Pathological complete response: 19.2% vs 7.2% (relative risk 2.69; 95% CI 1.86-3.90). Grade 3-4 adverse events: 71.6% vs 71.2%. Delayed surgery: 10.1% vs 10.8%.
cards.watchOut: pCR is a surrogate endpoint — a near-tripling of pCR does not by itself establish that patients live longer, and this card deliberately rests the claim on EFS. Equally, the interim OS analysis must be quoted with its failed threshold: at the NEJM report, 'durvalumab improves survival' was not yet a licensed sentence; the final analysis (next card) is what changed that.

cards.headline: MATTERHORN final overall-survival analysis (Lancet 2026; second, explicitly labelled report of the same trial): OS HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021) — the survival endpoint is now met
cards.summary: MATTERHORN final overall-survival analysis (Lancet 2026; second, explicitly labelled report of the same trial): OS HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021) — the survival endpoint is now met
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial — final overall-survival report, second report of the same trial (MATTERHORN, Janjigian 2026)
cards.people: The same 948 randomised participants (474 durvalumab plus FLOT; 474 placebo plus FLOT) at 147 centres in 20 countries, with stage II-IVA resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma; median age 62 years, 72% male. Overall survival in the intention-to-treat population was the key secondary endpoint and is the main endpoint of this report.
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly improved with perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT vs placebo plus FLOT: HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021, against a significance threshold of p<0.0499) — a relative measure (a 22% relative reduction in the hazard of death). Adverse events with an outcome of death possibly related to any trial treatment occurred in 6 (1%) of 475 participants in the durvalumab group and 2 (under 1%) of 469 in the placebo group. The authors conclude perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT is a new standard treatment option for resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. Funded by AstraZeneca.
cards.watchOut: This journal report is what licenses the survival claim — at slate mining the same analysis was ESMO-2025-presented only, and it is carded here because the Lancet report verifies it from a fetched record. It remains one trial: the HR's confidence interval (0.63-0.96) is compatible with anything from a large to a small survival benefit, and the possibly-treatment-related death counts (6 vs 2) run against the experimental arm even as overall mortality favours it.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of phase 3 perioperative checkpoint trials in gastro-oesophageal cancer (2025): FLOT-plus-immunotherapy beat FLOT alone on EFS (HR 0.732) — class-level support with cross-trial caveats
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of phase 3 perioperative checkpoint trials in gastro-oesophageal cancer (2025): FLOT-plus-immunotherapy beat FLOT alone on EFS (HR 0.732) — class-level support with cross-trial caveats
cards.type: Meta-analysis of phase 3 randomised trials with reconstructed individual patient data (Zhao 2025)
cards.people: Phase 3 randomised trials of perioperative chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint inhibition in locally advanced resectable gastro-oesophageal cancer, comparing FLOT-based and cisplatin/fluoropyrimidine-based backbones and different checkpoint agents, including MATTERHORN (durvalumab) and KEYNOTE-585 (pembrolizumab); survival curves were digitally reconstructed to obtain individual patient data.
cards.result: FLOT-plus-immunotherapy regimens showed superior event-free survival vs FLOT alone (HR 0.732; 95% CI 0.610-0.878; p<0.001) and vs cisplatin/fluoropyrimidine-plus-immunotherapy (HR 0.790; 0.647-0.966; p=0.021) — relative measures. No significant EFS difference was found between the FLOT-durvalumab and FLOT-pembrolizumab arms indirectly compared (HR 0.907; 0.637-1.290; p=0.586). Overall-survival curves diverged with increased heterogeneity across FLOT-only arms beyond 24 months, and the authors caution that the analyses lack patient-level covariate adjustment across trials; the analysis was performed while MATTERHORN's mature OS data were still awaited.
cards.watchOut: An indirect, reconstruction-based synthesis across different agents and backbones — it supports the strategy class, not durvalumab specifically, and its OS picture predates the MATTERHORN final analysis carded above. Cross-trial comparisons of this kind are hypothesis-framing, and the discordance the authors describe (some perioperative checkpoint trials failed) is part of the result.
cards.source: Zhao JJ et al. Checkpoint inhibitor benefit in perioperative gastro-esophageal cancer: A meta-analysis of phase III trials. Cancer treatment reviews. 2025. PMID: 40779895. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large double-blind trial, both endpoints now met — EFS HR 0.71 and final OS HR 0.78, with pCR as supporting surrogate only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large double-blind trial, both endpoints now met — EFS HR 0.71 and final OS HR 0.78, with pCR as supporting surrogate only
cards.people: MATTERHORN (n=948; primary report NEJM 2025 and final-OS report Lancet 2026 — two labelled reports of one trial), read with a phase 3 meta-analysis of perioperative checkpoint inhibition in gastro-oesophageal cancer (2025). Not to be confused with the unrelated mitral-valve MATTERHORN trial homed at pack #4169.
cards.result: Event-free survival: 2-year 67.4% vs 58.5% (HR 0.71). Overall survival: interim analysis not significant against its threshold; final analysis HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.96; p=0.021). Pathological complete response 19.2% vs 7.2% (surrogate). Grade 3-4 adverse events 71.6% vs 71.2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the single-trial cap applies despite both endpoints being met.
cards.watchOut: A second positive trial of perioperative durvalumab plus FLOT, or mature real-world survival data, would be needed to lift this above POSSIBLE under the stamp rules. The survival claim rests on EFS and OS — never on the pCR difference — and the possibly-treatment-related deaths (6 vs 2) belong in any consent conversation.
cards.source: Synthesis of Janjigian YY et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2025 (PMID: 40454643); Janjigian YY et al. Lancet (London, England). 2026 (PMID: 42716074); Zhao JJ et al. Cancer treatment reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40779895).

shelves.title: Avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST (NAVIGATOR, single-arm): 88–91% of 56 patients responded, median response 27.6 months — but cognitive effects in 57%, and no randomised evidence in this genotype
shelves.question: In adults with PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour, does avapritinib produce tumour responses compared with historical outcomes on other tyrosine-kinase inhibitors?
shelves.balance: Single-arm evidence only — there is no randomised trial of avapritinib in PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST, and none is likely: the mutation (5–10% of GISTs) is intrinsically resistant to imatinib and every previously approved tyrosine-kinase inhibitor, so historical response rates on standard TKIs are near zero. Against that background the NAVIGATOR phase 1 programme is striking: in the D842V population (n=56), 88% responded at first report (Heinrich 2020, PMID 32615108) and 91% at the long-term update of the SAME trial (Jones 2021, PMID 33465704 — two labelled reports of one trial, not two trials), with median duration of response 27.6 months and median progression-free survival 34.0 months. The harm side is real and belongs on the face: cognitive effects occurred in 57% of the D842V population in the long-term report, treatment-related grade 3–4 events in 57% of the safety population at first report, and memory impairment appeared among the dose-limiting toxicities at 600 mg. The randomised VOYAGER trial (PMID 34343033) is the discipline check: in molecularly UNSELECTED late-line GIST, avapritinib did not beat regorafenib — the benefit is specific to the D842V (and KIT-mutant) biology, not a class effect in all GIST. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single-arm, single-programme base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however large the response rate.

cards.headline: NAVIGATOR first report (Heinrich 2020): in 56 patients with PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST, 88% responded to avapritinib (5 complete responses) — in a population where standard TKIs are inactive
cards.summary: NAVIGATOR first report (Heinrich 2020): in 56 patients with PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST, 88% responded to avapritinib (5 complete responses) — in a population where standard TKIs are inactive
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1 trial, first report (Heinrich 2020, NAVIGATOR)
cards.people: NAVIGATOR, a two-part open-label phase 1 dose-escalation/dose-expansion study at 17 sites in 9 countries. The PDGFRA D842V efficacy population was 56 patients with unresectable D842V-mutant GIST who received avapritinib and had at least one target lesion and post-baseline assessment; the D842V safety population was 82 patients (dose-escalation plus dose-expansion, all doses). Maximum tolerated dose 400 mg; recommended phase 2 dose 300 mg once daily.
cards.result: Overall response in the D842V population: 49 of 56 patients (88%; 95% CI 76–95) — 5 (9%) complete and 44 (79%) partial responses. In the safety population, treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 47 of 82 patients (57%), most commonly anaemia (17%); there were no treatment-related deaths. No dose-limiting toxicities at 30–400 mg/day; at 600 mg two patients had dose-limiting toxicities, including grade 2 memory impairment in one.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: the 88% response rate is persuasive only because D842V-mutant GIST is documented to be refractory to imatinib and other standard TKIs — it is a comparison against a near-zero historical baseline, not against a randomised control. The D842V analysis population was separated out during the trial on the basis of enrolment trends and evolving knowledge, per the report itself.
cards.source: Heinrich MC et al. Avapritinib in advanced PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumour (NAVIGATOR): a multicentre, open-label, phase 1 trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32615108. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02508532. cards.headline: NAVIGATOR long-term update (Jones 2021) — SECOND REPORT OF THE SAME TRIAL: response rate 91% (51/56), median response duration 27.6 months, median PFS 34.0 months; cognitive effects in 57%
cards.summary: NAVIGATOR long-term update (Jones 2021) — SECOND REPORT OF THE SAME TRIAL: response rate 91% (51/56), median response duration 27.6 months, median PFS 34.0 months; cognitive effects in 57%
cards.type: Single-arm phase 1 trial, long-term update — second labelled report of the NAVIGATOR trial (Jones 2021)
cards.people: The same NAVIGATOR trial (NCT02508532) at a later data cut (9 March 2020; median follow-up 27.5 months): the PDGFRA D842V population is the same 56 patients (11 of them TKI-naïve), within an overall safety population of 250 patients with unresectable GIST.
cards.result: Overall response rate 91% (51/56); clinical benefit rate 98% (55/56); median duration of response 27.6 months (95% CI 17.6–not reached); median progression-free survival 34.0 months (95% CI 22.9–not reached); median overall survival not reached. Most frequent adverse events in the D842V population were nausea (68%) and diarrhoea (66%); cognitive effects occurred in 32 of 56 patients (57%).
cards.watchOut: This is NOT independent confirmation — it is the same 56 patients followed longer, and it must never be counted as a second trial. The 57% cognitive-effects rate is the harm that most needs counselling: effects on memory and cognition are a recognised avapritinib toxicity and were seen at the doses used in practice, not only at the abandoned 600 mg dose.
cards.source: Jones RL et al. Avapritinib in unresectable or metastatic PDGFRA D842V-mutant gastrointestinal stromal tumours: Long-term efficacy and safety data from the NAVIGATOR phase I trial. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 2021. PMID: 33465704. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02508532. cards.headline: VOYAGER (Kang 2021): in molecularly unselected third-line-or-later GIST, avapritinib did NOT improve progression-free survival versus regorafenib (HR 1.25; median 4.2 vs 5.6 months) — the D842V benefit does not generalise
cards.summary: VOYAGER (Kang 2021): in molecularly unselected third-line-or-later GIST, avapritinib did NOT improve progression-free survival versus regorafenib (HR 1.25; median 4.2 vs 5.6 months) — the D842V benefit does not generalise
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial in a DIFFERENT (molecularly unselected) population — context card (Kang 2021, VOYAGER)
cards.people: 476 patients with unresectable or metastatic GIST (molecularly unselected) randomised to avapritinib 300 mg once daily (n=240) or regorafenib 160 mg once daily, 3 weeks on/1 week off (n=236), as third-line or later therapy; crossover from regorafenib to avapritinib was permitted on progression.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival did not differ significantly (HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.99–1.57; 4.2 vs 5.6 months; P=.055) — the primary endpoint was not met. Objective response rates were 17.1% (avapritinib) and 7.2% (regorafenib); overall survival data were immature. Treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were similar (55.2% vs 57.7%).
cards.watchOut: VOYAGER does not contradict NAVIGATOR: it enrolled unselected late-line GIST, where most tumours lack the D842V target biology. Its role on this shelf is to stop the D842V response rate being read as evidence that avapritinib helps GIST generally — randomised evidence says it does not, outside the susceptible genotypes.
cards.source: Kang YK et al. Avapritinib Versus Regorafenib in Locally Advanced Unresectable or Metastatic GI Stromal Tumor: A Randomized, Open-Label Phase III Study (VOYAGER). Journal of clinical oncology. 2021. PMID: 34343033. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03465722 (trial); NCT02508532 also appears in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a very high, durable response rate in 56 D842V patients from one single-arm programme — with a 57% cognitive-effects burden — and randomised evidence that the effect is genotype-specific
cards.summary: Synthesis: a very high, durable response rate in 56 D842V patients from one single-arm programme — with a 57% cognitive-effects burden — and randomised evidence that the effect is genotype-specific
cards.people: On-question evidence: one single-arm phase 1 programme (NAVIGATOR) with 56 PDGFRA D842V-mutant patients, reported twice (2020 and 2021). Context: one randomised phase 3 trial in 476 unselected late-line patients (VOYAGER).
cards.result: Response: 88% at first report, 91% at long-term update (same patients); median response duration 27.6 months; median PFS 34.0 months. Harms: treatment-related grade 3–4 events 57%; cognitive effects 57% at long-term follow-up. In unselected GIST, no PFS benefit versus regorafenib (HR 1.25). PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for D842V-mutant disease — single-arm, single-programme evidence caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: The entire on-question base is 56 patients from one programme sponsored by the manufacturer (Blueprint Medicines, named as funder in the first report). The response magnitude against a refractory genotype is the strongest kind of single-arm evidence, but survival benefit versus any comparator has never been randomised in this genotype.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heinrich MC et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2020 (PMID: 32615108); Jones RL et al. European journal of cancer. 2021 (PMID: 33465704) — two reports of the one NAVIGATOR trial; Kang YK et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2021 (PMID: 34343033).

shelves.title: Daraxonrasib in previously treated RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer: published evidence is single-arm phase 1–2 only (35% response in a 26-patient subgroup) — phase 3 RASolute 302 is ⚠ congress-reported, not yet a journal report
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated RAS-mutant metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, does daraxonrasib (RMC-6236) improve survival compared with standard chemotherapy?
shelves.balance: The published evidence is a single-arm phase 1–2 programme — nothing randomised is in a journal yet. In the NEJM report (Wolpin 2026, PMID 42090791), 168 previously treated patients with RAS-mutated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma received daraxonrasib at 300 mg or less; the headline 35% objective response rate rests on a 26-patient subgroup (second-line, 300 mg, RAS G12 mutations), with median progression-free survival 8.5 months and overall survival 13.1 months in that subgroup — print that N whenever the 35% is quoted. Treatment-related grade 3-or-worse events occurred in 30%. Supporting syntheses are consistent but not independent: a daraxonrasib systematic review (PMID 42882807) found only the same phase 1–2 study plus the phase 3 trial as its evidence base, and a KRAS-targeted-therapy meta-analysis (PMID 42956271) pooled a pan-RAS(ON) response rate of 26.6% across early-phase cohorts. ⚠ CONGRESS/PRESS-REPORTED ONLY: the phase 3 RASolute 302 trial is reported in reviews and secondary sources as showing median overall survival 13.2 vs 6.7 months (HR 0.40, a relative measure) versus chemotherapy — as of this build (November 2026) NO full primary journal report of RASolute 302 was found on PubMed; only reviews citing it. Those phase 3 numbers are therefore NOT carded as published evidence and must not be quoted as established until the primary report appears. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) on the published single-arm base.

cards.headline: Phase 1–2 report (Wolpin 2026, NEJM): daraxonrasib in 168 previously treated RAS-mutated pancreatic cancers — the 35% response rate comes from a 26-patient subgroup (second-line, 300 mg, RAS G12)
cards.summary: Phase 1–2 report (Wolpin 2026, NEJM): daraxonrasib in 168 previously treated RAS-mutated pancreatic cancers — the 35% response rate comes from a 26-patient subgroup (second-line, 300 mg, RAS G12)
cards.people: Phase 1–2 multicentre study (RMC-6236-001) of oral daraxonrasib 10–400 mg once daily in advanced RAS-mutated solid tumours; this report covers the 168 patients with previously treated RAS-mutated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma who received 300 mg or less (300 mg was selected as the phase 3 dose). Primary endpoint was safety; antitumour activity was secondary.
cards.result: Treatment-related adverse events: any grade 96%, grade 3 or higher 30%; events in at least 10% included rash, diarrhoea, nausea, stomatitis/mucositis, vomiting and fatigue. In the subgroup of 26 patients with RAS G12 mutations treated second-line at 300 mg: objective response 35% (95% CI 17–56), median duration of response 8.2 months, median progression-free survival 8.5 months, median overall survival 13.1 months. In 38 patients with RAS G12, G13 or Q61 mutations: response 29% (95% CI 15–46), median overall survival 15.6 months.
cards.watchOut: SINGLE-ARM: there is no control group, so the survival figures (13.1 months in the 26-patient subgroup) cannot be compared with what second-line chemotherapy would have done in the same patients. The response estimate's confidence interval is wide (17–56%) because the subgroup is 26 patients. Funded by Revolution Medicines, the manufacturer.

cards.people: Systematic review (PRISMA 2020) of daraxonrasib in previously treated metastatic RAS-mutated pancreatic cancer, searching PubMed, Web of Science and ClinicalTrials.gov to July 2026: two studies met inclusion — RMC-6236-001 (n=168) and the phase 3 RASolute 302 trial (n=500 as reported) — 668 patients in total.
cards.result: For the published phase 1–2 study, the review's figures match the primary report (response 35% and median overall survival 13.1 months in the second-line RAS G12, 300 mg subgroup). The review also reports RASolute 302 results (overall survival 13.2 vs 6.6 months, HR 0.40; response 33.2% vs 11.8%) — but those numbers reach the review from congress/secondary reporting: no primary journal report of RASolute 302 was found on PubMed at this build, so they are fenced here and not carded as published evidence. Toxicity across the programme was mainly grade 1–2 dermatological and gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: A systematic review is only as published as its inputs: half of this one's evidence base is a trial whose primary report had not appeared in a journal when the review was written. Its risk-of-bias assessment treats RASolute 302 as a completed randomised trial, which it is — but the numbers available to readers remain congress-reported and could change at journal publication.

cards.headline: KRAS-targeted therapy meta-analysis (Fatima 2026): across 16 early-phase cohorts the pooled response rate was 38.9%, and 26.6% for pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors specifically — heterogeneous, largely single-arm data
cards.summary: KRAS-targeted therapy meta-analysis (Fatima 2026): across 16 early-phase cohorts the pooled response rate was 38.9%, and 26.6% for pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors specifically — heterogeneous, largely single-arm data
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of early-phase cohorts (Fatima 2026)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of KRAS/RAS-targeted therapy in locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: 1,008 patients from 16 cohorts across 7 trials; 15 single-arm cohorts (507 patients) contributed to the pooled proportion estimates; RASolute 302 was analysed separately and is not part of the pooled figures carded here.
cards.result: Pooled objective response rate 38.9% (95% CI 29.9–48.8) with high heterogeneity (I²=75.7%); by mechanism, pan-RAS(ON) inhibitors (the daraxonrasib class) pooled 26.6%, G12D-selective 31.0%, G12C-selective monotherapy 25.4%, and combination regimens 60.5%. Pooled disease control rate 87.6%. Grade 3-or-worse treatment-related adverse events occurred in 47.3% across the pooled cohorts. Response fell with later lines of therapy (32.5% after 3 or more prior lines).
cards.watchOut: This is a class-level pool, not a daraxonrasib trial: the 38.9% headline mixes drugs, combinations and treatment lines, and the heterogeneity (I²=75.7%) is high. The daraxonrasib-relevant figure is the pan-RAS(ON) subgroup (26.6%), which is consistent with — and derived from — the same single-arm cohorts as the primary report.
cards.source: Fatima F et al. shelves.title: PREOPANC-2: neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX vs gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy in resectable pancreatic cancer — no survival difference shown (HR 0.88, p=0.32); sibling of pack #4824
shelves.question: In adults with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, does neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX improve overall survival compared with neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy?
shelves.balance: No survival difference was shown. PREOPANC-2 (Janssen 2025, PMID 40945523) randomised 375 patients with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic cancer to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX or neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy (followed by adjuvant gemcitabine): median overall survival 21.9 vs 21.3 months (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69–1.13 — a relative measure; p=0.32). This is a null head-to-head between two active strategies, not evidence that either beats upfront surgery — that separate question, and the PREOPANC-1 and NORPACT-1 trials, are homed on pack #4824 and are not re-carded here. The choice between the two regimens therefore turns on toxicity and logistics: grade 3–4 diarrhoea was 23% with FOLFIRINOX vs 1% with chemoradiotherapy, neutropenia was similar (25% vs 22%), and serious adverse events were 49% vs 43%. Two prespecified/secondary analyses of the same trial add practical detail: staging laparoscopy at surgery cut non-therapeutic laparotomy (4.5% vs 17.1%; NNT 8), and venous thromboembolism occurred in 9% within a year and was associated with worse survival. PROPOSED: no difference shown between the regimens (the treatment made no difference to overall survival). The unpublished Alliance A021806 trial is not used as an anchor anywhere on this shelf.

cards.headline: PREOPANC-2 (Janssen 2025): neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX did NOT improve overall survival versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy — median 21.9 vs 21.3 months (HR 0.88; p=0.32)
cards.summary: PREOPANC-2 (Janssen 2025): neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX did NOT improve overall survival versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy — median 21.9 vs 21.3 months (HR 0.88; p=0.32)
cards.people: 375 patients aged 18 or older with resectable or borderline-resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and WHO performance status 0–1, randomised across 19 Dutch centres to neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX (8 cycles, then surgery, no adjuvant therapy; n=188) or neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy (3 cycles of gemcitabine with 36 Gy in 15 fractions during cycle 2, then surgery and 4 cycles of adjuvant gemcitabine; n=187). Six patients were excluded from the modified intention-to-treat population (369 analysed). Median follow-up 42.3 months.
cards.result: Median overall survival 21.9 months (95% CI 17.7–27.0) with FOLFIRINOX versus 21.3 months (16.8–25.5) with chemoradiotherapy (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69–1.13 — relative measure; p=0.32): no significant difference (the treatment made no difference to overall survival). Grade 3–4 adverse events: neutropenia 25% vs 22%, diarrhoea 23% vs 1%, leukopenia 8% vs 15%. Serious adverse events 49% vs 43%. Treatment-related deaths: 2 (1%) with FOLFIRINOX and 1 (1%) with chemoradiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A null result between two active neoadjuvant strategies: the confidence interval (HR 0.69–1.13) excludes a large FOLFIRINOX advantage but not a moderate one. The arms differ in more than the neoadjuvant regimen — only the chemoradiotherapy arm received adjuvant gemcitabine — so this is a comparison of two whole treatment strategies. Race and ethnicity data were not collected. This shelf does not answer whether either strategy beats upfront surgery (pack #4824).
cards.source: Janssen QP et al. Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX versus neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy in resectable and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (PREOPANC-2): a multicentre, open-label, phase 3 randomised trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2025. PMID: 40945523. Registry ID: EudraCT 2017-002036-17 (as stated in the record). cards.headline: PREOPANC-2 staging-laparoscopy analysis (Rompen 2026) — secondary report of the same trial: laparoscopy at surgery cut non-therapeutic laparotomy from 17.1% to 4.5% (NNT 8)
cards.summary: PREOPANC-2 staging-laparoscopy analysis (Rompen 2026) — secondary report of the same trial: laparoscopy at surgery cut non-therapeutic laparotomy from 17.1% to 4.5% (NNT 8)
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of the PREOPANC-2 trial (Rompen 2026) — not an independent trial
cards.people: Prespecified analysis within PREOPANC-2: of 369 randomised patients, 322 (87.2%) underwent surgical exploration after neoadjuvant treatment; 240 (74.5%) began with staging laparoscopy in the same session and 82 (25.5%) went straight to laparotomy.
cards.result: Occult metastases were found in 39 of 322 patients (12.1%) and were the reason surgery was aborted without resection in 90.5% of such cases. Non-therapeutic laparotomy was lower with staging laparoscopy (4.5% vs 17.1%; P=0.002; NNT 8). Tumour size 3 cm or more and baseline CA19-9 above 500 U/mL independently predicted occult metastases (risk 2.8% with neither factor, 14.8% with one, 28.9% with both).
cards.watchOut: Whether a patient received staging laparoscopy was not itself randomised — it was surgical practice within the trial — so the 4.5% vs 17.1% comparison is an observational contrast inside a randomised cohort, open to selection bias. It answers a surgical-workflow question, not the FOLFIRINOX-versus-chemoradiotherapy question.

cards.headline: PREOPANC-2 thromboembolism analysis (Willems 2026) — secondary report of the same trial: VTE in 9% within a year, more postoperative VTE after chemoradiotherapy (12% vs 3%), and VTE was associated with halved survival prospects (adjusted HR 2.13)
cards.summary: PREOPANC-2 thromboembolism analysis (Willems 2026) — secondary report of the same trial: VTE in 9% within a year, more postoperative VTE after chemoradiotherapy (12% vs 3%), and VTE was associated with halved survival prospects (adjusted HR 2.13)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of the PREOPANC-2 trial (Willems 2026) — not an independent trial
cards.people: Secondary analysis of 325 PREOPANC-2 patients, evaluating venous thromboembolism (symptomatic and incidental deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, splanchnic and catheter-related thrombosis) from randomisation to 12 months, and its association with overall survival.
cards.result: VTE was diagnosed in 28 of 325 patients (9%): 3% preoperatively and 8% postoperatively; 54% were symptomatic. Postoperative VTE was more frequent in the chemoradiotherapy arm (12% vs 3% with FOLFIRINOX; P=.02), but the 12-month cumulative incidence did not differ significantly (11% vs 6%; P=.06). Two patients in the chemoradiotherapy arm died of pulmonary-embolism-related causes. VTE was independently associated with reduced overall survival (adjusted time-varying HR 2.13, a relative measure; P=.002).
cards.watchOut: VTE ascertainment was retrospective within the trial, and the survival association (HR 2.13) is observational — VTE may mark more aggressive disease rather than cause the deaths. The arm difference rests on postoperative events only and the overall 12-month comparison was not significant (P=.06); do not read it as proof that chemoradiotherapy causes more clots overall.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 3 trial, three reports — no survival difference between the two neoadjuvant strategies; the regimen choice is a toxicity-and-logistics choice
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 3 trial, three reports — no survival difference between the two neoadjuvant strategies; the regimen choice is a toxicity-and-logistics choice
cards.people: One randomised phase 3 trial (PREOPANC-2, 375 randomised patients) reported in a primary paper and two secondary analyses (staging laparoscopy; thromboembolism). The neoadjuvant-versus-upfront-surgery question and PREOPANC-1/NORPACT-1 are homed on pack #4824 and deliberately not re-carded here.
cards.result: Overall survival: HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.69–1.13; p=0.32) — no difference shown (the treatment made no difference). Toxicity trade-offs: grade 3–4 diarrhoea 23% vs 1% favouring chemoradiotherapy; serious adverse events 49% vs 43%. Secondary findings: staging laparoscopy NNT 8 to prevent one non-therapeutic laparotomy; VTE incidence 9% at 12 months. PROPOSED: no survival difference between neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX and neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Three cards but one trial: the secondary analyses share the primary trial's patients and add no independent weight to the survival comparison. A future report of Alliance A021806 (perioperative mFOLFIRINOX vs upfront surgery) would address a different comparison and does not change this head-to-head null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Janssen QP et al. The Lancet. Oncology. 2025 (PMID: 40945523); Rompen IF et al. Annals of surgery. 2026 (PMID: 41673930); Willems RAL et al. shelves.title: Amifostine cytoprotection: grade ≥2 acute xerostomia 51% versus 78% without it in head-and-neck radiotherapy, and less cisplatin kidney and nerve toxicity in ovarian cancer — with no sign of tumour protection
shelves.question: In adults receiving radiotherapy (head-and-neck, thoracic) or cisplatin-based chemotherapy, does amifostine reduce moderate-to-severe xerostomia, mucositis, nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity versus no cytoprotection, without protecting the tumour?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for xerostomia and for cisplatin cumulative toxicity, with the mucositis claim split. In the phase III head-and-neck trial (Brizel 2000; 303 patients in the 2-year report), daily intravenous amifostine before each fraction cut grade ≥2 acute xerostomia from 78% to 51% and grade ≥2 chronic xerostomia from 57% to 34%, with median saliva production 0.26 g versus 0.10 g — but it did NOT reduce mucositis in that trial. In ovarian cancer (Kemp 1996, 242 patients), amifostine before cyclophosphamide/cisplatin reduced protracted creatinine elevations, ≥40% falls in creatinine clearance, neurologic toxicity severity and febrile-neutropenia hospital care, with pathologic response 37% versus 28% and median survival 31 months in both arms. A 17-trial meta-analysis found relative reductions in grade 3–4 mucositis, acute and late xerostomia and dysphagia with radiotherapy alone, but NO significant benefit in the concomitant-chemoradiotherapy subgroup. The tumour-protection fear is answered by an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 12 trials (1,119 patients): hazard ratio for death 0.98 (95% CI 0.84–1.14). The fetched records name the drug only as amifostine (generic); no brand or company is named in these records. Costs on the face: nausea/vomiting in 53% of patients (5% of doses), transient hypotension and allergic reactions.

cards.headline: Brizel 2000: amifostine cut grade ≥2 acute xerostomia from 78% to 51% and chronic xerostomia from 57% to 34% — but did not reduce mucositis
cards.summary: Brizel 2000: amifostine cut grade ≥2 acute xerostomia from 78% to 51% and chronic xerostomia from 57% to 34% — but did not reduce mucositis
cards.people: Patients with previously untreated head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma receiving once-daily radiotherapy (50–70 Gy); amifostine 200 mg/m² intravenously 15–30 minutes before each fraction versus radiotherapy alone. The companion 2-year report gives the analysed population as 150 amifostine and 153 control patients (303 total).
cards.result: Grade ≥2 acute xerostomia occurred in 51% with amifostine versus 78% without (P<.0001); grade ≥2 chronic xerostomia 34% versus 57% (P=.002). Median saliva production was 0.26 g versus 0.10 g (P=.04). Amifostine did not reduce mucositis. Two-year local-regional control was 58% versus 63%, disease-free survival 53% versus 57% and overall survival 71% versus 66% (amifostine versus control). Nausea and/or vomiting occurred in 53% of amifostine patients but with only 233 (5%) of 4,314 doses; hypotension and allergic reactions were the other common effects.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design (the 2-year report describes open-label amifostine), so patient-reported dryness is vulnerable to expectation bias; the objective saliva measurement points the same way. The mucositis null in this largest trial conflicts with the pooled meta-analysis card below — the split is printed, not smoothed over.
cards.source: Brizel DM et al. Phase III randomized trial of amifostine as a radioprotector in head and neck cancer. Journal of clinical oncology. 2000. PMID: 11013273.
