cards.headline: Wasserman 2005 (2-year follow-up of the Brizel trial): the xerostomia benefit persisted at 24 months, with no difference in locoregional control or survival
cards.summary: Wasserman 2005 (2-year follow-up of the Brizel trial): the xerostomia benefit persisted at 24 months, with no difference in locoregional control or survival
cards.type: Randomised phase III trial, 2-year follow-up report (Wasserman 2005) — second report of the Brizel trial, not an independent trial
cards.people: The same head-and-neck radiotherapy population as the Brizel 2000 card: 150 patients given open-label amifostine 200 mg/m² intravenously before each fraction and 153 controls, followed for chronic xerostomia and tumour outcomes at 18 and 24 months.
cards.result: Amifostine was associated with a reduced incidence of grade ≥2 xerostomia over 2 years (p=0.002), a higher proportion of patients with meaningful (>0.1 g) unstimulated saliva production at 24 months (p=0.011), and lower mouth-dryness scores at 24 months (p<0.001). Locoregional control, progression-free survival and overall survival were not significantly different between groups.
cards.watchOut: This is a follow-up report of the trial on the previous card — it extends the same evidence, it does not replicate it. Count the programme once when weighing the shelf.

cards.headline: Kemp 1996: in 242 women with advanced ovarian cancer, amifostine before cyclophosphamide/cisplatin reduced kidney, nerve and febrile-neutropenia toxicity — discontinuation for toxicity 9% versus 24%
cards.summary: Kemp 1996: in 242 women with advanced ovarian cancer, amifostine before cyclophosphamide/cisplatin reduced kidney, nerve and febrile-neutropenia toxicity — discontinuation for toxicity 9% versus 24%
cards.people: 242 patients with advanced ovarian cancer randomised to six cycles of cyclophosphamide 1,000 mg/m² plus cisplatin 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks, with or without amifostine 910 mg/m² before each cycle; haematologic, renal, neurologic and ototoxicity were evaluated, with pathologic tumour response and survival as efficacy measures.
cards.result: Amifostine reduced grade 4 neutropenia with fever/infection requiring antibiotics (P=.005), days in hospital (P=.019) and days on antibiotics (P=.031). Platinum-specific toxicities were reduced: protracted serum creatinine elevations (P=0.004), ≥40% reduction in creatinine clearance (P=.001) and severity of neurologic toxicity (P=.029). Discontinuation for protocol-specified toxicity was 9% with amifostine versus 24% without (P=.002). Pathologic tumour response was 37% versus 28% and median survival was 31 months in both groups. Principal side effects were emesis and transient blood-pressure falls.
cards.watchOut: A 1996 trial of a high-dose cisplatin regimen no longer typical; ototoxicity was evaluated but the abstract reports no separate ototoxicity result, so this shelf makes no hearing claim. The record names the drug only as amifostine; no product brand or company is given.
cards.source: Kemp G et al. Amifostine pretreatment for protection against cyclophosphamide-induced and cisplatin-induced toxicities: results of a randomized control trial in patients with advanced ovarian cancer. Journal of clinical oncology. 1996. PMID: 8683243. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gu 2014 meta-analysis (17 RCTs, 1,167 patients): relative risk 0.72 for grade 3–4 mucositis and 0.60 for late xerostomia with radiotherapy — but no significant benefit in the chemoradiotherapy subgroup
cards.summary: Gu 2014 meta-analysis (17 RCTs, 1,167 patients): relative risk 0.72 for grade 3–4 mucositis and 0.60 for late xerostomia with radiotherapy — but no significant benefit in the chemoradiotherapy subgroup
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Gu 2014)
cards.people: Seventeen randomised trials in 1,167 patients (604 amifostine, 563 control) with head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma treated with radiotherapy, pooled for mucositis, xerostomia, dysphagia, tumour response and haematologic toxicity.
cards.result: Amifostine reduced grade 3–4 mucositis (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.54–0.95), grade 2–4 acute xerostomia (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.52–0.96), late xerostomia (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.74) and grade 3–4 dysphagia (relative risk 0.39, 95% CI 0.17–0.92) — all relative measures. In the concomitant-chemoradiotherapy subgroup, none of these reductions was statistically significant. There was no tumour-protective signal: complete response relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.89–1.17). Grade 3–4 amifostine side effects averaged 5% nausea, 6% emesis, 4% hypotension and 4% allergy.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mucositis benefit is driven by radiotherapy-alone trials and disappears with chemoradiotherapy — the opposite emphasis from the Brizel trial's own null mucositis result is a genuine split in this literature, and relative risks are printed without the underlying absolute rates, which the review does not give.
cards.source: Gu J et al. Effect of amifostine in head and neck cancer patients treated with radiotherapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis based on randomized controlled trials. PloS one. 2014. PMID: 24788761. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bourhis 2011 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (12 trials, 1,119 patients): amifostine did not reduce survival — hazard ratio for death 0.98 (95% CI 0.84–1.14)
cards.summary: Bourhis 2011 individual-patient-data meta-analysis (12 trials, 1,119 patients): amifostine did not reduce survival — hazard ratio for death 0.98 (95% CI 0.84–1.14)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of individual patient data from randomised trials (Bourhis 2011)
cards.people: Individual data from 12 randomised trials (1,119 patients analysed; median follow-up 5.2 years) in non-small-cell lung, head-and-neck and pelvic cancers treated with radiotherapy alone (431 patients) or chemoradiotherapy (688 patients), randomised to amifostine or not.
cards.result: The hazard ratio for death was 0.98 (95% CI 0.84–1.14; P=.78) and for progression, relapse or death 1.05 (95% CI 0.90–1.22; P=.53), with no significant heterogeneity and no variation of effect by sex, age, tumour site, stage, histology, treatment type or route of administration. The authors concluded amifostine did not reduce overall or progression-free survival.
cards.watchOut: This card answers only the tumour-protection question; it does not add toxicity-benefit evidence. Four otherwise-eligible trials (435 patients) were excluded after data checking, which the authors report openly.

cards.headline: Synthesis: xerostomia and cisplatin-toxicity protection are real; mucositis protection is split; tumour protection is not seen
cards.summary: Synthesis: xerostomia and cisplatin-toxicity protection are real; mucositis protection is split; tumour protection is not seen
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase III head-and-neck radiotherapy programme reported twice (Brizel 2000 / Wasserman 2005; 303 patients), one randomised ovarian-cancer cisplatin trial (Kemp 1996; 242 patients), one 17-trial meta-analysis (1,167 patients) and one 12-trial individual-patient-data survival meta-analysis (1,119 patients).
cards.result: Grade ≥2 acute xerostomia 51% versus 78% and chronic 34% versus 57% in the direct trial; cisplatin kidney and nerve toxicity significantly reduced in the ovarian trial; pooled relative risks favoured amifostine for mucositis and xerostomia with radiotherapy alone but not with chemoradiotherapy; survival hazard ratio 0.98 with amifostine. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for xerostomia and cisplatin cytoprotection, with the mucositis split and the daily-infusion burden (nausea/vomiting in 53% of patients, transient hypotension) on the face.
cards.watchOut: The fetched records name the drug only by its generic name, amifostine; no brand or manufacturer is stated in them, so none is printed here. Ototoxicity protection was a stated aim of the Kemp trial but no separate hearing result is reported in its record — no ototoxicity claim is made on this shelf.

shelves.title: Dexrazoxane for anthracycline extravasation: surgery was avoided in 53 of 54 patients in the two prospective single-arm licensing studies — no randomised or comparative study exists
shelves.question: In patients with anthracycline extravasation from a central or peripheral line, does intravenous dexrazoxane (the extravasation formulation tested in the licensing programme) prevent tissue necrosis and the need for surgery versus conservative management?
mesh: Extravasation of Diagnostic and Therapeutic Materials
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — single-arm evidence only, and the shelf says so on its face: NO randomised or comparative study of dexrazoxane for anthracycline extravasation exists. The entire prospective base is two open-label, single-arm, multicentre licensing studies reported together (Mouridsen 2007): in 54 assessable patients with biopsy-verified extravasation treated within 6 hours with the 3-day dexrazoxane schedule, 53 (98.2%) avoided surgery-requiring necrosis and one (1.8%) needed debridement; 71% continued scheduled chemotherapy without postponement. A Belgian clinical-practice survey (Fontaine 2012, retrospective; 41 patients) points the same way: debridement avoided in 95% (39/41). The product is named in the licensing record as Savene (EU) / Totect (US); no manufacturer is named in the fetched record. Because there is no untreated comparator, the 98% figure cannot be read as a treatment effect — some extravasations resolve with conservative care alone, and this shelf cannot say how many. The liposomal-anthracycline slice is weaker still (17 published cases, dexrazoxane in only 3).

cards.headline: Mouridsen 2007 (the two prospective licensing studies): 53 of 54 patients (98.2%) with biopsy-verified anthracycline extravasation avoided surgery after dexrazoxane — single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: Mouridsen 2007 (the two prospective licensing studies): 53 of 54 patients (98.2%) with biopsy-verified anthracycline extravasation avoided surgery after dexrazoxane — single-arm, no comparator
cards.type: Two prospective, open-label, single-arm, multicentre studies reported together (Mouridsen 2007)
cards.people: Patients with fluorescence-positive, biopsy-verified anthracycline extravasation, treated with intravenous dexrazoxane [named in the record as Savene (EU), Totect (US)] on a 3-day schedule (1,000, 1,000 and 500 mg/m²) starting no later than 6 hours after the incident; 54 patients were assessable for efficacy (need for surgical resection), with follow-up for 3 months.
cards.result: In 53 of 54 assessable patients (98.2%) the treatment prevented surgery-requiring necrosis; one patient (1.8%) required surgical debridement. Thirty-eight patients (71%) continued scheduled chemotherapy without postponement; 22 (41%) were hospitalised because of the extravasation. Mild pain (19%) and mild sensory disturbances (17%) were the most frequent sequelae; other toxicity was transient transaminase elevation, nausea and injection-site pain, alongside the expected haematologic toxicity of the ongoing chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm by design: there is no conservative-management group, so the counterfactual — how many of these extravasations would have healed without an antidote — is unknown. Entry required biopsy verification and treatment within 6 hours, a selected, promptly-treated population. No manufacturer is named in the fetched record.

cards.headline: Fontaine 2012 (Belgian practice survey, retrospective): debridement avoided in 39 of 41 patients (95%) treated with Savene in routine practice, including 26 of 28 central-line extravasations
cards.summary: Fontaine 2012 (Belgian practice survey, retrospective): debridement avoided in 39 of 41 patients (95%) treated with Savene in routine practice, including 26 of 28 central-line extravasations
cards.people: 41 cancer patients treated with Savene (dexrazoxane) for anthracycline extravasation in Belgian hospitals, 2007–2010, identified by questionnaire to 44 hospitals; 28 of 41 (68%) extravasations were from central venous catheters.
cards.result: Surgical debridement was avoided in 26 of 28 central-access extravasations and in 95% (39/41) of all treated patients. Planned chemotherapy was maintained in 73% (30/41). Eight adverse events were reported in four patients: six grade 1–2 events (nausea, leucopenia, arm pain) and two grade 3 events (neutropenia, pancytopenia).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective survey data with questionnaire ascertainment — hospitals that used the antidote and replied are the denominator, and there is again no untreated comparison group. Concordance with the licensing studies is reassuring about feasibility, not proof of effect size.
cards.source: Fontaine C et al. Savene® (dexrazoxane) use in clinical practice. Supportive care in cancer. 2012. PMID: 22278308. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Caballero Romero 2018 (liposomal anthracyclines): only 17 published human cases, dexrazoxane given in just 3 — the liposomal slice rests on case-level evidence
cards.summary: Caballero Romero 2018 (liposomal anthracyclines): only 17 published human cases, dexrazoxane given in just 3 — the liposomal slice rests on case-level evidence
cards.type: Literature review of published cases (Caballero Romero 2018)
cards.people: Seventeen published human cases of extravasation of liposomal or pegylated liposomal anthracyclines (liposomal doxorubicin 9, liposomal daunorubicin 4, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin 4), identified from PubMed and Embase; general extravasation measures were applied in all patients and dexrazoxane in only three.
cards.result: All cases were completely resolved at 2–3 months except one patient, in whom dexrazoxane was not used. The reviewers concluded general measures may be inadequate and each case should be evaluated individually for (off-label) dexrazoxane until scientific evidence on its effectiveness and safety for these formulations is available.
cards.watchOut: This card marks the boundary of the evidence, not support for it: 17 cases, 3 antidote-treated, no comparison. It must not be pooled with the conventional-anthracycline licensing data above — the formulations' pharmacokinetics differ, as the reviewers state.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent single-arm story — surgery rarely needed after prompt dexrazoxane — with the size of the true effect unknowable without a comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent single-arm story — surgery rarely needed after prompt dexrazoxane — with the size of the true effect unknowable without a comparator
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective single-arm licensing studies (54 assessable patients), one retrospective practice survey (41 patients), and one case-literature review for liposomal formulations (17 cases). No randomised or comparative study exists in this literature.
cards.result: Surgery-requiring necrosis occurred in 1 of 54 prospectively treated patients (1.8%) and debridement was avoided in 39 of 41 survey patients (95%); chemotherapy continued on schedule in about 71–73%. shelves.title: Magnesium for cisplatin kidney protection: the large observational base points one way (adjusted odds ratio 0.80 in 13,719 patients; pooled odds ratio 0.24 in observational meta-analysis) — the randomised trials are small and mixed
shelves.question: In adults receiving high-dose cisplatin, does supplemental magnesium (intravenous or oral, added to standard saline hydration) reduce cisplatin-induced kidney injury (creatinine rise / KDIGO stage) versus hydration alone?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a mixed randomised/retrospective base, with designs labelled card by card and never pooled into one claim. The largest report is observational: a 5-centre US cohort of 13,719 patients (Gupta 2025) found cisplatin-associated AKI or death in 2.7% with first-day intravenous magnesium versus 5.3% without (adjusted odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97). A systematic review (Hamroun 2019) could meta-analyse only the 15 observational magnesium studies (1,841 patients) and found a pooled odds ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.19–0.32) — a much larger apparent effect than the best-adjusted cohort, which is itself a warning about confounding. The randomised evidence is two small trials pointing in different strengths: a double-blind phase II trial in ovarian cancer (Bodnar 2008, 40 eligible) showed significantly less GFR decline with magnesium on all three measures, while the pilot PRAGMATIC trial (30 patients, weekly low-dose cisplatin) found similar acute AKI (4.6% versus 1.3% of cycles) but less acute kidney disease over the course (6.7% versus 46.7%). The retrospective Kidera cohort (401 patients) found magnesium associated with a risk ratio of 0.175 for nephrotoxicity. Observational designs cap this shelf at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Gupta 2025 (5-centre cohort, 13,719 patients): cisplatin AKI or death in 2.7% with first-day IV magnesium versus 5.3% without — adjusted odds ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97)
cards.summary: Gupta 2025 (5-centre cohort, 13,719 patients): cisplatin AKI or death in 2.7% with first-day IV magnesium versus 5.3% without — adjusted odds ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97)
cards.people: 13,719 adults with cancer treated with a first dose of intravenous cisplatin at five US cancer centres (2006–2022); 3,893 (28.4%) received intravenous magnesium on the first cisplatin day (median dose 2 g). The composite outcome was cisplatin-associated AKI (≥2-fold creatinine rise or kidney replacement therapy within 14 days) or death, analysed with inverse-probability weighting and adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, concurrent nephrotoxic therapies, site, year and cisplatin dose.
cards.result: AKI or death occurred in 104 of 3,893 patients (2.7%) who received magnesium versus 520 of 9,826 (5.3%) who did not (adjusted odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97). Results were similar across sensitivity analyses, alternative AKI definitions and major adverse kidney events at 90 days. The authors state randomised trials are needed to confirm the finding.
cards.watchOut: Observational: magnesium was given by clinician/centre practice, not randomisation, so residual confounding (hydration volume, cisplatin dose intensity, centre effects) can manufacture part or all of a 20% relative odds reduction. This is the most conservative effect estimate on the shelf — compare it with the pooled observational odds ratio of 0.24 on the Hamroun card before quoting either.

cards.headline: Bodnar 2008 (double-blind randomised phase II, 40 patients): magnesium supplementation significantly blunted the GFR fall across six cisplatin courses (creatinine P=0.0069)
cards.summary: Bodnar 2008 (double-blind randomised phase II, 40 patients): magnesium supplementation significantly blunted the GFR fall across six cisplatin courses (creatinine P=0.0069)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial (Bodnar 2008)
cards.people: 41 women with epithelial ovarian cancer randomised (40 eligible) to paclitaxel 135 mg/m² plus cisplatin 75 mg/m² every 3 weeks for six courses, with either magnesium (5 g magnesium sulphate intravenously before each course plus oral magnesium subcarbonate 500 mg three times daily between courses) or matching placebo; GFR was tracked by creatinine, Cockcroft-Gault and MDRD formulae.
cards.result: Serum magnesium differed significantly between groups (p<0.0001), and the placebo group showed a significantly greater decrease in GFR by every measure: creatinine (p=0.0069), Cockcroft-Gault clearance (p=0.0077) and MDRD (p=0.032). The authors concluded magnesium supplementation was nephroprotective during cisplatin chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, surrogate GFR-formula endpoints rather than clinical AKI events, and a combined intravenous-plus-oral regimen — it cannot separate which route, if either alone, carries the effect. It is the only double-blind randomised card on this shelf and it is small.
cards.source: Bodnar L et al. cards.headline: PRAGMATIC pilot RCT (30 patients): acute AKI was similar (4.6% vs 1.3% of cycles) but acute kidney disease over the course was 6.7% with magnesium preload versus 46.7% without (hazard ratio 0.082)
cards.summary: PRAGMATIC pilot RCT (30 patients): acute AKI was similar (4.6% vs 1.3% of cycles) but acute kidney disease over the course was 6.7% with magnesium preload versus 46.7% without (hazard ratio 0.082)
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial, single-blind (Suppadungsuk 2022, PRAGMATIC)
cards.people: 30 patients with head-and-neck cancer receiving weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² for 7–8 weeks, randomised to pre-cisplatin saline hydration (500 mL 0.9% NaCl with KCl over 4 hours) with or without an additional 16 mEq magnesium in the infusion. Acute kidney injury was a creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 7 days; acute kidney disease was the same rise from baseline by the last measurement.
cards.result: Per-cycle AKI incidence was similar (4.6% control versus 1.3% magnesium), but acute kidney disease developed in 46.7% of controls versus 6.7% of the magnesium group (hazard ratio 0.082, 95% CI 0.008–0.79; P=0.03), and time to kidney disease was significantly shorter in controls (P=0.007). Tumour response and survival were comparable. Baseline creatinine was lower in controls (0.70 versus 0.87 mg/dL, P=0.01) despite randomisation.
cards.watchOut: A 30-patient pilot with a baseline creatinine imbalance against the magnesium arm and a very wide hazard-ratio confidence interval (0.008–0.79): the direction is encouraging, the size is not estimable. Weekly low-dose cisplatin is not the high-dose setting of the question's other cards.
cards.source: Suppadungsuk S et al. Preloading magnesium attenuates cisplatin-associated nephrotoxicity: pilot randomized controlled trial (PRAGMATIC study). ESMO open. 2022. PMID: 34953401. cards.headline: Kidera 2014 (retrospective, 401 patients): IV magnesium was associated with a risk ratio of 0.175 for grade ≥2 creatinine rise after high-dose cisplatin
cards.summary: Kidera 2014 (retrospective, 401 patients): IV magnesium was associated with a risk ratio of 0.175 for grade ≥2 creatinine rise after high-dose cisplatin
cards.people: 401 patients receiving first-line chemotherapy including high-dose cisplatin (≥60 mg/m²); nephrotoxicity was a creatinine rise of at least CTCAE grade 2 during the first course. Intravenous magnesium was given to 67 patients (17%).
cards.result: Nephrotoxicity occurred in 127 patients (32%). On multivariable analysis, performance status 2 (risk ratio 1.876, P=0.004) and regular NSAID use (risk ratio 1.357, P=0.047) increased risk, while intravenous magnesium was associated with a significantly reduced risk (risk ratio 0.175, P=0.0004) and with significantly less severe creatinine rises (P=0.012). Developing hypomagnesaemia during treatment was associated with greater creatinine increases (P=0.0025).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and small in the exposed group (67 patients): a risk ratio of 0.175 — an apparent 82.5% relative reduction — is far larger than the best-adjusted large cohort's odds ratio of 0.80, and that disagreement between observational estimates is the honest headline about this design class.
cards.source: Kidera Y et al. Risk factors for cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity and potential of magnesium supplementation for renal protection. PloS one. 2014. PMID: 25020203. cards.headline: Hamroun 2019 (systematic review): the only meta-analysable magnesium evidence was observational — 15 studies, 1,841 patients, pooled odds ratio 0.24 for cisplatin AKI
cards.summary: Hamroun 2019 (systematic review): the only meta-analysable magnesium evidence was observational — 15 studies, 1,841 patients, pooled odds ratio 0.24 for cisplatin AKI
cards.people: Fifty-one studies of 21 cisplatin-AKI prevention methods in adults; a meta-analysis was possible only for magnesium supplementation, using 15 observational studies in 1,841 patients, with AKI defined by KDIGO (2012) criteria.
cards.result: Magnesium supplementation showed a significant nephroprotective association for all combined AKI grades (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.19–0.32; I²=0.0%), and separately for grade 2 (odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.14–0.33) and grade 3 (odds ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.08–0.76) injury. The reviewers concluded that no prevention method had demonstrated indisputable efficacy, while highlighting magnesium's potential protective effect.
cards.watchOut: Every pooled study was observational — the review itself is the proof that the randomised base was too thin to pool. A pooled odds ratio of 0.24 from non-randomised data should be read as an upper bound on plausibility, not an effect estimate.
cards.source: Hamroun A et al. Prevention of Cisplatin-Induced Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Drugs. 2019. PMID: 31429065. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: every design points the same way and none is decisive — the randomised trials total 70 patients, the cohorts disagree on size by fourfold
cards.summary: Synthesis: every design points the same way and none is decisive — the randomised trials total 70 patients, the cohorts disagree on size by fourfold
cards.people: The carded evidence: two small randomised trials (40 and 30 patients), two retrospective cohorts (13,719 and 401 patients) and one systematic review whose magnesium meta-analysis rests on 15 observational studies (1,841 patients). Designs are labelled on each card and are not pooled here.
cards.result: Randomised: significantly less GFR decline (Bodnar) and less cumulative kidney disease (PRAGMATIC), on surrogate/course endpoints. Observational: adjusted odds ratio 0.80 in the largest cohort versus a pooled odds ratio of 0.24 across smaller observational studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction is consistent, mechanism (cisplatin-induced magnesium wasting) is coherent, but the effect size is unestablished and a definitive randomised trial does not yet exist in the carded record.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 0.24 pooled odds ratio or the 0.175 risk ratio as the effect of magnesium — both come from designs prone to confounding by hydration practice and centre. The Gupta cohort's 0.80 is the most defensible single number on this shelf, and it is still observational.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gupta S et al. JAMA Oncol. 2025 (PMID: 40272825); Bodnar L et al. Eur J Cancer. 2008 (PMID: 18796350); Suppadungsuk S et al. ESMO Open. 2022 (PMID: 34953401); Kidera Y et al. PLoS One. 2014 (PMID: 25020203); Hamroun A et al. Drugs. 2019 (PMID: 31429065).

shelves.title: Radiation-induced nausea and vomiting beyond the abdomen: one small total-body-irradiation trial (6 of 10 completed without rescue on ondansetron versus 0 of 10 on placebo) and field-based guideline stratification — the direct evidence outside the abdomen is thin
shelves.question: In adults receiving radiotherapy outside the abdomen — pelvic, thoracic, head-and-neck or total-body irradiation — does prophylactic 5-HT3-antagonist therapy (ondansetron, granisetron or palonosetron) prevent radiation-induced nausea and vomiting versus placebo or rescue-only treatment, and how does risk vary by irradiated field?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for the beyond-abdomen slice specifically. This pack is the PARTIAL companion to Shelf #6134, which homes the abdominal-radiotherapy question (Franzén placebo trial and the Priestman active-comparator trials — none of those reports is re-carded here). Outside the abdomen, the direct placebo evidence found is a single 20-patient total-body-irradiation trial (Spitzer 1994): oral ondansetron produced significantly fewer emetic episodes (P=.005), and 6 of 10 ondansetron patients completed 4 days of TBI without rescue versus 0 of 10 on placebo. A multicentre trial of ondansetron orally-disintegrating tablets for ESTABLISHED emesis during fractionated radiotherapy to thorax-to-pelvis sites (LeBourgeois 1999; N not documented in the record) found the active drug superior to placebo over 12 hours — treatment evidence, not prophylaxis. The only pelvic-field prophylaxis report carded is single-arm: palonosetron plus prednisolone during cervical chemoradiotherapy left a 57% probability of completing five cycles without emesis (Ruhlmann 2013, 48 patients). The MASCC/ESMO guidelines (2016, reaffirmed 2023) stratify prophylaxis by field — upper abdomen highest risk, with 5-HT3 antagonists the cornerstone for high and moderate emetic-risk radiotherapy — but state plainly that no new randomised prophylaxis data supported changed recommendations, i.e. the field recommendations rest largely on the abdominal evidence homed at #6134 plus expert consensus.

cards.headline: Spitzer 1994 (total-body irradiation): oral ondansetron gave significantly fewer emetic episodes than placebo (P=.005); 6 of 10 patients needed no rescue versus 0 of 10 on placebo
cards.summary: Spitzer 1994 (total-body irradiation): oral ondansetron gave significantly fewer emetic episodes than placebo (P=.005); 6 of 10 patients needed no rescue versus 0 of 10 on placebo
cards.people: 20 patients receiving 4 days of fractionated total-body irradiation as preparation for bone-marrow transplantation, randomised to oral ondansetron 8 mg or placebo, double-blind, with intravenous ondansetron as first rescue after repeated emetic episodes.
cards.result: Patients on oral ondansetron had significantly fewer emetic episodes over the 4 days (P=.005) and a significantly later onset of emesis or rescue (P=.003). Six of 10 ondansetron patients completed the study without additional antiemetic therapy, while none of 10 placebo patients did; six placebo patients given intravenous ondansetron rescue then needed no further antiemetics. No relation was seen between ondansetron blood levels and emetic episodes.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients in a transplant-conditioning setting — the smallest cardable trial, and the ONLY direct placebo-controlled prophylaxis trial outside the abdomen found this session. Total-body irradiation is also the highest-emetic-risk field, so the result does not transfer automatically to pelvic or thoracic fields.
cards.source: Spitzer TR et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 1994. PMID: 7964960. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LeBourgeois 1999: for established emesis during fractionated radiotherapy to thorax-to-pelvis sites, ondansetron orally-disintegrating tablets beat placebo over 12 hours (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: LeBourgeois 1999: for established emesis during fractionated radiotherapy to thorax-to-pelvis sites, ondansetron orally-disintegrating tablets beat placebo over 12 hours (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre trial of treatment for established emesis (LeBourgeois 1999)
cards.people: Patients who developed emesis and/or moderate-to-severe nausea during fractionated radiotherapy to sites between the thorax and the pelvis, randomised to ondansetron orally-disintegrating tablets 8 mg, 16 mg or placebo. The fetched record does not state the number of patients — N not documented.
cards.result: Both ondansetron doses were clinically superior to placebo in treating emesis and nausea successfully over the 12 hours after dosing, with no significant difference between 8 mg and 16 mg; in the first 2 hours, ondansetron patients had significantly fewer emetic episodes and significantly less nausea than placebo patients. The authors concluded the 8 mg orally-disintegrating tablet is effective for radiotherapy-induced emesis and nausea.
cards.watchOut: This is a treatment trial in patients already symptomatic, not a prophylaxis trial — it shows the drug class works against radiation emesis in these fields but does not measure prevention. The record gives no patient number and no event rates, so no quantitative claim beyond the reported significance is made on this card.
cards.source: LeBourgeois JP et al. Efficacy of an ondansetron orally disintegrating tablet: a novel oral formulation of this 5-HT(3) receptor antagonist in the treatment of fractionated radiotherapy-induced nausea and emesis. Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain)). 1999. PMID: 10591823. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ruhlmann 2013 (pelvic chemoradiotherapy, single-arm): palonosetron plus prednisolone left a 57% probability of completing 5 weekly cisplatin-radiation cycles without emesis — judged insufficient by its own authors
cards.summary: Ruhlmann 2013 (pelvic chemoradiotherapy, single-arm): palonosetron plus prednisolone left a 57% probability of completing 5 weekly cisplatin-radiation cycles without emesis — judged insufficient by its own authors
cards.type: Prospective single-arm phase II study (Ruhlmann 2013) — no comparator
cards.people: 48 patients with gynaecological cancer receiving fractionated pelvic radiotherapy with five cycles of concomitant weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m² at two Danish departments, given palonosetron plus prednisolone prophylaxis, with daily diaries of emesis, nausea grade and rescue use over 5 weeks (155 weekly cycles completed).
cards.result: The probability of completing five cycles without emesis (sustained no emesis) was 57%. Freedom from nausea fell from 42% of patients in cycle 1 to 23% continuously free after five cycles, and half the patients used rescue antiemetics at least once. The authors concluded this prophylaxis was insufficient for radiotherapy-plus-weekly-cisplatin nausea and vomiting and that adding a neurokinin-1 antagonist should be tested in a randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, and a chemoradiotherapy population — cisplatin contributes emetogenicity that pure pelvic radiotherapy does not, so the 57% figure cannot be read as the performance of palonosetron against radiation alone. Its value here is as the only pelvic-field prophylaxis report found, and as an honesty check on extrapolation.
cards.source: Ruhlmann CH et al. cards.headline: MASCC/ESMO 2016 RINV guideline: 5-HT3 antagonists remain the cornerstone for high- and moderate-risk fields — and the update found NO new randomised prophylaxis studies to change any recommendation
cards.summary: MASCC/ESMO 2016 RINV guideline: 5-HT3 antagonists remain the cornerstone for high- and moderate-risk fields — and the update found NO new randomised prophylaxis studies to change any recommendation
cards.type: Guideline consensus based on systematic literature review (Ruhlmann 2017, MASCC/ESMO 2016 update)
cards.people: Systematic review for the MASCC/ESMO Antiemetic Guidelines Update 2016: 926 records screened for radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (2009–2015), 18 publications finally included; the committee reclassified craniospinal radiotherapy from low to moderate emetic risk and adjusted other field risk levels by expert opinion.
cards.result: The only fully published randomised prevention studies found were two NEGATIVE studies (acupuncture and green tea). No data supported new antiemetic-prophylaxis recommendations; serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonists remained the cornerstone for high- and moderate-emetic-risk radiotherapy. The 2023 update (same committee) again retained only 20 publications from 343 references, changed the low-risk category to rescue-only, and left the drug choices unchanged.
cards.watchOut: A guideline card, not trial evidence: its field-by-field recommendations for non-abdominal sites rest on the abdominal trial base (homed on Shelf #6134), the small studies carded above, and expert consensus. The guideline's own literature yield — no new positive randomised prophylaxis trial in either update window — is the most informative number on this card.

cards.search: mascc/esmo 2016 rinv guideline: 5-ht3 antagonists remain the cornerstone for high- and moderate-risk fields — and the update found no new randomised prophylaxis studies to change any recommendation mascc/esmo 2016 rinv guideline: 5-ht3 antagonists remain the cornerstone for high- and moderate-risk fields — and the update found no new randomised prophylaxis studies to change any recommendation in adults receiving radiotherapy outside the abdomen — pelvic, thoracic, head-and-neck or total-body irradiation — does prophylactic 5-ht3-antagonist therapy (ondansetron, granisetron or palonosetron) prevent radiation-induced nausea and vomiting versus placebo or rescue-only treatment, and how does risk vary by irradiated field? guideline consensus based on systematic literature review (ruhlmann 2017, mascc/esmo 2016 update) systematic review for the mascc/esmo antiemetic guidelines update 2016: 926 records screened for radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (2009–2015), 18 publications finally included; the committee reclassified craniospinal radiotherapy from low to moderate emetic risk and adjusted other field risk levels by expert opinion. the only fully published randomised prevention studies found were two negative studies (acupuncture and green tea). no data supported new antiemetic-prophylaxis recommendations; serotonin (5-ht3) receptor antagonists remained the cornerstone for high- and moderate-emetic-risk radiotherapy. the 2023 update (same committee) again retained only 20 publications from 343 references, changed the low-risk category to rescue-only, and left the drug choices unchanged. a guideline card, not trial evidence: its field-by-field recommendations for non-abdominal sites rest on the abdominal trial base (homed on shelf #6134), the small studies carded above, and expert consensus. the guideline's own literature yield — no new positive randomised prophylaxis trial in either update window — is the most informative number on this card. ruhlmann ch et al. 2016 updated mascc/esmo consensus recommendations: prevention of radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. supportive care in cancer. 2017. pmid: 27624464. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antiemetics · humans · nausea · radiation injuries · radiotherapy · randomized controlled trials as topic · risk · vomiting

cards.headline: Synthesis: outside the abdomen the prophylaxis cupboard is nearly bare — one 20-patient TBI trial carries the placebo case, and field risk (not new trials) drives practice
cards.summary: Synthesis: outside the abdomen the prophylaxis cupboard is nearly bare — one 20-patient TBI trial carries the placebo case, and field risk (not new trials) drives practice
cards.people: The carded beyond-abdomen evidence: one placebo-controlled prophylaxis trial in total-body irradiation (20 patients), one placebo-controlled treatment trial in thorax-to-pelvis fractionated radiotherapy (N not documented in its record), one single-arm pelvic chemoradiotherapy prophylaxis study (48 patients), and the MASCC/ESMO guideline reviews (2016 and 2023). The abdominal-radiotherapy trials are homed on Shelf #6134 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Ondansetron prevented TBI emesis in the one small direct trial (6/10 versus 0/10 completing without rescue); ondansetron treated established thorax-to-pelvis emesis better than placebo; palonosetron-based prophylaxis in pelvic chemoradiotherapy was judged insufficient by its investigators (57% sustained no-emesis). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the class effect is plausible and guideline-endorsed by field risk, but direct prophylaxis evidence outside the abdomen is one small trial deep.
cards.watchOut: Do not import Shelf #6134's abdominal numbers (67% versus 45% complete control) into pelvic, thoracic or head-and-neck claims — emetic risk differs by field, which is precisely why this slice was built separately.

shelves.title: Lymphoedema surgery (lymphovenous anastomosis / vascularised lymph-node transfer): limb volume fell about 6–10% relative at 1 year versus a 3.2% rise on decongestive therapy alone in the one controlled prospective cohort — no completed randomised trial; the rest is prospective-cohort meta-analysis
shelves.question: In adults with established secondary lymphoedema (chiefly breast-cancer-related arm lymphoedema) despite complete decongestive therapy, do microsurgical procedures — lymphovenous anastomosis or vascularised lymph-node transfer — reduce limb volume, cellulitis episodes and compression dependence versus continued conservative therapy?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prospective/observational evidence only; no completed randomised trial of these operations versus conservative therapy was found (the international LYMPH randomised trial exists as a 2025 protocol, not results). This is the surgical PARTIAL companion to the conservative homes: weight lifting (Shelf #1786), bioimpedance surveillance (Shelf #3427) and decongestive therapy (Shelf #5421) — none of their reports is re-carded here. The one controlled prospective report (Zeltzer 2026, 92 patients) compared surgery plus decongestive therapy against decongestive therapy alone: relative interlimb volume difference changed by −6.21% (LVA), −9.61% (VLNT) and −7.00% (combined) versus +3.23% on conservative therapy alone at 1 year (all P<0.0001) — a non-randomised comparison. Meta-analyses of prospective series agree in direction: lymphovenous bypass gave a mean 14.26% limb-volume reduction at 1 year across 431 patients, with 46.3% reducing or stopping compression; and across 648 limbs followed >2 years, annual cellulitis events fell by about 1.1–1.3 episodes after LVA and 1.4–2.4 after VLNT. Without randomisation, selection (earlier-stage, motivated patients get surgery) can account for part of every one of these numbers.

cards.headline: Zeltzer 2026 (prospective controlled cohort, 92 patients): volume difference changed −6.21% (LVA), −9.61% (VLNT), −7.00% (both) versus +3.23% on decongestive therapy alone at 1 year
cards.summary: Zeltzer 2026 (prospective controlled cohort, 92 patients): volume difference changed −6.21% (LVA), −9.61% (VLNT), −7.00% (both) versus +3.23% on decongestive therapy alone at 1 year
cards.type: Prospective controlled cohort study (Zeltzer 2026) — non-randomised, observational comparison
cards.people: 92 patients with breast-cancer-related lymphoedema in four groups: lymphovenous anastomosis (n=30), vascularised lymph-node transfer (n=15), both procedures (n=13), and complete decongestive therapy alone as control (n=34); surgical groups also received decongestive therapy. Limb volumes were measured before surgery and 1 year after, expressed as percentage relative interlimb difference.
cards.result: Mean volume-differential change was −6.21% (±5.76) for LVA, −9.61% (±12.03) for VLNT, −7.00% (±6.56) for LVA+VLNT and +3.23% (±6.83) for decongestive therapy alone; each surgical group differed significantly from control (P<0.0001 for all three). The authors concluded the surgical options combined with decongestive therapy significantly reduced limb volume compared with decongestive therapy alone.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: patients were allocated by clinical pathway, so the surgical groups may differ in stage, duration and adherence from controls in ways the volume comparison cannot adjust away. The VLNT arm is 15 patients with a wide spread (±12.03). This is the only controlled card on the shelf — everything below it is uncontrolled series pooled.
cards.source: Zeltzer AA et al. Outcomes of Lymphovenous Anastomoses and Vascularized Lymph Node Transplant in the Combined Surgical Treatment of Lymphedema: A Prospective Cohort Study. Plastic and reconstructive surgery. 2026. PMID: 40707214. Registry ID: NCT06606145. cards.headline: Brown 2025 (meta-analysis of prospective studies, 431 patients): lymphovenous bypass reduced limb volume by a mean 14.26% at 1 year, and 46.3% reduced or stopped compression
cards.summary: Brown 2025 (meta-analysis of prospective studies, 431 patients): lymphovenous bypass reduced limb volume by a mean 14.26% at 1 year, and 46.3% reduced or stopped compression
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies (Brown 2025)
cards.people: Eight prospective studies (2009–2023) of lymphovenous bypass for lymphoedema, 431 patients, mean follow-up 21.8 months; retrospective analyses were excluded, and for multi-procedure studies only the bypass cohorts were analysed. Mean 3.4 anastomoses per patient.
cards.result: Lymphovenous bypass was associated with a 14.26% mean reduction in limb volume at one year (95% CI 6.63–21.88; p<0.0001) and with reduction or discontinuation of compression therapy in 46.3% (95% CI 24.9%–69.1%). Patients also reported subjective symptom relief and reduced cellulitis episodes.
cards.watchOut: Pre–post pooling of uncontrolled prospective series: regression to the mean, concurrent decongestive therapy and publication bias all push the estimate upward, and outcome metrics were not standardised across studies — the reviewers themselves open with the lack of high-level prospective data.
cards.source: Brown S et al. Lymphovenous bypass for the treatment of secondary lymphedema: A meta-analysis of prospective outcomes. Breast cancer research and treatment. 2025. PMID: 41396216. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Lymphedema · Female · Treatment Outcome · Prospective Studies · Lymphatic Vessels · Anastomosis, Surgical

cards.headline: Jungbauer 2025 (meta-analysis, 648 limbs, >2 years' follow-up): annual cellulitis events fell by 1.13–1.32 episodes after LVA and 1.38–2.43 after VLNT; VLNT cut upper-limb circumference by 42.7%
cards.summary: Jungbauer 2025 (meta-analysis, 648 limbs, >2 years' follow-up): annual cellulitis events fell by 1.13–1.32 episodes after LVA and 1.38–2.43 after VLNT; VLNT cut upper-limb circumference by 42.7%
cards.people: 23 studies of adults with secondary lymphoedema treated with lymphovenous anastomosis (216 limbs) or vascularised lymph-node transfer (432 limbs) with at least 24 months of follow-up; mean age 56.3 years, 99.9% female. Primary outcomes were annual cellulitis incidence and limb circumference change, by limb.
cards.result: Pooled mean reduction in annual cellulitis events: LVA −1.13 episodes (95% CI −1.70 to −0.57) upper limb and −1.32 (−2.08 to −0.55) lower limb; VLNT −2.43 (−3.36 to −1.50) upper and −1.38 (−2.11 to −0.65) lower. VLNT reduced limb circumference by 42.7% (95% CI 36.7–49.7) in upper extremities and 21.98% (19.8–24.4) in lower extremities.
cards.watchOut: Before–after event-rate comparisons in surgical series: cellulitis frequency is exactly the kind of outcome that regresses after enrolment at a bad patch, and patients offered surgery differ from those who are not. Circumference percentage reductions (42.7%) are not comparable with the volume-differential percentages on the Zeltzer card — different metrics, printed separately on purpose.
cards.source: Jungbauer WN et al. Lymphovenous Anastomosis and Vascularized Lymph Node Transfer Reduce Long-term Cellulitis Events in Patients With Secondary Lymphedema: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Annals of plastic surgery. 2025. PMID: 41071856. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nacchiero 2020 (meta-analysis, 48 studies, 1,281 subjects): LVA studies were 42 observational series and only 6 clinical trials — effectiveness signal consistent, design quality low
cards.summary: Nacchiero 2020 (meta-analysis, 48 studies, 1,281 subjects): LVA studies were 42 observational series and only 6 clinical trials — effectiveness signal consistent, design quality low
cards.people: 48 studies of lymphovenous (lymphaticovenular) anastomosis alone for primary and/or secondary lymphoedema, 1,281 subjects, searched to November 2019; the majority of included articles reported pre–post analyses.
cards.result: The pooled analysis favoured LVA effectiveness (odds ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.04–0.13; p<0.001), and all subgroup analyses — by anatomical site, clinical stage, duration of lymphoedema and microsurgical technique — were statistically significant (p<0.05). The authors called for further prospective trials with a common, clearly defined outcome measure.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 of 48 studies were clinical trials and the pooled odds ratio comes mostly from pre–post observational data — treat the 0.07 figure as a sign of consistency in a biased literature, not as an effect size. This card's real content is the design census of the field.
cards.source: Nacchiero E et al. Lymphovenous anastomosis for the treatment of lymphedema: A systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis. Lymphology. 2020. PMID: 33721924. cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery plus decongestive therapy beats decongestive therapy alone in the one controlled cohort, and every pooled series agrees — but the field has no completed randomised trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery plus decongestive therapy beats decongestive therapy alone in the one controlled cohort, and every pooled series agrees — but the field has no completed randomised trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective controlled cohort (92 patients, with a decongestive-therapy control group) and three meta-analyses of prospective/observational series (431 patients; 648 limbs; 1,281 subjects — overlapping literatures, not independent bases). Conservative-therapy evidence is homed on Shelves #1786, #3427 and #5421 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Volume: −6.2% to −9.6% relative interlimb difference at 1 year for surgery versus +3.2% for conservative care in the controlled cohort; 14.26% mean volume reduction in pooled bypass series. Cellulitis: about 1–2.4 fewer episodes per year in long-term pooled data. Compression: 46.3% reduced or stopped it after bypass. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, observational): consistent, clinically meaningful-looking benefits that remain vulnerable to selection bias until the randomised LYMPH trial (protocol published 2025) reports.
cards.watchOut: The three meta-analyses pool substantially the same primary series — agreement between them is not independent confirmation. Patients in these series typically had persistent lymphoedema despite conservative therapy, so the comparison that matters (surgery versus continued conservative care in comparable patients) is only directly made by the single Zeltzer cohort.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zeltzer AA et al. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2026 (PMID: 40707214); Brown S et al. Breast Cancer Res Treat. 2025 (PMID: 41396216); Jungbauer WN et al. Ann Plast Surg. 2025 (PMID: 41071856); Nacchiero E et al. Lymphology. 2020 (PMID: 33721924). Cross-reference: conservative care on Shelves #1786, #3427, #5421 (homed there, not carded here).

shelves.title: Paediatric antiemetics: adding aprepitant doubled delayed-phase complete response (51% versus 26%) in the phase 3 trial; palonosetron was non-inferior to ondansetron acutely, with a delayed-phase edge in one large trial and none in another
shelves.question: In children and adolescents receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding aprepitant (or fosaprepitant) to a 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone improve complete response versus the backbone alone, and is palonosetron superior to ondansetron in this age group?
mesh: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — each half of the question rests on essentially one programme. Aprepitant add-on: in the single phase 3 trial (Kang 2015, 302 analysed children aged 6 months–17 years), adding aprepitant to ondansetron ± dexamethasone raised delayed-phase (25–120 h) complete response from 26% to 51% (p<0.0001), with similar grade 3–4 adverse events (febrile neutropenia 15% versus 15% as the commonest serious event). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean the result. Palonosetron versus ondansetron is a SPLIT within the second half: the international phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Kovács 2016, 493 analysed) showed acute-phase complete response of 59% on palonosetron 20 µg/kg versus 59% on ondansetron — non-inferior, not superior — while a large Chinese randomised trial (Tan 2018, 555 analysed, all with dexamethasone) found acute-phase rates similar (69.7% versus 64.6%) but delayed-phase superiority for palonosetron 10 µg/kg (53.5% versus 32.8%), and a smaller Indian trial (200 children) found no significant differences in any phase. So: aprepitant add-on works in the delayed phase; palonosetron is at least as good as ondansetron acutely, with delayed-phase superiority shown in one of two head-to-head trials.

cards.headline: Kang 2015 (phase 3, 302 children): adding aprepitant to ondansetron ± dexamethasone raised delayed-phase complete response from 26% to 51% (p<0.0001)
cards.summary: Kang 2015 (phase 3, 302 children): adding aprepitant to ondansetron ± dexamethasone raised delayed-phase complete response from 26% to 51% (p<0.0001)
cards.people: 307 children aged 6 months to 17 years with malignancy receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy at 49 sites in 24 countries, randomised to age/weight-dosed aprepitant (day 1: 125 mg if 12–17 years, 3.0 mg/kg if younger; days 2–3: 80 mg or 2.0 mg/kg) plus ondansetron, or placebo plus ondansetron; dexamethasone was allowed in both arms. 302 patients were analysed (152 aprepitant, 150 control). Primary endpoint: complete response (no vomiting, retching or rescue) in the delayed phase, 25–120 hours.
cards.result: Delayed-phase complete response was achieved by 77 of 152 patients (51%) on aprepitant versus 39 of 150 (26%) on control (p<0.0001) — an absolute gain of 25 percentage points. Grade 3–4 adverse events were similar (commonest: febrile neutropenia 15% versus 14%; anaemia 9% versus 17%); the commonest serious event was febrile neutropenia (15% in both arms). The trial was funded by the aprepitant manufacturer, named in the record as Merck & Co., Inc.
cards.watchOut: One trial, manufacturer-funded, carries the whole aprepitant claim — hence the POSSIBLE cap. Dexamethasone use was optional and stratified, so the carded contrast is aprepitant added to a variably-steroid backbone, not a uniform triple regimen.
cards.source: Kang HJ et al. Aprepitant for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children: a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2015. randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial (kang 2015) 307 children aged 6 months to 17 years with malignancy receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy at 49 sites in 24 countries, randomised to age/weight-dosed aprepitant (day 1: 125 mg if 12–17 years, 3.0 mg/kg if younger; days 2–3: 80 mg or 2.0 mg/kg) plus ondansetron, or placebo plus ondansetron; dexamethasone was allowed in both arms. 302 patients were analysed (152 aprepitant, 150 control). primary endpoint: complete response (no vomiting, retching or rescue) in the delayed phase, 25–120 hours. delayed-phase complete response was achieved by 77 of 152 patients (51%) on aprepitant versus 39 of 150 (26%) on control (p<0.0001) — an absolute gain of 25 percentage points. grade 3–4 adverse events were similar (commonest: febrile neutropenia 15% versus 14%; anaemia 9% versus 17%); the commonest serious event was febrile neutropenia (15% in both arms). the trial was funded by the aprepitant manufacturer, named in the record as merck & co., inc. one trial, manufacturer-funded, carries the whole aprepitant claim — hence the possible cap. dexamethasone use was optional and stratified, so the carded contrast is aprepitant added to a variably-steroid backbone, not a uniform triple regimen. kang hj et al. aprepitant for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children: a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial. the lancet. oncology. 2015. pmid: 25770814. registry id: nct01362530. mesh: adolescent · adult · aprepitant · child · child, preschool · dexamethasone · double-blind method · drug-related side effects and adverse reactions · female · humans · induction chemotherapy · infant · male · morpholines · nausea · neoplasms · vomiting

cards.headline: Kovács 2016 (phase 3 non-inferiority, 493 children): acute complete response 59% on palonosetron 20 µg/kg versus 59% on ondansetron — non-inferior, not superior
cards.summary: Kovács 2016 (phase 3 non-inferiority, 493 children): acute complete response 59% on palonosetron 20 µg/kg versus 59% on ondansetron — non-inferior, not superior
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Kovács 2016)
cards.people: 502 paediatric patients aged 0 to <17 years receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy, randomised to palonosetron 10 µg/kg (169), palonosetron 20 µg/kg (169) or ondansetron 3 × 150 µg/kg (164) on day 1, for up to four cycles; 493 were in the first-cycle efficacy analysis. Primary endpoint: complete response in the acute phase (0–24 h) of cycle 1, against a −15% non-inferiority margin.
cards.result: Acute-phase complete response: 54% (90/166) on palonosetron 10 µg/kg, 59% (98/165) on 20 µg/kg and 59% (95/162) on ondansetron. Non-inferiority was shown for the 20 µg/kg dose (weighted difference 0.36%, 97.5% CI −11.7 to 12.4; p=0.0022) but not for 10 µg/kg (−4.41%, 97.5% CI −16.4 to 7.6). Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 69–82% across arms; drug-related events were mainly headache (≤2%).
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority design with a generous −15% margin: it licenses 'no worse than' within that margin, not equality, and says nothing about the delayed phase as its primary endpoint. The lower palonosetron dose failed its non-inferiority test — dose matters on this card.

cards.headline: Tan 2018 (randomised, 555 children, all with dexamethasone): acute complete response similar (69.7% vs 64.6%), but delayed-phase response favoured palonosetron 10 µg/kg (53.5% vs 32.8%)
cards.summary: Tan 2018 (randomised, 555 children, all with dexamethasone): acute complete response similar (69.7% vs 64.6%), but delayed-phase response favoured palonosetron 10 µg/kg (53.5% vs 32.8%)
cards.people: 565 patients aged 0–18 years receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, randomised to palonosetron 5 µg/kg (185), palonosetron 10 µg/kg (186) or ondansetron 3 × 150 µg/kg (194), all followed by dexamethasone; 555 were analysed. Complete response was assessed in acute (0–24 h) and delayed (24–120 h) phases.
cards.result: Acute-phase complete response was 69.1% (5 µg/kg palonosetron), 69.7% (10 µg/kg) and 64.6% (ondansetron). In the delayed phase, palonosetron 10 µg/kg (53.5%) was superior to palonosetron 5 µg/kg (39.8%) and to ondansetron (32.8%) (P<0.05). Drug-related adverse events were mainly headache (2.2–2.8% per group).
cards.watchOut: The delayed-phase superiority here was not replicated as a primary finding in the Kovács trial, and every patient here received dexamethasone — the comparison is palonosetron-plus-steroid versus ondansetron-plus-steroid in highly (not moderately) emetogenic regimens. Read together with the Chaudhary card, the delayed-phase claim is a split, not a settled win.

cards.headline: Chaudhary 2019 (randomised, 200 children): no significant difference in any phase — complete response overall 81% on palonosetron versus 72% on ondansetron (P=0.21)
cards.summary: Chaudhary 2019 (randomised, 200 children): no significant difference in any phase — complete response overall 81% on palonosetron versus 72% on ondansetron (P=0.21)
cards.people: 200 children (mean age 8 years) at a resource-limited paediatric oncology centre, randomised 100 per arm to palonosetron or ondansetron during their first cycle of moderate or highly emetogenic chemotherapy; outcomes were complete response (no vomiting) and complete protection (no nausea or vomiting, age >6) by phase, plus cost-effectiveness.
cards.result: Complete response for palonosetron versus ondansetron: acute 88% versus 84% (P=0.42), delayed 88% versus 79% (P=0.09), overall 81% versus 72% (P=0.21) — none significant. Complete protection showed the same pattern (overall 73% versus 60%, P=0.10). Efficacy and safety were comparable; the authors judged palonosetron more cost-effective and operationally suitable for busy centres because of its single-dose schedule.
cards.watchOut: A null trial on efficacy whose positive conclusion is about cost and convenience — do not cite it as evidence of superior control. Its higher absolute response rates than the phase 3 trials reflect a first-cycle, single-centre population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: aprepitant add-on clearly improves delayed control in one trial; palonosetron matches ondansetron acutely, and its delayed edge appears in one of two trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: aprepitant add-on clearly improves delayed control in one trial; palonosetron matches ondansetron acutely, and its delayed edge appears in one of two trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 aprepitant add-on trial (302 analysed children) and three randomised palonosetron-versus-ondansetron trials (493, 555 and 200 children). No fosaprepitant paediatric trial was carded — the carded NK1 evidence is oral aprepitant only.
cards.result: Aprepitant: delayed complete response 51% versus 26% (absolute +25 points). Palonosetron: acute-phase non-inferiority at 20 µg/kg (59% versus 59%); delayed-phase superiority in Tan 2018 (53.5% versus 32.8%) but no significant difference in Chaudhary 2019 (88% versus 79% delayed complete response). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) overall, with the palonosetron delayed-phase comparison explicitly split.
cards.watchOut: Age range spans 6 months to 18 years across trials with different emetogenicity mixes and steroid backbones — do not pool the percentages across cards. The aprepitant trial's funder is the manufacturer, stated on its card.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kang HJ et al. Lancet Oncol. 2015 (PMID: 25770814); Kovács G et al. Lancet Oncol. 2016 (PMID: 26795844); Tan J et al. Pediatr Blood Cancer. 2018 (PMID: 28941006); Chaudhary NK et al. J Pediatr Hematol Oncol. 2019 (PMID: 31026250).

shelves.title: Honey for radiation-induced oral mucositis: grade 3/4 mucositis 20% versus 75% (Biswal) and 15% versus 65% grade 3+ (Rashad) in two small unblinded trials — meta-analyses agree, but preparations differ by trial and none names a product
shelves.question: In adults with radiation-induced oral mucositis, does honey (topical/oral, the preparations tested in the trials) reduce moderate-to-severe mucositis, pain and weight loss versus standard oral care or placebo gel?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction, weak architecture. Two small randomised trials of 'pure natural honey' (no brand, maker or standardised preparation named in either record — current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness) found large reductions in severe mucositis: Biswal 2003 (40 patients, radiotherapy alone) grade 3/4 mucositis 20% versus 75% (p=0.00058), with 55% versus 25% maintaining or gaining weight (p=0.053); Rashad 2009 (40 patients, chemoradiotherapy) grade 3 mucositis 15% and no grade 4, versus 65% grade 3/4 in controls, with candida colonisation 15% versus 60%. Two meta-analyses of the wider trial literature (11 trials/715 patients; 19 trials/1,276 patients) pool the same direction — odds ratio 0.24 for grade 3 and 0.17 for grade 4 mucositis in one; relative risk 0.18 for intolerable mucositis in the prophylactic phase in the other — but the trials are small, heterogeneous in preparation and schedule, and largely unblinded (honey is hard to blind), and the MASCC/ESMO mucositis guideline assessment of this literature is 'suggestive but inconsistent', which is how this shelf presents it. Pain and weight effects are inconsistent across the pooled analyses.

cards.headline: Biswal 2003 (randomised, 40 patients): symptomatic grade 3/4 mucositis in 20% with topical honey versus 75% with radiotherapy alone (p=0.00058)
cards.summary: Biswal 2003 (randomised, 40 patients): symptomatic grade 3/4 mucositis in 20% with topical honey versus 75% with radiotherapy alone (p=0.00058)
cards.people: 40 patients with head-and-neck cancer receiving radiotherapy (2 Gy/day, 5 days/week, to 60–70 Gy) to the oropharyngeal mucosa, allocated to radiotherapy alone or radiotherapy plus topical pure natural honey — 20 mL taken 15 minutes before, 15 minutes after and 6 hours after each treatment. Mucositis was graded weekly on the RTOG scale. The record names no brand, maker or standardised honey preparation.
cards.result: Symptomatic grade 3/4 mucositis occurred in 20% of honey-treated patients versus 75% of controls (p=0.00058). Compliance was better in the honey group. Fifty-five percent of honey patients showed no change or a gain in body weight versus 25% of controls (p=0.053), most of whom lost weight.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, unblinded (patients applied honey themselves), single centre, and a control arm with no placebo gel or structured oral-care comparator — expectation and attention effects cannot be separated from any honey effect. The weight result is borderline (p=0.053) and is reported here as such.
cards.source: Biswal BM et al. Topical application of honey in the management of radiation mucositis: a preliminary study. Supportive care in cancer. 2003. PMID: 12673463. cards.headline: Rashad 2009 (randomised, 40 patients, chemoradiotherapy): grade 3 mucositis 15% and no grade 4 with honey prophylaxis versus 65% grade 3/4 without; candida colonisation 15% versus 60%
cards.summary: Rashad 2009 (randomised, 40 patients, chemoradiotherapy): grade 3 mucositis 15% and no grade 4 with honey prophylaxis versus 65% grade 3/4 without; candida colonisation 15% versus 60%
cards.people: 40 patients with head-and-neck cancer at a single Egyptian university hospital (2005–2006) receiving concomitant chemoradiotherapy with oral/oropharyngeal mucosa in the field, randomised to prior topical application of pure natural honey or no honey; mucositis was scored weekly and oral swabs cultured before, at completion of, and during irradiation when infection was evident. The record names no brand, maker or standardised preparation.
cards.result: In the honey group, no patient developed grade 4 mucositis and three (15%) developed grade 3; in controls, 13 patients (65%) developed grade 3 or 4 mucositis (p<0.05). Candida colonisation was 15% versus 60% (p=0.003) and positive aerobic pathogen cultures 15% versus 65% (p=0.007), during or after radiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Same structural limits as Biswal — 40 patients, unblinded, no placebo — in a chemoradiotherapy (not radiotherapy-only) population. Two concordant 40-patient trials are still only 80 randomised patients in total; the meta-analyses below widen the base but inherit these designs.

cards.headline: An 2021 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 715 patients): odds ratio 0.24 for grade 3 and 0.17 for grade 4 mucositis with honey — but no significant effect on weight loss or pain score
cards.summary: An 2021 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 715 patients): odds ratio 0.24 for grade 3 and 0.17 for grade 4 mucositis with honey — but no significant effect on weight loss or pain score
cards.people: Eleven randomised trials in 715 patients receiving radiotherapy for head-and-neck cancer, searched to July 2020; outcomes were mucositis incidence by grade, weight loss, pain scale and incidence of severe pain. The pooled trials used differing honey preparations and schedules.
cards.result: Honey reduced grade 2 mucositis (odds ratio 0.43), grade 3 (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.16–0.35; P<0.001) and grade 4 (odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.08–0.36; P<0.001) — all relative (odds) measures — while grade 1 mucositis was more frequent with honey (odds ratio 1.54), consistent with shifting severity downward. Unbearable pain was less frequent (odds ratio −0.20 as reported), but effects on weight loss and pain score were not statistically significant. The authors state more evidence is required for the pain and weight claims.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios overstate relative risks when events are common, and the underlying trials are the small, largely unblinded studies typified by the two cards above, with unlike preparations pooled — the pooling caveat the slate required is printed here rather than assumed away. One confidence interval in the record (grade 2) is internally inconsistent as printed and is not quoted.

cards.headline: Liu 2019 (meta-analysis, 19 RCTs, 1,276 patients): relative risk 0.18 for intolerable mucositis in the prophylactic phase, with lower pain scores — the largest pooled estimate
cards.summary: Liu 2019 (meta-analysis, 19 RCTs, 1,276 patients): relative risk 0.18 for intolerable mucositis in the prophylactic phase, with lower pain scores — the largest pooled estimate
cards.people: Nineteen randomised trials in 1,276 patients with radiochemotherapy-induced oral mucositis, covering prophylactic and therapeutic honey use; primary outcomes were mucositis grade and pain scores, with recovery time and quality of life secondary. Registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018108486, as stated in the record).
cards.result: In the prophylactic phase, intolerable mucositis was significantly prevented with honey (relative risk 0.18, 95% CI 0.09–0.41). Pain scores were lower with honey in the first month (weighted mean difference −3.25, 95% CI −4.41 to −2.09) and at end of treatment (−2.32, 95% CI −4.47 to −0.18). The authors recommended honey during and after radiochemotherapy for mucositis prevention and treatment.
cards.watchOut: A relative risk of 0.18 from pooling small unblinded trials is implausibly large as a true effect and should be read as 'direction consistent, size inflated' — it also conflicts with An 2021's null pain-score finding, a disagreement between the two meta-analyses that this shelf leaves visible.

cards.headline: Synthesis: severe mucositis is consistently less frequent with honey across every report — and every report shares the same weaknesses
cards.summary: Synthesis: severe mucositis is consistently less frequent with honey across every report — and every report shares the same weaknesses
cards.people: The carded evidence: two 40-patient randomised trials (radiotherapy alone; chemoradiotherapy) and two meta-analyses (11 trials/715 patients; 19 trials/1,276 patients) that pool those trials and their siblings. No carded trial names a brand, maker or standardised honey preparation — each tested a locally sourced 'pure natural honey', so preparations differ by trial and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.result: Grade 3/4 mucositis: 20% versus 75% (Biswal) and 15% grade 3 with no grade 4 versus 65% grade 3/4 (Rashad); pooled odds ratios 0.24 (grade 3) and 0.17 (grade 4). Pain: lower in one meta-analysis, not significant in the other. Weight: borderline in the one trial reporting it, null in pooled analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), matching the guideline characterisation of this literature as suggestive but inconsistent.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded application, no placebo gel in the anchor trials, heterogeneous preparations and probable publication bias all inflate the apparent effect; the honest claim is fewer severe mucositis cases in these trials, not the pooled relative risks at face value.

shelves.title: Hormone therapy after breast cancer — a SPLIT: HABITS was stopped early for more recurrences on hormones (hazard ratio 2.4 at extended follow-up), the Stockholm trial found no excess recurrence (relative hazard 0.82), and the two trials differed significantly from each other
shelves.question: In breast-cancer survivors, is systemic hormone therapy after treatment safe — what did the randomised HABITS and Stockholm trials show about recurrence, and why did they disagree?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — two randomised trials, two answers, and a statistically significant difference between the trials themselves (heterogeneity P=.02), so the disagreement is unlikely to be chance alone. HABITS (434 randomised; extended follow-up 447 assigned, 442 followed): hormone therapy increased new breast-cancer events — 26 versus 7 at the 2.1-year safety analysis that stopped the trial in December 2003, and at extended follow-up (median 4 years) 39 of 221 versus 17 of 221 (hazard ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.3–4.2; 5-year cumulative incidence 22.2% versus 8.0%). Stockholm (378 randomised; designed to minimise progestogen exposure): at median 4.1 years the recurrence relative hazard was 0.82 (95% CI 0.35–1.9), and at 10.8 years new breast-cancer events were 60 versus 48 (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9) — no significant difference overall, though contralateral breast cancers were more frequent on hormones (14 versus 4; hazard ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.2–10.9). Neither trial found increased mortality. The leading explanation offered by the trialists is regimen: HABITS used more continuous progestogen (estradiol with norethisterone), while Stockholm deliberately minimised progestogen. Both trials closed early, so neither answer is definitive; current guidelines typically consider systemic hormone therapy contraindicated after breast cancer, which is the practice context, not a carded result.

cards.headline: HABITS 2004 (trial stopped early): 26 new breast-cancer events on hormone therapy versus 7 without, at median 2.1 years — judged an unacceptable risk
cards.summary: HABITS 2004 (trial stopped early): 26 new breast-cancer events on hormone therapy versus 7 without, at median 2.1 years — judged an unacceptable risk
cards.type: Randomised open trial, stopped early (Holmberg 2004, HABITS safety report)
cards.people: 434 women with previous breast cancer randomised in Scandinavia to hormone replacement therapy or best treatment without hormones (345 with at least one follow-up report at this analysis); the main endpoint was any new breast-cancer event, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: After median follow-up of 2.1 years, 26 women in the hormone-therapy group and 7 in the non-hormone group had a new breast-cancer event. All women with an event in the hormone group, and two in the non-hormone group, had been exposed to hormone therapy, and most events occurred on treatment. The investigators judged the risk unacceptable and terminated the trial on 17 December 2003. (The companion Stockholm report quantifies this trial's recurrence relative hazard as 3.3, 95% CI 1.5–7.4.)
cards.watchOut: An early safety look at a trial stopped for harm: event counts at stopping are small (33 events) and stopping early tends to exaggerate the estimated risk. The extended follow-up card below is the fairer HABITS estimate — the two reports are one trial, not two.

cards.headline: HABITS 2008 (extended follow-up): 39 of 221 versus 17 of 221 new breast-cancer events — hazard ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.3–4.2); 5-year cumulative incidence 22.2% versus 8.0%
cards.summary: HABITS 2008 (extended follow-up): 39 of 221 versus 17 of 221 new breast-cancer events — hazard ratio 2.4 (95% CI 1.3–4.2); 5-year cumulative incidence 22.2% versus 8.0%
cards.type: Randomised trial, extended follow-up report (Holmberg 2008, HABITS) — second report of the same trial as the previous card
cards.people: 447 women randomly assigned in HABITS (442 followed, median 4 years), comparing hormone therapy for menopausal symptoms with best management without hormones; most hormone-therapy patients received continuous combined or sequential estradiol hemihydrate with norethisterone. The trial was a non-inferiority design powered to detect a 36% hazard increase.
cards.result: Thirty-nine of 221 women in the hormone arm and 17 of 221 in the control arm had a new breast-cancer event (hazard ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.3–4.2); 5-year cumulative incidence was 22.2% versus 8.0% — an absolute difference of 14.2 percentage points. Breast-cancer deaths were 6 in the hormone arm and 5 in controls, with distant metastases in 6 versus 4 (P=.51), so no mortality difference was shown.
cards.watchOut: Still the same single trial as the 2004 card — extended follow-up strengthens its internal estimate but adds no independent replication. The regimen was progestogen-containing throughout, which is central to the disagreement with Stockholm and limits generalisation to progestogen-sparing regimens.

cards.headline: Stockholm 2005: no association between hormone therapy and recurrence at 4.1 years (relative hazard 0.82, 95% CI 0.35–1.9) — and the two trials differed significantly (heterogeneity P=.02)
cards.summary: Stockholm 2005: no association between hormone therapy and recurrence at 4.1 years (relative hazard 0.82, 95% CI 0.35–1.9) — and the two trials differed significantly (heterogeneity P=.02)
cards.people: 378 patients with early-stage breast cancer randomised in Sweden (from 1997) to menopausal hormone therapy or none; unlike HABITS, the Stockholm protocol was designed to minimise progestogen combined with estrogen. This report also presents the HABITS comparison and the between-trial heterogeneity test.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 4.1 years, breast-cancer recurrence was not associated with hormone therapy (relative hazard 0.82, 95% CI 0.35–1.9), against HABITS' relative hazard of 3.3 (95% CI 1.5–7.4) at 2.1 years. Heterogeneity between the two trials was statistically significant (P=.02), indicating chance may not be the only explanation; the authors propose that estrogen/progestogen doses and regimens may be associated with recurrence.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.35–1.9) is wide — Stockholm does not prove safety; it fails to find harm within a range that still includes a near-doubling of risk. The trial was also stopped early (in 2003, after HABITS reported), truncating its power.

cards.headline: Stockholm 2013 (10.8-year follow-up): new breast-cancer events 60 versus 48 (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9) — but contralateral cancers 14 versus 4 (hazard ratio 3.6, P=0.013)
cards.summary: Stockholm 2013 (10.8-year follow-up): new breast-cancer events 60 versus 48 (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9) — but contralateral cancers 14 versus 4 (hazard ratio 3.6, P=0.013)
cards.type: Randomised trial, 10-year follow-up report (Fahlén 2013, Stockholm) — second report of the Stockholm trial
cards.people: Disease-free women with a history of breast cancer randomised to hormone therapy (n=188) or no hormone therapy (n=190) in the Stockholm trial, which minimised progestogen dose; the trial was stopped in 2003 after HABITS reported, and this is the long-term follow-up at 10.8 years.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in total new breast-cancer events: 60 on hormone therapy versus 48 on control (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9). Local recurrences were 11 versus 15 and distant metastases 12 versus 12, but contralateral breast cancers were 14 versus 4 (hazard ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.2–10.9; p=0.013). No differences in mortality or other new primary malignancies were found. The authors note both trials closed prematurely, so data do not allow firm conclusions.
cards.watchOut: The reassuring total conceals a significant contralateral-cancer excess — a new-primary signal in the opposite direction from the recurrence signal. With early closure and 378 patients, Stockholm cannot exclude clinically important harm, which is why this shelf is a SPLIT and not a reassurance.
