cards.headline: Kopetz 2026 (BREAKWATER Cohort 3, FOLFIRI backbone): response 64.4% versus 39.2% (odds ratio 2.76); PFS 15.2 versus 8.3 months (HR 0.44); overall survival hazard ratio 0.56
cards.summary: Kopetz 2026 (BREAKWATER Cohort 3, FOLFIRI backbone): response 64.4% versus 39.2% (odds ratio 2.76); PFS 15.2 versus 8.3 months (HR 0.44); overall survival hazard ratio 0.56
cards.people: 147 patients with previously untreated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer randomised 1:1 to encorafenib plus cetuximab plus FOLFIRI (73) or FOLFIRI with or without bevacizumab (74).
cards.result: Objective response was 64.4% versus 39.2% (odds ratio 2.756, 95% CI 1.420 to 5.348; one-sided p=0.0011) — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 25.2 percentage points. At the January 2026 cutoff, progression-free survival was 15.2 versus 8.3 months (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.70; p=0.0002) and overall survival favoured the combination (hazard ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.94; median not estimable versus 20.3 months). Serious adverse events occurred in 49.3% versus 44.1%.
cards.watchOut: A separate, smaller cohort with a different chemotherapy backbone (FOLFIRI, not mFOLFOX6) — supportive of the strategy, not a replication of the main comparison; survival medians were not yet estimable in the combination arm.
cards.source: Kopetz S et al. A randomised study of encorafenib, cetuximab, and FOLFIRI versus FOLFIRI with or without bevacizumab in BRAF V600E-mutant colorectal cancer: BREAKWATER Cohort 3. shelves.title: Sotorasib plus panitumumab in KRAS G12C colorectal cancer (CodeBreaK 300): PFS 5.6 versus 2.2 months (HR 0.49), response 30.2% versus 1.9%; overall survival not significant (HR 0.70, p=0.20)
shelves.question: In adults with previously treated KRAS G12C-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, does sotorasib + panitumumab versus investigator's-choice therapy improve progression-free survival?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on progression-free survival and response, not on proven survival. CodeBreaK 300 randomised 160 patients with chemorefractory KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer to sotorasib (960 mg or 240 mg) plus panitumumab or investigator's choice (trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib). At the approved 960-mg dose, median progression-free survival was 5.6 versus 2.2 months (HR 0.49, PMID: 37870968) and updated response was 30.2% versus 1.9%. The prespecified overall-survival analysis (PMID: 40215429) was NOT significant (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; p=0.20) in an analysis not powered for survival with crossover permitted. The phase 1b CodeBreaK 101 cohort (PMID: 38177853, response 30.0%) is carded as supporting evidence. KRAS G12C is present in only about 3-4% of metastatic colorectal cancers.

cards.headline: Fakih 2023 (CodeBreaK 300, primary analysis): progression-free survival 5.6 months on sotorasib 960 mg + panitumumab versus 2.2 months on standard care (HR 0.49); response 26.4% versus 0%
cards.summary: Fakih 2023 (CodeBreaK 300, primary analysis): progression-free survival 5.6 months on sotorasib 960 mg + panitumumab versus 2.2 months on standard care (HR 0.49); response 26.4% versus 0%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — primary analysis (Fakih 2023, CodeBreaK 300)
cards.people: 160 patients with chemorefractory KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer and no previous KRAS G12C inhibitor, randomised to sotorasib 960 mg daily plus panitumumab (53), sotorasib 240 mg daily plus panitumumab (53), or investigator's choice of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib (54); median follow-up 7.8 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 5.6 months (95% CI 4.2 to 6.3) in the 960-mg group and 3.9 months in the 240-mg group versus 2.2 months (1.9 to 3.9) on standard care (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.80, p=0.006 for 960 mg; 0.58 for 240 mg) — a 51% relative reduction in the hazard at the approved dose. Objective response was 26.4%, 5.7% and 0% respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related events occurred in 35.8%, 30.2% and 43.1%; skin toxicity and hypomagnesaemia were the commonest combination effects. Overall survival data were still maturing.
cards.watchOut: A small phase 3 trial (53-54 patients per arm) in a mutation present in only about 3-4% of metastatic colorectal cancers; the claim at this report rests entirely on progression-free survival and response.
cards.source: Fakih MG et al. Sotorasib plus Panitumumab in Refractory Colorectal Cancer with Mutated KRAS G12C. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 37870968. Registry ID: NCT05198934. cards.headline: Pietrantonio 2025 (CodeBreaK 300, overall-survival analysis): OS hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; p=0.20) — NOT significant; updated response 30.2% versus 1.9%
cards.summary: Pietrantonio 2025 (CodeBreaK 300, overall-survival analysis): OS hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; p=0.20) — NOT significant; updated response 30.2% versus 1.9%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial — overall-survival analysis (Pietrantonio 2025, CodeBreaK 300)
cards.people: The same 160 CodeBreaK 300 patients, with overall survival analysed as prespecified at about 50% maturity (82 deaths: 24, 28 and 30 across the three arms) after median follow-up of 13.6 months; crossover to the combination was permitted after the primary analysis.
cards.result: Overall survival did not differ significantly: hazard ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; two-sided p=0.20) for sotorasib 960 mg plus panitumumab versus investigator's choice, and 0.83 (p=0.50) for the 240-mg dose — on survival, the result is compatible with (the treatment made no difference). Updated objective response was 30.2% versus 7.5% versus 1.9%. No new safety signals were observed.
cards.watchOut: The trial was not powered for overall survival and crossover further dilutes it — 'not significant' here means unproven, in both directions; the shelf's positive claim remains progression-free survival and response only.
cards.source: Pietrantonio F et al. Overall Survival Analysis of the Phase III CodeBreaK 300 Study of Sotorasib Plus Panitumumab Versus Investigator's Choice in Chemorefractory KRAS G12C Colorectal Cancer. cards.type: Phase 1b trial (Kuboki 2024, CodeBreaK 101) — supporting evidence, labelled phase 1b
cards.people: 48 patients with chemotherapy-refractory KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer (dose exploration n=8; dose expansion n=40) treated with sotorasib 960 mg daily plus panitumumab 6 mg/kg every 2 weeks; single-arm.

shelves.title: Aspirin after resected colorectal cancer in an unselected population (ASCOLT)
shelves.question: In adults with resected non-metastatic colorectal cancer who have completed standard adjuvant therapy, does daily aspirin versus placebo improve disease-free survival, irrespective of tumour PI3K status?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aspirin/therapeutic use/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Aged · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Colorectal Neoplasms/drug therapy/prevention & control · Secondary Prevention/methods · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Oxaliplatin/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: In an unselected population the answer is no on the trial's own terms. ASCOLT randomised 1,550 patients (modified intention-to-treat) with resected Dukes' C or high-risk Dukes' B colon cancer or Dukes' B/C rectal cancer, after completion of standard adjuvant therapy, to aspirin 200 mg daily or placebo for 3 years: 5-year disease-free survival was 77.0% versus 74.8% (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.73–1.13; p=0.38 — the treatment made no difference), and serious adverse events were 12% versus 14%. ASCOLT's own preplanned translational analysis found no significant benefit in PIK3CA-mutated or COX-2-overexpressing subgroups either (all subgroup confidence intervals wide and crossing 1), although its pooled meta-analysis of the three published trials in PIK3CA exon 9/20-mutated tumours gave HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.39–0.96) — a biomarker-selected signal that belongs with Shelf #1849 (ALASCCA, aspirin restricted to PI3K-pathway-altered tumours), not with this unselected question. A 2026 systematic review pooling observational studies and RCTs likewise found no survival or disease-free-survival benefit (observational OS OR 0.92, DFS OR 0.90 — relative measures, both non-significant). The Add-Aspirin trial's colorectal cohort (950 registered) has reported feasibility only — tolerability and adherence, no colorectal efficacy result — so it is not carded as efficacy evidence here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for any unselected benefit.

cards.headline: ASCOLT: 5-year disease-free survival 77.0% on aspirin versus 74.8% on placebo (HR 0.91, p=0.38) — no difference in an unselected population
cards.summary: ASCOLT: 5-year disease-free survival 77.0% on aspirin versus 74.8% on placebo (HR 0.91, p=0.38) — no difference in an unselected population
cards.people: 1,550 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (791 aspirin, 759 placebo) aged 18 or older with Dukes' C or high-risk Dukes' B colon cancer or Dukes' B or C rectal cancer, resected and having completed at least 3 months of standard adjuvant chemotherapy, at 66 centres in 11 countries and territories (ten Asia-Pacific, one Middle East); median age 57 years, 58% male. Aspirin 200 mg daily or placebo for 3 years, followed for 5 years.
cards.result: 5-year disease-free survival was 77.0% (95% CI 73.6–80.0) with aspirin versus 74.8% (71.3–77.9) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.73–1.13; p=0.38 — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint; the hazard ratio is a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). Any-grade adverse events: 49% versus 51%. Serious adverse events: 95 (12%) versus 107 (14%). No treatment-related deaths in either group.
cards.watchOut: Patients with a clinically significant history of cardiovascular disease or stroke, contraindications to aspirin, or familial colorectal cancer syndromes were excluded — so this null applies to a comparatively low-bleeding-risk, unselected-for-biomarker population, and says nothing about PI3K-selected use (Shelf #1849).
cards.source: Chia JWK et al. Aspirin after completion of standard adjuvant therapy for colorectal cancer (ASCOLT): an international, multicentre, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2025. PMID: 39824200. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00565708, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: ASCOLT translational study: no significant aspirin benefit within ASCOLT's own PIK3CA-mutated or COX-2-overexpressing subgroups; a pooled three-trial exon 9/20 analysis favoured aspirin (HR 0.61)
cards.summary: ASCOLT translational study: no significant aspirin benefit within ASCOLT's own PIK3CA-mutated or COX-2-overexpressing subgroups; a pooled three-trial exon 9/20 analysis favoured aspirin (HR 0.61)
cards.type: Preplanned translational subgroup analysis of ASCOLT plus systematic meta-analysis
cards.people: ASCOLT participants who commenced study medication and had evaluable tumour tissue: 397 tumours assessable for PIK3CA (69 with a mutation in any exon; 45 with exon 9/20 mutations; 84 with PIK3CA or PTEN mutations) and 450 assessed for COX-2 (PTGS2) overexpression, 307 (69%) positive.
cards.result: Within ASCOLT, disease-free-survival hazard ratios for aspirin versus placebo were 0.93 (95% CI 0.35–2.47) for any PIK3CA mutation, 0.72 (0.21–2.46) for exon 9/20 mutations, 1.23 (0.47–3.19) for PIK3CA or PTEN mutations, and 0.99 (0.60–1.63) for COX-2 overexpression — none significant, all relative measures with wide intervals. The accompanying meta-analysis of trials in patients with PIK3CA exon 9/20 mutations showed reduced disease-free-survival events with aspirin (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.39–0.96 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: The subgroup analyses rest on very few events (for example 7 versus 4 disease-free-survival events in the exon 9/20 subgroup), so ASCOLT itself neither confirms nor excludes a biomarker effect; the pooled signal is driven by the biomarker-selected trials homed at Shelf #1849 and must not be read back onto the unselected population.
cards.source: Segelov E et al. Adjuvant aspirin for colorectal cancer with PIK3CA-mutated and COX-2 overexpressed tumours: the ASCOLT translational research study and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2026): pooled observational and randomised evidence shows no survival or disease-free-survival benefit from adjuvant aspirin in colorectal cancer
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (2026): pooled observational and randomised evidence shows no survival or disease-free-survival benefit from adjuvant aspirin in colorectal cancer
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (observational studies and RCTs)
cards.people: Ten studies comprising retrospective cohorts, population-based cohorts, prospective observational analyses and phase 3 RCTs of aspirin for secondary prevention after colorectal cancer (the record does not print a single pooled N).
cards.result: Pooled observational analyses showed no statistically significant improvement in overall survival (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78–1.08) or disease-free survival (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.74–1.08) among aspirin users — both relative measures, printed as reported without pooled absolute rates in the record. RCT estimates were likewise close to unity, with considerable heterogeneity across studies. The authors conclude current evidence does not support aspirin as adjuvant therapy for secondary prevention in unselected colorectal cancer.
cards.watchOut: Most of the pooled weight is observational, where aspirin users differ systematically from non-users (confounding by indication and healthy-user effects run in both directions); the randomised limb is dominated by ASCOLT itself, carded above, so this review corroborates rather than independently replicates the null.
cards.source: AlSawat AM et al. Aspirin after completion of standard adjuvant therapy for colorectal cancer (ASCOLT): A systematic review and meta-analysis. American journal of surgery. 2026. cards.summary: Synthesis: in an unselected population, adjuvant aspirin made no difference — the biomarker question lives elsewhere
cards.people: 1,550 randomised patients in ASCOLT, its 397-tumour translational substudy, and a 10-study systematic review.
cards.result: Disease-free survival 77.0% versus 74.8% (HR 0.91, non-significant); no significant subgroup benefit inside ASCOLT; pooled observational estimates at or near unity. Cross-point: aspirin restricted to PI3K-pathway-altered tumours (ALASCCA) is Shelf #1849 — a different, biomarker-gated question with a positive single trial. cards.watchOut: Do not let the pooled PIK3CA exon 9/20 hazard ratio (0.61) migrate into this shelf's verdict: it pools biomarker-selected populations and answers the #1849 question, not this one.

shelves.title: SIREC: metal stent versus single-dose brachytherapy for malignant dysphagia — stent relieves faster, brachytherapy relieves longer with fewer complications, at equal survival and cost (one randomised programme)
shelves.question: In adults with inoperable oesophageal cancer and dysphagia, does a self-expanding metal stent versus single-dose intraluminal brachytherapy differ in speed and durability of dysphagia relief, complications and quality of life?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brachytherapy · Deglutition Disorders · Esophageal Neoplasms · Esophageal Stenosis · Female · Humans · Male · Metals · Palliative Care · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Stents
shelves.balance: Single-trial-programme structure, stated plainly: SIREC (Homs 2004, nine Dutch hospitals, 209 patients) is the only randomised trial, and the quality-of-life (PMID: 15288288) and prognostic-model (PMID: 16111947) cards are further reports of it — their PMIDs appear here in the balance prose only as companion reports of the same programme, and the cards themselves carry their own records. The clinical answer is a timing trade-off: stent placement improved dysphagia more rapidly; brachytherapy gave better long-term relief, fewer complications (33% vs 21%, p=0.02; late haemorrhage 13% vs 5%) and better generic quality of life, with no difference in survival, recurrent dysphagia or total medical costs. The prognostic report supports stent when expected survival is short and brachytherapy when it is longer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE however clean the trial.

cards.headline: SIREC 2004 (the trial): dysphagia improved faster with a metal stent but long-term relief was better with single-dose brachytherapy; complications 33% vs 21% (p=0.02), driven by late haemorrhage 13% vs 5%; survival did not differ — N = 209
cards.summary: SIREC 2004 (the trial): dysphagia improved faster with a metal stent but long-term relief was better with single-dose brachytherapy; complications 33% vs 21% (p=0.02), driven by late haemorrhage 13% vs 5%; survival did not differ — N = 209
cards.people: 209 patients with dysphagia from inoperable carcinoma of the oesophagus or oesophagogastric junction at nine Dutch hospitals, randomised to self-expanding metal stent placement (n=108) or single-dose 12 Gy intraluminal brachytherapy (n=101), followed to death; intention-to-treat analysis, none lost to follow-up.
cards.result: Dysphagia improved more rapidly after stent placement, but long-term relief of dysphagia was better after brachytherapy. Complications were more frequent with stent (36/108, 33% vs 21/101, 21%; p=0.02), mainly late haemorrhage (13% vs 5%, p=0.05). Persistent or recurrent dysphagia (p=0.81) and median survival (p=0.23) did not differ. The trial report states total medical costs were much the same between the groups. The authors recommended brachytherapy as primary treatment where survival allows its slower benefit to accrue.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, 1999–2002 era stents (the QoL report names the covered Ultraflex stent) — modern stent designs and brachytherapy delivery may shift the complication balance; nine randomised patients never received their allocated treatment.
cards.source: Homs MY et al. Single-dose brachytherapy versus metal stent placement for the palliation of dysphagia from oesophageal cancer: multicentre randomised trial. Lancet. 2004. multicentre randomised trial (sirec, homs 2004) 209 patients with dysphagia from inoperable carcinoma of the oesophagus or oesophagogastric junction at nine dutch hospitals, randomised to self-expanding metal stent placement (n=108) or single-dose 12 gy intraluminal brachytherapy (n=101), followed to death; intention-to-treat analysis, none lost to follow-up. dysphagia improved more rapidly after stent placement, but long-term relief of dysphagia was better after brachytherapy. complications were more frequent with stent (36/108, 33% vs 21/101, 21%; p=0.02), mainly late haemorrhage (13% vs 5%, p=0.05). persistent or recurrent dysphagia (p=0.81) and median survival (p=0.23) did not differ. the trial report states total medical costs were much the same between the groups. the authors recommended brachytherapy as primary treatment where survival allows its slower benefit to accrue. one trial, one country, 1999–2002 era stents (the qol report names the covered ultraflex stent) — modern stent designs and brachytherapy delivery may shift the complication balance; nine randomised patients never received their allocated treatment. homs my et al. single-dose brachytherapy versus metal stent placement for the palliation of dysphagia from oesophageal cancer: multicentre randomised trial. lancet. 2004. pmid: 15500894. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · brachytherapy · deglutition disorders · esophageal neoplasms · esophageal stenosis · female · humans · male · metals · palliative care · quality of life · recurrence · stents

cards.headline: SIREC quality-of-life report 2004: generic quality of life favoured brachytherapy on four of five functional scales, and functioning declined more steeply after stent — same 209 patients, not a second trial
cards.summary: SIREC quality-of-life report 2004: generic quality of life favoured brachytherapy on four of five functional scales, and functioning declined more steeply after stent — same 209 patients, not a second trial
cards.type: Quality-of-life report of the SIREC randomised trial (Homs 2004)
cards.people: The same SIREC randomised cohort (stent n=108, brachytherapy n=101), with longitudinal disease-specific measures (dysphagia score, EORTC OES-23, pain scale) and generic measures (EORTC QLQ-C30, EQ-5D) collected at monthly home visits by a research nurse.
cards.result: Dysphagia again improved faster after stent but long-term relief was better after brachytherapy. Generic quality of life differed overall in favour of brachytherapy on four of five QLQ-C30 functional scales (role, emotional, cognitive, social; p<0.05). Functioning deteriorated over follow-up in both groups (physical and role functioning falling about 23–24 points on a 100-point scale over 0.5 years), more pronounced after stent; pain levels remained broadly stable.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same 209 patients, not independent evidence — the shelf counts the SIREC programme as one randomised trial with multiple reports, and monthly home-visit measurement in a dying population carries heavy missing-data weight.

cards.headline: SIREC prognostic-model report 2005: a simple score (tumour length, performance status, metastases, age, sex) identifies a poor-prognosis group in whom stent is at least equivalent — in good-prognosis patients brachytherapy gave better dysphagia-adjusted survival
cards.summary: SIREC prognostic-model report 2005: a simple score (tumour length, performance status, metastases, age, sex) identifies a poor-prognosis group in whom stent is at least equivalent — in good-prognosis patients brachytherapy gave better dysphagia-adjusted survival
cards.type: Prognostic-model report of the SIREC programme (Steyerberg 2005)
cards.people: Patient data from the SIREC trial (n=209) combined with a consecutive series (n=396) of patients receiving stent or single-dose brachytherapy for dysphagia from oesophageal cancer; survival modelled by Cox regression and dysphagia-adjusted survival (alive with no or mild dysphagia) by Kaplan-Meier analysis.
cards.result: Tumour length, WHO performance score and presence of metastases were significant prognostic factors (multivariable p<0.001); a simple score including age and sex separated poor, intermediate and relatively good prognosis groups. In the poor-prognosis group, dysphagia-adjusted survival differed by 23 days in favour of stent (77 vs 54 days, p=0.16 — not significant); in the other groups brachytherapy gave better dysphagia-adjusted survival. The authors propose the score to guide treatment selection, pending validation.
cards.watchOut: A model built partly on the trial it then interprets, with the key poor-prognosis contrast itself non-significant (p=0.16) — a sensible clinical heuristic (stent when life expectancy is short), not a validated decision rule.
cards.source: Steyerberg EW et al. Stent placement or brachytherapy for palliation of dysphagia from esophageal cancer: a prognostic model to guide treatment selection. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2005. PMID: 16111947. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial programme answers this question — stent for speed, brachytherapy for durability and fewer complications, at equal cost and equal survival; four reports on this shelf are one trial, and the stamp is capped accordingly
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial programme answers this question — stent for speed, brachytherapy for durability and fewer complications, at equal cost and equal survival; four reports on this shelf are one trial, and the stamp is capped accordingly
cards.people: Carded evidence: the SIREC multicentre randomised trial (209 patients) and two of its companion reports (quality of life; prognostic model). A single-trial programme, stated plainly per the slate instruction.
cards.result: Stent placement relieved dysphagia faster; brachytherapy relieved it better long-term, with fewer complications (33% vs 21%) and better generic quality of life; survival, recurrent dysphagia and total costs did not differ. The prognostic report supports choosing stent when prognosis is poor (weeks) and brachytherapy when it is better. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a single programme caps the stamp, however clean the trial.
cards.watchOut: Territory note: this is luminal GI-oncology palliation. Nothing here compares either treatment with chemoradiotherapy or best supportive care, and 2004-era devices bound the shelf's currency.

shelves.title: Pirtobrutinib after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure in CLL (BRUIN / BRUIN CLL-321)
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma previously treated with a covalent BTK inhibitor, does the non-covalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib improve response and progression-free survival versus investigator's-choice therapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy · Agammaglobulinaemia Tyrosine Kinase/antagonists & inhibitors · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Progression-Free Survival · Drug Resistance, Neoplasm/genetics · Mutation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pirtobrutinib (Jaypirca, Eli Lilly — the specific marketed product, named under the clarification exception) works after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure, on the evidence of one single-arm phase 1/2 cohort and one open-label phase 3 trial. In BRUIN, 73.3% of 247 covalent-BTKi-pretreated patients responded; in BRUIN CLL-321, pirtobrutinib lengthened progression-free survival versus investigator's-choice idelalisib/rituximab or bendamustine/rituximab (median 14.0 vs 8.7 months; HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.39–0.75 — a relative measure; the absolute median gain was 5.3 months) and delayed next treatment (median 24.0 vs 10.9 months). Overall survival was NOT improved (HR 1.09) — that null sits beside the PFS result on purpose: the trial allowed crossover, which contaminates survival, but no survival benefit has been shown. Tolerability favoured pirtobrutinib (grade 3 or higher events 57.7% vs 73.4%). Resistance is already documented: in the BRUIN genomic analysis, 68% of patients progressing had acquired at least one mutation, including new BTK gatekeeper (T474) and kinase-impaired (L528W) mutations that pirtobrutinib itself selects for — this is a further line of therapy, not a permanent answer.

cards.headline: BRUIN phase 1/2 CLL cohort (Mato 2023): 73.3% of 247 patients previously treated with a covalent BTK inhibitor responded to pirtobrutinib; median progression-free survival 19.6 months — single-arm, no comparator
cards.summary: BRUIN phase 1/2 CLL cohort (Mato 2023): 73.3% of 247 patients previously treated with a covalent BTK inhibitor responded to pirtobrutinib; median progression-free survival 19.6 months — single-arm, no comparator
cards.people: 247 patients with relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma who had previously received a covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, within the BRUIN phase 1–2 trial (317 patients with CLL/SLL received pirtobrutinib in total, forming the safety population). The pretreated group had a median of 3 previous lines of therapy (range 1–11), and 40.5% had also received a BCL2 inhibitor such as venetoclax.
cards.result: Overall response (partial response or better, independent review) was 73.3% (95% CI 67.3–78.7), rising to 82.2% (76.8–86.7) when partial response with lymphocytosis was included. Median progression-free survival was 19.6 months (95% CI 16.9–22.1). Among all 317 patients, the most common adverse events were infections (71.0%), bleeding (42.6%) and neutropenia (32.5%); atrial fibrillation or flutter occurred in 3.8% and major haemorrhage in 2.2%; only 2.8% discontinued for a treatment-related adverse event.
cards.watchOut: No comparator arm: a 73.3% response rate in a single-arm cohort shows activity, not superiority to any alternative, and the 19.6-month median PFS has no control beside it. Note the slate for this shelf quoted a 62% response figure from an earlier, smaller cohort cut; the full published record carded here reports 73.3%, and that is the figure used.
cards.source: Mato AR et al. Pirtobrutinib after a Covalent BTK Inhibitor in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 37407001. cards.headline: BRUIN CLL-321 phase 3 (Sharman 2025): progression-free survival HR 0.54 (median 14.0 vs 8.7 months) versus investigator's choice — but overall survival HR 1.09, no survival benefit shown
cards.summary: BRUIN CLL-321 phase 3 (Sharman 2025): progression-free survival HR 0.54 (median 14.0 vs 8.7 months) versus investigator's choice — but overall survival HR 1.09, no survival benefit shown
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial (Sharman 2025, BRUIN CLL-321)
cards.people: 238 adults with relapsed or refractory CLL/SLL previously treated with a covalent BTK inhibitor — the trial enrolled exclusively this population — randomised 1:1 to pirtobrutinib 200 mg once daily (119) or investigator's choice (119: idelalisib/rituximab 82, bendamustine/rituximab 37), in an open-label randomised phase 3 study, stratified by previous venetoclax use and del(17p).
cards.result: Progression-free survival (independent review) favoured pirtobrutinib: hazard ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.39–0.75; p=0.0002), median 14.0 months (95% CI 11.2–16.6) versus 8.7 months (8.1–10.4) — the hazard ratio is a relative measure; the absolute median difference was 5.3 months. Overall survival did not differ: HR 1.09 (95% CI 0.68–1.75; p=0.7202), with 18-month survival 73.4% versus 70.8%. Median time to next treatment or death was 24.0 versus 10.9 months (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25–0.52). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent events occurred in 57.7% on pirtobrutinib versus 73.4% on control, and discontinuation for adverse events in 17.2% versus 34.9%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design, and the control arm combined two quite different regimens chosen by investigators. Crossover to pirtobrutinib after progression contaminates the overall-survival comparison — which is a reason the null survival result is hard to interpret, not a reason to assume a hidden survival benefit.
cards.source: Sharman JP et al. cards.headline: BRUIN genomic resistance analysis (Brown 2026): at progression on pirtobrutinib, 68% of patients had acquired a new mutation — including BTK T474 gatekeeper mutations (26%) and L528W (16%) selected by pirtobrutinib itself
cards.summary: BRUIN genomic resistance analysis (Brown 2026): at progression on pirtobrutinib, 68% of patients had acquired a new mutation — including BTK T474 gatekeeper mutations (26%) and L528W (16%) selected by pirtobrutinib itself
cards.type: Genomic substudy of the BRUIN phase 1/2 trial (Brown 2026)
cards.people: Patients with relapsed or refractory CLL pretreated with a covalent BTK inhibitor enrolled in the BRUIN phase 1/2 trial, with DNA sequencing of peripheral blood at baseline, on treatment and at progressive disease; 88 patients were assessed at progression. This is a genomic substudy of the BRUIN programme carded above, not a separate treatment trial.
cards.result: At baseline, BTK mutations were present in 43% (predominantly C481S, 85% of BTK mutations), TP53 in 38%, and 17p deletion in 28%. At progression, 60 of 88 patients (68%) had acquired at least one mutation: 44% acquired BTK mutations and 24% other mutations. Of 55 acquired BTK mutations in 39 patients, gatekeeper T474 mutations accounted for 26% and the kinase-impaired L528W for 16%; the original C481 mutations decreased or cleared in 84% of cases. The authors emphasise complex clonal dynamics, including progression without an obvious genomic driver in some patients.
cards.watchOut: Percentages at progression describe the 88 patients with progression samples, not all treated patients, and assay sensitivity changed what counted as 'acquired' (with the most sensitive assay, all progressing patients had a detectable acquired mutation). Carded for the resistance picture, not as efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Brown JR et al. Genomic determinants of response and resistance to pirtobrutinib in relapsed/refractory chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Blood. 2026. PMID: 41055698. cards.headline: Synthesis: pirtobrutinib is active after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure and beat investigator's-choice therapy on progression-free survival, with no survival benefit shown — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: pirtobrutinib is active after covalent BTK-inhibitor failure and beat investigator's-choice therapy on progression-free survival, with no survival benefit shown — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports: the BRUIN phase 1/2 CLL cohort (247 covalent-BTKi-pretreated patients), the BRUIN CLL-321 randomised phase 3 trial (238 patients) and the BRUIN genomic resistance analysis.
cards.result: The randomised trial is the anchor: progression-free survival HR 0.54 with a 5.3-month absolute median gain, better tolerability than the control regimens, and no overall-survival difference (HR 1.09). The single-arm cohort's 73.3% response rate is consistent. One randomised trial plus a single-arm programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit), and acquired resistance — including mutations pirtobrutinib itself selects — limits how long the benefit should be expected to last.
cards.watchOut: The BRUIN mantle-cell lymphoma cohort is a separate question and is not carded on this shelf; nor are the later pirtobrutinib combination and first-line trials, which ask different questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mato AR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37407001); Sharman JP et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2025 (PMID: 40479620); Brown JR et al. Blood. 2026 (PMID: 41055698), all carded above.

shelves.title: Zanubrutinib versus ibrutinib in relapsed CLL (ALPINE)
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma, does zanubrutinib, versus ibrutinib, improve progression-free survival with fewer cardiac events?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Leukemia, Lymphocytic, Chronic, B-Cell/drug therapy · Pyrimidines/therapeutic use · Piperidines · Pyrazoles · Adenine/analogs & derivatives · Atrial Fibrillation · Disease Progression · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, definitive head-to-head trial (ALPINE, 652 patients) caps the stamp at POSSIBLE under the single-trial rule, however clean its result. Zanubrutinib was superior to ibrutinib on progression-free survival (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49–0.86 — a relative measure; 24-month PFS 78.4% vs 65.9%, an absolute difference of 12.5 percentage points), with higher response rates (85.6% vs 75.4% at the final analysis) and a sustained benefit at 42.5 months (PFS HR 0.68). The cardiac advantage is consistent across every report: atrial fibrillation/flutter was lower on zanubrutinib (7.1% vs 17.0% at the final analysis), cardiac events overall were fewer (25.9% vs 35.5%), and there were no cardiac deaths on zanubrutinib versus six on ibrutinib. Overall survival has not been shown to differ (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.55–1.06, medians not reached). The balance must also carry the published debate that the ibrutinib arm may have underperformed historical ibrutinib results, which would flatter the comparison — the within-trial randomisation still stands, but the size of the advantage should be read with that caveat. Zanubrutinib's other programmes ask different questions — SEQUOIA (treatment-naïve CLL, versus bendamustine–rituximab) and ASPEN (Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, versus ibrutinib) — and are cross-pointed here in prose only, not carded on this shelf. The other second-generation head-to-head, acalabrutinib versus ibrutinib (which showed non-inferiority, not superiority), is homed at pack #3445.

cards.headline: ALPINE interim analysis (Hillmen 2023) — first report of the trial: response rate 78.3% on zanubrutinib versus 62.5% on ibrutinib (p<0.001), with atrial fibrillation 2.5% versus 10.1%
cards.summary: ALPINE interim analysis (Hillmen 2023) — first report of the trial: response rate 78.3% on zanubrutinib versus 62.5% on ibrutinib (p<0.001), with atrial fibrillation 2.5% versus 10.1%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, preplanned interim analysis (Hillmen 2023, ALPINE)
cards.people: The first 415 patients enrolled in ALPINE (207 zanubrutinib, 208 ibrutinib), a global randomised open-label phase 3 trial in relapsed or refractory CLL; the preplanned interim analysis was scheduled about 12 months after the first 415 patients were enrolled, and median follow-up at this analysis was 15 months. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed overall response rate.
cards.result: Overall response was 78.3% (95% CI 72.0–83.7) on zanubrutinib versus 62.5% (55.5–69.1) on ibrutinib (p<0.001). Twelve-month progression-free survival was 94.9% versus 84.0% (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.23–0.69). Atrial fibrillation occurred in 2.5% versus 10.1% (p=0.001), and rates of cardiac events, major haemorrhage and adverse events leading to discontinuation or death were all lower with zanubrutinib.
cards.watchOut: An interim look at the first 415 of 652 patients, on a response-rate primary endpoint — superseded for progression-free survival by the two later reports carded below. Early atrial-fibrillation rates (2.5% vs 10.1%) grow with longer exposure in both arms; compare like with like across reports.
cards.source: Hillmen P et al. Zanubrutinib Versus Ibrutinib in Relapsed/Refractory Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma: Interim Analysis of a Randomized Phase III Trial. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2023. PMID: 36395435. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03734016. cards.headline: ALPINE primary PFS analysis (Brown 2023): zanubrutinib superior on progression-free survival (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49–0.86, p=0.002); 24-month PFS 78.4% versus 65.9%
cards.summary: ALPINE primary PFS analysis (Brown 2023): zanubrutinib superior on progression-free survival (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49–0.86, p=0.002); 24-month PFS 78.4% versus 65.9%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 head-to-head trial, primary PFS analysis (Brown 2023, ALPINE)
cards.people: 652 patients with relapsed or refractory CLL or SLL who had received at least one previous course of therapy, randomised 1:1 to zanubrutinib or ibrutinib until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, in a multinational phase 3 head-to-head trial; median follow-up 29.6 months at this final analysis of progression-free survival.
cards.result: Progression-free survival was superior with zanubrutinib (HR for disease progression or death 0.65, 95% CI 0.49–0.86; p=0.002, investigator-assessed, with similar independent-review results) — a relative measure; the absolute 24-month PFS rates were 78.4% versus 65.9%. In patients with 17p deletion, TP53 mutation or both, the HR was 0.53 (95% CI 0.31–0.88). The percentage of patients with an overall response was higher in the zanubrutinib group than in the ibrutinib group. Zanubrutinib had fewer adverse events leading to discontinuation and fewer cardiac events, including fewer cardiac events leading to discontinuation or death.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial: investigator-assessed PFS in an unblinded comparison can be biased, though the independent-review assessment agreed. This report's abstract does not give the overall-response percentages, so none are quoted on this card; the final-analysis card below gives the response rates from its own record.
cards.source: Brown JR et al. Zanubrutinib or Ibrutinib in Relapsed or Refractory Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. The New England journal of medicine. 2023. PMID: 36511784. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03734016. cards.headline: ALPINE final comparative analysis (Brown 2024): benefit sustained at 42.5 months — PFS HR 0.68, response 85.6% versus 75.4%, atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.1% versus 17.0%, and no cardiac deaths versus six
cards.summary: ALPINE final comparative analysis (Brown 2024): benefit sustained at 42.5 months — PFS HR 0.68, response 85.6% versus 75.4%, atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.1% versus 17.0%, and no cardiac deaths versus six
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial, final comparative analysis with extended follow-up (Brown 2024, ALPINE)
cards.people: All 652 ALPINE patients (327 zanubrutinib, 325 ibrutinib) at the final comparative analysis, with an overall median follow-up of 42.5 months and median exposure of 41.2 versus 37.8 months. This is the extended-follow-up report of the same single trial carded above, not a second trial.
cards.result: Progression-free survival benefit was sustained (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.54–0.84), including in del(17p)/TP53-mutated disease (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33–0.78). Overall response remained higher with zanubrutinib (85.6% vs 75.4%), with complete response rates of 11.6% versus 7.7%. Median overall survival was not reached in either group; fewer zanubrutinib patients had died (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.55–1.06 — not significant). Cardiac events were lower with zanubrutinib (25.9% vs 35.5%), atrial fibrillation/flutter occurred in 7.1% versus 17.0%, and there were no cardiac deaths on zanubrutinib versus six on ibrutinib.
cards.watchOut: Longer follow-up of one trial confirms durability; it does not add an independent trial. Overall survival remains unproven (confidence interval crosses 1), and the literature debate about whether the ibrutinib arm underperformed its historical results applies to every ALPINE report equally.
cards.source: Brown JR et al. Sustained benefit of zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib in patients with R/R CLL/SLL: final comparative analysis of ALPINE. Blood. 2024. PMID: 39316666. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03734016. cards.headline: Synthesis: zanubrutinib beat ibrutinib head-to-head on progression-free survival with fewer cardiac events — POSSIBLE (benefit) under the single-trial cap
cards.summary: Synthesis: zanubrutinib beat ibrutinib head-to-head on progression-free survival with fewer cardiac events — POSSIBLE (benefit) under the single-trial cap
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports, all from the single ALPINE trial (652 patients): its interim analysis, its primary progression-free-survival analysis, and its final comparative analysis at 42.5 months.
cards.result: ALPINE is the only BTK-inhibitor head-to-head to show progression-free-survival superiority: HR 0.65 at the primary analysis, sustained at HR 0.68, with higher response rates and a consistent cardiac-safety advantage (atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.1% vs 17.0%; no cardiac deaths vs six at final analysis). No overall-survival benefit has been shown. One trial, however large and clean, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (benefit). Adjacent zanubrutinib programmes — SEQUOIA in treatment-naïve CLL and ASPEN in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia — ask different questions and are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: All three cards are reports of one trial — read the shelf as a single-trial shelf with unusually complete follow-up, not as three independent confirmations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hillmen P et al. Journal of clinical oncology. 2023 (PMID: 36395435); Brown JR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36511784); Brown JR et al. Blood. 2024 (PMID: 39316666), all carded above.

shelves.title: Trilaciclib before chemotherapy shortens severe neutropenia in small-cell lung cancer — a supportive-care benefit, with no survival benefit shown
shelves.question: In adults receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, does trilaciclib given before chemotherapy reduce the duration and occurrence of severe neutropenia and other myelosuppression outcomes versus chemotherapy alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Brain Neoplasms/drug therapy,enzymology,secondary · Carboplatin/administration & dosage · Cisplatin/administration & dosage · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4/antagonists & inhibitors · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 6/antagonists & inhibitors · Double-Blind Method · Etoposide/administration & dosage · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy,enzymology,pathology · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Middle Aged · Myeloid Cells/drug effects · Paclitaxel/administration & dosage · Prognosis · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage · Pyrroles/administration & dosage · Small Cell Lung Carcinoma/drug therapy,enzymology,pathology · Survival Rate · Tissue Distribution
shelves.balance: The benefit is on myelosuppression and supportive-care endpoints — no survival benefit has been shown, and none may be implied: across the trials, overall survival was essentially unchanged (10.9 vs 10.6 months, HR 0.87, P=0.61 in the first-line etoposide/carboplatin trial; 12.0 vs 8.8 months, HR 0.69 with a confidence interval crossing 1, in TRACES). What trilaciclib (Cosela, as published) does consistently is protect marrow: duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1 fell from 7 to 2 days before topotecan and from 2 days to a mean of 0 days in TRACES, severe neutropenia occurrence fell, grade ≥3 adverse events were fewer (50% vs 83.8% in the first-line trial, driven by haematological toxicity), and supportive-care interventions and dose reductions fell in the pooled analyses. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the myeloprotection claim only.

cards.headline: Weiss 2019 (first-line etoposide/carboplatin): fewer grade ≥3 events on trilaciclib (50% vs 83.8%) and no detriment to tumour response or survival
cards.summary: Weiss 2019 (first-line etoposide/carboplatin): fewer grade ≥3 events on trilaciclib (50% vs 83.8%) and no detriment to tumour response or survival
cards.type: Phase Ib / randomised phase II trial (Weiss 2019)
cards.people: 122 patients enrolled with treatment-naïve extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (19 in the phase Ib dose-finding part and 75 receiving study drug in the randomised phase II part), receiving trilaciclib or placebo before etoposide/carboplatin on days 1–3 of each cycle.
cards.result: Improvements were seen across neutrophil, red-cell and lymphocyte measures. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 50% on trilaciclib versus 83.8% on placebo, primarily from less haematological toxicity; no trilaciclib-related grade ≥3 events occurred. Antitumour efficacy did not differ significantly: response 66.7% vs 56.8% (P=0.38), median progression-free survival 6.2 vs 5.0 months (HR 0.71, P=0.17), overall survival 10.9 vs 10.6 months (HR 0.87, P=0.61) — no survival benefit (the treatment made no difference to survival in this trial).
cards.watchOut: The randomised part is modest in size and the survival comparison is underpowered — 'no detriment shown' is not proof of no detriment. Myelosuppression endpoints, not survival, are what this programme was built to move.
cards.source: Weiss JM et al. Myelopreservation with the CDK4/6 inhibitor trilaciclib in patients with small-cell lung cancer receiving first-line chemotherapy: a phase Ib/randomized phase II trial. cards.headline: Hart 2021 (before topotecan, previously treated disease): severe neutropenia lasted 2 days versus 7 days in cycle 1, and occurred in 40.6% versus 75.9%
cards.summary: Hart 2021 (before topotecan, previously treated disease): severe neutropenia lasted 2 days versus 7 days in cycle 1, and occurred in 40.6% versus 75.9%
cards.people: 61 patients with previously treated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer randomised to intravenous trilaciclib 240 mg/m² or placebo before topotecan 1.5 mg/m² on days 1–5 of each 21-day cycle (32 trilaciclib, 29 placebo).
cards.result: Duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1: mean 2 days (SD 3.9) versus 7 days (SD 6.2) (adjusted one-sided P<0.0001). Occurrence of severe neutropenia 40.6% versus 75.9% (P=0.016). Grade ≥3 haematological events were fewer on trilaciclib, notably anaemia 28.1% versus 60.7%. Patient-reported fatigue outcomes favoured trilaciclib, and antitumour efficacy was comparable between arms.
cards.watchOut: Small trial (61 patients) in a heavily myelosuppressive second-line regimen — the absolute day counts belong to topotecan and should not be read across to first-line regimens.
cards.source: Hart LL et al. Myelopreservation with Trilaciclib in Patients Receiving Topotecan for Small Cell Lung Cancer: Results from a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase II Study. Advances in therapy. 2021. PMID: 33123968. Registry ID: NCT02514447. cards.headline: TRACES 2024 (phase III, China): duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1 was a mean of 0 days versus 2 days (P=0.0003)
cards.summary: TRACES 2024 (phase III, China): duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1 was a mean of 0 days versus 2 days (P=0.0003)
cards.people: 95 Chinese patients with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer (12 in the open-label safety run-in; 83 in the double-blind part: 41 trilaciclib, 42 placebo), receiving trilaciclib 240 mg/m² or placebo before etoposide/carboplatin or topotecan.
cards.result: In the double-blind part, duration of severe neutropenia in cycle 1 was mean 0 days (SD 1.7) versus 2 days (SD 3.0) (P=0.0003), with improvements in additional neutrophil, red-cell and platelet measures. After median follow-up of 14.1 months, median overall survival was 12.0 versus 8.8 months (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.22) and progression-free survival 4.8 versus 4.3 months (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.39) — neither significant, so no survival benefit is claimed.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China) phase III with a pharmacokinetic/safety primary structure; the survival hazard ratio's confidence interval is wide and crosses 1 — it must not be quoted as a survival signal.
cards.source: Cheng Y et al. Myeloprotection with trilaciclib in Chinese patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer receiving chemotherapy: Results from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III study (TRACES). cards.headline: Synthesis: marrow protection is consistent across regimens and countries; survival is unchanged wherever it was measured
cards.summary: Synthesis: marrow protection is consistent across regimens and countries; survival is unchanged wherever it was measured
cards.people: Three randomised placebo-controlled trials (first-line etoposide/carboplatin, second/third-line topotecan, and the Chinese phase III TRACES) in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer.
cards.result: Severe-neutropenia duration in cycle 1: 2 vs 7 days (topotecan trial) and mean 0 vs 2 days (TRACES). Grade ≥3 adverse events 50% vs 83.8% (first-line trial). Overall survival: HR 0.87 (P=0.61) and HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.40 to 1.22) — no survival benefit shown in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), confined to myelosuppression and supportive-care endpoints, per the slate flag.
cards.watchOut: All trials were industry-programme trials of one product in one disease; the licensed settings beyond extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer are not covered by the records carded here, and this shelf makes no claim about them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weiss JM et al. Annals of Oncology. 2019; Hart LL et al. Advances in Therapy. 2021; Cheng Y et al. Lung Cancer. 2024.

shelves.title: Glucarpidase cuts plasma methotrexate by about 99% within minutes — on single-arm evidence, with no randomised trial
shelves.question: In patients with delayed methotrexate clearance and methotrexate-induced kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate, does glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2) lower plasma methotrexate fast enough to change dialysis need and recovery versus supportive care with leucovorin?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/blood,chemically induced,prevention & control · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic/administration & dosage,adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Bone Neoplasms/blood,complications,drug therapy · Compassionate Use Trials · Drug Administration Schedule · Humans · Leucovorin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Methotrexate/administration & dosage,adverse effects,blood,therapeutic use · Osteosarcoma/blood,complications,drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Glutamyl Hydrolase/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: No randomised trial exists — the entire base is single-arm cohorts and compassionate-use programmes, graded accordingly, with small-N labelling applied per the slate flag (the pooled programme treated 476 patients, of whom 169 were efficacy-evaluable for the level fall). Glucarpidase (Voraxaze, as published — carboxypeptidase G2) does the pharmacokinetic thing dramatically and consistently: a median 99% reduction in plasma methotrexate from the first post-dose measurement (median 15 minutes) sustained to the last (median 40 hours) in the pooled analysis, and an immediate >97% reduction in the adult cohort. The clinical-outcome claims are cohort-grade only: 64% of patients with grade ≥2 renal impairment recovered to grade 0–1 at a median of 12.5 days in the pooled analysis, and 93% of the adult cohort had normalisation or improvement of creatinine — but with no comparator, how much of that recovery the enzyme caused, versus leucovorin and supportive care, cannot be known. The methotrexate-level fall is a pharmacokinetic surrogate. Timing matters: the consensus guideline states administration should optimally occur within 48–60 hours of the start of the methotrexate infusion.

cards.headline: Widemann 2014 (pooled compassionate-use, 476 treated): plasma methotrexate fell by a median of 99%, sustained; 64% with grade ≥2 renal impairment recovered to grade 0–1
cards.summary: Widemann 2014 (pooled compassionate-use, 476 treated): plasma methotrexate fell by a median of 99%, sustained; 64% with grade ≥2 renal impairment recovered to grade 0–1
cards.type: Pooled analysis of four single-arm compassionate-use trials (Widemann 2014)
cards.people: 476 patients with renal toxicity and delayed methotrexate elimination treated with intravenous glucarpidase in four multicentre single-arm compassionate-use trials (1993–2007); 169 were efficacy-evaluable (baseline methotrexate >1 µmol/L with HPLC measurement) and renal recovery was assessed in 436. Median age 20 years; osteosarcoma 36%, non-Hodgkin lymphoma 27%, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia 20%.
cards.result: Median pre-glucarpidase methotrexate was 11.7 µmol/L. From the first post-dose measurement (median 15 minutes) through the last (median 40 hours), plasma methotrexate showed a consistent 99% median reduction. A rapid and sustained clinically important reduction (to ≤1 µmol/L at all post-dose determinations) was achieved by 83 of 140 patients (59%). Of patients with renal impairment ≥ grade 2, 64% recovered to grade 0 or 1 at a median of 12.5 days after glucarpidase.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: the level fall is attributable to the enzyme (it is immediate and mechanistic), but renal recovery, dialysis avoidance and survival cannot be attributed — patients also received leucovorin and supportive care, and compassionate-use cohorts select for severity in both directions.
cards.source: Widemann BC et al. Efficacy of glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase g2) in patients with acute kidney injury after high-dose methotrexate therapy. Pharmacotherapy. 2014. PMID: 24132809. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Schwartz 2007 (adults and elderly, N = 43): an immediate >97% fall in serum methotrexate, creatinine normalised or improved in 93% — yet 23% died of complications of the methotrexate episode
cards.summary: Schwartz 2007 (adults and elderly, N = 43): an immediate >97% fall in serum methotrexate, creatinine normalised or improved in 93% — yet 23% died of complications of the methotrexate episode
cards.people: 43 patients aged 18–78 with delayed methotrexate elimination (serum methotrexate 1–1,187 µmol/L) who received glucarpidase, leucovorin rescue guided by methotrexate immunoassay, and standard supportive care (N = 43).
cards.result: Glucarpidase was well tolerated and produced an immediate >97% reduction in serum methotrexate, with 0.2%–35% of the total methotrexate dose recovered in urine as inactive metabolites. Forty of 43 patients (93%) had normalisation (25) or improvement (15) of serum creatinine. Frequent grade III–IV toxicities were haematological (60%) and mucositis (35%); 8 patients (19%) developed grade III–IV nephrotoxicity, and 10 (23%) experienced fatal complications associated with high-dose methotrexate therapy. Patients with ≥3 risk factors for delayed elimination had significantly poorer survival (HR 3.64).
cards.watchOut: N = 43, single-arm: the sobering mortality (23%) is the counterweight to the pharmacokinetic success — by the time adults receive the enzyme, much methotrexate injury may already be established, which is why the guideline stresses early administration.
cards.source: Schwartz S et al. Glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase g2) intervention in adult and elderly cancer patients with renal dysfunction and delayed methotrexate elimination after high-dose methotrexate therapy. The oncologist. 2007. PMID: 18055849. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ramsey 2018 consensus guideline: give glucarpidase on defined level thresholds, optimally within 48–60 hours of the start of the infusion
cards.summary: Ramsey 2018 consensus guideline: give glucarpidase on defined level thresholds, optimally within 48–60 hours of the start of the infusion
cards.people: Expert consensus guideline for patients with high-dose-methotrexate-induced acute kidney injury and delayed methotrexate clearance, in children and adults (a guideline, carded as the programme's decision framework — not as outcome evidence).
cards.result: For infusions of ≤24 hours, glucarpidase may be indicated if the 36-hour methotrexate concentration is above 30 µM, the 42-hour above 10 µM, or the 48-hour above 5 µM with significantly elevated creatinine; after a 36–42-hour infusion, if the 48-hour concentration is above 5 µM. Administration should optimally occur within 48–60 hours from the start of the infusion, because life-threatening toxicities may not be preventable beyond that point; the drug is less effective after more than 60 hours of exposure.
cards.watchOut: A consensus guideline built on the same single-arm base — it organises practice but adds no comparative evidence. Post-glucarpidase methotrexate immunoassays are also confounded by metabolites, a practical caveat the cohorts handled by HPLC measurement.
cards.source: Ramsey LB et al. Consensus Guideline for Use of Glucarpidase in Patients with High-Dose Methotrexate Induced Acute Kidney Injury and Delayed Methotrexate Clearance. The oncologist. 2018. PMID: 29079637. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the level fall is certain and immediate; every clinical-outcome claim rests on uncontrolled cohorts
cards.summary: Synthesis: the level fall is certain and immediate; every clinical-outcome claim rests on uncontrolled cohorts
cards.people: One pooled single-arm programme (476 treated, 169 efficacy-evaluable), one adult single-arm cohort (43 patients) and the consensus guideline built on them. No randomised trial exists.
cards.result: Plasma methotrexate reduction: median 99% (pooled) and >97% immediately (adult cohort). Renal recovery to grade 0–1 in 64% at a median of 12.5 days (pooled, uncontrolled). Adult-cohort mortality from the methotrexate episode: 23%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) with single-arm/small-programme labelling, per the slate flag.
cards.watchOut: A randomised trial in this rare, emergent indication is unlikely ever to be run; the shelf's honest ceiling is that glucarpidase certainly clears methotrexate from plasma and plausibly improves outcomes when given early — the size of any dialysis or survival effect is unknown.
cards.source: Synthesis of Widemann BC et al. Pharmacotherapy. 2014; Schwartz S et al. The Oncologist. 2007; Ramsey LB et al. The Oncologist. 2018.

shelves.question: In patients receiving taxane chemotherapy, does limb compression — alone or combined with cooling as cryocompression — prevent grade ≥2 chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy versus no intervention or cooling alone?

shelves.balance: This shelf asks the compression question that the library's existing cryotherapy shelf (the frozen gloves and socks shelf for paclitaxel neuropathy) does not: that shelf covers cooling alone, and compression — tight surgical gloves, alone or combined with cooling as cryocompression — is the unasked slice cross-pointed here. The POLAR randomised trial is the anchor: within each patient, the treated dominant hand was compared with the untreated other hand, and both cooling (grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 29% vs 50%) and compression (24% vs 38%) significantly reduced high-grade neuropathy on the treated hand, with no randomised difference established between cooling and compression themselves. The earlier surgical-glove compression programme points the same way (grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 21.4% on protected hands vs 76.1% on control hands in the within-patient phase II study; 13.8% in the single-arm confirmatory study), and a conventionally randomised compression trial (80 patients, gloves and elastic socks) found significantly lower neuropathy incidence after the fourth and sixth cycles. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): compression is a cheap, tolerable alternative where freezing is impractical — the evidence is promising, not settled.

cards.headline: POLAR 2025: on the treated hand, grade ≥2 neuropathy was 29% with cooling versus 50% untreated, and 24% with compression versus 38% untreated
cards.summary: POLAR 2025: on the treated hand, grade ≥2 neuropathy was 29% with cooling versus 50% untreated, and 24% with compression versus 38% untreated
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with within-patient control (POLAR, Michel 2025)
cards.people: 122 women with primary breast cancer receiving weekly paclitaxel- or nab-paclitaxel-based chemotherapy at Heidelberg, randomised 1:1 to cooling or compression of the dominant hand (frozen glove, or two surgical gloves one size too small, worn 30 minutes before, during and after administration), with the other hand untreated as the within-patient control; 101 patients were in the final analysis (52 cooling, 49 compression).
cards.result: Both interventions significantly reduced grade ≥2 sensory CIPN on the treated hand: cooling 29% (15 patients) versus 50% (26) on the untreated hand (P=.002; effect size 21.15 percentage points, 95% CI 5.98 to 35.55); compression 24% (12) versus 38% (19) (P=.008; effect size 14.29 points, 95% CI 2.02 to 27.24). CIPN was the main reason for treatment discontinuation in 16 of 24 patients who discontinued (67%), and patients with grade ≥2 CIPN had reduced global health status during and 6–8 months after therapy.
cards.watchOut: The control is the patient's own other hand, not a separate randomised no-treatment group, and patients were not blinded to which hand was treated; 21 of 122 randomised patients withdrew before the final analysis. The trial compares each intervention against no intervention — it does not establish cooling versus compression superiority.
cards.source: Michel LL et al. Efficacy of Hand Cooling and Compression in Preventing Taxane-Induced Neuropathy: The POLAR Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA oncology. 2025. PMID: 40048176. Registry ID: NCT06541769. cards.headline: Tsuyuki 2016 (surgical-glove compression, within-patient): grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 21.4% on protected hands versus 76.1% on control hands
cards.summary: Tsuyuki 2016 (surgical-glove compression, within-patient): grade ≥2 sensory neuropathy 21.4% on protected hands versus 76.1% on control hands
cards.people: 43 patients with primary or recurrent breast cancer receiving nab-paclitaxel 260 mg/m² enrolled, 42 evaluated; patients wore two surgical gloves one size too small on the dominant hand for 90 minutes, with the non-dominant hand as control (phase II multicentre case-control study).
cards.result: Occurrence of CTCAE grade ≥2 sensory peripheral neuropathy was 21.4% on glove-protected hands versus 76.1% on control hands, and grade ≥2 motor neuropathy 26.2% versus 57.1% (both significantly lower). No patient withdrew for compression intolerance. Fingertip temperature on the protected hand fell by 1.6–2.2 °C — compression also cools, which blurs the cooling-versus-compression distinction.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised between patients, and unblinded; the very large difference (21.4% vs 76.1%) comes from 42 patients on one nab-paclitaxel schedule in Japan. The fingertip cooling it produces means 'compression' here is partly cryocompression in effect.
cards.source: Tsuyuki S et al. Evaluation of the effect of compression therapy using surgical gloves on nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy: a phase II multicenter study by the Kamigata Breast Cancer Study Group. Breast cancer research and treatment. 2016. PMID: 27620884. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dongxue 2024 (conventionally randomised, N = 80): compression with tight gloves and elastic socks lowered neuropathy incidence after cycles 4 and 6
cards.summary: Dongxue 2024 (conventionally randomised, N = 80): compression with tight gloves and elastic socks lowered neuropathy incidence after cycles 4 and 6
cards.people: 80 patients with breast cancer receiving taxane chemotherapy at a Chinese hospital, randomised to routine care (40) or compression therapy (40) — surgical gloves one size too small on the hands and elastic socks on the feet from 30 minutes before to 30 minutes after infusion (N = 80).
cards.result: Before intervention and after cycle 2, neuropathy incidence, anxiety, depression and sleep scores did not differ significantly between groups. After the fourth and sixth cycles, the incidence of CIPN (grade ≥1 and ≥2), anxiety and depression scores, and sleep scores were significantly lower in the compression group than in the control group (P<0.05 for the reported comparisons).
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance without the absolute incidence figures for each cycle in its abstract, so this shelf does not quote absolute rates for this trial; open-label, single-centre, and the intervention bundles gloves with socks (hands and feet together).
cards.source: Dongxue G et al. Therapeutic effects of compression therapy on taxane-induced peripheral neuropathy incidence, negative emotions, and sleep disorders in patients with breast cancer. Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer. 2024. PMID: 38561474. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: compression reduces high-grade neuropathy on the treated limb in every design that has tested it — certainty is limited by within-patient and unblinded designs
cards.summary: Synthesis: compression reduces high-grade neuropathy on the treated limb in every design that has tested it — certainty is limited by within-patient and unblinded designs
cards.people: One randomised within-patient trial (POLAR, 101 analysed), one within-patient phase II study (42 evaluated) and one conventionally randomised trial (80 patients) — all in breast-cancer taxane treatment.
cards.result: Grade ≥2 sensory CIPN on treated versus untreated hands: cooling 29% vs 50% and compression 24% vs 38% (POLAR); surgical-glove compression 21.4% vs 76.1% (Tsuyuki). The conventional RCT found significantly lower incidence after cycles 4–6 without abstract-level absolute rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). This shelf complements, and does not duplicate, the library's cooling-only cryotherapy shelf for paclitaxel neuropathy.
cards.watchOut: Missing: a large conventionally randomised, blinded-outcome trial of compression (and of combined cryocompression devices) with follow-up for persistent neuropathy; feet are less studied than hands, and non-taxane neurotoxic regimens are untested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Michel LL et al. JAMA Oncology. 2025; Tsuyuki S et al. Breast Cancer Research and Treatment. 2016; Dongxue G et al. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2024.

shelves.title: Acupuncture for established painful CIPN: symptoms improve versus usual care, but real and sham acupuncture have not separated
shelves.question: In patients with established painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, does acupuncture (manual or electroacupuncture, as tested) reduce neuropathic pain and symptom scores versus sham acupuncture or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy* · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects* · Cancer Survivors* · Female · Humans · Neoplasms/drug therapy* · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/chemically induced* · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: The record splits on the comparator, and the stamp names that split. Against usual care, acupuncture improves CIPN-related quality of life and symptom scores (the Bao trial's FACT/GOG-Ntx scores rose significantly versus usual care at week 8, P=.001). Against sham acupuncture, real acupuncture has not separated: in the same trial, sham improved alongside real on quality of life (P=.01 versus usual care), there was no statistically significant difference between real and sham, and the trial's quantitative-sensory-testing report likewise found real and sham both better than usual care with no difference between them — expectancy and non-specific effects are doing measurable work here. A separate electroacupuncture programme (160 women with paclitaxel-induced neuropathy) found higher overall effective rates for 2 Hz (79.5%) and 2/100 Hz (81.1%) electroacupuncture than for oral mecobalamin (47.4%), with greater symptom-score reductions — a drug comparator, not a sham. Prevention claims are a different question and are not folded in. PROPOSED SPLIT, as above.

cards.headline: Bao 2020 (the sham-controlled anchor): 75 survivors with moderate-to-severe CIPN randomised to real acupuncture, sham acupuncture or usual care for 8 weeks
cards.summary: Bao 2020 (the sham-controlled anchor): 75 survivors with moderate-to-severe CIPN randomised to real acupuncture, sham acupuncture or usual care for 8 weeks
cards.people: Cancer survivors with persistent moderate-to-severe chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling or pain rated ≥4 on an 11-point scale) randomised 1:1:1 to 8 weeks of real acupuncture, sham acupuncture or usual care — 75 enrolled, as detailed in the programme's companion reports.
cards.result: This record is the trial's primary-endpoint report (neuropathy symptoms on the numeric rating scale); its abstract, as fetched, states the design and that the trial investigates acupuncture versus sham and usual care, without reproducing the primary numeric result — so this shelf takes its numbers from the programme's fully reported companion papers (next card) rather than quoting a figure this record does not contain.
cards.watchOut: Quoted plainly because it matters: the primary report's PubMed abstract is a summary stub. The shelf's numeric claims rest on the companion quality-of-life and sensory-testing reports of the same trial — one trial, several reports — and are labelled that way.
cards.source: Bao T et al. Effect of Acupuncture vs Sham Procedure on Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2020. PMID: 32159808. cards.headline: Bao 2021 (same trial, quality of life): FACT/GOG-Ntx improved versus usual care in both real (P=.001) and sham (P=.01) arms — with no difference between real and sham
cards.summary: Bao 2021 (same trial, quality of life): FACT/GOG-Ntx improved versus usual care in both real (P=.001) and sham (P=.01) arms — with no difference between real and sham
cards.people: 75 survivors of solid tumours with moderate-to-severe CIPN randomised to 8 weeks of real acupuncture, sham acupuncture or usual care; health-related quality of life was measured with FACT/GOG-Ntx, anxiety/depression, insomnia and fatigue scales (same trial as the previous card).
cards.result: At week 8, FACT/GOG-Ntx, anxiety and insomnia scores had improved significantly from baseline in the real and sham arms but not in usual care. Versus usual care, FACT/GOG-Ntx improved significantly in both the real arm (P=.001) and the sham arm (P=.01); there was no statistically significant difference between real and sham acupuncture, and no difference between arms in depression or fatigue at weeks 8 and 12.
cards.watchOut: Same 75 patients as the anchor card — not independent confirmation. The sham response is the finding: a non-insertion sham at non-acupuncture points produced the same quality-of-life gain, so point-specific efficacy for established CIPN remains unproven.
cards.source: Bao T et al. Health-Related Quality of Life in Cancer Survivors with Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy: A Randomized Clinical Trial. The oncologist. 2021. PMID: 34390283. cards.headline: Lu 2024 (electroacupuncture frequencies, N = 160): overall effective rates 79.5% (2 Hz) and 81.1% (2/100 Hz) versus 47.4% on mecobalamin
cards.summary: Lu 2024 (electroacupuncture frequencies, N = 160): overall effective rates 79.5% (2 Hz) and 81.1% (2/100 Hz) versus 47.4% on mecobalamin
cards.people: 160 women with paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy randomised to electroacupuncture at 2 Hz, 100 Hz or 2/100 Hz (40 per group; 37–39 analysed per group) or oral mecobalamin, treated for 4 weeks with 4 weeks of follow-up (N = 160). The stimulator used was the HANS-200E acupoint nerve stimulator, as published.
cards.result: FACT/GOG-Ntx scores fell in all groups after treatment, with greater reductions in the electroacupuncture groups than the medication group; pain (VAS) scores fell in the electroacupuncture groups. Overall effective rates were 79.5% (31/39, 2 Hz), 68.4% (26/38, 100 Hz), 81.1% (30/37, 2/100 Hz) and 47.4% (18/38, medication); the 2 Hz and 2/100 Hz rates were significantly higher than medication (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is an oral vitamin-B12 analogue (mecobalamin), not sham acupuncture, and there was no blinding of patients to needling — so this trial shows electroacupuncture beating a drug, not beating placebo needling. 'Effective rate' is a composite responder definition, not a pain-score difference.
cards.source: Lu C et al. [Electroacupuncture with different frequencies for paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy: a randomized controlled trial]. Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion. 2024. PMID: 39401811. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: benefit versus usual care is consistent; superiority over sham needling is not demonstrated — a SPLIT record
cards.summary: Synthesis: benefit versus usual care is consistent; superiority over sham needling is not demonstrated — a SPLIT record
cards.people: One sham-controlled trial programme (75 patients, multiple reports) and one electroacupuncture-versus-drug trial (160 patients) in established CIPN.
cards.result: Versus usual care: quality-of-life/symptom improvement significant for real acupuncture (P=.001) — and equally for sham (P=.01), with no real-versus-sham difference. Versus mecobalamin: electroacupuncture effective rates 79.5–81.1% versus 47.4%. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the comparator split on the face. Small trials throughout; blinding is imperfect by design.
cards.watchOut: A large sham-controlled trial powered on pain, with expectancy measured, is what would resolve the split; the existing expectancy analysis of the Bao trial found baseline expectancy was not significantly associated with week-8 pain in any arm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bao T et al. JAMA Network Open. 2020; Bao T et al. The Oncologist. 2021; Lu C et al. Zhongguo Zhen Jiu (Chinese Acupuncture & Moxibustion). 2024.

shelves.question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer about to receive radiotherapy, does submandibular gland transfer to the submental space (with shielding of the transferred gland) prevent radiation-induced xerostomia versus pilocarpine or no gland-sparing surgery?

shelves.balance: A pre-IMRT-era technique, and the caveat belongs on the face: the randomised comparison is transfer versus oral pilocarpine, and the phase II programme explicitly did not allow intensity-modulated radiotherapy — so the modern-comparator question (transfer versus IMRT parotid/submandibular sparing) has never been randomised, and this shelf does not pretend otherwise. Within its era, the record is consistent: the phase III interim analysis (120 patients) found stimulated salivary flow of 0.18 mL/min with transfer versus 0.05 mL/min with pilocarpine (P=.003) and better quality-of-life saliva scores, leading to premature closure; the functional-outcomes report (69 patients) found better swallowing and quality-of-life outcomes with transfer at every time point; and the multicentre phase II RTOG 0244 study found the technique reproducible (per protocol or acceptable variation in 77.3%) with 74% of patients prevented from acute grade ≥2 xerostomia — in a programme that also barred amifostine and pilocarpine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the pilocarpine-era comparison only.

cards.headline: Jha 2009 (phase III, interim N = 120): stimulated salivary flow 0.18 versus 0.05 mL/min favouring gland transfer over pilocarpine (P=.003) — the study closed early
cards.summary: Jha 2009 (phase III, interim N = 120): stimulated salivary flow 0.18 versus 0.05 mL/min favouring gland transfer over pilocarpine (P=.003) — the study closed early
cards.people: Patients with head-and-neck cancer in a prospective phase III multicentre randomised study of submandibular salivary gland transfer (transfer of the gland to the submental space, shielded during radiotherapy) versus oral pilocarpine during and for 3 months after radiotherapy; the interim intention-to-treat analysis covered 120 patients, with salivary flow and University of Washington quality-of-life scores measured.
cards.result: At 6 months, median baseline (unstimulated) salivary flow was 0.04 mL/min in the transfer arm versus 0.01 mL/min with pilocarpine (P=.001), and median stimulated flow was 0.18 versus 0.05 mL/min (P=.003). Quality-of-life scores for amount of saliva (P=.017) and consistency of saliva (P=.005) favoured transfer, leading to premature closure of the study.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis that stopped the trial early — early closure for benefit tends to exaggerate effects, and the full planned sample was never accrued. The comparator is pilocarpine, a drug — not modern IMRT gland sparing (see the balance).
cards.source: Jha N et al. Phase III randomized study: oral pilocarpine versus submandibular salivary gland transfer protocol for the management of radiation-induced xerostomia. Head & neck. 2009. PMID: 19107948. Registry ID: none in the record.
