cards.headline: RTOG 0244 (phase II, 49 enrolled): the transfer technique was reproducible across centres, and 74% of patients were prevented from acute grade ≥2 xerostomia
cards.summary: RTOG 0244 (phase II, 49 enrolled): the transfer technique was reproducible across centres, and 74% of patients were prevented from acute grade ≥2 xerostomia
cards.people: 49 patients with head-and-neck cancer undergoing primary surgery, neck dissection and submandibular gland transfer followed by radiotherapy with the transferred gland shielded, in a multicentre phase II study; 44 were analysable (81.8% men, 63.6% oropharynx, 61.4% stage IV, median age 56.5 years). Intensity-modulated radiotherapy, amifostine and pilocarpine were not allowed.
cards.result: Transfer was performed per protocol or within acceptable variation in 34 of 44 patients (77.3%), and radiotherapy in 79.5%. Nine patients (20.9%) developed grade ≥2 acute xerostomia; counting 2 further patients who started amifostine/pilocarpine, 11 of 43 (25.6%) were failures for the xerostomia endpoint — i.e. about 74% were prevented from acute xerostomia. Two-year overall survival was 76.4% and disease-free survival 71.7% (median follow-up 2.9 years in survivors).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: the 74% figure is judged against a prespecified acceptability threshold (grade ≥2 rate ≤51%), not against a randomised control. The explicit exclusion of IMRT dates the programme — it answers the pre-IMRT question.
cards.source: Jha N et al. A phase II study of submandibular gland transfer prior to radiation for prevention of radiation-induced xerostomia in head-and-neck cancer (RTOG 0244). International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics. 2012. PMID: 22541957. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rieger 2012 (functional outcomes, N = 69): swallowing and quality of life were better with transfer than pilocarpine at every assessment
cards.summary: Rieger 2012 (functional outcomes, N = 69): swallowing and quality of life were better with transfer than pilocarpine at every assessment
cards.people: 69 patients from the randomised programme (36 transfer, 33 pilocarpine) assessed for speech intelligibility, swallowing and quality of life before treatment and at 1, 6 and 12 months (N = 69).
cards.result: There were no differences between groups in speech outcomes. In all other comparisons, patients who received gland transfer had better swallowing outcomes and quality-of-life scores than patients who received oral pilocarpine, with significant between-group differences in swallowing and quality of life. The authors conclude transfer should be the treatment of choice between the two options studied.
cards.watchOut: A subset (69 of the programme's patients) with patient-reported and functional outcomes — unblinded by necessity (surgery versus tablets), so expectation effects on quality-of-life scores cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Rieger JM et al. Functional outcomes related to the prevention of radiation-induced xerostomia: oral pilocarpine versus submandibular salivary gland transfer. Head & neck. 2012. PMID: 21416547. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: transfer beat pilocarpine on flow, swallowing and quality of life — and the comparison that matters today was never run
cards.summary: Synthesis: transfer beat pilocarpine on flow, swallowing and quality of life — and the comparison that matters today was never run
cards.people: One phase III randomised programme (120 patients at interim analysis; 69 in the functional report) and one multicentre phase II reproducibility study (49 enrolled) — the Jha/Seikaly programme.
cards.result: Stimulated flow 0.18 vs 0.05 mL/min (P=.003); acute grade ≥2 xerostomia prevented in ~74% (phase II, uncontrolled); swallowing and quality of life favoured transfer throughout. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), fenced to the pre-IMRT, pilocarpine-comparator question, per the slate flag: transfer versus modern IMRT gland sparing has never been randomised.
cards.watchOut: Surgical candidacy is itself selective (the gland must be transferable and outside the high-dose field, and oncological safety of sparing a level-I gland constrains use); contemporary IMRT series are the missing comparator, not a detail.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jha N et al. Head & Neck. 2009; Jha N et al. International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics. 2012 (RTOG 0244); Rieger JM et al. Head & Neck. 2012.

shelves.title: Elective neck dissection in early oral cancer improved survival over watch-and-wait in two randomised trials
shelves.question: In adults with early (T1–T2, clinically node-negative) oral cavity squamous-cell carcinoma, does elective neck dissection at the time of primary surgery improve overall and disease-free survival versus watch-and-wait with therapeutic dissection on nodal relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Lymphatic Metastasis · Male · Middle Aged · Mouth Neoplasms/mortality,surgery · Neck Dissection · Neoplasm Staging · Neoplasms, Squamous Cell/mortality,surgery · Prospective Studies · Survival Analysis · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from different eras and health systems point the same way, and the trials are carded separately rather than pooled: in the Indian trial, 3-year overall survival was 80.0% with elective dissection versus 67.5% with watch-and-wait (hazard ratio for death 0.64 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates); in the UK SEND trial the survival hazard ratio was 0.71 but not significant alone, with disease-free survival significantly favouring elective dissection. The seven-trial randomised meta-analysis (HR 0.67 for death) supports the same conclusion. The cost, per the UK trial, is more facial/neck nerve damage and neck surgery in the majority whose nodes prove negative (occult disease was found in 19.1% of T1 and 34.7% of T2 necks). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: D'Cruz 2015 (SEND programme, NEJM RCT, first 500 patients): elective neck dissection improved 3-year overall survival to 80.0% versus 67.5% with watch-and-wait
cards.summary: D'Cruz 2015 (SEND programme, NEJM RCT, first 500 patients): elective neck dissection improved 3-year overall survival to 80.0% versus 67.5% with watch-and-wait
cards.people: 500 patients (of 596 enrolled) with lateralised stage T1 or T2 oral squamous-cell carcinoma and a node-negative neck, randomised to elective (ipsilateral) neck dissection at primary surgery (245) or therapeutic dissection after nodal relapse (255); median follow-up 39 months.
cards.result: At 3 years, overall survival was 80.0% (95% CI 74.1 to 85.8) with elective dissection versus 67.5% (95% CI 61.0 to 73.9) with therapeutic dissection — a hazard ratio for death of 0.64 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.92; P = 0.01), i.e. a 36% relative reduction in the hazard of death, beside the 12.5-percentage-point absolute survival difference above. There were 81 recurrences and 50 deaths in the elective group versus 146 recurrences and 79 deaths in the therapeutic group.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (Indian) trial in lateralised tumours, reported early at the data monitoring committee's prespecified point (first 500 of 596) — early-reported survival benefits can shrink with full follow-up.
cards.source: D'Cruz AK et al. Elective versus Therapeutic Neck Dissection in Node-Negative Oral Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2015. PMID: 26027881. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hutchison 2019 (UK SEND RCT, 250 randomised patients): disease-free survival favoured elective dissection (HR 0.66), overall survival did not reach significance in the trial alone (HR 0.71, p = 0.18)
cards.summary: Hutchison 2019 (UK SEND RCT, 250 randomised patients): disease-free survival favoured elective dissection (HR 0.66), overall survival did not reach significance in the trial alone (HR 0.71, p = 0.18)
cards.type: Nationwide randomised trial with meta-analysis (UK SEND, Hutchison 2019)
cards.people: 250 randomised patients (plus 346 in a concurrent preference cohort) with stage T1/T2 N0 oral cancer at 27 UK hospitals, having primary tumour resection with or without elective neck dissection (END).
cards.result: Occult neck disease was found in 19.1% of T1 and 34.7% of T2 patients. Five-year intention-to-treat hazard ratios were 0.71 for overall survival (p = 0.18) and 0.66 for disease-free survival (p = 0.04), favouring END; per-protocol results were HR 0.59 (p = 0.054) and 0.56 (p = 0.007). END patients had more facial/neck nerve damage; quality of life was largely unaffected. The concurrent observational cohort supported the randomised findings, and the authors' meta-analysis of all six randomised trials gave HR 0.64 for death and 0.54 for recurrence (both p < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: The UK trial alone was not powered to confirm the survival effect (overall-survival p = 0.18); its weight comes from consistency with the larger Indian trial and the six-trial pooling. Era and neck-management details differ between the two trials — they are carded separately, not pooled here.
cards.source: Hutchison IL et al. Nationwide randomised trial evaluating elective neck dissection for early stage oral cancer (SEND study) with meta-analysis and concurrent real-world cohort. British journal of cancer. 2019. PMID: 31611612. Registry ID: ISRCTN65018995 (stated in the record). cards.headline: Meta-analysis of RCTs 2022 (7 trials, 1,250 patients): elective dissection improved overall survival (HR 0.67) and disease-free survival (HR 0.64) and reduced nodal recurrence (OR 0.28)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of RCTs 2022 (7 trials, 1,250 patients): elective dissection improved overall survival (HR 0.67) and disease-free survival (HR 0.64) and reduced nodal recurrence (OR 0.28)
cards.people: Seven randomised trials (1,250 patients) comparing elective neck dissection at primary tumour resection with observation and therapeutic dissection on nodal recurrence, in early-stage clinically node-negative oral cancer.
cards.result: Elective dissection significantly improved overall survival (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86) and disease-free survival (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.89) — relative measures, consistent with the absolute difference in the largest trial (80.0% vs 67.5% at 3 years) — and reduced lymph-node recurrence (odds ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.66). After correcting for heterogeneity, disease-specific survival also improved (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.98).
cards.watchOut: The record for this synthesis carried no MeSH terms (see source line). The pooled trials span different eras and neck-management protocols; the two large modern trials are carded individually above.
cards.source: Elective Neck Dissection Versus Therapeutic Neck Dissection in Clinically Node-Negative Early Stage Oral Cancer: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of maxillofacial and oral surgery. 2022. PMID: 35712441. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised trials in different health systems and their pooled evidence agree — upfront elective dissection saves lives in early node-negative oral cancer, at the cost of more neck surgery up front
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised trials in different health systems and their pooled evidence agree — upfront elective dissection saves lives in early node-negative oral cancer, at the cost of more neck surgery up front
cards.people: Two large randomised trials (500 and 250 randomised patients) plus a 7-trial randomised meta-analysis (1,250 patients).
cards.result: Overall survival favoured elective dissection in the Indian trial (80.0% vs 67.5% at 3 years; HR for death 0.64) and in the pooled randomised evidence (HR 0.67); the UK trial's own survival result was directionally the same but not significant alone (HR 0.71, p = 0.18), while its disease-free survival was significant. Occult nodal disease in 19–35% of clinically negative necks is the mechanism. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Elective dissection means operating on the ~65–80% of patients whose necks prove negative — the trade is more upfront neck surgery and nerve damage (per the UK trial) for fewer relapses; sentinel-node biopsy is a separate strategy and is not the comparison on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of D'Cruz AK et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2015; Hutchison IL et al. British Journal of Cancer. 2019 (SEND); meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Journal of Maxillofacial and Oral Surgery. 2022.

shelves.title: Rolapitant for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: delayed-phase complete response 71% versus 60-62% across three phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does rolapitant (single-dose oral NK1 antagonist, as tested) added to a 5-HT3 antagonist plus dexamethasone improve complete response in the delayed phase versus the same backbone without an NK1 antagonist?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cisplatin/adverse effects · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced,drug therapy,pathology · Neoplasms/drug therapy,pathology · Spiro Compounds/administration & dosage · Vomiting/chemically induced,drug therapy,pathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: three phase 3 trials, carded as trials not papers (the HEC paper reports two trials, HEC-1 and HEC-2, and they are carded as one programme card with both results printed, not as two independent trials). Delayed-phase complete response favoured rolapitant in every trial: HEC-1 73% versus 58%, HEC-2 70% versus 62%, pooled HEC 71% versus 60%, and the moderately emetogenic/anthracycline-cyclophosphamide trial 71% versus 62% (odds ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.2-2.0). The meta-analysis of five randomised trials (n=2984) agrees (delayed complete response odds ratio 1.68, 95% CI 1.44-1.96 — a relative measure; the absolute gains are the 8-15 percentage points printed on the cards). Adverse events were similar to control, with fatigue, constipation and headache the commonest treatment-related events and no treatment-related deaths. Product naming (clarification exception): rolapitant (Varubi, TESARO) as published, a single 180 mg oral dose before chemotherapy.

cards.headline: HEC-1 and HEC-2 (2015, one paper, two trials): delayed complete response 73% versus 58% and 70% versus 62% with cisplatin-based chemotherapy
cards.summary: HEC-1 and HEC-2 (2015, one paper, two trials): delayed complete response 73% versus 58% and 70% versus 62% with cisplatin-based chemotherapy
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase 3 trials (HEC-1, HEC-2) reported in one paper — carded as one programme card
cards.people: Patients with cancer, cisplatin-naive, receiving cisplatin-based highly emetogenic chemotherapy: 532 randomised in HEC-1 (526 in the modified intention-to-treat population) and 555 in HEC-2 (544 analysed). All received granisetron plus dexamethasone, with a single oral rolapitant 180 mg dose or matching placebo before chemotherapy.
cards.result: Delayed-phase (24-120 h) complete response (no emesis, no rescue medication) in cycle 1: HEC-1, 192 (73%) on rolapitant versus 153 (58%) on control (odds ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.3-2.7; p=0.0006); HEC-2, 190 (70%) versus 169 (62%) (odds ratio 1.4, 95% CI 1.0-2.1; p=0.0426); pooled, 382 (71%) versus 322 (60%) (odds ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.3-2.1; p=0.0001) — odds ratios are relative measures; the absolute gains were 15, 8 and 11 percentage points. Adverse events were similar between groups; no serious treatment-emergent event was treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Two trials in one publication must not be counted as three trials with the MEC study, nor the pooled analysis as a fourth: the programme is HEC-1, HEC-2 and one MEC trial. HEC-2's own result was the weakest of the three (p=0.0426).

cards.headline: MEC trial (2015): delayed complete response 71% versus 62% (odds ratio 1.6) after moderately emetogenic or anthracycline-cyclophosphamide chemotherapy
cards.summary: MEC trial (2015): delayed complete response 71% versus 62% (odds ratio 1.6) after moderately emetogenic or anthracycline-cyclophosphamide chemotherapy
cards.people: 1369 patients randomised (1332 in the modified intention-to-treat population: 666 rolapitant, 666 control) receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy or anthracycline-cyclophosphamide regimens, all with granisetron and dexamethasone, plus a single rolapitant 180 mg dose or placebo before chemotherapy.
cards.result: Delayed-phase complete response in cycle 1 was achieved by 475 patients (71%) on rolapitant versus 410 (62%) on active control (odds ratio 1.6, 95% CI 1.2-2.0; p=0.0002) — an absolute gain of 9 percentage points. Adverse events were similar between groups (commonest treatment-related: fatigue, constipation, headache); the commonest grade 3-4 event was neutropenia (5% versus 3%), and no serious adverse event was treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The control was an active backbone (granisetron plus dexamethasone), not no prophylaxis — the 71% versus 62% contrast is the added value of the NK1 antagonist, and the benefit is concentrated in the delayed phase the trial was powered on.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (2018): across five randomised trials (n=2984), rolapitant raised delayed complete response with a relative odds ratio of 1.68
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (2018): across five randomised trials (n=2984), rolapitant raised delayed complete response with a relative odds ratio of 1.68
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Five randomised controlled trials totalling 2984 patients receiving chemotherapy, pooling rolapitant 180 mg plus a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone against placebo plus the same backbone.
cards.result: Complete response was higher with rolapitant in the acute phase (odds ratio 1.4, 95% CI 1.16-1.7) and the delayed phase (odds ratio 1.68, 95% CI 1.44-1.96), and complete protection was higher overall (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.3-1.76). All odds ratios are relative measures; on the trial cards the corresponding absolute gains are 8-15 percentage points. The authors conclude the combination is well tolerated and more effective than the backbone alone.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are the same programme carded above (including a phase 2 study) — the meta-analysis summarises the programme, it does not add independent trials, and a fixed-effect pool of sponsor-run trials inherits their design choices.
cards.source: Ahmed H et al. Meta-analysis of safety and efficacy of rolapitant, NK-1 receptor antagonist for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Current problems in cancer. 2018. PMID: 29310827. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent delayed-phase gain in all three phase 3 trials — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent delayed-phase gain in all three phase 3 trials — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HEC-1 (526 analysed), HEC-2 (544), the MEC trial (1332) and the five-trial meta-analysis (n=2984, overlapping).
cards.result: Every phase 3 trial found the same direction and a similar absolute size of benefit (8-15 percentage points of delayed complete response) from adding one 180 mg rolapitant dose to a granisetron-dexamethasone backbone, with no added serious toxicity signal. Three concordant large randomised trials justify LIKELY for the delayed-phase claim as tested.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is one sponsor's programme (TESARO) against an active backbone, in trial populations with good performance status; it does not compare rolapitant head-to-head with other NK1 antagonists, whose shelves are homed separately.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rapoport BL et al. Lancet Oncol. 2015. PMID: 26272769; Schwartzberg LS et al. Lancet Oncol. 2015. PMID: 26272768; Ahmed H et al. Curr Probl Cancer. 2018. PMID: 29310827. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Granisetron transdermal patch for CINV: non-inferior to oral, intravenous and ondansetron comparators in most trials — with a day-1 weakness in the Chinese phase 3
shelves.question: In adults receiving multi-day or moderately/highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does the granisetron transdermal system (patch, as tested) prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as effectively as oral/intravenous 5-HT3 antagonists (including palonosetron comparators), particularly in the long-delayed phase?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Antiemetics/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Granisetron/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/chemically induced,prevention & control · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Vomiting/chemically induced,prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: the claim tested is equivalence, not superiority, and comparators differ by trial, so the cards are kept per-comparator and never pooled into one efficacy number. The patch met its prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin against daily oral granisetron in multi-day chemotherapy (complete control 60% versus 65%), against intravenous/oral granisetron in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (complete response 75.0% versus 74.6%), against palonosetron in the acute phase of a crossover study (75.2% versus 79.8% of cycles), and against ondansetron in highly emetogenic chemotherapy (86.84% versus 90.36%). The exception is the Chinese phase 3 trial: complete control was numerically lower with the patch (47.52% versus 59.29%; p=0.0559), driven by a significantly worse day 1 (70.13% versus 91.03%) — the patch's slow onset is its real weakness, and the stamp stays at POSSIBLE because of it. Constipation was the commonest adverse event throughout. Product naming (clarification exception): the granisetron transdermal system (Sancuso patch, as published), one patch delivering granisetron continuously for up to 7 days.

cards.headline: Boccia 2011: patch non-inferior to daily oral granisetron in multi-day chemotherapy — complete control 60% versus 65% (margin 15%)
cards.summary: Boccia 2011: patch non-inferior to daily oral granisetron in multi-day chemotherapy — complete control 60% versus 65% (margin 15%)
cards.people: 641 patients randomised (582 in the per-protocol analysis) to one granisetron transdermal patch worn for 7 days or oral granisetron 2 mg/day for 3-5 days, before moderately or highly emetogenic multi-day chemotherapy.
cards.result: Complete control (no vomiting/retching, no more than mild nausea, no rescue medication) from chemotherapy initiation to 24 h after the final dose was achieved by 60% on the patch versus 65% on oral granisetron (difference -5%; 95% CI -13 to 3), inside the prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin. Both were well tolerated; constipation was the most common adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority with a wide 15% margin: the confidence interval still allows the patch to be up to 13 points worse, and complete control here is a stricter composite than the complete response used in the later trials — do not pool the percentages.
cards.source: Boccia RV et al. cards.headline: Yang 2016 (Chinese phase 3): complete control numerically lower on the patch (47.52% versus 59.29%; p=0.0559), with day-1 control significantly worse
cards.summary: Yang 2016 (Chinese phase 3): complete control numerically lower on the patch (47.52% versus 59.29%; p=0.0559), with day-1 control significantly worse
cards.people: 313 patients randomised (281 per-protocol) receiving moderately or highly emetogenic chemotherapy in China, to one transdermal granisetron patch for 7 days or oral granisetron 2 mg/day for at least 2 days.
cards.result: Complete control over the full observation period was achieved by 67 patients (47.52%) on the patch versus 83 (59.29%) on oral granisetron (p=0.0559, not significant). The gap was concentrated on day 1, when complete control in the full analysis set was 70.13% on the patch versus 91.03% on oral granisetron (significant); on later days control was similar. Differences also appeared in cisplatin-containing regimens and in women. Both treatments were well tolerated; constipation was the most common adverse event.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's cautionary trial: a transdermal system applied before chemotherapy may not reach effective levels for day-1 (acute) control, especially with cisplatin — the equivalence claim is strongest for the delayed days the patch was designed to cover.

cards.headline: Seol 2016 (phase 4 crossover versus palonosetron): acute-phase complete response 75.2% of patch cycles versus 79.8% of palonosetron cycles — non-inferior
cards.summary: Seol 2016 (phase 4 crossover versus palonosetron): acute-phase complete response 75.2% of patch cycles versus 79.8% of palonosetron cycles — non-inferior
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, crossover phase 4 trial versus palonosetron
cards.people: 196 patients receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, randomised to patch-then-palonosetron or palonosetron-then-patch across two cycles; 333 cycles (165 patch, 168 palonosetron) in the per-protocol analysis.
cards.result: Acute-phase (0-24 h) complete response (no emetic episodes, no rescue medication) was achieved in 124 patch cycles (75.2%) versus 134 palonosetron cycles (79.8%) (difference -4.6%; 95% CI -13.6 to 4.4), meeting non-inferiority against the second-generation comparator. Complete response did not differ significantly between sequences in either cycle. Both treatments were well tolerated; patient satisfaction results were internally mixed in the report and are not relied on here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label crossover with an acute-phase primary endpoint only: it does not test the patch's long-delayed-phase rationale, and satisfaction scores in an open-label patch-versus-injection comparison are expectation-prone.
cards.source: Seol YM et al. cards.headline: Kim 2015: patch non-inferior to intravenous-then-oral granisetron in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy — complete response 75.0% versus 74.6%
cards.summary: Kim 2015: patch non-inferior to intravenous-then-oral granisetron in moderately emetogenic chemotherapy — complete response 75.0% versus 74.6%
cards.people: 276 Korean patients randomised (234 per-protocol: 112 patch, 122 control) receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, 97.9% with gastrointestinal cancer and 76.9% receiving 3-day chemotherapy; the patch was worn on days 1-4 versus intravenous granisetron on day 1 then oral on days 2-4.
cards.result: Complete response from chemotherapy initiation to 24 h after the final dose was 75.0% on the patch versus 74.6% on intravenous/oral granisetron (95% CI for the difference -10.73 to 11.55), meeting non-inferiority, with sustained complete response from day 1 to day 4 and no difference in Functional Living Index-Emesis scores. Both treatments were well tolerated and safe.
cards.watchOut: A single-country, mostly gastrointestinal-cancer population on 3-day regimens: the day-by-day sustainment is reassuring for multi-day cover, but the trial does not address highly emetogenic single-day cisplatin.
cards.source: Kim JE et al. cards.headline: Sun 2023: patch non-inferior to ondansetron in highly emetogenic chemotherapy — complete response 86.84% versus 90.36%, with higher satisfaction scores
cards.summary: Sun 2023: patch non-inferior to ondansetron in highly emetogenic chemotherapy — complete response 86.84% versus 90.36%, with higher satisfaction scores
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind non-inferiority trial versus ondansetron
cards.people: 389 patients randomised before highly emetogenic chemotherapy (per-protocol 152 patch, 166 ondansetron); in the full analysis set the commonest diagnosis was lung cancer (40.27%) and 80.27% received cisplatin-based regimens.
cards.result: Complete response (no retching/vomiting/rescue medication) to 24 h after the last chemotherapy dose was 86.84% on the patch versus 90.36% on ondansetron (difference -3.52%; 95% CI -10.52 to 3.48), inside the prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin. Functional Living Index-Emesis satisfaction scores were significantly higher with the patch (1547.38 ± 306.00 versus 1494.07 ± 312.05 mm; p=0.0449). The patch was effective, safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is ondansetron, a weaker benchmark than palonosetron, and the 15% margin is generous; per-protocol analysis (318 of 389 randomised) can flatter non-inferiority.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an equivalent-delivery option for multi-day cover, not a better antiemetic — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: an equivalent-delivery option for multi-day cover, not a better antiemetic — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: five randomised trials against four different comparators (oral granisetron twice, intravenous/oral granisetron, palonosetron, ondansetron), 641, 313, 196, 276 and 389 patients randomised.
cards.result: Four of five trials met prespecified non-inferiority, supporting the patch as a delivery alternative that maintains control across multi-day and delayed periods without daily tablets or injections. The Chinese trial's day-1 deficit is the consistent mechanistic caveat: slow transdermal onset. Because the evidence supports equivalence with one discordant trial rather than superiority, and margins were wide, the stamp is POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Never quote a single pooled 'patch efficacy' percentage: endpoints (complete control versus complete response), comparators and chemotherapy settings differ across every card.

shelves.title: Octreotide for chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea: treatment trials positive (19 of 21 resolved versus 3 of 20 on loperamide), prophylaxis negative in RTOG 0315 — SPLIT
shelves.question: In adults with chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea (fluoropyrimidine- or cisplatin-based) that persists despite standard loperamide, does octreotide control diarrhoea (stool frequency / grade) versus placebo or versus continued loperamide — and does prophylactic long-acting octreotide prevent chemoradiation-induced diarrhoea in anorectal cancer?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Cisplatin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/chemically induced,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Octreotide/therapeutic use · Placebos
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is treatment versus prevention, and the two limbs must not be merged. Treatment limb: in two small 1990s randomised trials, octreotide controlled established chemotherapy diarrhoea — resolution in 19 of 21 patients versus 3 of 20 on loperamide in fluorouracil-induced diarrhoea (n=41), and diarrhoea in 5% versus 75% against placebo after cisplatin (n=43); Ns are printed on the face because these trials are small by modern standards. Prevention limb: the large modern trial went the other way — in RTOG 0315 (n=215), prophylactic long-acting octreotide did not reduce grade 2-4 acute diarrhoea during chemoradiation for anorectal cancer (44% versus 49% on placebo; P=.21) (the treatment made no difference), with no benefit in bowel function or quality of life. So: plausible rescue treatment on thin old evidence; prophylaxis tested and negative.

cards.headline: Cascinu 1993 (treatment, versus loperamide): diarrhoea resolved in 19 of 21 on octreotide versus 3 of 20 on loperamide (P<.005) — N = 41
cards.summary: Cascinu 1993 (treatment, versus loperamide): diarrhoea resolved in 19 of 21 on octreotide versus 3 of 20 on loperamide (P<.005) — N = 41
cards.type: Randomised trial of treatment for established fluorouracil-induced diarrhoea
cards.people: 41 patients with grade 2 (4-6 stools/day) or grade 3 (7-9 stools/day) diarrhoea after a fluorouracil-containing regimen (colorectal 28, gastric 6, pancreatic 5, breast 2), randomised to octreotide 0.1 mg subcutaneously twice daily for 3 days (21) or loperamide (20).
cards.result: Diarrhoea resolved in 19 of 21 patients on octreotide (1 within day 1, 4 by day 2, 14 by day 3) versus 3 of 20 on loperamide, all after day 3 (P<.005). Median stool frequency over the 3 days was 4, 3 and 0 on octreotide versus 5, 5 and 5 on loperamide. Hospitalisation for parenteral fluids was needed by 1 patient on octreotide versus 10 on loperamide. No side effects were observed in either arm.
cards.watchOut: N = 41, single-centre-era 1993 trial without stated blinding in the record: the effect size is very large, which in a trial this small should be read as promising rather than precise.
cards.source: Cascinu S et al. Octreotide versus loperamide in the treatment of fluorouracil-induced diarrhea: a randomized trial. Journal of clinical oncology. 1993. PMID: 8418225. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cascinu 1994 (treatment, versus placebo): diarrhoea in 5% on octreotide versus 75% on placebo in the next cisplatin course (p=0.01) — N = 43
cards.summary: Cascinu 1994 (treatment, versus placebo): diarrhoea in 5% on octreotide versus 75% on placebo in the next cisplatin course (p=0.01) — N = 43
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (patients with prior cisplatin diarrhoea)
cards.people: 43 patients who had already had diarrhoea in the 24 hours after a previous cisplatin administration, randomised to octreotide or placebo during the next cisplatin course.
cards.result: Patients given octreotide experienced less diarrhoea than those given placebo (5% versus 75%; p=0.01). There were no side effects. The authors conclude octreotide is more effective than placebo in controlling diarrhoea following cisplatin chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: N = 43, and the design enriches for patients already shown to get cisplatin diarrhoea — a selected population in whom a preventive-in-the-next-course effect is easiest to show; the abstract reports percentages without arm-level counts.
cards.source: Cascinu S et al. Control of chemotherapy-induced diarrhea with octreotide. A randomized trial with placebo in patients receiving cisplatin. Oncology. 1994. PMID: 8265106. cards.headline: RTOG 0315 (2010, prophylaxis): long-acting octreotide did not prevent chemoradiation diarrhoea — grade 2-4 diarrhoea 44% versus 49% on placebo (P=.21) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: RTOG 0315 (2010, prophylaxis): long-acting octreotide did not prevent chemoradiation diarrhoea — grade 2-4 diarrhoea 44% versus 49% on placebo (P=.21) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 215 patients with rectal or anal cancer undergoing chemoradiation, randomised to long-acting octreotide acetate 30 mg intramuscularly 4-7 days before radiation and again on day 22 (109) or placebo (106).
cards.result: After median follow-up of 9.64 months, grade 2-4 acute diarrhoea occurred at similar rates in both groups (44% on long-acting octreotide versus 49% on placebo; P=.21) (the treatment made no difference). There were no statistically significant differences in chemotherapy or radiation delivery, medical resource use, patient-reported bowel function or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: A prevention trial of a long-acting depot given before chemoradiation — a different drug exposure and question from short-course subcutaneous octreotide for established diarrhoea; its null result refutes prophylaxis, not rescue treatment.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treatment limb positive on two small old trials, prevention limb negative in the one large trial — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: treatment limb positive on two small old trials, prevention limb negative in the one large trial — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: treatment trials of 41 and 43 patients (1993-1994) and the RTOG 0315 prevention trial (215 patients, 2010).
cards.result: The evidence splits cleanly by question. For established fluoropyrimidine or cisplatin diarrhoea, octreotide beat loperamide and placebo in both small trials, with fewer fluid-resuscitation hospitalisations in the loperamide comparison. For prevention during chemoradiation, the adequately sized double-blind trial found no benefit at all. The stamp names the split rather than averaging it away.
cards.watchOut: The treatment limb has never been re-tested at modern scale or against modern supportive care, and neither 1990s trial enrolled irinotecan-diarrhoea patients — do not extend the claim to regimens untested here.

shelves.title: Probiotics for chemotherapy/radiotherapy diarrhoea: large positive trials for two named preparations, a null trial for a third — preparations are not interchangeable (SPLIT)
shelves.question: In adults receiving chemotherapy and/or pelvic radiotherapy, do orally administered probiotics (the named strains/preparations as tested) prevent or reduce grade 2 or worse treatment-induced diarrhoea versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antidiarrheals/therapeutic use · Colonic Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Diarrhea/drug therapy,etiology,prevention & control · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lactobacillus · Loperamide/therapeutic use · Male · Probiotics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Radiation Injuries/prevention & control · Radiotherapy/adverse effects · Risk Factors · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/radiotherapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is by preparation and setting, because probiotic preparations are NOT interchangeable: each card names the exact tested product/strains as published (clarification exception), and where a publication does not identify its product beyond genus composition, the card says so plainly; current commercial products may differ from what was tested in safety and effectiveness. Positive limb: the high-potency preparation VSL#3 (as named in the trial) cut radiation-induced diarrhoea from 51.8% to 31.6% in 482 analysed patients, and live Lactobacillus acidophilus plus Bifidobacterium bifidum cut grade 2-3 diarrhoea during cervical-cancer radiotherapy from 45% to 9% in 63 patients; a 100-patient colorectal trial of an unnamed-composition combination also reported significantly less diarrhoea. Null/mixed limb: a 28-patient 2025 trial of a named five-strain mixture found no significant benefit, and a 52-patient six-strain trial's clear effects were on inflammatory cytokines, not a demonstrated diarrhoea reduction. The chemotherapy-diarrhoea meta-analysis (13 trials, 1024 patients) pools these unlike preparations into a relative risk of 0.47 for total diarrhoea — a relative measure across heterogeneous products, printed here as the synthesis it is, not as a claim about any one product. Per the coordinator's note, an earlier VSL#3 radiation-diarrhoea report whose PubMed record has an empty abstract was excluded and is not carded; this shelf stands on the anchors below. Probiotic content for perioperative GI-surgery infections is homed on a separate shelf and cross-pointed in prose only.

cards.headline: Delia 2007 (VSL#3, radiation): diarrhoea in 31.6% on the probiotic versus 51.8% on placebo, and grade 3-4 diarrhoea 1.4% versus 55.4% as reported
cards.summary: Delia 2007 (VSL#3, radiation): diarrhoea in 31.6% on the probiotic versus 51.8% on placebo, and grade 3-4 diarrhoea 1.4% versus 55.4% as reported
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (radiation-induced diarrhoea prevention)
cards.people: 490 patients randomised (482 analysed: 243 probiotic, 239 placebo) receiving adjuvant postoperative radiation after surgery for sigmoid, rectal or cervical cancer. Tested product as published: the high-potency probiotic preparation VSL#3, one sachet three times daily from the first day of radiation (clarification exception — named as published).
cards.result: Radiation-induced diarrhoea occurred in 77 of 243 patients (31.6%) on VSL#3 versus 124 of 239 (51.8%) on placebo (P<0.001), an absolute reduction of about 20 percentage points. Grade 3 or 4 diarrhoea was reported in 55.4% of placebo patients versus 1.4% of VSL#3 patients as printed in the record (P<0.001). Daily bowel movements averaged 5.1 (±3) versus 14.7 (±6) (P<0.05), and mean time to rescue loperamide was 122 (±8) h versus 86 (±6) h (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The grade 3-4 percentages as printed (55.4% versus 1.4%) are strikingly asymmetric against the overall incidence figures and are reproduced here exactly as the record states them; the trial predates modern chemoradiation combinations, and VSL#3's formulation/ownership has changed since 2007 — current products may differ from the tested preparation.
cards.source: Delia P et al. Use of probiotics for prevention of radiation-induced diarrhea. World journal of gastroenterology. 2007. PMID: 17352022. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chitapanarux 2010 (live L. acidophilus + B. bifidum, cervical radiotherapy): grade 2-3 diarrhoea 9% versus 45% on placebo (p=0.002) — N = 63
cards.summary: Chitapanarux 2010 (live L. acidophilus + B. bifidum, cervical radiotherapy): grade 2-3 diarrhoea 9% versus 45% on placebo (p=0.002) — N = 63
cards.people: 63 patients with locally advanced cervical cancer receiving pelvic radiotherapy with weekly cisplatin, randomised to a probiotic containing live Lactobacillus acidophilus plus Bifidobacterium bifidum (32) or placebo (31), as named in the publication; the record does not give a brand or maker.
cards.result: Grade 2-3 diarrhoea occurred in 9% of the probiotic group versus 45% of the placebo group (p=0.002), anti-diarrhoeal medication use was significantly lower with the probiotic (the record prints this comparison with the group labels apparently transposed, p=0.03 — the direction stated in the authors' conclusion is reduced use on the probiotic), and stool consistency was significantly better (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: N = 63, single centre, and the record does not identify a commercial product, strain codes or dose — the result belongs to the tested preparation as described, and current products sold under the same species names may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Chitapanarux I et al. Randomized controlled trial of live lactobacillus acidophilus plus bifidobacterium bifidum in prophylaxis of diarrhea during radiotherapy in cervical cancer patients. Radiation oncology (London, England). 2010. PMID: 20444243. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Huang 2023 (colorectal chemotherapy, combination not strain-named in the record): probiotics significantly reduced diarrhoea (p<0.01) — N = 100
cards.summary: Huang 2023 (colorectal chemotherapy, combination not strain-named in the record): probiotics significantly reduced diarrhoea (p<0.01) — N = 100
cards.people: 100 patients with colorectal cancer treated with radical surgery and receiving chemotherapy, randomised to a probiotic combination (50) or placebo (50) from after surgery to the end of the first chemotherapy course. The record describes the intervention only as 'a probiotic combination' — no strains, brand or maker are given in the record, and the card says so plainly.
cards.result: Probiotic administration effectively reduced chemotherapy-induced gastrointestinal complications, particularly diarrhoea (p<0.01); the record does not print the diarrhoea rates for each arm. Chemotherapy reduced gut bacterial diversity, which probiotics significantly increased, and probiotics promoted short-chain fatty acid production (acetate, butyrate, propionate; p<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: An unnamed product with no arm-level diarrhoea rates in the record: this card supports the direction of the positive limb but cannot be used to recommend any purchasable preparation, and its microbiome endpoints are surrogates.
cards.source: Huang F et al. Postoperative Probiotics Administration Attenuates Gastrointestinal Complications and Gut Microbiota Dysbiosis Caused by Chemotherapy in Colorectal Cancer Patients. Nutrients. 2023. PMID: 36678227. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: de Souza 2025 (named five-strain mixture, GI-cancer chemotherapy): no significant benefit — grade 2/3 diarrhoea 44.44% versus 55.56% on placebo (P=1) (the treatment made no difference) — N = 28
cards.summary: de Souza 2025 (named five-strain mixture, GI-cancer chemotherapy): no significant benefit — grade 2/3 diarrhoea 44.44% versus 55.56% on placebo (P=1) (the treatment made no difference) — N = 28
cards.people: 28 patients with gastrointestinal cancer receiving fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin- and/or irinotecan-based chemotherapy, randomised 1:1 to placebo or 20 billion CFU daily for 90 days of a mixture of five viable strains as published: Lactobacillus acidophilus NCFM®, Lactobacillus paracasei Lpc-37™, Bifidobacterium lactis Bi-04™, Bifidobacterium lactis Bi-07™ and Bifidobacterium bifidum Bb-02™ (335 mg; strain designations as published, clarification exception).
cards.result: Grade 2/3 diarrhoea occurred in 44.44% on the probiotic versus 55.56% on placebo (P=1), and overall diarrhoea incidence was 64.29% versus 71.43% (P=1) (the treatment made no difference). Median diarrhoea episodes were 8 versus 9 (P=0.639). No subgroup benefited, and no infections related to the administered strains were detected.
cards.watchOut: N = 28 — far too small to exclude a moderate effect, so this null carded result disciplines the positive limb rather than refuting it; it is, however, the most precisely strain-specified trial on the shelf.
cards.source: de Souza GC et al. Efficacy of probiotics in preventing chemotherapy-induced diarrhea in gastrointestinal cancer patients. Arquivos de gastroenterologia. 2025. PMID: 41379184. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zaharuddin 2019 (named six-strain BCMC® mixture, post-surgical colorectal cancer): cytokines fell significantly; no diarrhoea advantage was demonstrated — N = 52
cards.summary: Zaharuddin 2019 (named six-strain BCMC® mixture, post-surgical colorectal cancer): cytokines fell significantly; no diarrhoea advantage was demonstrated — N = 52
cards.people: 52 patients with colorectal cancer randomised 4 weeks after surgery to placebo (25) or a six-strain mixture as published — Lactobacillus acidophilus BCMC® 12,130, Lactobacillus lactis BCMC® 12,451, Lactobacillus casei subsp BCMC® 12,313, Bifidobacterium longum BCMC® 02120, Bifidobacterium bifidum BCMC® 02290 and Bifidobacterium infantis BCMC® 02129 (27) — taken twice daily for 6 months (strain codes as published, clarification exception).
cards.result: No surgical infection occurred and no antibiotics were required in either group; chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea was observed in both groups, with no significant diarrhoea difference reported. Pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, IL-17A, IL-17C, IL-22) fell significantly from pre-treatment levels in the probiotic group (P<0.05), except IFN-γ. The authors conclude the product was safe and modified the intestinal microenvironment.
cards.watchOut: The demonstrated effects are immunological surrogates, not the diarrhoea endpoint of this shelf's question — carded to keep the shelf honest about what a well-specified modern trial did and did not show.
cards.source: Zaharuddin L et al. A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of probiotics in post-surgical colorectal cancer. BMC gastroenterology. 2019. PMID: 31340751. Registry ID: NCT03782428 (ClinicalTrials.gov). cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2019 (chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea): pooled relative risk 0.47 for total diarrhoea across 13 trials of unlike preparations (n=1024)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2019 (chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea): pooled relative risk 0.47 for total diarrhoea across 13 trials of unlike preparations (n=1024)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 13 randomised trials totalling 1024 patients with malignant tumours, pooling probiotics added to conventional symptomatic treatment for prevention or treatment of chemotherapy-induced diarrhoea.
cards.result: Probiotics reduced total diarrhoea rate (relative risk 0.47, 95% CI 0.35-0.63; p<0.00001) and grade III-IV diarrhoea (relative risk 0.16, 95% CI 0.05-0.42; p=0.0008), and shortened diarrhoea duration (mean difference -1.92 days) — all relative or pooled measures across different preparations; grade I-II diarrhoea did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.53-1.24; p=0.34). No enrolled study reported adverse reactions.
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative effect over heterogeneous, mostly small trials of different products cannot be assigned to any single preparation — it is the average of the split documented on the cards above, and publication bias in this literature is a standing concern.
cards.source: Lu D et al. Probiotics in preventing and treating chemotherapy-induced diarrhea: a meta-analysis. Asia Pacific journal of clinical nutrition. 2019. PMID: 31826366. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Humans · Probiotics/pharmacology

cards.headline: Synthesis: benefit is preparation-specific — two named preparations positive in radiotherapy, modern chemotherapy trials null or surrogate-only — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: benefit is preparation-specific — two named preparations positive in radiotherapy, modern chemotherapy trials null or surrogate-only — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Delia 2007 (482 analysed), Chitapanarux 2010 (63), Huang 2023 (100), de Souza 2025 (28), Zaharuddin 2019 (52) and the 13-trial meta-analysis (1024, overlapping).
cards.result: The honest summary is a split, not a class effect: the largest, oldest trial of one named high-potency preparation in pelvic radiation was clearly positive, a small trial of a second named preparation agreed, and a pooled analysis favours probiotics on relative measures — while the two most precisely specified modern chemotherapy trials showed no diarrhoea benefit. Any clinical use should copy a tested preparation and setting exactly, not substitute a look-alike product.
cards.watchOut: Excluded by the coordinator's instruction and not carded: an earlier VSL#3 radiation-diarrhoea report whose PubMed record has an empty abstract — the shelf stands on the carded anchors alone. Live-organism products in neutropenic or central-line patients carry a small infection risk that none of these trials was sized to measure.
cards.source: Synthesis of Delia P et al. World J Gastroenterol. 2007. PMID: 17352022; Chitapanarux I et al. Radiat Oncol. 2010. PMID: 20444243; Huang F et al. Nutrients. 2023. shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is adult versus paediatric programmes, carded as separate limbs as the slate directs. Adult limb: two randomised trials favoured the rinse — in 95 HSCT patients, Caphosol plus fluoride versus fluoride rinse alone cut days of mucositis (3.72 versus 7.22; P=0.001) and morphine dose (34.54 mg versus 122.78 mg); in 40 allogeneic HSCT patients, a supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse versus customary topical solutions lowered WHO oral toxicity (0.9 versus 1.8; P=0.02) and peak mouth pain. Paediatric limb: the largest and most rigorous trial went the other way — in 220 children and adolescents undergoing myeloablative HCT, Caphosol versus placebo saline did not reduce severe mucositis duration at all (4.5 ± 5.0 versus 4.5 ± 4.8 days; P=0.99) (the treatment made no difference). Product naming (clarification exception): Caphosol, a neutral supersaturated Ca2+/PO43- oral rinse, as published; the 2012 trial tested the same class of rinse (SCPR) against a non-saline customary-care control, which is part of why the adult limb is graded cautiously.

cards.headline: Papas 2003 (adults, HSCT): Caphosol plus fluoride cut mucositis days from 7.22 to 3.72 and morphine dose from 122.78 mg to 34.54 mg versus fluoride rinse alone
cards.summary: Papas 2003 (adults, HSCT): Caphosol plus fluoride cut mucositis days from 7.22 to 3.72 and morphine dose from 122.78 mg to 34.54 mg versus fluoride rinse alone
cards.people: 95 patients undergoing haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, randomised to a calcium phosphate mouth rinse (Caphosol, as published) with fluoride treatments or a standard regimen of fluoride rinsing with placebo tray treatments.
cards.result: Days of mucositis were 3.72 versus 7.22 (P=0.001), duration of pain 2.86 versus 7.67 days (P=0.0001), morphine dose 34.54 mg versus 122.78 mg, days of morphine 1.26 versus 4.02 (P=0.0001), and days to engraftment (ANC >200/mm3) 11.12 versus 12.56, all favouring the Caphosol-plus-fluoride group. The authors conclude the rinse is superior to fluoride rinse alone in reducing the frequency, intensity and duration of oral mucositis in HSCT.
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles Caphosol with the fluoride co-intervention against fluoride alone, in a 2003 transplant population whose conditioning and supportive care differ from current practice; the abstract does not print the arm sizes.
cards.source: Papas AS et al. A prospective, randomized trial for the prevention of mucositis in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Bone marrow transplantation. 2003. PMID: 12692611. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Markiewicz 2012 (adults, allogeneic HSCT): supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse lowered WHO oral toxicity (0.9 versus 1.8; P=0.02) and peak pain versus customary solutions — N = 40
cards.summary: Markiewicz 2012 (adults, allogeneic HSCT): supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse lowered WHO oral toxicity (0.9 versus 1.8; P=0.02) and peak pain versus customary solutions — N = 40
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (unblinded by practical necessity)
cards.people: 40 patients undergoing allogeneic HSCT, randomised to a supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse (SCPR) four times daily (20) or customary topical mouth solutions of salvia leaf extract, iodine-povidone and fluconazole (20), from conditioning until granulocyte count ≥0.2 g/L.
cards.result: The SCPR group had significantly lower mean WHO oral toxicity (0.9 versus 1.8; P=0.02), shorter disease course (3.2 versus 7.1 days; P=0.02) and lower peak mouth pain (0.85 versus 1.75; P=0.005). Analgesic need was shorter (1.1 versus 3.4 days; P=0.047) and total parenteral nutrition was needed by 0 versus 6 patients (P=0.02). Complication measures were lower but not significantly so.
cards.watchOut: N = 40 and unblinded (the preparations look and are prepared differently, as the authors state), against a multi-ingredient customary-care control rather than saline — expectation and control-choice effects cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Markiewicz M et al. Treating oral mucositis with a supersaturated calcium phosphate rinse: comparison with control in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Supportive care in cancer. 2012. PMID: 22736463. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Treister 2017 (children, myeloablative HCT): Caphosol did not reduce severe mucositis versus placebo saline — 4.5 versus 4.5 days (P=0.99) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Treister 2017 (children, myeloablative HCT): Caphosol did not reduce severe mucositis versus placebo saline — 4.5 versus 4.5 days (P=0.99) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Children's Oncology Group)
cards.people: 220 children and adolescents aged 4 to 21 years (median 13.7) undergoing myeloablative haematopoietic cell transplantation (74% allogeneic), randomised to Caphosol or placebo saline rinses four times daily from conditioning through day +20 (182 in the primary comparison as reported: 91 per arm).
cards.result: Mean duration of severe oral mucositis (WHO ≥3) was 4.5 (±5.0) days on Caphosol versus 4.5 (±4.8) days on placebo (P=0.99) (the treatment made no difference). Severe mucositis incidence was 63% (57/91) versus 68% (62/91) (P=0.44), and no secondary endpoint differed significantly. The authors conclude Caphosol did not reduce severe mucositis in this population.
cards.watchOut: Paediatric myeloablative conditioning is a more mucositis-intensive setting than the adult trials — the null may reflect population and regimen intensity as much as age, which is exactly why the limbs are carded separately rather than pooled.
cards.source: Treister N et al. Caphosol for prevention of oral mucositis in pediatric myeloablative haematopoietic cell transplantation. British journal of cancer. 2017. PMID: 27875526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small positive adult trials against one large rigorous paediatric null — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small positive adult trials against one large rigorous paediatric null — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Papas 2003 (95 adults), Markiewicz 2012 (40 adults) and Treister 2017 (220 children/adolescents).
cards.result: The adult transplant data favour the rinse on duration, pain and opioid use, but rest on 135 patients, one unblinded trial and non-saline controls. The paediatric programme — the biggest, double-blind, placebo-controlled test — found precisely no effect. Averaging these into a single verdict would misstate both limbs; the stamp is SPLIT, and any adult use should be presented as uncertain benefit, not established prevention.
cards.watchOut: Do not extrapolate either limb across the age/regimen divide, and do not merge this shelf with the cryotherapy, palifermin, benzydamine or photobiomodulation mucositis shelves homed elsewhere.
cards.source: Synthesis of Papas AS et al. Bone Marrow Transplant. 2003. PMID: 12692611; Markiewicz M et al. Support Care Cancer. 2012. PMID: 22736463; Treister N et al. Br J Cancer. 2017. PMID: 27875526. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Zinc sulfate for radiation-induced taste change: the largest trial (NCCTG, 169 patients) was negative, two small trials positive, one chemoradiation trial negative — SPLIT, set by the largest trial
shelves.question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer receiving radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, does zinc sulfate supplementation prevent or lessen treatment-induced taste alteration (dysgeusia) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Head and Neck Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Taste Disorders/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Zinc Sulfate/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — and per the slate flag, the balance is set by the largest trial, not the smaller positive ones. The NCCTG phase 3 double-blind trial (169 evaluable patients) found zinc sulfate 45 mg three times daily did not prevent taste alterations during oral/pharyngeal radiotherapy (73% versus 84% reported taste alterations in the first 2 months; p=0.16) and did not speed taste recovery. Against that stand two small positive trials: Ripamonti 1998 (n=18) found less worsening and faster recovery of measured taste thresholds on the same 45 mg three-times-daily dose started when taste change appeared, and Najafizade 2013 (n=35 completers) found thresholds rose significantly on placebo but barely on zinc 50 mg three times daily. A fourth trial in oral-cancer chemoradiation (Khan 2019, n=70) found no benefit for most tastes. Total evidence base is about 292 patients across four trials pointing both ways — SPLIT, weighted sceptical.

cards.headline: NCCTG N01C4 (2007, phase 3): zinc did not prevent taste alterations — 73% versus 84% reported them (p=0.16), and recovery was not faster — N = 169
cards.summary: NCCTG N01C4 (2007, phase 3): zinc did not prevent taste alterations — 73% versus 84% reported them (p=0.16), and recovery was not faster — N = 169
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (North Central Cancer Treatment Group)
cards.people: 169 evaluable patients receiving at least 2000 cGy of external-beam radiation to at least 30% of the oral cavity, randomised to zinc sulfate 45 mg orally three times daily or placebo throughout radiation and for 1 month after; taste change was assessed with the validated Wickham questionnaire.
cards.result: Taste alterations in the first 2 months were described by 61 zinc-treated patients (73%) and 71 placebo patients (84%) (p=0.16). Median interval to taste alterations was 2.3 versus 1.6 weeks (p=0.09). Zinc sulfate did not favourably affect the interval to taste recovery. The authors conclude zinc sulfate, as prescribed in this trial, did not prevent taste alterations in patients undergoing radiation to the oral pharynx.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is patient-reported taste alteration on a questionnaire rather than measured thresholds — the outcome the small positive trials used — so part of the split may be measurement, not biology; even so, this is the largest and most rigorous test and it is negative.
cards.source: Halyard MY et al. Does zinc sulfate prevent therapy-induced taste alterations in head and neck cancer patients? Results of phase III double-blind, placebo-controlled trial from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group (N01C4). International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics. 2007. PMID: 17394940. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ripamonti 1998: zinc started at the first taste change lessened worsening and sped recovery of measured taste thresholds — N = 18
cards.summary: Ripamonti 1998: zinc started at the first taste change lessened worsening and sped recovery of measured taste thresholds — N = 18
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (treatment at onset of taste change)
cards.people: 18 patients receiving external radiotherapy for head and neck cancer, randomised to zinc sulfate 45 mg three times daily or placebo from the onset of subjective taste alteration until 1 month after radiation ended; taste acuity was measured as detection and recognition thresholds for four taste qualities, before, weekly during, and 1 month after treatment.
cards.result: All patients had taste alterations at least once during radiation (at least 3 of 8 thresholds affected), and a third noticed change within the first week. Placebo patients had greater worsening of taste acuity during treatment than zinc patients, and zinc patients recovered taste acuity more quickly 1 month after treatment. Statistically significant differences emerged for urea detection and sodium chloride recognition thresholds during treatment, and for sodium chloride, saccharose and hydrogen chloride recognition thresholds after treatment. The therapy was effective and well tolerated in the authors' assessment.
cards.watchOut: N = 18 — the smallest trial on the shelf, with many thresholds tested and significance on only some of them; a treatment-at-onset design, unlike the NCCTG prevention design, so the two are not direct replications.
cards.source: Ripamonti C et al. A randomized, controlled clinical trial to evaluate the effects of zinc sulfate on cancer patients with taste alterations caused by head and neck irradiation. Cancer. 1998. PMID: 9587128. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Najafizade 2013: taste thresholds rose significantly on placebo after radiotherapy but barely on zinc 50 mg three times daily — N = 35 completers
cards.summary: Najafizade 2013: taste thresholds rose significantly on placebo after radiotherapy but barely on zinc 50 mg three times daily — N = 35 completers
cards.people: 35 patients (mean age 59.2 ± 16.5 years; 60% male) with head and neck cancers receiving radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy who completed the trial, allocated to zinc sulfate 50 mg three times daily or placebo from the start of radiotherapy until 1 month later; thresholds for four tastes were measured by the Henkin method at baseline, at the end of radiotherapy and 1 month later.
cards.result: After radiotherapy and at 1 month, taste perception thresholds for bitter, salty, sweet and sour tastes increased significantly in the placebo group (P=0.001), whereas in the zinc group only the salty threshold rose slightly (P=0.046). No relevant zinc side effects were reported. The authors conclude zinc supplementation can prevent radiation-induced taste alterations and call for larger studies.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH terms (fallback used on the source line), the number randomised (as opposed to completing) is not stated in the record, and threshold testing was not described as blinded in the record — a supportive but fragile small trial.
cards.source: Najafizade N et al. Preventive effects of zinc sulfate on taste alterations in patients under irradiation for head and neck cancers: A randomized placebo-controlled trial. Journal of research in medical sciences. 2013. PMID: 23914214. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Khan 2019 (oral cancer chemoradiation): zinc was not beneficial overall — significant only for sweet recognition at end of treatment and follow-up, and sour at end of treatment — N = 70
cards.summary: Khan 2019 (oral cancer chemoradiation): zinc was not beneficial overall — significant only for sweet recognition at end of treatment and follow-up, and sour at end of treatment — N = 70
cards.people: 70 patients with oral cancer receiving concurrent chemoradiotherapy, randomised to zinc sulfate capsules 50 mg three times daily after meals or placebo, from the first day of chemoradiation until 1 month after it ended; detection and recognition thresholds for four tastes were measured at baseline, end of treatment and follow-up.
cards.result: Sweet taste was most affected by treatment, then bitter and salty; sour was least affected. Detection-threshold differences between groups were not significant at any stage. For recognition thresholds, salty and bitter never differed significantly; sweet differed at end of treatment (p=0.010) and follow-up (p=0.038) and sour at end of treatment only (p=0.006). The authors' own conclusion: zinc sulfate was not found to be beneficial in preventing chemoradiation-induced taste alterations.
cards.watchOut: The record carries no MeSH terms (fallback used on the source line). Isolated significant tastes among many comparisons, against the authors' overall negative conclusion — carded as a negative trial, not mined for its two positive sub-results.
cards.source: Khan AH et al. Efficacy of zinc sulfate on concurrent chemoradiotherapy induced taste alterations in oral cancer patients: A double blind randomized controlled trial. shelves.title: Methadone as the first strong opioid for cancer pain: analgesia equal to morphine in three small comparative trials — paid for in drop-outs, dose instability and monitoring
shelves.question: In adults with cancer pain requiring a first-line strong opioid, does methadone provide analgesia equivalent to morphine, at what cost in adverse effects, dose instability and QT/monitoring burden?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methadone/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications · Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Palliative Care · Patient Dropouts · Patient Satisfaction
shelves.balance: Methadone gave analgesia equivalent to morphine as a first-line strong opioid — never superior — across the three comparative trials carded here (229 patients in total, so this shelf carries small-base labelling). In the double-blind multicentre trial (Bruera 2004), the proportion with at least 20% pain improvement at 4 weeks was 0.49 on methadone versus 0.56 on morphine, but opioid-related drop-outs were 22% (11 of 49) on methadone versus 6% (3 of 54) on morphine (P = .019). In the three-way randomised comparison (Mercadante 2008), pain, symptoms and adverse effects did not differ between methadone, sustained-release morphine and transdermal fentanyl, the opioid escalation index was significantly lower with methadone, yet methadone needed more up-and-down dose changes — the dose-instability cost named in the question. The small pharmacokinetic comparison (Gourlay 1986, N = 18) explains why: methadone's terminal half-life was 30.4 hours with wide between-patient variation (SD 16.3 hours) against 2.7 hours for morphine, so dosing intervals need individual adjustment and accumulation is a real risk without close monitoring. This shelf is the first-line slice only: methadone for refractory neuropathic cancer pain under specialist supervision is a different question, homed on the library's existing methadone shelf (#5754), whose Cochrane synthesis is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: methadone is a usable first-line alternative with equivalent analgesia, bought with more drop-outs, harder titration and a monitoring burden morphine does not carry.

cards.headline: Bruera 2004 (double-blind RCT, N = 103): methadone matched morphine on pain relief at 4 weeks (response 0.49 vs 0.56) but caused more opioid-related drop-outs (22% vs 6%)
cards.summary: Bruera 2004 (double-blind RCT, N = 103): methadone matched morphine on pain relief at 4 weeks (response 0.49 vs 0.56) but caused more opioid-related drop-outs (22% vs 6%)
cards.people: 103 patients in international palliative care clinics with cancer pain requiring initiation of a strong opioid, randomly assigned to methadone (49 patients; 7.5 mg orally every 12 hours plus 5 mg every 4 hours as needed) or morphine (54 patients; sustained-release 15 mg every 12 hours plus 5 mg every 4 hours as needed) for 4 weeks.
cards.result: More than three fourths of patients in each group reported a 20% or more reduction in pain intensity by day 8. At 4 weeks the proportion with a 20% or more improvement in pain was 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.64) with methadone and 0.56 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.70) with morphine, and patient-reported global benefit rates were nearly identical. The opioid escalation index at days 14 and 28 was similar between groups. Patients receiving methadone had more opioid-related drop-outs (11 of 49; 22%) than those receiving morphine (3 of 54; 6%; P = .019). The authors conclude methadone did not produce superior analgesic efficiency or overall tolerability at 4 weeks compared with morphine as a first-line strong opioid.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks only, in palliative-care clinics experienced with both drugs; the 22% drop-out rate on methadone is part of the result, not a footnote — tolerability in less experienced hands may be worse.
cards.source: Bruera E et al. Methadone versus morphine as a first-line strong opioid for cancer pain: a randomized, double-blind study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2004. PMID: 14701781. cards.headline: Mercadante 2008 (randomised three-way trial, N = 108): no difference in pain, symptoms or adverse effects between methadone, morphine and fentanyl — but methadone needed more dose changes, up and down
cards.summary: Mercadante 2008 (randomised three-way trial, N = 108): no difference in pain, symptoms or adverse effects between methadone, morphine and fentanyl — but methadone needed more dose changes, up and down
cards.people: 108 patients with cancer pain no longer responsive to opioids for moderate pain, randomly assigned to initial daily doses of 60 mg oral sustained-release morphine, 15 mg oral methadone, or 0.6 mg (25 micrograms/hour) transdermal fentanyl, followed at weekly intervals for 4 weeks; 70 patients completed the 4-week study period.
cards.result: No differences in pain and symptom intensity were observed between the three opioids, and no relevant differences in adverse effects during titration or chronic treatment. Five, five and four patients treated with oral morphine, transdermal fentanyl and oral methadone respectively required opioid switching. The opioid escalation index was significantly lower in patients receiving methadone (P < 0.0001), although methadone required more changes, up and down, in doses. Methadone was significantly less expensive (P < 0.0001); use and costs of supportive drugs were similar. The authors conclude all three opioids used as first-line therapy were effective and well tolerated, but that dose titration of methadone requires major clinical expertise.
cards.watchOut: Only 70 of 108 patients completed 4 weeks, and the population had already failed opioids for moderate pain — a step-up population rather than opioid-naive patients; cost findings are from an Italian health system of that era.
cards.source: Mercadante S et al. Sustained-release oral morphine versus transdermal fentanyl and oral methadone in cancer pain management. European Journal of Pain. 2008. PMID: 18353696. cards.headline: Gourlay 1986 (small comparative study, N = 18): methadone's half-life averaged 30.4 hours but varied widely (SD 16.3 hours) — the pharmacokinetic root of its dose instability
cards.summary: Gourlay 1986 (small comparative study, N = 18): methadone's half-life averaged 30.4 hours but varied widely (SD 16.3 hours) — the pharmacokinetic root of its dose instability
cards.people: 18 patients with severe cancer pain and metastatic disease (9 methadone, 9 morphine) in a comparative study of pharmacokinetics and efficacy, with blood opioid concentrations, visual analogue pain scores and end-tidal carbon dioxide measured before and after intravenous and oral doses.
cards.result: Terminal half-lives (mean ± SD) were 30.4 ± 16.3 hours for methadone and 2.7 ± 1.2 hours for morphine; clearance was 0.19 ± 0.13 L/min versus 1.16 ± 0.47 L/min. The long half-life of methadone was associated with prolonged pain relief, but its large variation necessitated careful adjustment of the dosing interval in individual patients. Oral bioavailability was 79 ± 11.7% for methadone versus 26 ± 13% for morphine, and also much less variable for methadone (coefficient of variation 15% versus 50%). Initial oral methadone doses ranged from 15 mg on alternate nights to 20 mg twice daily. There was no rapid escalation of daily opioid dose for either drug when adequate pain control was provided rapidly at the start.
cards.watchOut: N = 18 and chiefly a pharmacokinetic study — it explains methadone's handling, it does not by itself establish comparative analgesia; its N is printed on the face per the small-study labelling rule.
cards.source: Gourlay GK et al. A comparative study of the efficacy and pharmacokinetics of oral methadone and morphine in the treatment of severe pain in patients with cancer. Pain. 1986. PMID: 3528988. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three comparative reports (229 patients) agree methadone equals morphine for first-line cancer pain — the difference is tolerability, titration difficulty and monitoring, not analgesia
cards.summary: Synthesis: three comparative reports (229 patients) agree methadone equals morphine for first-line cancer pain — the difference is tolerability, titration difficulty and monitoring, not analgesia
cards.people: One double-blind multicentre RCT (103 patients), one randomised three-way comparison (108 patients) and one small comparative pharmacokinetic study (18 patients), all comparing methadone with morphine as a first-line strong opioid for cancer pain. Total evidence base 229 patients — a small base, labelled as such in the stamp.
cards.result: Pain response at 4 weeks: 0.49 methadone versus 0.56 morphine (Bruera 2004); no pain or adverse-effect differences in the three-way trial, with a lower escalation index but more dose changes on methadone (Mercadante 2008); methadone half-life 30.4 ± 16.3 hours versus 2.7 ± 1.2 hours (Gourlay 1986). Opioid-related drop-outs were 22% versus 6% in the double-blind trial. No trial shows methadone superior. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — equivalent analgesia, higher handling cost.
cards.watchOut: An older randomised report in this literature (Ventafridda 1986) has an empty abstract in its PubMed record and so is not carded — its numbers cannot be verified from the record this session. QT-interval outcomes were not reported in any carded record, so this shelf makes no quantitative QT claim; the monitoring burden it describes rests on the drop-out, dose-change and half-life data actually carded.
