shelves.title: Dexamethasone for breathlessness in advanced cancer: the definitive trial found no difference from placebo — and more harm
shelves.question: In adults with advanced cancer and dyspnoea, does systemic dexamethasone (the doses tested) reduce breathlessness intensity versus placebo, and what is the cost in hyperglycaemia, insomnia and other steroid effects over days-to-weeks horizons?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea/chemically induced,etiology · Humans · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The largest and best trial is null, and it was stopped for futility: in the ABCD trial (128 randomised), high-dose dexamethasone and placebo both improved dyspnoea by 1.6 points at day 7, with a between-group difference of 0 (95% CI -0.8 to 0.7; P = 0.48) — dexamethasone made no difference (the treatment made no difference) — while infections, insomnia and serious adverse events were all more frequent on dexamethasone. The earlier pilot RCT (Hui 2016, N = 41) found faster within-group improvement on dexamethasone but no statistically significant between-arm difference. The symptom-cluster secondary analysis (Yennurajalingam 2016, N = 114) found no significant change in the pain/dyspnoea cluster. The Cochrane review (Haywood 2019) pooled the only two trials then available (157 participants enrolled, 114 analysed) to a mean difference of -0.85 points (95% CI -1.73 to 0.03) at one week on very low-quality evidence — a confidence interval that includes no effect, and a pool the later ABCD trial outweighs. Hyperglycaemia is a recognised steroid cost in this population but was not quantified in the carded records, so this shelf does not put a number on it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine dexamethasone for unselected cancer dyspnoea is not supported; any benefit is unproven and the harm signal is consistent.

cards.headline: ABCD 2022 (double-blind RCT, N = 128, stopped for futility): dexamethasone made no difference to dyspnoea versus placebo (change -1.6 vs -1.6 points; difference 0, P = 0.48), with more adverse events
cards.summary: ABCD 2022 (double-blind RCT, N = 128, stopped for futility): dexamethasone made no difference to dyspnoea versus placebo (change -1.6 vs -1.6 points; difference 0, P = 0.48), with more adverse events
cards.people: Ambulatory patients with cancer and average dyspnoea intensity of 4 or more on an 11-point numerical rating scale at two Houston centres, randomly assigned 2:1 to dexamethasone 8 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days then 4 mg every 12 hours for 7 days (85 patients) or matching placebo (43 patients); 149 enrolled, 128 randomised and started treatment.
cards.result: Mean change in dyspnoea intensity from baseline to day 7 was -1.6 (95% CI -2.0 to -1.2) on dexamethasone and -1.6 (95% CI -2.3 to -0.9) on placebo, with no significant between-group difference (mean difference 0, 95% CI -0.8 to 0.7; P = 0.48). Enrolment was stopped after the second preplanned interim analysis when the futility criterion was met. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events were infections (11% of the dexamethasone group vs 7% of placebo), insomnia (8% vs 2%) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (4% vs none). Serious adverse events, all resulting in hospital admission, occurred in 28% (24 of 85) on dexamethasone versus 7% (3 of 43) on placebo. No treatment-related deaths occurred. The authors conclude high-dose dexamethasone did not improve dyspnoea more than placebo and should not be routinely given to unselected patients with cancer for palliation of dyspnoea.
cards.watchOut: High-dose regimen in ambulatory patients with dyspnoea of any cause — the result rules on routine use in unselected cancer dyspnoea, not on steroid-responsive causes such as lymphangitis or airway obstruction, which were not the trial's question.
cards.source: Hui D et al. Effect of dexamethasone on dyspnoea in patients with cancer (ABCD): a parallel-group, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial. The Lancet Oncology. 2022. PMID: 36087590. cards.headline: Hui 2016 (pilot double-blind RCT, N = 41): dyspnoea fell faster within the dexamethasone arm, but the between-arm difference was not statistically significant
cards.summary: Hui 2016 (pilot double-blind RCT, N = 41): dyspnoea fell faster within the dexamethasone arm, but the between-arm difference was not statistically significant
cards.people: 41 patients with cancer and dyspnoea of 4 or more randomised to dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily for 4 days then 4 mg twice daily for 3 days, or placebo, for 7 days followed by a 7-day open-label phase; 35 patients (85%) completed the blinded phase.
cards.result: Dexamethasone was associated with a reduction in dyspnoea numerical rating scale of -1.9 (95% CI -3.3 to -0.5, P = 0.01) by day 4 and -1.8 (95% CI -3.2 to -0.3, P = 0.02) by day 7; placebo was associated with -0.7 (95% CI -2.1 to 0.6, P = 0.38) by day 4 and -1.3 (95% CI -2.4 to -0.2, P = 0.03) by day 7. The between-arm difference was not statistically significant. Drowsiness improved with dexamethasone, and dexamethasone was well tolerated with no significant toxicities. The authors present this as feasibility and preliminary efficacy data requiring confirmation.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: within-arm improvements in a 41-patient feasibility trial are not evidence of a treatment effect — the between-arm comparison, the only valid one, was not significant, and the definitive ABCD trial from the same group later found no difference.
cards.source: Hui D et al. Dexamethasone for Dyspnea in Cancer Patients: A Pilot Double-Blind, Randomized, Controlled Trial. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2016. PMID: 27330023. Registry ID: NCT01670097. cards.headline: Yennurajalingam 2016 (secondary analysis of a randomised trial, N = 114): the pain/dyspnoea symptom cluster did not change significantly on dexamethasone
cards.summary: Yennurajalingam 2016 (secondary analysis of a randomised trial, N = 114): the pain/dyspnoea symptom cluster did not change significantly on dexamethasone
cards.type: Secondary (retrospective) analysis of a randomised trial (Yennurajalingam 2016)
cards.people: 114 participants with advanced cancer from a previous randomised dexamethasone-versus-placebo trial, analysed by symptom clusters identified with principal component analysis: fatigue/anorexia-cachexia/depression (FAD), sleep/anxiety/drowsiness (SAD), and pain/dyspnea (PD), with severity followed at baseline, day 8 and day 15.
cards.result: Changes in severity of the FAD and PD clusters correlated significantly over time. The FAD cluster improved significantly in severity at day 8 and day 15 after dexamethasone treatment, whereas no significant change was observed in the SAD cluster or the pain/dyspnea (PD) cluster. The authors suggest fatigue, anorexia-cachexia and depression may share a common pathophysiological basis and that further studies should target that cluster.
cards.watchOut: A secondary cluster analysis, not a dyspnoea trial: dyspnoea is bundled with pain in the PD cluster, so this card supports — but cannot by itself settle — the dyspnoea question; the parent trial is also one of the two trials inside the Cochrane pool carded here, so the reports overlap and must not be counted as independent.
cards.source: Yennurajalingam S et al. Effects of Dexamethasone and Placebo on Symptom Clusters in Advanced Cancer Patients: A Preliminary Report. The Oncologist. 2016. PMID: 26888692. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Haywood 2019 (Cochrane review): pooling the only two trials then available gave -0.85 points (95% CI -1.73 to 0.03) at one week — very low-quality evidence, compatible with no effect
cards.summary: Haywood 2019 (Cochrane review): pooling the only two trials then available gave -0.85 points (95% CI -1.73 to 0.03) at one week — very low-quality evidence, compatible with no effect
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials of systemic corticosteroids for cancer-related breathlessness in adults: two studies met the inclusion criteria, enrolling 157 participants (37 in one study and 120 in the other), of whom 114 were included in the analyses; both compared oral dexamethasone with placebo.
cards.result: At one week, corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone resulted in a mean difference of -0.85 in dyspnoea intensity compared with placebo (scale 0-10, lower = less breathlessness; 95% CI -1.73 to 0.03), on very low-quality evidence, and the reviewers were uncertain whether corticosteroids reduce dyspnoea. The two trials differed in agents, dosages, outcome measures and time points, preventing many planned analyses.
cards.watchOut: Published before the ABCD trial: its pool is the pilot-era literature only (and overlaps the Yennurajalingam parent trial carded here), so its point estimate must not be quoted without the later, larger null trial beside it.
cards.source: Haywood A et al. Systemic corticosteroids for the management of cancer-related breathlessness (dyspnoea) in adults. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 30784058. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the definitive trial is null and stopped for futility; the smaller literature is inconclusive — routine dexamethasone for cancer dyspnoea is unproven, with a consistent harm signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: the definitive trial is null and stopped for futility; the smaller literature is inconclusive — routine dexamethasone for cancer dyspnoea is unproven, with a consistent harm signal
cards.people: One large double-blind RCT (128 randomised), one pilot RCT (41 randomised), one secondary analysis of a randomised trial (114 participants, overlapping the Cochrane pool) and one Cochrane review of two trials (157 enrolled).
cards.result: Dyspnoea change at day 7 in ABCD: -1.6 on dexamethasone versus -1.6 on placebo (difference 0, 95% CI -0.8 to 0.7; P = 0.48) — the treatment made no difference. Pilot between-arm difference: not significant. Pain/dyspnoea cluster: no significant change. Cochrane pooled mean difference -0.85 (95% CI -1.73 to 0.03), very low quality. Harms in ABCD: serious adverse events 28% versus 7%; insomnia 8% versus 2%; grade 3-4 infections 11% versus 7%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Nothing carded here addresses dyspnoea from a specifically steroid-responsive mechanism (for example superior vena cava obstruction or lymphangitis carcinomatosa); the null applies to unselected cancer dyspnoea, which is the question this shelf asks.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hui D et al. The Lancet Oncology. 2022 (PMID: 36087590); Hui D et al. Journal of Pain and Symptom Management. 2016 (PMID: 27330023); Yennurajalingam S et al. shelves.title: Jaw-stretching devices for trismus: they widen an already stiff jaw, they do not prevent the stiffness — and patients find them hard to keep using
shelves.question: In patients with head-and-neck cancer at risk of, or with established, radiation/surgery-related trismus, do jaw-exercise programmes and stretching devices (as tested) preserve or improve maximal interincisal opening versus no exercise / usual care?
shelves.mesh: Exercise Therapy · Head and Neck Neoplasms/therapy · Humans · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome · Trismus/etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the split is treatment versus prevention. For established trismus, the meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (733 patients) found exercise therapy with a jaw-mobilising device significantly improved maximal interincisal opening; for prevention, the same analysis found no significant difference in trismus incidence versus usual care (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34). The head-to-head device trial (van der Geer 2020, N = 27) found no significant difference between the two named devices — mouth opening rose 3.0 mm with the TheraBite programme and 1.5 mm with the Dynasplint programme — and exercising was hard: pain, fitting problems and deterioration stopped many patients. The prevention feasibility trial (Zatarain 2018, N = 40) found adding the Jaw Dynasplint to conventional stretching lowered compliance (only 25% used it as prescribed) and trismus was diagnosed in 4 Dynasplint patients versus 2 controls. Device names are given as published, per the clarification exception: the TheraBite Jaw Motion Rehabilitation System and the Dynasplint Trismus System (the Jaw Dynasplint System in the prevention trial). PROPOSED SPLIT: jaw exercise with a device probably helps established trismus; it does not prevent trismus, and adherence is the binding constraint either way.

cards.headline: van der Geer 2020 (RCT, N = 27): no significant difference between TheraBite and Dynasplint — mouth opening rose 3.0 mm vs 1.5 mm, and many patients could not sustain the exercises
cards.summary: van der Geer 2020 (RCT, N = 27): no significant difference between TheraBite and Dynasplint — mouth opening rose 3.0 mm vs 1.5 mm, and many patients could not sustain the exercises
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, device versus device (van der Geer 2020)
cards.people: 27 patients with head-and-neck cancer and trismus randomly assigned to 3 months of stretching exercises with the TheraBite Jaw Motion Rehabilitation System or the Dynasplint Trismus System (devices named as published); five patients did not start the protocol, eight discontinued exercises and two were lost to follow-up. Maximal mouth opening, mandibular function and quality of life were measured at three study visits.
cards.result: No significant differences in change in mouth opening were found between the two devices. Mouth opening increased by 3.0 mm (interquartile range -2.0 to 4.0) with the TheraBite system and 1.5 mm (interquartile range 1.0 to 3.0) with the Dynasplint system. Exercising with either device was challenging because of the intensive protocol, pain during exercises, fitting problems and overall deterioration of medical condition. The authors conclude the factors influencing progression of stretching exercises must be taken into account when prescribing a similar regimen.
cards.watchOut: No no-exercise control group — this trial compares two devices, it does not test whether device exercise beats nothing; with 12 of 27 patients not completing, the completer gains flatter the programmes.
cards.source: van der Geer SJ et al. The use of stretching devices for treatment of trismus in head and neck cancer patients: a randomized controlled trial. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2020. PMID: 31701267. Registry ID: NTR 5589 (Dutch Trial Register number, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Zatarain 2018 (randomised feasibility trial, N = 40, prevention): adding the Jaw Dynasplint reduced compliance — only 25% used it as prescribed — and trismus occurred in 4 device patients vs 2 controls
cards.summary: Zatarain 2018 (randomised feasibility trial, N = 40, prevention): adding the Jaw Dynasplint reduced compliance — only 25% used it as prescribed — and trismus occurred in 4 device patients vs 2 controls
cards.people: 40 patients with head-and-neck cancer receiving primary or adjuvant radiation-based therapy, randomised to conventional stretching exercises or stretching plus the Jaw Dynasplint System (named as published) 3 times per day for 30 minutes, with daily recording of maximum interincisal opening and device use.
cards.result: At 6 months after starting the preventive regimen, 50% of patients in the Dynasplint arm and 75% in the conventional stretching arm remained on their assigned therapy. Trismus was diagnosed in 2 patients in the control arm and 4 patients in the Dynasplint arm. Only 25% (95% CI 11.1 to 46.9) of patients in the Dynasplint arm used the device as prescribed. The authors conclude the addition of the Jaw Dynasplint decreased compliance compared with conventional stretching and that the prescribed regimen is unlikely to prove efficacious as a preventive measure because of low compliance.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial by design: its effect sizes must not be read as definitive efficacy estimates in either direction — what it establishes is the compliance failure of the prescribed regimen, which is itself the clinically important finding.
cards.source: Zatarain LA et al. cards.headline: Shao 2020 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 733 patients): exercise with a jaw device improved mouth opening in established trismus but did not prevent trismus (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34)
cards.summary: Shao 2020 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 733 patients): exercise with a jaw device improved mouth opening in established trismus but did not prevent trismus (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Shao 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of exercise therapy combined with a jaw-mobilising device for prevention or treatment of cancer treatment-induced trismus in head-and-neck cancer: 13 RCTs involving 733 patients; six studies assessed maximal interincisal opening as the treatment outcome and seven assessed trismus incidence as the preventive outcome.
cards.result: In the treatment studies, exercise therapy adjuvant to a jaw-mobilising device significantly improved maximal interincisal opening (pooled estimates reported from 4.48 mm, 95% CI 0.20 to 8.75, to 14.20 mm, 95% CI 10.73 to 17.67, across the analyses as printed in the record). In the prevention studies, there was no significant difference in trismus incidence between standard usual care and exercise therapy with a device (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.34 — a relative measure). The authors conclude exercise therapy can improve mouth opening after trismus has developed but does not prevent trismus, and note the clinical exercise programmes were heterogeneous.
cards.watchOut: The pooled treatment estimates span a wide range and rest on heterogeneous programmes and devices; the prevention pool is small (the confidence interval runs from a 39% relative reduction to more than a doubling), so 'does not prevent' means no demonstrated prevention, not proof of impossibility.
cards.source: Shao CH et al. Exercise therapy for cancer treatment-induced trismus in patients with head and neck cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 2020. PMID: 32890607. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: devices help a stiff jaw open wider once trismus is established; they do not prevent trismus during radiotherapy, and patients struggle to keep using them
cards.summary: Synthesis: devices help a stiff jaw open wider once trismus is established; they do not prevent trismus during radiotherapy, and patients struggle to keep using them
cards.people: One device-versus-device RCT in established trismus (27 patients), one randomised prevention feasibility trial (40 patients) and one meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (733 patients) covering both limbs.
cards.result: Treatment limb: pooled mouth-opening improvement significant in the meta-analysis; head-to-head, TheraBite +3.0 mm versus Dynasplint +1.5 mm, not significantly different. Prevention limb: trismus incidence risk ratio 1.20 (95% CI 0.61 to 2.34) in the meta-analysis; in the feasibility trial, trismus in 4 of the device arm versus 2 controls with only 25% adherence to the prescribed device regimen. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the treatment-versus-prevention split.
cards.watchOut: Prevention and treatment populations must not be pooled into one verdict — that pooling is exactly what the split stamp exists to prevent; long-term durability of the treatment gains beyond the exercise period is not established by any carded report.

shelves.title: Pentoxifylline plus vitamin E for superficial radiation fibrosis: one small randomised trial and the founding centre's cohorts show slow regression — over years, not months
shelves.question: In patients with established superficial radiation-induced fibrosis (non-jaw sites), does combined pentoxifylline plus tocopherol (vitamin E) regress fibrosis area/volume and improve function versus placebo or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antioxidants/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Breast Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Pentoxifylline/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Placebos · Radiation Pneumonitis/drug therapy,pathology · Radiation-Protective Agents/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Tocopherols/administration & dosage,pharmacology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: GAP-E framing, labelled observational: the direct randomised base for superficial (non-jaw) radiation fibrosis is one small double-blind trial from the founding centre, and everything else carded here is that centre's uncontrolled cohort programme. In the randomised trial (Delanian 2003; 24 women, 29 fibrosis areas), combined pentoxifylline 800 mg/day plus tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 units/day for 6 months regressed fibrosis surface by 60% ± 10% versus 43% ± 17% on double placebo (P = .038), and each drug alone was ineffective — the combination is the intervention. The founding centre's earlier cohort (Delanian 1999; 43 patients, 50 areas) reported continuous regression on the same combination (surface area -53% at 6 months, -66% at 12 months), and its kinetics report (Delanian 2005; 44 patients) estimated a maximum effect of 68% surface regression reached after a mean of 24 months, with a rebound after stopping short treatment (+40% surface area at 1 year in the short-treatment group versus +8.5% after long treatment). The adjacent randomised limb in the same programme — pentoxifylline-tocopherol-clodronate for radiation plexopathy — was negative, a reminder that this programme's uncontrolled successes have not always survived randomisation. The jaw osteoradionecrosis question is a different shelf in this library and none of its cards is borrowed here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational cohorts plus one small randomised trial: combined pentoxifylline-tocopherol probably regresses superficial radiation fibrosis, slowly, over years of treatment.

cards.headline: Delanian 2003 (randomised placebo-controlled trial, 24 women, 29 fibrosis areas): combined pentoxifylline + tocopherol regressed fibrosis surface 60% vs 43% on double placebo at 6 months (P = .038); either drug alone was ineffective
cards.summary: Delanian 2003 (randomised placebo-controlled trial, 24 women, 29 fibrosis areas): combined pentoxifylline + tocopherol regressed fibrosis surface 60% vs 43% on double placebo at 6 months (P = .038); either drug alone was ineffective
cards.people: 24 women previously irradiated for breast cancer with 29 areas of superficial radiation-induced fibrosis involving skin and underlying tissues, randomly assigned to four balanced groups: (A) pentoxifylline 800 mg/day plus tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 units/day; (B) pentoxifylline plus placebo; (C) placebo plus tocopherol; (D) double placebo, for 6 months; 22 patients with 27 areas were analysed at 6 months.
cards.result: Mean fibrosis surface regression was significant with combined pentoxifylline/tocopherol versus double placebo (60% ± 10% versus 43% ± 17%; P = .038). The median slope for speed of surface-area and volume regression was significantly higher for the combined group than for the other three groups. All treatments were well tolerated. The authors conclude 6 months of combined pentoxifylline/tocopherol can significantly reduce superficial radiation fibrosis, that synergism between the two drugs is likely because each drug alone is ineffective, and that the results require confirmation in larger series.
cards.watchOut: Very small (24 women, one centre, breast-cancer fields only) and the placebo group itself regressed 43% — measurement drift and natural history eat much of the apparent effect; the between-group margin is about 17 percentage points of surface regression, not the headline 60%.
cards.source: Delanian S et al. Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of combined pentoxifylline and tocopherol for regression of superficial radiation-induced fibrosis. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2003. PMID: 12829674. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Delanian 1999 (uncontrolled cohort, 43 patients, 50 fibrosis areas — observational, labelled): continuous regression on pentoxifylline + tocopherol, surface area -66% and SOMA score -48% at 12 months
cards.summary: Delanian 1999 (uncontrolled cohort, 43 patients, 50 fibrosis areas — observational, labelled): continuous regression on pentoxifylline + tocopherol, surface area -66% and SOMA score -48% at 12 months
cards.type: Single-arm treatment cohort (observational — labelled as such) (Delanian 1999)
cards.people: 43 patients (mean age 59 ± 10 years) with 50 symptomatic areas of radiation-induced fibrosis of skin and underlying tissues after radiotherapy for head-and-neck or breast cancer a mean of 8.5 ± 6.5 years earlier, treated with pentoxifylline 800 mg/day plus tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 units/day orally for at least 6 months; fibrosis had developed in the first year after irradiation and gradually worsened without spontaneous regression. Mean measurable surface area at entry was 42 ± 34 cm² and mean SOMA score 13.2 ± 5.9.
cards.result: All assessable injuries exhibited continuous clinical regression and functional improvement. Mean fibrosis surface area and SOMA scores improved significantly (P < .0001) at 3 months (surface -39%, SOMA -22%), 6 months (-53%, -35%) and 12 months (-66%, -48%), and mean linear dimensions fell from 6.5 ± 2.5 cm at entry to 4 ± 2 cm at 12 months. Treatment was well tolerated. The authors conclude the combination reversed chronic radiotherapy damage.
cards.watchOut: No comparator: an uncontrolled cohort from the programme that invented the treatment cannot separate drug effect from measurement and selection effects — and its 6-month regression (-53%) is larger than the same centre's later randomised trial found against placebo, which is exactly why the randomised card governs the stamp.
cards.source: Delanian S et al. Striking regression of chronic radiotherapy damage in a clinical trial of combined pentoxifylline and tocopherol. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 1999. PMID: 10506631. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Delanian 2005 (long-term cohort, 44 patients — observational, labelled): maximum regression 68% after a mean of 24 months of treatment, with rebound when treatment stopped early
cards.summary: Delanian 2005 (long-term cohort, 44 patients — observational, labelled): maximum regression 68% after a mean of 24 months of treatment, with rebound when treatment stopped early
cards.type: Long-term treatment cohort (observational — labelled as such) (Delanian 2005)
cards.people: Women treated with pentoxifylline 800 mg/day plus tocopherol (vitamin E) 1,000 units/day for measurable superficial radiation fibrosis after breast-cancer radiotherapy: a long-treatment group of 37 patients (47 fibrosis areas, 24 to 48 months of treatment) and a short-treatment group of 7 patients (8 areas, 6 to 12 months), treated between April 1995 and April 2000 at the founding centre.
cards.result: Combined treatment was continuously effective, with exponential surface-area regression (-46% long-treatment and -68% short-treatment at 6 months; -63% and -62% at 18 months; -68% at 24 and 36 months in the long-treatment group). The mean estimated maximal effect was 68% surface-area regression, reached after a mean of 24 months (16 months for fibrosis under 6 years old versus 28 months for older fibrosis; P = .0003). Symptom severity (SOMA score) was halved in both groups. One year after stopping, mean surface area had increased by 40% in the short-treatment group (rebound) versus 8.5% in the long-treatment group. The authors recommend treatment of at least 3 years in severe fibrosis.
cards.watchOut: Same centre and overlapping treatment years (1995-2000) as the 1999 cohort carded here — patients may overlap between the two cohort reports, so they are concordant programme reports, not independent replications; there is still no comparator group.
cards.source: Delanian S et al. Kinetics of response to long-term treatment combining pentoxifylline and tocopherol in patients with superficial radiation-induced fibrosis. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2005. PMID: 16260695. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled trial (24 women) and two uncontrolled founding-centre cohorts (43 and 44 patients, possibly overlapping) — the entire carded base for non-jaw superficial radiation fibrosis. Total participants across cards are about 111, with only 24 randomised.
cards.result: Randomised: surface regression 60% ± 10% on pentoxifylline + tocopherol versus 43% ± 17% on double placebo at 6 months (P = .038), each drug alone ineffective. Cohorts: surface regression -53% to -66% by 6-12 months, maximal effect 68% at a mean of 24 months, rebound +40% one year after short treatment. shelves.title: Preventing acute radiation proctitis: prophylactic sucralfate does not work by either route — and mesalazine made things worse
shelves.question: In adults receiving pelvic radiotherapy (chiefly prostate), do prophylactic rectal/oral sucralfate regimens (or the other tested prophylactic agents in the same trial programmes) prevent acute radiation proctitis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Rectal · Dose-Response Relationship, Radiation · Double-Blind Method · Enema · Follow-Up Studies · Gastrointestinal Agents/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Proctitis/etiology,prevention & control · Prostatic Neoplasms/radiotherapy · Radiation Injuries/etiology,prevention & control · Radiotherapy, High-Energy/adverse effects · Retrospective Studies · Sucralfate/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Prophylaxis does not work, and the trials are consistent about it. Rectal sucralfate enemas made no difference to acute proctitis in the phase III double-blind trial (some degree of proctitis in 88% on sucralfate versus 95% on placebo; grade 2 in 61% versus 71%, all differences non-significant), and its 5-year follow-on found no significant difference in late toxicity either (late grade 2 probability 5% versus 12%, P = 0.26; late rectal bleeding 54% versus 59%). Oral sucralfate in the largest trial (338 patients) made no difference to any bowel symptom and was associated with more rectal bleeding (64% versus 47%, P = 0.001). In the three-arm trial, hydrocortisone foam was not superior to sucralfate (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2) and mesalazine gel was significantly worse (hazard ratio 2.5, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.7) — its arm was stopped early. This shelf asks the prevention question only: treatment of established chronic radiation proctopathy (hyperbaric oxygen, sucralfate enemas as treatment, formalin, argon plasma) is a different question, homed on the library's existing chronic radiation proctopathy shelf (#6870), and its treatment evidence must not be read across to prevention. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit): prophylactic sucralfate, rectal or oral, does not prevent acute radiation proctitis.

cards.headline: O'Brien 1997 (phase III double-blind RCT, N = 86): rectal sucralfate enemas made no difference to acute proctitis (grade 2 in 61% vs 71% on placebo; all differences non-significant)
cards.summary: O'Brien 1997 (phase III double-blind RCT, N = 86): rectal sucralfate enemas made no difference to acute proctitis (grade 2 in 61% vs 71% on placebo; all differences non-significant)
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (O'Brien 1997)
cards.people: 86 patients having radiotherapy for localised carcinoma of the prostate, randomised double-blind to a once-daily enema of 3 g sucralfate in 15 mL suspension or placebo suspension during radiotherapy and for 2 weeks afterwards, assessed by EORTC/RTOG acute toxicity criteria and a patient self-assessment diary.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between placebo and sucralfate for peak incidences of proctitis: 95% (placebo) and 88% (sucralfate) suffered some degree of proctitis (difference 7 ± 11%), with 71% and 61% reaching grade 2 (difference 10 ± 19%). Median time to onset of grade 2 proctitis was 33.5 versus 36 days and median duration 9.5 versus 15 days, again non-significant. Similar proportions rated the effect of radiotherapy on bowel habit as 'a lot' (35% versus 37%). The authors conclude rectal sucralfate does not substantially reduce acute radiation proctitis symptoms and its routine clinical use cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: Nonconformal radiotherapy era and a modest sample: the confidence intervals do not exclude a small benefit, which is why this shelf's stamp rests on the whole trial set, not this trial alone.
cards.source: O'Brien PC et al. A phase III double-blind randomised study of rectal sucralfate suspension in the prevention of acute radiation proctitis. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 1997. PMID: 9424000. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: O'Brien 2002 (5-year follow-on of the same trial, N = 86): no significant difference in late toxicity either — late grade 2 probability 5% vs 12% (P = 0.26), late bleeding 54% vs 59%
cards.summary: O'Brien 2002 (5-year follow-on of the same trial, N = 86): no significant difference in late toxicity either — late grade 2 probability 5% vs 12% (P = 0.26), late bleeding 54% vs 59%
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of a randomised trial (O'Brien 2002)
cards.people: The same 86 patients with localised prostate carcinoma randomised to daily rectal sucralfate (3 g in 15 mL) or placebo enema from the first day of radiotherapy to 2 weeks after completion, followed for a further 5 years on a 6-monthly basis with late RTOG/EORTC toxicity scoring and a patient self-assessment questionnaire. This is a follow-on report of the trial carded above, not an independent trial.
cards.result: With median follow-up of 5 years, the Kaplan-Meier probability of late grade 2 RTOG/EORTC toxicity was 12% (95% CI 2 to 22%) for placebo and 5% (95% CI 0 to 12%) for sucralfate (P = 0.26). The probability of late rectal bleeding was 59% (95% CI 45 to 73%) for placebo and 54% (95% CI 40 to 68%) for sucralfate. No statistically significant difference was found for any other patient self-assessment variable. Acute grade 2 or greater toxicity predicted later toxicity (hazard ratio 2.74, 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73 for late grade 1 or greater), and moderate or severe rectal pain during radiotherapy was the best single predictor (hazard ratio 3.44, 95% CI 1.68 to 7). The authors conclude the results do not support rectal sucralfate to reduce late toxicity of nonconformal radiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Counted as a follow-on of the 1997 trial, not a second trial; late-toxicity event counts are small, so the non-significant 5% versus 12% difference is compatible with anything from a real small benefit to none — the acute-phase null in the same patients is the firmer finding.
cards.source: O'Brien PC et al. Acute symptoms, not rectally administered sucralfate, predict for late radiation proctitis: longer term follow-up of a phase III trial — Trans-Tasman Radiation Oncology Group. cards.headline: Sanguineti 2003 (randomised three-arm trial, N = 134): hydrocortisone foam was not superior to sucralfate (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), and mesalazine gel was significantly worse (hazard ratio 2.5) — its arm was stopped
cards.summary: Sanguineti 2003 (randomised three-arm trial, N = 134): hydrocortisone foam was not superior to sucralfate (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), and mesalazine gel was significantly worse (hazard ratio 2.5) — its arm was stopped
cards.people: 134 consecutive patients undergoing three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy to 76 Gy for prostate carcinoma, randomised to once-daily enemas from day 1 of radiotherapy: sucralfate 3 g in 15 mL suspension (Antepsin, as published; 63 patients), mesalazine 4 g gel (Enterasyn, as published; 8 patients before the arm was discontinued) or hydrocortisone 100 mg foam (Colifoam, as published; 63 patients), with sucralfate as the control arm and time to grade 2 or worse acute rectal toxicity as the endpoint.
cards.result: Cumulative incidence of acute rectal toxicity at the end of treatment was 61.9 ± 6.1% (sucralfate), 87.5 ± 11.7% (mesalazine) and 52.4 ± 6.2% (hydrocortisone). The mesalazine arm was discontinued after the first 24 patients because seven of eight mesalazine patients developed acute rectal toxicity (five grade 3, two grade 2); mesalazine was significantly worse than sucralfate (hazard ratio 2.5, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.7; P = 0.03). Hydrocortisone did not differ significantly from sucralfate (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2; P = 0.2). The authors conclude topical mesalazine is contraindicated during radiotherapy and hydrocortisone enema is not superior to sucralfate in preventing acute rectal toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Randomisation was blind to the treating physician but not to patients, and there is no placebo arm — sucralfate is the comparator, so this trial ranks the three agents against each other rather than proving any of them beats nothing; the mesalazine harm signal rests on only 8 patients, albeit a striking 7 of 8.

cards.headline: Kneebone 2001 (double-blind RCT, N = 338): oral sucralfate made no difference to any bowel symptom — and rectal bleeding was more common on sucralfate (64% vs 47%, P = 0.001)
cards.summary: Kneebone 2001 (double-blind RCT, N = 338): oral sucralfate made no difference to any bowel symptom — and rectal bleeding was more common on sucralfate (64% vs 47%, P = 0.001)
cards.people: 338 patients with clinically localised prostate cancer receiving small-volume radiotherapy at four Sydney departments, randomised double-blind to 3 g oral sucralfate suspension or placebo twice daily during radiotherapy; 335 were evaluable (164 sucralfate, 171 placebo), keeping daily bowel-symptom diaries with RTOG/EORTC acute toxicity grading.
cards.result: After adjusting for baseline values there was no significant difference between groups for stool frequency (P = 0.41), consistency (P = 0.20), flatus (P = 0.25), mucus (P = 0.54) or pain (P = 0.73). Rectal bleeding was more frequent in the sucralfate group: 64% of patients noticed rectal bleeding compared with 47% on placebo (P = 0.001). RTOG/EORTC acute toxicity grades did not differ (P = 0.88; grade 0/1/2 in 13%/44%/43% on sucralfate versus 15%/44%/40% on placebo). The authors conclude prophylactic oral sucralfate does not ameliorate acute radiation proctitis symptoms and may increase acute bleeding.
cards.watchOut: The bleeding excess is unexplained by the authors and the placebo group had more liquid baseline stools (adjusted for in analysis); oral and rectal sucralfate are different exposures — this trial rules on the oral route, the O'Brien trials on the rectal route, and both are null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: across three randomised trials (558 patients), prophylactic sucralfate by either route did not prevent acute proctitis, hydrocortisone was not superior, and mesalazine looked harmful
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three randomised trials (558 patients), prophylactic sucralfate by either route did not prevent acute proctitis, hydrocortisone was not superior, and mesalazine looked harmful
cards.people: Three randomised trials — rectal sucralfate versus placebo (86 patients, with a 5-year follow-on report), a three-arm rectal-agent trial (134 patients) and oral sucralfate versus placebo (338 patients) — all in prostate radiotherapy.
cards.result: Acute grade 2 proctitis: 61% on rectal sucralfate versus 71% on placebo (non-significant). Oral sucralfate: no symptom benefit, bleeding 64% versus 47% (P = 0.001). Hydrocortisone versus sucralfate: hazard ratio 0.7 (95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), not significant. Mesalazine versus sucralfate: hazard ratio 2.5 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.7), arm stopped. Late toxicity at 5 years: no significant difference. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit) for prophylactic sucralfate.
cards.watchOut: All trials predate modern image-guided and intensity-modulated prostate radiotherapy, which lowers rectal dose and baseline proctitis rates; the null is about these agents at these doses, and says nothing about treating established chronic proctopathy, which is asked on a different shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Brien PC et al. Radiotherapy and Oncology. 1997 (PMID: 9424000); O'Brien PC et al. shelves.title: Frozen gloves and socks against taxane nail damage: striking protection in within-patient studies, no effect in the randomised trial — and the cold drives patients out
shelves.question: In patients receiving taxane chemotherapy, does local cryotherapy (frozen glove/sock, as tested) prevent taxane-induced nail toxicity (onycholysis, subungual haemorrhage, nail loss) versus the untreated contralateral hand/foot?
shelves.mesh: Cryotherapy/methods · Docetaxel/adverse effects · Humans · Nail Diseases/chemically induced,prevention & control · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Onycholysis/chemically induced,prevention & control · Paclitaxel/administration & dosage · Taxoids/adverse effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the split is by study design. The within-patient frozen glove and sock studies from the French programme (Scotté 2005, 45 patients; Scotté 2008, 50 patients) found much less nail toxicity on the protected side — onycholysis grade 1-2 in 11% of protected hands versus 51% of control hands, and grade 1-2 nail toxicity in 0% of protected feet versus 21% of control feet — using the Elasto-Gel frozen glove and sock as published. But the only conventionally randomised trial (McCarthy 2014) found no significant differences between gloved and ungloved hands, with a 60% withdrawal rate for discomfort and only 21 of 53 enrolled patients evaluable; and a 200-patient comparative study (Can 2012) also found no significant difference with frozen gloves and socks. The meta-analysis (Huang 2019; 3 RCTs and 6 prospective studies, 708 patients) pools to a lower total nail toxicity with cryotherapy (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.79 — a relative measure), driven largely by the within-patient studies. This shelf asks the nail question only: cryotherapy for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy is homed on the library's existing paclitaxel cryotherapy shelf and its compression/cryocompression companion shelf, and none of their neuropathy endpoints is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: cooling probably reduces docetaxel nail toxicity in patients who can tolerate it, but the randomised evidence is null and tolerability is the weak point.

cards.headline: Scotté 2005 (within-patient case-control study, N = 45): onycholysis grade 1-2 in 11% of frozen-glove hands versus 51% of control hands (P = .0001)
cards.summary: Scotté 2005 (within-patient case-control study, N = 45): onycholysis grade 1-2 in 11% of frozen-glove hands versus 51% of control hands (P = .0001)
cards.people: 45 patients receiving docetaxel 75 mg/m² alone or in combination chemotherapy, each wearing an Elasto-Gel frozen glove (84400 APT Cedex, Akromed, France — as published) for 90 minutes on the right hand, with the unprotected left hand as the within-patient control; onycholysis and skin toxicity graded each cycle by National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria with photography.
cards.result: Onycholysis and skin toxicity were significantly lower in the frozen-glove hand than the control hand (P = .0001). Onycholysis was grade 0 in 89% versus 49% and grade 1-2 in 11% versus 51% for the protected and control hands respectively. Skin toxicity was grade 0 in 73% versus 41% and grade 1-2 in 27% versus 59%. Median time to nail and skin toxicity did not differ significantly (106 versus 58 days for nail toxicity; 57 versus 58 days for skin toxicity). Five patients (11%) experienced discomfort due to cold intolerance. The authors conclude the frozen glove significantly reduces docetaxel nail and skin toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Within-patient and unblinded: the protected hand was always the right hand, and patients and assessors knew which hand was cooled; the design removes between-patient confounding but cannot exclude expectation and assessment bias.
cards.source: Scotté F et al. Multicenter study of a frozen glove to prevent docetaxel-induced onycholysis and cutaneous toxicity of the hand. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2005. PMID: 15994152. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Scotté 2008 (within-patient phase II study, N = 50): nail toxicity grade 1-2 in 0% of frozen-sock feet versus 21% of control feet (P = .002)
cards.summary: Scotté 2008 (within-patient phase II study, N = 50): nail toxicity grade 1-2 in 0% of frozen-sock feet versus 21% of control feet (P = .002)
cards.type: Phase II within-patient matched case-control study (Scotté 2008)
cards.people: 50 consecutive patients receiving docetaxel 70 to 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks, each wearing an Elasto-Gel frozen sock (as published) for 90 minutes on the right foot, with the unprotected left foot as the matched control; nail and skin toxicities assessed by National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria version 3.
cards.result: Nail toxicity was significantly lower in the frozen-sock foot than the control foot (grade 0: 100% versus 79%; grade 1-2: 0% versus 21%; P = .002). Skin toxicity was grade 0 in 98% versus 94% and grade 1-2 in 2% versus 6% respectively. Median times to toxicity did not differ significantly between feet. One patient experienced discomfort because of cold intolerance. The authors conclude cold therapy with the frozen sock significantly reduced docetaxel-induced foot nail toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Same design limits as the glove study — unblinded, protected side always the right foot, single programme; zero events on the protected side in 50 patients is a fragile count, and skin toxicity barely differed.
cards.source: Scotté F et al. Matched case-control phase 2 study to evaluate the use of a frozen sock to prevent docetaxel-induced onycholysis and cutaneous toxicity of the foot. Cancer. 2008. cards.headline: McCarthy 2014 (randomised trial, N = 53 enrolled, 21 evaluable): no significant differences between frozen-glove and control hands — and 60% withdrew because of discomfort
cards.summary: McCarthy 2014 (randomised trial, N = 53 enrolled, 21 evaluable): no significant differences between frozen-glove and control hands — and 60% withdrew because of discomfort
cards.people: 53 patients prescribed docetaxel every 3 weeks for a minimum of three cycles, enrolled after a 21-patient pilot, each acting as their own control with a frozen gel glove worn on one randomised hand from 15 minutes before infusion until 15 minutes after; hand and nail toxicities evaluated by two blinded assessors using CTCAE version 4. Only 21 participants provided evaluable data, with a 60% withdrawal rate due to patient discomfort with the intervention.
cards.result: Mean incidence and severity of toxicities in control versus intervention hands included nail discolouration grade 1 in 81% versus 67%, nail loss grade 1 in 19% versus 19%, nail ridging grade 1 in 57% versus 57%, and erythroderma grade 1 in 5% versus 5% of evaluable cycles. No significant differences were determined between hand conditions in time to event or in toxicity. The authors conclude that while frozen-glove cryotherapy for docetaxel cutaneous toxicities is safe, its limited efficacy, patient discomfort and logistical issues preclude its use in their clinical setting.
cards.watchOut: The 60% discomfort withdrawal guts the trial's power — only 21 evaluable patients — so its null is weak evidence against, just as the positive within-patient studies are weak evidence for; the withdrawal rate itself is a robust finding about tolerability in routine practice.
cards.source: McCarthy AL et al. Cryotherapy for docetaxel-induced hand and nail toxicity: randomised control trial. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2014. PMID: 24362908. Registry ID: NCT00911352. hand and nail toxicities evaluated by two blinded assessors using ctcae version 4. only 21 participants provided evaluable data, with a 60% withdrawal rate due to patient discomfort with the intervention. mean incidence and severity of toxicities in control versus intervention hands included nail discolouration grade 1 in 81% versus 67%, nail loss grade 1 in 19% versus 19%, nail ridging grade 1 in 57% versus 57%, and erythroderma grade 1 in 5% versus 5% of evaluable cycles. no significant differences were determined between hand conditions in time to event or in toxicity. the authors conclude that while frozen-glove cryotherapy for docetaxel cutaneous toxicities is safe, its limited efficacy, patient discomfort and logistical issues preclude its use in their clinical setting. the 60% discomfort withdrawal guts the trial's power — only 21 evaluable patients — so its null is weak evidence against, just as the positive within-patient studies are weak evidence for; the withdrawal rate itself is a robust finding about tolerability in routine practice. mccarthy al et al. cryotherapy for docetaxel-induced hand and nail toxicity: randomised control trial. supportive care in cancer. 2014. pmid: 24362908. registry id: nct00911352. mesh: adult · aged · antineoplastic agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · antineoplastic agents, phytogenic/administration & dosage,adverse effects · cryotherapy/methods · docetaxel · female · freezing · gloves, protective · hand · humans · male · middle aged · nail diseases/chemically induced,prevention & control · nails/drug effects · neoplasms/drug therapy · single-blind method · skin diseases/chemically induced,prevention & control · taxoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects

cards.headline: Can 2012 (comparative study, N = 200): no statistically significant difference in nail toxicity between frozen gloves/socks and control
cards.summary: Can 2012 (comparative study, N = 200): no statistically significant difference in nail toxicity between frozen gloves/socks and control
cards.people: 200 patients receiving taxane-based treatments, assigned to a frozen gloves/socks intervention group or a control group in a descriptive, interventional, cross-sectional study; frozen gloves and socks were applied only during hourly taxane infusions, and nail changes were graded with National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria. Most patients were women with breast cancer; groups were similar for diagnosis, taxane type and number of cycles.
cards.result: Grade 1 nail toxicity was found in 34% of patients, grade 2 in 11% and grade 3 in 5.5%. Nail toxicity was higher in women, in patients with diabetes, with capecitabine-docetaxel combinations and with breast or gynaecological cancers, and rose with the number of cycles, body mass index and neuropathy severity; body mass index, breast or ovarian cancer diagnosis and number of cycles were independent predictors. No statistically significant difference in nail toxicity incidence or time to occurrence of nail changes was found between the intervention and control groups.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised and cross-sectional in analysis, with cooling applied only during hourly infusions — shorter cooling than the 90-minute French protocol — so its null may reflect dose and design as much as the intervention itself.
cards.source: Can G et al. Taxane-induced nail changes: Predictors and efficacy of the use of frozen gloves and socks in the prevention of nail toxicity. European Journal of Oncology Nursing. 2012. PMID: 21784705. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Huang 2019 (meta-analysis, 708 patients): total nail toxicity risk ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.79) with cryotherapy — a relative reduction, pooled mainly from within-patient studies
cards.summary: Huang 2019 (meta-analysis, 708 patients): total nail toxicity risk ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.79) with cryotherapy — a relative reduction, pooled mainly from within-patient studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prophylactic management for taxane-induced nail toxicity: three randomised controlled trials and six prospective studies with 708 patients, comparing cryotherapy (and, in a separate limb, nail solution) with controls, with nail toxicity grading as the primary outcome.
cards.result: Nail toxicity and skin toxicity were significantly lower in cryotherapy patients than controls: grade 1 nail toxicity risk ratio 0.51 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.89), grade 2-3 nail toxicity risk ratio 0.36 (95% CI 0.11 to 1.12), total nail toxicity risk ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.79) and skin toxicity risk ratio 0.46 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.64) — all relative measures, with no single pooled absolute incidence applicable across the differing study populations. Nail solution also significantly lowered nail toxicity. The authors conclude cryotherapy and nail solution are effective prophylactic options for patients who can afford and comply with them, while calling for studies to establish routine protocols and long-term efficacy and safety.
cards.watchOut: The pool mixes the positive within-patient French studies with the null randomised and comparative reports, so the pooled relative risk inherits the strongest designs' biases rather than resolving the split; the grade 2-3 estimate is not itself significant (confidence interval 0.11 to 1.12).
cards.source: Huang KL et al. Prophylactic management for taxane-induced nail toxicity: A systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Cancer Care. 2019. PMID: 31184794. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: within-patient studies say cooling protects nails, the randomised and comparative studies say it does not — and patients often cannot tolerate the cold
cards.summary: Synthesis: within-patient studies say cooling protects nails, the randomised and comparative studies say it does not — and patients often cannot tolerate the cold
cards.people: Two within-patient French studies (45 and 50 patients), one randomised within-patient trial (53 enrolled, 21 evaluable), one 200-patient comparative study and one meta-analysis of 708 patients — the carded record on cryotherapy for taxane nail toxicity, distinct from the neuropathy question homed elsewhere in the library.
cards.result: Protected versus control sides: onycholysis grade 1-2 11% versus 51% (hands) and nail toxicity grade 1-2 0% versus 21% (feet) in the within-patient studies; no significant differences in the randomised trial or the 200-patient comparison. Pooled total nail toxicity risk ratio 0.49 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.79, relative). Tolerability: 11% cold-intolerance discomfort in the glove study, 1 patient in the sock study, and 60% withdrawal for discomfort in the randomised trial. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the design split.
cards.watchOut: Feet and non-docetaxel taxanes are thinly studied, frostbite has been reported with frozen gloves in the wider literature, and no carded study follows nails long enough to separate delayed toxicity from prevented toxicity.
cards.source: Synthesis of Scotté F et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2005 (PMID: 15994152); Scotté F et al. Cancer. 2008 (PMID: 18286527); McCarthy AL et al. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2014 (PMID: 24362908); Can G et al. European Journal of Oncology Nursing. 2012 (PMID: 21784705); Huang KL et al. European Journal of Cancer Care. 2019 (PMID: 31184794).

shelves.title: Dordaviprone in recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma: single-arm pooled response rate 20% by RANO-HGG with median response duration 11.2 months — no controlled evidence yet
shelves.question: In patients with recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, does single-agent dordaviprone (ONC201), versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses and clinical benefit?
shelves.mesh: Glioma/genetics/drug therapy/pathology · Brain Neoplasms/genetics/drug therapy/pathology · Histones/genetics · Mutation · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/genetics/drug therapy · Pyrimidines/therapeutic use/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, capped by design: every carded report is single-arm or uncontrolled, so response rates have no comparator and are framed as such throughout (GAP-E). The pooled integrated analysis of four trials plus an expanded-access protocol (n=50) found an objective response rate of 20.0% by RANO-HGG (30.0% by combined RANO criteria) with a median response duration of 11.2 months in a disease with no established therapy beyond radiation — the signal that supported FDA accelerated approval in August 2025 for recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. The large international compassionate-use cohort (n=174) is sobering real-world context: median survival after starting the drug was 4.7 months. The two paediatric phase 1 reports are dose/safety limbs of the same early programme (one, NCT03416530, also feeds the pooled analysis — the overlap is labelled, not hidden). Product naming, clarification exception: dordaviprone (Modeyso, Chimerix/Jazz Pharmaceuticals). Cross-points in prose only: the phase 3 ACTION trial in newly diagnosed disease is a different slice with no results published, and the non-midline H3 K27M cohort is an adjacent slice — neither is carded here.

cards.headline: Integrated analysis 2024: 50 patients pooled from four trials and an expanded-access protocol — response rate 20.0% by RANO-HGG (30.0% combined criteria), median response duration 11.2 months, grade 3 treatment-related events 20%
cards.summary: Integrated analysis 2024: 50 patients pooled from four trials and an expanded-access protocol — response rate 20.0% by RANO-HGG (30.0% combined criteria), median response duration 11.2 months, grade 3 treatment-related events 20%
cards.type: Integrated single-arm analysis of four trials plus expanded access, J Clin Oncol 2024
cards.people: Fifty patients (46 adults, 4 children) with recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma and measurable disease by RANO high-grade-glioma criteria, performance score ≥60 and ≥90 days from radiation (pontine and spinal tumours ineligible), who received oral single-agent dordaviprone (ONC201) in one of four clinical trials or one expanded-access protocol; radiographic endpoints by blinded independent central review. Single-arm pooled analysis — no concurrent control.
cards.result: The overall response rate by RANO-HGG was 20.0% (95% CI 10.0–33.7) and by combined RANO-HGG/LGG criteria 30.0% (95% CI 17.9–44.6). Median time to response was 8.3 months (range 1.9–15.9) and median duration of response 11.2 months (95% CI 3.8 to not reached). A ≥50% corticosteroid dose reduction occurred in 7 of 15 evaluable patients and performance-status improvement in 6 of 34 evaluable patients. Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% (fatigue commonest, 10%); there were no grade 4 treatment-related events, deaths or discontinuations.
cards.watchOut: Pooled single-arm data: a 20% response rate in recurrent disease is meaningful only against this tumour's dismal natural history, and eligibility (performance score ≥60, no pontine/spinal tumours, ≥90 days post-radiation) selected a fitter population than the clinic average — compare with the compassionate-use card below.
cards.source: Arrillaga-Romany I, Gardner SL, Odia Y et al. ONC201 (Dordaviprone) in Recurrent H3 K27M-Mutant Diffuse Midline Glioma. Journal of clinical oncology. 2024. PMID: 38335473. Registry ID: NCT02525692, NCT03134131, NCT03295396, NCT03416530, NCT05392374 (the five source studies, as listed in the record). cards.headline: Compassionate-use programme 2025: 174 patients treated internationally — median survival after starting dordaviprone 4.7 months, with thalamic site and older age the favourable prognostic factors (uncontrolled, labelled)
cards.summary: Compassionate-use programme 2025: 174 patients treated internationally — median survival after starting dordaviprone 4.7 months, with thalamic site and older age the favourable prognostic factors (uncontrolled, labelled)
cards.type: International compassionate-use cohort (observational), Eur J Cancer 2025
cards.people: One hundred and seventy-four patients (102 children, 72 adults) from 14 countries with H3K27-altered recurrent diffuse midline glioma treated through an academia-driven French compassionate-use programme (November 2021 to August 2023) after progression following radiotherapy; 37% received a second course of irradiation at relapse. Retrospective programme report — no control group.
cards.result: Median treatment duration was 57 days. Median overall survival from diagnosis was 15.5 months for the whole cohort (14.2 months in children, 19.6 in adults), and median survival after starting dordaviprone was 4.7 months (range 1–711 days). Thalamic tumour site and older age were favourable prognostic factors in multivariable analysis; re-irradiation was associated with longer survival after starting the drug only in children. The authors state plainly that efficacy needs validation in a controlled randomised trial.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled survival times in a compassionate-use population cannot be attributed to the drug — patients well enough to be referred internationally are selected, and concurrent re-irradiation confounds the paediatric read.
cards.source: Di Carlo D, Annereau M, Vignes M et al. Real life data of ONC201 (dordaviprone) in pediatric and adult H3K27-altered recurrent diffuse midline glioma: Results of an international academia-driven compassionate use program. European journal of cancer. 2025. PMID: 39700833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gardner 2022: first paediatric phase 1 (n=22) after radiotherapy — weight-scaled adult dose (625 mg weekly) is the recommended dose, no dose-limiting toxicities; a dose/safety limb of the same programme
cards.summary: Gardner 2022: first paediatric phase 1 (n=22) after radiotherapy — weight-scaled adult dose (625 mg weekly) is the recommended dose, no dose-limiting toxicities; a dose/safety limb of the same programme
cards.type: Paediatric phase 1 dose-escalation/expansion trial, Neurooncol Adv 2022
cards.people: Twenty-two children with H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma or diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma treated with single-agent dordaviprone after radiation (prior systemic therapy permitted) in an open-label multicentre phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion trial; the target dose was the adult recommended dose of 625 mg scaled by body weight.
cards.result: The recommended paediatric dose was the adult 625 mg dose scaled by body weight; no dose-limiting toxicities occurred. The commonest treatment-emergent grade 1–2 events were headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness and raised alanine aminotransferase. Median treatment duration was 20.6 weeks (range 5.1–129). Five patients (22.7%), all of whom started the drug after radiation and before recurrence, were alive at 2 years from diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study in a mixed newly-treated/recurrent population — its survival figures are not efficacy evidence for the recurrent-disease question, and this trial (NCT03416530) is also one of the sources pooled in the integrated-analysis card above.
cards.source: Gardner SL, Tarapore RS, Allen J et al. Phase I dose escalation and expansion trial of single agent ONC201 in pediatric diffuse midline gliomas following radiotherapy. cards.headline: Odia 2024: twice-weekly (two consecutive days) paediatric phase 1 — 12 patients on the D1D2 schedule, no dose-limiting toxicities or grade ≥3 treatment-related events; safety/pharmacokinetics only (same programme)
cards.summary: Odia 2024: twice-weekly (two consecutive days) paediatric phase 1 — 12 patients on the D1D2 schedule, no dose-limiting toxicities or grade ≥3 treatment-related events; safety/pharmacokinetics only (same programme)
cards.type: Paediatric phase 1 safety/pharmacokinetic study, Neuro Oncol 2024
cards.people: Paediatric patients with H3 K27M-mutant glioma and/or diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma after at least one line of therapy in a phase 1 dose-escalation/expansion study of the same programme (NCT03416530): 12 patients received dordaviprone on two consecutive days per week (D1D2) across three dose levels, with once-weekly patients serving as pharmacokinetic comparators. N = 12 on the D1D2 schedule, printed on the face.
cards.result: No dose-limiting toxicities and no grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred at any D1D2 dose level. Pharmacokinetic exposure was variable; the area under the curve over 48 hours was greater with D1D2 than with once-weekly dosing, without drug accumulation, and peak concentrations did not clearly increase with the doubled schedule. This report establishes tolerability of the alternative schedule, not efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: durable responses occur in about one in five recurrent patients on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with the controlled verdict still outstanding
cards.summary: Synthesis: durable responses occur in about one in five recurrent patients on single-arm evidence — POSSIBLE, with the controlled verdict still outstanding
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above: the pooled single-arm integrated analysis (n=50), the international compassionate-use cohort (n=174), and two paediatric phase 1 reports of the same early programme (n=22 and 12 on the twice-weekly schedule).
cards.result: The consistent picture: dordaviprone is well tolerated (grade 3 treatment-related events 20% in the pooled analysis, fatigue commonest; no dose-limiting toxicities in either paediatric study) and produces objective, sometimes durable (median 11.2 months) responses in about 20% of selected recurrent patients, while unselected real-world survival after starting it remains short (median 4.7 months). Single-arm evidence throughout caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The newly diagnosed question belongs to the phase 3 ACTION trial, whose design is published but whose results are not — it is cross-pointed here in prose and must not be cited as evidence for this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Accelerated approval rests on response rate and duration in uncontrolled data; a negative or null controlled readout would change this stamp, and the compassionate-use survival figures warn against extrapolating trial responses to all-comers.

shelves.title: Tovorafenib in relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma: FIREFLY-1 response rate 67% by RANO-HGG (51% by RAPNO), vision preserved in 80% of the optic-pathway subgroup — single-arm, single programme
shelves.question: In children with relapsed or refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma, does once-weekly tovorafenib, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses and preserve vision in optic-pathway disease?
shelves.mesh: Glioma/drug therapy/genetics · Brain Neoplasms/drug therapy/genetics/pathology · Proto-Oncogene Proteins B-raf/genetics · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Optic Nerve Glioma/drug therapy/pathology/diagnostic imaging · Visual Acuity/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, capped by structure: this is a single-arm, single-programme shelf — all three carded reports describe the same FIREFLY-1 (PNOC026) trial and are labelled as one programme throughout, on the established single-programme precedent. Within that limit the signal is strong and consistent across assessment criteria: response rate 67% by RANO-HGG and 51% by RAPNO (including minor responses) in arm 1 (n=77), median response duration 16.6 and 13.8 months respectively, and in the optic-pathway subgroup vision was preserved in 80% of patients and improved in 31%. The FDA granted accelerated approval in April 2024 for relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma from 6 months of age, with the frontline FIREFLY-2 trial required as the postmarketing study (a design for a different, frontline question — cross-pointed in prose, not carded). Product naming, clarification exception: tovorafenib (Ojemda, Day One Biopharmaceuticals). The harm face: hair colour changes (76%), raised creatine phosphokinase (56%) and anaemia (49%) are the commonest treatment-related events, grade ≥3 treatment-related events occurred in 42%, and 7% discontinued for toxicity. A separate 7-patient adult refractory-glioma series is below the floor and is not carded; its grade 4 intratumoural-haemorrhage event is noted here in prose so the harm record is not hidden.

cards.headline: FIREFLY-1 primary report 2024: arm 1 (n=77) — response rate 67% by RANO-HGG and 51% by RAPNO, median response duration 16.6 and 13.8 months; grade ≥3 treatment-related events in 42%
cards.summary: FIREFLY-1 primary report 2024: arm 1 (n=77) — response rate 67% by RANO-HGG and 51% by RAPNO, median response duration 16.6 and 13.8 months; grade ≥3 treatment-related events in 42%
cards.type: Single-arm phase 2 trial primary report (FIREFLY-1), Nat Med 2024
cards.people: Children and young people with BRAF-altered relapsed/refractory paediatric low-grade glioma in the ongoing phase 2 FIREFLY-1 (PNOC026) trial: arm 1 efficacy cohort n=77, arm 2 extension cohort n=60 (treatment access after arm 1 closed), safety assessed in all 137 treated patients. Tovorafenib 420 mg/m² once weekly (maximum 600 mg), an oral CNS-penetrant type II RAF inhibitor. Single-arm — no concurrent control.
cards.result: By independent review using RANO-HGG criteria, the overall response rate was 67%, meeting the prespecified primary endpoint, with median duration of response 16.6 months and median time to response 3.0 months. By RAPNO criteria (including minor responses) the response rate was 51%, median duration 13.8 months and median time to response 5.3 months. The commonest treatment-related adverse events were hair colour changes (76%), elevated creatine phosphokinase (56%) and anaemia (49%); grade ≥3 treatment-related events occurred in 42% of patients and 9 patients (7%) discontinued for treatment-related events.
cards.watchOut: Response criteria move the headline by 16 points (67% RANO-HGG vs 51% RAPNO) — quote both. Single-arm responses in a slow-growing tumour cannot separate drug effect from indolent biology for the minor-response fraction.
cards.source: Kilburn LB, Khuong-Quang DA, Hansford JR et al. The type II RAF inhibitor tovorafenib in relapsed/refractory pediatric low-grade glioma: the phase 2 FIREFLY-1 trial. cards.headline: FIREFLY-1 optic-pathway companion 2025: 42 of the same 77 arm-1 patients — response 64% by RANO-HGG, vision preserved in 80% of patients and improved in 31% (same trial, labelled)
cards.summary: FIREFLY-1 optic-pathway companion 2025: 42 of the same 77 arm-1 patients — response 64% by RANO-HGG, vision preserved in 80% of patients and improved in 31% (same trial, labelled)
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup companion report of FIREFLY-1, Neuro Oncol 2025
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of the 42 arm-1 FIREFLY-1 patients whose tumours were optic pathway gliomas (35 of 42 had at least two visual-acuity assessments); anti-tumour activity assessed independently by RANO-HGG, RAPNO and RANO-LGG criteria, data cutoff 5 June 2023. Same trial and population as the primary-report card — a companion limb, not an independent study.
cards.result: Response rates in the optic-pathway subgroup were 64% (RANO-HGG), 50% (RAPNO) and 55% (RANO-LGG), with clinical benefit rates of 95%, 88% and 90% respectively. Visual acuity per patient was preserved in 80% and improved in 31%; per eye, preserved in 87% and improved in 27%. The safety profile in this subgroup matched the overall trial population.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc subgroup of the same 77 patients — it adds the vision outcome that matters most in optic-pathway disease, but it is not confirmatory evidence, and 7 of 42 patients lacked the paired vision assessments.
cards.source: Nysom K, Kilburn LB, Leary SES et al. Radiographic and visual response to the type II RAF inhibitor tovorafenib in children with relapsed/refractory optic pathway glioma in the FIREFLY-1 trial. Neuro-oncology. 2025. PMID: 39700439. cards.headline: FDA approval summary 2025: accelerated approval on the same FIREFLY-1 data — efficacy population 76, RAPNO response rate 51% (95% CI 40–63), median response duration 13.8 months (same programme, labelled)

cards.type: FDA approval summary of FIREFLY-1, Clin Cancer Res 2025
cards.people: Regulatory review of FIREFLY-1 (NCT04775485), a single-arm open-label multicentre trial enrolling patients aged 6 months to 25 years with relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered paediatric low-grade glioma after prior systemic therapy; the efficacy population was 76 patients, with response (complete, partial or minor) by blinded independent central review using RAPNO criteria as the major outcome. Same programme as the two cards above — the regulator's read of the same data, not a new population.
cards.result: The overall response rate was 51% (95% CI 40–63) and median duration of response 13.8 months (95% CI 11.3 to not estimable). On 23 April 2024 the FDA granted accelerated approval for patients 6 months of age and older with relapsed or refractory paediatric low-grade glioma harbouring a BRAF fusion or rearrangement or a BRAF V600 mutation — the first approval of a systemic therapy for BRAF fusion/rearrangement disease. The frontline FIREFLY-2 trial was well underway as the required postmarketing study.
cards.watchOut: Accelerated approval is explicitly provisional on confirmatory evidence; the efficacy population (76) differs by one patient from the journal report's arm 1 (77) because of eligibility review — a reminder that the shelf's numbers are one trial's numbers, stated three ways.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one single-arm programme, three reports, a consistent response-and-vision signal — POSSIBLE by the single-programme cap
cards.summary: Synthesis: one single-arm programme, three reports, a consistent response-and-vision signal — POSSIBLE by the single-programme cap
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above, all describing the single FIREFLY-1 programme (arm 1 n=77; optic-pathway subgroup n=42; FDA efficacy population n=76; safety population n=137 including the extension arm).
cards.result: Tovorafenib produces responses in about half to two-thirds of children with relapsed/refractory BRAF-altered low-grade glioma depending on the criteria used, responses last a median of roughly 14–17 months, and in optic-pathway disease vision is usually preserved and sometimes improved — the outcome families care about most. But there is no randomised or controlled evidence, the frontline question (FIREFLY-2) is unanswered, and the single-programme structure caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Toxicity is frequent but mostly low-grade in kind (hair colour change, creatine phosphokinase elevation, anaemia), with grade ≥3 treatment-related events in 42% and discontinuation in 7%.
cards.watchOut: Long-term effects of chronic RAF inhibition on growth and development in young children are not yet characterised in this record; the adult refractory-glioma experience is a below-floor 7-patient series and is cross-pointed in the balance only.

shelves.title: Radical surgery in resectable mesothelioma: MARS 2 — surgery shortened survival (19.3 vs 24.8 months) and doubled serious harm; MARS — no benefit from extrapleural pneumonectomy
shelves.question: In adults with resectable malignant pleural mesothelioma, does radical surgery — extrapleural pneumonectomy (MARS feasibility programme) or (extended) pleurectomy decortication added to chemotherapy (MARS 2) — improve survival and quality of life versus chemotherapy / non-surgical management alone, and at what cost in perioperative mortality and morbidity?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Pleural Neoplasms · Middle Aged · Aged · Mesothelioma · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Pleura · Mesothelioma, Malignant · Combined Modality Therapy · Adult · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Lung Neoplasms
shelves.balance: LIKELY harm, on a two-trial base. Only two randomised trials of radical surgery in resectable malignant pleural mesothelioma exist, and both point against surgery. MARS (feasibility, 50 randomised): extrapleural pneumonectomy within trimodal therapy gave median survival 14.4 versus 19.5 months without it, adjusted hazard ratio 2.75 favouring no surgery, with 10 versus 2 serious adverse events. MARS 2 (phase 3, 335 randomised): (extended) pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy SHORTENED median survival versus chemotherapy alone (19.3 vs 24.8 months; restricted mean survival difference at 2 years −1.9 months, P=0.019) and produced 318 versus 169 grade 3-or-worse serious adverse events. The two operations are different limbs — pneumonectomy versus pleurectomy decortication — and are carded separately. Two clearly-labelled programme reports of the MARS 2 programme (patient experience, n=15; the embedded recruitment intervention) complete the record; they are not independent trials, and no cohort series have been used to pad the base.

cards.headline: MARS feasibility RCT (Treasure 2011): extrapleural pneumonectomy within trimodal therapy — median survival 14.4 months with EPP versus 19.5 months without; adjusted hazard ratio 2.75 favouring no EPP
cards.summary: MARS feasibility RCT (Treasure 2011): extrapleural pneumonectomy within trimodal therapy — median survival 14.4 months with EPP versus 19.5 months without; adjusted hazard ratio 2.75 favouring no EPP
cards.type: Multicentre randomised feasibility trial (MARS), extrapleural pneumonectomy vs no EPP, within trimodal therapy
cards.people: 112 patients with pathologically confirmed malignant pleural mesothelioma, fit for trimodal therapy, were registered after induction platinum-based chemotherapy; 50 were randomised — 24 to extrapleural pneumonectomy followed by hemithorax irradiation and 26 to no extrapleural pneumonectomy (12 UK hospitals, 2005–2008).
cards.result: Extrapleural pneumonectomy was completed satisfactorily in 16 of 24 assigned patients (not started in 5, abandoned in 3). Two patients in the EPP group died within 30 days and a third died without leaving hospital. The hazard ratio for overall survival was 1.90 (95% CI 0.92 to 3.93; P=0.082) unadjusted and 2.75 (95% CI 1.21 to 6.26; P=0.016) after adjustment — both point estimates favouring no EPP. Median survival was 14.4 months (EPP) versus 19.5 months (no EPP). Quality-of-life scores were lower in the EPP group without significant between-group differences (only 12 of 23 EPP and 19 of 26 no-EPP patients completed questionnaires). Serious adverse events: 10 in the EPP group versus 2 in the no-EPP group. The authors concluded a larger EPP trial was not feasible and that the data suggest no benefit and possible harm.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial — only 50 of the 112 registered patients were randomised (disease progression, inoperability and patient choice removed the rest), so survival estimates are imprecise; this is one of only two randomised trials of radical mesothelioma surgery in existence.
cards.source: Treasure T et al. Extra-pleural pneumonectomy versus no extra-pleural pneumonectomy for patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma: clinical outcomes of the Mesothelioma and Radical Surgery (MARS) feasibility study. The Lancet. Oncology. 2011. PMID: 21723781. Registry ID: ISRCTN95583524.
