cards.summary: MARS 2 phase 3 RCT (Lim 2024): (extended) pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy SHORTENED survival versus chemotherapy alone (median 19.3 vs 24.8 months) and roughly doubled serious adverse events
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label pragmatic randomised trial (MARS 2), (extended) pleurectomy decortication + chemotherapy vs chemotherapy alone
cards.people: 335 patients with resectable pleural mesothelioma (169 surgery plus chemotherapy, 166 chemotherapy alone; 87% men, 86% epithelioid), randomised after two cycles of chemotherapy across 26 UK hospitals (2015–2021). Surgery was pleurectomy decortication or extended pleurectomy decortication, followed by two to four further chemotherapy cycles.
cards.result: At median follow-up 22.4 months, median survival was SHORTER with surgery: 19.3 months versus 24.8 months on chemotherapy alone; the difference in restricted mean survival time at 2 years was −1.9 months (95% CI −3.4 to −0.3; P=0.019). Grade 3 or worse serious adverse events numbered 318 in the surgery group versus 169 in the chemotherapy group (incidence rate ratio 3.6, 95% CI 2.3 to 5.5), with more cardiac (30 vs 12), respiratory (84 vs 34) and infection (124 vs 53) events in the surgery group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable for major surgery) and conducted in the pre-immunotherapy chemotherapy era; the operation tested is (extended) pleurectomy decortication, a different and less radical operation than the extrapleural pneumonectomy of the MARS trial — the two trials are separate limbs, not replicates.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the entire randomised record is two trials — MARS (extrapleural pneumonectomy, n=50 randomised) and MARS 2 ((extended) pleurectomy decortication, n=335) — and both point the same way: no survival benefit, with MARS 2 showing significantly shorter survival and far more serious harm with surgery
cards.summary: Synthesis: the entire randomised record is two trials — MARS (extrapleural pneumonectomy, n=50 randomised) and MARS 2 ((extended) pleurectomy decortication, n=335) — and both point the same way: no survival benefit, with MARS 2 showing significantly shorter survival and far more serious harm with surgery
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No randomised trial has shown radical surgery to improve survival in resectable malignant pleural mesothelioma. MARS 2, the definitive trial, found median survival of 19.3 months with (extended) pleurectomy decortication plus chemotherapy versus 24.8 months with chemotherapy alone, with 318 versus 169 grade 3-or-worse serious adverse events. The smaller MARS feasibility trial of the more radical extrapleural pneumonectomy pointed the same way (adjusted hazard ratio 2.75 favouring no surgery; 3 perioperative/in-hospital deaths among 24 assigned to surgery). The two programme reports carded here (patient experience; recruitment) describe the MARS 2 programme only and add no comparative evidence. There is no third randomised report to card — this shelf is, by design, a two-trial shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Prophylactic tract irradiation in mesothelioma: no significant reduction in tract metastases in SMART (9% vs 16%), PIT (3.2% vs 5.3%) or the 2007 trial
shelves.question: In adults with malignant pleural mesothelioma who have undergone large-bore pleural interventions or chest-wall procedures, does prophylactic irradiation of the procedure tracts prevent procedure-tract metastases versus no prophylactic irradiation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lung Neoplasms · Male · Mesothelioma · Mesothelioma, Malignant · Neoplasm Staging · Neoplasms, Second Primary · Pain · Pleural Neoplasms · Postoperative Complications · Prognosis · Quality of Life · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Research Design · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Three randomised trials asked whether irradiating mesothelioma procedure tracts prevents tract metastases, and none found a significant reduction: SMART (203 patients, immediate vs deferred radiotherapy) 9% versus 16% tract metastases (odds ratio 0.51; P=0.14); PIT (375 patients, prophylaxis vs none) 3.2% versus 5.3% at 6 months (odds ratio 0.60; P=.44); and the earlier two-centre trial (61 patients) found no difference (P=0.748). SMART and PIT differ — SMART's control was deferred irradiation at metastasis, PIT's was no irradiation, and the procedures covered differ — so they are carded per-trial, not pooled. The consistent cost of prophylaxis was skin toxicity (grade 1 dermatitis in roughly half of treated patients). Low event rates mean a small preventive effect is not excluded; routine prophylaxis is nevertheless unsupported.

cards.headline: SMART phase 3 RCT (Clive 2016): immediate prophylactic radiotherapy 9% procedure-tract metastases versus 16% with deferred radiotherapy (odds ratio 0.51, P=0.14) — (the treatment made no difference) on the primary endpoint
cards.summary: SMART phase 3 RCT (Clive 2016): immediate prophylactic radiotherapy 9% procedure-tract metastases versus 16% with deferred radiotherapy (odds ratio 0.51, P=0.14) — (the treatment made no difference) on the primary endpoint
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label randomised trial (SMART), immediate vs deferred prophylactic radiotherapy after large-bore pleural procedures
cards.people: 203 patients with histocytologically proven mesothelioma who had undergone large-bore pleural interventions within the previous 35 days, randomised in 22 UK hospitals to immediate radiotherapy (102 patients; 21 Gy in 3 fractions within 42 days) or deferred radiotherapy (101 patients; same dose only if a procedure-tract metastasis developed).
cards.result: Procedure-tract metastases within 12 months occurred in 9% (immediate) versus 16% (deferred) — odds ratio 0.51 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.32; P=0.14), not statistically significant: (the treatment made no difference) that the trial could establish. The one serious related event was a painful tract metastasis inside the radiotherapy field needing hospital admission, in the immediate group. Immediate radiotherapy commonly caused grade 1 skin toxicity (54%) and tiredness/lethargy (39%). The authors concluded routine prophylactic radiotherapy after large-bore thoracic interventions is not justified.
cards.watchOut: SMART compared immediate with DEFERRED radiotherapy (given at metastasis), not with no radiotherapy ever — its question is timing as much as prevention. Open-label.
cards.source: Clive AO et al. Prophylactic radiotherapy for the prevention of procedure-tract metastases after surgical and large-bore pleural procedures in malignant pleural mesothelioma (SMART): a multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: PIT phase 3 RCT (Bayman 2019): chest-wall metastases at 6 months in 3.2% with prophylactic irradiation versus 5.3% without (odds ratio 0.60, P=.44) — (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: PIT phase 3 RCT (Bayman 2019): chest-wall metastases at 6 months in 3.2% with prophylactic irradiation versus 5.3% without (odds ratio 0.60, P=.44) — (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label randomised trial (PIT), prophylactic irradiation of tracts vs no prophylactic irradiation
cards.people: 375 patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma after a chest-wall procedure, randomised in 54 centres to prophylactic radiotherapy (186 patients; 21 Gy in 3 fractions within 42 days) or no prophylactic radiotherapy (189 patients). Open thoracotomies, needle biopsies and indwelling pleural catheters were excluded.
cards.result: Chest-wall metastases within 6 months occurred in 6 of 186 patients (3.2%) with prophylactic irradiation versus 10 of 189 (5.3%) without — odds ratio 0.60 (95% CI 0.17 to 1.86; P=.44): (the treatment made no difference). Radiation dermatitis in the prophylactic group was grade 1 in 51.6%, grade 2 in 10.2% and grade 3 in 0.5%. The authors concluded there is no role for routine prophylactic irradiation of chest-wall procedure sites.
cards.watchOut: Event rates were low in both arms (3–5%), so the confidence interval (odds ratio up to 1.86) cannot exclude a moderate effect in either direction; the trial's procedures excluded needle biopsies and indwelling catheters.

cards.headline: Earlier single-programme RCT (O'Rourke 2007): drain-site radiotherapy versus best supportive care in 61 patients — no significant difference in tract metastasis risk (P=0.748)
cards.summary: Earlier single-programme RCT (O'Rourke 2007): drain-site radiotherapy versus best supportive care in 61 patients — no significant difference in tract metastasis risk (P=0.748)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, immediate drain-site radiotherapy vs best supportive care, 12 months
cards.people: 61 patients with histologically diagnosed pleural mesothelioma and an invasive procedure within the preceding 21 days, recruited at two centres (1998–2004; median age 70); 31 were allocated to drain-site radiotherapy (21 Gy in 3 fractions) and the rest to best supportive care.
cards.result: Seven patients developed tract metastases at the drain site (4 radiotherapy, 3 supportive care) and four more at subsequent procedure sites; there was no statistically significant difference in drain-site tract metastasis risk between the arms (P=0.748) — (the treatment made no difference). The authors concluded prophylactic drain-site radiotherapy does not reduce tumour seeding by the margin earlier studies had suggested.
cards.watchOut: A small, two-centre trial (n=61) from an earlier era — on its own it could not exclude meaningful benefit or harm; its value is concordance with the two larger phase 3 trials.

shelves.title: Heparin vs saline port locking: split — saline met non-inferiority in the 802-patient trial but not on the smaller trial's margin; no significant occlusion difference in either
shelves.question: In adults with cancer and a totally implanted venous access port (or other long-term central venous catheter), does locking/flushing with normal saline alone maintain patency as safely as heparin locking — occlusion, catheter-related thrombosis and infection?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Bacteremia · Catheter-Related Infections · Catheterization, Central Venous · Catheters, Indwelling · Female · Heparin · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Sodium Chloride · Solutions · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — on the formal non-inferiority question. The larger port trial (Goossens 2013, 802 patients with cancer and non-valved implanted ports) met non-inferiority for saline versus heparin lock (300 units/3 mL): the dysfunction outcome occurred in 3.70% versus 3.92% of accesses (relative risk 0.94; upper confidence limit below the 1.4 margin), with catheter-related bloodstream infection of 0.03 versus 0.10 per 1,000 catheter days. The smaller Italian trial (Dal Molin 2015, 430 recruited) FAILED to demonstrate non-inferiority on its own 4-percentage-point margin (occlusions 14 saline vs 10 heparin), although it too found no significant difference. The Cochrane review across all central venous catheters (6 trials, 1,433 participants) found no conclusive efficacy or safety difference. Protocols differ per trial and are named on the cards; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is the harm the saline limb avoids by design.

cards.headline: Goossens 2013 RCT (802 patients): saline lock met non-inferiority versus heparin lock (300 units/3 mL) for port dysfunction — 'easy injection, impossible aspiration' in 3.70% versus 3.92% of accesses (relative risk 0.94)
cards.summary: Goossens 2013 RCT (802 patients): saline lock met non-inferiority versus heparin lock (300 units/3 mL) for port dysfunction — 'easy injection, impossible aspiration' in 3.70% versus 3.92% of accesses (relative risk 0.94)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised non-inferiority trial, normal saline lock vs diluted heparin lock, non-valved totally implantable ports
cards.people: 802 patients with cancer and a newly inserted non-valved totally implantable venous access port, randomised 1:1 to saline lock or heparin lock (300 units in 3 mL); 382 (saline) and 383 (heparin) patients were included in the analysis, with outcomes counted per port access.
cards.result: The primary outcome (easy injection with impossible aspiration at access) occurred at an incidence rate of 3.70% of accesses (95% CI 2.91% to 4.69%) with saline versus 3.92% (95% CI 3.09% to 4.96%) with heparin — relative risk 0.94 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.32), whose upper limit sits below the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1.4, so non-inferiority was established on the trial's own terms. Catheter-related bloodstream infection was 0.03 per 1,000 catheter days with saline versus 0.10 with heparin. The authors concluded saline is a safe and effective locking solution in implantable ports when combined with a strict insertion and maintenance protocol.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority was shown for one dysfunction definition under a strict maintenance protocol, in non-valved ports; the result does not automatically extend to valved ports, other catheter types, or lax flushing practice.
cards.source: Goossens GA et al. Comparing normal saline versus diluted heparin to lock non-valved totally implantable venous access ports in cancer patients: a randomised, non-inferiority, open trial. Annals of oncology. 2013. PMID: 23553060. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dal Molin 2015 RCT (430 patients): saline versus heparin locking of implanted ports — withdrawal occlusions 14 versus 10, and the trial FAILED to demonstrate saline's non-inferiority on its own margin, though no significant difference was found
cards.summary: Dal Molin 2015 RCT (430 patients): saline versus heparin locking of implanted ports — withdrawal occlusions 14 versus 10, and the trial FAILED to demonstrate saline's non-inferiority on its own margin, though no significant difference was found
cards.type: Multicentre randomised non-inferiority trial, normal saline vs heparin flushing/locking of totally implanted venous access devices
cards.people: 430 patients recruited at 14 Italian centres with totally implanted venous access devices, randomised to heparin or normal saline locking; after randomisation 203 patients were analysed in the saline group and 212 in the heparin group, with median follow-up of 204 days (saline) and 294 days (heparin).
cards.result: Withdrawal occlusions numbered 24 in total (5.78%): 10 in the heparin group and 14 in the saline group, plus one total occlusion in the saline group. Taking heparin as reference, the absolute risk difference was 2.67 percentage points with a 90% confidence interval that INCLUDED the 4% non-inferiority margin — so the study failed to demonstrate that saline is non-inferior, even though no significant difference between the hazards of occlusion was found. The authors called for further prospective trials.
cards.watchOut: This is the discordant limb of the shelf: 'no significant difference' is not non-inferiority, and this trial — smaller, with unequal follow-up between arms — could not exclude saline being up to its margin worse. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, the harm that motivates avoiding heparin locks, was not an outcome this abstract reports.
cards.source: Dal Molin A et al. Normal saline versus heparin solution to lock totally implanted venous access devices: Results from a multicenter, randomized, open-label, crossover trial. European journal of oncology nursing. 2015. PMID: 25933709. Registry ID: EudraCT 2009-013620-22. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Lopez-Briz 2014): 6 trials, 1,433 participants across central venous catheters — occlusion results conflicted by unit of analysis and no conclusive difference in efficacy or safety between heparin and saline flushing
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Lopez-Briz 2014): 6 trials, 1,433 participants across central venous catheters — occlusion results conflicted by unit of analysis and no conclusive difference in efficacy or safety between heparin and saline flushing
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, heparin vs 0.9% sodium chloride intermittent flushing in adults with central venous catheters
cards.people: Six randomised trials with 1,433 adults with central venous catheters (broader than implanted ports alone); heparin concentrations varied widely (10 to 5,000 IU/mL) and follow-up ranged from 20 to 180 days.
cards.result: Combined catheter-level analyses suggested fewer occlusions with heparin (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.94, a relative measure), but participant-level analyses did not (relative risk 0.21, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.70) and a line-access analysis found relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.40). Estimates for catheter-related thrombosis (relative risk 1.22), sepsis (1.02), mortality (0.77) and haemorrhage (1.37) were all imprecise and compatible with benefit and harm. The authors found no conclusive evidence of important differences in efficacy or safety and noted heparin costs more than saline.
cards.watchOut: This review pools all central venous catheters, not just implanted ports, and heparin doses across its trials span a 500-fold range — it frames the uncertainty around the two port-specific trials rather than settling the port question.
cards.source: Lopez-Briz E et al. Heparin versus 0.9% sodium chloride intermittent flushing for prevention of occlusion in central venous catheters in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25300172. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT on the formal question — the larger port trial met non-inferiority for saline, the smaller one failed to demonstrate it, and neither found a significant difference in occlusions; the practical difference between the locks is small either way
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT on the formal question — the larger port trial met non-inferiority for saline, the smaller one failed to demonstrate it, and neither found a significant difference in occlusions; the practical difference between the locks is small either way
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Goossens (802 patients) established saline's non-inferiority for port dysfunction (relative risk 0.94; upper confidence limit 1.32 against a 1.4 margin); Dal Molin (430 randomised) failed to demonstrate non-inferiority on its 4-percentage-point margin while also finding no significant difference (occlusions 14 saline vs 10 heparin). The Cochrane synthesis across all central catheters found no conclusive efficacy or safety difference. What is not in dispute: saline avoids heparin exposure (and with it heparin-induced thrombocytopenia risk) and costs less; what remains unproven is exact equivalence in every port type and maintenance protocol.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Navitoclax + ruxolitinib in myelofibrosis: spleen response 63.2% vs 31.5% in TRANSFORM-1 — but symptom score did not differ (P=.2852), with more cytopenia
shelves.question: In adults with myelofibrosis — JAK-inhibitor-naive, or with progression/suboptimal response on ruxolitinib — does adding the BCL-XL/BCL-2 inhibitor navitoclax to ruxolitinib, versus ruxolitinib alone (or versus continuing ruxolitinib), increase spleen-volume response, and does it improve symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Aniline Compounds · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Double-Blind Method · Nitriles · Primary Myelofibrosis · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on one randomised trial plus single-arm phase 2. TRANSFORM-1 (252 randomised, JAK-inhibitor-naive): spleen response at week 24 was 63.2% versus 31.5% — a clear benefit — but mean total-symptom-score change did not differ significantly (-10.2 vs -11.6, P=.2852), and grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia (54.0% vs 19.2%) and neutropenia (40.3% vs 8.8%) were much more common with navitoclax. The symptom null is printed beside the spleen result, as the evidence requires. In patients progressing or responding suboptimally on ruxolitinib, the evidence is single-arm REFINE phase 2 only (n=34; SVR35 26.5% at week 24, reversible thrombocytopenia 88%, platelet-gated escalation); the combined REFINE + TRANSFORM-2 report was refused for an effectively empty PubMed abstract, so no randomised post-ruxolitinib comparison is carded. The naive and post-ruxolitinib slices are labelled and their response rates are not pooled.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM-1 phase 3 RCT (Pemmaraju 2026): navitoclax + ruxolitinib doubled spleen response at week 24 (63.2% vs 31.5%) — but total symptom score did NOT differ significantly (-10.2 vs -11.6, P=.2852); the symptom null sits beside the spleen result
cards.summary: TRANSFORM-1 phase 3 RCT (Pemmaraju 2026): navitoclax + ruxolitinib doubled spleen response at week 24 (63.2% vs 31.5%) — but total symptom score did NOT differ significantly (-10.2 vs -11.6, P=.2852); the symptom null sits beside the spleen result
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (TRANSFORM-1), navitoclax + ruxolitinib vs placebo + ruxolitinib, JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis
cards.people: 252 JAK-inhibitor-naive adults with intermediate-2 or high-risk myelofibrosis and ECOG performance status 2 or better, randomised 1:1 to navitoclax (200 mg/day starting dose, or 100 mg escalated to 200 mg/day) plus ruxolitinib dosed per label (n=125) or placebo plus ruxolitinib (n=127); median follow-up 20.3 months; over 80% intermediate-2 risk and about 50% high-molecular-risk disease.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, at least 35% spleen volume reduction at week 24 (SVR35W24), was achieved by 63.2% with navitoclax + ruxolitinib versus 31.5% with placebo + ruxolitinib (P<.0001) — absolute rates as printed. Mean change in total symptom score at week 24 was NOT significantly different: -10.2 versus -11.6 (P=.2852). SVR35 at any time was 76.8% versus 44.1% (nominal P<.0001). A variant allele frequency reduction of at least 20% (exploratory) occurred in 58.5% versus 45.5%. Harm: grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia 54.0% versus 19.2%, grade 3/4 neutropenia 40.3% versus 8.8%, and any-grade diarrhoea 41.9% versus 16.8%; cytopenias were generally manageable and reversible with dose adjustments.
cards.watchOut: The trial proves a spleen-volume effect, not a symptom effect: the symptom-score comparison was null despite the large spleen difference, and the added cytopenia burden is substantial. Do not read the spleen result as patients feeling better.
cards.source: Pemmaraju N et al. TRANSFORM-1 phase 3 study: efficacy and safety of navitoclax plus ruxolitinib in patients with untreated myelofibrosis. Blood. 2026. PMID: 42378247. Registry ID: NCT04472598. cards.headline: REFINE phase 2 add-on (Harrison 2022): adding navitoclax to ongoing ruxolitinib in progression/suboptimal response — SVR35 in 26.5% at week 24 and 41% at any time; reversible thrombocytopenia in 88%
cards.summary: REFINE phase 2 add-on (Harrison 2022): adding navitoclax to ongoing ruxolitinib in progression/suboptimal response — SVR35 in 26.5% at week 24 and 41% at any time; reversible thrombocytopenia in 88%
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label single-arm add-on trial (REFINE cohort 1a), navitoclax added to ongoing ruxolitinib
cards.people: 34 adults with intermediate-/high-risk myelofibrosis who had progression or suboptimal response on a stable ruxolitinib dose (at least 10 mg twice daily for 12 weeks or more); navitoclax started at 50 mg once daily and escalated weekly to a maximum of 300 mg once daily only if platelets were at least 75 x 10^9/L — the platelet gating is part of the tested intervention. High-molecular-risk mutations in 58%; 52% had 3 or more mutations.
cards.result: SVR35 was achieved by 26.5% at week 24 and by 41% at any time, with an estimated median duration of SVR35 of 13.8 months. A 50% or greater total-symptom-score reduction (TSS50) was achieved by 30% (6 of 20) at week 24; bone marrow fibrosis improved by 1-2 grades in 33% (11 of 33 evaluable); anaemia response in 64% (7 of 11), including one transfusion-dependent patient. Median overall survival was not reached at median follow-up 21.6 months. The most common adverse event was reversible thrombocytopenia without clinically significant bleeding (88%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: there is no concurrent control, so these response rates cannot be compared directly with the randomised TRANSFORM-1 rates, and the population (post-ruxolitinib progression/suboptimal response) is a different slice from the naive population — the two slices are labelled and not pooled on this shelf.
cards.source: Harrison CN et al. Addition of Navitoclax to Ongoing Ruxolitinib Therapy for Patients With Myelofibrosis With Progression or Suboptimal Response: Phase II Safety and Efficacy. cards.summary: REFINE biomarker post-hoc analysis (Pemmaraju 2022): splenic responses occurred in both high-molecular-risk (31%) and non-high-risk (31%) patients; fibrosis or variant-allele-frequency improvement tracked with longer survival in exploratory analysis
cards.type: Post-hoc exploratory biomarker analysis of the REFINE phase 2 trial (same programme and patients as the REFINE card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same 34 REFINE cohort 1a patients (33 evaluable for biomarker analyses; 19 [58%] with high-molecular-risk mutations), followed to a median of 26.2 months for survivors.
cards.result: SVR35 at week 24 occurred in 5 of 16 (31%) high-molecular-risk patients and 4 of 13 (31%) non-high-molecular-risk patients. TSS50 at week 24: 4 of 11 (36%) high-risk versus 2 of 8 (25%) non-high-risk. Fibrosis improved by at least one grade in 7 of 18 (39%) versus 5 of 14 (36%). Patients who achieved fibrosis improvement or a variant allele frequency reduction of 20% or more had median overall survival not reached, versus 28.5 months in those who did not — an exploratory, post-hoc association the authors present as suggestive of disease modification, not proof of it. Changes in beta-2-microglobulin, TIMP-1, TNF receptor type II and VCAM-1 correlated positively with spleen-volume change.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and exploratory, in 33 evaluable patients from a single-arm trial: the survival-by-response association is vulnerable to responder bias (patients must survive long enough to respond) and must not be carded as a survival benefit of the drug.
cards.source: Pemmaraju N et al. Addition of navitoclax to ongoing ruxolitinib treatment in patients with myelofibrosis (REFINE): a post-hoc analysis of molecular biomarkers in a phase 2 study. The Lancet. Haematology. 2022. PMID: 35576960. Registry ID: NCT03222609. cards.headline: REFINE JAK-inhibitor-naive cohort (Passamonti 2026): navitoclax + ruxolitinib in untreated disease — SVR35 in 63% (20 of 32) at week 24 over 44 months of follow-up
cards.summary: REFINE JAK-inhibitor-naive cohort (Passamonti 2026): navitoclax + ruxolitinib in untreated disease — SVR35 in 63% (20 of 32) at week 24 over 44 months of follow-up
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label single-arm cohort (REFINE cohort 3), navitoclax + ruxolitinib, JAK-inhibitor-naive myelofibrosis
cards.people: 32 JAK-inhibitor-naive patients with primary or secondary myelofibrosis, splenomegaly, DIPSS intermediate-2 or high risk, ECOG 0-2 and platelet count above 100 x 10^9/L; navitoclax 100 mg or 200 mg once daily according to platelet count (150 x 10^9/L threshold), with ruxolitinib twice daily per label. Median follow-up 44 months.
cards.result: SVR35 at week 24 was achieved by 63% (20 of 32); median time to first SVR35 was 12 weeks. TSS50 at week 24 was achieved by 11 of 27 evaluable patients (41%). Bone marrow fibrosis improved by at least one grade in 13 of 27 (48%) at any time. Anaemia response was 38% (5 of 13) in transfusion-independent and 100% (2 of 2) in transfusion-dependent patients. A driver-gene variant allele frequency reduction of at least 50% occurred in 21% of 24 evaluable patients. No bleeding events or deaths were attributed to navitoclax.
cards.watchOut: A 32-patient single-arm cohort: its 63% SVR35 is consistent with, but adds no comparative weight to, the randomised TRANSFORM-1 result in the same naive population.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one randomised trial shows a large spleen-response gain with no symptom-score gain; the post-ruxolitinib evidence is single-arm phase 2
cards.summary: Synthesis: one randomised trial shows a large spleen-response gain with no symptom-score gain; the post-ruxolitinib evidence is single-arm phase 2
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: TRANSFORM-1 (n=252 randomised) is the only controlled evidence: SVR35 at week 24 of 63.2% versus 31.5%, with mean total-symptom-score change not significantly different (-10.2 vs -11.6, P=.2852) and substantially more grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia (54.0% vs 19.2%) and neutropenia (40.3% vs 8.8%). In the post-ruxolitinib slice, REFINE's single-arm add-on data (n=34) show SVR35 in 26.5% at week 24 with platelet-gated dose escalation and reversible thrombocytopenia in 88%; its biomarker and naive-cohort reports are programme reports of the same trial, not independent trials. Refused: the combined REFINE + TRANSFORM-2 report (PMID 42842696) was not carded because its PubMed record carries an effectively empty abstract (registry numbers only), so no numbers could be verified from the record this session — TRANSFORM-2's post-JAK-inhibitor randomised data therefore do not appear on this shelf, and the post-ruxolitinib slice rests on REFINE alone.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; the TRANSFORM-2 refusal above means the randomised post-ruxolitinib comparison is a known gap on this shelf, to be filled only from a verifiable full record.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib in Waldenstrom (ASPEN): primary endpoint non-significant — no complete responses, VGPR 28% vs 19% (P=.09); the difference is tolerability
shelves.question: In patients with symptomatic Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, does the selective BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib, versus ibrutinib, deepen responses (complete + very good partial response) and improve tolerability?
shelves.mesh: Adenine · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Cohort Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Piperidines · Prognosis · Pyrazoles · Pyrimidines · Survival Rate · Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia
shelves.balance: SPLIT, on a single programme (one trial, four reports). ASPEN's primary endpoint was non-significant: no complete responses in either arm and VGPR 28% versus 19% (P=.09) at the primary analysis, with major response rates 77% versus 78% — this shelf is not an efficacy win for either drug. The separation is tolerability over 44.4 months: atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.9% versus 23.5%, and less diarrhoea, hypertension and pneumonia with zanubrutinib, against more neutropenia (34.7% vs 20.4%). In MYD88 wild-type disease the evidence is a 26-patient single-arm zanubrutinib cohort (VGPR 27%, no complete responses). The CLL/SLL version of this comparison is homed separately at pack #6909.

cards.headline: ASPEN phase 3 primary report (Tam 2020): the primary endpoint was NON-SIGNIFICANT — no complete responses in either arm, VGPR 28% vs 19% (P=.09); major response 77% vs 78%
cards.summary: ASPEN phase 3 primary report (Tam 2020): the primary endpoint was NON-SIGNIFICANT — no complete responses in either arm, VGPR 28% vs 19% (P=.09); major response 77% vs 78%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (ASPEN cohort 1), zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib, MYD88-mutated Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
cards.people: 201 patients with symptomatic Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia and MYD88-mutated disease randomised 1:1 to zanubrutinib or ibrutinib; 199 received at least one dose.
cards.result: No patient in either arm achieved a complete response. Very good partial response (VGPR) was achieved by 29 (28%) on zanubrutinib and 19 (19%) on ibrutinib — a non-statistically significant difference (P=.09), so the trial's primary endpoint (complete + very good partial response by independent review) was not met. Major response rates were 77% and 78% respectively. Median duration of response and progression-free survival were not reached; 84% (ibrutinib) and 85% (zanubrutinib) were progression-free at 18 months. Atrial fibrillation, contusion, diarrhoea, peripheral oedema, haemorrhage, muscle spasms and pneumonia, and adverse events leading to discontinuation, were less common with zanubrutinib; neutropenia was more common with zanubrutinib, while grade 3-or-worse infection rates were similar (1.2 and 1.1 events per 100 person-months).
cards.watchOut: This is a null-primary-endpoint trial: any claim for zanubrutinib here rests on response-quality trends and tolerability, not on a demonstrated efficacy difference. Exact adverse-event rates for the primary report's safety population are given qualitatively in the abstract record carded here; the final analysis below gives the quantified long-term rates.
cards.source: Tam CS et al. A randomized phase 3 trial of zanubrutinib vs ibrutinib in symptomatic Waldenström macroglobulinemia: the ASPEN study. Blood. 2020. PMID: 32731259. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ASPEN final analysis (Dimopoulos 2023): at 44.4 months VGPR + complete response 36.3% vs 25.3%, still with no significant efficacy separation claimed; atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.9% vs 23.5% and neutropenia 34.7% vs 20.4%
cards.summary: ASPEN final analysis (Dimopoulos 2023): at 44.4 months VGPR + complete response 36.3% vs 25.3%, still with no significant efficacy separation claimed; atrial fibrillation/flutter 7.9% vs 23.5% and neutropenia 34.7% vs 20.4%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial final analysis (ASPEN, same trial as the primary report above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Cohort 1: the same 201 randomised patients (102 zanubrutinib, 99 ibrutinib, MYD88-mutated). Cohort 2 (MYD88 wild-type, zanubrutinib only): 28 patients, 26 efficacy-evaluable. Median follow-up 44.4 months.
cards.result: VGPR + complete response rates were 36.3% with zanubrutinib versus 25.3% with ibrutinib in cohort 1, and 30.8% with one complete response in cohort 2. In CXCR4-mutated patients (cohort 1), VGPR + complete response was 21.2% versus 10.0%. Median progression-free and overall survival were not reached. Adverse events more common with ibrutinib than zanubrutinib included diarrhoea (34.7% vs 22.8%), muscle spasms (28.6% vs 11.9%), hypertension (25.5% vs 14.9%), atrial fibrillation/flutter (23.5% vs 7.9%) and pneumonia (18.4% vs 5.0%); neutropenia was less common with ibrutinib (20.4% vs 34.7%). Zanubrutinib was associated with lower risk of adverse-event-related treatment discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Longer follow-up of the same single trial: the response-rate gap widened numerically but this remains one programme's data, and the primary-endpoint comparison at the primary analysis was non-significant.
cards.source: Dimopoulos MA et al. Zanubrutinib Versus Ibrutinib in Symptomatic Waldenström Macroglobulinemia: Final Analysis From the Randomized Phase III ASPEN Study. cards.headline: ASPEN MYD88 wild-type substudy (Dimopoulos 2020): single-arm zanubrutinib in MYD88 wild-type disease — VGPR in 7 of 26 (27%), major response 50%, no complete responses
cards.summary: ASPEN MYD88 wild-type substudy (Dimopoulos 2020): single-arm zanubrutinib in MYD88 wild-type disease — VGPR in 7 of 26 (27%), major response 50%, no complete responses
cards.type: Single-arm substudy cohort of the ASPEN trial (cohort 2), zanubrutinib in MYD88 wild-type Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
cards.people: 28 patients enrolled in ASPEN cohort 2 (23 relapsed/refractory, 5 treatment-naive), including 26 with centrally confirmed MYD88 wild-type disease and 2 with unknown status; all received zanubrutinib. Median follow-up 17.9 months.
cards.result: Among the 26 MYD88 wild-type patients, 7 (27%) achieved a VGPR and 50% a major response (partial response or better); there were no complete responses. Estimated progression-free survival at 18 months was 68% and overall survival 88%; median duration of response had not been reached. Two patients discontinued zanubrutinib because of adverse events. Treatment-emergent hypertension, atrial fibrillation and major haemorrhage were reported in 3, 1 and 2 patients respectively (one haemorrhage concurrent with enoxaparin).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and small (26 confirmed wild-type): there is no ibrutinib comparator in this genotype, so nothing here shows zanubrutinib is better than ibrutinib in wild-type disease — only that responses occur.
cards.source: Dimopoulos M et al. Zanubrutinib for the treatment of MYD88 wild-type Waldenström macroglobulinemia: a substudy of the phase 3 ASPEN trial. Blood advances. 2020. PMID: 33284944. cards.headline: ASPEN biomarker analysis (Tam 2024): CXCR4 and TP53 mutations marked worse prognosis; in TP53-mutated patients VGPR + complete response was 34.6% on zanubrutinib vs 13.6% on ibrutinib in post-hoc analysis
cards.summary: ASPEN biomarker analysis (Tam 2024): CXCR4 and TP53 mutations marked worse prognosis; in TP53-mutated patients VGPR + complete response was 34.6% on zanubrutinib vs 13.6% on ibrutinib in post-hoc analysis
cards.type: Post-hoc biomarker analysis of the ASPEN trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: Pretreatment bone-marrow next-generation sequencing from the ASPEN trial: 98 zanubrutinib and 92 ibrutinib patients with mutated MYD88, plus 20 zanubrutinib patients with wild-type MYD88. Of 329 mutations in 52 genes, CXCR4 (25.7%), TP53 (24.8%), ARID1A (15.7%) and TERT (9.0%) were most common.
cards.result: Patients with CXCR4 frameshift/nonsense mutations had lower VGPR + complete response rates (17.0% vs 37.2%, P=.020) and longer time to response (11.1 vs 8.4 months) than CXCR4 wild-type patients on BTK inhibitors. CXCR4 nonsense mutation was associated with inferior progression-free survival on ibrutinib (hazard ratio 3.39, a relative measure; P=.017) but not on zanubrutinib (hazard ratio 0.67; P=.598). In TP53-mutated patients, major response was lower on ibrutinib (63.6% vs 85.7% in TP53 wild-type; P=.04) but not on zanubrutinib (80.8% vs 81.9%); VGPR + complete response with zanubrutinib versus ibrutinib in TP53-mutated disease was 34.6% versus 13.6% (P<.05). The authors conclude CXCR4- or TP53-mutated patients had worse prognosis and zanubrutinib led to better clinical outcomes in these subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of one trial, with multiple comparisons and small subgroups: hypothesis-generating only, and it does not overturn the trial's non-significant primary endpoint.
cards.source: Tam CS et al. Biomarker analysis of the ASPEN study comparing zanubrutinib with ibrutinib for patients with Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Blood advances. 2024. PMID: 38315878. post-hoc biomarker analysis of the aspen trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence) pretreatment bone-marrow next-generation sequencing from the aspen trial: 98 zanubrutinib and 92 ibrutinib patients with mutated myd88, plus 20 zanubrutinib patients with wild-type myd88. of 329 mutations in 52 genes, cxcr4 (25.7%), tp53 (24.8%), arid1a (15.7%) and tert (9.0%) were most common. patients with cxcr4 frameshift/nonsense mutations had lower vgpr + complete response rates (17.0% vs 37.2%, p=.020) and longer time to response (11.1 vs 8.4 months) than cxcr4 wild-type patients on btk inhibitors. cxcr4 nonsense mutation was associated with inferior progression-free survival on ibrutinib (hazard ratio 3.39, a relative measure; p=.017) but not on zanubrutinib (hazard ratio 0.67; p=.598). in tp53-mutated patients, major response was lower on ibrutinib (63.6% vs 85.7% in tp53 wild-type; p=.04) but not on zanubrutinib (80.8% vs 81.9%); vgpr + complete response with zanubrutinib versus ibrutinib in tp53-mutated disease was 34.6% versus 13.6% (p<.05). the authors conclude cxcr4- or tp53-mutated patients had worse prognosis and zanubrutinib led to better clinical outcomes in these subgroups. post-hoc subgroup analysis of one trial, with multiple comparisons and small subgroups: hypothesis-generating only, and it does not overturn the trial's non-significant primary endpoint. tam cs et al. biomarker analysis of the aspen study comparing zanubrutinib with ibrutinib for patients with waldenström macroglobulinemia. blood advances. 2024. pmid: 38315878. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · waldenstrom macroglobulinemia · myeloid differentiation factor 88 · biomarkers · adenine · piperidines · pyrazoles · pyrimidines

cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial (ASPEN), a non-significant primary endpoint, and a tolerability argument — not an efficacy win
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial (ASPEN), a non-significant primary endpoint, and a tolerability argument — not an efficacy win
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: ASPEN is a single programme: one randomised trial reported four times (primary, final, wild-type substudy, biomarker analysis). Its primary endpoint was not met — no complete responses in either arm at the primary analysis and VGPR 28% versus 19% (P=.09), with major response 77% versus 78% and median progression-free survival not reached in either arm. At 44.4 months the VGPR + complete response rates were 36.3% versus 25.3%. What separates the drugs in this record is tolerability: less atrial fibrillation/flutter (7.9% vs 23.5%), diarrhoea, muscle spasms, hypertension and pneumonia with zanubrutinib, at the cost of more neutropenia (34.7% vs 20.4%). The same zanubrutinib-versus-ibrutinib comparison in relapsed/refractory CLL/SLL is a different question, homed at pack #6909 — cross-point only; no ASPEN report is carded there and no CLL report is carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Odronextamab in relapsed/refractory lymphoma: complete response 73.4% in follicular lymphoma, 31.5% in DLBCL — all single-arm (ELM-1/ELM-2)
shelves.question: In adults with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after at least 2 prior lines, does the CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody odronextamab, versus no concurrent control, produce objective and complete responses, including after CAR T-cell therapy?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on an entirely single-arm base (GAP-E discipline: no concurrent control anywhere). ELM-2 follicular lymphoma (n=128): objective response 80.0%, complete response 73.4%, median progression-free survival 20.7 months. ELM-2 DLBCL (n=127): objective response 52.0%, complete response 31.5%. ELM-1 post-CAR-T DLBCL (n=60): objective response 48.3%, complete response 31.7%. Cytokine release syndrome affected roughly half of patients (almost always low grade with the 0.7/4/20 mg step-up) and infections were reported in 64.6% of the DLBCL cohort. The FL and DLBCL slices are labelled, not pooled. An Author Correction to the DLBCL primary report (PMID 40240622) exists and is flagged on its card.

cards.headline: ELM-1 phase 1 (Bannerji 2022): odronextamab across relapsed/refractory B-cell lymphoma — objective response 51% overall; in follicular lymphoma at 5 mg or more, response 91% and complete response 72%
cards.summary: ELM-1 phase 1 (Bannerji 2022): odronextamab across relapsed/refractory B-cell lymphoma — objective response 51% overall; in follicular lymphoma at 5 mg or more, response 91% and complete response 72%
cards.type: Phase 1 single-arm dose-escalation/expansion trial (ELM-1), odronextamab in relapsed/refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
cards.people: 145 heavily pretreated patients (median 3 prior therapies; 42 [29%] previously treated with CAR T-cell therapy; 82% refractory to their last line) with CD20-positive relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies, treated at ten sites in the USA and Germany with step-up dosing in cycle 1 then weekly target doses of 0.1-320 mg, then maintenance every 2 weeks. Median follow-up 4.2 months.
cards.result: No dose-limiting toxicities were observed up to 320 mg weekly. Objective response rate was 51% (72 of 142). In follicular lymphoma patients receiving 5 mg or more, objective response was 91% (29 of 32) and complete response 72% (23 of 32). In DLBCL without prior CAR T therapy receiving 80 mg or more, objective response was 53% (8 of 15), all complete; in DLBCL after CAR T therapy at 80 mg or more, objective response was 33% (10 of 30) and complete response 27% (8 of 30). Cytokine release syndrome and neurological events were predominantly low grade; the most common grade 3-or-worse events were anaemia (25%), lymphopenia (19%), hypophosphataemia (19%), neutropenia (19%) and thrombocytopenia (14%); serious events occurred in 61%, most frequently cytokine release syndrome (28%). Four deaths were considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Phase 1, dose-ranging, short follow-up (median 4.2 months) and no comparator: the histology- and dose-specific response rates come from small subgroups and are the basis for dose selection, not estimates of benefit versus any alternative.

cards.headline: ELM-2 follicular lymphoma cohort (Kim 2024): objective response 80.0% and complete response 73.4% after at least 2 prior lines; cytokine release syndrome 56%
cards.summary: ELM-2 follicular lymphoma cohort (Kim 2024): objective response 80.0% and complete response 73.4% after at least 2 prior lines; cytokine release syndrome 56%
cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm cohort (ELM-2), odronextamab in relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma
cards.people: 128 patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after two or more lines of systemic therapy, treated with intravenous odronextamab in 21-day cycles with step-up dosing in cycle 1 until progression or unacceptable toxicity; 95% completed cycle 1 and 85% completed four or more cycles. Efficacy follow-up 20.1 months.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 80.0% and complete response rate 73.4% by independent central review. Median duration of complete response was 25.1 months; median progression-free survival was 20.7 months; median overall survival was not reached. Discontinuation because of adverse events occurred in 16%. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were cytokine release syndrome (56%; grade 3 or worse 1.7% [1 of 60] with the 0.7/4/20 mg step-up), neutropenia (39%) and pyrexia (38%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: response rates have no comparator and cannot show that odronextamab is better than other options in this setting. The step-up regimen changed during the programme, so cytokine-release rates are regimen-specific. An Author Correction to the companion DLBCL report (PMID 40240622) exists and is incorporated by reference here; it is not carded separately.

cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm cohort primary analysis (ELM-2), odronextamab in relapsed/refractory DLBCL
cards.people: 127 patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after at least two lines of therapy, treated with intravenous odronextamab in 21-day cycles with cycle-1 step-up dosing until progression or unacceptable toxicity. Efficacy follow-up 29.9 months.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 52.0% and complete response rate 31.5%. Median duration of response was 10.2 months and of complete response 17.9 months. With the 0.7 to 4 to 20 mg step-up (n=60), cytokine release syndrome was the most common event (53.3%; grade 3 or worse 1.7%). No immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome was reported. Infections occurred in 82 of 127 patients (64.6%; grade 3 or worse 38.6%), including COVID-19 in 18.1% (grade 3 or worse 12.6%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator. shelves.title: Lifileucel in advanced melanoma after checkpoint inhibition: response 31.4%, median response duration 36.5 months at 5 years — single-arm only
shelves.question: In patients with unresectable or metastatic melanoma progressed on anti-PD-1 therapy (and targeted therapy where appropriate), does one-time autologous tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy with lifileucel, versus no concurrent control, produce objective responses, and how durable are they at 5 years?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors · Immunotherapy, Adoptive · Lymphocytes, Tumor-Infiltrating · Melanoma · Skin Neoplasms
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on single-arm, single-programme evidence (GAP-E discipline). C-144-01: objective response 31.4% in 153 heavily pretreated patients, with median duration of response 36.5 months at the 5-year analysis and 5-year overall survival 19.7% — durable benefit for a minority, with no comparator to show it beats any alternative. The intervention is a package (resection, 22-day central manufacture, lymphodepletion, high-dose interleukin-2) and its harms are largely the package's: grade 3/4 events in 95.5% of the FDA safety population and a boxed warning. Product: lifileucel (Amtagvi, Iovance).

cards.headline: C-144-01 pooled analysis (Chesney 2022): lifileucel objective response 31.4% in 153 treated patients after checkpoint inhibition; median duration of response not reached at 27.6 months
cards.summary: C-144-01 pooled analysis (Chesney 2022): lifileucel objective response 31.4% in 153 treated patients after checkpoint inhibition; median duration of response not reached at 27.6 months
cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm pooled analysis (C-144-01 cohorts), one-time lifileucel TIL therapy in advanced melanoma after checkpoint inhibition
cards.people: 153 patients with advanced melanoma that progressed after immune checkpoint inhibitors and targeted therapy where appropriate (median 3.0 prior lines; 81.7% had received both anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA-4; high disease burden — median target-lesion sum 97.8 mm, lactate dehydrogenase above the upper limit of normal in 54.2%). The intervention is a package: tumour resection (at least 1.5 cm), central manufacture over 22 days, non-myeloablative lymphodepletion, a single lifileucel infusion, and up to six doses of high-dose interleukin-2.
cards.result: Independent-review objective response rate was 31.4% (95% CI 24.1 to 39.4), with 8 complete and 40 partial responses. Median duration of response was not reached at median follow-up 27.6 months, with 41.7% of responses maintained for at least 18 months. Median overall survival was 13.9 months and progression-free survival 4.1 months. In adjusted analyses, elevated lactate dehydrogenase and target-lesion sum above the median were independently correlated with response likelihood. The most common grade 3/4 treatment-emergent adverse events (at least 30%) were thrombocytopenia (76.9%), anaemia (50.0%) and febrile neutropenia (41.7%) — harms of the lymphodepletion/interleukin-2 package as much as of the cells.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, single programme: there is no comparator, and patients had to have resectable tumour, survive manufacture and be fit for lymphodepletion and high-dose interleukin-2 — a selected population whose results do not transfer to all patients progressing on checkpoint inhibitors.
cards.source: Chesney J et al. cards.headline: C-144-01 five-year analysis (Medina 2025): median duration of response 36.5 months; 31.3% of responders still responding at 5 years; 5-year overall survival 19.7%
cards.summary: C-144-01 five-year analysis (Medina 2025): median duration of response 36.5 months; 31.3% of responders still responding at 5 years; 5-year overall survival 19.7%
cards.type: Five-year long-term analysis of the single-arm C-144-01 trial (same programme and patients as the pooled analysis above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same C-144-01 treated population followed to the November 20, 2024 cutoff (responders n=48 of the treated patients).
cards.result: Objective response rate was 31.4% (complete response 5.9%, partial response 25.5%). Overall 79.3% of patients had some tumour-burden reduction; 16 patients had deepened responses, four converting from partial to complete response more than a year after infusion; 31.3% of responders completed the 5-year assessment with ongoing responses. Median duration of response was 36.5 months. Median overall survival was 13.9 months with 5-year overall survival of 19.7%. Responders had lower tumour burden and fewer liver or brain metastases than the overall population. Adverse events were consistent with the lymphodepletion and interleukin-2 profiles, declined rapidly within 2 weeks of infusion, and most grade 3/4 cytopenias resolved to grade 2 or better by day 30; no additional long-term safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Five-year follow-up of the same single-arm trial: durability among the 48 responders is the finding; it does not add a comparator, and responder characteristics (lower burden, fewer liver/brain metastases) mean durability cannot be promised to unselected patients.

cards.headline: FDA approval summary (Hu 2025): accelerated approval on a 31.5% response rate in the 73-patient approved-dose cohort; boxed warning for treatment-related mortality, prolonged severe cytopenia, severe infection, cardiopulmonary and renal impairment
cards.summary: FDA approval summary (Hu 2025): accelerated approval on a 31.5% response rate in the 73-patient approved-dose cohort; boxed warning for treatment-related mortality, prolonged severe cytopenia, severe infection, cardiopulmonary and renal impairment
cards.type: FDA approval summary of the single-arm C-144-01 trial (regulatory review of the same programme — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The FDA efficacy cohort: 73 patients treated within the approved dose range (7.5 x 10^9 to 72 x 10^9 viable cells) in C-144-01; the safety population was all 156 patients who received lifileucel in the primary and supportive cohorts.
cards.result: Objective response rate was 31.5% (95% CI 21.1 to 43.4), including 3 (4.1%) complete and 20 (27.4%) partial responses; median duration of response was not reached, and among the 23 responders, 56.5%, 47.8% and 43.5% maintained responses at 6, 9 and 12 months. Among all 156 treated patients, 95.5% had at least one grade 3 treatment-emergent adverse event and 87.8% at least one grade 4 event. The FDA granted accelerated approval on February 16, 2024 for adults with unresectable or metastatic melanoma previously treated with a PD-1-blocking antibody and, if BRAF V600-positive, a BRAF inhibitor with or without an MEK inhibitor. Product naming (clarification exception, as the publication gives it): lifileucel (Amtagvi, Iovance Biotherapeutics, Inc.).
cards.watchOut: Accelerated approval rests on response rate and durability in a single-arm trial; confirmatory evidence of survival benefit is not in this record. The near-universal grade 3/4 event rate reflects the whole treatment package.

cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm, single-programme evidence — about one in three respond, and responses can last years, at the cost of a toxic treatment package

cards.result: C-144-01 is the entire base: 153 treated patients, objective response 31.4% by independent review, median overall survival 13.9 months, and at 5 years a median duration of response of 36.5 months with 31.3% of responders still responding and 5-year overall survival of 19.7%. The FDA's approved-dose cohort (n=73) showed the same 31.5% response rate. There is no randomised or comparative report. The harms are largely the package's — resection, lymphodepletion and high-dose interleukin-2 — with grade 3/4 thrombocytopenia in 76.9% and a boxed warning covering treatment-related mortality, prolonged severe cytopenia, severe infection and cardiopulmonary and renal impairment.

shelves.title: Dostarlimab in dMMR rectal cancer: sustained complete response 68% at 12 months in AZUR-1 — organ preservation, single-arm evidence only
shelves.question: In patients with stage II-III mismatch-repair-deficient (dMMR) locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, does neoadjuvant single-agent dostarlimab for 6 months, versus standard chemoradiotherapy and surgery, produce sustained clinical complete responses that allow chemoradiation and surgery to be omitted?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · DNA Mismatch Repair · Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors · Neoadjuvant Therapy · Neoplasm Staging · Programmed Cell Death 1 Receptor · Rectal Neoplasms · Disease-Free Survival · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasm, Residual · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Chemoradiotherapy, Adjuvant · Capecitabine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on single-arm evidence throughout (GAP-E discipline applied to this PARTIAL slice). In the expanded phase 2 rectal cohort, all 49 patients who completed 6 months of dostarlimab had a clinical complete response and 37 had a sustained response at 12 months; in the global AZUR-1 trial the sustained 12-month clinical complete response rate was 68% (76% counting pathological complete responses in operated patients), with no recurrences among complete responders at median follow-up 26.3 months. The claim is organ preservation in a biomarker-defined minority under protocol surveillance — response-guided omission of chemoradiotherapy and surgery — not proof that standard therapy is unnecessary. The endometrial-cancer dostarlimab question is homed at live #853.

cards.headline: Phase 2 first report (Cercek 2022): all 12 patients who completed dostarlimab had a clinical complete response — an early, very small cohort
cards.summary: Phase 2 first report (Cercek 2022): all 12 patients who completed dostarlimab had a clinical complete response — an early, very small cohort
cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm study, neoadjuvant dostarlimab in dMMR locally advanced rectal cancer (first 12 completed patients)
cards.people: 12 patients with mismatch-repair-deficient stage II or III rectal adenocarcinoma who had completed 6 months of single-agent dostarlimab (every 3 weeks) and had at least 6 months of follow-up, in a prospective phase 2 study in which dostarlimab was to be followed by standard chemoradiotherapy and surgery, both omittable after a clinical complete response.
cards.result: All 12 patients (100%; 95% CI 74 to 100) had a clinical complete response, with no tumour on MRI, FDG-PET, endoscopy, digital rectal examination or biopsy. At this report no patient had received chemoradiotherapy or undergone surgery, and no progression or recurrence had been reported during follow-up of 6 to 25 months. No adverse events of grade 3 or higher were reported.
cards.watchOut: Only 12 completed patients — the 'all responded' framing of this early report must not stand alone; the expanded 2025 report and the global AZUR-1 trial below supply the denominators and the sustained-response rates. This cohort is inside the later expanded report of the same trial, not a separate trial.

cards.headline: Expanded phase 2, rectal cohort (Cercek 2025): all 49 rectal patients who completed treatment had a clinical complete response; 37 had a sustained complete response at 12 months
cards.summary: Expanded phase 2, rectal cohort (Cercek 2025): all 49 rectal patients who completed treatment had a clinical complete response; 37 had a sustained complete response at 12 months
cards.type: Phase 2 single-arm expanded study, neoadjuvant dostarlimab — rectal cohort 1 only carded here
cards.people: 117 patients analysed in the expanded phase 2 study of 6 months of neoadjuvant dostarlimab in stage I-III mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumours amenable to curative surgery. This card covers cohort 1 only — locally advanced rectal cancer: 49 patients completed treatment. (Cohort 2, nonrectal dMMR tumours, is a different slice and is not the question on this shelf.)
cards.result: In cohort 1, all 49 patients who completed treatment had a clinical complete response and elected nonoperative management; 37 had a sustained clinical complete response at 12 months, meeting the primary-endpoint criterion for efficacy. Across both cohorts, 103 patients completed treatment, 84 had a clinical complete response and 82 did not undergo surgery; recurrence-free survival at 2 years was 92% (95% CI 86 to 99) in the total 117 patients at median follow-up for recurrence of 20.0 months. Most patients (95%) had reversible grade 1 or 2 adverse events (60%) or no adverse events (35%), and the option of curative resection was not compromised in any patient.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: sustained complete response is judged against the protocol's own criterion, not against a randomised chemoradiotherapy/surgery control. Median follow-up for recurrence was 20.0 months, so late recurrences after nonoperative management remain the open durability question. The 2-year recurrence-free figure is for both cohorts combined and is labelled as such.
cards.source: Cercek A et al. Nonoperative Management of Mismatch Repair-Deficient Tumors. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40293177. Registry ID: NCT04165772. cards.headline: AZUR-1 global trial (Cercek 2026): sustained clinical complete response at 12 months in 68% by investigator review; cCR12 + pathological complete response 76%; no recurrences among complete responders
cards.summary: AZUR-1 global trial (Cercek 2026): sustained clinical complete response at 12 months in 68% by investigator review; cCR12 + pathological complete response 76%; no recurrences among complete responders
cards.type: Global single-arm registrational trial (AZUR-1), dostarlimab monotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer
cards.people: 154 patients enrolled with previously untreated stage II/III mismatch-repair-deficient/MSI-high locally advanced rectal cancer in the first global registrational study of dostarlimab monotherapy (500 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 9 cycles); 144 had at least 12 months of follow-up at the April 20, 2026 cutoff. Median follow-up 26.3 months (range 2-36).
cards.result: Of the 144 patients with at least 12 months of follow-up, 68% achieved sustained clinical complete response at 12 months (cCR12) by investigator assessment; pathological complete response was achieved in 12 of 15 patients (80%) who underwent surgery after dostarlimab alone, giving a cCR12 + pathological complete response rate of 76%. Central-review cCR12 was less mature, as first central-review complete responses were identified later. Of those who achieved cCR, 98% maintained it for at least 12 months. Overall 93% of patients were on study with no evidence of progression after treatment (dostarlimab with or without standard care); 71% achieved this with dostarlimab alone. There were no reported recurrences among patients in clinical or pathological complete response. Grade 3 or worse immune-mediated adverse events occurred in 4 patients (3%).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and interim: the 68% sustained-cCR rate — not the pilot's 100% — is the mature estimate, and central-review assessment lagged investigator assessment. This record carries no MeSH terms in PubMed, so the source line records that plainly.
cards.source: Cercek A et al. Clinical Complete Response with Dostarlimab Monotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: First Results from the Global AZUR-1 Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — sustained complete responses in about two-thirds to all rectal patients depending on the cohort, allowing omission of chemoradiation and surgery under surveillance
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — sustained complete responses in about two-thirds to all rectal patients depending on the cohort, allowing omission of chemoradiation and surgery under surveillance
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The rectal slice of the dostarlimab programme is: a 12-patient first report (100% clinical complete response), the expanded phase 2 rectal cohort (49 of 49 completed patients with clinical complete response, 37 with sustained response at 12 months), and the global AZUR-1 trial (68% sustained clinical complete response at 12 months among 144 patients with sufficient follow-up; 76% for cCR12 + pathological complete response; no recurrences among complete responders at median follow-up 26.3 months). This is a response-guided omission question: complete responders omitted chemoradiotherapy and surgery under protocol surveillance — it is not proof that standard therapy is unnecessary for all comers, and all evidence is single-arm. Dostarlimab in endometrial cancer (RUBY) is a different disease and setting, homed at live shelf #853 — cross-point only; the sintilimab and camrelizumab-apatinib rectal programmes are different regimens and are likewise cross-points, not carded here.

cards.search: synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — sustained complete responses in about two-thirds to all rectal patients depending on the cohort, allowing omission of chemoradiation and surgery under surveillance synthesis: single-arm evidence throughout — sustained complete responses in about two-thirds to all rectal patients depending on the cohort, allowing omission of chemoradiation and surgery under surveillance in patients with stage ii-iii mismatch-repair-deficient (dmmr) locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, does neoadjuvant single-agent dostarlimab for 6 months, versus standard chemoradiotherapy and surgery, produce sustained clinical complete responses that allow chemoradiation and surgery to be omitted? synthesis all reports carded on this shelf. the rectal slice of the dostarlimab programme is: a 12-patient first report (100% clinical complete response), the expanded phase 2 rectal cohort (49 of 49 completed patients with clinical complete response, 37 with sustained response at 12 months), and the global azur-1 trial (68% sustained clinical complete response at 12 months among 144 patients with sufficient follow-up; 76% for ccr12 + pathological complete response; no recurrences among complete responders at median follow-up 26.3 months). this is a response-guided omission question: complete responders omitted chemoradiotherapy and surgery under protocol surveillance — it is not proof that standard therapy is unnecessary for all comers, and all evidence is single-arm. dostarlimab in endometrial cancer (ruby) is a different disease and setting, homed at live shelf #853 — cross-point only; the sintilimab and camrelizumab-apatinib rectal programmes are different regimens and are likewise cross-points, not carded here. see the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data. synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Tucatinib + trastuzumab in HER2-positive colorectal cancer (MOUNTAINEER): response 39.3%, median response duration 15.2 months — single programme, uncontrolled
shelves.question: In patients with chemotherapy-refractory, HER2-positive, RAS wild-type unresectable or metastatic colorectal cancer, does tucatinib plus trastuzumab, versus no concurrent control (or tucatinib alone), produce objective responses?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Trastuzumab · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Cohort Studies · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Colonic Neoplasms · Rectal Neoplasms · Diarrhea · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Oxazoles · Pyridines · Quinazolines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single programme with an uncontrolled primary base (GAP-E discipline). MOUNTAINEER's combination cohorts (n=84): confirmed objective response 38.1% at the primary report and 39.3% at final analysis, median duration of response 15.2 months, median overall survival 23.9 months — in chemotherapy-refractory, HER2-positive (IHC/ISH as enrolled), RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer. Diarrhoea (64%) is the commonest harm; grade 3-or-worse hypertension occurred in 7%. The breast-cancer tucatinib question is homed at live #1859, and the first-line MOUNTAINEER-03 design paper is cross-pointed, not carded.

cards.headline: MOUNTAINEER primary report (Strickler 2023): tucatinib + trastuzumab objective response 38.1% in chemotherapy-refractory HER2-positive, RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer
cards.summary: MOUNTAINEER primary report (Strickler 2023): tucatinib + trastuzumab objective response 38.1% in chemotherapy-refractory HER2-positive, RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer
cards.type: Phase 2 open-label study (MOUNTAINEER): cohorts A/B tucatinib + trastuzumab (primary analysis set), cohort C tucatinib alone
cards.people: 117 patients enrolled with chemotherapy-refractory, HER2-positive, RAS wild-type unresectable or metastatic colorectal cancer; 114 with locally assessed HER2-positive disease received treatment and form the full analysis set (cohort A combination n=45, cohort B combination n=39, cohort C tucatinib alone n=30). HER2 testing definition (IHC/ISH as enrolled) is part of the tested intervention's identity. Treatment: tucatinib 300 mg orally twice daily plus trastuzumab (8 mg/kg loading, then 6 mg/kg every 21 days); cohorts B and C were randomised 4:3 to combination versus tucatinib alone after expansion.
cards.result: In the 84 patients of cohorts A and B, confirmed objective response rate by blinded central review was 38.1% (95% CI 27.7 to 49.3; 3 complete and 29 partial responses). In cohorts A and B the most common adverse event was diarrhoea (55 of 86, 64%) and the most common grade 3-or-worse event was hypertension (6 of 86, 7%); three patients (3%) had tucatinib-related serious adverse events (acute kidney injury, colitis, fatigue). In cohort C (tucatinib alone) diarrhoea occurred in 33% and grade 3-or-worse alanine/aspartate aminotransferase increases in 7% each. No deaths were attributed to adverse events; all deaths in treated patients were from disease progression.
cards.watchOut: The primary response rate is for the uncontrolled combination cohorts; the randomised B-versus-C element was not powered as a comparative efficacy trial, so 38.1% is an uncontrolled rate in a biomarker-selected, chemotherapy-refractory population.
cards.source: Strickler JH et al. cards.headline: MOUNTAINEER final analysis (Strickler 2026): confirmed response 39.3%, median duration of response 15.2 months, median overall survival 23.9 months at 32.4 months of follow-up
cards.summary: MOUNTAINEER final analysis (Strickler 2026): confirmed response 39.3%, median duration of response 15.2 months, median overall survival 23.9 months at 32.4 months of follow-up
cards.type: Final analysis of the phase 2 MOUNTAINEER trial (same trial as the primary report above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The 84 patients who received tucatinib plus trastuzumab in MOUNTAINEER, at median follow-up of 32.4 months.
cards.result: Confirmed objective response rate was 39.3%; median duration of response was 15.2 months; median progression-free survival was 8.1 months and median overall survival 23.9 months. Efficacy was relatively similar across central HER2-positive testing methods, and no clear association of response with co-occurring biomarker alterations was seen. Few patients discontinued because of adverse events and no treatment-emergent deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Final analysis of the same single programme: the survival figures are uncontrolled — a median overall survival of 23.9 months in a selected trial population cannot be compared directly with historical chemotherapy-refractory survival.

cards.headline: FDA approval summary (Casak 2023): accelerated approval on the pooled MOUNTAINEER combination cohorts — response 38%, median duration of response 12.4 months at approval
cards.summary: FDA approval summary (Casak 2023): accelerated approval on the pooled MOUNTAINEER combination cohorts — response 38%, median duration of response 12.4 months at approval
cards.type: FDA approval summary of the MOUNTAINEER trial (regulatory review of the same programme — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 84 eligible patients received tucatinib plus trastuzumab in MOUNTAINEER, as reviewed by the FDA (median follow-up 16 months at the approval analysis).
cards.result: Objective response rate was 38% (95% CI 28 to 49) and median duration of response 12.4 months (95% CI 8.5 to 20.5); 81% of responders had a response lasting more than 6 months. The most common adverse reactions (at least 20%) were diarrhoea, fatigue, rash, nausea, abdominal pain, infusion-related reactions and fever. The FDA granted accelerated approval on January 19, 2023 for unresectable or metastatic RAS wild-type, HER2-positive colorectal cancer after fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan, concluding the response magnitude and durability were clinically meaningful against an estimated survival of 6-7 months with available therapy — the first approval for HER2-positive colorectal cancer.
cards.watchOut: Accelerated approval on an uncontrolled response rate; the approval analysis's duration of response (12.4 months) differs from the final analysis (15.2 months) because follow-up matured — both are printed with their timepoints.

shelves.title: Camizestrant in ER-positive breast cancer: SERENA-6 switch at ESR1 emergence — progression-free survival 16.8 vs 9.2 months; SERENA-2 also positive
shelves.question: In women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, does the oral SERD camizestrant — switched to at ESR1-mutation emergence during first-line aromatase-inhibitor + CDK4/6 therapy, or given after endocrine progression — versus continuing/switching to standard endocrine therapy, prolong progression-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Aromatase Inhibitors · Breast Neoplasms · Circulating Tumor DNA · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4 · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 6 · Estrogen Receptor alpha · Mutation · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal · Follow-Up Studies · Aged, 80 and over · Breast Neoplasms, Male · Treatment Outcome · Benzimidazoles · Aminopyridines · Isoquinolines · Piperazines · Pyridines · Azetidines · Purines
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for progression-free survival, on two randomised trials in two labelled slices. SERENA-6: switching to camizestrant + continued CDK4/6 inhibitor at ESR1-mutation emergence (ctDNA tested every 2-3 months — the testing schedule is part of the intervention) gave median progression-free survival of 16.8 versus 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.45, a relative measure) and second progression-free survival of 25.7 versus 19.1 months; overall survival is not reported in the fetched records. SERENA-2: camizestrant after endocrine progression gave 7.2-7.7 versus 3.7 months against fulvestrant. Characteristic harms from phase 1 are visual effects (56%) and sinus bradycardia (44%), mostly low grade. No overall-survival benefit is claimed on this shelf.

cards.headline: SERENA-6 phase 3 primary report (Bidard 2025): switching to camizestrant at ESR1-mutation emergence — median progression-free survival 16.0 vs 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.44, a relative measure)
cards.summary: SERENA-6 phase 3 primary report (Bidard 2025): switching to camizestrant at ESR1-mutation emergence — median progression-free survival 16.0 vs 9.2 months (hazard ratio 0.44, a relative measure)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (SERENA-6), ctDNA-guided switch to camizestrant vs continuing aromatase inhibitor, both with CDK4/6 inhibitor
cards.people: 3,256 patients on first-line aromatase inhibitor + CDK4/6 inhibitor for at least 6 months were tested for ESR1 mutations in circulating tumour DNA every 2-3 months — the ctDNA surveillance schedule is itself part of the randomised strategy. The 315 eligible patients with an emergent ESR1 mutation and no radiologic progression were randomised 1:1 to switch to camizestrant 75 mg once daily + continued CDK4/6 inhibitor (n=157) or continue aromatase inhibitor + CDK4/6 inhibitor (n=158). Median follow-up 12.6 months at the interim analysis.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 16.0 months (95% CI 12.7 to 18.2) with the camizestrant switch versus 9.2 months (95% CI 7.2 to 9.5) with continued aromatase inhibitor; the hazard ratio for progression or death was 0.44 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.60; P<0.0001) — a relative measure, with the absolute medians printed beside it. Median time to deterioration in patient-reported global health status/quality of life was 21.0 versus 6.4 months (hazard ratio 0.54, relative). Discontinuation because of adverse events was 1.3% with camizestrant and 1.9% with aromatase inhibitor.
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis at 12.6 months in the minority who developed an ESR1 mutation without progression (315 of 3,256 tested): the strategy tested is surveillance-plus-switch, so the benefit cannot be claimed for camizestrant started without the ctDNA testing schedule.
cards.source: Bidard FC et al. First-Line Camizestrant for Emerging ESR1-Mutated Advanced Breast Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40454637. Registry ID: NCT04964934.
