shelves.title: Sacituzumab govitecan in pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer (TROPiCS-02): PFS 5.5 vs 4.0 months and overall survival 14.4 vs 11.2 months versus physician's-choice chemotherapy
shelves.question: In patients with endocrine-resistant, chemotherapy-pretreated hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, does the TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan, versus treatment of physician's choice chemotherapy, prolong progression-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Camptothecin · Capecitabine · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4 · Female · Humans · Immunoconjugates · Irinotecan · Middle Aged · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Vinorelbine
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit, on a single phase 3 programme. TROPiCS-02 (543 randomised, heavily pretreated: 99% prior CDK4/6 inhibitor, median three prior chemotherapy lines) found sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival versus treatment of physician's choice chemotherapy (5.5 vs 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.66 — a relative measure) and, in the final analysis, median overall survival (14.4 vs 11.2 months; HR 0.79, relative). Quality of life mostly favoured sacituzumab (physical functioning, dyspnoea) except diarrhoea, and a Q-TWiST analysis favoured it. The harms are neutropenia (grade ≥3 treatment-related 51% vs 38%) and diarrhoea (9% vs 1%). The small Japanese phase II cohort (n=42) did NOT meet its primary response endpoint and is carded labelled as a regional cohort, not confirmatory evidence. The triple-negative question (ASCENT) is homed at live #1852 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: TROPiCS-02 phase 3 primary report (Rugo 2022): sacituzumab govitecan improved median PFS versus physician's choice chemotherapy (5.5 vs 4.0 months; HR 0.66, relative) in heavily pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer
cards.summary: TROPiCS-02 phase 3 primary report (Rugo 2022): sacituzumab govitecan improved median PFS versus physician's choice chemotherapy (5.5 vs 4.0 months; HR 0.66, relative) in heavily pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (TROPiCS-02), sacituzumab govitecan vs treatment of physician's choice chemotherapy — primary PFS report
cards.people: 543 patients with endocrine-resistant, chemotherapy-treated HR-positive/HER2-negative locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic breast cancer randomised to sacituzumab govitecan (n=272) or physician's choice chemotherapy (eribulin, vinorelbine, capecitabine or gemcitabine; n=271). Median age 56 years, 95% had visceral metastases, 99% had a prior CDK4/6 inhibitor, and the median was three prior lines of chemotherapy for advanced disease.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: hazard ratio 0.66 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.83; P=.0003) for progression or death — a 34% relative reduction in risk. Median PFS was 5.5 months (95% CI 4.2 to 7.0) versus 4.0 months (3.1 to 4.4); PFS at 6 months was 46% versus 30% and at 12 months 21% versus 7% (absolute rates). Overall survival was not yet mature at this first interim analysis (HR 0.84; P=.14). Key grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were neutropenia (51% vs 38%) and diarrhoea (9% vs 1%).
cards.watchOut: Single programme; the comparator is a mix of four single-agent chemotherapies chosen by the physician, not one drug. The population is heavily pretreated (median three prior chemotherapy lines) — the result does not answer earlier-line use.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Sacituzumab Govitecan in Hormone Receptor-Positive/Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2-Negative Metastatic Breast Cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2022. PMID: 36027558. Registry ID: NCT03901339. cards.headline: TROPiCS-02 final overall-survival analysis (Rugo 2023): median OS 14.4 vs 11.2 months (HR 0.79, relative) with sacituzumab govitecan
cards.summary: TROPiCS-02 final overall-survival analysis (Rugo 2023): median OS 14.4 vs 11.2 months (HR 0.79, relative) with sacituzumab govitecan
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (TROPiCS-02) — protocol-specified final overall-survival analysis of the same trial as the card above, not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 543 randomised patients (272 sacituzumab govitecan, 271 chemotherapy) in 91 centres across North America and Europe; patients had received at least one endocrine therapy, a taxane and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and two to four prior chemotherapy regimens for metastatic disease. Median follow-up 12.5 months; 390 deaths had occurred.
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly improved with sacituzumab govitecan: median 14.4 months (95% CI 13.0 to 15.7) versus 11.2 months (10.1 to 12.7); hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.96; p=0.020) — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute medians. The benefit was consistent across Trop-2 expression subgroups. Objective response was 21% versus 14% (odds ratio 1.63). Time to deterioration of global health status/quality of life (median 4.3 vs 3.0 months; HR 0.75, relative) and fatigue (2.2 vs 1.4 months; HR 0.73, relative) also favoured sacituzumab. One fatal adverse event (septic shock caused by neutropenic colitis) was judged treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label trial; this is the final analysis of the same single trial, so the shelf's randomised base remains one trial of 543 patients.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Overall survival with sacituzumab govitecan in hormone receptor-positive and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative metastatic breast cancer (TROPiCS-02): a randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial. cards.headline: TROPiCS-02 quality-of-life report (Rugo 2024): better physical functioning and dyspnoea, worse diarrhoea, with sacituzumab govitecan
cards.summary: TROPiCS-02 quality-of-life report (Rugo 2024): better physical functioning and dyspnoea, worse diarrhoea, with sacituzumab govitecan
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes report of the TROPiCS-02 randomised trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The TROPiCS-02 randomised population (adults with HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer previously treated with a taxane, endocrine therapy, a CDK4/6 inhibitor and 2–4 lines of chemotherapy), assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30, EQ-5D-5L and PRO-CTCAE at baseline and on day 1 of each cycle.
cards.result: Compared with physician's choice chemotherapy, overall least-squares mean change from baseline was significantly better with sacituzumab govitecan for physical functioning and dyspnoea, but worse for diarrhoea. Time to first clinically meaningful worsening or death was significantly longer with sacituzumab for global health status/quality of life, physical functioning, fatigue, emotional functioning, dyspnoea, insomnia and financial difficulties, and longer with chemotherapy for diarrhoea. Few patients in either arm reported worsening to level 3 or 4 symptomatic events except diarrhoea frequency and hair loss, which favoured chemotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A secondary report of the one trial; patient-reported outcomes in an open-label trial can be influenced by knowing the treatment, and diarrhoea — the drug's characteristic harm — is the one domain that favoured chemotherapy.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Health-related quality of life with sacituzumab govitecan in HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer in the phase III TROPiCS-02 trial. The Oncologist. 2024. PMID: 38748596. cards.headline: Q-TWiST benefit–risk analysis (Rugo 2025): quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity 9.7 vs 8.1 months favouring sacituzumab govitecan
cards.summary: Q-TWiST benefit–risk analysis (Rugo 2025): quality-adjusted time without symptoms or toxicity 9.7 vs 8.1 months favouring sacituzumab govitecan
cards.type: Q-TWiST benefit–risk analysis of the TROPiCS-02 randomised trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The TROPiCS-02 population (pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer), with survival time partitioned into time with grade ≥3 toxicity, time after progression, and time without progression or grade ≥3 toxicity, using utility weights from the published literature.
cards.result: Sacituzumab govitecan significantly improved Q-TWiST versus physician's choice chemotherapy (mean 9.7 vs 8.1 months; difference 1.6 months; 95% CI 0.5 to 2.7; p=0.0067), and the relative Q-TWiST improvement (10.8%) met the established 10% threshold for clinical importance. Time spent in the toxicity state was numerically higher with sacituzumab and the difference stabilised over time.
cards.watchOut: A modelling analysis of the one trial using literature-derived utility weights; it integrates the trial's benefit and toxicity but adds no new patients.
cards.source: Rugo HS et al. Q-TWiST Analysis of Sacituzumab Govitecan vs. Chemotherapy in Previously Treated Patients with HR+/HER2- Metastatic Breast Cancer. Current Oncology. 2025. PMID: 40136373. cards.headline: ASCENT-J02 Japanese phase II cohort (Shimomura 2026): response rate 16.7% by independent review — the cohort's primary endpoint was NOT met (n=42)
cards.summary: ASCENT-J02 Japanese phase II cohort (Shimomura 2026): response rate 16.7% by independent review — the cohort's primary endpoint was NOT met (n=42)
cards.type: Single-arm phase II regional cohort (ASCENT-J02), sacituzumab govitecan in Japanese patients
cards.people: 42 Japanese participants with previously treated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer received sacituzumab govitecan 10 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 of 21-day cycles in the phase II cohort of an open-label phase I/II study. Median follow-up 7.5 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: independent-review confirmed objective response was 16.7% (95% CI 7.0 to 31.4; P=.1214 against the 10% threshold criterion as prespecified), while investigator-assessed response was 28.6%. Median PFS was 4.4 months by independent review and 5.6 months by investigator; median overall survival was 13.0 months. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 98% (grade ≥3 in 83%); there were no treatment-related deaths and one participant discontinued for neutropenia. The authors judged overall efficacy generally similar to TROPiCS-02.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=42), single-arm and its primary endpoint was not met — carded, labelled as a regional cohort, only to complete the record; it is not confirmatory evidence for the TROPiCS-02 result.
cards.source: Shimomura A et al. Sacituzumab govitecan in Japanese participants with HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer: primary results from the phase II ASCENT-J02 study. Japanese Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2026. PMID: 41887616. Registry ID: NCT05101096. cards.headline: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme (TROPiCS-02, n=543) shows sacituzumab govitecan prolongs PFS and overall survival versus single-agent chemotherapy in heavily pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer, priced in neutropenia and diarrhoea
cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 3 programme (TROPiCS-02, n=543) shows sacituzumab govitecan prolongs PFS and overall survival versus single-agent chemotherapy in heavily pretreated HR+/HER2− metastatic breast cancer, priced in neutropenia and diarrhoea
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: TROPiCS-02 is the entire randomised base: median PFS 5.5 vs 4.0 months (HR 0.66, relative) and final median overall survival 14.4 vs 11.2 months (HR 0.79, relative), with response 21% vs 14%. Quality-of-life and Q-TWiST reports of the same trial favour sacituzumab overall, diarrhoea excepted. Grade ≥3 treatment-related neutropenia (51% vs 38%) and diarrhoea (9% vs 1%) are the defining harms, and one treatment-related death from neutropenic colitis occurred. The Japanese ASCENT-J02 cohort (n=42) did not meet its response endpoint and adds no confirmation. The triple-negative question is a different shelf (live #1852, ASCENT).
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Asciminib first-line in newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML (ASC4FIRST): week-48 major molecular response 67.7% vs 49.0% vs investigator-selected TKIs — clear vs imatinib, not significant vs second-generation TKIs
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase, does asciminib (the STAMP inhibitor targeting the ABL myristoyl pocket, 80 mg once daily), versus investigator-selected ATP-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib or a second-generation TKI), increase major molecular response at week 48, and with what tolerability advantage? (The previously-treated question is asked at pack #4481.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Antineoplastic Agents · Fusion Proteins, bcr-abl · Imatinib Mesylate · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Myelogenous, Chronic, BCR-ABL Positive · Niacinamide · Pyrazoles · Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit on a molecular endpoint, on a single phase 3 trial. ASC4FIRST (405 randomised, newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML) found major molecular response at week 48 in 67.7% on asciminib versus 49.0% on investigator-selected TKIs — but the comparator is a stratified mix: the advantage was large against imatinib (69.3% vs 40.2%) and small and not significant against second-generation TKIs (66.0% vs 57.8%). Asciminib had fewer grade ≥3 adverse events (38.0% vs 44.4% on imatinib and 54.9% on second-generation TKIs) and fewer discontinuations (4.5% vs 11.1% and 9.8%). Major molecular response is a surrogate; no survival advantage is shown in these reports. This shelf asks only the FIRST-LINE question; asciminib after ≥2 prior TKIs (ASCEMBL) is homed at pack #4481 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: ASC4FIRST phase 3 primary report (Hochhaus 2024): major molecular response at week 48 in 67.7% on asciminib vs 49.0% on investigator-selected TKIs — driven by the imatinib stratum
cards.summary: ASC4FIRST phase 3 primary report (Hochhaus 2024): major molecular response at week 48 in 67.7% on asciminib vs 49.0% on investigator-selected TKIs — driven by the imatinib stratum
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (ASC4FIRST), asciminib vs investigator-selected TKI, first-line chronic-phase CML — primary report
cards.people: 405 patients with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase randomised 1:1 to asciminib 80 mg once daily (n=201) or an investigator-selected TKI (n=204; imatinib or a second-generation TKI chosen before randomisation, with randomisation stratified by that choice and by ELTS risk score). Median follow-up 16.3 months (asciminib) and 15.7 months (control).
cards.result: Major molecular response (BCR::ABL1 ≤0.1% on the International Scale) at week 48 occurred in 67.7% with asciminib versus 49.0% with investigator-selected TKIs (difference 18.9 percentage points; 95% CI 9.6 to 28.2; P<0.001) — absolute rates, printed both. In the imatinib stratum the rates were 69.3% versus 40.2% (difference 29.6 points; 95% CI 16.9 to 42.2; P<0.001). In the second-generation TKI stratum the rates were 66.0% versus 57.8% (difference 8.2 points; 95% CI −5.1 to 21.5 — not significant), and direct comparison against second-generation TKIs was not a primary objective. Grade ≥3 adverse events and discontinuations were less frequent with asciminib (38.0% and 4.5%) than with imatinib (44.4% and 11.1%) and second-generation TKIs (54.9% and 9.8%).
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison pools two different comparators. The 29.6-point imatinib-stratum difference must not be presented as the effect against modern second-generation TKIs, against which the difference was 8.2 points and not significant. The endpoint is a molecular surrogate at week 48, not survival.
cards.source: Hochhaus A et al. Asciminib in Newly Diagnosed Chronic Myeloid Leukemia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38820078. Registry ID: NCT04971226. cards.headline: ASC4FIRST Japanese subgroup (Takahashi 2025): week-48 major molecular response 81.0% on asciminib vs 47.1% on investigator-selected TKIs — in only 38 patients
cards.summary: ASC4FIRST Japanese subgroup (Takahashi 2025): week-48 major molecular response 81.0% on asciminib vs 47.1% on investigator-selected TKIs — in only 38 patients
cards.type: Regional subgroup report of the ASC4FIRST randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 38 Japanese patients in ASC4FIRST (asciminib n=21; investigator-selected TKI n=17, of whom 8 imatinib stratum and 9 second-generation stratum), randomised and stratified as in the main trial; cutoff November 28, 2023.
cards.result: Major molecular response at week 48 was 81.0% with asciminib versus 47.1% with investigator-selected TKIs, and in the imatinib stratum 100% versus 25.0%. Deeper responses (MR4.0 57.1% vs 11.8%; MR4.5 28.6% vs 5.9%) also favoured asciminib. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 42.9% on asciminib versus 50.0% (imatinib) and 55.6% (second-generation TKI), and discontinuations in 0% versus 37.5% and 11.1%. The authors judged outcomes consistent with the overall population.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of only 38 patients: percentages rest on very small denominators (the 100% imatinib-stratum figure is a handful of patients) and the analysis is descriptive, not powered.
cards.source: Takahashi N et al. Asciminib in patients with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukemia: results from the Japanese subgroup of ASC4FIRST. International Journal of Hematology. 2025. cards.headline: ASC4FIRST East Asian subgroup (Takahashi 2026): major molecular response at week 96 of 77.0% on asciminib vs 57.8% on investigator-selected TKIs (138 patients)
cards.summary: ASC4FIRST East Asian subgroup (Takahashi 2026): major molecular response at week 96 of 77.0% on asciminib vs 57.8% on investigator-selected TKIs (138 patients)
cards.type: Regional subgroup report of the ASC4FIRST randomised trial with week-96 data (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 138 patients from East Asian sites in ASC4FIRST, randomised to asciminib or investigator-selected TKIs (imatinib, bosutinib, dasatinib or nilotinib), stratified by risk category and prerandomisation-selected TKI.
cards.result: Major molecular response was 64.9% (asciminib) versus 45.3% (investigator-selected TKIs) at week 48 and 77.0% versus 57.8% at week 96 (common treatment differences 19.5 and 20.0 percentage points). In the imatinib stratum, week-96 response was 78.6% versus 46.2%. Grade ≥3 adverse events (41.9% vs 54.0%) and discontinuations (2.7% vs 9.5%) were lower with asciminib, consistent with the non-East Asian population.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup report of the one trial; it extends follow-up to week 96 within that subgroup only and does not add a second trial or a survival endpoint.
cards.source: Takahashi N et al. cards.result: ASC4FIRST is the entire first-line base, reported in the primary paper and two regional subgroup reports of the same trial. shelves.title: Isatuximab plus VRd in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma (IMROZ): 60-month PFS 63.2% vs 45.2% (HR 0.60, relative), with deeper MRD-negative responses
shelves.question: In patients aged 18–80 with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for transplantation, does adding the anti-CD38 antibody isatuximab to bortezomib–lenalidomide–dexamethasone (followed by isatuximab–Rd), versus VRd (followed by Rd), prolong progression-free survival and deepen responses, including in frail patients?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bortezomib · Dexamethasone · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lenalidomide · Multiple Myeloma · Neoplasm, Residual · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit, on a single phase 3 trial. IMROZ (446 randomised, transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma, age 18–80) found estimated 60-month progression-free survival of 63.2% with isatuximab-VRd (followed by isatuximab-Rd) versus 45.2% with VRd (followed by Rd) — hazard ratio 0.60, a relative measure, printed beside those absolute rates — with deeper responses (complete response or better 74.7% vs 64.1%; MRD-negative complete response 55.5% vs 40.9%). A frailty subgroup analysis found the PFS benefit held in frail and non-frail patients, and an MRD-dynamics report found deeper and more durable MRD negativity. Serious adverse events and discontinuations were similar between arms in the primary report. Transplant-ELIGIBLE isatuximab-VRd is a different question and is not carded here.

cards.headline: IMROZ phase 3 primary report (Facon 2024): estimated 60-month PFS 63.2% with isatuximab-VRd vs 45.2% with VRd (HR 0.60, relative) in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma
cards.summary: IMROZ phase 3 primary report (Facon 2024): estimated 60-month PFS 63.2% with isatuximab-VRd vs 45.2% with VRd (HR 0.60, relative) in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (IMROZ), isatuximab-VRd vs VRd, transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma — primary report
cards.people: 446 patients aged 18–80 with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for transplantation, randomised 3:2 internationally to isatuximab plus bortezomib–lenalidomide–dexamethasone (followed by isatuximab-Rd) or VRd alone (followed by Rd). Median follow-up 59.7 months.
cards.result: Estimated progression-free survival at 60 months was 63.2% in the isatuximab-VRd group versus 45.2% in the VRd group (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.60; 98.5% CI 0.41 to 0.88; P<0.001) — the hazard ratio is a relative measure; the absolute 60-month rates are printed beside it. Complete response or better was achieved by 74.7% versus 64.1% (P=0.01), and MRD-negative status with complete response by 55.5% versus 40.9% (P=0.003). No new safety signals were observed; the incidence of serious adverse events during treatment and of adverse events leading to discontinuation was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, open-label. The primary report does not give an overall-survival result, so no survival claim is made on this shelf; patients over 80 were not eligible.

cards.headline: IMROZ frailty subgroup (Manier 2025): PFS benefit held in frail patients (HR 0.518, relative) and non-frail patients (HR 0.615, relative)
cards.summary: IMROZ frailty subgroup (Manier 2025): PFS benefit held in frail patients (HR 0.518, relative) and non-frail patients (HR 0.615, relative)
cards.type: Post hoc frailty subgroup analysis of the IMROZ randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The 446 IMROZ patients classified by the simplified IMWG frailty score: 26.7% were frail (score ≥2; 26.0% of the isatuximab-VRd arm and 27.6% of the VRd arm) and 72.0% non-frail. Patients over 80 were excluded from IMROZ, so 'frail' here means frail within an 18–80 population. Median follow-up 59.7 months.
cards.result: Isatuximab-VRd improved progression-free survival versus VRd in frail patients (hazard ratio 0.518; 95% CI 0.294 to 0.912; P=0.0227) and in non-frail patients (HR 0.615; 95% CI 0.419 to 0.903; P=0.0131) — both relative measures from a post hoc subgroup analysis. Frail patients on isatuximab-VRd more often achieved MRD negativity with complete response (odds ratio 3.459; 95% CI 1.495 to 8.006). Rates of treatment-emergent adverse events leading to definitive discontinuation were similar between arms regardless of frailty.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgroup analysis. An erratum exists against this report (PMID 42383667); its PubMed record carries no abstract, so its content could not be verified this session and it is not carded — the numbers here are as published in the original report.

cards.headline: IMROZ MRD-negativity dynamics (Orlowski 2026): deeper MRD negativity at end of induction and during maintenance with isatuximab-VRd, up to 60 months
cards.summary: IMROZ MRD-negativity dynamics (Orlowski 2026): deeper MRD negativity at end of induction and during maintenance with isatuximab-VRd, up to 60 months
cards.type: MRD landmark/dynamics analysis of the IMROZ randomised trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The IMROZ randomised population (265 isatuximab-VRd followed by isatuximab-Rd; 181 VRd followed by Rd), analysed by landmark MRD status over time, including older (>70 years) and frail subgroups.
cards.result: Treatment with isatuximab-VRd led to deeper responses, with higher rates of MRD negativity and MRD-negative complete response at the end of induction and during maintenance versus VRd/Rd, up to 60 months of follow-up, with benefit across key subgroups including older and frail patients. Time to progression was significantly prolonged with isatuximab-VRd in patients who converted from MRD-negative to MRD-positive at any time point, and in the landmark analysis of patients who converted from MRD-negative at end of induction to MRD-positive. The authors suggest repeated MRD assessment may support decisions on treatment selection and continuation.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the one trial, reported qualitatively in its abstract without the underlying rates; MRD negativity is a depth-of-response measure, and this report does not by itself establish that MRD-guided treatment changes improve outcomes.
cards.source: Orlowski RZ et al. Isatuximab, bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone for multiple myeloma: dynamics of MRD negativity in the IMROZ study. Blood. 2026. PMID: 41758929. cards.headline: Phase 1b Isa-VRd programme report (Ocio 2023): overall response 98.6% in 71 efficacy-evaluable patients — the single-arm study that preceded IMROZ
cards.summary: Phase 1b Isa-VRd programme report (Ocio 2023): overall response 98.6% in 71 efficacy-evaluable patients — the single-arm study that preceded IMROZ
cards.type: Phase 1b single-arm programme study of isatuximab-VRd (a different, earlier study than IMROZ — no comparator)
cards.people: 73 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for, or with no immediate intent for, autologous stem-cell transplantation received four 6-week induction cycles of isatuximab-VRd followed by isatuximab-Rd maintenance; 71 were in the efficacy population.
cards.result: Overall response was 98.6%, with 56.3% achieving complete response or better and 36 of 71 (50.7%) reaching MRD negativity at 10⁻⁵ sensitivity. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 79.5% (58/73), and events leading to permanent discontinuation in 19.2% (14/73). Isatuximab pharmacokinetics were within the previously reported range. The authors concluded the data supported phase 3 study (IMROZ).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no control group: response proportions cannot be compared with VRd alone, and this study's population included patients with 'no immediate intent' for transplant, a slightly wider group than IMROZ's transplant-ineligible population.

shelves.title: Daratumumab vs active monitoring in high-risk smouldering myeloma (AQUILA; FLOOR-RISK — one trial): progression delayed (5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%), while ~59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years
shelves.question: In patients with high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma, does subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy for up to 36 months, versus active monitoring, delay progression to active multiple myeloma and prolong survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antineoplastic Agents · Disease Progression · Injections, Subcutaneous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Multiple Myeloma · Progression-Free Survival · Smoldering Multiple Myeloma · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK — the base is stated plainly: ONE phase 3 trial (AQUILA, 390 randomised) with one regional subgroup report and one review; there is no second trial. AQUILA found subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy for up to 36 months delayed progression to active myeloma or death versus active monitoring (HR 0.49 — a 51% relative reduction; 5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%, absolute rates) and 5-year overall survival was 93.0% versus 86.9% (deaths 15 vs 26; OS HR 0.52, relative). The counterweight belongs on the face: about 59% of monitored patients had NOT progressed at 5 years, so monitoring remains a strategy in which most patients in this trial avoided treatment for years, while daratumumab commits everyone treated to up to 3 years of therapy for a precursor condition. This is a delay-of-progression result under a treat-versus-monitor strategy — it is not prevention of myeloma. The commonest grade 3–4 event was hypertension (5.7% vs 4.6%).

cards.headline: AQUILA phase 3 primary report (Dimopoulos 2025): daratumumab delayed progression or death versus active monitoring in high-risk smouldering myeloma (HR 0.49, relative; 5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%) — FLOOR-RISK: the shelf's only trial
cards.summary: AQUILA phase 3 primary report (Dimopoulos 2025): daratumumab delayed progression or death versus active monitoring in high-risk smouldering myeloma (HR 0.49, relative; 5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%) — FLOOR-RISK: the shelf's only trial
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (AQUILA), subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy vs active monitoring, high-risk smouldering myeloma — primary report; the only trial on this shelf (FLOOR-RISK)
cards.people: 390 patients with high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma randomised to subcutaneous daratumumab monotherapy (n=194) or active monitoring (n=196). Treatment continued for 39 cycles, 36 months, or until confirmed progression, whichever came first. Median follow-up 65.2 months. Progression to active myeloma was assessed by an independent review committee using IMWG criteria.
cards.result: The risk of disease progression or death was 51% lower with daratumumab than with active monitoring (hazard ratio 0.49; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.67; P<0.001) — a relative reduction, printed beside the absolute rates: progression-free survival at 5 years was 63.1% with daratumumab and 40.8% with monitoring, meaning about 59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years. Deaths were 15 (7.7%) versus 26 (13.3%) (HR 0.52; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.98), and overall survival at 5 years was 93.0% versus 86.9%. The most common grade 3 or 4 adverse event was hypertension (5.7% vs 4.6%); adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.7% of the daratumumab group, with no new safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: a single trial with no confirmatory randomised report. 'High-risk' smouldering myeloma is a risk-model definition, and the benefit is delayed progression under a treatment strategy — roughly 59% of the monitoring arm had not progressed at 5 years, so many treated patients would not have progressed in that time anyway (the overtreatment counterweight).
cards.source: Dimopoulos MA et al. Daratumumab or Active Monitoring for High-Risk Smoldering Multiple Myeloma. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39652675. Registry ID: NCT03301220. cards.headline: AQUILA Japanese subgroup (Suzuki 2026): median PFS 59.1 vs 24.8 months favouring daratumumab — in only 28 patients, exploratory and post hoc
cards.summary: AQUILA Japanese subgroup (Suzuki 2026): median PFS 59.1 vs 24.8 months favouring daratumumab — in only 28 patients, exploratory and post hoc
cards.type: Regional subgroup report of the AQUILA randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 28 Japanese patients in AQUILA (15 daratumumab, 13 active monitoring), analysed as a small exploratory post hoc subgroup. Median follow-up 60.9 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 59.1 months with daratumumab versus 24.8 months with monitoring (hazard ratio 0.25; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.65 — a relative measure from very small numbers). Overall response was 86.7% versus 7.7%. Overall survival data were immature. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 5 patients (33.3%) on daratumumab, none leading to discontinuation, with no new safety concerns. The authors judged efficacy generally comparable to the global population.
cards.watchOut: Only 28 patients, post hoc and exploratory: the hazard ratio's confidence interval is wide and this subgroup adds consistency, not confirmation. Its PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.type: Narrative review / drug-profile report on daratumumab in smouldering myeloma (context only — not a trial report and not independent evidence)
cards.people: A narrative expert review of daratumumab (including the subcutaneous daratumumab–hyaluronidase formulation) in smouldering multiple myeloma, covering CD38 rationale, the Mayo 20/2/20 and IMWG 2020 risk-stratification models, the AQUILA trial, and ongoing daratumumab-combination studies.
cards.result: The review records that fixed-duration subcutaneous daratumumab delayed progression to active myeloma versus active monitoring in AQUILA, and frames the open questions: future triplet, quadruplet and immune-based combinations must be balanced against toxicity, infection, immunosuppression and overtreatment, and precise patient selection remains the key challenge. It reports no new patient data.
cards.watchOut: Carded, labelled as a review, only to complete the record of a one-trial shelf and to carry the risk-model and overtreatment context; it must not be counted as a second evidence report. Note its title's word 'preventing' is the review's framing — the trial showed delayed progression, not prevention.

cards.headline: Synthesis (FLOOR-RISK): the entire base is one trial — AQUILA (n=390) shows daratumumab delays progression versus monitoring (5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%) with a small survival difference, while about 59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years
cards.summary: Synthesis (FLOOR-RISK): the entire base is one trial — AQUILA (n=390) shows daratumumab delays progression versus monitoring (5-year PFS 63.1% vs 40.8%) with a small survival difference, while about 59% of monitored patients had not progressed at 5 years
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: There is exactly one randomised trial of daratumumab versus active monitoring in high-risk smouldering myeloma. AQUILA found progression or death HR 0.49 (relative), 5-year PFS 63.1% versus 40.8% and 5-year overall survival 93.0% versus 86.9% (15 vs 26 deaths), with hypertension the commonest grade 3–4 event (5.7% vs 4.6%). The Japanese subgroup (n=28) pointed the same way and the carded review adds context only. The result is a delay of progression under a treat-early strategy in a precursor condition — never prevention — and it must be weighed against treating many patients who, on the monitoring arm's own numbers, would not have progressed within 5 years.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. FLOOR-RISK: one trial, two reports of it, plus a review — if a third report is required without exception, this shelf should be held.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 in taxane-naïve mCRPC (PSMAfore): rPFS 11.60 vs 5.59 months, but ITT overall survival null (24.48 vs 23.13 months; HR 0.91) with 60.3% crossover
shelves.question: In men with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who have progressed on one androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor and have not received a taxane, does [¹⁷⁷Lu]Lu-PSMA-617, versus a change of ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide), prolong radiographic progression-free survival, and what happens to overall survival when crossover is allowed? (The post-taxane question is asked at live #1862.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant · Heterocyclic Compounds, 1-Ring · Aged · Lutetium · Androstenes · Dipeptides · Phenylthiohydantoin · Nitriles · Androgen Receptor Antagonists · Middle Aged · Benzamides · Taxoids · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Radioisotopes · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: SPLIT on its own endpoints, on a single phase 3 trial. PSMAfore (468 randomised, taxane-naïve PSMA-positive mCRPC after one ARPI) clearly prolonged radiographic progression-free survival with ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 versus a change of ARPI (updated median 11.60 vs 5.59 months; HR 0.49, relative) and delayed worsening of quality of life, pain and symptomatic skeletal events, with fewer grade 3–5 events (36% vs 48%). But the final intention-to-treat overall-survival analysis was NULL: median 24.48 vs 23.13 months, HR 0.91 (relative), P=0.20 — with 60.3% of the control arm crossing over to lutetium therapy after progression. The crossover-adjusted model estimate (HR 0.59) is model-based and does not displace the ITT result; both are printed. The post-taxane question (VISION) is homed at live #1862 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: PSMAfore phase 3 primary report (Morris 2024): radiographic PFS prolonged with ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 versus ARPI change in taxane-naïve mCRPC (updated median 11.60 vs 5.59 months; HR 0.49, relative)
cards.summary: PSMAfore phase 3 primary report (Morris 2024): radiographic PFS prolonged with ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 versus ARPI change in taxane-naïve mCRPC (updated median 11.60 vs 5.59 months; HR 0.49, relative)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (PSMAfore), ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 vs change of ARPI, taxane-naïve mCRPC — primary rPFS report
cards.people: 468 taxane-naïve patients with PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who had progressed once on a previous ARPI, randomised 1:1 at 74 sites in Europe and North America to open-label intravenous ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 7.4 GBq every 6 weeks for six cycles (n=234) or a change of ARPI to abiraterone or enzalutamide (n=234). Median number of lutetium cycles received was 6.0. Crossover from ARPI change to lutetium therapy was allowed after centrally confirmed radiographic progression; 134 (57%) crossed over by this report.
cards.result: In the primary analysis, median radiographic progression-free survival was 9.30 versus 5.55 months (HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.29 to 0.56; p<0.0001); in the updated analysis at the third data cutoff (median time from randomisation 24.11 months) it was 11.60 months (95% CI 9.30 to 14.19) versus 5.59 months (4.21 to 5.95) (HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.61) — hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute medians. Grade 3–5 adverse events were less frequent with lutetium therapy (at least one event in 81 [36%] of 227 vs 112 [48%] of 232; grade 5 in 2% in each group, none treatment-related with lutetium vs one treatment-related with ARPI change).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparator is a second ARPI after failure of a first — a strategy with limited expected activity — not chemotherapy. Crossover was built into the design, which shapes the survival analysis on the final-analysis card.

cards.headline: PSMAfore quality-of-life / pain / skeletal-events report (Fizazi 2025): lutetium therapy delayed worsening on all assessed scales and delayed symptomatic skeletal events
cards.summary: PSMAfore quality-of-life / pain / skeletal-events report (Fizazi 2025): lutetium therapy delayed worsening on all assessed scales and delayed symptomatic skeletal events
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes and skeletal-events report of the PSMAfore randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same 468 PSMAfore patients (234 per arm; 91% White), analysed by intention to treat at the third interim overall-survival analysis (median follow-up about 24.1 months in each arm), using FACT-P, EQ-5D-5L and the Brief Pain Inventory–Short Form.
cards.result: ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 delayed time to worsening in all assessed scales versus ARPI change: FACT-P total score median 7.46 vs 4.27 months (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.75), EQ-5D-5L utility 6.28 vs 3.88 months (HR 0.67), and BPI-SF pain intensity 5.03 vs 3.65 months (HR 0.72) — hazard ratios are relative measures. Median time to first symptomatic skeletal event was not reached with lutetium therapy versus 17.97 months with ARPI change (HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.26 to 0.63). The commonest grade ≥3 treatment-emergent event was anaemia (6% vs 7%). There were no treatment-related deaths in the lutetium group and one in the ARPI-change group.
cards.watchOut: Secondary endpoints of the one trial, in an open-label design where patients knew whether they received radioligand therapy — relevant when interpreting patient-reported outcomes.

cards.headline: PSMAfore final overall-survival analysis (Fizazi 2025): ITT overall survival NULL — median 24.48 vs 23.13 months, HR 0.91, P=0.20 — with 60.3% crossover to lutetium therapy
cards.summary: PSMAfore final overall-survival analysis (Fizazi 2025): ITT overall survival NULL — median 24.48 vs 23.13 months, HR 0.91, P=0.20 — with 60.3% crossover to lutetium therapy
cards.type: Final overall-survival and safety analysis of the PSMAfore randomised trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same 468 PSMAfore patients (234 per arm). Of those randomised to ARPI change, 141 of 234 (60.3%) crossed over to ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 — 75.4% of those with centrally confirmed radiographic progression.
cards.result: Overall survival did NOT differ significantly by intention to treat: median 24.48 months (95% CI 19.55 to 28.94) with ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA-617 versus 23.13 months (19.61 to 25.53) with ARPI change; hazard ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.14; P=0.20) — a relative measure, and not significant. The crossover-adjusted estimate by inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighting modelling was HR 0.59 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.91) — a model-based estimate that assumes the crossover mechanism is fully accounted for; it does not replace the ITT result. Exposure-adjusted grade ≥3 and serious treatment-emergent event rates were lower with lutetium therapy (60.8 vs 85.1 and 32.5 vs 49.9 per 100 patient-treatment years). In the lutetium arm, dry mouth occurred in 59.5% (135/227; grade ≥3 in 2/227) and anaemia in 27.3% (62/227; grade ≥3 in 14/227).
cards.watchOut: The ITT survival result is null and is the headline of this card; the crossover-adjusted HR 0.59 is a modelling exercise, not a randomised comparison, and must never be quoted without the ITT result beside it.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: PSMAfore is the entire taxane-naïve base. Radiographic PFS was prolonged (updated median 11.60 vs 5.59 months; HR 0.49, relative), time to worsening of quality of life and pain was delayed, symptomatic skeletal events were delayed (HR 0.41, relative), and grade 3–5 events were fewer (36% vs 48%). Final ITT overall survival was not significantly different (median 24.48 vs 23.13 months; HR 0.91; P=0.20) with 60.3% of the control arm crossing over; the crossover-adjusted HR 0.59 is model-based. Characteristic harms are dry mouth (59.5%) and anaemia (27.3%). The post-ARPI-and-taxane question (VISION) lives at live #1862 and is cross-pointed only.

shelves.title: Darolutamide + ADT without docetaxel in mHSPC (ARANOTE): radiological PFS HR 0.54 (relative); overall survival HR 0.81, not significant at the primary cutoff
shelves.question: In men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does darolutamide plus androgen-deprivation therapy — without docetaxel — versus placebo plus ADT, prolong radiological progression-free survival, and is overall survival improved? (The triplet question with docetaxel is asked at live #1868.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Pyrazoles · Androgen Antagonists · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Progression-Free Survival · Prostatic Neoplasms · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant · Aged, 80 and over · Sulfonamides
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit on radiological progression, on a single phase 3 trial — with overall survival not significant at the primary cutoff. ARANOTE (669 randomised) found darolutamide plus ADT — WITHOUT docetaxel — improved radiological progression-free survival versus placebo plus ADT (HR 0.54, a 46% relative reduction in risk of radiological progression or death), with overall survival HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.12 — not significant). Time to castration-resistant disease (HR 0.40, relative) and to pain progression (HR 0.72, relative) also favoured darolutamide, the benefit was consistent across disease-volume and risk subgroups, and fatigue was less frequent on darolutamide (5.6% vs 8.1%). This shelf is only the doublet-without-chemotherapy slice: the triplet question (darolutamide added to ADT plus docetaxel, ARASENS) is homed at live #1868, and ARASENS's survival result must not be borrowed for the doublet.

cards.headline: ARANOTE phase 3 primary report (Saad 2024): radiological PFS improved with darolutamide + ADT without docetaxel (HR 0.54, relative); overall survival not significant (HR 0.81)
cards.summary: ARANOTE phase 3 primary report (Saad 2024): radiological PFS improved with darolutamide + ADT without docetaxel (HR 0.54, relative); overall survival not significant (HR 0.81)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (ARANOTE), darolutamide + ADT vs placebo + ADT, no docetaxel — primary report
cards.people: 669 men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer randomised 2:1 to darolutamide 600 mg twice daily (n=446) or placebo (n=223), each with concomitant androgen-deprivation therapy and no docetaxel, enrolled March 2021 to August 2022. Primary cutoff June 7, 2024.
cards.result: Darolutamide plus ADT significantly improved radiological progression-free survival, with hazard ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.71; P<.0001) — a 46% relative reduction in the risk of radiological progression or death; the trial report does not give median rPFS in its abstract record. Overall survival was suggestive but NOT significant (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.12). Other secondary endpoints favoured darolutamide: time to metastatic castration-resistant disease HR 0.40 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.51) and time to pain progression HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.96) — both relative measures. Adverse events were similar between groups; fatigue was less frequent on darolutamide (5.6% vs 8.1%) and fewer patients discontinued for adverse events (6.1% vs 9.0%). Benefit was consistent across subgroups including high- and low-volume disease.
cards.watchOut: Single trial; the overall-survival confidence interval crosses 1 at this cutoff, so the shelf claims a radiological-progression benefit, not a survival benefit. The result must not be combined with ARASENS (the docetaxel triplet, live #1868).
cards.source: Saad F et al. Darolutamide in Combination With Androgen-Deprivation Therapy in Patients With Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer From the Phase III ARANOTE Trial. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2024. PMID: 39279580. Registry ID: NCT04736199. cards.headline: ARANOTE disease-volume/risk subgroups (Saad 2026): rPFS benefit in high-volume (HR 0.60), low-volume (HR 0.30), high-risk (HR 0.61) and low-risk (HR 0.40) disease — all relative measures, post hoc
cards.summary: ARANOTE disease-volume/risk subgroups (Saad 2026): rPFS benefit in high-volume (HR 0.60), low-volume (HR 0.30), high-risk (HR 0.61) and low-risk (HR 0.40) disease — all relative measures, post hoc
cards.type: Post hoc subgroup report of the ARANOTE randomised trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The 669 ARANOTE patients by disease volume (472 high-volume, 197 low-volume by CHAARTED criteria) and risk (400 high-risk, 269 low-risk by LATITUDE criteria), randomised 2:1 as in the main trial.
cards.result: Darolutamide consistently reduced radiological progression or death across subgroups: high-volume HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.80), low-volume HR 0.30 (0.15 to 0.60), high-risk HR 0.61 (0.44 to 0.86) and low-risk HR 0.40 (0.25 to 0.62), with similar trends for secondary endpoints including time to castration-resistant disease, PSA progression, pain progression and PSA <0.2 ng/mL rates. Treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between arms across all subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgroup analysis of the one trial; subgroup hazard ratios (especially low-volume, HR 0.30 on 197 patients) are imprecise and hypothesis-consistent rather than separately proven. Its PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Saad F et al. Darolutamide Plus Androgen-deprivation Therapy in Metastatic Hormone-sensitive Prostate Cancer by Disease Volume and Risk Subgroups in the Phase 3 ARANOTE Trial. European Urology. 2026. PMID: 42586872. Registry ID: NCT04736199. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: ARANOTE pain and quality-of-life analyses (Morgans 2026): delayed pain progression (HR 0.72, relative) and delayed deterioration of overall wellbeing (HR 0.76, relative)
cards.summary: ARANOTE pain and quality-of-life analyses (Morgans 2026): delayed pain progression (HR 0.72, relative) and delayed deterioration of overall wellbeing (HR 0.76, relative)
cards.type: Secondary/exploratory pain and quality-of-life analyses of the ARANOTE randomised trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The 669 ARANOTE patients (446 darolutamide, 223 placebo; treated at 133 centres in 15 countries), analysed by intention to treat for pain (Brief Pain Inventory–Short Form worst pain) and wellbeing (FACT-P total score) at the primary-analysis cutoff (median follow-up 22.8 months darolutamide, 20.3 months placebo).
cards.result: Darolutamide delayed time to pain progression (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.96) and extended time to deterioration in FACT-P total score (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.94) versus placebo — both relative measures. The commonest grade 3–4 adverse events were hypertension (4% vs 4%), anaemia (3% vs 4%) and aspartate aminotransferase increase (2% vs <1%); serious adverse events occurred in 24% in each group, and one treatment-related grade 5 event (death, not otherwise specified) occurred.
cards.watchOut: Secondary and exploratory endpoints of the one trial; the FACT-P deterioration endpoint was prespecified as exploratory. This report's phrase 'known survival benefits' refers to the darolutamide programme generally — ARANOTE's own overall-survival result at its primary cutoff was not significant (see the primary card).
cards.source: Morgans AK et al. shelves.title: Thalidomide for delayed-phase CINV: SPLIT by backbone — benefit on older 5-HT3 backbones (delayed response 70.6% vs 50.4%), null when added to a modern four-drug regimen after its failure
shelves.question: In patients receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy, does adding thalidomide to standard antiemetic prophylaxis (5-HT3 antagonist / NK1 antagonist / dexamethasone, with or without olanzapine) improve complete response and nausea control in the acute and especially the delayed phase, and at what cost in sedation, constipation and neuropathy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anorexia · Antiemetics · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Cross-Over Studies · Female · Fluorouracil · Gastrointestinal Tract · Humans · Leucovorin · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Organoplatinum Compounds · Prospective Studies · Thalidomide · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting
shelves.balance: SPLIT by backbone regimen and by trial generation. Two meta-analyses dominated by older, largely Chinese RCTs of thalidomide added to a 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone found higher complete-response and no-nausea rates, with the largest gains in the DELAYED phase (delayed complete response 70.6% vs 50.4%, RR 1.53 — a relative measure; delayed no-nausea RR 1.69, relative). The earliest primary trial (crossover, n=50 assessable, on a ramosetron + dexamethasone backbone with modified FOLFOX7) agrees for delayed nausea and emesis, at the cost of much more sedation/dizziness (42% vs 9.6%). But the one modern trial — thalidomide added to a FOUR-drug backbone (ondansetron, aprepitant, dexamethasone, olanzapine) in patients who had already failed that backbone — was NULL for its primary endpoint (no nausea 0–120 h: 16% vs 21% on placebo), though severe delayed nausea was less frequent and mild constipation more frequent. So the synthesis benefit belongs to weaker backbones; on a modern four-drug backbone, no added nausea control is shown. Thalidomide is teratogenic and requires strict pregnancy-prevention handling, and sedation, constipation and drowsiness/dizziness are its recurring harms — all on the face, not in a footnote. The olanzapine CINV shelves (live #769, #1789) ask a different agent's question.

cards.headline: Crossover RCT (Liu 2009): thalidomide added to ramosetron + dexamethasone improved DELAYED nausea and emesis complete response after modified FOLFOX7 — with far more sedation/dizziness (42% vs 9.6%)
cards.summary: Crossover RCT (Liu 2009): thalidomide added to ramosetron + dexamethasone improved DELAYED nausea and emesis complete response after modified FOLFOX7 — with far more sedation/dizziness (42% vs 9.6%)
cards.type: Prospective randomised crossover trial, thalidomide + ramosetron/dexamethasone vs ramosetron/dexamethasone alone (each patient both conditions)
cards.people: 52 chemotherapy-naive patients with malignant tumours enrolled, 50 (96%) assessable, in a prospective randomised crossover study: each patient received ramosetron 0.3 mg + dexamethasone 10 mg intravenously on day 1 in one cycle (A), and the same plus thalidomide 150 mg orally twice daily on days 2–5 in the other cycle (B), with the order randomised (A–B or B–A groups). The chemotherapy was a modified FOLFOX7 regimen. The primary endpoint was control of delayed (days 2–5) chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
cards.result: Complete response for delayed nausea (no nausea) was higher with thalidomide on day 2 (52% vs 24%; P=0.004), day 3 (58% vs 24%; P=0.001) and day 4 (60% vs 36%; P=0.016), and complete response for delayed emesis (no emetic episodes, no rescue therapy) on day 2 (86% vs 66%; P=0.019) and day 3 (76% vs 56%; P=0.035) — absolute rates, printed both. Complete response for anorexia was also higher with thalidomide on days 2–5. More patients reported sedation or dizziness with thalidomide (42% vs 9.6%; P=0.000). The authors concluded thalidomide improves prevention of chemotherapy-induced gastrointestinal side effects after modified FOLFOX7.
cards.watchOut: A 2009 crossover trial on a two-drug antiemetic backbone without an NK1 antagonist or olanzapine — its result does not predict added benefit on modern multi-drug prophylaxis (see the 2025 card). Crossover designs in CINV can carry period and expectation effects, and thalidomide's sedation was unblinding in practice.
cards.source: Liu Y et al. Thalidomide improves prevention of chemotherapy-induced gastrointestinal side effects following a modified FOLFOX7 regimen: results of a prospective randomized crossover study. Tumori. 2009. cards.headline: Modern four-drug-backbone RCT (Gowda 2025): adding thalidomide after failing ondansetron + aprepitant + dexamethasone + olanzapine was NULL for no-nausea (16% vs 21%)
cards.summary: Modern four-drug-backbone RCT (Gowda 2025): adding thalidomide after failing ondansetron + aprepitant + dexamethasone + olanzapine was NULL for no-nausea (16% vs 21%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, thalidomide + four-drug prophylaxis vs placebo + four-drug prophylaxis in cycle 2 after cycle-1 failure
cards.people: Adults who had failed four-drug prophylaxis (ondansetron, aprepitant, dexamethasone, olanzapine — OAOD) in cycle 1 of highly emetogenic chemotherapy (any nausea in 0–120 h) were randomised in cycle 2 to thalidomide 50 mg once daily for 5 days + OAOD (n=25) or placebo + OAOD (n=24). 105 patients were enrolled in cycle 1 and 49 randomised; median age 45 years; all received anthracycline/cyclophosphamide for breast cancer. The trial was registered with CTRI (CTRI/2021/08/035980, as printed in the record).
cards.result: The primary endpoint was NOT met: no nausea in 0–120 h was 16% with thalidomide versus 21% with placebo (p=0.72), and acute (32% vs 25%; p=0.58) and delayed 24–72 h (32% vs 25%; p=0.46) no-nausea rates also did not differ significantly — absolute rates, printed both. Severe nausea (VAS ≥7) in the delayed period was reduced with thalidomide (4% vs 30%; p=0.02), a secondary endpoint. Sedation and dizziness were not increased, but mild constipation was higher with thalidomide (84% vs 58%; p=0.047). The authors conclude adding thalidomide did not improve nausea control in patients who had failed the four-drug regimen.
cards.watchOut: Small (49 randomised) and in a selected population — patients who had already failed the strongest standard backbone, all on one chemotherapy regimen for breast cancer. Its null primary result governs the modern-backbone question; the severe-nausea finding is a secondary endpoint in a small sample.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Xie 2021): thalidomide + 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone raised complete response, most in the delayed phase (70.6% vs 50.4%; RR 1.53, relative) — 34 RCTs, 3,168 patients, largely Chinese
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Xie 2021): thalidomide + 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone raised complete response, most in the delayed phase (70.6% vs 50.4%; RR 1.53, relative) — 34 RCTs, 3,168 patients, largely Chinese
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, thalidomide add-on vs no thalidomide on 5-HT3-antagonist backbones in highly emetogenic chemotherapy
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of thalidomide as pre-medication for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting after highly emetogenic chemotherapy: 34 RCTs including 3,168 patients, comparing thalidomide plus a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist with or without dexamethasone against the same backbone without thalidomide. The review notes thalidomide's use for this purpose is a practice concentrated in China.
cards.result: Complete response was higher with thalidomide in the acute phase (74.4% vs 67.4%; RR 1.10), delayed phase (70.6% vs 50.4%; RR 1.53) and overall phase (68.4% vs 53.4%; RR 1.28) — risk ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute rates. No-nausea rates were also higher (acute 61.7% vs 55.5%, RR 1.12; delayed 50.5% vs 30.0%, RR 1.69; overall 44.6% vs 29.9%, RR 1.50 — relative). There was no significant difference in fatigue, headache, diarrhoea, rash, hepatorenal damage or myelosuppression, and KPS improvement, weight gain, appetite and sleep quality were more frequent with thalidomide.
cards.watchOut: The pooled backbones are 5-HT3 antagonist ± dexamethasone — weaker than modern three- and four-drug prophylaxis — and the trial base is concentrated in China and single-regimen studies, so the pooled benefit cannot be assumed on a modern backbone (the 2025 trial carded above found none). Its PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Wang 2020): thalidomide enhanced delayed and overall complete response for nausea (RR 1.69, relative) and vomiting (RR 1.38, relative); sedation, constipation and drowsiness/dizziness slightly more frequent
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Wang 2020): thalidomide enhanced delayed and overall complete response for nausea (RR 1.69, relative) and vomiting (RR 1.38, relative); sedation, constipation and drowsiness/dizziness slightly more frequent
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials, thalidomide vs control for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
cards.people: A meta-analysis of randomised trials of thalidomide for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting: 14 RCTs including 1,744 patients (42% male) reported risk ratios for the primary nausea/vomiting outcomes, and 30 studies monitored adverse events.
cards.result: Thalidomide statistically enhanced complete response in the delayed phase (nausea RR 1.69; 95% CI 1.47 to 1.94; vomiting RR 1.38; 95% CI 1.26 to 1.51) and overall phase (nausea RR 1.54; 95% CI 1.31 to 1.81; vomiting RR 1.31; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.46) — all relative measures; the acute-phase claim is not made for the primary outcomes in this synthesis. A dose subgroup analysis (100 vs 200 mg/day) showed no significant difference. All monitored adverse events were under grade 3; of the eight commonest, sedation, constipation and drowsiness/dizziness were slightly more frequent with thalidomide than controls.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis overlaps substantially with the 2021 meta-analysis carded above (the same underlying, largely Chinese RCT literature) — the two syntheses are not independent confirmations of each other. Its PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Synthesis: thalidomide's antiemetic benefit is real on older two-drug backbones and concentrated in the delayed phase — and absent on the one modern four-drug backbone tested; sedation and constipation price it, and teratogenicity governs its handling
cards.summary: Synthesis: thalidomide's antiemetic benefit is real on older two-drug backbones and concentrated in the delayed phase — and absent on the one modern four-drug backbone tested; sedation and constipation price it, and teratogenicity governs its handling
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Carded per backbone regimen, as the row requires: on ramosetron + dexamethasone (crossover RCT, 50 assessable) and in two overlapping meta-analyses of 5-HT3-antagonist backbones (34 RCTs, 3,168 patients; 14 RCTs, 1,744 patients), thalidomide improved delayed complete response and no-nausea rates (delayed CR 70.6% vs 50.4% in the larger synthesis). On a modern four-drug backbone in prior failures (49 randomised), the primary endpoint was null (no nausea 16% vs 21%). Harms: sedation/dizziness (42% vs 9.6% in the crossover trial), constipation (84% vs 58% in the modern trial), and the class harms of sedation, constipation and neuropathy with longer use; thalidomide is teratogenic and its use requires strict pregnancy-prevention handling, which belongs in any clinical decision to use it. The olanzapine add-on questions live at live #769 and #1789.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. The two meta-analyses share much of their underlying trial base and must not be counted as two independent bodies of evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Enzalutamide + radium-223 in first-line mCRPC (PEACE-3, one trial): final survival 38.2 vs 32.6 months — benefit conditional on mandatory bone-protecting agents
shelves.question: In men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases receiving first-line therapy, does adding six cycles of radium-223 to enzalutamide, versus enzalutamide alone, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival — and what bone-protecting-agent co-treatment does the combination require? (Single programme: the PEACE-3 / EORTC 1333 trial; bone-protecting-agent co-administration was mandated from March 2018 and is part of the tested intervention.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant · Nitriles · Benzamides · Radium · Phenylthiohydantoin · Aged · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Bone Neoplasms · Middle Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Progression-Free Survival
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — with a mandatory condition printed on the face: co-administration of a bone-protecting agent (zoledronic acid or denosumab), mandated mid-trial from March 2018 after the ERA-223 fracture signal, is part of the tested intervention as finally delivered, and this combination must not be presented without it. On a single programme (one trial, PEACE-3 / EORTC 1333, three reports), adding six cycles of radium-223 to first-line enzalutamide in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases improved radiographic progression-free survival (median 19.4 vs 16.4 months; hazard ratio 0.69 — a relative measure) and, in the final analysis superseding the interim read, overall survival (median 38.2 vs 32.6 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative; P=.0096, meeting the predefined significance level; 317 deaths at median follow-up 58 months). The cost: grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent events in 69.3% versus 57.6% at the final analysis, and fractures in 24.3% versus 13.4% across the trial's pre- and post-mandate eras — with a bone-protecting agent, 1-year fracture rates fell from 15.6% to 2.6% in the enzalutamide-alone arm (the combination-arm read is taken from the safety report as carded). Radium-223 versus placebo in symptomatic bone-metastatic disease (ALSYMPCA) is homed at live #1869 — cross-pointed in prose only.

cards.headline: PEACE-3 primary report (Tombal 2025): radiographic progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.69 (relative) — median 19.4 versus 16.4 months; interim overall-survival hazard ratio 0.69 (relative) at 80% of events, under non-proportional hazards
cards.summary: PEACE-3 primary report (Tombal 2025): radiographic progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.69 (relative) — median 19.4 versus 16.4 months; interim overall-survival hazard ratio 0.69 (relative) at 80% of events, under non-proportional hazards
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (EORTC 1333 / PEACE-3), enzalutamide + radium-223 vs enzalutamide alone, first-line mCRPC with bone metastases — primary report with interim overall survival
cards.people: 446 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and bone metastases receiving first-line therapy (including 11 who received abiraterone), randomised from November 2015 to March 2023 to enzalutamide alone or enzalutamide plus six monthly injections of radium-223. From March 2018, co-administration of zoledronic acid or denosumab was mandatory. The primary endpoint was radiological progression-free survival by investigator assessment.
cards.result: The hazard ratio for radiographic progression-free survival was 0.69 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.87; P=0.0009 — a relative measure), with median radiographic progression-free survival of 19.4 months (95% CI 17.1 to 25.3) on the combination versus 16.4 months (95% CI 13.8 to 19.2) on enzalutamide alone. At the preplanned interim analysis at 80% of overall-survival events, the hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.69 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.90; P=0.0031 — relative), with median overall survival 42.3 months (95% CI 36.8 to 49.1) versus 35.0 months (95% CI 28.8 to 38.9); because of non-proportional hazards this was to be tested further at the final analysis (carded next). Grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 65.6% (combination) versus 55.8% (enzalutamide); the most frequent grade 3-or-worse events in the combination arm were hypertension (34%), fatigue (6%), fracture (5%), anaemia (5%) and neutropenia (5%). Fractures (treatment-emergent or post-treatment, symptomatic or pathologic, with or without bone-protecting agent) were reported in 53 patients (24.3%) on the combination versus 30 (13.4%) on enzalutamide.
cards.watchOut: The overall-survival read in this report is an interim analysis taken under non-proportional hazards and is superseded by the final analysis carded next — quote the final figures for survival. Fracture rates span the era before bone-protecting agents were mandated, so they overstate the risk of the combination as finally delivered (with mandatory bone protection).
cards.source: Tombal B et al. Enzalutamide plus radium-223 in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer: results of the EORTC 1333/PEACE-3 trial. cards.headline: PEACE-3 final overall-survival analysis (Gillessen 2026): median overall survival 38.2 versus 32.6 months (hazard ratio 0.76, relative; P=.0096, meeting the predefined significance level); updated radiographic PFS hazard ratio 0.71 (relative)
cards.summary: PEACE-3 final overall-survival analysis (Gillessen 2026): median overall survival 38.2 versus 32.6 months (hazard ratio 0.76, relative; P=.0096, meeting the predefined significance level); updated radiographic PFS hazard ratio 0.71 (relative)
cards.type: Final overall-survival analysis of the PEACE-3 trial (same trial as the primary card — supersedes its interim survival read; not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same 446 randomised patients (224 enzalutamide alone, 222 combination), with the final overall-survival analysis triggered on May 1, 2025: median follow-up 58 months and 317 deaths. Bone-protecting-agent co-administration was mandatory for all patients from March 2018.
cards.result: The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.76 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.96; P=0.0096 — a relative measure) in favour of enzalutamide plus radium-223, reaching the predefined significance level of under 0.0248; median overall survival was 38.2 months (95% CI 33.1 to 44.8) on the combination versus 32.6 months (95% CI 29.3 to 38.2) on enzalutamide alone. The updated hazard ratio for radiographic progression-free survival was 0.71 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.89 — relative). Grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent adverse events were 69.3% (combination) versus 57.6% (enzalutamide), and treatment-related grade 3-or-worse events 28.9% versus 18.8%, with hypertension the most frequent. The authors state that co-administration of a bone-protecting agent is required to reduce skeletal complications.
cards.watchOut: Same single trial at final maturity — the survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.76) is smaller than the interim read suggested (0.69), which is exactly why both are carded and labelled; the final figures govern. The trial's population and delivery changed mid-course when bone protection became mandatory in 2018.

cards.headline: PEACE-3 fracture / bone-protecting-agent safety analysis (Gillessen 2025): after the ERA-223 signal, bone-protecting-agent use was mandated (rising from 46.1% to 97%); with a bone-protecting agent, 1-year fractures fell from 15.6% to 2.6% on enzalutamide alone
cards.summary: PEACE-3 fracture / bone-protecting-agent safety analysis (Gillessen 2025): after the ERA-223 signal, bone-protecting-agent use was mandated (rising from 46.1% to 97%); with a bone-protecting agent, 1-year fractures fell from 15.6% to 2.6% on enzalutamide alone
cards.type: Fracture / bone-protecting-agent safety analysis of the PEACE-3 trial (same trial as above — a safety report, not independent efficacy evidence)
cards.people: Patients in the PEACE-3 trial (enzalutamide plus radium-223 versus enzalutamide alone for first-line metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases), in an interim safety analysis of fracture rates before and after the independent data monitoring committee mandated bone-protecting-agent use in response to the ERA-223 trial (abiraterone with or without radium-223) fracture signal.
cards.result: Bone-protecting-agent use increased from 46.1% to 97% after the mandate. For patients who received bone-protecting-agent therapy, fracture rates significantly decreased in both study arms: at 1 year, fractures decreased from 15.6% to 2.6% with a bone-protecting agent in patients receiving enzalutamide monotherapy. The authors conclude the analysis underscores the high fracture risk in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and the necessity of complying with bone-protecting-agent guidelines in the androgen-receptor-pathway-inhibitor era.
cards.watchOut: An interim, era-based (before versus after the mandate) safety comparison, not a randomised test of bone protection — and the fetched record quantifies the 1-year fracture fall (15.6% to 2.6%) for the enzalutamide-alone arm, stating the decrease occurred in both arms without printing the combination arm's paired figures; no combination-arm numbers are invented here.
cards.source: Gillessen S et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — enzalutamide plus six cycles of radium-223 improved radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and, at final analysis, overall survival (38.2 vs 32.6 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative) in first-line bone-metastatic mCRPC — conditional on mandatory bone-protecting-agent co-treatment, without which fracture risk is unacceptably high
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — enzalutamide plus six cycles of radium-223 improved radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and, at final analysis, overall survival (38.2 vs 32.6 months; hazard ratio 0.76, relative) in first-line bone-metastatic mCRPC — conditional on mandatory bone-protecting-agent co-treatment, without which fracture risk is unacceptably high
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (a single programme: the PEACE-3 / EORTC 1333 trial — primary report, final survival analysis, and fracture safety analysis). Radium-223 versus placebo (ALSYMPCA) is homed at live #1869 and is not carded here.
cards.result: Radiographic progression-free survival: median 19.4 versus 16.4 months (hazard ratio 0.69 primary; 0.71 updated — relative measures with absolute medians alongside). Overall survival at final analysis (317 deaths, median follow-up 58 months): median 38.2 versus 32.6 months (hazard ratio 0.76; P=.0096 — relative), superseding the interim hazard ratio of 0.69. Harm: grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent events 69.3% versus 57.6% at final analysis, and fractures 24.3% versus 13.4% across pre- and post-mandate eras. The mandate is part of the intervention: bone-protecting-agent use rose from 46.1% to 97%, and with bone protection the enzalutamide-alone arm's 1-year fracture rate fell from 15.6% to 2.6%, with decreases in both arms. The combination as finally delivered is enzalutamide + radium-223 + a bone-protecting agent.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Capivasertib + abiraterone in PTEN-deficient mHSPC (CAPItello-281): PFS 33.2 vs 25.7 months on exactly 2 reports — survival not confirmed, diarrhoea in half
shelves.question: In men with PTEN-deficient (≥90% of viable malignant cells without cytoplasmic PTEN staining) metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, does adding the AKT inhibitor capivasertib to abiraterone (with prednisone/prednisolone and androgen deprivation therapy), versus placebo plus abiraterone, prolong radiographic progression-free and overall survival, and at what toxicity cost?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · PTEN Phosphohydrolase · Prostatic Neoplasms · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Aged · Androstenes · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines · Progression-Free Survival · Androgen Antagonists · Aged, 80 and over · Pyrazoles · Double-Blind Method · Pyrroles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, on exactly 2 reports of one trial. CAPItello-281 (1,012 randomised with PTEN-deficient tumours; only 25.3% of 6,003 validly tested tumours qualified) found radiographic progression-free survival of 33.2 versus 25.7 months with capivasertib plus abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone (hazard ratio 0.81, relative, P=0.034). Overall survival was NOT significant at the primary, confirmatory read (hazard ratio 0.90, relative, P=0.401, at 26.4% maturity); a later ad hoc descriptive update at 42% maturity gave hazard ratio 0.82 (relative, nominal P=0.044; medians 57.4 vs 46.5 months) — supportive only, not prespecified. Harms are common: diarrhoea 51.9% vs 8.0%, hyperglycaemia 38.0% vs 12.9%, rash 35.4% vs 7.0%, adverse-event-associated deaths 7.2% vs 5.2%.

cards.headline: CAPItello-281 primary report (Fizazi 2026): capivasertib + abiraterone improved radiographic PFS in PTEN-deficient mHSPC — median 33.2 vs 25.7 months, hazard ratio 0.81 (relative); overall survival was immature and NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.90, P=0.401)
cards.summary: CAPItello-281 primary report (Fizazi 2026): capivasertib + abiraterone improved radiographic PFS in PTEN-deficient mHSPC — median 33.2 vs 25.7 months, hazard ratio 0.81 (relative); overall survival was immature and NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.90, P=0.401)
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind randomised trial (CAPItello-281), capivasertib + abiraterone vs placebo + abiraterone, both with prednisone/prednisolone and ADT — primary report (report 1 of exactly 2 on this shelf)
cards.people: 1,012 patients with PTEN-deficient metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer were randomised 1:1 (507 capivasertib, 505 placebo), each plus abiraterone, prednisone/prednisolone and androgen deprivation therapy. PTEN-deficient meant ≥90% of viable malignant cells with no specific cytoplasmic PTEN staining. Of 6,003 patients with valid tumour test results, only 25.3% (1,519) had PTEN-deficient tumours — the screening funnel is part of this question.
cards.result: Investigator-assessed radiographic progression-free survival, the primary endpoint, was median 33.2 months with capivasertib plus abiraterone versus 25.7 months with placebo plus abiraterone — hazard ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.98; P=0.034), a relative measure beside the 7.5-month absolute median difference. Overall survival was a key secondary endpoint but immature at this analysis (26.4% maturity): hazard ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.15; P=0.401), a relative measure that was NOT statistically significant — the confirmatory survival read at primary analysis is therefore negative/immature, not positive.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base: this shelf rests on exactly 2 reports of this one trial, stated on the face. Post hoc analyses at higher PTEN-loss cut-offs (≥95%, ≥99%, 100%) are exploratory and are not carded as separate evidence.

cards.people: The same 1,012 randomised patients (507 capivasertib plus abiraterone, 505 placebo plus abiraterone), at an ad hoc data cut-off of 9 March 2026 with median follow-up 39 months in both arms and 17 months' additional follow-up.
cards.result: The report itself states these analyses — including overall survival, the alpha-controlled key secondary endpoint, and radiographic PFS — were descriptive and not prespecified in the protocol. Overall survival hazard ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.99; nominal P=0.044), a relative measure, with median overall survival 57.4 versus 46.5 months. cards.watchOut: Nominal P values from a descriptive, non-alpha-controlled analysis cannot upgrade the primary report's non-significant interim survival read into a confirmed survival benefit. This card is supportive only, exactly as the commissioning row directs.
