shelves.title: Bosutinib in chronic-phase CML (BFORE/BELA/BYOND): BFORE positive at 400 mg, BELA missed its primary endpoint at 500 mg, BYOND single-arm in pretreated disease
shelves.question: In adults with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic-phase CML — newly diagnosed, against imatinib (BFORE at 400 mg; BELA at 500 mg) — does the dual SRC/ABL inhibitor bosutinib produce faster and deeper molecular and cytogenetic responses than imatinib, and in patients resistant or intolerant to prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BYOND) what response does it produce, at what gastrointestinal and hepatic cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aniline Compounds · Antineoplastic Agents · Biomarkers, Tumor · Disease Progression · Female · Fusion Proteins, bcr-abl · Genetic Predisposition to Disease · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate · Leukemia, Myelogenous, Chronic, BCR-ABL Positive · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles · Phenotype · Philadelphia Chromosome · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Quinolines · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT across the first-line programme — one positive and one negative trial at two different doses, never averaged into a win. BFORE (bosutinib 400 mg, n=536): major molecular response at 12 months 47.2% vs 36.9% on imatinib (P=.02) and complete cytogenetic response by 12 months 77.2% vs 66.4% (P=.0075). BELA (bosutinib 500 mg, n=502): the primary endpoint was NOT met — complete cytogenetic response at 12 months 70% vs 68% (P=.601) — although major molecular response was higher (41% vs 27%; P<.001). BYOND (phase 4, n=163) is single-arm support in pretreated disease (confirmed major cytogenetic response by 1 year 75.8% after 1–2 prior TKIs, 62.2% after 3; diarrhoea in 87.7% — uncontrolled). Gastrointestinal and hepatic events price the drug: grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea 7.8% vs 0.8% and ALT increase 19.0% vs 1.5% in BFORE. Cross-points in prose only: asciminib packs #4481 and #7304 and ponatinib pack #7015 ask different questions.

cards.headline: BFORE phase 3 (Cortes 2018): bosutinib 400 mg beat imatinib on molecular and cytogenetic response at 12 months — MMR 47.2% vs 36.9%; CCyR 77.2% vs 66.4%
cards.summary: BFORE phase 3 (Cortes 2018): bosutinib 400 mg beat imatinib on molecular and cytogenetic response at 12 months — MMR 47.2% vs 36.9%; CCyR 77.2% vs 66.4%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (BFORE), bosutinib 400 mg vs imatinib in newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML
cards.people: 536 patients with newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia, randomised 1:1 to bosutinib 400 mg once daily (268) or imatinib (268); per protocol, efficacy was assessed in Philadelphia chromosome-positive patients with typical transcripts (246 bosutinib, 241 imatinib).
cards.result: The major molecular response rate at 12 months (primary endpoint) was significantly higher with bosutinib (47.2% vs 36.9%; P=.02), as was the complete cytogenetic response rate by 12 months (77.2% vs 66.4%; P=.0075) — absolute rates. Responses came earlier with bosutinib. Progression to accelerated/blast phase occurred in 4 patients (1.6%) on bosutinib vs 6 (2.5%) on imatinib. Grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea occurred in 7.8% vs 0.8%, ALT increase in 19.0% vs 1.5% and AST increase in 9.7% vs 1.9%; cardiac and vascular toxicities were uncommon. Discontinuation for drug-related toxicity: 12.7% vs 8.7%.
cards.watchOut: Endpoints are molecular and cytogenetic response rates, not survival; efficacy was assessed in the per-protocol typical-transcript population (487 of 536 randomised). The tested dose here is 400 mg — BELA, carded below, tested 500 mg and missed its primary endpoint.
cards.source: Cortes JE et al. Bosutinib Versus Imatinib for Newly Diagnosed Chronic Myeloid Leukemia: Results From the Randomized BFORE Trial. cards.headline: BELA phase 3 (Cortes 2012): bosutinib 500 mg MISSED its primary endpoint — CCyR at 12 months 70% vs 68% on imatinib (P=.601) — despite higher MMR (41% vs 27%)
cards.summary: BELA phase 3 (Cortes 2012): bosutinib 500 mg MISSED its primary endpoint — CCyR at 12 months 70% vs 68% on imatinib (P=.601) — despite higher MMR (41% vs 27%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (BELA), bosutinib 500 mg vs imatinib in newly diagnosed chronic-phase CML
cards.people: 502 patients with newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia, randomised 1:1 to bosutinib 500 mg daily or imatinib 400 mg daily.
cards.result: The complete cytogenetic response rate at 12 months did not differ (70%, 95% CI 64–76, vs 68%, 95% CI 62–74; P=.601) — the trial did NOT achieve its primary endpoint. The major molecular response rate at 12 months was higher with bosutinib (41% vs 27%; P<.001), and times to cytogenetic and molecular response were faster. On-treatment transformation to accelerated/blast phase occurred in 4 patients (2%) on bosutinib vs 10 (4%) on imatinib; CML-related deaths numbered 3 vs 8. Gastrointestinal and liver events were more frequent with bosutinib; neutropenia, musculoskeletal disorders and oedema were more frequent with imatinib.
cards.watchOut: A negative trial on its primary endpoint at the 500 mg dose — it belongs on the face beside BFORE's positive 400 mg read, and the two must not be averaged into a programme win.

cards.headline: BYOND phase 4 (Hochhaus 2020): bosutinib 500 mg in TKI-resistant/intolerant chronic-phase CML — confirmed major cytogenetic response by 1 year 75.8% after 1–2 prior TKIs, 62.2% after 3 — SINGLE-ARM, uncontrolled
cards.summary: BYOND phase 4 (Hochhaus 2020): bosutinib 500 mg in TKI-resistant/intolerant chronic-phase CML — confirmed major cytogenetic response by 1 year 75.8% after 1–2 prior TKIs, 62.2% after 3 — SINGLE-ARM, uncontrolled
cards.type: Phase 4 single-arm study (BYOND), bosutinib in pretreated CML — uncontrolled
cards.people: 163 patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia resistant or intolerant to prior tyrosine kinase inhibitors (156 with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic-phase disease), treated with bosutinib 500 mg once daily as starting dose; median treatment duration 23.7 months, with 56.4% of chronic-phase patients still on bosutinib at analysis.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — cumulative confirmed major cytogenetic response by 1 year — was 75.8% in chronic-phase patients after 1–2 prior TKIs and 62.2% after 3 prior TKIs. Cumulative complete cytogenetic response and major molecular response rates by 1 year in chronic-phase patients overall were 80.6% and 70.5%. No patient progressed to accelerated/blast phase on treatment. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events across all patients were diarrhoea (87.7%), nausea (39.9%) and vomiting (32.5%) — all uncontrolled rates.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with no comparator: response rates describe activity after prior TKIs and cannot be compared directly with the first-line randomised trials carded above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bosutinib's first-line record is one positive trial at 400 mg (BFORE) and one primary-endpoint miss at 500 mg (BELA), both showing faster, deeper molecular responses than imatinib at a gastrointestinal and hepatic price; BYOND adds single-arm evidence of activity after prior TKIs
cards.summary: Synthesis: bosutinib's first-line record is one positive trial at 400 mg (BFORE) and one primary-endpoint miss at 500 mg (BELA), both showing faster, deeper molecular responses than imatinib at a gastrointestinal and hepatic price; BYOND adds single-arm evidence of activity after prior TKIs
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (BFORE, n=536; BELA, n=502; BYOND, n=163 single-arm).
cards.result: BFORE met its primary endpoint at the later-standard 400 mg dose (major molecular response 47.2% vs 36.9%); BELA missed its primary cytogenetic endpoint at 500 mg (70% vs 68%) despite a higher molecular response rate. Both trials showed more diarrhoea and transaminase elevation with bosutinib. In pretreated disease, BYOND's uncontrolled confirmed major cytogenetic response rates (75.8% after 1–2 prior TKIs; 62.2% after 3) support activity without establishing comparative benefit. No card on this shelf reports a survival comparison.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Hypomethylating agents in higher-risk MDS (AZA-001/CALGB 9221/decitabine): azacitidine survival win (24.5 vs 15.0 months); decitabine response without a survival win
shelves.question: In patients with higher-risk myelodysplastic syndromes, do hypomethylating agents — azacitidine against conventional care regimens (AZA-001) or supportive care (CALGB 9221), and decitabine against best supportive care — prolong overall survival, delay leukaemic transformation and improve response, compared with the pre-hypomethylating standard?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic · Azacitidine · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myelodysplastic Syndromes · Proportional Hazards Models
shelves.balance: SPLIT across the class — the shelf must not be read as a uniform survival claim. Azacitidine carries the survival evidence: AZA-001 (phase 3, n=358) showed median overall survival 24.5 vs 15.0 months against conventional care (hazard ratio 0.58, relative; P=.0001), and CALGB 9221 (n=191) showed responses in 60% vs 5% against supportive care with delayed leukaemic transformation, in a trial whose crossover design qualifies its survival read. Decitabine (phase 3, n=170, tested on a 3-day inpatient schedule) improved response (17% vs 0%) and time to AML progression or death in the intermediate-2/high-risk slice (12.0 vs 6.8 months; P=.03) but the all-patient read was a non-significant trend (P=.16) with no overall-survival win shown. Cross-points in prose only: lower-risk MDS (live #674), oral decitabine–cedazuridine bioequivalence (pack #7019) and oral azacitidine maintenance in AML remission (pack #7018) are different questions.

cards.headline: AZA-001 phase 3 (Fenaux 2009): azacitidine prolonged overall survival in higher-risk MDS — median 24.5 vs 15.0 months vs conventional care (hazard ratio 0.58, relative; P=.0001)
cards.summary: AZA-001 phase 3 (Fenaux 2009): azacitidine prolonged overall survival in higher-risk MDS — median 24.5 vs 15.0 months vs conventional care (hazard ratio 0.58, relative; P=.0001)
cards.type: Phase 3 international open-label randomised trial (AZA-001), azacitidine vs conventional care regimens in higher-risk MDS
cards.people: 358 patients with higher-risk myelodysplastic syndromes, randomised 1:1 to azacitidine 75 mg/m² daily for 7 days every 28 days (179) or conventional care (179) — best supportive care, low-dose cytarabine or intensive chemotherapy, preselected by investigators before randomisation.
cards.result: After median follow-up 21.1 months, median overall survival was 24.5 vs 15.0 months (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.43–0.77; stratified log-rank P=.0001 — a relative measure). Deaths numbered 82 in the azacitidine group vs 113 in the conventional care group; 2-year survival by Kaplan–Meier estimate was 50.8% vs 26.2% (absolute rates; P<.0001). Peripheral cytopenias were the most common grade 3–4 adverse events for all treatments.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a preselected mix of three conventional strategies (supportive care, low-dose cytarabine, intensive chemotherapy), not a single control treatment; open-label design.
cards.source: Fenaux P et al. Efficacy of azacitidine compared with that of conventional care regimens in the treatment of higher-risk myelodysplastic syndromes: a randomised, open-label, phase III study. The Lancet. Oncology. 2009. PMID: 19230772. Registry ID: NCT00071799. cards.headline: CALGB 9221 randomised trial (Silverman 2002): azacitidine vs supportive care — responses 60% vs 5%, transformation as first event 15% vs 38%; crossover permitted, landmark survival 18 vs 11 additional months
cards.summary: CALGB 9221 randomised trial (Silverman 2002): azacitidine vs supportive care — responses 60% vs 5%, transformation as first event 15% vs 38%; crossover permitted, landmark survival 18 vs 11 additional months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (CALGB 9221), azacitidine vs supportive care in MDS, with crossover on worsening
cards.people: 191 patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (French-American-British criteria), randomised to azacitidine 75 mg/m²/day subcutaneously for 7 days every 28 days or supportive care (transfusions and antibiotics as required in both arms); supportive-care patients whose disease worsened could cross over to azacitidine.
cards.result: Responses occurred in 60% of the azacitidine arm (7% complete, 16% partial, 37% improved) vs 5% (improved only) on supportive care (P<.001 — absolute rates). Median time to leukaemic transformation or death was 21 vs 13 months (P=.007); transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia as the first event occurred in 15% vs 38% (P=.001). To remove the confounding of early crossover, a landmark analysis after 6 months showed median survival of an additional 18 months for azacitidine vs 11 months for supportive care (P=.03) — labelled as a landmark analysis, not the primary survival read. Quality of life significantly favoured patients initially randomised to azacitidine.
cards.watchOut: Crossover on worsening was built into the design, so the survival comparison is confounded by design — the 18 vs 11 month figure is a post-crossover landmark analysis and is labelled as such on this card.

cards.headline: Decitabine phase 3 (Kantarjian 2006): response 17% vs 0% on supportive care; time to AML progression or death favoured decitabine in intermediate-2/high-risk disease (12.0 vs 6.8 months; P=.03) but was a trend overall (P=.16)
cards.summary: Decitabine phase 3 (Kantarjian 2006): response 17% vs 0% on supportive care; time to AML progression or death favoured decitabine in intermediate-2/high-risk disease (12.0 vs 6.8 months; P=.03) but was a trend overall (P=.16)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial, decitabine (3-day schedule) vs best supportive care in MDS
cards.people: 170 patients with myelodysplastic syndromes, randomised to decitabine 15 mg/m² intravenously over 3 hours every 8 hours for 3 days (135 mg/m² per course, repeated every 6 weeks — the tested 3-day inpatient schedule) or best supportive care.
cards.result: Overall response was 17% with decitabine (9% complete responses) vs 0% with supportive care (P<.001 — absolute rates); a further 13% of decitabine patients achieved haematologic improvement, responses were durable (median 10.3 months) and were associated with transfusion independence. Median time to AML progression or death was 12.1 vs 7.8 months in all patients (P=.16 — a non-significant trend), 12.0 vs 6.8 months in International Prognostic Scoring System intermediate-2/high-risk disease (P=.03), 12.6 vs 9.4 months in de novo disease (P=.04) and 12.3 vs 7.3 months in treatment-naive patients (P=.08) — print both the slice and the all-patient read exactly. No overall-survival benefit is reported in this record.
cards.watchOut: The schedule tested (15 mg/m² every 8 hours for 3 days, inpatient) differs from the later 5-day schedule in common use — do not transfer this read to the 5-day regimen unlabelled. Response benefit without a demonstrated overall-survival win.
cards.source: Kantarjian H et al. Decitabine improves patient outcomes in myelodysplastic syndromes: results of a phase III randomized study. Cancer. 2006. PMID: 16532500. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (AZA-001, n=358; CALGB 9221, n=191; decitabine phase 3, n=170).
cards.result: Two agents, three randomised trials, one class question. AZA-001 is the only trial with a clean overall-survival win (hazard ratio 0.58, relative). CALGB 9221 supports azacitidine on response (60% vs 5%), delayed transformation and quality of life, with crossover qualifying its survival read. Decitabine produced responses (17% vs 0%) and delayed AML progression or death in the higher-risk slice, on a 3-day schedule no longer standard, without a demonstrated survival benefit. The class is therefore not a uniform survival claim.

shelves.title: Relugolix vs leuprolide in advanced prostate cancer (HERO): superior sustained castration (96.7% vs 88.8%) and far faster testosterone recovery; cardiovascular difference unpowered
shelves.question: In men with advanced prostate cancer requiring androgen deprivation, does oral relugolix 120 mg daily, versus leuprolide injections every 3 months for 48 weeks, achieve sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels faster and more completely, what happens to testosterone recovery after stopping, and with what cardiovascular-event profile?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal · Cardiovascular Diseases · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Leuprolide · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylurea Compounds · Prostatic Neoplasms · Pyrimidinones · Testosterone
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit on the trial's pharmacodynamic endpoint, on a single-trial base (HERO, three reports of one trial) — stated plainly: the primary endpoint is sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels, a pharmacodynamic endpoint, not a cancer-outcome endpoint. Relugolix 120 mg orally daily (Orgovyx, Myovant/Pfizer lineage as published) achieved sustained castration through 48 weeks in 96.7% vs 88.8% on 3-monthly leuprolide (difference 7.9 percentage points; noninferiority and superiority both met), with castrate testosterone on day 4 in 56.0% vs 0% — the no-surge, rapid-onset profile. Testosterone recovery after stopping was far faster (recovery to >280 ng/dL at 90 days in 54% vs 3.2% in the 184-man subset). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 2.9% vs 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.46, relative) — a secondary/safety analysis in a trial not powered for cardiovascular outcomes; it is printed labelled and must NOT be read as a proven cardiovascular benefit. Health-related quality of life did not differ significantly during treatment. Cross-point in prose only: degarelix, the injectable GnRH antagonist, is shelf #7441.

cards.headline: HERO phase 3 primary (Shore 2020): relugolix achieved superior sustained castration vs leuprolide — 96.7% vs 88.8% through 48 weeks; castrate on day 4 in 56.0% vs 0%
cards.summary: HERO phase 3 primary (Shore 2020): relugolix achieved superior sustained castration vs leuprolide — 96.7% vs 88.8% through 48 weeks; castrate on day 4 in 56.0% vs 0%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (HERO), oral relugolix vs 3-monthly leuprolide for 48 weeks in advanced prostate cancer
cards.people: 934 men with advanced prostate cancer (930 treated in the safety population as reported: 622 relugolix, 308 leuprolide), randomised 2:1 to oral relugolix 120 mg once daily or leuprolide injections every 3 months for 48 weeks.
cards.result: Sustained testosterone suppression to castrate levels (<50 ng/dL) through 48 weeks occurred in 96.7% (95% CI 94.9–97.9) on relugolix vs 88.8% (95% CI 84.6–91.8) on leuprolide — a difference of 7.9 percentage points (95% CI 4.1–11.8) meeting both noninferiority and superiority (P<.001 for superiority). Castrate testosterone on day 4: 56.0% vs 0%; all other key secondary endpoints also favoured relugolix (P<.001). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 2.9% vs 6.2% (hazard ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.24–0.88 — a relative measure from a secondary/safety analysis; the trial was not designed or powered as a cardiovascular-outcomes trial). In the 184-patient recovery subgroup, mean testosterone 90 days after discontinuation was 288.4 vs 58.6 ng/dL.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is testosterone suppression — a pharmacodynamic endpoint, not cancer control or survival. The cardiovascular-event difference is an unpowered secondary/safety analysis and is not a proven cardiovascular benefit.
cards.source: Shore ND et al. Oral Relugolix for Androgen-Deprivation Therapy in Advanced Prostate Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32469183. Registry ID: NCT03085095. cards.headline: HERO testosterone recovery (Tutrone 2024): recovery to >280 ng/dL at 90 days after stopping in 54% on relugolix vs 3.2% on leuprolide (nominal P=.002) — 184-man subset
cards.summary: HERO testosterone recovery (Tutrone 2024): recovery to >280 ng/dL at 90 days after stopping in 54% on relugolix vs 3.2% on leuprolide (nominal P=.002) — 184-man subset
cards.type: Testosterone-recovery analysis of a prespecified subset of the HERO phase 3 trial (same trial as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: 184 men from HERO who completed 48 weeks of treatment and were not indicated to continue androgen deprivation (137 relugolix, 47 leuprolide), followed for a 90-day recovery period after discontinuation.
cards.result: The cumulative incidence of testosterone recovery to >280 ng/dL at 90 days was 54% with relugolix vs 3.2% with leuprolide (nominal P=.002 — absolute rates in a subset). Median time to testosterone recovery was 86.0 vs 112.0 days, and recovery to at least 80% of baseline testosterone occurred in 39% vs 2.1%. Mean testosterone at 90 days was 288.4 vs 58.6 ng/dL. Adverse events during recovery were generally similar between groups. The authors note the short 90-day recovery follow-up as a limitation.
cards.watchOut: A 184-man subset of a 934-man trial, with nominal (not multiplicity-controlled) P values and only 90 days of recovery follow-up; faster recovery is a pharmacodynamic finding whose clinical consequences the trial does not establish.
cards.source: Tutrone R et al. Testosterone Recovery for Relugolix Versus Leuprolide in Men with Advanced Prostate Cancer: Results from the Phase 3 HERO Study. European urology oncology. 2024. cards.headline: HERO health-related quality of life (Tombal 2023): no significant difference vs leuprolide on EORTC QLQ-C30 or QLQ-PR25 during treatment; fewer hormonal symptoms during recovery
cards.summary: HERO health-related quality of life (Tombal 2023): no significant difference vs leuprolide on EORTC QLQ-C30 or QLQ-PR25 during treatment; fewer hormonal symptoms during recovery
cards.type: Health-related quality-of-life report of the HERO phase 3 trial (same trial as the cards above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The 934 HERO patients, assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and prostate module QLQ-PR25 during treatment and, in the recovery subset, during testosterone recovery.
cards.result: No statistically significant differences between relugolix and leuprolide were found in changes from baseline to end of treatment on either instrument. During the testosterone-recovery phase, hormonal treatment-related symptom scores were lower with relugolix, consistent with its faster testosterone recovery. Patient numbers in the recovery group were low, which the authors list as a limitation.
cards.watchOut: A programme report of the single HERO trial: quality of life was similar on treatment, so the oral antagonist's case rests on suppression speed, the absence of surge, and recovery speed — not on better on-treatment quality of life.
cards.source: Tombal B et al. Impact of Relugolix Versus Leuprolide on the Quality of Life of Men with Advanced Prostate Cancer: Results from the Phase 3 HERO Study. European urology. 2023. shelves.title: Degarelix vs LHRH agonists in prostate cancer (CS21): noninferior suppression, castrate by day 3 vs none, injection-site reactions 40% vs <1%; no established survival benefit
shelves.question: In men with prostate cancer requiring androgen deprivation therapy, does the GnRH antagonist degarelix (240 mg loading, 80 or 160 mg monthly), versus leuprolide (or goserelin in the pooled programme), achieve and maintain testosterone suppression without an initial surge, and what do the long-term extension and pooled disease-control data show?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Humans · Leuprolide · Male · Middle Aged · Oligopeptides · Prospective Studies · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Prostatic Neoplasms · Testosterone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE benefit, on a pharmacodynamic-endpoint base — stated plainly: the primary endpoint throughout is testosterone suppression, not cancer survival. In CS21 (phase 3, n=610), degarelix (240 mg loading, then 80 or 160 mg monthly) was noninferior to monthly leuprolide at maintaining testosterone at or below 0.5 ng/mL from day 28 to day 364 (97.2%, 98.3% and 96.4% respectively), with castrate levels by day 3 in about 96% on degarelix vs none on leuprolide — the no-surge, rapid-onset profile. The maintenance dose that survived is 80 mg monthly; the 240/160 arm was not the marketed regimen. Injection-site reactions are the pricing harm (40% vs <1% in CS21). Extension and 5-year reports show maintained suppression after continuing or crossing over from leuprolide. The pooled five-trial analysis (n=1,925) reports PSA progression-free survival favouring degarelix overall (hazard ratio 0.71, relative) but NOT significant in the baseline-PSA >20 ng/mL slice (hazard ratio 0.74; P=.052 — printed exactly), and an overall-survival read confined to a baseline-testosterone subgroup of that pooled analysis (hazard ratio 0.36, relative) — secondary and subgroup reads that must not present degarelix as improving survival. Cross-point in prose only: relugolix, the oral antagonist, is shelf #7440.

cards.headline: CS21 phase 3 primary (Klotz 2008): degarelix noninferior to leuprolide for sustained testosterone suppression (97.2% / 98.3% vs 96.4%); castrate by day 3 in ~96% vs none; injection-site reactions 40% vs <1%
cards.summary: CS21 phase 3 primary (Klotz 2008): degarelix noninferior to leuprolide for sustained testosterone suppression (97.2% / 98.3% vs 96.4%); castrate by day 3 in ~96% vs none; injection-site reactions 40% vs <1%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label parallel-group trial (CS21), degarelix 240/80 mg and 240/160 mg vs leuprolide
cards.people: 610 men with prostate adenocarcinoma of any stage for whom androgen deprivation was indicated (median age 72 years), randomised to degarelix 240 mg loading then 80 mg monthly, degarelix 240/160 mg, or intramuscular leuprolide 7.5 mg monthly for 12 months.
cards.result: Testosterone at or below 0.5 ng/mL at all monthly measurements from day 28 to day 364 (the primary endpoint) was achieved by 97.2% (degarelix 240/80), 98.3% (degarelix 240/160) and 96.4% (leuprolide) — noninferiority met. By day 3, testosterone was at or below 0.5 ng/mL in 96.1% and 95.5% of the degarelix groups vs none on leuprolide, and median PSA at days 14 and 28 was significantly lower with degarelix (P<.001). Injection-site reactions occurred in 40% on subcutaneous degarelix vs <1% on intramuscular leuprolide (P<.001); urinary tract infections (3% vs 9%) and arthralgia (4% vs 9%) were less frequent with degarelix, chills more frequent (4% vs 0%). No systemic allergic reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority trial on a testosterone-suppression endpoint — it establishes equivalent suppression with faster onset, not better cancer outcomes. The 160 mg maintenance arm was not the marketed regimen; 80 mg monthly is the dose that survived.
cards.source: Klotz L et al. The efficacy and safety of degarelix: a 12-month, comparative, randomized, open-label, parallel-group phase III study in patients with prostate cancer. BJU international. 2008. PMID: 19035858. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CS21 extension (Crawford 2011): suppression maintained on continued degarelix and after crossover from leuprolide; PSA progression-free survival hazard rate fell significantly after the switch
cards.summary: CS21 extension (Crawford 2011): suppression maintained on continued degarelix and after crossover from leuprolide; PSA progression-free survival hazard rate fell significantly after the switch
cards.type: Phase 3 extension trial of CS21 with one-arm crossover from leuprolide to degarelix (same programme as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Patients completing the 1-year CS21 trial who continued their degarelix maintenance dose (125 per dose) or were re-randomised from leuprolide to degarelix 240/80 mg (69) or 240/160 mg (65), at median follow-up 27.5 months; data shown on the approved 240/80 mg dose.
cards.result: Testosterone and PSA suppression during the extension were similar to the 1-year trial in both continuers and switchers. The PSA progression-free survival hazard rate decreased significantly after switching from leuprolide to degarelix, while the rate in continuers was consistent with treatment year 1; the same pattern occurred in patients with baseline PSA above 20 ng/mL. Adverse event frequency was similar between groups and decreased with time.

cards.headline: CS21 5-year extension (Crawford 2014): degarelix tolerated to 5 years with suppression maintained; PSA progression-free survival hazard rate fell after crossover (0.20 to 0.09; P=.002)
cards.summary: CS21 5-year extension (Crawford 2014): degarelix tolerated to 5 years with suppression maintained; PSA progression-free survival hazard rate fell after crossover (0.20 to 0.09; P=.002)
cards.type: 5-year results of the CS21 phase 3 extension trial (same programme as the cards above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Extension patients continuing degarelix 80 mg (125) or 160 mg (126), and patients re-randomised from leuprolide to degarelix 240/80 mg (69) or 240/160 mg (65), followed to 5 years.
cards.result: Adverse event frequency was similar between groups; events included initial injection-site reactions, hot flushes and increased weight, with no new safety concerns identified. Testosterone and PSA values during the extension were similar to the 1-year trial in continuers and switchers. The PSA progression-free survival hazard rate decreased significantly after crossover from leuprolide to degarelix (from 0.20 to 0.09; P=.002) and, in patients with baseline PSA above 20 ng/mL, from 0.38 to 0.19 (P=.019), while the rate in continuers did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: Long-term extension data without a continuing randomised comparator; tolerability and maintained suppression are the legitimate reads, not comparative efficacy.

cards.headline: Pooled five-trial analysis (Klotz 2014): PSA progression-free survival favoured degarelix overall (hazard ratio 0.71, relative) but NOT significantly at baseline PSA >20 ng/mL (hazard ratio 0.74; P=.052); overall-survival read is a pooled subgroup (hazard ratio 0.36 at baseline testosterone >2 ng/mL)
cards.summary: Pooled five-trial analysis (Klotz 2014): PSA progression-free survival favoured degarelix overall (hazard ratio 0.71, relative) but NOT significantly at baseline PSA >20 ng/mL (hazard ratio 0.74; P=.052); overall-survival read is a pooled subgroup (hazard ratio 0.36 at baseline testosterone >2 ng/mL)
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient analysis of five comparative randomised trials, degarelix vs leuprolide or goserelin
cards.people: Pooled individual-patient data from five prospective phase 3/3b randomised trials, n=1,925 (degarelix 1,266; leuprolide 201; goserelin 458), with 3 months (467 patients) or 12 months (1,458) of treatment.
cards.result: PSA progression-free survival was improved with degarelix overall (hazard ratio 0.71, a relative measure; P=.017). In patients with baseline PSA above 20 ng/mL the hazard ratio was 0.74 (P=.052 — NOT significant; printed exactly). Overall survival was higher with degarelix in the pooled analysis (hazard ratio 0.47; P=.023), particularly in the subgroup with baseline testosterone above 2 ng/mL (hazard ratio 0.36; P=.006) — a subgroup of a pooled analysis of trials designed on suppression endpoints, labelled as such. Joint-related, musculoskeletal and urinary tract adverse events were fewer with degarelix overall.
cards.watchOut: Secondary disease-control outcomes pooled across trials designed for testosterone suppression: the headline PSA slice at baseline PSA >20 ng/mL is not significant (P=.052), and the survival reads are pooled/subgroup analyses — none of this establishes that degarelix improves survival.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (CS21, n=610; its extensions; pooled analysis, n=1,925 across five trials).
cards.result: CS21 met noninferiority for sustained testosterone suppression over 12 months for both degarelix maintenance doses (the marketed dose is 80 mg monthly), with immediate onset and no surge. Extensions show maintained suppression in continuers and switchers to 5 years. The pooled analysis favours degarelix on PSA progression-free survival overall (hazard ratio 0.71, relative) but not significantly in the high-baseline-PSA slice (P=.052), and its survival findings are subgroup reads. Injection-site reactions (40% vs <1%) are the antagonist's pricing harm.

shelves.title: Pyrotinib in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (PHOEBE/PERMEATE/PHILA): large PFS wins in two China phase 3 trials; single-arm brain-metastases activity; diarrhoea the price
shelves.question: In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, does the irreversible pan-HER tyrosine kinase inhibitor pyrotinib — plus capecitabine after trastuzumab and taxanes, against lapatinib plus capecitabine (PHOEBE); plus capecitabine for brain metastases (PERMEATE); or added to trastuzumab–docetaxel first-line, against placebo (PHILA) — prolong progression-free survival and produce intracranial responses, at what diarrhoea cost?
shelves.mesh: Acrylamides · Adult · Aminoquinolines · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Capecitabine · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lapatinib · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit for progression-free survival, on single-region evidence — flagged on the face: all three trials were conducted in China, where pyrotinib is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved. Three settings, labelled separately and never pooled. After trastuzumab and taxanes (PHOEBE, phase 3, n=267): pyrotinib plus capecitabine prolonged median progression-free survival vs lapatinib plus capecitabine (12.5 vs 6.8 months; hazard ratio 0.39, relative). First-line (PHILA, phase 3, n=590): adding pyrotinib to trastuzumab–docetaxel prolonged median progression-free survival (24.3 vs 10.4 months; hazard ratio 0.41, relative). For brain metastases (PERMEATE, phase 2, n=78): intracranial response 74.6% in the radiotherapy-naive cohort and 42.1% after radiotherapy progression — single-arm, uncontrolled. Diarrhoea prices the whole programme: grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea in 31% vs 8% in PHOEBE and about a quarter of PERMEATE patients; grade 3-or-worse treatment-related events in 90% vs 76% in PHILA. Cross-points in prose only: neratinib extended adjuvant (pack #6406) and the tucatinib HER2CLIMB neighbourhood are different settings.

cards.headline: PHOEBE phase 3 (Xu 2021): pyrotinib + capecitabine prolonged progression-free survival vs lapatinib + capecitabine after trastuzumab — median 12.5 vs 6.8 months (hazard ratio 0.39, relative); grade ≥3 diarrhoea 31% vs 8%
cards.summary: PHOEBE phase 3 (Xu 2021): pyrotinib + capecitabine prolonged progression-free survival vs lapatinib + capecitabine after trastuzumab — median 12.5 vs 6.8 months (hazard ratio 0.39, relative); grade ≥3 diarrhoea 31% vs 8%
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre open-label randomised trial (PHOEBE, China), pyrotinib + capecitabine vs lapatinib + capecitabine
cards.people: 267 patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and taxanes, randomised at 29 hospitals in China to pyrotinib 400 mg daily plus capecitabine (134) or lapatinib 1250 mg daily plus capecitabine (132); results are from a prespecified interim analysis.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival by masked independent central review was 12.5 months (95% CI 9.7–not reached) with pyrotinib plus capecitabine vs 6.8 months (95% CI 5.4–8.1) with lapatinib plus capecitabine (hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.27–0.56; one-sided P<.0001 — a relative measure). The most common grade 3-or-worse adverse events were diarrhoea (31% vs 8%) and hand-foot syndrome (16% vs 15%). Serious adverse events occurred in 10% vs 8%; there were no treatment-related deaths in the pyrotinib group and one treatment-related sudden death in the lapatinib group.
cards.watchOut: Interim-analysis report, open-label, single-region (China); the comparator is lapatinib plus capecitabine, a regimen whose place has since narrowed — the read is against that comparator, in that era.

cards.headline: PERMEATE phase 2 (Yan 2022): pyrotinib + capecitabine for HER2-positive brain metastases — intracranial response 74.6% (44/59) radiotherapy-naive and 42.1% (8/19) after radiotherapy — SINGLE-ARM, uncontrolled
cards.summary: PERMEATE phase 2 (Yan 2022): pyrotinib + capecitabine for HER2-positive brain metastases — intracranial response 74.6% (44/59) radiotherapy-naive and 42.1% (8/19) after radiotherapy — SINGLE-ARM, uncontrolled
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre single-arm two-cohort trial (PERMEATE, China), pyrotinib + capecitabine in HER2-positive brain metastases — uncontrolled
cards.people: 78 women with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer and brain metastases at eight tertiary hospitals in China — 59 radiotherapy-naive (cohort A) and 19 with progression after radiotherapy (cohort B) — treated with pyrotinib 400 mg daily plus capecitabine, with no comparator arm.
cards.result: The confirmed intracranial objective response rate was 74.6% (95% CI 61.6–85.0; 44 of 59 patients) in cohort A and 42.1% (95% CI 20.3–66.5; 8 of 19) in cohort B — uncontrolled rates. The most common grade 3-or-worse treatment-emergent adverse event was diarrhoea (24% in cohort A, 21% in cohort B). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 2 patients (3%) in cohort A and 3 (16%) in cohort B; no treatment-related deaths occurred. The authors state the combination deserves validation in a randomised controlled trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm with a small post-radiotherapy cohort (n=19): intracranial response rates are uncontrolled and hypothesis-supporting only; no randomised comparison in brain metastases exists in this programme.

cards.headline: PERMEATE overall survival update (Yan 2024): median overall survival 35.9 months (cohort A) and 30.6 months (cohort B) at 30.9 months follow-up — uncontrolled, single-arm follow-up
cards.summary: PERMEATE overall survival update (Yan 2024): median overall survival 35.9 months (cohort A) and 30.6 months (cohort B) at 30.9 months follow-up — uncontrolled, single-arm follow-up
cards.type: Overall-survival update of the single-arm PERMEATE phase 2 trial (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same 78 PERMEATE patients (59 radiotherapy-naive, 19 post-radiotherapy progression), followed to a median of 30.9 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 10.9 months (95% CI 7.6–14.6) in cohort A and 5.7 months (95% CI 3.4–11.5) in cohort B; median central nervous system progression-free survival was 13.6 and 5.7 months respectively. Median overall survival was 35.9 months (95% CI 24.4–not reached) in cohort A and 30.6 months (95% CI 12.6–33.3) in cohort B — all uncontrolled. Among 14 cohort A patients with intracranial progression only who restarted pyrotinib plus capecitabine after local radiotherapy, median overall survival was 34.1 months (a small post-hoc slice). The authors again call for randomised validation.
cards.watchOut: Survival times from a single-arm trial cannot be compared with other regimens' trial results; carded to complete the PERMEATE record, not as comparative evidence.

cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (PHILA, China), pyrotinib + trastuzumab–docetaxel vs placebo + trastuzumab–docetaxel, first-line
cards.people: 590 women with untreated HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, randomised 1:1 at 40 centres in China to pyrotinib 400 mg daily (297) or placebo (293), each with trastuzumab and docetaxel; median age 52 years.
cards.result: At median follow-up 15.5 months, median progression-free survival by investigator assessment was 24.3 months (95% CI 19.1–33.0) with pyrotinib vs 10.4 months (95% CI 9.3–12.3) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.32–0.53; one-sided P<.001 — a relative measure). Grade 3-or-higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 267 (90%) of the pyrotinib group vs 224 (76%) of the placebo group. No treatment-related deaths occurred in the pyrotinib group; one treatment-related death (diabetic hyperosmolar coma) occurred in the placebo group. Overall survival was still under assessment at this report.
cards.watchOut: First-line setting — a different slice from PHOEBE's post-trastuzumab population; never pool the two. Single-region (China), and overall survival was immature at this report.
cards.source: Ma F et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: pyrotinib prolonged progression-free survival in two China phase 3 trials — after trastuzumab vs lapatinib (12.5 vs 6.8 months) and first-line added to trastuzumab–docetaxel (24.3 vs 10.4 months) — with single-arm intracranial activity in brain metastases; diarrhoea is the programme-wide price and no overall-survival read is yet established
cards.summary: Synthesis: pyrotinib prolonged progression-free survival in two China phase 3 trials — after trastuzumab vs lapatinib (12.5 vs 6.8 months) and first-line added to trastuzumab–docetaxel (24.3 vs 10.4 months) — with single-arm intracranial activity in brain metastases; diarrhoea is the programme-wide price and no overall-survival read is yet established
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (PHOEBE, n=267; PERMEATE, n=78 single-arm; PHILA, n=590).
cards.result: Two randomised phase 3 trials in distinct settings each showed a large relative progression-free survival benefit (hazard ratios 0.39 and 0.41). PERMEATE's intracranial responses (74.6% radiotherapy-naive; 42.1% after radiotherapy) are uncontrolled. Grade 3-or-worse diarrhoea affected roughly a quarter to a third of pyrotinib patients across the programme, and grade 3-or-worse treatment-related events reached 90% in PHILA. All evidence is from China, where the drug is approved; it is not FDA/EMA-approved, and neither phase 3 report establishes an overall-survival benefit.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Alpelisib plus fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer (SOLAR-1): progression-free survival 11.0 vs 5.7 months, overall survival not significant — one trial, with grade 3/4 hyperglycaemia in 36.6%
shelves.question: In patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing after endocrine therapy whose tumours carry a PIK3CA mutation, does adding the PI3Kα inhibitor alpelisib to fulvestrant, versus placebo plus fulvestrant, prolong progression-free and overall survival, and with what hyperglycaemia, rash and diarrhoea cost?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Breast Neoplasms · Class I Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinases · Diarrhea · Female · Fulvestrant · Humans · Middle Aged · Mutation · Progression-Free Survival · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Receptors, Estrogen · Receptors, Progesterone · Thiazoles
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-trial base (SOLAR-1, three reports). In the PIK3CA-mutated cohort (n=341), alpelisib plus fulvestrant prolonged median progression-free survival versus placebo plus fulvestrant (11.0 vs 5.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65, a relative measure). Final overall survival was numerically longer but NOT significant (39.3 vs 31.4 months; hazard ratio 0.86, relative; P=0.15, and the analysis did not cross its prespecified boundary). No progression-free-survival benefit was established in the cohort without PIK3CA mutations (hazard ratio 0.85, relative) — the benefit is biomarker-restricted. The price is substantial: grade 3/4 hyperglycaemia in 36.6% versus 0.7%, grade 3/4 rash 9.9% versus 0.3%, grade 3 diarrhoea 6.7% versus 0.3%, and discontinuation for adverse events in 25.0% versus 4.2%. Quality of life was maintained overall, with symptom subscales favouring placebo. BYLieve, the post-CDK4/6-inhibitor cohort study, is NOT carded as evidence on this shelf: it carries a published Expression of Concern (PMID 38142701) and is barred as load-bearing; this shelf rests on SOLAR-1 alone. Cross-points (prose only): capivasertib (pack #6403) and inavolisib (pack #6404) answer different biomarker questions.

cards.headline: SOLAR-1 phase 3 primary report (André 2019): in PIK3CA-mutated disease, alpelisib plus fulvestrant prolonged progression-free survival (median 11.0 vs 5.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative) — no benefit established without the mutation
cards.summary: SOLAR-1 phase 3 primary report (André 2019): in PIK3CA-mutated disease, alpelisib plus fulvestrant prolonged progression-free survival (median 11.0 vs 5.7 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative) — no benefit established without the mutation
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (SOLAR-1), alpelisib + fulvestrant vs placebo + fulvestrant, cohorts by PIK3CA mutation status
cards.people: 572 patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer previously treated with endocrine therapy were randomised to alpelisib 300 mg daily plus fulvestrant or placebo plus fulvestrant, in two cohorts by tumour PIK3CA mutation status; 341 had confirmed PIK3CA-mutated tumours.
cards.result: In the PIK3CA-mutated cohort, at median follow-up of 20 months, median progression-free survival was 11.0 months (95% CI 7.5 to 14.5) with alpelisib-fulvestrant versus 5.7 months (95% CI 3.7 to 7.4) with placebo-fulvestrant (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85; P<0.001 — a relative measure). In the cohort without PIK3CA-mutated cancer the hazard ratio was 0.85 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.25), so benefit was not established outside the mutated population. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events in the overall population: hyperglycaemia 36.6% versus 0.7%, rash 9.9% versus 0.3%; grade 3 diarrhoea 6.7% versus 0.3% (no grade 4 diarrhoea). Discontinuation of alpelisib/placebo for adverse events: 25.0% versus 4.2%.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is progression-free survival in the mutated cohort only; the non-mutated cohort's null read is part of the result, not a footnote — alpelisib is a biomarker-selected treatment. Hyperglycaemia is an on-target, frequent, high-grade harm that requires monitoring and often dose action.
cards.source: André F et al. Alpelisib for PIK3CA-Mutated, Hormone Receptor-Positive Advanced Breast Cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 31091374. Registry ID: NCT02437318. cards.headline: SOLAR-1 final overall survival (André 2021): median survival 39.3 vs 31.4 months in the mutated cohort — numerically longer but NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.86, relative; P=0.15; prespecified boundary not crossed)
cards.summary: SOLAR-1 final overall survival (André 2021): median survival 39.3 vs 31.4 months in the mutated cohort — numerically longer but NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.86, relative; P=0.15; prespecified boundary not crossed)
cards.type: Final overall-survival report of the SOLAR-1 phase 3 randomised trial (same trial as the primary card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same SOLAR-1 trial: men and postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer progressing on or after an aromatase inhibitor, randomised 1:1 to alpelisib 300 mg/day plus fulvestrant or placebo plus fulvestrant; overall survival was analysed in the PIK3CA-mutated cohort (n=341).
cards.result: Median overall survival in the mutated cohort was 39.3 months (95% CI 34.1 to 44.9) with alpelisib-fulvestrant versus 31.4 months (95% CI 26.8 to 41.3) with placebo-fulvestrant (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.15; P=0.15 — a relative measure); the analysis did NOT cross the prespecified O'Brien-Fleming efficacy boundary (P ≤ 0.0161), so no survival benefit is established. In the subgroup with lung and/or liver metastases, median survival was 37.2 versus 22.8 months (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.00 — a subgroup read, labelled as such). Median time to chemotherapy was 23.3 versus 14.8 months (hazard ratio 0.72, relative). No new safety signals appeared with longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A 7.9-month numerical median difference that is not statistically significant must not be read as a survival win; the lung/liver-metastases hazard ratio of 0.68 is a subgroup analysis of the same null overall result.
cards.source: André F et al. cards.headline: SOLAR-1 patient-reported outcomes (Ciruelos 2021): global quality of life was maintained and did not differ significantly between arms, while diarrhoea, appetite loss, nausea/vomiting and fatigue subscales favoured placebo
cards.summary: SOLAR-1 patient-reported outcomes (Ciruelos 2021): global quality of life was maintained and did not differ significantly between arms, while diarrhoea, appetite loss, nausea/vomiting and fatigue subscales favoured placebo
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes report of the SOLAR-1 phase 3 trial (same trial as the cards above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The 341 patients of the SOLAR-1 PIK3CA-mutated cohort, randomised 1:1 to alpelisib 300 mg daily or placebo, each plus fulvestrant; quality of life was assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and the Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form.
cards.result: Global Health Status/quality of life was maintained from baseline in both arms (overall change −3.50 points, 95% CI −8.02 to 1.02, with alpelisib versus +0.27, 95% CI −4.48 to 5.02, with placebo); the overall treatment effect was not significant (−3.77; 95% CI −8.35 to 0.80; P=.101), and time to 10% deterioration was similar (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.48, relative). Deterioration in social functioning and in the diarrhoea, appetite-loss, nausea/vomiting and fatigue symptom subscales occurred with alpelisib compared with placebo. Worst Pain improved numerically more with alpelisib (42% vs 32% at week 24; P=.090).
cards.watchOut: Patient-reported outcomes describe tolerability within the one trial; they add no independent efficacy evidence, and the symptom subscales that favoured placebo are the same toxicities that drive the 25% discontinuation rate.
cards.source: Ciruelos EM et al. Patient-Reported Outcomes in Patients With PIK3CA-Mutated Hormone Receptor-Positive, Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2-Negative Advanced Breast Cancer From SOLAR-1. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2021. PMID: 33780274. Registry ID: NCT02437318. shelves.title: Eribulin in pretreated metastatic breast cancer: SPLIT — EMBRACE survival win vs physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months); Study 301 not superior to capecitabine
shelves.question: In women with locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer previously treated with an anthracycline and a taxane, does the microtubule inhibitor eribulin, versus treatment of physician's choice in heavily pretreated disease (EMBRACE) or versus capecitabine in earlier-line advanced disease (Study 301), prolong overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents · Breast Neoplasms · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Furans · Humans · Ketones · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Metastasis · Survival Rate · Polyether Polyketides
shelves.balance: SPLIT across the programme's two trials. EMBRACE (heavily pretreated disease, 2–5 prior regimens): eribulin significantly prolonged median overall survival versus treatment of physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, a relative measure; P=.041). Study 301 (earlier-line disease, first- to third-line): eribulin was NOT superior to capecitabine for overall survival (15.9 vs 14.5 months; hazard ratio 0.88, relative; P=.056, not significant) or progression-free survival (4.1 vs 4.2 months). Quality of life in Study 301 was similar overall, with worse systemic-therapy side-effects on eribulin and worse nausea/vomiting and diarrhoea on capecitabine. The harms that price eribulin are neutropenia (52% vs 30% all grades in EMBRACE) and peripheral neuropathy, the commonest reason for eribulin discontinuation (5%). The two trials test different lines of therapy against different comparators and are carded as separate slices, never pooled. Cross-point (prose only): eribulin in liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma is live #1925, a different disease.

cards.headline: EMBRACE phase 3 (Cortes 2011): in heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer, eribulin prolonged overall survival versus treatment of physician's choice (median 13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, relative; P=.041)
cards.summary: EMBRACE phase 3 (Cortes 2011): in heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer, eribulin prolonged overall survival versus treatment of physician's choice (median 13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, relative; P=.041)
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label randomised trial (EMBRACE), eribulin vs treatment of physician's choice, heavily pretreated disease
cards.people: 762 women with locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer, previously treated with an anthracycline and a taxane and with two to five prior chemotherapy regimens (two or more for advanced disease), randomised 2:1 to eribulin mesilate 1.4 mg/m² on days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle (508) or treatment of physician's choice (254).
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly improved with eribulin: median 13.1 months (95% CI 11.8 to 14.3) versus 10.6 months (95% CI 9.3 to 12.5) with physician's choice (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.99; P=.041 — a relative measure). The commonest adverse events were asthenia/fatigue (54% of 503 eribulin-treated patients vs 40% of 247 on physician's choice, all grades) and neutropenia (52% vs 30%, all grades). Peripheral neuropathy was the commonest adverse event leading to eribulin discontinuation (24 of 503 patients, 5%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparator is a heterogeneous mix of whatever the physician chose — the win is against refractory-setting usual options, not against a single active standard; the survival hazard ratio's confidence interval (0.66 to 0.99) only just excludes 1.

cards.headline: Study 301 phase 3 (Kaufman 2015): eribulin was NOT superior to capecitabine in earlier-line advanced breast cancer — overall survival 15.9 vs 14.5 months (hazard ratio 0.88, relative; P=.056, not significant) and progression-free survival 4.1 vs 4.2 months
cards.summary: Study 301 phase 3 (Kaufman 2015): eribulin was NOT superior to capecitabine in earlier-line advanced breast cancer — overall survival 15.9 vs 14.5 months (hazard ratio 0.88, relative; P=.056, not significant) and progression-free survival 4.1 vs 4.2 months
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label randomised trial (Study 301), eribulin vs capecitabine, first- to third-line advanced disease
cards.people: 1,102 women with locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer previously treated with an anthracycline and a taxane, randomised to eribulin (554) or capecitabine (548) as first-, second- or third-line chemotherapy for advanced disease.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 15.9 months with eribulin versus 14.5 months with capecitabine (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; P=.056 — a relative measure, not significant). Median progression-free survival was 4.1 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.25; P=.30, relative). Objective response rates were 11.0% (eribulin) and 11.5% (capecitabine). Global health status and overall quality-of-life scores over time were similar in the two arms, and most adverse events were grade 1 or 2.
cards.watchOut: A negative superiority trial against an active single-agent comparator in an earlier-line population — it does not contradict EMBRACE, which tested a later line against physician's choice; the two results answer different questions and must not be averaged.

cards.headline: Study 301 quality-of-life report (Cortes 2015): no overall quality-of-life difference — eribulin caused worse systemic-therapy side-effects, capecitabine worse nausea/vomiting and diarrhoea
cards.summary: Study 301 quality-of-life report (Cortes 2015): no overall quality-of-life difference — eribulin caused worse systemic-therapy side-effects, capecitabine worse nausea/vomiting and diarrhoea
cards.type: Health-related quality-of-life report of Study 301 (same trial as the card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The Study 301 population (1,102 randomised); 1,062 patients (96.4%) completed the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-BR23 questionnaires at baseline, with compliance of at least 80% during follow-up to 24 months, progression or new treatment.
cards.result: Overall functioning and global quality of life did not differ between eribulin and capecitabine. Capecitabine produced significantly worse nausea/vomiting (minimally important difference 8; P<0.05) and diarrhoea (MID 7; P<0.05) symptom scores; eribulin produced worse systemic-therapy side-effects (dry mouth, altered taste, irritated eyes, feeling ill, hot flushes, headaches, hair loss; MID 10; P<0.01). Time to worsening was shorter with capecitabine for body image (by 2.9 months) and future perspective (by 1.4 months), and shorter with eribulin for systemic side-effects (by 2 months).
cards.watchOut: A tolerability report of the negative Study 301 comparison: it refines which side-effects each drug causes but adds no efficacy evidence, in an open-label trial where patients knew which drug they were receiving.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a split programme — a significant survival win in heavily pretreated disease against physician's choice (EMBRACE), and no superiority over capecitabine in earlier-line disease (Study 301)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split programme — a significant survival win in heavily pretreated disease against physician's choice (EMBRACE), and no superiority over capecitabine in earlier-line disease (Study 301)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Eribulin's survival evidence depends on the line of therapy and the comparator. After two to five prior regimens, eribulin prolonged median overall survival versus treatment of physician's choice (13.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio 0.81, relative; P=.041). As first- to third-line therapy it was not superior to capecitabine on survival (hazard ratio 0.88, relative; P=.056) or progression-free survival, with similar overall quality of life and a different side-effect profile (more systemic-therapy side-effects and neuropathy risk with eribulin; more nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea with capecitabine). Neither trial's result may be used to overwrite the other.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Dalpiciclib in HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer (DAWNA-1/2): FLOOR-RISK two-trial base — progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.42 and 0.51 (relative), survival immature, single-region (China)
shelves.question: In patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer — progressing after endocrine therapy, with fulvestrant (DAWNA-1), or untreated in the advanced setting, with letrozole or anastrozole (DAWNA-2) — does adding the CDK4/6 inhibitor dalpiciclib, versus placebo, prolong progression-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal · Breast Neoplasms · Cell Proliferation · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 4 · Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 6 · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fulvestrant · Humans · Middle Aged · Piperidines · Placebos · Progression-Free Survival · Protein Kinase Inhibitors · Pyridines · Pyrimidines · Erb-b2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinases · Receptors, Estrogen · Receptors, Progesterone
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) on a FLOOR-RISK base — stated on the face: the randomised evidence is exactly TWO phase 3 trials (DAWNA-1 and DAWNA-2), both conducted in China (dalpiciclib is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA), plus one labelled phase Ib dose-finding programme report that carries no comparative efficacy weight. Both phase 3 trials showed large relative progression-free-survival benefits: DAWNA-1, after endocrine therapy, with fulvestrant — median 15.7 vs 7.2 months (hazard ratio 0.42, a relative measure); DAWNA-2, first-line, with letrozole or anastrozole — median 30.6 vs 18.2 months (hazard ratio 0.51, relative). Overall survival was immature in both primary reports, so this shelf makes NO survival claim. The price is very frequent high-grade cytopenia: grade 3/4 neutropenia 84.2% (DAWNA-1) and 86% (DAWNA-2), grade 3/4 leukopenia 62.1% and 67%; grade 3/4 events overall in 90% versus 12% in DAWNA-2, with two treatment-related deaths in the dalpiciclib arm. No CDK4/6 classmate's data are borrowed: palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib answer their own questions (live #365 neighbourhood, cross-pointed in prose only).

cards.headline: DAWNA-1 phase 3 (Xu 2021): dalpiciclib plus fulvestrant after endocrine therapy prolonged progression-free survival (median 15.7 vs 7.2 months; hazard ratio 0.42, relative) — grade 3/4 neutropenia 84.2%
cards.summary: DAWNA-1 phase 3 (Xu 2021): dalpiciclib plus fulvestrant after endocrine therapy prolonged progression-free survival (median 15.7 vs 7.2 months; hazard ratio 0.42, relative) — grade 3/4 neutropenia 84.2%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (DAWNA-1), dalpiciclib + fulvestrant vs placebo + fulvestrant, post-endocrine-therapy setting (China)
cards.people: 361 patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had progressed after endocrine therapy, randomised 2:1 to dalpiciclib plus fulvestrant or placebo plus fulvestrant (double-blind).
cards.result: The interim primary analysis met its endpoint: investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 15.7 months (95% CI 11.1 to not reached) with dalpiciclib-fulvestrant versus 7.2 months (95% CI 5.6 to 9.2) with placebo-fulvestrant (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.58; one-sided P<0.0001 — a relative measure). The commonest grade 3 or 4 adverse events with dalpiciclib were neutropenia (84.2%) and leukopenia (62.1%). Serious adverse events occurred in 5.8% (dalpiciclib) versus 6.7% (placebo). Overall survival was not reported as mature in this primary report.
cards.watchOut: An interim progression-free-survival analysis with immature survival; the near-universal grade 3/4 neutropenia is largely laboratory-detected but is the dominant tolerability fact of the drug, and the trial is single-region (China).

cards.headline: DAWNA-2 phase 3 (Zhang 2023): first-line dalpiciclib plus letrozole or anastrozole prolonged progression-free survival (median 30.6 vs 18.2 months; hazard ratio 0.51, relative) — grade 3/4 events in 90% vs 12%
cards.summary: DAWNA-2 phase 3 (Zhang 2023): first-line dalpiciclib plus letrozole or anastrozole prolonged progression-free survival (median 30.6 vs 18.2 months; hazard ratio 0.51, relative) — grade 3/4 events in 90% vs 12%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (DAWNA-2), dalpiciclib + aromatase inhibitor vs placebo + aromatase inhibitor, first-line setting (China)
cards.people: 456 patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer and no previous systemic therapy in the advanced setting, randomised 2:1 (303 dalpiciclib, 153 placebo) at 42 hospitals in China; dalpiciclib 150 mg daily for 3 weeks on, 1 week off, plus letrozole 2.5 mg or anastrozole 1 mg daily.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 21.6 months, disease progression or death had occurred in 34% (103/303) on dalpiciclib versus 54% (83/153) on placebo. Median progression-free survival was 30.6 months (95% CI 30.6 to not reached) versus 18.2 months (95% CI 16.5 to 22.5) (stratified hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.69; one-sided P<0.0001 — a relative measure). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported in 90% (271/302) on dalpiciclib versus 12% (18/153) on placebo, driven by neutropenia (86% vs none) and leukopenia (67% vs none). Serious adverse events: 12% versus 7%. Two treatment-related deaths occurred, both in the dalpiciclib group (causes unknown as published). Overall survival was immature at this interim analysis.
cards.watchOut: Interim analysis of a single-region trial with immature overall survival; the 90% grade 3/4 event rate is dominated by neutropenia/leukopenia, and the two treatment-related deaths (unknown causes) belong on the face beside the progression benefit.
cards.source: Zhang P et al. cards.headline: Programme report — phase Ib dose-finding (Zhang 2024): dalpiciclib 150 mg was selected as the phase 3 dose with endocrine therapy; grade ≥3 events in 86.7–93.8% across cohorts (a report OF the dalpiciclib programme, not comparative evidence)
cards.summary: Programme report — phase Ib dose-finding (Zhang 2024): dalpiciclib 150 mg was selected as the phase 3 dose with endocrine therapy; grade ≥3 events in 86.7–93.8% across cohorts (a report OF the dalpiciclib programme, not comparative evidence)
cards.type: Programme report: multicentre open-label phase Ib dose-finding study of the dalpiciclib programme (uncontrolled — not comparative efficacy evidence)
cards.people: 104 patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative locally recurrent or metastatic breast cancer in five open-label cohorts: 58 received dalpiciclib (125 or 150 mg) plus letrozole/anastrozole without prior treatment for advanced disease, and 46 received dalpiciclib (125, 150 or 175 mg) plus fulvestrant after progression on endocrine therapy.
cards.result: No maximum tolerated dose was reached with either endocrine partner. Across cohorts, 86.7–93.8% of patients had a grade ≥3 adverse event, most commonly neutropenia and leukopenia. Dalpiciclib 150 mg was associated with numerically higher objective response rates (67.6% in patients untreated for advanced disease; 53.3% after endocrine therapy) and was selected as the recommended phase 3 dose — the dose used in DAWNA-1 and DAWNA-2.

shelves.title: Sintilimab plus chemotherapy first-line in advanced NSCLC (ORIENT-11/12): progression-free survival hazard ratios 0.48 and 0.54 (relative); survival benefit shown in nonsquamous disease — single-region (China)
shelves.question: In patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC without sensitising EGFR/ALK alterations, does adding the PD-1 inhibitor sintilimab to platinum chemotherapy — pemetrexed–platinum in nonsquamous disease (ORIENT-11) or gemcitabine–platinum in squamous disease (ORIENT-12) — versus placebo plus the same chemotherapy, prolong progression-free and overall survival?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Lung Neoplasms · Pemetrexed · Platinum
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on two phase 3 trials in two histologies, both single-region (China; sintilimab is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA) — the slices are labelled and never pooled. Nonsquamous (ORIENT-11): sintilimab plus pemetrexed-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (median 8.9 vs 5.0 months; hazard ratio 0.482, a relative measure) and, at final analysis, overall survival (median 24.2 vs 16.8 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative), despite 47% of the placebo arm crossing over to sintilimab. Squamous (ORIENT-12): sintilimab plus gemcitabine-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.536, relative); the carded primary report does not report a mature overall-survival read, so no survival claim is made for the squamous slice. Grade ≥3 adverse events were similar between arms in both trials (61.7% vs 58.8% in ORIENT-11; 86.6% vs 83.1% in ORIENT-12) — the chemotherapy backbone drives most high-grade toxicity. Cross-point (prose only): tislelizumab in NSCLC (pack #7299) is a separate agent's programme.

cards.headline: ORIENT-11 phase 3 primary report (Yang 2020): sintilimab plus pemetrexed-platinum prolonged progression-free survival in nonsquamous NSCLC (median 8.9 vs 5.0 months; hazard ratio 0.482, relative); response 51.9% vs 29.8%
cards.summary: ORIENT-11 phase 3 primary report (Yang 2020): sintilimab plus pemetrexed-platinum prolonged progression-free survival in nonsquamous NSCLC (median 8.9 vs 5.0 months; hazard ratio 0.482, relative); response 51.9% vs 29.8%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (ORIENT-11), sintilimab + pemetrexed-platinum vs placebo + pemetrexed-platinum, nonsquamous NSCLC (China)
cards.people: 397 Chinese patients with previously untreated, locally advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC without sensitising EGFR or ALK aberrations, randomised 2:1 to sintilimab 200 mg or placebo, each plus pemetrexed and platinum every 3 weeks for four cycles, then maintenance sintilimab/placebo plus pemetrexed; crossover was allowed.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 8.9 months, median progression-free survival (independent review) was 8.9 months with sintilimab-chemotherapy versus 5.0 months with placebo-chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.482, 95% CI 0.362 to 0.643; P<0.00001 — a relative measure). Confirmed objective response was 51.9% (95% CI 45.7 to 58.0) versus 29.8% (95% CI 22.1 to 38.4) — absolute rates. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 61.7% versus 58.8%.
cards.watchOut: A progression-free-survival primary report at short (8.9-month) median follow-up in a single-region population; the survival answer for this trial is in its final-analysis card below, not in this report.

cards.headline: ORIENT-11 final overall survival (Zhang 2022): sintilimab plus chemotherapy prolonged survival (median 24.2 vs 16.8 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative) despite 47% crossover from the placebo arm
cards.summary: ORIENT-11 final overall survival (Zhang 2022): sintilimab plus chemotherapy prolonged survival (median 24.2 vs 16.8 months; hazard ratio 0.65, relative) despite 47% crossover from the placebo arm
cards.type: Final overall-survival report of the ORIENT-11 phase 3 trial (same trial as the primary card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The same ORIENT-11 trial: 397 patients randomised to sintilimab plus pemetrexed-platinum (266) or placebo plus pemetrexed-platinum (131); patients in the placebo arm could cross over to second-line sintilimab monotherapy on progression, and 47% did.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 30.8 months, 243 deaths had occurred (57% of the sintilimab arm, 70% of the placebo arm). Median overall survival was 24.2 months with sintilimab-chemotherapy versus 16.8 months with placebo-chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85 — a relative measure); estimated 2-year survival was 50% versus 32% (absolute rates). After adjustment for the crossover effect, the hazard ratio was 0.52 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.69) — a sensitivity adjustment, labelled as such, not the headline. The survival benefit was largely consistent across prespecified subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Nearly half the control arm received sintilimab after progression, which biases the unadjusted comparison toward the null; the crossover-adjusted hazard ratio (0.52) is a modelling sensitivity analysis and is not the primary read.

cards.headline: ORIENT-12 phase 3 (Zhou 2021): in squamous NSCLC, sintilimab plus gemcitabine-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.536, relative) — no mature survival read in this report
cards.summary: ORIENT-12 phase 3 (Zhou 2021): in squamous NSCLC, sintilimab plus gemcitabine-platinum prolonged progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.536, relative) — no mature survival read in this report
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (ORIENT-12), sintilimab + gemcitabine-platinum vs placebo + gemcitabine-platinum, squamous NSCLC (China)
cards.people: 357 patients with locally advanced or metastatic squamous NSCLC without EGFR-sensitive mutations or ALK rearrangements, randomised 1:1 (179 sintilimab, 178 placebo) at 42 centres in China to sintilimab 200 mg or placebo plus gemcitabine-platinum every 3 weeks for four or six cycles, then maintenance sintilimab/placebo for up to 2 years.
cards.result: At median follow-up of 12.9 months, progression-free survival (independent review) favoured sintilimab-gemcitabine-platinum (hazard ratio 0.536, 95% CI 0.422 to 0.681; P<0.00001 — a relative measure). Grade 3 or worse treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 86.6% (sintilimab) versus 83.1% (placebo); treatment-emergent events leading to death occurred in 4.5% versus 6.7%. Overall survival was not reported as a mature result in this primary report.
cards.watchOut: Progression-free survival only in the carded report — do not extend ORIENT-11's survival result to the squamous population; high-grade toxicity is dominated by the gemcitabine-platinum backbone in both arms.

shelves.title: Anlotinib third-line or later in advanced NSCLC (ALTER0303 — one trial, three reports): survival 9.6 vs 6.3 months vs placebo, in a pre-chemo-immunotherapy-era population (China)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced NSCLC progressing after at least two lines of systemic therapy, does the multitarget antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitor anlotinib 12 mg daily, versus placebo, prolong overall and progression-free survival, and with what hypertension cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Indoles · Lung Neoplasms · Male · Middle Aged · Quinolines · Survival Rate · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a single-trial base — stated on the face: ONE trial (ALTER0303) with three reports (primary, quality-of-life, histology subgroup), conducted in China (anlotinib is approved there, not by the FDA or EMA). Anlotinib 12 mg daily prolonged median overall survival versus placebo (9.6 vs 6.3 months; hazard ratio 0.68, a relative measure; P=.002) and median progression-free survival (5.4 vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.25, relative). Quality of life favoured anlotinib on most scales. The era is part of the claim: the control was placebo in a post-second-line population enrolled in 2015–16, before chemo-immunotherapy became first-line standard, so this shelf is not evidence against modern later-line options. The commonest grade ≥3 events on anlotinib were hypertension and hyponatraemia. In the histology subgroup report, the survival benefit was significant in adenocarcinoma (9.6 vs 6.9 months; P=.0051) but not in squamous disease (10.7 vs 6.5 months; P=.2570, not significant) — a subgroup read, labelled as such.

cards.headline: ALTER0303 phase 3 primary report (Han 2018): anlotinib prolonged overall survival as third-line or later therapy (median 9.6 vs 6.3 months; hazard ratio 0.68, relative; P=.002) and progression-free survival (5.4 vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.25, relative)
cards.summary: ALTER0303 phase 3 primary report (Han 2018): anlotinib prolonged overall survival as third-line or later therapy (median 9.6 vs 6.3 months; hazard ratio 0.68, relative; P=.002) and progression-free survival (5.4 vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.25, relative)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind randomised trial (ALTER0303), anlotinib vs placebo, third-line or later NSCLC (China)
cards.people: 439 patients with advanced NSCLC progressing after at least two lines of systemic therapy, randomised 2:1 (296 anlotinib, 143 placebo) at 31 hospitals in China (enrolled 2015–16); anlotinib 12 mg daily or matched placebo. Patients with centrally located squamous carcinoma with cavitary features or uncontrolled brain metastases were excluded.
cards.result: Overall survival was significantly longer with anlotinib: median 9.6 months (95% CI 8.2 to 10.6) versus 6.3 months (95% CI 5.0 to 8.1) (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.87; P=.002 — a relative measure). Median progression-free survival was 5.4 months (95% CI 4.4 to 5.6) versus 1.4 months (95% CI 1.1 to 1.5) (hazard ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.31; P<.001, relative). Objective response and disease-control rates were considerably higher with anlotinib. The most common grade 3 or higher adverse events in the anlotinib arm were hypertension and hyponatraemia.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is placebo in a 2015–16 pre-chemo-immunotherapy-era population: the result shows anlotinib beats no active therapy after two lines, not that it beats modern later-line treatments. Single-region evidence.

cards.type: Quality-of-life report of the ALTER0303 phase 3 trial (same trial as the primary card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 437 of the ALTER0303 patients (294 anlotinib, 143 placebo) assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and lung-cancer module QLQ-LC13 at baseline, end of cycle 1, every two cycles and final visit; questionnaire completion ranged from 69.9% to 97.0%, and analyses covered the first six cycles.
cards.result: Baseline scores were similar between arms. Compared with placebo, anlotinib improved role functioning, social functioning, dyspnoea, insomnia, constipation and financial problems (differences of 10 points or more were prespecified as clinically meaningful); only the sore mouth or tongue symptom was worse in the anlotinib arm.
cards.watchOut: Quality-of-life data in a trial where the placebo arm progresses quickly are vulnerable to attrition (completion fell as low as 69.9%); this report supports tolerability, it is not a second efficacy trial.

cards.type: Histology subgroup analysis of the ALTER0303 phase 3 trial (same trial as the cards above — a subgroup report, not an independent trial)
cards.people: The ALTER0303 full analysis set by histology: 336 patients with adenocarcinoma, 86 with squamous cell carcinoma and 15 with another subtype, randomised 2:1 to anlotinib 12 mg daily (days 1–14 of a 21-day cycle) or placebo.
cards.result: In adenocarcinoma, median overall survival was 9.6 months with anlotinib versus 6.9 months with placebo (P=.0051) and median progression-free survival 5.5 versus 1.4 months (P<.0001). In squamous disease, median overall survival was 10.7 versus 6.5 months (P=.2570, not significant) and median progression-free survival 4.8 versus 2.7 months (P=.0004). Common adverse events were similar across the histology subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup analysis of a single trial: the squamous subgroup (n=86) is small, its survival read is not significant, and subgroup results must not be promoted to separate per-histology claims.
