shelves.title: Adjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy in resected NSCLC: survival benefit in stage II–III (IALT, ANITA, LACE) — none shown in stage IB, harm trend in stage IA
shelves.question: In patients with completely resected non-small-cell lung cancer, does adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy improve overall survival versus observation, and in which stages (IALT / ANITA / LACE)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Cisplatin · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lung Neoplasms · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) in stage II–III, not shown in stage I. IALT (1,867 randomised): 5-year survival 44.5% vs 40.4% with cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy (death HR 0.86, relative; absolute gain 4.1 points). ANITA (840 randomised, vinorelbine–cisplatin): median survival 65.7 vs 43.7 months (adjusted HR 0.80, relative; 5-year advantage 8.6 points). The LACE pooled individual-patient analysis (4,584 patients, including IALT and ANITA — labelled, not independent) gave HR 0.89 and a 5.4-point absolute 5-year benefit, varying by stage: IA HR 1.40 (harm trend), IB 0.93, II 0.83, III 0.83. Toxic deaths were 0.8% in IALT and 2% in ANITA, with neutropenia in 92% of ANITA's treated patients.

cards.headline: IALT RCT (Arriagada 2004): adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy after complete resection improved 5-year survival (44.5% vs 40.4%; death HR 0.86, a relative measure), with 0.8% chemotherapy-toxic deaths
cards.summary: IALT RCT (Arriagada 2004): adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy after complete resection improved 5-year survival (44.5% vs 40.4%; death HR 0.86, a relative measure), with 0.8% chemotherapy-toxic deaths
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (IALT), adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy vs observation after complete resection of NSCLC
cards.people: 1,867 patients with completely resected NSCLC randomised to three or four cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy or observation; 36.5% had pathological stage I disease, 24.2% stage II and 39.3% stage III. The cisplatin partner drug was etoposide in 56.5%, vinorelbine in 26.8%, vinblastine in 11.0% and vindesine in 5.8%; 73.8% of the 932 chemotherapy patients received at least 240 mg/m² of cisplatin. Median follow-up 56 months.
cards.result: Patients assigned to chemotherapy had significantly higher survival than those assigned to observation: 44.5% versus 40.4% alive at 5 years (469 vs 504 deaths; hazard ratio for death 0.86, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.98; P<0.03 — a relative measure, beside an absolute 5-year difference of 4.1 percentage points). Disease-free survival was also higher (39.4% vs 34.3% at 5 years; HR 0.83, 0.74 to 0.94). There were no significant interactions with prespecified factors. Seven patients (0.8%) died of chemotherapy-induced toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: Each centre chose its own stage range, cisplatin dose, partner drug and radiotherapy policy before randomisation, so IALT tests a cisplatin-based strategy rather than one regimen. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Arriagada et al. Cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with completely resected non-small-cell lung cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 14736927. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ANITA RCT (Douillard 2006): adjuvant vinorelbine–cisplatin after resection of stage IB–IIIA NSCLC prolonged survival (median 65.7 vs 43.7 months; adjusted death HR 0.80, a relative measure; 5-year advantage 8.6 percentage points), with neutropenia in 92% and 2% toxic deaths
cards.summary: ANITA RCT (Douillard 2006): adjuvant vinorelbine–cisplatin after resection of stage IB–IIIA NSCLC prolonged survival (median 65.7 vs 43.7 months; adjusted death HR 0.80, a relative measure; 5-year advantage 8.6 percentage points), with neutropenia in 92% and 2% toxic deaths
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (ANITA), adjuvant vinorelbine plus cisplatin vs observation in completely resected stage IB–IIIA NSCLC
cards.people: 840 patients with completely resected stage IB–IIIA NSCLC from 101 centres in 14 countries, randomised to observation (n=433) or vinorelbine 30 mg/m² plus cisplatin 100 mg/m² (n=407); 36% had stage IB disease, 24% stage II and 39% stage IIIA. Postoperative radiotherapy was per centre policy. Median follow-up 76 months.
cards.result: Median survival was 65.7 months (95% CI 47.9 to 88.5) with chemotherapy versus 43.7 months (35.7 to 52.3) with observation; the adjusted risk of death was significantly reduced (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.96; P=0.017 — a relative measure). Overall survival at 5 years improved by 8.6 percentage points, maintained at 7 years (8.4 points). Toxicity was dominated by neutropenia in 335 (92%) of treated patients and febrile neutropenia in 34 (9%); seven (2%) toxic deaths were recorded. Compliance was greater with cisplatin (median dose intensity 89%) than with vinorelbine (59%).
cards.watchOut: Only 367 of 407 chemotherapy-assigned and 431 of 433 observation-assigned patients received their assigned treatment, and vinorelbine dose intensity was low (59%) — the benefit was achieved despite incomplete delivery. Stage IB patients are included, and the LACE card below shows the stage IB effect is smaller and non-significant when pooled.
cards.source: Douillard et al. Adjuvant vinorelbine plus cisplatin versus observation in patients with completely resected stage IB-IIIA non-small-cell lung cancer (Adjuvant Navelbine International Trialist Association [ANITA]): a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2006. PMID: 16945766. Registry ID: ISRCTN95053737. cards.headline: LACE pooled individual-patient analysis (Pignon 2008): across the five largest trials (4,584 patients) adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy gave death HR 0.89 (relative) and a 5.4-percentage-point absolute 5-year benefit — but the benefit varied by stage, with a harm trend in stage IA (HR 1.40)
cards.summary: LACE pooled individual-patient analysis (Pignon 2008): across the five largest trials (4,584 patients) adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy gave death HR 0.89 (relative) and a 5.4-percentage-point absolute 5-year benefit — but the benefit varied by stage, with a harm trend in stage IA (HR 1.40)
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient-data analysis (LACE Collaborative Group) of the five largest adjuvant cisplatin trials in resected NSCLC — includes IALT and ANITA; not an independent trial
cards.people: Individual patient data pooled from the five largest post-1995 trials of cisplatin-based chemotherapy in completely resected NSCLC — 4,584 patients, including the IALT and ANITA populations carded above (this is a pooled analysis OF those trials, not an independent trial). Median follow-up 5.2 years.
cards.result: The overall hazard ratio for death was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.96; P=0.005 — a relative measure), corresponding to a 5-year absolute benefit of 5.4 percentage points, with no heterogeneity of effect among trials. The benefit varied significantly by stage (test for trend P=0.04): stage IA HR 1.40 (95% CI 0.95 to 2.06 — a harm trend), stage IB HR 0.93 (0.78 to 1.10), stage II HR 0.83 (0.73 to 0.95) and stage III HR 0.83 (0.72 to 0.94). By partner drug, vinorelbine combinations gave HR 0.80 (0.70 to 0.91) while etoposide/vinca-alkaloid combinations gave 0.92 and other combinations 0.97. The chemotherapy effect was higher in patients with better performance status and did not vary by sex, age, histology, type of surgery, planned radiotherapy or planned cisplatin dose.
cards.watchOut: Because LACE pools IALT and ANITA, its 4,584 patients must never be added to the two trial cards as if they were new patients. The stage IA hazard ratio of 1.40 has a confidence interval crossing 1 — it is a harm trend, not proven harm — but combined with the non-significant stage IB estimate it removes any basis for adjuvant chemotherapy in stage IA.
cards.source: Pignon et al. Lung adjuvant cisplatin evaluation: a pooled analysis by the LACE Collaborative Group. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2008. PMID: 18506026. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy after complete resection of NSCLC improves survival — IALT 5-year survival 44.5% vs 40.4% (HR 0.86), ANITA median 65.7 vs 43.7 months (HR 0.80), LACE pooled HR 0.89 with a 5.4-percentage-point absolute 5-year benefit (all hazard ratios are relative measures) — and the benefit is stage-dependent: clear in stage II–III, not shown in stage IB, with a harm trend in stage IA (LACE HR 1.40); the price is heavy neutropenia and roughly 1–2% toxic deaths

shelves.title: Lenalidomide-based first-line myeloma therapy: continuous Rd beat MPT (FIRST) and VRd beat Rd (SWOG S0777)
shelves.question: In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma not planned for immediate autologous transplant, does continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide (FIRST) — and does adding bortezomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone improve outcomes further (SWOG S0777)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Dexamethasone · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lenalidomide · Male · Melphalan · Middle Aged · Multiple Myeloma · Prednisone · Thalidomide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit), as a two-rung ladder from two trials (four reports, each trial's follow-up labelled as the same trial). FIRST (1,623 transplant-ineligible patients): continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide — final-analysis median OS 59.1 vs 49.1 months (HR 0.78, relative), with fewer haematologic and neurologic events but more infections than MPT, and grade 3/4 events in 70% vs 78%. SWOG S0777 (525 patients without intent for immediate transplant): adding bortezomib (VRd) beat Rd — median PFS 43 vs 30 months (HR 0.712) and median OS 75 vs 64 months (HR 0.709), persisting at 84 months (HR 0.709; median OS not reached vs 69 months) — all hazard ratios are relative measures. The cost of VRd was more grade ≥3 events (82% vs 75%) and more discontinuations (23% vs 10%).

cards.headline: FIRST primary report (Benboubker 2014): continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma — median PFS 25.5 vs 21.2 months (HR 0.72, relative); 4-year OS 59% vs 51%
cards.summary: FIRST primary report (Benboubker 2014): continuous lenalidomide–dexamethasone beat melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma — median PFS 25.5 vs 21.2 months (HR 0.72, relative); 4-year OS 59% vs 51%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial primary report (FIRST), continuous Rd vs Rd18 vs MPT in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma — FIRST limb
cards.people: 1,623 patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma ineligible for stem-cell transplantation, randomised to lenalidomide plus low-dose dexamethasone in 28-day cycles until disease progression (Rd continuous, n=535), the same combination for 72 weeks / 18 cycles (Rd18, n=541), or melphalan–prednisone–thalidomide for 72 weeks (MPT, n=547). The primary comparison was continuous Rd versus MPT.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 25.5 months with continuous Rd, 20.7 months with Rd18 and 21.2 months with MPT (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.72 for continuous Rd vs MPT and 0.70 for continuous Rd vs Rd18; P<0.001 for both — relative measures). Continuous Rd was superior to MPT on all secondary efficacy endpoints including overall survival at this interim analysis: 4-year overall survival was 59% with continuous Rd, 56% with Rd18 and 51% with MPT (absolute rates). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were somewhat less frequent with continuous Rd than MPT (70% vs 78%); continuous Rd had fewer haematologic and neurologic toxic events, a moderate increase in infections, and fewer second primary haematologic cancers than MPT.
cards.watchOut: The overall-survival comparison in this report is an interim analysis; the final analysis is carded separately below and supersedes it for survival. Fixed-duration Rd18 performed worse than continuous Rd on progression-free survival, so the result is about continuous treatment, not about lenalidomide exposure in general.
cards.source: Benboubker et al. Lenalidomide and dexamethasone in transplant-ineligible patients with myeloma. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 25184863. Registry ID: NCT00689936; EudraCT 2007-004823-39. cards.headline: FIRST final analysis (Facon 2018): at 67 months' follow-up, continuous Rd prolonged overall survival versus MPT (median 59.1 vs 49.1 months; HR 0.78, relative) — the same FIRST trial as the card above, not a second trial
cards.summary: FIRST final analysis (Facon 2018): at 67 months' follow-up, continuous Rd prolonged overall survival versus MPT (median 59.1 vs 49.1 months; HR 0.78, relative) — the same FIRST trial as the card above, not a second trial
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial final analysis (FIRST) — same trial as the primary report above, not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 1,623 FIRST patients (Rd continuous n=535, Rd18 n=541, MPT n=547), in the trial's prespecified final analysis with at least 60 months' follow-up; median follow-up 67 months. Over half of all patients who received second-line treatment were given a bortezomib-based therapy.
cards.result: Progression-free survival remained significantly longer with continuous Rd versus MPT (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.79; P<.00001 — a relative measure). Median overall survival was 10 months longer with continuous Rd than MPT (59.1 vs 49.1 months; HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.92; P=.0023 — a relative measure), and similar with Rd18 (62.3 months). In patients achieving complete or very good partial responses, continuous Rd gave an approximately 30-month longer median time to next treatment than Rd18 (69.5 vs 39.9 months). No new safety concerns, including risk for secondary malignancies, were observed.
cards.watchOut: This card and the FIRST primary report are two reports of one trial and one patient set; they must never be counted as two trials. Second-line bortezomib use in over half of retreated patients means the survival contrast is a first-line strategy contrast, not lenalidomide alone against no further therapy.
cards.source: Facon et al. Final analysis of survival outcomes in the phase 3 FIRST trial of up-front treatment for multiple myeloma. Blood. 2018. PMID: 29150421. cards.headline: SWOG S0777 primary report (Durie 2017): adding bortezomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (VRd) improved progression-free survival (median 43 vs 30 months; HR 0.712, relative) and overall survival (75 vs 64 months; HR 0.709) versus Rd alone
cards.summary: SWOG S0777 primary report (Durie 2017): adding bortezomib to lenalidomide–dexamethasone (VRd) improved progression-free survival (median 43 vs 30 months; HR 0.712, relative) and overall survival (75 vs 64 months; HR 0.709) versus Rd alone
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial primary report (SWOG S0777), VRd vs Rd in newly diagnosed myeloma without intent for immediate transplant — S0777 limb
cards.people: 525 patients with previously untreated multiple myeloma not planned for immediate autologous stem-cell transplant, randomised at 139 SWOG/NCTN institutions (264 to VRd, 261 to Rd); 21 VRd and 31 Rd patients were later deemed ineligible, mainly for baseline laboratory problems. VRd was eight 21-day cycles of bortezomib 1.3 mg/m² intravenously days 1, 4, 8 and 11 with lenalidomide 25 mg days 1–14 and dexamethasone; Rd was six 28-day cycles of lenalidomide 25 mg days 1–21 with dexamethasone 40 mg weekly.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was significantly improved with VRd (43 vs 30 months; stratified HR 0.712, 96% CI 0.56 to 0.906; one-sided P=0.0018 — a relative measure), as was median overall survival (75 vs 64 months; HR 0.709, 95% CI 0.524 to 0.959; P=0.025 — a relative measure). Overall response (partial response or better) was 82% (176/216 assessable) on VRd versus 72% (153/214) on Rd, with complete response or better in 16% versus 8%. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events occurred in 82% of VRd patients versus 75% on Rd, and 23% versus 10% discontinued induction because of adverse events; there were two treatment-related deaths on VRd and none on Rd.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the two arms' induction schedules differ in cycle length and dexamethasone dosing as well as in the bortezomib itself, so the comparison is of the VRd regimen as a whole against the Rd regimen as a whole. Fifty-two randomised patients were deemed ineligible after randomisation.
cards.source: Durie et al. Bortezomib with lenalidomide and dexamethasone versus lenalidomide and dexamethasone alone in patients with newly diagnosed myeloma without intent for immediate autologous stem-cell transplant (SWOG S0777): a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28017406. Registry ID: NCT00644228. cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial long-term follow-up report (SWOG S0777) — same trial as the primary report above, not an independent trial
cards.people: 460 patients evaluable for survival endpoints from the S0777 randomised set (225 eligible and analysable on Rd, 235 on VRd); all patients received Rd maintenance after induction (six 28-day Rd cycles or eight 21-day VRd cycles). Median duration of Rd maintenance was 17.1 months. Median follow-up 84 months.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 41 months for VRd and 29 months for Rd (stratified HR 0.742, 96% Wald CI 0.594 to 0.928; one-sided stratified log-rank P=0.003 — a relative measure). Median overall survival was still not reached for VRd versus 69 months for Rd (stratified HR 0.709, 96% CI 0.543 to 0.926; two-sided P=0.0114 — a relative measure). Both progression-free and overall survival remained improved with VRd after adjustment for age. No registry ID is in this report's PubMed record.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same trial and substantially the same patients as the primary report — labelled as such and never counted as a second trial. The evaluable set (460) is smaller than the randomised set (525) because ineligible patients were excluded.

shelves.title: Bortezomib plus melphalan–prednisone in transplant-ineligible myeloma (VISTA, one trial / three reports): longer progression-free and overall survival, neuropathy in 47% that mostly reversed
shelves.question: In patients with previously untreated multiple myeloma ineligible for high-dose therapy, does adding bortezomib to melphalan–prednisone prolong time to progression and overall survival, and at what neuropathy cost (VISTA)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols · Boronic Acids · Bortezomib · Disease Progression · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Melphalan · Middle Aged · Multiple Myeloma · Prednisone · Pyrazines · Survival Analysis · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — on ONE trial (VISTA, 682 randomised) reported three times, each report labelled as the same trial. VMP beat melphalan–prednisone on time to progression (24.0 vs 16.6 months, HR 0.48) and, at updated follow-up (median 36.7 months), on survival: HR 0.653 — a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death — with 3-year OS 68.5% vs 54.0% (absolute rates) and median OS not reached vs 43 months. Complete responses were 30% vs 4%. The pricing harm is peripheral neuropathy: 47% on VMP (13% grade ≥3), dose-related with a plateau at ~45 mg/m² cumulative dose, but 79% of events improved within a median 1.9 months and 60% resolved completely within 5.7 months; grade 3 events overall were 53% vs 44% with no excess of grade 4 events or treatment-related deaths.

cards.headline: VISTA primary report (San Miguel 2008): bortezomib plus melphalan–prednisone (VMP) prolonged time to progression versus melphalan–prednisone alone (24.0 vs 16.6 months; HR 0.48, relative), with complete responses 30% vs 4% and OS HR 0.61 — ONE trial, reported three times on this shelf
cards.summary: VISTA primary report (San Miguel 2008): bortezomib plus melphalan–prednisone (VMP) prolonged time to progression versus melphalan–prednisone alone (24.0 vs 16.6 months; HR 0.48, relative), with complete responses 30% vs 4% and OS HR 0.61 — ONE trial, reported three times on this shelf
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial primary report (VISTA), VMP vs MP in transplant-ineligible newly diagnosed myeloma — the single trial behind all three reports on this shelf
cards.people: 682 patients with previously untreated multiple myeloma ineligible for high-dose therapy, randomised to nine 6-week cycles of melphalan 9 mg/m² and prednisone 60 mg/m² on days 1–4, alone or with bortezomib 1.3 mg/m² on days 1, 4, 8, 11, 22, 25, 29 and 32 in cycles 1–4 and days 1, 8, 22 and 29 in cycles 5–9. The primary endpoint was time to disease progression.
cards.result: Time to progression was 24.0 months with VMP versus 16.6 months with MP (HR 0.48; P<0.001 — a relative measure). Partial response or better occurred in 71% versus 35%, and complete response in 30% versus 4% (P<0.001). Median response duration was 19.9 versus 13.1 months. The hazard ratio for overall survival was 0.61 for the bortezomib group (P=0.008 — a relative measure). Grade 3 events were more frequent with VMP (53% vs 44%; P=0.02), with no significant difference in grade 4 events (28% vs 27%) or treatment-related deaths (1% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: This shelf rests on ONE trial. The two cards that follow are the same trial's updated follow-up and its neuropathy subanalysis — labelled programme reports, not independent evidence. The survival result in this primary report was early (HR 0.61); the updated follow-up below is the mature survival estimate.

cards.headline: VISTA updated follow-up (Mateos 2010): after median 36.7 months, VMP's survival advantage was confirmed — a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death (HR 0.653), 3-year OS 68.5% vs 54.0% — and later bortezomib-based salvage still worked after first-line VMP (response 47%)
cards.summary: VISTA updated follow-up (Mateos 2010): after median 36.7 months, VMP's survival advantage was confirmed — a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death (HR 0.653), 3-year OS 68.5% vs 54.0% — and later bortezomib-based salvage still worked after first-line VMP (response 47%)
cards.type: Phase 3 trial updated follow-up report (VISTA) — same single trial as the primary report above, not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 682 VISTA patients (VMP n=344, MP n=338) after prolonged follow-up, including an evaluation of subsequent antimyeloma therapies given after the trial treatment.
cards.result: With median follow-up of 36.7 months there was a 35% relative reduction in the risk of death with VMP versus MP (HR 0.653; P<.001); median overall survival was not reached with VMP versus 43 months with MP, and 3-year overall survival rates were 68.5% versus 54.0% (absolute rates). Response rates to subsequent bortezomib-based therapy were 47% after first-line VMP versus 59% after MP, and among patients who received subsequent therapy median survival from its start was 30.2 months (after VMP, n=178) versus 21.9 months (after MP, n=233), with no difference in survival from salvage by which agent was used. Adverse-event rates were higher with VMP during cycles 1–4 but similar during cycles 5–9. Of peripheral neuropathy events on VMP, 79% improved within a median of 1.9 months and 60% resolved completely within a median of 5.7 months.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, same patients as the primary report — the two survival hazard ratios (0.61 early, 0.653 updated) are successive estimates of one effect, not two findings. No registry ID is in this report's PubMed record, although the primary report carries the trial's NCT number.

cards.headline: VISTA neuropathy subanalysis (Dimopoulos 2011): peripheral neuropathy occurred in 47% of VMP patients (13% grade ≥3), was dose-related with a plateau at a cumulative bortezomib dose of about 45 mg/m², and mostly reversed — 79% of events improved within a median 1.9 months and 60% resolved completely within 5.7 months
cards.summary: VISTA neuropathy subanalysis (Dimopoulos 2011): peripheral neuropathy occurred in 47% of VMP patients (13% grade ≥3), was dose-related with a plateau at a cumulative bortezomib dose of about 45 mg/m², and mostly reversed — 79% of events improved within a median 1.9 months and 60% resolved completely within 5.7 months
cards.type: Subanalysis of the phase 3 VISTA trial (peripheral neuropathy) — same single trial as the reports above, not an independent trial
cards.people: Patients in the VISTA trial who received VMP (the same single trial as the two cards above), analysed for the frequency, characteristics, reversibility and prognostic factors of bortezomib-associated peripheral neuropathy.
cards.result: Overall, 47% of patients receiving VMP developed peripheral neuropathy, including 19% grade 2 and 13% grade ≥3 (under 1% grade 4). Incidence was dose-related and reached a plateau at a cumulative bortezomib dose of approximately 45 mg/m²; median time to onset was 2.3 months. The neuropathy was reversible: 79% of events improved by at least one grade within a median of 1.9 months and 60% completely resolved within a median of 5.7 months, similarly in responding and non-responding patients. By multivariate analysis, baseline neuropathy was the only consistent risk factor (HR 1.785 for any neuropathy, 2.205 for grade ≥2, 2.438 for grade ≥3 — relative measures); age, pre-existing diabetes, stage, obesity and creatinine clearance did not affect the overall rate.
cards.watchOut: A subanalysis of the one VISTA trial, carded for its practical content on the regimen's main toxicity — it adds no efficacy evidence. The plateau and reversibility figures describe this twice-weekly intravenous schedule; they should not be transferred uncritically to weekly or subcutaneous bortezomib schedules, which this trial did not test.

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 reports, stated on the face: SHARP (602 randomised; median overall survival 10.7 vs 7.9 months, hazard ratio 0.69 relative) and the Asia-Pacific trial (226 randomised, predominantly hepatitis-B-related disease; 6.5 vs 4.2 months, hazard ratio 0.68 relative). Both were re-verified at slate-16 mining and fetched again this session. The two trials are regional/aetiological slices, never pooled. The benefit is real but modest in absolute terms (~2–3 months of median survival), and SHARP found NO significant difference in time to symptomatic progression (4.1 vs 4.9 months, P=0.77) — that null sits beside the survival gain, with partial response in only 2% and no complete responses, and diarrhoea, weight loss, hand–foot skin reaction and hypophosphataemia more frequent on sorafenib. A labelled SHARP biomarker programme report (no biomarker predicted sorafenib response) completes the record without counting as a third trial.

cards.headline: SHARP (Llovet 2008, 602 randomised): sorafenib prolonged median overall survival to 10.7 vs 7.9 months (hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and radiologic progression to 5.5 vs 2.8 months — but time to SYMPTOMATIC progression did NOT differ (4.1 vs 4.9 months, P=0.77)
cards.summary: SHARP (Llovet 2008, 602 randomised): sorafenib prolonged median overall survival to 10.7 vs 7.9 months (hazard ratio 0.69, relative) and radiologic progression to 5.5 vs 2.8 months — but time to SYMPTOMATIC progression did NOT differ (4.1 vs 4.9 months, P=0.77)
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SHARP), sorafenib vs placebo
cards.people: 602 patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma who had received no previous systemic therapy, in a multicentre phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled trial, randomised to sorafenib 400 mg twice daily or placebo. Primary outcomes were overall survival and time to symptomatic progression; the study was stopped at the second planned interim analysis after 321 deaths.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 10.7 months on sorafenib versus 7.9 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it: a gain of about 2.8 months). There was no significant difference in median time to symptomatic progression (4.1 vs 4.9 months; P=0.77). Median time to radiologic progression was 5.5 versus 2.8 months (P<0.001). Partial response occurred in 7 patients (2%) on sorafenib and 2 (1%) on placebo, with no complete responses. Diarrhoea, weight loss, hand–foot skin reaction and hypophosphataemia were more frequent on sorafenib.
cards.watchOut: Stopped at a planned interim analysis after 321 deaths. The survival gain came with no measurable delay in symptomatic progression — that null is printed in the headline because it prices the benefit: ~3 months of radiologic/survival gain without demonstrated symptom-delay.
cards.source: Llovet JM et al. Sorafenib in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. The New England journal of medicine. 2008. PMID: 18650514. Registry ID: NCT00105443. cards.headline: Asia-Pacific trial (Cheng 2009, 226 randomised, predominantly hepatitis-B-related disease): median overall survival 6.5 vs 4.2 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.68, relative); time to progression 2.8 vs 1.4 months
cards.summary: Asia-Pacific trial (Cheng 2009, 226 randomised, predominantly hepatitis-B-related disease): median overall survival 6.5 vs 4.2 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.68, relative); time to progression 2.8 vs 1.4 months
cards.type: Phase 3 multinational randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Asia-Pacific), sorafenib vs placebo
cards.people: 271 patients were enrolled at 23 centres in China, South Korea and Taiwan, and 226 with advanced (unresectable or metastatic) hepatocellular carcinoma, no previous systemic therapy and Child-Pugh class A liver function were randomised 2:1 to oral sorafenib 400 mg twice daily (150) or placebo (76), in a phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Overall survival, time to progression, time to symptomatic progression, disease control and safety were assessed (no predefined primary endpoint).
cards.result: Median overall survival was 6.5 months (95% CI 5.56 to 7.56) on sorafenib versus 4.2 months (3.75 to 5.46) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93; P=0.014 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it: a gain of about 2.3 months). Median time to progression was 2.8 versus 1.4 months (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.79; P=0.0005). The most frequent grade 3/4 drug-related adverse events among 149 assessable sorafenib patients were hand–foot skin reaction (10.7%), diarrhoea (6.0%) and fatigue (3.4%); dose reductions were driven by hand–foot skin reaction (11.4%) and diarrhoea (7.4%) and rarely led to discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: A different region and aetiology mix (predominantly hepatitis-B-related) from SHARP, with shorter survival in both arms — the two trials are labelled regional slices and are never pooled into one survival number. No predefined primary endpoint, as the record states.
cards.source: Cheng AL et al. Efficacy and safety of sorafenib in patients in the Asia-Pacific region with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: a phase III randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Oncology. 2009. PMID: 19095497. Registry ID: NCT00492752. cards.headline: Programme report — SHARP plasma biomarkers (Llovet 2012): baseline angiopoietin-2 and VEGF independently predicted survival in both arms, but NO biomarker significantly predicted response to sorafenib (a report OF the SHARP trial — not a third trial)
cards.summary: Programme report — SHARP plasma biomarkers (Llovet 2012): baseline angiopoietin-2 and VEGF independently predicted survival in both arms, but NO biomarker significantly predicted response to sorafenib (a report OF the SHARP trial — not a third trial)
cards.type: Programme report: prespecified plasma-biomarker analysis of the SHARP randomised trial (same trial as the SHARP card above — not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: Plasma biomarkers were measured at baseline in 491 of the 602 SHARP participants and after 12 weeks of treatment in 305, within the SHARP randomised trial carded above; ten candidate plasma biomarkers were analysed for prognostic and predictive value.
cards.result: Baseline angiopoietin-2 and VEGF concentrations independently predicted survival in the whole population and in the placebo cohort, as did macroscopic vascular invasion, ECOG performance status, baseline alpha-fetoprotein and alkaline phosphatase. In the sorafenib cohort there were only trends toward enhanced survival benefit with high soluble c-KIT or low hepatocyte growth factor (interaction P=0.081 and P=0.073 — neither significant). The authors concluded that none of the biomarkers tested significantly predicted response to sorafenib.
cards.watchOut: A biomarker analysis of one of the two trials on this shelf: it adds no efficacy evidence and must not be counted as a third report of the sorafenib-versus-placebo question — the randomised base remains exactly 2 reports.
cards.source: Llovet JM et al. Plasma biomarkers as predictors of outcome in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research. 2012. PMID: 22374331. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports exist (SHARP, n=602; Asia-Pacific, n=226), and both re-verified at mining and again this session: sorafenib prolongs survival by about 2–3 months of median overall survival in advanced HCC, with no demonstrated delay in symptomatic progression in SHARP
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports exist (SHARP, n=602; Asia-Pacific, n=226), and both re-verified at mining and again this session: sorafenib prolongs survival by about 2–3 months of median overall survival in advanced HCC, with no demonstrated delay in symptomatic progression in SHARP
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the two placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (828 randomised in total across two regions/aetiologies, never pooled), plus one labelled biomarker programme report of SHARP that adds no comparative evidence.
cards.result: SHARP: median overall survival 10.7 vs 7.9 months (hazard ratio 0.69, relative). Asia-Pacific: 6.5 vs 4.2 months (hazard ratio 0.68, relative). The relative effects are strikingly similar; the absolute gains are modest (~2.8 and ~2.3 months of median survival) and, in SHARP, bought without a significant difference in time to symptomatic progression (4.1 vs 4.9 months, P=0.77), with partial responses in only 2% and no complete responses, and with diarrhoea, weight loss, hand–foot skin reaction and hypophosphataemia more frequent on sorafenib. This is the founding systemic-therapy question for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: every later first-line HCC programme in the library was compared against sorafenib, while the sorafenib-versus-placebo question itself was asked nowhere — which is why this exactly-2-report base is rowed deliberately as FLOOR-RISK rather than padded. There is no third randomised report to card.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK stated exactly: 2 reports. If either trial had failed to verify this session, this pack would not have been built. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In treatment-naïve, physically fit patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, does adding rituximab to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide (FCR vs FC) improve progression-free and overall survival? (Slate row S16-3-03 — the CLL8 question.)

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): CLL8 randomised 817 fit, treatment-naïve patients with CLL to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide with or without rituximab. FCR improved 3-year progression-free survival (65% vs 45%; hazard ratio 0.56, relative) and overall survival (87% vs 83%; hazard ratio 0.67, relative); at median 5.9 years, median progression-free survival was 56.8 vs 32.9 months and overall survival not reached vs 86.0 months. Benefit was ABSENT in del(17p) and most durable in IGHV-mutated disease — both printed on the face. FCR induced low minimal residual disease more often than FC, and MRD level independently predicted outcome. The pricing harm is neutropenia (grade 3/4 34% vs 21%; prolonged first-year neutropenia 16.6% vs 8.8%), without more severe infections. This is the pre-BTK-inhibitor standard the library's targeted-therapy CLL shelves compare against. NOTE on the commissioning label: slate row S16-3-03 is this CLL8 question (rituximab + FC in CLL); it is not a rituximab-CHOP/DLBCL question, and no DLBCL report is carded here.

cards.headline: CLL8 primary report (Hallek 2010, 817 randomised): adding rituximab to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide improved 3-year progression-free survival to 65% vs 45% (hazard ratio 0.56, relative) and 3-year overall survival to 87% vs 83% (hazard ratio 0.67, relative); grade 3/4 neutropenia 34% vs 21%
cards.summary: CLL8 primary report (Hallek 2010, 817 randomised): adding rituximab to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide improved 3-year progression-free survival to 65% vs 45% (hazard ratio 0.56, relative) and 3-year overall survival to 87% vs 83% (hazard ratio 0.67, relative); grade 3/4 neutropenia 34% vs 21%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (CLL8), FCR vs FC in first-line CLL
cards.people: 817 treatment-naïve, physically fit patients (aged 30–81 years) with CD20-positive chronic lymphocytic leukaemia at 190 centres in 11 countries, randomised to six courses of fludarabine 25 mg/m²/day plus cyclophosphamide 250 mg/m²/day for the first 3 days of each 28-day course, with (408) or without (409) rituximab (375 mg/m² on day 0 of course 1, then 500 mg/m² on day 1 of courses 2–6). Open-label phase 3 trial; primary endpoint progression-free survival, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: At 3 years, 65% of the chemoimmunotherapy (FCR) group were free of progression versus 45% on FC (hazard ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.69; P<0.0001 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it), and 87% versus 83% were alive (hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.92; P=0.01). Grade 3/4 neutropenia was more frequent on FCR (136 of 404 [34%] vs 83 of 396 [21%]) and grade 3/4 leucocytopenia likewise (97 [24%] vs 48 [12%]); other side effects, including severe infections, were not increased. Treatment-related deaths were 8 (2%) on FCR versus 10 (3%) on FC.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and a physically fit, treatment-naïve population aged 30–81 — the result does not automatically transfer to unfit or older CLL populations treated with gentler regimens.
cards.source: Hallek M et al. Addition of rituximab to fludarabine and cyclophosphamide in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2010. PMID: 20888994. Registry ID: NCT00281918. cards.headline: CLL8 long-term follow-up (Fischer 2016, median follow-up 5.9 years — same trial, labelled): median progression-free survival 56.8 vs 32.9 months (hazard ratio 0.59, relative); benefit absent in del(17p); prolonged neutropenia in the first year 16.6% vs 8.8%; secondary malignancies 13.1% vs 17.4%
cards.summary: CLL8 long-term follow-up (Fischer 2016, median follow-up 5.9 years — same trial, labelled): median progression-free survival 56.8 vs 32.9 months (hazard ratio 0.59, relative); benefit absent in del(17p); prolonged neutropenia in the first year 16.6% vs 8.8%; secondary malignancies 13.1% vs 17.4%
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the CLL8 randomised trial (same trial as the primary card — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: The same 817 CLL8 participants carded above, followed for a median of 5.9 years; this is the long-term report of the one CLL8 trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 56.8 months on FCR versus 32.9 months on FC (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.69; P<0.001 — relative, absolute medians beside it); median overall survival was not reached on FCR versus 86.0 months on FC (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.89; P=0.001). In patients with mutated IGHV, FCR improved progression-free survival (hazard ratio 0.47) with an overall-survival hazard ratio of 0.62 that was not significant (P=0.1); the improvement applied to all cytogenetic subgroups OTHER than del(17p), where benefit was absent. Prolonged neutropenia during the first year after treatment was more frequent on FCR (16.6% vs 8.8%; P=0.007). Secondary malignancies including Richter transformation occurred in 13.1% on FCR versus 17.4% on FC (P=0.1).
cards.watchOut: Subgroup findings (IGHV-mutated durable remissions; del(17p) exception) are labelled as subgroups of one trial — the del(17p) absence of benefit is the clinically decisive exception and is printed on the face, not buried.
cards.source: Fischer K et al. Long-term remissions after FCR chemoimmunotherapy in previously untreated patients with CLL: updated results of the CLL8 trial. Blood. 2016. PMID: 26486789. cards.headline: CLL8 minimal-residual-disease analysis (Böttcher 2012, 493 patients with quantified MRD — same trial, labelled): median progression-free survival 68.7 / 40.5 / 15.4 months across low / intermediate / high MRD levels; FCR induced low MRD more often than FC, with no arm difference within any MRD category
cards.summary: CLL8 minimal-residual-disease analysis (Böttcher 2012, 493 patients with quantified MRD — same trial, labelled): median progression-free survival 68.7 / 40.5 / 15.4 months across low / intermediate / high MRD levels; FCR induced low MRD more often than FC, with no arm difference within any MRD category
cards.type: Minimal-residual-disease analysis of the CLL8 randomised trial (same trial — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: 493 CLL8 patients with prospectively quantified flow-cytometric minimal residual disease (1,775 blood and bone marrow samples), categorised 2 months after therapy as low (<10⁻⁴), intermediate (≥10⁻⁴ to <10⁻²) or high (≥10⁻²) MRD; a multivariate analysis of the randomised CLL8 trial carded above, not a separate trial.
cards.result: Median progression-free survival was 68.7 months (low MRD), 40.5 months (intermediate) and 15.4 months (high); compared with low MRD, the risks of progression were higher at intermediate and high levels (hazard ratios 2.49 and 14.7, both P<0.0001 — relative measures, absolute medians beside them). Median overall survival was 48.4 months in the high-MRD group and not reached at lower levels. MRD remained predictive in multivariate analyses including pre-treatment risk markers. Progression-free and overall survival did not differ between FCR and FC within each MRD category; FCR's advantage operated by inducing low MRD more frequently than FC.
cards.watchOut: MRD is a prognostic/surrogate analysis within one trial: it explains how FCR's benefit is mediated, and adds no independent comparative evidence. Registry ID is none in this report's own record (the trial's NCT00281918 appears on the primary and long-term reports).

cards.headline: Synthesis: ONE trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf) — CLL8 shows rituximab added to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide improves progression-free and overall survival in fit, treatment-naïve CLL, except in del(17p)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ONE trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf) — CLL8 shows rituximab added to fludarabine–cyclophosphamide improves progression-free and overall survival in fit, treatment-naïve CLL, except in del(17p)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the CLL8 trial (817 randomised) reported three times — primary report, long-term follow-up at median 5.9 years, and the MRD analysis in 493 patients. One trial, one programme, labelled as such throughout.
cards.result: Three-year progression-free survival was 65% vs 45% (hazard ratio 0.56, relative) and overall survival 87% vs 83% (hazard ratio 0.67, relative); at long-term follow-up median progression-free survival was 56.8 vs 32.9 months and median overall survival not reached vs 86.0 months. The benefit was absent in del(17p) and most durable in IGHV-mutated disease. The pricing harms are myelosuppression: grade 3/4 neutropenia 34% vs 21% at primary report and prolonged first-year neutropenia 16.6% vs 8.8% long-term, without an increase in severe infections or secondary malignancies. FCR is the pre-BTK-inhibitor standard against which the library's targeted-therapy CLL shelves are comparisons; this shelf is that standard's founding record, and it should be read as one trial reported three times, not three trials.
cards.watchOut: Single-programme shelf (one trial, three reports) — the count is stated exactly so the base is not mistaken for independent replication. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Bevacizumab in first-line non-squamous NSCLC: SPLIT — an overall-survival win in E4599, progression-free survival only in AVAiL, with fatal bleeding in E4599
shelves.question: In patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC, does adding bevacizumab to first-line platinum chemotherapy (paclitaxel–carboplatin in E4599; cisplatin–gemcitabine in AVAiL) improve overall and progression-free survival, and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Angiogenesis Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bevacizumab · Carboplatin/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy,mortality · Disease-Free Survival · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy,mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Paclitaxel/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A/blood
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by chemotherapy backbone. E4599 (878 randomised, paclitaxel–carboplatin): adding bevacizumab prolonged median overall survival (12.3 vs 10.3 months; hazard ratio 0.79, relative) and progression-free survival (6.2 vs 4.5 months), with the benefit concentrated in adenocarcinoma — but with clinically significant bleeding in 4.4% vs 0.7% and 15 treatment-related deaths, including 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage, in a population that excluded squamous tumours, brain metastases and significant haemoptysis. AVAiL (1,043 randomised, cisplatin–gemcitabine): bevacizumab improved progression-free survival (hazard ratios 0.75 and 0.85, relative) but overall survival was NOT significantly increased (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03 — the null is printed beside the E4599 headline), with ~62% receiving later-line therapy. The E4599/AVAiL contrast is the shelf.

cards.headline: E4599 primary report (Sandler 2006, 878 randomised): bevacizumab + paclitaxel–carboplatin prolonged median overall survival to 12.3 vs 10.3 months (hazard ratio 0.79, relative) and progression-free survival to 6.2 vs 4.5 months — with clinically significant bleeding in 4.4% vs 0.7% and 15 treatment-related deaths, including 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage
cards.summary: E4599 primary report (Sandler 2006, 878 randomised): bevacizumab + paclitaxel–carboplatin prolonged median overall survival to 12.3 vs 10.3 months (hazard ratio 0.79, relative) and progression-free survival to 6.2 vs 4.5 months — with clinically significant bleeding in 4.4% vs 0.7% and 15 treatment-related deaths, including 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage
cards.type: Randomised trial (E4599), paclitaxel–carboplatin + bevacizumab vs paclitaxel–carboplatin alone in advanced NSCLC
cards.people: 878 patients with recurrent or advanced (stage IIIB/IV) non-small-cell lung cancer (444 chemotherapy alone, 434 chemotherapy plus bevacizumab), treated with paclitaxel–carboplatin every 3 weeks for six cycles, with bevacizumab continued every 3 weeks until progression or intolerable toxicity. Patients with squamous-cell tumours, brain metastases, clinically significant haemoptysis or inadequate organ function/performance status were EXCLUDED. Primary endpoint overall survival.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 12.3 months with bevacizumab versus 10.3 months without (hazard ratio for death 0.79; P=0.003 — a relative measure, absolute medians beside it). Median progression-free survival was 6.2 versus 4.5 months (hazard ratio 0.66; P<0.001) and response rates were 35% versus 15% (P<0.001). Clinically significant bleeding occurred in 4.4% versus 0.7% (P<0.001). There were 15 treatment-related deaths in the bevacizumab group, including 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage.
cards.watchOut: A selected, non-squamous population: squamous histology, brain metastases and significant haemoptysis were excluded precisely because of bleeding risk — the 15 treatment-related deaths, 5 from pulmonary haemorrhage, occurred despite those exclusions and must sit beside the survival headline.
cards.source: Sandler A et al. Paclitaxel-carboplatin alone or with bevacizumab for non-small-cell lung cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 17167137. Registry ID: NCT00021060. cards.headline: E4599 histology analysis (Sandler 2010 — same trial, labelled): the survival benefit concentrated in adenocarcinoma (68.8% of patients; median overall survival 14.2 vs 10.3 months, hazard ratio 0.69, relative); other subtypes were too small for meaningful comparison
cards.summary: E4599 histology analysis (Sandler 2010 — same trial, labelled): the survival benefit concentrated in adenocarcinoma (68.8% of patients; median overall survival 14.2 vs 10.3 months, hazard ratio 0.69, relative); other subtypes were too small for meaningful comparison
cards.type: Retrospective histology analysis of the E4599 randomised trial (same trial as the primary card — labelled)
cards.people: The 878 E4599 participants carded above, analysed by tumour histology: adenocarcinoma in 68.8% (302 chemotherapy, 300 chemotherapy plus bevacizumab), 'not otherwise specified' 18.9%, large-cell undifferentiated 5.5%, bronchoalveolar carcinoma 2.6% and 'other' 3.9%. A retrospective histology analysis of the one E4599 trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Overall median survival was 10.3 months on chemotherapy alone versus 12.3 months with bevacizumab (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.93 — relative, consistent with the primary report). In adenocarcinoma, median overall survival was 14.2 months with bevacizumab versus 10.3 months without (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.83). Sample sizes for the other histologic subtypes were too small for meaningful comparisons. Safety profiles across histologies were consistent with the overall profile, with no unexpected trends.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective subgroup analysis of one trial: the adenocarcinoma concentration of benefit is a labelled subgroup finding, and the non-adenocarcinoma subtypes are explicitly inconclusive — not evidence of no benefit in them.
cards.source: Sandler A et al. Treatment outcomes by tumor histology in Eastern Cooperative Group Study E4599 of bevacizumab with paclitaxel/carboplatin for advanced non-small cell lung cancer. cards.headline: AVAiL final overall-survival analysis (Reck 2010, 1,043 randomised, cisplatin–gemcitabine backbone): progression-free survival benefit maintained (hazard ratios 0.75 and 0.85, relative) but overall survival was NOT significantly increased (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03 — null), with ~62% receiving later-line therapy
cards.summary: AVAiL final overall-survival analysis (Reck 2010, 1,043 randomised, cisplatin–gemcitabine backbone): progression-free survival benefit maintained (hazard ratios 0.75 and 0.85, relative) but overall survival was NOT significantly increased (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03 — null), with ~62% receiving later-line therapy
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial (AVAiL) final overall-survival analysis, bevacizumab (two doses) + cisplatin–gemcitabine vs placebo + cisplatin–gemcitabine
cards.people: 1,043 patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC receiving cisplatin 80 mg/m² plus gemcitabine 1250 mg/m² for up to six cycles, plus bevacizumab 7.5 mg/kg (345), bevacizumab 15 mg/kg (351) or placebo (347) every 3 weeks until progression, in a randomised phase 3 trial. Progression-free survival was the primary endpoint; this report is the final overall-survival analysis.
cards.result: The progression-free survival benefit was maintained: hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.87; P=0.0003) at 7.5 mg/kg and 0.85 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.00; P=0.0456) at 15 mg/kg (relative measures). Median overall survival was over 13 months in all groups, but overall survival was NOT significantly increased with bevacizumab: hazard ratio 0.93 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.11; P=0.420) at 7.5 mg/kg and 1.03 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.23; P=0.761) at 15 mg/kg. Updated safety was consistent with previous reports.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by backbone — the same drug-class question gives an overall-survival win on a paclitaxel–carboplatin backbone (E4599) and a progression-free-only result on a cisplatin–gemcitabine backbone (AVAiL)
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by backbone — the same drug-class question gives an overall-survival win on a paclitaxel–carboplatin backbone (E4599) and a progression-free-only result on a cisplatin–gemcitabine backbone (AVAiL)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: two trials — E4599 (878 randomised; primary report plus its labelled histology analysis) and AVAiL (1,043 randomised; final overall-survival analysis).
cards.result: E4599: median overall survival 12.3 vs 10.3 months (hazard ratio 0.79, relative), progression-free survival 6.2 vs 4.5 months, response 35% vs 15% — at the cost of clinically significant bleeding in 4.4% vs 0.7% and 15 treatment-related deaths (5 pulmonary haemorrhage) in a population already selected to exclude squamous tumours, brain metastases and significant haemoptysis; the benefit concentrated in adenocarcinoma. AVAiL: progression-free survival improved at both bevacizumab doses (hazard ratios 0.75 and 0.85, relative) but overall survival did not (hazard ratios 0.93 and 1.03), with about 62% receiving later-line therapy. Neither trial is in the immunotherapy era. The colorectal-cancer bevacizumab question is homed elsewhere in the library (live #1844) and is not folded in.
cards.watchOut: Two trials, two backbones, two different survival answers — never pooled into one bevacizumab headline. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Erlotinib versus placebo in pretreated NSCLC (BR.21): one trial, three labelled reports — a 2-month median survival gain and delayed symptom deterioration in an unselected population
shelves.question: In patients with stage IIIB/IV NSCLC after failure of one or two chemotherapy regimens, does erlotinib 150 mg/day prolong survival and improve symptoms versus placebo (best supportive care comparison)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/therapeutic use · Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung/drug therapy,mortality · Cisplatin/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · ErbB Receptors/antagonists & inhibitors · Erlotinib Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/drug therapy,mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Quinazolines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): BR.21 randomised 731 patients with stage IIIB/IV NSCLC after one or two chemotherapy regimens to erlotinib 150 mg/day or placebo. Erlotinib prolonged median overall survival (6.7 vs 4.7 months; hazard ratio 0.70, relative — a modest 2-month absolute gain) and progression-free survival (2.2 vs 1.8 months), with response in 8.9% vs <1%, delayed deterioration of cough, dyspnoea and pain, and better global quality of life (35% vs 26% improved). Five percent discontinued erlotinib for toxicity. In the elderly subgroup (163 patients ≥70), progression-free benefit was preserved but the overall-survival contrast was NOT significant (hazard ratio 0.92) and grade 3/4 toxicity was higher (35% vs 18%) — both printed on the face. This is the unselected-population EGFR trial, run before routine mutation testing.

cards.headline: BR.21 primary report (Shepherd 2005, 731 randomised): erlotinib prolonged median overall survival to 6.7 vs 4.7 months (hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and progression-free survival to 2.2 vs 1.8 months; response 8.9% vs <1%; 5% discontinued erlotinib for toxicity
cards.summary: BR.21 primary report (Shepherd 2005, 731 randomised): erlotinib prolonged median overall survival to 6.7 vs 4.7 months (hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and progression-free survival to 2.2 vs 1.8 months; response 8.9% vs <1%; 5% discontinued erlotinib for toxicity
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled double-blind phase 3 trial (BR.21), erlotinib vs placebo after 1–2 chemotherapy regimens
cards.people: 731 patients with stage IIIB/IV NSCLC and performance status 0–3 who had received one or two prior chemotherapy regimens (49% had received two; 93% had received platinum-based chemotherapy; median age 61.4 years), randomised 2:1 double-blind to oral erlotinib 150 mg daily or placebo. Primary outcome survival.
cards.result: Overall survival was 6.7 months on erlotinib versus 4.7 months on placebo (hazard ratio 0.70; P<0.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it: a gain of 2.0 months). Progression-free survival was 2.2 versus 1.8 months (hazard ratio 0.61; P<0.001). Response rate was 8.9% versus less than 1% (P<0.001), with median response duration 7.9 versus 3.7 months. Five percent of patients discontinued erlotinib because of toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: An unselected population — BR.21 was run before routine EGFR mutation testing, so its modest absolute gain (2 months of median survival) is the biomarker-unselected contrast to the library's first-line mutation-selected EGFR shelves. Pre-registration-era reporting: no registry ID in the record.
cards.source: Shepherd FA et al. Erlotinib in previously treated non-small-cell lung cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16014882. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BR.21 quality-of-life analysis (Bezjak 2006 — same trial, labelled): time to deterioration was longer on erlotinib for cough (4.9 vs 3.7 months), dyspnoea (4.7 vs 2.9) and pain (2.8 vs 1.9); global quality of life improved in 35% vs 26%
cards.summary: BR.21 quality-of-life analysis (Bezjak 2006 — same trial, labelled): time to deterioration was longer on erlotinib for cough (4.9 vs 3.7 months), dyspnoea (4.7 vs 2.9) and pain (2.8 vs 1.9); global quality of life improved in 35% vs 26%
cards.type: Quality-of-life analysis of the BR.21 randomised trial (same trial as the primary card — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: The 731 BR.21 participants carded above, with quality of life assessed by the EORTC QLQ-C30 and lung-cancer module QLQ-LC13; compliance was 87% at baseline and over 70% during treatment. The primary quality-of-life endpoints were time to deterioration of cough, dyspnoea and pain. A report of the one BR.21 trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Patients on erlotinib had significantly longer median time to deterioration for all three symptoms: cough 4.9 versus 3.7 months (P=0.04), dyspnoea 4.7 versus 2.9 months (P=0.04) and pain 2.8 versus 1.9 months (P=0.03). Improvement rates for cough, dyspnoea and pain on erlotinib were 44%, 34% and 42% respectively. Physical function improved in 31% on erlotinib versus 19% on placebo (P=0.01) and global quality of life in 35% versus 26% (P<0.0001). Patients with complete or partial response were more likely to report quality-of-life improvement than those with stable or progressive disease.
cards.watchOut: Symptom and quality-of-life benefits in a trial where only 8.9% responded: much of the symptom gain tracks disease control rather than tumour shrinkage, and quality-of-life compliance fell over time as patients progressed.
cards.source: Bezjak A et al. Symptom improvement in lung cancer patients treated with erlotinib: quality of life analysis of the National Cancer Institute of Canada Clinical Trials Group Study BR.21. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2006. PMID: 16921034. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: BR.21 elderly analysis (Wheatley-Price 2008, 163 patients aged ≥70 — same trial, labelled): progression-free benefit preserved (hazard ratio 0.63, relative) but the overall-survival contrast in the elderly was NOT significant (7.6 vs 5.0 months, hazard ratio 0.92), with grade 3/4 toxicity in 35% vs 18% in younger patients and toxicity discontinuations in 12% vs 3%
cards.summary: BR.21 elderly analysis (Wheatley-Price 2008, 163 patients aged ≥70 — same trial, labelled): progression-free benefit preserved (hazard ratio 0.63, relative) but the overall-survival contrast in the elderly was NOT significant (7.6 vs 5.0 months, hazard ratio 0.92), with grade 3/4 toxicity in 35% vs 18% in younger patients and toxicity discontinuations in 12% vs 3%
cards.type: Retrospective elderly-subgroup analysis of the BR.21 randomised trial (same trial — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: The 731 BR.21 participants analysed retrospectively by age: 163 elderly patients (≥70 years; 112 erlotinib, 51 placebo) and 568 younger patients (<70 years; 376 erlotinib, 192 placebo). A retrospective age analysis of the one BR.21 trial, not a separate trial.
cards.result: Progression-free survival benefit was preserved in the elderly (3.0 vs 2.1 months; hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.90; P=0.009 — relative, absolutes beside it), but overall survival in the elderly was 7.6 versus 5.0 months with a hazard ratio of 0.92 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.34; P=0.67 — NOT significant), versus a hazard ratio of 0.73 in younger patients (interaction P=0.31). Response rates were similar between age groups. Elderly patients had significantly more overall and severe (grade 3/4) toxicity than younger patients (35% vs 18%; P<0.001), were more likely to discontinue for treatment-related toxicity (12% vs 3%; P<0.0001) and had lower relative dose intensity.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective subgroup of 163 patients: the non-significant elderly overall-survival hazard ratio (0.92, interval 0.64 to 1.34) is compatible with benefit or none and must not be read as proof of no benefit in the elderly — but the higher toxicity and discontinuation rates in the elderly are direct findings and belong on the face.
cards.source: Wheatley-Price P et al. Erlotinib for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer in the elderly: an analysis of the National Cancer Institute of Canada Clinical Trials Group Study BR.21. shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer who have completed five years of tamoxifen, does five years of letrozole improve disease-free survival versus placebo?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf): MA.17 randomised 5,187 postmenopausal women who had completed five years of tamoxifen to five years of letrozole or placebo. Letrozole improved disease-free survival — estimated 4-year disease-free survival 93% vs 87% at the primary report and an updated hazard ratio of 0.58 (relative; distant disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.60). The trial was STOPPED EARLY at its first interim analysis, which inflates the apparent effect — stated on the face, with the updated hazard ratio beside the primary estimate. Overall survival was null overall (hazard ratio 0.82) and significantly improved only in node-positive patients (hazard ratio 0.61, relative) — a subgroup finding, printed as such. In women ≥70 there was no age interaction and no toxicity/quality-of-life difference at 24 months. Harms: more hormonally related side effects and new osteoporosis diagnoses (5.8% vs 4.5% at the primary report), with fracture rates similar.

cards.headline: MA.17 primary report (Goss 2003, 5,187 enrolled; trial STOPPED EARLY at the first interim analysis): estimated 4-year disease-free survival 93% on letrozole vs 87% on placebo; deaths 31 vs 42 (not significant); new osteoporosis diagnoses 5.8% vs 4.5%
cards.summary: MA.17 primary report (Goss 2003, 5,187 enrolled; trial STOPPED EARLY at the first interim analysis): estimated 4-year disease-free survival 93% on letrozole vs 87% on placebo; deaths 31 vs 42 (not significant); new osteoporosis diagnoses 5.8% vs 4.5%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MA.17), letrozole vs placebo after 5 years of tamoxifen — STOPPED EARLY at first interim analysis
cards.people: 5,187 postmenopausal women with hormone-dependent early breast cancer who had completed five years of tamoxifen therapy, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of a planned five years of letrozole; median follow-up at this report was 2.4 years. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival.
cards.result: At the first interim analysis there were 207 local or metastatic recurrences or new contralateral primary cancers — 75 on letrozole versus 132 on placebo — with estimated 4-year disease-free survival of 93% versus 87% (P≤0.001). A total of 31 women on letrozole and 42 on placebo died (P=0.25 — overall survival not significant). Low-grade hot flushes, arthritis, arthralgia and myalgia were more frequent on letrozole, and vaginal bleeding less frequent. New diagnoses of osteoporosis occurred in 5.8% on letrozole versus 4.5% on placebo (P=0.07), with similar fracture rates. After this first interim analysis, the independent data and safety monitoring committee recommended termination of the trial and prompt communication of the results to participants.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early at the first interim analysis on a disease-free-survival result — early stopping inflates the apparent effect size, so the 93% vs 87% estimate should be read alongside the updated analysis carded next. Pre-registration-era reporting: no registry ID in the record.
cards.source: Goss PE et al. A randomized trial of letrozole in postmenopausal women after five years of tamoxifen therapy for early-stage breast cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 14551341. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MA.17 updated analysis (Goss 2005 — same trial, labelled; median follow-up 30 months): disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.58 and distant disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.60 (relative); overall survival NULL overall (hazard ratio 0.82) but significantly improved in node-positive patients (hazard ratio 0.61, relative) — a subgroup finding
cards.summary: MA.17 updated analysis (Goss 2005 — same trial, labelled; median follow-up 30 months): disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.58 and distant disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.60 (relative); overall survival NULL overall (hazard ratio 0.82) but significantly improved in node-positive patients (hazard ratio 0.61, relative) — a subgroup finding
cards.type: Updated analysis of the MA.17 randomised trial (same trial as the primary card — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: The MA.17 participants carded above: 2,593 assigned to a planned 5 years of letrozole and 2,594 to placebo after completing 5 years of tamoxifen; median follow-up 30 months (range 1.5–61.4). Updated report of the one MA.17 trial, not a second trial; lymph-node status was a planned subgroup analysis.
cards.result: Disease-free survival favoured letrozole (hazard ratio for recurrence or contralateral breast cancer 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76; P<0.001 — a relative measure) as did distant disease-free survival (hazard ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.84; P=0.002). Overall survival did not differ overall (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.19; P=0.3). Among lymph-node-positive patients, however, overall survival was significantly improved with letrozole (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.98; P=0.04). Contralateral breast cancer incidence was lower on letrozole but not significantly. Women on letrozole had more hormonally related side effects; incidences of bone fractures and cardiovascular events were the same in both arms.
cards.watchOut: The overall-survival signal lives only in the node-positive subgroup — printed here as a subgroup finding, not a headline. The overall-population overall-survival result is null (hazard ratio 0.82, P=0.3).
cards.source: Goss PE et al. Randomized trial of letrozole following tamoxifen as extended adjuvant therapy in receptor-positive breast cancer: updated findings from NCIC CTG MA.17. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2005. PMID: 16145047. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MA.17 older-women analysis (Muss 2008, 1,323 women aged ≥70 — same trial, labelled): no interaction between age and treatment effect; no difference in toxicity or quality of life at 24 months in the ≥70 group
cards.summary: MA.17 older-women analysis (Muss 2008, 1,323 women aged ≥70 — same trial, labelled): no interaction between age and treatment effect; no difference in toxicity or quality of life at 24 months in the ≥70 group
cards.type: Age-subgroup analysis of the MA.17 randomised trial (same trial — labelled single-programme report)
cards.people: The 5,169 randomly assigned MA.17 patients divided by age — younger than 60 (2,152), 60–69 (1,694) and ≥70 years (1,323) — with quality of life measured by the SF-36 and the Menopause-Specific Quality-of-Life questionnaire. An age analysis of the one MA.17 trial, not a separate trial.
cards.result: At 4 years, disease-free survival showed statistically significant differences favouring letrozole only in patients younger than 60 (hazard ratio 0.46; P=0.0004 — a relative measure), but there was NO interaction between age and treatment, indicating a similar letrozole effect among all age groups. In patients aged ≥70 there was no difference in toxicity or quality of life at 24 months between letrozole and placebo. The authors concluded that healthy patients aged 70 or older completing 5 years of tamoxifen should be considered for extended adjuvant letrozole.
cards.watchOut: Absence of an age-by-treatment interaction is not proof the effect is identical at every age — the ≥70 stratum's own disease-free-survival contrast was not individually significant, and the card prints both facts rather than choosing one.
cards.source: Muss HB et al. Efficacy, toxicity, and quality of life in older women with early-stage breast cancer treated with letrozole or placebo after 5 years of tamoxifen: NCIC CTG intergroup trial MA.17. Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. 2008. PMID: 18332474. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ONE trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf) — MA.17 shows letrozole after five years of tamoxifen improves disease-free survival (updated hazard ratio 0.58, relative), with overall survival null overall and improved only in the node-positive subgroup; the trial was stopped early at its first interim analysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: ONE trial, three labelled reports (single-programme shelf) — MA.17 shows letrozole after five years of tamoxifen improves disease-free survival (updated hazard ratio 0.58, relative), with overall survival null overall and improved only in the node-positive subgroup; the trial was stopped early at its first interim analysis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the MA.17 trial (5,187 enrolled) reported three times — primary report, updated analysis at median 30 months, and the older-women analysis (1,323 aged ≥70). One trial, one programme, labelled as such throughout.
cards.result: Estimated 4-year disease-free survival was 93% vs 87% at the early-stopped primary report; the updated hazard ratios were 0.58 for disease-free survival and 0.60 for distant disease-free survival (both relative measures). Overall survival was null overall (hazard ratio 0.82) and significantly improved only in node-positive patients (hazard ratio 0.61) — a subgroup finding. In women ≥70 there was no age interaction and no toxicity or quality-of-life difference at 24 months. Harms on the face: more hot flushes, arthritis, arthralgia and myalgia on letrozole, and new osteoporosis diagnoses in 5.8% vs 4.5% at the primary report, with fracture rates similar and, in the updated analysis, the same as placebo. Context: live #942 homes the NEXT extension questions (tamoxifen to 10 years; letrozole after an aromatase inhibitor, MA.17R) — the founding MA.17 question, letrozole after tamoxifen versus stopping, is this shelf only and nothing from #942 is re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping at the first interim analysis inflates the apparent disease-free-survival effect — the updated hazard ratio beside the primary estimate is the corrective. Single-programme shelf (one trial, three reports). See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Adjuvant imatinib after GIST resection (Z9001 — one trial, three reports): recurrence-free survival 98% versus 83% at 1 year, no overall-survival benefit shown
shelves.question: In patients with completely resected primary gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) at least 3 cm in size and KIT-positive, does one year of adjuvant imatinib 400 mg/day improve recurrence-free and overall survival versus placebo (ACOSOG Z9001)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antineoplastic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Benzamides · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors/mortality,pathology,surgery,therapy · Humans · Imatinib Mesylate · Male · Middle Aged · Piperazines/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Pyrimidines/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit for recurrence-free survival; no overall-survival benefit shown), on a single-trial base labelled as such. Z9001 (713 randomised, double-blind) found 1-year recurrence-free survival of 98% on one year of adjuvant imatinib 400 mg/day versus 83% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure), with recurrence or death in 8% versus 20%. At a median 74 months the recurrence-free-survival advantage persisted (hazard ratio 0.6, relative) in the long-term pathology/molecular report, concentrated in KIT exon 11 deletion tumours, but adjuvant imatinib did not seem to alter overall survival — placebo patients crossed to imatinib at recurrence, so recurrence was deferred rather than shown to be prevented. The third card is a risk-score report built in SSGXVIII and validated in the Z9001 imatinib arm. All three cards are reports of, or using, the one Z9001 programme — never three trials. The duration question (3 years versus 1 year) is homed at live #1926.

cards.headline: Z9001 primary report (Dematteo 2009): one year of adjuvant imatinib improved 1-year recurrence-free survival to 98% versus 83% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure)
cards.summary: Z9001 primary report (Dematteo 2009): one year of adjuvant imatinib improved 1-year recurrence-free survival to 98% versus 83% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.35, a relative measure)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (ACOSOG Z9001) — primary report, 1 of 3 reports of this one trial on this shelf
cards.people: 713 patients with complete gross resection of a primary gastrointestinal stromal tumour at least 3 cm in size and KIT-positive by immunohistochemistry, randomised to imatinib 400 mg/day (n=359) or placebo (n=354) daily for 1 year after resection (ACOSOG Z9001, double-blind, multicentre). Placebo patients could cross to imatinib at recurrence. Accrual was stopped early because the interim results crossed the efficacy boundary; median follow-up was 19.7 months.
cards.result: 30 patients (8%) on imatinib and 70 (20%) on placebo had recurrence or died. Recurrence-free survival at 1 year was 98% (95% CI 96 to 100) on imatinib versus 83% (78 to 88) on placebo; hazard ratio 0.35 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.53) — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute 1-year rates. The most common serious events on imatinib were dermatitis (11 patients, 3%, versus 0), abdominal pain (12, 3%, versus 6, 1%) and diarrhoea (10, 2%, versus 5, 1%).
cards.watchOut: One trial, three reports: this shelf is a single-programme shelf and is labelled as such. Early stopping at an interim efficacy boundary can inflate the apparent effect, and crossover to imatinib at recurrence means the placebo arm is not a never-treated arm for survival.
cards.source: Dematteo RP et al. Adjuvant imatinib mesylate after resection of localised, primary gastrointestinal stromal tumour: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19303137. Registry ID: NCT00041197.
